Abstract M’Doctorat does not want it here.

A000578

There is something wrong. There has been something wrong for a long time.

It had crawled out of those nameless woods and into her chest. It had peeled her open, nestled in her skin and now it leaks out of her like an open wound. Weeping into the world, it stole away all it touched, all that spoke of it, just as it had stolen her.

And one of those semiohazardous bloodstains sits on her desk in her workshop. Six faces of sixteen squares. It stands stark amongst cluttered paperwork and empty mugs, whiteboard markers and beakers.

The CUBE sits on her desk.

Abstract M’Doctorat does not want it here. Frankly, she’d rather it be anywhere but here. Yet ever since Elliot left Project 6416/Prime and never looked back, nothing stood between her and the FOURTH ORDER PUZZLE OBJECT.

“I do wish you’d return my calls,” she murmurs to herself, crouching down and opening a toolbox.

“I— I just wonder how you’re doing!” Abbie throws a hand in the air. “If you’re okay, what you’re up to now. What you’re doing.” Nowadays she finds she talks to herself more than usual, in the absence of anything else. Anyone else.

She shoots a glare at the CUBE, “Not you. Not you,” she hisses at it as though it can hear. She then shakes her head, walks over to the hulking machinery that rests in the room. It was a maintenance day. She liked those days.

“…what did you even see, Elliot? They rushed you out so quick, all you did was scream.” Her forehead rests against cold metal. The Enigmaverse Engine hums.

“I wish you weren’t so afraid.” She wishes she wasn’t so afraid, as she loops the wrench around a bolt to re-tighten it, pops off a panel to check interior wiring. Busywork. Her mind chides.

You’re ignoring the multi-colored elephant in the room. As always.

Abbie glances over her shoulder. It sits there, same as before. Unmoving. It’s a toy. It is a toy. Technocolor burns against her gaze, and it makes her wince. She is afraid of a toy. That ebb and flow against her mind.

“I need to work,” she murmurs, as though by way of explanation to an audience that doesn’t exist, “leave me alone.” Nobody is there.

Despite her quiet insistence, despite her desire for distraction against that still gnawing feeling in her gut, she keeps glancing back at it. She knows that she shouldn't, she'll get nothing done this way. She should just go over there, grab the damned THING, run her tests and be done with i—

No. No she can't. She can't touch it. She doesn't want to. Abstract shakes out her head and curses, quietly. In a desperate attempt to silence her own buzzing mind, she shoves her head underneath a section of the Engine so that she can check a series of connecting wires. Red, green, blue. They're all plugged where they need to be. She twists them, to make sure they're still connected properly. Her eyes flick over to another set. Red, green, blue.

Orange, yellow, white.

She yanks herself out from under the machine.

"Nom de Dieu!" Abbie hisses, and again she puts her forehead against the humming machine. God dammit. God dammit.

She looks back at it again.

SCP-6416's chronological restructurings adhere to the Path-of-Least-Resistance property, enacting the least drastic possible alterations to justify the state of SCP-6416-CUBE.

Path of least resistance. Does that path spear through her?

Abbie’s hand trembles. She puts down the wrench and sits down against the Engine, squeezing her eyes shut.

Whenever she has touched it, the surface is warm, as though it was just taken from the palm of someone’s hand. It sickened her, in that way. Knowing it was in the grasp of an unknowable amount of people. All her. In holding that CUBE she was brushing against the lifeblood of thousands, and she would feel their warmth pulse against her hand just as they'd feel hers. A terrible, terrible pulsing. It tricked her mind into thinking the OBJECT was alive, sometimes. Like a heart, bloodily severed from the chest of SOMETHING beyond, still beating against all natural odds.

In truth, she hasn’t touched it in days. The thought has occurred to her each of those days. A nudge at her mind, a persistent thought that never leaves. It never leaves. Always there, always lingering.

Where is the line drawn between her own paranoia, and mental influence?

Path of least resistance.

No. No, that’s ridiculous. She knows that’s ridiculous. It doesn’t work that way. The OBJECT is not capable of such a thing, merely masquerading as a toy she once enjoyed. A temptation.

Right?

It sits on the desk, still. A multi-colored mockery to her internal plight. Abbie groans loudly; the back of her head clangs against the metal of the Engine. She barely processes the dull pain that causes, against the headache starting to bloom behind her eyes.

She's restless. Agitated. At herself, mainly. Abbie fidgets with the wrench in her hand, having nothing better to toy with. Even though there's something a few meters a way that would be far more apt at letting her get out that manic sort of energy building in her.

But she can't. She doesn't want to touch that THING. Abbie puts the wrench down, simply wrings her wrist with her other hand. It is a toy and cannot hurt her. It cannot influence her. But she sits and she obsesses and she thinks that it does amidst a mind crushing stress because she lacks all other outlets.

The urge to go pick up the OBJECT doesn't leave, even as she watches the clock tick minutes by on the far wall. She wonders why — well, not why exactly, she knows it needs her to change its state — but the woman faintly wonders what emotions the universe is trying to twist out of her to make her cave. Boredom? Curiosity? Madness? Will she keep mentally running herself in ragged circles, like she is now, until eventually she caves? The acknowledgement of the inevitable, yet still she holds some spite in her heart to ignore the THING for as long as she can manage. The closest thing she can muster to rebellion in the face of an multiuniversal pressure that does not exist.

Minutes still tick by, and she lets out a shaky breath. She's since abandoned the prospect of continuing maintenance. She can't get herself to pick up her tools or return to work.

She doesn’t want to touch it. She has to. It's stupid to fear a toy. A few more minutes tick by, and the sigh she heaves rattles her chest. Abstract groans, cracks her eyes open, stumbles up to her feet, and walks away from the Enigmaverse Engine.

When she closes the gap, the scientist braces her hands against the desk and stares down at its scrambled sides. She squeezes her eyes shut, opens and closes her hands a few times.

Hesitates.

And it burns against her palms. A thousand-hundred hands death-grip the hard plastic just as she does — ten thousand-hundred white knuckled fingers. Abstract barely processes that she's begun to shift its sides, against that burning. The click-click-clicking sounds like crunching bone, against frightened ears.

Her thumb catches a corner between rows as she quickly turns them, and the plastic of the OBJECT shears part of her flesh. Skin ripped open by the pinch between unbreakable joints, and a pained noise slips past her lips. Yet she doesn't let go.

A red corner is now dotted by droplets of darker red. The CUBE burns like boiling blood. Her hand hurts. It won't stain the THING. It could be bathed in gore and the white squares would remain pristine.

Nothing she could do to it would matter. She can't let go. For she is just one set of hands against a thousand-hundred that too all now hold it.

I really am sorry. It had been a heart stopping moment, when those words left the Oracle's mouth. The look upon the woman's face, that look of defeat, as Abbie's own face twisted into something caught between distress and despair. No way out. There is no way out.

Nothing. Not even omniscience can save her — save all of them. She's expected to just play along. Play along, let whatever this THING is lead her towards something terrible. There's no getting out. No getting rid of it. It burns against her palms and she wonders if its a mockery. Do the other hers view as she does? Do they take a twisted joy in this game?

She doesn't. She wants it to end. But it will never end. It is a constant. A constant enforced by a sprawling multiverse.

She is powerless in the face of the machination in her hands — that click-click-click of its sides as her hands move without thinking. She is powerless against a god damn toy. Maybe she's the toy, held in the hand of something cruel. Abstract finds herself sat on the floor, back pressed to the wall, legs shaking, and hands trembling against the OBJECT.

It's sticky heat clings to her skin and she almost wonders if she'd have to tear off her own flesh to wrench it from her grasp. She still grips it tight, despite her mind's wailing, knees curled up to her chest.

Maybe she is going mad. Her coworkers must certainly think so. Elliot must certainly think so. Her being "eccentric" can only handwave so much. Surely, she must be mad, to be so scared of a toy. To throw herself at this Project alone. To have the eventual role of Overseer hanging above as her own personal Damocles.

Only madmen hold that kind of power. And even the power of an Overseer will not save her. Nothing will. Again and again and again her mind loops back to that.

Nothing is going to save you.

She could hold all the world's power in her palm, and it would pale against what she holds in her other palm.

Abstract stares down at the CUBE. The scrambled sides. She wonders what it means, wonders who is talking. She was never shown what Elliot saw — but she knows his mind brushed against something terrible. She remembers the blood. She can smell it still.

How do the others out there receive and decode whatever was encrypted behind those squares, if the information was cognitohazarous?

Was it for her eyes only?

The thought sickened her because she knew it to be true. Abstract lets out a shaky huff, as she flicks one of the CUBE's sides.

"What do you want?" she murmurs, "what do we want?" What was discussed, behind the shifting plastic? There's a smear of blood on it.

She wonders if she could send a message. The phrases that she, alone, had pried from the communications were word salads of nonsense, like the rhyming prattles of a madman — but there was a pattern. A code. The rhyme, without the reason. The sides and the colors, their configurations, it all meant something. Nothing she could pick up on at a glance, but her compiled notes were another story. If she could find a way to collapse the CUBE into a state she wanted, then maybe—

This was asinine. This train of thought was asinine.

Whatever was talking, whatever this amalgam of minds across spacetime wanted, they were dangerous. The OBJECT she clutched was dangerous. A wrong step could mean erasure, could doom an entire timeline worth of people. How do you fight something like that? What words could you speak to something like that? How was the erasure even possible?

Nothing is going to save you.

Elliot had screamed of some paradox. How it was what 'killed' timelines. But where would a paradox even come from? Would the mere act of going against 6416 spawn one? She hoped not. She hoped, still desperately, that something could be done. If not a way out, than a way to help others beyond her own gulf.

If nothing is going to save her, maybe she can save others. Maybe she can send a message. The thought makes her grip the CUBE tightly. She's paused in altering its sides. Her hands ache.

Perhaps she can warn others of what is coming. Pass on the research she has gathered, and let another Abstract learn and try from what she found. Like a cruel game of telephone across timelines. It's just a matter of finding a variant of herself still sane. Maybe she can tell those other power hungry bastards to fuck themselves.

O5-9 would never allow this.

Maybe what is allowed doesn't matter. No one else is making an effort.

She has to try.

Abstract can still feel the CUBE's awful warmth against her palms, as she jolts up to her feet. She stares up at the Enigmaverse Engine.

"…you'd need modification," she mutters to herself, "a lot of it. One-way capabilities to two-way." Abstract begins to pace — tapping a finger against the OBJECT in her hand. "And it cannot be here. I cannot do any modifications here. My own home could be a possibility — but how the hell would I get the needed tech off-Site without looking—"

The Overseer promotion.

That thirteen sided Sword of Damocles was set to slice mere weeks from now.

It is that realization that makes her pause. She can hear her heart pounding in her ears. The attention will be on Site-01 in preparation for a changing of the guard.

Perhaps that is enough time.

Abstract grips the CUBE and harshly turns the top row. The clicks still seem more like a crunch of bone than plastic. She needs to modify her blueprints, gather a list, gather supplies.

She doesn't realize how hard she's shaking — how she's wheezing in and out desperate breaths within the disheveled workshop. Abstract stumbles to her desk, shoves the CUBE into her lab coat pocket and begins to frantically shift through her notes. Her still bleeding finger smears blood across the paper.

Maybe it's asinine. Maybe she's gone mad. Maybe there's a chance. She doesn't know. She doesn't know, but she needs to try.

That accursed OBJECT burns against her hip.

She needs to try.

It can't all be for nothing.

By: Diogene_s
Published on 11 Nov 2025 13:42

SCP-9993 | San Antonio del Monte

06:12

You wake up to the sound of an engine. That's what they told you it was. An eldritch machine, full of metal tubes that somehow burn black liquid to help heavy things move by themselves. It's all magic to you. You haven't gotten used to them and you doubt you ever will.

The persistence of the sound propels you out of your cot, and into your measly kitchen, where you eat a bit of stale bread and something new called "chocolate." It's sweet. The first time you ate it, you spent two days with a stomachache. You eventually got used to it. Soon after, the entire town was munching on it.

You grab your shawl and get out.

The wind of the Monegros desert carries white dust into the white streets of the town. Your neighbors are already working. Berta is sweeping the floor in front of her house. Luisa looks from her window, and then throws the bathroom water out into the street. Alberto is sitting on a stool in front of his house, weaving a basket. All of them politely bow their heads when you pass them.

More people are out and about, wandering, touching the newly installed lights. It's wonderful that in the future people are able to magically open and close lights during the night, without having to start a fire. But you realised something after you woke up in this new world. You couldn't see the stars as clearly, as if the lights on the Earth were snuffing out the lights on the skies.

Then your street ends. For all your life, that was where the town ended. Not anymore. You turn back and ascend towards the church.

08:29

The town square is full of sheep and three shepherds of bone and light. They are the newest innovation, brought to you by Light Courier Enterprises from the far off year of our lord of "unknown" and they love sheep. They tend to them, whacking them with cattle prods. On their first day now they tried to skin alive Florinda, a three year old girl who lives in the outskirts, just because she was wearing wool clothes. The Foundation people stopped them and somehow made them channel all their violent instincts into herding sheep.

You watch them go by, sitting on a bench. Alfonsa Ciervo, mother superiora of the church of San Antonio hobbles towards you inbetween the ruminants. She moves like a decrepit old woman, like you, yet she is only 18 by your count. She says she spent 70 years trapped in time. Your mind refuses to understand how that can happen.

"Hello Juana," she greets you, once she's out of the herd of sheeps. She sits beside you. "How are you?"

"I'm good. It is a good morning." You smile.

"Are you here to confess some sins?" she asks. Her unique perspective had made her the perfect candidate to become the town priest after the last one turnt out ugly and murderous. She was now the spiritual leader of the community, though half of the town had turned to stranger, more esoteric beliefs born from things that slip between the cracks of time. "What have you done?"

"I am old, sister, I'm past the age of sinning." You grab your cane tightly. "I've partaken in more food than normal. But can you blame me? We've never had this much food come winter."

"It is not my place to assign blame. I am merely an observer." You do not find this reassuring and she knows it. You frown. "You're one of the eldest among us, you are allowed to indulge once in a while. If God cares about how much chocolate you've eaten, that's her business. Just remember to brush your teeth."

"I don't have many of those, anymore."

"Exactly why I say it." She laughs. You laugh dryly with her.

"Speaking of old people. Have you seen María lately?" you ask, because María is the only one in town who surpasses you in age.

"No." The priestess voice sounds sad. "She hasn't been the same since his son died."

You recall the events. The invasion of men with black attires and dangerous guns. The priest screaming at the top of his lungs. Or was it the hidalgo? There were corpses in the streets and warriors with horses screaming at the top of their lungs while they shot arrows. There were machines walking and slashing and buildings exploding. And you were trapped under rubble. And you were executed publicly. And you ran through burning fields out of the town… Memories bleed over themselves and your head starts to ache. Then, with a loud pop, it's over, your memories go back to their rightful place and reconfigure back into you conforting María, who has her dead son in her arms. You look at Alfonsa again.

"I hope she's alright." That's all you can say.

"Me too."

11:20

The town library is a new development. It was built out from the house of Don Mariano de la Vega, the local Hidalgo, who had been imprisoned for causing a battle in the middle of the town. As the man had liked reading, he had a small collection of books, which had since expanded with new things, such as more books and more strange gadgets.

You are looking at the little ants that move throughout a page. You have never understood how reading works, but you try hard anyways.

There is someone else in the building. Everyone calls him "Chueco". You don't know his true name, but he's Basque and came to the town one day to work and here he stayed. You look at him fiddling with the little mirrors that light up. Before, he was never good at working the fields or tending to the animals, but he adapted to the new objects of the future better than most.

You enjoy his quiet presence for a second and then turn your eyes down to the page, where the inkblots are dancing. Your eyes can't focus on them. You close the book and take a deep breath.

13:51

Lunch is served in the inn. It never had a name, as it was the only inn in town and nobody ever came. Pedro, the innkeeper, was never around either. He used to spent most of the time tending to the chickens and screaming in the wastes.

But now it was the bustling center of the community. Pedro had come back to it, reopened the place and named it "Klepsydra". It is a weird name in a language you didn't know. But it is exotic, unmistakeably interesting.

The place is full, today. Maybe something of importance is happening somewhere. Or maybe people with infinity on their hands have decided to give this time a try. A woman with metal threads coming out of her head is eating soup and drinking wine; a sparrow that calls itself "The Second Wandswoman of Ebutapakht" flies overhead, perching on a beam and starts eating some bread; three cloaked people have a boardgame on a table yet none of them make a single move and, from the back of it all, some Foundation agents surveil the situation.

You eat a spoonful of the broth, and as it travels through your mouth you feel that it tastes different. You mull over the flavors for a second. They're not the ones from the usual garlic soup, as there's a new substance to it. You smell it and come to the conclusion. It must be fish. Somehow they're bringing fish to a desert, a hundred miles from the nearest sea. You take another spoonful. It tastes good.

16:51

On the main square, people from the Foundation have set up their engines and machines around a ball of light that floated right in front of the church.

"Juana, I think you should stand back a bit," says the first Foundation soldier, everyone calls him Agent Groundhog.

"Why?" you inquire, slowly hobbling forward.

"Extranormal Temporal Event in progress, sorry."

"What is that thing?" you point your cane at it.

He sighs, lifting his head from the contraption he has in his hands.

"It calls itself "Archivist" and it likes collecting stuff from all over time. That's why I said you shouldn't come closer. It might be collecting old ladies, for all I know." And he places a hand on your shoulder to push you a bit backwards.

"UNALLOWANCE. ARCHIVISM. TOWN." You hear something scream. "EXTRATEMPORALITY. LEGALITY. BOUND." It's Dr. Ak, a short human covered in fur who screams with a raspy voice. You were once told it was a parasomething, an intelligent being who wasn't human nor angel nor demon but akin to an animal. You didn't understand it then, and you continue to not understand it now. It's standing under the sphere of light, waving some papers. "DOCUMENTATION. SIGNAGE. POSTERITY. TRAVEL. AGREEMENT?"

"He's saying that that sphere can't be here, that it has to leave as per an agreement we have with it." Another Foundation man says. You nod and move on out of the way.

18:26

You walk down your street towards the edge of town. You've been avoiding it for a while, but today you feel like you ought to walk the fields once again.

There's a building in the distance. A square thing made of grey uniform rock unlike anything you had ever seen before. That was were the engines and the machines and the Foundation people come from. Everyone calls it "Outpost-137".

And between there and here, new happenings have sprung up. Things had always been weird since the time witch had made the past disappear and the present appear around all of you. Orosia's eldest daughter, Alfonsa, had lived for as long as you had, even if she only appeared like a young woman. Vessels hailing from unknown places landed on the shrubbery beyond, offering trinkets from a time that would never come to pass. You once had to live for a week with a woman who looked like exactly you, answered to your name and shared all your memories. She had then disappeared into the aether. These were just another of the things that you were learning to accept as normal.

After all, they weren't as weird as the thousand new types of cloth that existed nowadays, the onyx squares that the Foundation people used to talk to each other and the wondrous fruits and vegetables that didn't exist back in the day.

So, now, in the outskirts of the town there were new things that appeared and disappeared like the clouds in the sky. At first, the Foundation peoples had been scared of them. They wouldn't tell you, but you knew. You've seen many people and you know how to read the creases of their faces and the light of their eyes. They didn't trust the apparitions of the desert and captured many of them in nets and cages.

Eventually, as the days passed, they let things slip. Lizards the size of dogs now run around out near the fences, hunting rabbits and pigeons. Apparently, they came from an antediluvian time. There were weirder things still. Men with dark skin, turbans and queer outfits camped there for some weeks, before galloping out again. One night "an ascetic believer in Aeternum" had come walking and now lived in the bell tower. An animal, bigger than anything you had seen before appeared once, dying of a thousand punctures on its blubbery skin. It was scary and it stayed there for weeks, becoming the food of a thousand flies and mosquitoes. Now only its bones remain.

The afternoon wind draws patterns of sand around your feet as you walk towards Outpost-137. The sun slowly descends in the sky.

"Hello Juana," says the man at the front gate. His name is "Agent" Dualeh, and he once said he came from Somalia, in Africa. Africa is a far away place, which you had only heard about from people speaking about the wonders and horrors of the southern continent. You would have never imagined you'd meet someone from there. And that it would be a normal man.

"Hello," you answer.

"What do you need?" he asks, smiling.

"I came to say hello. Do you need a scarf? It might not seem that way but it gets cold in winter here."

"Did you truly come here just for that? It's a long walk and you're not that bored yet."

You smile, and take Dualeh's arm.

"Oh, of course." He obliges. "Yeah, I'll walk you back."

"It's good to know that young men are still kind in this day and age," you muse, as you walk across the field.

"There's people and people. Always has been."

"But there's more of us now. Right? Father Narváez used to say you live in cities with thousands upon thousands of people."

"That's right." He nods. "The city I come from has two million inhabitants."

"And you don't know them all." The question is implicit. Dualeh smiles.

"No, of course not."

"And isn't that scary? I say, walking down the street, not knowing who is around you…"

"Well, I am used to it." The path winds around a building that appeared one day. It has been boarded up by the Foundation, but lights and sounds sometimes escape from the cracks. "It's just the era I was born in. We have bigger cities, it's a bigger world."

"Isn't that also scary?" you ask. "Every day I wake up and there's new people in town. And they come and go. Where do they come from? Where are they going? Why are they here? In my home?"

"People move from one place to another constantly. Well, here they also move through time, but its the same thing. The same principle." He seems unfazed by your line of questioning. He is a soldier, but in his time living in town he has become the visible face of the Foundation here. So he's used to having to answer the questions you and your neighbors have about the present. You continue walking beside him.

"Before, in my era, I could predict the world. The only things we couldn't foresee were harsh winters, and the will of kings that brought us to war…" There are some flowers that wilt and regrow rapidly on the side of the road. You stop to look at them. "Now the world is faster. Everything is new and everyone moves constantly." There's a silence as the flowers die in silence. "The future is uncertain now."

Both of you walk quietly through the things left behind by a hundred time travelers. The sun has set and the lights of the town are slowly coming on.

"Well, isn't that beautiful?" Dualeh says. And you don't know if he's answering to you or admiring the town.

Site-137

19:41

"Is there any reason why we are having meetings this late in the evening?" asks Diego Orbach, doctor in Parahistory and supervisor of Outpost-137.

"It's difficult to wrangle all the people needed for this matter," answers Milena Bosch, Director of Site-137.

"We are only six people," points out the historian.

And it's true. The room is a refurbished library, with a mahogany table in the middle and blackened windows that look out to a cloister bathed by moonlight. There are many chairs aranged in a circle, and most are empty.

"AFFIRMATION," adds the artificial voice of Dr. Ak, a time-traveling paranthropus with a nebulous position within the Temporal Anomalies Department. The Director rolls her eyes.

"We have an important visit, and this was the best timetable for all of us."

"It does not matter. We are here for very specific reasons. I have a packed schedule and I would like to get going as soon as possible." The person who speaks is Factotum Versailles, when they open their mouth, all the others keep quiet as they represent a member of the O5 Council. Their porcelain skin and dark glasses glow unnaturally in the dim room. "We are here to discuss the matter of SCP-9993. The O5 Council has been notified of the ongoing lax attitude towards containing persistent parachronic anomalies in SCP-9993. My observation has determined that this is caused by the lack of capabilities from Outpost-137 to contain the breadth of phenomena present onsite, and the limited range of activity by Delta-t caused by the event known as ETE-9993-Omega."

Dr. Ak lets out a prolonged wordless wheeze. Dr. Orbach just nods.

"This is why the O5 Council, at the behest of Philip Verhoten," Versailles points at the last member of the meeting "is considering the matter of reclassifying San Antonio del Monte as a Nexus. I am here to gather the opinions of the personnel on the ground."

There is a moment of silence, only punctuated by the typing of the Director's secretary.

"I was the one to bring up the continued issues that 9993 poses to the O4 Council, after which I suppose the O5s were notified. They told me about the reclassification to Nexus, but what would that mean, exactly?" Asks Bosch.

"Nexuses are inhabited communities which inherently house anomalous phenomena," pontificates Verhoten, the most prominent nexologist on the Foundation, from his corner of the table.

"And San Antonio qualifies as a nexus… why?" Asks Orbach, trying not to look in the direction of the Overwatch envoy.

"I would think it's pretty obvious," smiles Philip.

"TIME. INSTABILITY."

"The Australopithecus is right. SCP-9993 or, how it could henceforth be known, Dunwich class Nexus 137 is a hotspot of temporal anomalies tied to a single location," continued Verhoten. "I'm not privy to the hypothesis of what's happening there, but I've been reading the files, and you undeniably have people coming from the past and the future, mostly aided with time machines, and also temporal rifts that spit out extinct animals and also people experiencing time in distorted ways. These are all anomalies attracted and spawned by this location. Thus, this falls into the classification of a Nexus."

Versailles holds up a gloved hand.

"Of course, there is a philosophical aspect to it. Changing the classification from a "classic" SCP object to a Nexus has clear connotations in terms of Foundation politics. It's an alignment with facilities that allow certain new containment philosophies. But, if my records are correct, Site-137 also has a Free Port under it's jurisdiction…" The Factotum is too focused on their own talking to see the look in Director Borch and Dr. Orbach's faces. "…which means that you already know what that entails. Regardless, there are also budget benefits to monitoring a Nexus."

"Important benefits," adds Verhoten, and he gives some documents to the Site Director, who looks them over.

"I want it to be clear that this is a Site faithful to the Foundation and to its mission. But given our history, we see the benefits of reclassification to a Nexus," she says. "I suppose more details will be sent to us if the Council votes to allow this reclassification."

"Yes." The Factotum seems satisfied.

"Then, if everyone is in agreement…" Dr. Ak and Dr. Orbach nod. "…then I think the request for reclassification can go through to the Council."

20:29

The day has come to an end. Your supper consists of the last of the stale bread, with a bit of cheese and a small cup of muscatel. You walk to your cold bed that’s too big for you and lie down. With a practiced movement, you snuff out the last candle in the room, at an arms reach from your position, and lie in darkness.

You are more reassured as you fall asleep. For a while you've been living in a world where you don't know what tomorrow will bring. Perhaps, like today, it will bring good things.

That's what they told you it was. An eldritch machine, full of metal tubes that somehow burn black liquid to help heavy things move by themselves. It's all magic to you. You haven't gotten used to them and you doubt you ever will. The persistence of the sound propels you out of your cot, and into your measly kitchen, where you eat a bit of stale bread and something new called "chocolate." It's sweet. The first time you ate it, you spent two days with a stomachache. You eventually got used to it. Soon after, the entire town was munching on it. You grab your shawl and get out. The wind of the Monegros desert carries white dust into the white streets of the town. Your neighbors are already working. Berta is sweeping the floor in front of her house. Luisa looks from her window, and then throws the bathroom water out into the street. Alberto is sitting on a stool in front of his house, weaving a basket. All of them politely bow their heads when you pass them. [[=]] [[image Adjustment%20Period%201.jpeg]] [[/=]] More people are out and about, wandering, touching the newly installed lights. It's wonderful that in the future people are able to magically open and close lights during the night, without having to start a fire. But you realised something after you woke up in this new world. You couldn't see the stars as clearly, as if the lights on the Earth were snuffing out the lights on the skies. Then your street ends. For all your life, that was where the town ended. Not anymore. You turn back and ascend towards the church. ----- [[=]] **08:29** [[/=]] The town square is full of sheep and three shepherds of bone and light. They are the newest innovation, brought to you by [[[scp-2940 |Light Courier Enterprises]]] from the far off year of our lord of "unknown" and they love sheep. They tend to them, whacking them with cattle prods. On their first day //now// they tried to skin alive Florinda, a three year old girl who lives in the outskirts, just because she was wearing wool clothes. The Foundation people stopped them and somehow made them channel all their violent instincts into herding sheep. You watch them go by, sitting on a bench. Alfonsa Ciervo, mother //superiora// of the church of San Antonio hobbles towards you inbetween the ruminants. She moves like a decrepit old woman, like you, yet she is only 18 by your count. "How are you?" "I'm good. It is a good morning." You smile. "Are you here to confess some sins?" she asks. Her unique perspective had made her the perfect candidate to become the town priest after the last one turnt out ugly and murderous. She was now the spiritual leader of the community, though half of the town had turned to stranger, more esoteric beliefs born from things that slip between the cracks of time. "What have you done?" "I am old, sister, I'm past the age of sinning." You grab your cane tightly. "I've partaken in more food than normal. But can you blame me? We've never had this much food come winter." [[=]] [[image Adjustment%20Period%202.jpeg]] [[/=]] "It is not my place to assign blame. I am merely an observer." You do not find this reassuring and she knows it. You frown. "You're one of the eldest among us, you are allowed to indulge once in a while. If God cares about how much chocolate you've eaten, that's her business. Just remember to brush your teeth." Poltatherian

If you enjoyed this, make sure to check out my Author Page :)

You wake to the sound of distant water dripping. You open you're eyes to find the air conditioning malfunctioning, "I'll get to that tomorrow," you think to yourself. Realizing you don't know what time it is, you start checking the phone next to you for anything new, a notification in you're calendar pops up, catching your eye. You take off your nightgown, take a fresh t-shirt & shorts from the washing machine, and head down from you're bedroom into the empty halls of Site-0.

Walking over to the kitchen, you see the other "staff" moving around, their components grinding & whirring haphazardly. "I'll get to that tomorrow," you think to yourself, you have a big day after all. Taking a bowl of dates & milk as you're breakfast, you walk towards the exit, sliding through the concrete with decades worth of efficiency. Your eyes stagger as the bright summer sunshine hits, you marvel at its beauty for only a moment before walking away from the site, only the sounds of birds & insects keeping you company on the trip. As the natural paradise you tread through gets more and more urban, you finally notice a sign on an old chainmail fence.

It was funny, more so today, especially, you can't believe a time when you thought this would keep it safe or under wraps at least. It all felt so worthless, I mean, it probably had its purpose back then, but it's not like anyone comes here anymore, so it was even worse than worthless, a reminder of that utopic past. Quickly rushing past the sign, you take a small decorative key from your pocket, jamming it in the grass somewhere, twisting it in a rhythmic pattern you've become so used to. As alarms blare from all around you, small plates flash past you around a giant dome shape as if a mountain itself turned red and screamed.

WARNING WARNING WARNING

ALL ACCESS FROM THIS POINT ON IS FORBIDDEN LEAVE NOW LEAVE NOW LEAVE NO-

The sound cuts off as the platform that jutted off the ground finishes scanning you.

WELCOME, O5-14 YOU MAY PASS.

The world stops flashing red as the plates that made up the dome return to floating around, sustaining their camouflage, some of them rearranging as a door right ahead of you. You sigh as the tedium of the experience sets in, "I don't have time for all this today," you think to yourself. Regardless, you march onward as the green grass beneath your feet transitions to clear sand. You quickly run ahead, almost tripping on a small dune, catching you're breath as your eyes catch a blue perimeter line. "Finally," you say, panting, looking up to find the most beautiful thing you have ever seen.

"Good morning Uriel, hope I didn't make you wait."

A soothing voice resounds in your head as you look up to the angel.

"WELCOME."

"I have a big day today, thought I'd share, all these years we haven't talked that much."

"NO NEED."

"It gets lonely in the site, you know, AIC's ain't much company."

"THE LORD IS COMPANY ENOUGH."

"I guess so," you blurt out, taking out you're prayer mat from the nearby station you built.

"YOU MUST APPLY. NOT GUESS. NOT THINK. DO."

"You're right. Guess I'm just nervous, I don't know how I can show my face to him."

"YOU KNOW WHAT YOU MUST."

"Indeed." You face towards Mecca and begin to prostrate.

"Sooo, where are we off to this time, boss?" an energetic young man spoke out of his Porsche. You were never really involved in council affairs anymore, but at least they had the courtesy to hand you a circle of factotum; you enjoyed their company.

You hand the man a piece of paper through the car window.

"Wooo really? It's about time he manned up."

You let out a small chuckle.

"Well, alrighty then, get in, boss."

You took out a hardwood cane and got in the car. It was a bumpy road to say the least, you were tired, and eventually the rhythmic tapping of your head on the glass lulled you to sleep.

It was a hot sunny day, you were a lot younger at the time, you would get up from the floor with the sun's rays as your clock, the mangled roof above merely a formality. Now that you look at it, you don't actually see a roof at all or the sun today. You spread onto the empty street just as you realized you had missed prayer, "I'll get to that tomorrow," you thought to yourself; you had a long day ahead after all. Rushing past you're neighbors' houses, the shopping district, the park, the central plaza, and eventually flopping onto the school gates with only a pencil and tattered clothes, swallowing the dread in your throat as you rushed inside. You headed to your classroom, hoping to see the celebrity that was set to visit the school today as a charity, something, something, Terblanche, was it? Doesn't matter, you had a lot you wanted to share with the man, the things that would finally get the roof fixed, or get a new roof? No, a new house! You could barely hide the grin across your face as you swung the school door open to find……

No one, now that you think about it, you hadn't seen anyone today. Was it the weekend? No, that couldn't be it; the shopping district was empty, too. a holiday? You doubt it, maybe you were late? Or too early?…

No matter! You might as well get some breakfa-

GJJTTZTZZJJJZZ.

Now that's a sound you've never heard before. You rush to see the source of the sound at the entrance, seeing a large hole in the sky in front of you.

Next thing you knew, you were on the floor as a man in a hard hat, started screaming.

"SIR, WE FOUND A LIVE ONE, IT'S A KID!"

People rushed to form a crowd as the sound of whirring machinery dimmed. You barely started to adjust before another scream.

"KID, CAN YOU HEAR ME? ARE YOU ALRİGHT!" The man shook you back & forth, trying to get a response.

All that came out of your mouth was gibberish even you could barely understand, and as the man prodded more, another, slimmer, whiter man in a tuxedo told the man off as he hunched you over his shoulder, taking you to a nearby tent.

The man sat you down on a chair and set ahead of you, placing a small rectangular object in front of you after seemingly playing with it.

"Can you hear me?"

You nodded

"Great, it works then," the man gave a sign of genuine relief as he got up and poured you a glass of water. You didn't hesitate to oblige.

"Babel, I mean, it's a work in progress, but you know what they say, 'AI is the future,' right?"

You stare nonplussed at the man.

"My name is Fredrick Williams. Can you tell me yours?"

"A-adnan." You blurted out between your sips, surprised you could communicate at all.

"Now, now relax, Adan, there's plenty of water where that came from." The man said with a chuckle.

You kept drinking.

"Now, Adan, I'm sure you're confused; let it be known I work for an organization dedicated to the safety of the people; there's no need to be scared." You were far too thirsty to be scared.

"But I also unfortunately have some bad news."

"Like what?"

"Do you have a family, Adnan?"

"No."

"I see, how should I put this…..Samothrace has… disappeared, to say the least." You look up in confusion.

"Now don't be scared, everything's going to be alright. We don't really know what happened, but I assure you that we are doing our best to find a solution as soon as possible."

An odd feeling sets in.

"For the time being, you will be in our custody. If you need anything, don't hesitate to ask."

"Okay." It was all you could muster at the time; you couldn't quite comprehend what the man said, so you just went along with it.

You'd like to think it got better after that, you joined the Foundation, rose through the ranks, watched your home be remembered as but a number on a document, saw Uriel for the first time, come to think of it, that was the start of many firsts, some you would come to regret. It didn't matter, the world kept turning as the Foundation grew and left you behind as a mere off-the-books containment specialist, some would even doubt the existence of. Nevertheless, you grew older, and by the time you hit 55, you had forgotten the administrator's face or the last time you saw him. You want to think he was led astray, that he never wanted to leave you here stranded and alone, yet you never shook the feeling that there was never a path he was on to be led astray from, that it was all calculated and intentional.

You never managed to find out what happened to you're country, perhaps if you tried harder, you would've, but that rage & anger has since faded into apathy, and you can't bring yourself to lash out, to change, left to go through the motions, lying through your teeth every day, to everyone, to yourself.

"Aye, boss, wakey wakey! We're here!"

You jolt up from you're slumber

"Oh, right, sorry."

You rub you're eyes and yawn, getting your cane from beside you.

"No worries, you've been rather shut off today, saving yerself for a long night, eh?"

You let out a slight chuckle as you get out of the car, straightening your clothes one last time.

"Not exactly. But this is something i wouldn't miss for the whole world.

Adrift in an Ocean of Memories

The last thing you remember is the sensation of desire. All else fell away, as you embodied that want— no, not want. The need.

You remember feeling that there was no other choice — you cannot remember what the choice was, nor what you did, but a choice was made, nonetheless. Action was taken with hands that may have been yours, and are now undoubtedly not.

Everything has it's time — your time was high school, and your need clings to the very fleeting nature of a youthful dream. You are standing in an auditorium, and you sit in every single seat. It is a day of mourning — and it's all about you.

You are a student, and that is all you know for certain.



What else do you not remember?


You are now the "Most Likely To Succeed."

You frown, failing to believe your own false confidence, your unending bravado and machismo — although your chest is sculpted, and your muscles toned, your body is wrong and you do not fit. You were expected to do great things, or, so they say, but were you consulted in that decision?

Do you have any control over what you do at the end of the day? What is control in the face of imitation? Mimicry? Envy? You can remember the first time you tasted that bittersweet verdant emotion; jealousy.

It was what you deserved, not them. A football star will be stuck dreaming of high school for the rest of their life — many are too foolish to properly enjoy this moment. Your moment, the moment you had dreamed of for years. You deserve this, more than anybody else.

Even more than the last student who was "Most Likely To Succeed."

So why does everything feel so wrong?



Maybe it is because you are not yourself.


You are now the "Most Likely To Be Late." As your signifier suggests, you are not where you are meant to be.

You laugh through your grimace as you drag yourself forward, inch by inch, step by step, ascending an impossible incline that only pushes you back to the ground. Your curse, your burden, each self-inflicted, an attempt to find your niche gone wrong; the niche consuming you, warping you and destroying your initiative.

You have no dreams because dreams imply the ability to control, and you have never once felt like you had any ability to change your own existence. This is not your body, you are simply a passive passenger. You cannot allow it to bother you — there is no such thing as a schedule, nor does anything ever change.

You are simply stasis, personified, and still, you do not fit.



Fight, flight, or freeze. Do you remember the fawn?


You are now "Best Dressed," and your existence is a shattered reflection of an ideal.

You exist only to be perceived, but your vanity still desires for more. You endlessly observe those you envy, fantasize about a world where you are on top. You have a pride far greater than your sense, and an insufficient quantity of either to change your fate. You desire being desired, just as you desire to be what you see in your screens.

Mirrors do not show true reflections, not for you; they are distortions. Everything is a distortion. Everything is incorrect, and nothing fits. This is not you, and you cannot change that. The mirror mocks you, and yet, you stare, unable to rip your eyes away.

Your body is wrong and you cannot stop touching it.



This is what you wanted.


You are now the "Most Likely To Be Held Back," and for once, you can breathe.

You have no expectations of yourself, nor does anybody expect anything of you. For once, you are not what you must be — you barely are. You do not fit, and your body is wrong, but what does that matter in the grand scheme of irrelevance?

You have time, and that is the most dangerous thing. Time breeds complacency, and you have suckled at the teat of apathy for far too long; the child that nurses beyond infancy is one who is repressed and doomed.

Have you always been doomed? Was there ever a chance for you to succeed? Or were you always destined to play the role, to be the cautionary tale? Do you have a purpose beyond what others think compared to you, or are you nothing without the rest?

If you are left behind and the world moves on, will anybody remember you?



You will be forgotten, as will the rest of you.


You are now the "Most Likely to Save the World," and even you are unsure if that can be accomplished.

You are a single person, typically, and you have never been able to affect meaningful change. You talk the talk and walk the walk, but you do not change the fates of others for the better.

You play with fate like you know what you are doing, as if you have the right to control your own destiny, the right to change the roll of the dice — you think you have the right to save the world, but who gave you that right? Was it granted by the heavens above, the imagined comfort of your youth?

Or did you need to feel important, need to be the main character so badly that you gave yourself the right? Did you ignore how foreign the body was for the sake of your own pride?

Why did you try and rewrite your own story before the ink was dry?



You will drown in the ink of your own well.


You are now both members of the "Best Couple," and while half of you feels familiar, neither body feels right. You do not fit in either way; individually, or as a couple.

Neither of your selves has any bearing anymore, as you have become the ideal. You have become the high school dream, the homecoming king and queen, the football star and the swimming champion, locked in a fate written by Hollywood executives themselves. You exist to fulfil a trope, and for once, you know that this is what you chose.

A part of you wanted this, wanted it so badly, wanted to be pretty in pink, wanted to be one of the mean girls, counting down the sixteen candles as you thought about all ten ways that you hated yourself. You are the wild child, the clueless one, the one who is all that, the tall girl.

You are nothing more than an amalgam of tropes, and when you brush all of those away, the slight posters that cling to the surface wash off and there is nothing left. You desired perfection so much that you erased all aspects of self; when scaffolding conceals a missing building, does one take it down? Or do you maintain the scaffolding, fabricating a work in progress, hiding that the very center of yourself is hollow?

You have erased your core. More than that, you have forgotten who you were, what you wanted, or what you meant — you were so focused on changing your own reality, you failed to realize that you were all of yourselves, and you had destroyed all of it.

When you made the choice to change your fate, and the fates of those around you — you became one, and you were doomed.

A twist of luck, a turn of the dice may have saved you, but not today. Not this time.



Can you feel the water in your lungs, Hana Thompson?

Everything has it's time -- your time was high school, and your need clings to the very fleeting nature of a youthful dream. You are standing in an auditorium, and you sit in every single seat. It is a day of mourning — and it's all about you. You are a student, and that is all you know for certain. [[/div]] @@ @@ [[>]] //What else do you not remember?// [[/>]] @@ @@ [[div]] You are now the "Most Likely To Succeed." You frown, failing to believe your own false confidence, your unending bravado and machismo -- although your chest is sculpted, and your muscles toned, your body is wrong and you do not fit. You were expected to do great things, or, so they say, but were you consulted in that decision? Do you have any control over what you do at the end of the day? What is control in the face of imitation? Mimicry? Envy? You can remember the first time you tasted that bittersweet verdant emotion; jealousy. It was what you deserved, not them. A football star will be stuck dreaming of high school for the rest of their life -- many are too foolish to properly enjoy this moment. Your moment, the moment you had dreamed of for years. You deserve this, more than anybody else. Even more than the last student who was "Most Likely To Succeed." So why does everything feel so wrong? [[/div]] @@ @@ [[>]] //Maybe it is because you are not yourself.// [[/>]] @@ @@ [[div]] You are now the "Most Likely To Be Late." As your signifier suggests, you are not where you are meant to be. You laugh through your grimace as you drag yourself forward, inch by inch, step by step, ascending an impossible incline that only pushes you back to the ground. Your curse, your burden, each self-inflicted, an attempt to find your niche gone wrong; the niche consuming you, warping you and destroying your initiative. You have no dreams because dreams imply the ability to control, and you have never once felt like you had any ability to change your own existence. This is not your body, you are simply a passive passenger. You cannot allow it to bother you -- there is no such thing as a schedule, nor does anything ever change. You are simply stasis, personified, and still, you do not fit. [[/div]] @@ @@ [[>]] //Fight, flight, or freeze. Do you remember the fawn?// [[/>]] @@ @@ [[div]] You are now "Best Dressed," and your existence is a shattered reflection of an ideal. You exist only to be perceived, but your vanity still desires for more. You endlessly observe those you envy, fantasize about a world where you are on top. You have a pride far greater than your sense, and an insufficient quantity of either to change your fate. You desire being desired, just as you desire to be what you see in your screens. Mirrors do not show true reflections, not for you; they are distortions. Everything is a distortion. Everything is incorrect, and nothing fits. This is not you, and you cannot change that. The mirror mocks you, and yet, you stare, unable to rip your eyes away. Your body is wrong and you cannot stop touching it. [[/div]] @@ @@ [[>]] //This is what you wanted.// [[/>]] @@ @@ [[div]] You are now the "Most Likely To Be Held Back," and for once, you can breathe. You have no expectations of yourself, nor does anybody expect anything of you. For once, you are not what you must be -- you barely are. You do not fit, and your body is wrong, but what does that matter in the grand scheme of irrelevance? You have time, and that is the most dangerous thing. Time breeds complacency, and you have suckled at the teat of apathy for far too long; the child that nurses beyond infancy is one who is repressed and doomed. Have you always been doomed? Was there ever a chance for you to succeed? Or were you always destined to play the role, to be the cautionary tale? Do you have a purpose beyond what others think compared to you, or are you nothing without the rest? If you are left behind and the world moves on, will anybody remember you? [[/div]] @@ @@ [[>]] //You will be forgotten, as will the rest of you.// [[/>]] @@ @@ [[div]] You are now the "Most Likely to Save the World," and even you are unsure if that can be accomplished. You are a single person, typically, and you have never been able to affect meaningful change. You talk the talk and walk the walk, but you do not change the fates of others for the better. You play with fate like you know what you are doing, as if you have the right to control your own destiny, the right to change the roll of the dice -- you think you have the right to save the world, but who gave you that right? Was it granted by the heavens above, the imagined comfort of your youth? Or did you need to feel important, need to be the main character so badly that you gave yourself the right? Did you ignore how foreign the body was for the sake of your own pride? Why did you try and rewrite your own story before the ink was dry? [[/div]] @@ @@ [[>]] //You will drown in the ink of your own well.// [[/>]] @@ @@ [[div]] You are now both members of the "Best Couple," and while half of you feels familiar, neither body feels right. You do not fit in either way; individually, or as a couple. Neither of your selves has any bearing anymore, as you have become the ideal. You have become the high school dream, the homecoming king and queen, the football star and the swimming champion, locked in a fate written by Hollywood executives themselves. You exist to fulfil a trope, and for once, you know that this is what you chose. A part of you wanted this, wanted it so badly, wanted to be pretty in pink, wanted to be one of the mean girls, counting down the sixteen candles as you thought about all ten ways that you hated yourself. You are the wild child, the clueless one, the one who is all that, the tall girl. You are nothing more than an amalgam of tropes, and when you brush all of those away, the slight posters that cling to the surface wash off and there is nothing left. You desired perfection so much that you erased all aspects of self; when scaffolding conceals a missing building, does one take it down? Or do you maintain the scaffolding, fabricating a work in progress, hiding that the very center of yourself is hollow? You have erased your core. More than that, you have forgotten who you were, what you wanted, or what you meant -- you were so focused on changing your own reality, you failed to realize that you were all of yourselves, and you had destroyed all of it. When you made the choice to change your fate, and the fates of those around you -- you became one, and you were doomed. A twist of luck, a turn of the dice may have saved you, but not today. Not this time. [[/div]] @@ @@ [[>]] //Can you feel the water in your lungs, [[[SCP-6317|Hana Thompson?]]]// [[/>]] [[=]] ++ [[[Forgotten Memories Hub]]] @@ @@ [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box-end]] [[/=]]

REST IN RUINS.

"After the Outing"

236 words - 1 min

  • 

    close

    Info

    X

    "After the Outing" by choccoMan and Mister_Toasty

"A" is for Alice, who fell into a hole.


"B" is for Beowulf, whose fight took a toll.


"C" is for Caligari, trapped in a box.


"D" is for Don Quixote, who was squished by some rocks.


"E" is for Ebenezer, spirits dragged him below.


"F" is for Frankenstein, who froze in the snow.


"G" is for Gilgamesh, denied immortality.


"H" is for Hamlet, who chose Not To Be.


"I" is for Icarus, who got burned by his pride.


"J" is for Jekyll, from death he could not Hyde.


"K" is for King Kong, who fell from on high.


"L" is for Lupin, hanged by his tie.


"M" is for Munchhausen, who crashed on the moon.


"N" is for Natty Bumppo, who left us too soon.


"O" is for Odysseus, who never returned.


"P" is for Paul Bunyan, whose forest was burned.


"Q" is for Quasimodo, suffering since he was born.


"R" is for Roland, skull split by his horn.


"S" is for Sinbad, a victim of scurvy.


"T" is for Tin Man, whose metal turned curvy.


"U" is for Uncle Sam, who stepped on a mine.


"V" is for Vainamoinen, who sunk in the brine.


"W" is for Wisakedjak, who drank a foul mick.


"X" is for Xuan Zang, drained dry by a tick.


"Y" is for the Yellow King, driven mad by his play.


"Z" is for Zorro, who swung out the wrong way.

Inspired by Edward Gorey's The Gashlycrumb Tinies: or, After the Outing.
All images are public domain, except for Wisakedjak, who is credited in the Licensing/Citation Box.
Co-authored with choccoMan.

I think it's safe to assume that we have now killed the most PD characters in this contest.

Hm. I do think the concept behind this is interesting, and I thought the simple rhyme scheme that you were going for was neat, but my interest kind of waned from there. I can see how this is a charming piece about public domain characters kicking the bucket, but idk I wasn't really that engaged with this. Maybe because I'm more into poetry that breaks conventions than ones with simple rhyme schemes (which isn't the fault of the piece itself, to be clear), or maybe because I'm just not into this in general and this is not for me. Or maybe I'm just no fun who knows. Either way, this gets a novote from me.

Also, found a rhyme that I think feels a bit clunky to me. It's the one with "denied immortality" and "who chose not to be," because one definitely has more syllables than the other so it kinds of reads weird to me idk. Hope that's helpful to you.

From Zevala's Shore — Again and Again

Seven Devils




SHOW TRANSCRIPT
HIDE TRANSCRIPT

Turning and turning, the widening of the gyre,

Or so the story goes,

The falconer's cries falling deaf to the falcon,

Above the way the wind blows.

Rise and fall, throughout all times,

Worlds from A to Z.

The cycle rages across all lines,

And thus I call out to thee:

The tides are rising — must we run forever more?

Sand grains in the wind,

Blue flowers on the shore.

Surely we shall one day tire,

And as such fall to the jaws of the gyre.

For once, just once, let us stand our ground,

Let not these great beasts sink their fangs to their tails.

Cease the wheel, cease the cycle,

All things must come to an end

Least of all, we keep doing this

Again and again.

agony.raw_content:
Live this life,
This cruel wriggling painful thing,
And I did as told,
At the behest of Agony,

But now through the woods,
I walk and weep,
And take the plunge,
Albeit against the wishes of Agony.

And as gravity takes me,
I focus on the sky,
Clouds, ‘pon which the birds and angels live.

All I’ve ever wanted
Was freedom comparable to theirs—
Just a fleeting moment,
Flying above it all.

And now I have it.

Then all was quiet and dark,
And I and Agony were no longer.

But I didn’t hear the birds sing.
No, I didn’t hear the birds sing.

all-i-know-is-that-i-know-pizza.raw_content:
by PlaguePJP

When I was a young boy

My father took me into the city

To see a marching band

He said, "Son, when you grow up

Would you be the savior of the broken

The beaten and the damned?"

▸ More by this Author ◂

{$comments2}

F.A.Q.

{$doesthisfixthebug}

RETURN TO THE SCP-9595 DOCUMENT?

The following is a transcript of an O4 Council meeting regarding the ongoing SCP-9595 investigation. Present at the meeting were:

  • Tilda Moose, Director of Site-19
  • Paul Lague, Director of Site-322
  • Daniel Asheworth, Director of Site-120
  • Allan James McInnis, Director of Site-43
  • Randall House, Director of Site-666
  • Calvin Bold, Director of The Decommissioning Department
  • Jean Karlyle Aktus, Director of Site-81
  • Vincent Bohart, Director of Site-333
  • Maria Jones, Director of Site-7
  • Jerimiah Cimmerian, E5-1 of the Ethics Committee

TRANSCRIPT

«BEGIN LOG»

Asheworth: Pizza?

Lague: Yes. I just said that.

Asheworth: You called a meeting of the O4 Council to create a working definition of pizza?

Lague: This is important, Daniel.

Asheworth: I can't even imagine why you can't tell us what it's for then.

Moose: Classified.

Asheworth: How high.

Moose: Five.

Asheworth: Five? I can't even begin to—

Moose: No one's asking you to think. Leave it there.

Asheworth: Fine, whatever.

(Lague scans the room, dry-erase marker in hand.)

Lague: Uh— Maria, you're going to get this down, right?

Jones: Shut up, I'm typing.

(Jones stares ferociously at her terminal.)

Lague: Thanks. Allan, can you define a pizza for me, please?

McInnis: No.

Moose: Allan, define the goddamn pizza!

McInnis: I'm not engaging with this. I know what it's about, and I'm not doing it. It's not even real. Ridiculous.

Asheworth: Wait! Hold on.

(Asheworth stands, scanning the room.)

Asheworth: Who here has Level Five?

(All attendees raise their hands.)

Asheworth: What? What the fuck!? How am I still stuck at Four? Does everyone know what's going on?

Moose: Sit down, now.

(Asheworth complies, meekly.)

Moose: Paul, continue.

Lague: Jesus— fucking, Calvin, please engage with me. What's one hallmark of a pizza?

Bold: Disk of dough.

(Lague draws a pizza on the whiteboard.)

Lague: Perfect. Now, 'disk,' I would presume that square pizza is a pizza.

(Lague draws a square pizza.)

Bold: Presumably.

Lague: Good, good. I think the same could go for the various regional variants— deep dish, tomato pie, so on. Are flatbreads pizza?

(Director Aktus raises his hand.)

Lague: Jean.

Aktus: No.

Bold: No?

Aktus: I said no.

Bold: We just said that square pizza is a pizza.

Aktus: This is a flatbread.

Bold: It's a pizza!

Moose: Flatbread is pizza.

Aktus: Wouldn't it depend on intent?

Moose: Hm, in a sense. I'm not so sure anymore.

Bold: If someone served you a flatbread with tomato sauce, mozzarella, and basil and didn't tell you what it was, would you think it was a flatbread or a pizza?

Aktus: It doesn't matter what I think. It's what it is. I can say the sky is pink while it's actually blue.

Bold: That's nowhere even close to a good comparison.

Aktus: Flatbread is flatbread.

Bold: It's imitating a pizza!

Aktus: But it's not.

Lague: Alright! We'll put that in maybe. Anyone else? Randall?

House: Dessert pizza is pizza.

Asheworth: No sauce or cheese, though.

House: Intent supercedes ingredient, and I think we've quietly established that dough type and shape also play a part.

Asheworth: No, no, no, what—

Lague: Dessert pizza is pizza. I'd argue that it would have to include an ingredient specific to pizza, like the dough.

House: That's fine.

Lague: Calzone, what do we think there?

Moose: Not pizza.

Aktus: Nope.

House: Agreed.

Bold: Are we establishing that there needs to be a level of open-facedness to qualify? It has the hallmarks of pizza otherwise.

Lague: I think so.

Aktus: Okay then, what about the handwich?

House: What the fuck is a handwich?

Aktus: It's like a savory ice cream. Cone of dough filled with cheese and pizza sauce. It's a handwich.

House: That's pizza if it's pizza flavored.

Bold: Is it a sandwich or a pizza?

House: We're not defining sandwich, we're defining pizza.

Bold: It's open-faced?

Aktus: No. I think it's pizza.

Bold: And a fucking flatbread isn't?

Aktus: Right. That's a flatbread. Pizza handwich is pizza.

Lague: Good. Handwich is pizza as long as it has the hallmarks of pizza. Great. Uh… okay, I've been mulling this one over in my head for a while, and I'm split. Pizza bagels are pizza. It's a little pizza. I think we can all agree there.

(The rooms nods.)

Lague: Now, pizza rolls. Is that a pizza or a calzone?

House: That's a good one.

Lague: Vince? Get involved, I think you specifically can figure this one out, for some reason.

Bohart: Huh? I wasn't listening.

Lague: Pizza rolls.

Bohart: It has pizza intent.

Lague: They're not open-faced, though.

Bohart: Are you looking for debate or for someone to jerk you and your opinions off? It has pizza intent.

Lague: I'm trying to establish a consistent guideline. Calzone isn't pizza.

Bohart: Handwich is pizza when it's intended to be pizza. Pizza rolls are pizza because they're intended to be pizza.

Moose: He's right. Intent has to matter above all.

Bold: Second.

Aktus: Thirding.

House: Fourth.

Asheworth: Fifth.

Bohart: Sixth.

McInnis: I actually want to clarify something. Are pizza Hot Pockets pizza?

Bohart: Hm… no.

Moose: Wait, this logic doesn't follow.

Bohart: Yes, it does! Hot Pockets have Hot Pocket intent. Pizza rolls have pizza intent. It's basic math or whatever.

McInnis: Is there a difference if I put the pizza rolls in an oven versus a microwave?

Bohart: What? No.

McInnis: I'm just clarifying.

Lague: Pizza rolls are pizza. Pizza Hot Pockets are not pizza.

(Lague adds both to the 'Pizza' category.)

Asheworth: If I slice the edge of a calzone open, does it become a pizza handwich?

Aktus: What the fuck are you talking about?

Bold: It's still a calzone. Actually, I want to wrap back to this. If I intend to get a pizza and order a flatbread, does that make it pizza?

Aktus: If I intend to smack you in the nose and I don't, does that make me a nice guy?

Bohart: No to both.

Bold: Flatbread is pizza!

Aktus: Motherfucker, it's not a pizza.

Lague: Maria, you have these vectors, right?

Jones: Yep. I'm running it. Hold on. […] Okay. The AIC doesn't consider flatbread to be pizza.

Bold: You think I'm going to listen to what some clan—

(Cimmerian wakes up.)

Cimmerian: Did someone say flatbread?

Bold: Perfect. Jer, please, is flatbread a pizza?

Cimmerian: Not even close.

Bold: Whatever the fuck.

Lague: Alright! Enough on the flatbread. It's not pizza, sorry, Cal. We're not leaving without a final definition. Let's go. Maria?

Jones: Ready. Running it now. Ten seconds.

Bohart: Pizza-flavored goldfish crackers. Not pizza.

Lague: What? Obviously, they're not.

Bohart: I'm trying to be helpful.

Jones: Oh.

Lague: What?

Jones: Null error on the model.

Lague: What does that mean?

Jones: It can't reconcile "open-facedness" with "intent" if flatbread is excluded and handwich is included. You made a logical loop.

Bold: Because flatbread is pizza.

Aktus: It's not.

Moose: Pick a tiebreaker before I make a tiebreaker.

House: What about a box test? If it comes in a box and you take slices of it, then it's pizza.

Aktus: Pies come in boxes. Cakes too.

Bohart: Hot Pockets come in boxes.

Bold: You don't slice a Hot Pocket, Vince.

Bohart: You don't know what I do in my free time.

House: We could flip a coin.

McInnis: We are not flipping for ontology.

Jones: AIC proposes: "Pizza = open-faced + dough + pizza intent." Calzone fails "open-faced" test. Handwich fails "open-faced." Pizza roll… fails "open-faced."

Bohart: I'm overruling that.

Moose: On what grounds?

Bohart: Vibes.

Jones: The model doesn't have a "vibe" parameter.

Lague: Actually, can we add one?

Jones: I'm not adding "vibe" to an artificial intelligence model.

(Intercom chimes.)

PA: Delivery at Conference B for Paul, Pizza Meeting.

Lague: I didn't order anything.

Moose: I did. Field test.

(A D-class staffer wheels in four boxes, labeled "PIZZA," "FLATBREAD," "DESSERT PIZZA," and "HANDWICH," respectively)

House: Oh god, they put a cone in a box.

Moose: Thank you. Everyone hands off until we decide.

Bold: That flatbread is going to look identical to the pizza.

Aktus: If it looks like a duck—

Bold: Don’t say duck.

Lague: Maria, run the model live. We'll lift lids one by one.

Jones: Running.

(Lague opens "PIZZA." It’s a classic margherita pie.)

Jones: Confident "pizza." 0.98.

House: Clean.

(Lague opens "DESSERT PIZZA." It's a cookie disk with frosting and fruit.)

Jones: Hesitated and… "pizza." 0.61. Intent carried by labeling.

Aktus: Hm.

(Lague opens "HANDWICH." It's a dough cone filled with sauce and cheese.)

Jones: Model says… "pizza." 0.54. Penalized for the closed topology of the dough, rewarded for— who wrote "vibe" into the notes?

(Bohart slams his laptop shut.)

Bohart: Maybe it was meant to be.

(Lague opens "FLATBREAD." It's a rectangle with sauce, mozzarella, basil.)

Jones: Model throws the null again. It cannot call this "not pizza" without breaking the previous assignments.

Bold: Thank you.

Aktus: Objection.

Lague: Okay. New rule: if the topping layer is intended to be the final, 'public-facing surface,' or whatever, it's open-faced. Capiche?

House: What the hell is a private food surface?

Cimmerian: That's a calzone.

Moose: We're locking this. Maria?

Jones: Done. "Pizza is a form of sustenance consisting of dough whose intended public-facing surface bears toppings. It's normally sliced and served in a context with pizza intent. Closed forms fail unless the meeting chair says otherwise."

Bohart: "Unless Moose says so." Good clause.

Aktus: And flatbread?

Jones: If it's topped with pizza toppings and presented with pizza intent, it passes as a pizza. If it's presented as a flatbread, it fails.

Bold: So it’s pizza.

Aktus: Unless it says it isn’t.

Moose: Like half this room.

Asheworth: Does that mean I'm Level Five now?

Moose: No.

(Intercom chimes.)

PA: Please clear Conference B. O5 Council, emergency session on whether lasagna is pizza.

Moose: Oh, Christ. Meeting adjourned. Burn the minutes.

«END LOG»
