    Title: Beau Goes For a Run
    Author: Mr Panik
    ⚠️ Content warning: This article contains a content warning: implied child abuse.

"Mom…I couldn't go through with— Mom, please, stop yelling…"

"…"

"I know… I'm sorry. I freaked ou— Mom, please!"

"…"

"Yeah, yeah, I know you pulled strings to get me the interview. Mom, I'll still help out, I swear!"

"…"

"I'll move to Pierre."

Beau's feet carried him through the cool air of Pierre's night. He'd taken to the street to burn off the anger of the argument he'd had with his mother, but it wasn't enough. It never was. He would run until he was exhausted like he did every time they fought and then he'd pass out on his bed only to wake up and repeat the same argument again the next day. When the frustration chaffed inside him so hard he wanted to tear his chest open, all he could think of doing was running.

So he ran.

As usual, his body gave way before his desperation did. After an aimless half-hour run followed by four circuits of the block the dog park was on, Beau collapsed on a bench, panting. He let himself slide sideways until he was lying down, then rolled over to stare at the sky. His chest heaved from the effort of the run, but that hadn't just been exercise. That'd been something else.

He closed his eyes, cutting the flitting shadows in the park from his view, and tried to dismiss his nerves to the back of his mind. The shadows chased one another back and forth across the road, liquid darkness that darted around his passing. He wasn't sure if he should have but he'd come to accept that they existed. What they were remained a mystery, though.

It had been months since Beau had left California, defeated; chased by nothing but the Santa Anas, heading towards nothing but the last resort. Most days, it still felt like he'd only just arrived. No matter how often he let himself get lost in work, no matter how often he reminded himself that he was safe in his own apartment with a roommate that wasn't insane, it didn't help. He struggled every month and every month his mother still managed to ask for more and more and more. He didn't want to blame her for her decisions, but he couldn't deny his feelings.

So he ran.

Money. It was always money that stuck its nose into his peace. Money in the shape of his mother's endless needs. She had a job in Pierre, like him, but after he moved out she'd suddenly needed his help way more than before. He didn't earn much working for SCP, but he helped her where he could. He'd have stayed living with her if he thought he'd survive it, but there was only so much his mind could take. So he left before the weight of his mother's collapse took him down too.

He sighed, firmly wiping sweat from his eyes. The wind began to cool him down and his breathing was beginning to steady.

"Hey there!"

Beau's eyes shot open to see who had spoken, but there was no one. "Hello?" He asked the night air, with the eerie emptiness standing silently witness. He shifted uncomfortably, sitting up to get a better view. This was Pierre; you never knew what could be watching you from out in the darkness.

"Down here."

Beau looked down, startled, and froze. His gaze came to rest on the scraggly opossum sitting calmly next to the bench. Beau said nothing. He wasn't sure if what was happening was weird enough for him to believe it, even in Pierre, but he was quite sure that opossum was speaking to him.

"Yup, you're looking at a talking opossum," the opossum said. "The name's Lloyd."

"H- hey, Lloyd. I'm Beau." Beau looked at the animal before him, confused. Pierre was properly strange on a good day, and knowing what was real and what wasn't hadn't been easy for him since before he even moved there.

The animal— Lloyd — yawned, his rat-like snout gaping out at the world. When he was done, he clicked his teeth a bit, shook his head and looked back up at Beau. "Nice to know you, Beau! You doing alright?"

"Uh," Beau looked around, wondering where the ventriloquist was, but knowing he wasn't going to find one. "I'm doing alright, I guess."

"You must be guessing if you passed out on a park bench at 10PM."

"Wasn't passing out. Just taking a break. I'll get back to running again soon."

"Well," Lloyd said, shuffling closer to bench. "Why are you out running so late?"

Lloyd did a little hop and managed to grab the edge of the bench. His body dangled for a moment, wiggling as his feet tread empty air. Beau reached over and lifted Lloyd up on the bench where he shook his coat out, turned in place and parked himself looking up at Beau. Beau returned the gesture by blinking blankly at him.

"Cat got your tongue?" Lloyd asked.

"Uh, no!" said Beau. "I just didn't expect to see anyone tonight. I was just getting some fresh air."

"Fresh air always helps clear the mind, yeah," Lloyd said, nodding and looking out across the dog park. "Those little guys sure do know how to have fun!"

"What do you mean?" Beau turned to look, but the shadows that had been hounding his periphery every night since he'd arrived disappeared as soon as he focused on them. "Damn."

"Eh, humans will catch up soon enough."

"What do you mean?"

"Just things on the other side of the here. Don't worry about it," Lloyd assured him. "But, seriously, what brings you out here tonight? Looks like you're carrying the world."

Beau paused, considering what to say. He didn't like speaking badly of his mother. She wasn't a bad person under everything. She was just at the end of her rope. She just needed some help, and there was nothing anyone could do to make his mother more reasonable. There was no amount of talking about how crazy she was that was going to make him feel better. And again, this was an opossum; talking to him would be insane.

"I'm just clearing my head after a fight with my mom," Beau said, eventually. "It's just easier to burn off that frustration out here."

"By hurting yourself with bad form? I watched you running up and down for a while, y'know?"

"I-I… I'm not a runner. Not really."

"Hmmmm," Lloyd nodded, thoughtfully. "Must have been a pretty rough argument."

"Is arguing about money ever calm?" Beau asked, sardonic to the bone.

"Not in my experience. People take money pretty seriously. Had a guy apologize to me once because I borrowed him some money," Lloyd scratched at his ear. "Maybe I'm just an opossum and I don't get it, but money seems to get in the way of a lot of good things in life."

"Yeah. It does."

Beau blinked hard, pushing away the thoughts of a life he could have had if he'd been anyone else, or just the one that didn't fumble when it mattered the most.

"Penny for your thoughts?" Lloyd asked, flicking his tail back and forth.

"It's just hard to think of my relationship with my mother as good." Beau murmured into the dark.

"Ah. That is a tough one." Lloyd looked as pensive as an opossum could for a bit then turned to Beau and said, "From what I've seen visiting with my neighbors over the years, family can be pretty complicated."

"You don't have a family of your own?"

"Not in the traditional sense, no," Lloyd said padding the air with a paw as if to swat away a concern. "But it's really no worries. I've got some good friends back home. But you sound like you've got no one."

"Yeah."

"Would it be too much to ask what happened with your mom?"

"I didn't get a job that she was really counting on." Beau was surprised he could say it as easily as he did. He'd never said it out loud. Not that plainly, at least. "I guess I would have been perfect for it, but I screwed up the interview."

"Money trouble's a theme for you, huh?"

"Yeah."

"Hmmmm," said Lloyd, looking out across the park again. The stillness of the night was impenetrable around them and for a moment they were they only living beings in the world. The crisp air swirled around them while ever clearer shadows played across the lawns in front of them. "You can't blame yourself forever. People screw up interviews all the time."

"Not everybody ends up hyperventilating in a bathroom because the world suddenly didn't look real."

Beau waited for some kind of confused or condescending quip. It never came. Lloyd just looked up at him and smiled. "This is real, Beau. I can tell you that much."

"Some days it's an effort to figure out what is and isn't, but thanks. That helps," said Beau. "I think."

Lloyd snickered for a second. "I think it's called derealization, by the way."

"Wh-What do you mean?"

"Derealization. It's a thing that happens to some people where the world looks a hundred miles away, or like it's not real. Some people say it's like interacting with the world through a pane of glass or like people look like cardboard cutouts," Lloyd looked up at him, but his smile seemed sad. "It happens to people who are under a lot of stress."

Beau couldn't speak. It was word-for-word what had happened to him. Nobody had believed him. He'd been sitting in his head alone with this for months, as alone as he'd been in the bathroom cubicle he passed out in. Moving to Pierre had scared him so much. He'd stayed inside for as long as he could before his mother had forced him out into the world to find work. In those early days when he wasn't sure what was real and what wasn't, bussing tables and running deliveries had been the most terrified he'd ever been.

It had only been when he'd eventually lost his second job in Pierre that he'd given SCP a call and he'd held onto that number since he found it in L.A. It was only there that he started learning what was in his head and what wasn't. It had brought him some kind of peace-of-mind knowing that he wasn't losing touch with reality completely.

"You're not crazy, Beau," Lloyd chimed. "You're just a guy with a lot on his plate."

"I guess."

"You really need to cut yourself some slack."

"People say that, but I'm just not where I wanted to be." The words tumbled out of his mouth, but it seemed that Lloyd had managed to break through the wall that usually held this all back. "I live in the middle of nowhere. I'm scared to talk to anyone that I'm not paid to. The only reason my roommate and I get along is because we both spend more time in our rooms than we should. I clean up after people for a living. I know I'm not supposed to look down on that, but it's just not where I wanted to be."

"Well, where do you want to be?"

"Not cleaning out Bagel Bob's cesspool walk-in."

"Bagel Bob's has great food, though!"

"I thought so too!" Beau's eyes widened. "Dee and I were cleaning it out and just don't eat there ever again. Trust me. Or do, I dunno. Who knows what's real anymore? Denise Does Dogs is still in business and I'm still not sure what she's doing with the dogs."

"Does it bother you that she's doing things with dogs?"

"It's just weird. Everything here is weird. Mr A. Lien's has had a 'Coming Soon' sign up there for months," Beau exclaimed. "Or a week. I don't know. Every time I look at it I just get stuck in time. Stuck here."

"And you don't want to be here," said Lloyd. Silence followed for a while as the two of them gazed out at the park across the road. He noticed the shadows at the edge of his vision start to take some clearer shape, slowly stretching into his full field of vision. Nothing became too much more defined, but he was surer now that there was something out there.

"Yeah," Beau nodded. "I could probably be doing better now if I'd just made things work in L.A."

"But why blame yourself for things not working out? What race are you running?" Lloyd asked, throwing his paws up. "L.A.'s been there for a while and it's probably not going anywhere soon. You're allowed to go back and try again when you're back on your feet. Who said you aren't?"

"Yeah, but because I freaked out, because I… derealized…" Beau tested the word in his mouth, confused by how correct it felt. "I'm a step back from where I needed to be. It's going to take me ages to save up again."

"Why did you sit down on this bench tonight, Beau?" Lloyd asked, casually looking away again. "Were you done running?"

"I needed a rest," said Beau.

"And are you mad at yourself for needing a rest?"

"W-Where are you going with this?"

"Your body was tired and needed a rest, so you rested," said Lloyd pointedly. "Why would you be mad at yourself for you needing a rest after things went badly for you? Because you shouldn't be. You didn't ask to break down. It just happened. Now you're recovering, but you're blaming yourself for needing to. That doesn't seem fair on you."

"Yeah, but if I'd gotten that job, there would have been more money to go around," said Beau. "My mom wouldn't be living in a tiny apartment. I'd be driving to work not cycling."

"You can't blame yourself for any of that and your mother isn't your yoke to bear." Lloyd managed to sound both gentle and stern as he spoke. "I know you love her and you seem like the type that really wants to help out, but what if that help is hurting someone?"

"How can that even happen?"

"Believe me, people respond weirdly to help. I've gotten some weird responses over the years for some of the help I've given people," said Lloyd. "Your mom needs to take action for herself so that she can start winning back her life. She's reliant on you. You're suffering. Everyone loses."

"And that's the difference between 'helping' and 'enabling,' isn't it?" Beau asked, but they both knew the answer and he was happy to sit in silence for a bit.

Beau considered Lloyd's words carefully. They may as well have been words whispered from another dimension considering how foreign they sounded. He'd always been there to carry the load when it was needed and he'd stayed in his mom's corner for every step of the way. Still, the needling in what Lloyd had said bloomed uncontrollably in Beau's mind as he realized the sad truth.

"I— I don't owe her anything," said Beau and slowly felt a smile form on his face.

"Yup!"

"Yup!" Lloyd said. "And you need to start accepting that you don't have to rescue her. You don't have to rescue anyone. You just have to be there for people when they need you. That's all."

The two sat quietly for a bit longer. Beau's mind was awash with thoughts of what he'd been through and how it'd really affected him. He cast his upwards at the pink-purple sky undulating in the night. It felt miles above him, though low thick clouds stretched in every direction. Occasionally, what seemed like lightning would streak silently across the sky, splitting the hazy night apart like the oil in a lava lamp. He watched calmly as the sky reattached itself, skittering energy sealing reality back together, and then he smiled, wondering if anyone else could see it.

He still needed to learn a lot, but running didn't feel right anymore. He and his mother would need to have a very difficult conversation; he couldn't put it off anymore. He didn't deserve to drown. Mulling over the same argument he'd been having with her since he was twelve had just driven him crazy. Things had to change.

"Thank you, Lloyd," said Beau.

"Don't mention it," Lloyd said, smiling up at him. "But I think I need to get going, actually. I'm meeting my new neighbors in the morning and it's still a way to go for me."

"I, uh, I can get can my roommate to drive you," said Beau, reaching for his phone.

"Oh, no need!" Lloyd said, shimmying his way off the bench. Beau watched as the bundle of fur popped down onto the grass again, bemused. Lloyd gave a large stretch then looked over at Beau. "You take care of yourself, Beau. I'm gonna enjoy the rest of the night."

"I… Be safe!" said Beau, watching as Lloyd waved at him and then set off into the night.

He watched until Lloyd's fluffy rear disappeared around the nearby corner, a few shadows loping playfully after him. The chill of the evening drew in around Beau, but for the first time in a while there was some kind of warmth he felt, like he was comfortable to be there for the first time since arriving.

Standing up, he stretched a little to get his muscles loosened up again and decided to head back. It was pretty late, but he had a day off the next day, so he didn't need to rush. The warmth in Beau's chest grew as he began to jog until a smile appeared on his face. Usually, he ran because he was frustrated, but tonight things had ended surprisingly well.

One foot in front of the other, Beau carried himself homewards; breathy, detached barking finally telling him what had been darting around in the shadows.

"Uh, my name's Beau. I'm 20. I spent the last year in L.A. but then I decided I needed to focus more on family, so here I am."

"And why did you choose Safe Cleanup Professionals?"

"I, uh, I'm really passionate about being of service to people. Really like helping people this w-way."

"I see. And how did you hear about us?"

"Oh! Yeah! I saw your ad while I was scrolling on my phone at the porn studio I auditioned for."

"And how did that audition work out?"

because-i-could-not-stop-for-death.creator: Uncle Nicolini
because-i-could-not-stop-for-death.raw_content:
Three brothers sit at a table in an otherwise empty bar, playing Skat.

There are bottles of alcohol, unopened, covered in dust and cobwebs sitting atop the counter.

The cards they play with are ancient and faded from neglect.

And still, they proceed in their merriment, awaiting company.

"He's late," says the first, a young man with a sleek mustache wearing a fine-tailored suit.

"He arrives precisely when he means to," the second speaks up, a balding man with spots on his head, dressed casually. "Not later, not sooner. You are too impetuous."

The third, a rail-thin old man, nearly desiccate in appearance and wearing rags, merely nods.

The three continue their game.

"I don't think we have much more time," the mustached brother speaks up again, putting his cards face-down on the table.

"We have as much time as we need." the bald brother reassures him, glancing over his hand.

The eldest brother plays a card, the Queen of Hearts, and says nothing.

The three continue their game.

Eventually, someone enters the bar.

He is tall, wears a blazer, and carries with him a cigarette and lighter.

"It's about time," the youngest chides him.

"Hush. Welcome, now we can finally play Durak," says the middle one.

The oldest smiles and gathers up the cards, shuffling them with the skill and grace only experience may grant one.

"Sorry I took so long. There was something I needed to take care of before coming here," the newcomer smiles, taking a seat at the table and lighting his cigarette ablaze.

"No worries, brother. We know how it is with you. Always the kind one."

The bar, the bottles, the cobwebs, and its four patrons, would stand for only one round of Durak before vanishing into the ether.

below.raw_content:
There is a bleak and boneless dark, which stretches slithering through the caverns below.

BELOW

There is a bleak and boneless dark, which stretches slithering through the caverns below. The wounds we give it are forever fleeting, scabbed over with earth and healed in our wake. Thus we are ever blind to our own footsteps, our past passings unknown except in lamplit memories of a place carved out within the black.

There is no rest below, for rest is the setting-down of lamps, and the stilling of limbs. Rest is when the stomach untwists and feels its emptiness, when the tongue rasps on bone-dry teeth, when we sit and fall and feel the stone grow around us, a calcification of the air and the skin, the sweet eternal embrace of the earth.

There is a Resting-Priest beside me. It walks with us, wearing our clothes, wearing our skin, but it has no lamp, and by this I know it to be a Resting-Priest. Here is one who stopped — who nestled into a smooth comfortable curve of granite, who felt the stone cup and cover, until it grew slow as a stalactite over the limbs and mouth and eyes. Here is one who was swallowed by the earth, and was spit out again, a hollowed emissary, an earth-born poison, an ever-present reminder of you don’t have to keep going following forever. Beneath that ashen skin is dust and diorite, and in those eye-sockets turn only marble, blind as death.

“Stop,” the Resting-Priest says. “Rest.”

Its voice is the whisper of sand falling through cracks, the shiver of gravel shifting — the sounds of eternal equilibrium momentarily disturbed.

We do not stop. We do not rest.

Instead, we tell stories.

It is the crooked one who begins, voice dry, cracked, heavy and brittle as slate.

“Once upon a time,” he says. “There was a young boy, who lived near a forest.” The words wash over me, press their meaning into my mind, and I try to feel what the crooked one is saying. A forest: A place where the darkness is cast by living things, where in every direction is life upon life upon life, where light falls from the sky and dapples on the soft green moss. A forest is unimaginable. To us, to me, after an aeon here below, after uncounted miles of hunger and thirst and lamp-cast shadows flickering across hard stone walls — a forest is heaven.

“The boy’s elders warned him not to tarry in the evening woods,” the crooked one says. “But the boy, being young and foolish, did not heed their words.

“Soon the darkness came, swift as a rockfall. The boy could not see, could not walk, could not find his way home. He stumbled over roots and scraped himself on branches. It seemed to him like the trees had woken from a long sunlight-dappled sleep, and now, having woken, they were hungry.

“In the distance he heard howls, and screeches, and other stranger sounds. He ran, blood pumping in his ears, stumbling and tripping in his haste. When he caught himself on a tree trunk, he felt the bark move beneath his hand, and when he pulled away he left a layer of skin behind.”

I wince. This story is different than usual: too dark, too close. Beside me, the Resting-Priest’s footsteps are heavy.

“The boy kept running, shielding his head with his arms, until his forearms were bloody from the hungry whipping branches, and his breath scraped in his throat. The boy ran until he could run no more.

“And then he stopped.”

The crooked one pauses for a moment, to catch his breath, or to let the tension build. In the silence the darkness presses in, but the light of my lamp, and the lamps of my fellows, carves us a small, warm place, a sanctuary against the weight without.

“He stopped, hands on his knees,” the crooked one continues. “And then he fell, into the curve of root and trunk, cold and hard on his back. The shape of it cupped his spine, and held his arms, and rested his tired legs.

“The boy felt the tree’s branches grow over and into him, and he knew that the forest would accept him here, now, defiant and exhausted, just as it would have accepted him if he had gone willingly to its embrace.

“The tree's roots grew over his body and under his skin, and at last the boy could rest.”

I am staring at the crooked one, agape. He meets my eyes, and I see the cold earth behind them. His lamp — light, warmth — falls to the ground and shatters.

“Stop,” the crooked one says. “Rest.”

One by one, more lamps fall to the ground. I run. What else is there to do? Rock flashes beneath my feet, black and grey and brown, erratic beating footsteps like a failing heart, pushing texture and pressure and pain through my nerves.

Behind me the stone is moving, slow and patient as nothing else is. I run faster, terror slipping silver-quick down my spine. My breath scrapes its way through my throat, feeling already half gravel. I am outpacing them, for now. I am alive — quick, they called it, long ago — not stone, not yet.

Anyone can outpace the earth for a span of time, for a day, a year, a century. But not forever.

I do not know how long I ran for. It doesn’t matter, in the end. Run as you might, the earth is above and beneath and around you, and it bears your weight and the weight of your footfalls with inexorable patience. There is no running from it, just as you cannot run from your own skin. It is the world. It is the end.

I stumble to a stop. Behind me, my footprints stretch back and back, dull iron-red in the dust, fading before my eyes into the ever-hungry earth. Before me—

As it turns out, the world has its own end.

Before me the darkness deepens, yawning back, jaws unhinging. The light of my lamp cuts into it, and dies. The air moves against my face, stirs the hairs on my skin. I shine my light up, down, to each side, and see it fail in the black whichever way I point it. Here is the void at the edge of the world. Here is the last darkness. I breathe, and hear the stone move behind me.

But out in the void, far, far, away—

Slow footsteps echo behind me. The sound travels into the dark and vanishes.

“Stop,” the crooked one — the Resting-Priest — says. “Rest.”

I turn to face it as it walks toward me.

“The boy was lost in the forest,” I say. “He ran and he ran, but he could find no respite. The shadows followed, tireless.”

The crooked one stops, and looks at me with blind stone orbs. There is nothing behind them, not will nor heart. Its movements are only an inevitable consequence of the shape of the world. Each step is taken without expenditure, as a rock rolling down a slope, as an object moving along the path of least resistance. I speak to no-one and nothing.


“He ran until he could run no more. He stopped, and felt the forest shift around him, wrapping root and vine about his limbs. He felt the cold shadows draw near.” A smile spreads across my lips, a warm and unfamiliar feeling. I take a step back, the rocks sharp beneath my bare feet. “But he did not die,” I say. “For in that moment—” I raise my arms, and grin.



“In that moment, when all was already lost, when everything was over, the struggle, the flight, the outpacing of the earth. He saw it.” I take another step back, feel the void opening up behind me, feel my body tip away from the world. This earth, this sloshing squirming darkness, these caverns below: they will not have me.



There is a curious warmth on my back. A breath of change stirs the air. A strange cast on the stone and the light. Old memories rise unbidden to my mind, of things I had thought lost long ago. The wind, the clouds, the sky—




I take another step back, and fall. And as I fall:

“Behold,” I say.

“The

rising


sun."

bernard-s-ballad.raw_content:
Poltatherian

If you enjoyed this, make sure to check out my Author Page :)

Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.










You wake up in a daze, still not sure whether or not you're alive. You get up and stare at your desk, scattered notes & pictures lining atop it. A garbage can full of used cigars and torn-up documents. It all used to mean something, used to represent a life that wasn't there anymore. All it brought you was pain, so you got rid of it. The pleading cries from inside a napkin with a drawing of saturn on it left unanswered.

Getting dressed in an all black suit, you head down to your kitchen and stare into the contents, grab a banana & a glass of water for breakfast as you rush to the garage and start the car, it needs some repairs but you don't want any, you remember every scratch of paint driving down the Italian coastline you couldn't bother to admire. You slam the brakes as a sign catches your eye. It's a school entrance.

It's graduation day in the Basilicata Catholic all-girls institute.

Birds chirping, choir girls singing, church bells ringing as the new adults of the world prepare to spread their wings in the school's bright pink halls. Though it must have been surprising for such students to see a not-so-new, decrepit, bald adult walking through the campus. The man quietly passed the celebrating students and headed to the lower floors, swiping a keycard while on the elevator, which led him down to a wine cellar. The man was you.

You entered the cellar, and the air smelled of must; the walls were covered in dust & and all you saw was her. You're shaking hands, grasping one of the bottles with alcohol still in them, forcing the lid open as you chug the contents with reckless abandon. After the bottle runs empty, you slide your fingers across the walls one last time before taking off you're cross.

You jam the cross into a small crack in one of the wine barrels, machinery whirring behind as the wall opens up.

The vault was a terrible thing, a bunker full of the Initiatives' most dangerous & powerful relics. It represented everything the Initiative didn't want to be. The halls were nowhere near the dusty mess the cellar it was kept in was; clear white halls shone as its golden accents drew the eyes towards weapon upon weapon upon weapon, all fire & brimstone hanging on the walls.

You fearfully drew your gaze away from the walls, looking straight ahead as you strode forward with a conviction you had never felt since the day you bowed & pleaded for unity to those who would become the tribunal. Turning corner after corner, the nature of the vault grew apparent, space was needed to hold such artefacts, and that retched deer had provided, non-euclidean though the space was. It didn't matter, you were here for better, more noble reasons than our dominion, you held that sacred feeling only humans could have closer than everyone, everything. Once that feeling was love. Love for the boring days, love for enjoyment, love for the insults, love for the arguments only siblings could have, love for family.

Now that feeling was grief, rage & anger at whatever you could think of. The deliveries were late, the missions dragged on and on, Adnan & Samuel made stupid decisions, it was THEIR FAULT, it was Saturn Deers fault it…..

"It was her own fault, you know. It was Ursula's fault that she was at the wrong place at the wrong time, and she paid for that."

You spin backward as a grating face meets yours, and your eyes narrow in disgust.

"EXCUSE ME???" You barked, only a basic sense of conscience preventing you from strangling whoever was behind you.

"You heard me, asshole, did you think I wouldn't know you were here? I BUILT THIS PLACE DAMMIT!"

"Oh, I'm well aware you wretch. Get out of my sight at once."

"And what if I don't? We fight and blow up the school? The chain reaction from the first 5 relics you saw alone would blow up Italy, so pipe down.

"Why are you here? To finish what you started?"

"I didn't kill your sister Bernie, to be frank, I couldn't care less. This place is just a favor."

"A favour, huh? You're even worse than what Henry told me."

"Well, Henry's dead and I'm not. Nothing much to be said after that, I'm just annoyed you ignored my message."

"The fucking napkin?"

"mmhmm. I tried to pay my respects, you know."

"Leave me alone. That's final."

The voice behind you takes a deep sigh and leaves.

You keep walking through the vault, eventually reaching a room headed with a blank pink plate. You open the door to find a single cigar laid atop a wooden pedestal, a note beside it. You took the note, placing a rose from your pocket in its place as you carefully opened it.






















The note was blank, and you couldn't help but laugh.

You walk out of the cellar, festivities have ended as the students move on with their lives, you examine the crayon drawings in the classrooms, the confetti on the ground, the uneaten food, the cheerful air as friends make plans, and the staff still left in the school begin to pack their things.

You head towards the reception desk, placing a cigar in front of the receptionist as a quick "Hello" escapes your mouth.

"Mr…Bernard, was it? You look just like her."

"Ah, yes, I'm sorry I didn't introduce myself properly; the students must be confused."

"It's perfectly all alright, sir. Ms. Amadeo was…dear to us all. I can't imagine what you must be going through. This is just as your school as it was at hers."

"Doesn't feel like it. The students here are definitely cut from her cloth.

"Perhaps, but her cloth grew with you, no?"

"Perhaps. Did she ever speak of me? Be honest."

The receptionist coughed as a nervous look etched itself across her face.

"Um, well, sir, she said you were a…."

"A What?"

"An annoying little cunt that can't keep himself out of trouble."

A slight slime creeps across your face.

"She would be happy to know I still am. Have a nice day, ma'am."




















"Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted."

bessie-bogan-and-the-crow-road-inn.raw_content:
In which the Mosaic’s favorite tavern flies into trouble.
(Tales of the Mosaic – 350 words)

Tessera

Bessie Bogan and the Crow Road Inn

written by Dr Angell
narration and music by Jezixo
art by Costodic

Few corners of the Mosaic were as convivial as the Crow Road Inn.

Word spread fast through the factory floors whenever Bessie Bogan’s feathered hut was seen soaring overhead, workers buzzing until shift’s end when, for but a couple pence, the inn’s tap would pour them a pint, and the stove would serve up a warm, hearty bowl of cow heel soup and a soursop sandwich. Her familiars conversed with regulars eagerly over the day’s gossip —who drowned in the river last Friday, what stranger appeared from the forsaken furnishing shop on Egbert Lane, or why Bessie’s dust pan ran away again— all while six-stringed fiddles, washboards and spoons played themselves to Bessie’s ballads: raunchy old tunes so jovial it made the most miserable wretches two-step on the tavern tables.

This, of course, would never do for the Proctors; gossip, music, and soursop sandwiches were antithetical to Progress, and should any of their workers be caught in a place so morally destitute, they would be cast from their living quarters to the river bank, fated to become gossip at the next gathering. But folks never stayed away for long, and if the Proctors hated anything more than indolence, it was waste. So one night, hired ruffians lurked in the shadows 'til no one was looking, and patrons were boisterous with drink. Then they hacked and sawed and snapped the wings off the Crow Road Inn.

The wingless hut sat still the next morning, helpless prey to the Proctors’ greatest weapon: the local food inspector, who wished to shutter the inn over Bessie’s lack of a license. As the inspector appeared, chains in hand, however, the old hut began to shake. The inky blue feathers of its thatched roof rustled, its timber walls rattled and groaned, and the inspector watched as it rose up on creaky crow legs. To his surprise, and utter distress, the Crow Road Inn wandered away.

Bessie came back from time to time, entertaining old patrons and friends, but her ballads were never as lively, and the sandwiches were never quite the same.

black-freighter-black-sea.raw_content:
Amanda is fifteen years old when she feels the pull of the deep for the first time.

It is July, and they have gone to the beach in the early hours of the morning to be. The others, mostly people from school that she has fallen in with by chance, are huddled around a cluster of plastic candles beneath the docks, but she breaks off silently and makes her way along the shore until the artificial orange glow and the shapes against it are out of sight. She has a need to be alone that she cannot place.

She comes to a place where the light of the waxing crescent hits the sea just so, sits with her back to the docks and their buildings, and watches the waves lap on the sand. The water splashes her toes every so often; a plane passes silently overhead. In the distance, a lone freighter glides westward to ports unknown.

The moon scuttles behind a cloud, leaving her with nothing but sound: the sea sloshing in steady rhythm on the shore, a lone insect buzzing somewhere to her right, the jeers and hollers of the others growing distant. She closes her eyes, takes a deep breath, feels the wet air fill her nostrils, opens her eyes as she exhales, lays on her stomach, gazes into the black water, thinks that she can make out something staring back at her from the deep, leans forward in an effort to get a closer look, stands up, slips out of her sandals, rolls her pant legs up to her knees, wades into the water, pays no mind to the sound falling away from her, keeps her eyes fixed on a shape beneath the waves that becomes clearer to her by the second, stretches her arms out to it, feels an alien and familiar sensation creeping up her back, and snaps back to awareness when the moon emerges and throws its light on the surface once again. The freighter is out of her sight.

She glances around her in confusion, looks into the sea, sees nothing, turns back to the shore, and stumbles back to dry land as quickly as she can manage. She contemplates going back to find the others, but she decides to head straight home instead after glancing once more at the water. Her trek along the shore has taken her to a part of town that she is unfamiliar with, but she eventually finds a street name that she recognizes, jogs back to the house, and slides through the front door without waking up her parents.

She is exhausted, but the night's events keep her up; sleep comes to her in frenetic bursts of concepts and colors. She dreams that she is trudging through a vast desert, and the sun is always bearing down on the back of her neck; she dreams that a monster with gaping maws for eyes has crawled out of a crack in the crust of the earth to swallow her whole; she dreams that she is trapped in her room, and the roof is crashing down on top of her; she dreams that she is floating through a dark tunnel with pale hands grasping at her from all directions; she dreams that the world has become so quiet that she can hear the electricity running up and down her nerves. She dreams of the deep.

Amanda is thirty-five years old when she feels the pull of the deep for the final time.

It is July, and she is on temporary leave from the Foundation, where she studies anomalous ocean life, to visit her family back home after the death of one of her uncles. It is three days after the funeral and two days before she is scheduled to return to work when she decides to take a walk along the beach in the early hours of the morning. She has spent the week visiting an endless procession of dimly-lit homes and consoling an endless procession of grieving relatives who knew old Uncle Bobby far better than she did; she must be alone, if only for a little while.

The moon is new, and darkness hangs over the surface of the water. The globular lights on the dock, which she has gathered were installed by the city last summer for safety, are too dim to illuminate much of the beach; she keeps between the edge of their off-white glow and the edge of the sea. She eventually comes upon a place that feels right, and she sits with her back to the spheres. The waves stop just short of her feet as they lap on the shore.

The sounds of the beach gradually recede, and she feels the familiar pull begin to take hold, the same pull that she felt on this beach so many years ago, the same pull that she felt every time she passed by the sea in the months and years that followed, the same pull that she could never escape when she went out to sea with her parents and their friends, the same pull that she fought against every time she had to go out to the beach for field work in college, the same pull that she swore she could feel somewhere in the back of her mind when she saw projected images of the sea during conferences. She sees a shape beginning to form in the deep, and the urge to gaze overpowers her.

She knows what she must do. She stands up, slips out of her shoes and socks, rolls her pant legs up to her knees, looks out at the sea of pitch before her and the thing waiting for her underneath, closes her eyes, steels herself, and opens her eyes with newfound resolve. She strides into the water, pauses when she feels it reach past her knees and seep into her pants, glances up at the sky, looks down at the shape growing in clarity beneath the waves, feels its sensation wash over her like the waves, takes a deep breath, dives headfirst into the water, powers through the chill that pierces her skin, swims into the deep, keeps her gaze fixed on the shape that is reaching out to meet her, beholds its many limbs and its one shimmering eye, reaches out with a trembling hand, and watches it dissolve into the black. Suddenly aware of how long she has spent in the water, she surfaces as quickly as she can.

She gasps for air as she breaks the even surface of the water. As soon as she can make out the direction the shore is in, she begins pushing towards it with everything she has. She dreads that she has gone too far out, that the current will sweep her away from land and toward oblivion, but little by little, the beach draws closer. She uses the last of her energy to heave herself onto the sand and lies there on her side for some time, breathing near-silently. She eventually rises, her clothes completely soaked through, and looks back at the sea. The shape is nowhere to be seen; she no longer feels the pull, and the water seems to shine despite the lack of moonlight. She picks up her sandals and sets off for home.

When she gets to sleep, she dreams of a freighter on the sea, its black frame cutting through deep blue water.

She dreams that she is trudging through a vast desert, and the sun is always bearing down on the back of her neck; she dreams that a monster with gaping maws for eyes has crawled out of a crack in the crust of the earth to swallow her whole; she dreams that she is trapped in her room, and the roof is crashing down on top of her; she dreams that she is floating through a dark tunnel with pale hands grasping at her from all directions; she dreams that the world has become so quiet that she can hear the electricity running up and down her nerves. She dreams of the deep.

----

Amanda is thirty-five years old when she feels the pull of the deep for the final time.



It is July, and she is on temporary leave from the Foundation, where she studies anomalous ocean life, to visit her family back home after the death of one of her uncles. It is three days after the funeral and two days before she is scheduled to return to work when she decides to take a walk along the beach in the early hours of the morning. She has spent the week visiting an endless procession of dimly-lit homes and consoling an endless procession of grieving relatives who knew old Uncle Bobby far better than she did; she must be alone, if only for a little while.



The moon is new, and darkness hangs over the surface of the water. The globular lights on the dock, which she has gathered were installed by the city last summer for safety, are too dim to illuminate much of the beach; she keeps between the edge of their off-white glow and the edge of the sea. She eventually comes upon a place that feels right, and she sits with her back to the spheres. The waves stop just short of her feet as they lap on the shore.



The sounds of the beach gradually recede, and she feels the familiar pull begin to take hold, the same pull that she felt on this beach so many years ago, the same pull that she felt every time she passed by the sea in the months and years that followed, the same pull that she could never escape when she went out to sea with her parents and their friends, the same pull that she fought against every time she had to go out to the beach for field work in college, the same pull that she swore she could feel somewhere in the back of her mind when she saw projected images of the sea during conferences. She sees a shape beginning to form in the deep, and the urge to gaze overpowers her.



She knows what she must do. She stands up, slips out of her shoes and socks, rolls her pant legs up to her knees, looks out at the sea of pitch before her and the thing waiting for her underneath, closes her eyes, steels herself, and opens her eyes with newfound resolve. She strides into the water, pauses when she feels it reach past her knees and seep into her pants, glances up at the sky, looks down at the shape growing in clarity beneath the waves, feels its sensation wash over her like the waves, takes a deep breath, dives headfirst into the water, powers through the chill that pierces her skin, swims into the deep, keeps her gaze fixed on the shape that is reaching out to meet her, beholds its many limbs and its one shimmering eye, reaches out with a trembling hand, and watches it dissolve into the black. Suddenly aware of how long she has spent in the water, she surfaces as quickly as she can.



She gasps for air as she breaks the even surface of the water. As soon as she can make out the direction the shore is in, she begins pushing towards it with everything she has. She dreads that she has gone too far out, that the current will sweep her away from land and toward oblivion, but little by little, the beach draws closer. She uses the last of her energy to heave herself onto the sand and lies there on her side for some time, breathing near-silently. She eventually rises, her clothes completely soaked through, and looks back at the sea. The shape is nowhere to be seen; she no longer feels the pull, and the water seems to shine despite the lack of moonlight. She picks up her sandals and sets off for home.



When she gets to sleep, she dreams of a freighter on the sea, its black frame cutting through deep blue water.

"Sounds like you've got a story, son."
A Foundation doctor finds common ground with a specter of the Red Brook Mine.

When questioned on the sudden end to the footage, Dr. Rune claimed the camcorder had died. Supposedly, he gave his account of an encounter with a Marshall, Carter, & Dark operation based in Virginia — known only as "Gunstone LLC." — before departing.

"You don't have to tell me twice, about the people who made that mine. I've seen what they've done to folks."

Dr. Atticus Rune is not a man unfamiliar with the horrors and the wild. Not in all his years of living amongst these woods and these mountains and all they held within their breadth.

And thus, he is not unfamiliar with what sat before him.

SCP-8306. Though Site-898 more often than not simply called it "The Foreman."

The ragged, coal-dust covered form of something that looked like the mind’s eye version of an old mine worker. Like the type of not-person you’d catch in the corner of your eye in a dream, with empty holes for eyes and a gaping maw. The being sat perched on a boulder by the side of the brook, bent forward with a dusty hand braced on one knee; like the way an old man leans in to listen. The Foreman had barely any expressions to read, but Rune could interpret intrigue, in the way that he spoke:

“Sounds like you’ve got a story, son.” a voice like mud over cobblestone. Rune squeezes his eyes shut, his inhale and exhale fogging in the February air.

“‘Cause I do, too.”

In a moment nothing short of impulse, Rune deactivates the camcorder. Its shutter thunks and he lets his arms fall to his sides. He can tell them the battery died. Wherever this was going, security didn't need more than a verbal summary. The Foreman notices this deliberate choice, and hums, awaiting response. With a sigh, one is supplied.

“On this mountain? With roaches like that? I bet you got plenty.” Rune scoffs tiredly. He’s hesitant to look this thing where its eyes should be, but slowly raises his head.

The Foreman pushes off the rock, heavy boots hitting the muck with a THUD. He approaches Rune, a raspy hum rising in his throat. “Why don’t you tell me yours, mm?” the entity walks a few steps past the doctor, before turning to look over his shoulder,

“We can walk ‘n' talk. It’s a crisp morn, after all.”

Rune watches, inhaling daybreak dew and breathing it back out. “You’re right,” he replies. “It is a nice mornin’.” He takes a few steps through the mud after the figure, but catches himself glancing over his own shoulder, back towards the site. The hesitation doesn’t last long. Pocketing the “dead” camcorder, Rune follows the Foreman into the mist rolling down the mountain, between the trees, and over the bog.

“Do you know anything ‘bout the things those ‘barons’ do outside these parts?” Rune asks after a time, the silence only punctuated by the sounds of their feet and the cawing of crows.

“Hmph,” there’s a faint squelch as the Foreman cocks his head to the side, “They infest these mountains like maggots. Tear ‘er up for all she’s worth. Though, I’ve only seen what they’ve done to this place." The entity raises a mud coated hand to gesture back towards Dutch Mountain, back towards the mine.

The Foreman trudges through the ankle deep mud as he walks the conifer-lined and moss filled swamp. He seems to ignore the bog bridges that the Site has constructed for their own ease of travel. Rune disregards them too, for now, wanting to remain in-step with the being beside him. It's polite.

“Won’t surprise ya to hear they do it up n’ down the coast, ‘nd they’re pulling the same as what I read about this place." Rune murmurs, "Break yer back n’ kill your lungs all for what might as well amount to Monopoly money,” he scoffs and shakes his head. He can taste coal dust on his tongue. It's a bitter familiarity.

“Point is, they leave a lot of desperate folks in their wake. Desperate people that are willin’ to do just about anything for money.”

A gurgling sound rings out, torn between a phlegm-filled cough and a bitter laugh that melts into the squelching of the Foreman’s boots in the muck.

“It don’t surprise me none that there’s more to them blinked bastards than Summit Anthracite. The little rat that used to rule these parts always spoke a’ his bosses.” The entity shakes his head, before turning to peer at Rune again with empty eyes.

“I reckon you’re from these mountains, by the way you talk. That right, son?”

“Hah, just ‘bout as local as someone can get for stolen land,” Rune chuckles tiredly and continues to avoid eye contact. “They’re a whole organization. The fucks you n’ I have been dealin’ with are a small part of it.”

The Foreman tilts his head, continuing to gaze at Rune as they trek deeper into the swamp. He brushes a hand against a moss covered boulder as he passes, streaking coal mud across it.

"Thieves and fools, the lot.” He huffs, “may the mountains be unkind.”

The Coalbed Swamp is quiet aside from the two. No birdsong, no rustling. Rune is familiar with the little yellow birds that are typically in abundance, but this morning? They’re absent.

It’s not natural for the forest to be so quiet. Rune knows that much, and it rings louder in his ears than any noise could. All of a sudden, he’s hyper-aware of his surroundings, scanning the landscape and itching for sound. “Mm. Usually they are. Y’can tell when the folks they’ve got have no idea what they’re doin’. Makes it really easy to spot ‘em, but then it’s worse when they turn ‘round and use the locals to get what they want. That’s what they did by me.”

The conifers blot out most of the morning light. There’s still fog curling around branches and mossy rocks. The only sounds are from the Foreman, low and wet wheezes accompanied by footsteps in the brush. The entity lets out long and low groan,

“That so?” the intrigue is back in his voice.

“Yeah. Down South a ways… they proposition ‘n pay the people most willin’ to catch and sell their own local legends. Items, animals, people; you name it. If it weren’t normal, they’d take ‘em for a hunk of cash.” When the woods are this quiet, it usually meant a predator was around. The wheezes and groans being the only thing to break the silence made Rune wonder if the man next to him was that. “‘Til I ratted ‘em out, that is,” he adds softly.

“Ha! Blew the ol’ whistle on ‘em, didja now, son?” The Foreman barks a laugh, he gives Rune a hearty pat on the back. It leaves coal dust on his coat and knocks Rune off balance. He slides forward through mud before catching himself just in time to not fall face first. The specter continues. “Good on ya, good on ya. Did you catch the name of the bastard you smoked out?” A tilt of the head, a crack of the neck.

Rune’s eyes stick to the ground now, watching his step. “The veiled name they were working over was "Gunstone LLC." or somethin’ like that. Foundation thinks there might be a connection 'tween 'em and what happened here.”

“Hmph,” the entity makes a low noise, hand returning to his side, “can’t say that name rings any bells, but I wouldn’t be surprised none if they’re two heads a’ the same snake.”

“Well, that’s relievin’. Means there ain’t somethin’ like it happening up here.” Rune shakes his head and grimaces. “It’ll be too soon if I never see nothin’ that depraved again.”

The Foreman continues through the swamp, leading Rune to an opening in the trees and rock. There’s an old, rotted campsite at its heart. The sight makes Rune raise an eyebrow. Is this marked down on any of the maps? Is it important enough to be? The barely maintained remains of a firepit, decayed logs around it, and a tattered, mossy linen tent. The only thing that looks like it’s seen use in the past years is the firepit, little embers dying out at its base. The Foreman makes a raspy hum and approaches it.

“I wouldn’t get your hopes up,” he sighs, “they were sendin’ what they robbed from here up North, cross state lines. Maybe to the cities, maybe somewhere else. Outta my reach regardless.”

Rune nudges at one of the logs with his foot. “Checks out,” he sighs, “There weren’t no consistency to where Gunstone sent things, but it sure as hell wasn’t anywhere close.” There’s a bit of silence before Rune sits himself down. “I’m guessin’ you like to stay local, then. If you don’t mind me askin’, anyway.”

A low, gurgling sound, seemingly one of contemplation, “I could go walkin’ down past the Mason-Dixon line if I so pleased, but I prefer to stick ‘round these parts.” The Foreman pokes himself into the old tent, removes a box of matchsticks from somewhere Rune can’t see in the low light. He sits in the dirt as he strikes it, and uses it to reignite the embers. A small fire starts to grow.

“Besides, there’s work to be done.”

Rune’s surprised that the fire stokes to life considering how rotted and damp this all is. His eyes settle on the flames.

”Work to be done,” he echoes, then huffs. “Right. MC&D — they’ll be back for this place — if not for the mine, then everything that’s been hauled up here.”

The Foreman laughs, "The Foundation might've declared war, in their eyes, when they took this place. Blue bloods never like to be undermined." The entity then leans forward. “Will you fight, if they come? Sounds like you have been already.” The Foreman cocks his head to the side.

Rune nods without a second of hesitation. “‘Course. I’ve been on their asses fer years now. ‘M not gonna stop the second they roll up,” he retorts, angrily.

"You still haven’t told me ya own story.” the entity points out, waving an mud encrusted hand at the man.

Rune's mouth pencils shut. He sits back, feeling exasperation seep into his bones. Heavy air. He's too tired to keep nodding the question off. “What I’d give for a drink right now,” he sighs to himself before rubbing his face and adjusting his glasses in the process, looking back up to the curious thing before him.

“Stop me if you’ve heard this one before,” he jokes tiredly, raising one hand and letting it flop back down. “My Pa was an Irish immigrant. My Ma was native. Neither were rich, but my Pa worked in the mine, so it kept us afloat. Whatever the hell ‘afloat’ is in a mining town,” he scoffs. “‘Till he got a leg injury in an accident, that is. It destroyed him, got him unemployed and us kicked outta home. The painkillers they gave him for the injury fucked him in the head, pipeline’d him to worse shit.”

The Foreman wheezes in a breath.

Rune wrings his hands around one another. “S’how I know how Gunstone works. He was desperate for money, and they had it in droves if he could give them any anomalous thing he could get his hands on. So… he did.”

As Rune speaks, the entity across from him crosses his legs and leans forward a little, simply making a quiet, “Ah…” in response.

Rune bites the inside of his cheek, trying to choose words carefully. “Started out small. First little items and trinkets, I imagine. I didn’t know. Not ‘til Ma left him over it. I wish I had." He rubs a hand against the side of his head. "Maybe then I could’ve stopped him from graduating to selling off living things. I don’t just mean animals and haints, either. I lost people. Friends who had no business bein’ bought n’sold they way they probably were."

There is venom on his tongue while he speaks, free hand finally gripping at the side of the log so tightly his knuckles turned bone. “Found out what my Pa was doin’ the hard way, and when I did I blew the whistle on ‘em. Haven’t stopped since. Those bastards want my head on a pike, but the Foundation fancied me a reliable source of information. So, now I’m here.”

Crackling embers waft out of the fire onto the dingy ground, and Rune watches their lights go out. “Satisfied?”

For a moment, the only thing that breaks the silent woods is the Foreman’s rasping breaths. There’s a pair of deer, down the path. They are still.

“…I see,” the entity’s head lowers. His voice is suddenly far quieter. Somber, even. “You got a wound in your belly that many do. I saw men fester and fall apart on these grounds from ‘em, cause no one was there to help clean out the shit. Got in their lungs, got in their heads.” he coughs.

“When they force you to bow so low, ya end up drowning in the muck.”

“Yeah, well, I’m not letting ‘em do that no more. Not where I can help it,” Rune retorts. “Something tells we’re alike in that way.” Rune dips his head low, a silent gesture of respect. He tries to ignore the deer. This safety net is fleeting. He is already too aware of what lives out in these woods.

The only thing that dares to show its face to a predator in silent woods is another.

“Damn straight.” The Foreman lets out a bitter chuckle, half choked by phlegm. “I couldn’t chase ‘em out on my lonesome, but I did what I could. Sent the bastard they put in charge down on chokin’ to his grave.” The apparition stands, body creaking like old wood. He removes a lantern from the remains of the tent, and kneels down by the fire to borrow embers. “Eyes for eyes, breath for breath.”

Oh, good. He sees the animals, too. Or at least that's what Rune assumes as he watches the entity work to light the lantern. He stands and brushes himself off.

“Good on ya,” Rune breathes with a nod. “Someone had to do it.”

"Is the Foundation joining the hunt too?"

He sticks his hands in his pockets, "I've caught word that the old RED CANARY investigation is getting revived. Little trinkets, traces of operations — things have cropped up over the years."

"Like you." The Foreman looks up.

"Like me, yeah." Rune sighs, gaze cast low.

The lantern’s light starts to steadily flicker to life, “Thanks for humoring an ol’ haint,” the Foreman rumbles, “Ain’t too often folks come for a talkin’, despite my interest in your affairs here.”

“‘Course. A happy accident, but I don’t mind,” Rune replies. Despite the Foreman’s claim, Rune doesn’t think he’s a haint. Supernatural, sure, but it doesn’t seem like the right category to place him into, if there is a ‘right’ one at all. “Been good to see ya with my own eyes.”

There’s a faint, rasping chuckle from the entity. The Foreman then straightens once more, pushing up to his feet with a grunt. He stares down the path.

“You’d best be movin’ along now.”

The two animals are facing them now, turned bodily to be staring straight down the path. The deer casts no shadow, cloud cover has turned the morning dark. The Foreman huffs, then turns to Rune, extending the old lantern to the man.

“Take this for the walk back.”

Rune hesitates, but doesn't need to be told twice. He grips the rusted handle, hears it squeal in protest. It's warm. The fire within squirms.

Rune mouths his thanks and dips his head.

"Just leave it by your window. I'll be back for it," the entity remarks, shifting to face the deer with backwards limbs.

Rune keeps this in mind as he turns his back to the barely-deer and the mine's specter. He hurries back the way he came and ignores the murmuring on the wind that trails his steps.

The lantern with writhing fire swings in his grasp all the way back.

Dr. Rune later stated: “We shared common ground.”

The barely maintained remains of a firepit, decayed logs around it, and a tattered, mossy linen tent. The only thing that looks like it’s seen use in the past years is the firepit, little embers dying out at its base. The Foreman makes a raspy hum and approaches it. “I wouldn’t get your hopes up,” he sighs, “they were sendin’ what they robbed from here up North, cross state lines. Maybe to the cities, maybe somewhere else. Outta my reach regardless.” Rune nudges at one of the logs with his foot. “Checks out,” he sighs, “There weren’t no consistency to where Gunstone sent things, but it sure as hell wasn’t anywhere close.” There’s a bit of silence before Rune sits himself down. “I’m guessin’ you like to stay local, then. If you don’t mind me askin’, anyway.” A low, gurgling sound, seemingly one of contemplation, “I could go walkin’ down past the Mason-Dixon line if I so pleased, but I prefer to stick ‘round these parts.” The Foreman pokes himself into the old tent, removes a box of matchsticks from somewhere Rune can’t see in the low light. He sits in the dirt as he strikes it, and uses it to reignite the embers. A small fire starts to grow. “Besides, there’s work to be done.” Rune’s surprised that the fire stokes to life considering how rotted and damp this all is. His eyes settle on the flames. ”Work to be done,” he echoes, then huffs. “Right. MC&D — they’ll be back for this place — if not for the mine, then everything that’s been hauled up here.” The Foreman laughs, "The Foundation might've declared war, in their eyes, when they took this place. Blue bloods never like to be undermined." The entity then leans forward. “Will you fight, if they come? Sounds like you have been already.” The Foreman cocks his head to the side. Rune nods without a second of hesitation. “‘Course. I’ve been on their asses fer years now. ‘M not gonna stop the second they roll up,” he retorts, angrily. "You still haven’t told me ya own story.” the entity points out, waving an mud encrusted hand at the man. Rune's mouth pencils shut. He sits back, feeling exasperation seep into his bones. Heavy air. He's too tired to keep nodding the question off. “What I’d give for a drink right now,” he sighs to himself before rubbing his face and adjusting his glasses in the process, looking back up to the curious thing before him. “Stop me if you’ve heard this one before,” he jokes tiredly, raising one hand and letting it flop back down. “My Pa was an Irish immigrant. My Ma was native. Neither were rich, but my Pa worked in the mine, so it kept us afloat. Whatever the hell ‘afloat’ is in a mining town,” he scoffs. “‘Till he got a leg injury in an accident, that is. It destroyed him, got him unemployed and us kicked outta home. The painkillers they gave him for the injury fucked him in the head, pipeline’d him to worse shit.” The Foreman wheezes in a breath. Rune wrings his hands around one another. “S’how I know how Gunstone works. He was desperate for money, and they had it in droves if he could give them any anomalous thing he could get his hands on. So… he did.” As Rune speaks, the entity across from him crosses his legs and leans forward a little, simply making a quiet, “Ah…” in response. Rune bites the inside of his cheek, trying to choose words carefully. “Started out small. First little items and trinkets, I imagine. I didn’t know. Not ‘til Ma left him over it. I wish I had." He rubs a hand against the side of his head. "Maybe then I could’ve stopped him from graduating to selling off living things. I don’t just mean animals and haints, either. I lost people. Friends who had no business bein’ bought n’sold they way they probably were."   There is venom on his tongue while he speaks, free hand finally gripping at the side of the log so tightly his knuckles turned bone. “Found out what my Pa was doin’ the hard way, and when I did I blew the whistle on ‘em. Haven’t stopped since. Those bastards want my head on a pike, but the Foundation fancied me a reliable source of information. So, now I’m here.” Crackling embers waft out of the fire onto the dingy ground, and Rune watches their lights go out. “Satisfied?” For a moment, the only thing that breaks the silent woods is the Foreman’s rasping breaths. There’s a pair of deer, down the path. They are still. “...I see,” the entity’s head lowers. His voice is suddenly far quieter. Somber, even.  “You got a wound in your belly that many do. I saw men fester and fall apart on these grounds from ‘em, cause no one was there to help clean out the shit. Got in their lungs, got in their heads.” he coughs. “When they force you to bow so low, ya end up drowning in the muck.” “Yeah, well, I’m not letting ‘em do that no more. Not where I can help it,” Rune retorts. “Something tells we’re alike in that way.” Rune dips his head low, a silent gesture of respect. He tries to ignore the deer. This safety net is fleeting. [https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/scp-6448 He is already too aware of what lives out in these woods.] The only thing that dares to show its face to a predator in silent woods is another. “Damn straight.” The Foreman lets out a bitter chuckle, half choked by phlegm. “I couldn’t chase ‘em out on my lonesome, but I did what I could. Sent the bastard they put in charge down on chokin’ to his grave.” The apparition stands, body creaking like old wood. He removes a lantern from the remains of the tent, and kneels down by the fire to borrow embers. “Eyes for eyes, breath for breath.” Oh, good. He sees the animals, too. Or at least that's what Rune assumes as he watches the entity work to light the lantern. He stands and brushes himself off. “Good on ya,” Rune breathes with a nod. “Someone had to do it.” "Is the Foundation joining the hunt too?" He sticks his hands in his pockets, "I've caught word that the old RED CANARY investigation is getting revived. Little trinkets, traces of operations -- things have cropped up over the years." "Like you." The Foreman looks up. "Like me, yeah." Rune sighs, gaze cast low. The lantern’s light starts to steadily flicker to life, “Thanks for humoring an ol’ haint,” the Foreman rumbles, “Ain’t too often folks come for a talkin’, despite my interest in your affairs here.” “‘Course. A happy accident, but I don’t mind,” Rune replies. Despite the Foreman’s claim, Rune doesn’t think he’s a haint. Supernatural, sure, but it doesn’t seem like the right category to place him into, if there is  a ‘right’ one at all. “Been good to see ya with my own eyes.” There’s a faint, rasping chuckle from the entity. The Foreman then straightens once more, pushing up to his feet with a grunt. He stares down the path. “You’d best be movin’ along now.” The two animals are facing them now, turned bodily to be staring straight down the path. The deer casts no shadow, cloud cover has turned the morning dark. The Foreman huffs, then turns to Rune, extending the old lantern to the man. “Take this for the walk back.” Rune hesitates, but doesn't need to be told twice. He grips the rusted handle, hears it squeal in protest. It's warm. The fire within squirms. Rune mouths his thanks and dips his head. "Just leave it by your window. I'll be back for it," the entity remarks, shifting to face the deer with backwards limbs. Rune keeps this in mind as he turns his back to the barely-deer and the mine's specter. He hurries back the way he came and ignores the murmuring on the wind that trails his steps. The lantern with writhing fire swings in his grasp all the way back. black-white-and-red.raw_content:
We roam dying woods;
snow-draped Doe
smells of innocence, of syrup,
soot-clad Beast,
palms yearning for her hooves.

The winter punctures my heart,
so I warm her with love,
survival from unity.
Eyes linger on me,
her wanting gaze,

And my mouth starts to bleed
jaws fight the weight
overflowing with her hot white passion,
when it runs down her fur
it takes the snow away.

My brain burns red;
lock my claws on her neck
gentle and soft, I squeeze
so her eyes plead in red
and fur tarnished black.

Now she is cold.
I stare at my hands
almost white in the moonlight.
I can't look at her
now coloured in red and black.

blood-beneath-the-leaves.raw_content:
The Leviathan arrived unnoticed, among many other ill omens, in the days when the Plague was ravaging Europe. It fell to earth in the Congo Basin, not far from the great lakes of the Rift Valley. The creature had tried to slow down as it descended - and had failed. She stirred once after the impact, before falling forever still. In the Basin this arrival was most unpleasant, though people found use for the corpse in short order.

The city of Carcosa was a side-effect. She sprouted from the corpse of the Leviathan like mold on bread. Or ants colonizing the vents of an old car rotting by the side of the road. The creature's body was sturdy. She was safe. Her bowels brought fourth meat in abundance, sinew, bone, teeth - anything one needed. Though not, it is true, ample personal space. But for those with a need to be apart, and a tolerance for the sweet stink of decay, the city offered security and prosperity. Hunter-gatherers filled with curiosity, explorers seeking wealth, and city dwellers from further afield who simply wanted a change, or needed one. So for seven hundred years the city grew.

When the Belgians came for rubber and blood they left the heart of the great Congo Basin alone, and their terror never reached the city. During the tumult of the 1960s, a formation of Strategic Air Command had visited Carcosa, meaning business. Their hands were guided by government witches and sanctioned diviners, which could not tolerate something so aberrant as the city. Beneath the cockpits of the bombers a cheerful slogan gleamed: “If we can’t kill it, it can’t die.” They departed as they came. They had not killed Carcosa.

So down to the present day.

Carcosa was a city of bones and clotted blood. All her sprawl was confined to what, in the creature’s life, amounted to a kneecap. How far down below the surface of the Earth did those dried out veins run? How deep were the dunes and drifts of yellow fat? Few had asked, and those who sought answers either did not come back, or came back different. For there was something deep within Carcosa very dangerous, and completely strange.

The Leviathan was not of our world, but what she carried here was not of any world at all. It was an Absence. Small, compared to the size of its host, small the way a pearl is small but carries all the value of the oyster. How had it come to reside in the stomach of a great star beast? There were none who could answer that, if any ever knew. The question itself was misguided. Relativity did not apply to such things as the Absence. One might just as well have said the Earth came to the Absence, as the other way around.

The void was a knot in creation, where lines crossed and times blurred. The denizens of Carcosa knew that when they went too deep, sickness followed. So they respected the dead beast of their home. They left the mystery alone.

Some people can’t do this. To such wanderers, a mystery is a scab to pick at. A beacon to follow. Even a mystery like the Absence, something entirely unpleasant, unknown, unknowable.

In 1919, a young man and his dog came to the heart of the beast, the heart of the world. They came to drag Truth out of her well. Tintin was a journalist. Snowy was a terrier. They were two such who could not turn aside from an unanswered question. They came to the Congo and - changed.

When Tintin returned to the surface, there was Absence in his eyes, and in the eyes of Snowy - entirely too much intelligence. Perhaps something broke, or boiled away. Something like restraint, or fatigue, or fear - because after they returned, they could no longer be stopped. No longer be dissuaded or dismayed. Evil-doers, thieves, and scoundrels on a dozen continents learned that Tintin was not a reporter, he was a force. To find the truth, to reveal the treasure, and expose all to which he and that dog set their minds.

They left tumult in their wake without malice, exactly like footsteps disturbing an anthill, or a child casting aside a forgotten toy. Their human and canine characteristics magnified and purified. Concentrated. For years after they looked into the void, Tintin and Snowy crossed the globe bringing the light of the Absence to bear on everyone in their paths. They flickered and danced across the pages of history. The stories about them became improbable, and then unbelievable. Finally, they disappeared.

A century passed, and the Archival Division began to ask - why?
