bonds-of-blood-and-wire.raw_content:
When a member of his estranged family reaches out to him, Andrew wants nothing more than to reconcile with them, but are they truly willing to accept him, or are they just hoping go bring him back into the fold?

More by this Author

Andrew lay next to his partner, Oz, around two in the afternoon. Oz was reading, still making his way through the old Makhanite tome Andrew gave him a few months earlier. Andrew was reading a cyberpunk novel.

As far as Andrew knew, this author wasn’t under the Veil, but their description of one particular implant, the mechanical eyes possessed by the protagonist, was shockingly accurate. His sibling, Riely, had one that was nearly identical in form and function.

Andrew put the book down. He didn’t like being reminded of his sibling. He didn’t get to see them anymore. That’s what happened when your family disowned you for falling in love with a Nälkän.

Andrew tried to make his family understand. He tried to tell them that it didn’t change anything about his own faith, or between him and them, but there was no getting through to them. In the end, Andrew accepted that. He loved Oz, and if his family couldn’t accept that, then they couldn’t accept him.

Andrew’s phone rang. He sighed, fully expecting it to be a robocall. However, as he picked up his phone, he saw the caller ID. He froze.

It was Riely.

“What is it?” Oz asked. He looked over at Andrew, and, in doing so, also saw who had called. “Holy shit,” Oz whispered.

Andrew’s mind went into overdrive. Had someone died? It was hard to imagine any other situation in which Riely would call him. Who could it have been? Mom? Dad? A more distant relative? Would a more distant relative be sufficient reason for Riely to call him?

Either way, Andrew needed to answer. If something like that had happened, he needed to know.

“Want to do it on speaker so I can support you?” Oz asked.

Andrew shook his head. “This is someone who meditates to the sound of radio static. Riely will be able to tell the phone is on speaker.” He rose from the bed. “I’ll take it outside.”

Andrew didn’t just leave the bedroom. Oz’s enhanced ears would still be able to hear Riely, which would upset them. Andrew went all the way out of the apartment. Even then, Oz would probably hear his side of the conversation, but he wouldn’t hear Riely’s.

Andrew tried to answer the phone, only to see that he had already waited too long and missed the call.

Crap. Riely probably thought he’d ignored the call intentionally. He rushed to call them back.

Fortunately, they answered. “Sorry for not answering,” Andrew said. “I needed to take the call outside.”

“It’s okay,” Riely said.

“What’s going on? Did something happen to Mom or Dad?”

The question seemed to surprise Riely. “What? No. Nothing like that. Everyone’s fine.”

Andrew sighed. “Oh, thank WAN.”

“It should have occurred to me that you might think that. Sorry for scaring you.”

“It’s okay. What do you need?”

Riely hesitated. “Recently,” they began, “I’ve been thinking. A lot. There was… a failed project. I shouldn’t say exactly what. The specifics don’t matter. The important thing is that it prompted me to do some introspection. To contemplate what’s important. To reevaluate some of my choices, and, well, I realized that I’ve missed you.”

They were words Andrew had dreamed of hearing. Words that he had accepted he would never hear.

Words that were hard to believe.

“Not that I only started missing you recently,” Riely continued. “I have the whole time, of course, but, well… I wanted to maybe talk about spending some time with you. I don’t think you’ve visited Portlands since you finished at Deer?”

“I haven’t.”

“There’s been a lot of change-over at the Anderson Robotics Museum. A lot of new body modifications are on display, and a new war mech. Maybe I could take you there someday soon?”

It seemed too good to be true. Could Riely truly just call one day, suddenly willing to make peace? To see him again? They said something else had happened to set this off. A failed project. What could that be? They didn’t seem intent on telling Andrew, and prying might upset them.

“Andrew?”

“Sorry. I was just, thinking.”

“I understand.”

“I don’t mean that in a bad way. I’m just surprised. You all took such a firm stance.”

“I know. I know I said some hurtful things. If you need some time to think about this—”

“I don’t,” Andrew hurried to say. “I’d love to see you again.” Part of him wanted to request they go somewhere outside of Portlands. Going back into the anomalous world meant he’d once again be in danger of being recognized and subject to mistreatment, but that museum was a place they’d often gone as children. For it to be the first place they went after reconciling felt fitting.

“Thank you.” The smile was audible in Riely’s voice. “Are you free Saturday?”

“I should be.”

“How about I come pick you up around one?”

“Alright.”

“Where should I pick you up?”

Andrew debated for a moment whether to give Riely their apartment’s address. There was no guarantee Riely wouldn’t go back on their change of heart. Even if they did, though, it was hard to imagine them actively endangering Andrew by revealing his location. Andrew’s family cut him off when he began dating Oz, but they hadn’t actively contributed to the harassment that drove them out of Three Portlands.

Once Riely had the address down, the call ended.

Andrew returned to the bedroom. Oz looked at him, expectantly.

“It wasn’t bad news,” Andrew said. “They were reaching out. They said they’d rethought things, and that they wanted to spend some time together.”

Oz smiled. “That’s awesome.”

“We’re going to visit the Anderson Robotics Museum on Saturday.”

That gave Oz pause. “Are you sure you should go into town?”

“Not completely, but I think it will be fine. It’s been a few years since the video. I don’t think it’s likely that anyone will recognize us.”

“Okay,” Oz said, after a moment. “I’ll trust your judgement.”

“You can come along, if you want,” Andrew said.

“With you and Riely?”

“Yes.”

“That will probably be awkward.”

“I know, but it could also pay off. Maybe actually meeting you will help Riely see that you’re not some scary evil disease cultist.” Andrew reached down and took Oz’s hand. “I mean, it worked on me.”

Oz took a moment to think. “How about this? When they come to pick you up, I see both of you off. They’ll meet me then. Any more than that, we’ll save for later, okay?”

“Okay,” Andrew said. “Thank you.”

Oz stood and pulled Andrew into a hug. Oz was impossibly strong, and there was a hint of that strength in his embrace, but only a hint. Even though he was strong enough that he could snap Andrew’s spine—despite its metallic reinforcements—Oz always knew how to apply just the right amount of force to make Andrew feel held, and not a newton more.

That Saturday, Riely knocked on the door to Andrew’s apartment. Andrew took a deep breath. He was ready to go, and Oz was ready to meet Riely.

Andrew opened the door. Oz sat on the couch several feet behind him. Riely looked up at Andrew and smiled, then noticed Oz. They glanced over at him. He waved. With agonizing awkwardness, they waved back.

“Hey,” Andrew said.

“Hello,” Riely said. “Are you ready to go?”

“Yeah,” Andrew said. However, instead of following them outside the door, he stepped aside. “Before we do, though, it occurred to me that you’ve not actually met him in person. I figured I should introduce you. Riely, this is Oz. Oz, this is Riely.”

Oz stood and approached the door. Riely reflexively stepped back, then seemed to catch themself.

Oz was an imposing presence, six and a half feet tall and with bodybuilder muscles. His body just barely passed for baseline human. Any more augmentation, and he’d be jumped by sysops the next time he went outside.

Riely looked up at Oz as he approached. Oz extended his hand. “I’m Oz,” he said, with a cordial smile. “It’s nice to meet you.”

Riely eyed his hand as if worried it carried a deadly pathogen. Given the myths they believed about Nälkäns worshiping disease, that may well have been precisely what Riely was worried about.

Still, their sense of politeness won out. They reached out and gingerly shook Oz’s hand. Oz stepped back, and Riely was visibly relieved.

“You’ll get back around dinner time,” Oz said. “Would you like me to cook something for the three of us?”

“He’s a really good cook,” Andrew said. “His dumplings are amazing.”

“No, thank you,” Riely said, a bit too quickly. “I have other plans for dinner.” They looked up at Andrew. “In fact, we should get going to make sure I don’t have to cut our museum visit short in order to get to them.”

There was a momentary, awkward pause, before Andrew said, “Okay.”

The two left, heading toward Riely’s car. They got inside. Riely pulled a bottle of hand sanitizer out oof the glove box and squirted a generous glob onto their hand. They rubbed it in.

“He’s really not that bad once you get to know him,” Andrew said.

Riely didn’t say anything.

“Just, please try to give him a chance, okay?”

Riely still didn’t say anything. Andrew allowed the subject to drop as they left the apartment.

Andrew hadn’t been back in Three Portlands since he moved out of it. Leaving was a difficult choice. Outside the free port, they were technically in Foundation territory, and there was a non-zero chance they could be accosted and contained.

Unfortunately, that was the lesser evil compared to what they faced in town. Above the Veil, no one knew, much less cared, about the interfaith nature of their relationship. While most Portlandsers didn’t care either, many Nälkäns and Mekhanites did. The couple had been outed on the Intranet very early in their relationship, and, during their remaining time living in Portlands, they were often harassed by zealots from both faiths.

Riely parked their car outside the department store that housed the closest Way. Andrew was out of practice performing its knock—a precise series of hand motions—and Riely had to do it for him.

They stepped inside the portal it created.

Andrew took a long, deep breath of Portlands air, whose strange scent he never would have thought he could miss.

It was sunny, which was a rare treat here. They’d emerged in a park. On a nearby jungle gym, a mixture of children, including humans and sidhe, played. One of them was an awakened monkey whose effortless mobility had the other children in awe.

Even among the ‘human’ children, one had horns, another wings that poked through a pair of holes on the back of her shirt.

“I know you haven’t been here in a while,” Riely said. “Would you like to stop by the Dragon’s Den before we head to the museum?”

The Dragon’s Den was a restaurant owned by an actual family of dragons, who famously used their fire breath to keep their grills alight and their fryers boiling.

“Didn’t you say you wanted to get straight to the museum?”

“I wanted to make sure we left early enough to have time for both,” Riely said. “We don’t have to go, if—”

“No, no, I definitely want to go. God, to think it’s been two whole years.”

Riely smiled. “Alright, then. It’s on the way.”

The Dragon’s Den’s entrance was round, stylized to seem like the entrance to a cave. Inside, there were few windows. It was lit by wall-mounted lights meant to look like torches.

Everywhere, there were faux jewels and precious metals meant to evoke the idea of a dragon’s hoard. Just about every surface was either studded with false gems or painted silver or gold. The dishware and cutlery were likewise decorated to seem valuable. The plates were ornate. The cups were gold-colored chalices. The building was a bit too warm for human comfort, but that was to be expected from a dragon’s lair.

The treasure may have been fake, but the dragon in the kitchen was very real. The building was designed so that the kitchen was visible from the main dining area, and a twenty-foot, bright red dragon was currently at work, along with two human assistants.

The dragon didn’t breathe directly on the food. She was using her flame breath to keep the grills and stoves alight. Perhaps the smokey flavor the food acquired from this wasn’t that different from what any grill could achieve, but it was excellent regardless.

A waiter came to take their orders almost immediately. Andrew ordered one of the restaurant’s absolutely amazing burgers. Riely ordered a meat pie.

“So,” Riely said, as they waited for their food, “how have you been since I last saw you?”

Andrew could have given a very incendiary answer to that question. Alright, apart from having been disowned by my family, but saying something like that would just drive Riely away again. This was an opportunity to genuinely rebuild things between them, and Andrew couldn’t waste that for the sake of spite.

“I managed to find a work-from-home job,” Andrew said. “Software development. Anomalous, thank WAN. Pretending not to know about paratech while working on problems it could easily solve would drive me insane.”

“I’m glad you were able to find something you liked,” Riely said.

It would have been much easier to find a paratech job if I hadn’t been driven out of Three Portlands.

No, that wasn’t fair. At least, not to Riely. Andrew’s family cutting ties hadn’t driven him and Oz out of Three Portlands. The active harassment of other Nälkäns and Mekhanites had done that.

“Thank you,” Andrew said. “What have you been up to?”

“Working on my graduate degree. Oh, I never told you, did I? I managed it. I got into Deer’s paratech graduate program.”

“Congratulations,” Andrew said. No graduate program was easy to get into, but this was especially impressive. After all, hundreds of universities had graduate programs in computer science. Less than half a dozen had programs in paratech.

“What did you wind up specializing in?” Andrew asked. “Body modifications?”

“What else? My thesis is about modifications that augment the raw power of the human brain. You’d be surprised how little research there is in that area. Brain augmentations are usually designed to give the wearer a specific skill, or to transfer a person’s entire mind somewhere else. There’s a lot of untapped potential when it comes to simply making people smarter.”

“Interesting,” Andrew said. “Hopefully I’ll be able to install something of yours, someday.”

“Hopefully a lot of people will,” Riely said. “There are a lot of ways it could make the world better. I believe the human mind deserves better than the brain’s limitations.”

“By WAN’s hum,” Andrew said.

They talked for a little while longer. During lulls in their conversation, they glanced over at the dragon at work in the kitchen. They managed to catch the moment Riely’s pie went into the oven. They also saw dozens of burgers come on and off the grill, though there was no telling whether they’d seen Andrew’s in particular.

When their food arrived, they ate.

The food was just as good as Andrew remembered. The fries had the perfect amount of crispiness. The burger was juicy, enhanced by flavorful “Dragon Sauce.”

Riely clearly enjoyed theirs as well. The look on their face reminded Andrew of something Oz once said, back when they were college roommates struggling to tolerate one another. Most Mekhanites were hypocrites, prone to railing against the evils of the flesh while still enjoying the animal pleasures their bodies allowed them.

There was at least some truth to it. For sure, most Mekhanites avoided fleshly pleasures to some extent. It had taken a lot of time, and a lot of help from Oz, before Andrew could enjoy food or intimacy without feeling a twinge of guilt. Still, very few Mekhanites forsook such pleasures completely, as their doctrines would suggest they should.

Eventually, they finished their food. Riely paid for both of them, despite Andrew’s offer to pay for his own meal. From there, they walked a few blocks north to the museum.

The Anderson Robotics Museum was a large, grey building covered in decorative, often-glowing metallic parts that insinuated that the whole building was an enormous machine. It rested on the edge of the large campus of buildings out of which Anderson Robotics was based.

Admission was free. After all, the whole place was a glorified commercial for Anderson Robotics products. They wanted as many people as possible to see it.

“When do we need to leave for you to make those dinner plans you mentioned?” Andrew asked as they entered.

“Five or so.”

“Alright.” That left them with plenty of time to spend in the museum.

There were countless robots and other paratech devices on display throughout it. The most natural path through the museum led them by the ‘autos’ first. These were autonomous machines whose primary job was to move things around. Most of them resembled non-anomalous machines of some sort, especially cars, but none of them required human operators of any kind.

The museum’s most impressive display was in the section on paratechnical weapons. There weren’t many things on display here. Generally, Anderson Robotics didn’t like to call attention to the fact that they were war profiteers. However, they were willing to make an exception in order to show off their thirty-foot war mech.

The machine was humanoid in shape, albeit very broad and squat, with two extra pairs of arms. Only the lowest pair ended in grasping devices that might be called hands. The others ended with weapons. One was a blade. One was a gatling gun. The other two were metallic tubes that, according to the plaque at the front of the display, fired rockets and grenades.

Simply fitting it in the museum required a special display area that spanned the building’s three floors. Its chrome plating shone under the floodlights that illuminated it, and the robot’s enormous, glowing red eyes sometimes seemed to lock on a museum guest.

“You said this one was new?” Andrew said. “It’s bigger than the one I remember.”

“I did,” Riely said. “They removed the old one last year and replaced it with their latest model.”

Andrew looked up at it. “Remind me who they sell these to?”

“That’s in dispute,” Riely said. “There was a scandal last year when Valravn was caught with one. Anderson swore the thing was stolen, and there’s technically no proof it wasn’t, but not everyone believed them.”

There were several other areas in the museum, including a large section for robotic laborers and servants. Both of the siblings were most interested in the area dedicated to cybernetic implants, so they deliberately saved it for last.

It was a large section of the museum, with multiple rooms dedicated to different parts of the body. They were arranged head to toe, so the first room displayed various head and brain augmentations. As soon as they entered, Riely’s face lit up, and they hurried over to a large brain implant.

Andrew followed them. “You look excited,” he said once he reached them.

“This is an unreleased product,” Riely said. “I didn’t expect it to be here. It’s an intelligence-enhancing implant.”

“Like the ones your thesis is about?”

“Exactly. It’s a very impressive machine, and I’ve seriously considered getting one. However, it has a crucial flaw. One no one currently knows how to fix. I’m hoping to be the one who figures it out.”

“What is it?”

Riely smirked. “Can you guess?”

Andrew looked at the device. The thing was huge. It wasn’t inside the model head so much as it was on it, with a large metallic mass visible. Andrew saw the problem right away. “It’s not Veil-friendly.”

“That’s it,” they said. “I’m surprised you figured it out so quickly.”

“I’ve been worrying about the Veil every day for two years.”

“Right,” Riely said. “Of course.”

The device’s maintenance panel was open, which meant the complex array of switches, buttons and wires that made it work were mostly visible.

“What do those buttons do?” Andrew asked.

“The big red switch just turns it on and off. That slider near the bottom allows you to turn the sensory enhancements up and down.”

“Shouldn’t it have thought controls that do that, like our eye implants do?” Every commercially available sensory implant could be turned off with a thought command. It was a basic safety feature.

“It does. The slider is a backup. There have been a few news stories recently about thought controls failing and trapping people in some pretty brutal situations. Remember Ethan?”

“From the Deer College Maxwellist group?”

“Yes.”

“Please tell me something horrible happened to him.”

Unlike Riely, Ethan played an extremely direct role in driving Andrew and Oz out of Three Portlands. He’d ejected Andrew from the campus Maxwellists for ‘heresy.’ He’d also gossiped about the couple to parties who eventually did far worse.

“It was horrible,” Riely admitted. “All of his sensory implants got stuck on their maximum settings.”

“All five senses at once?”

“Yes. His eyes became microscopes. His field of vision was so narrow that he may as well have been blind. He could taste his own breath so strongly that it made him vomit. It lasted hours before he was able to find his phone and call for help.”

That did sound brutal. Part of Andrew felt bad for wishing Ethan had suffered.

Part of him did not.

“He was able to get to a hospital and get it fixed,” Riely said, “but the industry is making a show of prioritizing safety. As I’ve gone further and further into my field, I’ve found one of the most frustrating things about designing brain modifications is how reliable they need to be. You essentially need to be able to promise they’ll never break. Not that I blame people. I wouldn’t install an unreliable brain implant either, but it can be very frustrating when a device is several times larger or more expensive just so it can be a fraction of a percent less likely to malfunction.”

“That’s understandable.”

“I should have known you’d spot the Veil-issue right away, though. I probably would have too if I got out of town more.”

I wouldn’t spend much time outside Three Portlands, either, if I had a choice.

“I hardly ever leave town these days,” Reily continued. “Heck, this is the first time I’ve been off campus in over a week, and, honestly, it’s an indulgence. I should be working on my thesis right now.”

“Oh,” Andrew said.

“Not that I regret reaching out to you!” Riely rushed to clarify. “I’ve been that busy for the past year, and will be until the day I turn my thesis in. Every nanosecond of ‘me’ time between now and then will be an indulgence.”

“I see.” Andrew smiled. “Well, I’m glad I was worth an indulgence.”

“I didn’t want to wait,” Riely said. “Given the note we ended things on, you probably thought I hated you. I wanted to change that as soon as I could.”

“I see,” Andrew said. “Well, thanks for reaching out. It means a lot.”

Riely smiled. “I’m glad.”

“Would you mind telling me what brought me to your mind?”

“It was just a bout of introspection,” Riely said. “Some events made me think about who I was choosing to have in my life. Given some of the people whose company I tolerated over the past few months, I realized I didn’t have the right to keep shutting you out.” They looked down. “I won’t pretend I understand your decision, but it pales in comparison to some of the people I put up with for the past several months.”

There was a moment of silence.

“Thank you,” Riely added. “For forgiving me so easily.”

“I was never the one who was mad.”

Riely turned to face Andrew, and pulled him into a hug. He hugged them back. There were people around, but Andrew didn’t care. This reunion was too long-awaited. After almost six years, he had his sibling back.

Still, the hug did not last forever, and, eventually, they made their way to the next room. “Do you mind…” Riely began, as they walked. It seemed to take quite a bit of effort for them to find the right words. “Can you help me understand? Of all people? A Sarkite? How?”

“Nälkän,” Andrew said.

“If you say so.”

If Oz had been here, he wouldn’t have let the issue drop with just that, but Andrew decided to let it go. “It began with us spending time together because we had no choice. We were paired up as roommates at Deer. A computer error prevented either of us from being reassigned.”

“I know that part. Afterwards, though?”

“After months of living with him, well, he didn’t act like the flesh-hungry, disease-worshiping monster I expected him to be. He acted like a normal person, and, eventually, I had to accept that was what he was. I started being decent to him, and he started being decent to me in turn.”

“How did you get from that to a romantic relationship?”

Andrew shrugged. “How does anyone? Don’t get me wrong. Their faith isn’t perfect. No faith is…”

Riely pursed their lip as Andrew said that, as if holding in an objection, but they let him continue.

“They’re a lot less different than us than you think,” Andrew continued. “They augment their bodies just as much as we do. You could build a museum as big as this one and only display a fraction of the ways they use their magic to improve themselves.”

Riely considered that for a moment. “Their methods are very different from ours, though.”

“We’ve always had Mekhane to guide us. They had to figure everything out for themselves. If you keep that in mind, the amount they’ve accomplished is downright impressive. They’ve found so many ways to subvert Yaldaboth’s designs.”

“Even as they worship her.”

“They don’t.”

“I know that’s the official story, but if they did worship her, would they admit it?”

“Oz would.”

“How can you be so sure?”

“Oz is the most brutally honest person I’ve ever met. If he worshiped Yaldaboth, he’d brag about it, and mock anyone who got upset.”

“Why does Yaldaboth grant them power if they don’t serve her designs?”

Andrew had once asked Oz an identical question, and Andrew gave Riely the exact same answer. “Why do you give your blood to a mosquito?”

Riely looked at him like he’d said something totally nonsensical.

“They hate gods,” Andrew said. “The food analogy I just used, they use it, too. They view themselves as parasites. Nälkä means ‘hunger,’ specifically for the flesh of gods.”

“All gods?”

“Depends on the Nälkän.”

“What about yours?”

“Name a god, I’ve heard him joke about eating them.”

“I hope that doesn’t include WAN herself?”

Andrew considered lying and saying it did, but he didn’t want to lie to Riely. He was trying to rebuild his relationship with them. Their renewed bond shouldn’t be founded on lies.

“Oz makes fun of everything,” Andrew said. “He can be serious when he needs to be, but no topic is above his sense of humor.”

“And you tolerate this?”

Once, those jokes had horrified Andrew as much as they now did Riely, but after so many years, Andrew knew when not to take Oz seriously. “I know he’s joking,” Andrew said.

“Is he? If he’s the enemy of all gods, doesn’t that make him WAN’s enemy? Doesn’t that mean he opposes our faith’s true and final purpose, the great Rebuilding? If we were on the cusp of it, wouldn’t he try to stop us?”

This was not the first time Andrew contemplated that question. Unlike Oz’s jokes, it still made him nervous. Nervous enough that he’d never had the courage to raise it with Oz himself.

“I don’t know,” Andrew said. “Fortunately, it’s not very likely to be an issue any time soon.”

It took Andrew a second to realize Riely had stopped following him. He turned to face them. Their eyes were wide, like Andrew had just uttered a blasphemy beyond description. “Fortunately?” Riely asked. “Our God remaining broken for longer is fortunate to you?”

“That’s not what I meant,” Andrew rushed to say. “Of course I don’t think WAN’s state is fortunate in general, but it does make it unlikely I’ll ever have to confront that specific problem.”

“How can you be content with that?” Riely asked. “Don’t you long for the great Rebuilding?”

“Of course I do!”

“Then the question must have occurred to you.” Riely stepped closer to him. Thankfully, they had the sense to keep their voice down. “You’re too smart not to have thought of this. If WAN’s Rebuilding were imminent, you would be forced to choose between her and him.”

“No, I wouldn’t, because he’s not our enemy, or hers.”

“How could that possibly be true? The Sarkites would never sit back and allow us to rebuild our god. They fear us too much to ever permit us to obtain that kind of power.”

“Can you blame them, after everything we’ve done to them? Are they wrong to believe Mekhane’s rise might lead us to embark on a genocidal crusade against them?”

“Genocide? Of course that’s how they characterize it, but surely you know better.”

“No, I don’t. We attacked them first, and our intent, from the beginning, was to destroy them all.”

It took Riely a moment to respond to that. They took a deep breath. “Please just assure me of one thing. If, today, there were a struggle over whether Mekhane’s imminent return would be allowed or prevented, would you side with us, even if it meant a war with them?”

Andrew hesitated. Riely noticed that Andrew hesitated. “That’s a complicated question.”

“No, it isn’t. For a Mekhanite, ‘do you want to rebuild the Broken God’ should be the easiest question in the world.”

“Of course, I do!”

“Even though Oz would become your enemy?”

“I don’t believe it has to mean that. I truly believe there can be peace between us. It won’t be easy, or soon, but I want to bring about a day when they would welcome Mekhane as a powerful ally against the ultimate foe we share. That’s what I meant, earlier, when I said it was ‘fortunate’ that none of this will transpire within our lifetimes. We’ll need that time to build that peace, to make it so Mekhane’s rise won’t drive them to fear their destruction and make a desperate last stand.”

“Nothing is worth delaying her rise, over,” Riely said, with an awful gravity in their voice. “WAN has been broken too long, already. If you’ve come to believe otherwise, you’ve fallen farther than I knew. So, I ask you again, if it came down to it, which side would you choose?”

Once again, Andrew was tempted to say something just to smooth this over. He didn’t know if he could get Riely to understand his actual thoughts. However, even if he did lie, Riely knew him too well. If Andrew said anything but the truth, they would sense it.

“I believe there’s a plan,” Andrew said.

“A plan?”

“Do you remember what I told you about how things started between me and Oz? How we were originally roommates in Deer because a computer error assigned us together, and Deer’s systems absolutely would not allow either of us to be reassigned?”

Their eyes widened as they grasped the implication. “You can’t be serious.”

“I am. I don’t believe that was a coincidence. There are already Nälkäns and Mekhanites striving to bring peace. I believe WAN meant for me and Oz to be part of that effort, and that she wants it to succeed. I don’t believe she wants innocent blood on her hands.”

“No one who sought to prevent the rise of our god could be innocent.”

“Unless they acted out of sheer terror. Justified terror. Terror forged by us. From our mistakes. Our crimes.”

“And how long would you keep our god broken while you pursue this project? A century? A millennium?”

“That part is out of my control.”

That triggered a long, dry laugh.

Andrew raised a brow. “What?”

It seemed for a moment like Riely intended to answer, but then they shook their head. “We’re near the end of our route through the museum,” they said. “We shouldn’t stay much longer. As I said, I have dinner plans I cannot be late for.”

“It’s barely three o’clock.”

Riely didn’t say anything to that. They just walked toward the gift shop and the exit to the museum.

When Andrew and Riely were children, the gift shop was one of their favorite parts of this place, second only to the giant war mech. Sometimes, they’d spent close to an hour inside it. They’d beg their parents to buy them toy replicas of the body modifications they were too young to receive but already viewed with religious awe.

This time, they didn’t linger for even a second. They walked right out of the shop and toward the Way where they’d left Riely’s car.

Fortunately, Riely was still willing to give Andrew a ride home.

Andrew tried to take that opportunity to restart the conversation between them, but Riely shut him down each time. Half an hour later, Riely dropped Andrew off at his apartment. They pulled up to it and unlocked the door. “Go.”

“You’re really going to do it all over again? After everything you said?”

It took Riely a moment to respond to that. “If you oppose our faith’s ultimate goal—”

“That’s not what I said!”

“If I’d called you with news that we were on the cusp of bringing WAN back, would you have joined us? Or would your absurd belief that she’d prefer to remain broken have driven you to do nothing, or even oppose us?”

“The odds of any of this happening in our lifetimes are miniscule. Why are you so hung up on this hypothetical?”

“It’s not hypothetical.”

“Until it actually happens—”

“It nearly happened last week!”

That silenced Andrew for several seconds. “What?”

“There was a project. A massive, inter-denominational effort between each major branch of the church to restore her. Mekhanites of each strain put aside our differences and gave it everything we had. The largest hivemind we Maxwellists could create, combined with more than a dozen pieces of her old body the others had collected.

“We did everything we could to get more people to aid us. We didn’t just take Maxwellists, or Mekhanites. Many of us called on other friends. Heretics of various kinds. Anyone who owed us a favor big enough. We even brought new people under the Veil just to plug them into our network. Plenty of those people were wonderful, but others weren’t. Their heresies were not simply a matter of questioned dogma. Some of them were slavers. Murderers. Architects of evils as great as any Sarkic plague. It made me nauseous to work with such people. People who had no right to be part of Mekhane’s flock. I had to hold my nose around all of them…”

Riely looked down.

“But not you. I wasn’t allowed to reach out to you. At least, I presumed so. Truth be told, I wasn’t brave enough to ask. Even though you were still a follower of Mekhane, still a Maxwellist, and still my brother, I was more willing to work with people who shoved innocents into a giant mechanical stomach than I was to work with you.”

They looked Andrew in the eye. “I felt awful, afterward. Once it failed, I cursed myself for not reaching out to you. Perhaps one more pair of hands could have made the difference, and even if they didn’t… I thought you deserved to be there. That you would have helped us. That I’d gone too far by rejecting you.”

“Riely…”

“But you wouldn’t have helped us. If I’d called you about the project, asked for your help, you’d have refused, because you don’t think the time is right? At the very least, you’d have told him, and, thus, sent him running to some Sarkic nest with the warning they needed to stop us. Do you deny it?”

Andrew wanted to deny it. He wanted to assure them that their goals, their priorities, hadn’t drifted apart that much, that he would still side with his own people if it came to blows between them and the Nälkäns.

But, once again, it would be a lie. Riely was right. If an opportunity to bring WAN back appeared before him now, he would do whatever kept Oz safe, even if that meant delaying her return.

“Please, Andrew, deny it. Please.”

He wanted to. With everything he had, he wanted to.

But he couldn’t.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“Go,” Riely repeated.

Without another word, Andrew got out of Riely’s car and walked back up to his apartment.

Oz was waiting at the door to their apartment. As soon as Andrew entered, Oz pulled him into a hug.

“I take it you overheard?” Andrew asked.

“I couldn’t really make out what you were saying,” Oz said, “but I could tell there was an argument.”

Andrew nodded, eyes moist.

“I’m so sorry this didn’t work out.”

“It’s not your fault.”

“I know.” Oz stepped back. “C’mon.” Oz led Andrew into the bedroom. Both of them lay on the bed.

“I think Riely was right,” Andrew admitted.

“About what?”

“The argument was over… whether I was still an ally of the church’s ultimate purpose. Whether I would be with them when it came time to rebuild the Broken God.”

“Why wouldn’t you be?”

“Because I don’t know what she would do to you.”

“To me?”

“If the Broken God was rebuilt today,” Andrew continued, “it would spark a war between our faiths. A reborn Mekhane would be attended by a crusade’s worth of zealous Mekhanites, who would have the privilege of explaining this new world she’d awoken in. They’d tell her what they believe about you. She’d act accordingly, and you, along with every other Nälkän, would die.”

Oz took Andrew’s hand. “You figured out I was alright,” Oz said. “Surely your god is at least as smart as you.”

“It took me months to unlearn my prejudice against you. Against such a crusade, you wouldn’t survive that long.”

Oz rolled onto his side and pulled Andrew close. “You’ve told me there’s a piece of WAN inside every human mind, even mine. Wouldn’t that mean she’ll know everything you know? Heck, everything I know?”

“But what if it’s not every other Mekhanite on earth who’s wrong about what she would want? What if it’s me?”

Oz stroked Andrew’s back. It felt good. Like being pet. “A Mekhane who wanted to kill me, and all those innocent people, wouldn’t be the god you worship. If a group of Mekhanites did build such a god, you wouldn’t be a traitor for opposing it.”

“But what if it was the Broken God? The being who granted humanity reason and sacrificed herself to imprison Yaldaboth? What if that being wasn’t okay with you, or us?”

“Then fuck her. She’s not the god you serve. She’s not a god you would ever serve. You wouldn’t owe her anything.”

Andrew buried his face in Oz’s chest. Oz’s augmentations made his metabolism run higher than that of other people, which made him wonderfully warm. “Maybe.”

“Look,” Oz continued, “if Mekhane is the goddess you hope she is, then once she’s rebuilt, you’ll be able to follow her with a clear conscience. She won’t exterminate a group of people just because her followers told her we’re evil. She’ll value honesty, reason, and open-mindedness, just like you do. She’ll look into it, just like you did, and she’ll realize most Mekhanites are wrong about us, just like you did. After that, she’ll do the right thing, no matter how it makes her followers feel.”

“Maybe.”

“And if she turns out to be evil enough to do all that fucked up shit, we’ll stand against her together, like we have everything else.”

Andrew shook his head. “She’d still be a god. We’d have no hope—”

“Have you forgotten who you’re talking to? I come from a long tradition of spitting in the face of gods.”

Andrew had nothing to say to that. He didn’t want to think about who would win a battle between a rebuilt Mekhane and Earth’s Nälkäns. No matter who won, something very important to him would be destroyed.

“For what it’s worth,” Oz said, “I think your interpretation of her makes more sense.”

Andrew looked up at Oz. “Why?”

“This being gifted humanity with reason and sacrificed herself to help us. Why would she lead a genocidal crusade?”

“You’d really give her the benefit of the doubt. Don’t you hate gods?”

“I hate things that want to control me. Don’t get me wrong. If something calling itself Mekhane or WAN does that, there’s absolutely going to be a problem. You know how I roll. Omnomnom.”

That made Andrew laugh. Riely would have been furious to see it.

“But,” Oz continued, “that hypothetical megalomaniac has nothing to do with you, or your faith.”

Andrew lay there for a moment. Oz continued stroking his back.

Neither of them could know how Riely’s project would have gone, or how any future effort to restore the Broken God would go. It was possible that something horrible would one day rise and call itself Mekhane. Indeed, as much as Andrew didn’t want to believe it, it was possible that the Mekhane of eons past had been a very different person than Andrew hoped.

But Oz had a point. No matter what kind of being emerged from the Great Rebuilding, Andrew, and Oz, had a path forward. Either a new golden age to usher in, or a tyrant to oppose.

“You’re right,” Andrew said. “Thank you.”

“Hey Andrew, guess what?” Oz said.

“What?”

“I love you.” He leaned forward and planted a kiss on Andrew’s forehead.

Somehow, despite the years they’d been together, Oz could still make Andrew blush. “I love you, too.”
