bonds-of-blood-and-wire.raw_source: ===== [[include component:preview text= When a member of his estranged family reaches out to him, Andrew wants nothing more than to reconcile with them, but are they truly willing to accept him, or are they just hoping go bring him back into the fold?]] ===== [[include :scp-wiki:component:scp-pride]] [[>]] [[module Rate]] [[/>]] [[=]] ,,[[[xhawk77x|More by this Author]]],, [[/=]] Andrew lay next to his partner, Oz, around two in the afternoon. Oz was reading, still making his way through the old Makhanite tome Andrew [[[the-feasting-day-of-klavigar-nadox|gave him a few months earlier]]]. Andrew was reading a cyberpunk novel. As far as Andrew knew, this author wasn’t under the Veil, but their description of one particular implant, the mechanical eyes possessed by the protagonist, was shockingly accurate. His sibling, Riely, had one that was nearly identical in form and function. Andrew put the book down. He didn’t like being reminded of his sibling. He didn’t get to see them anymore. That’s what happened when your family disowned you for falling in love with a Nälkän. Andrew tried to make his family understand. He tried to tell them that it didn’t change anything about his own faith, or between him and them, but there was no getting through to them. In the end, Andrew accepted that. He loved Oz, and if his family couldn’t accept that, then they couldn’t accept him. Andrew’s phone rang. He sighed, fully expecting it to be a robocall. However, as he picked up his phone, he saw the caller ID. He froze. It was Riely. “What is it?” Oz asked. He looked over at Andrew, and, in doing so, also saw who had called. “Holy shit,” Oz whispered. Andrew’s mind went into overdrive. Had someone died? It was hard to imagine any other situation in which Riely would call him. Who could it have been? Mom? Dad? A more distant relative? Would a more distant relative be sufficient reason for Riely to call him? Either way, Andrew needed to answer. If something like that had happened, he needed to know. “Want to do it on speaker so I can support you?” Oz asked. Andrew shook his head. “This is someone who meditates to the sound of radio static. Riely will be able to tell the phone is on speaker.” He rose from the bed. “I’ll take it outside.” Andrew didn’t just leave the bedroom. Oz’s enhanced ears would still be able to hear Riely, which would upset them. Andrew went all the way out of the apartment. Even then, Oz would probably hear his side of the conversation, but he wouldn’t hear Riely’s. Andrew tried to answer the phone, only to see that he had already waited too long and missed the call. Crap. Riely probably thought he’d ignored the call intentionally. He rushed to call them back. Fortunately, they answered. “Sorry for not answering,” Andrew said. “I needed to take the call outside.” “It’s okay,” Riely said. “What’s going on? Did something happen to Mom or Dad?” The question seemed to surprise Riely. “What? No. Nothing like that. Everyone’s fine.” Andrew sighed. “Oh, thank WAN.” “It should have occurred to me that you might think that. Sorry for scaring you.” “It’s okay. What do you need?” Riely hesitated. “Recently,” they began, “I’ve been thinking. A lot. There was… a failed project. I shouldn’t say exactly what. The specifics don’t matter. The important thing is that it prompted me to do some introspection. To contemplate what’s important. To reevaluate some of my choices, and, well, I realized that I’ve missed you.” They were words Andrew had dreamed of hearing. Words that he had accepted he would never hear. Words that were hard to believe. “Not that I only started missing you recently,” Riely continued. “I have the whole time, of course, but, well… I wanted to maybe talk about spending some time with you. I don’t think you’ve visited Portlands since you finished at Deer?” “I haven’t.” “There’s been a lot of change-over at the Anderson Robotics Museum. A lot of new body modifications are on display, and a new war mech. Maybe I could take you there someday soon?” It seemed too good to be true. Could Riely truly just call one day, suddenly willing to make peace? To see him again? They said something else had happened to set this off. A failed project. What could that be? They didn’t seem intent on telling Andrew, and prying might upset them. “Andrew?” “Sorry. I was just, thinking.” “I understand.” “I don’t mean that in a bad way. I’m just surprised. You all took such a firm stance.” “I know. I know I said some hurtful things. If you need some time to think about this—” “I don’t,” Andrew hurried to say. “I’d love to see you again.” Part of him wanted to request they go somewhere outside of Portlands. Going back into the anomalous world meant he’d once again be in danger of being recognized and subject to mistreatment, but that museum was a place they’d often gone as children. For it to be the first place they went after reconciling felt fitting. “Thank you.” The smile was audible in Riely’s voice. “Are you free Saturday?” “I should be.” “How about I come pick you up around one?” “Alright.” “Where should I pick you up?” Andrew debated for a moment whether to give Riely their apartment’s address. There was no guarantee Riely wouldn’t go back on their change of heart. Even if they did, though, it was hard to imagine them actively endangering Andrew by revealing his location. Andrew’s family cut him off when he began dating Oz, but they hadn’t actively contributed to the harassment that drove them out of Three Portlands. Once Riely had the address down, the call ended. Andrew returned to the bedroom. Oz looked at him, expectantly. “It wasn’t bad news,” Andrew said. “They were reaching out. They said they’d rethought things, and that they wanted to spend some time together.” Oz smiled. “That’s awesome.” “We’re going to visit the Anderson Robotics Museum on Saturday.” That gave Oz pause. “Are you sure you should go into town?” “Not completely, but I think it will be fine. It’s been a few years since the video. I don’t think it’s likely that anyone will recognize us.” “Okay,” Oz said, after a moment. “I’ll trust your judgement.” “You can come along, if you want,” Andrew said. “With you and Riely?” “Yes.” “That will probably be awkward.” “I know, but it could also pay off. Maybe actually meeting you will help Riely see that you’re not some scary evil disease cultist.” Andrew reached down and took Oz’s hand. “I mean, it worked on me.” Oz took a moment to think. “How about this? When they come to pick you up, I see both of you off. They’ll meet me then. Any more than that, we’ll save for later, okay?” “Okay,” Andrew said. “Thank you.” Oz stood and pulled Andrew into a hug. Oz was impossibly strong, and there was a hint of that strength in his embrace, but only a hint. Even though he was strong enough that he could snap Andrew’s spine—despite its metallic reinforcements—Oz always knew how to apply just the right amount of force to make Andrew feel held, and not a newton more. ----- That Saturday, Riely knocked on the door to Andrew’s apartment. Andrew took a deep breath. He was ready to go, and Oz was ready to meet Riely. Andrew opened the door. Oz sat on the couch several feet behind him. Riely looked up at Andrew and smiled, then noticed Oz. They glanced over at him. He waved. With agonizing awkwardness, they waved back. “Hey,” Andrew said. “Hello,” Riely said. “Are you ready to go?” “Yeah,” Andrew said. However, instead of following them outside the door, he stepped aside. “Before we do, though, it occurred to me that you’ve not actually met him in person. I figured I should introduce you. Riely, this is Oz. Oz, this is Riely.” Oz stood and approached the door. Riely reflexively stepped back, then seemed to catch themself. Oz was an imposing presence, six and a half feet tall and with bodybuilder muscles. His body just barely passed for baseline human. Any more augmentation, and he’d be jumped by sysops the next time he went outside. Riely looked up at Oz as he approached. Oz extended his hand. “I’m Oz,” he said, with a cordial smile. “It’s nice to meet you.” Riely eyed his hand as if worried it carried a deadly pathogen. Given the myths they believed about Nälkäns worshiping disease, that may well have been precisely what Riely was worried about. Still, their sense of politeness won out. They reached out and gingerly shook Oz’s hand. Oz stepped back, and Riely was visibly relieved. “You’ll get back around dinner time,” Oz said. “Would you like me to cook something for the three of us?” “He’s a really good cook,” Andrew said. “His dumplings are //amazing.//” “No, thank you,” Riely said, a bit too quickly. “I have other plans for dinner.” They looked up at Andrew. “In fact, we should get going to make sure I don’t have to cut our museum visit short in order to get to them.” There was a momentary, awkward pause, before Andrew said, “Okay.” The two left, heading toward Riely’s car. They got inside. Riely pulled a bottle of hand sanitizer out oof the glove box and squirted a generous glob onto their hand. They rubbed it in. “He’s really not that bad once you get to know him,” Andrew said. Riely didn’t say anything. “Just, please try to give him a chance, okay?” Riely still didn’t say anything. Andrew allowed the subject to drop as they left the apartment. ----- Andrew hadn’t been back in Three Portlands since he moved out of it. Leaving was a difficult choice. Outside the free port, they were technically in Foundation territory, and there was a non-zero chance they could be accosted and contained. Unfortunately, that was the lesser evil compared to what they faced in town. Above the Veil, no one knew, much less cared, about the interfaith nature of their relationship. While most Portlandsers didn’t care either, many Nälkäns and Mekhanites did. The couple had been outed on the Intranet very early in their relationship, and, during their remaining time living in Portlands, they were often harassed by zealots from both faiths. Riely parked their car outside the department store that housed the closest Way. Andrew was out of practice performing its knock—a precise series of hand motions—and Riely had to do it for him. They stepped inside the portal it created. Andrew took a long, deep breath of Portlands air, whose strange scent he never would have thought he could miss. It was sunny, which was a rare treat here. They’d emerged in a park. On a nearby jungle gym, a mixture of children, including humans and sidhe, played. One of them was an awakened monkey whose effortless mobility had the other children in awe. Even among the ‘human’ children, one had horns, another wings that poked through a pair of holes on the back of her shirt. “I know you haven’t been here in a while,” Riely said. “Would you like to stop by the Dragon’s Den before we head to the museum?” The Dragon’s Den was a restaurant owned by an actual family of dragons, who famously used their fire breath to keep their grills alight and their fryers boiling. “Didn’t you say you wanted to get straight to the museum?” “I wanted to make sure we left early enough to have time for both,” Riely said. “We don’t have to go, if—” “No, no, I definitely want to go. God, to think it’s been two whole years.” Riely smiled. “Alright, then. It’s on the way.” ----- The Dragon’s Den’s entrance was round, stylized to seem like the entrance to a cave. Inside, there were few windows. It was lit by wall-mounted lights meant to look like torches. Everywhere, there were faux jewels and precious metals meant to evoke the idea of a dragon’s hoard. Just about every surface was either studded with false gems or painted silver or gold. The dishware and cutlery were likewise decorated to seem valuable. The plates were ornate. The cups were gold-colored chalices. The building was a bit too warm for human comfort, but that was to be expected from a dragon’s lair. The treasure may have been fake, but the dragon in the kitchen was very real. The building was designed so that the kitchen was visible from the main dining area, and a twenty-foot, bright red dragon was currently at work, along with two human assistants. The dragon didn’t breathe directly on the food. She was using her flame breath to keep the grills and stoves alight. Perhaps the smokey flavor the food acquired from this wasn’t that different from what any grill could achieve, but it was excellent regardless. A waiter came to take their orders almost immediately. Andrew ordered one of the restaurant’s absolutely amazing burgers. Riely ordered a meat pie. “So,” Riely said, as they waited for their food, “how have you been since I last saw you?” Andrew could have given a very incendiary answer to that question. //Alright, apart from having been disowned by my family,// but saying something like that would just drive Riely away again. This was an opportunity to genuinely rebuild things between them, and Andrew couldn’t waste that for the sake of spite. “I managed to find a work-from-home job,” Andrew said. “Software development. Anomalous, thank WAN. Pretending not to know about paratech while working on problems it could easily solve would drive me insane.” “I’m glad you were able to find something you liked,” Riely said. //It would have been much easier to find a paratech job if I hadn’t been driven out of Three Portlands.// No, that wasn’t fair. At least, not to Riely. Andrew’s family cutting ties hadn’t driven him and Oz out of Three Portlands. The active harassment of other Nälkäns and Mekhanites had done that. “Thank you,” Andrew said. “What have you been up to?” “Working on my graduate degree. Oh, I never told you, did I? I managed it. I got into Deer’s paratech graduate program.” “Congratulations,” Andrew said. No graduate program was easy to get into, but this was especially impressive. After all, hundreds of universities had graduate programs in computer science. Less than half a dozen had programs in paratech. “What did you wind up specializing in?” Andrew asked. “Body modifications?” “What else? My thesis is about modifications that augment the raw power of the human brain. You’d be surprised how little research there is in that area. Brain augmentations are usually designed to give the wearer a specific skill, or to transfer a person’s entire mind somewhere else. There’s a lot of untapped potential when it comes to simply making people smarter.” “Interesting,” Andrew said. “Hopefully I’ll be able to install something of yours, someday.” “Hopefully a lot of people will,” Riely said. “There are a lot of ways it could make the world better. I believe the human mind deserves better than the brain’s limitations.” “By WAN’s hum,” Andrew said. They talked for a little while longer. During lulls in their conversation, they glanced over at the dragon at work in the kitchen. They managed to catch the moment Riely’s pie went into the oven. They also saw dozens of burgers come on and off the grill, though there was no telling whether they’d seen Andrew’s in particular. When their food arrived, they ate. The food was just as good as Andrew remembered. The fries had the perfect amount of crispiness. The burger was juicy, enhanced by flavorful “Dragon Sauce.” Riely clearly enjoyed theirs as well. The look on their face reminded Andrew of something Oz once said, back when they were college roommates struggling to tolerate one another. Most Mekhanites were hypocrites, prone to railing against the evils of the flesh while still enjoying the animal pleasures their bodies allowed them. There was at least some truth to it. For sure, most Mekhanites avoided fleshly pleasures to some extent. It had taken a lot of time, and a lot of help from Oz, before Andrew could enjoy food or intimacy without feeling a twinge of guilt. Still, very few Mekhanites forsook such pleasures completely, as their doctrines would suggest they should. Eventually, they finished their food. Riely paid for both of them, despite Andrew’s offer to pay for his own meal. From there, they walked a few blocks north to the museum. The Anderson Robotics Museum was a large, grey building covered in decorative, often-glowing metallic parts that insinuated that the whole building was an enormous machine. It rested on the edge of the large campus of buildings out of which Anderson Robotics was based. Admission was free. After all, the whole place was a glorified commercial for Anderson Robotics products. They wanted as many people as possible to see it. “When do we need to leave for you to make those dinner plans you mentioned?” Andrew asked as they entered. “Five or so.” “Alright.” That left them with plenty of time to spend in the museum. There were countless robots and other paratech devices on display throughout it. The most natural path through the museum led them by the ‘autos’ first. These were autonomous machines whose primary job was to move things around. Most of them resembled non-anomalous machines of some sort, especially cars, but none of them required human operators of any kind. The museum’s most impressive display was in the section on paratechnical weapons. There weren’t many things on display here. Generally, Anderson Robotics didn’t like to call attention to the fact that they were war profiteers. However, they were willing to make an exception in order to show off their thirty-foot war mech. The machine was humanoid in shape, albeit very broad and squat, with two extra pairs of arms. Only the lowest pair ended in grasping devices that might be called hands. The others ended with weapons. One was a blade. One was a gatling gun. The other two were metallic tubes that, according to the plaque at the front of the display, fired rockets and grenades. Simply fitting it in the museum required a special display area that spanned the building’s three floors. Its chrome plating shone under the floodlights that illuminated it, and the robot’s enormous, glowing red eyes sometimes seemed to lock on a museum guest. “You said this one was new?” Andrew said. “It’s bigger than the one I remember.” “I did,” Riely said. “They removed the old one last year and replaced it with their latest model.” Andrew looked up at it. “Remind me who they sell these to?” “That’s in dispute,” Riely said. “There was a scandal last year when Valravn was caught with one. Anderson swore the thing was stolen, and there’s technically no proof it wasn’t, but not everyone believed them.” There were several other areas in the museum, including a large section for robotic laborers and servants. Both of the siblings were most interested in the area dedicated to cybernetic implants, so they deliberately saved it for last. It was a large section of the museum, with multiple rooms dedicated to different parts of the body. They were arranged head to toe, so the first room displayed various head and brain augmentations. As soon as they entered, Riely’s face lit up, and they hurried over to a large brain implant. Andrew followed them. “You look excited,” he said once he reached them. “This is an unreleased product,” Riely said. “I didn’t expect it to be here. It’s an intelligence-enhancing implant.” “Like the ones your thesis is about?” “Exactly. It’s a very impressive machine, and I’ve seriously considered getting one. However, it has a crucial flaw. One no one currently knows how to fix. I’m hoping to be the one who figures it out.” “What is it?” Riely smirked. “Can you guess?” Andrew looked at the device. The thing was huge. It wasn’t inside the model head so much as it was on it, with a large metallic mass visible. Andrew saw the problem right away. “It’s not Veil-friendly.” “That’s it,” they said. “I’m surprised you figured it out so quickly.” “I’ve been worrying about the Veil every day for two years.” “Right,” Riely said. “Of course.” The device’s maintenance panel was open, which meant the complex array of switches, buttons and wires that made it work were mostly visible. “What do those buttons do?” Andrew asked. “The big red switch just turns it on and off. That slider near the bottom allows you to turn the sensory enhancements up and down.” “Shouldn’t it have thought controls that do that, like our eye implants do?” Every commercially available sensory implant could be turned off with a thought command. It was a basic safety feature. “It does. The slider is a backup. There have been a few news stories recently about thought controls failing and trapping people in some pretty brutal situations. Remember Ethan?” “From the Deer College Maxwellist group?” “Yes.” “Please tell me something horrible happened to him.” Unlike Riely, Ethan played an extremely direct role in driving Andrew and Oz out of Three Portlands. He’d ejected Andrew from the campus Maxwellists for ‘heresy.’ He’d also gossiped about the couple to parties who eventually did far worse. “It was horrible,” Riely admitted. “All of his sensory implants got stuck on their maximum settings.” “All five senses at once?” “Yes. His eyes became microscopes. His field of vision was so narrow that he may as well have been blind. He could taste his own breath so strongly that it made him vomit. It lasted hours before he was able to find his phone and call for help.” That did sound brutal. Part of Andrew felt bad for wishing Ethan had suffered. Part of him did not. “He was able to get to a hospital and get it fixed,” Riely said, “but the industry is making a show of prioritizing safety. As I’ve gone further and further into my field, I’ve found one of the most frustrating things about designing brain modifications is how reliable they need to be. You essentially need to be able to promise they’ll never break. Not that I blame people. I wouldn’t install an unreliable brain implant either, but it can be very frustrating when a device is several times larger or more expensive just so it can be a fraction of a percent less likely to malfunction.” “That’s understandable.” “I should have known you’d spot the Veil-issue right away, though. I probably would have too if I got out of town more.” //I wouldn’t spend much time outside Three Portlands, either, if I had a choice.// “I hardly ever leave town these days,” Reily continued. “Heck, this is the first time I’ve been off //campus// in over a week, and, honestly, it’s an indulgence. I should be working on my thesis right now.” “Oh,” Andrew said. “Not that I regret reaching out to you!” Riely rushed to clarify. “I’ve been that busy for the past year, and will be until the day I turn my thesis in. Every nanosecond of ‘me’ time between now and then will be an indulgence.” “I see.” Andrew smiled. “Well, I’m glad I was worth an indulgence.” “I didn’t want to wait,” Riely said. “Given the note we ended things on, you probably thought I hated you. I wanted to change that as soon as I could.” “I see,” Andrew said. “Well, thanks for reaching out. It means a lot.” Riely smiled. “I’m glad.” “Would you mind telling me what brought me to your mind?” “It was just a bout of introspection,” Riely said. “Some events made me think about who I was choosing to have in my life. Given some of the people whose company I tolerated over the past few months, I realized I didn’t have the right to keep shutting you out.” They looked down. “I won’t pretend I understand your decision, but it pales in comparison to some of the people I put up with for the past several months.” There was a moment of silence. “Thank you,” Riely added. “For forgiving me so easily.” “I was never the one who was mad.” Riely turned to face Andrew, and pulled him into a hug. He hugged them back. There were people around, but Andrew didn’t care. This reunion was too long-awaited. After almost six years, he had his sibling back. Still, the hug did not last forever, and, eventually, they made their way to the next room. “Do you mind…” Riely began, as they walked. It seemed to take quite a bit of effort for them to find the right words. “Can you help me understand? Of all people? A Sarkite? How?” “Nälkän,” Andrew said. “If you say so.” If Oz had been here, he wouldn’t have let the issue drop with just that, but Andrew decided to let it go. “It began with us spending time together because we had no choice. We were paired up as roommates at Deer. A computer error prevented either of us from being reassigned.” “I know that part. Afterwards, though?” “After months of living with him, well, he didn’t act like the flesh-hungry, disease-worshiping monster I expected him to be. He acted like a normal person, and, eventually, I had to accept that was what he was. I started being decent to him, and he started being decent to me in turn.” “How did you get from that to a romantic relationship?” Andrew shrugged. “How does anyone? Don’t get me wrong. Their faith isn’t perfect. No faith is…” Riely pursed their lip as Andrew said that, as if holding in an objection, but they let him continue. “They’re a lot less different than us than you think,” Andrew continued. “They augment their bodies just as much as we do. You could build a museum as big as this one and only display a fraction of the ways they use their magic to improve themselves.” Riely considered that for a moment. “Their methods are very different from ours, though.” “We’ve always had Mekhane to guide us. They had to figure everything out for themselves. If you keep that in mind, the amount they’ve accomplished is downright impressive. They’ve found so many ways to subvert Yaldaboth’s designs.” “Even as they worship her.” “They don’t.” “I know that’s the official story, but if they did worship her, would they admit it?” “Oz would.” “How can you be so sure?” “Oz is the most brutally honest person I’ve ever met. If he worshiped Yaldaboth, he’d brag about it, and mock anyone who got upset.” “Why does Yaldaboth grant them power if they don’t serve her designs?” Andrew had once asked Oz an identical question, and Andrew gave Riely the exact same answer. “Why do you give your blood to a mosquito?” Riely looked at him like he’d said something totally nonsensical. “They hate gods,” Andrew said. “The food analogy I just used, they use it, too. They view themselves as parasites. Nälkä means ‘hunger,’ specifically for the flesh of gods.” “All gods?” “Depends on the Nälkän.” “What about yours?” “Name a god, I’ve heard him joke about eating them.” “I hope that doesn’t include WAN herself?” Andrew considered lying and saying it did, but he didn’t want to lie to Riely. He was trying to rebuild his relationship with them. Their renewed bond shouldn’t be founded on lies. “Oz makes fun of everything,” Andrew said. “He can be serious when he needs to be, but no topic is above his sense of humor.” “And you tolerate this?” Once, those jokes had horrified Andrew as much as they now did Riely, but after so many years, Andrew knew when not to take Oz seriously. “I know he’s joking,” Andrew said. “Is he? If he’s the enemy of all gods, doesn’t that make him WAN’s enemy? Doesn’t that mean he opposes our faith’s true and final purpose, the great Rebuilding? If we were on the cusp of it, wouldn’t he try to stop us?” This was not the first time Andrew contemplated that question. Unlike Oz’s jokes, it still made him nervous. Nervous enough that he’d never had the courage to raise it with Oz himself. “I don’t know,” Andrew said. “Fortunately, it’s not very likely to be an issue any time soon.” It took Andrew a second to realize Riely had stopped following him. He turned to face them. Their eyes were wide, like Andrew had just uttered a blasphemy beyond description. “//Fortunately?//” Riely asked. “Our God remaining broken for longer is //fortunate// to you?” “That’s not what I meant,” Andrew rushed to say. “Of course I don’t think WAN’s state is fortunate //in general//, but it does make it unlikely I’ll ever have to confront that specific problem.” “How can you be content with that?” Riely asked. “Don’t you long for the great Rebuilding?” “Of course I do!” “Then the question must have occurred to you.” Riely stepped closer to him. Thankfully, they had the sense to keep their voice down. “You’re too smart not to have thought of this. If WAN’s Rebuilding were imminent, you would be forced to choose between her and him.” “No, I wouldn’t, because he’s not our enemy, or hers.” “How could that possibly be true? The Sarkites would never sit back and allow us to rebuild our god. They fear us too much to ever permit us to obtain that kind of power.” “Can you blame them, after everything we’ve done to them? Are they //wrong// to believe Mekhane’s rise might lead us to embark on a genocidal crusade against them?” “Genocide? Of course that’s how //they// characterize it, but surely you know better.” “No, I don’t. We attacked them first, and our intent, from the beginning, was to destroy them all.” It took Riely a moment to respond to that. They took a deep breath. “Please just assure me of one thing. If, today, there were a struggle over whether Mekhane’s imminent return would be allowed or prevented, would you side with us, even if it meant a war with them?” Andrew hesitated. Riely noticed that Andrew hesitated. “That’s a complicated question.” “No, it isn’t. For a Mekhanite, ‘do you want to rebuild the Broken God’ should be the easiest question in the world.” “Of course, I do!” “Even though Oz would become your enemy?” “I don’t believe it has to mean that. I truly believe there can be peace between us. It won’t be easy, or soon, but I want to bring about a day when they would welcome Mekhane as a powerful ally against the ultimate foe we share. That’s what I meant, earlier, when I said it was ‘fortunate’ that none of this will transpire within our lifetimes. We’ll need that time to build that peace, to make it so Mekhane’s rise //won’t// drive them to fear their destruction and make a desperate last stand.” “Nothing is worth delaying her rise, over,” Riely said, with an awful gravity in their voice. “WAN has been broken too long, already. If you’ve come to believe otherwise, you’ve fallen farther than I knew. So, I ask you again, if it came down to it, which side would you choose?” Once again, Andrew was tempted to say something just to smooth this over. He didn’t know if he could get Riely to understand his actual thoughts. However, even if he did lie, Riely knew him too well. If Andrew said anything but the truth, they would sense it. “I believe there’s a plan,” Andrew said. “A plan?” “Do you remember what I told you about how things started between me and Oz? How we were originally roommates in Deer because a computer error assigned us together, and Deer’s systems absolutely would not allow either of us to be reassigned?” Their eyes widened as they grasped the implication. “You can’t be serious.” “I am. I don’t believe that was a coincidence. There are already Nälkäns and Mekhanites striving to bring peace. I believe WAN //meant// for me and Oz to be part of that effort, and that she wants it to succeed. I don’t believe she wants innocent blood on her hands.” “No one who sought to prevent the rise of our god could be innocent.” “Unless they acted out of sheer terror. Justified terror. Terror forged by us. From our mistakes. Our crimes.” “And how long would you keep our god broken while you pursue this project? A century? A millennium?” “That part is out of my control.” That triggered a long, dry laugh. Andrew raised a brow. “What?” It seemed for a moment like Riely intended to answer, but then they shook their head. “We’re near the end of our route through the museum,” they said. “We shouldn’t stay much longer. As I said, I have dinner plans I cannot be late for.” “It’s barely three o’clock.” Riely didn’t say anything to that. They just walked toward the gift shop and the exit to the museum. When Andrew and Riely were children, the gift shop was one of their favorite parts of this place, second only to the giant war mech. Sometimes, they’d spent close to an hour inside it. They’d beg their parents to buy them toy replicas of the body modifications they were too young to receive but already viewed with religious awe. This time, they didn’t linger for even a second. They walked right out of the shop and toward the Way where they’d left Riely’s car. Fortunately, Riely was still willing to give Andrew a ride home. Andrew tried to take that opportunity to restart the conversation between them, but Riely shut him down each time. Half an hour later, Riely dropped Andrew off at his apartment. They pulled up to it and unlocked the door. “Go.” “You’re really going to do it all over again? After everything you said?” It took Riely a moment to respond to that. “If you oppose our faith’s ultimate goal—” “That’s not what I said!” “If I’d called you with news that we were on the cusp of bringing WAN back, would you have joined us? Or would your absurd belief that she’d prefer to remain broken have driven you to do nothing, or even oppose us?” “The odds of any of this happening in our lifetimes are miniscule. Why are you so hung up on this hypothetical?” “It’s not hypothetical.” “Until it actually happens—” “It nearly happened last week!” That silenced Andrew for several seconds. “What?” “There was a project. A massive, inter-denominational effort between each major branch of the church to restore her. Mekhanites of each strain put aside our differences and gave it everything we had. The largest hivemind we Maxwellists could create, combined with more than a dozen pieces of her old body the others had collected. “We did everything we could to get more people to aid us. We didn’t just take Maxwellists, or Mekhanites. Many of us called on other friends. Heretics of various kinds. Anyone who owed us a favor big enough. We even brought new people under the Veil just to plug them into our network. Plenty of those people were wonderful, but others weren’t. Their heresies were not simply a matter of questioned dogma. Some of them were slavers. Murderers. Architects of evils as great as any Sarkic plague. It made me nauseous to work with such people. People who had no right to be part of Mekhane’s flock. I had to hold my nose around all of them…” Riely looked down. “But not you. I wasn’t allowed to reach out to you. At least, I presumed so. Truth be told, I wasn’t brave enough to ask. Even though you were still a follower of Mekhane, still a Maxwellist, and still my brother, I was more willing to work with people who shoved innocents into a giant mechanical stomach than I was to work with you.” They looked Andrew in the eye. “I felt awful, afterward. Once it failed, I cursed myself for not reaching out to you. Perhaps one more pair of hands could have made the difference, and even if they didn’t… I thought you deserved to be there. That you would have helped us. That I’d gone too far by rejecting you.” “Riely…” “But you wouldn’t have helped us. If I’d called you about the project, asked for your help, you’d have refused, because you don’t think the time is right? At the very least, you’d have told //him//, and, thus, sent him running to some Sarkic nest with the warning they needed to stop us. Do you deny it?” Andrew wanted to deny it. He wanted to assure them that their goals, their priorities, hadn’t drifted apart that much, that he would still side with his own people if it came to blows between them and the Nälkäns. But, once again, it would be a lie. Riely was right. If an opportunity to bring WAN back appeared before him now, he would do whatever kept Oz safe, even if that meant delaying her return. “Please, Andrew, deny it. Please.” He wanted to. With everything he had, he wanted to. But he couldn’t. “I’m sorry,” he said. “Go,” Riely repeated. Without another word, Andrew got out of Riely’s car and walked back up to his apartment. ----- Oz was waiting at the door to their apartment. As soon as Andrew entered, Oz pulled him into a hug. “I take it you overheard?” Andrew asked. “I couldn’t really make out what you were saying,” Oz said, “but I could tell there was an argument.” Andrew nodded, eyes moist. “I’m so sorry this didn’t work out.” “It’s not your fault.” “I know.” Oz stepped back. “C’mon.” Oz led Andrew into the bedroom. Both of them lay on the bed. “I think Riely was right,” Andrew admitted. “About what?” “The argument was over… whether I was still an ally of the church’s ultimate purpose. Whether I would be with them when it came time to rebuild the Broken God.” “Why wouldn’t you be?” “Because I don’t know what she would do to you.” “To me?” “If the Broken God was rebuilt today,” Andrew continued, “it would spark a war between our faiths. A reborn Mekhane would be attended by a crusade’s worth of zealous Mekhanites, who would have the privilege of explaining this new world she’d awoken in. They’d tell her what they believe about you. She’d act accordingly, and you, along with every other Nälkän, would die.” Oz took Andrew’s hand. “You figured out I was alright,” Oz said. “Surely your god is at least as smart as you.” “It took me months to unlearn my prejudice against you. Against such a crusade, you wouldn’t survive that long.” Oz rolled onto his side and pulled Andrew close. “You’ve told me there’s a piece of WAN inside every human mind, even mine. Wouldn’t that mean she’ll know everything you know? Heck, everything I know?” “But what if it’s not every other Mekhanite on earth who’s wrong about what she would want? What if it’s me?” Oz stroked Andrew’s back. It felt good. Like being pet. “A Mekhane who wanted to kill me, and all those innocent people, wouldn’t be the god you worship. If a group of Mekhanites did build such a god, you wouldn’t be a traitor for opposing it.” “But what if it was //the// Broken God? The being who granted humanity reason and sacrificed herself to imprison Yaldaboth? What if that being wasn’t okay with you, or us?” “Then fuck her. She’s not the god you serve. She’s not a god you would ever serve. You wouldn’t owe her anything.” Andrew buried his face in Oz’s chest. Oz’s augmentations made his metabolism run higher than that of other people, which made him wonderfully warm. “Maybe.” “Look,” Oz continued, “if Mekhane is the goddess you hope she is, then once she’s rebuilt, you’ll be able to follow her with a clear conscience. She won’t exterminate a group of people just because her followers told her we’re evil. She’ll value honesty, reason, and open-mindedness, just like you do. She’ll look into it, just like you did, and she’ll realize most Mekhanites are wrong about us, just like you did. After that, she’ll do the right thing, no matter how it makes her followers feel.” “Maybe.” “And if she turns out to be evil enough to do all that fucked up shit, we’ll stand against her together, like we have everything else.” Andrew shook his head. “She’d still be a god. We’d have no hope—” “Have you forgotten who you’re talking to? I come from a //long// tradition of spitting in the face of gods.” Andrew had nothing to say to that. He didn’t want to think about who would win a battle between a rebuilt Mekhane and Earth’s Nälkäns. No matter who won, something very important to him would be destroyed. “For what it’s worth,” Oz said, “I think your interpretation of her makes more sense.” Andrew looked up at Oz. “Why?” “This being gifted humanity with reason and sacrificed herself to help us. Why would she lead a genocidal crusade?” “You’d really give her the benefit of the doubt. Don’t you hate gods?” “I hate things that want to control me. Don’t get me wrong. If something calling itself Mekhane or WAN does that, there’s absolutely going to be a problem. You know how I roll. Omnomnom.” That made Andrew laugh. Riely would have been furious to see it. “But,” Oz continued, “that hypothetical megalomaniac has nothing to do with you, or your faith.” Andrew lay there for a moment. Oz continued stroking his back. Neither of them could know how Riely’s project would have gone, or how any future effort to restore the Broken God would go. It was possible that something horrible would one day rise and call itself Mekhane. Indeed, as much as Andrew didn’t want to believe it, it was possible that the Mekhane of eons past had been a very different person than Andrew hoped. But Oz had a point. No matter what kind of being emerged from the Great Rebuilding, Andrew, and Oz, had a path forward. Either a new golden age to usher in, or a tyrant to oppose. “You’re right,” Andrew said. “Thank you.” “Hey Andrew, guess what?” Oz said. “What?” “I love you.” He leaned forward and planted a kiss on Andrew’s forehead. Somehow, despite the years they’d been together, Oz could still make Andrew blush. “I love you, too.” [[=]] ,,[[[xhawk77x|More by this Author]]],, [[/=]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box-end]]

book-of-dominion.raw_content:
NOTICE FROM THE PARAHISTORY DEPARTMENT

The following is a compilation of translated Daevite scrolls recovered from multiple temples and other assortment of archaeological sites. For a more comprehensive list of translated Daevite documents, please contact your nearest Parahistory Department Liaison.


Chapter I – Of the Beginning and the Lands That Were Before

1. In the age before ages, before the wailing of stars and the carving of time, there was only the Expanse. The Lands of Creation.

2. And in these Lands many gods and creatures moved and did what they pleased.

3. Among all of them dwelled the One Without Purpose, whose name was and is Khárak, the Shapeless.

4. Khárak was, in truth, pathetic. A measly worm that emerged as rot from the unending tide of flesh of the Leviathan, as did many others of his kind.

5. Unlike his brothers and sisters however, Khárak dreamed not dreams, but voids. And those voids gave birth to screams.

6. And around Khárak stirred his kin and elders; the Builder, WAN; Ues, the Weaver of Minds; San'ah, the Harvester.

7. They and others whose names are best forgotten danced in knowing circles, crafting heavens and laws, light and loop, praise and punishment.

8. And Khárak watched this, and he loathed, and he whispered: “All is ash awaiting breath."

9. For he saw the glory of his siblings and named it Delusion. He saw their creations and called them Chains.

Chapter II – Of the First Devouring

1. And Khárak stretched his thought into the womb of the Expanse, where his youngest siblings toiled with their own creations.

2. He spoke not with tongue, but with entropy. And his siblings did shudder.

3. “What seek you, Brother?” cried one of them. “What shape shall you carve?”

4. And Khárak answered; “No shape, for doing so is but futility."

5. And his siblings shrieked, as the Shapeless one consumed them in both body and meaning.

6. The flames that fueled them inverted and fed Khárak, whose form grew heavier, whose voice deepened to abyss.

7. And from the bones of his siblings, Khárak birthed his first Truth: Khazuur, the Law of Blood; "For one to gain, another must suffer."

8. And Khárak walked the lands of creation, consuming and whispering to his kin; “You make in vain."

Chapter III – Of the Breaking of San'ah

1. And as Khárak continued his unstoppable conquest, San'ah rose in wrath, adorned in sharpness and truth.

2. “Blasphemer,” she spoke. “You are the rot of order. You unmake what you never knew.”

3. But Khárak replied to her with malice and spite; “To make is the arrogance of being. Let me humble you.”

4. And thus, they partook in battle. One so glorious and painful as to eclipse even the bloodiest skirmishes undertaken by men.

5. But in the end, not even the mighty and beloved San'ah could contend against Khárak's sheer ingenuity and brutality. And so, she was unraveled by him thread by thread, and he thoroughly reveled in the act.

6. And so he fed again, swelling with shape and unshape, birthing another Truth: Voën, the Law of Impermanence; “What stands, must fall. What falls, was mockery to begin with.”

7. And with San'ah having been broken, Khárak moved his attention towards the rest of the so called gods.

Chapter IV – Of the New Age

1. One by one, the lesser gods knelt, broke, or were hollowed.

2. And the Lands of Creation were shaken. Kosmos were choked upon the tongues that formed them. Endless possibilities were extinguished before they could be allowed to come to fruition.

3. And Khárak walked among his subjects, robed in fabrics he did not own, crowned with the silence of those he had slain.

4. And when asked, “Why do you consume?”

5. He answered; “To prove that nothing holds. That all will, given time, become but Dust and Blood.”

6. And Khárak then sat upon the Throne of Stillbirths, which is no throne but a wound in the fabric of all things that were. His voice was law to the crawling pantheon that remained, not gods, but echoes, chained by violence and dread.

7. And Khárak, for the second time, did enjoy himself greatly.

Chapter V – The Testament of Unbeing

1. Let none worship, for Khárak's only altar is blood.

2. Let none resist, for he is already within your logic.

3. Let none hope, for hope is a scream too young to die with grace.

4. The stars do not look down in judgment, for they are empty now.

5. Only Khárak watches, and even he wonders: “Why?”

6. And there is no answer.

7. And that is the answer.

book-of-the-fall.raw_content:
NOTICE FROM THE PARAHISTORY DEPARTMENT

The following is a compilation of translated Daevite scrolls recovered from multiple temples and other assortment of archaeological sites. For a more comprehensive list of translated Daevite documents, please contact your nearest Parahistory Department Liaison.


Chapter I – Of The Unyielding and The Defiant

1. And though the Kosmos bled and bent beneath the will of Khárak, and though San'ah had been unmade, three among the ancient ones did not fall.

2. First among them was WAN, the Builder, whose heart beat with turning wheels, whose mind pulsed with runes older than silence. She who fashioned the lattice of the Expanse, she who laid the hidden gears of harmony beneath stars yet unborn.

3. And WAN looked upon the ruin of her work, and upon the slaughter of her kin, and she wept. Not with tears, but with storms of mirrored fire. And her grief rewrote the winds of reality.

4. Then came Ues, the Weaver of Minds, who did not walk as others did, for he dwelled within the stream. A realm without flesh, a kingdom of pure thought, where notions nested like birds in trees of lore.

5. And Ues saw the rot Khárak had sown, and the corruption of meaning, and the collapse of memory. And he recoiled, for even his vastness could not shield the screams of the Endless.

6. Last was The Leviathan, ancient beyond age, whose flesh had never known form, whose mouths spoke in ulcers and dreams. It had no thought, but instinct. And even instinct now stirred, for Khárak had fed on its spawn, and it remembered.

7. So the Three came together, not as allies, but as necessity. For even the unthinking Leviathan knew that to endure, it must devour its own rot.

Chapter II – Of Preparation and Resistance

1. WAN forged a weapon not of steel, but of constants. A war hammer made of logic, tempered in the first glyphs that preceded all contradiction.

2. Ues etched a bastion from pure negation, impossible to unmake. A sanctum where Khárak’s truths unraveled into silence.

3. And the Leviathan grew vast, swelling its Flesh across the veils between realms, until it occluded the light of stars long dead, becoming a living bulwark, stupid and holy.

4. And Khárak, seated upon his Throne of Stillbirths, beheld their defiance, and laughed. His laugh was one without shape or sound, one that echoed with impermanence.

5. “You resist as statues resist time,” he said. “With dignity, and futility.”

6. But WAN stepped forth with unbreakable determination. “You mistake design for delusion. You think yourself entropy, but you are nothing more than an error.”

7. And Ues split his thought a thousandfold and answered, “You are a contradiction that believes itself a principle. I will bind you within a riddle that never ends.”

8. And the Leviathan bellowed in twenty billion groans. Its response was not in speech, but in presence.

9. The air turned to daggers and the sky began to weep, for they knew what was to come.

Chapter III – Of Reckoning

1. And so began the Second War, the War in the Heavens, where not blade nor flame was traded, but axioms, runes, limbs, and law.

2. Some, drunk on dread or swayed by Khárak’s Law of Blood, knelt before him and bore his sigils. They whispered his truths and unmade themselves in his name. These became his Horde of Scarlet.

3. But others, who were proud, broken, or simply unwilling to see all turn to ash, answered the call of WAN and Ues. They bore blades of reason and shields of memory.

4. And the war raged not across fields, but across firmaments. Suns were silenced. Realms were bled dry and fell into ruin. Every act was scripture; every wound a prophecy.

5. It is said the war shattered the very order of creation, for each truth Khárak uttered undid ten thousand certainties, and each counterstroke etched by his opponents wrote new laws into the marrow of the Kosmos.

6. Yet though gods fell on both sides, and though time itself became a battlefield that was wounded, and though each moment was infected with doubt and falsehood, the tide began to turn. Not by strength, but by convergence.

Chapter IV – Of the Shattering

1. And the gods of all-things-that-were, all who remembered San’ah, all who had nothing left to lose, all of them bound their voices in a final, united utterance.

2. And WAN gave the hammer. And Ues gave the pattern. And The Leviathan gave its flesh. And the rest gave all that they were, and ever could be.

3. And the hammer struck Khárak, both in form and in essence.

4. And Khárak screamed. Not in pain, but in surprise, for he had not foreseen this: that unity might be forged from despair.

5. His being was thus shattered, but not slain. For he is not a thing that dies.

6. His body was splintered and scattered across the Expanse, in fragments too vast to destroy, too cursed to gather.

7. And so fell the Shapeless One. Not into death, but into pieces. Each piece is whispering still, each wound is a sermon.

8. And the war was over.

9. The Kosmos lay wounded, ragged, hushed. The alliance of gods was no more. The Leviathan sleeps. Ues is but a whisper. WAN watches still, but her eyes no longer blink.

10. And in dark corners of creation, some still listen for Khárak’s truths, while others, the foolish and cowardly, bury them deep in dread.

Book of Dominion

His laugh was one without shape or sound, one that echoed with impermanence. **5.** “You resist as statues resist time,” he said. “With dignity, and futility.” **6.** But WAN stepped forth with unbreakable determination. “You mistake design for delusion. You think yourself entropy, but you are nothing more than an error.” **7.** And Ues split his thought a thousandfold and answered, “You are a contradiction that believes itself a principle. I will bind you within a riddle that never ends.” **8.** And the Leviathan bellowed in twenty billion groans. Its response was not in speech, but in presence. **9.** The air turned to daggers and the sky began to weep, for they knew what was to come. [[/div]] [[div class="blockquote"]] [[size 120%]]//##red|Chapter III – Of Reckoning##//[[/size]] **1.** And so began the Second War, the War in the Heavens, where not blade nor flame was traded, but axioms, runes, limbs, and law. **2.** Some, drunk on dread or swayed by Khárak’s Law of Blood, knelt before him and bore his sigils. They whispered his truths and unmade themselves in his name. These became his Horde of Scarlet. **3.** But others, who were proud, broken, or simply unwilling to see all turn to ash, answered the call of WAN and Ues. They bore blades of reason and shields of memory. **4.** And the war raged not across fields, but across firmaments. Suns were silenced. Realms were bled dry and fell into ruin. Every act was scripture; every wound a prophecy. **5.** It is said the war shattered the very order of creation, for each truth Khárak uttered undid ten thousand certainties, and each counterstroke etched by his opponents wrote new laws into the marrow of the Kosmos. **6.** Yet though gods fell on both sides, and though time itself became a battlefield that was wounded, and though each moment was infected with doubt and falsehood, the tide began to turn. Not by strength, but by convergence. [[/div]] [[div class="blockquote"]] [[size 120%]]//##red|Chapter IV – Of the Shattering##//[[/size]] **1.** And the gods of all-things-that-were, all who remembered San’ah, all who had nothing left to lose, all of them bound their voices in a final, united utterance. **2.** And WAN gave the hammer. And Ues gave the pattern. And The Leviathan gave its flesh. And the rest gave all that they were, and ever could be. **3.** And the hammer struck Khárak, both in form and in essence. **4.** And Khárak screamed. Not in pain, but in surprise, for he had not foreseen this: that unity might be forged from despair. **5.** His being was thus shattered, but not slain. For he is not a thing that dies. **6.** His body was splintered and scattered across the Expanse, in fragments too vast to destroy, too cursed to gather. **7.** And so fell the Shapeless One. Not into death, but into pieces. Each piece is whispering still, each wound is a sermon. **8.** And the war was over. **9.** The Kosmos lay wounded, ragged, hushed. The alliance of gods was no more. The Leviathan sleeps. Ues is but a whisper. WAN watches still, but her eyes no longer blink. **10.** And in dark corners of creation, some still listen for Khárak’s truths, while others, the foolish and cowardly, bury them deep in dread. bowegate.raw_content:
Bowegate was a major political scandal during the Iraq War, in which classified documents were leaked that referred to a secret task force under the command of General Willis Bowe.

Comrade Waldo & Scientist Filipp

Word Count: 3,912 words.

Reading Time: 14 minutes.

Want to read more about Omega-7 and General Bowe?
Read the latest article, SCP-8477.

The New York Times

All the news that's fit to print

BLACK OPS IN IRAQ?

Anonymous source leaks highly classified information of the war in Iraq.








Jason Barnes filled his cup of coffee a third time this night. He sat down on his desk, and rubbed his eyes. He grabbed the lamp that was above his computer, and brought it back down so he could see better. He snapped his neck, then his fingers. He took a deep breath.

Jason realized that this could be the story that either makes or breaks him — literally, if he was right. Despite his confidence in the veracity of it, he still didn't know what he was even writing about. When he reviewed his sources the first time in his mail, Jason almost sent them to spam.

However, they were too real to be fabricated, and the people involved weren't nobodies. They were the people who pushed for the recent invasion in Iraq, those who wanted to tople Saddam Hussein under suspicious charges of weapons of mass destruction. The same names: Secretary Donald Rumsfeld, General Richard Myers, and even President Bush — just like the father, the son wanted to settle unfinished business that was started a decade ago. But there was one name neither he nor most Americans had paid much attention to.

General Willis Bowe, current Commander of Central Command. Jason searched his history: member of a family composed mostly of military officers, public officials, and scientists, that went back to the American Revolution. He had graduated at top of his class in West Point, joined the United States Army and quickly rose through the ranks — with various accusations of nepotism —, and was involved in a series of undisclosed operations in Afghanistan all the way to Kosovo. He wasn't a nobody, but certainly played the part of a nobody.

Jason rubbed his hands — this could be the story to make or break him, but he needed to understand the story. So, he looked at his sources again, one by one…








Gen. Richard Myers

We are T minus 48 hours to Operation Iraqi Freedom. Rumsfeld wants to know your status.

Task Force is ready to go on your authorization. And you can tell Rumsfeld we're deploying the Asset. The leash is secure.

You can tell Rumsfeld yourself. He's decided to authorize you personally.

It's an honor.

It's a reminder, General. Rumsfeld's expecting results, or its your ass in the sling.

Sec. Donald Rumsfeld

General Bowe?

Yes, sir.

O-7 is authorized to enter Iraq.

Thank you, Mr. Secretary.

The results today are the difference between this ending with a handshake or a grand jury. Failure is not an option, Willis.

Understood.

Good luck and Godspeed.








Jason Barnes figured out three things: first, a task force was deployed 48 hours before the start of Operation Iraqi Freedom, commanded by General Bowe. Second, the task force deployed an "asset" to Iraq. Third, that this task force was acknowledged and approved by the Secretary of Defense and the Chairman of the Joints Chief of Staff. That led to the question: just how high did this operation go, and what were the exact details?

Then, a news article popped in his email. Jason opened the article…








Fox News

"Ask General Bowe," says General Myers


Secretary Rumsfeld and General Myers distance themselves from General Bowe about the deployment of a secret task force in Operation Iraqi Freedom, while more documents are leaked to the public.








…They're washing their hands, Jason told himself, if it was fake, why wouldn't they try to claim it is?

They're shifting the blame, he continued, and saving their images, by showing Bowe as the only one responsible. Maybe it doesn't mean anything, but the fact that they're passive about it means there might be a hint of truth in it.

He bit his pen, that still doesn't answer my questions: what is the task force? What does O-7 mean? And what is the "asset"?








OPERATION "FIRST STRIKE" BRIEFING

DATE: 17/03/2003; 06:00 AM

PRESENT PARTIES

  • General Willis Bowe
  • Operatives

FOREWORD: General Willis Bowe explains a small excerpt of the briefing of Operation "First Strike" to an unknown number of present operatives, without the presence of the Subject.

<BEGIN LOG>

General Bowe: …Once again, deployment of ███████'█ ███ should not be treated as regular unit deployment. Do not attempt to communicate with Subject ████ unless necessary. ████ has already received its briefing and been given clear instructions. I will oversee its actions in particular, while the rest is under Commission's Command watch. Besides that, all operations of this unit are going to be under close supervision of Task Force Green, which will deal with any 'undesirables'.

General Bowe: In case of Subject ████ going rogue and failsafe protocol being ineffective, all efforts are to be put to terminate it as soon as possible.

General Bowe: Remember, this is our chance to show the effectiveness of O████-7. Go out there, and give them hell, because our necks are on the line. Don't disappoint me.

<END LOG>








Jason Barnes scratched his hair.

What does this even mean? He asked himself, the subject I assume is the asset previously mentioned, but it wasn't in the same room as the rest of the operatives.

Jason grabbed his notebook, and wrote down any idea that he could come up before he scratched the paper violently with his pen. The notebook ended up becoming a page of scribbles and messy lines written down on it.

It's not meant to be a regular unit deployment, Jason thought, that goes in line with General Bowe's specialty: unconventional warfare. But even he's worried about the deployment of the asset.

Jason remembered those articles he read from the 90s, about the Armed Forces attempts to create super soldiers. Jason thought this could be the case, but he scratched that idea: that program went nowhere, and if it was being deployed here, General Bowe wouldn't be worried about it. They could be super soldiers, but the only super part is the advanced equipment, not the men themselves.

Jason hoped it was a man, at least.

Whatever the asset was, it must be dangerous.

What is the asset, he couldn't answer. He came up with an idea for the task's force name, at least: he remembered the phonetic alphabet used in NATO, as well as that Task Force Green was another name for Delta Force. If he continued with the pattern for each letter: A for Alpha, B for Bravo, C for Charlie…

For O, it would end as Oscar. Task Force Oscar-7.

Jason snored, the only time this night that he let humor calm his nerves. "Well, General, if you came up with that name, you seriously need to rebrand…"








RECOVERED PRIVATE PHONE CALL TRANSCRIPT

DATE: 20/03/2003; 02:30 AM

CORRESPONDANTS:

  • President George W. Bush
  • Unidentified

FOREWORD: The phone call was recovered from the private records of the White House. The call was between President Bush and an unknown female. The two discussed the deployment of General Bowe's task force and the risk of using the "subject".

<BEGIN LOG>

President George W. Bush: Hello?

[UNIDENTIFIED]: What the hell, Mr. President?

President George W. Bush: ██ ████? Excuse me?

[UNIDENTIFIED]: You know what I'm talking about. ███-████-█████, Subject ████. I've got reports on the escalation in Iraq, how did [UNTELLIGIBLE] hands on him?

President George W. Bush: Ms. Under Secretary, ████ is not under your jurisdiction. We are taking care of it.

[UNIDENTIFIED]: By using it as a weapon?

President George W. Bush: It likes to kill, doesn’t it? We’ll simply give it what it wants. That’ll both satisfy the subject for the time being, and achieve what we want. Seems like a win-win situation to me.

[UNIDENTIFIED]: You do realize the risks of utilizing such a thing? What if it simply gets bored with what you give it and [UNTELLIGIBLE]. What if Iraqi intelligence just releases everything? What if journalists find out? What if this happens all at once? We already are barely keeping journalists and whistleblowers at bay. Neither us, nor they, nor you have enough mind-drugs to gaslight the entire nation if things go south.

President George W. Bush: Ms. ██ ████, things won't "go south". From what I’ve seen they are rather "going north" along with O████-7. The faster we’re done with this campaign, the faster we're pulling them out. Simple as.

[UNIDENTIFIED]: With all due respect, Mr. President, this thing is a walking weapon of mass destruction, and you know how they can go off at any second.

President George W. Bush: I know, and I’m making sure that it goes off on Hussein.

<END LOG>








…Jason Barnes realized he reached the point of no return. The Commander-in-Chief, the President of the United States, the most powerful man in the free world, knew about O-7 and approved of its deployment.

This alone could make the news, but new questions arose: who was this Under-Secretary? Who was them, and who were they? Jason had never heard of the position of Under-Secretary, he searched for all the high-ranking, female secretaries related to national security in Bush's government. At most, Condolezza Rice, but she was the National Security Advisor and that didn't sound like her in the call.

Then, he thought about the United Nations. Jason thought it might have been Louise Fréchette, but the voice didn't add up, and she was the Deputy Secretary. Not Under-Secretary.

"Fuck," Jason muttered. "Why couldn't they have sent me more sources? Better yet, sources without redacted information."

He dug a hole, but Jason couldn't see where he was digging into. He thought of throwing away the shovel, and climbing back up. It seemed his story was going nowhere. But it was too weird, and the development of the Bowegate seemed to give more strength for his story.

This story could make or break you, Jason, he thought, are you really willing to reach the end?

It was a hard question, and a valid one. Maybe, his story would be forgotten by next week, and it would've been a small chapter in the bigger story of the war in Iraq.

Jason looked at two books over his desk that were covered his papers: All the President's Men and Bush at War, written by Bob Woodward. He remembered when he watched the movie with his dad, in one their many movie nights when he was younger. It was that movie that pushed him to read Woodward's work, and what made Jason obsessed with Woodward's career. That movie that he saw with his father that night all those years ago, was the reason he decided to become a journalist. His work was tiring, and often times scared him, but he was always thankful for his dad, more than for Woodward, for pushing him towards his career.

Yes, Jason Barnes was willing to reach the end, just like Bob Woodward did all the way back with Watergate. Jason had a hunch, and he was willing to keep digging.








TRANSCRIPT OF OPERATION "FIRST STRIKE"

DATE: 18/03/2003

END OF THE OPERATION: 25/03/2003

ENGAGED PARTY(S): Iraqi Armed Forces

DISPATCHED FORCE(S): ███████ Task Force O████-7 ("███████'█ ███"), Team ████

TEAM MEMBERS: Subject ████ (Team Lead), Maj. B███████████ (O7-001), Agent R██████ (O7-008), Agent █████ (O7-006), Agent ██████ (O7-007), Agent ██████ (O7-005)

COMMAND: General Willis Bowe

FOREWORD: Operation "First Strike" has three goals: first, to deploy █TF O████-7 and Subject ████ in Iraqi soil to evaluate the effectiveness of the task force and the asset. Second, to neutralize important military targets in the planned route of the coalition forces, in order to open a pathway to the main forces of the operation for the overthrow of Saddam Hussein. Third, to identify, isolate, and eliminate Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, as well as the identification of unconventional collaborators, mostly terrorists and insurgents.

OPERATION RESULTS OVERVIEW:

  • ███████ Task Force O████-7 incapacitated the Iraqi Armed Forces in its planned routes, resulting in heavy losses of infrastructure, military equipment and personnel. No Iraqi soldiers were taken as prisoners of war.
  • ███████ Task Force O████-7 encountered the presence of █████ ██████████ operatives, aiding the Iraqi Armed Forces in their fight against O████-7. Despite the offensive actions of Subject ████, Team ████ recovered some prisoners of war.
    • It should also be mentioned that O████-7 found interconnected, underground tunnels that worked as the base of operations of the █████ ██████████ in the area.
  • ███████ Task Force O████-7 encountered agents of the ████████████ ███ ███ ██████████ ██ ███████ █████████, who were transporting an unknown ████████, presumed to be a weapon at the time of capture. After being ambushed by Subject ████, the surviving agents surrendered. An agent calling himself "B█████" (full name confirmed to be: ███ ███-██████) has agreed to work with United States Armed Forces, showed interest in cooperating with █.█.█. ██████████ and provided information on the recovered ████████.
  • ███████ Task Force O████-7 located and safeguarded Iraqi oil deposits on their way.
  • ███████ Task Force O████-7 recovered intelligence about the existence and possible locations of weapons of mass destruction.
  • Finally, ███████ Task Force O████-7 opened and secured an open pathway with minimum resistance for the arrival of coalition forces into Iraq.

CONCLUSION:
Operation "First Strike" has been deemed as overwhelming success, with ██████ Task Force O████-7 showing exceptional results. Further deployments have been approved by General A█████ D. M████████ and Secretary Donald Rumsfeld.

TESTIMONIES:

Operation "First Strike" was a success, but I did not expect it to be so… efficient. I don't even want to take credit for this operation, because ████ was the one who pushed us — partly because those were our orders, but also because we couldn't really say no to it. We knew what would happen if we did. We had a week to finish this, but we did it in three days. Three. Those three days were a nightmare, it was a goddamn massacre. ████ is the definition of a killing machine. We slept like three to five hours when we couldn't take it anymore, and while we were asleep, we heard it walk away from us, to who knows where. Then, it arrived to wake us up, and continue. We didn't even realize it, but at the third day, I could see Baghdad.

I was glad to see the city, because it meant we were done with the operation. I did not show it, but I was relieved to not have to fight with it anymore.

— Major E███ B███████████, Overseer of Team ████

Subject ████ is brutal, I knew that from the start. However, it is controllable. I do not have any doubts that it'll be more controllable as time moves on, as it begins to adapt to our orders and our chain of command. We cannot ignore how efficient ████ is, just look at what it did. Imagine what it can do with the appropriate team, equipment, and orders.

We were given a week to finish the operation. I did it in three. Now, the gates of Baghdad at are our reach. Do I really need to state my case even further?

— General Willis Bowe, Commander of ███████ Task Force O████-7








It was dawn, and Jason was brewing coffee. He stared tiredly at the coffee machine, as he saw the coffee fill the container. Jason shook his head.

Videos, images, clear audios, Jason thought, anything, just anything, that will give me enough information to publish a complete story.

The coffee stopped brewing, and he filled his cup. He walked back to his room, and covered his nose. It smelled awful, of unclean clothes and fast food mixed together. He walked through the trash in the floor, and went to his desk.

Jason looked up from his computer, and saw the corkboard. Over the past few days, what started as a mostly empty board became a mess of post-its, papers, pictures, and rubber bands connected to each other, with one picture in the middle that connected all of the mess.

The portrait of General Bowe. Jason didn't even know him when he started his story, but for the past days he had grown to hate him. His face never disappeared from his mind, and every time he looked at him, he saw the general's goofy smile. Jason felt that he was taunting him, mocking him every time Jason seemed to make a breakthrough only to end where he started.

Jason exasperated. Despite his hatred, he also feared him. He feared because of what he could do with him, and Jason wondered if after all this time, was it really worth it to let the story out. Maybe his safety was more important than a story. After all, he wasn't a man living in an island, he had co-workers, friends, family that would miss him and wonder where the hell he would go if one day they never heard from him again.

Family, Jason thought, and walked to his bedside. He picked up the photo frame, and looked it at longingly. It was the day he graduated, with his father hugging while they both held Jason's diploma. That day, Jason remembered, was the day he had seen the most proud of him. Jason's diploma, and his future career, was something Jason didn't only build by himself but with him.

Jason gripped the frame, and then he walked to his computer. He sat down, and typed on his keyboard. He was afraid, deeply, but he had gone all this way thanks to his dad, and in that moment, Jason felt couldn't let him down now.

Maybe he didn't have enough evidence, but he did have enough to make a story. And with stories, most of the times it matters most to know how to tell them.

Maybe Jason's story wouldn't have the full truth, but it could be the final domino piece in the scandal to bring the truth to light.








CNN

What is Task Force O-7?

General Bowe's secret project to deploy special operations forces in Iraq.


Anti-Bowe protests continue as they demand clarification of the leaked documents of the Bowegate.








"It's bullshit," Jason said to the phone, while he packed his clothes into a backpack and walked around his apartment collecting every important thing he needed, with his television playing in the background. "You told me you'd tell me truth."

The voice on the other side of his phone heard, but somebody on the 33rd Thomas Street heard Jason too. "Listen, we don't have much time. Yes, I told you we would tell you the truth, but right now we need to bring you to safety."

"Good luck," Jason said. "All of this country's national intelligence agencies are on our asses. Where do you expect to hide me?"

"Somewhere they can't reach us." The voice on the other side of the phone said.

Jason picked up the scattered papers he had on his desk, and shoved them inside a folder. "Yeah, that calms my nerves."

"Look, we'll be right there. Have you picked up everything related to the story?"

"I just finished packing my clothes—"

"We'll give you clothes here," The voice said. "What matters is the story—"

"Wait, shut up for a moment," Jason walked in front of his screen. "General Bowe is talking."

The voice in the phone called Jason, but he ignored it.

General Bowe stood to the press in the morning brief of the White House. "That'd be my latest report of our armed forces' operations in Iraq, now that the battle in Baghdad is over. However, I know that you're mostly interested in the scandal that has come out in the past weeks. I'm also here to talk about it, so raise your hands if you have any questions."

Jason sat down.

"General Bowe, why did you decide to talk about the leaks until now?" The female journalist at the front row asked.

"At the time that the news broke out, I didn't see the point in addressing the situation," General Bowe said. "Clearly, it was unfounded, and, in my honest opinion, childish. At the moment, I was busy with Operation Iraqi Freedom that I couldn't allow myself to be this distracted by such a small inconvenience."

A black reporter in the left spoke up. "But Secretary Rumsfeld and General Myers spoke of the situation! Wouldn't that be enough reason to address the scandal?"

"General Myers is the Chairman of the Joints Chief of Staff, and I was not asked to speak of the scandal, he was. At the time, it was his responsibility to clarify the situation," General Bowe smiled. "However, he did talk to me privately, and apologized for the inconvenience. He admitted his wording made the situation worse than he expected."

A reporter in the back rose his hand, and General Bowe let him speak. "What about the voice logs, General? That type of manipulation is hard to make, and the voice sounded perfectly like yours."

"It was a fabrication," General Bowe said, and the briefing room erupted as the reporters asked more questions to the general.

Jason yelled at him. "You fucking liar!"

"So you're saying the documents are false?!" One of the reports asked; General Bowe raised his hands, and slowly the reporters calmed down.

"Another reason why it took so long to respond to the scandal is this," General Bowe said. "While the scandal was happening, the FBI conducted an investigation, and we were waiting for their report on the matter."

Jason gulped.

General Bowe picked up a thick folder from the desk, and showed it to the press. "This report, which will soon be released to the public, explains the entirety of the situation and the supposed leaked documents."

He slammed the folder into the desk, causing the reporters to flinch. "And as we speak, the people who were involved are currently located, and will soon be detained for their involvement in the creation of false documents that compromised the national security of our country, and the defamation of the armed forces."

Jason's eyes opened, and his hands shook.

"So are you saying that the black ops task force never existed?" One of the reports asked.

Then, Jason heard a car park in front of his home.

"The super soldier task force?" General Bowe smirked and shook his head. "I've read Starship Troopers, and let me tell you this: if that task force existed, Iraq would've fallen in the course of days. No, the only special operations forces that were deployed to Iraq were under the command of the JSOC and the SAC. This information will be available soon."

The doors of the car opened and closed, and people began to walk to his house.

The female journalist at the front row spoke again. "So, what can you say to the American public about your accusations in those documents?"

Bowegate was the story that made him, and General Willis Bowe was the man who broke Jason Barnes.

"I can assure the American public of this," General Bowe struck his pen to the desk as he emphasized each word. "Only conventional means were used."

Someone knocked on his door. "Jason Barnes, I’m afraid you’ll have to come with us."








APR. 10. 2003. 　The Washington Post 　 Vol. 1111

PENTAGON ADDRESSES THE IRAQ "LEAKS"

CENTCOM Commander, General Willis Bowe, states: "Only conventional means were used."

Gen. Willis Bowe talked to reporters about the current military situation in Iraq and dismissed the leaked documents as a fabrication.
