breaking-on-a-floppy-disk.raw_content:
There are types of darkness that can be hard to get out of your head.

xexnoncores

This work contains CWs for: ideations of suicide/self-harm, and mentions of drugs.

Breaking On A Floppy Disk by xexnoncores

⚠️ content warning

A text file found on a floppy disk taped to a book in the Wanderer’s Library. It has no distinguishing features besides being covered in granite dust, with “PROP”, “1998”, and “MC&” written on the front with faded marker.

Its author and owner are unknown.

I think to myself of what it means to “move on” in the most violent ways possible, the most egregious ways possible, the most demanding ways possible. Insomuch as one’s self-contained hatred of their own body poisons the well of all their endeavors, so too does it inform and venomize the rules which such bodies are instructed to act under.

It is in the nature of “moving on” to have been hurt in the first place, to bleed. And oh how easily I bleed, how easily my lungs and mouth pour with scarlet when smashed against the flesh of others. It is easy to fool me into a self-administered fugue state, bordering on the line of sanity and helplessness, into useless breakdowns of no help to anyone. Into displays of non-functioning miserable enough to push onlookers to a self-hanging, because I am a grown adult who slipped the facade of normality. It is so easy to force my skull wide open with the twisting sensations of my chest, of a freeze-response that only works halfway, because even a deer in the headlights can jump out of a car’s way to watch the crash.

Does this make me someone who is doomed to forever reassure myself of unassailed slights against my person? An ouroboros of neuroticism at every stray look, every neutral response, every hanging message that goes unanswered? Shall I state to my coworkers the plain truth that when they forget to do something for me that I dream of the noose, for their disapproval of me could lead to a string of complaints that I’ll never be able to stop? In what universe can I tell my boss that his flat “alright” makes me consider slitting my wrists because of the pain his imagined disappointment causes me? If he’s not satisfied with my every move, I feel like a failure. I need his endorsement to do my job. It’s his invisible signature on all the checks I’m carrying.

I’m good at my job. I am allegedly good at my job. People smile at me, rank me highly in peer reviews, I keep getting bigger and bigger bonuses—but none of it matters. None of it adds. I am only subtracting from myself as I continually work and interact with others; I am only waiting on them to respond to me, to praise me, to end the thought cycle in my head of “Do you like me? How can I make you not hate me? Please don’t hate me. Please. Please. Please.”

I have to “move on” every day from these unintentional failures of theirs. These expected failures of theirs, because I can’t be a madman and ask them 24/7 about this. They do not mean anything by their inaction, supposedly. That’s the most logical explanation, because they have jobs, families, and obligations too. I do not think they care about me around the clock—they shouldn’t, actually.

That both brings me great comfort and great pain, because it means I should not care, that their machinations are not as embedded in my fate as I imagine, but what if I should? What if I should say something to avoid them all ostracizing me at the Christmas parties? Should I confront one of them about their habitual cold shoulder? Confront the one who makes niceties with me in front of the bosses but refuses to say a good word about my work otherwise? Will that get me in trouble? Will that have been for the greater good? Will I have been brave, or will I have done something stupid? That determiner will be up to the other person, because it is under them I must consider such a path forward. No man is an island.

“Moving on” is difficult when I don’t know who I am. What I come off as to people. It’s nauseating, and wholly unproductive for me to consider this line of inquiry when I am seriously working, for when I’m not interacting with any face—but it still gnaws at me. It still cleaves me in two as I beg for mercy, for a silent relief from others, a relief I know is juvenile, and not theirs to give, but why has my cursed brain assigned to them such a function? How can I not know who I am and yet care about what others think of me?

Is something wrong with me?

I don’t think people are supposed to live like this.

Why can’t I exist like a normal human being?

I’m so pathetic.

I don’t know if I’m evil for being like this. If some demon is gnawing my heart as I type.

Someone must have wished me harm when I was born, because why else would I be like this?

One of our suppliers sent us a dossier today about some new drug they’re developing. Says it can make people read minds with the downside of a chance to turn you into stone, more-so with repetitive use. And it’s a big chance, apparently; they’re not sure if they can scrub that out enough to make it desirable enough to market.

It’s been tempting me for a while now. I’ve been clean ever since I started this job (which has been a challenge—nobody in the office will stop you as long as you perform) but how much does something like this…count towards that? Don’t people take medication for stuff like depression and anxiety in manageable doses? This is just like that, isn’t it? Isn’t it?

Just one time…

I know how stupid it is to imagine that something like a pill could fix me, but if I knew whether everyone was telling me the truth or not, I think I would be happy.

I think I would be stable again.

bromus-inermis-renovationis.raw_content:
Paraflora Classification Log

Status: Conservation Dependent

Scientific Name: Bromus Inermis Renovationis

Height: 40 to 85 cm

Habitat: Chugwater, Wyoming

Bromis Inermis Renovationis is a subspecies of Bromis Inermis native to Chugwater, Wyoming. This Rhizomatous grass is best characterized by its similarity to Bromis Inermis, up to and including growth cycle, reproductive tract, and general botanical features (leaves, stem, etc.).

Bromis Inermis Renovationis's paraflora classification is derived from its capabilities in rejuvenation. More specifically, it is notable for its capability to rapidly accelerate the process of hemostasis. Though it cannot assist with the entirety of the process to heal wounds, its capability to rapidly cause hemostasis gives it notoriety in medical applications, specifically in the case of minor abrasions.

This process appears to be due to a rapid acceleration of an unknown enzymatic compound which attracts platelets at a faster pace. Additionally, it appears to heighten the tightening of blood compounds in the region to slow the process of blood loss. Potential cancerous implications are currently being explored.

Researcher Lorri lets out a defeated sigh as she sorts through a myriad of files, all related to Paraflora. There was a certain drawl to her appearance indicative of apathetic nihilism.

"Working late again darling? I can get you a drink if ya' need." Marvin was cleaning off a glass about 3 feet to the right of Lorri behind the bar. They had done this dance many a time before. "Ya' know, you really oughta spend some time of that there time of yours doing this in your lab."

"Actually, this is what I do in my lab. I just do it here to." Lorri never minded Marvins remarks. Despite breaking her focus, she could always tell it was what she needed.

"Sometimes I wonder how your brain can handle all that junk inside darling. Always thinkin bout' those plants and how they work, it's like yer whole life is about leaves." Marvin turned to leave back behind the bar, likely to organize some glasses.

As Lorri gazed right through the Paraflora log in front of her, Director Richter could be heard entering into the bar with a look of contempt on her face. Lorri shifted her head for a moment tentatively before she went back to staring down the documents in front of her. The assorted files dribbled memories of lab work into her head, painting imagery of a distant snowfall quietly clumping up in drifts on the windowsill over time. Though not quite assuring or otherwise pacifying, it left a feeling of heaviness down the edges of her throat.

Swallowing down her dissatisfaction until it formed a lump down the bottom of her esophagus, Lorri spoke. "If you're looking for Johnston, I don't know her whereabouts. I apologize." A slight stutter punctuated her statement as she shifted her thumbs between various files. As she contemplated whether to listen or to respond to whatever Richter says, she suddenly felt the edge of Richter's warm palm caressing the tip of her thumb — the distal end. Richter seemed intrigued by a specific file.

"Lorri." The sappy feel of sympathy oozed out of Richters mouth. Suddenly, Lorri found herself feeling even smaller then before. "I don't mean to impose on your studies, and I'm sure you find these details amusing, but-"

"Is there something wrong with my work?" Lorri's retort escaped her without her realizing it. Like a snake hidden in the depths of her throat, it suddenly has challenged Richter in a way unfamiliar to either. Though Richter wasn't the best with emotions, Lorri read it clear as day on her face that all she sensed was fear. Lorri shrank down into her barstool seat before quickly regaining her composure. "Sorry, sorry, I didn't mean to come off as defensive or anything-"

"Perfectly alright, don't stress yourself out." Richter removed the file from the stack and glazed it over with scrutiny. "Bromis Inermis Renovationis. Forgive me if I sound overly astute, but is this not just the grass outside?"

"It's similar, sure, but there's intricate differences between the strains. My studies into them have been somewhat microbial, but I do think there is enough distinction to warrant it as a form of Paraflora. My research has shown that it has numerous thaumaturgical properties, and I think that if we-"

"Lorri, I don't mea-"

"Wait, hold on, it's not what you think." Lorri quickly composed herself once more. Though she hadn't meant to get lost in her ramblings, it appeared she had found herself back to square one. "I'm not going back to distribution or investment or anything of the sort. I just think we here could benefit a little if we gave this little guy a shot."

"'Little guy.' That's an odd way to refer to a strain of grass." Richter's skepticism was on full display. As she was about to read further, a familiar figure approached.

"Evening dear. It appears we have company at this lil' hole-in-the-wall." Marvin emerged from behind the soda bar with a familiar look of warmth in his grin. Richter, having done this routine too many times to count, merely waved him off as a sign of deterrence. Once she regained her focus onto the report, she regained her look of reproach.

"Marvin, could we have a moment?"

"Certainly dearest. I'll prepare you your classic." With that, Marvin whisked away. Lorri, looking into her not-quite-empty cup, stared through the table right into the loam packed into the soil below. As she attempted to stutter out anything meaningful, Richter finally found her words.

"Lorri, I know botany means a lot to you. I don't want to take that away from you. This is your life's work! I know how that feels." Richter's face loomed with distant desires for a moment before regaining composure. "I'm just worried about how the council will feel if they see this as the epicenter of your work."

Lorri looked back into Richters eyes as she fumbled with her mouth. "Can I ask you something?"

"Shoot me."

"Do you think my work is useless?"

Richter looked away for a moment. Lorri had heard enough. She silently stood up and defeatedly gathered her assorted files. It was clear in her head what the director had meant. Her bachelor's began to swirl through her head. The central DOGMA, forming enzymes, illustrating compounds, creating molecules, organelles and all, soon to be fully realized biotic organisms. They all played into one another in a harmonious way. Imagery of how sound it was appeared in her head, swirled in stasis; a firm concept which stood unshaken until she was scouted.

Then, suddenly, without warning, a whole new world found her. A world filled with all sorts of anomalies she couldn't even begin to wrap her head around. She had spent so much of her undergrad refining her understanding of what was real that the second it was tampered with, her mindset began to crumble.

"The anomalous has that feeling, doesn't it?" Richter finally broke her silence. As if she read her mind, Richter had already said enough to bring Lorri back to the ground where she stood. "Let's head outside, I have a feeling you may need some fresh air."

As Richter rose from her stool, she gently took the various documents from Lorri's hand. Tapping them onto the bar table, she made sure they all stood even to one another. Before handing it back, she took the log for Bromis Inermis Renovationis and looked a little closer once more. Then, she threw her coat back on — log still in hand — and walked towards the door.

"No drink for ya dear? That's a shame." Marvin's quip reminded Lorri of her tab, so she haphazardly scrambled to grab some change from her spare pocket. As if Marvin had known, he hadn't prepared Richter's drink after all.

"Just put it on my tab Marvin, we got places to be." Richter's voice echoed across the building as she went out the side door. A gust of cool wind nipped at Lorri's cheek — she knew she wasn't ready for whatever was going to hit her. Yet, she had to survive whatever happened, no matter what. "Thanks Marvin, I'll see ya soon."

"Anytime, dear." Marvin's voice cooed quietly as Lorri sped towards the side door.

As Lorri exited out the side door, she saw Richter sitting on the sidewalk, faced towards the empty parking lot. It wasn't snowing at the moment, but clouds were trickling in over head. Nimbostratus: essential for the environment yet so dreary to look at. Lorri wasn't quite the fan. Richter seemed unfazed by it all as she threw a pebble into a snow drift.

Lorri sat next to Richter. A slight shiver escaped her before she sniffled and spoke. "My work means a lot to me. You know that, right?"

Richter sighed. A gaze filled with long lost desire clouded her vision. Her eyes were fogged over as she stared down into the space in front of her. "I see a lot of myself in you."

Lorri was taken aback. Out of all the things to come out of her mouth, that wasn't anywhere near the top of the list. "What do you mean?"

"Did I ever tell you what my field of study was? It's anthropology — sociocultural to be exact. I assume you're familiar?"

"Mostly, yeah. You study cultures n' stuff, right?" Lorri was admittedly rather uninformed of the field, yet she familiarized herself slightly when she first joined Site-78. She wanted to attempt to glean some amount of attention from the site director, so she took it upon herself to learn as much as she could. However, without it being botany, it didn't necessarily pique her interest. Inevitably, she gave up.

"Pretty much. It's a little more intricate then that, but that'll suffice. I do dabble in the other subfields, but most my work is about understanding why people do the things they do." Richter shuffled awkwardly in her spot, heaved out a sigh, then continued. "Which is why this job is so hard for me."

Lorri's head shifted to the side as she sat confused. "What do you mean?"

"Being an anthropologist, for me, is about so much more then just studying people. It's about connecting to people, giving them the time of day to truly understand them. Too many times, people find themselves glancing over others perspectives and evaluating them based only on the resulting product. I don't think that's right. I don't think we as people should be evaluating ourselves based on our own metrics. We don't take the time to understand each other, and it shows.

"Over time, throughout my studies, I began to realize I had a unique sense of empathy towards others. My cultural studies over time shifted from studying other cultures to taking the time to appreciate my own. I was a wonder-kid — my ethnographies had depth to them that were so intricate, so attentive, that I was bound to be noticed eventually. Forgive my lack of humility."

"Nono, you're okay." Lorri didn't want to make Richter shy away, so assurance arose from her throat. "I've skimmed one of your ethnographies about Colorado; I can see the appeal."

"I appreciate that." Richter looked away, not wanting to meet Lorri's eyes. "Sometimes, I fear I've lost that part of me. Coming here, my mindset has changed." Richter's eyes looked towards a distant light post. The first flurries of snow had begun to hop along the sky like bunnies as they traveled towards the ground to settle in. Like a blanket, they slowly covered the hem of Lorri's skirt.

"When I first started working for the foundation, I thought I'd be surveying for the sake of understanding. In a way, that was what I was doing. However, it soon became clear that it wasn't what I was supposed to do." Richter stood up and paced back and forth as she continued to speak. "My ethnographic reports were frequently marked for heavily featuring 'extraneous materials'. I hadn't changed my approach at all, and yet, I found myself facing more scrutiny then ever before.

"Soon, I noticed a pattern. There were points in my writing they enjoyed, portions and excerpts they highlighted as 'useful'. I then began to analyze these patterns, which is when it hit me — they were interested in containment above all else."

Richter paused for a moment. Lorri cleared her throat before speaking once more. "I mean- obviously?"

"You're not wrong to say that." Richter looked away from Lorri, evidently trying to formulate her thoughts. "What I mean to say is, they weren't interested in understanding the anomalous. Rather, they were interested in putting it away. They wanted to take my passion, my desire, my life's work, and hand wave it in favor of raw data for their own purposes."

Lorri shrugged her shoulders back as she attempted to come up with a response that came from a perspective of sympathy. Instead, she found herself coming off rather direct. "I don't mean to be blunt, but the question came to mind naturally. Why are you still here?"

Richter stifled a chuckle. "I suppose somewhere along the way I lost sight of what I was searching for."

Richter walked back to the sidewalk and plopped down to the concrete. Lorri and Richter sat together, only a few inches apart. The snow, once gentle, had begun to pick up pace into a flurry. Though the winds remained stagnant, those tiny icicles continued to emerge from clouds like particles moving throughout a cell.

Thoughts began crowding Lorri's brain — to loud to tune out. What even is a cell? How can a cell develop into a collection of cells and how do those collections become things? How do they evolve and change and respond? How did that inevitably lead to culture? To morals? What are morals?

Like a tornado, thoughts raced through Lorri's head in this silence, as if it were grabbing her and shaking her by her vices. She felt unnerved. A sense of melancholy began to choke her, both metaphorically and literally as the spit which she had long forgotten finally reminded her of its existence.

As she coughed up and attempted to regain her composure, Richter glanced over and had to hold back a giggle. After letting her calm down, Richter continued. "Your study of botany is so intricate. You get so focused on the minor details. Look here. 'This process appears to be due to a rapid acceleration of an unknown enzymatic compound which attracts platelets at a faster pace.' Verbatim."

Lorri, finally composed, responded. "Is there something wrong with postulating based on minor details? It's not the most incorrect assumption. It may even be true."

Richter took a moment to collect herself. To Richter, It was clear her thoughts were still not quite hitting Lorri. "It's not that you're incorrect, it's that you're stuck in your ways."

"What do you mean?"

"You have a tendency to focus so heavily on the empirical, and yet you find yourself working with the anomalous. You asked me why I linger still, there's your answer."

Lorri was dumbfounded. Her answer failed to clarify anything. "What is your answer? Why can't you just give it to me directly instead of dancing around with double entendres and random pontifications. Why can't you just tell me."

Without realizing it, Lorri had grown agitated. Once she realized, a look of fear once more overcame her. This was her superior, and she was talking down to her. After sputtering nonsense sounding somewhat similar to "my apologies", she tugged her knees into her chest and looked down.

Richter didn't respond immediately. That moment, which lasted less than a minute, felt like hours in Lorri's head. "You're trying to apply the real to what is truthfully unknown. You're what I used to be. Clinging onto what you know and trying so desperately to avoid what you don't."

Lorri didn't look up immediately. She didn't look up at all. After a pause, Richter continued. "If you want to survive here, you can't be so stuck to reality. You're going to be surrounded by the anomalous constantly. As you rise the ranks, you're going to find yourself facing stranger and stranger flora and you have to be able to understand it may not always be understandable, and that's okay-"

"How can you be so content with that! How could you possibly forsake your entire identity, everything you have built for yourself all for the sake of something you'll never even begin to get a secure grasp on! How could you possibly do that!" Lorri was suddenly standing, fist shaking, exasperated. It was clear that she was facing internal turmoil. Despite this, Richter — having been in the same position once — found herself sympathizing with said turmoil.

"I don't know. I found my own way." In the corner of her eye, Lorri saw Richters eyes look more fluid then normal. Was she tearing up? "There are days I yearn to return to my own ways. Days where I look upon my purpose and see myself attempting to contain and catalogue and secure and when I look upon myself I get so angry with myself. Days where I remind myself constantly I have an anthropological background just to try and feel human again and grounded in layers of hume I can't even begin to fathom.

"I don't know in so many ways where I am. Enigmatic entities surface every day here in this tiny town in the middle of butt-fuck nowhere and there's no way for me to stop it! How could I possibly place myself in the shoes of people who disappear or heal themselves with magical funky grass which emerged out of anomalous unknowable chance! Who knows anything!"

Richter paused. She was out of breath. Lorri stared evenly, clearly unnerved but also attentive. Finally, Richter spoke. "But I do it anyways. I can't change this place. My purpose here will always be to contain. But I can continue to try to do better anyways. I can try to formulate ideas and pass proposals for this tiny town to feel a little more normal."

For a moment, the two of them stared at each other. Lorri tried to open her mouth, and yet, no response emerged. "You know, we do have a lot in common, research wise. More then I'd suspect at first glance."

Richter stifled a laugh. "You think?"

"Of course I do. We share a thought process. It's comforting."

The two sat in silence for a moment. The silence rang in their ears which almost cleared their heads. Lorri did have one thought though. A very pressing one. "This grass. This one right here. Bromis Inermis Renovationis. It could save a lot of people."

Richter knew where this was going. "It could. But it won't."

A sense of infantilization overcame Lorri. Empathy and morality filled her conviction before she spoke out profusely. "How can you do that. How can you live with that."

Richter sighed. "I don't know. I don't know why we don't share these things. I've told you before and I'll tell you again — we can't. I don't know why we can't. I'm sure it'd make life easier for a lot of people. But we can't."

She paused for a moment. Tension flowed through Richter's body. "I wish we could. I really wish we could. It's just the way it is.

"Like I said. All I can do is try to formulate proposals."

Both sat silently. After that moment passed, Lorri spoke. "I suppose that'll do." She looked away for a moment before continuing. "I don't know if I can do that. Amnesticize me for all I care, I can't help but want to help."

Richter scrutinized her. It was clear she was speaking emotionally. "I don't think you want that, do you?"

Lorri was read. Read like a newspaper in some old-timer film. "You're not wrong to presume that."

"I suppose you can try to make sense of things anyways. Or you won't, be stuck in your ways like that numbskull Chudley."

"Heh, I suppose there is that desire. In microbiology I mean."

Richter finally got confused. "In microbiology?"

"A desire to know what is unknown. It'll be a while before I break my though process."

Richter shook her head and smirked. "No, don't lose that drive. Keep that one close."

Lorri tilted her head once more. Contradictory information appeared to process in her mind. "What good would that do me?"

Richter sighed before continuing. "You need to want to know the unknown. That's how we study the unknown. That one, keep that one close." Lorri gazed at her before looking down once more.

Richter stared at Lorri as she continued to stare blankly at the concrete. Something was simmering on Lorri's mind — that much was evident to Richter. All Richter knew to do was scoot closer. She reached out her hand and let snowflakes trickle into it, watching them melt immediately in the warmth of her hand. She needn't push Lorri, she knew she would talk if she wished to.

"When I was a kid, I wanted to be an enchantress." Lorri spoke absentmindedly, not paying particular attention to what she was saying. Richter didn't press.

"I always dreamt myself being a brilliant witch, one who could draw out from abundant mana. I would wear the most dignified robes — ruby red, obviously — and have a staff made of enchanted tungsten. In the center of my staff, a ruby would float, imbued with my magical capabilities.

"I would dream up the most magnificent magical spells. At first, I fell into the pitfalls of fireballs and beams of pure arcana, yet that soon bored me. I chiseled the branches that fell from the local tree in the park to make faux wands. Eventually, I let myself experiment more with spells made for other reasons. Some were reactionary, like one that cleaned dishes perfectly. Others were personal."

Lorri joined Richter in trying to catch snowflakes. She reached out her palm and caught a couple. Once her hand got moist, she wiped it onto Richter's jacket, causing both to giggle. After quieting down, she continued.

"My first experience with the anomalous was when I was 8. I found a floating rock. It wasn't a ruby, hardly even notable. I've researched it recently, it is a perfectly ordinary rock. It just floats. Little me wouldn't like that much, at least I think she wouldn't."

Richter broke her silence. "Why wouldn't she?"

Lorri glanced into Richter's eyes, a small smirk gracing her face before she looked back towards the concrete below. She went back to catching snowflakes before going on. "I made these brilliant diagrams in my bedroom. My mom used to think I was some genius, plotting out these auspicious plans like some mystical engineer. The magic I imagined made sense. Every spell had origin.

"I wanted to study the magic. I wanted to know where it came from. In a way, I was a scientist long before I was a scientist. I've never been bored of science. I liked knowing things. I wanted things to make sense. I guess in a way, it was inevitably I'd accept the foundations proposal to work for them. I was cocky, I thought I'd figure it out."

Richter raised her eyebrow, glancing over to Lorri with skepticism. Lorri felt it. "When I was younger, I kept that rock a secret. It was mine alone. No one else knew of it. I painted it red and put some rhinestones on it. I put it in the center of my 'magical staff' and pretended to cast spells with it. None of them worked, that rock wouldn't bring miracles.

"As I grew older, I grew to resent that rock. Even now, I have it packed away in a box, somewhere hidden in the top of my closet. I never got rid of my staff though. It sits in the corner of my room, the weak wood wilting away and crumbling off. You have no idea how much I have to vacuum." They giggled together at the thought.

"A month after I started, I was asked if the anomalous lived up to my expectations. I said they didn't, but I never elaborated. I was asked what my favorite anomaly is. I didn't answer. Some form of standard questions they ask all the new hires. Their wide eyes and blown minds probably answered enthusiastically, but for me it was all the same. I wasn't remotely surprised." Lorri gulped. "I suppose that's a lie."

Lorri's voice had begun cracking. Her eyes glazed over, moisture gathering. Richter wasn't sure how to respond. She wiped her hand on her own pants before placing it on Lorri's slightly shaking hand. Lorri had to catch her breath. Richter gave her three gentle squeezes. Lorri, finally stabilized, continued.

"I kind of always expected the anomalous to be weird. I mean, it's in the name. I long expected stuff of such stature to exist. If anything, I'm sure there's more, much more to know. Many anomalies I'll never have the clearance to access are probably hidden away, leaning their omnipresence all over my life yet somehow always just out of sight. I knew that's not what they were asking.

"I'm sure that rock didn't get picked up right away. It hardly hovered, it was only a couple inches off the ground. It wasn't even that hidden away, it was a couple feet away from the bike path at best. I was following a pack of red ants move about and they just so happened to place their hill beneath the rock. I suppose it was advantageous somehow. When I found it, my first thought wasn't fear, but intrigue. I stayed up at least 3 days, acting like it didn't exist in the day and fiddling with it at night."

Richter was listening intently. She had no intention of sharing her secrets despite her mandate to report this kind of stuff. Lorri, in a way, knew she wouldn't. They had a mutual understanding. Richter gave her hand one more squeeze while Lorri composed herself, then Lorri continued.

"It wasn't terribly interesting. My report for it would've been shorter then the one for the grass. It floats about 5 inches away from the nearest surface, in a gap it'll hover. Otherwise, it was a perfectly normal rock. All the way down to its core, the composition is nothing more then a chunk of quartz. It would be foolish to give it any more attention then a designation in the log of anomalous items. If I told the foundation, they would've likely just thrown it in a box. Better yet, they'd melt it down and throw it out."

Lorri began shifting her feet in and out. Richter could sense she was about to get personal, so she let her hand go for a moment and rubbed her back, being gentle on the spine. After the reassurance, she grabbed the back of her hand once more, letting her thumb go back and forth.

"Promise not to laugh?"

"No promises, but I'll try."

Lorri giggled, then continued. "If I could cast one spell — just one — I'd cast one to create a set of basalt columns."

Richter had to stifle her giggle, leading to Lorri elbowing her side. After Richter feigned a recoil, Lorri continued. "As a teen, I had the chance to see a beautiful set of basalt columns. I even got to climb them for a bit, but I chose not to. It isn't something people think to visit, so many people often don't.

"Mortality is so funny. If it didn't exist, I'd have no reason to do anything anywhere, as everything would happen to me inevitably. Yet, since it does, there's no way for me to experience everything I want to, and even less of a chance to experience the things I don't know I want. It makes me cry sometimes."

Lorri had begun to tear up. Richter stayed silent, trying not to interrupt. Lorri found it in herself to continue.

"I think a lot of people would be astounded by the sight of those columns. Many more probably wouldn't care. They stuck with me because I didn't appreciate them then. I hope to go back one day.

"I guess in a strange way, that rock feels the same way to me."

"Can I ask how so?"

"That rock is something that I'll likely be the only one to know. Eventually I'll die, someone will find it in a box and pick it up, then throw it out. They likely won't even notice it floats. But whenever I try to think back to my favorite anomaly, all I can think about is that rock. I probably sound idiotic saying this, but that rock changed my life. Without it, I would've never have guessed to assume the anomalous existed. Without it, I would've never devoted myself to being discovered. I would've never been assigned Site-78. I would've never met you."

Richter stared at Lorri as she continued to refuse eye contact. A couple tears flowed down her cheek, her boots now glistening from the melted snow. She was shivering a little.

"Sometimes, I think about switching my speciality. Something more practical could get me more noticed. I'd experience much, much more. Every time I think like that, I think back to those basalt columns. I didn't appreciate them back then. I worry if I think to much like that, I'll forget to appreciate what I have here."

Lorri pulled her hand away. She sat up and walked a couple paces away from Richter. Taking a moment to wipe her eyes, she stammered out "I'm not really sure why I told you that."

Richter's gazed softened. "I think you know why you did."

Lorri turned back to face Richter. The pair stared at each other for a moment. "I know this grass may seem pointless. In the same vein, that rock is also pointless. And yet, that rock sits in my room, still covered in those rhinestones."

Her voice trailed off for a moment before she found the strength to go on. "And even though this grass looks pointless, and maybe I'm the first person to notice anything about it, but I'm sure someone will see what it does and have their life changed. I hope that person has the chance to experience even a portion of all the wonders I've experienced since I met you."

Lorri closed her mouth, no longer giving Richter her gaze. After a moment of silence, it was suddenly broken by the sound of Richter's ignition. She had turned on her car remotely, already heating it up. She walked over to Lorri. "You look like you'll need a ride. I'll take you back."

Lorri looked back up, eyes still glazed over, looking up at Richter. She had a soft smile, a knowing gaze, and a comforting aura. She chuckled to herself, interrupted by the occasional sniffle, before walking towards her car. As she opened the passenger door, she wiped her boots and dusted the snow off her jacket. Before getting in, she turned around and looked up towards the sky, giving the snow one last glance. She happened upon the moon, noticing it was full. She quickly turned away, though in the corner of her eyes she couldn't quite tell if it seemed to have a red tint to it. She didn't give it another glance — she didn't want to know.

Paraflora Classification Log

Status: Conservation Dependent

Scientific Name: Bromus Inermis Renovationis

Height: 40 to 85 cm

Habitat: Chugwater, Wyoming

Bromis Inermis Renovationis is a subspecies of Bromis Inermis native to Chugwater, Wyoming. This Rhizomatous grass is best characterized by its similarity to Bromis Inermis, up to and including growth cycle, reproductive tract, and general botanical features (leaves, stem, etc.).

Bromis Inermis Renovationis's paraflora classification is derived from its capabilities in rejuvenation. More specifically, it is notable for its capability to rapidly accelerate the process of hemostasis. Though it cannot assist with the entirety of the process to heal wounds, its capability to rapidly cause hemostasis gives it notoriety in medical applications, specifically in the case of minor abrasions.

This process appears to be due to a rapid acceleration of an unknown enzymatic compound which attracts platelets at a faster pace. Additionally, it appears to heighten the tightening of blood compounds in the region to slow the process of blood loss. Potential cancerous implications are currently being explored.

Bromis Inermis Renovationis is currently being explored as a potential onsite abrasion treatment. Further testing is needed before confirmation. Medical distribution pending. For more information, consult Director Richter.

P-H Vixter & 7eventy7evenfold

It's easier to just walk away,
I know you'll see brighter days, along the way.

Author page of 7eventy7evenfold, P-H Vixter notwithstanding xP

The weather outside was somewhat cloudy, and the blue sky was tinted grey. The sun was there, but could barely brighten up a thing. The air was still and humid, and breathing it in did not give the sensation of oxygen. It was there, though, or else everyone would be dead by now.

A black car stopped by, an AMC Ambassador, a new brand of the time. The driver's seat opened, and the driver extracted himself. He was a man with a classy suit and bow tie, a black trilby and a set of invisible eyes.

What stood before him was a Waffle House, his favorite in his routine. They make quality food like no other around in town. The man was an exhausted individual, with a bandage wrapped around his right hand; the result of last week's trouble, something he had just finally got sorted out.

He moved to the other side and opened the passenger's seat, taking his rolled up newspaper and antique cane — something he didn't quite need anymore, but kept regardless — and closing the door with a gentle thud. He moved towards the Waffle House and made his entrance. He took a seat and ordered simply orange juice and scrambled eggs. He just didn't feel like eating waffles today, it gets repetitive when it's the only thing you ever do eat.

He unrolled his newspaper and opened it wide, and read whatever contents happened to be inside. Nothing too noteworthy, just your average daily report. It did have the headline of a new CEO for Coca-Cola Co, and a minor department he had founded named SODA that came to light. About as creative as naming a movie about cars "Cars," he thought to himself, chuckling.

The door opened and closed, and someone made their way in. The man didn't pay attention to it, perhaps just another random costumer. But then, he heard his voice, and recognized it. This voice belonged to a man who shared a cigarette with him back in the Hub. He wouldn't accurately guess how long it has been since then, since the Hub has its own separate spacetime. But still, he recognized it like yesterday.

He put the now-finished newspaper down and called out to the man, who was talking to one of the servers for waffles to-go. He recognized his voice too, and turned to meet an old pal.

"Oh, 7, is that you?" The man said to the other across the distance, he approached. He was both surprised and excited.

"Indeed it is, 8. Come, take your seat."

He sat to the other side, and placed his packed waffles on the table. They both were almost indistinguishable from each other. Same clothes, same manners, same non-existent, shadowed eyes.

"How has it been?" 8 asked.

"I'm getting the hang of it. Did last week's duty and now waiting for this to heal." 7 showed his wrapped up hand. "Other than that, just my daily life."

The waiter came, and served the orange juice and scrambled eggs. With a simple thank you, he went away.

"How about you?" He continued.

"Well, I did get an order from Boss a few hours ago. Just wanted to get something to eat on the way. I need to stop Church of the Broken God from spawning a few dozen memetic agents, apparently."

"Doesn't sound easy."

"I'm old folk, I've handled harder. But you are new, you better get ready for whatever is written for you," he half-joked. 7 could hear the tone of his voice. That was a hint to something.

7 let out a pretty convincing fake laugh, and took a piece of the scrambled eggs. "You know, sometimes not existing feels like a curse, I do these humane things to keep my mind together, munching on this food knowing I don't have to eat. How long will this continue?"

"Every story needs a character to convey that story. We both know that we dealt with pretty smelly nonsenses before." 8 explained. "And that's because a story doesn't necessarily have to follow logic or order, whether it be surface level or axiomatic level. We both are pieces of something much bigger, personifications projected into reality to convey a message."

"And what are we truly?" 7 asked, continuing to eat his eggs like this is an ordinary conversation.

"I am the Boss' self-perception of his absence. Embodying the feeling of having the continue even after death."

"And that means you are dead?"

"Precisely. I died back in 1913 due to a heart attack from… Work stress 'n' stuff."

"But you are still here, in front of me."

8 gave a small pause, readying himself for something bigger. "When I died, I went into oblivion, where I was allowed to act linearly in a place beyond the concept of time and space. And then it got reflected down wholly, allowing my motions to persist in this world despite death claiming me. If I am talking to you, 7, and not a brick wall, that means I was able to predict the future accurately enough to have this conversation with you."

7 finished his eggs, now taking small sips from his orange juice. "And what about me?"

"I wouldn't know. But I do know of our Batman-alike. He created a city by himself, for himself. Protecting it like it's his whole purpose, embodying the little bit of heroism Boss has."

"And what about me?" 7 repeated himself, coming off as disrespectful.

"…I can't tell yet. It's yours to discover." 8 stood up, and fixed his tie. Slowly making his way out to the exit. "But I will help you with one thing: the first Waffle House was founded in 1995. The year's 1973." He gave a know-it-all smile, and finally fully left.

7 Didn't say anything, keeping his unreactive face.

He stared out of the window, seeing things normal people wouldn't. It's just people walking, but he saw more than that. He saw their colors. He saw their small movements and twitches and instantly recognized the emotions they've felt for the past 5 years. He saw the world more than just stone and water, he saw it as a pathway, a medium necessary to act as a ground for the supernatural. He saw the stars from the other side of the observable, supposedly infinite sized universe during daylight hours. He looked at statues and saw the maker's intent in them.

But despite all of this, he was a low-class given the ability to grow and develop, a smaller piece of Boss personified and branched off, destined to create a story for itself. He looked at the now-finished plate. The aftertaste vanished so fast he didn't even notice. He didn't need to eat. It was for the sake of the story. The Cars movie wasn't even conceptualized yet, and yet he knew about it.

He sighed and turned his attention to the exit door. 8, someone who predicted the 60 years past his death with immense accuracy, someone with much more significance than the man who remained stationary in his resting place. Who knows how much more capable he was compared to 7, but he was already dead. He was like a star seen at the night sky. Those stars died millions of years ago and yet they can still be seen because their light is reaching earth just now.

And yet, after all that, he forgot to take his waffles.

7 smirked at it. One day, he will get better. One day, he will make a story for himself, and once that story is over, he will no longer be a Nobody.

He finished his orange juice and got up, picking the packed waffles from the table on 8's behalf. He would leave it to the Hub once his work is over, and 8 would pick it up from there.

He made it to the exit, and checked the time. Merely 3 minutes passed. No matter. He better visit these SODA guys soon.

builder-of-ages.raw_content:
What is a beginning?

One might as well ask what is an ending? They seem so purposeful, so…grand. The starting gun, and the last door, of whatever it is they measure. But what are they, really? What is the start? Do we ask science, or faith, or that sodden clay of memory? In the great chain of relation and causation, at what point does anything truly start or end? There is an impulse to put perception forward…it begins when we notice, when we see, when we record…but what hubris is this. That mankind is so great that all reality must kneel and accept our attention when it is given, and find fulfillment with its touch. Still, with very few exceptions, we are what we are. We must eventually pick a place, plant our flag, and call it the start, ignoring the mocking call of our own hypocrisy above our heads like so many cawing crows.

So I tell you that this beginning was in Minoa, knowing the lie in the truth of it. Not even a clean beginning, but the place with the footfalls of history leave fine marks to follow, a place where the prey can finally be known and named. Reading the ripples in the lake, never seeing the stone now sunk to its depths.

Minoa was old, even then. It had always been old, somehow. Like a man born a doddering ancient, age seemed written in to the bones of the place. Others would make much of the strange stones in walls, or the odd carvings one could find in the lonely hills. However, for those who called themselves Minoan, they just…were. Like sheep grazing near a cathedral, in their souls they knew that the age of the place had secrets they lacked even the senses to truly know, so they accepted with a bland, indifferent pride. Even the name was old, the roots lost ages ago. Like the small, brittle stones carved with eyes one found on the beach, it just…was. Found, whole, and accepted.

That is not to say all accepted. Many probed, and dug, and questioned. Minoa was always a place that seemed to encourage horizon gazing, and it seemed to echo down into the souls of some as well. They pried, and puzzled, and many found a good enough answer. Some, though, refused to plant their flag, and continued. They pushed deeper, and found hints of those who had done the same before. Like layers of sediment, they started to probe the age of the place, and found…oddness. Hints, stories, warnings, names increasingly simple, yet profound, like watching a steer somehow wither and curl back into a calf. In time, they seemed less like human names, and more simple…sounds. Its when they seemed to call for organs beyond the human voice that most turned away.

If any truly found the bottom of those layered ages, if any pushed past the catacombs, the tunnels, the squat halls with carvings seemingly impossible for the human hand, none spoke of it. It was, as so much was, accepted. There was no bottom. The roots of Minoa were the navel of the world, and to press too deep would be to find oneself treading in the gardens of the gods, unbidden and unwanted. They robed themselves with “impossible” and used it to hide from the truth like children from nighttime horrors. Was it this that pushed them out, those before and after, to ply the sea and strike forth, endlessly? Was it more comfortable to brave the endless, unknown ocean than face their unknown foundations? Or was it because of it, instead of in spite of it? To constantly probe beyond, to extend the map, like a poison leeched into their souls over generations? As we have established, what you choose to believe must be good enough.

There was a king. There had been many before, but there would be none after. He was not particularly good, nor evil, any more than any king. In truth, little was expected of him…but he did have one thing so few kings have: fear. Many have had fear, yes, but this fear was boundless. It was not a raving, rabid thing…but it touched everything. In time, it clustered around his own looming mediocrity. It whispered to him, mocking with the shadow of the unattainable. It made him unable to rest. It made his eyes roam, and his reach start to stretch. Unknowing, the king learned one of the few truths to be found:

Fear Brings Change.

It was near the island that he found it. Or him, as it were. A remote spit of rock and brush, rumored to be the haunt of a by-blow of the divine, a giant of terrible power and hunger. The king was dismissive, until a few ancients whispered of the giant's true nature, and of the wonders it was rumored to hold. Treasure, glory, or the call of a vast, internal horizon, whatever the case was, the king went to the forbidden place. As he approached the cave, the carvings and raised stones made him tremble with awareness, echoing the deep, forgotten stones of forgotten ages in his own city…but much fresher.

Read of cyclops, of jotun and titan rising in challenge to great lords and heroes. Lies, and their lover, Myth, are so much sweeter. The truth has so much more stammering, slipped footing, and tumbling flight…yet we must make do. He was massive, head and shoulders above any man the king had ever seen…but he was a man. Of what kind, the king could not say…he was strange, and his voice creaked like unoiled leather, yet his great weariness was easy to see. The giant began to speak, as if the king was not even an expected guest, but as someone returning to a room after stepping out for a moment. He mumbled, and rambled off, speaking to the king as if he was supposed to know much more than he did. The giant, truly, spoke at him, not with. Addressing him with all the self-reflective focus of a man pouring his thoughts to a potted plant.

He spoke of the Sea People, and of what oceans they had truly sailed. His ancestors, as most would count, though of the king or the giant's, he was unclear. Of the great mountain who's worn, drowned bones would form the king's home. His voice wandered, speaking of the fog of the past and even the future with the ease of a man appraising grapes. The king felt his fear coil and shift, like a sleeping wolf hearing a lamb's bleat. The giant's cave was cluttered with madness. Objects and carvings, some beyond the king's understanding, some damnably suggestive in what he could puzzle out. The giant strode through this cave of horrible wonders with all the reverence of a stray dog wandering through a temple.

In time, he finally stopped, and stooped to paw through the drifts of relics. From it, he drew a metal mass. It was nearly the size of the giant's head, and faceted like a round gemstone, though it was a tarnished, brassy metal. Along the edges of each facet ran thin grooves, and each face was scratched and carved with odd shapes. The giant rambled, telling the king this was what he sought. He said it was a gallstone of god, and when the king asked of which, the giant laughed with a icy dismissal. Take and place it, and the uppermost face would do as gods do, and make. Here, time. Here, fate, and wealth, and light, all that was could be found here. Though it could not truly make, never new things, merely stretching and twisting that which was. The kings eyes widened, thinking of life, power, safety. The giant laughed, letting it fall from his hands like a forgotten stone, and called it little more than a curse. The monument to a failed test, one life had failed before it even understood. A curse so many fought to bear.

The king tried to ask, to probe, to understand, but the giant would not respond. He gestured to the orb, mumbling that it was his time, now. A poison, like madness, carried not in blood, but fate. It was the king's, now. It would always be. The giant started to walk deeper, and the king scooped up the metal thing, following…and finding the depths of his cave sprawling ever forward, warped and strange. The giant had vanished, though his mad ranting wafted through the caves and tunnels, the galleries and pits. In time, the echos seemed to twist as well, racing ahead of their source, or seeming to slither like bats around the king's head. He fled, clutching the metal mass, praying to whatever would listen to make the sounds and footsteps behind him only echos, only his own panicked feet flapping and skittering behind him. He spilled from the cave, exhausted and panting like a dog, drinking in the night sky of stars, feverishly checking to see if they were all still in their places. His fear and exhaustion dragged him into the oblivion of sleep, there hounded not by echos, but by their sources. He woke screaming, clutching the metal ball, feeling rain on his face, warm as blood.

The cave was gone. Just a spray of rubble, and a notch in the stone, little bigger than a doorway.

The king fled, charging the isle as a cursed place, forbidden to all, a haunt of the darkness and secrets that even the gods recoiled from.

Prosperity is so grand in the present, yet a footnote in the past. Tell us not of the glory, but of the fall. Not the grand, gilded halls, but what hands pried it loose as the blood of men and the screams of women soaked the streets. The king found the giant had not lied. The metal object could grow and stretch many things. Not merely that of the physical, but of the invisible as well, all seemed as simple to spool forth as the rolling of bones. He became not a king, but The King, the true King of Ages, and though the names changed, the island never knew another. Wise, powerful, wealthy, fruitful, nothing was beyond his grasp. Yet, like a garden, not all that is planted is what springs up. Despite all it could give, his fear grew in turn, and its fell children of greed, paranoia, and rage. The more he made, the more he had, the more room existed for his fear to grow.

The kingdom grew, and grew. Becoming a legend, bearing the name of the eternal king at times, and others when those beyond looked upon the swelling wonders and despaired. Walls, canals, great towers, all were built, drawn from the seemingly bottomless coffers of the King. Even the roads would have been the wonder of any other place…but all paled to the great palace. It was a kingdom within the kingdom, a place where the might of the eternal King was brought to full force. Legions lived within, and many whispered that the endless depths stretched even beyond the veil of life, that the King could call audience with that which no man could truly know. Generations lived and died within, and the priests who served him soon found little reason to worship beyond him. He could stretch lives, spill forth gold, and find secrets lost before the bones of the world were laid. What else could he be, but a god given flesh?

Like all budding gods, he fell to himself.

It should not have happened. He should have learned…but even with his endless life, the ball always brought new wonders. New places, new things, new beings…he had grown complacent. He had started to believe his priests, that he was the master, the alpha and omega, beyond the world. Even as the strange places formed, and the beasts distorted, he always felt it was his own will, somehow, bloomed forth. His divine power, finding amusement in the world like a boy finding shapes in clouds. He knew, below his will, that the giant had not lied…but he had not told the truth. That what shape pointed to heaven would be the focus of power…but that the others were not idle. Quietly, slowly, they still worked. Like seeping water, or the creep of plague, they moved unseen, and remained even when rooted out. What cares a god for a cut on his toe…until the poison in the blood finally makes itself felt.

The King was wandering, seeing what new turns of color and shape had come to his newest garden. He was alone, and watching the flutter of gem-fleshed birds as they gibbered with half-human voices, the bending stems of bleeding flowers throbbing below them. It was a sound, a laugh, and the King turned to rebuke who would dare trespass…and saw himself, sneering back at him, framed by glass trees. It was the King…but also not. They looked the same, but the King knew, for all his reflected might, this other was more. The King had gained, and twisted, and stolen as he wished…but this other, he was whole and entire. Perfected. Where he was grafted, stitched, and stretched…this other was as a perfectly cut gem. The Other smiled at him, mocking him with his reflected perfection. The King recoiled, he shouted, he wept. Never had the metal ball made something new, never had it made something whole-cloth…and nothing so perfect, so achingly flawless. The King saw himself as he could never hope to be, and being whom he was unworthy to be the shadow of. For the first time in ages, he felt the cold grip of fear once again. Even as the Other left, the King shook with fear, coiled in a ball at the base of a silver tree. That was where they found him.

The Other became his shadow…or, in the depths of his terror, the King was his. He would find others smiling, or confused, wondering why he had come back so soon. Find himself congratulated for his wise rule, his find comments…in rooms he had never been, with people he had not yet met. He saw the Other walk in his halls, sit on his throne, yet none seemed to notice the change. The King began to wonder in the depth of his fear…for how long? For how long had this other usurped his rule, under the nose of all? For how long had the metal ball betrayed him. Even his priests seemed confused…and he wondered at their slyness. Was this some trick, some vile plot by those fawning advisors? The power of the gods had always rested with the priesthood…was this some attempt to replace him with some glowing copy?

The fear coiled tight. He dared not rid himself of the ball, but neither could he trust it anymore. He sent forth agents of his will, to collect wise men from far shores, and bring them before the King, to wring from them some solution to this madness. His bidding was done, even as the Other continued his simulacrum rule. It seemed unaware, which suited the King all the better. The wise men came, secreted spirited into the depths of the endless palace, and there he forced their wills against the mad thing that had usurped his life, and the cursed ball that had spawned it. Some thought him mad, and for their effrontery they were introduced to some of the more horrific things the ball had spawned. One was pressed down a great vase, that narrowed endlessly at the bottom. The screams and rending of bones as he was impossibly drawn in to nothing soon silenced the doubts of many, though did little to truly banish them.

In time, a proposal was made. If each facet of the metal ball had its own power, then their removal would stand to end it. The King blanched at the idea, but they soothed him by saying this would truly bring more power. Each could, when separated, be used by itself, and limit the radiant effects that seemed to source of the problem. The King then pressed, would this too end the stalking shadow of the Other? Would breaking the ball's power truly undo the thing that walked and ate and spoke in his stead? Of course, said the wise men…but it was truly fear who spoke through them, and fear will always voice whatever it is one wishes.

The work began, and for a time, it was good. Slowly, each facet was cut and worked free, and each seemed to retain its power, when properly positioned. However, the core of the ball refused their attentions. It was impossibly hard, and resisted even the most exotic of attempts. The priesthood was in a fury, as well. This was a mote of the god's power, given to the world, which they sought to rend and alter. The King's rage silenced them, sending them fluttering away in terror…but fear is a quiet, slow hunter when needs must. The king rejoiced in the depths of his eternal palace, setting his facets on the much reduced orb, his own fear smothered with seemingly redoubled power. For a time, it was good.

One night, wishing to test his newly rediscovered delight, he went to the ball…and his heart froze in his chest. There he stood. The Other, standing over the ball, gently gliding his fingers over the gilded settings around it that held each removed facet. He seemed at perfect ease, a smile on his lips, favoring the King with the flicker of a knowing smile. The King felt his life drain though his body, his heart stilled in an icy grip. The Other reached, and lifted the heart of the ball, tossing it gently in his hand as a boy will an interesting stone found by the road. He placed it back, heedless, and left the King's supposed sanctum of sanctums. It had not spoken, truly, the King had never heard it speak, but the message was all too clear. For all his work, it meant nothing. The ball still lived, and within it the power flowed forth. It had merely changed…but still lay beyond his ability to control. The terror coiled up and smothered the King, driving him into senseless oblivion. That was how they found him, for a time.

The King's wrath was beyond understanding. It lashed like a summer storm, savage and unpredictable. His fear drew him far from the shores of reason, and anyone could become the sudden, brief source of his swelling madness. In time, though, it crystallized around a single idea: if he could not be rid of it, then he would at least control it. He would force the ball, and the Other, to kneel to his will. He would turn the power against itself, and force the Other to come, and beg his indulgence. The King had learned that, without the facets, the ball seemed…undefined. It would simply force growth. Unfocused, undirected, and could spawn true madness if not properly contained. Still…the Other. He must keep it from stealing his life as it had. Finally, he drew back his priesthood, and pressed upon them a most terrible duty.

First, the palace would be prepared. Every door was to be opened, no seal or passage barred. Then, every opening to the outside was to be sealed and bricked tight, except one. All would be forced from the palace, save for the King and his priests, and then they would wait. Once the Other came, they would fall upon him. A great and terrible helm, horned and twisted, would be placed on its head, and iron nails would be driven through it, deep into the flesh and bone, fixing it forever. Then they would take it deep, deep into the belly of the place, to the chamber of the orb and its facets. There they would remain, to stand guard until their end, while the King and the remaining priests left, to seal the palace, and bury it, to build a new city atop it…save for the one door. That would remain, in the bowels of the new palace, for them to watch, and wait for the Other to return, for the ball to send its hateful avatar to beg his forgiveness.

Madness, of course, but they feared to refuse him, and Fear Brings Change. It also brings opportunity.

The priesthood did as the King willed…that is to say, as far as the King knew and could confirm, they followed the letter of his law. What was actually done…that was questioned in time. For a time, it was good. The Other was gone, his (relatively) modest palace building quickly, and his rule was (as far as he knew) strong. So the commoners wept at the expense and mad tyranny of the King. So he noticed gray finally creeping into his hair. So his will seemed more foggy each year…at least he was at peace. A grand, smothering peace. Too much peace, in time. There was no appeal. No voices came to the great buried door. No one knocked, begging for forgiveness…nothing. It is one thing for a king to be hated…it is far, far another to be ignored.

The King pressed his priesthood to plunge the depths of the old palace, to find what had happened. The sly priests pressed subjects into service for the task, as the halls had grown strange and dangerous with the crawl of years. When subjects could not be found, then slaves would be acquired…and so it went. The King waned, and in time he, finally, fell, and with him the maze of horror and its dark inhabitants that had lead to that fall…or so the old stories went. From the wreckage came little, except gaunt, twisted men with mad glints in their eyes…and a small metal object, not much bigger than a fist. What had become of the rest, none could truly say…lost, stolen, or returned to whatever outer dark that spawned them, all the stories were true to someone. The heart, though…that was enough for them. They had learned the lesson of growth. That expansion was its own reward…and worthy of worship.

So then time, and the roll of ages, that march that some hate and some praise, as if either would stay its relentless roll. The priests survived, for a time. Cults rose and fell, and the heart was reshaped, presented as no more than a trifle, an object of luck, to be carried in the hope that its power would expand fortune. If you wish to hide a tree, hide it in a forest…and if none exists, plant one. Copies of the heart were spread throughout the great borrowers swelling empire…and perhaps the spirit of it bled into their souls. The great legions did spread endlessly…and even the crumbling fragments after their fall were defined by their expressionistic impulses. In time, even the memory of the empire fell, and the heart passed into other hands.

Like a ship at sea, it wandered. So many did not fully understand what the heart could do, and fewer still sought to purposefully use its power. Even when it did express its endless dream of greatness, almost nobody connected the strange metal bauble and the madness it lay in. Most of its smaller works were destroyed…but some remained. In the reeking catacombs of plague and death…in the mad tombs of desert kings, and black tunnels into which the dying were thrown to complete their journey, it would lay, often unknown…until some new force drew it away. Fate, desire, or some curse, what forced hands and nature to always find and move the heart, choose whatever truth you most love. As always, it cared not.

In time, the heart was found in the sodden ruins of a city of madness, and the new wise men took it, presumed to understand it, and stamped their supposed understanding with the number 184. What truth do these men and papers hold…as much as you believe them to. How much do they truly know? Do they know of the facets, and wonder at their purposes, and removal? Do they question what became of the cult of the Endless Horizon, and its other names? Do they question why all seems so distant…and why the flickering lights, such a comfort to a forgotten King, are so very far away? Perhaps…but this is a terrible danger. Trying to know, illuminates what one does not know…and a lack of knowing brings fear. And with that fear,

Change.

They truly fear that, more than anything else. A sterile forever is better than the chaos of otherwise. They have chosen their truth, planted their flag, and decided that there will be no other. This is the truth, for they say it is so, and it ever shall be, world without end, amen. They don't even know enough to understand their folly. Yet we must hold to something…to set our flag, and choose. We must pick our beginnings…and pray to chose our ends. However, all seek that hidden truth…there must be a way. A way to cheat the march of years, a way to slide behind the last door without opening it. The new wise men, with their numbers, and their rules, they form a cage and affect an air of detachment…like hunters pretending not to notice the rabbit, for fear of spooking the game. They hope, sometimes in spite of themselves, that one day this, or another, or something will lift them up, and show them something worthy of being called Truth.

As is, was, and ever will be, the wise men play and squabble over and within an idiot god's broken dream.

What is a beginning?



One might as well ask what is an ending?  They seem so purposeful, so...grand.  The starting gun, and the last door, of whatever it is they measure.  But what are they, really?  What is the start?  Do we ask science, or faith, or that sodden clay of memory?  In the great chain of relation and causation, at what point does anything truly start or end?  There is an impulse to put perception forward...it begins when we notice, when we see, when we record...but what hubris is this.  That mankind is so great that all reality must kneel and accept our attention when it is given, and find fulfillment with its touch.  Still, with very few exceptions, we are what we are.  We must eventually pick a place, plant our flag, and call it the start, ignoring the mocking call of our own hypocrisy above our heads like so many cawing crows.



So I tell you that this beginning was in Minoa, knowing the lie in the truth of it.  Not even a clean beginning, but the place with the footfalls of history leave fine marks to follow, a place where the prey can finally be known and named.  Reading the ripples in the lake, never seeing the stone now sunk to its depths.
