It should not have happened.  He should have learned...but even with his endless life, the ball always brought new wonders.  New places, new things, new beings...he had grown complacent.  He had started to believe his priests, that he was the master, the alpha and omega, beyond the world.  Even as the strange places formed, and the beasts distorted, he always felt it was his own will, somehow, bloomed forth.  His divine power, finding amusement in the world like a boy finding shapes in clouds.  He knew, below his will, that the giant had not lied...but he had not told the truth.  That what shape pointed to heaven would be the focus of power...but that the others were not idle.  Quietly, slowly, they still worked.  Like seeping water, or the creep of plague, they moved unseen, and remained even when rooted out.  What cares a god for a cut on his toe...until the poison in the blood finally makes itself felt.



The King was wandering, seeing what new turns of color and shape had come to his newest garden.  He was alone, and watching the flutter of gem-fleshed birds as they gibbered with half-human voices, the bending stems of bleeding flowers throbbing below them.  It was a sound, a laugh, and the King turned to rebuke who would dare trespass...and saw himself, sneering back at him, framed by glass trees.  It was the King...but also not.  They looked the same, but the King knew, for all his reflected might, this other was more.  The King had gained, and twisted, and stolen as he wished...but this other, he was whole and entire.  Perfected.  Where he was grafted, stitched, and stretched...this other was as a perfectly cut gem.  The Other smiled at him, mocking him with his reflected perfection.  The King recoiled, he shouted, he wept.  Never had the metal ball made something new, never had it made something whole-cloth...and nothing so perfect, so achingly flawless.  The King saw himself as he could never hope to be, and being whom he was unworthy to be the shadow of.  For the first time in ages, he felt the cold grip of fear once again.  Even as the Other left, the King shook with fear, coiled in a ball at the base of a silver tree.  That was where they found him.



The Other became his shadow...or, in the depths of his terror, the King was his.  He would find others smiling, or confused, wondering why he had come back so soon.  Find himself congratulated for his wise rule, his find comments...in rooms he had never been, with people he had not yet met.  He saw the Other walk in his halls, sit on his throne, yet none seemed to notice the change.  The King began to wonder in the depth of his fear...for how long?  For how long had this other usurped his rule, under the nose of all?  For how long had the metal ball betrayed him.  Even his priests seemed confused...and he wondered at their slyness.  Was this some trick, some vile plot by those fawning advisors?  The power of the gods had always rested with the priesthood...was this some attempt to replace him with some glowing copy?



The fear coiled tight.  He dared not rid himself of the ball, but neither could he trust it anymore.  He sent forth agents of his will, to collect wise men from far shores, and bring them before the King, to wring from them some solution to this madness.  His bidding was done, even as the Other continued his simulacrum rule.  It seemed unaware, which suited the King all the better.  The wise men came, secreted spirited into the depths of the endless palace, and there he forced their wills against the mad thing that had usurped his life, and the cursed ball that had spawned it.  Some thought him mad, and for their effrontery they were introduced to some of the more horrific things the ball had spawned.  One was pressed down a great vase, that narrowed endlessly at the bottom.  The screams and rending of bones as he was impossibly drawn in to nothing soon silenced the doubts of many, though did little to truly banish them.



In time, a proposal was made.  If each facet of the metal ball had its own power, then their removal would stand to end it.  The King blanched at the idea, but they soothed him by saying this would truly bring more power.  Each could, when separated, be used by itself, and limit the radiant effects that seemed to source of the problem.  The King then pressed, would this too end the stalking shadow of the Other?  Would breaking the ball's power truly undo the thing that walked and ate and spoke in his stead?  Of course, said the wise men...but it was truly fear who spoke through them, and fear will always voice whatever it is one wishes.



The work began, and for a time, it was good.  Slowly, each facet was cut and worked free, and each seemed to retain its power, when properly positioned.  However, the core of the ball refused their attentions.  It was impossibly hard, and resisted even the most exotic of attempts.  The priesthood was in a fury, as well.  This was a mote of the god's power, given to the world, which they sought to rend and alter.  The King's rage silenced them, sending them fluttering away in terror...but fear is a quiet, slow hunter when needs must.  The king rejoiced in the depths of his eternal palace, setting his facets on the much reduced orb, his own fear smothered with seemingly redoubled power.  For a time, it was good.



One night, wishing to test his newly rediscovered delight, he went to the ball...and his heart froze in his chest.  There he stood.  The Other, standing over the ball, gently gliding his fingers over the gilded settings around it that held each removed facet.  He seemed at perfect ease, a smile on his lips, favoring the King with the flicker of a knowing smile.  The King felt his life drain though his body, his heart stilled in an icy grip.  The Other reached, and lifted the heart of the ball, tossing it gently in his hand as a boy will an interesting stone found by the road.  He placed it back, heedless, and left the King's supposed sanctum of sanctums.  It had not spoken, truly, the King had never heard it speak, but the message was all too clear.  For all his work, it meant nothing.  The ball still lived, and within it the power flowed forth.  It had merely changed...but still lay beyond his ability to control.  The terror coiled up and smothered the King, driving him into senseless oblivion.  That was how they found him, for a time.



The King's wrath was beyond understanding.  It lashed like a summer storm, savage and unpredictable.  His fear drew him far from the shores of reason, and anyone could become the sudden, brief source of his swelling madness.  In time, though, it crystallized around a single idea: if he could not be rid of it, then he would at least control it.  He would force the ball, and the Other, to kneel to his will.  He would turn the power against itself, and force the Other to come, and beg his indulgence.  The King had learned that, without the facets, the ball seemed...undefined.  It would simply force growth.  Unfocused, undirected, and could spawn true madness if not properly contained.  Still...the Other.  He must keep it from stealing his life as it had.  Finally, he drew back his priesthood, and pressed upon them a most terrible duty.



First, the palace would be prepared.  Every door was to be opened, no seal or passage barred.  Then, every opening to the outside was to be sealed and bricked tight, except one.  All would be forced from the palace, save for the King and his priests, and then they would wait.  Once the Other came, they would fall upon him.  A great and terrible helm, horned and twisted, would be placed on its head, and iron nails would be driven through it, deep into the flesh and bone, fixing it forever.  Then they would take it deep, deep into the belly of the place, to the chamber of the orb and its facets.  There they would remain, to stand guard until their end, while the King and the remaining priests left, to seal the palace, and bury it, to build a new city atop it...save for the one door.  That would remain, in the bowels of the new palace, for them to watch, and wait for the Other to return, for the ball to send its hateful avatar to beg his forgiveness.



Madness, of course, but they feared to refuse him, and Fear Brings Change.  It also brings opportunity.



The priesthood did as the King willed...that is to say, as far as the King knew and could confirm, they followed the letter of his law.  What was actually done...that was questioned in time.  For a time, it was good.  The Other was gone, his (relatively) modest palace building quickly, and his rule was (as far as he knew) strong.  So the commoners wept at the expense and mad tyranny of the King.  So he noticed gray finally creeping into his hair.  So his will seemed more foggy each year...at least he was at peace.  A grand, smothering peace.  Too much peace, in time.  There was no appeal.  No voices came to the great buried door.  No one knocked, begging for forgiveness...nothing.  It is one thing for a king to be hated...it is far, far another to be ignored.



The King pressed his priesthood to plunge the depths of the old palace, to find what had happened.  The sly priests pressed subjects into service for the task, as the halls had grown strange and dangerous with the crawl of years.  When subjects could not be found, then slaves would be acquired...and so it went.  The King waned, and in time he, finally, fell, and with him the maze of horror and its dark inhabitants that had lead to that fall...or so the old stories went.  From the wreckage came little, except gaunt, twisted men with mad glints in their eyes...and a small metal object, not much bigger than a fist.  What had become of the rest, none could truly say...lost, stolen, or returned to whatever outer dark that spawned them, all the stories were true to someone.  The heart, though...that was enough for them.  They had learned the lesson of growth.  That expansion was its own reward...and worthy of worship.



------



So then time, and the roll of ages, that march that some hate and some praise, as if either would stay its relentless roll.  The priests survived, for a time.  Cults rose and fell, and the heart was reshaped, presented as no more than a trifle, an object of luck, to be carried in the hope that its power would expand fortune.  If you wish to hide a tree, hide it in a forest...and if none exists, plant one.  Copies of the heart were spread throughout the great borrowers swelling empire...and perhaps the spirit of it bled into their souls.  The great legions did spread endlessly...and even the crumbling fragments after their fall were defined by their expressionistic impulses.  In time, even the memory of the empire fell, and the heart passed into other hands.



Like a ship at sea, it wandered.  So many did not fully understand what the heart could do, and fewer still sought to purposefully use its power.  Even when it did express its endless dream of greatness, almost nobody connected the strange metal bauble and the madness it lay in.  Most of its smaller works were destroyed...but some remained.  In the reeking catacombs of plague and death...in the mad tombs of desert kings, and black tunnels into which the dying were thrown to complete their journey, it would lay, often unknown...until some new force drew it away.  Fate, desire, or some curse, what forced hands and nature to always find and move the heart, choose whatever truth you most love.  As always, it cared not.



In time, the heart was found in the sodden ruins of a city of madness, and the new wise men took it, presumed to understand it, and stamped their supposed understanding with the number 184.  What truth do these men and papers hold...as much as you believe them to.  How much do they truly know?  Do they know of the facets, and wonder at their purposes, and removal?  Do they question what became of the cult of the Endless Horizon, and its other names?  Do they question why all seems so distant...and why the flickering lights, such a comfort to a forgotten King, are so very far away?  Perhaps...but this is a terrible danger.  Trying to know, illuminates what one does not know...and a lack of knowing brings fear.  And with that fear,



Change.



They truly fear that, more than anything else.  A sterile forever is better than the chaos of otherwise.  They have chosen their truth, planted their flag, and decided that there will be no other.  This is the truth, for they say it is so, and it ever shall be, world without end, amen.  They don't even know enough to understand their folly.  Yet we must hold to something...to set our flag, and choose.  We must pick our beginnings...and pray to chose our ends.  However, all seek that hidden truth...there must be a way.  A way to cheat the march of years, a way to slide behind the last door without opening it.  The new wise men, with their numbers, and their rules, they form a cage and affect an air of detachment...like hunters pretending not to notice the rabbit, for fear of spooking the game.  They hope, sometimes in spite of themselves, that one day this, or another, or something will lift them up, and show them something worthy of being called Truth.



As is, was, and ever will be, the wise men play and squabble over and within an idiot god's broken dream.

    Part III of the Human Error series.

    King Solomon's jurisdiction over His ancient and bygone Holy Foundation is a topic of heated debate amongst members of the Council of 108.

    The epigraph is Frank Ifield's I Remember You

7eventy7evenfold

I remember too, a distant bell,
And stars that fell, like the rain,
Out of the blue~

When my life is through, and the angels ask me to recall,
The thrill of them all,
Then I will tell them I remember you

If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold...

Dolloran Light awoke in her bed at dead of night with a horrible gut feeling and went to her laptop for an answer. That normally answered her gut feelings, so…

Yup. It worked. There was an email from Fahrenheit in her inbox and it was no good. He might've just fought a dream demon and he was sickly. Except, she started to worry. Not that she wasn't already worried! God, no!

But, she just got rid of the wicked thing. Is it back? Or, let me rephrase that one; did it ever even leave?

Her heart felt heavier and guiltier than it already was about the death of one Ray Hancock and she decided there was no better option than to take her time off. So, she did what any good employee would do, and called her godlike, supernatural boss on her personal phone because she secretly hated SCiPnet and email.

Ring, ring.

"What is the matter, Director Light?" a menacing voice answered. Does he even sleep? That's a stupid question, of course he doesn't.

"I wanna take you up on that vacation offer to go save Fahrenheit—" oops. "…'s flowers! I have a nice date planned for him and want to make it really sweet and all."

There was an awkward moment of silence.

"Light. You think O5-10 and I do not read SCiPnet emails?" Light frowned, and he chuckled, ever so softly. He actually chuckled! His first laugh.

"Did you just—"

"Go tend to Fahrenheit. I will be the Acting Director of Site-02 for the time being." And with that command, he hung up, leaving her to her devices.

"…oookay then, let meee…"

She dialed Fahrenheit's number, which picked up near instantly. It was a date.

Light waited outside of a coffee shop in Cortez, wearing an oversized lab coat and sweatpants. Because that's not inconspicuous at all.

Fahrenheit approached after too many minutes of waiting donning an equally ginormous Metallica tee and scummy ripped jeans. The first thing he had to say about Light's get-up was—

"Because that's not inconspicuous at all."

She rolled her eyes. "What? It's just my old researcher coat." They shared a long embrace. "Guess what I found in my car on the way here?"

Fahrenheit shrugged.

"A box with weird, cool spiral glasses in it. Signed from Wondertainment herself! They're like animated somehow and are safe to wear." She smiled. "She said she heard what happened somehow and wanted to give me something to help, so." She put them on, before realizing she probably shouldn't wear those in public. "They're sweet."

"I miss the old Wondertainment," Fahrenheit let out. "I liked his toys a little better."

"Yeah, well he was a tool," she spoke with antipathy, before noticing the inkblots on his face. They had grown. "You okay?"

"Better since last night, yeah. Quick, tell me something only the real Dolloran Light would know!"

She froze up. "Uh, uh… shit! I dunno!"

He giggled. "Now I know I'm not having an evil wet dream again."

They entered laughing with each other.

"So after I shot them all it felt like everything just started closing in on me and turning into this awful, inky feeling thing. But it also felt like grass." He burned himself on coffee. "And it covered me up all over. I couldn't see or hear shit. Gun was useless."

Light rubbed her thumb on his hand.

"And I reached for that crucifix I had shot, but it felt weird, like pointy and rough. I started swinging it around and it let up so I could move freely again and it was just, there. In front of me. And the crucifix was a wooden dragon."

She looked frightened. "What did it look like up close?"

Fahrenheit raised his eyebrow. "Really big, just as ugly. Must've been eleven, twelve feet tall. Dozen eyes and a whole lot of arms or tentacles or something and this awful, rigid mouth. It looked how the ink felt. I started trying to stab it but it backhanded me against the wall into a praying position, which saved me because that's what I started doing." Fahrenheit looked around while sipping. "…I'm glad nobody is awake right now. I brought that dragon by the way." He removed it from his pocket and placed it on the table. She looked intrigued, before he took it back. "It's my dream dragon!"

She chuckled. "Hey, Burnie? I need to say something," she uttered nervously, before chugging her drink, scalding her throat.

"What's up?"

"I think I somehow gave a demon to you by ridding myself of mine."

He was confused.

"I— I mean, not intentionally, obviously, but like one that feeds on turmoil. I stopped having it that night whenever I decided to not let my mom and grandma's deaths bother me so much, and since yours is giving you trouble about your faith, it's trying to hurt us about our weak points that way."

It clicked.

"Damn." He took another drink. He was dry, so he instead pulled out a bottle of coke.

"Okay, how long has that been in your pocket?"

He shrugged. "Y'know. I've always had some doubts about my faith. Working for the Foundation, despite confirming all and more religions are true at once, kinda just did it in for me. It was a matter of time."

"It's okay." She didn't know what else to say.

"I mean, Jesus how many gods are out there at this point and how many have we locked up or killed? They can't be all-benevolent. If they had as much love as power, that thing wouldn't even be hurting us. Hell, we'd all be in Heaven." He swigged his coke. "I mean, I used to be a faithful Christian, but 343's death some years back and the shit we go through for no reason..? Kinda killed that. I'm just confused. I feel like I worry so much every day about if I'm picking the right path because of how many are out there."

Dolloran hugged Fahrenheit. "I understand how you feel. I'm scared too." She swallowed. "I lost my faith after I saw the way my grandma died. I don't think 343 would leave her in that awful state unless He had one helluva plan."

Fahrenheit sat still, eyes trained on his bottle. "Yeah. How could any one of them do such awful things to the people in this world if they were caring?" Fahrenheit paused. "And how the hell did they even come to be? Everything needs a start, even the anomalous."

They say quietly, absorbing the atmosphere of the coffee shop.

"There's no way to know for sure how the world was even made, Burnie. Swann said horror writers, Joseph Smith says God organized shit that already existed, and every other belief has weird thoughts about it, but we won't ever know. Even He dodged the question."

They shared an understanding look.

"I guess so. I just wish I had an answer. There are so many options too, and yet not a single one is suitable. Ugh, it's unbearable."

Light hugged him again. "That's okay. You don't have to pick one to be happy in life, okay? You'll still always have me. And TacTheo. And the rest of the Foundation." Fahrenheit smiled.

"Okay." They shared a kiss over the table. "You wanna go do something? I feel like we could both use an actual vacation and not a glorified traumadump."

"Sure. Monster trucks?" She put on her glasses.

Fahrenheit smiled. "Monster trucks."

"That was awesome!" Dolloran exclaimed! "Thanks Burnie!"

"Yeah man! That was great." Fahrenheit and Dolloran were exhausted from such the long two days and it was their time to part. "I guess I'll see you again soon sweetie."

They shared a long hug and a little kiss before parting. Fahrenheit's mind was thus easier. He had no more need for an afterlife or a creator. He had his life, and that made it worth it. He was happy.

The mahogany halls of Site-02 were quiet, barely echoing the voices of years passed and the construction taking place many rooms over. Aaron Siegel oversaw the ruckus and ensured it was of utmost satisfaction. He flipped open his phone and texted The Administrator, informing him it was going well.

Just then, he observed an awful, bordering on Satanic screeching in the general direction of the cafeteria. He closed his phone and stashed it, assigning a trusted employee to continue while he departed to investigate the sound.

When he arrived, ink was stained and splattered across every corner of the kitchen. Pots and pans were scattered about and clearly, someone had been hungry. Siegel heard shuffling behind him.

He reeled around with a right hook, stunning the wicked ratcher, which had — in a last ditch effort — began to target him, as the other two's minds were at ease. It let out a disgusting roar, spitting ink over Siegel's white dress shirt. At least it didn't stain his black tie or pants. He jumped up onto it while undoing his belt, before attempting to strangle it; it seemed as if, by will, the belt fizzled right through the thing's "neck." Siegel fell off.

Landing squarely on the floor, he opened his eyes and narrowly avoided a stomp, rolling over onto his stomach and quickly jumping back to his feet. He tried to punch again, but his arm was caught by the wicked ratcher, who suspended him in the air with its tendrils and began to siphon the shame and the guilt from his very soul. His skin melted off, flake by flake, until he was nothing but a skeleton.

At that crucial moment, Siegel remembered the eyebags Light had the day before, and Fahrenheit's email to her. "I've got you, you ruddy old bastard." He pointed up his finger and three giant stone spikes, manifested from the marble floor, drove through the body of the ratcher, immobilizing it.

Siegel pulled out a cigar and took a long drag, before extinguishing it on its eye and drawing a longsword. "SOLOMON" was engraved onto its blade. The beast let out an awful roar, before Siegel plunged the weapon deep in its heart.

The wicked ratcher disappeared. Siegel gasped, falling to his knees and clutching his chest.

Siegel woke up with a cigar in his mouth, smiling. "Called it. Good job, Light."

+ An illustration
- NX Site-02 Directorer

"I mean, I used to be a faithful Christian, but 343's death some years back and the shit we go through for no reason..? Kinda killed that. I'm just confused. I feel like I worry so much every day about if I'm picking the right path because of how many are out there." Dolloran hugged Fahrenheit. "I understand how you feel. I'm scared too." She swallowed. "I lost my faith after I saw the way my grandma died. I don't think 343 would leave her in that awful state unless He had one helluva plan." Fahrenheit sat still, eyes trained on his bottle. "Yeah. How could any one of them do such awful things to the people in this world if they were caring?" Fahrenheit paused. "And how the hell did they even come to be? Everything needs a start, even the anomalous." They say quietly, absorbing the atmosphere of the coffee shop. "There's no way to know for sure how the world was even made, Burnie. Swann said horror writers, Joseph Smith says God organized shit that already existed, and every other belief has weird thoughts about it, but //we// won't ever know. Even He dodged the question." They shared an understanding look. "I guess so. I just wish I had an answer. There are so many options too, and yet not a single one is suitable. Ugh, it's unbearable." Light hugged him again. "That's okay. You don't have to pick one to be happy in life, okay? You'll still always have me. And TacTheo. And the rest of the Foundation." Fahrenheit smiled. "Okay." They shared a kiss over the table. "You wanna go do something? I feel like we could both use an actual vacation and not a glorified traumadump." "Sure. Monster trucks?" She put on her glasses. Fahrenheit smiled. "Monster trucks." ----- "That was awesome!" Dolloran exclaimed! "Thanks Burnie!" "Yeah man! That was great." Fahrenheit and Dolloran were exhausted from such the long two days and it was their time to part. "I guess I'll see you again soon sweetie." They shared a long hug and a little kiss before parting. Fahrenheit's mind was thus easier. He had no more need for an afterlife or a creator. He had his life, and that made it worth it. He was happy. ----- //The mahogany halls of Site-02 were quiet, barely echoing the voices of years passed and the construction taking place many rooms over. Aaron Siegel oversaw the ruckus and ensured it was of utmost satisfaction. He flipped open his phone and texted The Administrator, informing him it was going well.// //Just then, he observed an awful, bordering on Satanic screeching in the general direction of the cafeteria. He closed his phone and stashed it, assigning a trusted employee to continue while he departed to investigate the sound.// //When he arrived, ink was stained and splattered across every corner of the kitchen. Pots and pans were scattered about and clearly, someone had been hungry. Siegel heard shuffling behind him.// //He reeled around with a right hook, stunning the wicked ratcher, which had -- in a last ditch effort -- began to target him, as the other two's minds were at ease. It let out a disgusting roar, spitting ink over Siegel's white dress shirt. At least it didn't stain his black tie or pants. He jumped up onto it while undoing his belt, before attempting to strangle it; it seemed as if, by will, the belt fizzled right through the thing's "neck." Siegel fell off.// //Landing squarely on the floor, he opened his eyes and narrowly avoided a stomp, rolling over onto his stomach and quickly jumping back to his feet. He tried to punch again, but his arm was caught by the wicked ratcher, who suspended him in the air with its tendrils and began to siphon the shame and the guilt from his very soul. His skin melted off, flake by flake, until he was nothing but a skeleton.// //At that crucial moment, Siegel remembered the eyebags Light had the day before, and Fahrenheit's email to her. "I've got you, you ruddy old bastard." He pointed up his finger and three giant stone spikes, manifested from the marble floor, drove through the body of the ratcher, immobilizing it.// //Siegel pulled out a cigar and took a long drag, before extinguishing it on its eye and drawing a longsword. "SOLOMON" was engraved onto its blade. The beast let out an awful roar, before Siegel plunged the weapon deep in its heart.// //The wicked ratcher disappeared. Siegel gasped, falling to his knees and clutching his chest.// ----- Siegel woke up with a cigar in his mouth, smiling. "Called it. Good job, Light." burning-water.raw_content:
Rhythmic drums, unyielding pulses like veins of a perpetual machine, heralding the end times: a world consumed by blood, greed, and fire. The boy ran away as far as he could, away from the shrieking, the guttural growls, the pitiful last cries from neighbors and family alike. He ran until the fire became ice and nothing else could be seen around, apart from the white maws of a frozen void. And as he fell to his knees, exhausted, he could feel the monster's pain, and it felt familiar. It was that raging grief that comes only through great loss and injustice. Feeling kinship for the first time in a very long time, he welcomed the embrace of the jaws of winter, and the moonless night howled, sealing their pact.

Cristina fell to the ground. Landing on the sand wasn't painful, but it still took her a while to process what had happened: the hammock had come loose on one end. She looked around — a beautiful beach with pink sands and crystal-clear waters. Cristina breathed deeply, and the warm offshore breeze caressed her lungs.

"The weather is always lovely at this part of the Seas of Id…" The voice behind her felt both soft and distant, like the shifting clouds in the sky above her. Some had the shapes of animals, others of persons… and even some resembled concepts like Love, Fear, and Hunger. Cristina got lost in those shapes; she was particularly fascinated by the cloud shaped like Rebellion, but it was suddenly scattered by a luminous particle moving at high speed. More particles soon followed, reaping engines slicing through the peace of the sky.

"I hate those pesky drones, destroying dreams and lives alike…" The voice now felt closer.

"Drones?"

"You must be careful when you dream within a dream… You wouldn't want to swim back to the Nightmare Depths, would you?" The voice felt now behind her, warm and strong. She turned around to find herself facing a tall man with a big smile. Dark and long curly hair fell over his shoulders; his dark skin glowed under the blazing sun. He held a bottle of beer in each hand and offered one to Cristina while taking a sip from the other.

"I hope you enjoy Corona, it's my favorite."

"I do, though I prefer Indio."

"Then have it your way. Don't be afraid to shape your own dreams."

Cristina took another look at the bottle in her hand. The light Corona beer was now dark; an Indio bottle had taken its place. "Who are you?" Asked the witch.

"First, we drink. Skol!" And they drank the beers in one gulp. For Cristina, it was like tasting a little piece of heaven. His gaze drifted into the oniric sea before them; he seemed thoughtful—perhaps even sad. "Cristina… do you think monsters are born or made?"

"What are you talking about?"

"My father… I think he acted guided not by wisdom but by fear. Perhaps there was another way. Long time ago, perhaps. He created his own monster and now… now the wolves are the gates. Again." He finished what was left of his beer in a single sip and let the can fall onto the sand. "When the time comes, Cristina, you must do as my brother Viðarr did and put an end to that old dog's suffering…"

"What are you talking about?" A bolt of lightning fell over the waters, and Cristina, startled, dropped the bottle. The storm broke over the crystal-clear sea, now boiling with violent rhythm.

"Atl tlachinolli, Cristina." The tall man looked at the burning water, smiling with satisfaction. "I'm sorry about your god of Sun and War. But this won’t end here. When you find it, make good use of my hammer. Even though it's lost, don't worry about returning it; It'll remember its way back home in time."

"I don't understand…"

"But keep this in mind. A hammer is both a tool and a weapon. It is easy to forget that not everything is a nail. You can use it in many ways… and in the right hands, it can tender even the hardest of flesh… Cristina…" A thunder fell just right next to her; the pink sands melted into a kaleidoscope of glass.

"Wake up!"

Cristina opened her eyes. The shrieking sound of an old anti-air siren rumbled in her ears. She sighed and exited the rusted makeshift bunker that was her room. Outside, a big purple bipedal capybara waited for her with a tray of coffee and pan de muerto.

"Good morning, Lady Cristina. Would you like some coffee and brunch?"

"Only the coffee…" she grabbed the cup somewhat rudely, "…and don't call me 'lady'."

"Sorry, Comandanta." The capybara made a gesture either mocking or imitating a military salute. "The Paly Lady sent me to check on you."

"Tell her I'm fine, will go to the frontlines now."

Cristina walked through the ruined streets of the once lively Tomb City, rubble rustling under her boots. Two months had passed since the invasion began; the initial deluge of blood and fire had simmered down into the stagnant agony of a siege, and tiredness and desperation were beginning to take their toll even on the dead. With dead Huitzilopochtli now floating —perhaps still dreaming— somewhere in the orbit of Mercury, Mictlán had lost its strongest ally, giving the Ravens the chance to push further into the Underworld. Still, the defenders of the realm had fought tooth and nail to cut off their advance, forcing the enemy into a brutal trench war with no one side able to gain any more terrain. Bound to play this game of guile and patience, Valravn could have taken the easy way out and flipped over the entire board, obliterating the topmost layer of Mictlán, but their drones had been conservative in their bombardment. They don't want to burn down their prize, at least not yet. Cristina dreaded to think about the day they finally decided to unleash that heavy rain.

A raven-shaped drone flew above her. She closed her eyes and breathed, making momentary peace with the possibility of imminent destruction. Instead of missiles, the payload was pamphlets. One of them landed on her hand. Cristina read it, exhaled an angry snort, and then crumpled it with her fist.

Kneel and Surrender.

Do not resist Order and Progress.

Váyanse a la verga, she thought, and continued her stroll towards the trenches. While climbing down an once elegant, but ruined staircase, she crossed paths with a pack of xolotls driving a makeshift armored cart. An antiquated horseless carriage, it had been reinforced with steel plates and mounted with WWI-era rusted machine guns. "Comandanta!" The canine driver yelled at her and shook the wheel just in time to avoid a crash. "Good to have you here in time for the party!" Times were truly dire if the Syndicate of Psychopomp Transportists had been given free rein to drive their post-apocalyptic contraptions inside the city.

She finally reached the frontlines at the city outskirts, where the trench warfare was methodical but brutal, an ultraviolent game of chess. She found Lorena, the pyromancer, overseeing the battlefield.

"How's everything, Lore?"

The fire-maiden neither answered nor turned her gaze away from the trenches. Her hands made a swift movement, and a section exploded into a fiery storm. Distant, painful screams followed soon.

"Nice shot," observed Cristina. The fire-maiden finally turned back and reproached her with a look. "Really, Cristina? I told you to get some fucking rest."

"I'll rest when I'm dead."

"That's what everyone down here thought. How's that working for them?"

Cristina shrugged. "Is Baruch down there?"

"Yes, right down in the trenches, hunting for some roasted Ravens." A powerful, beastly roar had joined as the bassline for the chorus of panicked screams and percussive gunshots. "You two make a terrific team," commented Cristina.

Lorena's answer was a brief smirk. She had always been a passionate fighter, and now her fire burned to avenge Huitzilopochtli. Still, Cristina worried that eventually, that very fire would either burn her candle into nothingness or explode her powder into senseless destruction. The witch sighed, wondering if they could break the siege before it broke them.

Another drone flew by, raining more propaganda. Lorena gestured again, and the falling pamphlets began to burn like fireflies in the night. The drones… Cristina took the last sip from her coffee before throwing the cup far away into the trenches. "Lorena, where's Guadalupe?"

"Last time I checked, Lupe was on the radio station," answered the daughter of the sun, "probs trying to do something about those damn metal mosquitoes."

At the radio station, Cristina found the ex-Foundation agent surrounded by old radio gear, tinkering obsessively with rusty circuits and bulbs. "Cristina!" They greeted her without turning away from the machinery, "Cristina, I cracked it!"

"Antes que nada, buenos días." La Comandata took a seat over a pile of rusty audio equipment. "Let me guess, the drones are somehow controlled by a dream…"

"They are using an oneiric frequency to control the drones… Wait!? How did you know!"

"It came to me in a dream, " the witch answered.

"For real?" Guadalupe raised an eyebrow.

"Never mind, are you thinking the same thing I am?" Cristina asked with a playful smile.

"I'll talk with the alebrijes." They nodded complicitly, "It should be ready soon."

Cristina sighed with relief. If they could neutralize the drone fleet, that would make the war even. "Thanks, Guadalupe… for everything. Get some rest, please."

"I'll do. But you have to rest too, deal?"

"Deal, but there is something I need to do first."

"What?"

"I was thinking of sending our guests a nice postcard," Cristina cracked her neck and fingers. As she was leaving the radio room, she noticed a bunch of tools littering a table. One caught her attention.

"Are you going to use this hammer? Can I borrow it?"

"Hmmm, sure, but… why would you need this hammer?"

"In case I find a nail."

Miles away, on the other side of the battlefield, Hersir Thorsten's tent was plagued by a nine-fingered vermin. Nate Hansen, former Midwestern Regional President of Valravn, had been crashing at his camp for two months straight, compulsively leeching alcohol and non-stop talking shit. Thorsten often wondered which one of his long list of sins Nate was a punishment for.

"We've been rotting in this hellhole for two months already, aren't you tired of this?" Nate poured another stream of mead into his glass. He overflowed the glass, spilling the mead over the maps and battle plans scattered across the table, much to Thorsten's dismay.

"A siege is a game of patience," replied the Hersir, trying his best not to think about his ruined documents.

"Alright, but why are we doing a fucking siege? We should bombard these savage zombies to Kingdom Come."

"We were sent here to secure the Necropolis, not to turn it into rubble." Thorsten tried to discreetly take away the mead bottle, but Nate held onto it as if it were his life.

"You were sent here to conquer this place for the High Table. And I was sent here to make sure you do your job." Since the beginning, the two were bound to clash. Thorsten could never respect a suit that shunned combat, while Hansen, despite Thorsten's legendary status among the Ravens, could only ever see the Hersir as hired muscle, another disposable grunt.

"You were sent here as a punishment for being a drunken idiot." The Hersir finally snapped. For the most part, he tried to be diplomatic, and it almost worked when Hansen was sober. Drunk Hansen, on the other hand, seemed to be emboldened by a suicidal bravado. "You insulted a very important client, and that cost you both your position and your finger."

"Should I remind you I have the total authority to relieve you of your command at any time?" Hansen's alcoholic smugness could almost be admired.

Thorsten could have easily ripped the bottle away from Nate… he could have even ripped the whole arm, but he didn't want to make more of a mess. He sighed. "You could have done it any time during these two months. But you haven't and never will. You know why?"

"Enlighten me." Hansen was now drinking straight up from the bottle.

"Because you are a spineless coward. But I have to admit it will be very amusing to see you trying and failing to lead a military operation."

Hansen looked at the Hersir in a mixture of disbelief and amusement, then downed nearly half the bottle in one gulp and spat onto the fine carpet of the tent. "You know what? I don't understand the hype around you. You are supposed to be this living legend: The Wolf of Winter! But you act more like a puppy… a true wolf would have eaten its enemies' head in one bite!"

"A true wolf? Funny that you mention that…" Thorsten smirked.

"I already hate this bitch Cristina so much. I'd just blow up her and her snake friends with our drones. Kaput. And then we’d return to Eurtec, covered in gold and laurels."

"Rule number one of war, Nate: Respect your enemies. This is exactly the attitude that brought you down in the first place."

"Come on, Thorsten! She is the only thing standing between us and glory. Once we conquer Mictlán, the Table will see the mistake they made. They'll give me back my old job, and I'll get a new finger. A bionic one!"

"Sure, Nate… sure." In his vast experience, the old warrior had learned that some battles were not worth fighting.

Nate's phone rang and he rushed to check it. Thorsten took the opportunity to finally grab and quickly hide the mead bottle away.

"Fuck, fuck, fuck! This is bad!" Nate's face was livid. "Our drones are down everywhere… They jammed the oneiric signal! The dreamers are convulsing! Fuck, fuck, fuck. The Table is going to blood-eagle me."

"Clever girl." Thorsten smiled. For the first time in weeks, things were starting to get interesting again. "She never ceases to amaze me."

"Why the fuck are you smiling? Let's make something clear: if I'm going down, you are coming with me…" Nate wanted to keep shitalking, but the words stuck in his throat. It was only for a brief moment, but he thought he saw a cold gleam in Thorsten’s gaze—predatory eyes that stirred a primal terror within him. The Wolf of Winter. He tried to regain composure. Ridiculous, Nate thought, he is nothing but a brute.

At this point, Thorsten was not even paying attention to his unwelcomed guest. Through the entrance of the tent, he had noticed a faint glow, seemingly coming from above. He stepped to get a look outside: officers and soldiers were running chaotically, failing to respond to the drone crisis. Thorsten looked up; the painted ceiling of the Underworld cavern had been adorned with a message, etched in glowing letters:

Kneel and Surrender?

Kneel and Surrender your ass, Ravenfuckers!

Thorsten got back to the tent, smiling internally. He hadn't felt so young in ages. "You know what, Nate? You may be an idiot, but you may have a point. It's time to end this dance once and for all."

"Finally!" Nate exclaimed sardonically. "I was wondering when you would grow a pair."

Thorsten decided to ignore that last part. "Tell all the troops to get ready. Prepare the heavy artillery…"

"Hell yeah!" Nate raised his fist.

"And a big white flag."

"What?"

Fallen drones littered No Man's Land. The bulk of Mictlán's army, difuntos, alebrijes and xolotls alike, remained entrenched but alert and ready for a fight. The Pale Lady and Cristina's group stood in the open, waiting for the Ravens to arrive at the site of the parley.

"I don't like this," said Baruch the jaguar-nahual, "this has to be the most obvious trap ever."

"They could blow us up with artillery at any time," observed Guadalupe.

"If it comes to that, I'll raise a shield to protect us," Cristina wanted to reassure them as much as she wanted to reassure herself.

"Are you sure it will hold?"

"For the most part…"

A guttural shriek pierced the silence, while the sound of drums and marching boots rumbled through No Man's Land. Thousands of voices, chanting gutturally in a dead language, echoed as the Raven army approached the defenders of Mictlán. An imposing figure led the army, a two-meter-tall frame encased in power armor. His footsteps were heavy, rising louder and stronger above the rest of the percussive cacophony. He dragged a remarkably large battle-axe, leaving a scar through the sacred soil of the underworld: a weapon of such a size and wickedness that it would have looked ridiculous if wielded by anyone else. Two women flanked the giant, one had a metallic arm and donned a white, expressionless mask hiding murderous intent. The other was a spectral apparition, an ancient herald of dread and ruin. Behind the Valkyrie and La Llorona, a flag bearer carried the white flag of truce, and a man in a suit struggled to keep the warrior's pace. The boots finally stopped their march, and while the guttural choir ceased chanting, the cruel echoes still haunted the air.

"Is all this circus really necessary?" complained the suit.

"Shut up, Nate." Murmured Thorsten, and he raised his voice and weapon to address his enemies. "I am Hersir Thorsten, commander of the 13th Armored and the 25th Infantry Division of the Valravn Corporation. I have come here to parley with the Ruler of Mictlán."

"That would be me," replied the Pale Lady. "You shall address me as any of my many names and titles: La Santa Muerte, La Catrina, La Patrona, La Dama Pálida, La Niña Blanca, La Flaquita, La Huesuda, La Tiznada, La Parca, La Malquerida, La Viuda Blanca, La Dueña de los Alebrijes, la Madrina, Azrael, and Mictecacíhuatl. Or just Catrina. And here standing besides are Las Viboras, Defenders of Mictlán: Lorena, the three-times blessed Daughter of the Sun, Baruch, Jaguar-warrior of Clan Bah, Guadalupe, Righter of Wrongs and Defector from the Foundation, and Cristina, Best Student of the Black Queen, the Thief of Books, la Bruja, and Comandanta of my armies."

"Cristina!" exclaimed Thorsten in an oddly sincere and warm tone. "It is an honor to finally meet you!"

"Is it, though?" snarked the witch.

"Of course, since we started this little dance of Ravens and Vipers, I couldn't help but admire your martial talents. This is the most fun I've had in centuries."

"And I have no idea who the hell you are."

"Meh, I'm nothing but a simple man. Standing beside me are Valravn's finest: Sister Sifvar," he first gestured towards the Valkyrie, and then towards La Llorona, "and Sister Amelia." He then rolled his eyes and pointed to the suited man, "That one, standing over there, is Nate. Don't mind him."

"I am the Midwestern Regional President of Valravn," protested Nate.

"Former Midwestern Regional President of Valravn," corrected Thorsten. "Anyways, Cristina, let's waste no more time. You have masterfully disabled our drone fleet, a hard hit for our offensive capabilities. Unfortunately for you, I still have plenty of ways to reduce the Tomb City to ashes. Let me show you." He then nodded to Sifvar, and the Valkyrie pressed a button on her armpad. Almost immediately, a missile rose from one of the launchers at the Valravn base directly to the Necropolis. It hit one of the palace bell towers, shattering its pieces across the Lady's citadel. Screams of terror echoed through the ranks of the dead, and the old merc cruelly smiled. "As you see, I can reduce this whole place to rubble at any time, but that is not what I want."

Mierda. Cristina said internally. Still, she was determined to remain firm. "We have endured the siege. We will endure your missiles. We will endure everything you throw at us. We will never surrender."

"I know," Thorsten kept smiling. "And I wouldn't want it any other way. What is the point of a battle just by pressing buttons? No, no, Hel no! I wouldn't want that! I have come here to challenge you, Champion of Mictlán."

"Challenge me?"

"To a duel. Axcan quema, tehuatl, nehuatl… Now, you and I. Until someone dies or kneels. If I win, Mictlán surrenders; if you win, we pack and leave you alone."

"Have you fuckin lost your mind?" Nate shouted hysterically, "Why would you risk the mission in a stupid duel? We got them! Just bomb them to oblivion! Enough! You are getting court-martialed. I hereby relieve you of your position! Sifvar! Amelia! Arrest this madman!"

Thorsten didn't even turn to look at Nate. "Sifvar, I need silence," he spoke calmly but annoyed. The Valkyrie just nodded and drew a kukri knife. For a moment, it felt as if she was about to slice his throat, but instead, she hit him hard in the face with the pommel. The former Midwestern Regional President of Valravn fell to the ground, sobbing and grabbing his broken nose as blood ran from it, tainting the Holy grounds of Mictlán.

"Honestly," Thorsten continued, "I don't know why the High Table wants this place so badly. Neither do I know what unholy business Zenith is planning to do with this sacred place. And I couldn't care less. I have fought their wars long enough to understand they are meaningless! Devoid of any higher purpose beyond their money! Fuck the High Table! And Fuck Zenith! I want this place for me! And I will earn it like a warrior!" His eyes shone when speaking those last words, and, for a brief moment, Cristina perceived a strange aura around Thorsten. It felt like the rage and hunger of a primordial beast, the fangs of a conqueror and a devourer.

"You seem too eager to betray your masters. Why should we trust you to keep your word?" asked Cristina.

"We mercenaries may not have loyalty. But we do have honor. The High Table may believe gold is enough to buy my obedience, but I have never truly given them my word. I am, however, giving it to you now."

The revolutionary group remained silent, unsure of how to approach the bizarre challenge. After a few eternal moments, Guadalupe decided to be the first one to speak: "I don't like this guy," they said in a quiet voice.

"Me neither, but what options do we have?" answered Lorena.

"Not much really," La Comandanta felt a shiver down her skin. She could sense the air charged with something… ancient and ominous.

"Cristina," the Pale Lady grabbed her arm, "you felt it too, right? I don't think deceit is what we should fear from this one. This man is on a mission. A sacred one. That doesn't make him righteous, but we must accept his challenge."

Cristina sighed. “I know.” There was no way they could win a conventional war, especially if the Ravens chose to unleash the full force of their arsenal. But settling it with a duel… that almost seemed too good to be true.

Never mind, she thought. Even if it was some twisted trap or a cruel joke, she had to take the chance and make the most of whatever happened next. Improvisation had always been one of her magical talents—at least, that’s what Allison used to say.

She turned to face the axe-wielding giant.

“Thorsten, we accept your challenge.”

An alebrije had brought a finely decorated art-decó makeup case. The Lady of Death opened and took out a brush. "This makeup is part of me. It has my soul and my skin. It will bind you to the Xolotl, it will bind you to my roots. It will open to you the doors of primordial magic, but you will have to discover that on your own. It is a gift that I can only give to those dearest to me, for it will make you a living Catrina. It is both a war paint and a costume for celebration. Let it protect you both in war and peace."

And the Lady began to humbly apply the makeup over Cristina's face. Behind this seemingly mundane act, there was something holy, ancient, and deep taking place. It was an act of death and rebirth, the true power of symbols. La Catrina, the playful and colorful embodiment of the bittersweet joy of Día de Muertos. La Santa Muerte, the terrifying yet merciful Saint of Death, revered equally by both the victims and the victimizers. And the deep and primordial roots of Mictecacíhuatl, a being so antique that it defied comprehension. A trinity of symbols overlapping on each, a superposition that should be paradoxical yet still made perfect sense, such was the mysterious nature of the gods. "Now you are ready to go, querida."

Cristina nodded and raised her fist with quiet resolve. Then, wielding a macuahuitl, she walked to the No Man's Land, where the Hersir awaited her. Around them, her friends, the dead, alebrijes, and xolotls, as well as the Valkyrie, La Llorona, the suit, and the Raven mercenaries, all of them awaited eagerly the spectacle that would decide the fate of this war.

"I have waited for so long for this moment," Thorsten kept smiling like a child about to open a gift. "Cristina, this is such a beautiful moment."

"Let's get this over with."

"As you wish." The sound of servo motors running was barely enough to warn Cristina of the upcoming attack. Thorsten moved his axe with speed and precision, unlikely for a weapon and a man of that gargantuan size. Cristina felt adrenaline rushing through her veins. She avoided the strike, but it was a close call.

"You are faster than you look, gonna give you that," said La Bruja.

"Good that you are quick too, would be a shame if this dance ended so soon…" Thorsten looked down, confused—his legs had begun to sink into the ground, trapping him. Cristina jumped on him, trying to break his guard with her weapon, but the Hersir blocked her attack and pushed her away. Then he effortlessly broke away from the trap.

But Cristina had not wasted her time. She could feel it in her skin, the Pale Lady's makeup gifting her a new connection to the taumathurgical forces of Mictlán. She was now confident and felt in control. At her command, multiple stone pillars, carved with the angry faces of forgotten spirits, rose from the ground and fell over his enemy. The Hersir jumped back, narrowly avoiding getting crushed.

"Bravo! Marvelous play!" exclaimed Thorsten. He seemed mostly unbothered, and that was starting to annoy Cristina.

"Look, you may be big and strong, but I'm a witch. My tricks are infinite, and you are fighting on my terms. You may start to consider kneeling if you value your life."

"Kill me, if it's so easy. But don't pretend you're not enjoying this like me."

"Is this a game for you?" Her annoyance gave way to rage, as all the horrors unleashed by the Ravens flashed through her memory. Guatemala. Bolivia. México. "After all the lives you have taken? All the suffering you have caused? Does that not matter to you?" Cristina shouted.

"Atl tlachinolli. Burning Water… the Nahua captured it perfectly. What a beautiful way to encapsulate the paradoxical nature of War."

"Shut up!" Cristina charged again with her macuahuitl, but she was easily parried.

"War is a paradox. Terrible but also inevitable and… quite fun. It brings out both the best and the worst of humanity. And it is often necessary to make war to keep the peace. It shouldn't, but that contradiction makes perfect sense. Burning Water. But don't play dumb, you already know this, guerrillera."

"You can wax poetically all you want, but you are just another greedy fascist who only cares for himself! Do you have any idea of what is at stake here? Do you know what will happen if Mictlán falls?"

"I know Mictlantecuhtli threatened to break the Pillars of Earth. But it won't be necessary, I'll do it myself."

Those last words caught Cristina off guard, and Thorsten saw the opening; his axe lunged like a bird of prey upon its quarry. But then, he felt an impact on his weapon and lost his grip. To his surprise, it was not the macuahuitl that had parried his attack; Cristina had suddenly conjured a gleaming cloud on her hand, from which a double-barreled shotgun emerged. She fired it without hesitation and blew away his opponent's weapon. Then, she did not waste time and rolled across the ground to position herself behind him, firing again at the main servomotor of the armor.

"You parried my axe with a bullet!" Thorsten shouted, genuinely excited.

"I warned you that my tricks were limitless. And now you can't move in this armor with the servo-motors ruined." A regular round fired by a regular person wouldn't have damaged the reinforced mechanism of the Hersir's armor. Fortunately, Cristina was anything but a regular person.

Thorsten just smiled and shrugged; the armor fell to the ground. He now faced the witch, unarmored and bare-chested.

"Do you kneel now?" The witch pointed the macuahuitl at his throat.

"And ruin all this fun? You know that is not happening."

"Perhaps I misjudged you. You are not greedy, you are just insane!" And then she plunged the bladed weapon into his ribs. But to her surprise, she did not feel the cut in the flesh, nor did she see blood pouring. Instead, the blades of the macuahuitl shattered. At the impact zone, his skin had become dark and dense, a hardened fiber.

"What? How?"

"Nanomachines, girl."

"Come on!"

The hardened punch she received in the face would have killed her if she hadn't raised a kinetic barrier just in time to absorb it. Still, she flew a few meters into the air.

"Cristina!" Shouted Baruch, and he tried to rush towards her, Lorena and Guadalupe following him. But their path was promptly blocked by a kukri-wielding Sifvar and Amelia's biomechanically implanted claws. "No one shall interfere with the duel," threatened the Valkyrie.

"She is right," The Pale Lady touched Baruch's shoulder, "This is Cristina's fight and only hers."

"But…"

"She is still alive. And I have faith in her."

Baruch felt relieved as he saw Cristina standing, albeit with difficulty. But now Thorsten approached her with raised arms, which now glowed in the shape of a pair of spectral, beastly claws.

"What the hell are you?" murmured the witch.

"I don't want to kill you, Cristina," Thorsten spoke for the first time in a somber tone. Gone was his past playful demeanor. Shit, thought Cristina, he is serious now. Her confidence, strong like steel just a few moments ago, lay now shattered by the punch she just received. She was not facing an ordinary foe, but the abominable offspring of unholy magic and technological depravity.

"I won't kneel."

"Perhaps you'll change your mind if we take a trip together to the origin." Thorsten's raised claws pierced the painted sky, and the curtain fell, cut into pieces; they were now standing at the Cempasuchitl Fields. A wolf howled, and a blinding snow began to swallow the orange flowers. "Behold Fimbulwinter, the prelude of Ragnarok! Man shall become the wolf of man!"

"Why on Earth do you want to destroy the Pillars?"

"Atl tlachinolli. Paradox. The men who destroyed my village and enslaved my family spoke of mercy. And yet they carried a tortured god on a cross. But I get it now, the paradox makes perfect sense."

Cristina's magic absorbed another fist, but she could still feel part of the pain. "I can no longer hear my gods; there is no Thor in the storm, nor Wotan in the skies. Perhaps they are dead, or perhaps they have forsaken us. Perhaps they were always traitors and deceivers. Doesn't really matter. The only Rule of Nature is that the strong shall devour the weak." He continued pummeling Cristina. "The Christian God was stronger than my gods, but even He was replaced by a bigger fish: The God of Money!"

Cristina's arms weighed like anchors, yet she kept her kinetic guard up. Thorsten continued punching both with fist and words: "Your gods are also weakened, barely a shadow of their former selves. Think of the fate of hummingbird god, Huitzilopochtli…"

"Don't you dare say that name!" Cristina's voice almost broke.

"Even if you could defeat me, do you think you can hold Mictlán forever? Think, Cristina, think! Worse things will come for you! Worse Gods will rise, even crueler than the God of Money! I am your only lifeline!"

He threw another punch, but this time it didn't hit Cristina. Instead, it fractured the cempasuchilt, the broken fragments of orange-stained glass shattered all over them. When the broken rain finally stopped, they were now standing on the humid roots of the inverted Ceiba Tree hanging over the Necropolis of Mictlán. Above them stood the mighty Pillars of Earth, extending endlessly into the eternal abyss of shadows.

"This world is tainted beyond repair. Why do you insist on it? Valhalla is just a faint memory, lost forever, and soon Mictlán will follow. Yet the Sillicon Nornir foretold me it would be a witch who would show me the way to a new age. Whether you accepted or not, this was Fate." He extended his hand to Cristina.

"Let this world burn, Cristina. Let the Fifth Sun and the Nine Worlds die, and from their ashes we shall build something new. Something more beautiful than ever. Mictlán and Valhalla shall rise together. Here we will build the Ark carrying the worthy to the new world, Idavoll… Avalon."

Above Thorsten, a colossal wolf with translucent, sanguineous fur rose. It was the spectre of Fenrir, eyeing the Pillars with frenetic hunger; its jaws dripping saliva in bloodlust and anticipation. "The old world is dying and the new world struggles to be born…" the Hersir grinned manically like the jaws of a wolf, "now is the time of monsters."

Cristina looked very small, faced against the giant warrior and the gaping jaws of the beastly incarnation of entropy. Still, she began to laugh, blood dripping from her nostrils. "So you have given up on this world, and this is why you want to start Ragnarok. Good grief." She spat a bloody glob at his opponent’s feet. "You know what, Thorsten? For a second, I thought you were making sense… and then you came up with this nihilist bullshit. Give me a fucking break! Pathetic…"

"I have brought with me the Wolf that will devour the Sun and the Moon. One way or another, Ragnarok is inevitable."

"You are forgetting something."

"Am I?"

"You are not the only one with a pet."

It emerged from the shadow of time, the stealthy silhouette had been stalking its foe, waiting for the perfect time to ambush it. When the moment came, it sprang from its dark hiding place, madly howling with fangs bared. Xolotl, Lord of Monstrosities, bit Fenrir in the neck, and the Hersir writhed as if he could feel such pain. The two primordial canids clashed in a violent embrace, and the cacophony of their howls and barks reached the deepest confines of the universe.

"Also," the witch stood and smiled defiantly, "your gods never went silent. You were just too stubborn to listen!"

Cristina raised her hand, and the old rusty hammer materialized from a cloud of electrons and quarks. "Impossible," muttered the Hersir, still recovering his breath.

Cristina hit Thorsten in the ribs, and sparks and thunder illuminated the primordial darkness. For the first time in centuries, the Vessel of Fenrir felt true pain again.

"I wonder if those nanomachines can withstand this level of electrical power. Only one way to find out." And she kept hammering the Hersir, each strike a lightning bolt of thousands of volts. And every time the hammer hit the vessel, a thunderbolt struck the dire wolf’s skin as well; Fenrir howled in rage and pain as Xolotl's jaws and claws tore away his burned flesh.

Overwhelmed, Thorsten tried to back away, but the ancient roots of the world-tree came to life, entangling his arms and legs. "These are the roots of Mictecacíhuatl. Perhaps my gods are stronger than they look," Cristina smirked, "Now, kneel."

"You know that is not happening!"

"I said: Kneel!"

The roots pulled Thorsten down, and he finally fell to his knees. He sighed, "So it had to be this way."

The nanotech's hardened fiber was no more; the electrical shock had disabled it, softening the Hersir's impenetrable skin. Cristina picked one of the obsidian blades broken from the macuahuitl and made a wide cut in Thorsten's chest. She then reached her hand deep inside. As she did it, she felt the void of darkness burning her skin as the howls of Fenrir became increasingly erratic and pitiful.

But she didn't stop. With all of her strength, the witch grabbed and pulled the still pulsating heart of the Hersir. Holding his heart, he saw visions of the past: a burning village, a small child taken from his family, centuries of war hardening him to become the vessel of the Wolf. "If Valhalla is what you want, then I shall give it to you!" And she stabbed the heart with the obsidian blade.

"Cristina…" There was no anger or grief in Thorsten's voice. Instead, there was… relief, "Thanks." That was his final word, and his body fell lifeless. Cristina turned her head to face Xolotl, standing triumphantly with the bloodied head of Fenrir hanging from its jaws. The defeated specter howled one last time before dissipating back into entropy. Cristina reached out her hand to pat Xolotl's nose, and the eyeless guard dog of the Underworld nodded to the witch. Then, he turned around to return to his dwelling in the depths of Time. Cristina closed her eyes and breathed. When she opened them, she was back at Mictlán, surrounded by the bewildered spectators.

"Cristina! You did it!" Her friends rushed to hug her, and they almost lost their balance. Even the Pale Lady and some alebrijes joined the group hug.

"Sifvar!" Nate had somewhat recovered from her punch, more or less managing to stand, "They're distracted! I command you to attack! We have to avenge Hersir Thorsten." Amelia materialized behind the former regional president and grabbed him by the neck. Sifvar walked next to his ear. "In case you don't understand what Amelia is communicating, I'll spell it to you: Don't you dare say his name. If you ever manage to be one tenth of the man Thorsten was, then perhaps your life would be worth a dime, maggot. The Hersir gave us one last order, and we are obeying him. Till the end." La Llorona dematerialized again, and Hansen dropped to his knees, sobbing.

The Valkyrie turned around to face Cristina, who had broken free from the celebration to seal the negotiations.

"You… you bested the Hersir in combat…" Sivfar spoke in a mix of shock, rage, and admiration.

"Are you leaving, Raven?"

"We are. But I'm taking the Hersir's body with me. That is not a question."

"Be my guest," replied the witch.

It took eight of Sivfar's men and an unusually large body bag to carry Thorsten's body away. As the Ravens walked away, Amelia appeared next to Sivfar, who had turned around to address the witch one last time: "Comandanta Cristina, the next time we meet… I'll kill you."

"Say whatever makes you feel better, bitch. Just fuck off already." Cristina returned the murderous gaze of the shield-maiden with equal intensity and hate.

"War is over!" The Pale Lady shouted with an ancient, otherworldly voice that rang with the force of a chorus of thousands of souls, its echo stretching into the depths of infinity. She had stepped between the two would-be opponents, who in turn recoiled instinctively. Then, she returned to her usual soft and gentle tone and spoke to the valquirie and her companion, "Sivfar, Amelia, queridas… As the Queen of Death, it is my duty to remind you that it is beneath both the Valkyrie and the Cihuateoteo to be slaves of the Raven. Break away before you follow your hersir."

La Llorona's ghostly face showed no emotion, but she lowered her gaze slightly. The valkyrie merely turned her back on the Lady, ignoring her words. "Let's go, Amelia."

And as the last Raven left Mictlán never to return again, Cristina finally fell to her knees. She was about to cry, she could finally breathe free, she could finally… finally get some fucking rest.

Cristina woke up in an elegant room; she recognized it as one of the guest suites of the Lady's Art Deco palace.

The door opened, and the Pale Lady walked in, followed by the purple capybara butler.

"Good morning, Lady Cristina. Would you like some coffee and brunch?" asked the capybara.

"Don't call me… You know what… yeah fuck it, give me everything."

The butler bowed and then pranced out of the room.

"He means well," said the Pale Lady as she sat on the side of the bed.

"Did all of that really happen?" Cristina had awoken with this strange, surreal feeling that the last few months, years… perhaps her whole life had been nothing but a dream.

"Cristina, querida, thanks for everything." The Holy Death took her hand. "There is no way we will ever be able to pay you."

"It is not necessary to pay, I did this as a promise, do you remember?" It was all real, she finally believed. "But I would have done it anyway; this is what I do. This is what Las Víboras do. We kick oppressors and fascists' asses wherever we find them."

The Lady laughed, "You and your friends are really something else."

"Yes, they are the best… My friends! Where are they? Is everyone safe?"

"Worry not, they are getting some well-deserved rest just like you. Soon we'll be having a big feast to celebrate this victory!"

"Amazing!" Cristina couldn't remember the last time she had a decent meal. "I need some good food! What are you having?"

"The main course will be pozole…"

"A huevo!"

"Made from the flesh of our dead enemies…"

"…"

"There will also be a vegan option if you prefer that."

"Thanks."

"Anyways, I'll be on my way. Need to supervise the xolotls so they don't eat all the ingredients before we can cook," the Paly Lady stood graciously and walked to the door. "Meanwhile, you get more rest, querida."

"Wait, Catrina!" Cristina said as the Lady was about to leave the room.

"Yes, querida?" replied the Holy Death.

"I have been thinking about his words. He was an evil, broken, deranged man, but at least on some level, his rambling made sense. We won today… but what will come tomorrow? We can't keep like this forever."

"Atl tlachinolli, Cristina. Sometimes, the only way forward is to embrace the paradox. In the wise words of a trickster: 'To be seen, you have to cover your face… to be named, you have to deny your own name, you gamble your present to secure a future, and… to live… you die.'"

"I know that speech, Catrina…"

"Maybe the way forward is to protect what we have to the last end. Or maybe we have to learn to let things go. Or perhaps there is another unknown option, but whatever the case is…"

"We will decide for ourselves."

"Indeed, querida. Indeed."

When the butler capybara came back with the coffee and pan de muerto, he found Cristina already asleep. I guess she can ask her pyromaniac friend to heat the coffee when she wakes up, he thought as he left the tray on the nightstand.

"Oh, you are here! I didn't notice you before. Pardon me, querida, for not giving you a proper welcome. Are you here to join the celebrations?

"I'm not here to party, Catrina."

"Cristina would certainly be very happy to see you…"

"I’ve fulfilled my promise. Now is just a turn."

"I know you won't listen, but… may I give you one last warning before you fuck everything again?"

"I'm not in the mood for this. Answer my question, Lady of the Death: Where is Gears?"

The Raven and the Hummingbird

She looked around — a beautiful beach with pink sands and crystal-clear waters. Cristina breathed deeply, and the warm offshore breeze caressed her lungs. "When the time comes, Cristina, you must do as my brother Viðarr did and put an end to that old dog's suffering..." "What are you talking about?" A thunder fell just right next to her; the pink sands melted into a kaleidoscope of glass. "Wake up!" ----- Cristina opened her eyes. The shrieking sound of an old anti-air siren rumbled in her ears. Cristina walked through the ruined streets of the once lively Tomb City, rubble rustling under her boots. Two months had passed since the invasion began; the initial deluge of blood and fire had simmered down into the stagnant agony of a siege, and tiredness and desperation were beginning to take their toll even on the dead. With dead Huitzilopochtli now floating —perhaps still dreaming— somewhere in the orbit of Mercury, Mictlán had lost its strongest ally, giving the Ravens the chance to push further into the Underworld. Still, the defenders of the realm had fought tooth and nail to cut off their advance, forcing the enemy into a brutal trench war with no one side able to gain any more terrain. Bound to play this game of guile and patience, Valravn could have taken the easy way out and flipped over the entire board, obliterating the topmost layer of Mictlán, but their drones had been conservative in their bombardment. //They don't want to burn down their prize, at least not yet//. Cristina dreaded to think about the day they finally decided to unleash that heavy rain. A raven-shaped drone flew above her. She closed her eyes and breathed, making momentary peace with the possibility of imminent destruction. Instead of missiles, the payload was pamphlets. One of them landed on her hand. Cristina read it, exhaled an angry snort, and then crumpled it with her fist. [[=]] ++++ Kneel and Surrender. ++++ Do not resist Order and Progress. While climbing down an once elegant, but ruined staircase, she crossed paths with a pack of xolotls driving a makeshift armored cart. The canine driver yelled at her and shook the wheel just in time to avoid a crash. "Good to have you here in time for the party!" Her hands made a swift movement, and a section exploded into a fiery storm. Distant, painful screams followed soon. "Nice shot," observed Cristina. The fire-maiden finally turned back and reproached her with a look. "Really, Cristina? I told you to get some fucking rest." "I'll rest when I'm dead." "That's what everyone down here thought. The witch sighed, wondering if they could break the siege before it broke them. Another drone flew by, raining more propaganda. "I was thinking of sending our guests a nice postcard," Cristina cracked her neck and fingers. As she was leaving the radio room, she noticed a bunch of tools littering a table. One caught her attention. "Are you going to use this hammer? Can I borrow it?" "Hmmm, sure, but... why would you need this hammer?" "In case I find a nail." ----- Miles away, on the other side of the battlefield, Hersir Thorsten's tent was plagued by a nine-fingered vermin.
