Thorsten smiled. For the first time in weeks, things were starting to get interesting again. "She never ceases to amaze me." "Why the fuck are you smiling? Let's make something clear: if I'm going down, you are coming with me..." Nate wanted to keep shitalking, but the words stuck in his throat. It was only for a brief moment, but he thought he saw a cold gleam in Thorsten’s gaze—predatory eyes that stirred a primal terror within him. //The Wolf of Winter.// He tried to regain composure. //Ridiculous//, Nate thought, //he is nothing but a brute.// At this point, Thorsten was not even paying attention to his unwelcomed guest. Through the entrance of the tent, he had noticed a faint glow, seemingly coming from above. He stepped to get a look outside: officers and soldiers were running chaotically, failing to respond to the drone crisis. Thorsten looked up; the painted ceiling of the Underworld cavern had been adorned with a message, etched in glowing letters: [[=]] ++++ Kneel and Surrender? ++++ Kneel and Surrender your ass, Ravenfuckers! [[/=]] Thorsten got back to the tent, smiling internally. He hadn't felt so young in ages. "You know what, Nate? You may be an idiot, but you may have a point. It's time to end this dance once and for all." "Finally!" Nate exclaimed sardonically. "I was wondering when you would grow a pair." Thorsten decided to ignore that last part. "Tell all the troops to get ready. Prepare the heavy artillery..." "Hell yeah!" Nate raised his fist. "And a big white flag." "What?" ----- Fallen drones littered No Man's Land. The bulk of Mictlán's army, //difuntos//, alebrijes and xolotls alike, remained entrenched but alert and ready for a fight. The Pale Lady and Cristina's group stood in the open, waiting for the Ravens to arrive at the site of the parley. "I don't like this," said Baruch the jaguar-nahual, "this has to be the most obvious trap ever." "They could blow us up with artillery at any time," observed Guadalupe. "If it comes to that, I'll raise a shield to protect us," Cristina wanted to reassure them as much as she wanted to reassure herself. "Are you sure it will hold?" "For the most part..." A guttural shriek pierced the silence, while the sound of drums and marching boots rumbled through No Man's Land. Thousands of voices, chanting gutturally in a dead language, echoed as the Raven army approached the defenders of Mictlán. An imposing figure led the army, a two-meter-tall frame encased in power armor. His footsteps were heavy, rising louder and stronger above the rest of the percussive cacophony. He dragged a remarkably large battle-axe, leaving a scar through the sacred soil of the underworld: a weapon of such a size and wickedness that it would have looked ridiculous if wielded by anyone else.  Two women flanked the giant, one had a metallic arm and donned a white, expressionless mask hiding murderous intent. The other was a spectral apparition, an ancient herald of dread and ruin. Behind the Valkyrie and La Llorona, a flag bearer carried the white flag of truce, and a man in a suit struggled to keep the warrior's pace. The boots finally stopped their march, and while the guttural choir ceased chanting, the cruel echoes still haunted the air. "Is all this circus really necessary?" complained the suit. "Shut up, Nate." Murmured Thorsten, and he raised his voice and weapon to address his enemies. "I am Hersir Thorsten, commander of the 13th Armored and the 25th Infantry Division of the Valravn Corporation. I have come here to parley with the Ruler of Mictlán." "That would be me," replied the Pale Lady. "You shall address me as any of my many names and titles: La Santa Muerte, La Catrina, La Patrona, La Dama Pálida, La Niña Blanca, La Flaquita, La Huesuda, La Tiznada, La Parca, La Malquerida, La Viuda Blanca, La Dueña de los Alebrijes, la Madrina, Azrael, and Mictecacíhuatl. Or just Catrina. And here standing besides are Las Viboras, Defenders of Mictlán: Lorena, the three-times blessed Daughter of the Sun, Baruch, Jaguar-warrior of Clan Bah, Guadalupe, Righter of Wrongs and Defector from the Foundation, and Cristina, Best Student of the Black Queen, the Thief of Books, la Bruja, and Comandanta of my armies." "Cristina!" exclaimed Thorsten in an oddly sincere and warm tone. "It is an honor to finally meet you!" "Is it, though?" snarked the witch. "Of course, since we started this little dance of Ravens and Vipers, I couldn't help but admire your martial talents. This is the most fun I've had in centuries." "And I have no idea who the hell you are." "//Meh//, I'm nothing but a simple man. Standing beside me are Valravn's finest: Sister Sifvar," he first gestured towards the Valkyrie, and then towards La Llorona, "and Sister Amelia." He then rolled his eyes and pointed to the suited man, "That one, standing over there, is Nate. Don't mind him." "I am the Midwestern Regional President of Valravn," protested Nate. "Former Midwestern Regional President of Valravn," corrected Thorsten. "Anyways, Cristina, let's waste no more time. You have masterfully disabled our drone fleet, a hard hit for our offensive capabilities. Unfortunately for you, I still have plenty of ways to reduce the Tomb City to ashes. Let me show you." He then nodded to Sifvar, and the Valkyrie pressed a button on her armpad. Almost immediately, a missile rose from one of the launchers at the Valravn base directly to the Necropolis. It hit one of the palace bell towers, shattering its pieces across the Lady's citadel. Screams of terror echoed through the ranks of the dead, and the old merc cruelly smiled. "As you see, I can reduce this whole place to rubble at any time, but that is not what I want." //Mierda.// Cristina said internally. Still, she was determined to remain firm. "We have endured the siege. We will endure your missiles. We will endure everything you throw at us. We will never surrender." "I know," Thorsten kept smiling. "And I wouldn't want it any other way. What is the point of a battle just by pressing buttons? No, no, Hel no! I wouldn't want that! I have come here to challenge you, Champion of Mictlán." "Challenge me?" "To a duel. //Axcan quema, tehuatl, nehuatl//... //Now, you and I//. Until someone dies or kneels. If I win, Mictlán surrenders; if you win, we pack and leave you alone." "Have you fuckin lost your mind?" Nate shouted hysterically, "Why would you risk the mission in a stupid duel? We got them! Just bomb them to oblivion! Enough! You are getting court-martialed. I hereby relieve you of your position! Sifvar! Amelia! Arrest this madman!" Thorsten didn't even turn to look at Nate. "Sifvar, I need silence," he spoke calmly but annoyed. The Valkyrie just nodded and drew a kukri knife. For a moment, it felt as if she was about to slice his throat, but instead, she hit him hard in the face with the pommel. The former Midwestern Regional President of Valravn fell to the ground, sobbing and grabbing his broken nose as blood ran from it, tainting the Holy grounds of Mictlán. "Honestly," Thorsten continued, "I don't know why the High Table wants this place so badly. Neither do I know what unholy business Zenith is planning to do with this sacred place. And I couldn't care less. I have fought their wars long enough to understand they are meaningless! Devoid of any higher purpose beyond their money! Fuck the High Table! And Fuck Zenith! I want this place for me! And I will earn it like a warrior!" His eyes shone when speaking those last words, and, for a brief moment, Cristina perceived a strange aura around Thorsten. It felt like the rage and hunger of a primordial beast, the fangs of a conqueror and a devourer. "You seem too eager to betray your masters. Why should we trust you to keep your word?" asked Cristina. "We mercenaries may not have loyalty. But we do have honor. The High Table may believe gold is enough to buy my obedience, but I have never truly given them my word. I am, however, giving it to you now." The revolutionary group remained silent, unsure of how to approach the bizarre challenge. After a few eternal moments, Guadalupe decided to be the first one to speak: "I don't like this guy," they said in a quiet voice. "Me neither, but what options do we have?" answered Lorena. "Not much really," La Comandanta felt a shiver down her skin. She could sense the air charged with something... ancient and ominous. "Cristina," the Pale Lady grabbed her arm, "you felt it too, right? I don't think deceit is what we should fear from this one. This man is on a mission. A sacred one. That doesn't make him righteous, but we must accept his challenge." Cristina sighed. “I know.” There was no way they could win a conventional war, especially if the Ravens chose to unleash the full force of their arsenal. But settling it with a duel… that almost seemed too good to be true. Never mind, she thought. Even if it was some twisted trap or a cruel joke, she had to take the chance and make the most of whatever happened next. Improvisation had always been one of her magical talents—at least, that’s what Allison used to say. She turned to face the axe-wielding giant. “Thorsten, we accept your challenge.” ----- An alebrije had brought a finely decorated art-decó makeup case. The Lady of Death opened and took out a brush. "This makeup is part of me. It has my soul and my skin. It will bind you to the Xolotl, it will bind you to my roots. It will open to you the doors of primordial magic, but you will have to discover that on your own. It is a gift that I can only give to those dearest to me, for it will make you a living Catrina. It is both a war paint and a costume for celebration. Let it protect you both in war and peace." And the Lady began to humbly apply the makeup over Cristina's face. Behind this seemingly mundane act, there was something holy, ancient, and deep taking place. It was an act of death and rebirth, the true power of symbols. La Catrina, the playful and colorful embodiment of the bittersweet joy of Día de Muertos. La Santa Muerte, the terrifying yet merciful Saint of Death, revered equally by both the victims and the victimizers. And the deep and primordial roots of Mictecacíhuatl, a being so antique that it defied comprehension. A trinity of symbols overlapping on each, a superposition that should be paradoxical yet still made perfect sense, such was the mysterious nature of the gods. "Now you are ready to go, //querida//." Cristina nodded and raised her fist with quiet resolve. Then, wielding a macuahuitl, she walked to the No Man's Land, where the Hersir awaited her. Around them, her friends, the dead, alebrijes, and xolotls, as well as the Valkyrie, La Llorona, the suit, and the Raven mercenaries, all of them awaited eagerly the spectacle that would decide the fate of this war. "I have waited for so long for this moment," Thorsten kept smiling like a child about to open a gift. "Cristina, this is such a beautiful moment." "Let's get this over with." "As you wish." The sound of servo motors running was barely enough to warn Cristina of the upcoming attack. Thorsten moved his axe with speed and precision, unlikely for a weapon and a man of that gargantuan size. Cristina felt adrenaline rushing through her veins. She avoided the strike, but it was a close call. "You are faster than you look, gonna give you that," said La Bruja. "Good that you are quick too, would be a shame if this dance ended so soon..." Thorsten looked down, confused—his legs had begun to sink into the ground, trapping him. Cristina jumped on him, trying to break his guard with her weapon, but the Hersir blocked her attack and pushed her away. Then he effortlessly broke away from the trap. But Cristina had not wasted her time. She could feel it in her skin, the Pale Lady's makeup gifting her a new connection to the taumathurgical forces of Mictlán. She was now confident and felt in control. At her command, multiple stone pillars, carved with the angry faces of forgotten spirits, rose from the ground and fell over his enemy. The Hersir jumped back, narrowly avoiding getting crushed. "Bravo! Marvelous play!" exclaimed Thorsten. He seemed mostly unbothered, and that was starting to annoy Cristina. "Look, you may be big and strong, but I'm a witch. My tricks are infinite, and you are fighting on my terms. You may start to consider kneeling if you value your life." "Kill me, if it's so easy. But don't pretend you're not enjoying this like me." "Is this a game for you?" Her annoyance gave way to rage, as all the horrors unleashed by the Ravens flashed through her memory. Guatemala. Bolivia. México. "After all the lives you have taken? All the suffering you have caused? Does that not matter to you?" Cristina shouted. "//Atl tlachinolli//. Burning Water... the Nahua captured it perfectly. What a beautiful way to encapsulate the paradoxical nature of War." "Shut up!" Cristina charged again with her macuahuitl, but she was easily parried. "War is a paradox. Terrible but also inevitable and... quite fun. It brings out both the best and the worst of humanity. And it is often necessary to make war to keep the peace. It shouldn't, but that contradiction makes perfect sense. //Burning Water//. But don't play dumb, you already know this, //guerrillera//." "You can wax poetically all you want, but you are just another greedy fascist who only cares for himself! Do you have any idea of what is at stake here? Do you know what will happen if Mictlán falls?" "I know Mictlantecuhtli threatened to break the Pillars of Earth. But it won't be necessary, I'll do it myself." Those last words caught Cristina off guard, and Thorsten saw the opening; his axe lunged like a bird of prey upon its quarry. But then, he felt an impact on his weapon and lost his grip. To his surprise, it was not the macuahuitl that had parried his attack; Cristina had suddenly conjured a gleaming cloud on her hand, from which a double-barreled shotgun emerged. She fired it without hesitation and blew away his opponent's weapon. Then, she did not waste time and rolled across the ground to position herself behind him, firing again at the main servomotor of the armor. "You parried my axe with a bullet!" Thorsten shouted, genuinely excited. "I warned you that my tricks were limitless. And now you can't move in this armor with the servo-motors ruined." A regular round fired by a regular person wouldn't have damaged the reinforced mechanism of the Hersir's armor. Fortunately, Cristina was anything but a regular person. Thorsten just smiled and shrugged; the armor fell to the ground. He now faced the witch, unarmored and bare-chested. "Do you kneel now?" The witch pointed the macuahuitl at his throat. "And ruin all this fun? You know that is not happening." "Perhaps I misjudged you. You are not greedy, you are just insane!" And then she plunged the bladed weapon into his ribs. But to her surprise, she did not feel the cut in the flesh, nor did she see blood pouring. Instead, the blades of the macuahuitl shattered. At the impact zone, his skin had become dark and dense, a hardened fiber. "What? How?" "Nanomachines, girl." "Come on!" The hardened punch she received in the face would have killed her if she hadn't raised a kinetic barrier just in time to absorb it. Still, she flew a few meters into the air. "Cristina!" Shouted Baruch, and he tried to rush towards her, Lorena and Guadalupe following him. But their path was promptly blocked by a kukri-wielding Sifvar and Amelia's biomechanically implanted claws. "No one shall interfere with the duel," threatened the Valkyrie. "She is right," The Pale Lady touched Baruch's shoulder, "This is Cristina's fight and only hers." "But..." "She is still alive. And I have faith in her." Baruch felt relieved as he saw Cristina standing, albeit with difficulty. But now Thorsten approached her with raised arms, which now glowed in the shape of a pair of spectral, beastly claws. "What the hell are you?" murmured the witch. "I don't want to kill you, Cristina," Thorsten spoke for the first time in a somber tone. Gone was his past playful demeanor. //Shit//, thought Cristina, //he is serious now//.  Her confidence, strong like steel just a few moments ago, lay now shattered by the punch she just received. She was not facing an ordinary foe, but the abominable offspring of unholy magic and technological depravity. "I won't kneel." "Perhaps you'll change your mind if we take a trip together to the origin." Thorsten's raised claws pierced the painted sky, and the curtain fell, cut into pieces; they were now standing at the Cempasuchitl Fields. A wolf howled, and a blinding snow began to swallow the orange flowers. "Behold Fimbulwinter, the prelude of Ragnarok! Man shall become the wolf of man!" "Why on Earth do you want to destroy the Pillars?" "//Atl tlachinolli//. Paradox. The men who destroyed my village and enslaved my family spoke of mercy. And yet they carried a tortured god on a cross. But I get it now, the paradox makes perfect sense." Cristina's magic absorbed another fist, but she could still feel part of the pain. "I can no longer hear my gods; there is no Thor in the storm, nor Wotan in the skies. Perhaps they are dead, or perhaps they have forsaken us. Perhaps they were always traitors and deceivers. Doesn't really matter. The only Rule of Nature is that the strong shall devour the weak." He continued pummeling Cristina. "The Christian God was stronger than my gods, but even He was replaced by a bigger fish: The God of Money!" Cristina's arms weighed like anchors, yet she kept her kinetic guard up. Thorsten continued punching both with fist and words: "Your gods are also weakened, barely a shadow of their former selves. Think of the fate of hummingbird god, Huitzilopochtli..." "Don't you dare say that name!" Cristina's voice almost broke. "Even if you could defeat me, do you think you can hold Mictlán forever? Think, Cristina, think! Worse things will come for you! Worse Gods will rise, even crueler than the God of Money! I am your only lifeline!" He threw another punch, but this time it didn't hit Cristina. Instead, it fractured the cempasuchilt, the broken fragments of orange-stained glass shattered all over them. When the broken rain finally stopped, they were now standing on the humid roots of the inverted Ceiba Tree hanging over the Necropolis of Mictlán. Above them stood the mighty Pillars of Earth, extending endlessly into the eternal abyss of shadows. "This world is tainted beyond repair. Why do you insist on it? Valhalla is just a faint memory, lost forever, and soon Mictlán will follow. Yet the Sillicon Nornir foretold me it would be a witch who would show me the way to a new age. Whether you accepted or not, this was Fate." He extended his hand to Cristina. "Let this world burn, Cristina. Let the Fifth Sun and the Nine Worlds die, and from their ashes we shall build something new. Something more beautiful than ever. Mictlán and Valhalla shall rise together. Here we will build the Ark carrying the worthy to the new world, Idavoll... Avalon." Above Thorsten, a colossal wolf with translucent, sanguineous fur rose. It was the spectre of Fenrir, eyeing the Pillars with frenetic hunger; its jaws dripping saliva in bloodlust and anticipation. "The old world is dying and the new world struggles to be born..." the Hersir grinned manically like the jaws of a wolf, "now is the time of monsters." Cristina looked very small, faced against the giant warrior and the gaping jaws of the beastly incarnation of entropy. Still, she began to laugh, blood dripping from her nostrils. "So you have given up on this world, and this is why you want to start Ragnarok. Good grief." She spat a bloody glob at his opponent’s feet. "You know what, Thorsten? For a second, I thought you were making sense... and then you came up with this nihilist bullshit. Give me a fucking break! Pathetic..." "I have brought with me the Wolf that will devour the Sun and the Moon. One way or another, Ragnarok is inevitable." "You are forgetting something." "Am I?" "You are not the only one with a pet." It emerged from the shadow of time, the stealthy silhouette had been stalking its foe, waiting for the perfect time to ambush it. When the moment came, it sprang from its dark hiding place, madly howling with fangs bared. Xolotl, Lord of Monstrosities, bit Fenrir in the neck, and the Hersir writhed as if he could feel such pain. The two primordial canids clashed in a violent embrace, and the cacophony of their howls and barks reached the deepest confines of the universe. "Also," the witch stood and smiled defiantly, "your gods never went silent. You were just too stubborn to listen!" Cristina raised her hand, and the old rusty hammer materialized from a cloud of electrons and quarks. "Impossible," muttered the Hersir, still recovering his breath. Cristina hit Thorsten in the ribs, and sparks and thunder illuminated the primordial darkness. For the first time in centuries, the Vessel of Fenrir felt true pain again. "I wonder if those nanomachines can withstand this level of electrical power. Only one way to find out." And she kept hammering the Hersir, each strike a lightning bolt of thousands of volts. And every time the hammer hit the vessel, a thunderbolt struck the dire wolf’s skin as well; Fenrir howled in rage and pain as Xolotl's jaws and claws tore away his burned flesh. Overwhelmed, Thorsten tried to back away, but the ancient roots of the world-tree came to life, entangling his arms and legs. "These are the roots of Mictecacíhuatl. Perhaps my gods are stronger than they look," Cristina smirked, "Now, kneel." "You know that is not happening!" "I said: Kneel!" The roots pulled Thorsten down, and he finally fell to his knees. He sighed, "So it had to be this way." The nanotech's hardened fiber was no more; the electrical shock had disabled it, softening the Hersir's impenetrable skin. Cristina picked one of the obsidian blades broken from the macuahuitl and made a wide cut in Thorsten's chest. She then reached her hand deep inside. As she did it, she felt the void of darkness burning her skin as the howls of Fenrir became increasingly erratic and pitiful. But she didn't stop. With all of her strength, the witch grabbed and pulled the still pulsating heart of the Hersir. Holding his heart, he saw visions of the past: a burning village, a small child taken from his family, centuries of war hardening him to become the vessel of the Wolf. "If Valhalla is what you want, then I shall give it to you!" And she stabbed the heart with the obsidian blade. "Cristina..." There was no anger or grief in Thorsten's voice. Instead, there was... relief, "Thanks." That was his final word, and his body fell lifeless. Cristina turned her head to face Xolotl, standing triumphantly with the bloodied head of Fenrir hanging from its jaws. The defeated specter howled one last time before dissipating back into entropy. Cristina reached out her hand to pat Xolotl's nose, and the eyeless guard dog of the Underworld nodded to the witch. Then, he turned around to return to his dwelling in the depths of Time. Cristina closed her eyes and breathed. When she opened them, she was back at Mictlán, surrounded by the bewildered spectators. "Cristina! You did it!" Her friends rushed to hug her, and they almost lost their balance. Even the Pale Lady and some alebrijes joined the group hug. "Sifvar!" Nate had somewhat recovered from her punch, more or less managing to stand, "They're distracted! I command you to attack! We have to avenge Hersir Thorsten." Amelia materialized behind the former regional president and grabbed him by the neck. Sifvar walked next to his ear. "In case you don't understand what Amelia is communicating, I'll spell it to you: Don't you dare say his name. If you ever manage to be one tenth of the man Thorsten was, then perhaps your life would be worth a dime, maggot. The Hersir gave us one last order, and we are obeying him. Till the end." La Llorona dematerialized again, and Hansen dropped to his knees, sobbing. The Valkyrie turned around to face Cristina, who had broken free from the celebration to seal the negotiations. "You... you bested the Hersir in combat..." Sivfar spoke in a mix of shock, rage, and admiration. "Are you leaving, Raven?" "We are. But I'm taking the Hersir's body with me. That is not a question." "Be my guest," replied the witch. It took eight of Sivfar's men and an unusually large body bag to carry Thorsten's body away. As the Ravens walked away, Amelia appeared next to Sivfar, who had turned around to address the witch one last time: "Comandanta Cristina, the next time we meet... I'll kill you." "Say whatever makes you feel better, bitch. Just fuck off already." Cristina returned the murderous gaze of the shield-maiden with equal intensity and hate. "War is over!" The Pale Lady shouted with an ancient, otherworldly voice that rang with the force of a chorus of thousands of souls, its echo stretching into the depths of infinity. She had stepped between the two would-be opponents, who in turn recoiled instinctively. Then, she returned to her usual soft and gentle tone and spoke to the valquirie and her companion, "Sivfar, Amelia, //queridas//... As the Queen of Death, it is my duty to remind you that it is beneath both the [[[https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/scp-8503 | Valkyrie]]] and the [[[https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/scp-7712| Cihuateoteo]]] to be slaves of the Raven. Break away before you follow your hersir." La Llorona's ghostly face showed no emotion, but she lowered her gaze slightly. The valkyrie merely turned her back on the Lady, ignoring her words. "Let's go, Amelia." And as the last Raven left Mictlán never to return again, Cristina finally fell to her knees. She was about to cry, she could finally breathe free, she could finally... finally get some fucking rest. ----- Cristina woke up in an elegant room; she recognized it as one of the guest suites of the Lady's Art Deco palace. The door opened, and the Pale Lady walked in, followed by the purple capybara butler. "Good morning, Lady Cristina. Would you like some coffee and brunch?" asked the capybara. "Don't call me... You know what... yeah fuck it, give me everything." The butler bowed and then pranced out of the room. "He means well," said the Pale Lady as she sat on the side of the bed. "Did all of that really happen?" Cristina had awoken with this strange, surreal feeling that the last few months, years... perhaps her whole life had been nothing but a dream. "Cristina, //querida//, thanks for everything." The Holy Death took her hand. "There is no way we will ever be able to pay you." "It is not necessary to pay, I did this as a promise, do you remember?" //It was all real//, she finally believed. "But I would have done it anyway; this is what I do. This is what Las Víboras do. We kick oppressors and fascists' asses wherever we find them." The Lady laughed, "You and your friends are really something else." "Yes, they are the best... My friends! Where are they? Is everyone safe?" "Worry not, they are getting some well-deserved rest just like you. Soon we'll be having a big feast to celebrate this victory!" "Amazing!" Cristina couldn't remember the last time she had a decent meal. "I need some good food! What are you having?" "The main course will be pozole..." "//A huevo!//" "Made from the flesh of our dead enemies..." "..." "There will also be a vegan option if you prefer that." "Thanks." "Anyways, I'll be on my way. Need to supervise the xolotls so they don't eat all the ingredients before we can cook," the Paly Lady stood graciously and walked to the door. "Meanwhile, you get more rest, //querida//." "Wait, Catrina!" Cristina said as the Lady was about to leave the room. "Yes, //querida//?" replied the Holy Death. "I have been thinking about his words. He was an evil, broken, deranged man, but at least on some level, his rambling made sense. We won today... but what will come tomorrow? We can't keep like this forever." "//Atl tlachinolli//, Cristina. Sometimes, the only way forward is to embrace the paradox. In the wise words of a trickster: '//To be seen, you have to cover your face... to be named, you have to deny your own name, you gamble your present to secure a future, and... to live... you die.'//" "I know that speech, Catrina..." "Maybe the way forward is to protect what we have to the last end. Or maybe we have to learn to let things go. Or perhaps there is another unknown option, but whatever the case is..." "We will decide for ourselves." "Indeed, //querida//. Indeed." When the butler capybara came back with the coffee and //pan de muerto//, he found Cristina already asleep. //I guess she can ask her pyromaniac friend to heat the coffee when she wakes up//, he thought as he left the tray on the nightstand. ----- [[span style="color:#0c0c0c; font-size: 5%"]] "Oh, you are here! I didn't notice you before. Pardon me, //querida//, for not giving you a proper welcome. Are you here to join the celebrations? "I'm not here to party, Catrina." "Cristina would certainly be very happy to see you..." "I’ve fulfilled my promise. Now is just a turn." "I know you won't listen, but... may I give you one last warning before you fuck everything again?" "I'm not in the mood for this. Answer my question, Lady of the Death: Where is Gears?" March 20th, 1918

The world had answered the tempting call of darkness a few hours ago, bringing a further sense of glumness to the metropolis just when the two businessmen arrived from an exhaustive plane travel. Both wore large overcoats of a faded, uninspired shade of beige, spick and span dress pants, and a black pair of shoes. Their dry mouths and eyes, bitter taste clawing against their throats, and the ravishing vertigo were the perfect company to that style, because they captured even more the morbid, potentially regrettable curiosity that led them to Cape Town; one with such a life of its own it completely overshadowed the primary affairs they would have to solve before facing the ecstasy they were craving for, deep down. That nauseating feeling grew stronger and stronger each time it was denied.

They had never met Nathan Terblanche in person before, as a few exchanges through letters and telephone calls were sufficient to coordinate the next steps to be taken in the exploration of Hawthorne Island. But once it was done, Fritz did his research, and so did Liam too after he was invited to be in the presence of the world's richest man.

Nathan graduated in psychology at the University of Cape Town. His family passed thaumaturgic knowledge and mysterious artifacts from one generation to another. Such circumstances seemed to make Nathan more than a magician; he was a walking outrage ready to free people from Plato's cave, people would say. Men advised one another to see Nathan in their free time and shuddered, and where Nathan went, the rest vanished. To think about his alleged doings — prophecies no other person would ever dare making, the miracle that brought the Savior back to life — felt like having such autonomy over one's body you could order it to release adrenaline whenever needed.

It was sinful; to be blessed by God and be under the Devil's spell at the same time.

"The map, please." Fritz asked while taking a pack of Marlboro out of his pocket and lighting up a creased cigarette. "We're late. Don't wanna mess this up after everything."

Liam nodded, arranging his fedora before opening his suitcase to get the map and give it to the older man, the Administrator of the SCP Foundation. He scratched his neck and quickened his step, fearless to explore the lone wolves that are the alleys and sidewalks past midnight. Both Liam and the lunatic full moon above them decided to follow Fritz's guidance; it was glowing in a beautiful red, a unique vermilion that wouldn't be matched for centuries, as if the skies had painted it with ink, still fresh and quite effervescent.

The venue was the mansion of the Terblanche family. Its ownership was passed to Nathan after his father assumedly entered an irreversible comatose state many years ago, and said the connoisseurs of the 'esoteric arts' that its level of reality itself would meet negative scores, given Nathan's willingness to conceive any wishes with his mere thought. Hidden by trees, buildings, and factories, there it was, waiting to be found by those who left it all behind; it was seemingly the highest point in the city, floors and more floors of pure treasure swirling into and out of each other, with the open windows revealing such an amount of colors, some unknown to the human eye, that it felt as if two suns were dancing through the skies and Hubble's recent discoveries were nothing but a glimpse of the true chaotic nature of the cosmos.

From that noisy imagery, the God-shaped silence came; a silent void in the form of a voice, a playful and inviting voice that turned their heads immediately to its direction. For how long he was there, it didn't matter; what mattered was that he was, simply. The man made of gold.

He was slender, tall — roughly 6'5" — and of a skin so pale it rivaled the aspect of the winter's snow. Bright blue eyes of a snake and silky hairs of amber matched elegantly his pompous style of a red and black trench coat made of the most polished fabric, with an old wooden cane in his hands to support his walk. He was surrounded by several types of cars that the two men could swear were not there before, of the working class and the bourgeoisie, of waste and wealth; naturally antagonistic but united by something way, way above of both — not the top of the pyramid, but the pyramid itself.

Nathan had a slight smile on his face and calmly waved to Liam and Fritz, who crossed the road in a hurry. They looked the man in the eye deeply — his soul had nothing to hide. His smile widened.

"Good night, dear Fritz. And before you say it, please let me assure you the pleasure is all mine."

He nodded, then Nathan turned to Liam with a glimpse of surprise in his eyes.

"And I see you brought a friend indeed. Care to tell me your name, son?"

"Turner, Sir. Liam Turner of the Overseer Council."

Fritz completed, "He's our most recent addition."

Nathan nodded. "It's a courageous move to put a Negro in such a high position at times like this, isn't it?"

Fritz looked at Liam. He was still, arms crossed.

"Now now, this is not a complaint. In fact, dare I say I'm quite ahead of my colleagues when it comes to this matter."

"Good to know, sir," Liam replied with a smile, "but that aside, shall we enter? We're quite late."

A chuckle. "Of course son, but don't be so orthodox. I would never begin an exhibition when everyone hasn't arrived."

"Exhibition?" Fritz interrupted. "I thought we would discuss our partnership first."

And Nathan replied in an instant, "One can do both at the same time."

The insides of the house were of more impelling fascination and allurement than the looks of the outside. Endless stairs led to choking rooms above, and their size seemed to let out a shrunken creak as it was studied, each of which seemed to echo in a different direction. Regardless of where they were looking, Liam and Fritz's eyes would only meet instruments of glass and metal, and then instruments of both combined in a yet stranger nature.

A smell one's mind could only recognize as a light scent of vivid tumors hovered in the air, and as Nathan's cane stepped on the floor, its clicking sound resembling the one of a clockwork, varied forms appeared amidst the pillars of creation sustaining the main room. And as their faces were revealed, the men could only remember the antagonism they thought of earlier: people of both the bourgeoisie and the working class united to celebrate Nathan, but in a quite sinister view — one only the likings of capitalism could offer as the vampire that feeds off its intestine in an all-embracing hunger.

The looks of those people seemed not exaggerated but rather monsterified to the greatest extent; those one may consider 'poor' barely had teeth in their mouths or clothes to wear, and their skins — dear God, their skins were whirling, churning, and then struggling against air itself, as if it could burn them, trying to banish them from a world they could never belong to. And those one may consider 'rich' were worse! Liam and Fritz had to cover their mouths to avoid vomiting as their superiority could be tasted, and it tasted like piss and blood mixed with caviar and rotten cigarattes. The bourgeoisie was taller too, and their columns were bulging through the skin and curving, bending to their own self-rightness to the point the heads were meeting the floor made of gold. And both rich and poor people were separated in several pairs of a rich and a poor person each, always firmly holding hands and dancing a dance they would not acknowledge to themselves that they had seen.

"Who— what are these people?"

"Dear Fritz, do not raise your voice like that." He put his hand over the man's shoulder. "And remember, it is rude to talk about someone who's listening."

"But Sir," Liam intervened in a hurry, "it's even ruder to ignore what's going on—"

He turned to Liam calmly. "What is wrong, son?"

"What isn't?" Said Fritz.

And one of the figures replied and cursed the room to silence, "Those who have seen Nathan before look on sights which others saw not."

The two men swallowed, and nothing else could they do besides watching in horror as Nathan gave an unsanctified smile and became the soul and center of that blasphemous chamber beyond time, overflowing with so many contradictions that the room soon felt embraced by the quasars that feed the greatest galaxies. And as the world began to revolve and sunder and displace science, thousands of muffled screams coming from unspoken things were heard and accompanied by maddening and sentient prayers that would inaugurate the thunderous crunching of drums, played by the gigantic nightmares from the edge of the universe to devour even the slightest part of reality one would wrongly call normalcy.

That was the beginning of the 'special exhibition' — at some point the men wouldn't dare to guess when, the lights went out and the moon opened its eyes and glittered beyond those windows made of cooling sun while howling, transmuting the blueness of Nathan's eyes into a purplish dream that evoked faceless symbols in the air and hurried to thrust their skin as a syringe's needle injecting the sacred waters of Heaven in their blood — and all fear suddenly disappeared, crushed by the lasting satisfaction of a monotonous humming from the burning angels they couldn't see, as the place became completely enamored not by darkness, but by the broken lamp itself, until all they saw was themselves; first two replicas of them, and in a second two of thousands, each one with their own individual but shared senses that together got to see the big picture of Nathan — and only Nathan — being blessed by thunder and stars crawling from the sky like snakes and an eternal rain falling as if tears, in a world Lucifer regretted his choices and was forgiven.

Then it all stopped again, and their minds became glass shards inside of a renovated skin, led by a speechless heart to a bland and simple office of one desk and two chairs, where Liam and Fritz were sitting before Nathan, who just finished preparing a cup of hot coffee for himself. Fritz's countenance was pale, and his skinless hands trembled whilst Liam stared right into the soul of Nathan Terblanche — and I assure it would be more precise to tell you what he didn't see rather than what he did, as ten thousand unspoken names and ten thousand unborn faces can correlate the contents of reality and mind just enough.

"Your friend doesn't seem well," Nathan said, "so let's get this over with for you to go back home."

And just when Liam was about to answer, Fritz intervened; he slowly lowered his head to look at the several papers in front of them.

"The SCP Foundation and Terblanche Enterprises shall cooperate with each other for the following one-hundred years."

Fritz nodded — he thought he was asleep and decided to simply keep going. It would have to end at some point.

Nathan proceeded to calmly open one of the desk's drawers and picked a simple sheaf of papers, stapled together in the top left corner, and handed it to Fritz. He held it and began to go through the pages as he saw the covering sheet reading simply, “Confidential Report on Special Items—Classified.”

"It's a special one, and it will surely help you." Nathan smiled. "It was my father's favorite."

Fritz's teary eyes grew wide, and in a moment of both sudden shock and realization, he began to laugh. He couldn't stop laughing and laughed with Nathan for what seemed like hours. He laughed as he left the mansion with Liam and laughed as they entered the plane in the morning. He laughed when he arrived at his house, and he laughed even more as Nathan opened the front door for him to get inside.

May 31st, 2024
Merlo Family Residence, Portland, Oregon

Sasha Merlo does not have a bad security system.

An Assistant Site Director for the Foundation already warrants the kind of protection usually afforded to federal judges and local politicians, but Merlo is the subject of special attention from internal security — given her personal vendetta with a real-life Bond villain, it is more than earned. Since the last time Vincent Anderson decided to visit, her apartment building has become one of the hardest targets in suburban Portland. Every room in the house has at least one panic button that can summon a full combat MTF within minutes, and the closet of the master bedroom has been fortified into a saferoom strong enough to hold off a squadron of battlemages long enough for that to matter.

Unfortunately, it is still an apartment building in suburban Portland, which carries with it certain intrinsic vulnerabilities, especially when dealing with the American government and its agents.

She knew this better than anyone; knew that the UIU was far more capable than they chose to appear. She had been a UIU agent once, and had spent a considerable part of her Foundation career working with the Unit. It had long been her habit to act as if they knew where she lived.

So Merlo wasn't exactly surprised when she came home to find the federal agent sitting in her living room, chatting amicably with her husband, Gabe.

It even made sense. If ever there was a situation that would prompt a home visit by the FBI, the imminent shift in consensus normalcy brought about by her nemesis — and by her failure to stop him — was certainly one.

So although she wasn't prepared, Merlo wasn't surprised that the UIU agent was there.

But she was surprised that it was Robin Thorne.

Once upon a time, Merlo would have counted Thorne as her closest ally within the UIU. That was before she had betrayed their trust, of course — left them in the dark so she could stage an illegal raid in Three Portlands in another failed attempt to capture Anderson. The two had barely spoken since, although Merlo had hoped that their cooperation on the final, finally successful raid on Anderson's headquarters might lead to some rapprochement. Thorne being in her house now made that prospect seem less likely.

"Perfect timing, honey," Gabe said cheerfully, although Merlo could tell that his smile was somewhat forced. "I was just telling Agent Thorne that you should be home any minute now."

Merlo pinched the bridge of her nose and sighed. "Thorne, if you're here to give me another lecture about my Ahabian tendencies, you can save your breath. I realize that none of this would have happened if I'd just let the Unit arrest him for the Caldwell incident."

Thorne looked at her blankly. "I have no idea what you're talking about."

Merlo blinked. "You haven't heard?"

They shrugged. "I've been taking some personal leave. I haven't heard anything about anything since this weekend."

She frowned. "You aren't here about Anderson?"

They shook their head. "No. Why, did he escape?"

"I should be so lucky," she muttered. "No, he only just orchestrated the biggest shift in consensus normalcy since the atom bomb from inside his damn cell. Figured you were here to chew me out about it. Seems like that's all anyone wants to do the last few days."

"Nope. I'll leave that to Spencer. Sounds like something he'll want to break out the special profanity for."

"Special profanity?" Gabe asked.

"He collects them," Thorne explained. "By his reckoning, he knows more insults, blasphemies, vulgarities, and curse words than anyone else alive. A lot of them can't even be used on this side of the Veil."

"Great, that'll be something to look forward to then." Merlo dropped into a seat across from Thorne. "Why are you here, Thorne?"

The other agent bit their lip. "I need your help, Sasha."

Merlo took a long, hard look at Thorne. There was something deeply off about the wizard's demeanor. Their eyes kept flitting about the room, even as their gaze lingered just a little too long on the exits. And there was a telltale tension in the air, a weight pressing down on reality that Merlo had learned to recognize from working with Navarro — Thorne was holding an evocation in their mind, ready to cast in an instant, even as they fidgeted on the couch and tried to appear nonchalant.

Thorne was expecting a fight.

She glanced at Gabe, making eye contact for just a moment, and was gratified to see him tip his chin ever-so-slightly in silent acknowledgment. He had picked up on it too.

"What seems to be the trouble?" Merlo asked.

"Maybe we could take a walk and discuss it?" Thorne suggested. As they spoke, they moved their hand to brush a strand of hair out of their face, but finished the motion by tapping their ear twice — an obvious coded gesture.

Merlo watched Gabe's face as he motioned with his eyes towards the blue table lamp, which concealed the nearest panic button.

"Sure, there's a dog park at the end of the block we can walk to." She blinked twice, answering Gabe's silent question in the negative. "Gabe, honey, why don't you get started on dinner. I don't think we'll be long."

As soon as they were outside, Thorne began muttering under their breath, a long string of mixed Latin, Celtic, Greek, and Old English words. Merlo could only pick out every third word or so, but just from that it was fairly obvious that Thorne was casting obfuscation wards around them to prevent eavesdropping.

Once they were done, Thorne reached into their jacket and pulled out the semi-spectral form of an albino robin, which they gingerly held in front of their face with both hands. "Circle aloft and stay out of sight. If you spot anything that seems off, break for the second nearest Way immediately and wait for me back at the federal building."

The familiar twittered a question in Celtic.

"Then tell Spencer everything."

The not-bird tilted its head to examine Merlo, then chirped another query.

"Yes, even that." Without waiting for a response, Thorne tossed the creature into the air, where it hovered for a moment before remembering that it was supposed to pretend to use its wings to fly.

Merlo watched bemusedly as the familiar drifted up and out of sight. "Paranoid enough?"

"Never," Thorne said. "The Foundation killed my mother."

"That's impossible." The words slipped out immediately, before Merlo could even think about it. "I was at the funeral, Thorne. She was killed by a Lighthouse Mafia gunman. Everyone knows that."

"Just like everyone knows wizards aren't real?" Thorne retorted. "The gunman was an escaped convict operating under the compulsion of a homicide geas that killed him via auto-memetic Cuchulainn syndrome. Before he died he was able to tell my mom that he had been recruited and released from prison — he thought by a three letter agency, but it's pretty obvious who it actually was."

"How on earth could you possibly know that?"

"Because before she died, she was able to record her last moments in this." Thorne held up a sunstone necklace that was hanging from their neck.

"And where's that been for the last 16 years?"

"Forgotten in evidence lockup. I had to break in to get it out."

Merlo studied the wizard with a new wariness, considering for the first time that they might actually be crazy. She was starting to regret telling Gabe not to call for an MTF. Her own personal panic button was in the front pocket of her jeans, but it might as well be on the far side of the Moon for all the good it would do her if Thorne decided to start throwing evocations around — the federal wizard might not have their mother's talent as a battlemage, but even the younger Thorne could easily turn her skull inside-out with a few words and some willpower.

"Okay, let's assume that all of that is true. That doesn't mean the Foundation is responsible. There's plenty of groups that could have pulled that off — the GOC, the Pentagram, probably a couple different CI cells."

"Oh please, Sasha, pull your head out of the sand for a second and try to think like a cop again. Means, opportunity, motive — they're all lacking the third one."

"The Chaos Insurgency—"

"Oh, you mean the one that's just a Foundation false flag?"

"It is not!" Merlo whirled on the wizard, disregarding personal safety to get directly in their face. "The Foundation does not engage in assassination, and certainly not against its allies. It just doesn't."

Thorne stared at her, steely-eyed and unwavering. "Tell that to Ross and Creed. Or did you mean that the Foundation only tries to assassinate its own agents?"

Merlo recoiled as if she had just been slapped. "That's not the same," she hissed. "That was the work of a rogue Ethics Committee member."

"And how many rogue elements are there in the Foundation?" Thorne asked. "How many secrets and lies and conspiracies that you don't even know of? The Foundation is not a monolith, and you are far too smart to believe the party line bullshit you're spewing at me, Sasha Merlo."

Thorne reached into their jacket again and pulled out their badge. The Eye of Providence seemed to wink at Merlo in the evening twilight. "You used to carry this badge, just like me, just like my mother. Do you remember? Do you remember taking an oath to serve the interests of truth and justice? To defend the innocent? Do you remember why any of us do this in the first place? Or has the Foundation taken your honor too? Filled your head with so much nonsense about necessary evils and hard choices that you don't even know what's right anymore?"

"I remember!" Merlo shouted. She took a breath. "I remember," she said again. "But think about what you're saying, Thorne. Do you have any idea what the consequences will be if you're right? If the Foundation really is behind your mother's death, then there is almost nothing they won't do to keep that secret."

"I know, and I don't care," Thorne said. "All I care about is this: what are you willing to do to help me prove it?"

When the history of the 8th Occult War is written, there are many moments that will eventually be cited as proximate causes. This isn't one of them. But it should be. Unbeknownst to anyone — certainly not to the two agents standing in an empty dog park in Portland, Oregon — a fateful decision is about to be made that will all-but-guarantee a collision course between the largest single normalcy organization and the dominant global superpower.

Sasha Merlo decides to do the right thing and help the child of an old friend.

She sighed. "I can check our files for any corroborating evidence."

She reached into her jacket and pulled out her secure phone, a chunky, featureless phablet with a full physical keyboard. She took a moment to pop the battery out and flip it around — a necessary precaution, as in its default configuration the phone wouldn't actually work except as a hand grenade, triggered by pressing the power button three times in rapid succession. She knew a couple agents who had lost fingers that way, and she didn't intend to join their ranks.

"I'm gonna start with your mom's old personnel file," Merlo explained, fingers flying through her secure login prompt. "It'll be an unreadable mess of codeword classifications, but we might be able to infer something even from the codewords I don't have clearance for."

She waited the few agonizing seconds for SCiPnet to respond to her query. "Here, see…" She turned the phone to show it to Thorne. "Grand Slam is gonna be the SATF Program, and Triton Point is for Site-246. No idea what Wise Guys is, but it looks like a sub-clearance of Grand Slam — maybe for the original Delta-3? Same with Love Doctor, that one only shows up in connection with Grand Slam or Wise Guys. Lightfoot Ballad is a complete mystery, but it only shows up twice in the 90s."

Thorne nodded. "That's when she left the Foundation, it's probably related to that."

"Makes sense."

"Are there any file sections from 2008? What are those classified under?"

Merlo tapped at the keyboard to scroll through the rest of the file. "Looks like… Blind Pythagoras, that's for the UIU, and Angry Bovine is MOOT. Here's one I haven't heard of… Lightfoot Elegy. It's the last clearance assigned to the file."

"Would that be related to Lightfoot Ballad?" Thorne asked.

"Probably."

"That's gotta be it then. Can you see what other files have that codeword on them?"

"Yeah, we've got…" Merlo paused, heart sinking as the results loaded in. "Ah, fuck."

"What?"

She didn't say anything, just handed the phone to Thorne.

"A file on the Oregon State Penitentiary and something redacted?"

"It's a person of interest file," Merlo explained. "Completely expunged, so there's just the RAISA metadata left. I've never seen that before."

"Sounds like someone trying to cover something up," Thorne said softly.

"Yeah, it sure does."

Thorne handed the phone back to Merlo. "Can you get anything out of them?"

Merlo shook her head. "No. It's above my clearance level. I'd need to get authorization from Holman—"

"No."

"Thorne, be reasonable. We've both worked with him for years, you can't seriously believe that he would—"

"That he would what? That he would authorize an illegal operation in Three Portlands?"

"That's different, and you know it."

"All I know is that my mom didn't trust him. Until we have proof that he wasn't involved, I'm going to follow her lead on this."

"Fine. But without Director-level clearance, you aren't getting those files."

Thorne rubbed their thumb against the sunstone necklace, their expression betraying the fact that they were clearly contemplating something distasteful.

"…Who's the current Director of Site-246?" They asked.

"The Draintrap? Cody Westbrook. Why?"

Thorne shook their head. "You're better off not knowing. Will anyone know you've been looking for these files?"

"Maybe. The RAISA request will be logged, and it might trip a flag if anyone is worried about someone digging. But I can pull some more of our files on the Unit to cover my tracks. If anyone asks, I'll just say that I was doing research for an assessment on whether we should try to recruit you and Spencer."

"Not happening."

"Well, yeah, that's obvious now, but it wasn't the last time Holman asked me about it." Merlo turned off the phone and reversed the battery again. "Don't worry too much about me, I know how to answer questions from internal affairs. Seems like that's half my job these days."

Thorne nodded. "Thank you, Sasha. For everything. For believing me."

"You'll forgive me if I'm not as pleased about it as you are." Merlo blew out a long breath. "I really didn't want you to be right."

"I know. I wish I wasn't."

"What's next?" Merlo watched dispassionately as a young yuppie couple approached, walking one of those trendy labradoodle hybrids with a rididuculous name — probably a snickerdoodle or something equally stupid.

Thorne stared pensively off into the distance. "Now I get to see if my badge has the right memetics to convince the TSA that I'm an Air Marshal. Otherwise, I'm walking to Minnesota."

Gabe asked. "He collects them," Thorne explained. "By his reckoning, he knows more insults, blasphemies, vulgarities, and curse words than anyone else alive. A lot of them can't even be used on this side of the Veil." "Great, that'll be something to look forward to then." Merlo dropped into a seat across from Thorne. "Why are you here, Thorne?" The other agent bit their lip. "I need your help, Sasha." Merlo took a long, hard look at Thorne. There was something deeply off about the wizard's demeanor. Their eyes kept flitting about the room, even as their gaze lingered just a little too long on the exits. And there was a telltale tension in the air, a weight pressing down on reality that Merlo had learned to recognize from working with Navarro -- Thorne was holding an evocation in their mind, ready to cast in an instant, even as they fidgeted on the couch and tried to appear nonchalant. Thorne was expecting a fight. She glanced at Gabe, making eye contact for just a moment, and was gratified to see him tip his chin ever-so-slightly in silent acknowledgment. He had picked up on it too. "What seems to be the trouble?" Merlo asked. "Maybe we could take a walk and discuss it?" Thorne suggested. As they spoke, they moved their hand to brush a strand of hair out of their face, but finished the motion by tapping their ear twice -- an obvious coded gesture. Merlo watched Gabe's face as he motioned with his eyes towards the blue table lamp, which concealed the nearest panic button. "Sure, there's a dog park at the end of the block we can walk to." She blinked twice, answering Gabe's silent question in the negative. "Gabe, honey, why don't you get started on dinner. I don't think we'll be long." As soon as they were outside, Thorne began muttering under their breath, a long string of mixed Latin, Celtic, Greek, and Old English words. Merlo could only pick out every third word or so, but just from that it was fairly obvious that Thorne was casting obfuscation wards around them to prevent eavesdropping. Once they were done, Thorne reached into their jacket and pulled out the semi-spectral form of an albino robin, which they gingerly held in front of their face with both hands. "Circle aloft and stay out of sight. If you spot anything that seems off, break for the second nearest Way immediately and wait for me back at the federal building." The familiar twittered a question in Celtic. "Then tell Spencer everything." The not-bird tilted its head to examine Merlo, then chirped another query. "Yes, even that." Without waiting for a response, Thorne tossed the creature into the air, where it hovered for a moment before remembering that it was supposed to pretend to use its wings to fly. Merlo watched bemusedly as the familiar drifted up and out of sight. "Paranoid enough?" "Never," Thorne said. "The Foundation killed my mother." "That's impossible." The words slipped out immediately, before Merlo could even think about it. "I was at the funeral, Thorne. She was killed by a Lighthouse Mafia gunman. Everyone knows that." "Just like everyone knows wizards aren't real?" Thorne retorted. "The gunman was an escaped convict operating under the compulsion of a homicide geas that killed him via auto-memetic Cuchulainn syndrome. Before he died he was able to tell my mom that he had been recruited and released from prison -- he thought by a three letter agency, but it's pretty obvious who it actually was." "How on earth could you possibly know that?" "Because before she died, she was able to record her last moments in this." Thorne held up a sunstone necklace that was hanging from their neck. "And where's that been for the last 16 years?" "Forgotten in evidence lockup. I had to break in to get it out." Merlo studied the wizard with a new wariness, considering for the first time that they might actually be crazy. She was starting to regret telling Gabe not to call for an MTF. Her own personal panic button was in the front pocket of her jeans, but it might as well be on the far side of the Moon for all the good it would do her if Thorne decided to start throwing evocations around -- the federal wizard might not have their mother's talent as a battlemage, but even the younger Thorne could easily turn her skull inside-out with a few words and some willpower. "Okay, let's assume that all of that is true. That doesn't mean the Foundation is responsible. There's plenty of groups that could have pulled that off -- the GOC, the Pentagram, probably a couple different CI cells." "Oh please, Sasha, pull your head out of the sand for a second and try to think like a cop again. Means, opportunity, motive -- they're all lacking the third one." "The Chaos Insurgency--" "Oh, you mean the one that's just a Foundation false flag?" "It is not!" Merlo whirled on the wizard, disregarding personal safety to get directly in their face. "The Foundation does not engage in assassination, and certainly not against its allies. It just doesn't." Thorne stared at her, steely-eyed and unwavering. "[[[portland-vice|Tell that to Ross and Creed]]]. Or did you mean that the Foundation only tries to assassinate its own agents?" Merlo recoiled as if she had just been slapped. "That's not the same," she hissed. "That was the work of a rogue Ethics Committee member." "And how many rogue elements are there in the Foundation?" Thorne asked. "How many secrets and lies and conspiracies that you don't even know of? The Foundation is not a monolith, and you are far too smart to believe the party line bullshit you're spewing at me, Sasha Merlo." Thorne reached into their jacket again and pulled out their badge. The Eye of Providence seemed to wink at Merlo in the evening twilight. "You used to carry this badge, just like me, just like my mother. Do you remember? Do you remember taking an oath to serve the interests of truth and justice? To defend the innocent? Do you remember why any of us do this in the first place? Or has the Foundation taken your honor too? Filled your head with so much nonsense about necessary evils and hard choices that you don't even know what's right anymore?" "I remember!" Merlo shouted. She took a breath. "I remember," she said again. "But think about what you're saying, Thorne. Do you have any idea what the consequences will be if you're right? If the Foundation really is behind your mother's death, then there is almost nothing they won't do to keep that secret." "I know, and I don't care," Thorne said. "All I care about is this: what are you willing to do to help me prove it?" ---- When the history of the 8th Occult War is written, there are many moments that will eventually be cited as proximate causes. This isn't one of them. But it should be. Unbeknownst to anyone -- certainly not to the two agents standing in an empty dog park in Portland, Oregon -- a fateful decision is about to be made that will all-but-guarantee a collision course between the largest single normalcy organization and the dominant global superpower. Sasha Merlo decides to do the right thing and help the child of an old friend. ---- She sighed. "I can check our files for any corroborating evidence." She reached into her jacket and pulled out her secure phone, a chunky, featureless phablet with a full physical keyboard. She took a moment to pop the battery out and flip it around -- a necessary precaution, as in its default configuration the phone wouldn't actually work except as a hand grenade, triggered by pressing the power button three times in rapid succession. She knew a couple agents who had lost fingers that way, and she didn't intend to join their ranks. "I'm gonna start with your mom's old personnel file," Merlo explained, fingers flying through her secure login prompt. "It'll be an unreadable mess of codeword classifications, but we might be able to infer something even from the codewords I don't have clearance for." She waited the few agonizing seconds for SCiPnet to respond to her query. "Here, see..." She turned the phone to show it to Thorne. "Grand Slam is gonna be the SATF Program, and Triton Point is for Site-246. No idea what Wise Guys is, but it looks like a sub-clearance of Grand Slam -- maybe for the original Delta-3? Same with Love Doctor, that one only shows up in connection with Grand Slam or Wise Guys. Lightfoot Ballad is a complete mystery, but it only shows up twice in the 90s." Thorne nodded. "That's when she left the Foundation, it's probably related to that." "Makes sense." "Are there any file sections from 2008? What are those classified under?" Merlo tapped at the keyboard to scroll through the rest of the file. "Looks like... Blind Pythagoras, that's for the UIU, and Angry Bovine is MOOT. Here's one I haven't heard of... Lightfoot Elegy. It's the last clearance assigned to the file." "Would that be related to Lightfoot Ballad?" Thorne asked. "Probably." "That's gotta be it then. Can you see what other files have that codeword on them?" "Yeah, we've got..." Merlo paused, heart sinking as the results loaded in. "Ah, fuck." "What?" She didn't say anything, just handed the phone to Thorne. "A file on the Oregon State Penitentiary and something redacted?" "It's a person of interest file," Merlo explained. "Completely expunged, so there's just the RAISA metadata left. I've never seen that before." "Sounds like someone trying to cover something up," Thorne said softly. "Yeah, it sure does." Thorne handed the phone back to Merlo. "Can you get anything out of them?" Merlo shook her head. "No. It's above my clearance level. I'd need to get authorization from Holman--" "No." "Thorne, be reasonable. We've both worked with him for years, you can't seriously believe that he would--" "That he would what? That he would authorize [[[austringers|an illegal operation in Three Portlands]]]?" "That's different, and you know it." "All I know is that my mom didn't trust him. Until we have proof that he wasn't involved, I'm going to follow her lead on this." "Fine. But without Director-level clearance, you aren't getting those files." Thorne rubbed their thumb against the sunstone necklace, their expression betraying the fact that they were clearly contemplating something distasteful. "…Who's the current Director of Site-246?" They asked. "The Draintrap? Cody Westbrook. Why?" Thorne shook their head. "You're better off not knowing. Will anyone know you've been looking for these files?" "Maybe. The RAISA request will be logged, and it might trip a flag if anyone is worried about someone digging. But I can pull some more of our files on the Unit to cover my tracks. If anyone asks, I'll just say that I was doing research for an assessment on whether we should try to recruit you and Spencer." "Not happening." "Well, yeah, that's obvious now, but it wasn't the last time Holman asked me about it." Merlo turned off the phone and reversed the battery again. "Don't worry too much about me, I know how to answer questions from internal affairs. Seems like that's half my job these days." Thorne nodded. "Thank you, Sasha. For everything. For believing me." "You'll forgive me if I'm not as pleased about it as you are." Merlo blew out a long breath. "I really didn't want you to be right." "I know. I wish I wasn't." "What's next?" Merlo watched dispassionately as a young yuppie couple approached, walking one of those trendy labradoodle hybrids with a rididuculous name -- probably a snickerdoodle or something equally stupid. Thorne stared pensively off into the distance. "Now I get to see if my badge has the right memetics to convince the TSA that I'm an Air Marshal. Otherwise, I'm walking to Minnesota." "Nicolette Krupps — you know that girl. Liaison with the FSD? Light brown hair, about this long?" Carmine held his fingertips to his shoulders.

"Sure? Vaguely." I squinted at him.

"Would you fuck her?"

It was a casual question to Carmine, not one worthy of weight or pretense. Twelve years in Administration will do that to you — years of working on the fly, of spitting out orders and seeing everyone in the vicinity scuttling around to follow with very few questions asked. You get used to it, and then you learn to just kinda say shit.

"She's helped me with some stuff, so I talk to her sometimes." He quote unquote 'clarified'.

"What? Are these statements supposed to relate to each other somehow?"

Carmine had always oscillated between being extremely direct and hopelessly unclear. This was some hellish abomination of both stitched together.

"Obviously."

"Is the first one a hypothetical, a request, or are you preempting a suggestion?"

"If you wouldn't say yes to the hypothetical, then why the fuck would I bother with the request or the suggestion afterwards?"

Another logical, yet entirely non-clarifying question — all of the sudden we were two or three layers deep into this ridiculous word game.

"Okay, so…" I took a deep breath.

I'd wondered about my potential attraction to women for a while, even before Carmine. After we got together, I'd given it up pretty early on — solely because I took him as the type to go headhunting the moment I even breathed in the direction of anyone else.

"Hypothetically, I would, sure."

He was always so possessive, so in control. I was surprised to learn that he, as he'd put it, didn't give a shit.

"Okay?" He looked at me expectantly, "How's about literally?"

He'd explained it to me before in typical Carmine fashion: "So, you're not going anywhere, I'm the right hand man of this site, I got nothing to be ashamed of, I'm not scared of no other men, my dick's probably bigger than theirs, and they're never knocking you up in a million years. What else is there?"

"Why?" I cocked my head to the side.

"I just think it would be mutually beneficial." He shrugged.


Carmine always had close ties with the Fire Suppression Department. Something to do with his fucked up family, was his explanation. I never doubted that per se, but there were certainly reasons I could see why others wouldn't buy it.

To everyone else, the FSD only comes to you – selling you a better life at the Foundation that you know won’t ever be fully realized, or worst case scenario, threatening you with a worse life that you know could be realized at any time. Nobody approaches the Fire Suppression Department, unscalded and free of embers, just for a chat.

Well, nobody except him.

The modus operandi of the FSD was, and had always been dealing in loyalty — it was the only currency they accepted, and they set the price every time. For everyone else, demanding more for less was extortion. But, the way he did it, it was a friendly favor — a preemptive one that "didn't mean anything" until he needed it to.

He’d gotten better at playing games over the years, and by 2005, he’d given up on bargains. Why would he, when he could get a five-finger discount?


Nicolette was supposed to arrive at 9 o'clock that night and Carmine, always a class act in respect, looked at his watch. He saw he had fifteen minutes and coaxed me to a sitting position on the edge of the bed. When I looked up at his face, his expression was almost blank — somber, downturned eyes nearly pure black in the low light of the bedroom.

He told me to open my mouth and I did. Perhaps I was distracted by speculation over what was to come, but I could barely comprehend how I'd ended up there. I receded into my own mind. Anything to dull the unwanted sensation of tingly warmth in the pit of my stomach. An eternity passed before he was done with me.

I stared daggers into him, grimacing as I swallowed, only receiving a look of feigned sympathy in return. He quickly shifted his focus to tucking his shirt and straightening his tie. It was all a mind game with him — marking his territory, like a dog pissing on a fire hydrant.

Nicolette arrived, and Carmine made a show of it. He made a point to welcome her to our 'lovely (by on-site housing unit standards) home', all while ensuring that she saw him buckling his belt while I wiped saliva from my swollen lips and failed to smooth down my ruffled hair.

After the curtain fell on Carmine's little production, he flashed Nicolette his made-for-TV smile and wished us a fun night before exiting stage left. All while I sat on the bed, desperately wanting to disappear.

"Seriously?" Nicolette whispered the moment the door clicked behind him.

"I— I'm sorry!" I apologized rather frantically, knowing instantly that she knew. "He does stuff like this sometimes…"

Her brows furrowed, "Yeah, well… I figured it would be pretty fucking obvious to y'all that I, a gay woman, don't particularly take interest in the idea of licking his cum out of your mouth."

"None of—" I vaguely waved my hand towards the door, as if his presence still lingered. "that was my idea, for the record."

"You still went along with it, though."

I stared at her, trying and failing to come up with a defense for why I'd done so. I could almost sense the blank spaces in my mind, inhabited by truths I'd never admit to myself. Eventually, she broke the silence herself.

"Whatever. Ugh, just go brush your teeth. Wash your hands too, while you're at it." She folded her arms.

I stared at myself in the bathroom mirror and wiped the blood off my split lip. As if I needed another reminder of the humiliating ritual I'd been put through. I scrubbed my tongue until it hurt, yet the residual bitterness still lingered.

When I finally emerged from the bathroom, Nicolette was lounging on the bed. Shirt off, bra and pants still on. I was almost surprised to see her — it would've been beyond understandable if she took the chance for an Irish goodbye, yet she stayed regardless. She stared at me, but I couldn't read her expression — even as she stood up and walked over to me, pulling me closer until the tips of our noses touched.

She inhaled, then pulled away.

"What now?" I asked, letting my arms fall to my sides.

"You smell like eau de toothpaste, with not-so-subtle notes of semen. Sorry."

She walked to her bag, pulled something out and tossed it to me.

"Here. Drink some of this."

It was a silver flask, engraved with a monogram — NJK for Nicolette Jane Krupps. Poison in a pretty package with her name on it.

"You know my liver's mostly scar tissue at this point?" I protested. Liver cirrhosis really was a bitch.

"Relax. You only need a swig. Just like, gargle with it. Like mouthwash, right?"

I swiped it from her hand.

Vodka. It burned like hell. I couldn't help but choke, gulping down air.

"God, this is a mess…" Nicolette chuckled, taking the flask back and downing most of what remained. "Some Russian you are…" The flask was tossed to the far end of the bed.

I hummed in response, already feeling just a little bit tipsy. Purely psychosomatic, but I felt woozy nonetheless.

She grabbed me by the arms without warning, pulling me down to face her. We fit together awkwardly — my rather broad figure against her lithe frame; almost a foot of height between us. This time, she didn't bother smelling my breath before shoving her tongue down my throat.

Nicki's hands were already around my chest, unclasping my bra. Just as she started to pull the straps from my arms, I crossed my arms over my chest — panic setting in.

Growing up, I'd never thought much of my tuberous breasts — not until I was seventeen, changing clothes next to a friend at the lake we'd visit in the summer. "You look weird," she'd said, with an expression of snide intrigue on her face. She'd glanced down at my chest, "Like, you still look like a kid, kinda. Not really, but…" I had opened my mouth to speak, but found that I was unable to. "Weird." Then, she went back to putting her clothing on as if nothing had happened.

My heart jumped, then fell.

It was a well-known fact that anomalous Foundation personnel were often fetishized, and I was no exception. Some wanted novelty, some wanted bragging rights, and the worst of them saw me as a safe outlet for a desire that, without compromise, would violate multiple codes of ethics. If I presented myself and invited everyone who wanted me to have a turn, no doubt I'd be rubbed raw and bleeding from every orifice by the time it was over. At least then, the novelty would be gone…

Of course I couldn't completely write off the possibility that some simply found my features attractive, but it was one I doubted every time I looked in the mirror.

Sometimes I wish I knew what my birth mother looked like — if she looked anything like me. Unfortunately, GRU-P wasn't in the practice of wasting film on photos of their D-Class equivalents. I'd seen pictures of my "father", though. Tons of them. They do that when you're the premier researcher of anomalous genetics, believe it or not. I remember the relief I felt when I saw him and could only identify him as a stranger.


"I wanna see how fast I can make you cum." Nicolette mused.

She stood on her toes and kissed me before I could swallow, licking the residual fluid out of my mouth. I froze. The liquor on her breath reeked of a night I'd been trying to forget for the past decade. My stomach suddenly felt queasy.

"No, but seriously. That was like — I don't know, a minute? Hold on, let me try something…"

Nicolette pulled down my skirt without pretense, and prompted me to step clear of where it pooled on the ground — I did it without thought nor question. As for my pantyhose, they were only yanked halfway down before she dropped to her knees.

I could've at any time, but I knew I never would. My vision blurred when I felt her nails scratch my thighs. Feeling her hair in my clenched fist made it better. It helped, but the shaking never really stopped. My queasy stomach told me to pull her off of me. The heavy feeling in my chest told me to apologize profusely. I hate that I just…couldn't. It felt wrong to do so, ungrateful. She should've left the moment she came in, but she didn't. Even though she noticed what Carmine had done. I had no idea why she was prostrating like this, not when I'd done nothing to deserve it. My hand in her hair moved to the back of her head — she moaned when I pulled her closer. Resigning myself to focusing only on the physical sensations made me realize how much my body had responded to her. I let my mind go blank — I wasn't surprised that it didn't take much more.
