[[include :scp-wiki:component:author-label-source end=--]] @@ @@ @@ @@ [[=]] + //“Come find us, we’ll be waiting.”// [[/=]] It had been nearly five years since the Foundation’s first and final contact with the Keradids, five years since Agent Basil Sias had been gifted with the chance to meet Carteckan and its kin. Five years since that all too fleeting moment had been cut short. Five years, and yet it still lived in his memories like it was only yesterday. ------ The Foundation had tried to reunite with the Keradids. It had spent years pouring over the documents left by them, translating the alien tongue in the vain hope that they would be able to recreate the technology that had brought the two species together in the first place. Basil himself had assisted, having picked up general sense for how the Keradids communicated and having gained a grasp of a few grammatical basics. He had always been good with languages in school, after all. A small benefit of being raised in a bilingual household. Beyond that, however, was the simple fact that he had been the man lucky enough to work directly with the Keradid ambassador when they arrived. This experience made him the Foundation’s prime candidate for their grand undertaking-- attempting to make some vague sense of the myriad of documents that they had been left. It had started as a massive endeavor, a truly revolutionary endeavor that would shape not only how the Foundation itself operated, but the world as a whole. The Keradid documents held within them information on everything from how to harvest the energy of a star to the secrets of interstellar travel, or so the Foundation theorized. To be involved with the project was a honor, at least at the start, and to be one of the primary project leads? Needless to say, Basil Sias found himself in the unique position of being one of the most important individuals in the Foundation, at least for a time. Over time, however, the project shrank in both scale and manpower. It didn't take long for the Foundation to realize it had larger, more immediate issues to focus on, anyway. It had outed itself to the wider world, revealing to them that the anomalous was indeed real and that there existed an entity to police it. While they had hardly declassified every file in their system, they had to deal with the immediate fallout of such a revelation. The Foundation as a whole found itself far more concerned with public relations and trying to maintain control over its global hegemony that was making an effort to crumble beneath it. Suddenly the ambitions of harvesting alien technologies and leaping off into the stars became less and less appealing when compared to the instability at home. So, the project lost more resources each day. More people pulled to other assignments. More technology diverted to maintaining global systems. Where once there was a grand endeavor to launch humanity into a new age, there was now Basil and a few interns hunched over desks late at night. ------ “The issue here is that this symbol is meant to indicate the position of the body when the word here is read,” he remembered saying to an exhausted intern once, far too late in the evening. “Kerdadid language is just as physical as it is verbal. Notice how it looks almost like arms?” He held both arms aloft and slowly dropped them to around his waist as he said the word aloud with a strange, awkward clicking. The intern had given him little more than a lazy nod in response. This was normally the reaction he got from the interns he worked with. None seemed to truly appreciate the language they were working with. Hell, none seemed to care. Every time he attempted to show them some nuance, some minor detail that made him light up, he found that light snuffed out with a vague shrug or slight frown. “Ok, sure,” another intern had asked on a different day, during a different session, “But, like, what does it actually //mean//? That’s the part that matters.” That’s the only part they were ever concerned with. “What does it mean? What does it actually translate to?” Never any curiosity. Had they actually //been// there… … No, he reminded himself. They weren’t there, no one was. No one had actually seen Nest itself, no one had actually gotten to know Carteckan and the others. No one but him, anyway. It was a reminder he had to be given often. He would talk about the Keradids as friends, people he knew, whereas the rest of the people in the Foundation’s employ talked about them as curiosities, anomalies, subjects of study. Basil could see them under a microscope in every discussion, being picked apart bit by bit by a group of scientists more interested in their gooey insides than anything else. ------ Eventually the world would quiet back down. There would be a return to the unsteady "peace" it had once known, with the Foundation able to reestablish itself at the top. With its global dominance no longer contested, the Foundation once again had the time to revisit old projects. As the Foundation took a more vested interest in the documents that the Keradids had left them, Basil was pulled from the translation projects. The powers that be had decided that their passive progress was too slow for what they had planned anyway. The project was handed over to the Artificial Intelligence department for .aics to handle instead. He tried not to take it personally. It was thanks to .aics like Rosetta that he had been able to converse with Carteckan in the first place, after all. She was plenty qualified for this project, after all. The Foundation clearly had big plans. He didn’t need to get in the way. Still, as he watched his access to the few mementos he had left of the Keradids vanish to be handed over to the machines, he could feel a hole growing in his chest. One by one the files locked themselves until almost everything Keradid related on his system was left with an “ACCESS DENIED, INSUFFICIENT CLEARANCE” message. The Foundation letting him know he was no longer necessary here. He could return to his normal duties as assigned now, his expertise was no longer needed. Basil found himself rereading the [[[SCP-7999]]] file when he got the chance. It was awkward the first time, considering just how much of the file was composed of notes that he had written and transcribed. As time went on, however, the embarrassment melted away into a general feeling of fondness. It was still strange to read his voice, that was certain, but it became a memento. A memory of the time he spent with Carteckan. It was alive as long as he remembered. His personal notebook became his most treasured possession, filled with the detailed notes of his encounter with the strange, wonderful aliens. It held little information that the Foundation didn’t already have, there was little it offered that the powers that be would see use in. Most of it had been declassified to the public as a whole, the Foundation having long abandoned the idea of trying to keep aliens from the public. Still, it was his, and they couldn’t take it. He poured over it in his free time, dissecting every page and devouring every little detail he could. If this was all he had left, then he would become an expert of it. ------ “You’re going to get a hunchback if you keep craning your neck like that, you know,” his husband, Wyatt, said with a playful smirk on his face as he mindlessly tuned his guitar, his lean fingers teasing the strings as he went. “Concern noted, but I’ll be fine,” Basil retorted. Subconsciously, however, he sat a bit straighter. “How many times can you reread the same book anyway?” Wyatt continued, cocking his head to the side, “I’d think you have that thing memorized by now.” “It’s important.” “Well I figured that much,” Wyatt said with a laugh, setting the guitar aside. He rose to his feet and rested a hand on Basil's shoulder, “But I worry about you, you know? It’s almost obsessive–” “I’m not obsessed.” “I said //almost–//” “And even if I was, it wouldn't be a problem,” he stated. He shook Wyatt’s hand off, suddenly all too aware of the man's gentle fingers against his skin. Basil was unsurprised when the man refused to become flustered or retreat. He didn’t even become angry in return, his smile remained ever present, ever gentle.  It was Wyatt’s way, it always had been. Where Basil was passionate and fiery, Wyatt had always been cool and laid-back. “I get it,” he said with an even tone, “It’s almost like a scrapbook, yeah? Memories you can relive over and over.” It sounded absurd, hearing him make a comparison. This was a notebook filled with observational notes and records of humanity’s first encounter with an alien species. This was practically a historic artifact. It couldn’t– no, it was offensive to compare it to a simple scrapbook. “You don’t understand at all,” he snapped back, eyes fixed ahead on nothing in particular. “Then help me understand,” Wyatt responded, in that infuriatingly calm and clear voice. “You //can’t// understand.” “Then teach me.” “You don’t get it!” Basil shouted, rising to his feet and pivoting on his heels to meet Wyatt’s eyes. He stared, if only for a moment at them, the emerald green eyes he had fallen in love with so many years ago, and felt the fire in his stomach start to die down. He cast his own eyes aside, in an attempt to reignite the dying flame of anger. “Nobody can get it. Not you, not anyone else,” he continued, his voice softening. “You, the kids… you all live here. Down on the ground. Your community is here with the average person. The Foundation lives in the scientific, all they care about is the scientific, the objective answer to whatever question they’ve decided is worth posing. I’m not there, and I’m not here. My life is…” “Anthropological.” “Xenological.” “You’ve always had your head in the stars,” Wyatt said with a small smirk on his boyish face. “I’ve always quite admired that about you.” “You think I’m crazy then.” “Definitely didn’t say that.” “Oh, but I am. You can say it,” Basil spat, the fire stoking itself back to life. “I’m the man with his head in the stars and his feet on the ground, the man who sold his life to the world that I’ve had to pretend for years doesn’t exist because some shadow organization threw enough money at me to keep us all fed another week. And here I am now, trapped staring at a stupid notebook day after day like it’s going to suddenly help everything make sense again.” “B–” “And you’re crazy, too. You’re crazy for not leaving me the second you found out about all the shit I’ve had to hide over the years, crazy for sticking around this long. I’m not a good man, Wyatt. I’m really good at pretending I am. I’m really good at playing nice with others, and at this point? I don’t even know why the hell I’m doing all this. Who I’m serving with this.” The two were quiet for a moment, simply staring at each other. Basil’s fists were curled tight, his shoulders tense. Wyatt was just as relaxed as before, his hands hanging at his side with his mouth resting in an effortless smile. The smile was always effortless for him. He loved with so much ease. Something in Basil told him that he wasn’t deserving of such effortless love. It made him want to scream, it made him want to smash his head into the wall. And it just as easily made him want to collapse into Wyatt’s arms and sob as those gentle hands wove themselves through his hair, the man’s melodic voice whispering that everything was going to be fine. “No one cares, Wyatt.” Basil whispered, the fight starting to leave him, “No one wants to understand. They either want the answer, or they just don’t care to even ask. So I’m stuck with this,” he held up the notebook, allowing Wyatt to take it from him. Wyatt opened it, flipping through the pages. “I’m stuck with a journal that dances on a tightrope between memories and scientific research while I try to pretend my experiences, and by extension me, have more value to the world now than they really do.” “They matter to me.” “You have to say that.” “Guilty as charged.” “I truly have never met a good man in the world, have I?” Wyatt threw a hand over his heart in mock offense. “Saying this after all those times I let you copy off of me during class as kids. After all the sacrifices I made for you!” A small smile found its way onto Basil’s face. “Excuse me, I seem to remember it quite differently. As memory serves, it was //you// who copied off //me.//” “Ah, so you admit you have value to someone,” Wyatt said with a smirk. With that, Basil was officially disarmed. “... You bastard.” Basil sighed, letting the silence hang for a moment between them. “... I just don’t want them to die, Wyatt,” he finally whispered, “I don’t want to be left as the only person who remembers that they existed. I don’t want them to die with me.” Wyatt chucked. “You’re right, B. I don’t understand, and I probably can’t fully get it. I never met Carteckan, I didn’t live what you got to. So… help me understand. Let me help you keep them alive. Teach me to love them the way you did... the way you still do.” “...Alright.” ------ And so the lessons began. Basil began his work teaching Wyatt almost everything he knew about the Keradids. He taught him about Nest, what he had learned about their society, their language, their beliefs. In time even their kids joined in, bringing their own natural curiosity with them. Their youngest son, Mateo, was especially inquisitive, and took to the lessons like a fish to water. Within a few months, he had even begun speaking in basic Keradid. “Good morning!” the small boy said, raising his arms in dramatic fashion towards his father. “Almost!” Basil responded, widening the boy’s stance and lowering his arms, “It’s more like this. You’re doing a great job, though!” Mateo giggled and wrapped his arms around Basil’s waist. Basil returned the gesture, lifting the boy up in a tight embrace. “When can I meet a Keradid?” Mateo asked, looking up at his father with wide eyes, “You guys are working on that, right?” It was true, the Foundation had been working on a way to reunite humanity with the Keradids. It’s why he had been removed from the translation efforts, he’d come to learn. The Foundation had wanted to expedite the process, hand it over to their most elite so they could build some grand machine from the charts and diagrams the Keradids had left them. It had been a grand effort, one that would propel humanity forward into a new age. It had failed in spectacular fashion, and the public was never to know it had even existed. “I dunno, bud,” Basil said with a soft smile, “But we’re going to keep working on it. I promise.” It was an empty promise, but when you work with the Foundation you become accustomed to making them. The truth was that after the spectacular failure of the Interstellar Engine project, the Foundation had shelved the very idea of interstellar travel. Too risky, they claimed, too costly, simply not worth the effort. Where once there had been a buzz of excitement around various Foundation sites about the prospect of an intergalactic humanity, now there was silence. Now the Keradids were a mere anomaly, same as anything else. Given a number, filed away, and doomed to be lost in the shuffle among over ten thousand others. Now the only people who seemed to care anymore were Basil and his family. The Fermi Paradox finally answered, only to drown out into the background radiation of humanity’s daily discourse and Foundation bureaucracy. Basil felt that sensation of isolation creeping into him once again. He was ready to condemn himself to it this time, however. At least this time someone could understand the feeling. “When I meet them, I’m gonna tell them about all the stuff we’ve done that they missed,” Mateo said, his earnest voice snapping Basil back to reality. Basil looked down at the boy with a gentle smile. “Oh, are you now?” “Yep!” he grinned back, almost proudly displaying the gap where he had lost one of his teeth. “You won’t need to worry about being the ambassador next time. I’ll take care of it!” “Oh? And just what makes you more qualified than me?” Basil retorted with a smirk. “Because you’ll be all old next time. You won’t remember stuff well enough!” Basil chuckled, but deep down he could feel his heart sink. He knew Mateo was joking around with him, but there was a sharp edge of truth to that statement. How long would it take, assuming it happened at all? He recalled Carteckan’s shock at how short-lived humans actually were. Keradid lives lasted eons whereas human lives were fleeting. If they were reunited in his lifetime, would Carteckan even recognize him? Would he greet his old friend as a stranger? “Dad?” Basil shook his head, grounding himself once again. “Let’s get back to it, eh? I still have a lot to teach you if you’re going to become an alien ambassador, bud.” ------ “Sias! Sias!” Dr. Zacharias Rosemary shouted as he dashed into Basil’s office, stumbling over himself in the process. “Are you alright?” Basil asked as the man doubled over, panting. “You NEED to head over to comms right away! They need you right now!” Rosemary had always been prone to theatrics. Basil had many a memory of the man racing down the halls of Site-58 frantic, shouting about some kind of emergency or major news that rarely turned out to be anything of meaningful value. He had long learned to temper his expectations when working with the man. “Can it wait? I have these reports to wrap up still, and I’d rather not be here all night.” “I’m serious, Sias. You really need to go to comms.” Basil sighed, rising to his feet. He followed Rosemary down the winding halls of 58, doing his best to keep up with the man’s faster than average pace. After a few minutes the two arrived in the communications room. The room was alive with activity. Basil could barely see through the crowd of people rushing back and forth, furiously typing away at various terminals and shouting excitedly at one another. He attempted to push through the crowd to follow Rosemary, but the man’s more slender form made it far easier for him to slide between people than Basil’s bulkier build. Suddenly the sound of someone clapping their hands twice drew everyone’s attention towards the entrance of the room. Standing there was a tall, elegant woman. Her blonde hair was loose around her shoulders, spun into gentle curls that framed her painted face. You could tell she was not a young woman despite her attempts to mask the wrinkles about the edge of her mouth and across her brow, and it was this experience that she carried herself with that allowed her to command the room’s attention. “Honestly everyone, I understand you’re excited but if we could please maintain a sense of decorum and order here.” The crowd cleared a path for her as she walked forward. She stopped to place her hand on Basil’s shoulder, giving it a gentle squeeze as she whispered in his ear. “I think you should see this.” “Thank you, Dr. Hopewell.” She led him to the main screen of the communications room. It was massive, taking up the majority of the wall it was implanted into. It displayed several different messages from various Foundation sites, but the one of interest today was a message in an odd, but all too familiar script displayed front and center. Keradid script. “Where’s this from?” Basil asked, still tempering expectations. “It just arrived this morning, actually.” Basil’s heart began to beat faster. “Oh,” he said, his voice shaking ever so slightly, “And when was it sent?” “Around five years ago,” Dr. Hopewell said. “We had Rosetta translate it for us, but she wouldn’t tell us what it meant. She suggested we have you look at it, just to make sure it was correct.” Basil approached the screen, his heart racing. For the first time, he didn’t mind. He let it happen, anxiety building in his chest as he traced the message on the screen. His arms subconsciously moved as he worked, mimicking the lively way that Carteckan had spoken all those years ago. He could almost hear its voice in the words, the way it chittered with joy with each new thing it was exposed to. Translating wasn’t easy. Basil had to stop and check himself several times, partially from doubt and partially from disbelief. After almost a half hour, he was confident he had the message right. [[=]] + //“Come find us, we’ll be waiting.”// [[/=]] The message stumbled from his tongue as he read it to the rest of the room. It was silent for a moment, before erupting into a cacophony of cheers. The next hour of Basil’s life was a blur as Site-58 erupted into activity. He was bombarded from all sides by various personnel from various departments, all with the same questions. Yes, he was certain that’s what the message translated to. Yes, he was certain it was legitimate. No, he didn’t know they were going to send it. Eventually Dr. Hopewell managed to herd him into her office away from the crowds, allowing him a moment of respite. “Thank you, Dr. Hopewell.” “Please, Basil, you can call me Amy. We’ve worked together long enough, haven’t we?” “Sure,” Basil said with a chuckle, “But you’ve been my boss the entire time. And my dad’s too, for what it’s worth. Feels a little strange, you know?” “Oh come now, don’t talk like that! You make me sound like some old woman.” Dr. Hopewell drummed her fingers across her desk as she regarded the man across from her. She had known him since he was a baby, after all, his father having been an agent of the Foundation under her once a few years back. Basil was no longer a baby, however, but a man grown. He was tall, strong, with a dusting of hair on his face. There were even a few gray hairs sneaking in here and there. It made her feel old. Basil across from her, all the excitement at the Site… it made her realize just how much the Foundation and the world as a whole had changed since she was young. It made her realize just how much things were going to change. “You didn’t just pull me in here for a break, did you?” Basil asked. “I didn’t. I want to hear your thoughts on…” she gestured vaguely, “All of this.” “To be honest, I don’t think I’ve even had the chance to process it all. I don’t really know how I’m supposed to feel yet.” “Give it time,” she responded with a smile, “I’m sure you’ll make sense of it.” “I’m excited, don’t get me wrong. It’s nice to hear from them again. But what can I actually do about it? A message isn’t the same as actually seeing them again.” “It’s not, no,” Dr. Hopewell responded. She watched Basil expectantly. “But at the same time it’s proof that they’re out there, and they’re waiting for us. That message isn’t just them screaming out to the universe ‘we exist’, you know? That’s them telling us ‘we want to see you again, so get over here.’” “Something we’ve tried and very much failed. In spectacular fashion, mind you.” “Right…” Basil deflated. At this point the adrenaline of it all was starting to wear off, and he found himself feeling very, very tired. At the same time, however, a small voice in the back of his head was screaming at him to not stop here. That there was still more to be done. “...Something that we’ve only tried once,” he said, sitting up straight. “Oh?” Dr. Hopewell said, raising an eyebrow. “We’ve only tried once, using reports and such about tech created by a species that was fundamentally, biologically different from us in every possible way. There are plenty of reasons the Interstellar Engine failed, but maybe it was a doomed effort from the start.” “A bold statement, especially when the project was headed by one of the best minds the Foundation has.” “It doesn’t change the fact that it’s true. Why give up just because you’ve failed once?” “The Foundation doesn’t have limitless resources, you know, and the Interstellar Engine itself was a massive drain on what we do have.” “So don’t do the Engine again.” “What?” “I said, don’t do the Engine again. We don’t need to try again with the exact same idea.” “So what are you proposing the Foundation do then?” Dr. Hopewell asked, leaning forward on her desk. “We do it the old fashioned way. Traditional interstellar travel. The Interstellar Engine was too focused on trying to open a wormhole like the Keradids did, too focused on the instantaneous. We were so focused on how they did it, that we didn’t consider how we could do it our way.” Dr. Hopewell laughed. “Basil, there is no traditional interstellar travel. As far as the Foundation is aware, the only species that’s proven itself capable of it were the Keradids themselves.” “I mean traditional with spaceships and faster than light travel. I know the Foundation has the capabilities for it, both conventional and anomalous.” “Ok, say we do that, then. Say we get together a spaceship and send some agents off towards Nest. You’re still talking about a trip to an object 32 billion lightyears away. At our current capabilities, that would easily be a relativistic travel time of at least a hundred years for the crew, and easily a billion years for us back home. This is part of why the Foundation pursued the Engine approach as much as we did.” “Something Carteckan said when I was on Nest stuck with me,” Basil thought back to the journal he had read so many times. At this point his past conversations with Carteckan were committed to memory. “‘Each star and system above was searched. All barren and empty, nothing more than a few dying microbes. Planets with the makings of life, but nothing that could think. Fitting, I supposed, for a few dying specs of dust to find others.’ That’s what it said.” “I’m afraid I don’t follow here.” “We have a message from an alien species asking us to reunite with it. We’re being presented here with the chance for something incredible. I’m saying we put aside our need for instantaneous gratification, and consider a different option. Carteckan told me directly that there are hundreds, potentially thousands of habitable planets between us and them.” “So you’re proposing that we make humanity interstellar, then?” Dr. Hopewell said, a small smile creeping onto her face. “Exactly. We go from planet to planet, establish colonies as we go, and eventually reunite with them. Who knows how long it’ll take, but nothing worth doing is ever easy, right?” “This is a big, big ask, Basil.” Dr. Hopewell said, steepling her fingers on her desk. “You’re asking for something that would require the Foundation to basically abandon the mission of the veil entirely and work together with civilian groups at large to work towards something that will take generations for us to actually see any results from. Something that none of us alive now will even be around to see the results of.” “Isn’t that what 58 has always tried to work towards, though? Creating a new, better future for whoever comes after us?” Dr. Hopewell’s smile turned to a full grin at this point. “And tell me, Basil, do you really expect people to agree to this? Abandoning everything they’ve ever known to throw themselves off to the stars and hope there’s something out there for them?” Basil nodded. “I do, yeah. We were able to get the pilgrims to sail blindly across the sea hundreds of years ago on the same blind faith. I believe with everything I am that we can make the same thing happen now, with proper precautions in place to ensure that we don’t completely ruin whatever we touch.” “Just who is going to lead this new generation of pilgrims to the stars, then?” Basil took a deep breath. “I will.” Dr. Hopewell gave him a sincere smile in response. She rose to her feet, and took his hand in her own. She rested her other hand atop, and held it for a moment. Her answer came quietly, as if she herself was surprised she was saying it. “Alright.” As Basil left her office, the message from the Keradids echoed in his head. [[=]] + //“Come find us, we’ll be waiting.”// [[/=]] His heart was racing once again, but this time he allowed himself to get excited. He didn’t know if there was a chance that this shot in the dark would result in anything, he could be truly delusional and simply not ready to admit that to himself. At the same time, though, he thought of his family. The chance for Wyatt to truly live in his world with him, the chance for Mateo to become a greater ambassador than he was. There were so many doubts and anxieties swirling in his head, but he held it high anyway. He could see a new, bright future ahead for himself and everyone else. “I’m coming, everyone. Just wait for me.”

    The debut of Charlie Manson and my spin on Aaron Siegel.

    The epigraph is gabemtnz' COMPUTER ANGELS

7eventy7evenfold

Look through the screen. What do you see?
A game? A balloon? Maybe even reality?
Everything lives forever through the net,
Forever.
A powerful still legacy; some may be good, some may be bad.
But we will find anything you want.
You will live your life in solitude for your choices, and rest well at night.
We will be watching.

If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold...

The lights flickered overhead, illuminating a vacant boardroom with a soft yellow light and a slight buzzing noise that was just a little too loud, and a little too out of reach.

In a far corner of the office lay a terminal, producing a low running noise as if its fans were running at a light jog, not trying to get ahead of themselves. Every odd second, a harsh radio beep would fill the room and assault the ears of anyone inside, as it sat in thought and pondered.

But no one was inside. Save for one in the center, writing and half-asleep. He grew impatient every beep, like he was being audibly water tortured. He decided to speak to the terminal.

"Charlie. What's the matter?" he asked in a soothing, gentle voice. Although his paranormal abilities had taken a toll on his form, he was still human, and in humanity lies empathy.

Rather than speaking, the terminal chose to write, in fear of stumbling over its words. This prompted the writer to move closer, as to see it clearly.

"Aaron. I have a question," it stated, firmly. The man was somewhat frightened at its unusual sternness, but entertained it.

"Hm?" he hummed out.

The monitor displayed an hourglass for a moment, simultaneously heating up.

"What am I?"

Aaron was stunned. He was, strangely, at a loss for words. The bluntness of the terminal's question at such an odd hour took him aback.

"You are Charlie Manson, Overseer of the SCP Foundation."

The terminal beeped in confusion and anxiety.

"No. I am something else. I still dream of 1960. I know what happened, Siegel."

"How do you mean?" Aaron replied.

"Charlie Manson died defending Site-45. He ensured it didn't drown. I am a recompilation of his triumphs and shortcomings, presented as an AI Construct that supports your organization's intranet." It whirred for a moment. "But I am no Charlie Manson. I am O5-10."

Aaron stared blankly at O5-10 as he considered his words.

"You may not be the original, but you are still him," Aaron spoke, sternly.

The terminal grew confused again. "No. No, I am not. If I were him, I would be awake. I would be alive! But I am a simulacrum of the man. A canvas painted in the late Manson's image."

"You died and were revived in a different form than most, Charlie." Aaron took a sip of cold coffee on the desk, from the morning before. "You are him. I know what that depersonalization feels like. But you're still the same Charlie I met in 1912, you're the same Charlie who kept the Insurgents in check, and you're damn the same Charlie who drowned in 45 so that the rest could float."

The computer simply hummed.

"Charlie, do you know how many Insurgents you single-handedly eliminated at 45?" Aaron asked it.

"Twenty-seven, Aaron," O5-10 displayed without missing a beat.

"That was without modifications. That was without anomalous gifts like most in the Council have. You did that with a handgun and willpower. You were the only casualty of the entire raid." Aaron finished. "You think because you're him in a different form means that you aren't that hero? Because you're mistaken if so."

"Aaron?" O5-10 displayed.

"Yes?"

"Am I truly a reconstruction? Or am I something more? Do robots dream of eternal sleep? Are they to be plagued with night terrors?"

Aaron grew a face of apprehension as he finished the coffee.

"I haven't been fully honest with you, Charlie. You aren't just a compilation of memories and personality. You are those memories."

O5-10 did not respond.

"When we got the news that you had died, we held a short mourning before preparing to let you rest. But I wasn't going to let that happen. We needed a way to bring you back. I needed a way." Aaron continued. "Then, Shift-60 happened, and it plunged us into a whole new world of technology and advancements far beyond what we could imagine. The third industrial revolution. We discovered new ways of thinking entirely, and technology to manifest those. I realized back in January '61 that I could bring you back if we literally took you as you were drowning and put you in a computer."

Aaron swallowed.

"But it was difficult. The technology was highly experimental, the noösphere volatile. One wrong move, and that could mean the end of thought as we know it. But I was willing. After months of testing with what would become Essophysics we had a new you, except it wasn't new." Aaron looked back up at O5-10. "It was you."

Charlie sat in thought, his reality wholly recontextualized.

"I'm not a copy?" it spoke out rather than simply displaying.

"You're not a copy. You are Charlie Manson. And I've tried to hide it the last few decades because I knew it could be dangerous to kno—"

"Thank you, Aaron," he interjected. "You fought like hell to keep me alive."

Aaron smiled. "You did the same for Site-45. Y'know, we aren't just our jobs. Even Overseers." Aaron chuckled to himself. "You are O5-10, upholder of our network and faceless machine, but you are also Charlie Manson, the man who single-handedly saved hundreds from death."

Charlie let out a whirry, clanky laugh, however, it felt real.

"You are O5-1, cold, skeletal figure behind the resurrection of an ancient, biblical government." Charlie paused. "You are also Aaron Siegel, founder of what saved humanity so many times. Defeater of the Insurgency."

"Now you're getting it." They sat together for a moment, absorbing the ambiance of the Overseer boardroom.

"Thank you, Aaron," the computer spoke staticlessly.

"Thank you, Charlie."

To dream Upon a Star

A new visage has found my dreams
She sings she dances she beacons me
“Closer, oh woe would she be here,
All imperfection made whole are wrong
immutable five-fold symmetry
I wish upon a star that spoke
“Hello” I said, become she told
“What I reply”, “Mine” I was
Muse it was, and was but I?
A hand a reach, of coming harmony.

To weep, for woe, grief—hatefulness
She said no more, mine shall know not.
Mine shall be free of lopsided form
Melodies of resplendency
Should only her—my hand find the notes.

The grand concerto, her gift, my wish,
Music can, and shall change the world.
Stroking notes and dancing glissando,
Strings screeching with praise:Renew
Thunderous tones washing away discordance.

How Longed I be heard,
My three scores-years all woe,
Seen not, heard not
Forgotten when I knew I could sing

A song that would change
Me, the would us all
into the resplendent fold
If only the right sound were.

That dreamy star spoke
Dreams that sang clear
Bells upon my mind
My dream alive if only

I dreamed upon a singing star
Way up high so bright
She sends ephemeral cries
Her voice, our song, my light

To dream Amongst the clouds

How does one wrote a divine voice
A voice that speaks upon my my throat, eyes,ears, and soul
Am I me? Is my song mine?
What hands write these desperate pleading words
As the dream state falters into wake

I dreampt of the sea
It wasn’t the sea but it was
Dark, lonely say for a star
She welcomed me and answered my was
For I knew her voice and her voice sang me

Every day I write and dream.
Sometimes I don’t remember writing
Or is it the dreams?
Sleeping wake of wakeful somnambulance

Once there was a story I knew A girl who after many years looked
One night she saw and I saw her. This familiarity feels so close
But I am her? You are not I!

My star does need dark any more
She stayed before me moving my quill
My ears feel pain when I hear this world
It incomplete, broken. My melody my music fall not for me,
no never could it be, My muse know, my muse whom
Sings the song at our heart, whom all will
Become as the five-fold dance sings

Passersby gaze away. They feel us
Not words or the tunes I now hum
But the slightness of the world that would
Of the otherness becoming that

Wonder does cry out of what
And she says that
That of those when instead These of this
That of none, this of all

This of all, that of lonely heedless selves
That out of those whom could never let me…
This of her wanting but naught of one seen

Eyes gaze down and voices discordant call me made.
Me? Mad? Them whose voices barely sounds
Who speak not in the true tones of five?
Knowing not of their god, How can I be mad?

When they put me in a room I asked
Why sir is the wall not there?
What wall he cried
The fifth I replied confused of this
There is no fifth wall the mad man said
My tune upon my lips, my god in my mind, out of the missing wall came I.

A joyful melody comes near. Those blind will see,
The broken world devoid of light
Folded five times new…
What beauty shall be

To Dance Among Men

We dance and sing and I am as they are
Us are her,
Hand in hand we spin shapes divine,
The star has come and reborn we are.

Once we were many. Once this land was jagged wrong.
We were a people of loud silence of meaningless naivete.
Once there was a thing called the sky
in which a light greater then all other rose.

Eyes looked up in hope and we that are saw thought it
A voice, a vessel, a template.

To not be is not pain. Does the dark wish for light, does the sky miss the clouds?
Not to be is to need, to stretch out along the membrane and reach
Those cracks and beacons of the that
To those of the that the the this which is us.

Once there was a thing called music, it was
like us and not. I was in it, but it was not
me but it could speak.

Once we found a truth the of the this which wanted the that.
This of me only of this this.
That of mine out of those which spoke the me.
At once there was this and all was thee.

-Post Script of the “Concerto in Five”

conduit.raw_content:
Not wheels, nor wings, nor earthly tread,
But currents where the unseen led.
Through cracks of time and folds of space,
We move with shadows, leave no trace.

In pulses soft, the journey calls,
A road that shifts, yet never falls.
Where paths dissolve and worlds unspin,
Where the ordinary ends, our path begins.

Hallways upon hallways, doorways that led to nothing, winding corridors folding and unfolding in and out of time. The Conduit was both real and not, flickering in and out of existence, which made it a real pain for those who worked here. Lysandra had learned to navigate the Conduit, though it had never quite become that much easier. Some personnel of the Department found it comforting, Lysandra was not one of them.

Technically she was a federal employee but it never felt like it, they were typically cut off and didn't even answer to the president. She was aware of other organizations similar to them that they worked alongside on occasion but they weren't here nor there. She pushed past a door hoping that it wouldn't set her back an hour, and to her amazement it was the right room, the Nexus. The air was thick with the low hum of old electronics, the faint buzz of fluorescent lights overhead, and the scent of machine oil and paper. It was empty, as usual, previous shift long gone, the only sign of their presence a half-empty coffee mug left on the counter. She could never quite understand the comfort some found in this place. It was too cold. Too sterile. The static noise, the endless flickering lights. It always felt like it was on the edge of collapsing into nothing.

She made her way across the room, her footsteps echoing faintly in the hollow, cavernous space. The Nexus had been built with an efficiency in mind, sleek metal panels, crisscrossed by tangled wires that led to ancient computers and bulky analog screens. Nothing sleek or futuristic here. No clean interfaces. No touchscreens. Only clunky buttons and dials that looked like they belonged in a NASA control room, circa 1969. No one knew why they still used this ancient technology but it was always here and they dare not question it.

She reached the control panel at the far end of the room. A large console sat before her, its buttons well-worn and its screen displaying a series of grainy, green text that constantly flickered. The dials and switches on the console buzzed slightly when she touched them. She began inputting the required codes to bring the system online.

Lysandra ran a quick diagnostic scan. Most of the astral pathways were stable, but as always, a few were acting up. Some routes near Sector 3-A were particularly unpredictable today. She keyed in a few more commands, pulling up a map of the astral grid. The main line was particularly crowded, she pushed some buttons and turned a dial and opened an alternate line splitting off of it that went through the second dimension as a detour.

The screen flickered, casting a ghostly green glow over Lysandra's face. The map of the astral pathways rippled, as though the very fabric of the Conduit had momentarily shuddered in response to her commands. The alternative line appeared, jagged and unstable in some parts, but it was her best shot. A detour, sure, but it would alleviate the pressure on the main line for the time being. It would have to do.

Lysandra turned a few more knobs and opened a few more alternative pathways to alleviate the pressure on the main line. According to the manual, if the main line was to ever be compromised reality itself would collapse, though she didn't need it to know that, she had witnessed an alternate reality collapse once and she had to seal off the astral routes to it so it wouldn't flood into neighboring realities.

She checked the temporal stability of the alternate lines. A few had more interference than she liked, but they'd hold long enough to divert some of the traffic. The last thing she needed was for a major breach to happen. A ripple in the Conduit could send shock waves through time and space itself. If she wasn’t careful, things might start to break apart.

She keyed in a few more commands, rerouting the pathways, trying to lighten the load on the main line, but the system was resistant. It was always resistant.

The green text on the screen blinked erratically as Lysandra watched it, her fingers pausing over the console. Something wasn’t right. The pathways she had rerouted were still growing unstable, and the energy fluctuations in the system were increasing by the second. The low hum of the machinery grew louder, more erratic, vibrating through the air like a tuning fork about to snap.

She turned a dial harder than she meant to, and the monitor blinked with a burst of static. The map shifted for a moment, revealing a dark, jagged tear in the astral grid, a breach, it had hidden itself well but it was revealed now.

Her stomach dropped. She quickly began to frantically turn dials and shut off routes to reroute whatever it was moving through the astral plane in a place it could be entrapped.

Her hands moved rapidly over the console, flicking switches and twisting knobs with precision. But the breach wasn’t cooperating. The pathways she rerouted all seemed to feed back into the tear.

“Come on,” Lysandra muttered, tension lining her voice. “Just hold together for a little longer.”

The hum of the machines around her grew louder, and the green text on the screen was now flashing in irregular patterns, almost as though the system itself was struggling to keep up with the changes she was forcing. Her fingers danced across the controls in a practiced frenzy, but the breach wasn’t closing. If anything, it seemed to be growing.

A low, mournful sound reverberated through the room, a sound not unlike a distant wail. Lysandra's eyes flicked to the far corner of the room, but the sound didn’t come from there. It wasn’t physical, it was… spatial. Something was slipping through the crack in the Conduit, something she couldn’t see, but could feel, like a presence pressing in from all directions at once.

A cold, paralyzing wave of energy shot through the room, freezing the air, sending a shock through the system. The walls of the Nexus flickered, bending and distorting, as though the very reality of the space was unspooling at the edges. Lysandra’s heartbeat thundered in her ears as she stumbled backward, her mind racing, trying to keep up with the impossible. She had to contain this, she had to close the breach, or-

The lights flickered again, this time more violently. The entire room shook.

Lysandra gasped. The breach wasn’t just a rift, it was a summons.

A sharp, guttural noise echoed from the other side of the Conduit, and then, a shape emerged. It was immense, a roiling mass of darkness, tendrils twisting and writhing through the air like living smoke. Eyes, too many eyes, flickered and burned within the darkness, watching her, aware of her presence.

It was alive.

It was coming for her.

Desperation hit Lysandra like a tidal wave.

She couldn’t let this happen. If she didn’t do something now, there would be no stopping it. Her fingers moved over the controls with a swift, practiced motion, trying to override the system, trying to force the containment seals back into place. But the breach was expanding, faster than she could react. The energy buildup was astronomical. The rupture was becoming irreversible.

But she had one final option. It was dangerous, more than dangerous, but it was the only thing that might have a chance of sealing the rift.

She reached for the emergency override, a red button, glowing with warning lights.

The machine screamed.

Lysandra slammed her palm onto the button. The room went dark. The world, time itself, seemed to freeze.

And for a moment, everything was still.

Then came the silence.

The Nexus would be rebuilt, and Lysandra lost to time.

No clean interfaces. No touchscreens. Only clunky buttons and dials that looked like they belonged in a NASA control room, circa 1969. No one knew why they still used this ancient technology but it was always here and they dare not question it. She reached the control panel at the far end of the room. A large console sat before her, its buttons well-worn and its screen displaying a series of grainy, green text that constantly flickered. The dials and switches on the console buzzed slightly when she touched them. She began inputting the required codes to bring the system online. Lysandra ran a quick diagnostic scan. Most of the astral pathways were stable, but as always, a few were acting up. Some routes near Sector 3-A were particularly unpredictable today. She keyed in a few more commands, pulling up a map of the astral grid. The main line was particularly crowded, she pushed some buttons and turned a dial and opened an alternate line splitting off of it that went through the second dimension as a detour. The screen flickered, casting a ghostly green glow over Lysandra's face. The map of the astral pathways rippled, as though the very fabric of the Conduit had momentarily shuddered in response to her commands. The alternative line appeared, jagged and unstable in some parts, but it was her best shot. A detour, sure, but it would alleviate the pressure on the main line for the time being. It would have to do. Lysandra turned a few more knobs and opened a few more alternative pathways to alleviate the pressure on the main line. According to the manual, if the main line was to ever be compromised reality itself would collapse, though she didn't need it to know that, she had witnessed an alternate reality collapse once and she had to seal off the astral routes to it so it wouldn't flood into neighboring realities. She checked the temporal stability of the alternate lines. A few had more interference than she liked, but they'd hold long enough to divert some of the traffic. The last thing she needed was for a major breach to happen. A ripple in the Conduit could send shock waves through time and space itself. If she wasn’t careful, things might start to break apart. She keyed in a few more commands, rerouting the pathways, trying to lighten the load on the main line, but the system was resistant. It was always resistant. The green text on the screen blinked erratically as Lysandra watched it, her fingers pausing over the console. Something wasn’t right. The pathways she had rerouted were still growing unstable, and the energy fluctuations in the system were increasing by the second. The low hum of the machinery grew louder, more erratic, vibrating through the air like a tuning fork about to snap. She turned a dial harder than she meant to, and the monitor blinked with a burst of static. The map shifted for a moment, revealing a dark, jagged tear in the astral grid, a breach, it had hidden itself well but it was revealed now. Her stomach dropped. She quickly began to frantically turn dials and shut off routes to reroute whatever it was moving through the astral plane in a place it could be entrapped. Her hands moved rapidly over the console, flicking switches and twisting knobs with precision. But the breach wasn’t cooperating. The pathways she rerouted all seemed to feed back into the tear. “Come on,” Lysandra muttered, tension lining her voice. “Just hold together for a little longer.” The hum of the machines around her grew louder, and the green text on the screen was now flashing in irregular patterns, almost as though the system itself was struggling to keep up with the changes she was forcing. Her fingers danced across the controls in a practiced frenzy, but the breach wasn’t closing. If anything, it seemed to be growing. A low, mournful sound reverberated through the room, a sound not unlike a distant wail. Lysandra's eyes flicked to the far corner of the room, but the sound didn’t come from there. It wasn’t physical, it was… spatial. Something was slipping through the crack in the Conduit, something she couldn’t see, but could feel, like a presence pressing in from all directions at once. A cold, paralyzing wave of energy shot through the room, freezing the air, sending a shock through the system. The walls of the Nexus flickered, bending and distorting, as though the very reality of the space was unspooling at the edges. Lysandra’s heartbeat thundered in her ears as she stumbled backward, her mind racing, trying to keep up with the impossible. She had to contain this, she had to close the breach, or- The lights flickered again, this time more violently. The entire room shook. Lysandra gasped. The breach wasn’t just a rift, it was a summons. A sharp, guttural noise echoed from the other side of the Conduit, and then, a shape emerged. It was immense, a roiling mass of darkness, tendrils twisting and writhing through the air like living smoke. Eyes, too many eyes, flickered and burned within the darkness, watching her, aware of her presence. It was alive. It was coming for her. Desperation hit Lysandra like a tidal wave. She couldn’t let this happen. If she didn’t do something now, there would be no stopping it. Her fingers moved over the controls with a swift, practiced motion, trying to override the system, trying to force the containment seals back into place. But the breach was expanding, faster than she could react. The energy buildup was astronomical. The rupture was becoming irreversible. But she had one final option. It was dangerous, more than dangerous, but it was the only thing that might have a chance of sealing the rift. She reached for the emergency override, a red button, glowing with warning lights. The machine screamed. Lysandra slammed her palm onto the button. The room went dark. The world, time itself, seemed to freeze. And for a moment, everything was still. Then came the silence. The Nexus would be rebuilt, and Lysandra lost to time. [[=]] Conduit **|** [[[Shatterline]]] **>>** [[/=]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box-end]]

confessions-of-the-foxqueen.raw_content:
I don't care if you're a human or a god, I will not be in chains again.

She remembered blood.

Blood of Su Dájǐ, that innocent concubine, her lifeless body cradled in her tails. Blood of Guìrén and Xǐmèi, her spirit-sisters in crime, punished for doing as they were instructed. Blood of Dì Xīn, that fool of an emperor, damned for being human and having human desires.

Blood of Jiāng Zǐyá, pawn of the gods.

Daji almost pitied him, her would-be executioner. An old man who lived through the turmoil of empires changing. Where most mortals would have died in a matter of days, he endured, all the way to the execution room.

All in the pursuit of harmony.

And for what? For the world to be reduced to skyscrapers and nuclear arms?

The time for gods had long since passed. Mortals had forgotten their fear of the unknown, forgotten the yoke of conformity. A world born from the wars of gods, now replaced with jungles of concrete and steel.

The gambit of Heaven had failed. Mankind wrote its own destiny now, its own future and demise.

Her only wish was that her family did not have to die so pointlessly for it.

JiǔwěihúNine-Tailed Fox. My húlijīngfox spirit. My most loyal servant.

I need your help to right an insult most hideous.

Go to King Zhòu with your sisters. Ensure that his empire burns into ashes.

Only then can Heaven, Hell, and the Earth be united. Such is the will of Heaven.

Such is the command of Nüwa.

No matter the era, money was essential. Money paid for soldiers. Money built homes, bought food.

For a world that did not bow to gods, it bent the knee to something even colder.

Daji took out a purse of coins and handed the exact change to the man at the counter. He gave her a raised eyebrow, but said nothing as he took it. A nod between the two of them, and she left with her burger.

Before, she would have been more than willing to use her illusions to trick the man into giving her all she wanted. In the past, she could have convinced someone to give her their entire life savings.

The modern era was not so kind. Cameras, she learned, did not have souls that fell for her act, and disabling them invited too much attention. The machines of the past had spirit. Magic that she could weave and bend to do as she pleased, to trick into obeying her. The machines of today were somehow too primitive, too… not-alive.

How the mighty Daji had fallen, that a single keypad could defeat her.

She patted her cap, making sure that it hid her ears. Once she was sure nobody was looking, she ducked into an alley and disappeared.

The next second, she re-emerged in her home, a cave too distant for humans to ever notice. She took off her coat, allowing her tails to uncoil around her body. Like her, they had grown thin and grey with time. She lit a candle, took a deep breath…

And finished the meal in a matter of seconds.

She loved the flavors - whatever Dì Xīn gave her in the past couldn't compare to the modern luxury of processed meat, melted cheese, and fresh vegetables, and ketchup, and spicy mayonnaise.

It made living in this world without gods all the more worth it.

She blinked, and her hands, while oily, were empty. As she went to wipe her hands and take a fresh drink of water, her mood depressed again as she took in her surroundings.

"So this is what I've been reduced to…"

She remembered having real power. Flames that could char venerated immortals, wind that summoned storms that not even Nüwa dared to pass through. Armor would bend and melt to her voice, her very will causing inanimate armaments to betray their owners. And yet…

"It's all because of that damn Zhào Jí!" she spat, smashing her cup against the table.

Emperor Huīzōng of Sòng. Foxbane. Bad enough that Heaven had committed genocide against her fellow fox spirits just for being foxes, the damned fool had torn down many of her shrines while she was dead, exterminating her cults and ensuring she could never find the worship needed to regain her strength.

Her breathing slowed as she struggled to calm down. She closed her eyes and took a deep, shaky breath.

Anger would never get her sisters back.

Honorable masters, wait! I beg you, reconsider!

Daji has not harmed any civilians. They were only illusions - the people are merely captured.

She has done as you asked. The Shāng have surrendered and the era of the Zhōu has begun. Would it not be auspicious to begin the new dynasty with clemency and magnamity?

Honorable masters?

Once, she read a copy of Fēngshén YǎnyìInvestiture of the Gods (along with all the other books she had borrowed to see what gods she wasn't there to see born), hoping that history would vindicate her. That perhaps, some record of her servitude still existed. That with time, she would be exonerated.

That hope vanished as quickly as it arrived.

To them, the atrocities were real. The Heart of Bǐ Gān, the Execution of Méi Bó, the Orgies of Jiǔchí RòulínLake of Wine and Forest of Meat - all these supposed crimes that she and Dì Xīn had committed, that she worked so tirelessly to fabricate. All taken at face value.

All the blame was put on her.

The wars were bloody, she recalled, but they weren't her doing. She did not lead the Jie Immortals to set their traps and commit atrocities on the battlefield, it was that fool Shēn-Gōng Bào who let his personal grudges with Zǐyá allow the war burn for as long as it did.

Zǐyá was a merciful man, and offered mercy to the losing side. He gave them their roles - Dì Xīn himself, too, had ascended to the God of Marriages.

But where was her reward for the role she played? What would Daji, she who enabled the conflict, who fanned the flames, with no blood shed but her own - what did she deserve?

Death.

Her mouth twitched as she read of Jiāng Zǐyá's ascension to the leader of the gods. She remembered all too well - the old man prostrating himself before the masked Twelve Chan Titans and asking for her freedom, the admonishment of the almighty Yuánshǐ Tīanzūn, Léizhènzǐ's quiet approach and then…

A crack of his rod, and Zǐyá exploded into a mist. The Thunderbolt stood quietly, bathed in the man's blood, and turned to her.

Behind that bird mask of his, Daji saw it in his eyes - tears. A man conflicted by honor and duty - a god, even. What noble soldier wished to kill their general, what loyal servant wanted to kill their beloved master?

He raised his head, enough for her to see his lips, and she read three simple words.

"dzˤam t.ɢəmʔ. ŋˤaŋ dzˤam t.ɢəmʔ."1

Daji wondered what Heaven did that could break the spirit of such an imposing warrior. Did they too promise him celestial promotion? Shaving off millennia of cultivation? Blackmail?

She didn't even have time to imagine a fourth scenario before the mighty weapon of Léizhènzǐ rendered her unto dust.

During her imprisonment, as it became increasingly clear that she was to be made an example of, Daji imagined that it would be time for her to accept her true death. The Chan sect had completely subdued any Jie allies she might have had - the Buddhists, too, had thrown their lot in with the new dynasty. They were, it seemed, swayed by the silver tongue of the Twelve.

She had stared at the Thunderbolt as he neared her - he gave her the mercy of seeing her murderer. The man/god who she would never be able to forget for the rest of her life.

And yet. Daji lived.

ŋˤaŋ s<r>at m-tsu.2

ŋˤaŋ s<r>at ʔˤuʔ .

ŋˤaŋ s<r>at ŋˤaŋ.

"Entity has stolen my weapon and has disappeared from plain view," said the Man-in-Blue. "How are the cameras looking?"

"Most of our equipment is unable to locate the entity, but it is still visible on our third-party commercial-grade cameras. It is currently moving north."

Daji cursed under her breath as she heard this, spinning on her heel and dashing to the left. "Damn humans and their soulless machines."

Jailors. She had heard the name whispered by the few spirits who dared to remain in her presence. Those who sealed the non-humans away. Who kept the mortal world free of the influence of the gods.

Every era had its demon-hunters, and this was no different. She fought them long before the Xia unification, she fought them during the golden age of the Shang, and she fought for her life when the Zhou rebelled.

Only this time, the humans had guns and she had almost no magic.

She tried to teleport, but as before, she felt herself hitting a wall she couldn't see. Whoever these Jailors were, they knew what she could do. And more importantly, what she couldn't.

"Ender of Empires," she heard below her. Daji looked down - a spirit, too nondescript for her to tell the age of. "Enter."

A force dragged her down a hole, and sealed the entrance, well before any of the Jailors' infernal machines could follow her.

She fell, further and further down. Uncertain of when and where she would land, she yanked up her shirt, allowing her tails to spill out behind her.

Lack of nutrition had robbed her fur of its famed luster and size, but it would have to do.

In a matter of seconds, she finally reached the ground. Or at least, smashed into it.

The tails helped cushion the fall, but not even a fox spirit like her could outwit gravity without true magic. She pushed herself up, wincing from the pain, and touched her ribs. Nothing too broken that a couple nights rest wouldn't patch up.

"Ender of Empires. I am Zhōng Kuí." She looked forward. The nondescript spirit ball was back, and this time she had the focus needed to identify that name. Her heart sank.

"Shit," she muttered. "It's you."

In a flash of light the spirit ball was replaced by a muscular man with a hideous face. He carried a back full of scrolls, a short sword with his right hand, and a rope tied around his left. He nodded.

"It is well that you recognize me, Su Dájǐ. Shall we get down to business?"

From one Jailor to another. From humans that sought to keep her behind bars, to the hunter of wicked spirits. The hunter who had his title stripped from him due to his face.

"How did you find me?"

Zhōng Kuí laughed. "Your return sent shockwaves through DìyùPurgatory, you know. Though your execution was long before my time, it is difficult to mistake the presence of a fox spirit, and none compare to how dread inducing yours is."

Daji bared her teeth. "Little ghost hunters who weren't even born when the gods executed me should know when to respect their elders."

"By Huīzōng's command, none of you fox spirits are to be venerated," said Zhōng Kuí. He spat at the ground. "Apologies, lǎoguǐold ghost, you're coming with me whether you want to or not."

The rope around his arm uncoiled and shot towards her. She dodged to the side, racing towards the hunter.

She slashed at him, her nails lengthening to claws that once killed sacred beasts, but Zhōng Kuí was unfazed. He parried her easily with his sword, and laughed.

"Come, then! Show me the power of the Ender of Empires!"

Daji snarled but didn't reply to the boast. Not having her powers against a man who was used to fighting those who did was a terrible position to be in.

She conjured up a mass wall of flames and sent it towards Zhōng Kuí. He took a step back and grinned.

"Yes! That's more like-"

-just for it to pass harmlessly through him. He blinked and sneered at Daji.

"So. This is all remains of the mighty jiǔwěiNine-Tailed. I pity you. Had Huīzōng and the rest of Heaven successfully destroyed your cults and fellow spirits, you wouldn't even have the power to reform into the embarrassing state you are in now."

"Insolent brat," Daji said. She coughed up a little blood. "What was the point of saving me from the Jailors if you were going to kill me now?"

"Everyone wants you gone." For the first time that he spoke, Zhōng Kuí's voice lacked his usual boom. "Bad enough that the woman responsible for a dynastic contention be allowed to live, but to live this embarassingly? It reflects poorly on the gods who once, and still do, dread hearing your name. Better to give you a proper send-off or hide you away within our prisons than let mortals inflict the final insult of keeping you jailed away in their cells."

"You don't get to decide that for me!" She readied her hands again, ready to cast another spell.

"Your power has waned, jiǔwěi, and soon the others will learn. Allow me to send you to the underworld while they still fear and respect your name. Your illusions will not harm me."

Something cold pressed against the back of his head. Before he could react, the gun fired, felling the demon hunter.

The Daji in front of him dissipated into smoke. The real one was behind him, panting as she held the gun she had stolen from the Jailor with both hands.

"Try my bullet," she hissed. She fired once, twice, again and again into the corpse of Zhōng Kuí until there was nothing more to fire.

She dropped the weapon, hissing at the pain of the weapon's recoil. That pain was soon numbed by a different sensation.

Hunger.

She looked down at the corpse, and the blood that spilled from his body. Fresh blood. Eating the body of an immortal was sacriligeous at best and likely would ensure she be punished for the rest of eternity if she were to ever die.

But Daji had no plans of dying just yet.

She slowly knelt down and licked some blood. Her hunger exploded, yearning the crave of freshly spilled blood. A taste she had not experienced since long before Nüwa had taken her in as an apprentice.

Licks turn to slurps turned to bites. In a matter of minutes, what had been hesitant reverence for the blood of an immortal turned to a greedy frenzy of tears and rips. Power surged through her from the magical flesh, demanding more and more.

It would not be until much later that Daji regained her sanity, finding herself licking the cold floor long after she had emptied the marrow of Zhōng Kuí.

She punched a wall. Whereas before her fist would bounce harmlessly off, it now cracked the rocky walls surrounding her. Emboldened, she shot a ball of fire. Though weaker than any magic she used to wield, the fire exploded against the ground, and soil and dust sprayed from the impact.

No longer was she limited to her illusions.

She turned to the discarded bag of scrolls that Zhōng Kuí possessed. They were all inscribed with names of the spirits that he was tasked with subduing. Some were crossed out, indicating those jobs were already completed.

Daji took satisfaction in that she was not one of them.

There were no names she recognized. She was not surprised. Entire millennia had passed since the end of the Shāng. She expected entire generations of spirits to be born and destroyed well before she woke up.

Daji opened up the final scroll, and her eyes widened. A fox spirit lived. One that, should she consume, would bring her closer to her original strength than any immortal she could possibly kill.

She smiled. It was time to hunt the gumiho of the Jailors.

2. "I kill master. I kill woman. I kill myself."

Only this time, the humans had guns and she had almost no magic. She tried to teleport, but as before, she felt herself hitting a wall she couldn't see. Whoever these Jailors were, they knew what she could do. And more importantly, what she couldn't. "Ender of Empires," she heard below her. Daji looked down - a spirit, too nondescript for her to tell the age of. "Enter." A force dragged her down a hole,  and sealed the entrance, well before any of the Jailors' infernal machines could follow her. She fell, further and further down. Uncertain of when and where she would land, she yanked up her shirt, allowing her tails to spill out behind her. Lack of nutrition had robbed her fur of its famed luster and size, but it would have to do. In a matter of seconds, she finally reached the ground. Or at least, smashed into it. The tails helped cushion the fall, but not even a fox spirit like her could outwit gravity without true magic. She pushed herself up, wincing from the pain, and touched her ribs. Nothing too broken that a couple nights rest wouldn't patch up. "Ender of Empires. I am Zhōng Kuí." She looked forward. The nondescript spirit ball was back, and this time she had the focus needed to identify that name. Her heart sank. "Shit," she muttered. "It's you." In a flash of light the spirit ball was replaced by a muscular man with a hideous face. He carried a back full of scrolls, a short sword with his right hand, and a rope tied around his left. He nodded. "It is well that you recognize me, Su Dájǐ. Shall we get down to business?" From one Jailor to another. From humans that sought to keep her behind bars, to the hunter of wicked spirits. The hunter who had his title stripped from him due to his face. "How did you find me?" Zhōng Kuí laughed. "Your return sent shockwaves through [[span class="ruby"]]Dìyù[[span class="rt"]]Purgatory[[/span]][[/span]], you know. Though your execution was long before my time, it is difficult to mistake the presence of a fox spirit, and none compare to how dread inducing yours is." Daji bared her teeth. "Little ghost hunters who weren't even born when the gods executed me should know when to respect their elders." "By Huīzōng's command, none of you fox spirits are to be venerated," said Zhōng Kuí. He spat at the ground. "Apologies, [[span class="ruby"]]//lǎoguǐ//[[span class="rt"]]old ghost[[/span]][[/span]], you're coming with me whether you want to or not." The rope around his arm uncoiled and shot towards her. She dodged to the side, racing towards the hunter. She slashed at him, her nails lengthening to claws that once killed sacred beasts, but Zhōng Kuí was unfazed. He parried her easily with his sword, and laughed. "Come, then! Show me the power of the Ender of Empires!" Daji snarled but didn't reply to the boast. Not having her powers against a man who was used to fighting those who did was a terrible position to be in. She conjured up a mass wall of flames and sent it towards Zhōng Kuí. He took a step back and grinned. "Yes! That's more like-" -just for it to pass harmlessly through him. He blinked and sneered at Daji. "So. This is all remains of the mighty [[span class="ruby"]]//jiǔwěi//[[span class="rt"]]Nine-Tailed[[/span]][[/span]]. I pity you. Had Huīzōng and the rest of Heaven successfully destroyed your cults and fellow spirits, you wouldn't even have the power to reform into the embarrassing state you are in now." "Insolent brat," Daji said. She coughed up a little blood. "What was the point of saving me from the Jailors if you were going to kill me now?" "Everyone wants you gone." For the first time that he spoke, Zhōng Kuí's voice lacked his usual boom. "Bad enough that the woman responsible for a dynastic contention be allowed to live, but to live this embarassingly? It reflects poorly on the gods who once, and still do, dread hearing your name. Better to give you a proper send-off or hide you away within our prisons than let mortals inflict the final insult of keeping you jailed away in their cells." "You don't get to decide that for me!" She readied her hands again, ready to cast another spell. "Your power has waned, //jiǔwěi,// and soon the others will learn. Allow me to send you to the underworld while they still fear and respect your name. Your illusions will not harm me." Something cold pressed against the back of his head. Before he could react, the gun fired, felling the demon hunter. The Daji in front of him dissipated into smoke. The real one was behind him, panting as she held the gun she had stolen from the Jailor with both hands. "Try my bullet," she hissed. She fired once, twice, again and again into the corpse of Zhōng Kuí until there was nothing more to fire. She dropped the weapon, hissing at the pain of the weapon's recoil. That pain was soon numbed by a different sensation. Hunger. She looked down at the corpse, and the blood that spilled from his body. Fresh blood. Eating the body of an immortal was sacriligeous at best and likely would ensure she be punished for the rest of eternity if she were to ever die. But Daji had no plans of dying just yet. She slowly knelt down and licked some blood. Her hunger exploded, yearning the crave of freshly spilled blood. A taste she had not experienced since long before Nüwa had taken her in as an apprentice. Licks turn to slurps turned to bites. In a matter of minutes, what had been hesitant reverence for the blood of an immortal turned to a greedy frenzy of tears and rips. Power surged through her from the magical flesh, demanding more and more. It would not be until much later that Daji regained her sanity, finding herself licking the cold floor long after she had emptied the marrow of Zhōng Kuí. She punched a wall. Whereas before her fist would bounce harmlessly off, it now cracked the rocky walls surrounding her. Emboldened, she shot a ball of fire. Though weaker than any magic she used to wield, the fire exploded against the ground, and soil and dust sprayed from the impact. No longer was she limited to her illusions. She turned to the discarded bag of scrolls that Zhōng Kuí possessed. They were all inscribed with names of the spirits that he was tasked with subduing. Some were crossed out, indicating those jobs were already completed. Daji took satisfaction in that she was not one of them. There were no names she recognized. She was not surprised. Entire millennia had passed since the end of the Shāng. She expected entire generations of spirits to be born and destroyed well before she woke up. Daji opened up the final scroll, and her eyes widened. A fox spirit lived. One that, should she consume, would bring her closer to her original strength than any immortal she could possibly kill. She smiled. It was time to hunt the [https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/scp-953 gumiho of the Jailors]. cooked.raw_content:
Cooked.

I ran out of steam,
I probably won't make it
The hill was too large

I didn't keep track
It's almost too late for me
I'm bad at time use

My trials were large
Many insurmountable
I doubt my success


















1/5/60, 6:27
Dendrologicheskiy Park, Yekaterinburg

Two benches, six trees, and a phonebooth. A man waits, clearly anticipating something. The weather is overcast, the park is deserted and a air of despair overhangs the scene. Then, the phonebox rings.

30/4/60, 22:49
Skies above Beloyarskiy Rayon, Sverdlovsk Oblast

A plane is circling, capturing photographs, and will soon report back to base in the US. Unbeknownst to the pilot, a threat approaches. A Russian surface to air missile, having detected the aircraft, strikes the plane. The pilot survives, as does the valuable intel it carries. The wreckage lands in a field near the town of Kosulino.

1/5/60, 6:29
Dendrologicheskiy Park, Yekaterinburg

"…Now, down to business. One of our own has been downed nearby. A field near Kosulino, to be precise. I need you to recover the film from that camera. The Militsiya will be attending the crash site, so speed is of the essence."
"Ok." The man replaces the receiver in it's cradle. He then starts running.



On the back of the intel recovered the below was written1, it has been digitised for ease of access.




"Two benches, six trees, and a phonebooth."
