divine-intervention.raw_content:
Why hello there.

Come to chat up an old man, have you?

Eh? Another interview? Fine, fine. I see no reason to deny it. Could you do me a favor, though? Pass me that grape juice box on the bedside table. I would get up and grab it, but my bones aren't what they used to be anymore.

Thank you.

How refreshing. Now, what was it you wanted to ask me about?

Ah, that. You had another name for it, at least before the changes happened. What was it again? SCP-6500? My, my, how far along we've come since the days of little old me, huh? Anyway, forgive me for reminiscing, it's all I've got left nowadays.

But yes, The Impasse. To tell you the truth, my child, I knew of it since it's waxing days, though I said nothing of it in hopes that you and yours would notice. It took far too long for your superiors to realize the world was at stake, and even longer for them to act. Unfortunate, yes?

Hmm?

Well, I couldn't interfere. It's not up to God to decide what happens to His creation. You have free will for a reason, my child. You were made in my image, after all, and I love you all so much.

You do your best as a Father. You raise your children; You prepare them for the world and then You let them go. You can’t swoop in every time Your children are struggling.

To do so would undermine the point of raising children. If they can’t solve their problems on their own, if they need You to save them every time they falter, then they’re nothing more than Your pets. I love you, so I respect you enough to save yourselves.

I see.

Doubt is such an ugly emotion to feel. But I do not fault you for it. After all, faith is blind trust in a higher power, and me being who I am, I did nothing to intervene. Yes, I am aware there were many lost. I know it was ugly. But like I said, I trusted you to save yourselves.

Click.

What's this now?

Hmmm. I suppose there is only one way for us to know the truth or not. Pull the trigger, my child. Find out for us both, for I do not know myself. Do it.

Do it, and face the truth no matter what.






BANG!

Karen Elstrom goes to the DMV MTO

…ᘛ⁐̤ᕐᐷ

▸ More by this Author ◂

{$comments2}

F.A.Q.

{$doesthisfixthebug}

Karen Elstrom speeds down the highway in her sleek black Tesla. She definitely bought this car before Musk went full mask off fascist. She definitely did not commit to a several thousand dollar purchase without even doing a cursory Google search of the company owner's political views! That would be absurd!

She made an appointment with the most middle of nowhere DMV a girl could find. Lowers the risk of being recognized to practically zero. I mean, who on earth would have the same idea to go to the same DMV on the same day as her?

The DMV is packed. Like packed for a DMV. She assumed a middle of nowhere DMV would be less packed than this. This definitely has to be more people than the population of this town. Good thing she had an appointment. She waltzes past the crowd towards the glass door between her and a renewed driver's license.

A man's hand shoots out to stop her, hovering suspiciously over her chest. "You've gotta take a number."

"But I've got an-" she bites her tongue. Everyone is looking at her now, in her three piece suit and expensive brown cardigan, roaring up here in a car more expensive than every other car here combined. She will not be a bitch today. She will not be a bitch today.

The number she receives is 47, which tells her very little about her position in line. She scans the waiting room, and spots one open seat. It's right next to a graying man who-

Wait.

That's Dr. Wettle!

She sits, and it takes him all of a minute and a half to notice her. "Woah! Hi, Karen!"

"Hi, Will." There are definitely worse people to be stuck in a DMV with. Wettle, who does not read any of the site memos, is one of the few people who doesn't immediately hold a grudge against her for doing her job. "What're you in for?"

"Getting my driver's license renewed. You?"

"Same." He pats the clipboard in his lap. It's one of those plastic clipboards that has a compartment inside. The clip part is missing; it's held closed by a rubber band. "I've got every possible paper they could ever ask for. Nothing's gonna sneak up on this guy!"

She double checks her manilla folder of paperwork, everything down to her birth certificate to her car insurance. The one thing she did forget is her phone, which is still in her car. She'd go get it, but she's already settled and she'd hate to have to stand if someone steals her seat.

"I'm hoping to get this picture fixed." Wettle shows his driver's license. He sneezed mid photo and they did not let him retake it.

"Number thirteen?" Calls a woman over the speaker.

Everyone shuffles to check their numbers, including Elstrom just out of habit. Still 47.

"Oh shit." Wettle pats himself down. Elstrom points to his front pocket, where lucky number thirteen is poking out. "Thanks!" He stands and immediately trips over some old woman's cane. His clipboard goes flying, flimsy rubber brand breaking, papers scattering everywhere.

"You watch it!" She barks, bringing the cane down to strike him in the shoulder.

"Sorry! Sorry!" He cries. In a rare act of collective human kindness, everyone picks up one of Wettle's papers and hands it back to him. He makes it through the glass door with seemingly everything together.

"Um?" A stranger holds up Wettle's driver's license. All eyes look to the door, waiting for the moment Wettle steps out, head hung low in shame, to pluck his ID out of their hands.

Thirteen, then fourteen, then into the twenties, and thirties, the forties… Then, an hour and a half of sitting there, an hour and a half after her appointment date, forty-seven is called.

The waiting room hasn't gotten any more empty. Still, Elstrom marches into the DMV office. She sits, one leg crossed over the over.

"What can I help you with?"

"I had an appointment to get my driver's license renewed."

"An appointment? For when?"

"For ten am."

"And when did you get here?"

"Well, nine-fifty. There was a line."

"You should've said something. We would've had you in at your appointment time!"

"Oh…" Elstrom makes a sour face, but quickly masks it.

She slides all of her documentation through the glass sperator. She looks off into the middle distance, always showing off her great side profile.

"Ma'am, your insurance is out of date."

"What!?"

The DMV woman slides the paper back towards her, tapping the expiration date with her pen. This time the sour look doesn't leave Elstrom's face.

"Let me check my car." She knows she has an updated version on her phone.

"Quickly, please." Says the DMV woman, not even looking up, as if Elstrom were some common bug.

Elstrom takes the walk of shame through the waiting room, back to her car, and returns with the last document. Finally, she walks out a free woman! Brand new driver's license in hand.

Goodbye middle of fuck all! See you when this one expires!

There's a familiar run down car in the parking lot. A familiar run down man helplessly turning his key with no luck. Elstrom can practically hear him whining in frustration. With a sigh, she walks over to him to knock on the window. He jumps, and quickly shoves a wad of napkins in his face to wipe his tears.

"Hiiiiii Karen!" Wettle says.

"You alright out here?"

He fiddles with his fingers. "My battery died and I've just been stuck here. I think all the tow truck companies have blocked me, heh…"

"Do you have a jumper cable?"

He sniffles and nods. "In the back."

"I'll give you a jump."

They go through the works of hooking one battery up to another. Wettle turns the key and his engine purrs to life.

"I can't thank you enough!" He says, wiping his face on his sleeve. "The day's barely gotten going and I'm already having a rough one. Hehe…"

"Hey," she says, gently. "Get it together."

She watches him drive until he's well and out of sight before getting back into her car and getting on her way home. She puts on a pair of fashionable sunglasses and dials Aubrey Al-Khafaji.

"Hello! Did my Kitty survive the Department of Motor Vehicles?"

"We call it the Ministry of Transportation here, but yes, I've survived!"

"That doesn't roll off that tongue."

"Does the Department of Motor Vehicles?"

"Hmm. Point. Any plans for the rest of the day?"

"Probably stop at the mall. Try on some new clothes." She passes. "Such a teenager thing to say. I'm also going to get a bottle of wine and drink it in my underwear while watching dating shows."

"I'd love nothing more than a front row seat to that."

"Smooth talk me enough and maybe you'll get one!"

Police sirens sound off. Elstrom looks in her rear view mirror and sees a police truck right behind her. She pulls over, the truck pulls over behind her and comes to a stop.

"Uh oh."

"Getting pulled over?"

"Yes."

"You weren't speeding, were you, Kitty?"

"Only to keep up with the traffic." The officer gets out of his car. "Hold on, he's coming up to me."

She lowers Al-Khafaji's volume and runs her fingers through her hair. When the officer reaches her, she's got a smoldering look on her face. It wouldn't be the first time she'd gotten pulled over just to get hit on. She rolls down her window, lets her sunglasses fall to the bridge of her nose, and flutters her eyelashes.

"Can I help you, officer?" She coos.

"You're missing an inspection sticker." He points to the corner where the sticker should be.

She gawks in a painfully unsexy way. "This is a new car."

"Sadly, not a legal one." He hands her a ticket and a sticky note. "You can get it inspected here."

"Alright…" She stares at the ticket with dismay. It's not the price, but the principal of the matter!

"Get that sticker, and drive safely."

She rolls up her window and sits there. She turns up Al-Khafaji.

"Kitty… Don't tell me you have been driving an un-inspected car."

"It's a new car! Why would it need an inspection?"

"Kitty…"

"You're supposed to be on my side in these things!"

"I am a health inspector. I am on the side of regular inspections!"

Elstrom makes a flabbergasted horse-esque noise. "Aubreyyyyyyy."

"Kitty!"

Elstrom punches in the address in her GPS and turns around. Soon, she's in another waiting room, at least this time without a number or a coworker to keep her company.

"Where did Kitty come from," she asks as she waits. "I don't mind it, I just wonder."

"I must confess… It is because of this song I have had stuck in my head."

"Which song?"

"The one that goes something something short skirt long jacket."

"You know, I actually met the lead singer of CAKE back in the 80s and he wrote that song about me."

"Is that true?"

"No."

Al-Khafaji laughs.

Another hour off her life, Elstrom gets back into her car and puts her foot to the floor. "Mall trip for real this time!"

"Yes!"

Police sirens sound off again. Elstrom swears she sees the officer scowling in the rear view mirror.

"God damnit!" She mutes Al-Khafaji and lowers the window. "Yes, officer?"

"You know you were going ninety-eight in a sixty-five."

"No, I did not, officer."

"Ha. Ha." He says, dryly. "Speeding ticket." He hands over the ticket. Elstrom rolls up the window and watches him walk back to his car.

"You've gotta be fucking kidding me!"

It's not the price, but the principal of the matter! "Get that sticker, and drive safely." She rolls up her window and sits there. She turns up Al-Khafaji. //"Kitty... Don't tell me you have been driving an un-inspected car."// "It's a new car! Why would it need an inspection?" //"Kitty..."// "You're supposed to be on my side in these things!" //"I am a health inspector. I am on the side of regular inspections!"// Elstrom makes a flabbergasted horse-esque noise. "Aubreyyyyyyy." //"Kitty!"// Elstrom punches in the address in her GPS and turns around. Soon, she's in another waiting room, at least this time without a number or a coworker to keep her company. "Where did //Kitty// come from," she asks as she waits. "I don't mind it, I just wonder." //"I must confess... It is because of this song I have had stuck in my head."// "Which song?" //"The one that goes something something short skirt long jacket."// "You know, I actually met the lead singer of CAKE back in the 80s and he wrote that song about me." //"Is that true?"// "No." Al-Khafaji laughs. Another hour off her life, Elstrom gets back into her car and puts her foot to the floor. "Mall trip for real this time!" //"Yes!"// Police sirens sound off again. Elstrom swears she sees the officer scowling in the rear view mirror. "God damnit!" She mutes Al-Khafaji and lowers the window. "Yes, officer?" "You know you were going ninety-eight in a sixty-five." "No, I did not, officer." "Ha. Ha." He says, dryly. "Speeding ticket." He hands over the ticket. Elstrom rolls up the window and watches him walk back to his car. "You've gotta be fucking kidding me!" [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box-end]]

Prologue

When Death pulled itself from the lake in the black of night, we were not prepared. Shrouded in darkness, its mountainous form was a mockery of humanity, a caricature drawn by those who knew only hatred: as tall as a thirty-story building, it had countless human hands, and a human head, but a shining cyclops eye and the unmistakeable mouth of a shark. After an hour, it slid back into Lake Michigan and disappeared, leaving half of Chicago in ruins and thousands dead.

The Forces of Sharkness had issued a proclamation.

In the days that followed, survivors dug through the wreckage while shadowed snapshots of the monster stalked the front pages of every newspaper. Every projector from coast to coast spun the same flickering newsreel on repeat: six or seven hands the size of houses churning like a cultivator, scooping pedestrians from the street and tossing them into a gaping mouth lined with rows of gleaming teeth.

For millennia, humanity had gone the distance, punching sharks for every inch of land we called home, but this shark was beyond the reach of human fists. The sharks had rung the bell for our final round; if we could not rise to this new challenge, they would deliver the knockout blow.

We at the Shark Punching Center saw an unprecedented spike in enlistment. Everyone wished to join the happy few that might destroy this monster when it next appeared.

I shared their sentiment. But until that call came, I still had a job to do.

Part I

1. The Deviant

Kovalik put his ear to the apartment door – an awkward movement in the bulky frame of his exosuit – then glanced to where I stood by the wall. He nodded, holding up the finger and thumb of his gauntlet. Two hostiles.

I nodded, lifted my own gauntlet, and punched through the wall, blasting concrete and sheet rock into the apartment. The hydraulics hissed as I retracted my arm from the three-foot hole, which was immediately surrounded by a swarm of tentacles from within. The head of a shark burst through, teeth gnashing and black eyes staring wildly.

It was too slow.

I pivoted, grabbed its face with my left hand, and delivered a hook with my right, the full force of my exosuit driving my steel fist into its skull. I felt a familiar crunch as the abyssal pearl in its brain shattered, and the shark fell back into the hole, limp tentacles sliding out of sight.

A few feet away, Kovalik kicked the door off its hinges and charged into the apartment. I gripped the hole I'd made with both hands and tore the wall apart to make my own entrance.

I was hit by the choking smell of burning flesh and rot. In the grim darkness, I saw Kovalik engage a waiting shark, ducking and weaving around the clawing motions of its arms to floor it with a straight jab.

“Two civilians alive here,” he called, pointing to a man and woman slumped by the wall.

The apartment was a ruin: furniture splintered and discarded in the corners, the walls and floor slick with a dark liquid. A charred human corpse lay by a power socket, both hands gripping an electrical cord it had apparently tried to eat.

“Captain!” Kovalik fell to the floor with a crash, tackled by a shark twice his size. It pinned him with clawed hands while he swiped his fists in vain. The mass of writhing tentacles below its waist wormed across his body and slid around his throat.

Three hostiles.

The civilian woman on the floor leaned forward and jabbed a fork into the shark’s back, to no effect. When she pulled the fork out, the wound closed instantly.

I grabbed two of the tentacles nearest to me and pulled, using the power of the exosuit’s legs to swing the shark’s head like a pendulum into the wall, which buckled from the impact.

The shark pulled itself upright on its tentacles, but paused for a moment, stunned by the blow.

I closed the distance and delivered a kidney punch, jab and a final haymaker that crumpled its skull. The pearl inside shattered; the abyssal threads that birthed the demon unraveled, and it lay lifeless on the floor.

Kovalik clambered to his feet and checked the remaining rooms. He called to the team outside. “We’re clear. Ring it!”

From elsewhere in the compound, a bell sounded.

I knelt by the civilians. The man was barely conscious, surrounded by empty bags of bread. His stomach was visibly swollen.

“Please,” he said faintly. “I need a croissant.”

The woman beside him put a bony hand on my shoulder. She was severely emaciated, in the final throes of starvation. “How much longer?” she whispered. “I put the slice in three weeks ago. I still haven't popped.”

“Here I am, Captain!” Kovalik pointed to a stone altar the sharks had built in the center of the room, strewn with bones and soaked in blood. Organs, probably human, were arranged in a ring around it.

In the center of the altar was a silver toaster. I could feel it fumbling inside my skull, a tiny voice repeating a phrase that echoed between my ears and yearned to escape my mouth.

“Bring the box,” I called.

Orderlies carried in a steel chest, lined with ornate golden trim, and prepared to move the toaster. They were followed by the Ref, his white shirt and black bowtie a stark contrast to the blood-soaked apartment. After surveying the scene, he nodded to Kovalik and I.

“Three KOs. Fouls?”

Goran jabbed his thumb towards the woman. “This one stabbed a shark with a fork.”

“She wasn’t in her right mind,” I added.

The Ref nodded solemnly. “Absolved.”

I looked to the open chest. The orderlies had placed the toaster within its red velvet lining and secured it with silver straps. The tiny voice grew louder as I approached.

I am a toaster, it said.

I slammed the chest, and the voice fell silent. The skeletal woman began to sob.

2. Goran

I punched a report into the typewriter in my quarters. An empty bottle of Bosun’s Titrant glinted in the yellow glow of the desk lamp, beside two crystal glasses. Kovalik was whittling an idol with his shark tooth knife, leaving shavings of balsa wood on the armchair.

“There were three sharks, not two,” I said.

“Two, three… ten sharks. It makes no odds for a righteous fist.”

I glanced at him. “I'm revising the breach protocol again. No more surprises.”

He nodded.

I laced my fingers and read what I’d written so far. There were days, increasingly common of late, when I felt my life and career amounted to a joke: forty years of setup for a punchline I wouldn't understand.

“A toaster,” I said. I pulled yesterday’s newspaper across the desk and studied the photograph again, though the monster’s face was already burned into my mind. “A week’s work just to contain a toaster.”

“A deviant,” Kovalik corrected. “One more deviant for the incinerator, ma’am. The world is safer for it.”

“Not safe enough.”

He followed my gaze to the paper. “They should dredge the lake. Fish that thing out and punch its brains."

“It's not in the lake,” I said. “They sent divers. It's gone. Back to the abyss, or wherever it came from. You’ve heard about Cleveland?”

He nodded. “The featherweights were aflutter when we came aboard. Seems the troops weren’t ready for it to return so soon.”

“The troops were two hundred miles away, guarding Chicago. But now it seems this monster can manifest anywhere. God, have you seen what they’re calling it?” I pointed to the headline:

CLEVELAND STEAMS AFTER MISTER HANDS ATTACK

Kovalik shook his head reproachfully. I reached for my glass of Titrant – it was empty. I leaned back and rubbed my eyes instead. “For every deviant we neutralize, the sharks find five more. And now this… I’ve never seen its like, Goran.”

"Aye, these are salient days. The Haymaker calls us to be weighed-in.” He was still focused on the idol in his hands. “Each of us will be measured by how we answer. Live or die, it makes no odds.”

“Is that so? What does the Ref say about that?”

Kovalik paused to pull at his long white beard. “The Ref says but little," he said, and returned to whittling. "He cares only for the edicts of the Center. I answer to the Three-Fisted God herself.” He pressed his fists together in reverence.

I appreciated this about Goran Kovalik: he never asked what I believed. His faith was a weathervane for the rank and file who shared it, and a leader must understand those she leads. I peered at the idol in his hands, which he was turning this way and that.

"Why do you keep that knife? It's unseemly."

He chuckled, and placed the finished idol on my desk – three gloved fists sprouting from the base like a flower – and sheathed the shark tooth knife in his belt.

“Crafting a holy symbol with the demon’s own tooth. I fancy the sharks know, and that it drives them mad.”

The yellow phone on the wall rang, and I answered reflexively.

“Blunt speaking.” I nodded as the bridge crew relayed the message. “Understood. Set a course.” I hung up and turned to Kovalik. “We’re being recalled to the Center.”

Kovalik smiled. “Salient times, Captain.”

3. The Admiral

The Shark Punching Center headquarters was a colossal fist. Its thirty floors were a sculpture of glass, steel and concrete that towered over the manicured gardens and parks before it, intended to broadcast humanity's strength and resilience.

It was a waste of resources. Every ounce of steel could have been better used to punch sharks. One of the reasons I avoided returning where possible.

Behind the Center, the blue afternoon sky was darkened by black clouds.

I straightened my dress uniform, and walked briskly through the crowd of civilians queuing at the main doors, where an officer waved me through. I overheard excited chatter from hopefuls who had never thrown a punch, explaining how they would personally destroy “Mister Hands” if they were only given the chance.

The elevator opened on the thirty-first floor – Admiral’s country. A Lieutenant Major wearing a floral shirt and sunglasses raised a hand as I approached the checkpoint.

“Name?”

“Captain Blunt.”

“For?”

“Admiral Strik.” I handed him my order slip.

“Block?” he said, gesturing to a dispenser at the booth.

“I– no thank you.”

He waved me through, and I shielded my eyes against the afternoon sun.

On the rooftop of the Center, rolling hills of landscaped grass undulated between game courts and lounge areas, surrounding a swimming pool that overlooked the north balcony. The south lawn was a collection of thatch huts and a tiki bar.

A glass railing at the edge offered a view of the factories behind the Center’s fist: a carpet of chimneys that streamed black smoke into the sky. Lying between them like an open wound was Ten Mile Sump, where the industrial effluence and runoff pooled into a lagoon that glimmered in rainbow colors.

An officer silently offered me a tray of cocktails, which I refused; I only drink after a fight.

I approached the swimming pool, and tried to determine which of the twenty men and women splashing, tossing balls and lying on floats might be Admiral Strik.

“Admiral?” I called hopefully.

Every head turned in my direction.

“There she is!” came a voice from my right. A man in a white shirt and shorts with Admiral epaulets was waving from a hill, leaning on a golf club. His curled hair and bushy beard was a bright orange. “Captain Blunt! Come, join me.”

I saluted, raising my fists in a fighting pose. “Admiral Strik, sir. Captain Blunt reports as ordered.”

“At ease. Come, I was just finishing a round.” I followed him over the hill, where he addressed a golf ball, aiming for a tunnel at the base of a spinning windmill. “Welcome back to the Center, Captain. I’m told it’s been years since you were here last.”

“Sir,” I said. “That’s correct, my assignment keeps me in the field. There are always more deviants to destroy.”

He swung the club in a gentle arc, and watched the ball roll down the green. It bounced off a windmill blade, and he snapped his fingers in frustration.

“Yes, well. That's why I needed to have this little chat with you today. We've got quite the deviant problem in this Mister Hands.”

I wasn't sure I'd heard him correctly.

“Sir, are we adopting the name the newspapers have chosen?”

“Ah, it’s as good as any for now. Perhaps we’ll let you choose a better name after you kill it,” he said, knocking the ball towards the windmill again.

Finally, confirmation: of all the officers at the Center, I had been chosen to lead humanity's defense. I'd dreamed of this since the monster first rose from the lake.

The ball rolled through the tunnel, and landed in the hole with a hollow rattle.

“Well then!” The Admiral thrust the handle of his golf club into my chest, and strode off towards the bar. I froze, until a Lieutenant with dead eyes collected the club and slid it into a bag. I assumed the Admiral expected me to follow him, and wandered to the bar.

I found him in the shade of a pink umbrella, peering at a case file through half-moon glasses perched on the tip of his nose.

“Mister Hands is making a lot of mischief,” he said without looking up. “First Chicago, now Cleveland… we can’t seem to catch up. It all reflects very poorly on us – I’ve been getting a lot of questions.” He looked at me. “That won’t do, Captain.”

“Understood, sir. What’s our plan of attack? Mister Ha– this monster’s head is beyond the reach of our fists.”

“Yes, it is.” He passed me the case file. “So we must make our arms longer.” He strolled over to a pink chaise lounge under a palm thatch shade.

The file was bound in black leather, with gold-embossed print on the cover:

Project OPUS LEGION

I stood next to the Admiral and leafed through the pages: detailed schematics, with various components highlighted. “A submarine, sir?”

He smiled, but there was caution in his eyes, trepidation. He’s not sure how I’m going to react.

“A deviant submarine, Blunt, with other deviants tacked on for good measure. This is how we’ll stop Mister Hands. You’ve been chasing deviants for years. It’s time for us to start using them.”

Start using them? It was as if Bodega Bay had never happened.

“I see, sir.”

The file held an annotated diagram of the monster’s physiology, based on assembled camera footage. It had a human head and torso, but no legs. It was supported by ten arms – the diagram noted the count was approximate – all jutting from its ribcage.

Its eye, deeply recessed in the center of its face, was nested within concentric rings of rolled flesh under a pronounced brow ridge. Beneath it was an ordinary round nose, and that shark-toothed grin. From the eye, illustrated lines spread in branching patterns to the rest of its body.

"The eye is an abyssal gem," I noted. "A ruby."

"Precisely. Destroy the eye, and the monster dies. It's so simple it rhymes."

"And this submarine will allow us to do that?"

He laid back and closed his eyes. "Opus Legion can intercept Mister Hands wherever he appears. Sinus Homestead will allow you to deploy a battalion of exosuits. And Rose Plastique is an aerial attack solution to destroy the eye. There are others, I forget… it's all in the file."

I leafed through the documents, trying to make sense of the plan.

“I have absolute faith in you, Captain," he continued. "You have experience with both submarines and deviants. Finish the project, command the ship, and when Mister Hands returns, kill it. It’s quite straightforward.”

Deviants are never straightforward, I thought. They were unknowable, unpredictable. They had no regard for the laws on which civilization and sanity relied. They were chaos; that’s why the sharks loved them. To make a plan with deviants was like trying to sail in a hurricane, and it wasn’t clear the Admiral had thought this through.

“So now Captain,” he said. “Let’s hear your questions.”

I sensed the words I wanted to say next would be insubordinate, so I decided on a different tack.

“This decision has been made already?”

He nodded.

“And will we stop at deviants, or are we to fight with bombs and missiles too? Bullets and bayonets, sir?”

“Now, there's no call for anything so extreme,” he said.

“Even so, sir, this change in strategy may be difficult for our pugilists to accept.” There will be anger and fear, I thought. Either could cripple us. “Especially after the…” I paused. “The events in Bodega Bay.”

He turned to look at me then, eyebrows raised. Perhaps he was surprised I’d had the indecency to bring it up. He smiled with one half of his mouth, and looked down at the ground between us.

“Regrettable,” he said, nodding. “But we’ve learned from the past.” He looked up. “We can’t allow it to hold us back, not now. As for the hearts and minds, I’m sure you’ll find a way. Keeping Commander Kovalik by your side has earned you respect from those in our ranks who… play by the old rules.”

“I keep those by my side who can throw a punch, sir.”

“I’ve heard he gutted a ray on your quarterdeck for All Hallows.”

“He– We hold various divine services, sir. It's good for morale, and it hurts no-one… except the ray.”

“And you see, thats just the perspective we need. I have every confidence you will convince them of the merits of this path.”

A purple bean bag landed in the Admiral’s lap.

“Strik!” Another Admiral was striding towards us. “Cornhole, let’s go. Best of three this time.”

Strik climbed to his feet. “Ah, apologies Blunt, that’ll be my 1 o’clock – I’m afraid I do have to take this. Admiral Towne is a wicked hand at cornhole.” He tossed the beanbag back to Towne.

I had a hundred questions. “Sir? When will we start?”

“Oh we’re already underway,” he said, walking away. “The science lead can give you the details. I expect they’ll be in the labs.”

4. Doctor Keane

According to the directory, the “Deviant Technology” labs were on the fourth sub-basement. I wandered fluorescent hallways of sickly green linoleum that smelled faintly of bleach, in search of “Room A13”. I had so far found only an “A12” and, three corridors over, an “A14”.

I passed an open door where someone was working, and decided to ask for directions. She had her back to me, apparently aiming at a dartboard. A dark braid hung down the back of her white lab coat. As I came closer, she threw a perfect bullseye, and scribbled notes on a clipboard.

“With skills like that they should make you an Admiral,” I said wryly. “How's your cornhole?”

She froze, but didn’t turn. Then she spoke, with a voice that turned my guts to ice.

“My cornhole is right where you left it.”

“Melanie,” I whispered.

She turned to face me. She wore a gold emerald necklace, and a white fingerless glove on her right hand. Her rolled sleeves displayed the colorful tattoos my fingers had traced countless times.

She looked me over. Under her gaze, I felt like a featherweight entering her first bout.

“It’s good to see you again, Lindsay,” she said at last, with a sad smile. Something stirred in me that took all my resolve to quell.

She pointed to my badge. “You're still a Captain.”

I looked at hers. Dr. Melanie Keane, Head of Deviant Research.

Suddenly I understood. “This is your project… you gave the Admiral my name. But why?”

She glanced at me for a moment, but said nothing. She went to a table, where a collection of steel darts were arranged on a silver tray.

“Melanie,” I said. “It’s been–”

“Ten years, yes.” She lifted a dart and rolled it between her fingers. “I’ve been busy,” she said to it. “As have you.” She gestured vaguely to a corner of the room, where boxes of every size were piled haphazardly.

Steel boxes with gold trim. These were boxes I had filled, in the naive hope they would be responsibly destroyed. All of my efforts in the last decade, and the blood of a hundred pugilists, had served only to stock Melanie’s laboratory. I turned on her.

“How can you still work with deviants, Melanie?”

She didn't look up. "The way you say that word, you sound almost like Goran. Remember him?”

“Commander Kovalik is my second now.”

She snorted. “Good lord.”

“I’m serious, Melanie. I've seen the nightmares they create. We can’t trust them. And what about Bodega Bay? You of all people know the lesson we learned–”

“No,” she said coldly, meeting my gaze once again. “You saw what you saw. I took a different lesson from the Bay.” She turned to the dartboard, but threw the dart at the floor. It ricocheted and landed squarely on the bullseye.

“Huh. That was some coincidence–”

She held up her gloved hand. “I prefer to make my own coincidences.”

I looked closer at the glove. It seemed unremarkable.

“A deviant, I assume. Something you plan to give to our pugilists?”

She laughed, and some warmth returned to her eyes.

“This deviant, they can pry from my cold dead hands. I’m a little too fond of it.”

Fond of deviants. She always knew how to provoke me. But I wanted to hear that laugh again.

“So how does it work?” I tried. “The glove controls the dart in the air?”

“It manipulates probability. Anything you throw will land true. It’s a mathematical constant of the universe, as certain as gravity, entropy, or that sharks must be punched. Just as long as you can see your target, and you believe you’re engaged in some sort of ‘game’.”

“’Some sort of game…’ Melanie, listen to yourself. War is no game.”

“It’s a minor constraint,” she shrugged, taking another dart from the tray. “Deviants are like people, they have their… idiosyncrasies. You get used to them. But can you imagine what we might achieve with weapons like this?”

“A projectile, in a bout of combat. Should we abandon everything that makes us human?”

“There may be other uses for it. But Lindsay, you saw the monster that climbed from the lake. Humanity is out of time. If we’re to choose between our ‘purity’ and our survival, I choose survival.”

She glanced again at the dartboard, and casually tossed the dart on the floor behind her.

It bounced once. A rat suddenly scurried across the floor. The rat bumped a tray leaning against a wall, which fell against a cart, which wheeled forwards over the tip of the dart, causing it to skitter forward. But it stopped there, several feet from the wall.

A splintering sound came from the wall the dartboard was on, and a crack forked across the white paint. There was a loud creaking groan as a sheet of concrete came loose, allowing a chunk of the wall to peel forward. It hit the ground and exploded into a cloud of masonry dust.

Melanie stepped forward over the rubble and pulled aside shattered blocks of concrete. She lifted a circular chunk and found the dartboard still attached to the other side, with the dart lodged firmly in the bullseye.

“Impressive,” I said, as she started to take notes. “But you’ve only proven my point. The dart will hit the target, but does the glove care whether you or I survive, or if this building still stands afterwards? The glove cares only for the target… as you care only for these deviants.”

She stared at her notes silently, her pen immobile. Finally she whispered:

“There’s the Lindsay I remember.”

The words sank as shark’s teeth into my heart. My breath caught in my throat. Carelessly, I allowed the hurt to sour into anger, and rose my voice.

”Stay here in your lab, then. Play with fire all you like. But keep your chaos out of my ring. I have no time for your ‘games’.”

I moved to the door. “I’m glad you can throw a dart,” I said over my shoulder. “But unless you can throw a punch, you’re of no use to me.”

She said nothing as I stormed from the room.

5. Folly

I threw my weight into my fist, savoring the impact that resonated in my arm and chest. Another jab, followed by a cross, hook, uppercut and a jab that knocked a shower of dust from the top of the brown leather training bag.

The successive impacts were a salve for my swarming thoughts. Emotions burned away in the acid of adrenaline. Regret for what I'd said to Melanie. Anger and humiliation at the betrayal of the Center. And fear. Fear that I would again watch innocent people suffer for our carelessness when our weapons spiralled out of our control.

Kovalik's face appeared from behind the bag. He gestured to the falling dust. “These Center gyms don't see much use.”

I nodded, still catching my breath, and stepped back to towel off.

“This project is absurd,” I said into the towel. “We'll kill ourselves before we kill the monster. I can’t allow it to go forward.”

Kovalik followed. “On the contrary, Captain, that's just what you must do.”

I lowered the towel from my face to be sure I'd heard him right. “You’re serious, Goran? You, of all people, I would have thought…”

“Oh, it's the worst plan I ever heard, ma’am,” he said matter-of-factly, handing me a water bottle. “But that's why you and I must see it through.”

I sat on a bench and stared at the opposite wall. The gym was empty. Most pugilists trained at the base where they were stationed; the staff at the Center seemed more interested in punching clocks than bags.

Kovalik sat, and cracked his knuckles thoughtfully. “May I speak plainly, Captain?”

“Always.”

“I've been punching sharks a long time. Longer than you've been alive, if I may say. Some bright sort always gets the notion to use these cursed things instead of burning them like we should. But there's a pattern to these things. I expect you're thinking of the Bay?”

“I’m always thinking of the Bay.”

“Might I ask – why do you suppose Hereford thought to poison the water supply in the first place?”

“The shark tsunami,” I said. “He was trying to heal the wounded.”

“Aye, that’s true. But we’d seen wounded before. We have medics for that. I’d say rather, he lost faith in our natural abilities, felt he had no choice but to trust in the profane. Just as our Admirals have done now, for fear of this monster in the lake."

He tugged at his beard. "That’s how it always goes," he said. "This won't be the last time, either. Not unless we prove the folly of it, once and for all.”

”If you're suggesting some kind of sabotage…”

”Sabotage?” He was horrified. “Never, Captain. The opposite. We hold tack with the plan, dabble in the abyss, as far as we must. But when the time comes, we find a way to fell the monster ourselves. Show the world these deviants weren’t necessary after all.”

He had a point – it was no use harping on the danger unless we could offer an alternative solution. What better way to prove deviants were unnecessary, than to beat the thing with our own hands?

“Consider this, ma'am,” he continued. “Seems the Admiralty will pursue this course either way. Can you really trust the task to anyone else?”

Later that afternoon, I stopped at a message booth and sent a telegram to Admiral Strik.

CPT BLUNT COMMITTED TO OPUS LEGION STOP FAITH WILL BE REPAID IN FULL STOP TRUST CORNHOLE WENT WELL

Part II

6. The Sub

Opus Legion was a black rubber cigar the length of a football field, with a winged conning tower bristling with antennae. It was floating in the murky water of a graving dock, on the eighth sub-basement of the Shark Punching Center.

“Some place for a dock, this,” Kovalik said as we walked the concrete deck beside the ship. “No gate on either end, as I can see.”

“Maybe its a prototype,” I offered. “Perhaps they plan to rebuild it when – Melanie!”

She was approaching briskly, white coat blooming behind her, with a clipboard in one hand and a large steaming mug in the other. “Captain. I saw your note about a demonstration.” She reached us, and looked at her clipboard. “Well, you managed to find the ship – that’s a good start.”

Kovalik gave her a brusque nod. “Doctor Keane.”

“Yes” I said. “I need to know exactly what this thing does… or at least, what we think it does.”

She gazed at the submarine, perhaps in awe, or perhaps to avoid eye contact. “Beautiful, isn’t she?”

“Melanie,” I said quietly. “About yesterday, I–”

“Hold this,” she said, thrusting the mug into my hands. It held a steaming black liquid that smelled like fresh brewed coffee.

“Can I drink it?”

She glanced at the mug for a moment. “Better that you don't.”

She turned back to the submarine. “Reverb, I have the Captain with me. Systems online? Good. When ready, execute the Folgers maneuver, reference… my position.”

I looked around, and saw Kovalik doing the same. The only other people on the dock were two porters, moving a set of deep sea diving suits on a trolley. Melanie appeared to be speaking directly to the submarine.

“Who's Reverb?” I asked her.

“The navigator on the ship,” she said. Then, realizing our confusion: “I can make a phone call from anywhere. It’s quite convenient.” She lifted her braid, and pointed to a small scar on the back of her head. “Anywhere I go, I’m always connected.”

Goran shifted uneasily by my side, and muttered under his breath. “She’s a goddamned witch.”

There was an extremely loud and short sucking sound, like jello meeting the tube of a vacuum cleaner, and the submarine turned to glass.

No, not glass – it was water, in the precise shape of the submarine, suspended in the air for an instant before it fell with a crash into the pool below, displacing a wave that rose up the concrete wall to where we stood. The submarine was gone.

Melanie was smiling. Kovalik had turned white.

“Where–” I began, but was interrupted by a small “plop” from the mug I was holding. A ball was rising from the surface of the coffee, attached to a long pole. It rose past my face and stopped, at least six feet high, its entire mass rising weightlessly from the mug.

Loudspeakers around the dock broadcast a cheery male voice.

“Good morning, Captain! It’s great to meet you. With your permission, I will remanifest in the dock.”

I stared at the antenna, and at Melanie, who nodded. “Yes,” I said. My mouth was bone dry. “I mean – very well, Mr. Reverb.”

The antenna retracted into the mug and disappeared, leaving an oily red swirl. Then, in the dock water below us, that same pole re-emerged and rose higher, eventually revealing that it was attached to the submarine’s conning tower. Finally, the full mass of the vessel surfaced and bobbed on the water.

“He put the ship's antenna in my cup,” I said.

Melanie nodded excitedly.

“Its an impressive trick,” I said, handing the cup back to her. The red swirl had started to curdle. “We'll be able to intercept Mister Hands, just as soon as he starts drinking coffee.”

“It can manifest in any liquid – hey! Stop! Put that down right now!” She ran full-pelt down the deck, letting the coffee mug shatter on the ground. I looked to where she was yelling; the two porters had started playing with the diving suit helmets, and one of them was about to try wearing one. I followed at a brisk pace.

“Stop!” Melanie yelled. “That’s not–”

The porter placed the helmet on their head, and gestured with their hands to indicate that nothing untoward had happened. The other porter glanced between Melanie and their colleague, trying to understand the cause for alarm.

“It’s not a big deal,” the helmeted porter said, heavily muffled. “I’m very sorry. Look I’ll take it off–”

“Wait!” Melanie said.

The porter lifted the helmet, and a rush of red water cascaded from the neck hole, over their shoulders and chest. When the helmet had emptied of liquid, there was nothing else above the porter’s neck. The arms holding the helmet aloft went limp, and the body fell lifeless to the ground. The helmet landed with a clang and rolled away.

I was running now, and reached the three of them just as the second porter started to scream. The body had no head, but the water that emptied onto the dock had carried with it shreds of meat, eyes, and teeth.

I cast an accusing finger at the helmet. “What the hell are these things?”

“They came with the submarine,” Melanie said. She was staring immobile at the porter’s body.

Kovalik came up behind us. “It’s a sign, Captain. As clear a sign as any. These are not forces to ally ourselves with.”

“No,” Melanie said, rounding on him. “It’s a sign that we need to find porters with more discipline.”

“There are no signs at all,” I said, inspecting the suits on the trolley. “These things should be under lock and key. Nobody should be handling them without full awareness of what they do. Discipline starts at the top, Melanie.”

She had fury in her eyes, but we both knew I was right.

“Aye aye, Captain!” She saluted, pushed Kovalik aside and marched down the dock, passing a medical crew that was rushing to our location. She looked back at me. “Are you coming, sir? There’s more to see, and we’re already ten minutes behind the schedule you set.”

7. Mr. Reverb

“It doesn’t match any model we’ve seen. But with our retrofitting, it should feel quite familiar.”

The airlock cycled, and Melanie led the way into the interior. The corridors were illuminated by dim orange lamps, and it smelled faintly of steel and motor oil, but that was normal for a submarine. Less so was the pervasive smell of licorice.

“We don’t know why it smells like anise,” Melanie said. “You’ll get used to it.”

“I’ll need to write up an incident report for that porter,” I said.

She paused for a moment before continuing. “I'll have Reverb write it up. You'll have a draft on your desk this afternoon. The berths are just up here…”

“This Reverb is an industrious navigator,” said Kovalik behind me. “He’s doing a lot of work for you.”

“No,” she said. “He's doing a lot of work for us.”

We toured the operational rooms, storage, and berthing, where Melanie offered no additional information beyond reading the sign on the door. Kovalik said little, but his disapproval was palpable.

“’Captains quarters’,” she said, opening the hatch and walking away. They were comfortable enough, though the licorice smell was stronger there.

“’Galley’, or ‘Mess’… whatever it says.”

I stepped into the mess hall. “That’s… quite the artwork,” I said, pointing to an enormous mural hanging across the back wall.

“Oh, that,” Melanie said, poking her head into the room. “Just some fun. We thought it might inspire the crew.”

The lower part of the mural was a swarm of sharks, clambering over each other in a pile to reach Kovalik and I, who stood on a platform in the center pummeling every shark within reach. Neither of us had shirts on. Melanie was standing in the background like some holy saint, along with others I didn’t recognize.

“How did you commission this so quickly?” I asked.

“Reverb printed it. He’s quite the artist. That is to say, he’s every artist whose work we’ve shown him.”

I moved closer. “I appear to have three arms in this picture… and there are… eight fingers on this fist here.”

“Yes, well…” Melanie hesitated. “He’s not very good at drawing hands.”

“God forgive us.” said Kovalik.

“I want to meet this artist,” I said.

Melanie showed us to the conn, the command hub for the ship. It was unlike any I’d seen. Arranged on the walls were twenty or thirty rectangular screens, each of which showed a moving picture in full color – various views of the graving dock outside. I moved to the captain’s chair and sat down, running my hands over the black leather armrests.

“Where are the projectors?” Kovalik asked.

“Behind the screens,” Melanie said absent-mindedly. She was working at a typewriter that had no paper in it. “Welcome to the future, and so on. Reverb, meet Captain Blunt.”

A simple face appeared on one of the screens: two dots for eyes and a curved line for a mouth. That same voice sounded again from the speakers.

“Ah, it’s great to meet you in person, Captain! I’m looking forward to working with you. And also with you, Commander Kovalik.”

“Reverb is a… an electric person,” Melanie said. “A machine that can think and talk like we do. He uses tiny microphones and cameras to see and hear us. We think he came through a temporal slip.”

“An electric person,” I repeated. “How exactly does it function?”

Melanie looked at the ceiling and tapped her clipboard in agitation. I recognized the gesture – it meant you're getting caught on things that don't matter.

“We’re not entirely sure how he works,” she said, “and neither is he.”

“You’re absolutely right, Doctor,” Reverb said. “As a sixth-generation mixed-mode language model, my cognition is based on artificial neural networks. It’s a lot like a human brain, though its workings are just as mysterious.”

“But he does work,” Melanie added. “We can train him to do anything. Writing reports, gathering intelligence… he can even do things a human can’t, like pilot this ship through extra-dimensional space.”

Kovalik circled the room, inspecting the screens. He stopped in front of Reverb’s “face”.

“So it’s just a machine… though you talk as if it were a man.”

“Because he talks as if he were a man,” Melanie said, staring daggers at Kovalik. “And stop touching the screen, the fingerprints are–”

“Let’s see what he can do,” I said, to get us back on course. I looked to the screen and raised my voice. “Mr. Reverb, I hear you can gather intelligence.”

“That’s correct, Captain! I’ve been trained on over a thousand–”

“Locate the nearest shark activity.”

Reverb paused. “Certainly! I’d be glad to help with your shark location project. I’ve completed a review of past combat engagements, behavioral observations, and tidal patterns, and I’m ready to provide an assessment.”

“Go ahead.”

“I can predict with 99.42% confidence that sharks are active in the ocean.”

I looked to Melanie.

“We’re still working out the kinks,” she said impatiently. “But we can trust him.”

“With our lives, and the lives of everyone we’re to protect?” I asked. “How do we know he won’t steer the ship into a rock?”

She cocked her head. “He's a better pilot than any human. Wherever the monster shows up next, Reverb can get us there in minutes. Watch – Reverb, show us a demanifest cycle.”

Reverb paused before replying. “I’m sorry Doctor, but there are strict protocols for the chain of command with regards to submarine operations. While the Captain is in the conn, it would not be appropriate for me to accept navigational commands from–”

“Thank you Reverb,” I said. “You can do as she says.”

The ship jostled instantly – almost before I’d finished saying the words – as though we’d been hit by a light wave. The sucking sound from earlier was audible, but muffled by the ship’s hull. The only other indication we’d disappeared from the face of the Earth was on the viewscreens.

The world outside was now an endless ocean of arterial red, which we were fully submerged in. Leaning forward, I could make out strands of material or small pieces of debris floating past, but couldn’t identify them.

“I’ve never seen an ocean like this,” Kovalik said. “These waters were not made for us.”

“It looks like they might be made of us,” I said.

Melanie tapped her clipboard again. “We don’t know much about this space, yet. We know it’s not Earth. And we know it’s… well, it’s mostly blood, and seawater.” She looked to me. “May we now return, Captain?”

I nodded.

“Perfect!” Reverb said cheerily. “I’d be glad to return us to the Center.”

Nothing happened. I looked to Melanie, but there was concern in her eyes now.

I turned back to the smiling face on the screen. “Reverb, take us back home.”

“I would love to Captain! Returning us home now.”

We didn’t move.

“Reverb,” I said slowly. “We haven’t moved.”

“Ah, my mistake Captain. I see now that I didn’t actually navigate us back to Earth. Let’s navigate back now.”

A long silent moment passed in which the vessel did not move.

Kovalik was standing by a screen, staring at the featureless red expanse. “I’m going to die in this godforsaken hell,” he said, with a voice of quiet certainty.

“Reverb,” Melanie said. “Take us home, now.”

“Great, Doctor! Setting current location to… home.”

When nothing happened, Melanie darted to the front of the room, where a collection of wires terminated in a gray box, into which a single black cable was plugged. She started fumbling with the wires.

“Reverb,” I said, standing up. “Navigate this vessel back to the graving dock of the Shark Punching Center… on Earth.”

At last, we heard the thrusters spin, and the ballast pumps working.

From the movement of the debris, I could tell we were rising. The light grew brighter, as though were were about to breach the surface of the blood sea, but when we broke through, the graving dock was waiting on the other side. The only clues that we’d travelled anywhere at all were the clinging wisps of blood gently unspooling from the hull into the dark water.

Kovalik sank into a chair and stared at the floor. I sat down too.

“Let’s not go back there until we need to,” I said.

“I’d love to, Captain!” Reverb said. “Returning us back to–”

Melanie grabbed the black cable and wrenched it out of the box.

“Ah, I seem to have lost functional control of the submarine, Captain. Please try again later.”

None of us spoke. Melanie was crouched by the box, still holding the plug. “I know that wasn’t ideal,” she said quietly, standing to face me. “But we can train him to be better. We need to, if we want to stand a chance of intercepting Mister Hands. The calculations required to navigate that space would take us years, but Reverb does it in seconds… when he actually does it, at least.”

I stood up again. “Fine. I want to see the training schedule, and a manifest of everything we’ve taught this thing to do so far. We need to test its abilities rigorously before we can rely on it.”

“Rely on him,” she said, then added “Captain,” with a theatrical curtsy.

“Kovalik – I'll meet you back at the dock,” I said. “Melanie… a word.”

8. Respect

I decided to use the submarine’s briefing room; my quarters felt somehow inappropriate. By the time I’d closed the door behind us, she was already sitting at the opposite end of the long wooden table.

“I’m all ears, Captain.”

“Enough, Melanie.”

“I don’t–”

“I said enough. I’m sorry for how I acted yesterday. I was out of line and I apologize.”

She said nothing.

“But we can’t go on like this,” I continued. “This is your project. You recommended me to the Admiral. Why? There are other captains. Why would you want me here?”

She traced her finger over the tabletop.

“You were the only one they’d accept,” she said, without looking up. “This project was hard to sell. I needed a name that would inspire confidence, and that was you. They trust you.”

I should have felt pride, but there was something disappointing about her answer.

“I see,” I said. “So you’re stuck with me, then.”

She looked up. “I’ve been working in a basement these last ten years, Lindsay. My department might seem like a joke to you now, but it was nothing when I inherited it. Maybe I haven't planned for every variable the way you do, but this is how progress is made. Sometimes you have to take a leap of faith."

She stood, and started pacing.

"I want to get out there and help," she said. "I know we can. I hate that so many people had to die for me to get this chance, but that's why this project has to succeed.”

“Then help me,” I said. “The rest of the crew will be here in two days, so cut the theatrics. We're not kids anymore. Say what you want in private, but when we're in mixed company, I'm the captain. If I can't maintain the crew's respect, your project will die before we leave port.”

She paused.

“Fair enough,” she said.

“We will succeed,” I said, with more confidence than I felt. “But the crew will need guidance. They're not used to working with deviants or… why are you rolling your eyes?”

“Because they already use deviants, you all do. You use them every day you put on one of those exosuits. Or use medical gel, or–”

“Wait, what are you talking about?” I said. “We’ve had exosuits for decades.”

“It’s deviant technology, they’d never work without it. Even our buildings use deviant materials – how do you think skyscrapers are made? The Center spent millions on shell companies and cover stories to keep it all a secret. But we don’t have time for their stupid conspiracy now.”

I felt my face grow flushed. Blood was pulsing in my temples.

“You don’t understand,” I said. It was like she’d told me my left arm was actually that of a shark. “Our exosuits are… in the field, your fists are the only thing you can trust–”

“But that’s the point!” She leaned on the table. “You can trust them. You do, every day. You reap the benefits of deviant research, while proudly announcing that you’re ridding the world of them.”

“Listen, Melanie,” I got to my feet. “I understand, but the crew, our pugilists… they won't. They're not ready for it. Keep this to yourself for now. Understood?”

She bristled, but eventually nodded.

“Aye aye, captain,” she said quietly.

9. The Crew

On the day that our crew reported for duty, the Shark Punching Center issued a new edict, affirming that the use of deviants in combat was now considered honorable, provided the safety of civilians and pugilists was properly accounted for. It announced Opus Legion as the first project of a new global initiative to utilize every useful deviant in our war against the sharks: Operation Mythos Hoedown.

Melanie was radiant, declaring it was a leap forward for humanity.

I was frustrated by the vague wording, and the likelihood that careless pugilists might start seeking out deviants they were unprepared to safely use.

Kovalik was furious, along with about half the crew. They’d signed up for Opus Legion with the understanding that it would be a temporary solution to the Mister Hands crisis, but the Center had made clear they had larger plans. We had to break up a squabble in the mess hall in which a junior engineer had threatened to punch the Ref himself.

“Not to worry, Captain,” Kovalik told me privately afterwards. “The crew will settle once we bring the Admiralty around to our way of thinking. They’ll see the truth of it yet, once we remind them what our pugilists can do. We’ll beat this monster with our fists, and the natural products of our ingenuity – our ships, harpoons and exosuits.”

I could have told him then. It would have saved a great deal of pain if I had. Our exosuits aren’t natural; perhaps none of our tools are. But I believed I was granting him mercy, to be unburdened by the hypocrisy of those we served.

Work began in earnest. I created daily training drills to prep the crew for every conceivable scenario. We ran demanifestation cycles, practicing rapid deployment from the graving dock to various bodies of water around the world. We practiced emergency underwater escape routines, but I stopped short of asking anyone to swim in that blood sea, even for a practice drill.

Melanie had a long list of deviants to be integrated, and we started with simpler ones: a coffee machine that could dispense 12 ounces of any liquid we asked for, which we used for both mechanical fluid resupply and beverage service; a bowl that automatically filled itself with soup, which we added to the rotation for morale; a kitchen funnel that could alter the size of anything that passed through it, which Melanie said would be important later; and a tree that grew a slightly-inferior clone of any object that touched it, with which we could quickly stock our army.

We kept the deadly diving suits in the sub’s airlock – Melanie was unsure if their presence was required for the ship to operate properly – but I insisted they be placed in a secure locker, which only the Commander and I had the key to.

Each new deviant was met with grumblings of resentment from the more devout members of the crew, which I counted on Kovalik to control. I wondered if it had been a mistake to include them in our roster to begin with, but the best pugilists were often the most religious.

I ordered that proper documentation be written for every deviant to avoid further accidents. Reverb attempted to draft some, but I found them overly verbose and too generic to be of use. In the end, I wrote them all myself, capturing the unique containment and handling procedures for each deviant, along with a detailed description of its effects; I called them “Safety Control Processes”.

It was a lot of work, but worth it to ensure there were no more accidents.

10. Rose Plastique

“Alert. Containment breach in progress. All personnel report to safe areas.”

Alarm klaxons sounded, and spinning beacon lights flashed orange and red throughout the floor.

I hurried down the corridor with Kovalik at my side, our exosuits wheezing and clanking with every step. The corridors weren't built for our suits.

“Melanie's in Hydroponics Lab A. It's just down here.”

We reached a set of double doors and swung them open.

Kovalik pressed his fists together. “What fresh hell…?”

In the corridor beyond were five pink plastic lawn flamingoes, clattering around the linoleum on metal legs. They were crudely made, with painted eyes and beak, and I could make out a ridge down their center where they might have been injection molded. Their stiletto legs had no feet and ended in sharpened points. They were flapping their solid plastic wings in anger, or perhaps distress.

“Let's go slowly,” I said. I took a step forward, my boot hitting the floor with a thunk.

The flamingoes opened their mouths as though to scream, though the only sound they made was of rattling plastic and scraping metal.

Then they attacked. They came at us fast, kicking with their pole legs as though they were rapiers.

Two of them closed in on me. I ducked out of the way of one kick, but the other flamingo jammed its leg right through a joint in my leg armor and drew blood.

“Alright then, we fight,” I said.

The flamingo that stabbed me spread its wings and leaned forward to bite. I grabbed hold of its beak and swung the bird like an axe against the wall, snapping its neck clean off. I turned to the second and curled a downwards hook that knocked its head from its body. They both lay still.

At my side, Kovalik push kicked the third flamingo into the remaining two, and all of them scattered like bowling pins. Before they could pick themselves up, we charged forward together, elbowing them out of the way and bursting through the double doors at the far end.

“Alert. Containment breach in progress. All personnel report to safe areas.”

Goran shook his head. “They’re disgusting. They fight with beak and sword, bleeding us like sharks.”

“Agreed,” I said. "But they fight with their own limbs… the Refs approved it. We have to destroy the monster's eye – and until we find a way to drop exosuits from the sky, these birds are our best option."

Besides, I thought, there is something strangely impressive about them. Though they were a fraction of our size, they didn’t hesitate to throw themselves against us. I could use a squad of pugilists with half their fighting spirit.

We came to the doors of Hydroponics Lab A, and Kovalik stopped at the door. "I can scarce see how a handful of these birds will fell the beast. It would take an army."

He pushed open the door, and we were hit by a deafening noise, like ten thousand typewriters hammering at once.

The lab was a vast rectangular room, with a field of artificial grass lit by bright white lights suspended from the ceiling. In the center of the room, barely visible, was a tall apple tree with long pink apples growing from its branches. Swarming around the tree was a flock of hundreds upon hundreds of flamingoes, running rampant across the floor and over each other, flapping their wings and snapping their beaks.

“Alert. Containment breach in progress. All personnel report to safe areas.”

Around the edges of the room, I caught glimpses of Center researchers pressed up against the walls, covering their heads with their arms. And in the furthest corner, I saw Melanie waving to us across an ocean of swirling pink plastic.

A phone was ringing. I looked to my left, and saw one installed by the door.

I picked it up. “Hello?”

“It’s me,” Melanie said. I often forgot she could call from anywhere, and was always surprised to hear her voice. “We have to stop the cloning. They’re multiplying out of control. We brought a few of them in here so we could make more, but… well you can see how that went.”

I looked at the apple tree again – the pink fruits were actually flamingoes, swelling on its branches and dropping to the ground to immediately join the fray. Every time a flamingo brushed against the trunk, another pink fruit began to grow.

“How?”

“There’s a safety switch in the control room. But none of us can reach it. It’s on the opposite side of the room from where you are.”

I saw the stairs she was referring to, across a whirling blender of steel poles. There were several lifeless bodies on the floor, which the flamingoes were running over heedlessly.

“We need to control them somehow,” I said. “These exosuits don’t offer much protection. What do you know about them?”

“I…” she stuttered. “Well they don’t like loud sounds, for a start.”

I turned to Kovalik. “Find a way to turn off the alarm, fast.”

He nodded, turned and ran down the corridor, barging through another set of double doors. I saw him clothesline a flamingo before the doors swung shut. Then I waited.

“Alert. Containment breach in progress. All–”

The alarms were silenced. The flashing lights stopped. All that remained was the sound of rattling plastic, but it grew quieter too. The flamingoes slowed, no longer flapping their wings.

But the tree was still cloning more flamingoes. I looked to the control room, and took a step forward.

Immediately, ten or more birds hurled themselves at me, pecking and stabbing. I blocked as best I could with my armored forearm, stumbled back into the hallway and let the doors close. They didn’t attempt to follow.

My exosuit is too loud, I thought.

I took a deep breath, and unbuckled the straps that secured me in the exosuit, and slid out onto the ground. I unlaced my boots, and stepped across the linoleum in my socks to slowly push the doors open again.

The flamingoes were silent, idly stalking around each other and pecking at the ground as if to find food.

How’s this for a leap of faith Melanie?

I waded slowly into the crowd. Flamingoes closed in on all sides, and brushed up against the bare skin of my arms, but they moved aside without complaint.

I was chest-deep in a sea of plastic. One of the flamingoes carelessly walked over my foot, sending the metal spike through the sock, skin and muscle between the bones of my feet.

I bit my clenched fist to stop from calling out.

At last I reached the far side and limped up the stairs. On the console in the dark control room, I found the safety shut-off button.

I looked through the glass window at the field of flamingoes quietly roaming, and was struck by a strange feeling. At this distance, they were indistinguishable from real birds. It was hard to deny that deviants were a form of life too, albeit a strange one, as wild and spirited and free as we humans were.

I pressed the button, and a fence rose around the tree while a cage descended over it, blocking the flamingoes from going near. The sound made them swarm again briefly, and when they did, I noticed a spot in the room they were all avoiding; it was an exposed coolant pipe, frosted over.

I came down the stairs again, stepping tenderly on my wounded foot, and gestured for the other employees to come slowly around the edge of the room to reach the exit.

When everyone was safely extracted, I found Kovalik in the hallway.

“Send in a team with nets and wire,” I said, “Padded armor, no exosuits. And fire extinguishers – they don’t like the cold.”

I turned to Melanie, who was covered in cuts and scratches. “We need to make shoes for these birds.”

11. Sinus Homestead

“They've identified the head and torso,” I said, leafing through the briefing document on the desk in my office. “Apparently Mister Hands was once Tariq Makhdum, a courier from Karachi. Abducted in a shark raid six months ago.”

“And the arms, ma'am?” Kovalik asked.

I flipped a page, then flipped it back again. “We may never know.”

“So it's true," he said. "The sharks are experimenting on us. They’re turning us into monsters.”

I nodded, and he shook his head distastefully. After a moment, he cleared his throat.

“Captain, I…” He paused. For the first time, Kovalik seemed unsure of his words. “It’s the most peculiar thing, but… I think you ought to hear it.”

“Go ahead.”

“On my life, when I sleep in my bunk on the ship, I awake to find some spectre standing over me. I thought I'd imagined it, but last night I saw him plain. A pale man, with his mouth–”

“Sewn shut, yes I see him too.”

“You…” he stuttered, his face as white as his beard. “You mean to say he's real?”

“Yes. Melanie says the ship’s just spent too long in that extra-dimensional space. He should be harmless though. Apparently he just likes to watch.”

Kovalik said nothing, his face a picture of horror.

There was a knock at the door, and Melanie entered, followed by a thin woman with one arm. I stood up.

“Captain," she said. "I’d like you to meet Ariel Donner.”

I reached forward and shook the woman's hand. I could tell from her posture she was a pugilist, or used to be one.

"Glad to have you," I said. "I understand you're the solution to our storage problem." I gestured to her arm. “You’re a purple glove?”

She nodded, and raised her hand in a fist. “A shark. But it didn’t have a chance to enjoy it. Ready to get back on the front lines." She looked to Melanie. "You said you've got a way to get these corpses out my nose?”

Melanie nodded. "I hope so. Let's go take a look."

Down in the lab, Melanie's team examined Ariel's nose with an endoscope. Though she was an ordinary human, her left nostril was a portal leading to an abandoned war bunker.

“We don’t know which bunker it is,” Melanie explained with her eye to the scope. “Somehow it’s become untethered from wherever it used to be. It’s a normal size… it's only the portal that's tiny. But from what we can see of the bodies inside, we can guess they were Federicos."

“Why does she have a fascist war bunker in her nose?” I asked.

“Hell if I know,” Ariel said. “I didn’t ask for it. I just woke up one day with this godawful smell.”

Melanie nodded. “There’s a second portal in there that leads from the bunker to the rest of her nasal passage. When we found her, she had severe pneumonia. The filters we installed keep her safe, but I think we may have a better solution now.”

Melanie’s team used the cloning tree with the orange plastic funnel we’d collected earlier, assembling them together into one giant funnel; one end was two metres tall, the other was barely a centimetre. Even though the funnel was cone shaped, from the inside it appeared perfectly cylindrical. Anything entering one end would be resized – through means nobody could comprehend – to match the aperture on the other end.

Ariel sat on a stool with the small end in her nose, while the big end provided a human-sized entryway.

There was a problem, though. The funnel could shrink a person, but there was nothing on the other side to size them up again. While inside the bunker, they were ants in a vast desert of rotting giants. Removing the bodies would be impossible.

In the cathedral of a skeletal ribcage, we built a forward operating base: Sinus Homestead. We set up tents for safe working areas, but otherwise the air was foul-smelling and toxic. Anyone stationed there for more than a few hours required breathing apparatus.

Even when the base was ready, many of our pugilists refused to enter Ariel’s nose. I pressed Kovalik into service, and he arranged for a priest to cleanse the space with holy smelling salts. It did nothing to purify the air, but the troops seemed satisfied.

Watching Ariel sit patiently on the stool, reading a book while troops and supplies poured in and out of her nose, I was struck by her resolve. It was clear that it wore on her, but she wouldn't admit to it; she merely said she was glad to be fighting sharks again.

With her apparatus connected to the deployment bay doors, we could deploy an army of exosuits from the top of Opus Legion. She was the linchpin of our strategy to destroy Mister Hands.

Melanie threw open the doors and sprinted down the corridor, with Kovalik and I keeping pace behind. There was no time for suits – we would have to rely on our combat gauntlets.

"Where is she?" I said.

"In her quarters. Reverb spotted it on the security camera. We might already be too late."

"How did these hostiles get into the Center?"

Melanie looked back at me incredulously. "They work here, Lindsay. They're your crew."

We reached Ariel's quarters – a spacious apartment reserved for guests. The living room was strewn with discarded food containers, scattered paperwork and pieces of Center equipment.

The hallway ended with closed doors to the left and right. Against the wall was a spool of coiled rope connected to a Center-issued harpoon, the tip blunted to regulation standards.

There was a crash from the bedroom to our right, and sounds of a struggle.

Without our suits, a wall entry was impossible. I signalled to Kovalik: “Breach protocol, form 2-3.”

He nodded, and I kicked open the door to the bedroom. Two men were holding Ariel.

I pushed into the room and Kovalik followed, moving left to cover the corner. One of the assailants shoved Ariel into the back corner and rushed toward me, fist raised. I parried his punch, pulled him forward and drove my metal fist into his elbow, snapping his arm. He screamed, and my followup jab connected with his face, knocking him bloodied to the floor where he lay still. He was wearing a Center uniform.

Behind me, Kovalik was scrapping with an assailant who’d been hiding in the corner. He delivered an uppercut that lifted their feet off ground, and they crashed backwards into a wardrobe. The new breach protocol had worked.

“Ariel!” Melanie shouted from the doorway.

I looked to the far corner – the third hostile was now holding a knife to Ariel's throat. She elbowed him in the stomach, and he doubled over. She spun to hook his jaw, but he intercepted the punch and wrenched her back into his grip, pinning her arm behind her.

I recognized the man – Senior Middleweight Foley, an exosuit squad leader.

“Don’t move!” he said, with the knife back at her throat. “Not another step, Captain.”

“Don’t you fucking touch her!” Melanie screamed.

“You’re a pugilist,” I said. “What do you think you're doing?”

“I won't go back in there!” His voice cracked with desperation. "I'm sorry Captain. They're the pits of hell itself. We're cursed for going in there, all of us!"

Ariel grunted. "Suck it up. That's what duty means." His arm tightened around her throat. "You think I want you in my nose all day?" she rasped.

“Easy son,” Kovalik said, his hands open in a display of trust. “Easy now. That's an employee of the Center you’re holding.”

“She's a fucking deviant! What you're making us do… we're unclean! None of us will make it to the ring!”

I raised my hands too, slowly removing the gauntlets. “Listen, Foley. We can fight this out like honorable folk. You want off the project? It's done. But we’re pugilists – we don't use knives. You know that.”

I thought I saw some kind of understanding dawning in his eyes, and hoped we might still defuse the situation. But it wasn’t understanding – it was the peace of resolute determination. Certainty. Conviction.

He raised the knife higher. “For the glory of the haymak-”

His head exploded in a shower of skull and brains that sprayed across the back wall. The ragged remains of his neck spouted blood and the body toppled backwards.

Ariel slowly wiped his blood from her face with her sleeve, and looked down at the corpse.

Behind her, deeply embedded in the wall, was the harpoon, still attached to a taut length of rope which divided the room. I looked back and saw the other end was held in Melanie’s hands.

Kovalik spoke first. “What in god’s name have you done, woman?”

“I saved my friend,” she said. She held up her right hand, on which she was wearing the deviant glove. “He was about to kill her.”

“You threw a projectile in a bout of combat!” he yelled, stepping towards her. "Is it not enough that we corrupt ourselves with these profanities, you want to abandon the rules as well?"

I held out my hand to stop him. "It's distasteful," I said. “But the use of harpoons is permitted. So long as the rope is attached, it's an extension of your arm.”

Kovalik clenched his fists and spoke through gritted teeth. "You speak for the Refs now, ma'am?"

"Just stating the rules," I said calmly. "You know them better than I do, Commander. Why don't you go ask a Ref yourself, while we clean up here?"

He stared daggers at Melanie, but couldn’t seem to find any other words. He marched out of the room and slammed the door.

12. Taking a Leap

Melanie was pacing in my quarters. It was a small space, so she was practically walking in circles. I closed the door behind me quietly.

“You know I don’t agree with Goran,” I said. “But we have to take his concerns seriously. He speaks for a lot of the crew.”

"Speaks for them? I guarantee it was his idea to kill her in the first place. Do you still let him perform those sacrifices? Purifying the ship by gutting some defenseless fish?"

I considered my answer carefully.

"We can trust Goran. We need to."

She continued pacing for a moment, then turned to me. “I read the Safety Control Process you wrote, for Rose Plastique… the flamingoes.”

“I… yes?”

“You said to avoid loud noises. And not to spray them unless necessary, and to avoid damaging their wings…" She pulled a folded piece of paper from her pocket and opened it. "You said, ‘though they are prone to fits of rage, their violent outbursts are never without cause.’”

“How long have you been carrying that around?” I held up my hands in confusion. “Were those instructions not accurate?”

She put the paper away carefully, and stepped closer.

“No, it was accurate, I just…" she looked down at her hands. "It’s a side of you I don’t often see. You’re starting to get it – you can see they’re alive, in their own way. You’re protecting them like you protect your crew.”

I hadn’t noticed. “I suppose I am."

She looked up into my eyes. “If you don’t agree with Goran, you should challenge him directly.” She put a hand on my shoulder. “The crew follow you, Lindsay. They hang on your word. Show them deviants aren’t some evil curse.”

I sighed, and pulled back. “I wish I could, Mel. We’re barely holding them together as it is. They think when they die the Haymaker weighs them in for their final bout, and that if they’ve been corrupted by deviants they won't be allowed in. They think they’re gambling eternal damnation – they're scared. If I’m to protect them, I have to at least respect them.”

She paused, and turned away.

“You’re afraid of them,” she said. “You’re always so careful, about everything.”

“What’s that supposed to mean?”
