She sat down on my bunk. “I know I was cruel to you, after…” she trailed off and said nothing for a moment.

“Say it.”

She looked up. “What I mean is, Bodega Bay was hard on you, on all of us, and maybe we dealt with it in our own ways. Even though you weren’t in command–”

“It doesn’t matter,” I said reflexively. “Hereford took the fall, but we can’t pretend we didn’t agree with him.”

“Of course. We wanted to help those people, that's what made it so painful. Watching them age backwards, until they were just–”

“Stop,” I said, my heart pounding. “Please Mel, I can't.”

“Look, we all fucked up, okay? I'll carry that weight forever. But the way it affected you… it changed you. You were unsure. You started to hesitate – I had never known you to do that before. And I know it’s unfair, but… I missed the old you. The Lindsay that would jump into action without a second thought.”

I sat on the bunk next to her. From the all-encompassing smell of licorice, something else came through. Eucalyptus mint: she was still using the same shampoo. Its icy sting recalled warm, quiet nights when I would fall asleep with my nose nestled in her neck. The only time I felt safe.

“But this isn't about what I want,” she said. “Or what I miss.” She looked in my eyes. “You can’t afford to hesitate anymore, Lindsay. There won’t always be time for you to weigh the risks. We all need you to remember how you were before. How to take a leap. Even if you don’t know the outcome. To be–”

I kissed her.

It was strange, awkward. I used to do it every day without a thought, but it now felt harder than climbing a mountain. My hands were shaking. Her body was a foreign language to me now; I’d miscalculated.

“There’s the Lindsay I remember,” she whispered.

She put her arms around my neck, and kissed me back – warmly, desperately – and the doubt was gone. I remembered again how we fit together, and how completely the world beyond our arms would dissolve when she was holding me.

She paused, put her head against mine. “I lied, earlier. About why I recommended you for the project. There were other captains. But you were the only one I thought I could actually convince. The only one who might come to see the beauty in the things we can’t understand.”

We sat in silence for a time.

“Mel… do you think we can start over?”

She sat up slowly, pulling at her braid with one hand after the other. Then she came back to me.

“Ask me again after we kill this thing, okay?”

In that moment, I could have beaten the monster to a pulp with my bare fists.

13. The Battle of Toronto

“Hello, all hands! I’m delighted to share with you all an urgent message from Center command. Please report to battle stations immediately. The monster known as Mister Hands has returned.”

Crew moved swiftly around the ship with practiced fluidity, slipping around each other in the cramped corridors without colliding. I found Melanie and Kovalik waiting in the conn.

“Give us the report, Reverb,” I said.

“Certainly. The report is as follows. Mister Hands attacks again, stop. Emerged Lake Ontario, stop. Attacking Toronto, stop. Divisions 8 and 10 engaged. And that’s the end of the message!”

“This is it,” I said. I lifted the intercom. “All hands, prepare for battle.”

“It’s not ready,” Melanie said, frantically leafing through papers on a clipboard. “There's… at least twenty components still to collect. The clockwork, the butler, the exclusion suit–”

I looked to Kovalik.

"We are being called to the ring,” he said. “We have no choice but to answer."

I nodded. “The sub is ready. We go now.”

We surfaced in the middle of Lake Ontario. Toronto’s squat brown buildings peppered the shore a mile away, windows glinting in the sun. Hulking before them on the shore, in the pale flesh, was our foe.

Seeing him now in person – even through the medium of the viewscreen – felt different. He was far bigger than my mind could have imagined, and he moved too quickly. He was a mountain of fingers and teeth, and we hoped to fell him with pebbles. As we watched, the monster’s eye glowed brightly, and a beam of fire lanced out, slicing a building in half.

The lights in the conn were dim and red for battle. I was ready for a fight.

“Sound the bell,” I said.

The Ref hit the bell.

“Round one!” He yelled.

“Ho!” echoed the crew in unison.

The Ref retrieved his ceremonial steel chair from against the wall, unfolded it, and took a seat.

“Reverb,” I said. “Get us in closer. Evasive maneuvers as needed.”

We dematerialized and resurfaced. We were still some five hundred feet from the creature, but he filled the viewscreen. Five or six of his hands were shaking a building, apparently trying to pry it from the ground. The columns on the building's facade fell like timber and shattered on the streets.

“Deploy exosuits,” I ordered.

On the top of Opus Legion, the deployment bay doors opened. An army of fifty exosuits marched out of Ariel's nose and up the stairs.

In their subaquatic heavy combat armor and rebreather helmets, they barely looked human. A thousand feet of coiled rope hung on each armored back beside colossal harpoon guns. They dropped into the water and tore off towards the shore, propelled by airjets around their waist.

Mister Hands finally tore the top of the building off, and hurled it into another. His hands reached inside and pulled out civilians that he threw into his mouth.

He didn't notice the exosuits assembling around him, marching against the flow of fleeing civilians like rocks in a stream. On the magnified viewscreen I saw a civilian fall at the feet of a Bravo squad member, apparently thanking them for the rescue, but the pugilist pushed them aside and readied their harpoon gun. Well trained, I thought.

“Let’s get his attention, I said. “Launch the noisemaker.”

“Aye aye, Captain,” called Lieutenant Savage, from the weapons console to my left.

A rocket launched from the rear of the submarine, streamed high into the sky and exploded with an enormous bang. Colored lights trailed from the explosion, crackling loudly. Mister Hands stopped mid-chew. He pulled his massive body around to look at us.

“Fire harpoons.”

Fifty harpoons fired at once from the exosuits, piercing the monster’s hands, arms, head, neck and back. His red eye couldn’t express surprise, but his hands flailed wildly in apparent confusion.

The ropes went taut, and for a moment, he was held perfectly still.

Then he gathered his strength, and started to wriggle loose. A rope snapped. Then another.

“Target the eye,” I said.

Ten designated exosuits arranged in formation on the shore fired harpoons directly at his eye, but they glanced off his brow, dug into the rings of his eye socket, or pierced his nose. His eye was too protected.

Another rope snapped, then ten more. One of his hands came free and swept the other ropes away. Exosuits that were too slow in detaching from the rope were hurled into the air and crashed into buildings or the lake.

Mister Hands started clambering across the streets again.

“They’re not enough,” Melanie said. “We need the torpedoes.”

I thought of what the flamingoes might do, raining down on the city. The shoes we’d made for them had a tendency to fly off.

“We just need more exosuits,” Kovalik said. “We’ve still got a hundred in reserve. Send them all, Captain.”

“Wait! He’s turning back. He’s coming back to the lake.”

For a moment, Mister Hands seemed to be looking directly at us. Then he looked left to right, seemingly scanning the water for something. He must have found what he wanted, because he pulled himself into the lake and disappeared beneath the surface.

“Mister Hands is no longer in the lake,” said Reverb.

“All hands, stand down but remain alert,” I said. “The monster has retreated.”

The crew cheered. Civilians on shore were shouting and waving.

Our exosuits strode back into the water, climbed the side of the ship and filed back into Sinus Homestead to re-arm.

“Great news, Captain! The Toronto mayor would like to speak with you, likely as an expression of gratitude for defending–”

“Thank you, Mr. Reverb,” I said. “The mayor can wait. Once everyone is aboard, take us back to the Center.”

“Aye aye, Captain!”

Melanie shook her head. “We got lucky. We all know we weren’t ready for him.”

14. Theta Team

“Captain, a moment if I may.”

“Make it quick, Goran. We have to restock and prepare. He could strike again at any moment.”

“The harpoons would have worked, ma’am. This is the opportunity of which we spoke, some time ago.”

“Goran, I–”

“Please ma’am, if you’ll hear me out.”

Crew members streamed past us in the corridor.

“Not here,” I said. “My quarters.”

I closed the door behind us.

“Let’s hear it then.”

“You saw how the harpoons held it. That’s just the strategy we need. We can finish this without resorting to… well we both know the torpedoes are not to be used. I saw how you hesitated and it was well you did. Who knows who they might injure? They might even side with Hands himself – they crawled out of the same abyss.”

“Do you have an alternative solution? There’s no other way to strike the eye.”

“We can climb it, ma’am. We’ll use the exosuits. Theta Team will climb its face while Bravo squad holds it down. We’ve already run the training drills, they know what to do. I only ask that you trust in our people, ma’am. Have they not fought for by our side for years?”

“It’s risky,” I said. “And truth be told, Goran, I don't share your disgust for deviants. We need to use whatever works right now.”

“But you care for safety, Captain, do you not? If I may, the woman I've known some fifteen years would recognize the danger these torpedoes pose to civilians, and to our own pugilists.”

“Watch your tone, Commander. You go too far.”

“Captain…” He was desperate. “Ma’am… I implore you to listen. We must stop this while we still can. You may trust the deviants, but can you trust whoever uses them next? Do you trust the Admiralty to exercise restraint?”

I pictured Admiral Strik in his white golfing shorts, using Melanie's glove to cheat at cornhole.

I pinched the bridge of my nose. “Look, Goran…” I put a hand on his shoulder. “I'll give it some thought. Clear?”

He smiled with relief and nodded. “Aye, ma'am. We'll show our true colors this day. Salient times indeed.”

The emergency alarm sounded.

”Captain to the conn immediately. Captain to the conn.”

When I entered the conn, everyone was staring at the viewscreens. We were back in the blood sea, but we weren’t alone.

“He doesn’t seem to have noticed us,” Melanie said. “Or he just doesn’t care we’re here.”

Mister Hands was barely visible through the murky red soup, pulling himself through the blood and water with all of his limbs. Then he breached the surface and disappeared.

“Mr Reverb, do you know where he went?”

”Yes, Captain. Based on his trajectory, he would have surfaced from Ten Mile Sump, the lagoon situated next to the headquarters of the Shark Punching Center.”

“We’re out of time,” I said. “It’s now or never.”

15. Battle for the Center

We surfaced in the middle of Ten Mile Sump. Oil-slick water slid over Opus Legion’s hull. It was not water anyone should swim in.

Mister Hands had already pulled himself from the lagoon and was approaching the great silver fist of the Center headquarters. He plowed through two factories, which crumbled to ruins in his wake.

The Ref rung the bell. “Round two!”

“Ho!”

Two battleships were stationed on the lagoon already, on either side of us. They fired deck-mounted harpoon guns that tore deep into the monster’s back. He turned to face them, and his hands flailed wildly, ripping the harpoons out as quickly as they fired them in. He pulled the roof off a nearby factory and hurled it at a battleship, catching it midship and tearing the harpoon gun off the deck.

“We have to get behind him,” I said. “Reverb, find somewhere we can surface. All hands, prepare for exosuit deployment.”

We were sucked into the ocean of blood once again, and broke the surface. The water drained from the viewscreen cameras to reveal rolling hills of green and a minigolf course.

We were in the Admiralty pool. Panicked admirals in swimsuits were swimming away from the surfaced submarine, climbing over each other to get out of the pool and running in every direction.

The bay doors opened and a squad of exosuits crashed into the water. They vaulted onto dry land and ran to take positions around the edge of the roof, collapsing the pool walls under their weight and tearing up the turf.

We dematerialized and reappeared at the edge of the lagoon to offload additional squads. Reverb sent us to three other locations, deploying over a hundred armored pugilists at strategic locations.

“Is that all of them?”

“Almost,” said Kovalik. “There’s one squad left to deploy Captain.”

Mister Hands seemed to spot us for the first time. He dropped the slabs of concrete he was holding and turned to face us. His eye burned a bright red, and a spear of white-hot light danced across the lagoon, vaporizing the water.

He was too slow. Reverb remanifested us half a mile away. We watched exosuits moving into position at his feet, while his eye stayed fixed on us.

“Keep him distracted,” I said. “It’s working.”

Mister Hands charged another piercing beam of fire, and Reverb remanifested us again. Then another beam split the lake – but we were already on the south side, then the north, then back at his feet again.

He paused for a moment, perhaps thinking. He reached his many hands up to his back, where some kind of sack was attached. He pulled out several orbs and threw them into the sky – over the lake, over the factories, and several towards the Center.

“What are those?” Kovalik asked.

“Ah, great question, Commander! While it’s impossible to know for sure, there are couple of likely candidates for what the pods might contain. For instance–”

A pod fell onto the shore in front of us and burst in a shower of water. It was full of sharks.

“That’s the last exosuit squad deployed, Captain,” said Kovalik. “They’ll engage the sharks first.”

We watched a pod arc high into the air above us. I looked to another screen; the deployment bay doors on top of Opus Legion were still open.

“Reverb, close the deployment bay doors.”

“Sure Captain! Closing them now.”

The doors didn't move. The pod burst in the air, and five sharks rained down from the sky.

I stood. “Reverb! Close the deployment bay doors!”

“Ah, my apologies, Captain. I see now that I didn't close the doors.”

The conn shook as four sharks landed directly on the ship and climbed towards the open doors on our back.

“I'll close the doors now,” Reverb said.

Two sharks slithered inside before the doors clamped shut.

“Intruder alert!” Kovalik shouted into the intercom. “All hands prepare to repel boarders!”

I watched on the screen as the two sharks trashed the cargo room, claws ripping down shelves and tentacles whipping crates around. One of them disappeared through the hatch, deeper into the ship. The other snapped at Ariel and Sergeant Austin, who were fending it off with a metal shield.

“Rob!” Ariel’s voice came through the speakers in the conn. “Get in my nose, lure it in!” she yelled. “Trust me!”

She put her nose to the funnel, and Sergeant Austin darted inside without hesitation.

“Come on you bastard!” Austin yelled behind him. He threw his shield at the shark and caught its back. It turned from the hatch and followed him into the funnel.

I took a step closer to the screen, my fists clenched.

Ariel pulled away from the funnel and reached her thumb and index finger into her nose, slowly peeling out a long thin tentacle, followed by the rest of the shark, which was now the size of her thumb. She dropped it on the ground and drove the knuckles of her fist into it.

Melanie pointed at the other screens. “Captain, look!”

The second shark was tearing through the corridors of the sub, shredding pipes, wires, and crew members.

Lieutenant Savage pointed to one of the screens. “It's headed straight for–”

The shark burst into the conn, wrapping its giant mouth around the Lieutenant and biting his torso in half.

Melanie threw her clipboard: the edge of it crushed one of the shark's black eyes.

It stumbled forward, tripping over Reverb's wires and landing on the floor at the Ref's feet. He stood, folded his steel chair and drove it into the shark’s skull, crushing the pearl inside.

The Ref nodded, then went to kneel by the lifeless body of Lieutenant Savage.

“He's looking right at us,” Kovalik shouted. On the screen, Mister Hands was looming over the ship. “Evasive maneuvers, Reverb!”

“I'm sorry Commander, I seem to have lost control of the ship.”

“His wire’s unplugged!” Melanie yelled, pointing.

The conn shook violently as two sets of hands grabbed hold of us, and pulled the submarine clean out of the water. We were lifted hundreds of feet in the air, held over his head.

The room turned upside down. I hit the ceiling hard, and struggled for breath. “Hold on to something!” I rasped.

For a moment, nothing happened. On the screen, I saw the back of Hand’s head, the empty sack of shark pods, and his pale bony back. In the divots of his bones, glimmers of rainbow light were reflecting in the sun: pooled water from the lagoon.

Then he launched us into the sky.

Every loose object in the conn slammed against the wall, including Kovalik, the Ref, the shark’s corpse and both halves of Lieutenant Savage. I held onto a pipe with both hands. Then my feet and legs started to float behind my head.

We were in freefall.

The ground was speeding towards us – we were flying towards a set of brick buildings.

I pushed away from the pipe and drifted across the room, grabbing hold of the center console and using it to pull myself forward, to the grey box at the front of the conn. My hands scrambled along the floor for the black cable.

Every viewscreen was filled with the building we were about to hit.

My fingers closed around the black cable and pulled it up to find the plug.

I jammed the plug into the socket as we crashed through the factory roof.

We were in the blood sea again, and all was silent.

“Thank you Captain! I’ve regained control of the ship. It seems we have taken significant damage.”

I looked around the conn; Melanie, Kovalik and the Ref were still alive, but battered and bloody.

I could barely catch my breath. “The pools of water on its back,” I said. “Take us there, and deploy the thumpers.”

We rushed back to the surface, breaking through from the puddles on Mister Hands’ back. Deployment flaps opened on the sides of the ship, and crews leaned out to secure ten heavy jackhammers, which dug with metal claw feet into his skin.

Then we were gone, and resurfaced back in the lagoon. The hammers began to pound on the flesh and bones of the monster’s back.

He reared up with a long roar, all of his hands reaching back to pull the drills off.

“Now!” I said.

A hundred exosuits fired their harpoons in unison. Every one of his hands was snared and pinned. The exosuits on the Admiralty rooftop harpooned the back of his head and pulled it back. He was stuck.

“Now, Captain!” Melanie said. “Fire the torpedoes!”

Kovalik raised his hand. “Not yet! Look, there’s Theta team!”

A squad of ten exosuits was moving swiftly, scaling the chest of Mister Hands like a vast mountain.

I thought of the flamingoes, and how hard it had been to contain them before. I saw the lifeless bodies on the floor of the Hydroponics Lab, skewered by a hundred daggers. There were exosuits surrounding the monster now, even climbing on him – if we deployed, they would certainly face the birds' wrath as well.

I hesitated.

“Lindsay! What are you doing?”

A harpoon rope snapped, then another. A hand came free. Sharks on the shore pounced on some of the exosuits and forced them to let go of their harpoon ropes. Mister Hands’ head started to roll forward again. Theta team were barely at his neck. They weren’t going to make it.

“Fire the torpedoes,” I said.

Opus Legion reared its nose out of the water, opened the torpedo bays, and fired a streaming volley of gas-propelled plastic lawn flamingoes – fifty, a hundred, two hundred, until the bays were empty. In the air, a timer device snapped the wires that bound them, and their wings spread wide. Pink plastic rained down over Mister Hands just as his head broke loose of the last harpoon and snapped forward.

The flamingoes fell like a carpet on the top of his head, and immediately started to peck and kick. The boots flew off immediately – they were stabbing, piercing, slicing at his flesh, a maelstrom of razor sharp metal perforating the skin and muscles of his face. Car-sized chunks of his body sloughed off and fell to the ground where they exploded in fountains of blood.

The flamingoes hit our people, too. They landed among the battling exosuits and sharks and attacked everyone alike. On the telescopic viewscreen I watched in horror as a flamingo landed directly on the head of a Theta team member, and speared its foot directly through their helmet like opening a tin can.

“Good god,” Kovalik said. “Those are not punches. This is… unnatural.”

The Ref was hunched over the console, his bushy beard smeared with blood from his nose, watching the viewscreen with bloodshot eyes. He shook his head. “Unsporting. Most unsporting.”

Mister Hands pulled himself forward, then reached up to his head and wiped the flamingoes off, taking half of his face with it. His forehead and brow, and most of the upper flesh protecting the eye, fell forward into the lagoon.

Before I could issue another order, he screamed.

The microphones on the submarine cut out, but we could hear it through the hull: the sound of a thousand elephants dying at once.

The ruby in his eye socket turned an iridescent green, and a massive shockwave rippled the air. It shattered windows, sent exosuits flying, and lifted a wave on the lagoon that crashed over us.

An arc of lightning forked from his eye to the surface of the lake, and in an instant the oily water turned to bubbling, vicious green acid.

The two battleships immediately started to capsize, their hulls dissolving like paper. Those unlucky exosuits who were still in the water evaporated.

We could hear the acid eating our own hull. Cracks and metallic groans echoed around the room.

“Get us out of here, Reverb!”

“Certainly Captain!”

Silence. We floated in an expanse of blood once again.

16. Conviction

“Status report.”

“Captain, I’m sorry to report we’ve suffered extreme damage. The primary and secondary thrusters appear to be inoperable. There are hull breaches and flooding in the lower decks, and the life support system reports a critical pressure loss, indicating lines have been severed.”

“What does that mean? We’re losing air?”

“You're absolutely right. We have approximately two hours of air remaining.”

Ariel appeared at the hatch with Sergeant Austin. “What’s the plan?”

Melanie wiped blood from her eyes. I couldn’t tell if it was hers. “We have to rematerialize,” she said. “Get back to Earth and regroup.”

“Ah, that’s a great idea, Doctor! Unfortunately, without thrusters I can only return us to our previous position, and resurfacing in Ten Mile Sump while it's still in an acid state would rapidly dissolve the hull.”

“We don’t have armor for that kind of thing?” Kovalik asked.

”It was never built for acid,” Melanie said quietly.

Kovalik shook his head and began to pace back and forth. ”This is a curse. We have been blighted, and no mistake.”

”Its eye is exposed!” said Melanie. “If we could fire something at it–”

”A projectile?” said the Ref. “In a combat engagement? It can't be done.”

”Will you stop with your pedantic rules for one moment? The Center is being destroyed as we speak. This is humanity's survival we’re talking about–”

Kovalik slammed his hand against a console. ”It’s your fault we're in this godforsaken sea of blood to begin with, witch! In a cursed vessel no less, inhabited by blasted ghosts!” He gestured to the corner of the room, where the pale man with his mouth sewn had been standing; he disappeared the moment we looked at him. “We are out of the ring!” Kovalik shouted. “We are entirely out of the ring!”

”My fault?” Melanie whispered. “If we had launched the flamingoes when I said to–”

“She’s right Goran,” I said. “This is my fault. I shouldn’t have hesitated.”

”No Captain.” His eyes were wide, manic. I’d never seen Kovalik this way. “We have been punished. Punished for allowing a wretched crone, an emissary of sharkness to poison our minds, and our weapons of war!” He waved his hands at the screens. “Do you think it an accident that a shark’s creation swims in the same red waters we do? Ask yourself, where did this vessel even come from? And when last did you see Melanie Keane? I knew her many years ago, and this woman is not her.”

“Goran–”

“To think we were inches from victory, a pure victory with our own hands! We turned our back on our sacred tools. Our exosuits–”

”Your precious exosuits are powered by deviant energy cores,” Melanie said. “The neural interface is a thaumaturgic contract. Even the fists are hardened with the sap of Yggdrasil.”

He stopped dead.

”Lies!” he hissed, pointing a finger at her. “She lies, Captain–” He looked to me for support, but I gave none, merely shaking my head.

His face fell. ”No… surely not.”

“It's true,” I said. “They use deviant technology. They always have.”

He floundered for a moment, but then found some understanding. “All these years… Captain, don't you see? This is why the monster was sent in the first place! It is our divine punishment. Oh, we are cursed. We are cursed!”

I noticed that other crewmembers had appeared at the hatch. This display of emotion was getting out of hand.

"Goran,” I said, stepping between them. “I understand the anger, the betrayal, the fear. I felt it myself when I learned the truth. I shouldn’t have kept it from you. But this is the only way for us to survive. We rely on our suits – we can rely on these deviants. If we're to survive, this is what we must become.”

He looked at me sideways. "'Become'… A strange choice of words, Captain.” He paced to the other end of the room. “Of course your mind has been changed. They’ve warped it, don't you see?” He pointed to the floor. “We’ve all seen that mural downstairs, in the mess hall. Captain Blunt, victorious–”

“You’re in that mural too–”

“Captain Blunt, the savior with three arms. Aye, they painted you as the Haymaker herself. Fuddled your mind with visions of glory. You would let them corrupt your fists so that you may steal the throne of God.”

“That’s enough, Goran. This is absurd.”

“Oh but it is absurd, Captain. It is hubris. It is blasphemy. My friend, you have fallen far. But it was not your doing.”

His face showed a strange kind of calm, then. I'd seen it before, in the eyes of the pugilist that almost killed Ariel. Conviction.

“But I yet know the way to save your soul,” he said. “To save all our souls. The Haymaker is merciful. She forgives those who are willing to sacrifice.”

"What more can we possibly sacrifice?" I said, gesturing to the devastation that surrounded us. “The people in the Center need us to–”

”Look if you're both quite finished–” Melanie inserted herself between us, and turned to me. “Lindsay, we have to talk about–”

"I will show you," said Kovalik behind her. “Glory to the Haymaker. Accept this sacrifice to purify our vessel.”

He didn’t hesitate.

In one movement, he unsheathed the shark tooth knife and dragged it across Melanie’s throat, which ran red with a thick sheet of blood.

“Foul!” yelled the Ref. “Unforgivable! Disqualification!”

I didn’t hear his words, didn’t see the crew tackle Kovalik and wrestle the knife from his hands, or the squabble that broke out between the other crewmembers. In that moment there was only Melanie and I, alone in a sea of darkness. I caught her as she fell, pressed my hands to her neck in a frail attempt to stop the bleeding. Her blood pulsed over my hands in hot waves. I pleaded with her to stay with me, to stay awake, to fight. Her wide eyes stared into mine, her mouth opening and closing silently. If she had last words to say, she couldn’t say them.

Her mouth hung open, and the blood stopped pulsing. Her eyes no longer stared at me, but through me. I felt Ariel at my side, saw her hand reach for Melanie’s neck to help. I put my hand on her arm and shook my head.

I stood, my hands sticky with Melanie’s blood. Goran was restrained by two officers.

“She’s gone,” I said, my voice thick. “Ref, count her out, please.”

The Ref nodded, and knelt by Melanie. He raised a hand above his head and brought it down to the bloodstained floor, three times.

“One… two… three.”

He put a hand on her chest. “May your golden gloves shine forever in the hall of fame.” He stood, and put his hand on my shoulder. “She boxes with God now, ma’am.”

“Boxes with God?” Kovalik laughed, his arms still trapped by the officers. “Ha! Chum for the abyss. We’d all be chum too, had I not cleansed this vessel!”

The pain turned to fury. I stepped forward and drew back for a punch, but the Ref put his hand on mine.

“Unsporting,” he said quietly.

I unclenched my fist, and grabbed Kovalik’s collar. “A knife, Goran. A shark tooth knife. You’re no pugilist. You’re barely human. If you want to be a shark so badly, go and join them.” I looked to the officers. “Take him to the port airlock.”

There were better ways to handle the situation, but in that moment I had allowed the rage to consume me. I was no longer a captain. I was merely pain and grief and loss, and I would have my revenge. Melanie would have talked me back from the edge; without her, I was uncontrollable.

We dragged him through the corridors. Crewmembers were lying on the floor, huddled in corners. Word spread through whispers; what Melanie had said, and what Goran had done.

We came to the ship's port side airlock and the officers opened the door.

“No,” he said. “Kill me if you must Captain, I did what needed done. But this blood sea is not of our world. It is unclean! It is impurity itself!”

“Then you'll fit right in,” I said, and hooked him in the face. He stumbled back into the airlock. I closed the door and started the cycle process.

Through the porthole I saw bloody water pouring in through the chamber’s floor, and was surprised to find Kovalik retrieving the key to the locker which held the deviant diving suits. He wrenched it open and managed to pull on one of the suits as the water splashed around his waist. He grabbed a helmet and stared at it for a moment. When the water reached his chest, he put it on.

“So now you choose survival,” I said numbly.

He stood wearing the suit, staring at his hands. Through the helmet glass I could just make out his face, but his expression was inscrutable. When the outer door finally opened he climbed through, floating out of sight into the ocean.

“Well go on then," I said. "We’re all chum for the abyss now.”

Fights broke out across the ship as the crew learned what I'd done and those loyal to Kovalik tried to mutiny, but they were subdued by those still loyal to me. Half the crew had their hands full containing the other half.

I was little help; I wandered through the corridors in a dream.

17. Answer the Call

Death surrounded me once again.

I stood over the captain’s chair, numb. The mutineers were secure, but our petty squabble had achieved nothing. The Center was being torn apart – humanity’s defense against the sharks was being crippled while we sat stranded in an ocean of blood, much of which was our own.

I looked around the conn, and realized I was waiting for Kovalik to ask a question, or for Melanie to make a sly comment. I couldn’t understand that they were both gone.

"What are you looking at!?" I said to the pale man in the corner, the ship's ghost. He disappeared silently, and I was alone again.

The rest of the ship was quiet. With nothing left to do, the crew had taken to standing idly by. The air had already grown thin. There was no escape, and no way to repair what was broken.

The yellow phone on the captain’s console started to ring.

I had never heard it ring before. I stared in confusion, then lifted the receiver slowly.

“…Hello?”

“Lindsay.”

It was her voice.

“Melanie… where… how are you doing this? I watched you die.”

There was a long pause, filled with hissing static, clicks and pops.

“I told you, Lindsay. I can make a call from anywhere. I’m always connected.”

I had no words.

Eventually some of them tumbled out of my mouth. “Come back to me.”

“We know I can’t do that, Lindsay. But I want you to know it wasn’t your fault. Just my dumb mouth again. You did try to warn me.”

“Mel, where are you?”

A long silence, more clicks.

“I don’t think I could tell you if I tried. But it’s not bad. There are no sharks here.”

I looked around the conn.

“We’ve lost,” I said quietly.

“Maybe,” she whispered. “I would tell you I’m sorry I brought you into this, but I’m not. The last few weeks were the most fun I’ve ever had."

Hissing static and clicking.

"I am sorry about one thing though," she said. "I never did learn to throw a punch the way you can. You put your whole weight into it. You don’t hold anything back. Still, you were wrong. You told me war isn’t a game. But it has a referee, and rules. Of course it’s a game, Lindsay. It’s one you’re really, really good at.”

I slowly came to understand what she was telling me. But I couldn’t bear to let her go. The phone was glued to my ear. Nothing in the universe could pry it away in that moment.

“I need you, Mel. Tell me how I can find you. I promise I will.”

Another long pause of static and clicks.

“I’m going to go now, Lindsay. Nail the bullseye for me, okay? And… I love you.”

The line went dead.

Part III

18. Round Three

Slowly, I returned the receiver to its cradle, and looked down at where Melanie’s body still lay, in a pool of blood. There, on her right hand, was the white leather glove.

I knelt at her side and tugged it free. “’From your cold dead hands’… right Mel?”

I pulled the glove onto my hand. It was still warm.

I straightened my uniform and hit the intercom. “Attention. This is your Captain speaking. As you may know, Goran Kovalik is no longer aboard this vessel. We’ve all suffered losses. I know you're afraid. Some of you think we're damned. I can't tell you one way or the other. For what it’s worth, I think the Haymaker would be proud of how you've all fought."

I paused. "But to tell you the truth I don't care anymore. You have two choices. Report to Ms Donner’s nose where we have food and supplies, and mostly breathable air, or take a swim in the ocean of blood. Either way, it ends now. I'm going to kill Mister Hands. Thank you.”

The crew filed through the corridors to the cargo bay and climbed one after the other into the funnel. The mutineers, too, were forced kicking and screaming into Ariel’s nose.

“Will you be okay?” I asked her.

She gave a thumbs up. “There's enough air in there for days, and the filters will protect me. It'll be harder for them. We don't have enough masks for everyone. But I’ll keep them safe.”

“Captain Blunt?” It was Sergeant Austin at my side. “What happens to us all, if she…”

“If I die?” Ariel asked. “I was wondering the same thing.”

“We’re not going to find out,” I said, putting a hand on his shoulder. “Whether or not I succeed, Reverb will send out a call. The Center will come for you eventually. Just stay put.”

“What will you do?” Ariel asked. “You can’t face that thing alone.”

“I won’t allow the Center to fall,” I said. “And I’m not alone.”

I went to the conn one last time. I took slow deep breaths; there was hardly any air left.

“Reverb, on my mark, you’re going to surface in the lake. Stay just long enough to let me out. The moment my feet leave the ship, you’re to return to the blood sea. If this works, you’ll know when it's safe to resurface. If it doesn’t… someone will clear the lake eventually.”

“Certainly, Captain.”

With the last of the crew secured, Ariel placed a plug over her nose, and nodded to me.

I reached over and rang the bell myself. “Round three.”

“Ho!” said Ariel.

19. The Punch

From the conning tower airlock, I felt Opus Legion surface one last time. There had been no exosuits left to take, but I couldn’t have risked it anyway.

I pushed open the top hatch, and a rush of foul-smelling air came in from the acid lake. I climbed out onto the surface of my ship, and down the tower ladder onto the rubber hull. The acid was already dissolving the submarine; there was no time to lose.

I looked out at Mister Hands, who was flailing furiously among ruined factories, his face bloody and his eye, red once again, partially exposed. Behind him, the glass and steel fist of the Center was still standing, its four round knuckles thrust triumphantly into the sky.

I took a deep breath, and focused on the eye.

“It’s you and me now, Tariq,” I said. “The game is… boxing. Let’s play.”

I held up my right hand, made a fist, and started to run.

As the edge of the ship grew closer, I felt a flicker of doubt. But whether it worked or not, I had nothing left to lose.

I didn't hesitate.

I jumped, throwing a haymaker with every pound of my body, directly at Mister Hand’s red eye, which was half a mile away and across a lake of acid.

Just as my feet left the hull, a huge wave rippled across the lagoon and caught Opus Legion. Its nose tilted upward, throwing me high into the air. I saw the ship turn to water as Reverb took the crew to safety.

I fell towards the acid lake.

The water of the ship mixed with the acid in some unusual reaction, causing a geyser that erupted beneath me, sending gas and debris flying upwards. A metal door that hadn’t yet dissolved collided with me and threw me higher still.

There was a crack of lightning, and a gale of wind from a freak tornado that sucked me upwards, higher and higher into the black clouds above. The wind howled in my ears. I could see nothing.

Something collided with my shoulder and sent me spinning. Then something else hit me in the head. Another collided with my stomach and I wrestled with it – feathers, feet, a huge beak.

It was a bird: a pelican. A flock of pelicans was stampeding past me through the clouds, and as I fell I landed squarely on one bird’s back.

Immediately my weight sent the bird careening downwards and we fell together. We broke through the clouds, and though we were closer to Mister Hands, we were falling too fast toward the acid lake below.

Seeing us, Mister Hands let out a roar, his hot breath forming a thermal that the bird's wings found purchase in, allowing us both to glide some of the remaining distance before the bird again started to drop.

We fell, hurtling towards his hands at a hundred miles an hour, just as the remaining flock of flamingoes took flight, swarming into the sky toward us. I was battered and pounded by wave after wave of flying plastic, and the pelican disappeared from beneath me, but the flamingoes slowed my descent, and when they finally cleared I landed with a thump into the soft fleshy palm of one of Mister Hands’ hands.

He looked down at me greedily, and tried to toss me into his mouth, but he threw too hard.

I sailed through the air over his gaping mouth – a chasm of darkness and teeth under my feet – and flew past it, over his nose and down toward his eye.

The crystal was a tall and thin octagonal shape, twice my height and as thick as a car. My bare fist and the entire weight of my body collided with it, and instantly shattered the bones in my hand and forearm without leaving a dent.

With my right hand useless, I slid helplessly down the concentric flesh rings and out of his eye socket, but caught hold of the edge with my left hand, and planted my legs on the bridge of his nose.

I had nothing left. All I could do was hold on, and my strength was failing. The giant head swayed to and fro as the monster turned and pulled himself toward the Center again.

I looked up at the eye. It was attached to the flesh of his head only at the top and bottom: there was a cavity behind it.

I pulled with my left arm and thrust my feet against his nose, heaving my weight up into the eye socket. Instinctively I tried to hold on with my right hand, and a wave of nauseating pain washed over me. I got one foot up onto the first fold of his eye socket and pushed, grabbing the next ring with my left hand, slowly inching my way up towards the eye.

I made it to the crystal and pulled myself up into the space behind it. There was just enough space there to wedge myself in, with my back pressed against his flesh and my feet against the crystal. I took a breath, summoned my strength and kicked as hard as I could.

The crystal seemed unharmed, though it rippled with a strange light, and the swaying stopped – Mister Hands had paused what he was doing.

I’ve got your attention now.

I kicked again, and again. My feet barely glanced off the glass surface, but Mister Hands hated it. He let out a mournful cry. Then he seemed to realize what was happening, and tried to grab me.

I huddled behind the crystal and closed my eyes as a hand the size of a house collided directly with his eye socket, smashing into his head like a meteor. I looked up and saw the crystal had been cracked. Waves of magical energy were radiating from it.

He seemed even more confused now. He sent another hand, and another, rising up and crashing directly into his own eye. The more damage they did, the angrier he got, and the more determined he was to crush whoever he thought was doing this to him.

Hand after hand, fist after fist – he pummeled his own face while I spent every ounce of energy I had left to stay hidden behind the crystal.

A thick crack splintered through the crystal from root to tip, and the hands stopped. He let out a long, slow moan, and lifted himself up to his full height. He was teetering as if drunk, his body trembling and shuddering.

I looked out from behind the crystal to see that he was slowly turning around again to face the Center – he was right next to it, his head just above the rooftop level where the Admiralty had long since abandoned their games.

Then the hands that were keeping him upright buckled, and we fell forward together. I steeled my nerves, came out from behind the crystal and coiled my legs, ready to jump.

His face collided directly with the knuckle of the Center’s fist, and I was hurled from his eye socket, over the glass railing and onto the golf lawn, where I rolled awkwardly and crashed into the spinning windmill.

I looked back to see Mister Hands still reeling from the impact. The crystal splintered and exploded, sending a circular shockwave of energy that threw me against the windmill a second time.

Then his lifeless head slid out of view. The building shook as his body hit the ground.

In the distance, the shockwave rolled over the ruined factories and across Ten Mile Sump, which turned back into the disgusting oil-slick water it had been before.

Silence.

I lifted myself with my good hand, barely able to stand. I limped slowly to the south lawn, where a fresh piña colada had been abandoned on the bar by a fleeing Admiral.

“KO,” I said, and took a sip.

I spat it out. It was far too sweet.

Epilogue

The sun shone through the black clouds and warmed my face. Circling gulls squawked loudly above. I sat on the black rubber hull of Opus Legion, slowly sipping my coffee.

In the distance, the colossal corpse of Mister Hands was still sprawled across the ground at the foot of the Center. It was now covered by hundreds of orange dots: work crews swarming like ants, taking him apart piece by piece. They had already found a number of deviant elements buried in his physiology, and they expected to find many more. Every one of them would be analyzed and then repurposed in our ongoing war.

The sharks had called us to the ring, and we had answered. For our courage and willingness to adapt, humanity had been granted a reprieve. As I looked at the tangled jumble of arms, I wondered what horrors the sharks might send next, and what horrors we might have waiting for them when they did.

I stood, and returned inside, moving awkwardly down the ladder with my arm in a sling. Crew members buzzed around me in the corridors, cleaning and repairing. All of them greeted me with a salute.

Many of them greeted me with reverent pressed fists.

Witnesses had spread the story of how Mister Hands was defeated, and since few had knowledge of Melanie's glove or its capabilities, the common understanding was that the Haymaker herself had blessed my fist and delivered us to victory.

I had shed all concern for protecting their faith, and as a result I had somehow become a saint.

The conn was thankfully deserted. I slowly lowered myself into the captains chair. Every part of my body ached.

I stared at the yellow phone, wondering if it would ring again.

Do Not Go Gentle Into That Shark Night

SCP-8226 Auxiliary Logs

Dogs In Sheep's Clothing

SCP-8226 Observation Log Series
Recorded on static trail cams within the pastures of the Carpathian Mountains, Southern Transylvania. These logs were captured over the span of several weeks, with recordings remotely transmitted to Foundation analysts. All of the following logs are believed to be of a single SCP-8226 instance within the same herd.

Log 8226-A - "The Lamb"

02:14: An abnormally small lamb is seen lying prone behind a bush, separated from its flock by about 20 meters. The neck is hyperextended and its eyes are rolled upward, fixated on the sky. Occasional convulsions are observed1.

2:16: A doe, the presumed mother, approaches the lamb while bleating repeatedly. It nudges the lamb's side, but fails to rouse it.

2:28 SCP-8226 enters the frame from the northeast, the opposite direction of the ewe. Its maw is stained, and multiple claw-wounds have torn into its fur. These items disappear over the next several minutes, and SCP-8226 returns to the appearance of a normal sheep.

2:34: SCP-8226 pauses briefly and approaches the doe. It presses its head against the mother's flank and gently guides it away.

2:37: The doe hesitates and circles back once more, before it and SCP-8226 return to the herd.

3:10 The lamb continues exhibiting tremors, rigid limbs, and upward eye fixation. SCP-8226 returns to frame without the mother and lies next to the lamb without making contact.

5:36: The lamb is now completely still, covered in flies around its eyes and mouth. It emits a final bleat.

6:38: SCP-8226 rises and positions itself over the lamb, unhinging its jaw beyond normal anatomical limits. In a single motion, the lamb is consumed whole. No residue remains

6:54: After lingering for several minutes, SCP-8226 rises and walks back in the direction of the herd.

Log 8226-B - "The Ram"

21:05: An aged ram is lying on its side in a quiet field with no other animals visible. Its breathing is shallow. The sky above it is clear.

21:45: Entering the frame silently, SCP-8226 settles next to the ram, which lifts its head and bleats. SCP-8226 does not respond.

23:10 The ram attempts to rise, but collapses in a few short steps. SCP-8226 moves beside it and coaxes it into a resting position.

00:58: The two figures remain sitting upright, until the ram leans into SCP-8226's flank. No further movement observed for three hours.

04:34: SCP-8226 shifts out from beneath the ram, which is no longer visibly breathing. Lowering its head, SCP-8226 opens its mouth and consumes the ram from the head down. No residue remains.

04:43: SCP-8226 exits frame.

Log 8226-C - "The Doe"

13:01: The herd is seen moving through a valley. One doe lags behind, stumbling downhill and vocalizing repeatedly. The herd does not slow.

13:04: The doe freezes and continues calling out. SCP-8226, lingering near the back of the herd, pauses and approaches the struggling doe.

13:18: The doe collapses and begins crying out. SCP-8226 approaches and lies down beside her and begins licking her back. The doe's bleats soften slightly.

13:25: The herd disappears behind a distant hill. The doe has stopped bleating and begins whimpering. SCP-8226 maintains physical contact, with its head atop her back. It continues licking intermittently.

13:54: Without warning, SCP-8226 snaps the back of the doe's head mid-lick. The doe goes limp. SCP-8226 opens its mouth and slides the body in. It then stands, shakes, and continues on in the direction of the herd.

Recovered Document 8226-D - "The Dying"

The following document was uncovered in historical archives near the location of the documented SCP-8226 instance and herd.

--

To whom takes the time to read the words of an aged shepherd:

As the wind grows cold and stale, my legs no longer carry me across the hillside as they once did. On my best days, I can only sit by the old fir and watch the flock from afar. Though I would like to think they still know me, I can no longer call them home as I once did.

In my youth, I had crafted a new breed- not for guarding nor hunting nor companionship, persay- but rather, for mercy.

Too many winters I watched my flock suffer slow deaths. Those sick, frail and lost things each cried out for an end that would come ever-so-slow, and I had naught the strength nor - lord forgive me- the heart, to answer each one. Therefore, I prayed not for this strength, but rather, for a kindness that could walk among my flock when I one day could not.

With those prayers and careful hands, I crafted the dogs.

They are quieter things than I expected. They do not bark nor chase nor even herd. Instead, they wait. Wait until they smell the scent of pain, of hopelessness. They walk beside the dying and offer what I could not: an end without terror, cold, or solitude.

It is far from pretty work, but it is holy in its own way.

Now, my legs cannot carry me alongside the herd. My arms can no longer lift my crook. My lungs cannot whistle for them.

But the dogs still walk. They walk with the lambs and the rams, the does and the dying. They walk through dark and frost and cold and wind, where only mercy is kind enough to go.

And tonight, one sits beside me.

He has not moved within an hour. He watches the stars with me. His breath is steady, and I feel no fear.

Yet, I know that when I sleep, he will finish the work that I began.

And it will be the last kindness I ever know.
