    Part I of the Human Error series.

    I'm the only person on the wiki as of writing this with a character named Dolloran. That's funny.

    The epigraph is Fall Out Boy's The Carpal Tunnel Of Love

7eventy7evenfold

We keep the beat with your blistered feet,
And we bullet the words at the mockingbirds, singing

Slept through the weekend, and dreaming,
Of sinking with the melody of the cliffs of eternity,
Got postcards from my former selves saying "How've you been?"

If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold...

Dolloran Light drove endlessly in the vast desert of Colorado, her transgressions pursuing. She dare not to lighten the gas pedal, lest her troubles arrive, latch onto her, and stain her clothes a sickly dark. She passed Nexus Site-02, but halted not, in the knowledge that she would be too slow in the face of the past. She drove on past the Site, not allowing herself even an attosecond of thought about the consequences of failure. Her mind was wholly focused on the objective. If she failed to get ahead, then the parasite 'neath her would surely dismantle her persona whole and kill her, inside out, laying waste to the Director.

She passed Nexus Site-02, but halted her mind for that one attosecond. "Did I not just come through here?" she thought for a moment, though a moment too long. The wicked ratcher caught up alongside her Mustang, tearing off the door and allowing itself a seat at her passenger. When she turned, she felt a shooting pain from her stomach, but could not scream, nor even breathe. She could not think. She could not see. She could not drive.

Dolloran Light woke up in her bed a dream loser, rubbing her blackened, bagged eyes as the alarm clock pierced her ears like a missile would a fort's defenses. She tried to hit it, but was so disoriented she missed seven times before scraping it. O, for the love of…

She grabbed it, ensuring her grip, before throwing the whole damn thing across the room. She was probably due for a new one anyway. Rising and stretching, she realized that she hadn't worn her pajamas to bed the previous night; she had worn her sweatpants. Too bad. She slipped on some bunny sneakers and droned away like a zombie to the kitchen — barely able to control her own limbs — to put on some coffee. Then, it was to the computer.

From:
To:
CC:
Subject:
bestdirector7@scip.net
FahrenheitTacTheo@scip.net
{$cc}
visiting!

hihi burniieee I miss youu!! I know you're busy at like eta-77 and all and I know it must be so stressful,,, I just wanna say I'm still thinking about you :>. listen I've got big news oka? remember how you told me when you were first leaving the coalition that if tactheo ever got boring you'd consider noospheric imaging?? well guess WWHATTTTT??? upper management told me an odd day ago that essophysics is gonna be moving into 02's free port!!! isn't that exciting? aaaaaaa

so they're gonna be starting in like 5 days and I want you to come visit so we can talk again or something okay well i've got to get to work now get back to me whenever you're done killing god or whatever it is you do. BYEE I love you!
Dolloran Light
Director, Nexus Site-02
Dream On

She was scared. She had begun to lose hope that he would be visiting at all. She lumped down in her chair and started picking at her nails worried, knowing that she wouldn't be able to get him over if he didn't even see the email. Oh well…

She walked back over to the kettle and lowered the heat, not wanting to burn her drink. Not too much, anyways. It would be all she had for the day, probably.

She sat in her chair for the five more minutes she had before work, taking moderate sips of coffee and scrolling through her gallery. She went over old pictures of them together, family photos — what little she had — and cat videos. Suddenly, she sprung from her seat, snorting hot coffee over her laptop — like a Christmas miracle, an email from Fahrenheit was sitting in her inbox.

From:
To:
CC:
Subject:
FahrenheitTacTheo@scip.net
bestdirector7@scip.net
{$cc}
Re:visiting!

I was busy on a diplomatic thing in Israel. Hey, did you know they invented USBs? Anyways, yes! I saw your email while I was over there and arranged to be sent back to Cortez rather than Canada when the whole thing was finished, I couldn't respond because I didn't have the time to think of anything good to say x_x

See you soon. Love you <3
████ Fahrenheit
Field Agent, Reliquary Area-27
Invenient Novum Numen

She was going to die of excitement before she ever had the chance to see him. Either that or be killed by her superiors for being late. Slipping on a way-too-big tee, she grabbed her coat, badge, and #1 Site Director! mug, and ran out the door at lightspeed.

"Sorry I'm late Sir Mr. O5-1 Sir!"

She sat in her office across from Aaron Siegel, the skeletal figure attending for the purpose of oversight, one of many for the following weeks.

"Is there an excuse for your tardiness, Director Light?"

"…I burnt myself badly on my tea," she muttered out. A bold-faced lie, and one which he could see right through, given her less-than-clinical attire and the fact that — although she had tea now — he could smell coffee on her. He also took note of her incredibly dark eye bags, but figured it's what the coffee was for. Her facade would at least convince somebody else, so,

"You're excused. Try to be on time, next time? We have our schedules filled and we cannot afford to plaster the Director on every milk carton in Cortez while trying to establish essophysics in her Site. Good morning."

He left the room. She let out a heavy sigh, like she had been holding her breath the entire encounter. Actually, she probably was. Suddenly, her phone rang out. She reached for her pocket, groping around and dodging two pennies and a fuzzball.

"Hello?" she said, out of breath. I was right!

"Hey Doll, it's me. Uhh, how do you get into the Nexus again? I'm at the cactus."

Damn. "Okay, ditch the car, but don't worry, it won't be taken. First, walk around it four times counterclockwise while whistling the intro to Star Wars."

"…"

"You're jerking me around, right?"

"Yeah." They burst into hysterics. "Here's what you actually have to do…"

"So this is Site-02 in Y2K? I expected it to be a lot more… expansive." He let out a chuckle.

"Yup. It's surprisingly small for how it sounds. A few small rooms adds up to a medium place. I think the hardest part of installing essophysics here is going to be breaking the 'size spell' in order to expand the place a bit." They shared a look. "Walk with me."

They strolled past the mahogany corridors of the Administrative Quarters, through the marbled cafeteria and into the construction zone. Fahrenheit was briefed on the procedure and Light was given a firm handshake.

"So, you said that you got me here to explain a bit more about the noöspheric imaging offer, but this is essophysics. What's the difference?" he asked, stumped.

"Well, noöspheric imaging is essentially mapping out constructs in the realm of thought, in layman's terms. Essophysics is a broad spectrum," she explains. "Basically, there's the umbrella term — which includes imaging — that has everything related to the noösphere. And then you have the singular term, which is ideas manifesting in the real world. For examples, O5-4 is representative of Death, and this bill I'm about to hand you is representative of five dollars I owe you."

She slips a five dollar bill out of her pocket.

"But, you don't owe me—"

"I feel generous." He took it happily and they laughed.

"O-hokaayy then, I guess." He looked informed, but he wasn't any more knowledgeable than one minute ago. "Thanks for the briefing, Director Light."

She stared at him.

"Let's go catch up over breakfast. I think they're serving biscuits."

"So then Abel comes up and slashes me, straight across the abdomen. I would've died if it weren't for a Nine-Tailed Fox squad bumrushing his ass and running me to the medbay. They held me there for three whole hours. I've never met a group so willing to save a janitor." She took a bite and didn't savor it a moment before swallowing it. "That's one of the two times I ever met Abel. He was only temporarily in 02 because of a nasty breach a month before.

Fahrenheit was in awe of her story.

"You said that you started out believing you were working for the CIA right?" Fahrenheit asked. "How did you figure that if you had to access a Free Port every time?" he inquired, before drilling into his sausage, egg and cheese Heaven.

"Well, you used to not have to. It's a long story with the original Insurgency, basically—"

Light's pager rang out, demanding her presence at construction.

"What's it say?"

"There's been an accident."

They arrived in the room, where something had clearly gone wrong. Tape had already been deployed to sector off an area, and something had fallen. She connected the dots.

A Goldbaker-Reinz employee, accompanied by O5-4, approached Light, giving her a clipboard and pen to sign.

"Director Light, please sign here. This shows that you acknowledge a fatality has occured in the workplace and hold legal accountability for the time being until it is known who is responsible for the accident."

"Mhm."

"And this one states that you will respect the victim and family's wishes should they have any esoteric requests."

"But I don't know them."

The employee cocked his head. "What are the orders from here?"

"Call the Clean-Up GoI or something. Consult O5-1 for something else."

She signed the lines all the while training her eyes on the box, and the blood that had slowly leaked out since the idiot started talking. The GB-R man left, and O5-4 placed his brittle hand on her shoulder, before vanishing. She caught a whiff of gunpowder. Nobody seemed to have noticed him at all.

The world seemed to spin, and yet simultaneously crawl to a snail's pace.

"Why did that happen? Today was going so good and I was so happy and then a dude just dies in my Site and now I'm probably gonna be fired and—"

Fahrenheit hugged her. "It's okay Doll. You're not gonna be fired over this because you're not the one who secures that. And, if it's any comfort, he's in a better place now."

"You don't know that," she remarked.

"I'm in Tactical Theology. He's an honest construction worker. I do know that."

Light stood against the guardrail, looking at the drop-off. She took her eyes off of the box and saw Siegel, across the room, looking at her. He walked away.

Light sat in her office biting her nails and poking her lunch. She was scared for her job and for her life. What was going to happen to her?

She saw something moving — watching her — through the curtains. She could've sworn she did, anyways. But when she looked up to see, nobody was there.

After a few moments, Siegel knocked on the door, then let himself in. He sat across from her.

"O5-10 went back and found out who failed to secure the box. He's been amnesticized and let go. You are legally absolved."

She didn't respond.

"Why no response?"

"Is Four in today?" she meekly asked.

"O5-4 is not overseeing essophysics' installation. He is occupied with Marshall, Carter, & Dark in Hong Kong. Why do you ask?"

She took a bite out of her burger. "I was just wondering. What's his name, by the way?"

"…"

"I meant the one who died."

"Ray Hancock."

"Okay. Thank you."

He rose. "Good afternoon." He walked on over towards the door before being stopped.

"Hey, tell Four thanks."

Siegel looked back at her, and then understood. He gave a short nod and then exited. She meekly sipped tea from her #1 Site Director! mug, running it dry. Its message seemed a whole lot more solemn now.

It just wasn't supposed to happen. Why did it happen so out of nowhere?

Fahrenheit came in.

"Hi, you feeling any better?" he asked sweetly.

"A little… I just don't understand. Why does this have to happen?"

Fahrenheit sat on her desk. "Death happens, a lot. Whether or not you're in the Foundation, it follows everyone. It's an inevitable constant that we have to face. Every single thing will die one day." He took a sip of his coke. "It's the most important thing in the world."

"Hey Burnie? I want to talk about myself," she shyly told him.

"Well, talk away."

"When I was barely sentient, my mom died in a car crash. I had to be caretaken by my senile grandma up until '64, though admittedly I was more of her's. That's when I became a janitor here. Whenever that breach happened and that E-11 squad held me in the medbay before getting me out of there, they gave me the choice between amnesticizing myself and being 'normal' again, or committing to this life." She swallowed. "I chose the red pill."

She teared up, just barely, before wiping it on her sleeve. "I still think it's the worst thing I've ever done. My grandma deserved family to be with her in her final months, not some trained Jailor schmucks. And I haven't ever had a break in my life. I raised myself and now I even have to raise my own Site, one that raised me." She took a few moments to catch her breath, chuckling.

"And the things I've seen here. I don't know why that poor man affected me so badly. I've seen people fall into patterns, I've seen gods come back to Earth and make the Foundation their bitch, I've seen people stretched and torn apart into pieces forty-two."

She looked up at Fahrenheit.

"I think there's just something about a normal, random, workplace accident, killing one good man with a family. In my Site. That wrecks me. Something entirely in our control." She looked perplexed. "It wasn't a puzzle we couldn't solve — some pataphysical riddle or an Insurgent plan or even some freak outbreak. It was just human error." She took another bite. "His name was Ray Hancock, and I hope he's in a better place now."

Fahrenheit seemed lost in thought for a moment, before reaching out his hand. She took it. They hugged for a minute.

"I can't say I can relate to how you feel. I mean, I'm in Spheres Within Spheres. We only deal with theology. Being Director must be so difficult for you, because you have a little piece of it all on your plate. You're gonna be okay, though. You're a tough cookie. You should've known that the second you survived Abel of all things, up close." Fahrenheit detached himself from her desk and grabbed the Foundation crest she had earned as a reward.

"There's a reason you have this, y'know? And that scar on your belly is kickass."

She smiled warmly.

"Thanks. Let's go to the roof."

The permanent desert sunset stretched across the horizon, the enlarged sun peering up above the technicolor skyline and greyish cliffs as if to tease "I see you!" Fahrenheit and Light sat, legs dangling off the roof and fingers intertwined, and chatted about everything. The cold wind blew, breezing against their ears and hair, and making it almost hurt to inhale too hard.

"I'm so stressed out over this damn job, y'know? I just get so focused on trying to complete the task at hand that if I take even one second to stop and think about something else, I slip up and everything falls apart." Light stole Fahrenheit's coke and finished it off for him. He laughed.

"Yeah, I get that. Every other job that isn't a diplomatic affair with an afterlife or the Middle East, I know the op is a coin flip between recovering some Akiva-heavy artifact or having the universe depend on me appeasing or killing some god. That doesn't feel good. It gets to a guy's head… I can relate, sweetie."

"Thanks. It means a lot." They embraced for a moment, enjoying each other's patient company.

"Hey, you notice how cold it is out here?" Fahrenheit asked. "What's that about?"

"Huh. Never did. I dunno."

Light remembered a conversation they had earlier.

"I should probably entertain your breakfast question. I'm probably not gonna be paged again."

Fahrenheit cocked his eyebrow.

"Don't tell anyone I'm telling you all of this, it's above your clearance." They shared a good laugh. "Back in the '40s, the Insurgency and the Sarkics made a little blood deal and decided to start a curse to enchant these three square miles of land with a loop that could be escaped with specific actions only the Foundation would know. It was intended to be used as a backup O5 thing. It got cancelled after the Insurgency split up from the Red Right Hand and the Sarkics lost trust in us. 02 finally got built in the '50s as a small base used as an HQ for joint ops between Foundation MTFs and GOC Strike Teams. They repurposed it in 1961 to be used as a full Site after some O5 supposedly remembered it was supposed to be a cursed land, so now it's a Nexus Site, and soon to be the essophysics HQ."

She thought to herself for a second, as if trying to remember something.

"If my memory serves me, with good binoculars, you can see this building and us again in the distance. Or if you keep walking. You'll never reach the mountains that you see off in the distance," she pointed out at the world. "They're always at the same distance from you."

Fahrenheit found keen interest in the topic.

"That's really neat! I like that. You sure know a lot about the Site, huh?" he quipped.

"Well, I'm the Director. It's my job." They laughed. "You oughta tell me some fun stuff about Area-27 sometime. Bet it has cooler lore than that administration hell is."

"Well, I would right now, but it's about time I actually head back there. Commander is about to be here with a chopper. Sorry…"

"It's okay! I'll see you around. I love you Burnie."

"Love you too," he assured. "Goodnight."

As he left the rooftop — though not before Light told him how to get out — she sat still for another few minutes. When she finally decided to turn around and go, she saw him again. O5-4. His golden skeleton, alight with violet flame.

Now, it could just be because he has a skeleton jaw, but it almost seemed like he was smiling.

Light sat in her bed with her laptop and emailed Siegel, needing a rest for her weary mind.

From:
To:
CC:
Subject:
bestdirector7@scip.net
doyouknow@scip.net
privateeyesaboveallholy@scip.net
Incident
Hello, Siegel. I just had a question about the loss today. It seems weird and obvious, but has the Foundation issued Ray's family an adequate notice? I want to ensure that the Veil Protocol is maintained while also avoiding the downplay of what happened today, and quite frankly, I find it unbelievable you could die from an accident at a coffee shop. Thank you.
Dolloran Light
Director, Nexus Site-02
Dream On

She clicked send and waited in anxiety— for all of ten seconds before she was issued a response. He's gotta be using an .aic, what?

From:
To:
CC:
Subject:
keeperofbees@scip.net
bestdirector7@scip.net
overseefairandwholly
Re:Incident

All needs have been appropriately met; the wishes of cremation have been fulfilled and the remains have been sent to the family, who have been informed that Mr. Hancock died in a tragic workplace accident.

Off the record, I do not hold you accountable for what happened to Ray today. Although you are the Director and should have caught the mistake, I have noticed your stress and weariness in recent weeks, and I know better than anyone how much that can wear a person down. You should take a vacation, Light.

Back on the record, I know what you're thinking, and no, I'm not using an AI Construct to respond. I've always been an exceptionally swift reader and typer. Goodnight.
selbstjohnbobby6adam7
Obama's Running Mate, USA
Stun, Cobalt, Precede

She was fulfilled. With an easy mind, she fell to her pillow, passing out on contact.

Dolloran Light drove endlessly in the vast desert of Colorado. She had a moderate cruise selected and chose not to take her transportation so quick, for fear of an accident. She gazed in her rear-view and noticed black mass, in the far far distance, barely managing to keep pace. This satisfied the dream loser, who had made a detour at a gas station to grab a burger and a coke.

When she reentered the solemn path, she once more passed Nexus Site-02, deciding to take another pit-stop. She exited the vehicle and jubilantly greeted the helipad security, thanking him for his tireless service. "I appreciate your help at this Site. You have been of wondrous assistance."

She entered her automotive and pressed on the gas, becoming one with that good night, painted like a canvas with ethereal mountains. Not once more did she pass Site-02.

It's a long story with the original Insurgency, basically--" Light's pager rang out, demanding her presence at construction. "What's it say?" "There's been an accident." ----- They arrived in the room, where something had clearly gone wrong. Tape had already been deployed to sector off an area, and something had fallen. She connected the dots. A Goldbaker-Reinz employee, accompanied by O5-4, approached Light, giving her a clipboard and pen to sign. "Director Light, please sign here. This shows that you acknowledge a fatality has occured in the workplace and hold legal accountability for the time being until it is known who is responsible for the accident." "Mhm." "And this one states that you will respect the victim and family's wishes should they have any esoteric requests." "But I don't know them." The employee cocked his head. "What are the orders from here?" "Call the Clean-Up GoI or something. Consult O5-1 for something else." She signed the lines all the while training her eyes on the box, and the blood that had slowly leaked out since the idiot started talking. The GB-R man left, and O5-4 placed his brittle hand on her shoulder, before vanishing. She caught a whiff of gunpowder. Nobody seemed to have noticed him at all. The world seemed to spin, and yet simultaneously crawl to a snail's pace. "Why did that happen? Today was going so good and I was so happy and then a dude just dies in my Site and now I'm probably gonna be fired and--" Fahrenheit hugged her. "It's okay Doll. You're not gonna be fired over this because you're not the one who secures that. And, if it's any comfort, he's in a better place now." "You don't know that," she remarked. "I'm in Tactical Theology. He's an honest construction worker. I do know that." Light stood against the guardrail, looking at the drop-off. She took her eyes off of the box and saw Siegel, across the room, looking at her. He walked away. ----- Light sat in her office biting her nails and poking her lunch. She was scared for her job and for her life. What was going to happen to her? She saw something moving -- watching her -- through the curtains. She could've sworn she did, anyways. But when she looked up to see, [https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/nobody-has-seen-it-all nobody was there]. After a few moments, Siegel knocked on the door, then let himself in. He sat across from her. "[https:scp-wiki.wikidot.com/computer-angel O5-10] went back and found out who failed to secure the box. He's been amnesticized and let go. You are legally absolved." She didn't respond. "Why no response?" "Is Four in today?" she meekly asked. "O5-4 is not overseeing essophysics' installation. He is occupied with Marshall, Carter, & Dark in Hong Kong. Why do you ask?" She took a bite out of her burger. "I was just wondering. What's his name, by the way?" "..." "I meant the one who died." "Ray Hancock." "Okay. Thank you." He rose. "Good afternoon." He walked on over towards the door before being stopped. "Hey, tell Four thanks." Siegel looked back at her, and then understood. He gave a short nod and then exited. She meekly sipped tea from her //#1 Site Director!// mug, running it dry. Its message seemed a whole lot more solemn now. ----- //It just wasn't supposed to happen. Why did it happen so out of nowhere?// Fahrenheit came in. "Hi, you feeling any better?" he asked sweetly. "A little... I just don't understand. Why does this have to happen?" Fahrenheit sat on her desk. "Death happens, a lot. Whether or not you're in the Foundation, it follows everyone. It's an inevitable constant that we have to face. Every single thing will die one day." He took a sip of his coke. "It's the most important thing in the world." "Hey Burnie? I want to talk about myself," she shyly told him. "Well, talk away." "When I was barely sentient, my mom died in a car crash. I had to be caretaken by my senile grandma up until '64, though admittedly I was more of her's. That's when I became a janitor here. Whenever that breach happened and that E-11 squad held me in the medbay before getting me out of there, they gave me the choice between amnesticizing myself and being 'normal' again, or committing to this life." She swallowed. "I chose the red pill." She teared up, just barely, before wiping it on her sleeve. "I still think it's the worst thing I've ever done. My grandma deserved family to be with her in her final months, not some trained Jailor schmucks. And I haven't ever had a break in my life. I raised myself and now I even have to raise my own Site, one that raised me." She took a few moments to catch her breath, chuckling. "And the things I've seen here. I don't know why that poor man affected me so badly. I've seen people fall into patterns, I've seen gods come back to Earth and make the Foundation their bitch, I've seen people stretched and torn apart into pieces forty-two." She looked up at Fahrenheit. "I think there's just something about a normal, random, workplace accident, killing one good man with a family. In //my// Site. That wrecks me. Something entirely in our control." She looked perplexed. "It wasn't a puzzle we couldn't solve -- some pataphysical riddle or an Insurgent plan or even some freak outbreak. It was just human error." She took another bite. "His name was Ray Hancock, and I hope he's in a better place now." Fahrenheit seemed lost in thought for a moment, before reaching out his hand. She took it. They hugged for a minute. "I can't say I can relate to how you feel. I mean, I'm in Spheres Within Spheres. We only deal with theology. Being Director must be so difficult for you, because you have a little piece of it all on your plate. You're gonna be okay, though. You're a tough cookie. You should've known that the second you survived Abel of all things, up close." Fahrenheit detached himself from her desk and grabbed the Foundation crest she had earned as a reward. "There's a reason you have this, y'know? And that scar on your belly is kickass." She smiled warmly. "Thanks. Let's go to the roof." ----- The permanent desert sunset stretched across the horizon, the enlarged sun peering up above the technicolor skyline and greyish cliffs as if to tease //"I see you!"// Fahrenheit and Light sat, legs dangling off the roof and fingers intertwined, and chatted about everything. The cold wind blew, breezing against their ears and hair, and making it almost hurt to inhale too hard. "I'm so stressed out over this damn job, y'know? I just get so focused on trying to complete the task at hand that if I take even one second to stop and think about something else, I slip up and everything falls apart." Light stole Fahrenheit's coke and finished it off for him. He laughed. "Yeah, I get that. Every other job that isn't a diplomatic affair with an afterlife or the Middle East, I know the op is a coin flip between recovering some Akiva-heavy artifact or having the universe depend on me appeasing or killing some god. That doesn't feel good. It gets to a guy's head... I can relate, sweetie." "Thanks. It means a lot." They embraced for a moment, enjoying each other's patient company. "Hey, you notice how cold it is out here?" Fahrenheit asked. "What's that about?" "Huh. Never did. I dunno." Light remembered a conversation they had earlier. "I should probably entertain your breakfast question. I'm probably not gonna be paged again." Fahrenheit cocked his eyebrow. "Don't tell anyone I'm telling you all of this, it's above your clearance." They shared a good laugh. "Back in the '40s, the Insurgency and the Sarkics made a little blood deal and decided to start a curse to enchant these three square miles of land with a loop that could be escaped with specific actions only the Foundation would know. It was intended to be used as a backup O5 thing. It got cancelled after the Insurgency split up from the Red Right Hand and the Sarkics lost trust in us. 02 finally got built in the '50s as a small base used as an HQ for joint ops between Foundation MTFs and GOC Strike Teams. They repurposed it in 1961 to be used as a full Site after some O5 supposedly remembered it was supposed to be a cursed land, so now it's a Nexus Site, and soon to be the essophysics HQ." She thought to herself for a second, as if trying to remember something. "If my memory serves me, with good binoculars, you can see this building and us again in the distance. Or if you keep walking. You'll never reach the mountains that you see off in the distance," she pointed out at the world. "They're always at the same distance from you." Fahrenheit found keen interest in the topic. "That's really neat! I like that. You sure know a lot about the Site, huh?" he quipped. "Well, I'm the Director. It's my job." They laughed. "You oughta tell me some fun stuff about Area-27 sometime. Bet it has cooler lore than that administration hell is." "Well, I would right now, but it's about time I actually head back there. Commander is about to be here with a chopper. Sorry..." "It's okay! I'll see you around. I love you Burnie." "Love you too," he assured. "Goodnight." As he left the rooftop -- though not before Light told him how to get out -- she sat still for another few minutes. When she finally decided to turn around and go, she saw him again. O5-4. His golden skeleton, alight with violet flame. Now, it could just be because he has a skeleton jaw, but it almost seemed like he was smiling. ----- Light sat in her bed with her laptop and emailed Siegel, needing a rest for her weary mind. [[include :scp-wiki:component:dynamic-emails start=-- |from= bestdirector7@scip.net |to= doyouknow@scip.net |cc= privateeyesaboveallholy@scip.net |subject= Incident ]] Hello, Siegel. I just had a question about the loss today. It seems weird and obvious, but has the Foundation issued Ray's family an adequate notice? I want to ensure that the Veil Protocol is maintained while also avoiding the downplay of what happened today, and quite frankly, I find it unbelievable you could die from an accident at a coffee shop. Thank you. [[include :scp-wiki:component:dynamic-emails end=-- |name= Dolloran Light |title= Director, Nexus Site-02 |signoff= Dream On |signoff-icon= https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/local--files/component:dynamic-emails/Default_Profile_Icon.png ]] She clicked send and waited in anxiety-- for all of ten seconds before she was issued a response. //He's gotta be using an .aic, what?// [[include :scp-wiki:component:dynamic-emails start=-- |from= keeperofbees@scip.net |to= bestdirector7@scip.net |cc= overseefairandwholly |subject= Re:Incident ]] All needs have been appropriately met; the wishes of cremation have been fulfilled and the remains have been sent to the family, who have been informed that Mr. Hancock died in a tragic workplace accident. Off the record, I do not hold you accountable for what happened to Ray today. Although you are the Director and should have caught the mistake, I have noticed your stress and weariness in recent weeks, and I know better than anyone how much that can wear a person down. You should take a vacation, Light. Back on the record, I know what you're thinking, and no, I'm not using an AI Construct to respond. I've always been an exceptionally swift reader and typer. Goodnight. [[include :scp-wiki:component:dynamic-emails end=-- |name= selbstjohnbobby6adam7 |title= Obama's Running Mate, USA |signoff= Stun, Cobalt, Precede |signoff-icon= https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/local--files/component:dynamic-emails/Default_Profile_Icon.png ]] She was fulfilled. With an easy mind, she fell to her pillow, passing out on contact. ----- //Dolloran Light drove endlessly in the vast desert of Colorado. She had a moderate cruise selected and chose not to take her transportation so quick, for fear of an accident. She gazed in her rear-view and noticed black mass, in the far far distance, barely managing to keep pace. This satisfied the dream loser, who had made a detour at a gas station to grab a burger and a coke.// //When she reentered the solemn path, she once more passed Nexus Site-02, deciding to take another pit-stop. She exited the vehicle and jubilantly greeted the helipad security, thanking him for his tireless service. "I appreciate your help at this Site. You have been of wondrous assistance."// //She entered her automotive and pressed on the gas, becoming one with that good night, painted like a canvas with ethereal mountains. Not once more did she pass Site-02.// [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box-end]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:earthworm | previous-url=/ | previous-title= | next-url= https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/wooden-dragons | next-title= Wooden Dragons | hub-url=/ | hub-title= Human Error ]]

Starving. Hungry. Gnawing needles of hunger piercing fetid flesh pocked by ghostly maggots.

The Hound trembles, skittering through the legs of pedestrians unseen, sniffing the air for scraps. Nothing. The winding streets of Portlands are bare of the shards of soul the feral Hound once feasted upon. The pet graveyard, the sewers, pounds, even the dreaded clinic where it perished were empty of spirits.

The souls of dog, cat, rat, all eaten by something larger, a shadow cast over Portlands, a biting, consuming wind.

Hungry.

Its nose scents something in the air. The smell of coming death, of decay, of cloying sweetness. Larger prey than it, but wounded. Sickly. It will have to do.

The Hound runs. The streets blur past, the flickering flames of living humans burn past, the world of black and grey and living white tunneling and warping as it gallops faster than it ever did in life, bounding over rooftops and across clotheslines, keeping on the scent, howling wildly into the air. The hunt begins.

Across the city, Saoirse is startled awake by the sound of a wolf's cry.

Dashing, rushing, closing in.

A mile away, then a half mile, then a street, then a single wall.

The heady musk of a soul slipping out of a mortal body fills its nose as it flicker-jumps between worlds, a burning eye fixed on its target, maw open and salivating as it pounces on the last meal in the city.

Saoirse was still rubbing the sleep from her eyes when death on four legs barreled out of her living room wall. A wolf-like thing, as much of a dog as a dog's shadow, lunged towards her neck, its jaw snapping and salivating.

Time seemed to slow down as it sailed through the air. Even as her mind struggled to process this abrupt change from dream to reality, an alien instinct kicked in and broke her out of shock, foreign battle-reflexes imprinted on her soul forcing her body off of the couch and rolling onto the floor.

The beast's jaws clamped down on the pillow that her head had rested on a moment before, scattering stuffing everywhere as it ripped into what it thought was her throat. It took a second before the Hound processed that it had missed.

By then, Saoirse was already up on her feet, muscle memory racing a million miles ahead of her mind as she flipped the coffee table onto its side, trying to create a barrier between herself and the threat, something to slow it down. Not sparing a second, she ran down the hallway and into her bedroom, slamming the door behind her and swearing all the while.

Panting, dripping in cold sweat, she slumped against her bed. Her mind was finally starting to catch up to her instincts, processing what had happened. Some thing had appeared out of nowhere, trying to attack her, eat her. It was in her house. It was in her living room. There was nowhere to go. Saorise just got out of the hospital, she couldn't afford to go back again, or worse, back to the graveyard in her own coffin.

Saorise heard it prowling down the hall, claws click-clacking on the floor, coming to a stop just outside the door. She saw the shadow of a shadow looming through the crack under the door. She held her breath.

Then, hazy as smoke, its head appeared through the door, and Saoirse screamed. Far in the distance, her shriek was echoed by a flock of crows — her flock — but they were too far away, comfortably perched in the trees of a nearby park to do anything but screech in sympathy.

The animal was huge — easily the size of a Great Dane. Clearly starving, too, but through its too-tight skin she could also see the corded muscle of a predator, steel cords stretched tight by starvation. It possessed a single eye centered over its snout, gleaming red and narrowing as it stared at her. Its jaws were foamy and frothy with thick strands of dripping saliva, droplets evaporating as they landed on the bedroom rug, steaming.

The beast hunched down, hackles raised, and filled the room with a low, echoing growl. Saorise looked around for anything that she might be able to use as a weapon. Her eye landed on the disassembled skateboard on her desk. She lunged for it.

Hungry. So very hungry.

The prey-thing had dodged it once, but wouldn't again. Instinct woven into its being tells the Hound to wait for an opening, to pounce when the prey is distracted. And it does.

As its prey races away, the Hound jumps, aiming for center-mass to bring it to the ground, to pin it down, to carve and tear the mortal soul from its body. It makes contact, its jaws close around the prey's black hide, and it tastes victory for a split-second, before its prey slips out of its bite, like it was made of air. Its jowls and tongue burn as if struck by cold iron where they made contact with the hide, but the pain is distant compared to the hunger.

Undeterred, it pushes forward and pounces again, its weight knocking the prey to the ground, but something is wrong.

The Hound tries to claw at the hide, tries to tear through it to get to the living flesh, but again it slips off. Its paws burn and sear where they make contact, and the dog yelps with pain.

This is not what it wanted. Its quarry is not the easy prey it had anticipated.

The dog backs away, keeping its eye on its prey, hackles raised. Fear wars with hunger as it paces, growling a funeral dirge as it has for countless other souls, more to bolster its own spirit than to frighten its prey's own. It feels scared.

The thing freezes, eyes doe-wide, and stares at the Hound, its gaze inscrutable. With its long, awkward limbs, the thing slowly strips off its black pelt, revealing the pallid flesh underneath. It holds up its own hide in front of itself, as if that would ward away the beast.

An opening.

Starvation wins out against fear, and the Hound lunges once more. Its prey is cocky, its prey is stupid. Its black hide was the one thing protecting it, and it was willingly removed.

It flicker-jumps to the side, so it can come at its prey from the flank. It prepares itself to feed.

The wolf vanished mid-stride before her eyes, its corporeal form evaporating into mist as it dissipated into nothingness. But Saoirse saw its path, she could see its paw-prints on the rug as it made them. It was trying to get around the battle jacket.

Saorise dove in the direction she thought the devil-dog would be, the jacket outstretched, and impacted a mass where there shouldn't be any. As soon as she felt the wolf's weight between her arms, she wrapped it tight in her battle-jacket — her divine mantle — and squeezed, immobilizing the thing in its grip. It reappeared, mist forming from nothing, yelping, barking at the surprise attack.

It took all of Saorise's strength to wrestle the hound to the ground, trying to keep its gnashing teeth as far from her face as she could, her muscles burning.

She laid on the floor of her room for what felt like hours, waiting for Anand to arrive, the wolf thrashing and snarling underneath her.

It wasn't going anywhere. She made sure of it.

The makeshift restraints gave Saorise enough breathing room to study the monster in greater detail. There was no way it was a normal dog — even by Portlands standards. Its whole body was hazy somehow, corporeal, but only inasmuch as looked like it was made out of smoke and shadow, bound together in a loose mold, tight enough to infer the broad strokes of definition and texture. There was also the single eye, a red-irised, malevolent orb floating in that black misty mass, and of course the fact it was able to phase through walls with seemingly little effort at all.

She mentally flipped through her relatively slim index of mythical canines, trying to identify the snarling thing in her grasp, hoping it would give her an understanding of what to do with it. Cerberus? Missing two heads. Coyote? Not a dog, also a bit too far north for that. The Hound of Baskerville? Was the dog even magical in that one?

Her train of thought was interrupted by a cacophony of bird chatter and wing-beats as the soul-flock poured into the room.

"Saoirse! Forgive us our tardiness, but we are arrived!" Anand croaked, landing on an open windowsill.

Saoirse panted between the cyclopean wolf's apocalyptically loud barks. "Yeah, I can see that! Do you- Do you have- any idea what this is?"

Anand cocked her head in contemplation. "I… believe I did, once. Though I know not now. Certainly, it is some kind of psychopomp." She declared, as if that was clarification enough.

"A what? And…" Saoirse's frustrated reply was interrupted by the bucking of the beast, "how do I get it to go away?"

"There is time for questions later. As for removing the beast, you must slay it. It is your duty."

Saorise went rigid, and shook her head. "I'm not going to kill a dog!"

Said dog snapped at her face, spattering her with ectoplasmic spittle.

"It is no mere dog. Perhaps once, but no longer. It is a creature wearing the shape of a hound, a beast which feasts on souls. As Phantom Queen, as Protector of the Dead, it is your duty to slay any such creature which might feed on your subjects." The rest of the soul-flock stared at Saoirse as Anand spoke, their half-lidded eyes silently judging her.

Saorise's mouth twisted. Her arms burned. "It's a dog, Anand. It's clearly starving — can't I like, I don't know, feed it? Throw it a bone or something?"

If crows could sigh, Anand would have. Instead, she approximated the gesture with a ruffle of her wings. "Saoirse, for thousands of years I hunted creatures such as these. If I were in your stead, I would have slayed it without a moment of hesitation. Why should this one earn the Queen's mercy?"

"Because I don't want to kill it! I don't want to kill anything! Ever! " Saoirse's voice projected louder than she had intended, her tones echoing the clash of spears and shields, with the spilled blood of the dying and the orders of their execution as she spoke.

The hound froze at the sound of her voice. It whimpered, the white of its eye showing, as if recognizing her as an apex predator for the first time.

Anand stamped her feet and flapped her wings in frustration. It was a while before she was coherent enough to speak in anything but meaningless, peeved croaks. "Saoirse. You are Queen, and my fealty is to you. But you must understand — you are a goddess of war. The day will come when you have to kill, even if you intend to spare a life. Sometimes, the only way to save the life of one is to end another."

"Maybe you're right, but I'm not going to kill this dog, not now. So find another way."

Anand turned her head from Saoirse to study the beast, which had resumed thrashing against its denim bonds. After a moment of silent contemplation, she hopped back out of the window, leaving Saoirse, the hound, and her flock behind. The rest of the crows continued to stare at Saorise, barely moving even to ruffle their feathers. Generations of opinions weighed heavily on Saorise through their gaze, but she pointedly ignored their looks. A few minutes of wrestling with the dog later, her arms beginning to scream from exertion, Anand returned, carrying the wriggling body of a squirrel.

"What is…" Saoirse trailed off as Anand pinned the writhing squirrel to the floor with her claws and plunged her beak into its body. The squirrel immediately ceased in its struggle, limbs sagging and eyes going glassy. Her ghostly beak did not leave a speck of blood in its wake, phasing through the squirrel's flesh as easily as the dog had the door. Anand jerked her head back, and tore loose an exact copy of the rodent, translucent and eerie, its spectral nose twitching nervously at this change of circumstances. Anand held the ghost aloft in her beak, freshly harvested from a still-warm corpse.

Moving as if fighting a stiff wind — the squirrel's ghostly tail and fur fluttering in its nonexistence — Anand dragged the spirit to the Saoirse. At the scent of the squirrel's specter, the hound stopped struggling and let out a hungry whine.

"Feed it." She said flatly. "Feed it, and understand the lesson I teach you."

Shaking, without taking her eyes off of the dog, Saoirse picked up the squirrel's ghost. It was a tiny, flimsy thing, but within it she could sense a tangled web, a knot of memories and emotions. All of the nervous energy the animal had had in life, all of the fear of winter and the joy of summer, a lifetime of tiny experiences cut short by her order, if not her hand directly. It was so small, so delicate.

Such a beautiful little thing.

Tears welling up in her eyes, she tenderly cupped its spirit in her hands, and delivered the squirrel's soul into the dog's maw.

Rich, vital essence fills the Hound's body, and it immediately feels reinvigorated in a way it hasn't in weeks. The fog of hunger clears, mostly. Not as big of a meal as it had hoped, but one far less terrifying than the one it had initially sought. It was a tasty morsel gifted to it by the not-prey and its strange pack, which the Hound realizes all had the same spiritual scent. Involuntarily, its tail begins to wag, long-forgotten memories of its lost life tugging at its mind.

The not-prey stares at the Hound, and relaxes in its grip, unwrapping it from its pelt. Gingerly, fearfully, it shakes off vestigial thing-stuff out of its fur and backs out of the room. It doesn't glance back before it shifts out of the material world, and races away through the monochrome world of Dead Portlands.

It isn't sure what to make of this. A predator of predators, disguised as dying prey. A hunter of hunters that shared its kill. A distant, aching familiarity, to someone long forgotten. A firm lesson, rising up out of the bubbling soup of memories from its former life.

Don't bite the hand that feeds you.

Saoirse quietly sobbed as she flopped face-down on her bed, her cries muffled by her pillows. Anand let her be, for a time, perching on the headboard to survey for any further threats in the bedroom. Eventually, the teenage goddess flipped over, staring up at her predecessor's corvine form.

"I… I understand, Anand." Saoirse said, her expression blank.

The crow approximated a look of compassion, black eyes half-lidded and downcast. "I am sorry, child. It is a lesson that does not come easy for some."

"It's the circle of life. The food chain. Something had to die for it to eat. It eats souls, and there aren't any of those in the city, right? So it was between the dog, me, or something else dying. That's how it works."

"Yes." Anand cawed, mournfully.

Saoirse groaned, staring at the posters on her wall. "This isn't right. Why me? Why did it attack me? Why couldn't it just hunt squirrels or something by itself, like you did?"

"You are the bridge to the crossroads, Saorise. You straddle the line between the living and the dead, of both and yet of neither. Creatures such as that hound — they are creatures of the spirit. To attack the living is beyond their typical abilities, only the dead and dying are prone to their predations." Anand shuffled her feet on the headboard. "I— you, now, the Morrigan, are uniquely vulnerable, a target on both sides of the crossroads."

"…Oh."

"Hm. I would reckon that with the dearth of spirits in this city, the ecosystem has become unbalanced. It is a lean time for these beasts. It may not be inappropriate to say that every psychopomp, every demon, every magic-eating glutton in all of Three Portlands has considered attacking you, attacking us, absorbing our essences for themselves. This hound was but the first. It was a harbinger of future things to come."

"So, like everything else, it's about the missing souls." Saoirse covered her face with both hands and let out a low, muffled scream. "What am I even supposed to do, Anand?"

"For now, you rest. And then, you must do your duty." Anand's voice was flat and brooked no argument, a divine command from the ex-divine, a fire of determination glinting in her avian eyes.

"I'm not killing animals, Anand! I can't."

"Saoirse, it is your charge. A heavy burden, to be sure, but it is yours." Anand puffed up her feathers, agitated. "I understand you are not overjoyed, but this is your life now!"

"It's wrong!" Saoirse shouted, her voice filling the room with clamor of war drums.

Anand jumped back from the goddess, but continued. "You eat meat, do you not? You would kill in self defense, would you not? It is necessary. Right and wrong do not play into this."

"Yes, they do." Saoirse took a deep breath before continuing, the beating of drums fading into silence. "How many times did you try and find another way to do 'your duty'?"

"Never. It was fate. There was no other way."

"Wasn't my dying supposed to be fate, too?"

Anand gave no response, so Saoirse continued.

"Look. I agreed that I'd be the new Morrigan. I agreed that I'd take on your responsibilities and your powers. But I won't use them to kill." In a smaller voice, she added, "Not unless there's no other way."

"Saoirse, there is—" Anand's reply was cut off as Saoirse continued.

"There is another way. I don't care if we have to change fate or whatever to do it, but there is. Maybe we take the psychopomps out of the city. Maybe we, I dunno, find a way to feed them normal food. But the fact is, I fed that dog, and it didn't attack me." Saoirse paused, then repeated softly: "It didn't attack me. It was just lonely, and hungry, and scared, and we gave it a chance, and it took it and didn't attack me."

"Why are you so resistant to this, child? It cannot be a mere moral issue."

"Because! Because…" Saorise's voice trailed off, her mouth moving but producing no sound. Tears filled the corners of her eyes, and she rested her head on her knees, trying to avoid eye contact with the spirits of the dead. She took a shuddering breath before finding the courage to continue.

"Because… because when my mom was in the hospital, when she was really sick, it got really bad. She had to… they put her on life support, they put her on ventilation, she couldn't breathe by herself. The doctors said that… he said that she wouldn't recover. He said that science couldn't help and that… that the magic carried too much of a price to pay."

She wiped her snotty nose with the heel of her hand. "It was up to Dad, in the end. He looked so… aged, after. He looked old, walking me back home from the hospital after Mom… after she was gone. He didn't speak to me for two days. He didn't speak at all. It was just too much for him, and… I don't want to feel that. I don't want to feel that hurt, I don't want to hurt people. That's why."

A long, silent minute creeps past before Saorise looks up from her knees to Anand. Maybe it was her imagination, but she thought that the crow's flinty eyes softened, when it next spoke. "There is no convincing you otherwise on this, is there?"

Saoirse shook her head tentatively, and Anand gave another shrugging sigh, shaking her head. "Very well. There seems to be little I can do in this matter, but… I hope you are correct, child. I hope that your new path works."

"Me too." The new goddess sat up on the bed, dabbing at her eyes with the sleeve of her shirt. She took a breath, calming herself down. Slowly, she changed the subject: "So. What do we do now — about the missing souls, I mean."

"You rest. You learn. You pray that no other psychopomp comes for you, and tests your vow of pacifism. And we — "Anand gestured with one wing to the murder of her sisters, perched on various furniture around the room" — we search. We shall find where the rest of us have gone, and then we shall hope that you have grown into enough of your gifts to take it back."

The girl. Not-predator-not-prey. The Hound doesn't know what to make of her, yet. A thing that small, that unassuming and vulnerable, yet something so strong, intelligent… kind…

By all rights, it should have learned its lesson, and stayed as far away as it could from the girl, yet something compels it not to. It finds itself dogging her footsteps in the days to come, lurking in the shadows, watching unseen. It sees others following, as well, lurking in the same dark corners it is. Following the same scent that lured it there in the first place.

It is lurking in the alley outside of her apartment when it hears chittering. A rat-king, gnarled and twisted with so many squeaking mouths, perched outside of her window, looking for a way in past the newly fitted wards.

The Hound clambers up the fire escape and swallows it whole, and the girl sleeps peacefully another night.

In the morning, a skili swoops overhead on tattered wings, its eyes round and staring as the girl comes back from a walk in the park. The Hound jumps and catches it when it flies too low, snatching it out of the air like a plastic Frisbee. Another small morsel, but more than it has had in months.

The girl walks home, safe and sound, never knowing the Hound is near.

The Hound grows content. Hunger loosens its fire-cold grip on its ghostly belly, and is replaced by the stirring of a long-forgotten feeling, memories dredged up where they had almost been cast away. Memories of another girl, of warm hugs, of games in the park, of treats echo from its mortal life, and it doesn't know what to make of them.

Surely, it only follows the girl because the hunting is good.

Once, she nearly glimpses it, on a walk home from her school. The Hound is no longer careful. She walks with one of the birds in her soul-pack, the connection between them obvious to the Hound's eye and nose. The bird croaks into her ear and she wheels around, staring in the direction of the Hound. Instinctively, it hides behind a thin light-pole, cloaked in its shadow.

The girl is quiet for a beat, and then unleashes a peal of laughter, a sound of unfettered joy. It is a good sound. A familiar sound. A sound that makes its tail instinctively wag. It cannot see her, its eye obscured by the pole, so she must not see it. It is so well hidden. She must be laughing at something else.

When it finally breaks from cover, she is gone. It finds her again that night, as it takes up its post in the alley. Where it can smell anything that might come for her — any potential prey.

But there was a new scent, a fresh, different scent.

She has left something outside the window, on the fire escape. A mess of blankets, arranged in a loose nest, and a bright green tennis ball, nestled in its center. It calls to the Hound, dredging up more memories of a time long forgotten. Of a girl who cried the last day it saw her. Who cuddled next to him in a narrow sunbeam. Who threw such a ball for it, over and over again. How it loved that game, hunting and not hunting.

The Dog picks up the tennis ball, curls up in the blankets, and settles in for the night.

[[include :scp-wiki:component:author-label-source end=--]] [[=]] **« [[[mirror-isnt-big-enough|Honey, This Mirror Isn't Big Enough for the Two of Us]]] || [[[phantom-queen-hub|Hub]]] || Vampires Will Never Hurt You >>** [[/=]] [[div]] Starving. Hungry. Gnawing needles of hunger piercing fetid flesh pocked by ghostly maggots. The Hound trembles, skittering through the legs of pedestrians unseen, sniffing the air for scraps. Nothing. The winding streets of Portlands are bare of the shards of soul the feral Hound once feasted upon. The pet graveyard, the sewers, pounds, even the dreaded clinic where it perished were empty of spirits. The souls of dog, cat, rat, all eaten by something larger, a shadow cast over Portlands, a biting, consuming wind. //Hungry.// Its nose scents something in the air. The smell of coming death, of decay, of cloying sweetness. Larger prey than it, but wounded. Sickly. It will have to do. The Hound runs. The streets blur past, the flickering flames of living humans burn past, the world of black and grey and living white tunneling and warping as it gallops faster than it ever did in life, bounding over rooftops and across clotheslines, keeping on the scent, howling wildly into the air. The hunt begins. Across the city, Saoirse is startled awake by the sound of a wolf's cry. Dashing, rushing, closing in. A mile away, then a half mile, then a street, then a single wall. The heady musk of a soul slipping out of a mortal body fills its nose as it flicker-jumps between worlds, a burning eye fixed on its target, maw open and salivating as it pounces on the last meal in the city. ----- Saoirse was still rubbing the sleep from her eyes when death on four legs barreled out of her living room wall. A wolf-like //thing//, as much of a dog as a dog's shadow, lunged towards her neck, its jaw snapping and salivating. Time seemed to slow down as it sailed through the air. Even as her mind struggled to process this abrupt change from dream to reality, an alien instinct kicked in and broke her out of shock, foreign battle-reflexes imprinted on her soul forcing her body off of the couch and rolling onto the floor. The beast's jaws clamped down on the pillow that her head had rested on a moment before, scattering stuffing everywhere as it ripped into what it thought was her throat. It took a second before the Hound processed that it had missed. By then, Saoirse was already up on her feet, muscle memory racing a million miles ahead of her mind as she flipped the coffee table onto its side, trying to create a barrier between herself and the threat, something to slow it down. Not sparing a second, she ran down the hallway and into her bedroom, slamming the door behind her and swearing all the while. Panting, dripping in cold sweat, she slumped against her bed. Her mind was finally starting to catch up to her instincts, processing what had happened. Some //thing// had appeared out of nowhere, trying to attack her, //eat// her. It was in her house. It was in her living room. There was nowhere to go. Saorise just got out of the hospital, she couldn't afford to go back again, or worse, back to the graveyard in her own coffin. Saorise heard it prowling down the hall, claws //click-clacking// on the floor, coming to a stop just outside the door. She saw the shadow of a shadow looming through the crack under the door. She held her breath. Then, hazy as smoke, its head appeared //through// the door, and Saoirse screamed. Far in the distance, her shriek was echoed by a flock of crows -- her flock -- but they were too far away, comfortably perched in the trees of a nearby park to do anything but screech in sympathy. The animal was huge -- easily the size of a Great Dane. Clearly starving, too, but through its too-tight skin she could also see the corded muscle of a predator, steel cords stretched tight by starvation. It possessed a single eye centered over its snout, gleaming red and narrowing as it stared at her. Its jaws were foamy and frothy with thick strands of dripping saliva, droplets evaporating as they landed on the bedroom rug, steaming. The beast hunched down, hackles raised, and filled the room with a low, echoing growl. Saorise looked around for anything that she might be able to use as a weapon. Her eye landed on the disassembled skateboard on her desk. She lunged for it. ----- Hungry. So very hungry. The prey-thing had dodged it once, but wouldn't again. Instinct woven into its being tells the Hound to wait for an opening, to pounce when the prey is distracted. And it does. As its prey races away, the Hound jumps, aiming for center-mass to bring it to the ground, to pin it down, to carve and tear the mortal soul from its body. It makes contact, its jaws close around the prey's black hide, and it tastes victory for a split-second, before its prey slips out of its bite, like it was made of air. Its jowls and tongue burn as if struck by cold iron where they made contact with the hide, but the pain is distant compared to the hunger. Undeterred, it pushes forward and pounces again, its weight knocking the prey to the ground, but something is wrong. The Hound tries to claw at the hide, tries to tear through it to get to the living flesh, but again it slips off. Its paws burn and sear where they make contact, and the dog yelps with pain. This is not what it wanted. Its quarry is not the easy prey it had anticipated. The dog backs away, keeping its eye on its prey, hackles raised. Fear wars with hunger as it paces, growling a funeral dirge as it has for countless other souls, more to bolster its own spirit than to frighten its prey's own. It feels scared. The //thing// freezes, eyes doe-wide, and stares at the Hound, its gaze inscrutable. With its long, awkward limbs, the thing slowly strips off its black pelt, revealing the pallid flesh underneath. It holds up its own hide in front of itself, as if that would ward away the beast. An opening. Starvation wins out against fear, and the Hound lunges once more. Its prey is cocky, its prey is stupid. Its black hide was the one thing protecting it, and it was willingly removed. It flicker-jumps to the side, so it can come at its prey from the flank. It prepares itself to feed. ----- The wolf vanished mid-stride before her eyes, its corporeal form evaporating into mist as it dissipated into nothingness. But Saoirse saw its path, she could see its paw-prints on the rug as it made them. It was trying to get around the battle jacket. Saorise dove in the direction she thought the devil-dog would be, the jacket outstretched, and impacted a mass where there shouldn't be any. As soon as she felt the wolf's weight between her arms, she wrapped it tight in her battle-jacket -- her divine mantle -- and //squeezed//, immobilizing the thing in its grip. It reappeared, mist forming from nothing, yelping, barking at the surprise attack. It took all of Saorise's strength to wrestle the hound to the ground, trying to keep its gnashing teeth as far from her face as she could, her muscles burning. She laid on the floor of her room for what felt like hours, waiting for Anand to arrive, the wolf thrashing and snarling underneath her. It wasn't going anywhere. She made sure of it. The makeshift restraints gave Saorise enough breathing room to study the monster in greater detail. There was no way it was a normal dog -- even by Portlands standards. Its whole body was //hazy// somehow, corporeal, but only inasmuch as looked like it was made out of smoke and shadow, bound together in a loose mold, tight enough to infer the broad strokes of definition and texture. There was also the single eye, a red-irised, malevolent orb floating in that black misty mass, and of course the fact it was able to phase through walls with seemingly little effort at all. She mentally flipped through her relatively slim index of mythical canines, trying to identify the snarling thing in her grasp, hoping it would give her an understanding of what to do with it. Cerberus? //Missing two heads.// Coyote? //Not a dog, also a bit too far north for that.// The Hound of Baskerville? //Was the dog even magical in that one?// Her train of thought was interrupted by a cacophony of bird chatter and wing-beats as the soul-flock poured into the room.   "Saoirse! Forgive us our tardiness, but we are arrived!" Anand croaked, landing on an open windowsill. Saoirse panted between the cyclopean wolf's apocalyptically loud barks. "Yeah, I can see that! Do you- Do you have- any idea what //this// is?" Anand cocked her head in contemplation. "I... believe I did, once. Though I know not now. Certainly, it is some kind of psychopomp." She declared, as if that was clarification enough. "A what? And..." Saoirse's frustrated reply was interrupted by the bucking of the beast, "how do I get it to go //away//?" "There is time for questions later. As for removing the beast, you must slay it. It is your duty." Saorise went rigid, and shook her head. "I'm not going to kill a dog!" Said dog snapped at her face, spattering her with ectoplasmic spittle. "It is no mere dog. Perhaps once, but no longer. It is a creature wearing the shape of a hound, a beast which feasts on souls. As Phantom Queen, as Protector of the Dead, it is your duty to slay any such creature which might feed on your subjects." The rest of the soul-flock stared at Saoirse as Anand spoke, their half-lidded eyes silently judging her. Saorise's mouth twisted. Her arms burned. "It's a //dog//, Anand. It's clearly starving -- can't I like, I don't know, feed it? Throw it a bone or something?" If crows could sigh, Anand would have. Instead, she approximated the gesture with a ruffle of her wings. "Saoirse, for thousands of years I hunted creatures such as these. If I were in your stead, I would have slayed it without a moment of hesitation. Why should this one earn the Queen's mercy?" "Because I don't want to kill it! I don't want to kill ##D11D1D|//anything!// Ever!## " Saoirse's voice projected louder than she had intended, her tones echoing the clash of spears and shields, with the spilled blood of the dying and the orders of their execution as she spoke. The hound froze at the sound of her voice. It whimpered, the white of its eye showing, as if recognizing her as an apex predator for the first time. Anand stamped her feet and flapped her wings in frustration. It was a while before she was coherent enough to speak in anything but meaningless, peeved croaks. "Saoirse. You are Queen, and my fealty is to you. But you must understand -- you are a goddess of war. The day will come when you have to kill, even if you intend to spare a life. Sometimes, the only way to save the life of one is to end another." "Maybe you're right, but I'm not going to kill this dog, not now. ###D11D1D|So find //another way.//##" Anand turned her head from Saoirse to study the beast, which had resumed thrashing against its denim bonds. After a moment of silent contemplation, she hopped back out of the window, leaving Saoirse, the hound, and her flock behind. The rest of the crows continued to stare at Saorise, barely moving even to ruffle their feathers. Generations of opinions weighed heavily on Saorise through their gaze, but she pointedly ignored their looks. A few minutes of wrestling with the dog later, her arms beginning to scream from exertion, Anand returned, carrying the wriggling body of a squirrel. "What is..." Saoirse trailed off as Anand pinned the writhing squirrel to the floor with her claws and plunged her beak into its body. The squirrel immediately ceased in its struggle, limbs sagging and eyes going glassy. Her ghostly beak did not leave a speck of blood in its wake, phasing through the squirrel's flesh as easily as the dog had the door. Anand jerked her head back, and tore loose an exact copy of the rodent, translucent and eerie, its spectral nose twitching nervously at this change of circumstances. Anand held the ghost aloft in her beak, freshly harvested from a still-warm corpse. Moving as if fighting a stiff wind — the squirrel's ghostly tail and fur fluttering in its nonexistence — Anand dragged the spirit to the Saoirse. At the scent of the squirrel's specter, the hound stopped struggling and let out a hungry whine. "Feed it." She said flatly. "Feed it, and understand the lesson I teach you." Shaking, without taking her eyes off of the dog, Saoirse picked up the squirrel's ghost. It was a tiny, flimsy thing, but within it she could sense a tangled web, a knot of memories and emotions. All of the nervous energy the animal had had in life, all of the fear of winter and the joy of summer, a lifetime of tiny experiences cut short by her order, if not her hand directly. It was so small, so delicate. Such a beautiful little thing. Tears welling up in her eyes, she tenderly cupped its spirit in her hands, and delivered the squirrel's soul into the dog's maw. ----- Rich, vital essence fills the Hound's body, and it immediately feels reinvigorated in a way it hasn't in weeks. The fog of hunger clears, mostly. Not as big of a meal as it had hoped, but one far less terrifying than the one it had initially sought. It was a tasty morsel gifted to it by the not-prey and its strange pack, which the Hound realizes all had the same spiritual scent. Involuntarily, its tail begins to wag, long-forgotten memories of its lost life tugging at its mind. The not-prey stares at the Hound, and relaxes in its grip, unwrapping it from its pelt. Gingerly, fearfully, it shakes off vestigial //thing//-stuff out of its fur and backs out of the room. It doesn't glance back before it shifts out of the material world, and races away through the monochrome world of Dead Portlands. It isn't sure what to make of this. A predator of predators, disguised as dying prey. A hunter of hunters that shared its kill. A distant, aching familiarity, to someone long forgotten. A firm lesson, rising up out of the bubbling soup of memories from its former life. //Don't bite the hand that feeds you.// ----- Saoirse quietly sobbed as she flopped face-down on her bed, her cries muffled by her pillows. Anand let her be, for a time, perching on the headboard to survey for any further threats in the bedroom. Eventually, the teenage goddess flipped over, staring up at her predecessor's corvine form. It is a lesson that does not come easy for some." "It's the circle of life. The food chain. Something had to die for it to eat. It eats souls, and there aren't any of those in the city, right? So it was between the dog, me, or something else dying. That's how it works." "Yes." Anand cawed, mournfully. Saoirse groaned, staring at the posters on her wall. "This isn't right. Why me? Why did it attack me? Why couldn't it just hunt squirrels or something by itself, like you did?" "You are the bridge to the crossroads, Saorise. You straddle the line between the living and the dead, of both and yet of neither. Creatures such as that hound -- they are creatures of the spirit. To attack the living is beyond their typical abilities, only the dead and dying are prone to their predations." Anand shuffled her feet on the headboard. "I-- you, now, the Morrigan, are uniquely vulnerable, a target on both sides of the crossroads." "...Oh." "Hm. I would reckon that with the dearth of spirits in this city, the ecosystem has become unbalanced. It is a lean time for these beasts. It may not be inappropriate to say that every psychopomp, every demon, every magic-eating glutton in all of Three Portlands has considered attacking you, attacking //us//, absorbing our essences for themselves. This hound was but the first. It was a harbinger of future things to come." "So, like //everything else//, it's about the missing souls." Saoirse covered her face with both hands and let out a low, muffled scream. "What am I even supposed to do, Anand?" "For now, you rest. And then, you must do your duty." Anand's voice was flat and brooked no argument, a divine command from the ex-divine, a fire of determination glinting in her avian eyes. "I'm not killing animals, Anand! I //can't//." "Saoirse, it is your charge. A heavy burden, to be sure, but it is yours." Anand puffed up her feathers, agitated. "I understand you are not overjoyed, but this is your life now!" "It's ##D11D1D|//wrong//!##" Saoirse shouted, her voice filling the room with clamor of war drums. Anand jumped back from the goddess, but continued. "You eat meat, do you not? You would kill in self defense, would you not? It is //necessary//. Right and wrong do not play into this." "##D11D1D|Yes, they do.##" Saoirse took a deep breath before continuing, the beating of drums fading into silence. "How many times did you try and find another way to do 'your duty'?" "Never. It was fate. There was no other way." "Wasn't my //dying// supposed to be fate, too?" Anand gave no response, so Saoirse continued. "Look. I agreed that I'd be the new Morrigan. I agreed that I'd take on your responsibilities and your powers. But I won't use them to kill." In a smaller voice, she added, "Not unless there's no other way." "Saoirse, there is--" Anand's reply was cut off as Saoirse continued. "There is another way. I don't care if we have to change fate or whatever to do it, but there is. Maybe we take the psychopomps out of the city. Maybe we, I dunno, find a way to feed them normal food. But the fact is, I fed that dog, and it //didn't attack me.//" Saoirse paused, then repeated softly: "It didn't attack me. It was just lonely, and hungry, and scared, and we gave it a chance, and it took it and //didn't attack me.//" "Why are you so resistant to this, child? It cannot be a mere moral issue." "Because! Because..." Saorise's voice trailed off, her mouth moving but producing no sound. Tears filled the corners of her eyes, and she rested her head on her knees, trying to avoid eye contact with the spirits of the dead. She had to... they put her on life support, they put her on ventilation, she couldn't breathe by herself. The doctors said that... he said that she wouldn't recover. He said that science couldn't help and that... that the magic carried too much of a price to pay." She wiped her snotty nose with the heel of her hand. "It was up to Dad, in the end. He looked so... aged, after. He looked old, walking me back home from the hospital after Mom... after she was gone. He didn't speak to me for two days. He didn't speak at all. It was just too much for him, and... I don't want to feel that. I don't want to feel that hurt, I don't want to //hurt// people. That's why." Du's On First?

Security Footage, Replication Studies Office, Site-43
11 October 2024

[Dr. Bastien LeBlanc enters Dr. William Wettle's office.]

Dr. LeBlanc: Hey, I've got a bunch of forms to deal with. Just need to check over some things with you.

Dr. Wettle: Sure, go on.

[Dr. Wettle waves dismissively as Dr. LeBlanc takes a seat.]

Dr. LeBlanc: OK. Request for a psych eval of a contained subject so that we can run some tests on it. Who is it that signs off on these, is it Ngo?

Dr. Wettle: No.

Dr. LeBlanc: Great, I'll send that off to her. Th—

Dr. Wettle: No.

Dr. LeBlanc: What?

Dr. Wettle: It's not Ngo. It's— hang on…

Dr. LeBlanc: Oh, I thought you said Ngo.

Dr. Wettle: I did say no.

Dr. LeBlanc: Then why—

Dr. Wettle: It's her deputy, I think. I forget his name.

[Dr. Wettle starts typing a query into his computer.]

Dr. LeBlanc: Oh! Dr. Nott, I think.

Dr. Wettle: Not him!

Dr. LeBlanc: Great, I'll—

Dr. Wettle: No!

Dr. LeBlanc: It is Ngo?

Dr. Wettle: No, it— n…

[Dr. Wettle stammers, then scowls and resumes typing.]

Dr. Wettle: Niven! That's the name. Damien Niven. Send it to him.

Dr. LeBlanc: Right, got it. Uh, then there was some stuff for Security & Containment…

Dr. Wettle: Oh.

Dr. LeBlanc: I thought O moved to P&S?

Dr. Wettle: What?

Dr. LeBlanc: Ji O moved to the MTF forces last year.

Dr. Wettle: What's G.O. stand for?

Dr. LeBlanc: No, that's her name.

Dr. Wettle: What's Ngo got to do with it?

Dr. LeBlanc: Nothing! The agent's name is O.

Dr. Wettle: Oh? Did you forget something?

Dr. LeBlanc: I'm fine. I just don't know who I'm sending this security paperwork to.

Dr. Wettle: Why have we got security paperwork?

Dr. LeBlanc: One of the keycard readers broke.

Dr. Wettle: Why?

Dr. LeBlanc: It was Lab W, actually. Lab Y is fine.

Dr. Wettle: Why did it break, Bastien?

Dr. LeBlanc: That would be because someone kept shaking the casing until it came loose.

Dr. Wettle: Fuck's sake. Isn't that a maintenance problem, not a security problem?

Dr. LeBlanc: Might be both. Does this report need to go to Torosyan and Kuroki?

Dr. Wettle: No.

Dr. LeBlanc: You want it sent to Ngo?

Dr. Wettle: NO!

Dr. LeBlanc: OK, I'll send it.

Dr. Wettle: No. Shut up. Shut the fuck up.

[Dr. Wettle takes a deep breath.]

Dr. Wettle: Send it to Torosyan only. Kuroki's already pissed at me for some reason.

Dr. LeBlanc: Didn't you photocopy your badge that one time? And those other six times?

Dr. Wettle: Shut up. What else?

Dr. LeBlanc: Uh, research proposal involving the DUAL Core.

Dr. Wettle: Send it to Du.

Dr. LeBlanc: I know it's to do, to be done by who?

Dr. Wettle: Zinyi Du in Quantum Supermechanics is who's doing it, Bastien.

Dr. LeBlanc: Isn't it pronounced Xinyi?

Dr. Wettle: Fuck knows!

Dr. LeBlanc: There's only one Ngo, and I don't think she'd like that.

Dr. Wettle: I hate you.

Dr. LeBlanc: What, the archivist who retired a decade ago?

Dr. Wettle: What?

Dr. LeBlanc: Yu Ong. Harry mentioned him to me. Miserable guy, apparently.

Dr. Wettle: You. Not Yu.

[Dr. LeBlanc opens his mouth, but Dr. Wettle interrupts him.]

Dr. Wettle: And not Nott the psychologist either. Don't start.

Dr. LeBlanc: Not not the psychologist? So it is the psychologist?

Dr. Wettle: …what other forms you got?

Dr. LeBlanc: Uh, fourth is a requisition form for general lab equipment.

Dr. Wettle: Oh, I know this one. Forth is in Temporal Anomalies.

Dr. LeBlanc: I haven't got any forms about temporal anomalies, luckily.

Dr. Wettle: Requisitions are what A&O do.

Dr. LeBlanc: I thought Du was in QS.

Dr. Wettle: Keep going.

Dr. LeBlanc: Some kind of general questionnaire about the department's activities, but the person I'm supposed to return it to is blank.

Dr. Wettle: Well, go take it across the hall then.

Dr. LeBlanc: Why would I take it across the hall?

Dr. Wettle: That's Blank's office.

Dr. LeBlanc: I mean, the bit of this paper that should have a name is blank.

Dr. Wettle: Well, go give it to him, then!

Dr. LeBlanc: Should I just write in a placeholder name there?

Dr. Wettle: NO! Fuck that, I don't want to go anywhere near that fucking guy.

Dr. LeBlanc: OK, I'll write in Ngo, then.

Dr. Wettle: No, uh…

Dr. LeBlanc: Noè's dead.

Dr. Wettle: Jesus Christ!

Dr. LeBlanc: He's also dead.

[Dr. Wettle shouts inarticulately.]

Dr. Wettle: Listen, you fucker. No Ngo. Not Nott. Nothing to do with Du. I don't know, and I don't care any more. Just send it to someone who actually gives two fucks!

Dr. LeBlanc: Ah, Dr. Fuchs is in Memetics. Should I give it to him?

[Dr. Wettle storms out of the office. Dr. LeBlanc follows slowly behind, meeting Dr. Gabrielle O'Connor outside.]

[Dr. O'Connor reluctantly reaches into her pocket and hands Dr. LeBlanc a $5 bill.]

Dr. O'Connor: I regret betting on that. It's way too easy to make that guy tie himself in a knot.

Dr. LeBlanc: I don't think Dr. Nott knows how to tie people up.

[Transcript ends.]
