Fuck that, I don't want to go anywhere near that fucking guy. **Dr. LeBlanc:** OK, I'll write in Ngo, then. **Dr. Wettle:** No, uh... **Dr. LeBlanc:** Noè's dead. **Dr. Wettle:** Jesus Christ! **Dr. LeBlanc:** He's also dead. //[Dr. Wettle shouts inarticulately.]// **Dr. Wettle:** Listen, you fucker. No Ngo. Not Nott. Nothing to do with Du. I don't know, and I don't care any more. Just send it to //someone// who actually //gives two fucks//! **Dr. LeBlanc:** Ah, Dr. Fuchs is in Memetics. Should I give it to him? //[Dr. Wettle storms out of the office. Dr. LeBlanc follows slowly behind, meeting Dr. Gabrielle O'Connor outside.]// //[Dr. O'Connor reluctantly reaches into her pocket and hands Dr. LeBlanc a $5 bill.]// **Dr. O'Connor:** I regret betting on that. It's way too easy to make that guy tie himself in a knot. **Dr. LeBlanc:** I don't think Dr. Nott knows how to tie people up. //[Transcript ends.]// [[/div]] [[=]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box-end]] [[/=]]

Dusty Pearl

An unpublished poem by Dr. Pearl N. Langstrum

From dawn till dusk

You ponder still

Identity your rock

Identity your dream

You crawl through your days

Clacking away at your little keyboard

Scribbling on your clipboard

Listening to their sorrow while you are so bored

But you never truly feel like they do

Do you?

Would you know?

When you are not one of them?

When you are not like them?

They wouldn't accept you

Because they wouldn't know you

They'd see your real face and throw away the key

So why risk it?

You can't be different

For you are just paint on a wall

Dusty pearls gleam in the twilight after all

The Manticore Hotel!

MANTIMANIA

Mania Ever More

Hege Falling

So, you listened and hoped beyond hope she would find a way to right the dissonance of her flesh placed upon her by the world.

Where There Is A Flame Someone Is Bound to Get Burned

Seas of Orcadia Hub

But Just Because It Burns Doesn’t Mean You’re Gonna Die

Make Me a Rainbow, I'll Shine Down On My Mother

I wish they would start already.

Astral beams of light rippled across the translucent, stained crystal panes. Each frame flushed a grand space with dancing flutters of history and mythologized scenes from past ages. Bleached white and gold organo-metallic polymers gave life to the never-ending panacea. Together, flowing across the immense and heavily packed hall. Banners of rich color combinations flutter in an artificial breeze from where they are wrapped carefully around sculpted columns.

Beads of sweat were already pooling from the pores in-between her crimson scales. Brynhild’s digits trembled from where they wrapped around the trident, the other hand purposely laid flat against her thigh. The temptation to reach up and pull on the collar itched at the back of her skull. It wouldn’t take much, just enough to get some air into her uniform.

No.

Instead, she straightened her spine and focused.

The towering columns lining the center of the room, carefully shaped and carved with the flowing embodiment of concepts made manifest, Rustics, posed as the great monarchs who came before. Each were studded with precious gemstones in the place of eyes and teeth.

She wondered, for but a moment, if the magic within them would bring them to life under the right circumstances. They weren’t cognitive threads, that much she was sure of. It was a question for someone else; they moved far too fast for her to read.

Arches of water pour out into waterfalls; tumbling to earth and creating cooling mist where they strike grooved channels far below.

She got lost in watching the trickling rainbow reflected by the falling water, eyes tracing the path downwards to follow the channels. She was just close enough to one of the waterfalls to catch little flecks of cooling moisture every now and again but not close enough to enjoy the mists. If the line was just a little farther back, if she leaned just a little bit, she’d be in the cool spray.

Don’t think about it. Focus.

The channels, miniature canals, snaked in carved patterns on the floor, dancing with light and Rustics in the shape of further scenes and murals upon which the occupants of the chamber stand. She wondered what the little oscillations in the flow of the symbols felt like, or if they produced any sensation at all.

The whole atmosphere brimmed with excitement threatening to flow over. It buzzed in her bones, begging her to move.

I will have to spend the entire evening in an ice flow after this.

She pivoted her eyes without moving her head to find something else to focus on.

Any minute now the bells will ring.

The frescoes, murals and carved etchings embedded in the walls changed with every glance that Brynhild gave them. This was normal, but the rapid oscillation was not. There were new marks in that maelstrom, and a part of her tingled with envy at those getting to feel them for the first time. Perhaps they were supercharged by the atmosphere and concentration of Magisters and Adepts.

Or perhaps that was her wandering, itching mind that was trying to admire the depths of beauty of the room without being pulled into the Rustic-laced cognitive threads embedded in every piece of art. A task that was proving far more difficult with every passing moment.

The silk vines of history and myth were calling her name, offering her experience that she would never normally have.

Come on now. What is taking so long?

Officers of the academy stood at attention all around her. Around a hundred Hlérsyngva, the Sea singers, the Finnfolk, in their finest uniforms lined on either side of the algal carpets and the canals of trickling water. Here she was in the middle of them all, Brynhild of the Growing Storm, trying her best to stand utterly, completely still. A task which seemed to be amusingly difficult.

Her uniform itched. It was like she had a rash from the alchen vines, those promiscuous things that creeped and crawled upon the great huts, the abodes of the nomads erected upon the backs of greater-mudcrab’s in the outer cylinders. The itching was made all the worse by the sweat causing fabric to cling to scaley skin.

If I move, I'll get the tongue lashing of my life. If I get lost in a cognitive thread I might move. If they don’t start soon, I might melt. I could have gone into a path that didn’t require self-torture, but noooo.

As if for emphasis, Grinwald walked up and down both lines of officers.

There was no one in the world Brynhild respected more.

I'll Tell You My Sins And You Can Sharpen Your Knife

A thread of magic snagged against the wandering thought spooling out into memory. Colored pencils etched into the pages of a sketchpad, filling in the frame of a warmly lit equipment room. It smelled of metal, oil, and copious amounts of sweat.

You stood there nervously, a tiny thing in the shadow of the black-scaled woman. Her gills lay flat to you and her lips were curled down. The way she stood, with legs held slightly apart in a powerful stance, and the appraising look gleaming in her eyes told the story of her life. A hard Finnwoman, no-nonsense, holding your fate in her hands.

“So, you’re the Agrusa child?” she asked, looking you over yet again with pursed lips.

Too afraid to mess up the words, you simply nodded. You wished your legs and hands would stop trembling.

“Do you have a name?”

“B-b-brynhild, ma’am.” You winced at your stammering voice.

She sighed, gills pulsing once, as if you were a tremendous inconvenience.

“I don’t suppose you’ve had any training before you got here?” She turned away from you to an equipment rack.

Your heart sank; she was going to throw you out.

“A little… but I’m only eleven.”

Wood and metal shifted. You looked up, just in time for a blur of brown to flick through the air.

It was reflex really. Instinct that set your path in stone.

Before you knew what was happening, you had snatched the wooden frame of a practice trident from the air. Twirled it once and set the butt against the stone.

You stood there, staring at the practice weapon, then your hands, dumbfounded, and then looked up at Grinwald.

Her arms were crossed over her chest and there was a smile plastered across her lips. Her gills were fluttering.

“Better than most and you have the instincts.” The smile vanished into an intense, narrow-eyed gaze. “But talent won’t carry you alone. Life in the mud and sand requires discipline, patience, sweat, blood. Tell me now, no lies, is this what you want?”

Your spine stiffened, eyes filling with flame. “Yes. I want to live up to my name.”

She nodded once. “Then we start now.”

I Will Find My Way, If I Can Be Strong

The colored lines and pages faded away as Brynhild returned to the moment. Right as Grinwald was about to walk past.

The older Finnwoman’s lips were puckered so tight you could have balanced a quill perfectly atop them.

A shift of the hips, closing her feet too much, rippling her gills, shifting her head, it wouldn’t take much to set the old soldier off.

Despite the discomfort grinding against Brynhild’s red, scaly skin, the twitch of webbing in her fingers, toes, and the flutter of her gills, she was excited. Infernos burned a vicious dance in her eyes. The rapid beat of her heart gave it away beneath all the distant gazes; thankfully no one could hear just how fast it hammered.

There were so many eyes and expectations on her. She shifted her eyes up to the stain-glass pane of Agrusa, her many-great grandmother.

The threads wormed deep into her mind, snagging perception. A thousand images flaring against the threads of time and history. Grasping the calloused hand of the gold-scaled Triemedes, the Unifier and giant upon whose shoulders they all stood. Dances upon boat and distant ancient shores, — salt burning in her nostrils from the sea. She was teaching the one who would save us all.

The great sweeping storms of the scarlet desert where heat burned against her neck and dried out scales. The frigid depths of black in the bay where the great serpent of knowing gnashed at their heels.

The wind blew against her hair, roars of a Kraken’s engine filling the sky. She stood upon the prow of the great, shimmering thaumic machine as it barreled through the writhing storm. Barometric pressure smeared heavily against her skin.

Five terrible arms cleaved through cloud and rain, memory evaporating in its antimemetic conceptual wake. She roared, Krakens streaming towards annihilation.

On the shores of the Southern Basin, she bought enough time. In her fading moments, conceptual ideal eroding in the Odr’s wake, she basked in the coming glory of legacy. Then it came. The Astral Fire of Finnfelheim smeared the sky and struck the Starfish into the depths of its writhing prison.

The threads faded away as Brynhild returned to the moment. This is who she was. She was the last in the line of Agrusa.

A twinge of tight longing crawled up her spine before being banished as she focused on the moments that led her here.

Her eyes drifted to another panel, a great coral spire shining in the brilliant light of the afternoon singularity. A place that existed now in naught but stories.

The threads wrapped around her mind once again.

She was shouting, magic pouring off her numbed fingers as she streaked through the freezing sky on a sicklemoon hammerhead. Magic she’d never known, worming beneath every inch of flesh. It ached, carving a hollow cavern in her belly.

She rode, dipped, dove, and weaved through a fog heavy sky – droplets of water shattering against her scaley skin like needles. The Northern White Wyvern roared in her ears, the blast of her singularity driven thaumic beams smashing holes in its fibrous membranes.

Then she was riding great winged beasts through the highland lochs and fjords of the northern realms, yipping and hollering with wind blowing through her wild crimson hair. Trekking strange mountains far to the west with a woman of soft golden character and stunning blue eyes. Laying in bundles of twigs and bush gazing upon hatching eggs producing birds wrapped in thunder.

Gleaming metal gates framing proud, glimmering walls that towered like sheer cliffs above the Mediterranean. Behind the walls scaling up off into the horizon, a sprawling city of crystalline metal stretched as far to her left and right as she could see. The sky above was filled with the streaking shapes of hundreds of sundfljúgavagns1. Far away standing proudly defiant on the horizon, a tower, glimmering with light and Magistry.

Then it all burned in a ferocious firestorm of swirling smoke and falling metal. The heat it radiated near-blasting against her face Fraying and dissolving beneath the threads of fate.

Brynhild crashed back to reality, many other names and stories flashing through memory burning through the panes.

She had seen these moments countless times and focused now on the emotional heights instead of the details. Though some, like the grandiose scope of Finnfelheim, dizzied her even now.

These were monuments to the blood that ran through her veins. She had stood here beneath their grandeur when she was but a small child, staring and losing herself in the threads of a past that was so close and yet so very far away.

She understood, in theory, how they worked. It was a signature component of her people’s artistic traditions. Cognitive threads carried through the millions of tiny Rustics embedded in every pane, brush stroke, ink line and chiseled carving of stone, metal and crystal. Of course, it largely depended on the artist, but memory, stories, and emotional evocation were the point.

For the brief seconds and minutes when she was swept away in their conceptual threads, she could live alongside them. Feel the magistry sinking deep into her bones, feel it all around her in the moments her ancestors lived through.

In those spaces she felt like she belonged.

And now, as they almost always did when she emerged, their deeds and glory sat heavy upon her shoulders, threatening to crush her beneath their expectations.

She tightened her grip on her many great aunt’s trident, scales and webbing pressing into the smoothly polished organo-metallic alloy.

She stood in the shadows of their deeds determined to live up to their reputation.

But there was a problem — well, multiple really. But there was one that stood out above the rest and weighed heavily upon her.

She was near Astrally dead.

Must Be Homesick For The Real

The pencils shift across the page, carrying you through those initial days of training. The hard days in the sand and mud, sweating. Bruised and battered. Grinwald’d knock you down, tell you to get up, and do it again. Again, and again until you learned, until you rolled out of reach and turned it back against her.

Each step conquered earned a “good job”. Then she shifted approach and did it all over again. Training stopped being about single moves, became a dance of technique and drills as you grew.

When you were caught out of line, forgot to clean up the practice yard, or missed practice, you’d scrub the stone and crystal floors of the equipment room until they shined. No excuses.

You had a schedule: Wake, mischief, eat, mischief, learn, mischief, practice, mischief, eat, mischief, academics, clean, eat, bathe, sleep and surprise, more mischief.

When you finally beat her for the first time in a spar, you got a pat on the back, and the next day off.

She was hard, but fair. More than that. She listened. She fought for you when no adult would.

She caught you once breaking down in the equipment room on the anniversary of that night. You were sat cross-legged on the stone, wiping your eyes and sniffling when she walked in.

For a moment it seemed she was about to scream and yell. But she didn’t. She sat on the ground, didn’t touch you.

“What is it?” she asked, in the softest tone she’d ever used. She listened, as you cried and spat it all out.

She didn’t utter a word, just sat there with a faraway look haunting her eyes.

And next year when that black day rolled around again? You showed up in the barracks, she took one look at you and said the words you’ll never forget.

“Go home. No lessons today.” It wasn’t pity in her eyes. It was something you wouldn’t understand until you were much older. Understanding.

You tried to ask why, but she just locked the door and walked off clutching a golden locket suspended from chain around her neck.

It wouldn’t be until much later that you’d see the little dark scaled spawnling's Rustic painting suspended inside.

Slick oil pigment moved along the confines of a dry canvas, pressed by a narrow brush along pre-marked lines as the palace training yard smears into definition.

Grinwald's imperious shadow arcs over you in the light of the singularity's afternoon adjustments. The metallic chill of the trident's heft seeped into your small fingers; a blunted child's toy to the giant that is your opponent.

A short Finnman stood between the two of you, preparing the field for your coming struggle.

The drop of a rock could have shattered the tension resting upon the oil film pulsing around you.

Seated on the spartan steps and benches are, perhaps, two hundred or more observers, come to watch the last of your line, you. The blood of champions burned in your veins and that made all the difference.

Their expectations pressed the meniscus of the film down, crushing against your shoulders.

None were heavier than the princess’s; seated on the stairs. She was a centerpiece all her own in her flowing twines and ribbon robes of fine silk, auric scales and hair gleaming in the singularity’s light.

Your eyes traced to the crowd. Her father, the King of all the Hlérsyngva, sat among the Magisters and Ministers. His wife, Queen Astrid, obscured by the reflection of the bright light of the singularity upon her golden scales, sat beside him, soft smile invisible to you in this moment. But it was there, you were sure.

“Begin.” The Finnman said, snapping you back into the moment.

You circled each other in measured steps, trying to keep up with every gigantic step she takes.

You sought the slightest opening in Grinwald’s impenetrable defense. Scanned the twitch of her muscles.

Motion, a feint designed to bait you into striking.

A year ago, it worked, and many times since, but not today. No, the opening came in the aftermath.

You didn’t take the bait, she shifted, and you sprang your trap.

You burst right, drew the reactive swing. The blunted tips of the training trident flicked past as you stutter stepped to her left. All the while the trident twirled in one hand like a baton.

One, two, three you hit her leg and hips with the twirling metal. Enough to bruise, but not much more. You weren’t strong enough yet to fracture. You wouldn’t have even if you were.

Grinwald grunted in surprise, pivoting to force you away, but you were behind her now, jabbing the butt of your trident into her spine.

She stumbled forward with another grunt. You spun on one heel, rebounding trident arm thrusting in a direct dash to follow through.

“Iss,” hissed from Grinwald’s lips, the Rustic burning in the air in the milliseconds before you reached her. Perhaps there was a smile there, however briefly. Your trident smacked into the film of ice formed between you and her, biting cold surging through the metal and stinging your fingers hard.

All those lessons squirmed back in, as you reached for threads of your own. You tried to yank your trident back with one hand while drawing the symbol in the air. All that theory, the practiced motions to counter opponent’s magistry… and nothing came. Tiny embers trickled off your fingers, ineffectual.

Grinwald’s trident knocked yours aside, snapping it out of your hands as the ice shattered into cold fragmented panes.

Metal collided with your chin in a retaliatory spin.

You were knocked into the air, electrostatic shocks from another spell squirming through nerve and muscle.

Landed with a hard thud and rolled in the sand. Flesh twitched beyond control for far too long. Stunned confusion twisted in your mind before flaring into a flame of determination in an abdomen that was defiant of these events.

You weren’t done; you refused to give up at one surprising blow and misfire.

Iron taste of blood polluted your tongue. You rolled, dodging the hammering butt of the trident seeking to knock you out. Teeth clenched, you tried to rise, summoning another thread to try and pull your trident back into your hands, but it only wiggled ineffectually across the yard.

You stared at it, then down at your fingers, at the abject failure of your attempts.

Panic crept into your small chest, tight with icey fear as you looked up. The expression rippling across King Aske’s gills and face dropped a pit into your stomach.

It was over.

Grinwald’s trident leveled, inches from your throat. “Match,” she barked tersely. Disappointment burned in her dark eyes; gills closed to you. You couldn’t meet her gaze, looked down at your feet as she pulled you up. Hot shame crawled up the back of your neck and through your flattening gills.

The crowd’s murmurs and affectations faded as the light changed in the sky, drawn forth by broader brushes.

You hadn’t moved a muscle for an hour, staring straight down. Everyone was gone. So was your confidence and any idle hopes of having lived up to your family name. You stared absently at your fingers. All that training, Grinwald’s lessons, for nothing.

Of course, they’d lose interest the moment you couldn’t do the most basic expectation of your people’s world, magic.

Dark bruises lay upon your chin, chest, and legs from Grinwald’s blows. They ached and throbbed as you limped absently through the palace halls. Too ashamed to go see the healers.

They’re Marks of what shame you’ve brought upon your hallowed house. Upon the man and woman who took you in for your worth and potential.

How many skittering messenger and servant constructs skittered past you in your stupor? How many stopped in your path, thaumo-mechanical servos whirring as their crystal lenses dilated to adjust for your presence?

Something compelled you to stop outside the cracked door of Grinwald’s office, posted next to the King’s personal quarters. A deep rattling urge to apologize, for the failure that you embodied, swirled in your belly like a maelstrom. Raising a webbed hand to knock, you stopped hearing the voices within. Ministers, Grinwald, the King, and the Queen.

“We ran the evaluations during the spar, Majesties; the outcome is unimpeachable.”

“Surely it must be a mistake.” His majesty’s normally upbeat tone sat grimly in your stomach as you leaned against the wall next to the door. Felt all the vibrations of the palace, of their voices filter into your skull. Pressed your hot and swollen face against the cool crystal and stone.

“It’s not. She tried to draw on fire and recall basic concepts in and of themselves. Sparks, embers, and the twitching of metal but nothing more. I fear it’s a worst-case scenario.” It’s the voice of a young Magister, Skreyja. A man who always looked at you as if you were far beneath him. His abject distaste for your very presence was never noticed by anyone else, and he shared that gaze for the Princess.

Hot shame wormed in the terse flattening of your gills and clenched teeth.

“Not for lack of trying, she was able to do something. I’m confident with a little more training…” Grinwald’s voice.

“Training won’t fix the root problem. Her Astral density is the lowest I’ve ever seen, nearly zero.” A different magister now.

“She can’t be dysthaumic. She’s of Agrusa’s line, noble magister-warriors.” The King’s voice again.

“Denying it will not unmake the truth, Majesty.”

A deep sigh through the doors. “This will devastate her.”

“There are ways around such things, no? She is my second daughter and I am loathe to abandon her dreams so easily.” Astrid’s voice, soft and harmonious in your ears.

“Your ward of the state, Majesty,” Skreyja’s corrected. “Adoption does not make her of royal blood or your daughter by the accords of unification.”

A sudden, intense burst of silence filled the interior space, permeating out and reaching you. The words echoed in your mind, an indirect punch to the gut.

“If Majesty cares for her to such a degree,” the other Minister, not Skreyja, began gently and far more diplomatically, “then it would be wise to recommend a different path for her life. Without Magistry she will be vulnerable, weak and easily laid low by a skilled warrior who can. It’s a risk in the defense force or even the Royal guards. Not to mention this sign of disfavor from the Mither.”

You hung your head, biting back the tears.

“Nonsense,” Grinwald barked tersely. “In the yesteryears of our ancestors, your words would be true, but there are approaches to compensate as Queen Astrid suggested. She is more physically skilled at her age than any recruit we’ve had in a lifetime of remembrance. Strong, and fast. With the right tools, she would have had me today. She deserves, on merit alone, to see her ambitions unfold.”

“The compensation will never be enough Grinwald, you know this. Think of the cost if something were to happen? You’d risk the last in the line of Agrusa, prevent the preservation of the bloodline, for a single child’s ambitions and feelings against the will of the Mither and needs of the Work?”

“If the bloodline is dry of access to the Rustic weave, perhaps it’s time to consider deemphasizing the despotism of our so-called ‘sacred bloodlines’ for the good of all. A slot filled with no merit is nothing but nepotism manifested,” Skreyja purred.

“Must you speak about her like she’s farmstock?” Astrid snapped. “Mither’s harvest she’s a spawnling!”

“A spawnling with a limited future and value to the greater work we all seek,” he rebuffed.

“She is far more than that and you faen well know it Skreyja. I will not stand by and let you smash a spawnling’s dreams beneath whatever ambitions you’re puckering and plucking from your carrion filled—” Grinwald snarled.

“Enough!” Aske’s staff rang with a metallic echo in your ears, cutting further debate off.

You didn’t hear the rest, already limping towards your quarters with barely suppressed despair dripping from your eyes. As soon as the door shut, you collapsed onto the silken algal sheets of the bed.

Silent sobs racked your body, wallowing at just how abjectly broken you were.

To be without the ability to do magistry? A critical component of your people’s lives. Used to access everything from transport, building and facility access, even direction of the vehicles you so desperately wanted to command.

You were dead to the Mither’s gifts and voices. She had rejected you, left you as nothing more than an incubator to carry the next generation of your bloodline.

So deep in wallowing were you, you heard neither the knock, nor the opening of the door and subsequent footsteps. A webbed hand pressed gently into your back, startling you from the spiral to look up. Through blurry tears, you saw the Princess looking down at you.

She had placed a stack of books upon the sea-oak end-table.

Her gills pulsed three long times, surveying your bruises.

“You’re hurt still, why didn’t you go to the healers?” Her voice was gentle, as if fully cognizant that you could break at any moment.

“I wanted to be alone.” The response poured so fast from your lips that you flinched at the harshness of wishing her away conveyed in your tone.

Ever the curious and yet socially oblivious creature, Hege simply ignored you. “Sit up, so I can heal you.”

The command was blunt, and you obeyed without really thinking about it.

The soothing warmth of healing Rustics wormed into your flesh with more than a bit discomfort. That was of course a mark that Hege was not an experienced healer. You watched, feeling all the worse as you were reminded by burst blood vessels mending beneath the skin of what you could not do.

“Now, tell me, why you are shedding such copious tears? I did not take you for one to weep after a defeat?”

Of course she wouldn’t know. She’s blessed with more magistry in her pinky than I have in my entire body. you thought bitterly as the words stung with potential implications laden behind them.

But then you banished them, remembering that she was simply matter of fact, something you’d learned very quickly after you first met. No ulterior intent, a refreshing characteristic compared to even Grinwald’s games of careful words.

You lived in a political world of disagreements between officials over how best to accomplish the purpose and drive of the Mither’s ever present will.

Nonetheless, the truth was hollowing a hole in an abdomen too small to support it.

“I-I-I’m dysthaumic.” You hung your head, a few more tears dripping off one scale covered cheek.

“Of course you are, I could have told you that the moment we began magistry lessons,” Hege’s voice scoffed, gills pulsing three times in annoyance. “Any magister worth their salt can detect the threads of a spawnling learning the concepts. The simple act of forming a Rustic in the mind spawns a twitch in the fabric of the Magistry weave.”

You looked up at her, anguish twisting to disbelief in the open disposition of your membranes. You were broken and she was dumping mechanistic details of her special interest upon you.

“Dysthaumia is rare, but not unheard of. It is nothing to despair over, simply a condition beyond your control.”

“It’s disqualifying. I can never be in the defense force now. I can never live up to my ancestor’s name.”

Hege snorted air out of her nostrils. “Who told you that? The Ministers? Magisters?”

“Yes… No. I overheard it. I’m sure they’ll tell me in the morning. Aske will send me away.”

“Don’t be ridiculous Brynhild. The ministers are political fools and father wouldn’t dare. Brynhild, look at me.”

You obeyed, raising your head to look up at Hege.

“Good. Wipe your tears. You may cry further, but not until you hear what I have to say.”

You wiped your eyes and sniffled. She watched waiting for you to gain some measure of composure and dignity.

“You do not need magistry to become what you most desire. It would help yes, but there are ways around such limitations.”

“But… even if I do, the Mither has forsaken me…”

Hege sighed languorously.

“Nonsense. Utter nonsense.”

“Bu—”

“No buts. Noone knows the Mither’s will but the Priestesses, and I have never met a priestess who didn’t talk in riddles of the old tongues! Especially to the ministers. Pure conjecture and speculation. I’ll have none of that sort of emotional speculation from you.”

You stared at her, bewildered, unsure if she was simply trying to cheer you up or if, for once in her life, she actually had an ulterior motive you couldn’t see.

She pulled diagrams and sheets of algal sea-paper off the end table and spread them out on the bed between the two of you. You admired her confidence in that moment, the ache in your chest lessening for her presence and assuredness of purpose.

Eyes tracked to the paper, admiration becoming abject disbelief. As the paint began to fade, she told you of all the tools she had already designed, all the ways she would make you equal to a warrior capable of great magistry. Make you capable of functioning in this world with accommodations that would be so smooth, that sun-fish butter would feel chunky in comparison.

You were grateful for her… but the opportunity was purely nepotism. If you had never been taken in because of your family legacy, then you never would have this chance. Advantaged over who knows how many others among your people who were dysthaumic.

You hated it. For what it meant you were taking rather than giving.

Though The Road May Wander, It Will Lead Me To You

Bells chimed in Brynhild’s ear, stirring her back to reality as the thoughts and echoes of memory lingered.

They let me in, not on merit, but because of who is around me, where my blood runs through the undersky, and who I had make me tools.

They thought she would be nothing more than a lowly officer, a pity case for some bureaucratic post. Just an incubator for the next great Agrusa. But here she was, with all of Hege’s tools and devices.

I trained, fought, struggled in the dirt, sparred, pressed my body to its limits.

She proved them all wrong. She was the top of the class in all areas except one. The one that always haunted her, Magistry.

But you didn’t need Magistry to be a great commander. Not with Hege’s tools. Not with her tactical and strategic mind. She was going to prove it.

Her eyes dart to the stain glass window of her great-great-grandaunt. Segrusa, grand general of the southern provinces in the height of their people’s glory.

Today I go to make my name, Auntie. Today I finally get to make something of myself. I will secure command of a Kraken.

There were talks, ambitions in play in the upper echelons of the defense force. Arcane whispers of reaching out to make contact with the world. Humans, speakers of the mud and dirt, be damned. They were going to find the refugees from the South who scattered to the winds. Who knew what grand feats they had accomplished, how they had survived the drowning of Finnfelheim.

There must be some, no, many alive.

Now was the time to strike while the will was there.

Change was coming, opening from isolationism. Too long had they hidden from the world, sank into the dark of the night and depths. Even now the pendant burned against her chest beneath the uniform, the neglect of the Mither’s ethos shaming her flesh. Shaming all of them. That purpose with which they had been burdened, all their kind, demanded a return to form. The four golden eyes burned like fire in the back of her mind, ever watching.

The King must know it’s time. It’s been time. But for too long he failed to act due to politics, the old guard, the cowards whose scars at human hands linger on the tide.

But change was here in the shape of a golden-scaled girl.

The din of the hall began to settle around her, briefly drawing her back to the moment. It lasted but a moment before the halls of memory called her back in, urged by the dancing murals and their threads of memory.

Fifty-two cycles ago, princess Hege Aquaillian was born. The name seared in her skull, ache tightening in her ribcage. She almost lost composure. Almost flinched. Gritting her teeth at the thought of her former friend.

Fourty-four cycles ago, Brynhild lost everything she’d ever known. How she’d been taken in by the Royal Family, how she lost everything, orphaned by a horrible fire. The hand around the trident trembled as the inferno caught again in her mind.

When It All Burned Down

Watercolor pigments swirl atop a faded canvas, drawing you back to the past.

Your heart thrummed in your ears, tiny footsteps carrying you down the street as fast as you could run.

You were late, of course you were late. You should have stopped at the market after lessons. You had the sandstars in your pockets after all. But no, you didn’t when you should have.

No, you were returning home with the herbs of your mother's asking, kicking yourself for forgetting and delaying dinner another two hours. Roasted floatbirds, grilled eastern-lumifish from the outer cylinders — filled with nuts and those waxy green stalks of which their name always tingled delightfully on your tongue. A favorite meal.

Your stomach growled, mouth salivating at the unbidden echoes of taste and smell wafting across tiny nostrils. You couldn't notice the glow above the buildings, unnaturally intense. It’s not until you were a street away that the sound of whirring pitches snapped you from your salivating reverie. Sirens, shouts, voices, a menacing crackling buzz in the air.

Rounding the corner; acheing tiny legs skid to a halt as the horror rose before you. Flames, huge orange, red, and yellow tongues lapped at the sky. Responders, servicemen and women in green uniforms flared against the backdrop of the inferno. Sundfljúgavagns painted in bright orange and red tones, maneuvering and spreading the air with Rustics that spewed gouts of thick water into the relentless conflagration.

Your home was burning. Precious abode of crystal and wood with all its paintings, little comforts and rich familial history, swallowed by a firestorm.

The bag of herbs hit the ground. Brushstrokes along the canvas whipped the insidious tongues of heat back and forth in the atmosphere.

You stared, gills flaring open in total horror. Frozen, internally screaming at your flesh to move, to fly into the blaze and save them.

Minutes later you writhed in a burly Finnwoman’s arms, screaming “Móðir! Faðir! Systir!” reaching for the place you once called home. Desperate hot tears wormed down your face.

Through the tears you saw a young Finnman, yellow-green scales shimmering in the light of the flames. You didn’t know his face but could see the smirk in his eyes as he turned and walked away.

When the smoke and flame cleared, the burnt-out shell of your home rose at the whims of the cruel brushstrokes of fate. There was nothing left for you in this hellish husk of memory, only ash, charred flesh and bone that you no longer recognized.

A trident, your family’s ancient heirloom was all that remained salvageable. You clung to it like its loss would unravel you fully from the world.

Everything you love consumed, leaving you and you alone the last of your bloodline.

They looked at you with such sorrow. Pity, sympathy filling their eyes and gills as you knelt in the grass and cried your heart out.

Hours later the stencils and narrow tipped brushes carried you to a mural lined room within a service station. Depicitions of heroic sacrifice danced upon the walls, hollow in their messaging now with the failure that cost you everything. Laying on a finely crafted, fabric stretched couch, red eyed and dissociated.

What would happen to you now?

Where would you go?

Who would take you in?

You were eleven namedays of passing, no skills, no value to the community or family unit.

You were too young for that and now damaged by loss.

All you had was a name, an important name, but no weight or added deeds behind it. Who would possibly take in such a sink of resources? Not on merit, but out of pity. All hope of the future evaporated. Tears wormed out of your eyes, flanks and gills rising and falling in stuttered, despairing gasps.

Then, voices, hushed whispers, scuffling feet and rippling parchment. Stunned gasps through the door to the front of the station. Someone shushing the cacophony in muted whispers.

“Let me see her.”

Momentary flow of pigments, as the door opened, a pair of cloaked figures in the dim light of the early morning. They stood in the squat service lobby with its shell shaped chairs and intricate murals.

One shorter, round and portend. Hidden by the shadow of their cloak. A Finnman most like, they rarely stretched more than 6 hands high.

The other was tall, elegant, and bright despite the concealing robe. Radiant like the sun, soothing, if only a little, the grief churning in your belly.

The looming stranger glided into the room with you, door closing behind them.

Sitting up; crimson scales and green hair dancing in the reflection of mirrors and murals, you looked up at them. Your jade eyes widened. Gills opened, fins extended, staring at the royal crest luminescing and holding the cloak in place. Traced its trajectory as the figure kneeled before you.

Flush embarrassment squirmed up the back of your neck, a strange and unfamiliar heat as they lowered their hood. You should have bowed, gotten down on your hands and knees. But you were frozen in place.

She was beautiful, with golden scales, auric hair with the fine definition of silk in the braid that tied it to her skull. Her eyes paralyzed you, the brightest, purest gold you’d ever drowned in.

Air rushed in through green lips filling your belly; realization dancing like stars in your view as it clicked who knelt before you.

“M-m-majesty,” you dared to whisper.

There was such compassion in the way that all-consuming smile spread across her lips, in how it reached her eyes.

Queen Astrid the Kind, beloved wife of the ruling King Aske. There was no pity in her eyes, no sympathy, just pure empathy and understanding. She radiated calm, certainty, and comfort that threatened to make the tears flow again from your eyes. Painful images of your mother and her loving presence drug into the front of your staggered mind.

“Hello, Brynhild, my name is Astrid.” She didn’t belittle you with descriptors such as “little one”. She simply offered her name as if you didn’t already know it.

“Hello,” you managed meekly, voice faintly croaking.

“Do you mind if I sit here and talk with you for a minute or two?” she asked so gently of you.

You nodded, acheing for the company of her presence, her gentle voice, her steadying aura.

She sat next to you on the couch, a tower next to your tiny form.

“You don’t need to speak.”

You scooted closer to her, aware of the dozen possible cultural taboos it would be to touch her without permission. She immediately smashed them into a thousand pieces. An arm bundled around your tiny shoulders. Her warmth, her kindness a blanket across you, washing away the numbness and locks blocking the grief and emotions squirming beneath your skin.

She rocked you gently as the dams wavered beneath her support. Then, she spoke.

“Everything you are feeling, it is valid. That sense of aimless, listless, sudden deprivation of everything you’ve ever known. Of everything you’ve ever loved. Your loss, your sadness is valid. But through this trial, sweet Brynhild, I want you to remember that this loss is not a burden upon you. These feelings do not define your worth. You are not suddenly less for being away, for failing to stop it. You are not a burden for having nothing but a name to offer now, as easy as these thoughts are to fall into. Your potential is endless, and the house you will rebuild will be all the stronger.”

You burst into tears, all the dams breaking. Sobbed into her cloak, gills stuttering with your breaths.

On and on you shed those broken tears until you had no more to shed.

Then you listened to her coos and wordless notes of comforting song. A voice of soothing tone against your ears, shivering against her.

Though her words rang in your ears, a hollowness grasped your bones.

“What if, what if I have nothing left to give?” You choked out quietly into the fabric of her robes. “What if nothing ever comes of me? If I cannot rebuild a house whose greatness I will never see?”

Her great webbed hand gently held the back of your skull, long harpists fingers parting the strands of your locks.

“Such things a spawnling should not worry about,” she cooed quietly. “But you will, for the sight runs heavy through me and I have foreseen it.”

You absorbed her words, stunned by the declaration. “How?” you sniffled, sitting back to look up at her warm and loving features.

“That would be telling.” A wry, clever upturn of the lips and rippling gills. “You have had a great ordeal this night, but I would ask of you to make a choice. It needs not be made now, but it is of importance.”

You sat up a little straighter, the offering of an important choice stiffening your spine. Puffed out your chest in the pride of being given a task by someone of such importance.

“What is it, Majesty?”

“Please, call me Astrid.” She smiled warmly again with an undertone of curiosity at your sudden discipline shining in her eyes.

“My daughter has just passed her seventh nameday. The life of a princess is a lonely thing, with no friends and great expectations. Do you have any friends?”

You shook your head. You weren’t quite old enough yet to go to school with peers. Your sisters had been your friends and now they were gone.

“Would you like to be her friend? Would you want to come and live with us awhile?”

The question was like being hit with a Kraken’s beam weapon, it knocked the wind from your lungs.

You looked up with wide eyes and flared gills.

“You’d… you’d take me in?”

“It would be a great shame on my house and name to not do so. No spawnling should go without a home, without friends, without structure and parents to love them.”

You trembled and burst into tears again, nodding fiercely against her robes.

“Then it shall be.” She rocked with you until they came in with all the papers filled out. Took your hand and walked you out on towards your new home with the fading lines of the brush and stencil.

But no matter what was said to you that night, you could not help feeling you were a burden, only given another chance because of who you came from.

But I won't Lose Hope

"Whose bones shall carry us into the night?" Bells rang as words filled the hall and jolted Brynhild back to reality.

A priestess, standing on the dais cried out to the audience. Her skin glistened, twirling tattoos of ten thousand vibrant Rustic marks swirling across her barren scales. The voice echoed in the fractally endless rafters of the palace.

Brynhild had to force her eyes straight ahead, feeling the heat crawl up the back of her neck.

"Aquailian!" The response danced off her tongue, electrified with the aura of the power worming through all their bones.

There she saw him, the King of the Hlérsyngva, Watcher of the Deep, Arbiter of the Mither’s Will and the Thousand Eyed Watch of the Creation. He was once a jolly, portund Finman. But now he showed his age and the strain of his post. The gold of his scales had dulled. His hair was greying at the roots, and bags hung heavy beneath his eyes as he walked past.

Heavy is the crown.

Grasp of webbed digits clenched around her trident as her gaze fell upon his escort and accompaniment.

Nearly two heads shorter than her, the crown princess. Her former friend and heir to the Astral Throne. In equal parts Brynhild attempted to shift her gaze up without moving and yet at the same time strained her eyes to see. The princess’s golden locks wove into a single long braid; scales flush and brilliantly shining in the dancing auroras of light. Her twine robes flowed like a river of stardust behind her, gleaming with waltzing Rustics.

Heat flared along the back of Brynhild’s neck beneath green locks of hair.

“Aquailian!” Boomed around her. She missed the call this time and cursed herself mentally for being so inattentive.

Hege’s head turned, roving across the lines of soldiers like a lighthouse illuminating a convoy of ships on a clear night. Their eyes meet; the pearlescent depths of blue threatening to swallow and drown Brynhild in the depths of memory.

I Know You Got My Back, And You Know I Got You

Acryllic strokes over metal primers sat in glaze upon a far-off wall in your mind, dragging the images of the past to the forefront. Crystalline hallways, dimmed lights of canal bound Rustics illuminating your small face. Queen Astrid led you beneath and along the mural lined architecture, the images grabbing at your mind with their threads of color and history.

You drifted as if through a dream, nearly missed the man with yellow-green scales who greeted the Queen with a bow. As you passed, he gazed upon you with utter disdain, forcing your skin to crawl.

Astrid never noticed.

Though you barely remembered it, you came to a stop outside a dim-lit door. What you’d later come to know as Grinwald’s office. A hushed exchange spilled into the hallway as Astrid gestured at you in your nigh dissociated state. Grinwald took one look at you, raised an eyebrow, and then shrugged.

“I can make no promises.”

Then you were moving again, tiny hand clasped in Astrid’s immense palm.

She showed you a room, a place all your own. It had a bed, kitchenette with amenities aplenty, shelves and drawers and places to sit.

She left you there, to your own devices, numb, and full of dread for the empty days ahead. Of course, she promised to introduce you to her daughter in the days to come but for now you were all on your own to get some rest. Your first parental instruction, take as much time as you needed to grieve.

Or so you thought as you lay on the sea algal sheets, wanting nothing more than to return to a place that no longer existed.

“Hello.” the voice was soft, beautiful and resonant in your finned ears.

You bolted upright, nearly tangling in the silken sheets. A double take rocked your head. In the middle of your quarters, with a tiny twisting cube of light and color hovering just above her hand, was a miniature copy of the Queen.

The eyes were a sharp contrast to the gold of her mother’s, clear blue but less overtly kind. Filled with mischievous, curious, and adventurous spirit that instantly screamed of trouble to come. Your eyes traced up trying to identify how she got into your Rustic lit, crystalline room. To your great befuddlement, there was an open duct grate. You looked back down to the rather soaked nature of her nightgown and did the obvious math.

“Hi…” you replied cautiously, still shaking off the bafflement of her daring feat. “Did you crawl through the vents?”

“Yes, I did. I know them like the back of my hand.” She held up the webbed appendage for emphasis. She was entirely too pleased with herself. Lips upturned at the corners; gills fluttering in amusement.

“I heard Móðir and Faðir talking this evening about what had happened… and took it upon myself to come meet my newest neighbor and soon to be friend and partner in mischief.”

Her vocabulary dizzied your head and confirmed your suspicions. She was the princess, daughter of the king and queen. And here she was so… casually breaking into your room and talking to you as if you were the next curiosity for her to interrogate. You weren’t sure whether to be offended or delighted at her rather forward entry into your space. But you were sure of something, beneath that triumphant gaze, there was a deep sadness in her eyes, in the way she slouched and covered herself with cloth.

Unusual for one so close to the heart of the Mither, to cover up like that.

Then you processed again that she was the princess. Unannounced and in your room. Some part of you internally began to panic, if guards came looking, they might cast blame upon you.

“Should… should you be talking to me? Should you even be in here? Won’t they be looking for you?”

“At this hour? Hardly.” Her voice lilted in rebellious defiance at the suggestion. “No one, not the ministers, magisters, or fadir can cage my mischief!”

“What about your Móðir?”

“She would never!”

You stared at her once again, keenly aware of how slack your jaw had become.

You were going to tell her to leave, you really were… but your curiosity got the better of you.

“Mischief?” you asked; unconsciously leaning forwards.

“Chaos, experiments, sating of curiosity and bending of rules.” She held up a webbed digit as she listed each item. “The keys to progress!”

“Why me? Aren’t there—” You stopped yourself, remembering Astrids words. There were no other spawnlings around, she must be very lonely.

“Because you need something to do. Something other than the mundanities of life here in the palace. If you sit idly in here, the grief will consume you.” Her words cut to the bone, seeing straight through you.

“Uhm…”

“Don’t you want to be part of something greater,” She interrupted as you stumbled over your words. “There is no greater blessing than making chaos to ensure progression.”

She had you dead to rights, though you had no idea what she meant by “chaos to ensure progression.” But that hardly mattered, the princess of all the Seasingers had made you an offer, just like her Móðir, and, well, you didn’t see any better options for how to spend your coming days.

“Alright,” you said quietly, fidgeting with your hands. “What do you need me to do?”

Her lips curled up, gills pulsing. “That’s the beauty, I don’t know yet, but I can tell we will do great things. I am Hege.” She offered you her tiny extended fin.

You extended yours next to hers. “Brynhild.”

So began your bond with a thaumic genius to be, and a royal pain to her advisors.

The paints danced across the page, as your friendship grew.

Your first bit of mischief was sneaking through the grates to the generator systems deep in the heart of the palace. To your utter amazement, you found dozens of diagrams hewn into the organo-metallic polymer walls. She asked you to move components larger and heavier than she could manage, and you obliged, lifting her on your shoulders to tall places she couldn’t reach.

Your Song Sends Me Higher

Watercolor brushstrokes burn across a wrinkled canvas with burns along the edges of the memory it encompasses. Moments frozen in time of love, of growing together with your friend, watched over by one who became a Mother in place of the one you lost. Sweeping your heart again with acheing love and deep wells of grief.

The first time you ever heard Hege sing was a black week, the day after you lost your second Móðir.

Queen Astrid the Kind, beloved mother of all seasingers, collapsed in the gardens six fortnights hence the hour in which gloom burned upon all in the palace.

In the fifteen turns of your name since she took you in, she had been strong and healthy. She regularly lifted you and Hege on her back, and carried you about the palace grounds, playing games and pointing out things you’d never see otherwise at your height.

She grew steadily frailer, weak in constitution. Some days she was bound strictly to bed. She had good and bad days, but the Magisters had no answers, despite a parade of new and old healers. Then, she collapsed.

You weren’t there. Training with Grinwald when the messenger burst through the doors into the middle of your sparring. The blood drained from your watercolor faces, and you rushed across the palace compound to their aid.

They tried to deny you, they had denied Hege and Aske at first, sought to hide and cover up how bad things were. But Grinwald opened doors you could not.

When you stepped into that suffocating chamber of black, she was pale, drained of all the luster. A sharp ache deep in your chest bore its fangs upon seeing her skeletal frame in those sheets. Then her eyes opened and she smiled weakly at you and Hege.

The king ushered you out, to give her space to rest. To recover. But not Hege. King Aske never truly took to you the degree the Queen did. The other spawnling of the house who kept his favorite daughter from blowing herself up. His acknowledgement and distance from you mistaken for an adoptive father who struggled with the ides of his expectations. But no, you were wrong, and he proved it now.

You were not family. You were a ward of the state. Unable to do magic, you were of diminished value. The tears came hard that night, hoping beyond hope that the ship would right itself again.

But everything just went downhill from there.

Hege was beside herself, vanishing into the depths of her quarters. You knew her well enough to grasp, in those fleeting moments where she called upon you, she was deep in denial.

Tomes scattered over every open surface and floor. Half scribbled notes, formulations, and arrangements that were utter nonsense to you.

Desperation stank on her scaled flesh, refusing to stop clawing at some potential hope beyond both your reach.

But she was doomed to fail.

And you? Well, you threw yourself into your training, the rage, the anger at fate, at the Mither’s lack of answering your own tear-filled prayers. It weighed so heavily on an acheing young heart.

Grinwald was always there. Never questioned the intensity with which you needed to train. Only stopped you before you collapsed, listened and sat with you through the sobs.

When they would let you in.

You’d seen Skreyja’s momentary twitching sneers buried beneath the polite refrain of political gainsay. You didn’t know if she meant him or some other force beyond.

Yet still you didn’t fully understand.

In the dark of the room her eyes glew bright, unfocused and seeing something more. You realized as you sat there, she saw all the things beyond time and you.

“I will try,” was all you could manage, voice breaking in the oppressive dark.

She squeezed your hand, gazing through you with sad and tired eyes. In that moment there was something deeper, something more. Something that felt as if you were gazing upon all creation in the golden light of her brilliant quadruple orbs.

This made no sense, as when you blinked, she only had two, which closed.

When you left that suffocating space you heard the magisters speak to Aske in hushed, small whispers.

She sang for you, what you’d lost twice now. For the pain of fleshy connection you didn’t share. The wayward cast of the King’s love away from your heart.

You laughed in the early afternoon, making camp with her. Bantering about how furious Skreyja would be with your escapade. But there was a stiffness to her words and gestures that scratched at the back of your skull.

Strange murmurs sat in your belly when you looked at Finnwomen now. Befuddling, longing desires for touch, the collision of lips and flesh that dragged fire squirming up the back of your neck, storms in your belly and rapid oscillations of gills that you couldn’t hide.

It was at its worst around Hege.

You didn’t know why.

It was the first time you were truly beginning to grasp feelings for her. The soft love of friendship beginning to burn in your chest like aldrnari’s fire. You wondered then, as you often did, if she was beginning to feel the same.

Her eyes stared at the growing embers of the campfire, avoiding your gaze. For a moment, you were afraid she knew of the strange, bottled desire sitting deep in your guts.

Your mind reminded you she’d been distant the past few days, covering more of her flesh than usual. This happened from time to time, but you’d learned early on that asking got you nowhere. She simply didn’t want to talk about it.

They were her first words of the night.

You looked at her, before looking off towards the glimmering snowcaps turning the question over in your mind.

“Often. There’re so many expectations on me. I—I worry I won’t be able to live up to my name,” you admitted. “That I’ll have nothing to offer—and whenever magic is asked after, I—” you trailed off letting the words fail.

“I want to bury myself in sand beneath the sea and lay there until the Undersky claims me. “I know,” you responded simply. You did; you really did. After discovering your dysthaumia, you understood the impulse. Not in the context she spoke of, but there were things that were beginning to stand out. “We could.”

“Could?” She looked up at you.

“Run-away together. To the Witch of the Croon, or to the world beyond. Brynhild and Hege against the wider world. No titles, no princess and line of Agrusa, just us.”

Her eyes softened, gills gently pulsing.

The compliment burned in your mind, heart hammering in your chest.

“But these are idle dreams.”

“I know,” you said simply, leaning back against the tree. Knowing she would never abandon your people.

You looked at her then, really looked at her. You both were almost fully grown, and it was hard not to notice how small Hege was. That wasn’t all, where protrusions had grown more weighty in your chest, hers had stayed flat and you had no explanation for that. Perhaps you even dismissed it, it was rare for Finnwomen to be that small. Maybe it was also rare for them to be that flat of chest? But neither of you were particularly normal by your people’s standards, and it endeared her more to you.

It resonated with that same acheing discomfort, skin itching and sitting wrong across your bones.

Pierced deep into that well of despair and insecurity buzzing around your dysthaumia and dragged it into the light.

Your stomach twisted in knots in your belly, feeling the rawness of her emotion intertwining with your own. Harmonic penitence.

It clicked in that moment why she never let you linger on the alienness of dysthaumia.

Of how wrong it felt, doing everything she could to make it easy to be yourself. All that effort to allow you to pursue what you desired despite it.

It’s because she suffered a wrongness deep inside her, an incorrectness and inadequacy of the flesh that was apparently beyond her reach to correct.

Something you didn’t fully understand, couldn’t because your shape was perfectly you. Yet in that moment you understood, in the way her song touched your dysthuamia; the way It burned through the harmony and rhythm of her wordless notes into your crimson scaled flesh.

So, you listened and hoped beyond hope she would find a way to right the dissonance of her flesh placed upon her by the world.

And she did.

The swirl of color brightened across the page as you recalled the third time she sang to you. The hope of resolution within grasp, and the joy burning in the notes. You knew then that she had found her glowing solution. Celebrated with her, dancing in the artificial moonlight of that hot summer night in her quarters.
