She tried to focus on the excitement again. But the ceremony, the song, lingered in her mind.

Names rattled off in order of alignment. One by one, with each name called anticipation built in Brynhild's chest. Her moment seemed to barrel down atop her at furious speed and yet crawled towards her like a seaslug.

"Brynhild, House of Agrusa." Stomps rose from the crowd as she marched with perfect physical form down the aisle.

Her approach halted before the King, and the Crown Princess. She presented her trident as she’d been taught, in a series of perfect twirls and spins, before kneeling. In that moment of artful display, her eyes met Hege’s in a brief exchange of distant congratulations.

"By the Mither's blessing I bequeath upon you command as an officer of the Royal Guard. You will be assigned to the family retinue." The anticipation of the room abruptly deflated, as if the swim bladder of a float fish had been abruptly popped. The world around Brynhild trickled away, time slowing to a halt.

Her stomach bottomed and then dropped. Dread gnashed its teeth against the walls of her belly.

It must be a mistake. This can’t be.

Hege's gaze flicked to her father. Her gills flared open, eyes wide in shock, lips curled strangely. It was a new expression.

Was it anger?

Disbelief?

Horror?

"Congratulations my dear Brynhild, it's a role of great honor," Aske commended her, picking up on the room’s shock. "As is the tradition, we shall feast and sing once all candidates have received their assignments."

There was nothing to celebrate about this. She’d been sidelined. Benched. Her lack of Magistry, being taken in but not accepted as family, all of it haunted her. Skreyja, Aske. This must be their conspiracy to keep her leashed, to keep the wounds between them from healing.

Her future, and any hope of mending what had happened with Hege was gone in an instant. She’d never be able to prove herself, get the distance they both needed.

All opportunity evaporated with a single slip of paper. As she rose to return to her position in the formation, that hollow ache in her bones that first arose in that fire so many years ago ripped a hole deep inside.

She had the deepest sinking feeling that Hege would be her direct assignment.

And A Thousand Years Would Be Worth The Wait

Brynhild stood to the side of the door of Hege’s tower, Grinwald positioned on the other side.

She was alert, but more relaxed than she would be in any other location, which was a paradox in and of itself given what had happened here ten years earlier.

Though she couldn’t feel them, the many lines of fluttering Rustics weaving through the walls and door beheld a dizzying number of protective and destructive concepts ready to discharge upon an intruder at a moment’s notice.

Many were of Hege’s own design. Others were already there long before.

Brynhild did everything in her power not to look at the princess, going so far as to stare at the overly dramatic plant in one corner. It was starting to wilt, despite having been watered not an hour earlier.

Hege wasn’t making it easy to not look at her. She’d parked herself at a positively ancient sea-maple table. It had more ornate woodworking than the doors of the grand throne hall and it was right in the center of the room.

And with a sudden flick of her fingers, a watering can lifted off a shelf and sprinkled its contents on the primadonna plant.

The princess was grinding thumb and forefinger into the scales of her temples, just as she had done when they were children when presented with a conundrum. Her mumbles were incomprehensible, but almost certainly pertained to some arcane innovation prototype.

The Rustics were practically pouring from her lips into the paper.

Both Brynhild and Grinwald straightened when Hege abruptly slammed the tome closed and then dramatically sighed.

“No, no, no. It’s not in this one either.” She slumped in the chair, then tilted her head forward to press forehead to the wood.

Brynhild glanced at Grinwald, who met the look with a raised eyebrow.

‘You know her better than I do. What’s about to happen?’ was the implied question.

Brynhild shrugged. ‘Could be anything.’

‘Anything’ here meant she either walked upstairs or decided to run off to the library to find what she actually needed.

Hege straightened and abandoned the chair before Grinwald could mime further questions, walking towards the pair. Grinwald opened the door for Hege when it was clear she wasn’t going to veer up the stairs.

But she didn’t step out. She stopped before them, looking at Grinwald and ignoring Brynhild.

“Grinwald, you can go home for the night.”

“Majesty?” Grinwald blinked, looking at Hege, and then glancing at Brynhild.

“Its fine. I need to make a trip across the grounds to the library, but I don’t need you both.”

Grinwald hesitated, meeting Brynhild’s gaze. Brynhild realized then that Grinwald must have picked up on the tension between them for the past ten years. How could she not have?

“Majesty, if it would make you more comfortable, I could go and Grinwald stay with you for the night.”

“It wouldn’t,” Hege said, still not looking at Brynhild. Heat crawled up the back of Brynhild’s neck.

When Aske had died… she fully expected Hege to reassign her. But she hadn’t. And now, here she was telling Grinwald to go and Brynhild to stay.

What is she doing?

“If Majesty is sure—”

“I am.” Hege cut Grinwald off.

Grinwald simply nodded, gave Brynhild an inscrutable look, and departed. Hege waited until she was fully out of sight before stepping out of the tower.

Brynhild followed, at an appropriate distance as they trekked silently through the quiet crystal and metal halls of the palace. A thick knot of tension sat suspended across the gap between them.

Brynhild wanted to say something. Anything. Apologize. Tell Hege she missed her. But the words never came, and her mouth refused to move.

She found them, abruptly, in the gardens with their glimmering scultures, rare and exotic plants, and amenities aplenty. They walked past the spiraling flowering plants and corals deeper in. It wasn’t the normal straight route to the library. And there it was, the spot where, so very long ago, Brynhild had held Hege as they mourned Astrid’s departure.

At the foot of the hill next to the rocks they once climbed every evening, Hege came to a sudden stop. Brynhild almost noticed too late and came to a wheeling stop to avoid running her over. She backed up slowly, keeping space between the two of them.

She watched the muscles in Hege’s neck tense and relax, tense and relax.

“Brynhild?” she finally asked. The tone was gentle, the same intonation she’d once frequently used before a deep conversation. She hadn’t used it to address Brynhild since that night. Heat crawled up the back of Brynhild’s neck.

“Yes, majesty?” Brynhild defaulted to the formal address in this moment, not wanting to violate that space that had been so clearly demarcated between them in both their roles.

She realized, too late, the mistake.

Her stomach sank in her scaled belly as Hege’s shoulders bunched up tightly to her frame. Silence sat heavy between them for a moment.

“Nevermind.” Hege started walking again, and the opportunity slipped away.

Brynhild’s chest tightened in a vice. Breathing suddenly hard as she fully grasped the slipped chance.

Idiot, why did I address her like that? Why?! Why didn’t I use her name! She was looking to talk as just friends. What are you doing?

She let her shoulders sag as they walked, well as much as they could while she was still on alert.

The Library stood proudly before the two of them, ancient heavy doors rich with scenes of history and myth that threatened to drown Brynhild’s mind in memory.

Hege stood before it, hand resting on the ringed handle glimmering with gold and gemstones.

“Brynhild?” she asked again in that same soft tone. Brynhild’s heart welled, a second chance presenting itself in the luminous light of the flickering Rustic torches.

“Yes, Hege?” The desperation almost leaked into Brynhild’s voice. Almost.

No bunching of shoulders this time, a quiet relaxation in the princess’s muscles.

“I’m not ready… Yet. But someday, I will be.” The statement flamed around Hege’s frame, as if the words were carving into the air and thus Brynhild’s mind.

Brynhild didn’t know what to say, or if saying anything would be any good. So, she simply acknowledged it for what it was.

“Okay. I’ll be here.”

Wind rustled through chimes as Hege turned her head to look at Brynhild with one crystal blue eye.

Flame wicked and thundered in Hege’s irises. It swirled all around Brynhild, on the cusp of swallowing her in the depths of being that lay within.

Then Hege was looking forward again and Brynhild was staring at the back of her neck.

“Go get some rest. I’ll be fine on my own for now.”

Brynhild blinked, and hesitated.

“Are you sure?”

“Very. You’ve earned a rest.” She opened the door and walked into the Library before Brynhild could debate further.

The trip back to her room was a blur of halls and moving artworks. Brynhild barely registered the soft mattress or the silk algal sheets as she stared at the dark ceiling.

All she knew then was that there was resolution on the horizon. Maybe they could finally heal from that horrible night ten years ago.

Lights Out, Follow The Noise

The night that changed everything between the two of you was a matte painting of throbbing, hot colors and emotion.

You arrived before the gleaming, sea-oak door marked in burning letters with Hege’s name. Rustics twirled over every inch of wood, carved and freely flowing fluorescent lights dancing in the reflections of your crimson scales.

You knocked, the marks grasping and clinging at your curled fist. Whispers simmered in your finned ears. Threads of memory coiled in your skull drawing forth names and key aspects.

A mechanical click cut through the thickening silence. The door unlocked. It opened of its own accord, without your interference. In the moment in-between it was almost as if a woman’s voice filled your ears, whispering some future yet unseen.

Then you were standing in the middle of Hege’s kitchenette.

You rubbed the side of your skull, having lost any memory of moving across the crystal-inlaid-wood floor.

The lingering aromas of a homemade meal brushed against your nostrils. Books and half-finished experimental aggregations of metal, wood, and crystal sat on the counters, tables, and floor.

“Hege?” You called into the space, scanning for the traces of her golden scales amongst the chaos of a thaumic-genius’s habitation.

Only silence greeted you.

“She must be upstairs,” you murmured to yourself, looking to the fractally spiraling steps of the tower she called her own.

You considered going up them to knock on her bedchamber door but banished it just as quickly. You’d not been up there since the throes of adolescence and maturation spindled you into a ball of sapphic desire.

Nor had she invited you that far since.

Unspoken boundaries between you that carved an acheing throb in your heart, but you weren’t about to risk what connections you had.

Then, she screamed.

A sharp, surprised squeal that pitted your gut with alarm.

Instinct and training seized hold, bounding the stairs in heavy stomps. Your heart thundered in your chest, heavy breaths filling your ears. She was in danger; she needed you now.

The door creaked and thumped beneath your webbed digits, flying open with a loud bang.

You froze, eyes wide in shock at the state of the room, at Hege.

Outwardly spiraling fractals connected by lines of glowing light consumed the floor. Circles, Rustics pulsing with heat and light, all of it flowing inwards through objects and places of power towards the center.

Gasping for air in the middle of it all was Hege. She was half bent over. Runic marks flowed across every inch of her barren flesh. She looked up at the bang of the door, expression twisting.

Her gills were flared wide open, eyes wide and dripping with dread.

Your own horror writhed across your flared open gills, extended fins, and gaping mouth in her mirrors.

“Oh fukka!” Hege cried and fell to the floor writhing in spasms of muscle and flesh.

There and then she exposed the truth to you without meaning to. The reason for her height and the discomfort of her flesh.

Shown before she was ready, if she would have ever been.

Time slowed to a crawl as more than 40 years of observation and lightly dismissed detail clicked into place. Heat crawled up the crimson matte paint of your neck, shame at being exposed to her deepest, darkest secret without being invited into that confidence.

But now she was in danger, and you had to do something.

“Hege!” you cried, shifting as if to move into the room.

“Don’t!” she shouted at you; her voice filled with such commanding emotion. You recoiled, as if struck by a wayward hand. "I don't know what will happen if someone else steps in!"

You panicked, trying to think of what to do. "I should get your father, he'll kno—"

"No! You especially should not do that."

You took another step back, finally looking away. Your gills oscillated in three second intervals.

"I don't know why it feels like this, but it's what I want. It's what I need, Brynhild. I can't let it stop. I can’t keep going like this. Please, please don't do something that will stop it."

The fear in her voice, the warble in her vocal cords, it told you what she was doing. How important it was.

Fleshcrafting.

What now?

Why did you have to barge in?

Why didn’t you call out first, see if she needed you?

"Do you want me to go? I won't leave you like this but I can…"

"No. Stay, I don't — in case something does go wrong, I don't want to be alone. Just don't look at me." Another sharp gasp and the sound of shifting flesh filled the air. “I don’t ever want to be seen like this again.”

The sound of her change seared in your mind forever, as the paint faded. You spent the rest of the night sitting in the doorframe once it was all done.

She’d cried.

Cried until the false moon was high in the night sky. Then she asked you to go.

Nothing was ever the same between you after. A chasm, a void in your chest where inseparable friendship once laid as she put distance between you.

Every Word Shot Down In Flames

Brynhild jolted into wakefulness. Roaring klaxons filling the air of the palace.

She bolted from bed, instinct taking over as the trident came free of its holder on the wall, leaping across the gap to her hand. She burst through the door of the chamber, charging out into the hallway like a moon-sickle hammerhead. Adrenaline screamed in her veins as she looked left and right.

Magisters and guards were running back and forth like anchovies swept up by a riptide current. Brynhild’s hand snatched out and grabbed a minister.

“What’s going on?!” She practically roared in his face. He shrunk in her grasp.

“Fire! The Library is on fire!”

Brynhild’s eyes widened. “Hege. Hege.”

“Hege?” The blue-scaled Finnman asked wide-eyed.

“She sent me away for the evening while she was in the Library.”

His eyes widened.

Brynhild dropped him, turned, and sprinted. Ministers and Magisters swerved, tripped, fell, and tumbled to get out of her accelerating mass.

Her heart drummed in her chest. Feet pounded against stone, metal, and crystal. The growing crowd of confused faces parted before her like when Triemedes parted the Orcadian Lochs to put Terran deep in the earth.

She skidded to a halt on the grass, staring up at the firestorm filling the night sky. The grand spiral columns of the royal library were stained with growing smoke and ash. Its structure groaned over the roaring Klaxons. Service workers were already rushing to the building with their Rustics and vehicles, but the fire was already huge.

Brynhild lept forward, straight over several Finnmen frozen on the lawn. Someone’s hands slipped off her arm, trying to get her to stop, but she didn’t. The doors to the Library crumpled beneath her hands, flaying apart and weakened by the heat in a shower of splinters.

She pressed the hem of her top over her mouth to protect her airway from the smoke.

“Hege!” she shouted, voice drowned by the roar of the flames. A ceiling beam collapsed somewhere ahead, a shower of masonry and crystal smashing into the floor and shaking the structure. The lustrous golden timepiece was melting, shelves tumbling down into showers of sparks and wood.

Brynhild waded into the inferno, clearing a path with her trident, ignoring the heat pulsing against her flesh.

She found the lump deep in the shattered shelves, blackened and burnt.

“Hege!” Brynhild cried over the roar of the flame. She braced and lifted the once ornate and beautifully decorated shelf. It rose with a great groan pulling it up and over her head.

With a great roar, she flung it. Wood shattered as it smashed a clean path through the maze of burning debris.

Brynhild lifted the broken and burnt body from the rubble, wrapping it delicately in her cloak. No pulse, no breathing, no trace of life.

In that moment, despite the inferno blazing around her, Brynhild’s heart broke. Shattered into a million pieces. She cradled Hege close. Rocked her, whispering.

“Don’t go. Please don’t go without me.”

Tears tried to pour from her eyes, evaporating in the rampant heat as she walked towards the smoke occluded doors. Didn’t run, walked. All around her structural beams gave way, shelves collapsed, tumbling with calamitous noise.

She emerged from the smoke like a ship cutting through the grimmest fog.

Her scales were dried out by the heat and fire, shallow surface burns throbbing against her forearms and legs.

She stood framed by the flames, smoke pouring from the once great hall of knowledge behind her. She stared up to the sky above, and then down at the mass of Finnfolk, multi-colored scales a rainbow in the dancing luminescence of the hateful fire.

The din and roar of chattering voices, hundreds of eyes staring at the flames, frozen in inaction. Some pointed at Brynhild, others soon joining, and then all eyes were on her and her once precious cargo.

Brynhild stared out at them, those who had stood by and watched while the fire consumed all that she had left. Her face twisted in acheing grief. She took a deep shuddering breath.

“The Line of Aquailian is gone,” Brynhild sung with deep sorrow burning in the air from her voice. “H-Hege is gone.”

The world seemed to stand still, even the flames seemed to freeze in acknowledgement of what had been taken. The crowd stared, gills opening wide, hands flying to mouths.

A line unbroken for more than 10,000 years, extinguished in a single, final night.

Brynhild’s legs moved of their own volition carrying her forward down the stairs. Reality swirled about her head; vision blurred with the weight of what was gone. The crowd parted before her, webbed digits reaching, touching the bundle that was their princess. Their hope for an ambitious future was taken from them on this terrible night.

Grinwald’s grim face met her at the edge of the crowd, a cadre of guards surrounding Brynhild.

A whisper in her ear. “Where will you take her?” Acknowledgement, quiet as it was powerful, of Hege being her last link of family in this darkened world.

A voice that wasn’t Brynhild’s own swam through her throat into the world.

“To the heart of the temple, where I shall claim her bones.”

Grinwald stepped back in surprise, the color of the air swarming with the weight of sudden realness beyond what any had ever seen in these halls. Then it was gone.

“As the Mither wills.” Grinwald’s hands shook, but Brynhild was in a nightmare all her own and beyond hearing. The singular purpose of bringing her precious cargo to safety overwhelmed all other drivers.

Everything else was a blur, as she found herself once more in that temple to time. The mirror of the throne room in its ornate Rustic murals and columns shaped into statues and depictions of rulers of the past. The Priestesses, barren flesh borne to the eyes of the Mither, let her in but barred Grinwald and the guards with tridents.

Through the haze of numb purpose she heard, “The goddess forbids all but the aggrieved this night.”

The Mither’s word was law. Brynhild walked step by step across the crystal path through time and the great Astral sea stained into the temple ground. She stopped before the immense carved statue of the Mither that dominated the room. Here her legs gave out and she collapsed to the floor clinging to the bundle.

Here beneath the four golden eyes of the creation goddess upon a great mass of fertile dirt, she wept. Wept for all that had been taken from her, every link in her familial chain cruelly snatched away by the jaws of the Undersky.

What was she without Hege?

Without Astrid?

Without her parents?

Without the care and adoration crafted into a shield against the cruelties of the world?

A dysthaumic girl, barely a young adult, in the eyes of the world. A failure of a royal guard who wasn’t there when she was needed most.

“I’ve lost everything,” Brynhild croaked out, body shaking with tears. “I failed you Hege. I should have been there. I could have gotten you out. Why did I leave? Why did I go when you told me to? Why didn’t I stay?”

Brynhild slumped, squeezing the bundle against her. She pulled the cloth away to rub the burnt and ashened flesh of the body’s cheeks. Brittle flakes disintegrated as she wept, tears streaking ash into the cloth.

The goddesses’s golden eyes stared down at her, weighing all her failures on the scales of the Astral Sea. She wept, realizing then and there what she should have realized so long ago. She loved Hege. She loved her. Deep and binding love of romantic and platonic entwining with the flesh now cold and lifeless. They were the hope for the future, the burning pyre signaling to all that a better future was coming.

“Goddess, I failed you,” she weeps to the lifeless statue.

It was all gone. Her love, broken and burnt in the flames of their people’s written knowledge.

“Why didn’t you take me too?” She looked up at the statue, looming. “I have nothing left.” She gasps for air pressing her face into the cloth, chest pressing into the dirt.

The air cracked with the thunderous rumbling of something of immense mass moving. She froze, slowly looking up, Shadows changed on the floors and walls of the temple. Lit candles and censers were buffeted by wind and then extinguished. The star-studded crystal floors around the winding path dropped into the waves of Astral Star sea. Dust, rock, and twirling galaxies danced above.

Brynhild trembled and slowly looked up. The crystal and organo-metallic green skin of the statue flushed into shifting flesh, oscillating into an infinite changing array of tentacles, claws, and writhing limbs.

A grand green hand scooped through the stars beneath the soil, lifting Brynhild and her bundle through nebulae and clouded planets into a warm and loving sky. She was frozen as the hand came to a halt, held before four auric spheres in an incomprehensible face embodying the fabric and web of creation.

“Child,” she spoke to Brynhild, voice consuming her entire existence in the rasping song of infinite worlds. “All is not as it seems.”

Brynhild stared, wide-eyed, as one of many arms shifted, pointing. At first Brynhild thought the goddess was pointing at her, and then she realized the Mither was pointing at the bundle. Brynhild looked down at the body and then back up at the monolith of writhing flesh and concept.

“Mither, please, what do you mean?”

“Deceit pollutes the air of my children. The time has come to fulfill oaths and promises to protect the future you swore in cycles past.”

“I don’t understand!” Brynhild closed her eyes, a fist smacking the soil. “What do you mean?!”

When she opened her eyes again, the temple had returned. The statue once more Inert, finger still pointing at the cloth wrapped form. The goddess was silent.

Brynhild laid the body on the ground, hands shaking as she unwound the algal-derived fabric, looking closer now.

As she was scanning the shape, she saw it.

The body did not have a certain something. A feature that Hege had not gotten rid of on that faithful night. The thought made Brynhild turn her head away in hot shame.

Confusion grasped her brain.

Then realization.

“It’s not her.” Her hands shook harder as she rose, staring down at the body. “It’s not her… but where is she?”

A stranger? A sacrifice? Some poor minister? Magister? A child easily mistaken for her?

Brynhild looked up at the Goddess statue slowly, grappling with the truth of the situation.

The light of the false sun streamed through windows as she wandered the halls of the palace, lost and aimless. She’d stood in Hege’s quarters for hours, hoping for some clue to jump out.

Some had tried to stop her in the grandiose hallways, get her to come sit somewhere, eat something. None of it penetrated the fog of confused grief.

Now she wandered without a purpose, no idea where to look, unsure of who to trust, who would know.

It was late into that morning that she was shaken from the trance.

A commotion ahead. She flattened herself into the long shadows as Skreyja and a group of guards rounded a corner, hauling Grinwald along behind them.

“What is the meaning of this?! Unhand me! I am captain of the Royal Guard, and you cannot haul me out of my quarters in this manner!”

“A captain of the Royal Guard who failed the singular most important task required of them. Oath to protect the line of Aquailian at all costs,” Skreyja’s voice dripped with contempt. “Now she is dead, and no one was there to save her. The blame falls upon you and the other Royal Guards. Where were you? Asleep in your chambers? Drunk in the palace mead hall?”

“This is outrageous!”

“It’s perfectly reasonable to hold negligence to account dear Grinwald.”

“You don’t have the authority—”

“The monarchal line is dead, and we are without executive head of state. By right as Chief Magister, change of regime and designation of a new head falls to me.”

Grinwald stared at him as they came to a stop in the hallway.

He took her chin in his slimey hand. “It is time for us all to wake up, leave the past behind and forge a new era. One where we take the fight to the demons above. Thank you for volunteering to be one of the first soldiers.”

Brynhild was abruptly slammed, memory flashing through her mind. The fire that took her parents, the after reports of accelerants in strange places in the house.

Skreyja there in the moment when she was taken away.

His lurking presence, building disagreements with Astrid. Her abrupt illness, rapid decline and changes in policies.

Aske’s sudden departure after assigning Brynhild to Hege.

The cannisters in the library. Identical to the ones used in her own home. Brynhild clenched her fist, fourtyfour years of history slamming into her stomach like a Kraken’s beam weapon.

He did this. He hurt, no, killed his fellow Sea Singers. For what? Power? Ambition? She fought with every fiber of her being not to leap out then and there. This crime could not go unmet.

“No… no it…” Grinwald’s face twisted through anguish, disbelief, dismay, and then cold rage. “It was you. You did this. It was always you. I should have known, I should have kept you under closer watch. The fires, Astrid, Aske, now her too. When did you fall? When did he corrupt you?”

Skreyja released her and stood up, wiping his hand on his robes. “You three, take her away for the transports to the outer cylinder.”

Grinwald fought tooth and nail against the guards dragging her.

“This is not over! The Mither will not forget this Skreyja! One day, the whole world will come to know what you’ve done!”

Skreyja ignored her, already moving on to the four guards that remained. Brynhild’s attention dragged back to Grinwald, tempted to leap out and free her old teacher from the grasp of these traitors. Their eyes met in the black, Grinwald’s widening.

She shook her head furiously, gills oscillating in rapid strokes. ‘Don’t throw your life away now, find a way out and get help.’ The unspoken message passed between them.

Then she was gone.

“Griss, Ledrhals, Stella, and you… whatever your name is, go deal with our loose end. Do not fail. Then find the Agrusa child. Force your way into the temple if you must.”

“So, finish off the princess and we swap the body with the simulacrum?”

“Easy work by all other comparisons.”

“Fools!” Skreyja stepped forward and slapped Griss across the face, almost knocking her to the ground. “That ‘easy work’ slew twenty-five of my best men with an Elder Mark! She is a force to be reckoned with. Kill her quickly, if she’s alive. Do not underestimate her and fail me, she will end you.” He simmered for a moment. Then he turned with a flourish of his cloak, and vanished into the halls beyond, leaving the guards looking bewildered.

All the other words blurred together as the truth smashed into Brynhild.

Hege was alive.

She knew what she needed to do, fingers tightening around Segrusa’s legendary trident.

She slipped closer in the shadows. The group of traitors turned to descend the stairs down into the depths of the dungeons for their grisly task. They were completely unaware that Brynhild of the Growing Storm crept behind them.

She was going to destroy them and there wasn’t a soul in the world who could stop her now.

[[include :scp-wiki:info:end]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:earthworm | first=false | last=false | hub=yes | previous-url=https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/where-there-is-a-flame-someone-is-bound-to-get-burned| previous-title=Where There Is A Flame Someone Is Bound to Get Burned | next-url=https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/but-just-because-it-burns-doesn’t-mean-you’re-gonna-die| next-title=But Just Because It Burns Doesn’t Mean You’re Gonna Die | hub-url=https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/seas-of-orcadia-hub| hub-title=Seas of Orcadia Hub ]] [[span style="font-family: Gwendolyn; font-size: 3rem"]]//**Make Me a Rainbow, I'll Shine Down On My Mother**//[[/span]] [[span style="color:orange"]]//I wish they would start already.//[[/span]] Astral beams of light rippled across the translucent, stained crystal panes. Each frame flushed a grand space with dancing flutters of history and mythologized scenes from past ages. Bleached white and gold organo-metallic polymers gave life to the never-ending panacea. Together, flowing across the immense and heavily packed hall. Banners of rich color combinations flutter in an artificial breeze from where they are wrapped carefully around sculpted columns. Beads of sweat were already pooling from the pores in-between her crimson scales. Brynhild’s digits trembled from where they wrapped around the trident, the other hand purposely laid flat against her thigh. The temptation to reach up and pull on the collar itched at the back of her skull. It wouldn’t take much, just enough to get some air into her uniform. [[span style="color:orange"]]//No.//[[/span]] Instead, she straightened her spine and focused. The towering columns lining the center of the room, carefully shaped and carved with the flowing embodiment of concepts made manifest, Rustics, posed as the great monarchs who came before. Each were studded with precious gemstones in the place of eyes and teeth. She wondered, for but a moment, if the magic within them would bring them to life under the right circumstances. They weren’t cognitive threads, that much she was sure of. It was a question for someone else; they moved far too fast for her to read. Arches of water pour out into waterfalls; tumbling to earth and creating cooling mist where they strike grooved channels far below. She got lost in watching the trickling rainbow reflected by the falling water, eyes tracing the path downwards to follow the channels. She was just close enough to one of the waterfalls to catch little flecks of cooling moisture every now and again but not close enough to enjoy the mists. If the line was just a little farther back, if she leaned just a little bit, she’d be in the cool spray. [[span style="color:orange"]]//Don’t think about it. Focus.//[[/span]] The channels, miniature canals, snaked in carved patterns on the floor, dancing with light and Rustics in the shape of further scenes and murals upon which the occupants of the chamber stand. She wondered what the little oscillations in the flow of the symbols felt like, or if they produced any sensation at all. The whole atmosphere brimmed with excitement threatening to flow over. It buzzed in her bones, begging her to move. [[span style="color:orange"]]//I will have to spend the entire evening in an ice flow after this.//[[/span]] She pivoted her eyes without moving her head to find something else to focus on. [[span style="color:orange"]]//Any minute now the bells will ring.//[[/span]] The frescoes, murals and carved etchings embedded in the walls changed with every glance that Brynhild gave them. This was normal, but the rapid oscillation was not. There were new marks in that maelstrom, and a part of her tingled with envy at those getting to feel them for the first time. Perhaps they were supercharged by the atmosphere and concentration of Magisters and Adepts. Or perhaps that was her wandering, itching mind that was trying to admire the depths of beauty of the room without being pulled into the [[[SCP-2381| Rustic-laced cognitive threads]]] embedded in every piece of art. A task that was proving far more difficult with every passing moment. The silk vines of history and myth were calling her name, offering her experience that she would never normally have. [[span style="color:orange"]]//Come on now. What is taking so long?//[[/span]] Officers of the academy stood at attention all around her. Around a hundred Hlérsyngva, the Sea singers, the Finnfolk, in their finest uniforms lined on either side of the algal carpets and the canals of trickling water. Here she was in the middle of them all, Brynhild of the Growing Storm, trying her best to stand utterly, completely still. A task which seemed to be amusingly difficult. Her uniform itched. It was like she had a rash from the alchen vines, those promiscuous things that creeped and crawled upon the great huts, the abodes of the nomads erected upon the backs of greater-mudcrab’s in the [[[SCP-4700 | outer cylinders]]]. The itching was made all the worse by the sweat causing fabric to cling to scaley skin. [[span style="color:orange"]]//If I move, I'll get the tongue lashing of my life. If I get lost in a cognitive thread I might move. If they don’t start soon, I might melt. I could have gone into a path that didn’t require self-torture, but noooo.//[[/span]] As if for emphasis, Grinwald walked up and down both lines of officers. There was no one in the world Brynhild respected more. ----- [[span style="font-family: Gwendolyn; font-size: 3rem"]]//**I'll Tell You My Sins And You Can Sharpen Your Knife**//[[/span]] A thread of magic snagged against the wandering thought spooling out into memory. Colored pencils etched into the pages of a sketchpad, filling in the frame of a warmly lit equipment room. It smelled of metal, oil, and copious amounts of sweat. You stood there nervously, a tiny thing in the shadow of the black-scaled woman. Her gills lay flat to you and her lips were curled down. The way she stood, with legs held slightly apart in a powerful stance, and the appraising look gleaming in her eyes told the story of her life. A hard Finnwoman, no-nonsense, holding your fate in her hands. “So, you’re the Agrusa child?” she asked, looking you over yet again with pursed lips. Too afraid to mess up the words, you simply nodded. You wished your legs and hands would stop trembling. “Do you have a name?” “B-b-brynhild, ma’am.” You winced at your stammering voice. She sighed, gills pulsing once, as if you were a tremendous inconvenience. “I don’t suppose you’ve had //any// training before you got here?” She turned away from you to an equipment rack. Your heart sank; she was going to throw you out. “A little… but I’m only eleven.” Wood and metal shifted. You looked up, just in time for a blur of brown to flick through the air. It was reflex really. Instinct that set your path in stone. Before you knew what was happening, you had snatched the wooden frame of a practice trident from the air. Twirled it once and set the butt against the stone. You stood there, staring at the practice weapon, then your hands, dumbfounded, and then looked up at Grinwald. Her arms were crossed over her chest and there was a smile plastered across her lips. Her gills were fluttering. “Better than most and you have the instincts.” The smile vanished into an intense, narrow-eyed gaze. “But talent won’t carry you alone. Life in the mud and sand requires discipline, patience, sweat, blood. Tell me now, no lies, is this what you want?” Your spine stiffened, eyes filling with flame. “Yes. I want to live up to my name.” She nodded once. “Then we start now.” ---- [[span style="font-family: Gwendolyn; font-size: 3rem"]]//**I Will Find My Way, If I Can Be Strong**//[[/span]] The colored lines and pages faded away as Brynhild returned to the moment. Right as Grinwald was about to walk past. The older Finnwoman’s lips were puckered so tight you could have balanced a quill perfectly atop them. A shift of the hips, closing her feet too much, rippling her gills, shifting her head, it wouldn’t take much to set the old soldier off. Despite the discomfort grinding against Brynhild’s red, scaly skin, the twitch of webbing in her fingers, toes, and the flutter of her gills, she was excited. Infernos burned a vicious dance in her eyes. The rapid beat of her heart gave it away beneath all the distant gazes; thankfully no one could hear just how fast it hammered. There were so many eyes and expectations on her. She shifted her eyes up to the stain-glass pane of Agrusa, her many-great grandmother. The threads wormed deep into her mind, snagging perception. A thousand images flaring against the threads of time and history. Grasping the calloused hand of the gold-scaled [[[The Seas of Orcadia Part 1 How I met Your Mither | Triemedes]]], the Unifier and giant upon whose shoulders they all stood. Dances upon boat and distant ancient shores, -- salt burning in her nostrils from the sea. She was teaching the one who would save us all. The great sweeping storms of the scarlet desert where heat burned against her neck and dried out scales. The frigid depths of black in the bay where the great serpent of knowing gnashed at their heels. The wind blew against her hair, roars of a Kraken’s engine filling the sky. She stood upon the prow of the great, shimmering thaumic machine as it barreled through the writhing storm. Barometric pressure smeared heavily against her skin.  Five terrible arms cleaved through cloud and rain, memory evaporating in its antimemetic conceptual wake. She roared, Krakens streaming towards annihilation. On the shores of the Southern Basin, she bought enough time. In her fading moments, conceptual ideal eroding in the Odr’s wake, she basked in the coming glory of legacy. Then it came. The Astral Fire of Finnfelheim smeared the sky and struck the Starfish into the depths of its writhing prison. The threads faded away as Brynhild returned to the moment. This is who she was. She was the last in the line of Agrusa. A twinge of tight longing crawled up her spine before being banished as she focused on the moments that led her here. Her eyes drifted to another panel, a great coral spire shining in the brilliant light of the afternoon [[[SCP-3703 | singularity]]]. A place that existed now in naught but stories. The threads wrapped around her mind once again. She was shouting, magic pouring off her numbed fingers as she streaked through the freezing sky on a sicklemoon hammerhead. Magic she’d never known, worming beneath every inch of flesh. It ached, carving a hollow cavern in her belly. She rode, dipped, dove, and weaved through a fog heavy sky – droplets of water shattering against her scaley skin like needles. The Northern White Wyvern roared in her ears, the blast of her singularity driven thaumic beams smashing holes in its fibrous membranes. Then she was riding great winged beasts through the highland lochs and fjords of the northern realms, yipping and hollering with wind blowing through her wild crimson hair. Trekking strange mountains far to the west with a woman of soft golden character and stunning blue eyes. Laying in bundles of twigs and bush gazing upon hatching eggs producing birds wrapped in thunder. Gleaming metal gates framing proud, glimmering walls that towered like sheer cliffs above the Mediterranean. Behind the walls scaling up off into the horizon, a sprawling city of crystalline metal stretched as far to her left and right as she could see. The sky above was filled with the streaking shapes of hundreds of [[[SCP-3706 | sundfljúgavagns]]][[footnote]] Vehicles of the sky and sea.[[/footnote]]. Far away standing proudly defiant on the horizon, a tower, glimmering with light and Magistry. Then it all burned in a ferocious firestorm of swirling smoke and falling metal. The heat it radiated near-blasting against her face Fraying and dissolving beneath the threads of fate. Brynhild crashed back to reality, many other names and stories flashing through memory burning through the panes. She had seen these moments countless times and focused now on the emotional heights instead of the details. Though some, like the grandiose scope of Finnfelheim, dizzied her even now. These were monuments to the blood that ran through her veins. She had stood here beneath their grandeur when she was but a small child, staring and losing herself in the threads of a past that was so close and yet so very far away. She understood, in theory, how they worked. It was a signature component of her people’s artistic traditions. Cognitive threads carried through the millions of tiny Rustics embedded in every pane, brush stroke, ink line and chiseled carving of stone, metal and crystal. Of course, it largely depended on the artist, but memory, stories, and emotional evocation were the point. For the brief seconds and minutes when she was swept away in their conceptual threads, she could live alongside them. Feel the magistry sinking deep into her bones, feel it all around her in the moments her ancestors lived through.   In those spaces she felt like she belonged. And now, as they almost always did when she emerged, their deeds and glory sat heavy upon her shoulders, threatening to crush her beneath their expectations. She tightened her grip on her many great aunt’s trident, scales and webbing pressing into the smoothly polished organo-metallic alloy. She stood in the shadows of their deeds determined to live up to their reputation. But there was a problem -- well, multiple really. But there was one that stood out above the rest and weighed heavily upon her. She was near Astrally dead. ----- [[span style="font-family: Gwendolyn; font-size: 3rem"]]//**Must Be Homesick For The Real**//[[/span]] The pencils shift across the page, carrying you through those initial days of training. The hard days in the sand and mud, sweating. Bruised and battered. Grinwald’d knock you down, tell you to get up, and do it again. Again, and again until you learned, until you rolled out of reach and turned it back against her. Each step conquered earned a “good job”. Then she shifted approach and did it all over again. Training stopped being about single moves, became a dance of technique and drills as you grew. When you were caught out of line, forgot to clean up the practice yard, or missed practice, you’d scrub the stone and crystal floors of the equipment room until they shined. No excuses. You had a schedule: Wake, mischief, eat, mischief, learn, mischief, practice, mischief, eat, mischief, academics, clean, eat, bathe, sleep and surprise, //more mischief//. When you finally beat her for the first time in a spar, you got a pat on the back, and the next day off. She was hard, but fair. More than that. She listened. She fought for you when no adult would. She caught you once breaking down in the equipment room on the anniversary of //that// night. You were sat cross-legged on the stone, wiping your eyes and sniffling when she walked in. For a moment it seemed she was about to scream and yell. But she didn’t. She sat on the ground, didn’t touch you. “What is it?” she asked, in the softest tone she’d ever used. She listened, as you cried and spat it all out. She didn’t utter a word, just sat there with a faraway look haunting her eyes. And next year when that black day rolled around again? You showed up in the barracks, she took one look at you and said the words you’ll never forget. “Go home. No lessons today.” It wasn’t pity in her eyes. It was something you wouldn’t understand until you were much older. Understanding. You tried to ask why, but she just locked the door and walked off clutching a golden locket suspended from chain around her neck. It wouldn’t be until much later that you’d see the little dark scaled spawnling's Rustic painting suspended inside. Slick oil pigment moved along the confines of a dry canvas, pressed by a narrow brush along pre-marked lines as the palace training yard smears into definition. Grinwald's imperious shadow arcs over you in the light of the singularity's afternoon adjustments. The metallic chill of the trident's heft seeped into your small fingers; a blunted child's toy to the giant that is your opponent. A short Finnman stood between the two of you, preparing the field for your coming struggle. The drop of a rock could have shattered the tension resting upon the oil film pulsing around you. Seated on the spartan steps and benches are, perhaps, two hundred or more observers, come to watch the last of your line, you. The blood of champions burned in your veins and that made all the difference. Their expectations pressed the meniscus of the film down, crushing against your shoulders. None were heavier than the princess’s; seated on the stairs. She was a centerpiece all her own in her flowing twines and ribbon robes of fine silk, auric scales and hair gleaming in the singularity’s light. Your eyes traced to the crowd. Her father, the King of all the Hlérsyngva, sat among the Magisters and Ministers. His wife, Queen Astrid, obscured by the reflection of the bright light of the singularity upon her golden scales, sat beside him, soft smile invisible to you in this moment. But it was there, you were sure. “Begin.” The Finnman said, snapping you back into the moment. You circled each other in measured steps, trying to keep up with every gigantic step she takes. You sought the slightest opening in Grinwald’s impenetrable defense. Scanned the twitch of her muscles. Motion, a feint designed to bait you into striking. A year ago, it worked, and many times since, but not today. No, the opening came in the aftermath. You didn’t take the bait, she shifted, and you sprang your trap. You burst right, drew the reactive swing. The blunted tips of the training trident flicked past as you stutter stepped to her left. All the while the trident twirled in one hand like a baton. One, two, three you hit her leg and hips with the twirling metal. Enough to bruise, but not much more. You weren’t strong enough yet to fracture. You wouldn’t have even if you were. Grinwald grunted in surprise, pivoting to force you away, but you were behind her now, jabbing the butt of your trident into her spine. She stumbled forward with another grunt. You spun on one heel, rebounding trident arm thrusting in a direct dash to follow through. “Iss,” hissed from Grinwald’s lips, the Rustic burning in the air in the milliseconds before you reached her. Perhaps there was a smile there, however briefly. Your trident smacked into the film of ice formed between you and her, biting cold surging through the metal and stinging your fingers hard. All those lessons squirmed back in, as you reached for threads of your own. You tried to yank your trident back with one hand while drawing the symbol in the air. All that theory, the  practiced motions to counter opponent’s magistry… and nothing came. Tiny embers trickled off your fingers, ineffectual. Grinwald’s trident knocked yours aside, snapping it out of your hands as the ice shattered into cold fragmented panes. Metal collided with your chin in a retaliatory spin. You were knocked into the air, electrostatic shocks from another spell squirming through nerve and muscle. Landed with a hard thud and rolled in the sand. Flesh twitched beyond control for far too long. Stunned confusion twisted in your mind before flaring into a flame of determination in  an abdomen that was defiant of these events. You weren’t done; you refused to give up at one surprising blow and misfire. Iron taste of blood polluted your tongue. You rolled, dodging the hammering butt of the trident seeking to knock you out. Teeth clenched, you tried to rise, summoning another thread to try and pull your trident back into your hands, but it only wiggled ineffectually across the yard. You stared at it, then down at your fingers, at the abject failure of your attempts. Panic crept into your small chest, tight with icey fear as you looked up. The expression rippling across King Aske’s gills and face dropped a pit into your stomach. It was over. Grinwald’s trident leveled, inches from your throat. “Match,” she barked tersely. Disappointment burned in her dark eyes; gills closed to you. You couldn’t meet her gaze, looked down at your feet as she pulled you up. Hot shame crawled up the back of your neck and through your flattening gills. The crowd’s murmurs and affectations faded as the light changed in the sky, drawn forth by broader brushes. You hadn’t moved a muscle for an hour, staring straight down. Everyone was gone. So was your confidence and any idle hopes of having lived up to your family name. You stared absently at your fingers. All that training, Grinwald’s lessons, for nothing. Of course, they’d lose interest the moment you couldn’t do the most basic expectation of your people’s world, magic. Dark bruises lay upon your chin, chest, and legs from Grinwald’s blows. They ached and throbbed as you limped absently through the palace halls. Too ashamed to go see the healers. They’re Marks of what shame you’ve brought upon your hallowed house. Upon the man and woman who took you in for your worth and potential. How many skittering messenger and servant constructs skittered past you in your stupor? How many stopped in your path, thaumo-mechanical servos whirring as their crystal lenses dilated to adjust for your presence? Something compelled you to stop outside the cracked door of Grinwald’s office, posted next to the King’s personal quarters. A deep rattling urge to apologize, for the failure that you embodied, swirled in your belly like a maelstrom.  Raising a webbed hand to knock, you stopped hearing the voices within. Ministers, Grinwald, the King, and the Queen. “We ran the evaluations during the spar, Majesties; the outcome is unimpeachable.” “Surely it must be a mistake.” His majesty’s normally upbeat tone sat grimly in your stomach as you leaned against the wall next to the door. Felt all the vibrations of the palace, of their voices filter into your skull. Pressed your hot and swollen face against the cool crystal and stone. “It’s not. She tried to draw on fire and recall basic concepts in and of themselves. Sparks, embers, and the twitching of metal but nothing more. I fear it’s a worst-case scenario.” It’s the voice of a young Magister, Skreyja. A man who always looked at you as if you were far beneath him. His abject distaste for your very presence was never noticed by anyone else, and he shared that gaze for the Princess. Hot shame wormed in the terse flattening of your gills and clenched teeth. “Not for lack of trying, she was able to do //something//. I’m confident with a little more training…” Grinwald’s voice. “Training won’t fix the root problem. Her Astral density is the lowest I’ve ever seen, nearly zero.” A different magister now. “She can’t be dysthaumic. She’s of Agrusa’s line, noble magister-warriors.” The King’s voice again. “Denying it will not unmake the truth, Majesty.” A deep sigh through the doors. “This will devastate her.” “There are ways around such things, no? She is my second daughter and I am loathe to abandon her dreams so easily.” Astrid’s voice, soft and harmonious in your ears. “Your ward of the state, Majesty,” Skreyja’s corrected. “Adoption does not make her of royal blood or your daughter by the accords of unification.” A sudden, intense burst of silence filled the interior space, permeating out and reaching you.  The words echoed in your mind, an indirect punch to the gut. “If Majesty cares for her to such a degree,” the other Minister, not Skreyja, began gently and far more diplomatically, “then it would be wise to recommend a different path for her life. Without Magistry she will be vulnerable, weak and easily laid low by a skilled warrior who //can//. It’s a risk in the defense force or even the Royal guards. Not to mention this sign of disfavor from the Mither.” You hung your head, biting back the tears. “Nonsense,” Grinwald barked tersely. “In the yesteryears of our ancestors, your words would be true, but there are approaches to compensate as Queen Astrid suggested. She is more physically skilled at her age than any recruit we’ve had in a lifetime of remembrance. Strong, and fast. With the right tools, she would have had me today. She deserves, on merit alone, to see her ambitions unfold.” “The compensation will never be enough Grinwald, you know this. Think of the cost if something were to happen? You’d risk the last in the line of Agrusa, prevent the preservation of the bloodline, for a single child’s ambitions and feelings against the will of the Mither and needs of the Work?” “If the bloodline is dry of access to the Rustic weave, perhaps it’s time to consider deemphasizing the despotism of our so-called ‘sacred bloodlines’ for the good of all. A slot filled with no merit is nothing but nepotism manifested,” Skreyja purred. “Must you speak about her like she’s farmstock?” Astrid snapped. “Mither’s harvest //she’s a spawnling!//” “A spawnling with a limited future and value to the greater work we all seek,” he rebuffed. “She is far more than that and you faen well know it Skreyja. I will not stand by and let you smash a spawnling’s dreams beneath whatever ambitions you’re puckering and plucking from your carrion filled--” Grinwald snarled. “Enough!” Aske’s staff rang with a metallic echo in your ears, cutting further debate off. You didn’t hear the rest, already limping towards your quarters with barely suppressed despair dripping from your eyes. As soon as the door shut, you collapsed onto the silken algal sheets of the bed. Silent sobs racked your body, wallowing at just how abjectly broken you were. To be without the ability to do magistry? A critical component of your people’s lives. Used to access everything from transport, building and facility access, even direction of the vehicles you so desperately wanted to command. You were dead to the Mither’s gifts and voices. She had rejected you, left you as nothing more than an incubator to carry the next generation of your bloodline. So deep in wallowing were you, you heard neither the knock, nor the opening of the door and subsequent footsteps. A webbed hand pressed gently into your back, startling you from the spiral to look up. Through blurry tears, you saw the Princess looking down at you. She had placed a stack of books upon the sea-oak end-table. Her gills pulsed three long times, surveying your bruises. “You’re hurt still, why didn’t you go to the healers?” Her voice was gentle, as if fully cognizant that you could break at any moment. “I wanted to be alone.” The response poured so fast from your lips that you flinched at the harshness of wishing her away conveyed in your tone. Ever the curious and yet socially oblivious creature, Hege simply ignored you. “Sit up, so I can heal you.” The command was blunt, and you obeyed without really thinking about it. The soothing warmth of healing Rustics wormed into your flesh with more than a bit discomfort. That was of course a mark that Hege was not an experienced healer. You watched, feeling all the worse as you were reminded by burst blood vessels mending beneath the skin of what you could not do. “Now, tell me, why you are shedding such copious tears? I did not take you for one to weep after a defeat?” [[span style="color:orange"]]//Of course she wouldn’t know. She’s blessed with more magistry in her pinky than I have in my entire body.//[[/span]] you thought bitterly as the words stung with potential implications laden behind them. But then you banished them, remembering that she was simply matter of fact, something you’d learned very quickly after you first met. No ulterior intent, a refreshing characteristic compared to even Grinwald’s games of careful words. You lived in a political world of disagreements between officials over how best to accomplish the purpose and drive of the Mither’s ever present will.
