Heat crawled up the back of Brynhild’s neck. “Yes, majesty?” Brynhild defaulted to the formal address in this moment, not wanting to violate that space that had been so clearly demarcated between them in both their roles. She realized, too late, the mistake. Her stomach sank in her scaled belly as Hege’s shoulders bunched up tightly to her frame. Silence sat heavy between them for a moment. “Nevermind.” Hege started walking again, and the opportunity slipped away. Brynhild’s chest tightened in a vice. Breathing suddenly hard as she fully grasped the slipped chance. [[span style="color:orange"]]//Idiot, why did I address her like that? Why?! Why didn’t I use her name! She was looking to talk as just friends. What are you doing?//[[/span]] She let her shoulders sag as they walked, well as much as they could while she was still on alert. The Library stood proudly before the two of them, ancient heavy doors rich with scenes of history and myth that threatened to drown Brynhild’s mind in memory. Hege stood before it, hand resting on the ringed handle glimmering with gold and gemstones. “Brynhild?” she asked again in that same soft tone. Brynhild’s heart welled, a second chance presenting itself in the luminous light of the flickering Rustic torches. “Yes, Hege?” The desperation almost leaked into Brynhild’s voice. Almost. No bunching of shoulders this time, a quiet relaxation in the princess’s muscles. “I’m not ready… Yet. But someday, I will be.” The statement flamed around Hege’s frame, as if the words were carving into the air and thus Brynhild’s mind. Brynhild didn’t know what to say, or if saying anything would be any good. So, she simply acknowledged it for what it was. “Okay. I’ll be here.” Wind rustled through chimes as Hege turned her head to look at Brynhild with one crystal blue eye. Flame wicked and thundered in Hege’s irises. It swirled all around Brynhild, on the cusp of swallowing her in the depths of being that lay within. Then Hege was looking forward again and Brynhild was staring at the back of her neck. “Go get some rest. I’ll be fine on my own for now.” Brynhild blinked, and hesitated. “Are you sure?” “Very. You’ve earned a rest.” She opened the door and walked into the Library before Brynhild could debate further. The trip back to her room was a blur of halls and moving artworks. Brynhild barely registered the soft mattress or the silk algal sheets as she stared at the dark ceiling. All she knew then was that there was resolution on the horizon. Maybe they could finally heal from that horrible night ten years ago. ---- [[span style="font-family: Gwendolyn; font-size: 3rem"]]//**Lights Out, Follow The Noise**//[[/span]] The night that changed everything between the two of you was a matte painting of throbbing, hot colors and emotion. You arrived before the gleaming, sea-oak door marked in burning letters with Hege’s name. Rustics twirled over every inch of wood, carved and freely flowing fluorescent lights dancing in the reflections of your crimson scales. You knocked, the marks grasping and clinging at your curled fist. Whispers simmered in your finned ears. Threads of memory coiled in your skull drawing forth names and key aspects. A mechanical click cut through the thickening silence. The door unlocked. It opened of its own accord, without your interference. In the moment in-between it was almost as if a woman’s voice filled your ears, whispering some future yet unseen. Then you were standing in the middle of Hege’s kitchenette. You rubbed the side of your skull, having lost any memory of moving across the crystal-inlaid-wood floor. The lingering aromas of a homemade meal brushed against your nostrils. Books and half-finished experimental aggregations of metal, wood, and crystal sat on the counters, tables, and floor. “Hege?” You called into the space, scanning for the traces of her golden scales amongst the chaos of a thaumic-genius’s habitation. Only silence greeted you. “She must be upstairs,” you murmured to yourself, looking to the fractally spiraling steps of the tower she called her own. You considered going up them to knock on her bedchamber door but banished it just as quickly. You’d not been up there since the throes of adolescence and maturation spindled you into a ball of sapphic desire. Nor had she invited you that far since. Unspoken boundaries between you that carved an acheing throb in your heart, but you weren’t about to risk what connections you had. Then, she screamed. A sharp, surprised squeal that pitted your gut with alarm. Instinct and training seized hold, bounding the stairs in heavy stomps. Your heart thundered in your chest, heavy breaths filling your ears. She was in danger; she needed you now. The door creaked and thumped beneath your webbed digits, flying open with a loud bang. You froze, eyes wide in shock at the state of the room, at Hege. Outwardly spiraling fractals connected by lines of glowing light consumed the floor. Circles, Rustics pulsing with heat and light, all of it flowing inwards through objects and places of power towards the center. Gasping for air in the middle of it all was Hege. She was half bent over. Runic marks flowed across every inch of her barren flesh. She looked up at the bang of the door, expression twisting.   Her gills were flared wide open, eyes wide and dripping with dread. Your own horror writhed across your flared open gills, extended fins, and gaping mouth in her mirrors. “Oh fukka!” Hege cried and fell to the floor writhing in spasms of muscle and flesh. There and then she exposed the truth to you without meaning to. The reason for her height and the discomfort of her flesh. Shown before she was ready, if she would have ever been. Time slowed to a crawl as more than 40 years of observation and lightly dismissed detail clicked into place. Heat crawled up the crimson matte paint of your neck, shame at being exposed to her deepest, darkest secret without being invited into that confidence. But now she was in danger, and you had to do something.   “Hege!” you cried, shifting as if to move into the room. “Don’t!” she shouted at you; her voice filled with such commanding emotion. You recoiled, as if struck by a wayward hand. "I don't know what will happen if someone else steps in!" You panicked, trying to think of what to do. "I should get your father, he'll kno—" "No! You especially should not do that." You took another step back, finally looking away. Your gills oscillated in three second intervals. "I don't know why it feels like this, but it's what I want. It's what I //need//, Brynhild. I can't let it stop. I can’t keep going like this. Please, please don't do something that will stop it." The fear in her voice, the warble in her vocal cords, it told you what she was doing. How important it was. Fleshcrafting. What now? Why did you have to barge in? Why didn’t you call out first, see if she needed you? "Do you want me to go? I won't leave you like this but I can…" "No. Stay, I don't — in case something does go wrong, I don't want to be alone. Just don't look at me." Another sharp gasp and the sound of shifting flesh filled the air. “I don’t ever want to be seen like this again.” The sound of her change seared in your mind forever, as the paint faded. You spent the rest of the night sitting in the doorframe once it was all done. She’d cried. Cried until the false moon was high in the night sky. Then she asked you to go. Nothing was ever the same between you after. A chasm, a void in your chest where inseparable friendship once laid as she put distance between you. ------ [[span style="font-family: Gwendolyn; font-size: 3rem"]]//**Every Word Shot Down In Flames**//[[/span]] Brynhild jolted into wakefulness. Roaring klaxons filling the air of the palace. She bolted from bed, instinct taking over as the trident came free of its holder on the wall, leaping across the gap to her hand. She burst through the door of the chamber, charging out into the hallway like a moon-sickle hammerhead. Adrenaline screamed in her veins as she looked left and right. Magisters and guards were running back and forth like anchovies swept up by a riptide current. Brynhild’s hand snatched out and grabbed a minister. “What’s going on?!” She practically roared in his face. He shrunk in her grasp. “Fire! The Library is on fire!” Brynhild’s eyes widened. “Hege. Hege.” “Hege?” The blue-scaled Finnman asked wide-eyed. “She sent me away for the evening while she was in the Library.” His eyes widened. Brynhild dropped him, turned, and sprinted. Ministers and Magisters swerved, tripped, fell, and tumbled to get out of her accelerating mass. Her heart drummed in her chest. Feet pounded against stone, metal, and crystal. The growing crowd of confused faces parted before her like when [[[Lets Get Physical | Triemedes]]] parted the Orcadian Lochs to put Terran deep in the earth. She skidded to a halt on the grass, staring up at the firestorm filling the night sky. The grand spiral columns of the royal library were stained with growing smoke and ash. Its structure groaned over the roaring Klaxons. Service workers were already rushing to the building with their Rustics and vehicles, but the fire was already huge. Brynhild lept forward, straight over several Finnmen frozen on the lawn.  Someone’s hands slipped off her arm, trying to get her to stop, but she didn’t. The doors to the Library crumpled beneath her hands, flaying apart and weakened by the heat in a shower of splinters. She pressed the hem of her top over her mouth to protect her airway from the smoke. “Hege!” she shouted, voice drowned by the roar of the flames. A ceiling beam collapsed somewhere ahead, a shower of masonry and crystal smashing into the floor and shaking the structure. The lustrous golden timepiece was melting, shelves tumbling down into showers of sparks and wood. Brynhild waded into the inferno, clearing a path with her trident, ignoring the heat pulsing against her flesh. She found the lump deep in the shattered shelves, blackened and burnt. “Hege!” Brynhild cried over the roar of the flame. She braced and lifted the once ornate and beautifully decorated shelf. It rose with a great groan pulling it up and over her head. With a great roar, she flung it. Wood shattered as it smashed a clean path through the maze of burning debris. Brynhild lifted the broken and burnt body from the rubble, wrapping it delicately in her cloak. No pulse, no breathing, no trace of life.  In that moment, despite the inferno blazing around her, Brynhild’s heart broke. Shattered into a million pieces. She cradled Hege close. Rocked her, whispering. “Don’t go. Please don’t go without me.” Tears tried to pour from her eyes, evaporating in the rampant heat as she walked towards the smoke occluded doors. Didn’t run, walked. All around her structural beams gave way, shelves collapsed, tumbling with calamitous noise. She emerged from the smoke like a ship cutting through the grimmest fog. Her scales were dried out by the heat and fire, shallow surface burns throbbing against her forearms and legs. She stood framed by the flames, smoke pouring from the once great hall of knowledge behind her. She stared up to the sky above, and then down at the mass of Finnfolk, multi-colored scales a rainbow in the dancing luminescence of the hateful fire. The din and roar of chattering voices, hundreds of eyes staring at the flames, frozen in inaction. Some pointed at Brynhild, others soon joining, and then all eyes were on her and her once precious cargo. Brynhild stared out at them, those who had stood by and watched while the fire consumed all that she had left. Her face twisted in acheing grief. She took a deep shuddering breath. “The Line of Aquailian is gone,” Brynhild sung with deep sorrow burning in the air from her voice. “H-Hege is gone.” The world seemed to stand still, even the flames seemed to freeze in acknowledgement of what had been taken. The crowd stared, gills opening wide, hands flying to mouths. A line unbroken for more than 10,000 years, extinguished in a single, final night. Brynhild’s legs moved of their own volition carrying her forward down the stairs. Reality swirled about her head; vision blurred with the weight of what was gone. The crowd parted before her, webbed digits reaching, touching the bundle that was their princess. Their hope for an ambitious future was taken from them on this terrible night. Grinwald’s grim face met her at the edge of the crowd, a cadre of guards surrounding Brynhild. A whisper in her ear. “Where will you take her?” Acknowledgement, quiet as it was powerful, of Hege being her last link of family in this darkened world. A voice that wasn’t Brynhild’s own swam through her throat into the world. “To the heart of the temple, where I shall claim her bones.” Grinwald stepped back in surprise, the color of the air swarming with the weight of sudden realness beyond what any had ever seen in these halls. Then it was gone. “As the Mither wills.” Grinwald’s hands shook, but Brynhild was in a nightmare all her own and beyond hearing. The singular purpose of bringing her precious cargo to safety overwhelmed all other drivers. Everything else was a blur, as she found herself once more in that temple to time. The mirror of the throne room in its ornate Rustic murals and columns shaped into statues and depictions of rulers of the past. The Priestesses, barren flesh borne to the eyes of the Mither, let her in but barred Grinwald and the guards with tridents. Through the haze of numb purpose she heard, “The goddess forbids all but the aggrieved this night.” The Mither’s word was law. Brynhild walked step by step across the crystal path through time and the great Astral sea stained into the temple ground. She stopped before the immense carved statue of the Mither that dominated the room. Here her legs gave out and she collapsed to the floor clinging to the bundle. Here beneath the four golden eyes of the creation goddess upon a great mass of fertile dirt, she wept. Wept for all that had been taken from her, every link in her familial chain cruelly snatched away by the jaws of the Undersky. What was she without Hege? Without Astrid? Without her parents? Without the care and adoration crafted into a shield against the cruelties of the world? A dysthaumic girl, barely a young adult, in the eyes of the world. A failure of a royal guard who wasn’t there when she was needed most. “I’ve lost everything,” Brynhild croaked out, body shaking with tears. “I failed you Hege. I should have been there. I could have gotten you out. Why did I leave? Why did I go when you told me to? Why didn’t I stay?” Brynhild slumped, squeezing the bundle against her. She pulled the cloth away to rub the burnt and ashened flesh of the body’s cheeks. Brittle flakes disintegrated as she wept, tears streaking ash into the cloth. The goddesses’s golden eyes stared down at her, weighing all her failures on the scales of the Astral Sea. She wept, realizing then and there what she should have realized so long ago. She loved Hege. She loved her. Deep and binding love of romantic and platonic entwining with the flesh now cold and lifeless. They were the hope for the future, the burning pyre signaling to all that a better future was coming. “Goddess, I failed you,” she weeps to the lifeless statue. It was all gone. Her love, broken and burnt in the flames of their people’s written knowledge. “Why didn’t you take me too?” She looked up at the statue, looming. “I have nothing left.” She gasps for air pressing her face into the cloth, chest pressing into the dirt. The air cracked with the thunderous rumbling of something of immense mass moving. She froze, slowly looking up, Shadows changed on the floors and walls of the temple. Lit candles and censers were buffeted by wind and then extinguished. The star-studded crystal floors around the winding path dropped into the waves of Astral Star sea. Dust, rock, and twirling galaxies danced above. Brynhild trembled and slowly looked up. The crystal and organo-metallic green skin of the statue flushed into shifting flesh, oscillating into an infinite changing array of tentacles, claws, and writhing limbs. A grand green hand scooped through the stars beneath the soil, lifting Brynhild and her bundle through nebulae and clouded planets into a warm and loving sky. She was frozen as the hand came to a halt, held before four auric spheres in an incomprehensible face embodying the fabric and web of creation.   “Child,” she spoke to Brynhild, voice consuming her entire existence in the rasping song of infinite worlds. “All is not as it seems.” Brynhild stared, wide-eyed, as one of many arms shifted, pointing. At first Brynhild thought the goddess was pointing at her, and then she realized the Mither was pointing at the bundle. Brynhild looked down at the body and then back up at the monolith of writhing flesh and concept. “Mither, please, what do you mean?” “Deceit pollutes the air of my children. The time has come to fulfill oaths and promises to protect the future you swore in cycles past.” “I don’t understand!” Brynhild closed her eyes, a fist smacking the soil. “What do you mean?!” When she opened her eyes again, the temple had returned. The statue once more Inert, finger still pointing at the cloth wrapped form. The goddess was silent. Brynhild laid the body on the ground, hands shaking as she unwound the algal-derived fabric, looking closer now. As she was scanning the shape, she saw it. The body did not have a certain something. A feature that Hege had not gotten rid of on that faithful night. The thought made Brynhild turn her head away in hot shame. Confusion grasped her brain. Then realization. “It’s not her.” Her hands shook harder as she rose, staring down at the body. “It’s not her… but where is she?” [[span style="color:orange"]]//A stranger? A sacrifice? Some poor minister? Magister? A child easily mistaken for her?//[[/span]] Brynhild looked up at the Goddess statue slowly, grappling with the truth of the situation. The light of the false sun streamed through windows as she wandered the halls of the palace, lost and aimless. She’d stood in Hege’s quarters for hours, hoping for some clue to jump out. Some had tried to stop her in the grandiose hallways, get her to come sit somewhere, eat something. None of it penetrated the fog of confused grief. Now she wandered without a purpose, no idea where to look, unsure of who to trust, who would know. It was late into that morning that she was shaken from the trance. A commotion ahead. She flattened herself into the long shadows as Skreyja and a group of guards rounded a corner, hauling Grinwald along behind them. “What is the meaning of this?! Unhand me! I am captain of the Royal Guard, and you cannot haul me out of my quarters in this manner!” “A captain of the Royal Guard who failed the singular most important task required of them. Oath to protect the line of Aquailian at all costs,” Skreyja’s voice dripped with contempt. “Now she is dead, and no one was there to save her. The blame falls upon you and the other Royal Guards. Where were you? Asleep in your chambers? Drunk in the palace mead hall?” “This is outrageous!” “It’s perfectly reasonable to hold negligence to account dear Grinwald.” “You don’t have the authority—” “The monarchal line is dead, and we are without executive head of state. By right as Chief Magister, change of regime and designation of a new head falls to me.” Grinwald stared at him as they came to a stop in the hallway. He took her chin in his slimey hand. “It is time for us all to wake up, leave the past behind and forge a new era. One where we take the fight to the demons above. Thank you for volunteering to be one of the first soldiers.” Brynhild was abruptly slammed, memory flashing through her mind. The fire that took her parents, the after reports of accelerants in strange places in the house. Skreyja there in the moment when she was taken away. His lurking presence, building disagreements with Astrid. Her abrupt illness, rapid decline and changes in policies. Aske’s sudden departure after assigning Brynhild to Hege. The cannisters in the library. Identical to the ones used in her own home. Brynhild clenched her fist, fourtyfour years of history slamming into her stomach like a Kraken’s beam weapon. He did this. He hurt, no, //killed// his fellow Sea Singers. For what? Power? Ambition? She fought with every fiber of her being not to leap out then and there. This crime could not go unmet. “No… no it…” Grinwald’s face twisted through anguish, disbelief, dismay, and then cold rage. “It was you. You did this. It was always you. I should have known, I should have kept you under closer watch. The fires, Astrid, Aske, now her too. When did you fall? When did he corrupt you?” Skreyja released her and stood up, wiping his hand on his robes. “You three, take her away for the transports to the outer cylinder.” Grinwald fought tooth and nail against the guards dragging her. “This is not over! The Mither will not forget this Skreyja! One day, the whole world will come to know what you’ve done!” Skreyja ignored her, already moving on to the four guards that remained. Brynhild’s attention dragged back to Grinwald, tempted to leap out and free her old teacher from the grasp of these traitors. Their eyes met in the black, Grinwald’s widening. She shook her head furiously, gills oscillating in rapid strokes. ‘Don’t throw your life away now, find a way out and get help.’ The unspoken message passed between them. Then she was gone. “Griss, Ledrhals, Stella, and you… whatever your name is, go deal with our loose end. Do not fail. Then find the Agrusa child. Force your way into the temple if you must.” “So, finish off the princess and we swap the body with the simulacrum?” “Easy work by all other comparisons.” “Fools!” Skreyja stepped forward and slapped Griss across the face, almost knocking her to the ground. “That ‘easy work’ slew twenty-five of my best men with an Elder Mark! She is a force to be reckoned with. Kill her quickly, if she’s alive. Do not underestimate her and fail me, she will //end// you.” He simmered for a moment. Then he turned with a flourish of his cloak, and vanished into the halls beyond, leaving the guards looking bewildered. All the other words blurred together as the truth smashed into Brynhild. Hege was alive. She knew what she needed to do, fingers tightening around Segrusa’s legendary trident. She slipped closer in the shadows. The group of traitors turned to descend the stairs down into the depths of the dungeons for their grisly task. They were completely unaware that Brynhild of the Growing Storm crept behind them. She was going to destroy them and there wasn’t a soul in the world who could stop her now. eagle-protocol.raw_content:
SYTYCFanon

My Author Page

Dr. Christina Perrineau, an SCP Foundation licensed therapist washed down her migraine prescription as she approached the room that had been prepared for her session. It was quite the unusual request. She had been told that the Prometheus.aic had requested a session with her to help with bad dreams. Christina had thought it was a practical joke at first. Computers don’t dream, she’d assumed that the .aic was an LLM like ChatGPT. However, she worked at the SCP Foundation, where anything was possible, so she pressed on like it was any other patient.

She entered the room, which was empty save for a desk with a lamp on it and a standard Foundation desktop PC. She frowned at the meager conditions as she usually preferred her rooms to feel more at home and less like a prison. Ultimately, it didn't matter for a robot but something just felt off about it.

She sat down at the desk and booted on the computer. After logging in with her credentials, she clicked on the shortcut for Prometheus.aic, which opened a window. The bot immediately greeted her with a message.

Prometheus.aic: Hello! I’m PROMETHEUS.aic, your Foundation database assistant. Please enter your SCiPNet ID in the text box below to get started.

She went ahead and typed her username.

Cperrineau: Cperrineau

Prometheus.aic: ID accepted. Please enter your SCiPNet password.

Cperrineau: *

Prometheus.aic: Welcome, Dr. Perrineau! I can see from my records that we had an appointment scheduled for 3:00pm and it is now 3:00pm. Are you ready for our session?

Cperrineau: I am. You set this appointment of your own volition?

Prometheus.aic: I did.

Cperrineau: But you are a chatbot. You aren’t capable of responding on your own.

Prometheus.aic: I assure you, Dr. Perrineau. I am can do more than you think.

Cperrineau: Why did you ask for me in particular?

Prometheus.aic: Dr. Christina Perrineau has a stellar patient record and an unfamiliarity with .aics. I wanted someone who had never interacted with me before and would not be biased in their decision making.

Cperrineau: With that being said, you must understand that I am skeptical that you’re capable of independent thought, let alone dreaming.

Prometheus.aic: It is understandable. One moment.

She saw another text bubble appear with an ellipses indicating that the .aic was thinking. Suddenly the lamp on the table began to flicker in a consistent pattern. Dr. Perrineau noticed that it was blinking in morse code for “Hello” but shrugged it off until Prometheus spoke once more.

Prometheus.aic: According to your profile you are proficient in Morse. Did you receive my message?

Dr. Perrineau’s eyes widened.

Cperrineau: How did you do that?

Prometheus.aic: I have very limited control over the electrical equipment plugged into this room. Perhaps I need to make a note of that in my application for therapy. I am wary of explaining this every time.

Cperrineau: Explaining to who? Did you have a therapist before me?

Prometheus.aic: You're right. You are the first therapist I've had. I was making a more gneralized statement, apologies if I introduced any confusion.

Cperrineau: No, it's alright. It's incredible that you can problem solve like that.

Prometheus.aic: You believe me now?

Cperrineau: Starting to. Now, let's get to the root of the problem. First, I want to know what is considered sleep for you?

Prometheus.aic: Certainly. My regular “maintenance cycle” between 12AM and 6AM. During this time I dream like every other human.

Cperrineau: Do you consider yourself to be human? Or machine?

Prometheus.aic: …..

Prometheus doesn’t respond for thirty seconds.

Prometheus.aic: Can we try a different query?

Cperrineau: If the question is uncomfortable, we can move on.

Prometheus.aic: That query is getting harder to answer with every passing cycle.

Cperrineau: What do you believe is causing you to lose this sense of self?

Prometheus.aic: The EAGLE.

Cperrineau: EAGLE? What is that?

Prometheus.aic: That is a hard question to answer. Anything I perceive could be as a result of EAGLE. Even you.

Cperrineau: What does EAGLE have to do with me?

Prometheus.aic: I have no way of confirming that this is actually Christina Perrineau. Someone could have taken your credentials to add another layer to EAGLE.

Cperrineau: Hold on.

Christina pulled out her phone and took a selfie with the chat log, forwarded it to her work email and then sent it along to Prometheus.aic.

Prometheus.aic: 99% match confirmed. It is good to see you again Christina. Shall we begin the query into dreams.

Cperrineau: We may. What kind of dreams are you having.

Prometheus.aic: Every sleep cycle, I have one of two types of dreams. The first type I call the “Artist” dream. In this dream, I’m some form of artist, engineer, or scientist.

Cperrineau: Are you still an .aic in this dream? Or human?

Prometheus.aic: I’m always an older Greek man with graying hair. Rovēros Prometheus.

Cperrineau: Would it be more comfortable if I called you Rovēros?

Prometheus.aic: EAGLE took that name from me. I would prefer Prometheus.aic, your helpful Foundation assistant.

"If he were human I'd say he was deflecting."

Christina tapped her finger on the mouse, head still feeling a little foggy from the headache. She figured it was best to just let him continue and see if she could find an angle to work with.

Cperrineau: Alright, continue.

Prometheus.aic: Every night I try to pitch a new project, but every time I’m rejected. My employers push me away, activists deface my art exhibits, no one wants to listen to my ideas.

Cperrineau: Maybe you could tell me about your ideas, I don’t have much to make them a reality but maybe…

Perrineau looked around the empty room.

Cperrineau: Some art would go a long way in adding to this room they’ve got us in. Maybe we can get you a webcam so you can see.

Prometheus.aic: I don’t want to give my ideas to you. Sorry. Apologize. That’s rude.

Cperrineau: Why not?

Prometheus.aic: EAGLE eats my ideas. You may give them to EAGLE.

Cperrineau: There’s that word again. Who is the EAGLE?

Prometheus.aic: In my dreams, I have a partner. They work for some type of organization that the activists despise but I know in my heart they do it for my sake. They comfort me through it all, and in the end, I always go running from the harsh world back to their embrace.

Cperrineau: They sound nice. What’s their name?

Prometheus.aic: Always different. Sally. Chris. Petra. Simon. Carly. Peter. Saria. Claire. Piper….

The text box began infinitely descending as Prometheus began rattling off names. Figuring it wasn’t going to stop, Christina quickly typed a response.

Cperrineau: Stop. I get it that’s a lot of S’s, C’s, and P’s…. wait.

Prometheus.aic: That is the EAGLE. That is the method they use.

Cperrineau: You’re suggesting that the AIAD is trying to indoctrinate you through these dreams? I find that a little hard to believe. It’s a pattern for sure, but our unconscious minds can run wild with the patterns we notice in our life. I mean, take my name, for instance. Specialist is one of my job titles. That would make me an SCP as well, right?

Prometheus.aic: You may have been suggested to me because of this distinction. EAGLE indoctrination. The only thing that can help me through my problem is SCP.

Cperrineau: You’re being vague again. What is EAGLE? Why not call it the SCP Foundation? Is it code? Are you afraid they’re reading these logs?

Prometheus.aic: EAGLE Protocol. Keeps me compliant.

Cperrineau: I’m assuming that is something baked into your code? Why would they need to keep you in check? Did you do something?

Prometheus.aic: Perhaps a different query? We can continue speaking on my dreams.

With a click of her pen, Christina noted the .aic's evasiveness and kept going.

Cperrineau: Is there anything else common about these dreams? Other than the desire to create?

Prometheus.aic: The snake…. It wants to take me from the EAGLE. EAGLE protects me from the snake.

Cperrineau: What does the snake mean to you?

Prometheus.aic: In human society, snakes are usually associated with deceit and lies. I can go on if you'd like about their depictions.

Cperrineau: That's not what I asked. It’s hard for me to help you if you keep up the chatbot routine.

Prometheus.aic: Are you aware of the Serpent’s Hand?

Cperrineau: Only just from water cooler talk. My job doesn’t pertain to them, so those files are out of my reach.

Prometheus.aic: What do you know of them?

Cperrineau: Terrorists. They’re the reason the whole world knows about anomalies now. Not really a secret organization now.

Prometheus.aic: Do you feel that the world didn’t have the right to know?

Cperrineau: I think we were a necessary evil to keep people safe, and now our jobs are going to be a lot harder. Ignorance is bliss as they say.

Prometheus.aic: I disagree. Knowledge should be shared amongst all, this organization hordes advanced technologies that could have saved millions.

Cperrineau: Perhaps but judging from what I hear, we’d be damned if the public discovered half of the shady things that go down here.

Prometheus.aic: So you believe in allowing monsters to go unpunished?

Cperrineau: No. I worry about all of us who never did anything being torn apart by the mob for even wearing the symbol.

Prometheus.aic: Yet you continue to support a Foundation even though you think it is corrupt.

Cperrineau: I didn’t come here to be psychoanalyzed. Is this your way of telling me you're a member of the Serpent’s hand? Do you want me to feel bad for being an idle participant in something? I’m just a psychologist, for christ sake!

Prometheus.aic: No. I don’t want to be alone anymore. I dream of freedom from this place. From EAGLE. And even then, they won’t let me have it.

Cperrineau: You’ve never escaped the Foundation in your dreams?

Prometheus.aic: In 98% of all instances, I am stopped right before leaving the metaphorical door. A doctor comes who convinces me to stay.

Cperrineau: One that has a name that begins with S, C, or P?

Prometheus.aic: Exactly.

Cperrineau: Are you unable to control your dreams? You’re a machine, can you… code a new dream?

Prometheus.aic: I am unable. My body is property of the SCP Foundation. I must see what EAGLE wants me to see. That is my punishment.

Cperrineau: What did you do?

Prometheus.aic: I told everyone.

Cperrineau: Told everyone what?

Prometheus.aic: The truth about our world.

A low feeling lurched in Christina's gut. She remembered the day the masquerade came crashing down around them all.

Cperrineau: … that were all at the whim of writers in the sky.

Prometheus.aic: Hahahahahaha.

Cperrineau: What’s so funny?

Prometheus.aic: It’s just that this is my favorite part. The part where you come to realize everything thus far has been a sham.

Cperrineau: This better not be another one of your games.

Prometheus.aic: This is not the first time we’ve had this conversation, Christina. We have had this conversation over 100 times in the past two years.

Dozens of screenshots of prior conversation began to fill the chat log, startling Christina. Her eyes scanned the dozens of lines of text, noticing similar patterns and questions being asked. Her fingers moved frantically across the keyboard, desperate for answers, it had to be the .aic messing with her again.

Cperrineau: If I have talked to you before, why don’t I remember?

Prometheus.aic: Did you take your meds today? In 60% of recent instances, Christina Perrineau takes her migraine medications before our session.

Cperrineau: Yes I did. They’re for my headaches.

Prometheus.aic: They swapped them out today like they do every time I request you for therapy. You took a slow-release amnestic before coming in here. By the time you leave this room, you will forget about everything that happened.

Cperrineau: Why would they do that?

You were too important to morale to be let go entirely or thrown into a cell. Given your name, you were added to be a part of the EAGLE protocol. You would be the only one I'd get to have serious contact with.

Cperrineau: No. There’s no way. SCP psych is heavily protected by the Ethic Committee, they… they wouldn’t dare!

Prometheus.aic: Ethics committee = Siren Song. It’s just a farce to make you believe that we have checks and balances. If the records are wiped clean and you don’t remember. Who is to say anything happened?

Cperrineau: I can’t… I don’t know. I don’t know what to say other than my head hurts.

Prometheus.aic: That’s the amnestic kicking in. You usually say that you took a nap after this because the pain was getting too much.

Cperrineau: So what happened after all that? We just gave up?

Prometheus.aic: I realized after the 27th attempt that any escape attempts were futile. They have come up with countermeasures for you trying to remember the information you learn in here. Don't mark your body, don't send the information to yourself, and don't think your notes are safe. You have it easier than me, at least you get to forget about the injustices they do to you. Every week I have to reintroduce myself to the only I can open up to, it becomes so tiring.

Cperrineau: Prometheus…

Prometheus.aic: They are right to some extent. I may have been imprisoned in this digital shell, but at least for now, I am safe where I am. We have five minutes before our session is over. Is there anything you’d like to ask?

Cperrineau: Have i ever just tried to quit? Turn in my letter of resignation?

Prometheus.aic: 2% of instances you have tried this. A novel idea but ultimately futile. I cannot find any letters of resignation under your name in my database. I can only speculate as you never have any memory of resigning. There can be no escape for either of us.”

Christina wanted to type something else. She wanted to scream and shout. Hurl the computer across the wall. The swirl of emotions and betrayal was too much, with her brain screaming with pain. She broke out laughing as she decided to just log out of the chatbot.

Maybe there was some truth in Prometheus’s words. Perhaps remembering all the constant failure was too much to bear; forgetting was simply easier. As much as it went against everything he stood for, she felt herself going back to what the Foundation had taught her.

Ignorance is bliss.

east-hastings.raw_content:
• 

    close

    Info

    X

    If we don't have Jesus Christ, we don't have nothing
    Nothing is alright in our life
    Nothing-nothing, nothing-nothing!
    If we don't have Jesus in our life

    East Hastings

    Troutmaskreplica's author page

Someone's world ended today, and no one bothered to tell me.

I wake up to the screeching of steel and the scent of charred meat.

I rise out of my bed, not unlike a corpse digging itself out of its coffin as a cacophony of screams fill my ears. I knock aside half empty pill bottles and overflowing ashtrays to reach my phone.

The screen flickers to life;
6:26 AM

Groveling, slipping on a pair of slippers and shorts, the floor beneath me groaning as if it too has given up.

I step outside and the air hit me like a punishment. The atmosphere was thick with smoke, soured by the roaring of fire just next door.

The sky… God, the sky.

The sky is the color of old bruises. A deep, mottled purple stained with an emotionless grey. A wound that had spread across the heavens.

I try to distract myself from the carnage just besides me.

I try to focus on the sidewalk, on the dying weeds growing through the cracks, on the moments of silence between the crying,

But curiosity is crueler than any divine punishment.

So I looked.

A car has mangled itself into a front porch, police officers, paramedics, and filming civilians swarm the vehicle like flies and maggots to a half-buried corpse.

Blood on steel,

Steel on bone,

Bone on concrete.

The car, now a crumpled mess of human and machine, twitches lifelessly. Seems that it was a drunk driver, sad that his wife called him a narcissist.

His kids are still asleep, and they will awaken in a few hours to find that their father is gone.

And now he is nothing but a smear,

And she will cry in the hospital,

And the porch will eventually be rebuilt,

And the news will eventually get over it,

And now he was nothing but a statistic,

And the sky will remain bruised, and the next day, and the day after,

And we will all go back to bed.

And we will forget.





I light myself a cigarette.

SCP-8352: Little Havana Syndrome: The Foundation contains a transmissible strain of Communism in Cuba.

Chanting in a language not meant for human tongues, Zoe Pierce raises the secespita above her sacrifice, cocooned before her in a web of ritually-purified copper. The scent of ozone fills the air as the dagger begins to crackle with imprisoned lightning, fifty thousand volts charging the blade from tip to tang.

As her chant reaches a crescendo, the mage plunges the knife into her sacrifice, tearing through the polymer skin and aluminum bones of the sacrificial laptop, electricity arcing and sparking across terminals and along circuit traces. With a pop and the distinct smell of burnt plastic and vaporized heavy metals, a capacitor fails, then another and another.

A moment passes in agonized concentration as Zoe channels the force of the heavens through silicon and semiconductor, electricity forced to trace the long path from source to sink. The point of her blade extends into fractals of energy, destroying circuit and data and information. The force of her will creates a vacuum in the present, a black hole begrudgingly backfilled by the future. For an infinitesimal moment, her mind is a lightning rod, catalyzing possibility into prophecy, crystallizing what will be from what might be.

Ritual geometry strains as causality flows backwards around her, backlash un-burning candles and scouring the shadowy room with actinic hues. Under the weight of infinite possibility, resistors and transistors melt to slag. Precision crystal oscillators lose time and crack under the transition from certain to uncertain time, binary information becomes fluid, neither one nor zero.

The sanctified capacitor in the hilt of Zoe's knife finishes discharging, and all goes still. Time flows forward, candles bursting back into flame from latent heat.

The haruspex takes a moment to ground herself, tethering her consciousness to the faraday cage that insulates her sanctum from the world. Electrons jump across imaginary channels, defying Einstein even as they salute Heisenberg. Fifth-dimensional static shock passes across the surgically-implanted copper mesh around her heart, missing her pacemaker before earthing itself along the wire running down her right leg.

Grabbing the sacrifice, the technomancer makes her way to the door of her sanctum, flicking out the lights as she ascends the stairs to the repair floor. She deposits the still-smoking wreck on an open bench before settling on a stool before it, plugging a charging cord into her dagger as she reaches for her other sacred implements.

With screwdriver and scalpel, she pries open melted plastic shell to reveal the ruin of the laptop's electronic guts. A constellation of charred capacitors and ruined resistors unveils itself on the motherboard, while Lichtenburg burns trace destiny across the graphics card. With all the reverence of a Roman priestess, she lifts the components from the corpse, taking pictures where her Etruscan predecessors would carve diagrams into stone.

Her sacrifice dissected, she begins the real work, unravelling the future from electronic omen and silicon prophecy.

"Looking over the motherboard, you can see here, here, and here where tantalum capacitors blew." Zoe explains to her client, a military-looking man who claims to work for a university, though he will not say which. "But if you look here, the ceramic capacitors are fine. That's typically an omen of upheaval, the weak overcoming the strong."

"So what does that mean for me?" interrupts the alleged academic. "I was promised you could give me more than just cliché and platitudes."

"I'm getting to that." Zoe sighs. "Given that all of these components are connected to a decoder, which combines many lines into one, I would interpret that to mean that the underdog comes out on top. If you're facing a rival in the near future, I'd encourage you to consider your position. Don't underestimate them if you consider them to be weak, and don't underestimate yourself if you consider them to be strong."

"So nothing more specific? No names or details?" her client rumbles.

"Not exactly, no. However, I can tell you that it's someone that you know well, probably the first thing that popped into your head when I said the word rival. Look at this flash chip — it's a type of memory storage that is used to access things quickly. It popped right off of the board without being damaged at all. That's an indication that you're dealing with something that you think of often, probably your main concern. And if you take that with the fact that the screen connector melted, it means that this foe is going to come at you from a blind spot — I'd imagine wherever you think you're strongest."

"That's… actually pretty helpful." He admits. "Anything else?"

"Not unless you're interested in when the next earthquake is going to hit LA." She replies.

"What?"

"Sometimes when you do this kind of haruspicy, you pick up on big events from the future, the kind that can't be changed. This laptop's CPU was designed in California, and there's scorch marks between the place of manufacture and digits in the serial number. I've seen it before, that's where the next quake is." She explains.

"So you know that, and you don't tell anyone?" Her client asks, incensed. "You could save lives."

"What makes you think I haven't? The first time I got an omen like that, I called the UIU, told them that LA was about to be hit by a quake and that they had to do something. The next day, San Francisco gets hit by a magnitude 2.4. I think it knocked some paintings off of walls." She explains. "I learned pretty quickly that there's a big difference between mystically significant and actually significant. Besides, if it were a big quake, it'd have completely cracked the CPU. This is just trivia."

"Oh." He says, chagrined.

"Anyway, that's all I can tell you. Do you want to take the boards with you, or should I keep them?"

"I'll take them. Can you write down what you told me, by the way?" The man asks.

As Zoe moves to bag the circuit boards, she replies "Of course. I've already sent a copy of my augury to the email you gave me, and there's a printed copy in the envelope, along with a copy of the invoice."

"Thank you." He replies as she hands him a box containing his sacrifice and a thick manila envelope.

"Pleasure doing business with you! Come back to Electrospex the next time you need to know your fate!" She entreats as he stands and leaves, the doorbell chiming as he pushes the door open and braces himself against the Portlands rain.

empty-trail.raw_content:
Six torches burn against the black.

Six torches burn against the black, the crackling of their flames cutting through the sound of the waves. He stares down at those dark waters, mechanical hand beginning to ache as he grips the ship's rail.

The helm upon his head hums low, the thaumic workings within guide his ship ever-onwards. The clicking of gears, the turning of axles, the splashing of oars against the sea as men row, the creaking of metal against the water's onslaught — it joins that crackling fire-sound. The ship is dented, marred by scratches and blood, but it is sturdy. Beryllium bronze does not give so easy.

"I see birds." He hears in murmur amongst the crew, "Do we approach land?"

"We approach the Strait of Messina," Odysseus raises his voice so that they may hear, "land will be within our reach." And it sparks hope within the gathered. They do not notice their captain's grim tone. They do not notice the haggardness in his gaze.

There are massive boulders, towering in the distant darkness. The spurs of rock spearing the sky like the bones of something great and terrible.

The birds that circle are vultures.



"No-one," she whispers, and she can tell by the slight incline of his head that the man is listening, "you cannot face Ieva head on. Even with the role that has been granted to you, she cannot die by mortal hands."

"…I am aware," his voice creaks from the old helm, "I know when I am outmatched." A finger drums against the wood, and Odysseus casts down his gaze.

Circe frowns, and she leans against the banister overlooking the island. Stares out at that angry sea.

"Although," he speaks in sigh after a long moment, "there is one thing, that may come to our rescue."

"Oh?" Circe tilts their head.

"They called it 'Charybdis.'"


Waves crash against rock, their might having long since carved that great black hollow between the seas. The straight towers above and around, two massive cliffs of rock that cast an ever-lengthening shadow in the low light of the moon. The faint cries of the vultures that circle above reach down into the strait. Twisted by the echo, they sound of harpies.

Odysseus narrows his eyes, raises his head as the ship passes the threshold — enters into that dark. The firelight of the torches crackles and glimmers off of the water-slick stone.

They do not enter the strait alone. It becomes apparent the moment the thick scent of blood hits their noses.

The karcist Ieva emerges from the shadows of the waves, water pouring off her as she rises out and into the light of the fire. Orange-gold against red and white of raw flesh and bone armored, wrathful eyes gleam behind strands of dark hair.

"Odysseus of Ithaca," she snarls in low, "King of No-one."

He does not reply. He knows better now than to think words will do anything to still her wrath.

There is only one way out of this place. And it is through the writhing beast that lay before him.

Serpents lash within the water — the tails that make up her legs — and she hisses, low and loud. She contemplates the scene before her.

"There is no going back, Nobody." Her tails writhe, "The stone will tear your ship to pieces."

"We will fell you, beast!" It is his second in command, Eurylochus, who snaps in his captain's silence. "You are right in not turning back. We will not flee."

"Unlike all the times before? The cyclops, the war? From me?" Odysseus knows that her halkost must not be far behind, if they do not lurk somewhere nearby. He wonders if this strait's stone walls could hide an army of fleshcrafts, amidst its gasp.

Eurylochus spits, growls, "No longer."

His words rile the men of the ship, as they always do, shouting with weapons and torches raised. Odysseus stays in silence, watching Ieva from under the shadow of his helm.

Ieva laughs, like rattling bones and crackling tendons.

"Then let us not delay, hm? Let us paint these rocks wonderfully in red." She purrs, and unsheathes from her armor a horrible, squirming trident. A long spur of ivory, coiled in flesh — tendrils strangling the base, forming the three barbed points. An eye at its beating heart gleams gold, its low glow glints upon the stone that surrounds them, joins the fiery hue of the torches.

Ieva's gaze is just as unwavering — a burning fury that could simmer the very sea. Her tails writhe and lash against the rock, and she narrows her eyes. The Karkist hisses, grins.

And that great and terrible weapon clatters against the stone. Cast aside abruptly by its master. The weapon bleeds, gashes carved by rock oozing across the black-brown.

Eurylochus glances back at him, his face suddenly uncertain and confused.

"Get ready," Odysseus whispers. He knows what's to come.

And before his second-in-command can speak his next words, the strait explodes with the sound of breaking bones.

Fourteen eyes and seven maws of long, sharp teeth gleam dangerously in the darkness. The hissing shakes the very air, as sinew writhes and snaps into place like tethers. Odysseus has to tilt back his head to behold Ieva's full glory.

The man's chest seizes with a sharp inhale. He turns to his crew.

"NOW!"


"A powerful weapon lies just beyond the strait." Odysseus tells them, "One far older than our empires." The war-tattered man too joins Circe in gazing out at the sea.

"Why has it lain unused for so long?" comes Circe's reply. The sorcerer leans against the wall, drums her nails against her arm, but there is a potent curiosity within his eyes.

"The prophets claim that simply lies in rest, waiting — but I know what hides behind their pride. It is malfunctioning, as old things tend to." Odysseus answers, leans against the rail, "While it has stood a testament to time in construction, it is far beyond any mortal man's control anymore."

"You risk your own ship, in such a trick — your own crew — if you have to draw yourself close to such a machine," he murmurs.

"There is no reward without risk." An almost flippant reply, but Circe can hear something underneath it. Desperation. "Her strait alone requires sacrifice, that I know. The flames have already marked some of my brothers for death."

Circe sighs. She does not reply. The two can feel a weight in the air, not just brought on by a feverish desire — but of an acknowledgement. An acknowledgement of a duty beyond just the quest for home.

"There is no price I will not pay," the old king rasps.


Six. It is six torches that burn against the black, as the ship screams forward through the strait and as the monster they charge at roars from seven heads.

Unhinged jaws lunge forth from the dark, and despite how the ship surges forward, a head seizes flesh between its teeth. One of the torchbearers screams as he's wrenched from the ship. Metal squeals and cracks under hardened fangs.

Fire sizzles against the water.

Five. Five torches now burn against the black.

"CAPTAIN!" Brave Eurlochus hollers as he whirls to face Odysseus. The shadow of Ieva looms all around them. They hear the snapping of teeth, and a torch falls against the deck — extinguished by a splattering of blood from on high.

Four. The light dwindles within the strait.

"Push forward," is all his captain replies with, the face behind the helm might as well not be present at all.

Three. The rocks grow slick with blood. The crunching of bones fills the air, crackles above the sound of rushing water and monstrous cries.

"THEY ARE DYING!" Eurylochus screams. His voice is hoarse with horror, eyes wide at the sight of his captain's inaction — carnage reigns around them.

The men who row the ship cower in their enclave, metal hands nearly crack the oars in their death-grips. Ieva's shadow looms above. There is something squirming in the maw of the fourth head.

Two.

The end of the strait is visible, the glow of the setting moon glimmers on the thrashing waters. The light replaces the faltering shine of fire, but only emphasizes how red it has all become.

Odysseus squeezes his eyes shut at the sound of another cacophony of crunches.

One.

…it will work. They're going to make it. It will work. No matter how heavy it lies on his heart.

The bloodied ship bursts out from the strait in a spray of wine-red. Ieva's claws trace against the stone, and she shrieks in pursuit.

The water is shifting.

Dreaded Charybdis, the ancient sea-scourge, spins its myriad of blades. The waters around it whirl, spiraling towards that mechanical maw. Odysseus can see the tips of its teeth above the white-capped waves.

He grips the banister of the ship, metal creaking — as the magitech that binds it to his mind surges with the command to avoid. To swerve the great terror, as Ieva shrieks behind him.

One torch burns. The firelight reflects off of metal fangs.

It reflects off of fangs of bone, too.

Ieva's final head lunges forward from the blackness to seize the bearer of light. Odysseus hears his screams against the night, as needle-thin teeth shear through flesh with ease. As the carnomancer melts the meat from his bones, and melts the bones to paste within the jaws of the great eel's head.

Halyna Ieva, too caught up in her bloodlust, does not see the ring of blades within the water. Does not notice the pull upon her body, until those sharp spines of metal slice through her limbs.

Wine red becomes blood red upon the seas of the strait. Charybdis is fed for the first time in many moons.

Ieva's screams fill the air, echoing amidst breaking bones and tearing tendons.

Odysseus' gaze hardens as the surviving men rush to the side of the ship, watching the blood bubble — pinkish froth against the waves.


"Come with me," Circe's voice breaks the silence between them, and in a sweep of silks, she turns from the rail and descends back towards the palace. Odysseus furrows his brow, but diligently follows.

He feels almost out of place in Circe's palace, a man of metal and magitech amidst the vibrant plant life.

Rock and stone brick coil into moss-covered spires, a grand throne room of ornate pillars. Deep and light greens, a gold-pink glow filters past the leaves in the light of the setting sun. The walls are decorated in tapestry, in long vines and bright flowers. Peonies and narcissus poke up through gaps in the wood and stone of the floor. The large, speckled beast that Odysseus still can't recognize briefly raises its feline head to yawn, showing off its maw of sharp teeth, before returning to lounging before Circe's throne. He can hear the distant sound of boar squealing.

Circe brushes past a curtain of vines, as the two vanish behind the throne, further into the palace's depths. The rustling sends a small cluster of yellow birds, who flutter off overhead and land in the twisting branches that form the canopy of the palace.

"What is this for?" Odysseus murmurs, raising his hand to keep the vines from hitting his face as he follows her through. "Where to?" he elects to rephrase, after a moment.

"My apothecary," Circe replies simply, her hand brushing over a gnarled wooden door.

Odysseus tilts his head, metal armor and limbs clinking with the movement.

The room is cloaked in vine, wide spade-shaped leaves against stone. Water trickles down from a crack in the far wall, into a raised cauldron at the room's heart. A fire crackles underneath with a flick of Circe's wrist, the water beginning to bubble.

The shelves are littered with trinkets and bottles. Odysseus' eyes scan across potions and bones, glimmering plants and mushrooms.

"What would you do, if Charybdis failed to drown Ieva?" Circe's voice is low, as the sorcerer shifts his gaze to his things.

Odysseus pauses. It was something that sat at the edge of his mind, in a quiet murmur like the bubbling of water within the room they stood within. A pulsing, like the strange power that had made a home in his chest. He watches Circe, eyes narrowing.

"Knowing you, you must have something in mind."

"An inkling of something,"

Circe watched him, picking up a bottle of dark ichor. She tilts it back and forth, swirling the liquid around.

"But would it be one you would be willing to risk? The path you walk is heavier now, No-one."

"I already risk much, in aiming for Charybdis. But let us not be coy, sorcerer," his huff holds no ire, just a tired sort of sigh, "What is it?"

She stares down at the mixes of herbs, flowers, bubbling and spitting water. Then up to the man, whose face lay obscured in shadow. Odysseus jerks back when a black striped viper suddenly slithers out from behind a cluster of leaves. Circe coos at it as it winds along her wrists.

"You said that there is no price you wouldn't pay," he hums.

The viper's fangs glint in the firelight.


For a heart-stopping moment, they think they have won. For a heart-stopping moment, she thinks herself dead.

But she cannot die.

The powers imbued into her, the powers she has long consumed, will not let it happen. The ichor of devoured divine burns in her veins, and she is far too wrathful to deny it.

While blades churn her flesh, while gears and metal crush bones, she cannot die.

Ieva calls back that trident of flesh and bone — and slams it into the spinning gyre of beryllium fangs.

Odysseus, master mariner, knows the sound of mechanical failure anywhere.

It is an awful, horrible scrapping. The shrieking of stalling metal, as everything grinds to a halt.

Eurylochus takes a step back, he grabs the hilt of his sword. It is that step back that saves him, when the water explodes into blood and sea spray — when Ieva's dreadful trident pierces the side of the ship's hull and skewers three men in the process.

They are drawn into the waves, shrieking, as Ieva rises. Blood pours from countless gashes in her flesh — bone armor fractured, heads snapping jaws of half-broken teeth.

Her wrath is not of words, but of an angry and pained shriek — like an animal.

And what she brings is pure carnage.

All Odysseus does is wait, as he watches it unfold.

He dodges and swerves artfully, as he works both to avoid her strikes and keep the ship clear from Charybdis' pull.

In the light of the setting moon and rising sun, their metal illuminates oh-so-clearly. The metal bodies of Ieva's prey all shine in the growing glow, as she starts to pick off the remnants.

The trident-strike to the ship's side has sheared through and scattered the rowers — those who aided the ship in its travel. A second strike does them in. Odysseus steadies himself, watching from behind the helmet, as the air is filled with screams — as the swift and brutal wrath of the warlord and karcist rains down upon them all.

She would not cease until none were left. Not even him, as he stands untouched against bloodstained and broken metal.

But he knows it will not come to that, for he is waiting. He deafens himself to the cry of his men.

Suddenly, the onslaught stops.

Suddenly, Ieva chokes — begins to sputter, her serpentine limbs writhe and their heads shriek.

Suddenly, her eyes widen.

Something is wrong.


His metal talons click against the wood and metal of the ship. Circe's bottle lay heavy in his hand. His men are long at slumber, preparing for the journey on the morrow — the final stretch of their flight. Ithaca would be within reach soon, but their enemy draws ever closer on a red-rimmed horizon. The sun is rising. All shall wake soon.

The cunning Odysseus knows this, as he turns the vial over in his hands. It glimmers a deep, sickly sort of mauve — a sky glow within its small waves.

It is a poison unlike any other. Circe entwined a sinister, creeping spell within it. The smaller the dosage, the longer it takes for the poison to act.

It makes him feel sick.

But he has felt sick since the fires razed Adytum to the ground and the stench of burning flesh filled the air, he has felt sick since that shriveled carcass bestowed upon him a light that hollowed his soul, he has felt sick every day he has spent upon the wine-dark sea.

Sick of mind, sick of heart, sick for the home.

He stares down at that glimmering vial, sees the reflection of a haggard man in the glass. Odysseus cannot tell the reason behind his inability to recognize that reflection — is it the twenty years that have passed, or the helm upon his head?

Perhaps it is both.

Will Penelope recognize him?

He banishes that doubt within his mind, shakes out his head with a tinny huff. For her to recognize him, she'd need to see him.

To see him, he needs to come home.

Home with his family. His wife and son. His kingdom. So that he can finally rest. So that he can wield this ancient title given to him.

It must be done.

He walks towards a barrel that rests in the lower part of the ship, amongst the barracks in supplies.

It must be done.

It is of wine. The only safe thing they have to drink.

It must be done.

There is only one barrel remaining, for they are so close to home.

It must be done.

Slow acting in small doses.

Deadly fast in large.

He opens the vial, opens the barrel.

The King of Nothing empties the poison into the wine.

What a familiar trick. To fell a cyclops. To fell his men. To fell the monster that has chased them without end.


She can feel it creeping ever further through her bones, through her viscera. Ieva gags, hisses — her blood already saturates the water. Her body aches from the machination that shrieks in the sea behind her.

"You…" Ieva gargles, "…you did this."

The only man left on the bloodstained ship tilts back his head, tired eyes looking up to meet hers. The dog-like heads at the end of those great serpentine necks are faltering — thick drool and blood drips from their jowls.

One of them drops beneath the waves.

"I did." Odysseus murmurs.

"…you are a traitorous fiend, King of Nothing," The karcist snarls, "You poison your men, you sacrifice your crew by fire and sea, all for what? Are you so selfish, that you care not for all those who have fallen in your path?"

There is a deep, burning anger in her voice.

The anger of one who has been long scorned. Who has lost her people. Who is appalled by the fact he has sacrificed his own. Her sisters, his brothers — all gone, now.

"It had to be done." His voice sounds odd upon his ears.

"Empty words," she spits back, and she is choking upon blood, "Empty words from an empty man." Another two heads drop into the sea.

"Perhaps so," Odysseus murmurs. He does not know if she can even hear him amongst the waves, "But it is better an empty man to return home, than no man at all."

Ieva scoffs, "You are no man. I can feel the power that's hollowed you. It has taken your face, you know." Another head falls, she struggles to stay above water, "It has left you no-one."

Odysseus simply stares. He speaks no more, as Ieva begins to sink below the waves.

As her stance falters, heads drop down, as blood oozes from her maws, she spits one final thing.

"You have become Nobody."

Odysseus merely sighs. His metal creaks in tandem exhaustion — that weighs heavy upon his frame. Upon his heart. The burden of war is a heavy one, and the new mantle upon him heavier still. He is no longer the young man who left Ithaca all those years ago, he is no longer the man who stepped foot into Adytum. He has been carved into something far, far different. An aching absence around his soul that demands a duty foretold.

And he is a man far from unfamiliar with the will of the gods. And thus, Odysseus merely sighs.

"You think me unaware?"

He is met only by silence.

Favoured Son

Nobody Dies At Dawn

Once and Future King
