— I began mockingly. ?code, a, ёе йолги ТежоМ—

Johnson looked at her thoughtfully. The victim was swollen as if she had been underwater for a long time. Age indeterminate. A girl. The body lay at my feet.

Flash.

There was a body at my feet. A girl. She looked to be in her twenties or thirties. Only emptiness surrounded us. Absolute nothingness was all-consuming. It felt like we were hanging in mid-air. I pulled out my ID and was about to throw it forward, expecting the object to hang in mid-air, but at the last moment I changed my mind. We're not in space, for God's sake.

I crouched down beside the body and ran a bloody finger across her forehead. Her eyes opened. They were covered with a veil that perfectly matched the pale desolation of the place.

- Then you had no face.

- It would only get in the way.

A shadow covered the eyeballs.

Flash.

At my feet lay a body. Charred to such a degree that it was impossible to identify any features. However, the amount of smoke in the room was astonishingly small. Even cigarettes in the mouths of the coroner, the patrolmen, and myself could not bring the smoke level down to normal levels.

A fierce desire to drop everything and go home, take a boiling bath, light candles similar to those burning here, and indulge in a peaceful slumber burned in my heart. But I couldn’t. I had a corpse in my arms, a firearm in my holster, and an ID card in my pocket—I felt it, convincing myself to stay.

- Listen, Ferrero, maybe you should stop burning the wall with your gaze and get down to business? - The doc was clearly on edge, there was no point in fueling his anger.

- Yes, yes. You work there too, - I answered absentmindedly. My thoughts were not here.

- I've already finished. The victim's burns don't allow any clear conclusions to be made. We'll have to wait for the autopsy.

I wanted to shout passionately that I didn't care, but I stopped myself in time. Where did this rage come from?

— We'll wait if necessary.

Doc nodded and stood by the door. I looked around the room: glowing embers in the walls, smoky quartz in the windows, fire in the lamps - everything was as usual. I thought that the adjoining rooms would provide better evidence. I walked into the kitchen and ran my finger along the stove, leaving a bloody trail in the thick layer of soot.

I took the cigarette out of my mouth and flicked the ashes onto the floor. Something didn't add up. There was nothing out of the ordinary about the house, no sign of a fire out of control—the fire was within normal limits—but how did the victim burn? Had he been burned somewhere and brought here? And God, how my wrists hurt.

A shadow passed outside the window.

Flash.

Emily was lying at my feet. A blood stain was spreading across her blouse. The knife in my hands seemed weightless.

“Why…” she croaked, “…we decided not to…”

Her eyes rolled back, her breathing slowed. I began to carve numbers into her arms. The only numbers. The most important numbers. But you can’t write them in a row. You can’t write them correctly. Then they’ll find it. It wants to be found. You have to resist. But it’s too late. It was my decision. “35-40,” “20-25,” “33,” “I.”

Hand in pocket. No need, words in head. Finger on blouse. Big bloody "M". Shadow behind, but I won't turn around. "A". It goes around. "Y".

Flash.

There was a body lying at my feet. A man, about thirty-five, maybe forty. The orange robe looked terribly unnatural on him.

- Well, look. D-2025354033-1, the effect is clearly visible on it.

- But what effect? ​​You still haven't told me a word about the anomaly.

Junior research fellow Kenneth was not exactly a bright young man, but he was a smart guy and with enough persistence he could achieve a lot.

- Because you yourself must understand what the point is. Examine him. Don't be afraid, it's not dangerous.

The guy walked up to the man and began examining him. He opened his eyelids and looked into his wildly darting eyes. He tried to unclench his hands – he didn’t succeed, but he saw the black edge of the leather cover with bloody stains. He opened the victim’s mouth and listened. He felt his muscles. He grunted with satisfaction.

“Don’t forget to look in your pants,” I egged the guy on.

He frowned, stood up and walked away from the body.

- I think I get the gist of it. He's having dreams that seem real to him, right?

- So far so good.

— The source is that thing in his hands. A passport, an ID, a wallet — something like that, right?

- Right.

- It doesn't work on touch, otherwise you wouldn't let me anywhere near it. So either there can only be one victim, or it's somehow tied to that person's personality.

- Three out of three, congratulations, and now let's get out of here. I've been coming here for two weeks now, and he always lies motionless, it makes me shiver.

We left the cell and headed towards the dining room. Lunch was approaching - you can't miss that.

"So, does the item only affect one person or is it connected to the victim?" Kenneth asked after a few seconds.

- Second. He was a former officer from some backwater town. Mike - or Mark, I don't remember exactly. Last name Ferrero. He investigated all sorts of small stuff until his wife died. I don't remember how it happened, but I remember that the causes were not natural. Since then, he literally lived at work. And then there was another murder in the same town. Just before that, he was promoted to detective and given a brand new ID. Guess what the cover of this document is, by the way.

- Black leather.

— Bingo. Anyway, our valiant detective arrived at the crime scene, started investigating, put his hand in his pocket and collapsed in the middle of the room, right next to the corpse. They couldn't shake him awake, the medics just threw up their hands. But he was still lying there, not breathing, not needing food or water. A statue. Anyway, that's when we intervened. We found the object, but couldn't get it out of the guy's hands, so now we're keeping them together.

- What about the crime? Well, the one he was investigating? Is it somehow connected to the object?

- Who knows, I didn't really look into it. It seems like it's still hanging. There was some kind of ritual or something like that. Listen, you noticed correctly - we need to wake up our people and make them figure it out. If it's a ritual, then maybe everything is really connected.

A smile lit up the boy's face.

Finally reaching the dining room, we filled our plates and went to the table.

"The fried baby feet turned out surprisingly appetizing this time, tell me?" I began.

- Yeah. By the way, try the crushed brain garnish, it's absolutely delicious today.

A shadow emerged from under the table.

Flash.

Always wearing sunglasses, dark loose hair, red lipstick, the color of fresh blood, and... Sorry, nothing else comes to mind. - I see. Thank you for your help, Mr. Kipnes. You will be contacted later, but for now you can go and rest. - Yes, thank you... He turned and slowly walked into his apartment. The information, of course, was not so great. Half of the women in the city could fall under such a composite sketch, starting right with me. I glanced to the side and saw a mirror. The body of the murdered man was reflected in it, taking on some inexplicably creepy shape. My tired face was also reflected in it. Sleepless nights were not doing me any good. I went to the curtain, pulled it back and stared at the view from the fifth floor through the closed window. Yes, the window option was out. A shadow flitted in the corner of my eye. Flash. There was a body lying at my feet. A girl. She looked to be about twenty or twenty-five years old. Her face, smooth, without a single wrinkle, was cut crosswise. The vertical cut ran right across the skin of her mouth and nasal tubercle, the horizontal one crossed her eye sockets. The coroner raised his dry, featureless face to me: “— ,” he said, not in a particularly cheerful tone. “— .” I decided that now was not the time for stupid jokes, so I answered simply: — , — after which he left the old man alone. The inside of the room, although ordinary, still gave off something unhealthy. The leather sofa seemed to have turned pale, and the hair on the carpet resembled the fur of a dead animal. I quickly retreated to the kitchen. Passing by the window, I glanced at my reflection in the glass: the same tiredly sagging skin on my face, the same wrinkles, the same twisted flesh in the mouth in a dissatisfied grimace, and the same narrowed eye sockets. The kitchen was empty. There were still drops of darkish water in the sink, reminiscent of sweat on the forehead - something had recently been washed in it. I ran my hand over the leather of the refrigerator and looked at the knives - all the bones were sticking out in their grooves. Approaching the window, he peered into the ordinary landscape: emptiness, only a light haze hovers in the air. In the distance, a devilish bloody grin can be seen. Flash. I lay at my feet. My chest and wrists were covered in blood, horror frozen on my face. I asked myself: — What do I think? Domestic suicide, suicide or ritual? - It's clearly not suicide, why would I stick a knife into my chest if I've already cut my wrists? Besides, where is the suicide weapon? - I thought for a moment, and then continued. - It's also strange for a domestic suicide: if I throw a knife at myself in anger, why would I then cut my wrists? I'm betting on a ritual. I considered my words, then sat down to examine the body more closely. Coat, trousers, boots – all in dark tones. Only the once white, now scarlet shirt stood out from the overall picture. In the left pocket of the trousers there was a wallet: inside were a dozen bills of various denominations and my photo. In the right lay a police ID card, glistening with blood, and a piece of chalk. I stood up and walked away from myself. I decided that I clearly had nothing to catch with me, and therefore, perhaps, I should go and question the witness. I stood surrounded by me and me. I asked myself to move away and began the questioning. — What time exactly did I hear the scream? — At 17:30. — And you immediately called the police? - Yes, I was very scared. — Did I hear you leaving the apartment after the murder? - No, but I don’t believe that I could somehow remain there unnoticed, which is probably why I left very quietly. A tired look, as if he had last seen a bed a thousand years ago. I don't remember. The floor is uncomfortable. It's hard to breathe. My whole body aches. Actually, I came to say that it was time to pack up. I don't think we'll be able to dig up anything else here. — I'll need help moving the body. "A corpse!? There's a corpse in my apartment? Where!?" - Yes, poor girl. Well, I hope someone will help you, and I'm off. - Beast. There was a dark silhouette on the detective's back. He cast his crimson gaze at me. "Now I remember." Flash. Piles and heaps of bodies went up, disappearing beyond the edge of my perception. I felt my body, looked in my pockets, touched the torn page, ran my hand over my ID. I wiped the sweat from my forehead, leaving a red streak there. I hadn't seen so many bodies in a long time. “It seems this one had a lot of little sisters,” I stated gloomily. “Yes, I don’t envy the others,” Mike said slowly. “You say that as if hell isn’t waiting for us now,” Ferrero replied. “Oh no, hell will come later,” said Michelle. A shadow slid between the bodies. Flash. There was a bloody thing at my feet, outlined in chalk. I walked over to the potential clue and lifted the edge of the carpet. My gaze was caught by a strange mark on the floor, where the bare carpet met the carpet. I looked away from the street and scanned the room. Drop after drop flew up into the air, disappearing into the twilight. On the other side, it was raining again. Unable to stand there any longer, I left the bathroom, then crossed the room, pulled the curtain down, and looked out the window. At least now it became clear where the victim was kept. Bending down to examine her better, I smelled a terrible smell of decomposition. The liquid here was black as pitch. The sink was filled with something unknown, the same was true of the bathtub. All the taps were open, but the water was barely dripping. She looked to be in her twenties or thirties. Only emptiness surrounded us. Absolute nothingness was all-consuming. It felt like we were hanging in mid-air. I pulled out my ID and was about to throw it forward, expecting the object to hang in mid-air, but at the last moment I changed my mind. We're not in space, for God's sake. I crouched down beside the body and ran a bloody finger across her forehead. Her eyes opened. They were covered with a veil that perfectly matched the pale desolation of the place. - Then you had no face. - It would only get in the way. A shadow covered the eyeballs. Flash. At my feet lay a body. Charred to such a degree that it was impossible to identify any features. However, the amount of smoke in the room was astonishingly small. Even cigarettes in the mouths of the coroner, the patrolmen, and myself could not bring the smoke level down to normal levels. A fierce desire to drop everything and go home, take a boiling bath, light candles similar to those burning here, and indulge in a peaceful slumber burned in my heart. But I couldn’t. I thought that the adjoining rooms would provide better evidence. I walked into the kitchen and ran my finger along the stove, leaving a bloody trail in the thick layer of soot. I took the cigarette out of my mouth and flicked the ashes onto the floor. Something didn't add up. The knife in my hands seemed weightless. “Why…” she croaked, “…we decided not to…” Her eyes rolled back, her breathing slowed. I began to carve numbers into her arms. The only numbers. It was my decision. “35-40,” “20-25,” “33,” “I.” Hand in pocket. No need, words in head. Finger on blouse. Big bloody "M". Shadow behind, but I won't turn around. "A". It goes around. "Y". Flash. There was a body lying at my feet. A man, about thirty-five, maybe forty. The orange robe looked terribly unnatural on him. - Well, look. D-2025354033-1, the effect is clearly visible on it. - But what effect? ​​You still haven't told me a word about the anomaly. Junior research fellow Kenneth was not exactly a bright young man, but he was a smart guy and with enough persistence he could achieve a lot. - Because you yourself must understand what the point is. He's having dreams that seem real to him, right? - So far so good. — The source is that thing in his hands. A passport, an ID, a wallet — something like that, right? - Right. - It doesn't work on touch, otherwise you wouldn't let me anywhere near it. So either there can only be one victim, or it's somehow tied to that person's personality. - Three out of three, congratulations, and now let's get out of here. I've been coming here for two weeks now, and he always lies motionless, it makes me shiver. We left the cell and headed towards the dining room. Lunch was approaching - you can't miss that. "So, does the item only affect one person or is it connected to the victim?" Kenneth asked after a few seconds. - Second. He was a former officer from some backwater town. Mike - or Mark, I don't remember exactly. Last name Ferrero. He investigated all sorts of small stuff until his wife died. I don't remember how it happened, but I remember that the causes were not natural. Since then, he literally lived at work. And then there was another murder in the same town. Just before that, he was promoted to detective and given a brand new ID. Guess what the cover of this document is, by the way. - Black leather. — Bingo. Anyway, our valiant detective arrived at the crime scene, started investigating, put his hand in his pocket and collapsed in the middle of the room, right next to the corpse. They couldn't shake him awake, the medics just threw up their hands. But he was still lying there, not breathing, not needing food or water. A statue. Anyway, that's when we intervened. We found the object, but couldn't get it out of the guy's hands, so now we're keeping them together. - What about the crime? Well, the one he was investigating? Is it somehow connected to the object? - Who knows, I didn't really look into it. It seems like it's still hanging. There was some kind of ritual or something like that. Listen, you noticed correctly - we need to wake up our people and make them figure it out. If it's a ritual, then maybe everything is really connected. A smile lit up the boy's face. Finally reaching the dining room, we filled our plates and went to the table. "The fried baby feet turned out surprisingly appetizing this time, tell me?" I began. - Yeah. By the way, try the crushed brain garnish, it's absolutely delicious today. A shadow emerged from under the table. Flash. Transyvalania, Carpathian Mountains.

May 29th, 1453.
Jonathon Harker.

Dear Jonathan Harker,
I hope this letter finds you in good health.
How is it in England this time of year? I always preferred summer; long sunny days make me happy. My sweet Lady Elisabad fell pregnant, The doctor confirmed it about two weeks ago as I write this letter. I hope to introduce a healthy child to a thriving country by the start of winter. I do worry my ailments may be contagious. This worry lingers and gnaws at my thoughts, it threatens my beloved. It dampens the joy of the news for me.

The soil has degraded further this spring. I have organised an increase of imports from neighbouring principalities; I fear we can only survive on trade for so long. Reserves are dwindling. It’s been a full season since I’ve witnessed fresh meat served at the local tavern, or even sold in the market. The bread has become difficult to chew.

Another shepherd has found one of their sheep dead. Bled dry, again. The weary old man holds madness in his eyes. He whispers of the devil lurking in his fields; a drinker of blood. I am drawing up plans to relocate his flock. I hesitate; I desperately want to keep a close eye on him, maybe I could get more information about this supposed devil out of him. His late wife is buried on the property and his flock relies on the nearby forest for food. Still, it’s a risk we have to take. The predator responsible, whatever it truly is, may live within the trees.

Last night I was informed of a case of demonic possession. A man from a local village suddenly fell over in the town square, and his body convulsed. My men took him off the road and into Christ’s church. He was stuck with hallucinations; he believes he had spoken with his dead wife. However, I believe these general hallucinations are brought on by poisoned bread. He complained of his skin burning after father splattered him with holy water. My men had found bread in his hand.

My dear lady was witness to a case where an unfortunate young girl was found rigid after consuming bread she had stolen. I suspect the little crops were infected by a fungus, something that poisons the mind and the body. At closer inspection, it acts as a hallucinogenic. It is likely we are witnessing a wide spread of an untamed infection; though it resembles a demonic possession. This Is the 6th case this spring. The people fear mass possession, I fear it’s a case of ergot fungus. I’ve sent for them to bring me the bread they found. I am very interested in taking a very closer look at the quality of the soil, and then the bread. My father left me some equipment in his estate. I do not know the origin. I hope to shine light on this affliction and the land that has forsaken me.

This reeks of foul play.

A priest from you-know-what approached me. I have faint memories of a conversation, although I’m not too sure what I said in my drunken stupor. Immorality plagues them. Cursed people. They lack integrity. I do not wish to work with them. I catch myself flirting with the idea of it. I do not have long. I’m only getting sicker.

Sincerely, Vlad Dracula.


9th June, 1443.
Jonathon Harker.

Dear Jonathon Harker,
Harker, much has happened since I last wrote to you. The ritual was successful; however, I feel like I was deceived about its true nature. I fear they did not have my best interest in mind. As soon as it started, I could taste the coppery air, thick with humidity. For a second I felt the prick on my neck. For a fleeting moment, venom pumped through my veins. Leeches sunk their sharp teeth into my flesh, gnawing into my chest. They sucked the viscous blood out of me when my heart stopped, I could feel my life slipping.

Ever since, food has tasted foul. I can hardly stand the scent of it. There are days the mere sight of it makes my toes curl. Chewing it feels wrong, and I can’t bring myself to swallow it. My teeth are changing. They are growing more sensitive, I have noticed that lukewarm foods are the most comfortable. Small chips are forming near my canines. The white colour around the cracks are discoloured. I suspect this is the result of poor nutrition. I do not like this.

Something peculiar has been happening to me since. They told me this would give me time I so desperately craved. Maybe I was naive to believe they would heal my ailments. Today, I had to turn away a starving peasant. I often offer such people food and lodging within my castle for a short time, but the scent of her neck was so exquisitely decadent. So alluring. For a moment, I forgot she was a person. It felt like having a morsel of food in my mouth. I stared at her strangely, so long that she herself noticed. When, at last, she asked me what was wrong, her voice broke me out of my trance. It felt like a dream. The hazy ambience almost hid the truth from me. I did not want to feel the call of her flesh again, so I sent her away.
Ever since that awful night, I have suffered. Hunger gnaws at me. Its gnashing claws rake my stomach. It has become a constant, unrelenting presence.

Those dirty priests knew what they were doing. Food was the last thread that connected me to my mother, The last thing we did together. and they tarnished it. With every ounce of my being, I hate them. Oh how I lust to drain them of their blood.
Given all that has happened, I genuinely had a productive few months. My father experimented with adding mechanical upgrades to a horse drawn thresher. Today I moved the rusted mechanical prototype off the field. Certainly, an overdue task. Preliminary testing on the soil will be completed before summer begins. Maybe I can remedy this soon.

I did find something interesting I wanted to share with you. I examined the soil my men collected after escorting the Shepard temporary accommodation. It was ravaged by crystalline structures, Salt. Now I know someone tampered with my lands. I may know who did it. I have sent men to tail them. I have a plan for them.
I have sent men to survey farmland from across my county. I plan to analyse the information they have gathered. However I have tasked them with weeding out their tainted degeneracy; those depraved heathens will not be able to hide. Not from me. I will rid my lands of them.

Sincerely, Vlad Dracula.

6th May 1443

Jonathon Harker

Dear Harker,

Hello Harker, Recently, I have fallen further into illness. I do not know what affliction invades me. Just now, I caught a fleeting glimpse of my hollow face in the flicker of candle light. My muscles hurt too much to crank my father’s light machine. I discovered soil sprinkled in my bedding when I awoke. I don’t know where it could have come from.

I’m considering moving most of my father’s strange contraptions down into the family vault, though I do wish to keep the preserver up in the dining hall. I do enjoy the rather odd little device, and the taste of chilled red wine after a meal.
I do hope that my carriage returns in a timely manner. It is hard to see at night. Its black inky colour conceals it, so that the only signs of its presence are its gold highlights and the rattle it makes as it starts and stops.

Tonight, It carries lady Eloise Elisabad. I hope the mechanical nature of the carriage does not startle her as it did the first time she rode it, all those years ago. There is no driver, you see. No horses. No obvious signs of locomotion. It’s quite a fascinating machine, and a convenient one. The markets would be a nightmare without it. My father had hoped to study it. Had he been able to, perhaps he would have made a mechanical apparatus to recreate its locomotion.

I received a report on the lands. They are healing, to some extent, but that’s less comforting as it should be. I have analysed the progression of the fungus. Its spread is too calculated and precise to be natural. Someone is tampering with my domain.

I will learn who, and they will be dealt with.
Over the last few weeks, my fingers have grown numb, as I’ve scribbled notes, and ground herbs, forever burning, replacing, and testing, always testing. Nothing I try cures the blight. I’ve examined the fungi using another contraption, an advanced version of a flea glass, which uses three lenses in front of one another to magnify anything I wish. Somehow, nothing works. Methods of management have been sent out to the farmers.
There’s only one more thing to do.
Sincerely, Vlad Dracula.


6th may 1444

Jonathon Harker.

Dear Harker.
My friend, since I last wrote to you, great difficulty overcame me, Not long after the turning of the year, she became frail. I knew something was wrong when she didn’t respond to that mechanism that signals the morning, I vividly remember her setting it. Yet she stirred as it floated over her head, blaring and shining light into her eyes.

The birth of our son took a lot out of her. She was terribly changed. The roses in her cheeks are fading, and she is weak and languid. I already see the pallor of death creeping over her, despite the doctor's efforts. He told me not to worry; that he would handle it. I told myself; a doctor's confidence is sacred.

She died. He lied. Though my soft kiss briefly breathed life into her eyes, like a soft breeze onto dying embers, it wasn’t enough. She perished, and he died with her.
A momentary lapse in judgement. I drank his blood. I waited for him to die before I stopped. It took mere moments for me to regret it, but the deed was done.Ever since the day I first tasted that indescribably exquisite nectar , I have been caught in a brutal cycle of temptation, sin, and remorse. Each time this cycle repeats, I grow more accustomed to murder. I cannot explain how divinely luxurious it tastes. Each time I feed, it fills me with ecstasy.

A few months back, I received a report. One of my men spent time within the ranks of those heathens after they tracked them down. They hid in the southernmost village of my domain. How could they truly believe they could hide from me? Dracula? No. I bided my time. Last night we struck. I tried to enter the home in which they hid, but an unseen force blocked me. They cackled behind an open door, but they did not laugh long. They did not laugh when I sent in my men to drag them out, or when I slaughtered them in the street.Two heathens remained. I could smell their wretched scent. They were hiding in a closet. They had locked themselves behind a metal reinforced door while we were killing their comrades. I remained unable to enter.

So what did I do? The bald heathen almost coughed up a lung when he realized I’d found a way in. The sweet allure of fear in his neck was palpable. It excited me. It made my stomach rumble. I pressed my nose up to the closet and sniffed so loudly he heard, and screamed. You should have seen the look on the imbicile's face when the man who hid with him gave me permission to enter. I’m sure my man hated pretending to be such a nasty little pest. Not a drop of blood remained in that room when I was done, ignoring my men. I have rid my lands of those sick creatures.

On a brighter note, I recently dug into my fathers diagrams. I used them to build irrigation across all of my farmlands. I have spent months flooding salt out of my domain. It was a costly affair, but certainly worth it. The people have no more excuses to avoid paying their taxes. They owe me that much for all my hard work

Sincerely, Dracula.

My first attempt at a poem on the Wiki. Felt good to flex these muscles again. :>

My author page: Cthulhu Corner

Within the mighty forests green,
A fairy meek and mild
Appears before her honored guests
And offers them a child.

The child is carved of olive wood,
And not of flesh and bone;
Must raise the child with care, she says,
And love him as their own.


The boy behaved as best he could,
But couldn't make the grade.
His parents wouldn't lend a hand,
Just said he was "delayed"

He had no map to follow, no
Example to compare;
Supposed to simply know just what
Was proper, just, and fair.

He looked at all the boys and girls
With whom he went to school,
And tried in vain to imitate
The ways they'd act so cruel.


But soon, his efforts weren't enough,
And retribution came;
And all the while knowing not
For what he was to blame.

The other children laughed and played,
But he was not allowed;
No shelf could stay undusted, not
One field remain unplowed.

And every day reminding him,
While he would cry in vain,
That he was truly broken and
That wood he would remain

Until one day, they cast him out
And washed their hands of him
"It's not our fault its wooden brain
Has rendered it so dim."


When people saw him coming, they
Would hide their young away;
As though it was the child's fault
His parents lost their way

And every time they met his gaze,
Their judgments burned his soul.
But he could not determine if
He'd ever be made whole.

Then, falling to his wooden knees,
He finally pled for aid.
With shaking voice, and in between
His choking sobs, he prayed:

"Oh Spirit, let me waken from
This nightmare of a life.
Allow me now to start again,
Unburdened by my strife."

Well, silently, and with a flash,
She came to him that night.
She let him cry and scream and rage
And held him near and tight.


Some say that she still searches for
Another family,
Or anyone whose home and heart
Have room enough for he.

His parents wouldn't lend a hand, Just said he was "delayed"  _ He had no map to follow, no Example to compare; Supposed to simply know just what Was proper, just, and fair.  _ He looked at all the boys and girls With whom he went to school, And tried in vain to imitate The ways they'd act so cruel.  _  _ But soon, his efforts weren't enough, And retribution came; And all the while knowing not For what he was to blame.  _ The other children laughed and played, But he was not allowed; No shelf could stay undusted, not One field remain unplowed.  _ And every day reminding him, While he would cry in vain, That he was truly broken and That wood he would remain  _ Until one day, they cast him out And washed their hands of him "It's not our fault its wooden brain Has rendered it so dim."  _  _ When people saw him coming, they Would hide their young away; As though it was the child's fault His parents lost their way  _ And every time they met his gaze, Their judgments burned his soul. But he could not determine if He'd ever be made whole.  _ Then, falling to his wooden knees, He finally pled for aid. With shaking voice, and in between His choking sobs, he prayed:  _ "Oh Spirit, let me waken from This nightmare of a life. Allow me now to start again, Unburdened by my strife."  _ Well, silently, and with a flash, She came to him that night. She let him cry and scream and rage And held him near and tight.  _  _ Some say that she still searches for Another family, Or anyone whose home and heart Have room enough for he. Food/Porn

    close

    Info

    X

    Author: SocksesForFoxes
    Content Warnings: Eating Disorders, Objectification, Inappropriate Sexualization, Body Horror

⚠️ content warning

It starts when boys watch the way you eat. They like the way you lick your lips, the way you suck the powder of your snacks off your fingertips. When you eat something sweet and squeeze your eyes shut, they stop and stare. It’s unnerving for all of you.

As you get older and understand what this is, briefly you are flattered. You can be enticing merely by sucking an oyster from a shell, biting down on a berry. You get very popular as a dinner date. But soon, you become irritated. Overwhelmed, yes, but also bored. It’s kind of a cliché, you know? Any time you put something in your mouth you’re someone’s slut, when sometimes a girl just wants to eat some fucking ice cream.

Sometime in your thirties you start hiding to eat. Not literally, not like a spy sitting behind a bush, but you’ve become very uncomfortable eating in public. If you can’t be alone at work, you don’t eat lunch. Whenever someone retires, you sit in a corner, pull a napkin over your lips to take two bites of a brownie, and carry it around to prove you aren’t dieting.

Because that’s becoming an issue, the resentment from women who think you’re on a diet you refuse to share. It’s the first such issue in — maybe ever. You’ve never had a weight problem before, not since the mild amount of baby fat your mother fussed about dropped away in your preteens.

Of all your problems, food was something you didn’t have to think about. A missed meal here and there when you worked late, some cheesecake and cocktails at a girlfriend’s on the weekend. It all evened out, the number on the scales staying the same for a solid decade after college. Other people had disordered eating, yours was just a bit cluttered.

In fact, you worried so little about it you stopped weighing yourself. So it’s hard to tell how suddenly the problem came on: slowly, you think, over years. But now it seems to be speeding up.

You remember the day your pants felt a little loose. Then, maybe a year after that, those pants were falling down. You’d gotten out your oldest, most wishfully skinny clothes, and been surprised that they fit after all. By the next year not only were they all that fit, you’d had to buy new clothes.

By the time the problem has become noticeable to you, it has started to really alarm you. Perhaps you tried to worry about it before but it was drowned out by other anxieties. The new clothes are Size 0 and that sounds ominous, like after this there’s nowhere further to go.

You decide: screw it, you’re going to start eating more fast food, and if you have to bolt it down in your car, so be it. You start losing shirts to spilled tacos and slider sauce. You learn to keep a spare outfit in the backseat.

Even the paper sacks full of grease are somehow not putting weight back on you. At this point, though, the problem is still… mostly not a problem. People think you are on a diet and exercising and have an enormous amount of self-discipline.

You know this is not true and worry you are sick with something, even though the doctors check for everything obvious. They assure you that your metabolism is perfect, and you are in wonderful — no, admirable— health. A woman’s waistline, they tell you, is a reliable indicator of other issues.

So you thank people for noticing, even as the comments get more barbed. You can’t tell if the women are looking at you with envy, pity, or disgust, which flavor of bitter judgment it is they’ve made about you. You get used to them disliking you, though this too is a cliché that grates on you. But the men… them you find intolerable.

You’ve seen that look before, and you like it now even less. You could slip through a banister, are swayed by a stiff breeze. You’re barely more substantial than a water cracker, and they think you’re fucking delicious.

You start counting your calories in a notebook. If calories input are greater than calories burned, you are scientifically guaranteed to gain weight. You calculate your activity needs (none, now, you are too tired), take the base of 2000 calories, and add 500 as a margin of error. You add another 500 every week this fails to work.

You think about nothing but food now. Calories, fat, protein, complex carbohydrates. This has become your job, to get enough in your body to keep it your body. The last time you weighed yourself the number of pounds on the scale was a shockingly low two-digit number, but you have been eating more than enough to increase that mass. You must be.

You gave up on eating healthy weeks ago, panicking at the meager number a salad added to your total. You subsist on sausages, butter, sugary syrups. You have grown accustomed to a constant feeling of nausea and disgust. You take vitamins as an apology to yourself.

There is no need to keep checking the scale. All you need to do is eat, even if the food feels like styrofoam in your mouth, even if it strains your shrunken stomach. You have dreams about chewing, chewing and swallowing, and wake up covered in sweat. But you know that if you keep eating, the next weigh-in will show improvement.

It does not show improvement. You go to the health clinic, thinking today will be the day that you are declared unwell, that they will hook you to tubes of glucose. Your hand is trembling, not from the cold (though you feel cold all the time) but from the lack of energy. Your fingers are like sticks of sucked-down candy.

The nurse behind the counter smiles beautifully at you, and you are grateful, thinking she must be exceptionally kind; no one has smiled at you that way in months. “Oh hello!” she says. “What a pretty girl you are!” She is lovely herself, glowing with health, and looks around your age.

You meet her again at the scales where you weigh in. The number is lower. You wonder how long your organs, your brain and heart, can go on functioning. You look at the nurse expectantly, biting your lip.

She does not seem alarmed by what she sees on the blood pressure cuff, which you take as a good sign. She had to fetch the child’s cuff to fit your arm; less encouraging. She frowns at you, but perplexed, not angry. “Why are you here today?”

You lift your shirt to show her what used to be a softly rounded belly, then the flatness of abs, and has since sunk into something concave. Cavernous. “I have a weight problem.”

The sweet nurse gasps. “No, you are not fat! You look amazing! So, so good!”

You shake your head and point to the scale. “I’m medically underweight?”

“Oh?” the nurse says vaguely. “Are you?” You can see your reflection in the plastic anatomical chart hanging on the wall behind her. There is not much difference, your figure not only starkly defined but almost two-dimensional. “Well, keep up the good work!” She doesn’t see your face crumple; she’s hurrying away to help someone else.

The doctor, a man, asks if you’re a model. When you say you aren’t, he offers to make some calls to find an agent. His cousin knows some people.

You grasp the spare planes of your face, which resemble a skull from most angles. “I don’t even look human!” you scream. “I hate this, I can’t bear it!”

The doctor agrees, “That’s what’s so profoundly appealing. You don’t look like anything. Like you shouldn’t exist.” He diagnoses you as a work of art, a thing of beauty that belongs to all mankind. Your career, metaphorically but still destructively, explodes.

It’s impossible to tell, really — if your fans love your body so much because you hate it, or if they love it despite that, because it’s you. Eating, not eating, it all looks good on you, baby.

When the doctor says art, what he really means is you’ve got It, that power they talk about like it’s magic, when they want and hate it too much to name it outright. What they mean is, looking at you makes their dicks stand to attention. You have the physiological mind control of stealing blood from a guy’s brain. Taking something you didn’t ask for is still stealing.

Any of the unwanted could tell you how lucky you are. They'd curse you for thinking of it as a curse. If you asked it, these men would give you their money, their attention, their compulsively grasping hands. They have tried to give it, unasked. It is fair trade to give yourself: it costs you nothing but a pound of flesh. It is only inevitable that what is wanted should be consumed.

Any woman would die to be you.

Your corpse is the most elegant thing anyone has ever seen, they agree, and in ads for champagne with glasses whose legs are as thin as yours, its proportions are breathtaking.

for-brandon.raw_content:
"What I don't say now will be gone forever. I have one page left, the fire is burning, and I can't let it go to waste."

  • 

    close

    Info

    X

    Title: for Brandon
    Author: TheChunk
    More from This Author: The Chunk's Author Page

    ⚠️ Content warning: This article contains themes of grief and personal loss.

⚠️ content warning

I skipped work today, Brandon. Can you believe it? You had always said that the day I took off work would be the day the world ends. But today the world wouldn’t even pause. There were a million different people going to work this morning alongside me, drinking their coffee and reading the news as though all was well in the world. Maybe for them it really was, but I couldn't pretend to be one of them. I got as far as the subway, but my legs wouldn't let me make it to the platform. So I came to the only place I can always find on foot. I didn't call out sick. I didn't send an email. Let them look for me all they want: they'll never find me here.

I'm sure you'd laugh if you could see me now. Though it never took much to make you laugh at me, did it? Eight years of poring over city maps and blueprints, and I can't even find my way out of a scrapyard in Queens. But there's no map for this place. I've tried to draw one many times, stumbling over the corridors of rusted iron and thick black dust, but the lines never meet where they should. There's always an exit–sometimes it's close, sometimes it's far, but the only way to find it is to feel your way through. Today I'm just stumbling more than usual.

I've wanted to bring you here since the day I found this place. I know, at a glance it hardly seems remarkable, in the way that nothing in Queens ever seems remarkable. It's just piles of junk metal, right past a gate that's around a corner, behind a bodega, through a parking lot, and under an overpass. As though that doesn't describe all of Queens, from Astoria to South Ozone Park.

But it goes on for miles. It goes on for miles that Queens doesn’t have. Towers of steel, and sheets of rust, and a quiet that I’ve never heard elsewhere. I’ve sketched its corners for years, and I still don't know if it ends.

I would have brought you here when I had the chance, but I couldn't stop myself from waiting. Waiting for the right words, for the right moment, for the right opportunity. But I waited too long, and now there's nothing left to wait for.

Tonight I've gone deeper than I've ever gone before, but I've given up on answers. I've given up on sketches, and notes, and research. I've given up on waiting. It's getting dark, my phone is dead, and all I have now is this letter. So I've burned my notebooks. I’ve thrown them in a trash bin and set them alight. There's only one thing left to write, but I need the light to write it by, and the fire adds such a soft light to such a gray place.

I know I must look foolish, waiting until now. Every day for the last two years I could have written. So why tonight, Brandon? Words are best spent on those who can read them. But what I don't say now will be gone forever. I have one page left, the fire is burning, and I can't let it go to waste.

They say that when you lose someone, you're supposed to talk to people. You're supposed to share memories, and swap stories, and laugh, and cry, and stick together until the world starts to make sense again. But there's no one left in the department who knew you. The Department of Urban Studies is still just a place where people stop on their way to somewhere else. A place where people count the days until they leave.

I used to tell Miriam that once someone leaves the department, I forget them. I've gotten requests for letters of reference from researchers whose names I didn't recognize. They all blend together after a while, like drops of water in a river that have already flowed to the sea. I’ve said this loud, and I’ve said it often. I hope I never said it to you.

I could have built something out of the place, but I've never been much of a builder, have I? Things just tend to crystalize around me. It's as though the entire department has come to take my shape, just because I refuse to move out of the way. At this point, every junior researcher has been trained by me, and they follow my lead, whether I ask them to or not. They print hard copies of all their emails, and they keep the condiments in the break room in alphabetical order. They never ask why. They just accept that that’s the way it is.

But you're still a part of the department too, Brandon. No one on my team has met you, but they’ve all felt your presence. When they read the section in the site dress code prohibiting excessive makeup, they’re reading about you, whether they know it or not. No, you weren’t the first man at the site to wear makeup. But you were the first to do it so badly that they had to take action, weren't you? It’s in the site handbook now. It will be there forever.

I've left all your notes up in the break room. All the haikus scrawled on post-its on the cabinets and refrigerator. The glitter from your pen has faded, but the handwriting could only be yours: the I’s you would dot with hearts. The J's you would dot with hearts. The T’s you would cross with hearts. That's too many hearts, Brandon! No one can read them!

No one can read them, but I won't take them down.

Did you know that everyone on my team knows your name? When I explain to them that staff are no longer allowed to eat cinnamon buns out of the garbage–even if they’re “in a box and mostly whole”–I call it Brandon’s Law. I never tell them more. I’d rather leave them wondering. No one’s ever really known you who hasn't been left wondering.

I’m afraid I've made a habit out of wondering. I’ve been visiting this scrapyard for two years. I'm starting to think that wondering is all it was made for.

Why did I wait, Brandon? Why did I stay silent? This is exactly the kind of anomaly that could get the department up on its feet. We’d get funding. We’d get recognition. We’d get a reason for people to stay. But I never told anyone: Not Miriam. Not Director Davis. Not you.

The sun has already passed behind the skyline, and the tracks around me have started to fade from sight. There are a thousand footprints in the dust, but all of them are mine. Though I could follow them forever, they'll only ever lead me back in circles.

The night you asked me if you should quit was the night I found this place. It's not the reason I was late to see you, though. I was late because I knew you would be late. And what's the point of waiting in one place when there's so much of Queens left to explore?

The entrance was different back then. It's always different. A different shape, in a different place. But always right past a gate that's around a corner, behind a bodega, through a parking lot, and under an overpass. That part never changes. I don't think the junk piles were as high back then. Nor were the paths so narrow, nor the air quite as still. I barely had the time to explore it that night. After all, I might have been late, but I couldn't allow myself to be as late as you. But it was the first thing I would have told you about when I saw you, the first thing I could share: a discovery. A project. Maybe, in the best of all possible worlds, a collaboration that would last for years.

But you weren't late that night. You were already waiting for me, with a serious face, and the blouse you only ever wore when you had bad news. When you told me what you were thinking of doing, I could have taken you straight here. It was just a short walk away, past a gate that's around a corner and…well, you know the rest by now. We could have had a containment proposal drafted by midnight. Discoveries like this don't come often. They’d have paid us to explore this place for a decade just to prove there’s nothing on the other side.

But that wasn't what you wanted, was it, Brandon? This place was never built for you. I could give you every reason to stay and hope you would listen, but I could never make you want it. I could never make you want to be here the way I wanted you to be here.

When you asked me if you should leave, did you expect me to say no? Did you expect me to repeat the same things the rest of them said: that there’s no money in academia? That there’s nowhere to go from the Foundation but down? I could have done it, and you would have believed me. It might have even been true.

If you'd asked me what I’d wanted, I’d have told you to stay forever. I’d have told you that there's more to uncover in this city than can ever be found, and you could have a job here for life if you'd only ask. I’d have told you that this department needs to run on something other than quotas, and deadlines, and regret, and that no man can hold on to regret for long when you’re around.

But that's not what you asked me.

You asked me something else that night: you asked if I thought you were childish. When I said no, it wasn't to reassure you. I said no because I meant it. You’ve never been childish, but you've always been sweet. Sweet, and kind, and brave in all the little ways that men are never brave.

I'm the one who's childish, Brandon. I'm the one who never learned to use his words, the one who sulks and pouts when he has to be a grown-up about these things.

For all of my waiting, and all of my wondering, I still knew. I knew on your last day that I may never see you again. I knew when I saw you off at the front gate, with a handshake instead of a hug, that I was getting it wrong, and I may never have another chance to get it right. But never doesn't feel like never until it comes. There’s a part of my childish brain that still believes, however many times I tell it otherwise, that if I send you an email, you might still reply. That if I call you on the phone right now, you may answer. That if I send you this letter, I may get one back from you, written in smudged ink on rosy stationary, creased because you sat on it before you sent it, just like you would always do with the budgetary reports.

But you were gone for a reason. You were building your own world, far away from here, in places I would never visit, with friends I would never meet. You were finally free. So who was I to try to claw you back?

You had moved on. I was sure of it. Your silence told me that you had a thousand more concerns, and that to reach out now would just be an intrusion.

Did my silence make you think the same of me?

I told Miriam that of all the employees who ever left the department, you were the only one I’d miss. I told her because I hoped that she would tell you. I hoped that she would tell you, but I don't think she did.

So now my letter is almost done, and there’s no one left to read it. By now it's too dark to read anyway. The fire is almost out, and my hand is finding the lines in this notebook from muscle memory alone. My handwriting has always been straight, but I don't know if that will be enough this time.

Everyone still compliments me on my handwriting. For being straight. For being even. For being regular. You were the only one who teased me for it. Two more years of practice, you said, and I could get a job as a desktop printer. Well, it's been more than two years, Brandon. Seems I'm overdue for that promotion.

Maybe that’s why I never posted my haikus next to yours. Taped to the cabinet beside your sticky notes, they looked too official, too imposing, more like an order than a feeling. But thank you for reading them anyway. Did you find them in the garbage while you were looking for cinnamon buns? Or did you find cinnamon buns in the garbage while you were looking for haikus?

You know, there's a second half to Brandon’s Law. I never tell the staff this part, but I know it for myself. No, you're not allowed to eat cinnamon buns out of the garbage. But if someone else has already started, you have to help them finish. Because come on! They were in a box. And mostly whole. We couldn't just let a thing like that go to waste.

When you asked me if you should quit, you never asked me what I wanted. Maybe you didn't have to ask what you already knew. Because I might be bad at saying what I mean, but I’m even worse at hiding it.

I would write all night, but the page is done, and nothing more would fit in the margins. The fire is dead, the wind is quiet, and somewhere very far away from here is the hum of the streets, and the trains, and the buses that keep the world moving.

I may have said goodbye already, years ago at the front gate, but I didn't know how to mean it then. I wish I didn't know how to mean it now. So thank you, Brandon. For being a colleague. For being a friend. For being a bigger part of my life than you could know, and for allowing me the chance to be a tiny part of yours.

So I came to the only place I can always find on foot. I didn't call out sick. I didn't send an email. Let them look for me all they want: they'll never find me here. I'm sure you'd laugh if you could see me now. Though it never took much to make you laugh at me, did it? Eight years of poring over city maps and blueprints, and I can't even find my way out of a scrapyard in Queens. But there's no map for this place. I've tried to draw one many times, stumbling over the corridors of rusted iron and thick black dust, but the lines never meet where they should. There's always an exit–sometimes it's close, sometimes it's far, but the only way to find it is to feel your way through. Today I'm just stumbling more than usual. I've wanted to bring you here since the day I found this place. I know, at a glance it hardly seems remarkable, in the way that nothing in Queens ever seems remarkable. It's just piles of junk metal, right past a gate that's around a corner, behind a bodega, through a parking lot, and under an overpass. As though that doesn't describe all of Queens, from Astoria to South Ozone Park. But it goes on for miles. It goes on for miles that Queens doesn’t have. Towers of steel, and sheets of rust, and a quiet that I’ve never heard elsewhere. I’ve sketched its corners for years, and I still don't know if it ends. They print hard copies of all their emails, and they keep the condiments in the break room in alphabetical order. They never ask why. They just accept that that’s the way it is. The J's you would dot with hearts. The T’s you would cross with hearts. That's too many hearts, Brandon! No one can read them! No one can read them, but I won't take them down. For Every Soldier, A Child

Pandora Bowe knelt at the grave of a man she did not know. She wept, knowing the one she wanted watched, just out of sight. She laid flowers, stem by stem, allowing the last thorns to prick her finger, blood pooling on her thumb. She made a show of wiping her tears away, the blood smeared under her somehow pristine mascara.

Always performing. Pandora stood, staring at the tombstone. Nothing more than ends to a mean.

"Did… did you know Nathan?"

Pandora turned, acting surprised as she saw her target before her. Like a loquacious and malicious predator, she toyed with them. "I'm sorry, I didn't want to disturb anybody with my visit. I thought that I would be alo—"

"No, please— " The woman before her gasped and let out a sob. She was pleading, begging, desperate for answers. "I just can't believe he's gone. One day he was—"

"You're Nathan's wife?" Pandora waited, patiently.

"Y— yes." Of course she was. "Did you work with Nathan?"

Nathanial Flitterman was a Foundation agent, part of MTF Theta-12, one of the nameless, meaningless divisions that was most likely somehow under Pandora's command. Not that she made a habit out of visiting the graves of the fallen fodder, mind you, but there was something greater at stake here.

I wonder how much she knew. Pandora nodded. "Did he… what did he tell you about his work?"

"That it was dangerous. I knew that I just—"

"It's okay," Pandora mimicked, her voice matching the widow's in tone and timbre. She crossed the little gap remaining between them, holding the woman close. As she did, Pandora rolled her eyes. "I wasn't ready for his passing either. I can't imagine what you must be going through, nor… you had a son together, right?"

As the woman sobbed into Pandora's shoulder, a fact that irritated her, she could barely string together sounds, let alone a coherent sentence.

I'm going to have to dry clean this. What a worthless woman, she is nothing more than an accessory to her dead husband. Even in death, he is still more relevant than she. Of course, there was more to Agent Flitterman than just a nameless pawn in one of countless games; there was something that Pandora had spent far too much money on to let it go to waste. Thus, here she was, standing in the midst of a field of graves she couldn't give a shit about, supporting a weeping widow.

It's pitiful. I don't even visit my own father's grave, to think I came all this way just for a simpering, sobbing timewaster.

Pandora had enough of the woman's seemingly endless tears. It was time to be more actively supportive.

"Mrs. Flitterman, let me take you somewhere warmer. We can talk more there. Is there a cafe, a park or maybe you—"

"My house," Mrs. Flitterman supplied through sniffling. "It's not far."

"Lead the way." Pandora nodded, having already known that to be the case. Without waiting for the widow, she began to guide her towards her house, nodding all the while to the woman's depressed babbling.

The things I do for people. Pandora brushed snot off of her lapel in disgust. What can I say, I am truly generous.

The hovel was run-down, bland and average, the ideal vision of a failed suburban dream. Despite this, Mrs. Flitterman seemed to take pride in her surroundings, each frame on the mantle dusted, as if that made a difference. Pandora had been in many homes just like this, she knew exactly who the Flittermans were.

The imperfect American dream, resolute in the face of economic depression, withering away as our country rots from Washington. She scrambles to hold onto the visage of normalcy, ignorant that the white picket fence peels with each winter. She was waiting on a husband who lied, a man who told her no truths and was as absent as he is now.

The grandfather clock in the hallway chimed, as Mrs. Flitterman returned, carrying a tray of tea. Pandora had not asked for any. She acquiesced.

"You have a… welcoming house." Pandora smiled gently, sipping on her tea. God, this is bland.

"Thank you. I… it was hard, with Nathan being away so often. I tried my best, but, there are just some things only a man can do, you know?"

"I do." Pandora nodded. Not that I can think of any.

"You said that you worked with my Nathan? Can you… nobody told me anything. One day he was calling, saying good night to Joshua, and the next—" Mrs. Flitterman began to choke up, fighting away another wave of sobs. "They sent him home in a box, miss… I'm sorry, I don't think I got your name."

That's correct. Pandora forced her face to one of sympathy. "My name is General Bowe, and I was Nathan's commanding officer."

"A General came all this way, because of Nathan?" The woman was astounded, rightly so.

It didn't really matter that Pandora lacked the official rank, nor the station to use the title; it was her birthright, one she claimed with pride. Speaking of birthrights…

"He was an incredible man. Doing dangerous work, keeping our country safe from terrorists and threats around the world."

Mrs. Flitterman nodded, as if her greatest xenophobic suspicions were confirmed. "Was it…"

"He died bravely." Pandora pulled on the twisted threads the woman projected, their family tapestry unravelling before her eyes. "He was stopping a bomb, set by… I'm sorry, but the name of the terrorist cell is classified. I hope you can understand, regardless of that, your husband served his country to the very end."

"Thank you for telling me," the widow eked out, staring at the portrait sitting on the mantle. "I had no idea he was doing such important work."

He wasn't. Pandora kept that to herself, amongst many things. He worked at the Foundation, firing bullets at what we told him to, throwing his life in harms way to move the needle slightly to our side. He didn't make a difference, he didn't make a mark, he barely gave me a reason to remember him.

Pandora reminded herself of her mission. But what a salient reason indeed.

She leaned forward in her seat, setting the teacup on the coffee table, upon a coaster. An air of intensity began to brew, as Pandora manipulated the woman's emotions like a puppet on strings. She paused, waiting for Mrs. Flitterman to make the first move.

"What is it?"

And there it is. Pandora looked up at the woman, passion burning behind her eyes, the same fervent feeling she once held for the flag radiating out.

"Mrs. Flitterman, your husband was working with me, directly, on a project of international importance. We were creating a device, a machine that could protect the United States from a threat before the enemy could even launch their weapons." A quarter-truth, at best, but enough to bait the hook.

"I had no idea…" Mrs. Flitterman shook her head, worried. "Why… why are you telling me?"

For as bland as she is, at least she knows to jump when I call.

"I wouldn't, not under any other circumstances but…" Pandora paused, building the tension in the room. "Nathan told me many stories about your son—"

What was his name? Pandora hesitated, trying to recall the uninspired choice that Mrs. Flitterman had said just a few minutes prior.

"Joshua?"

Thank you.

"Yes, he told me so much about Joshua. He cared about your son more than anything else in the world. There is nothing that can compare to a father's love for his son, did you know that?"

"He… he never seemed like—"

"Nonsense," Pandora interrupted, plying the woman further. "I have seen fathers, mothers, countless parents who all love their families. I have seen men and women sacrifice themselves, just so their loved ones back home might live to see another day, and I have watched those same men and women fight until their dying breath because they cannot wait to come home."

Mrs. Flitterman began to cry, and Pandora pushed the advantage.

"But Nathan? Nathan blew all of them away. He was so dedicated, so assured that what he was doing now would protect both of you, give Joshua the life that he deserved… he would have done anything. In fact, he did."

"I'm sorry, I don't understand. What do you mean?"

This is almost too easy.

"Nathan was at the center of our research, and we had calibrated the device to him. Unfortunately, he passed before we could ensure that the device functioned properly." Pandora put her hand on the other woman's knee, trying her best not to show any distaste for the cheap tights. "They want to cancel the project entirely. I told them that we could rework the machine to another biological signature, but they refused to give me the funding unless I could prove that the device would work as intended."

That should be enough. Pandora sat back in her chair, sighing intentionally, lips tight.

"So… what are you saying? That… that Nathan died before you could—"

"It was terrible. He died fighting to save the rest of his team, he didn't care about the cost. His bravery was incomparable, but…" Pandora nodded, as if the woman had found some profound idea. "Yes, you are right. He died before we could do anything, and now a decade of research is going to go to waste. I've tried to plead the case, but unless we can prove that it works— I'm sorry, I don't need to burden you with my problems, this isn't something you can fix. I apologize, sincerely. It seems that my emotions got the best of me."

Pandora was tired of the charade, no matter how well she might have played it. There was little joy to be found in treading the same boards, tugging the same strings, playing the same hapless citizens like a lyre. Still, she was close to her goal, and knew exactly what was needed to get what she wanted.

So, Pandora waited. Silently. The clock in the hall swung back and forth, noisily passing by the seconds, as Pandora stared at her reflection in the disgusting cup of fluid the woman had called 'tea'. She was ready to leave, when, just as she knew would happen, Mrs. Flitterman lit up.

"Wait!" Mrs. Flitterman grabbed Pandora's hand, excitedly. "You said that it was linked to Nathan's genetics, right? His DNA?"

"It was, which is why—"

"What about Joshua?"

Thank you for making this easy.

"I… yes, that would work, but I wouldn't want to—"

"What would you need from him?" Mrs. Flitterman was in a fervor, staring at the portrait of her dead husband. "If there's something that Joshua can do to honor his father's legacy, a way that we can make it all worthwhile… We have to. For Nathan's sake."

Pandora sat back, waiting an appropriate amount of time that a more sensitive person might to consider the merits of testing a weapon with a child, before nodding.

"I… I think that would work. It wouldn't be much, just a few tests, all conducted over a weekend, four days at most but… Mrs. Flitterman, I… I think you just saved the United States billions of dollars. This is… incredibly selfless of you."

"Let me go get Joshua, I'm sure he'll understand." As the frantic woman scurried away up their stairs, Pandora allowed herself to smile. It didn't take all that long this time, she mused, checking her watch.

Once the mother had proposed the idea to use her own son, in the legacy of his father — a choice Pandora knew that she would make, just as all mothers would — the rest of the afternoon was a formality.

As Pandora walked down the steps to the Flitterman's house, she contacted a nearby Foundation site, and arranged a time for them to come pick up Joshua Flitterman. The boy had been reluctant at first, but when Pandora explained that he would get to play a video game to shoot down terrorists, the boy nodded in excitement, readily obliging.

Of course, there were no terrorists, nor was it a game. Pandora pulled the schematics up on her phone, reviewing the machine — yes, even with a child, it should still work. Once they got it up and running, he would be transferred into a conceptual-digital consciousness, ready to influence the Noosphere directly. While Nathan was the preference, due to his MTF training and loyalty to the cause, Pandora was sure that a few months in the digital purgatory would turn Joshua into quite the pliable thing, ready to come when she called, fighting on her behalf. From there, well — the sky was the limit.

Actually, this may be for the best. A child has not only an imagination, but their minds are more willing to accept the unknown. Joshua…. yes, he may be exactly what I was looking for. If I can change the very thoughts people are having…

Pandora grinned devilishly, putting the phone back into her pocket. As soon as she left their yard, Pandora forgot about Mrs. Flitterman, unimportant, her use having dried up.

Funny. Mrs. Flitterman will soon do the same for Joshua.

Pandora watched the sun crest from behind a cloud, blinding her eyes as she reveled in the warmth. She had done it, taken a loss and turned it back into a victory — just as she had, countless times before.

For each end, a means. For each soldier, a child. All ready, waiting for my command.

Maybe, today was a good day.

foresee-obstacles.raw_content:
We played hide and seek in waterfalls
We were younger, we were younger

Dr. Lunar Ludarium turns her computer off and packs up her stationary as the clock ticks silently in the distance. Suddenly, her exit is blocked by Dr. Kazuki Minerva.

"Where you headed?" He asks, like he has any right to know.

"None of your business," Lunar responds, not even glancing in his direction as she moves things around in her purse.

"Its 8:30PM Loo. You don't usually stay this late unless you've got something on your mind." He awkwardly places a hand on her shoulder, much to her dismay.

"Since when did you psychoanalyse people?" Lunar glances at Kazuki.

"When you don't talk to anyone, you've got a lot of time to think. So…" Kazuki removes his hand and leans against the wall of the cubicle. "What's wrong?"

Lunar stares at the man. The utter audacity he must have to think she could tell him anything. His expression is unreadable, neither one of pity or of concern but something in the muddled grey. Lunar stands and walks through the now open exit of the cubicle.

"I don't have to tell you anything." She mutters as she does.

"But it would help, wouldn't it?" He retorts. Lunar turns and glares at Kazuki, who now leans against the cubicle's outer wall.

"You wouldn't understand."

"Then you could talk to someone who does."

"Bye." Lunar turns and leaves, her pace hastened with annoyance. Kazuki lingers in the empty halls of Site-3 for another half hour. He wonders if he went about talking to her the wrong way.

We playеd hide and seek in waterfalls
We wеre younger, we were younger

Lunar steps out into the open night, the freezing, whispering winds flowing through the streets with ease. She takes a deep breath and turns right. It isn't long before the solid stone transitions into uneven dirt as the breeze is silenced by foliage.

"Screw him." She mutters on instinct. Her expression shifts to confusion for a second, contemplating if Kazuki's questions affected her. It returns to forced indifference, mentally denying the thoughts.

Lunar turns the corner and strides through the shallow river, passing from one forest to another. She walks a familiar unmarked trail, one which reeks of wayward souls of lingering unprocessed emotions. A bug chirps as it is crushed by her boot. A twig falls in her path and is snapped in two.

Her footsteps echo now, the winds incapable of sound.

She places her hand on the greyed oak, running it along the recognisable markings. She stares at the path ahead, one which gets drastically steeper with each step, one where the wind flows freely. She takes a deep breath.

Lunar climbs the small cliff.

We played hide and seek in waterfalls
We were younger, we were younger

The yard of identical sedimentary shapes stretches out across the clearing, long since abandoned for the flashy beachside view. A crow lands on a tree branch five metres away from Lunar, who stands in front of the newest looking stone in the yard.

The words etched onto it are familiar to her, all too so. She sighs, opens her purse, removes a small candle and places it in front the rectangular rock. With a concealed lighter, she ignites a small flame, which illuminates the the recognisable words.

Mandrigoria Golden

1982-2000

May She Rest In Piece

She breathes in deeply as the memories flicker into view.

"Hey dude." She manages to push through. "A lot of… crazy shit has happened… recently. But hey, I see you're doing well."

The grave cannot respond.

"Ha. You've still got it." Lunar sighs "Greatest comedian ever."

The grave cannot respond.

"Anyways, happy birthday man! How old are you now, 30?"

The grave cannot respond.

"That's crazy. It feels like just yesterday when we were kids."

The crow chirps.

"We used to do some much together… and then we… drifted apart…"

The grave cannot respond. The flame starts to flicker out.

"It… you meant so much to me. If only you… if only the world hadn't taken you from me."

Lunar lets one tear fall. The flame flickers more intensely.

"I know I never said it when you were here but…"

The flame flickers out. The grave cannot respond.

"I love you."

Lunar can only stare at the rock in front of her. Below it lay no body, for it had been incinerated long ago. She didn't want it to, but how could she have a choice? She was just a friend at the time. That's all they ever were. Lunar stands and leaves the graveyard.

There is nothing left to say.

She will return.

Again…

And again…

And again…

And again…

And again…

Forever.

We played hide and seek in waterfalls
We were younger, we were younger

Someday we will foresee obstacles
Through the blizzard, through the blizzard

Twenty-Fifth

SNAPSHOTS OF THE HAZE

TBD

[[size 90%]]And again...[[/size]] [[size 70%]]And again...[[/size]] [[size 50%]]And again...[[/size]] [[size 30%]]And again...[[/size]] [[size 10%]]Forever.[[/size]] ------ [[=]] //We played hide and seek in waterfalls// //We were younger, we were younger// //Someday we will foresee obstacles// //[[[https://youtu.be/GEmLF0DgjLQ|Through the blizzard, through the blizzard]]]// [[/=]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:earthworm | first=false | last=false | hub=yes | previous-url=https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/twenty-fifth | previous-title=Twenty-Fifth | next-url=/ | next-title=TBD | hub-url=/ | hub-title=SNAPSHOTS OF THE HAZE ]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box-end]]

            position: initial;
            width: var(--body-width-on-desktop, 45.75rem);
            max-width: var(--body-width-on-desktop, 45.75rem);
            max-height: 100%;
            margin: 0 auto;

            top: 0;
            left: 0;

            min-width: var(--sidebar-width-on-desktop, 13.6rem) !important;
            max-height: 100vh;
            padding-right: 2.5rem;
            padding-left: 0.5rem;

            transition:

            background-color: rgba(var(--sidebar-bg-color, 255, 255, 255), 1);

        }

            transition:

            background: url("https://scp-wiki.wdfiles.com/local--files/component%3Acollapsible-sidebar/sidebar-tab.svg");

            background-size: 1rem 12.875rem;
            pointer-events: none;

            left: calc(var(--sidebar-width-on-desktop, 14.5rem) * -1);
            width: 0rem;
            transition:
                left 300ms cubic-bezier(0.4, 0.0, 0.2, 1),
                background-position 300ms cubic-bezier(0.4, 0.0, 0.2, 1),
                opacity 300ms cubic-bezier(0.4, 0.0, 0.2, 1);

            background-position: center left calc(var(--sidebar-width-on-desktop, 14.5rem) * -1);
            font-size: 0em;

            position: absolute;
            z-index: 9;
            top: var(--final-header-height-on-desktop, 0);
            left: 0;
            width: var(--sidebar-width-on-desktop, 14.5rem);

            background-color: rgb(var(--swatch-alternate-color, 0, 0, 0));
