0600

"AUFWACHEN!"

Ames Fabré jumped out of his bed and fell right to the cold, hard floor as the Wehrmacht soldier stood above him. For the first few seconds, he just looked at the man, standing there armed like a scared animal, before finally scrambling up to his feet and throwing his blanket back on the bedding. Wordlessly, he collected himself, sneaking only a brief glance at the clock at the wall. He realized he was supposed to wake up five minutes ago.

The daily routine had exhausted him beyond all ability to resist. Hours and hours of daily spellcasting, with only minutes to eat or drink something in between. He knew what aim these industrialized rituals served, they all knew. And they all knew just how powerless they were to stop what was to come.

"Raum Einunddreißig. Jetzt!"

At the very least, he refused to fall into despair. During every session of mindless chanting, rune or sigil he had drawn, every sacrifice he made, he thought of his family. Charging at a guard and getting himself killed wouldn't help them. He promised them they will meet again once this is over, he promised his wife to embrace her, he promised his son to talk to him once more. Will they even recognise him after all of this? He lacked the answer, but he didn't lack hope. Every free minute, he hoped and prayed that something, someone, was going to stop this before the final ritual. But the time was drawing near.

MA OO

OOO AAAI

A EEE OOO

ON AAAAAN

He exclaimed, to the room full of mystics, occultists, Kabbalists, Gnostics and Angeologists. The ritual circle between them, drawn in a mixture of blood and salt, now radiated heat too hot to bear. The robes each of them wore made existence in it for longer than a few minutes even harder. But neither Jean nor anyone else in the room could even dare to exit for a break without permission from the guards. They've all seen what happened to the few who attempted it, or at least heard it. The guards took take them out of the room first, before the shots rang out. As the chanting and ritual movements continued, Jean finally saw what all of them have been dreading now for months. A glow. A bright, white glow, right from the center of the ritual circle.

In that moment, his hope had finally left him, for the last and final time. He fell to his knees, clutching his chest. As the figure before him materialized, there was only a single word on his lips.

"Mon Dieu!"

0730

Samuel Collins' squad could see the grey, brutalist building in the distance. The facility extended in all directions, branching out into sub-buildings and snaking surface tunnels of reinforced steel. There was a method to the madness of Fritsch-IV, even if they couldn't comprehend it from the ground. They've all seen the aerial photographs, after all. The whole complex was a sigil, thaumaturgic in nature. What for? Who cared. They were there to blow up the Obskurakorps scum, not psychoanalyze them.

"I'm detecting a sudden rise in Elan-Vital, Captain. Readings suggest a massive thaumaturgic ritual, likely still ongoing." Private Adi Wilson whispered as he gazed in a mixture of shock and amazement down at the EVE meter in his hands. The bulky device showed levels that, normally, could only be picked up were it strapped to a participant of a particularly resource-intensive ritual. And here he was picking it up from a mile and a half away. "Are you sure it is safe to continue, Captain?"

Collins furrowed by brows, but shortly afterwards, shook his head "We're not abandoning our mission now, Private. Continue forward!" He barked out, making the sign of the cross. "Protection spells, boys. We'll need them."

As the crew descended down the hill and into a thick forest below, that assumption was proven correct. Only a few meters inside and the trees around them were covered by cognitohazardous sigils. Nothing lethal, of course, all of them had undergone their inoculations years ago. Still, all who even caught a glimpse of them felt an omnipresent feeling of warmth and headsplitting headaches, looking down at the ground being only a brief remedy. And a very deadly one as well.

"Stop!" Collins grabbed the private in front of him, as he almost walked face-first into a steel wire, designed to catch any fool staring at the ground off guard. It connected right to a M39, perfectly at head height "Keep your heads up, boys. Shrapnel's gonna hurt much more than whatever this is"

Finally, the trees parted and the complex was once more visible. Much closer now, the squad could see some kind of white glow, coming out of the majority of its windows. Anxiously getting into positions, the commandos found…no one outside. There were only a few transport trucks parked in front of the facility, no security detail or watchtowers. The only sign of life was a faint chanting coming from somewhere deep inside, escaping the open windows as an echo. Still looking through his iron sights, Collins ordered the team to check their antimemetic munitions.

"Full magazines, Captain" The antimeme specialist whispered, confirming that no firefight had taken place outside of the squad's memory. A headcount proved no discrepancies either. "Should we prepare the Eve-Bomb, Captain"

"Affirmative"

And so, their weapon of choice began its assembly. It was a simple, metal sphere, covered in thaumaturgic symbols and containing passages from half a dozen spells. All that was needed was some careful handling and a few nuts to screw it into place. Once ready, it would neutralize all magic in a 2 kilometer radius. That, and level a few city blocks on its way. Just as two squad members struggled with attaching the detonation mechanism, however, something changed. Wilson's face, already covered in sweat, turned pale as he shook his EVE detector.

"Captain, we have an- we have a problem" He said, wiping his eyes and looking at the building. The glow in its windows had ceased, and so had the chanting. "Captain, the readings are at…the readings are at zero, Captain"

"Wha-"

Only a flash of light followed.

0910

Two men sat at a balcony overlooking the alps, one balding and one still with his full set of hair. Both wearing an undercut. The former had, just earlier that day, downed close to a full bottle of champagne. The latter found no use for such degenerate practices, he much preferred opiates and amphetamines, like a true Aryan.

"According to our schedule, The Rite should now be completed, Mein Fuhrer. Obskurakorps units are ready to strike on all fronts the moment we have confirmation" The balding man answered, suppressing a smile.

"Wunderbar! I'm impressed with you, Himmler. Seems I had been correct with giving you a second chance after the…fiasco, back in Tibet" He answered, with a serious tone to his voice. Somehow, Herr Himmler found little appreciation in the Fuhrer's words "I can picture it already, the black boots of the master race stomping their way across Moscow, wiping the untermenschen under their boots…"

"So can I, Mein Fuhrer. I assure you, we're only months away from bearing witness to that"

He smiled. Today was the start of a new era. Today was victory.

0923

Somewhere in Europe, a shockwave was felt.

Somewhere in Germany, a church had crumbled.

Somewhere in Berlin, the ground had shattered.

1115

Heather was running as fast as his feet allowed him.

The corridors of Site-01 seemed to drag on forever. The newly recruited assistant felt as if he was the minotaur, running through the infinite smooth, cold walls of a labyrinth designed specifically to trap him. Unlike the minotaur, however, he had a task to perform.

"Fuck! Sorry, sorry, 7's that way, right?" The guard, currently picking himself up from the floor, stared at him dumbfounded. Heather shook his head "Nevermind, I'll be on my way."

In an office at the end of the hallways sat an older woman, her movements robotic and her skin seemingly stretched too thin for her skeleton. She was spending her working hours like every day, signing documents, approving budget changes, reviewing intelligence findings. A lot of intelligence findings, as the bags under her eyes gave away. She hardly even reacted as her door blew open and the red-headed, young gentleman barged in.

"Madam, we've received reports from sites all over the world, they're recording sudden swings in Akiva, EVE, even Hume meters are malfunctioning. Anomalies, mostly theological, are being reported all over, we're having breaches left and ri-" The young man stopped, as the firm voice of 05-7 cut him off.

"Calm down, Andrew. I want you to slowly explain to me, which sites have reported these fluctuations, and which are currently undergoing a breach. Do you understand?" She asked with a calm voice and an almost relaxed tone, looking straight at the shaking and panting man before her.

"That's the issue, Madam. All of them have. And… and Sites-19, -17, -45, -63 are, Madam"

For the first in decades, 05-7's dried skin cracked into a look of genuine concern.

1208

Collins' head was ringing, and his body felt on fire. He couldn't feel his right leg, and wished he could say the same about the rest of his limbs. Opening his eyes, he was met with nothing but light. Not the same blinding light that struck him earlier, nor that of the pearly gates. It was a light of something large, descending far from beyond the clouds.

"Wilson!" He yelled with the last remnants of his voice. At least his throat was intact "Private Wilson! Specialist Michaels!"

But no one answered him, not even the sound of branches swaying in the wind. The explosion had levelled all the trees around him. His brief moment of lucidity was very quickly fading, as the pain and blood loss began to have their effect on him. It was a miracle that he had even lived this long, he thought to himself.

"A miracle…" He whispered, looking up above him. At the bright ship, or plane, or city. He saw the chariots, the wheels, the wings ascending from it, just as his vision began to blur. As his heart gave out, a smile appeared on his mouth.

"Give 'em hell, boys"

1545

"Fine! Fine! If you want to go out like the vermin, go ahead!"

Hans Reuter stormed out of the Reichpost building, cursing back all the cowards who remained in hiding. Berlin was under attack, and he wasn't going to make himself into a sitting duck now. A wave of relief rushed over him as he saw his Benz 770, still in one piece, waiting for him as expected. He knew the coating of holy water and the dozen protection spells weren't for nothing. It was just a matter of time until either the judeo-bolsheviks or the filthy western capitalists stooped so low as to send infernal forces for him. Demonology is an Aryan science, God damn it!

"Herr-Herr Reuter, I-I-I am so glad to see you I" His chauffeur was covered in tears and sweat, his heartbeat seemingly audible. His words were muffled by the screams and roars happening all around the car. "Wha-why-where are we-was that-"

"Shut up! Out of Berlin, now!" His employer yelled, swinging luger like a club. "Don't even think about slowing down or stopping, understand?"

He didn't answer, just hitting the gas. The city around them was in utter chaos. Black figures soared through the sky. Clouds of smoke billowed across the sky. Some from the direction of the Kroll Opera, some from the Schutzstaffel headquarters. Around them, hundreds of civilians ran, most not even knowing what they were running from. Neither of the men knew how they haven't even hit a single one yet.

"Halt!" An Ordnungspolizei officer yelled at them, blowing into a whistle. It seemed that he was trying to set up an evacuation route, with a few others joining him in that fruitless pursuit. Before Hans could tell his driver to ignore it, or run him over, he suddenly looked downwards. Right at a crack on the ground. "What in heaven's-"

A figure emerged from the hole, covered in fur wet with a red liquid. It was as tall as a lamppost, had the horns of a goat and the maw of a wolf, but the gait of a man. Seconds after it ascended, it just grabbed him, right by the throat. Right after, it squeezed it, crushing the flesh and muscle while spraying blood across both it and the now-dead man. The other officers opened fire, the bullets tearing holes through its body. It, meanwhile, slowly turned its head towards the car. It did not even flinch as the gunshots continued.

"Go! Go, before it breaks through the spells!"

And just like that, the car turned around and started going in the opposite direction. As they drove away, the figure remained in the back view mirror, staring at them. Without consulting his driver, Hans tore it down. No looking back now, he said it himself. They either get out of the city, or they're sharing the fate of that officer.

And it seemed that they had gotten away. The chaos was more or less equal across Berlin, but not, at the outskirts, they could see the safety of the countryside. No plumes of smoke, no distant demonic figures. As they passed a factory, only earlier in the day used to print propaganda, they sighed in relief.

By the time they turned their heads down towards the road again, it was too late, a rift having opened in the ground. Its insides glowed in hues of red and orange. By the time the brake was hit, the front wheels were already at the edge of the abyss.

The last thing they smelled was the sulfur.

2015

05-7's office was a mess of papers, stamps and spilled ink. With the council unable to host its emergency meeting until the next day, due to over half of 05's being currently present outside of Site-01, she and her colleagues were now the supreme authority within the Foundation. She herself was in charge of declining or approving emergency measures, be they the mass amnesticization of whole towns or use of D-class as field agents. The times were desperate. At least she had the opened package of pervitin on her desk to help her. It was the only thing she appreciated the Germans for.

Her hand slammed down the "DECLINE" stamp on the proposal for the usage of anomalous weapons to combat the angelic entities currently present over most of France, just as the door to her office swung open.

"We've received a letter, Madam. Addressed straight to the Overwatch Council." Heather said, panting. Unlike her, he lacked access to drugs which could help him get through. His face was covered in sweat and his hair was messier than usual. "It was found wedged under the front door, we're…not sure who it is from, or how it got there. We showed it to a D-I mean D-Class-to test for cognitohazards, none found"

"Thank you" was all she had to say as she nodded her head. She looked at the opened envelope and slowly extracted the piece of paper. The first thing she saw was the logo. A pentagram, surrounded by stems of wheat. Finally, she thought to herself. The Initiative was going to tell her what in the heavens was going on.

To all members of the Overwatch Council

The Allied Occult Initiative has been made aware of a thaumaturgical ritual of unknown purposes, performed this morning at a facility presumed to be under control of the SS-Ahnenerbe Obskurakorps, an occult branch of the Schutzstaffel organization. According to all available data, the ritual has resulted in the increased effeciency of all known thaumaturgic rituals and, more importantly, the sudden severance of barriers between religious beings and the material world. As reported by troops under our command, this includes both Angelic and Infernal entities.

We currently estimate that the Global Veil System, as dictated by the 1885 convention of the General Assembly of Thaumaturgists and Theologists, may collapse over the coming weeks.

In light of this crisis, the AOI leadership requests an emergency meeting with representatives of the Overwatch Council of the Special Containment Procedures Foundation, with the goal of coming to a consensus regarding the response and recovery efforts, in addition to the future of the veiled world.

With highest regards
Derry Cornelius Al-Fine, Head Negotiator of the Allied Occult Initiative.

/

Paradise Lost

To be continued...

Shrapnel's gonna hurt much more than whatever this is" Finally, the trees parted and the complex was once more visible. Much closer now, the squad could see some kind of white glow, coming out of the majority of its windows. Anxiously getting into positions, the commandos found...no one outside. There were only a few transport trucks parked in front of the facility, no security detail or watchtowers. The only sign of life was a faint chanting coming from somewhere deep inside, escaping the open windows as an echo. Still looking through his iron sights, Collins ordered the team to check their antimemetic munitions. "Full magazines, Captain" The antimeme specialist whispered, confirming that no firefight had taken place outside of the squad's memory. A headcount proved no discrepancies either. "Should we prepare the Eve-Bomb, Captain" "Affirmative" And so, their weapon of choice began its assembly.  It was a simple, metal sphere, covered in thaumaturgic symbols and containing passages from half a dozen spells. All that was needed was some careful handling and a few nuts to screw it into place. Once ready, it would neutralize all magic in a 2 kilometer radius. That, and level a few city blocks on its way. Just as two squad members struggled with attaching the detonation mechanism, however, something changed. Wilson's face, already covered in sweat, turned pale as he shook his EVE detector. "Captain, we have an- we have a problem" He said, wiping his eyes and looking at the building. The glow in its windows had ceased, and so had the chanting. "Captain, the readings are at...the readings are at zero, Captain" "Wha-" Only a flash of light followed. [[=]] +  **0910** ----- [[/=]] Two men sat at a balcony overlooking the alps, one balding and one still with his full set of hair. Both wearing an undercut. The former had, just earlier that day, downed close to a full bottle of champagne. The latter found no use for such degenerate practices, he much preferred opiates and amphetamines, like a true Aryan. "According to our schedule, The Rite should now be completed, Mein Fuhrer. Obskurakorps units are ready to strike on all fronts the moment we have confirmation" The balding man answered, suppressing a smile. "Wunderbar! I'm impressed with you, Himmler. Seems I had been correct with giving you a second chance after the...fiasco, back in Tibet" He answered, with a serious tone to his voice. Somehow, Herr Himmler found little appreciation in the Fuhrer's words "I can picture it already, the black boots of the master race stomping their way across Moscow, wiping the untermenschen under their boots..." "So can I, Mein Fuhrer. I assure you, we're only months away from bearing witness to that" He smiled. Today was the start of a new era. Today was victory. [[=]] +  **0923** ----- [[/=]] Somewhere in Europe, a shockwave was felt. Somewhere in Germany, a church had crumbled. Somewhere in Berlin, the ground had shattered. [[=]] +  **1115** ----- [[/=]] Heather was running as fast as his feet allowed him. The corridors of Site-01 seemed to drag on forever. The newly recruited assistant felt as if he was the minotaur, running through the infinite smooth, cold walls of a labyrinth designed specifically to trap him. Unlike the minotaur, however, he had a task to perform. "Fuck! Sorry, sorry, 7's that way, right?" The guard, currently picking himself up from the floor, stared at him dumbfounded. Heather shook his head "Nevermind, I'll be on my way." In an office at the end of the hallways sat an older woman, her movements robotic and her skin seemingly stretched too thin for her skeleton. She was spending her working hours like every day, signing documents, approving budget changes, reviewing intelligence findings. A lot of intelligence findings, as the bags under her eyes gave away. She hardly even reacted as her door blew open and the red-headed, young gentleman barged in. "Madam, we've received reports from sites all over the world, they're recording sudden swings in Akiva, EVE, even Hume meters are malfunctioning. Anomalies, mostly theological, are being reported all over, we're having breaches left and ri-" The young man stopped, as the firm voice of 05-7 cut him off. "Calm down, Andrew. I want you to slowly explain to me, which sites have reported these fluctuations, and which are currently undergoing a breach. Do you understand?" She asked with a calm voice and an almost relaxed tone, looking straight at the shaking and panting man before her. "That's the issue, Madam. All of them have. And... and Sites-19, -17, -45, -63 are, Madam" For the first in decades, 05-7's dried skin cracked into a look of genuine concern. [[=]] +  **1208** ----- [[/=]] Collins' head was ringing, and his body felt on fire. He couldn't feel his right leg, and wished he could say the same about the rest of his limbs. Opening his eyes, he was met with nothing but light. Not the same blinding light that struck him earlier, nor that of the pearly gates. It was a light of something large, descending far from beyond the clouds. "Wilson!" He yelled with the last remnants of his voice. At least his throat was intact "Private Wilson! Specialist Michaels!" But no one answered him, not even the sound of branches swaying in the wind. The explosion had levelled all the trees around him. His brief moment of lucidity was very quickly fading, as the pain and blood loss began to have their effect on him. It was a miracle that he had even lived this long, he thought to himself. "A miracle..." He whispered, looking up above him. At the bright ship, or plane, or city. He saw the chariots, the wheels, the wings ascending from it, just as his vision began to blur. As his heart gave out, a smile appeared on his mouth. "Give 'em hell, boys" [[=]] +  **1545** ----- [[/=]] "Fine! Fine! If you want to go out like the vermin, go ahead!" Hans Reuter stormed out of the Reichpost building, cursing back all the cowards who remained in hiding. Berlin was under attack, and he wasn't going to make himself into a sitting duck now. A wave of relief rushed over him as he saw his Benz 770, still in one piece, waiting for him as expected. He knew the coating of holy water and the dozen protection spells weren't for nothing. It was just a matter of time until either the judeo-bolsheviks or the filthy western capitalists stooped so low as to send infernal forces for him. Demonology is an Aryan science, God damn it! "Herr-Herr Reuter, I-I-I am so glad to see you I" His chauffeur was covered in tears and sweat, his heartbeat seemingly audible. His words were muffled by the screams and roars happening all around the car. "Wha-why-where are we-was that-" "Shut up! Out of Berlin, now!" His employer yelled, swinging luger like a club. "Don't even think about slowing down or stopping, understand?" He didn't answer, just hitting the gas. The city around them was in utter chaos. Black figures soared through the sky. Clouds of smoke billowed across the sky. Some from the direction of the Kroll Opera, some from the Schutzstaffel  headquarters. Around them, hundreds of civilians ran, most not even knowing what they were running from. Neither of the men knew how they haven't even hit a single one yet. "Halt!" An Ordnungspolizei officer yelled at them, blowing into a whistle. It seemed that he was trying to set up an evacuation route, with a few others joining him in that fruitless pursuit. Before Hans could tell his driver to ignore it, or run him over, he suddenly looked downwards. Right at a crack on the ground. "What in heaven's-" A figure emerged from the hole, covered in fur wet with a red liquid. It was as tall as a lamppost, had the horns of a goat and the maw of a wolf, but the gait of a man. Seconds after it ascended, it just grabbed him, right by the throat. Right after, it squeezed it, crushing the flesh and muscle while spraying blood across both it and the now-dead man. The other officers opened fire, the bullets tearing holes through its body. It, meanwhile, slowly turned its head towards the car. It did not even flinch as the gunshots continued. "Go! Go, before it breaks through the spells!" And just like that, the car turned around and started going in the opposite direction. As they drove away, the figure remained in the back view mirror, staring at them. Without consulting his driver, Hans tore it down. No looking back now, he said it himself. They either get out of the city, or they're sharing the fate of that officer. And it seemed that they had gotten away. The chaos was more or less equal across Berlin, but not, at the outskirts, they could see the safety of the countryside. No plumes of smoke, no distant demonic figures. As they passed a factory, only earlier in the day used to print propaganda, they sighed in relief. By the time they turned their heads down towards the road again, it was too late, a rift having opened in the ground. Its insides glowed in hues of red and orange. By the time the brake was hit, the front wheels were already at the edge of the abyss. The last thing they smelled was the sulfur. [[=]] +  **2015** ----- [[/=]] 05-7's office was a mess of papers, stamps and spilled ink. With the council unable to host its emergency meeting until the next day, due to over half of 05's being currently present outside of Site-01, she and her colleagues were now the supreme authority within the Foundation. She herself was in charge of declining or approving emergency measures, be they the mass amnesticization of whole towns or use of D-class as field agents. The times were desperate. At least she had the opened package of pervitin on her desk to help her. It was the only thing she appreciated the Germans for. Her hand slammed down the "DECLINE" stamp on the proposal for the usage of anomalous weapons to combat the angelic entities currently present over most of France, just as the door to her office swung open. "We've received a letter, Madam. Addressed straight to the Overwatch Council." Heather said, panting. Unlike her, he lacked access to drugs which could help him get through. His face was covered in sweat and his hair was messier than usual. "It was found wedged under the front door, we're...not sure who it is from, or how it got there. We showed it to a D-I mean D-Class-to test for cognitohazards, none found" "Thank you" was all she had to say as she nodded her head. She looked at the opened envelope and slowly extracted the piece of paper. The first thing she saw was the logo. A pentagram, surrounded by stems of wheat. Finally, she thought to herself. The Initiative was going to tell her what in the heavens was going on. > **{{To all members of the Overwatch Council}}** > > **{{The Allied Occult Initiative has been made aware of a thaumaturgical ritual of unknown purposes, performed this morning at a facility presumed to be under control of the SS-Ahnenerbe Obskurakorps, an occult branch of the Schutzstaffel organization. According to all available data, the ritual has resulted in the increased effeciency of all known thaumaturgic rituals and, more importantly, the sudden severance of barriers between religious beings and the material world. As reported by troops under our command, this includes both Angelic and Infernal entities.}}** > > **{{We currently estimate that the Global Veil System, as dictated by the 1885 convention of the General Assembly of Thaumaturgists and Theologists, may collapse over the coming weeks.}}** > > **{{In light of this crisis, the AOI leadership requests an emergency meeting with representatives of the Overwatch Council of the Special Containment Procedures Foundation, with the goal of coming to a consensus regarding the response and recovery efforts, in addition to the future of the veiled world.}}** > > > **{{With highest regards}}** > **{{Derry Cornelius Al-Fine, Head Negotiator of the Allied Occult Initiative.}}** [[include :scp-wiki:component:earthworm | first=true | last=false | hub=no | previous-url=/ | previous-title=/ | next-url=/tbd | next-title=To be continued... | hub-url=/paradise-lost | hub-title=Paradise Lost ]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box-end]]

Her Future in Bloom

The sloshing of the gasoline can was the only companion Beatrice had walking through the long, lying halls of her childhood home. These walls had once been so safe, so kind and so warm; the gardens surrounding the home had once seemed deep and endless — a majestic world her father had grown just for them.

Just for her.

Reaching his office where this all started, his sanctum where he'd kept his secrets, she dumped the empty can on the ground and lifted the next one. Father knew everything that happened in this place; he was deeply connected to his garden, and to the swamps of Louisiana beyond, but he wasn't omnipotent.

She watched him on the security cameras for a while as he tended the beehives that surrounded their garden. How many had died because of him? Because of her. She wanted to cry about it, but couldn't. There was work to do. She took a second to cycle through the security cameras to make sure none of her father's associates were on the property at all.

She didn't want anyone getting hurt.

Beatrice spins and spins and spins, the world around her a carousel of color. She swings her arms wide as she spins, the hundreds of plants in the beds around her are like a beautiful gown. He grew them just for her, he said!

"Beatrice?" His voice is warm and curious as he rounds the corner from his work bench, her giggles having summoned him. "Mea flosculissima!"

"Papa!" She barely stops her spin and using its momentum sends herself running towards him. "Papa, come play!"

Her father laughs as she throws her arms around his waist. She's not the little girl she was before, and even though she misses the days he could lift her up, now he places a warm hand against her cheek and says, "And who will finish making your birthday gift, Bea?"

"I just want to spend time with you, papa! You don't have to make me anything," She laughs. "Let's go play tag with the Bugles!"

"Turning ten is a big occasion, Beatrice." Her father looks down at her warmly. "It'll be the start of your whole life, so I'm going to make it very special for you. Then we can play with the bugles as much as you want. Why don't you go count how many leaves the azaleas have?"

"They're endless, Papa," says Beatrice, her giggle carrying clearly through the warm spring air.

"Are you sure about that? Maybe go have a closer look."

He turns away, heading for his work bench again, but he's smiling so warmly over his shoulder at her that it doesn't matter what the gift is. He grew this kingdom just for her!

Maybe the plants knew what was coming; any of those capable of motion rattled and skittered their protest. The Bugles lazily snatched at the gas can, but she held it at a distance. She loved this garden, but it wasn't going to stop this from happening.

How many women had he killed for this place? How many had just been failed experiments leading to his pièce de résistance — Beatrice herself? How many of these women had been fertilizer and nothing else?

It didn't matter.

He'd grown it all for himself, so she would do what she wanted with it — just like he'd always done what he wanted with her. She just hadn't realized it. For years his evil had seeped its way into her life, into her breath and into her touch. Each loving gift he'd given weighed on her as she passed their sources in the garden.

The Lying Belladonna fluttered their flowers at her as she doused them, remembering her excitement at receiving the soaps he'd made for her tenth birthday. The strange symbols stamped onto the soap had been so interesting back then, and now she just knew why they were there. She'd always known he had books about occultism — thaumaturgy, as the Foundation liked to call it — but she'd never thought she was the reason he was reading any of it.

She headed towards to the Dead Men's Bugles. Playing tag with them had been a game she used to play and now the rage that burned in her when she looked at them needed release. The Bugles seemed to know what was happening, like they could smell the gasoline. Their vines were more like tentacles and the more they reached out for her, the more the prickly hairs that ran along their length poised to strike.

She stopped outside its reach and watched for a second as the plant recoiled at first, then reached repeatedly for the gas can.

"Alright." She said and launched the can into the air and a trail of gasoline traced through the air behind it, splashing down onto the violent flora below. The Bugles rattled erratically as the gas droplets hit them, but the can kept its arc and landed squarely in the middle of the Bugles' main mass. The vines retracted, trying desperately to toss the cannister out, but it just sent more gasoline all over itself.

She would make sure that there would be nothing left. He would never do this again. All the Foundation files she'd found with all the medicines her father was making were on his work bench. Or at least, the medicines he told them he was making. How much did they know?

She'd thumbed through them, but she'd only understood some of it. She was only halfway to seventeen and most of the thaumaturgy went above her, but it didn't matter. The two files that lay on top of all of them were all that mattered to her.

First, Rappaccini's Poison. It was the recipe for a life she had never asked for — a life of death, and loneliness and cold. She'd never be able to touch anyone or anything. It didn't matter why he'd done it. Not to her. It was done and it couldn't be undone.

Beneath that were more personal notes. She'd never seen them before and she'd never heard the names of the women listed in there before either. Evelyn Miller. Helen Williams. Giulia Conti. Antonia Marinelli. Eleanora Russo. Eudokia…

Her mind raced as she doused the generators in gasoline. How long had this been going on? How much had he lied about? How long had the Foundation let him get away with this? Did they even know?

Tears stung her eyes, but she forced herself to believe it was the gasoline fumes. He didn't get to ruin more of her. Blinking away tears, she fixed her eyes on those two books as she fished a lighter out of her pocket and approached his workbench.

Her past lay before her and it left her with nothing but the results of a life she'd never asked for.

Her thumb flicked across the flint of the lighter and a flame flashed into being a second later. Without needing to see where it landed, she threw it and braced herself as flames blossomed into the air and the Dead Men's Bugles began to screech.

"PEPPINO!"

Beatrice's cat stumbles away from her, yowling as it collapses against the wall. Blood and bile bubble from his mouth as she reaches towards him. Peppino swats at her hand, leaving a trail reddened with blood behind. He yowls louder, flicking the same paw uncontrollably like something was stuck to it.

"Peppino! Peppino, please!"

The fit had come on so quickly. A moment ago she was holding him, playing with him to pass the time for the afternoon, but now he jerks uncontrollably, weaker by the second. Her sobs come quicker as she cradles her hand, watching helplessly as Peppino's feet slip from beneath him.

She quickly reaches to catch him again. Beneath her fingers she sees his fur come loose and the skin beneath redden quickly where her hand grabs him. His yowl is weaker this time. He can't get away, but the skin she touches twitches uncontrollably and her sobs break into hysterics.

"Peppino!"

"Beatrice!" Her father's voice calls from down the hall. "Beatrice!"

She lifts Peppino into her arms, tears flooding her face as she turns to see her father enter the room, "Papa, help!"

The door swings open and he enters. In a moment, she sees her father's eyes drink the situation in, — her tears, Peppino's slowly weakening body twitching in her arms, the blood pouring from the cat's mouth — and he freezes.

"Papa!" She scrambles towards him. She knows he can save Peppino. "Help him! Papa, help him!"

"Stay away!" Rappaccini yells and quickly steps out the room, the fear in his eyes paralyzing her.

"Papa?" She asks as the door slams closed. A moment passes and she hears the door lock. Peppino stops moving. "PAPA!"

Beatrice coughed as the thickening smoke finally reached her. There, in the center of the garden where her father kept his research table, she sat and waited for it to end. What more was there for her? She didn't want to be another notebook for him. Not again. Not like before.

All the pages of his notes lay before her, the detritus of a life she never knew he had. Many were in English. Many in Italian. These she understood, but her eyes kept resting on the oldest notes she could see, titled Eudokia. She recognized the script as Latin and she recognized the hand it was written in — his.

Who any of these women were would only ever be a mystery, but she knew that they had died so she could… succeed.

Her file was the thickest and as her eyes had scanned them earlier. It detailed every soap he'd crafted, every tea he'd brewed and every damned gift he'd given her that had soaked this curse into her very being. Every lie he'd told had burned her eyes like the smoke that drew in across the sky like a pall. She was afraid of it, but what choice did she have? The flames would cook her body and make sure she never hurt anyone again. It would end his work.

"BEATRICE!" Her father's voice rang out across the flames that crackled louder by the second. "BEATRICE! WHERE ARE YOU?"

An explosion rocked the house and she gave a shriek, diving under the table. Ash and rubble clattered down around her, but the villa wouldn't be done that easily. Alarms rang out from across the grounds, but she couldn't say who they were alerting. She hadn't even known they were there.

The garden, on the other hand, was ablaze on all sides. The heat pressed in and as she sat under the table, the panic rose in her as the world drew in tight around her.

She was going to die.

"Beatrice!" Her father rounded a corner, vaulting over burning vines that shriveled under the flame. He scanned the area and she tried to hide, but the movement caught his attention and he stormed towards her. He knew his beekeeper uniform would keep him safe from her. It had been months since he'd touched her and now she knew why. She was everything he'd ever wanted her to be — his.

"No!" She shrieked and scrambled further into his little research station. "Stay away!"

"Beatrice, we have to leave!"

"No! I won't!" She stood, coughing, but wielding Eudokia's notes at him. "How long have you been doing this? How long?"

He stood still, his eyes resting on the notes for just a second before another explosion rocked the house. She looked away to shield her head from falling debris, but a second later she felt his arms wrap around her.

"NO!" She yelled, thrashing against his strength. She may as well have been a bouquet from how easily he lifted her into the air and over his shoulder. Who was this man? He hadn't picked her up in years, but now she was a paper doll in his arms.

She aimed a kick as she fell over him, but he took the blow to the shoulder stoically. She hit him again and again, but he carried her swiftly back into the burning garden. With each strike she panicked more, her hands colliding with nothing but the thick beekeeping uniform.

Tears ran freely now, her voice turning hoarse from the smoke and the sobbing. She knew what needed to happen.

With a great yell she reached behind her and grabbed the front of his beekeeping mask, shoving the netting towards his face. Now he cried out.

Beatrice felt his skin brush her fingertips and he recoiled and let go. She hit the ground with a hard thud, but she didn't stop moving for a second. She didn't have the time to risk him overpowering her.

She jumped up at him again, her hands reaching for his face as he tried to keep her off. His foot struck her stomach and she fell backwards. A nearby flower-bed erupted into flames, blasting flames across his uniform.

He stumbled and slipped. In the light of the flames in the clearer air closer to the ground, she saw the reddened skin under his beekeeping helm and she dived at him again. She yanked hard at it and she felt the material tear. A second later, her hands closed over his face.

"Beatri— No!" He yelled, but it didn't matter. The skin beneath her fingers blistered and she watched his fearful eyes run red. She sat on him, gripping his face and digging her nails into the side of his head.

Blood burbled from his mouth. The grip he had on her arms was already weakening, but she wasn't going to risk anything. Blood dribbled out of his ears, through her fingers and onto the floor as his body spasmed beneath her. He wasn't fighting to get her off him anymore; he was fighting to keep his grip on life.

But Giacomo Rappaccini was good at his job. His flesh blackened beneath Beatrice as red-green spittle dried at the side of his mouth.

His eyes locked with hers for a moment before glazing over. The flames licked the air closer to her and she allowed herself to fall off him as his final death rattle escaped between her fingers.

She lay next to his twitching body, slowly letting go of its functions, and she waited for the flames to take them both.

But the sound of an approaching helicopter caught her attention.

She sat up, peering through the smoke at the sky and watched as a helicopter passed over, showering Beatrice's garden with water. Her heart sank and she turned her attention toward a new sound rising across the crackling fire. The thundering footsteps forged a path through the smoke and she watched as armed men in gas masks appeared from the smoke, with machine guns raised at her.

"Gardener 1, reporting," the lead gunman said. "We've got her."

Peppino hops onto the coffee table sniffing at the gift wrapped in soft, lilac paper. The yarn binding it catches his attention for a bit before Beatrice lifts him into her arms.

"Nosey boy," she chides, then plants a kiss on his head.

"He seems more interested in it than you," Rappaccini says to her and she sighs. "Why don't you open it?"

"I will," she says. "I'm just nervous."

"For your sixteenth birthday gift? Why?"

"You always give me such amazing gifts. I just wish I could the same for you." She scratches Peppino behind the ear and he purrs deeply. "I want to be more involved, papa!"

Rappaccini smiles and takes her hand. "Mea flosculissima, you're my life's work. You couldn't be more involved if you tried. Now indulge an old man, if you please."

He slides the gift forward and Beatrice smiles sheepishly, but sets Peppino down and lifts the gift. She can feel the sloshing contents and her heart warms. She knows it's perfume. She'd been complaining that real women wore perfume and she didn't have any.

Wordlessly, gratefully, she unties the yarn and folds open the paper to reveal a small wooden box with a glass window revealing the bottle inside.

"It's beautiful!" She whispers and she beams at him then flips the box open to the release the teardrop crystal bottle from inside. It's heavy as she raises it and the deep purple liquid inside glows warmly at her from within. "Thank you, papa!"

He places his hand on her cheek like he did when she was young and for a moment, she loses herself in the gaze of the man who'd loved her here in their secluded garden for years.

"Anything for you, mea flosculissima. Anything."

heres-a-beer.raw_content:
“Alright. Listen,” Clef said, without looking up at him. “I know what you’re thinking. I can explain.”

Kondraki blinked at him slowly and blearily in the bathroom light. It was midnight. Day 2 of living together. Clef fucking knew it was going to come up but didn’t know when. There wasn’t a whole lot Ben didn’t know about him— they’d been somehow involved informally on and off for twenty five years. But Clef had put off moving in for a damn reason.

“Quick question,” Kondraki asked. It was his capital-D Director voice, and Clef fucking loathed hearing it in this context. “Are you fucking okay? Do you need to go to medical?”

Clef spat bloody vomit into the toilet and rubbed his face. “Nope.”

“You look really bad,” Kondraki said.

“Thanks,” said Clef flatly. That tank top he’d worn to bed was soaked through with sweat and streaks of blood. The shower was streaked with blood. The kitchen wasn’t even Kondraki’s right now, he knew that damn well without looking at it, who knew if the hallway was stretching endlessly or not. Fuck.

“Where’s the door to our room?” Kondraki asked.

“It’s your damn apartment, you tell me,” Clef said. It was a half-hearted attempt at a joke that only made sense to him.

“It’s gone.” Again. Director voice. He wanted an explanation, and Clef reflected on his options, and also reflected on how much he wished Kondraki had never been given an authoritative position so he never developed a Director voice to present to him when there was only the two of them around.

“Right,” said Clef. God it was like pulling teeth to say it, he hated saying it. “You know I’m a Type Green, right?”

“…Vaguely,” Kondraki said. This was exactly as much as Clef wanted him to know.

“Right. So every so damn often I have nightmares, I don’t know what to tell you. It’s why I avoided moving in for so long.”

There. He could put the pieces back together from the bare minimum that supplied, surely. Clef wasn’t going to fucking dwell on it, did not want to take questions.

“I didn’t know that was even possible,” Kondraki said, a little perplexed.

“Oh, it’s possible,” Clef said. “Unfortunately.” He sighed. “Look, Konny, I’ll give it to your straight. I still have the lease on my own apartment. I understand if you don’t want me to fucking wreck your bachelor pad every damn time this happens, if we want to take the oppurtunity with this and quit while we’re ahead here.”

No response. Kondraki knelt beside him, his grey-black hair mussed, and he leaned against the wall with his arms crossed, looking at him. Clef wanted to punch him and didn’t. He also didn’t make eye contact. He didn’t know how to deal with some of this shit and never could fucking figure it out.

“If you don’t mind me asking—”

“I might mind you asking,” Clef said. A matter of warning.

“Fine. Do you have… I mean. Look, I hate to ask, but… do you have an SCP filing number? Containment procedures? That sort of… thing? Reality bender stuff?” Kondraki asked.

“Oh, fuck you, Ben,” Clef growled. Jesus he hated this bastard and hated that he had no idea what it was like to be contained and documented in that way and more than anything he hurt. It hurt for him to know and he didn’t know what to do. It gnawed at the bottom of his stomach but he knew this had to happen. Fuck.

Kondraki sighed. “Alright. How do you usually…”

“I put it back. I memorize where shit is and what it is and I just put it back.”

Kondraki nodded. “Alright, well,” he said, and shrugged, then settled against the wall conspicuously. “I’m watching.”

Clef slid his eyes over to look at him. His face was honest and neutral. He wasn’t screwing with him. Clef almost wished he was.

“Close your eyes and I’ll do it,” said Clef.

“Nope.”

“Why not.”

“I’m curious. I want to see it.”

Clef cracked a smile. “You think I’m joking.”

“Nope. The opposite, actually. I believe you and I want to see it.”

“Why.”

Ben dug his glasses out of the pocket of the sweatpants he slept in, and put them on. “Because I think it’s a big part of you.”

“Don’t fucking tell me what it is to me,” Clef spat. Sure, it was a little too aggressive, but damn that was a stretch. “This shit doesn’t mean anything to me. Wish I had been born without it. If they were smart about it they would have put me down a long time ago.”

“Alright. Then I want to see it because I think it’s important.” He crossed his arms again.

“It’s not fucking important, either. I’ve worked damn hard to make sure it’s not important,” Clef said.

“If it wasn’t we wouldn’t be having this conversation, and you wouldn’t be throwing up blood and manifesting shit in our apartment in your sleep. It’s bizarre you’re acting as ashamed as you are about this, honestly,” Kondraki said.

“I think it’s completely fair to be ashamed of it,” he said, and with utter disdain in his heart he realized he was on the brink of tears, almost.

Why was he on the brink of tears?

Ben looked perplexed, and then maybe a little saddened for him in some remote, complex way Clef didn’t understand. His eyes scanned him up and down, still knelt in front of the toilet, hair soaked with sweat. Clef could tell he was trying to pick what to say— whether to argue with him or pass it by. Then he smiled teasingly.

“I’m not touching that,” he chuckled. “That… You know my opinion on that, I don’t need to tell you. You’re gonna have to unpack that with a shrink or something. I just work here, this is a damn Wendy’s.”

That made Clef smile, too. Diffused a little of the tension. Ben was good at that sort of shit.

Kondraki adjusted himself and pressed his head against the tile wall. “It’s crazy that you know I’m a huge into hauntings kind of guy, and a huge creepy stuff type guy, big anomaly and paranormal guy, and then you actually talk to me about how you can manifest reality at your fingertips and won’t even let me see it. Not even for a second, like it’s your asshole or something.”

Clef grunted, but was smiling a little. He was taking a different route rather than unearthing any more of that.

“Like surely I can see it as a treat, right? What if it wasn’t important, but it was a treat. For me.” He touched the middle of his disgusting, ratty Ghostbusters shirt. Kondraki had been wearing that to bed for the entire time Clef had known him, and he’d gotten a front row seat to seeing it deteriorate into dryer lint and bits of thread.

Clef shook his head.

“You know what? One second.” Kondraki got to his feet laboriously and left the bathroom. Clef flushed the toilet and took a moment to meditate on the taste of copper in his mouth, and the residual fear and adrenaline making his chest tight. He closed the toilet lid and leaned against the wall, then closed his eyes for a minute.

God he was exhausted. These nightmares took a ton of energy out of him when they happened. He wasn’t looking forward to putting everything back, but then again he never was. In his old apartment he intentionally had as little stuff as possible, just so he could reverse it with as little effort as possible, but he’d had to put a lot more memorization into Kondraki’s apartment over the years to get to the point where he could fix it correctly. He’d raised his son here, after all. It was more lived in.

Clef liked it. It was harder on him from a technical ability standpoint to put back together if he broke reality, but he liked that it felt like an actual person lived there, and had a life there. The other day he’d helped Kondraki move an old dresser to the curb, and they’d found three chewed-on crayons behind it from when Draven had chewed on crayons— Draven, who was now an agent. Clef had trained him himself.

“These could’ve been from last year, honestly. Task forces and all that,” Clef had said. Kondraki had sworn at him but he’d seen him desperately attempting to not smile, and that had been enough for Alto in his heart.

He heard Kondraki come back and roll a glass bottle across the floor to him.

“Here’s a beer,” he said. “Now show me.”

Clef smiled and opened his eyes again. The brown bottle rolled to a stop against his thigh. Kondraki had grabbed one for himself, too, and slid back down to the floor across from him. He popped the top off of his on the side of the toilet seat— it was ridged with half-moons already, this was far from the first time the two alcoholics had shared an intimate 3am toilet beer together— and drank from it deeply and thirstily.

Clef picked his up wearily. He knew what it meant if he opened it, but god did a beer sound good after that. Like it might help numb the horrible mix of emotions he was currently feeling. The apartment wasn’t going to correct itself, anyway.

He reached the beer out and popped it on the toilet seat.

“Shame,” Kondraki said. “I was hoping you’d do it with magic.”

“Your standards for reality bending are incredibly low,” said Clef. He took a deep swig of his own.

“You should correct me then,” said Kondraki. “Let me see what you can do. Give me a new car or something.”

A tiny toy car perfectly resembling Kondraki’s sedan manifested on the floor to their left. Kondraki did a double take, and Clef found himself mildly satisfied by his look of genuine surprise.

“Oh, you’re very funny,” Ben said, and Clef was about to make it disappear when Kondraki picked it up and examined it closer, turning it slowly in his hands, and something deep inside Clef was struck by the sincerity. The way he held it with respect, like it was a piece of art Alto had made for him instead of something he had memorized over the years they’d known each other. It wasn’t something he’d expected.

Kondraki squinted at the side. Clef had replicated a string of dents and every scratch on it, as well as the marks in the passengers’ seat where Draven had spilled nail polish as a teenager. “Jesus Christ, you’re detailed.”

“Have to be,” said Clef. He took another swig of his beer. It was washing the taste of vomit and blood out of his mouth and he appreciated it deeply. “People fuck up, Ben. They fuck up the details and that’s how they get killed, but you can avoid all that by just…not doing it in the first place.”

“Question,” Kondraki asked. “Is this drivable? Did you like, put parts in it? Because it’s fucking heavy.” He weighed it in the palm of his hand.

“That is a…” He didn’t know the scale estimate, or the answer, really. He just took the car he had memorized and made it comically small on a whim. “…I don’t know. It’s a scale model of your car and whatever that means.” He made it disappear from Kondraki’s hands into nonexistence and took another swig of his beer.

“That was already pretty impressive, I hope you realize that,” said Kondraki.

“You think that is impressive?” Clef said, genuinely. Maybe he was just desensitized to it, between his use, Lilly’s use back when she’d been alive, all the Greens he’d hunted in the GOC, all the Greens he’d seen in the Foundation… But he really thought Ben would have higher expectations.

“Yeah, I do,” said Ben, as if it was a challenge that Clef had put him up to. “I do think that’s pretty damn impressive. Are you gonna fix my bathroom or what?”

Clef felt a sense of self consciousness he hadn’t anticipated settle in on him. Damn it, he had to get it over with.

If Ben wouldn’t close his eyes than he would. He couldn’t bear to look him in the eye while he did it and he didn’t know why. He pictured the bathroom as he had it memorized and did it quickly. Heard Kondraki react to the reversal with a sharp inhale like it was actually something to be impressed by and tried to ignore it.

Clef opened his eyes. Ignored Kondraki. Checked his work, because that was the responsible way to do it, if you had to. Checked to make sure the grime had made it back where it needed to be, the dust made it back in the corners, the slight scratches on the tiles, the marks on the mirror and the objects in the drawers.

Then he looked back at him, dead eyed. Embarrassed.

“I don’t think you know how amazing you are. That was crazy. You know I don’t say that shit lightly, either,” Ben said, very seriously. “That was some… remarkable power, Al, quite frankly.”

“Stuff it, Romeo,” said Clef.

“I mean it. Jesus you’re fucking rude about this.”

“Yep,” Clef said. He took another long swig of his beer and looked away. “Fixed the other stuff too.”

Ben looked surprised. He got to his feet and peeked around the corner into the hallway.

It was fixed. He’d fixed all of it in the blink of an eye.

“I’m not gonna pretend to get it, is what I’m saying,” Ben said delicately, following behind him into the kitchen twenty minutes later— Clef didn’t think there was even twenty minutes of shit to say about his reality bending, but Kondraki was verbose as usual. “From what I understand, it’s complicated. As an identity thing, I mean. The Green stuff.”

Clef rolled his eyes. “You’re reading too many Serpent’s Hand manuscripts if you think it’s an identity thing, Konny, don’t be fucking soft. These bastards want you stupid so you don’t shoot them between the eyes.” He double checked his work in the kitchen, quickly, eying the colors and materials in the ceiling and walls, the scratches on the sink, the objects in the drawers. Superficially all correct. He’d check the small details and look at it all again with fresh eyes in the morning, but he was fairly sure he got everything.

“It is though, isn’t it?” Kondraki said. “Like, to be honest, this kind of… it kind of reminds me of when we talked about dating for the first time, do you remember that? And you didn’t like the idea of dating a guy, not because you didn’t want to but because—”

“Oh, fuck off,” Clef said again. “It’s not the same thing and you know that.” He’d only put four plates in the stack in the third cabinet instead of five. He added another out of thin air and ignored Ben’s gaze while he did it. “I’ll tell you what it is, it’s cosmic lying. That’s what it is. Fucking embarrassing and dangerous, not at all the same thing.” He shut the cabinet door shut and turned to face him.

Ben shrugged. He smirked. “I don’t think it’s lying. And it’s dangerous, sure, but that doesn’t mean it’s embarrassing.”

Clef squatted and checked the contents of the cabinet under the sink. All the same. “My commander in the Gock would’ve called it a ‘severe lapse of judgment and control’.”

Ben took a long sip of his beer, and said, “Well, if there’s anything we know about the Gock, it’s that their judgement and control is impeccable.” He opened a cabinet to his right. “You forgot to put my three pounds of weed and brick of cocaine back, by the way.”

Clef laughed despite himself; he was good. Ben was really good. He put one hand on the counter above him and hoisted himself up laboriously. “Oh, that’s fine, I think you’ve had enough. I didn’t forget Draven’s, though.”

Ben stopped mid-sip of his beer. “What?”

Clef snapped his fingers. Kondraki’s cigarette lit itself.

They stood on the fire escape at Ben’s apartment now, which he’d decorated with blue and white lights and festive Dreidel stick-ons on the window behind them. Ben carefully removed the lit cigarette from his mouth, returned the lighter he was struggling to get to work to his pocket, and studied it carefully. He looked at Clef and grinned.

“That’s still really fucking cool. You gotta do that for Hanukkah,” Ben said.

Clef laughed softly, almost like he was charmed, or somehow flattered. “I haven’t seen a religion yet where changing reality is kosher,” he said. He removed his own cigarette from his lips and exhaled the smoke slowly.

“Sure it is. It’s my house and my menorah, and I say it is.”

“Oh, that’s a strong argument to have with a higher power, Konny. ‘My house, my rules’. That works all the time in the Containment blocks.”

“Draven would be fine with it. And he’s the more religious Jew in the family,” said Ben. He slowly inhaled, then exhaled, then said, “I don’t think I had any super hard rules on the kid, but I mean, the ones I did have, I like to think the ‘my house, my rules’ logic was sound.”

The night was cold and dark. Ben was wearing his hair down, the way he did when they were off work, and it came past his shoulders in a mess of lethargic curls, dark and streaked with grey. Alto thought that he himself had been old and fat for a long damn time, but Konny— he could have sworn Konny had been young and fat once. And it was crazy how beautiful he still was.

Clef was lucky, that was for sure. He thought he was damn lucky. He leaned his head on Ben’s shoulder, as if he was resigning himself to something he couldn’t quite articulate, and looked out off the fire escape into the alleyway.

“Sure,” Clef said. “You run a Site like that, too. I hope you know that. Not a whole lot of rules, but, you know…” He smiled. “If you break them, you’re required to break them in a cool way.”

“Obviously,” Ben said. He kissed the top of Clef’s head in the dark, and Clef moved his head and met his lips, and they kissed again, for a moment. Then Ben said, “You’re my favorite haunting, you know. I hope that makes sense.”

“It doesn’t,” said Clef, smirking.

“Cool,” said Kondraki, smiling. “How about I just say I love you, then?”

“Don’t get sappy on me now, Kondraki,” Clef said, but as he said it he put one liver-spotted hand over Ben’s on the railing of the fire escape, and warmed the other man’s curled fingers in his palm. “Oh, ‘my favorite haunting’, he says, always so goddamn prosaic about it. I love you, too.”

I can explain.” Kondraki blinked at him slowly and blearily in the bathroom light. It was midnight. Day 2 of living together. Clef fucking knew it was going to come up but didn’t know when. There wasn’t a whole lot Ben didn’t know about him— they’d been somehow involved informally on and off for twenty five years. But Clef had put off moving in for a damn reason. “Quick question,” Kondraki asked. It was his capital-D Director voice, and Clef fucking loathed hearing it in this context. “Are you fucking okay? Do you need to go to medical?” Clef spat bloody vomit into the toilet and rubbed his face. “Nope.” “You look really bad,” Kondraki said. “Thanks,” said Clef flatly. That tank top he’d worn to bed was soaked through with sweat and streaks of blood. The shower was streaked with blood. The kitchen wasn’t even Kondraki’s right now, he knew that damn well without looking at it, who knew if the hallway was stretching endlessly or not. Fuck. “Where’s the door to our room?” Kondraki asked. “It’s your damn apartment, you tell me,” Clef said. It was a half-hearted attempt at a joke that only made sense to him. “It’s gone.” Again. Director voice. He wanted an explanation, and Clef reflected on his options, and also reflected on how much he wished Kondraki had never been given an authoritative position so he never developed a Director voice to present to him when there was only the two of them around. “Right,” said Clef. God it was like pulling teeth to say it, he hated saying it. “You know I’m a Type Green, right?” “…Vaguely,” Kondraki said. This was exactly as much as Clef wanted him to know. “Right. So every so damn often I have nightmares, I don’t know what to tell you. It’s why I avoided moving in for so long.” There. He could put the pieces back together from the bare minimum that supplied, surely. Clef wasn’t going to fucking dwell on it, did not want to take questions. “I didn’t know that was even possible,” Kondraki said, a little perplexed. “Oh, it’s possible,” Clef said. “Unfortunately.” He sighed. “Look, Konny, I’ll give it to your straight. I still have the lease on my own apartment. I understand if you don’t want me to fucking wreck your bachelor pad every damn time this happens, if we want to take the oppurtunity with this and quit while we’re ahead here.” No response. Kondraki knelt beside him, his grey-black hair mussed, and he leaned against the wall with his arms crossed, looking at him. Clef wanted to punch him and didn’t. He also didn’t make eye contact. He didn’t know how to deal with some of this shit and never could fucking figure it out. “If you don’t mind me asking—” “I might mind you asking,” Clef said. A matter of warning. “Fine. Do you have… I mean. Look, I hate to ask, but… do you have an [https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/scp-4231 SCP filing number]? Containment procedures? That sort of… thing? Reality bender stuff?” Kondraki asked. “Oh, fuck you, Ben,” Clef growled. Jesus he hated this bastard and hated that he had no idea what it was like to be contained and documented in that way and more than anything he hurt. It hurt for him to know and he didn’t know what to do. It gnawed at the bottom of his stomach but he knew this had to happen. Fuck. Kondraki sighed. “Alright. How do you usually…” “I put it back. I memorize where shit is and what it is and I just put it back.” Kondraki nodded. “Alright, well,” he said, and shrugged, then settled against the wall conspicuously. “I’m watching.” Clef slid his eyes over to look at him. His face was honest and neutral. He wasn’t screwing with him. Clef almost wished he was. “Close your eyes and I’ll do it,” said Clef. “Nope.” “Why not.” “I’m curious. I want to see it.” Clef cracked a smile. “You think I’m joking.” “Nope. The opposite, actually. I believe you and I want to see it.” “Why.” Ben dug his glasses out of the pocket of the sweatpants he slept in, and put them on. “Because I think it’s a big part of you.” “Don’t fucking tell me what it is to me,” Clef spat. Sure, it was a little too aggressive, but damn that was a stretch. “This shit doesn’t mean anything to me. Wish I had been born without it. If they were smart about it they would have put me down a long time ago.” “Alright. Then I want to see it because I think it’s important.” He crossed his arms again. “It’s not fucking important, either. I’ve worked damn hard to make sure it’s not important,” Clef said. “If it wasn’t we wouldn’t be having this conversation, and you wouldn’t be throwing up blood and manifesting shit in our apartment in your sleep. It’s bizarre you’re acting as ashamed as you are about this, honestly,” Kondraki said. “I think it’s completely fair to be ashamed of it,” he said, and with utter disdain in his heart he realized he was on the brink of tears, almost. Why was he on the brink of tears? Ben looked perplexed, and then maybe a little saddened for him in some remote, complex way Clef didn’t understand. His eyes scanned him up and down, still knelt in front of the toilet, hair soaked with sweat. Clef could tell he was trying to pick what to say— whether to argue with him or pass it by. Then he smiled teasingly. “I’m not touching that,” he chuckled. “That… You know my opinion on that, I don’t need to tell you. You’re gonna have to unpack that with a shrink or something. I just work here, this is a damn Wendy’s.” That made Clef smile, too. Diffused a little of the tension. Ben was good at that sort of shit. Kondraki adjusted himself and pressed his head against the tile wall. “It’s crazy that you know I’m a huge into hauntings kind of guy, and a huge creepy stuff type guy, big anomaly and paranormal guy, and then you actually talk to me about how you can manifest reality at your fingertips and won’t even let me see it. Not even for a second, like it’s your asshole or something.” Clef grunted, but was smiling a little. He was taking a different route rather than unearthing any more of that. “Like surely I can see it as a treat, right? What if it wasn’t important, but it was a treat. For me.” He touched the middle of his disgusting, ratty Ghostbusters shirt. Kondraki had been wearing that to bed for the entire time Clef had known him, and he’d gotten a front row seat to seeing it deteriorate into dryer lint and bits of thread. Clef shook his head. “You know what? One second.” Kondraki got to his feet laboriously and left the bathroom. Clef flushed the toilet and took a moment to meditate on the taste of copper in his mouth, and the residual fear and adrenaline making his chest tight. He closed the toilet lid and leaned against the wall, then closed his eyes for a minute. God he was exhausted. These nightmares took a ton of energy out of him when they happened. He wasn’t looking forward to putting everything back, but then again he never was. In his old apartment he intentionally had as little stuff as possible, just so he could reverse it with as little effort as possible, but he’d had to put a lot more memorization into Kondraki’s apartment over the years to get to the point where he could fix it correctly. He’d raised his son here, after all. It was more lived in. Clef liked it. It was harder on him from a technical ability standpoint to put back together if he broke reality, but he liked that it felt like an actual person lived there, and had a life there. The other day he’d helped Kondraki move an old dresser to the curb, and they’d found three chewed-on crayons behind it from when Draven had chewed on crayons— Draven, who was now an agent. Clef had trained him himself. “These could’ve been from last year, honestly. Task forces and all that,” Clef had said. Kondraki had sworn at him but he’d seen him desperately attempting to not smile, and that had been enough for Alto in his heart. He heard Kondraki come back and roll a glass bottle across the floor to him. “Here’s a beer,” he said. “Now show me.” Clef smiled and opened his eyes again. The brown bottle rolled to a stop against his thigh. Kondraki had grabbed one for himself, too, and slid back down to the floor across from him. He popped the top off of his on the side of the toilet seat— it was ridged with half-moons already, this was far from the first time the two alcoholics had shared an intimate 3am toilet beer together— and drank from it deeply and thirstily. Clef picked his up wearily. He knew what it meant if he opened it, but god did a beer sound good after that. Like it might help numb the horrible mix of emotions he was currently feeling. The apartment wasn’t going to correct itself, anyway. He reached the beer out and popped it on the toilet seat. “Shame,” Kondraki said. “I was hoping you’d do it with magic.” “Your standards for reality bending are incredibly low,” said Clef. He took a deep swig of his own. “You should correct me then,” said Kondraki. “Let me see what you can do. Give me a new car or something.” A tiny toy car perfectly resembling Kondraki’s sedan manifested on the floor to their left. Kondraki did a double take, and Clef found himself mildly satisfied by his look of genuine surprise. “Oh, you’re very funny,” Ben said, and Clef was about to make it disappear when Kondraki picked it up and examined it closer, turning it slowly in his hands, and something deep inside Clef was struck by the sincerity. The way he held it with respect, like it was a piece of art Alto had made for him instead of something he had memorized over the years they’d known each other. It wasn’t something he’d expected. Kondraki squinted at the side. Clef had replicated a string of dents and every scratch on it, as well as the marks in the passengers’ seat where Draven had spilled nail polish as a teenager. “Jesus Christ, you’re detailed.” “Have to be,” said Clef. He took another swig of his beer. It was washing the taste of vomit and blood out of his mouth and he appreciated it deeply. “People fuck up, Ben. They fuck up the details and that’s how they get killed, but you can avoid all that by just…not doing it in the first place.” “Question,” Kondraki asked. “Is this drivable? Did you like, put parts in it? Because it’s fucking heavy.” He weighed it in the palm of his hand. “That is a…” He didn’t know the scale estimate, or the answer, really. He just took the car he had memorized and made it comically small on a whim. “…I don’t know. It’s a scale model of your car and whatever that means.” He made it disappear from Kondraki’s hands into nonexistence and took another swig of his beer. “That was already pretty impressive, I hope you realize that,” said Kondraki. “You think //that// is impressive?” Clef said, genuinely. Maybe he was just desensitized to it, between his use, Lilly’s use back when she’d been alive, all the Greens he’d hunted in the GOC, all the Greens he’d seen in the Foundation… But he really thought Ben would have higher expectations. “Yeah, I do,” said Ben, as if it was a challenge that Clef had put him up to. “I do think that’s pretty damn impressive. Are you gonna fix my bathroom or what?” Clef felt a sense of self consciousness he hadn’t anticipated settle in on him. Damn it, he had to get it over with. If Ben wouldn’t close his eyes than he would. He couldn’t bear to look him in the eye while he did it and he didn’t know why. He pictured the bathroom as he had it memorized and did it quickly. Heard Kondraki react to the reversal with a sharp inhale like it was actually something to be impressed by and tried to ignore it. Clef opened his eyes. Ignored Kondraki. Checked his work, because that was the responsible way to do it, if you had to. Checked to make sure the grime had made it back where it needed to be, the dust made it back in the corners, the slight scratches on the tiles, the marks on the mirror and the objects in the drawers. Then he looked back at him, dead eyed. Embarrassed. “I don’t think you know how amazing you are. That was crazy. You know I don’t say that shit lightly, either,” Ben said, very seriously. “That was some… remarkable power, Al, quite frankly.” “Stuff it, Romeo,” said Clef. “I mean it. Jesus you’re fucking rude about this.” “Yep,” Clef said. He took another long swig of his beer and looked away. “Fixed the other stuff too.” Ben looked surprised. He got to his feet and peeked around the corner into the hallway. It was fixed. He’d fixed all of it in the blink of an eye. ------ “I’m not gonna pretend to get it, is what I’m saying,” Ben said delicately, following behind him into the kitchen twenty minutes later— Clef didn’t think there was even twenty minutes of shit to say about his reality bending, but Kondraki was verbose as usual. “From what I understand, it’s complicated. As an identity thing, I mean. The Green stuff.” Clef rolled his eyes. “You’re reading too many Serpent’s Hand manuscripts if you think it’s an identity thing, Konny, don’t be fucking soft. These bastards want you stupid so you don’t shoot them between the eyes.” He double checked his work in the kitchen, quickly, eying the colors and materials in the ceiling and walls, the scratches on the sink, the objects in the drawers. Superficially all correct. He’d check the small details and look at it all again with fresh eyes in the morning, but he was fairly sure he got everything. “It is though, isn’t it?” Kondraki said. “Like, to be honest, this kind of… it kind of reminds me of when we talked about dating for the first time, do you remember that? And you didn’t like the idea of dating a guy, not because you didn’t want to but because—” “Oh, fuck off,” Clef said again. “It’s not the same thing and you know that.” He’d only put four plates in the stack in the third cabinet instead of five. He added another out of thin air and ignored Ben’s gaze while he did it. “I’ll tell you what it is, it’s cosmic lying. That’s what it is. Fucking embarrassing and dangerous, not at all the same thing.” He shut the cabinet door shut and turned to face him. Ben shrugged. He smirked. “I don’t think it’s lying. And it’s dangerous, sure, but that doesn’t mean it’s embarrassing.” Clef squatted and checked the contents of the cabinet under the sink. All the same. “My commander in the Gock would’ve called it a ‘severe lapse of judgment and control’.” Ben took a long sip of his beer, and said, “Well, if there’s anything we know about the Gock, it’s that their judgement and control is impeccable.” He opened a cabinet to his right. “You forgot to put my three pounds of weed and brick of cocaine back, by the way.” Clef laughed despite himself; he was good. Ben was really good. He put one hand on the counter above him and hoisted himself up laboriously. “Oh, that’s fine, I think you’ve had enough. I didn’t forget Draven’s, though.” Ben stopped mid-sip of his beer. “What?” ------ Clef snapped his fingers. Kondraki’s cigarette lit itself. They stood on the fire escape at Ben’s apartment now, which he’d decorated with blue and white lights and festive Dreidel stick-ons on the window behind them. Ben carefully removed the lit cigarette from his mouth, returned the lighter he was struggling to get to work to his pocket, and studied it carefully. He looked at Clef and grinned. “That’s still really fucking cool. You gotta do that for Hanukkah,” Ben said.   Clef laughed softly, almost like he was charmed, or somehow flattered. “I haven’t seen a religion yet where changing reality is kosher,” he said. He removed his own cigarette from his lips and exhaled the smoke slowly. “Sure it is. Ben was wearing his hair down, the way he did when they were off work, and it came past his shoulders in a mess of lethargic curls, dark and streaked with grey. Alto thought that he himself had been old and fat for a long damn time, but Konny— he could have sworn Konny had been //young// and fat once. And it was crazy how beautiful he still was. Clef was lucky, that was for sure. He thought he was damn lucky. He leaned his head on Ben’s shoulder, as if he was resigning himself to something he couldn’t quite articulate, and looked out off the fire escape into the alleyway. “Sure,” Clef said. “You run a Site like that, too. He kissed the top of Clef’s head in the dark, and Clef moved his head and met his lips, and they kissed again, for a moment. Then Ben said, “You’re my favorite haunting, you know.
