When he couldn't keep his eyes open anymore, Ace retreated back to the dubious shelter of his tent and the dubious solace of sleep. ---- At first, Ace thought he'd only gotten another hour or two. But that couldn't be right; the fire was cold. He stared up at the stars and, with uncharacteristic sluggishness, determined from their positions the time of day. How could it be //earlier// than it'd been when he first fell asleep? Oh. With numb surprise and a bit of embarrassment, Ace realized that he'd slept for close to twenty hours. His stomach realized it too and immediately demanded compensation. At least all that sleep had finally eased his aching muscles a bit, and it had certainly helped with the exhaustion. One make-up meal later, Ace got to work on re-starting the fire. He didn't see any sign of returning coyotes while he gathered sagebrush in the dark, but he did catch some glimpses of his brothers' bodies. They seemed to be showing a lot more bone than they had before; maybe that meant all the meat was gone, and the scavengers would go elsewhere in search of fresher pickings. Only Bob was still whole, but even he had started to rot on the inside, if the green creeping into his swelling skin was any indication. Only when the fire was finally started did Ace begin to suspect that something was wrong. He'd been shivering in the dark, of course, but that was normal. It gets cold in the desert at night, when the crystal-clear sky steals all the heat from the sun-baked sand. But even now, sitting a foot from the fire, he was //still// shivering. And despite that, his bloody clothes were soaked with clammy, clinging sweat. "Oh no," Ace groaned. A hand flew to the scabbed-over gash on his chest, and then to the one on his leg. Then, in the newfound firelight, he noticed a problem on the hand itself: an angry red rash that he shortly found over almost half of his body. Though that was certainly nothing to smile about, it still gave him a strange (but slight) relief. Mosquito-borne diseases were something he might stand a chance against, but a gangrenous chest wound? There'd be nothing for that but a merciful bullet to the head. But then again, a fever and rash might not be the worst of it. He ought to try and find some civilization, someplace that might have a doctor, but he couldn't very well do that at night, not when he didn't even know where he currently was, much less which direction to go in. Maybe in the morning he could send up some smoke signals, see if anyone else was in the area. But that wouldn't work at night, so the best he could do for now was stay hydrated and give his body the rest that, even after the minor effort of building another fire, it was already aching for. ---- That was a mistake. The next day, Ace was almost too dizzy to walk, and he felt sure that the combined forces of his fever and the heat would fry him before he got to anything interesting, no matter which direction he went. He kept the fire going, at least, and made sure to feed it the greenest, smokiest stuff he could find, but if anybody saw it, they didn't care to investigate. The non-Bob bodies, even the dead coyote's, were mostly gone by then, and it looked like the flies had finally abandoned Kevin. Bob was getting badly bloated, though; Ace wondered if he might eventually burst like a beached whale. That was yet another good reason to relocate, but Ace was no longer sure he could even manage it. He was already sweating out so much water from the fever, and already having a hard enough time walking and seeing straight, that he might end up too depleted from breaking camp to put it back up again. Then he'd have no shade, no warmth at night, and nothing between himself and any hungry coyotes but a limited supply of bullets and an increasingly impeded aim. All he could do was sit, scratch, sip, and sleep. ---- This time, he couldn't even stand. He couldn't eat, either; the last of Doug's beef jerky came right back up, bringing with it entirely too much of his limited water supply. If that kept up, it might very well be a death sentence. Moving while he still could, Ace half-crawled back to what little was left of Kevin. The maggots had all died or grown their wings and flown away, leaving nothing but stripped bones and empty clothes behind. The water in his still-sealed canteen furnished a moment of hope, but both soon evaporated; he took one look inside, then it upended onto the sand. Half a dozen leeches shriveled in the sun. For too long, Ace tried to rebuild his makeshift signal fire, which was quickly starting to seem like his only hope of salvation from whatever plague Kevin's last act had infected him with. Eventually, Ace's trembling limbs and spinning head forced him to just give up on lighting the fuel, even if he could have managed to gather enough of it. He laid in the tent and groaned. He choked down some food and water, then choked most of it right back up. And when the sun fell down once again, he faded into something too fitful to really call sleep. ---- Thirst. Hunger. Vomiting. Spinning, sweating, shivering. Spasming. ---- Something moved in his chest wound. ---- He awoke, for what he knew would be the last time. It was night, but what night, there was no way to know. The fire was out. The water was gone. The food was gone. His vision was starting to go; everything seemed to fade and waver, like he was looking through water. Two huge, black buboes pressed on either side of his neck. Maggots slithered in his chest. His right hand twitched uncontrollably. His left hand was numb. He took one horrible breath, and it scraped his dry and burning throat like a sandstorm. He coughed, once and weakly. He couldn't move. He couldn't think. He couldn't even talk; all that came out when he moved his swollen lips and sandpaper tongue was a weak, strangled gasp. But Ace Cliff was a fighter, and he was going to fight this, too. He sucked another dry inhalation, then forced it back out as a quiet groan. Again and again, he did this, pouring his last dregs of energy into the lungs that heaved inside his infected chest. Each cry was just a little louder, and each one was just a little more desperate. Perhaps there was a hint of anger there, at first, but it died in the desert air. What more could it do, when the soul it had once sustained was trapped in a body so utterly broken? Not for much longer, though... Still, Ace labored. He would breathe his last breath wide awake, and he would make it a cry of hate, of vengeance, of pain. A rebuke of the man who'd broken him, of the thing that had called itself his father, of the whole cruel world of dust and blood that had hated him for his whole short life. But for what? For who? There was no one here to hear it, no one but the coyotes howling outside his door, no one but the carrion-eaters that would feast on his flesh and gnaw his bones, no one but the wind and sand that would bury them. But he had to try, he had to... to what? Why? A single tear, maybe the last drop of water in his whole ravaged body, appeared at the corner of one unfocused eye. It was too much. Too many years of violence. Too many masks, too many names. Too many lies. Too much blood. With one final, shuddering gasp, all of it broke at once. He screamed. Not a yell of defiance, not an angry shout. It was nothing more or less than the desperate, directionless, mindless wail of a frightened baby, alone and abused in a cold and evil world. The last cry of his dying body was just as painful, pathetic, and pure as its first. And with that, Ace Cliff died. ---- But this was not the end. He opened his eyes, slowly. Lazily, they focused, picking out one detail at a time. First, there was the crackling fire. Tendrils of sweet smoke tickled his nose. The warmth felt good; homely and welcoming, like a blanket, not the cruel glare of the desert or the sick heat of a fever. Next, he noticed his legs, crossed beneath him. He was sitting up, not dying on his back. There was no blood where his boot had plunged again and again into Kevin's ruptured guts. There was no pain in his bones, muscles, or skin. He licked his lips, and they were wet and uncracked. Without the agony to anchor it, this body felt unreal, insubstantial. He wiggled his fingers and watched them move. Third, he began to wonder where he was, and looked up to see the walls of a wickiup, furs and hides spread over a wooden frame. They looked like bearskins. That thought reminded him of something... Finally, his eyes came to rest on the other occupant of the shelter, and he could not imagine how he failed to notice her first. She was huge, probably the size of Bob, at least. A native woman, not at all young but not quite old. She sat across the fire from him, and its light cast deep shadows onto a face marred more by more scars than wrinkles. Her long, black-brown hair seemed to merge with the bear furs she wore... or maybe that was simply //her// fur. She met his eyes and smiled. Her eyes were a deep, woody brown. Her teeth were long and sharp. That did not scare him; if the Mother Bear had wanted to eat him, she would have. Instead, she had brought him to her den... wherever it was, in this world or the next. Remembering, somewhat belatedly, his past experience with desert goddesses, he averted his eyes. "Who are you?" she asked. Her voice was deep and growling, but not unkind. He opened his mouth. He closed it. "You do not know?" He shook his head. He knew full well who he was. He just didn't like the answer. "You are my child." He could not help himself; he looked up, eyes wide with hope and surprise. Then he felt ridiculous, and hung his head back down. This was not his mother, he knew that. His mother was a broken skeleton, and she was still in the shallow grave where his father had put her twenty years ago. This was the Mother Bear; everyone was her child, in a way. "And when the mother bear hears the cry of her child, the hunter dies." So that last pathetic scream into the night had not been for nothing. The thought should have comforted him, but instead it filled him with rage; who was this woman, that claimed to be his mother, but had only come for him in the lowest moment of his life? Who was she to claim the hunter dead, when the only killing ever done to the Flynn family had been by his hand or his father's? She was the Mother Bear, that's who she was, and that's why he choked down that anger and indignation instead of letting it fly, but the goddess still surely saw some of it on his face. The inscrutable grin of the late Ace Cliff had fled from there; he could no longer hide his pain behind it. She grunted. He tensed. "You wonder why I do not kill him," she said. "Why I do not break his bleeding crown and beat him to death with it." These were not questions. They were statements of fact. He began to feel very afraid; he hadn't meant to challenge a goddess, not in her own den. On an instinct well-honed by life in his father's house, he curled in, ready to be struck. He //felt// the fist approach before he saw it, a boulder-sized bludgeon of stone bones and oak-hard flesh, hurtling towards his chest with enough force to crack it like a walnut. He closed his eyes, and... opened them. The Mother Bear's fist had halted, an inch from his skin. Smoothly, she turned it up, so he could see the claws on her fingertips. Then they unfurled, and he could see an egg, white as starlight, nestled in her scarred palm. She drew the hand -- the paw -- away, and his eyes stayed fixed on that strange and delicate egg. It seemed to shine brighter than the fire below it. As he watched, the goddess turned her hand sideways, and the egg rolled off it and into the heart of the flames. There was a great flash of light, and a loud rush of air. The egg hatched in the heat, and from it grew a shining tree of white-hot flame. Its countless branches stretched up and out, twisting and forking until they almost touched the walls of the shelter, which they surely would have set ablaze. It was not a big tree, not within this wickiup, but he //understood//, as one sometimes does in dreams, that it was really the biggest thing in the universe... no, it was //bigger// than the universe. He was only seeing an image of it, like a photograph, if a photograph glowed and moved. All along the branches, he could see tiny figures of light and fire, moving back and forth like ants or beetles. Enraptured, he leaned closer to the nearest branch. At the far end, mere inches from his face, he saw one shape -- tall, burning, red -- standing tall, with six smaller ones standing before it. A little ways beyond them, he saw a seventh. It had the outline of a man, and that man was kneeling, in pain or in prayer, before the other figures. Somewhere behind him, close to where this branch met the trunk, he saw another shape, dim, flickering, feminine, and huge; taller than the red one at the end. He looked more closely at the kneeling man. So. This branch was the world, his world. The others, perhaps they were others. And all of it nestled in that egg, that the Mother Bear could crush in her fist. His eyes tried to trace the tree, up and up, and he felt his mind begin to reel. How could anything be so immense? Why was it being shown to him? Who was he, that it would... oh. Gazing back now, he saw the shadow that he cast on the wickiup's wall, illuminated now by the tree of light. It was huge, far taller than him, and dark, dark enough to swallow him whole. From its head grew two twisted antlers, and even their shadows dripped with blood. It ran down the side in steaming rivulets, soaking the bearskins. Looking the other way now, he saw that the Mother Bear's shadow was different, too. Through the twisting branches of the tree, he spied the shadow of a bear, a bear as big as a mountain. It raised its cleaving claws, and his shadow raised its own, and above his head they grappled. A bloody roar echoed from somewhere, like thunder on the horizon. The wickiup trembled; the tree shivered, as in tornado winds. Everything shook until he thought the whole structure might come down, smothering the light and him with it. "I //am// killing him!" the Mother Bear shouted. Then the shadows released each other, and the shaking ceased. He watched as they shrunk back down to the same shapes and sizes of those that cast him. Now her voice was barely above a whisper. "By sending you." He gaped at her for a long few seconds. Then he coughed out something like a laugh, and something like a scream, and very much like a sob. What did she think he was? She had scraped him up from an undignified death, and now wanted to send him off to kill not just his father, but the world-burning Devil himself? That was a joke. An insult. A farce. He closed his eyes again, expecting her to hit him for real this time, or maybe just send him back to his dying body from this ridiculous fever dream. That was easier to accept than world trees and cosmic shadows. “It must be you, child,” the Bear urged. Her tone was firm, but not harsh… she almost sounded sorry. Almost. “Just let me die, then,” he muttered, more quietly than he’d wanted to. “He needs me to live anyway. If I go, so does he.” "No," she snarled, baring her fangs, "he does not deserve a slow and peaceful death. He must scream and suffer and bleed for what he has done. His flesh must be torn and his rotten bones snapped, his eyes gouged and teeth shattered, his body and soul clawed and bitten and broken until he knows one ounce of the agony he has inflicted." “I can’t,” he whispered, voice crackling. “He’s too powerful. Too //big//. He’ll beat me and take my blood. He’ll…” he couldn’t finish, for the thought of what else his father might do to him, had already done to him long ago, hurt too much. “You can, and you will. My paw will guide you and protect you from him. This I promise.” He shook his head, violently. “No! Why does it have to be me? There’s other people that could do this, there’s gotta be! Why are you making me do this?!” For a long time, neither said anything. He wept, head in hands, and she only frowned in silence. When the Bear finally spoke, it was in a whisper, almost conspiratorial. Almost… fearful? “I did not choose you,” she said to the sobbing, broken man. “That… was your grandmother.” Thunder cracked so loud that, at first, he thought he had been hit. His eardrums rattled as loudly as the wickiup frame. If he'd been standing, he'd have jumped high enough to bump his head on its ceiling. Instead, he fell unceremoniously on his back. Looking up now, he saw that a torrent of rain had poured through the shelter's smoke hole and extinguished the fire. The glowing tree was gone, and there was no sign of the mother bear on the other side of its steaming coals. Where she had been, he saw a doorway that her bulk had blocked. Through it, there was only darkness. A bolt of lightning split the night! Again, the whole world seemed to tremble at its fury. In the blinding flash, he saw for a split second through the pounding rain outside. Out there in the dark, in a world almost invisible through the pour, he glimpsed someone. He found himself standing. He walked, without knowing why. The rain soaked him to his core; it was cold, and the weight of it seemed to turn his clothes to chains, chains that grew tighter and heavier as they reeled him towards the woman in the night. And she was a woman, though as he staggered closer, he saw she was too small to be the Mother Bear. He called to her, some wordless question or plea that was swallowed up instantly by the stormy cacophony. Did she need his help? Did he need hers? Did it matter, in this drowning nightmare? Lightning lanced across the sky, crackling back and forth across a storm cloud that stretched from horizon to horizon. In its flicker, he saw her clearly now: a small woman, with dark and tangled hair, wearing a dress soaked dark with something thicker than rain. She had her back to him, so he tried to call out again. The voice died in his throat, though, for it was then that he noticed her hands. As she raised them slowly to the sky, he saw... that they had no fingers. The world exploded. Only when the sight returned to his scalded eyes did he realize what they'd seen; a bolt had descended from the heavens and struck the fingerless woman. The thunder around it had hit him like a train, and now he was on his back, staring up into the full force of the storm. Lightning cracked one more time, and even through the water that filled his eyes, he could see the clouds above twisting, swirling, coming together into the shape of an enormous, toothy maw. The whole sky was alive, a single primordial monster too large to understand, a Leviathan of water and darkness and fury. He screamed, then, but his terror was drowned by a greater cry, a resounding command woven from the howling wind, the pounding rain, and most of all the roaring thunder: [[=]] [[size larger]]**YOU ARE MY KNIFE**[[/size]] [[/=]] ---- And with that, Xavier Flynn was born again. Without moving a single muscle, he could tell that he was healed. No pain burned in his rejuvenated body, and only one thought blazed in his clarified mind: he had to kill his father. In the same way that a bullet must kill what it is fired at, he had been launched from a gun forged of divine wrath, and sent screaming down a straight line toward destiny. Some fearful part of him resisted — some part always had — but now there was another force moving his feet out of that tent and down the dusty road to Montauk. For every drop of fear that pulled him away from the horror that waited there, there was a gallon of rage. That final bolt of dream-lightning had pumped it into him, and though it had not always been his, it certainly was now. The time to run had passed. The time of fear had passed. Now it was time for vengeance. Vengeance, for himself and all his pain. For the dead brothers beaten down before him and turned into monsters like their father, //by// their father. For all the people that they had hurt and killed. For each of their mothers, broken and buried. And for their mothers’ mother, that fingerless woman in the rain, that shadow of the primeval storm. Xavier did not recognize his grandmother, for she had died — //for his father had murdered her// — long before his birth, but he //felt// her in the fury of that storm. He had taken it into himself. It made every muscle twitch in anticipation. His fingers were curling, ready to pull the triggers. His legs were almost jogging toward that doomed bastard’s familiar house. And his face, now freed from Ace’s eerie, empty grin, had become a scowl as deep as the sea. With every step, something bumped against his chest. He didn’t have to look at it; he knew what it was. A bear paw on a leather cord, a parting gift from the Mother. Something that would protect him from his father. Its swinging weight counted his footsteps, counted the beats of his burning heart, counted the seconds that Rory Flynn had left to live. They were not many. @@ @@ @@ @@ @@ @@ @@ @@ @@@@ [[include :scp-wiki:component:earthworm | previous-url = cowboys-from-hell | previous-title = Cowboys from Hell | next-url =/ | next-title = By Demons Be Driven | hub-url = / | hub-title = Vulgar Displays of Power ]]

I NEVER TOLD YOU WHAT I DO FOR A LIVING

Canon Hub » From 120's Archives Hub » I Never Told You What I Do For A Living


March 26th, 1895

Amsterdam, Koninkrijk der Nederlanden



Wishing you were here…

The Municipal University of Amsterdam unsettled Jonathan, but he couldn't quite explain why. The main building of the university was cold, almost freezing in the spring nighttime. Unlike many places back home — none the least Jameston Estate — the staff were yet to have lightbulbs installed, leaving the narrow halls of the old building lit only by the dim glow of gas lamps, swaying faintly above him as his footsteps joined the creaking of the floorboards. It reminded him of his father's old home, back in London, sans the permeation of the stench of cigar smoke and weeks-old fruit. That same polished oak, the red bricks exposed for all inside to see, the lightest of coats of condensation forming on the inside of the windows…

He passed by door after door, each with a plaque of some currently employed academic, or denoting their purpose — His Dutch was subpar, but he was certain he could piece together what a toilet was. — in bronze. He paid most no mind. Pieter Hermans, Joop Luns, Hendrik Van Dijk… He passed them all in a matter of moments, unlikely to ever hear or think of the names again.

He stopped, eyes locked onto the door he had almost just walked past. It had no plaque, the place where one had evidently sat before visible against its weathered surroundings. A nail had been loosely hammered into the wood, and a small chalkboard had been hung from it with a piece of string. Scrawled in neat chalk writing, the current occupant's name was written.

Professor Abraham Van Helsing

Doctor in Filosofie en Recht (Tussen Anderen)

Just the man he'd been looking for. He took a deep breath, gathered himself, and knocked on the door. A small commotion from the other side, as the person inside evidently stood hastily and walloped their knees off the table. After a short bout of cursing he wasn't sure he wanted translated, heavy footsteps followed. The door's handle rattled, and swung inward, revealing the professor.

Van Helsing was an impressive man, for someone well into his sixties. What he'd always lacked in height he'd made up for in compactness. Even through the large tweed jacket he had draped over himself, you make out the broadness of his shoulders, the slight shape his arms had to them… The slight rotundness he'd gained as of recent. Had he been a decade or three younger, Jonathan could picture him with a rugby ball in his hands. His head, similarly, was rather boxy, with a rather pronounced jaw and hard features, framed by a receding head of formerly red hair and a pair of round, unframed spectacles. His expression was one of confusion and mild discomfort, but his midnight blue eyes quickly widened and the corners of his mouth rose as he looked at his visitor's face.

"Mein Gott!" He exclaimed, his decades in Basel shining through still. "Jonathan Harker! In the flesh, before my eyes!" He stepped aside, beaming as widely as his tight mouth would allow. "Come in, Herr Harker. Do come in, I must hear how you've been since we last spoke!"

"Gladly." Jonathan returned the smile, far wider than his former teacher's, and stepped into his office.

☾

Van Helsing's office was a mess. This was, by his own admission, his fault. His recently rediscovered duties as a university professor had left him short on time and energy to properly unpack the belongings he had intended to display here, and the floor was covered with trunks. The only piece of furniture with any sort of display was the desk, which was stacked with books. A small, framed picture of a much younger Van Helsing sat to the left side of the workspace. As Jonathan took a seat, he noticed a paper, in English, had been slid to one side. The large, curved font emblazoned across the top read: SUPRANATURAL CHRONICLER'S PAPER, FOURTY-SIXTH ISSUE. He didn't bother to read on. He knew a Foundation misinformation campaign when he saw one, especially when it was written and published just down the hall from his own office.

Van Helsing sat down heavily into the chair across from Jonathan, its wooden frame creaking under his weight. He ducked down slightly, and pulled a bottle of bourbon and two tumblers from somewhere out of sight. "Will you have some?"

"Oh, gladly." Jonathan placed a hand on a glass as Van Helsing unscrewed the top of the bottle and poured the brown liquid in. "It's been a long while since I've touched alcohol."

"Oh?" Van Helsing raised an eyebrow as he poured himself a glass, before lifting it to his lips and taking a hefty swig. "I would've thought all the time you'd spend im Gerichtssaal would make the drink more appealing."

"It did, for a time." Jonathan took a sip of his own drink, trying not to let his face speak to the taste. "But… Well, circumstances change. The money arrives a little less frequently, and I've good reason to not be down in the pub every evening, moaning about clients."

"You've married, then?" Van Helsing waggled his eyebrows at him. "No longer… what was it Seward called you… the rosebud. No longer the rosebud you were in Cambridge, eh? You're here to invite me to your firstborn's christening, then?"

"To be married." Jonathan corrected, placing the glass to one side. He could feel the amnestics in his pocket almost burning, ready to be used the second things went pear-shaped. "And… no. Well, you're free to come, whenever we decided on the time and place. I'll write you. But, no. Not why I'm here."

Van Helsing nodded. "I see. Then, if I may ask, why are you here?"

"Do you remember the world before the Veil?"

Van Helsing blinked. "Veil?"

Jonathan sighed. "Sixth Occult War. 1864 through 1868. Four years of the most brutal warfare the world may well ever see. Magic and whatnot. Subsequently hidden from the public eye."

"Ah, ja, I remember it." The aging man's expression hardened slightly, his brow furrowing. "I remember reading the accounts of what occurred in Berlin… horrible. Although, I will say, I haven't kept up with those parts of the world since the Convention in 1868. No need to, I've been too busy."

"Too busy to keep up with current affairs?"

"It's been a long twenty-five years, Jon." Van Helsing took another sip of his drink. "I've taught in universities across the globe. Britain, the States, Switzerland, China… I simply haven't had the personal time to…" He gesticulated vaguely about himself. "…Drop by the Library or somewhere and ask what exactly I've missed."

The two sat in silence for a moment, before a look of concern crossed Van Helsing's face. "Warte, how did—"

"I'm with the Foundation." Jonathan said, hands interlocked on the table. "Surely you remember that name."

"Scheibenkleister." Van Helsing sighed, and finished what remained of his drink in a single go. "Yes, I'm unfortunately familiar."

"Unfortunately?"

"I have associates in the Hand, as they call themselves. I've wandered the Serpent's stacks myself, many a time." Van Helsing's eyes shot over to Jonathan's almost untouched glass. "So, if you've come to try and drag me into the fold, you can tell them that they can have me the day my soul goes to God and my body's in the earth."

"Harsh." Jonathan murmured.

"Not unnecessarily so." Van Helsing retorted. "I've always been a believer in the freedom of knowledge, have I not?"

"You may have mentioned, back in Cambridge."

"Good, you remember. Then my reasons are self-explanatory. Du lenhst sie ab."

Jonathan sat silently for a moment, half looking at the old man. He stared back, any of the warmth in his face when he'd opened the door replaced with a cool neutrality. He'd always wished Van Helsing allowed himself to get angry. At least anger passed in a burst. The man's disappointment was like being crushed under a ton of bricks.

"Also jetzt, I believe we have nothing further to discuss on this matter, Zellkind." Van Helsing began to rise from his seat with a slight grunt. "If you may, leave my office and ne-"

"You care about the preservation of knowledge too, don't you?"

Van Helsing paused. "I suppose. It's… in the same domain."

"I see. It's good to know you hold those ideals with such little genuine care for them. I can see why you bounce from place to place so often now. If anyone found out…"

Van Helsing's jaw tensed. "Cease this."

"Then listen to what I have to say." Jonathan rose to his feet, looking Van Helsing dead in the eye. "The Foundation knows you're something of a scholar of the occult, alongside everything else you've ever put your mind to. As it stands, we're actively losing touch with a part of it, as we have been for centuries."

"…Necromancy." Van Helsing muttered.

"Correct." A smirk grew on Jonathan's face. "We believe two things. One, we have found a potential source, one with knowledge that could easily preserve the field, and our understanding thereof, for years to come. Two, you may be able to help us access it. Of course, for a healthy sum when all is said and done."

Something in Van Helsing's expression shifted, and his eyes widened slightly, excited by the prospect like a child being told a secret. "…Why me, specifically?"

"You've had… prior experiences with such phenomena, haven't you? Those stories you used to pull out when you went into Seward's English lectures, they were always about it. Zombies in Utrecht, skeletal serpents along the Nile, an encounter with Death Himself in New York… I'd always assumed you just had a rather morbid creative mind, but knowing what I do now…"

"I will say," Van Helsing interjected. "The one about the zombies wasn't entirely true. That was in Charleroi. Horrid place, somehow one of the nicest in Belgium."

Jonathan nodded. "True. But, anyways, you have a… strangely large involvement with undeath at large, however circumstantial those encounters may be."

"Why such an interest in necromancy?" Van Helsing asked, stepping around the table and looking Jonathan directly in the eyes. "Do you not have greater beasts zu jagen?"

"On the whole, yes. But we… have our fingers in many pies, so to speak. This happens to be one that's caught our attention as of late."

Van Helsing was silent. His lips narrowed and his gaze seemingly left the room, headed into his own mind. He rested his chin in the space between his fist and thumb, brow furrowed. He remained in that position for an awkward few seconds.

"I can give you the night, if you need it." Jonathan picked up his glass, grimaced, and necked the remainder of its contents. "Of course, I have… other things to attend to, back in England, so—"

"I'll take up your offer, vielen dank." Van Helsing removed his hand from his chin and snapped his fingers, pointing at Jonathan. "Under one condition."

"I'm in no position to accept terms, but I can hear it out for you."

"Whenever we find something, wenn wir etwas finden, I want it put into your little academic world below the Veil. To anyone who may find it useful in preventing harm, to the Library for its preservation, to all."

Jonathan sighed. "Freedom of knowledge, yes."

"Does it annoy you, mein Junge?"

"No, it doesn't. I'll just… let you discuss that with my superior." He paused. "But, you will come, yes?"

Van Helsing beamed at him. "It's a good thing I haven't unpacked my belongings after all! I'll let the rector know I will be needing ein paar Monate Urlaub, and I shall gather myself."

"No need for that." Jonathan grinned, and pulled the bag from his pocket. "Take this to the kitchen. Put it in whatever it is they're cooking the staff for breakfast tomorrow. Nobody'll ever remember you were here. The Foundation'll handle any documentation about you, don't worry about that."

Van Helsing nodded. "I suppose I shall pack, then. Could you help, vielleicht?"

"Gladly." Jonathan handed the older man the bag of memory-affecting drugs. "Makes the job quicker. Our boat leaves for Dover at dawn, so we have a few hours."

"So we can brauchen unsere Zeit." Van Helsing gestured to the remainder of the bottle of bourbon. "I don't think a drink before we leave would be such a bad thing, ja?"

"…You know what?" Jonathan handed Van Helsing his empty glass. "A toast."

He smiled, and poured them both another round, offering the brimming glass to Jonathan before raising his own. "To our future collaboration, mein Freund."

Jonathan raised his own glass, and clinked it against Van Helsing's, a small drizzle of the contents spilling over the edge and onto his shoes. "Cheers."

"Zum wohl!" Van Helsing replied, as they both lifted the glasses to their mouths and drank.

Dieu et mon droit

Jameson Estate wasn't the Foundation's. At least, not entirely.

In the years since the folding of HMFSCP and the Commission on Unusual Cargo into the wider body of the Foundation, Britain had been left without a directly answerable agency to serve their interests and keep the average citizen safe from the things that went bump in the night. Fearing the worst, they had made the decision to found one anew. A separate entity from the standard law enforcement of the wider kingdom, Military Intelligence 13 was founded somewhen in the 1880s, and properly made a presence in the core territories of the empire, leaving their larger, more distant holdings, such as Australia and Canada, to their own devices.

To this end, they had facilities all over the isles, covert and clandestine, much like the Foundation. Jameson Estate was one of the more important ones, at least in the latter's eyes. It was the primary site for diplomatic relations between the two, located on an old estate of some lord whose name and legacy had long since been forgotten, about an hour's train ride away from London. They shared the grounds, and split the manor at its heart down the middle. Foundation north, MI13 south. It was a rather agreeable situation, considering the two's cause and effect relationship.

It also happened to be Jonathan's home, four nights of the week. And, as Abraham followed him up the lawn, he couldn't help but voice some concerns.

"Nicht sehr versteckt, is it?" He said, feeling the morning sun's heat creep along the back of his neck. "Any ruffian with half a brain is going to be curious about what's going on inside the manor all these rather smart looking people keep coming to and from, ja?"

"Hardly matters if they have the brains to not act on their curiosity." Jonathan glanced over his shoulder, smiling faintly. "You'd be surprised by easy it is to make people believe such a grand affair is not more than conversion for government use. And it's not entirely wrong, either."

"You lie to people a lot, then?"

"Professor, I work with the Department of Censorship and Disinformation. Legal side of things, police and court documents, and such. It's my job to lie to them." They crossed the threshold of the lawn, and stepped onto the driveway, the crunch of gravel disturbing the early morning quiet. "Besides, is it really that bad if they aren't supposed to know anyway?"

The tension of disagreement arose in the back of Abraham's mouth, but he bit in back. Not here. Not now. Speak to him later. Speak to him CIVILLY.

The two crossed the driveway and climbed the stairs to the front door in silence, the mood growing heavy as they went. The front door was open, and a line of men in police uniforms passed them by, carrying a collection of wooden crates toward a truck they had passed. They murmured their hellos, which Jonathan returned, and they stepped inside.

The main hall of the manor had been stripped bare, devoid of almost any furnishing that wasn't serving a practical use. It felt bare, especially considering the grandiosity of the staircase at the center still had its ornate banisters and carpet. It was slightly sad, like a stag stood in the burnt remains of its home after a raging forest fire. Jonathan paid it no mind, immediately made for the stairs. Abraham followed, glancing around as they went. A quick right, and through a door emblazoned with what he now knew to be the Foundation's logo.

The Foundation's wing of the building was quiet. Not silent, but while you could hear the murmurings of conversation on the other side of every door in the place, it almost seemed adverse to entering the hallways fully. It all quickly died upon the faded, intricate patterns on the decades-old carpeted floor. Light trickled in the windows, illuminating the floating clouds of dust that filled the place. It reminded Abraham of a boarding school he'd been sent to in his youth, sans the Catholic priests and overabundance of religious iconography.

"Watch your step. The floor's a little bit lumpy underneath." Jonathan said, reaching for the handle of a door, a plaque below its glass panes labelled "DCD." He entered, and Abraham followed. Inside, a small crowd of people were huddled around a table at the center of the vast room, desks by the walls left unattended. Jonathan made his way over to them and joined the circle, while Abraham hovered behind him. "Morning, everyone."

"Back from your little jaunt over to Holland, sir?" One of the men in the circle jabbed an elbow into Jonathan. "How did it go?"

"Look for yourself, Holmwood." He nodded his head toward Abraham, and the man he'd been speaking to looked over his shoulder. He gave Abraham a small hmm, and went back to murmuring to the people around him. A few moments, Jonathan extracted himself from the circle and came back to the professor.

"What's all the Theater about?" Abraham tried to peek at the table, curious as to its contents.

"Nothing much. Just a small incident with a cult of Mekhanites up in Jarrow."

"…What are either of those things?"

"None of your concern." Jonathan tapped the side of his nose. "You're currently in the headquarters of the Foundation's censorship efforts. At least, for now. They're talking about moving the Department to somewhere in Dahomey. Just know that asking questions of most of the people here isn't going to get you many straight answers."

Good to know you won't be the only one feeding me nonsense. Abraham thought, as Jonathan gestured for him to follow him, as he moved to leave. Let's see how far that'll get them.

He followed Jonathan, and the two left the room, making for a nearby stairwell. They began their ascent, side by side, before almost colliding with a pair of women where it turned a hundred and eighty degrees before continuing up.

"Bloody ha—" He paused, looking at the two women. They were both of average height, and one was much thinner than the other, almost gaunt. The more healthy-looking of the pair was blonde, with a strong jaw pale blue eyes. She smiled at Jonathan, whose face softened slightly as he returned it. "Ah, sorry, dear. Didn't see you coming."

"Oh, no, that's fine. It's my bad." She raised her hands sheepishly. She had a rather strong accent, one Abraham recognized. Somewhere between Bavarian and Welsh. He knew where she got the former from. A look of recognition crossed her face as she looks to him, but she said nothing. He remained silent, in kind. "I presume this is the professor?"

He nodded, turning to look at him. "Professor, this is my fiancé. Wilhelmina Murray."

"Just 'Mina is fine." She gestured to her companion. "And this is—"

"Carmilla." The thin woman said, deadpan, with a twang of what he recognized as Austrian. "Carmilla de Ville."

Abraham could've sworn he heard Mina sigh, but her mouth didn't move. "Well, it's a pleasure to meet both of you junge Damen. Are you also with the D-C-D?" He pronounced each letter separate and deliberate.

"No." Carmilla replied. She looked almost bored, her pale face seemingly locked into a perpetual frown. "I am an agent, observational. I usually work overseas, back in my home in Graz. On occasion, I am required to make a visit to some site or another for reports, but I am never away for too long."

Mina shook her head. "I think I'm more… asset, than member? At least, now I am."

"Curious." Abraham cocked his head ever so slightly. "Why so?"

"I, uh, developed some sort of…" Mina trailed off for a moment. "Psychic abilities? I think that's what they've said it is. A few years ago, after a bit of a… bad fever." Jonathan nodded. "Aye, psychic. Must've been latent until recently, which is apparently unusual." Abraham glanced at Carmilla, who avoided his gaze.

"A psychic, you say?" Abraham returned his attention and curiosity to Mina. "Exciting. A tad dangerous, too, if memory serves correct. I knew one once. A Manchu fellow, from Harbin, went by Chyi. I learned a great deal about the mind from him, I'd be more than willing to share."

"Only if I don't know what I'm doing." Mina shot Jonathan what Abraham assumed to be a glare. "Which I think I do, by and large. But… thank you for the offer. I'll keep it in mind."

Abraham and Carmilla watched the pair stroll off in silence, before the young woman turned to him and started, in German. "You were a former teacher of Jonathan's, I presume?"

"Correct." He adjusted the cuffs of his shirt, and turned to resume his walk back up the stairs. "And you, a friend of Mina's?"

She was silent for a moment. "Yes. I think that's the best word. Coworker is a bit too distant. She seems to know of you as well. Have you met previously?"

Abraham grimaced. "Yes, albeit I doubt Jonathan's entirely aware of that, and I'd much rather not share the details of our meeting. Her father was a good friend of mine, and I'd rather not break a promise to a dead man."

Carmilla nodded. "Honorable. A rare thing to find in people, these days."

"This line of work especially." Abraham grumbled. "Can't wholly believe a word that would come out of most of these people's mouths. Oh, and if I may ask, where is the Director's office? I'm meant to be meeting with them soon."

"Up these stairs. Hallway should take you to the right. Final door at the end, although I think he's a bit busy at the moment. Stay, talk a bit more. You seem an interesting man."

"Why, thank you." He smiled at her, a gesture she didn't return. "I'd much rather be seen as interesting than a simple intellectual, as I think most would."

"Undoubtedly," She continued. "Although, I will say, you seem somewhat familiar. By any chance, were you in Rome… maybe, five, six years ago? July, it was. Near the Vatican."

"I… was, yes. Summer of 1888." He nodded. "What brought you to Rome? It's not as far from Styria as, say, Moscow, but still something of a trek."

She hesitated before speaking, casting a wary look behind him. "An uncle of mine is a member of the Swiss Guard. Used to be, I suppose. He's still quite the man of God, but… he's grown a bit old for the position in his age. He lives there, now. Owns a little bakery in Ostia."

Abraham nodded. "Swiss Guard, eh? Quite the position. I believe I almost qualified, in my younger years. Never did train with the army, though. War never seemed appealing to me."

"Guerre est enfer, he used to say. Never partook, but it always did weigh on his mind." She turned back toward the stairs, and looked to him. "Shall I walk you to the Director's office?"

"Lead the way, madam." He gestured for her to do so, and began to follow as she climbed the remainder of the stairs. The rest of the walk was rather silent, save for the mumbled greetings of people as they passed them by. Before long, they'd arrived at a oak door, a series of ornately carved vines and flowers set into the surface. A pair of armed guards stood at either side of the entrance, staring at Abraham. "Who might you be?" One of them asked, in a thick Cockney accent.

"Abraham Van Helsing." He extended a hand to the guard, who ignored it. He smiled, brushing it off. "I believe I have a meeting with your leader. The Overseer, as it were." The two guards exchanged a look, and the other spoke. "He'll be with you in a moment. He and Sargent Dawson are discussing other matters prior to whatever yours may be."

"I suppose I should take my leave." Carmilla said, eyeing the door with something close to nervousness. "I do wonder what goes on behind these doors, sometimes."

"Much bureaucracy, occasional conversations of interest, and more headaches than any part of the position ought to be worth." Abraham muttered. "But, who knows? Maybe you'll find yourself in one like it, some day."

"Oh, I'd sooner die than involve myself in the administrative processes of this organization. A fate far worse than death, that." She smiled at him, and for but a moment, he could've sworn her teeth were far more pointed than the average human's had any right to be. But, before he could say a word, she turned away. "I'll take my leave. A pleasure to meet you, Doctor Van Helsing." And just like that, she was gone. Back down the hall from where they'd came. He frowned, and leaned himself against the wall opposite the door. The two guards kept their eyes trained on him, hands close by their revolvers. Nobody made any moves, save the darting of eyes between the three.

Finally, after almost a minute of silence, the door of the office cracked open, and a man emerged from behind the dark oak. He smiled and nodded to Abraham, and extended a hand. "Hello, Doctor Van Helsing. I don't believe we've met. My name is John Hadfield. It's a pleasure."

☾

The Director's office was rather bare, compared to Abraham's own. It was a wide, beige room, with a large window overlooking the lawn they'd approached from, sun filtering in through the glass. A desk sat, facing away from the glare, largely undecorated beyond a simple nameplate with Mister Hadfield's title on it. O5-4. "The Annalist," too, apparently.

Hadfield himself reminded Abraham of a much younger, leaner version of himself. While the Overseer's hair was much browner than his own, and he'd never been particularly gifted with facial hair, much less a beard as full as his, it almost felt like looking in a mirror. Of course, his fashion sense was much less refined than Abraham's had been, but nobody could be perfect. Joining them was a rather elderly woman, with long-since greyed hair and a surprisingly unwrinkled face. She was sat across from where the Overseer had seated himself, beside an empty chair Abraham assumed his to take. He quickly made his way over, and nodded to the woman, smiling.

"Mister Van Helsing, this is Dame Leah Dawson." Hadfield gestured to her with an open hand. "She is the member of the MI13 responsible for oversight of all activity here in the estate, Foundation or otherwise, and in the surrounding county of Kent."

"I'm also the head of most of the technological research this organization does, but most of that isn't for your ears." She returned Abraham's smile, her voice much younger than the rest of her looked, and extended a hand, which he shook. "I take it you're Doctor Van Helsing, then?"

"That would be me, yes," He returned his gaze to Hadfield. "I take she's to be assisting us?"

"No," Hadfield paused, thinking. "Well, yes. But, no, not directly. Not… well, not physically."

"I think it's best you try and explain what's going on, John." Dawson placed her elbows on the desk, her bones cracking slightly as she moved. "For his sake, and both of our dignity."

"Very well then." Hadfield took a deep breath, and rose from his seat as he began to speak. "Doctor Helsing, I want you to think back to the 1st Century BC. More specifically, 48 through 30 BC. The start of the last great conflicts known to make use of necromancy, the Third Occult War, and the civil war it helped spiral the Roman Republic into, that being the War of Actium."

"Does he always talk about such things like he's telling a story to children?" Abraham whispered to Dawson, the Overseer too enraptured in the history flowing from his mind and mouth to take notice.

"Yes." She replied bluntly. "Humor him. He has a rather vested interest in 'parahistory,' as he calls it."

"Ever since the end of those wars, since Egypt fell under Rome's control, since the burning of Alexandria and the sacking of Crocodilopolis, the art has been in decline. Now, not without good reason. However, this aversion spread, and the Catholic Church would quickly come to frown upon the practice. "Even after, it was an ideology they spread across the world, and one many chose to adopt. Valencia, Cangzhou, Mainpuri, all saw thousands of documents consigned to oblivion." He spread his arms, and Abraham rolled his eyes. "Now, almost two millennia later, we find ourselves understanding the arts of undeath close to as poorly as we do the stars above, or the depths of the sea below. Is that not a tragedy, Doctor?"

"Agreed." Abraham nodded. "A grave failure of the Old World, I must admit."

"Oh, undoubtedly." Hadfield's voice was heavy with a rather genuine frustration. Not at anyone in particular, but similar to that of a student who would much rather their education end already. "We do not even have records of necromancy in the Americas, or in Australia, beyond anything their mythologies may tell us. Of course, their failure to document their own histories is by and large outside of our control, but I digress." He waved a hand. "Whereabouts was I?"

"How we lost most of our knowledge of necromancy, and things to that effect." Abraham sighed. "Interesting as it is, I'd much like if we got to the point now. Although I would like to talk history more sometime, just… more casually, as it were."

Hadfield nodded. "I believe I could make the space in my schedule for such an arrangement. As for the rest, well… I feel Miss Dawson is best equipped to explain the situation."

Dawson cleared her throat, and continued. "Thank you, sir. Now, I will preface, I am a necromantic construct myself. An Effro-celain, 'waking corpse.' Though most formal folk than I prefer the term 'lich' these days. I digress. Soul tied to a body that should've died a long time ago. Now, I've been around since the… 10th Century. In and out of the general public, as needed, and I've managed to collect a good few sources of general magical lore, some of it based around necromancy. Now, obviously, it's mostly written in the various forms of English that have been spoken on this island, and the various languages we've pushed aside to replace with it, but there's always one key element among them. A name."

Abraham felt his stomach turn as she described her condition. He wasn't fond of undeath, much less those who'd twisted it for their own benefit, however polite they seemed to be. However, he was in good company, and elected to ignore the sense of disgust growing in his gut for the time being. "Do all the grimoires bear the same title, or am I mistaken?"

"No, although many do lack one entirely." Dawson straightened herself in her seat. "But most of the necromancy detailed is attributed, usually by no more than two degrees of separation, to someone by the name of 'Bladud.' Sometimes 'Blaiddyd,' if the text is in a Celtic tongue, as they ought to be."

Abraham sat silently for a moment, his memory churning what it could toward the surface before answering. "The Historia Regum Britanniae. That Bladud? The supposed "mage-king" of the Britons?"

"The very same." Dawson nodded in approval of his recognition. "Of course, this makes the assumption it is him, and not some other ancient scholar writing under a pseudonym. It also assumes he existed at all."

"We do have somewhat solid evidence to suggest he did." Hadfield interjected. "Written records from Athens, his name in Ogham across the eastern coast of Ireland, even a painting matching his description in Cairo."

"Thank you, John." She continued. "Obviously, with what little we know, we're eager to find any way we can learn more—"

"You want me to go hunt after some ancient Celt, who may or may not exist, or ever still be alive if he did, to try and… extort his esoteric wisdom from him?" Abraham squinted. "Am I correct?" Dawson and Hadfield shot each other a look, and nodded. He sighed. "Look, as much as I appreciate a nice jaunt to and fro about the country, I… Well, I'm not Blackwood, God rest the poor fool's soul. I don't do adventure."

"I prefer the term 'investigation' here." Hadfield interrupted. "And I think this is a little bit more… well, Blackwood did what he did for fun. There is a reason here."

Abraham paused, and shrugged. "True. But, still, I'd rather not end up with it all being for naught, ja? No matter how much you offer to pay me."

"Well…" Hadfield frowned. "We cannot quite guarantee that there will be returns on our efforts here, as much as it pains me. We're dealing with a rather heavy hypothetical here, and while I have my hopes, I believe it's best to keep the expectations of others realistic in this regard."

"My point stands. I'd be parading about the countryside, looking for something or someone who may not even exist." Abraham crossed his arms, frowning. "You have to offer etwas für mich. Unless, you'd rather look elsewhere for somebody qualified, that is?"

Hadfield was silent for a moment, and looked to Dawson. She shrugged, and he sighed. "Consider, what if he is real? Or was, assuming the works he created survived longer than he has. What if you're not the one to uncover it? What then?" Abraham's eyes narrowed. "What did Jonathan tell you about me?"

"Nothing I think you wouldn't want me to know." He raised a hand. "He did, however, tell me of your little condition to your agreement. Complete freedom of the knowledge acquired." Dawson's eyes narrowed, but she said nothing as he continued. "While I am not in a position to offer it with a complete guarantee, I can certainly raise some form of the idea with the rest of the Council, and I can see if it holds any water there. Oh, and the attachment of your name to the recovery, for as long as possible. That much I can guarantee if all else goes well."

Abraham sat silently, pondering the sudden offer. His name, going down in scholarly history for his efforts… If there was something there to be found, anything, it would be another addition to the stack of his bibliography, in a way. One more important than yet another response to Nietzsche, or another paper on metaphysics nobody would read. It could all be for naught, yes, but at the same time…

"I think we may have some sort of a deal, then." He rose from his seat, and extended a hand to Hadfield. "I'll do it."

Hadfield smiled widely, and took his hand, shaking it firmly. For but a moment, Abraham could've sworn he saw a form shift just below the bottom of the window. A large, black shape, almost in the shape of a bat's wing. Likely just the leaves of a bush, poorly visible with the sun streaming in from behind them, but he did wonder. "I thank you, Professor. I believe this may be the beginning of a fruitful, and potentially long, partnership."

Dorian de Ville's eyes ran down the page one more time. Crossifica stood over him, her usual forced smile the only part of her face visible in the dying light of the fire. He, on the other hand, frowned rather strongly.

"Were she not my own blood, I would fly to England this instant and throw her into the Thames." He grumbled. "Daring to call me a miscreant for attempting to help."

"I'm sure she's simply anxious for your arrival, sir." Crossifica leaned forward, bringing the rest of her face into view, her skin the same shade of brown it had been the day he'd met her in the light. "Nerves do grip one's thoughts and actions like a vice, after all. Well, most. I have no doubt you have your—"

"Yes, yes, thank you." He brushed her off, and set the first page aside, perusing the contents of the rather official looking document that followed absently. "Have you heard from the Archbishop about my appeal for an audience? Anything?"

"He's… dead, sir." She faltered slightly. "His successor hasn't been raised to the rank yet. Not until after his funeral… tomorrow, I think it is."

"Hmmm." Dorian rose from his seat, setting the stack of papers on the table beside his armchair. From beside it, he picked up his glass and a small cube of meat from a tray. He held the cube above the glass, and crushed it, watching as a stream of red liquid trickled from his fist into the glass. A quick shake of the hand to get rid of excess droplets, and he raised the half-full glass to his mouth, feeling the taste wash over his tongue. It reminded him of caramel, almost, but the buzz it gave was much closer to his old favorite: whiskey. "He can wait, then. I've certainly done so for long enough."

"You sent the letter a week before the poor man died, signor de Ville." Another woman called from the far side of the room, on a couch closer to the fire. "I doubt he had the time to read it before his heart gave out."

"Beatrice, could you not be so brazen about the man's death? It's tragic, and I doubt his soul wo—" She started, before the other woman sat up and raised a hand to silence her. "Don't go on about his soul, and resting, and all that. I, for one, hope the bastard's rotting in hell." She ignored the indignant noise Crossifica made. "Don't act like he doesn't deserve it. He killed those men. He got that boy hanged. Doubt he stopped there. Straight into the Styx with him."

Dorian nodded his approval. "Quite fair. But still, not ideal." He glanced around the room, his eyes lingering on every shadow, searching for another presence. "Where is Assunta? I could've sworn she was here when you both entered."

"She was 'feeling hungry.' She left to get something to eat." Beatrice strolled over toward the pair, leaning against Crossifica as she placed her arm around her shoulder. "Went toward the pantry."

Dorian sighed. "Lord give me strength." He winced slightly as the words left his mouth, the utterance of the holy name leaving his mouth alongside the faintest hissing sound as his tongue burned. He let it pass, and raised his voice to a roar, which almost anyone inside the nigh-empty castle would've been able to hear. "ASSUNTA! GET BACK HERE!" The sound of crashing footsteps from the floor above them came almost at once, and quickly made their way down and around toward the door of the study, before it was thrown open and the light from the hallway spilled into the room.

Beatrice and Crossifica had always looked rather similar. Brown hair, green eyes, both on the taller side, towering over Dorian by almost a solid ten inches. Had it not been that Beatrice was much paler than Crossifica by nature, one almost could've mistaken them for sisters. Crossfica's mother had come from somewhere in Egypt, according to the Sister Superior of the convent he'd found the three girls in, while the former couldn't have been any more Venetian unless she'd crawled out of a canal as a newborn and offered a trade deal to the nearest shopkeeper. Assunta, on the other hand, had been moved to the convent from somewhere in Rome. Largely, the elderly nun had said, for the good of the diocese's name.

As she stood there, hunched slightly, blonde hair framing her face, blue eyes above a mouth stained red with blood, one hand on the door and the other holding the remains of an uncooked chicken with its head bitten clean off, he was reminded of why that was.

"For Christ's sake, Assunta, that was a fresh carcass! Unwashed!" He threw his hands up, grimacing. "Do you have any idea what sorts of diseases that thing could have? And how in God's name did you get BLOOD on you? That thing was bled before I bought it!"

"Won't kill me, will they?" She panted, the blood from her face dripping down from her chin onto the hardwood floor. "Also, the steaks are good. Very nice quality."

"I won't even ask how many of them you ate, and your biology, blessed as you seem to be, won't stop salmonella from making you want to remove your intestines with a hacksaw for the next week. And— " He flicked a hand, index finger extended, and the chicken and blood vanished. " —Stop walking about the place like some sort of deranged member of the peasantry."

"I wasn't done with that." She growled, as she straightened herself. He turned away, shooting her a dirty look from the corner of his eye. "You are now. Now, please, do join us for a moment."

Assunta opened her mouth, possibly to make some snide comment about how she'd rather not, before closing it again and falling into line beside Beatrice, pouting slightly. "Excellent." Dorian clapped his hands together, and smiled at the three women, his slightly pointed teeth giving him more of the appearance of a hungry animal than a pleased man. "I encourage you all to gather any important belongings by daybreak. We must take a longer visit abroad than usual, and will likely not be returning for a time. Weapons, in-progress works, the like."

"To England, I assume? As Lady Carmilla said in her message?" Crossifica interjected. Assunta's eyes lit up at the name, and she turned to look at her fellow attendant, smiling. "Carmie's in England?"

"Yes, she is, and yes, we are." He sighed. "The fetid cancer upon this world that the island of Britain is, I believe it may hold the key to what I've sought, and thus… Well, you understand the importance I place on such things." The three women nodded. "Now, I shan't bother you further. Go, collect yourselves."

Assunta was out of the room before he'd even finished his sentence. Beatrice and Crossifica sauntered out at a much more leisurely pace, muttering to one another about what they'd do once they got to the United Kingdom. Always wanted to see London, Dorian made out, just before the door slammed shut behind them. Dorian settled back into his seat, crushing another cube into his glass, and picked back up the initial message.

Abraham. Van. Helsing. That name had been stuck in his head for the better part of a decade, and every time it shifted in his mind, it brought the sting of the old wound back. He could almost see it again. Saint Peter's Basilica, the light of the setting sun casting long shadows down its steps. A small crowd of bishops and Swiss guardsmen, their eyes bearing down on him as he walked toward the threshold back to Rome. And that fat Dutch bastard, watching from behind them all. The blood hit his throat, but he almost couldn't make out the taste as he rolled the name over and over in his head.

If nothing else came of the trip, Dorian swore to make sure of two things. The first was that Van Helsing remembered the name he'd known him by for the rest of his days. Dracula, wedged into the doctor's mind as his had been in Dorian's.

The second was that he was going to make sure the old man died screaming.
