She will live her life on her own terms, and not even Cupid himself will take that away from her. ]] ===== [[module CSS]] :root {     --header-title: "SITE-35";     --header-subtitle: "SUPPORT, CONSOLE, PROTECT"; } [[/module]] [[>]] [[module Rate]] [[/>]] It had only been [https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/turning-out a year] since Sylvie met her beloved friend, and yet so many things have changed. For one thing, Sylvie was now swamped with research work. She had to chemically synthesize multiple anomalous compounds that came by her desk each day, each with exciting new reactions to try. She examined different extradimensional objects that came down from the Ectodimensional Studies section from across the site; sometimes they were eldritch monstrosities with at least ten thousand tentacles, other times they were hard to look at without getting a migraine. Sylvie could even take on research projects of her own now, without the supervision of senior researchers that took her under their wing. It felt like yesterday that Sylvie was first introduced to Site-35, with its plaster walls covered with lovely little drawings made by the children who were kept there. She could still remember first meeting Caoimhe and her warm hazel eyes and auburn hair. //How has time gone by so fast?// It was all so overwhelming. Had she spent enough time with her friend, so that it all truly mattered? Had she done enough? The future had become so much more uncertain as each day passed. Sylvie had gotten exactly what she wanted. It was everything that she ever desired and more. But there was still that little hole in her heart, a hole that could never be filled. What was she missing? Sylvie sighed in exasperation, and opened the door to her dorm room. Inside were various posters of 70s rock musicians and bands plastered all over the walls, from Jimi Hendrix to Black Sabbath and Deep Purple, each poster giving off a psychedelic feel. There were old vinyl discs stuck into one corner of the room. Her bed, with a cushioned headboard and covered in bold red and green patterns, sat in the other corner. Caoimhe was already there, sitting on the edge of the bed and scrolling through her phone. She looked up as Sylvie closed the door. “Hiya, Sylvie!” She waved at her enthusiastically. Sylvie gave a little wave and a slight smile back. “Hey.” “How’ve you been? I feel like a walking corpse with the amount of shite on my plate lately.” Sylvie shrugged. “It’s been going. All those research projects, you know.” “I can tell with the bags under your eyes.” Caoimhe pulled out a deck of UNO cards, and patted the spot next to her. “Wanna play?” Sylvie’s smile grew even wider. “You bet.” Playing UNO was a great pastime for Sylvie and Caoimhe. It was a necessary distraction from the outside world and whatever Sylvie had going on at any given moment, especially for the backstabbing, deceit, and other trickery that culminated in trying to strangle your friends. It was a classic game for having fun and feeling absolutely miserable at the same time, right up there with Monopoly. Caoimhe shuffled the cards, and dealt seven for each person. Then the game began. Cards were stacked, swapped, and thrown across the room. What started as a quick round became a flurry of emotions, the tension in the room sizzling into a boiling pot with a mixture of laughter and loathing disdain. These exhilarating yet frustrating competitive challenges, they became shared experiences that created lasting memories between the two friends that Sylvie will always cherish for as long as she lives. It was Sylvie’s turn now. She looked at her cards, saw a +2, and knew what she had to do. She placed the card down onto the pile, and didn’t say a word. Caoimhe stared at it, nodded her head, and placed another +2 on top of it. “…Really?” Sylvie frowned. Caoimhe grinned. It was always that damn smile. “Yep.” “I thought I said no stacking.” “I thought you said we were free to pull, and I quote, ‘any bullshit to trip the other person up.’ Does that count?” Her grin grew even wider. Sylvie couldn’t help but concede. “I guess so. Anyway,” as she pulled her cards from the deck, “oh look at //that//.” She placed down a wild draw four card. “Blue. Now we’re even.” Caoimhe laughed with a gentle, melodic tone like a songbird’s call on a sunny day. It was music to Sylvie’s ears. “You’re fun, you know that?” Sylvie smiled back. “So are you.” They kept playing, raging, and bonding. There was nothing that Sylvie could ask for other than this. She had it all, and she would do anything to keep it. But that hole was still there. It was spreading, expanding to the point that it covered her whole chest. What was she missing? This was what she wanted, wasn’t it? Other people didn’t have this feeling, right? But Sylvie wasn’t like them. Their trajectory was simple, obtaining all the ingredients for the recipe of living a happy life with the people they love. But as Sylvie couldn’t feel that way for her friend, or for anybody really, it wouldn’t be the same. How could she try to navigate this path her own way? There were so many unknown variables, so many hidden obstacles that were waiting for her to bump into. It shouldn’t have to be this hard. Living a happy life with someone that she cared about should be simple, and quiet. Mundane, and carefree. Those impulsive thoughts that couldn’t be kept down, they slowly crept into her mind, and kept coming, getting faster and faster, overwhelming her as the surroundings around her began to blur and become unfocused. //I can’t lose her, I can’t lose her, I can’t—// Look at the cards. She had to look at the cards. Staring at their bright colors, the only distinctive spot in the blurred room around her. Sylvie focused on those colors, painting her mind into a bright and vivid canvas. Now as the painter in her thoughts, she drew a sunny summer day, the two of them in a field full of sunflowers, with clear skies without a cloud in sight. They held each other’s hands, strolling down this field, feeling the wind in their hair. Sylvie picked a sunflower and pulled it out, showing it to Caoimhe, who accepted it gracefully. She loved it. And they were both happy together. She went back to the colors, back to the game again, and the internal tension inside her simmered down. Caoimhe was waiting on her. “Sorry, I was just thinking about which card I should put down,” Sylvie said. “That’s okay! Let’s keep going, shall we?” Caoimhe grinned. They went back-and-forth, never missing a beat. An electric energy in the room that would not slow down. Sylvie could see her friend, giddily placing another card down to change the tides of the game. She was so happy. That pure, unbridled joy, it was the light that always brightened Sylvie’s day. Those little moments, those small everyday details, they were what made Caoimhe so special to her. And there was no telling what would happen if she had to let it all go. ---- The water splashed all over the floor, as a mop was forcibly inserted into a yellow bucket. A janitor’s bucket, the kind with wheels that one could drag around. As the mop was lifted up, two burly hands began to wring it out, squeezing the excess water as it dribbled back down into the bucket. The work wouldn’t be exciting, or interesting in the slightest, but it had to be done nevertheless. [https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/i-only-loved-the-idea-of-you Cliff] sighed, as he continued to do what he always did. Here he was, going through the same motions, doing the same tasks, all the same. All of these daily tasks compiled in the same script that inevitably melted together into one indistinguishable mess of a life. The dull tick, tick, ticking of the clock that pounded his skull, the grey-toned tables that meshed into one, the piercing white lights from above, no variety to it all, it made the environment even more monotonous than it already was. He got used to it after a while, but he couldn’t do this forever. Could he? What else could he do? With every bridge that he burned, every opportunity slipping from his fingers like sand, it became too easy to fall back into these routines. He dunked his mop into the bucket, harder this time. Cliff kept sweeping, back and forth and back and forth. Patterns that repeated over and over again, lines of splattered liquid that crossed into each other. Every once in a while, he looked around the room for anything memorable, any minute changes that could make his day a little more interesting. But, as always, there was nothing. Only chatter between faceless researchers. He plunged the mop again. A few droplets of water splashed on his shoes this time. How fun. As the clock kept ticking and time kept turning, Cliff once again dragged himself back into the inner depths of his thoughts and his regrets. He imagined the different paths that he could’ve taken, the things he could’ve done to carve a better future. If only he made the right choices, and stopped basing his desires on his idealized fantasies. If only he tried to reach out to the people that he cared for, and wasn’t so naive. //If only I knew how to love someone.// But that didn’t matter anymore. There wouldn’t be any future for him regardless. This was it. As Cliff reached the upper left corner of the cafeteria, he looked up one final time, to see two familiar faces scamper in from the hallway. The blonde one was stammering, and looked embarrassed, while the other one had her hands on her knees, laughing to her heart’s content. It reminded Cliff of what could’ve been. It always did. “Christ, I look like my old neighbor with how much I’m prying,” he mumbled to himself. Should he go up to them? Say something? At least he had people to talk to, right? But he was already doing too much by staring at them. The conversation would be awkward, and short-lived, and he would go back to playing his part once again. But it would be something. Time would move with or without him either way, so what’s the harm in trying something new? Cliff began to saunter his way over to the two researchers, making sure to be discreet and inconspicuous. He went over to the far end of the furthest table, and started to sweep around the area with his mop. Eventually, the researcher with the braided auburn hair spotted him and turned to the blonde one, who looked back and nodded. The blonde researcher gave a little wave, shifting her weight from one foot to the other. “Hi again.” “Afternoon,” Cliff greeted. “Don’t think I’ve ever introduced myself. I’m Cliff.” “Sylvie.” She swayed slightly from side-to-side while standing. “Nice to meet you, Sylvie. And you are?” The other researcher reached out to eagerly shake hands. “I’m Caoimhe. I’m Sylvie’s friend. Nice to see ya again!” Cliff nodded. “Yeah, it is.” “Do you need anything else?” Sylvie asked. He could tell she did not want to be there. That was something he could relate to. “No, I’m only here to say hi. It’s not often that anyone else does the same for me.” Caoimhe nodded. “We’ll let you know if we spot anyone littering or if there’s any trash around. I respect the work you do, and I think more people should respect you back.” He smirked. “Appreciate it. See you around.” He gave another wave, and they both waved back. He could see Sylvie hiding behind Caoimhe as he left to continue his work. Although those two were a painful reminder of the life he should have lived, Cliff was happy for them nonetheless. It was nice to know that there were people out there who didn’t have to second guess themselves, who didn’t have to lose everything because they could never figure out why everything didn’t match, why these aspects of life weren’t the same as what was presented and expected by those around them. But in the end, it didn’t really matter for Cliff, did it? He made his choices. So he grabbed his mop and his bucket, and carried on. ---- Sylvie sat in the office of the head of Psychology & Parapsychology, the familiar mahogany desk and black-painted walls giving her a sense of comfort. She’d been taking appointments a lot recently, which for anyone else would be concerning but it wasn’t really that bad for her. It was nice to air out her feelings in private, without having to reveal them to the people that she cared about the most. This room was a safe space, a place where she didn't have to hide. Across from Sylvie was a man in his early 30s, with dark-rimmed glasses and a distinctive Shire mullet. He was typing on his computer, most likely editing some documentation for another of his clients on the paranatural side. Sylvie could see that he still wore the black ring on his right middle finger and the white ring on his left, as he always did. He, of course, was Michael Prescott, the head of P&P and her therapist. And if someone were to tell Sylvie that he was also everyone else’s therapist at the site, she would believe them. It was astonishing to learn how many clients he worked with each day. He took a sip from the black mug on the corner of his desk, and placed it back down. “So, how has everything been going for you?” Sylvie shrugged. “Alright, I guess.” He stopped typing, and turned to look at her. “I know things have been… difficult for you in the past few days, but I’m here to help no matter what it is.” “Yeah, yeah I know, but,” and she turned away from him, “it’s all so //frustrating//. I thought I had it all figured out. But it’s like I’m back at square one all over again.” Michael seemed to ponder for a moment, before clasping his hands together. “We’ve navigated this before. I don’t believe that your situation will change for the worse. And even if it does, I’m still here if you need to talk.” Sylvie began to fiddle with her thumbs. “There’s always that chance that something horrible is going to happen. And I hate that I can’t shake that feeling off. Everyone else doesn’t have to deal with what I have. They only have to worry about what their future will be like as a couple. Childcare, familial issues, what the wedding is going to be like, all that. We both know I’ll never have that. I don’t know how to spend time with her. She’s still the romantic, while I’m the complete opposite.” She could feel her heart pounding. “What if she somehow finds someone else? Someone better than me in every single aspect? How would I handle that? How would you handle that? Tell me. Go on.” No response seemed to come from the other end. The air felt heavy and stale, forcing down a pressure on them both, time standing still, a cold chill crawling up her spine. And Michael only stared. She knew why, of course, that was merely the way he had to process some things, but with the way things looked now it felt as if the weight of her words was going to crush her into a pile of slurry. Michael looked down at his rings, then looked back up at Sylvie. “I know how you feel. You’re in the background. And then they get into those certain topics, and you feel like you’re being shut out.” She felt sick. “Yeah. Like I’m a shadow on the wall.” “It’s a hard thing to accept, knowing that you’ll never be what they expect you to be. But I’m here to help. I always am.” “What if she leaves me behind?” She could barely get out every word. “She wouldn’t. Because I know her, and I know you. Can’t you see how much she cares about you?” “That’s the problem! I see it. But I don’t know if I’m giving the same to her.” “Are you comfortable elaborating on that, for me?” Michael inquired. “No, no, it’s fine. I’m fine.” “Are you sure?” “Yeah, I am.” She tried to look as calm as possible. “I think this is something that she and I should work out between each other. It’s not like we’re falling apart.” Sylvie began to stand up, but Michael placed a hand on her shoulder. “We can still talk about it, if you want to. I’m here to talk.” She nodded. “I know. I’ll make sure to email you when I need you again.” Sylvie pushed her chair in, and left the room at a brisk pace, not looking back. This shouldn’t be a repeat of last time. It didn’t have to be. She could handle it herself. ---- The familiar scent of roasted carrots filled the whole kitchen, only undercut by the aroma of cooked chicken sprinkled with paprika and black pepper. This was Cliff’s father’s recipe, and it was the only thing that he remembered fondly about the old times. Back before he had to cut himself off from everyone around him. Before his family found out that he ‘did it’ with the boy next door. Before his father never saw him the same way again. Even now, when he was free to feel like himself again, those same thoughts of his complete and total seclusion kept flooding back to him. All he needed was an impression of closeness with other people. But not in the way that most people would think of it. He had no desire for that. Sometimes he went days staying inside his home without any interaction with other people, only to come crawling back to the site for work and for the break room to talk with his coworkers. There were days that he desired for connection, and days that he didn’t. It was hard to describe. It was harder to describe it to someone else. How does one describe a fundamental difference that only a rare amount of people could understand? Cliff sighed, and went back to the skillet. He let his food simmer, watching it turn to a crisp golden brown. He flipped the chicken, sprinkled in a tinge of thyme, and reduced the heat to medium-low. Once the chicken was cooked thoroughly for another two to three minutes, he made sure to scrape up all the darker bits. He turned the heat off, and backed up to see his work. There it was, in all of its homemade glory. He grabbed a plate, carefully removed the chicken and the carrots from the skillet, and served himself, as he always had. He sat down, and stared at the chair across the table on the other side, where someone once sat. Someone who was no longer there. The only person who understood him. The only person who was there for him when no else was.   He imagined him sitting there, slurping Ramen noodles, his favorite food. Cliff perfectly recalled every detail from all those years ago, from his dirty blonde hair to that perfect smile that always brightened up his day. There he was, so full of life, full of pure, unbridled energy that couldn’t be suppressed. Cliff remembered this day. It was one of their last days together, the last good moment that he had with him, before he had to leave everything he loved behind for a second time. He remembered it like it was yesterday. “Yo, Noah, check this out,” his past self pushed the newspaper closer to him. Noah looked it over, before grabbing it and showing it back to him. On the page was an advertisement for wedding rings. “Changed your mind, huh?” “Nah, I just thought they looked nice.” He grinned. Noah shook his head. “You’re the one who didn’t want it.” “Having a lawn with a white picket fence or a dog or vacations to Venice would be nice, but not as nice as being with you.” “Oh, stop it! You’re going to make me blush.” “You’re too easy to fluster,” Cliff said. “One of these days, I’ll get you to crack. One day,” Noah wiggled a finger at him in jest. But that never happened. In fact, he never felt it at all. They ate in silence. Eventually, Cliff gathered up the courage to say something that he always kept to himself. “…Can I ask you something?” Noah gulped down his food. “Sure, yeah.” “Have you ever felt… nothing when I teased you before? Nothing at all?” “No, why?” He raised an eyebrow. “I’m just thinking about something. You know, hypothetically. Would it be weird if someone didn’t have that spark? No feelings for anyone at all?” Cliff posed the question that he wrestled with for the longest time. Noah simply sat there. “I mean, I guess? I don’t know what that would be like. It sounds depressing, I can’t imagine how lonely I would feel if I didn’t have you, or anyone really.” “Yeah, that would suck.” Cliff tried his hardest to keep the pit in his stomach from growing any wider. Those recollections, a roaring river of regret, cascaded through his mind to this day. It had been years since. Noah had probably forgotten about it all by now, and moved on with someone else. And yet here he was, still reminiscing on what could’ve been. He pulled out his phone, and went on Grindr for the third time today. Why he kept trying to match with other men when he knew that it wouldn't work out to begin with was something that couldn’t be answered easily. Maybe it was for the thrill of it, for one more one-night stand. One more short moment after another to feel the warmth that he once felt. And then when the sun came and the morning birds made their call, he fell right back to the hole that he dug for himself. Was he that much of a creep? Was he that much of a slut? Cliff didn’t choose Noah as much as he did for him. He was the one who asked first, he was the one who always worried about him, who was there to be his guiding light in the everlasting dark. But Cliff didn’t give the same. He never gave enough. He had to leave, because he made Noah’s life harder than it had to be. And his presence in it wasn’t enough to make up for it. That was the whole point of a partnership, right? To carry the burden together. But it would never be enough. Not with any part of him. Cliff blinked and looked around the room, now realizing that he was lost in his thoughts yet again. Grabbing his fork, he took a bite of the chicken. It was getting cold. Reducing the amount of leftovers in the fridge would be a good idea from now on. He shoved his phone back into his pocket, and returned to chowing down on the dinner that he made, without anyone else to share it with. He tried to not think about it this time. ---- Sylvie sat in a desk chair in her friend’s dorm, waiting for her to return from a meeting. Looking around the hodgepodge of various assorted items scattered around the desk, she focused on a bobblehead in the back right corner. Its dark, lifeless beady eyes seemed to stare into her soul. She felt like it was judging her. Caoimhe had an important project that could lead to her getting a lot of recognition, and with that came new people that she could meet, more important things to pay attention to, and less time that they could spend together. If that project got approved, what would happen then? So many things were changing around her, and yet everything felt the same. Sylvie was stuck, anchored in the same place and unable to move forward. Was she worrying over nothing? Nothing about their friendship seemed to change throughout the year since they met. At least, not outwardly. She wondered what Caoimhe was thinking. They both knew how worried she’d get sometimes. Some days it felt like her brain was testing her body chemistry and cranking it up to overdrive, heating her up in an inner oven of her own making. And every time all this catastrophizing turned out to be nothing. Just like this one. At least, she hoped it would be. But what if it was legitimate, this time? It became obvious that Sylvie’s constant fretting made the scales tip over to one side, as Caoimhe now had to console her and take care of her more often. One side gave too much, and the other gave nothing at all. The most important part of their friendship to her was the small joys. Walking down the park together, hand in hand, feeling the warm breeze and seeing the flowers bloom. Playing UNO together, watching each other scream in frustration. Getting close to one another while watching a movie. Their friendship wasn’t like most, but it was //theirs//. But as Sylvie appreciated the good things, she scrutinized the other side as well; all her imperfections. The way she clung to Caoimhe like a seahorse barely hanging onto a piece of coral, orbiting around her each day to stave off her feelings of desolation. Every moment that she tried her damndest to not make a mistake in front of her, or at least to make sure that she would never know about them. Managing all her problems herself and then being unable to admit that she needed help until much later. She could see every crack starting to form, ones that could collapse the entire foundation if left unchecked. Sylvie once tried to confess a bit of it to her friend, but they both shrugged it off and went on with their days. Maybe it was nothing after all, like everything else she was obsessed over. But it could turn out into something. It could slip by her unnoticed, and eventually cause something worse to happen in the future. And it would be her fault. And her friend would leave her for good, and she would have nothing left, and— The door to the room opened, snapping her out of her inner turmoil. She turned to see her friend leap into her arms, squealing in delight. “Did you get it?” Sylvie eagerly asked. “Yes! They approved my project. I got it!” Caoimhe tackled her onto the bed, cheering in excitement. They embraced each other, laughing all the way. But it got approved. Sylvie knew what would happen next. Yeah, that’ll work.” He then pulled out a letter, and began to read off of it, with Sylvie listening intently at every word he spoke. “I was only with you because I was trying to figure out myself. I was trying to love the person that I wanted to turn out to be, and living a happy life with someone else was part of that. I should’ve realized that our relationship was more than a checklist, but there’s nothing that can be done now.” “I think if younger me knew that there were more ways to love and appreciate someone than what we’re presented with, maybe things could’ve been different. I could’ve been there for you. I could’ve treated you as you wanted to be instead of how I thought I had to. It would’ve been nice to know that being close with someone doesn’t have to strictly be a black and white thing. But for what it’s worth, at least you’re better off without me.” He rolled the letter back up, and placed it in his pocket. “See? It’s not what you should be telling her, but it’s the truth. It’s what I should’ve said to him. You need to tell her exactly why you’re feeling this way, and then you can figure it out together with her after that,” Cliff explained. “Right, right.” Sylvie frowned. “What about you?”  Cliff raised an eyebrow. “What about me?” “I don’t know, I just think you should be more forgiving to yourself, that’s all.” “Eh.” He waved it off. “That’s past the point. I made my decisions, and you should be making better ones.” “Would Noah want that?” Sylvie asked him. He glared at her. “You don’t know shit about Noah.” “Yeah, you’re right, sorry.” She sighed. “But I’d think he’d forgive you, wouldn’t he? But even if he didn’t, I think he’d want you to at least forgive yourself. You helped me out this much, so I think I should return the favor.” Cliff paused for a moment. “You’d really do that?” “Yeah. Yeah I would,” she replied. In a split second, Sylvie could see Cliff’s expression shift, like a weight that he’d been holding for years had finally been lifted. “I’ve never had anyone do that for me. Thanks, I guess.” “I can’t leave a fellow aro behind, you know? We gotta stick together,” Sylvie said. He tried to conceal the smile that was creeping in, but it was there. “I don’t know how anyone can help me of all people. I still don’t know what’s in store for me. Who I should be in spite of everything.” “Well, we can figure that out together, right?” She held out her hand. He accepted it. “Sure. Why not.” ---- It was the 26th. One year ago on this day, Sylvie and Caoimhe found each other in the lab, working together on various experiments. They were an unlikely pair, but their chemistry for each other mixed together to form a bond that could never split apart. Throughout all of this, Caoimhe was her usual bubbly self, always looking after her, always cheering her up after every failed experiment with lackluster results, always being the light to brighten up her day. If she had anything negative to say about Sylvie, she must have been very good at hiding it. But that never showed. There were no signs, no change in her expression, nothing but that bright and jovial smile. The only changes that moved in flux were Sylvie’s thoughts about everything they had and everything that could be taken away. But communication was key. If the problem couldn’t be solved alone, reaching out would be the next best thing. She went down the hallway connecting all the personnel dormitories, her mind racing, her heart lumped in her throat. There were so many things that could happen. So many things that could go wrong. But she couldn’t run in circles anymore. There was no other way. The door opened, and she stepped into her friend’s room. It looked to be even more of a mess, with papers scattered around her desk and the wastebasket overflowing with soda cans, with a few having fallen out onto the floor. Sylvie knew Caoimhe was extra busy as she was still working on that project for the higher-ups. She had no idea who those higher-ups were, but they had to be important, right? With all this bureaucracy and red tape, it could get difficult to track names and faces. But that didn’t matter at this moment. She shouldn’t make her friend’s life even harder by sitting this out. Caoimhe was sitting at her desk, head in hands, staring at a large set of papers stapled together. Sylvie came up and sat beside her, looking over her shoulder. “What’s all this?” She asked. “What do you think?” Caoimhe threw the papers up in the air. “Sorry, I’m just really frustrated right now. Nothing’s been working, and I’m supposed to show this to my supervisor in a week from now. I don’t know what to do.” Sylvie had never seen her like this. Never this exhausted. “I can help you out with that, if you need any suggestions or anything.” “No, I’ll be fine, you don’t need to worry about me.” She shrugged it off. “I should be, actually. It’s okay to ask for help. Take it from me, I could also use some help right now.” Caoimhe looked at her curiously. “Is something up?” “More like something’s down. I need to talk to you about something, and it’s really important, and I know that I shouldn’t be distracting you from your work, but I just need to let this out of my system.” Her smile came back in full force. “Anything that distracts me from this hawkshite is a plus. C’mon.” She pulled her arm as she rolled her desk chair to the middle of the room, where they had more space to talk without feeling cramped. She swiveled the chair around to face her. “You can take your time, alright? No rush here. Say what you want to say.” Sylvie sat there, contemplating on what to say, analyzing every single word that could be phrased in different ways. But it was obvious what needed to be said. She didn’t have to overthink it this time. It had to come from her heart. “I’d first like to say that whatever I’m feeling is not because of you. It’s my fault. All of it is. I didn’t feel like I was doing enough for you. I never defined any of this with you, and I know it's ours and that’s all it needs to be, but I’m scared, Caoimhe. I’m scared of being left behind. I’m a big fucking baby. I’m not proud of who I am at all.” She could feel herself shaking again. “I just wanted to live a quiet, carefree life with you. I shouldn’t have to worry about how people see me. See us. Because it’s not what they expect. I feel like I’d fall apart without you, not even for a week, and that’s not healthy. You’re off to that important project, and I’m sitting here by myself because I don’t have anyone else. I’m sorry for dragging you down all this time. I’m not worth it.” She could feel the tears coming again. Why was she so weak? Why was she so worthless? Maybe the world was right about her. Maybe— A soft, warm embrace fell onto her like a blanket, allowing her to let it all out, the floodgates opening all the tears that she was holding back. “You are worth it. You’ve been the most important person in my life, Sylvie. I’m serious. Do you remember the time when I fractured my leg, and you volunteered to do both my work and yours at the same time, regardless of how taxing that would be? Do you remember rushing over to my dorm after my mom had to be taken to the hospital, doing everything you can to support me when I thought she was going to die? Do you remember all those times where you took me out bowling, or ate at your favorite restaurant, or when we laughed at all your baby photos? Do you even remember //any of that//? You’ve done more than enough.” Caoimhe pulled away from her. “If anything, I’m not the one pulling my weight. But I don’t think it matters how much we’re doing to let each other know that we care. What matters is that we care. You still care a lot about me. And I’m the same. Even more so. Because you’re the coolest person I know. You’re my best friend. That’s not ever going to change. I’m not going anywhere, okay?” Sylvie nodded, wiping her tears away. “Okay. Thank you. Sorry for all of that.” “No need to apologize. Better to just say it than keep it buried inside, eh?” “Yeah.” Sylvie stood up. “Shit! I forgot. I still have that surprise for you today.” “What surprise?” Caoimhe asked. “For our anniversary. I thought we should make it more special, bring a few more people to celebrate with.” Caoimhe hugged her again, squeezing her as hard as she could. “That is class! You’re the best, Sylvie.” “Yeah, okay, okay, can you stop squeezing me please—” Later in the day, they all gathered up in Sylvie’s room. Caoimhe, Cliff, and Michael were all there, playing cards and having a good time. They had a giant chocolate cake and everything. Once they had downtime, Sylvie went up to Cliff, who was leaning against the wall. “Hey. I want to say thanks. For helping me out.” Cliff nodded. “Least I could do.” He took a sip of his drink. “Well, I better get going. Thanks for inviting me.” He turned to the door, before Sylvie grabbed his arm. “I think we should talk, first. I still need to put in my part of our deal.” Cliff simply stood there. “I do appreciate it, but you can’t help me. No one can.” “I’ll try my best. You don’t have to feel like you’re  left out of the conversation anymore. I know what that’s like. You can hang out with us. Hang out with me.” He turned his head to the right. “Can you find me a guy who doesn’t think I’m there to only have sex?” “I’ll look around. You know that guy over at T&C, the one with the lip piercing? Caoimhe told me that he was a tattoo artist before he got here. I think that’s pretty cool.” Cliff chuckled. “I don’t think I’m ready for that, yet.” “Yeah. All I’m saying is that I hope that you find someone who makes you feel loved in a way that you’re comfortable with. Or if you don’t want to partner with anyone, that’s okay too. I still question myself sometimes, even though I got it mostly figured out, but that’s fine, because we’re always discovering something new about ourselves each and every day. You’re you, and that’s all that matters.” He fully turned towards her. “You’re a kind soul, you know that?” “Yeah. Thanks. Thank you. The door is this way.” They walked out the door together, and as Sylvie held it open for him, Michael watched them from the chair by the back wall. He knew it would work eventually. It wasn’t how he wanted it to go, but it turned out right in the end. To turn out, to figure out this aspect of your life, it was hard to navigate. It always was. But with others by your side, to be there to support you no matter what, to make you feel like you belong, it lightened the burden. There will always be others out there just like Sylvie. Just like Cliff. Just like Michael. It’s what gave the world its beauty with a variety of experiences and identities that made up all of its shades of colors. Even if the world didn’t want them, they still existed. They will always exist, and they will always be free to live as they want to, to dance and cry and run and laugh and smile and //live.// In the end, it will all turn out for the better. And just this once, love lost. [[include component:wikimodule |ratings= --]]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box-end]]

Is This Land Still Made For You And Me?

by Jay Santos Everwood

This land's your homeland, it's not my own land,
From the Keys of Florida to the 'burbs of Portland,
From the Texas praries to the Great Lake waters;
Is this land still made for you and me?

As I was running that endless rat race;
I felt around me growin' prejudice;
I saw in this country roaring hatred;
Is this land still made for you and me?

I've roamed and rambled and I followed the footsteps
Of this country's millions a' migrant workers;
And all around me a voice was asking;
Is this land still made for you and me?

When the voice came sounding, and I was listening,
And the crowds a'screaming and fanatics roaring,
As the fog creeped in now, voices were chanting:
"Deport all immigrants you see!"

As I went walking I saw two rallies,
And on one side it said "Deport All Migrants."
And on the other side it said "Kill the poor."
Which side is meant to be for me?

In steeple shadows, on city corners,
I see my people despised as foreigners,
Get locked away, or being deported,
Is this land still made for you and me?

Nobody living can make me ashamed
Of where I come from or who I am now;
Nobody living can make me turn back
…









This land has been made hell for me.







SCP-9726

Wonder World!TM

Wonderday

(That's Friday)

April 11 2025

9:00 AM WWST

Your name is Dr. Isabel Helga Anastasia Parvati Wondertainment, V.

You are President, CEO, and CCO of Doctor Wondertainment Incorporated, and Big Boss Lady.(The role is purely ceremonial. There is no whimsy in governance, after all. You have Mr. Mayor to do all of that for you!) of your own little corner of the Mnemosyne Expanse called "Wonder World!TM".

And you're dealing with the one thing you dread facing.

A creative block.

You lean back against the purple swivel chair, which squeaks from exertion, and look towards the big big window of your office.

The smiling sun of Wonder World!TM beams delicious rays of lemonade-y light down onto your sprawling headquarter and the beautiful town it overlooks. The rainbow ficuses that flank either side of the glass pane dance to a silent tune, basking in the warmth and taste of the nutrients the star you created gives.

Such sights surely should have sparked some inspiration in you…

… But they haven't!

A frustrated whine slips past your lips before you can stop it, the hurried clamp of your hand - partially obscured by your favorite (if oversized) technicolor coat - against your mouth coming moments too late.

Dang it! you think to yourself, crossing your arms against your chest while a pout forms against your lip. This won't do! Won't do at all!

You're the face of Wondertainment as a whimsical empire! You're supposed to be a source of inspiration and awe! The inherent joy of creativity, personified!

You're not supposed to feel this executive dysfunction! How heartbroken would people be, if they found out that even you felt the bubbling frustration…

The gnawing anxieties…

The mind-numbing void of Doubt that came with not being able to Have An Idea?

A cute yip, and then a sudden weight against your lap, distracts you from your thoughts.

Looking down, you see your Welsh corgi companion, Jeremy — Well, one of them; even you have trouble keeping track of them sometimes! — staring up at you with big, brown puppy-dog eyes. He lets out a worried whimper as he splays his pawsers against your knees, headbutting your torso with his cold nose.

Your bad mood ebbs away, and you give Jeremy a smile.

"Hi, puppa," you greet him, reaching behind his big ol' golden ears and giving them a few scritches. His tiny lil tail wags and thumps against your left knee in appreciation. "Mama's okay; she's just having trouble with her job."

Jeremy tilts his head at you, his tail still going at it like a propeller plane ready for takeoff. He places a paw against your hand, making a noise that you know means "Play?".

"I can't, Jeremy," you say with a pained sigh. "I have to think of something for our next lineup by tonight, and that means no distractions!"

A series of heart-tugging whines leaves his throat, his eyes becoming more pleading.

Your thin brow scrunches up in thought, and you wheel your chair towards your office door before pushing it open with your foot.

"Emma?" you call out.

"Yes, Miss Isabel?" the chipper voice of Emma Aieselthorpe-Brown - your faithful assistant-slash-secretary - responds from her desk, looking up curiously from her Wondertainment Whimsytop.(A purple laptop with your logo on it, powered by the innate marvel of technology's potential instead of boring things like "RAM" and "SSDs"!).

"Please cancel all of my calls for the day," you say to her, releasing Jeremy from your lap, watching him run excitedly towards the now-confused woman.

"But ma'am, you… don't have any calls scheduled today," she informs you with some worry.

You roll your eyes, feeling a smile against your lips. "So make up some calls, and then cancel them!" you suggest with a giggle. "And then take your break early," you finish, gesturing towards the dog that currently has both paws on Emma's right knee, stubby tail wiggling in excitement. "Jeremy needs his playtime!"

A normal assistant would probably balk at such requests.

But no one in Wonder World!TM was "normal". Otherwise, the name would be false advertising!

"Right away, Miss Isabel," Emma chirps, letting Jeremy hop onto her lap as the brunette begins typing away in the scheduling application.

You give an appreciative smile her way, before rolling backwards towards your desk.

Your left leg sticks back out at the last possible moment, your foot pressing against the cherry oak and stopping your chair dead in its tracks.

Success!

You spin a triumphant 180°…

… And then immediately that good reverie fizzles out like a flat soda, your eyes set upon the blank papers and violet ballpoint once more.

Rats.

You hunch back over the desk, and tap the end of the pen against your cheek, your tongue sticking out the side of your mouth while your brow bunches up once more.

Something sports-related? No no no, too masc-dominated; need something unigender, you begin to think, idly scribbling a "cool W" on the corner of the paper.

Something to do with horses? That's been popular with all genders recently. You ponder for a moment, tip of the pen nearly touching the parchment to begin writing…

And then you stop, shaking your head.

No no. Tried that before; all the magical horse manure…

You shudder and shove that thought in the back of your mind.

You groan again, balling your tan hands against your cheeks. Think, Izzy, think! You've never missed a deadline before.

…

Wait.

…

Missed a deadline.

…

…

Missed a.

…

…

…

Mister!

"Aha!"

Of course! You could make a new collectors' line of Misters!

After all, the Foundation might be making their own. But a genuine Wondertainment Mister's charm could never be replicated!

Invigorated and stimming with a tapping foot, you begin jotting down a preliminary little message.


Wow! You've just gotten a member of the Universal Little Mister Collectors' Line! Infinite worlds? Infinite possibilities!

Collect them all to become Mister Multiverse!

  • 01. Mr. Cowpoke
  • 02. Mr. Starstruck
  • 03. Ms. LLM
  • 04. Mr. Polar
  • 05. Mr. Ascension
  • 06.


…

You stop, frowning.

Yggdrasil possesses a lot of branches, sub-branches, and entanglements.

You'd have to make hundreds… thousands… hundreds of thousands of Misters to fully encompass them!

That would oversaturate the market! And be expensive as heck!

Even a Toon like you didn't have infinite money on hand!!

What's the point?, you feel the Doubt quietly hiss in the very back of your mind.

Sighing, you take the piece of paper off the sheaf. You start sliding it towards the shredder…

And then stop yourself.

You look towards the pneumatic tube system by your desk.

The Random Universe Mail Shoot, or RUMS.

(Forced acronym? Maybe. But you couldn't think of a better one, so it stuck.)

… You don't have to let this idea go to waste.

You can let one of the other Wondertainments build off of it!

Grinning, you roll up the purple stationary and wheel over towards the contraption Mr. Brass helped you construct. You pop the cover, which lets out a hiss of compressed air, and place the document into the tube's container. You shut the cover firmly - making sure you hear the CLICK - and wait a few moments.

Three seconds later, you hear the pipe rumble, and the container rocket upwards with a SHUP, so fast you're barely able to register its speed!

Waiting until you no longer hear the rattling above your head, you nod to yourself and come back to your desk.

Okay, so those Mister ideas didn't pan out!

But you're not deterred.

You should be.

You start jotting down on the next piece of paper.


Wowzers! You're now in possession of one of your very own Mistercores, a limited edition vibe and aesthetic-based line of Little Misters!

Collect them all to become Mister Wavecore!

  • 01. Mr. Vaporwave
  • 02. Ms. Cottagecore
  • 03. Mr. Low and Mrs. Poly
  • 04. Mr. Weirdcore
  • 05. Mr. Cassette Futurism
  • 06. Ms. Sparkly
  • 07.


…

No no no, that won't work, either!

These things wax and wane all the time, sometimes within a single day!

Who knows how difficult it'll even be to market some of these?

Not to mention how difficult it'll be to narrow down which aesthetics to make a Mister off of!

Wondertainment will never sell a Miss Traumacore, thank you very much!

You should have taken up that offer… the Doubt sadistically whispers, the taste of static like rotten Pop Rocks against your tongue.

You swallow with a grimace.

No.

You made your thoughts on that very clear when…

THUNK

The RUMS container has returned from… wherever it went.

Huffing, you go back towards the system, unseal the cover, put the paper in, and send it off once more.

CLICK!

SHUP!

How long can you keep offloading your ideas onto others?

You let out another groan, and return to your workstation.

Okay, enough messing around! you think to yourself! Time to lock in!

You're wasting your time…

Holy cow! You got yourself a Genre Mister! Perfect for reading a good book with!

Collect them all to become Mister Genre!



…

Too derivative!

THUNK!

CLICK!

SHUP!

You keep rushing.

Wowee! You're now the proud owner of a Gaming Mister! Which style are you nostalgic for?

Collect them all to become Mister Video!



…

Too much R&D work!

THUNK!

CLICK!

SHUP!

Your need for validation will consume you whole.

Groovy! You're procured a Generational Mister ! All days are the good ol' days in someone's eye!

Collect them all to become Mister Generation!



…

Too Gregorian (and possibly problematic)!

THUNK!

CLICK!

SHUP!

You'll never be able to realize these ideas to their fullest potential.


Wow, congrats! You have been granted an exclusive part of Doctor Wondertainment's upcoming Little Misters sub-series, GOI Misters !

Get ready to collect them all and become Mister Interest!

"AAAUGH!"

This ran into the same issue as the Universal Misters!

There are just too many dang Groups running around in this universe alone!

And some of them you definitely don't want to associate with the brand.

Especially that creep at Westhead—

"Hey there, champ!"

You suddenly feel static permeate around you, followed by the whine of a CRT television.

You spin around, and see Steamboat Willie playing on one of your many leisure screens clustered in the corner by your office door. The jovial mouse himself being front and center.

Only "Willie" isn't doing his jaunty whistle at the ship's helm.

He's staring directly at you. Grinning with too many teeth, his hands behind his back, and his neck turning at a 90° angle with a warbling but no less sickening crunch.

"You should be careful with your thoughts!" "Willie" chides you, the voice grainy but unmistakably not that of Ol' Walter's. "You never know what might be listening!"

This is your second chance…

Your hands grip against the armrests of your chair, all pleasantries drained from your gaze.

"I thought I told you you weren't welcome here," you say, words clipped. The possessed rodent only lets out a mirthless chuckle and wags a finger at you.

"You never formalized that," the parasite puppetering the animation icon sneers at you. "So I'll come and go as I please, missy…"

You're going to push them away, like you always do…

Your knuckles whiten, very un-whimsical thoughts zipping through your mind as the amused snake smirks at you.

"What. Do. You. Want?" you grit out, which only seems to make the parasite more emboldened. A dull, unmelodic hum leaves its puppet's lips, and it steps closer, hands pressed up directly against the glass barrier.

Television snow distorts where its fingertips rest.

"Oh, nothing too grand. Just a small little deal I have on offer." The faux-affable words leave the mouth that doesn't belong to it like crunching glass, making your hair prickle upwards.

TAKE IT!

"And I'll tell you what I told you last time," you say coolly, getting up from your chair and beginning to make your way towards the television with purpose.

The inksuit reels back from you. Very subtly, but your keen eyes are able to catch its fingers twitch apprehensively. Just as quickly, however, the leech's humorless grin returns, the beady eyes it stole levelling with yours.

"I don't want your cloying, saccharine blemish anymore," The Westhead snarls at you, before it straightens up, sickening pops emitting from its mouthpiece's spine. "I simply want to offer to… alleviate your current struggles."

TAKE IT!

That earns him a scoff from your lips, though it successfully halts you, only a couple of feet away from the screen. "And what could you possibly know that can help me?" you barb out.

The ghoul is not deterred, though, its chuckles like bubbling tar.

"Well, why make ideas yourself," it begins, arms behind its back as its pawn sways in place. "When you can get other people — other things — to think for you?"

TAKE! IT!

Unburden yourself!

"Absolutely not!" you respond immediately, only noticing you raised your voice when its echo bounces off your office walls. The bastard's lips only curl up further, the rows of teeth too dense to make out from the fuzz and grain.

"You stupid, stubborn cunt," it spits at you, its true venom finally seeping into its words. "I'm trying to help you. What you're doing isn't sustainable, not profitable."

Another offer of help ignored.

"Tell me. How many toys have you sold that weren't seized and locked away from the brats you market towards?"

Typical.

"How much money has Wondertainment even made?"

This is why people hate you.

"Is your company even close to being in the black, after all the setbacks you've faced?"

"…"

"What's the matter?" It jeers. "Rat got your tongue?"

If your glare could get any stronger, it'd probably melt the television into scrap.

"I don't do this for the money," you growl lowly.

The creep has the audacity to laugh at that.

"That's what they all say," it chuckles at you, unbearable smugness in its words. "And then the gears stop taking the oils of passion, and - in their desperation - the creatives submit to soaking the machine's teeth with their blood, their sweat, their meat, subsuming themselves until all that's left is compliant viscera and…"

Its snatched voice fades away from your ears, the Doubt in your mind practically screaming at you now.

Useless failure

Slapping away the hands that try to feed you

This is all you'll be remembered for

"Get out."

You find yourself surprised by how harshly the words leave your throat. Though perhaps not as surprised as the Westhead, who takes a small step backwards behind the screen, even if the contemptuous look it gives you doesn't waver.

What are you doing

That only makes something within you spike higher, past a ceiling you never knew you had.

You briskly close the distance between the two of you, your gaze never breaking away from the intruder as you extend your left hand - palm first - directly at it.

Stop it

It doesn't move back any further. Though you can see its false digits twitch, see it lean backwards…

See genuine nervousness crack against its holier-than-thou air, as purple lightning sparks from your palm.

Pure, unadulterated Wonder.

STOP IT

"Get the hell out!" you shout, ignoring the bile that even that mild profanity leaves on your taste buds. The glow from your hand becomes almost blinding, forming an obscuring, violet glare against the CRT.

"AND DON'T EVER, EVER, COME BA—!"

"Miss Isabel?"

You blink.

The lavender orb immediately dematerializes, your arm sagging like a deflating balloon towards your side, as you see Emma's worried face - along with three of your Jeremies - poke out from the doorway.

You look back at the TV, and see Willie glancing around in a panic, before hesitantly returning to the script as if nothing happened.

"You sounded angry," your assistant says in a quiet voice, and you notice her hair buns seem a bit frazzled. "Very angry. Is everything okay?"

You're going to scare her off.

You look down at yourself, the light brown hand you were seconds away from using as a weapon of last resort… now unremarkable, except for who it was attached to.

You let out a breath you didn't know you were holding, and give a shaky smile in her direction. "I'm fine, Emma," you reassure as you click the television off. "I just had to kick out an unwanted guest."

She won't believe you.

Emma nods uncertainly, anxiousness bunching up her eyes, before the door is pushed open by the excited and panting corgis that quickly circle around you.

"Did the Jeremies give you any trouble?" you ask her, eager to change the subject as you bend down to pet each of your canine friends.

Deflecting coward

Emma laughs, the tension fully broken now, and shakes her head. "Other than them wanting to sniff Mr. Fish during walkies, not at all," she says, taking a moment to smooth down her hair with one hand.

You chuckle at that. I really need to train them better, you think.

Another failure on your part

"Anyway," your secretary continues. "Stressing yourself out isn't going to make the ideas come quicker. Why don't you call it early today, Miss Isabel?" She smiles up at you, that same soothing smile that carried you through hell and high water.

Relief washes over you, and you nod.

"Thank you, Emma," you say gratefully. "Let me take care of one more thing, and then I'll take the rest of the day off. Mr. Board and Mr. Director will understand, surely."

You can only push your luck so many times until you're told "no"

"Of course, Miss," she says with a nod, before shutting the door. You sigh, which segues into a high pitch yawn. You stretch your arms out with a cute noise as you relieve the tension in your back.

A head-clearing stroll outside would be good for you.

You walk up to RUMS one last time, carefully folding the paper still in your right hand.

THUNK!

CLICK!

SHUP!

Hope one of the Corneliuses, Hollies, Judies, or other Izzies put these drafts to good use.

They won't.

You clasp your hands together once the tube stops shaking, instantly catching your dogs' attention. You grin down at them.

"Who wants mama to buy some Pup Whip Cups?"

A good cuppa - double-roasted, with two sugars, milk, whipped cream, sprinkles, and a Wonder Cherry© on top - sounds delicious right now!

A chorus of excited yips follow behind you as you and the Jeremies walk out of your office.

Before you leave, you steal one last glance towards your desk.

Can you really put this off again?

…

I'll manage, you silence them firmly.

You flick the lightswitch down, and head out to spend of the rest of the day with your best friends.

"Mama's okay; she's just having trouble with her job." Jeremy tilts his head at you, his tail still going at it like a propeller plane ready for takeoff. It/Her/Them



2025

26 July

Grand Cove: Grand Bend, Lambton County, Ontario, Canada

Jay found her on the porch of the little bungalow, sitting on the swing. Ilse had insisted on having one installed just days after moving in. She'd seen them in the movies, projected through her window.

For decades before Jay had been born, everything in its partner's life had been projected through glass. They had lived second-hand through more than one lifetime. The demiwoman out of the incinerator was due a few indulgences.

Besides, ridiculous artifact of days gone past though it was, Jay had to admit that the swing was kind of great. Most of the personal touches in Ilse's house had a similar vibe. It gave the whole sleepover a subtle time-lost quality, like a dream from another life.

Ilse looked up as Jay sat down beside them, but didn't speak. In the darkness — it was night, and the house was on a corner lot tucked out of view — those big blue eyes were pools of starlight. Jay put their arm around Ilse's shoulders, and asked one of those stupid questions that did so much load bearing in human relations.

"Can't sleep?"

Ilse shrugged. "I probably could, if I put my mind to it."

Jay reached up to ruffle its partner's orange mop. "Well, that's true of anything."

Ilse smiled. "You are the wind beneath my wings."

"And what's he?" Jay jerked a thumb at the bungalow, where Researcher James, age six, was fast asleep. He snored a little, but at least his growth had been arrested past the point where he slept through the night.

"The bags beneath my eyes?" Ilse suggested innocently.

Jay suppressed a laugh. "That's not nice!"

Ilse's eyes narrowed impishly. "I'm practicing not being nice. One condition of my release is blending in with the modern world."

Month by month, the restrictions placed on Ilse to prevent their anomalous existence from disturbing the mundane status quo were being lifted. She was well on her way to living as normal life as you could live without ever actually getting any older.

"I'll bet it's a disappointment," Jay mused, "coming out of the incinerator to this era specifically."

"No." Ilse shook their head. "It's been anything but a disappointment. And I've seen worse."

Jay cocked their head to one side. "Worse than everyone trying their best to end the world?"

"Yes." Ilse slipped out from under Jay's arm, and walked to the rail. They were still in their night clothes, old fashioned and frilly. Jay, by contrast, wore a robe. "I've seen what comes after. Worlds that really did end."

"The deadlines."

Ilse nodded. "Half of humanity dead in one." She left a beat, to acknowledge the customary omission of Timeline 5243-B. "Ninety nine point repeating nine percent dead in another. Millions dead, everyone dead, and…"

"You never talk about the other two."

Ilse glanced back at them.

"Well, I never saw one. And I'm not actually allowed to so much as mention the other."

"You've told me plenty of things that aren't allowed," Jay reminded them gently. "I've done the same for you."

"This is different." Ilse sighed. "I agree with the reason these things are kept secret. I wish I didn't know about them."

"Are they worse? Worse than the other five?"

Ilse looked up, past the eaves of the house. At the stars. "It's… subjective."

"Subjective how?"

The little redhead's voice took on a quality of distance, though she didn't move a muscle. "There was a world where everyone lived in abject misery. No hope. No peace. Just endless death in red, drifting farther and farther from the possibility of repair. No rest, no comfort, nothing."

"How is that not obviously the worst of the lot?"

"It was, for everyone else."

Ilse tapped the rail.

Jay slipped off the swing, and walked to stand next to her. "You were stuck in the incinerator."

Ilse was still searching the stippled heavens. "Yes, but that wasn't it."

"Then what?"

"You know I was an Overseer in -A."

"You might have mentioned it, several times." Mostly when she wanted to choose what they had for dinner.

"I made a genuine difference there." Ilse wrung the rail with their thin fingers. "I helped rebuild the world."

"You might get your chance to do that here, soon."

Ilse acknowledged the gallows humour with a nod, but would not be distracted from whatever point she was trying to make. "In -C I held them all together. Told them stories about what was still out there, beyond the black. Reminded them what was worth waiting for, no matter how long it took."

Jay ruffled her hair again. It was so hard not to. "You've always been selfless."

Ilse grimaced. "I spent seven decades focusing on nothing but myself. But that's not the point. -D wasn't much different from the world we live in now. Little hiccoughs in the usual course, nothing humanity couldn't survive. Maybe even forget."

"And -E?"

A dark cloud Jay was already well acquainted with crossed those ageless features. "I'm still not ready to talk about that. The point is, they weren't all bad. Some of them were little hells, or big. But for me… at the time, I could have told you with confidence which was worse. Not anymore."

"Why? What changed?"

Ilse was still looking up, only now it was at them. "Jay, there was a time when I was never really alone. Seven realities at once, all blurring across my field of view. Seven humanities to keep me company. But one by one they all dropped away, until I was left with just one me, and just one everybody else."

"That's all most people ever have."

"And it's more than I need. Because Jay?" Ilse leaned in close, and their bodies began coordinating defence against the evening chill. "I could lose a thousand eternities without caring at all. There's only one line I want to walk, now. The others are all equally barren to me. They fall short on the only thing that matters, the thing that makes this world the best of all of them, for me."

Jay stared at her. It didn't know what to say. Ilse leaned in further, rested her head on their chest. They held each other at the rail for a few moments, then a few moments longer.

"This is the only world where I have you," Ilse finally finished.

"Yeah," Jay sniffled. "Obviously I got that already, dummy."

Ilse would not be deflected. Jay found it one of their most endearing qualities. "All those worlds slipped away. All the people I could have been without you are gone. I don't miss them anymore. This world will never end, Jay. Not for me. You're what to get for the demiwoman who was everything."

"You're so humble," Jay tried to laugh. The emotion in their voice crowded it out. "I'm… I'm thankful every day that I met you."

"Me too." Ilse squeezed Jay's side, its empty left sleeve hanging loose over her wrist. "I get to wake up every morning and talk to you. It's an upgrade across the board. I wouldn't trade you for an eternity, Jay. No matter how dark the days get, we'll always have each other."

"That, plus coffee," Jay yawned, and the spell was broken. "Think you can sleep now?"

"And miss more of the Earth's final moments?" She didn't say: and ours? but Jay heard it anyway.

"You said it yourself. You've seen those final moments enough times."

"You're right." Ilse nodded against Jay's chest. "This time belongs to us."

Jay rested its chin against her scalp, and smiled as their hearts beat in sync. "Ilse Reynders, I do believe that some day, all of time will."

The little redhead's voice took on a quality of distance, though she didn't move a muscle. "There was a world where everyone lived in abject misery. No hope. No peace. Just endless death in red, drifting farther and farther from the possibility of repair. No rest, no comfort, nothing." "How is that not obviously the worst of the lot?" "It was, for everyone else." Ilse tapped the rail. Jay slipped off the swing, and walked to stand next to her. "You were stuck in the incinerator." Ilse was still searching the stippled heavens. "Yes, but that wasn't it." "Then what?" "You know I was an Overseer in -A." "You might have mentioned it, several times." Mostly when she wanted to choose what they had for dinner. "I made a genuine difference there." Ilse wrung the rail with their thin fingers. "I helped rebuild the world." "You might get your chance to do that here, soon." Ilse acknowledged the gallows humour with a nod, but would not be distracted from whatever point she was trying to make. "In -C I held them all together. Told them stories about what was still out there, beyond the black. Reminded them what was worth waiting for, no matter how long it took." Jay ruffled her hair again. It was so hard not to. "You've always been selfless." Ilse grimaced. "I spent seven decades focusing on nothing but myself. But that's not the point. -D wasn't much different from the world we live in now. Little hiccoughs in the usual course, nothing humanity couldn't survive. Maybe even forget." "And -E?" A dark cloud Jay was already well acquainted with crossed those ageless features. "I'm still not ready to talk about that. The point is, they weren't all bad. Some of them were little hells, or big. But for me... at the time, I could have told you with confidence which was worse. Not anymore." "Why? What changed?" Ilse was still looking up, only now it was at them. "Jay, there was a time when I was never really alone. Seven realities at once, all blurring across my field of view. Seven humanities to keep me company. But one by one they all dropped away, until I was left with just one me, and just one everybody else." "That's all most people ever have." "And it's more than I need. Because Jay?" Ilse leaned in close, and their bodies began coordinating defence against the evening chill. "I could lose a thousand eternities without caring at all. There's only one line I want to walk, now. The others are all equally barren to me. They fall short on the only thing that matters, the thing that makes this world the best of all of them, for me." Jay stared at her. It didn't know what to say. Ilse leaned in further, rested her head on their chest. They held each other at the rail for a few moments, then a few moments longer. "This is the only world where I have you," Ilse finally finished. "Yeah," Jay sniffled. "Obviously I got that already, dummy." Ilse would not be deflected. Jay found it one of their most endearing qualities. "All those worlds slipped away. All the people I could have been without you are gone. I don't miss them anymore. This world will never end, Jay. Not for me. You're what to get for the demiwoman who was everything." "You're so humble," Jay tried to laugh. The emotion in their voice crowded it out. "I'm... I'm thankful every day that I met you." "Me too." Ilse squeezed Jay's side, its empty left sleeve hanging loose over her wrist. "I get to wake up every morning and talk to you. It's an upgrade across the board. I wouldn't trade you for an eternity, Jay. No matter how dark the days get, we'll always have each other." "That, plus coffee," Jay yawned, and the spell was broken. "Think you can sleep now?" "And miss more of the Earth's final moments?"  She didn't say: and ours? but Jay heard it anyway. "You said it yourself. You've seen those final moments enough times." "You're right." Ilse nodded against Jay's chest. "This time belongs to us." Jay rested its chin against her scalp, and smiled as their hearts beat in sync. "Ilse Reynders, I do believe that some day, all of time will."
