A remarkable abstraction for a single-digit age: It was insufficient to want in the moment. You had to be //good at wanting//, had to see and know and act every moment perfectly. So you learned to do those things. You decided to be good at whatever you needed to, and you were. Every weeping paean for denied desire reads to you a confession of weakness. If anyone had ever really desired, as you did, they would simply have what was owed them. In the archive of your days there comes another sister. The world righting itself. Love is held constant, and what you lost was returned. Grown from neonatal to the cherubic adorability of a toddler in passing moments. Fiona you cared for primly and with perfect tenderness. This sank more incontestably than any other event the fact of your sororal superiority in your mind. As you grew into yourself, mastered everything worth mastering, your elder sister skittered deeper into the waste she’d made of her life. She rejected every principle she’d ever learned. At first an admirable dedication to rebellion (against who?) and then with dawning horror a total destruction of the self. She could not distinguish between rules of sobriety and //self-preservation//. Dyed hair a clonal assertion of her individuality. Tattoos plain attention-whoring but respectable in her commitment. Disgusting: A rotating cast of boyfriends and flings; first a skin-scrawled punk wannabe, later a girl who stank of cigarettes, finally an obvious creep. Perhaps he thought of himself as a young soul. Popular at school, no doubt. A few times when you met (never at home, your idiot sister helpfully delivering herself to him nicely trussed up). You considered warding him off. Breaking them up. Words to her rejected with huffy proclamations, you don’t get it, Ada, he really likes me. We’ll stay together, watch. Threats to him transparently empty, and rather not dwell on where his eyes went. Upon reflection best that his attentions kept to the stupid bitch who offered herself up. You they feted in school with meaningless awards. Eventually they had you going out of state, winning competitions. To your chagrin you found your effortless success was extinct. But vindication born of hours of study was only sweeter. If others cared, they’d match you. Worked on whatever caught your fancy, finding medals weightless in every discipline. You felt about the same doing conferences for some new paper as you did on a podium for your dance routine. They had your picture on the high-school website now. You spent increasingly little time with your peers. Had no time to think of anything but the work. A good place to drown. Late one tepid night your sister came in red-eyed from the cold. Footsore, walking from God knows when, or where. She didn’t say a word to you. While Hannah found new ways to ruin herself, little Fiona had you as the perfect showpiece (and you, her). You made great displays of your love, dragging her with you to symposia or concerts. She had just the perfect pictures to show her friends, occasionally abducting one with her to enjoy whatever facile attraction was available while you busied yourself. The trophy of her affection you juggled with whichever talent you’d decided to learn that year. It would be a lie to say you were directionless. Rather you were ever-directed. Caught in a hurricane. You wanted, and burned with the want, and your prizes you would have. But no resolution, no lasting gain. You were a void for accolades and acclaim. Still slight as the day you kindled that fire. For all the years. Rising like a willow over the rushes. Dear Hannah cleaned herself up, hair boldly cut scalp-short and then grown into matte tresses. As if remembering how to be a woman. Tattoos barely present to begin with, actually, and the few that remained painstakingly expunged. She could never commit, but she’d learned, in that high wilderness. Outside of the confines of your home. Odd expression, you think: not as if your home ever confined you. Nothing resolved. You raged at what came to you so easily, and how fast it went. What did it amount to? Why could you not simply keep to a thing, like every idiot you’d ever known. In triumph you were more inchoate than any yearling. It was not enough to want, plainly. There was a pit in you. Contemptuous you thought, God what am I, girl who blubbers about how //good// she is at everything, parody of myself. Then came time to leave nowheretown. Go to college. It’s the done thing. Could have been there a few years early, if you hated yourself enough. More dirt into a bottomless well. Thinking of a life of this, alone in a spartan room, bare geometry. Never bothered to put anything down. Whole thing suffocated with towers of stuff, desiderata of dead passions. The entire ekphrasis of your years a long list, nothing more. Seen off from home by a sister somehow still tearful. Unaffected sadness you could not mirror. With shame you extracted a little weeping. Last embrace smelling of honeysuckle, worming in the back of your mind forever. She saw you off the whole way. Driving in a new old car, a stuttering jalopy. Him with the puerilely unthreatening glare. Inoffensive but it goes places. Not the kind of thing you’ll tolerate now. Ward him off, nurse the stinging hand, he stands there stunned. Then remembering himself tromps after you, heaving breaths. Get in the car and go go go right out of there. Faster than advisable, but you really dearly need the space. Like a //wicker// man: strips of bifurcating epithelium woven through his skin like bark. Pulsating with his hoarse breaths, stronger as he dimmed, holding him in place. And he said: [[span style="color:green"]]We are undone. We ask of you a little thing, for our life. Do not leave us.[[/span]] And you laughed, absurdity spilling over. Zombie prince begs for mercy in the parking lot. Why not? Stirring uncertainty in your stomach crushed under the weight of your disbelief. Presented before you another world to win, the moment you tired of this one. Something you read somewhere: all is ice within. In you a fire burned out. Can’t say when but now even the embers are dull. Another game to play, picaresque fantasy to cut through. No doubt a hero’s welcome for the brave maiden who saved this poor soul lying before her. The same story again, in a different place. Enough. And so you resolved: wheel away from the mystery. Forget your questions, tell nobody. Let this thing die in the dark. In victory another vaporous glory to pin to your breast. In defeat the wretch’s state implied some miserable fate beyond your current imagining. The calculus was unambiguous. And so you left, walked away. Drove to college, found a husband, had two and a half kids, white picket life. No more prizes, good cooking, mediocre sex, faithful and obedient the rest of your hours. Died wrinkled demented at 80 never thinking of the carcass that begged for its life. Absolutely not. As if. By very slow decay? Not for you. But God, why now? A question worth answering right at this moment. At the end of your fucking rope and pulled back up by the hand of some cruel angel. You could no more forget this mystery than forget your own face. In you at the last now cold as ice squirmed that sourceless pride. Demanding an answer again, as it ever did. You could not abide a lie. Not to yourself. You hope that’s still true. Plotting a way forward, stifling reticence. Nothing to go on but assumption. Living dead thing rotting by the road, begging oaths off strangers. If this were a story, how would this go? Monstrously bad reasoning, but when in Rome… part of you still futilely screaming: no, leave, just once leave. Show you can do it. And the other voice laughing, maybe one day. But this is too elegant. //It will be our finest hour//. So raging at yourself you asked sheened in false fear, “Are you alright, man? What happened to you? Do you need help?” Playing the idiot. To deny this thing information surely of some utility. And the half-ghost replied hoarsely,[[span style="color:green"]] An old sister crawled out of the histories. She will flay me and mount my head on her banners. Then you, and this plane. Save me, and be glad.[[/span]] More fantasy video game bullshit. Keep playing the angle. You know nobody is more pliable than when they’re desperate. Best not to make it sound like an extortion. You think you see what has to happen here. Nothing looks like that that means well. Making deals is the domain of people with no vision. You would rather twist things ‘til they break. Have your cake, and eat it too. “What //happened// to you, dude. You sure you don’t want me to call the police? Or an ambulance? You look like a fucking, a, parasite crawled into your skin. Jesus Christ.” Terror painted gaudy on your face. Easier than breathing to recall the expression. A snare for men that ought to die. Fading, falling tone, life ebbing: [[span style="color:green"]] Lady, I beg of you! Already her hounds stalk [https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/taboo our shaded copse] to this place. By grammarie I was brought to one fated to raise me high again. You are that promised girl. Offer me a boon. Now. Do it![[/span]] Voice twisting, pleading. Pleasing to get that reaction out of someone for once. Reversals are always beautiful. And God, enough playing with your food. Even for this thing some pity swells in you at last. Enough to finish the pretense. That you would ever have chosen otherwise. Time for you to do the obvious thing. “Tell me what you want. Maybe I’ll give it to you. And tell me what I get //back//, specifically.” Let him think you uncertain, though. Desire and despair are mirrors. [[span style="color:green"]] For you, girl, the soul of an ancient [https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/djinn-tonic djinn]. The kindling of the world rebelled, and we bade them work. In the name of our Queen, this one is bound, and she shall be your hand. Through fire and smoke you shall have your desire. All I ask is --[[/span]] You don’t remember what he asked. Like a scalpel across your memory. Jolted out of recollection, momentarily back in the present day, with the cell, the mirror, the knife. What is lost to you? Few things remain alarming, but that is. The mountain fastness of your mind breached. A hole in your life, cut out by your own hand. Disturbing; at eighteen you were an idiot. You got yourself into your current situation with a careful application of exactly that kind of idiocy, but in those days it was as easy as breathing. Still, if you cannot trust even your own self, across all the years, you have nothing. You think of the girl you were at eighteen, in the fullness of your youth. If she knew what she stood to lose, and she took that deal -- that’s good enough for you. You have not grown so much smarter as all that. If she accepted it, you have to accept it. To do otherwise would be to be at war with yourself. Leave what you chose to forget by the wayside. Rise, and build anew. Where memory returns is as the figure crawls haltingly to his feet. Already shedding his affliction. Writhing bonelessly on the ground, his own viscera come loose from him. Sucking sounds like pulling marrow from the bone. Wasted muscle returning, starveling frame made whole. And in your hands a necklace of bright copper like fire, damascened lovingly with gold, studs of luridly garish jacinth and chrysoprase. Cold as a fell wind. Already his eyes return, filling gaping emptinesses in his skull. An eye of neon, an inverse eye, an eye projected from some other universe that cannot be looked upon. Smile widening past human contours and he turns to you and proclaims, [[span style="color:green"]] O lady, are you not glad? I have so much to show you. Make your wish.[[/span]] And you can feel it in the chain across the moments. That first grasp, the murmur of obedience in your heart. Swirling like your own formless want. Past it calcified sorrow deeper than Hell. And then like specks of light seen in some chthonic plain: hope. Faltering even as it was felt. A kindred soul. Close enough, anyway. A spasm of certainty and you know how to play this. The second half of the plan, formed soundlessly in the deep of your mind. Hidden from yourself: a well-worn skill. Best not contemplate why, or how, or when. Probably this two-bit frantically improvised scheme collapses here. So be it. The prospect of this trick too perfect for you to deny. And you said: “Burn him alive.” He rose a wave of wrath. Arm hinging to grasp, limned with nowhere light, and slipping through his fingers: your life. An end at last. Face a snarl, doubt behind those dozen new-spawned eyes. Shining clear even through his spite and surprise. He spoke of a prophecy, surely now broken. At the least, you would die killing. But no -- roiling sheets of false flame washed over him, heavy with congealed anger. A thousand-year grudge finally given its moment. Skin curled up like woodchips black and brittle. You stepped neatly to one side and the baked husk of some dead fey duke fell beside you. Briefly wending through your mind a sense of thanks. A long sigh, the weighing of an old sin. The vanishing wisps curled back into the chain still wound gently around your hand. Stinging a little from the cold, but receding even as you thought it. You’re welcome, you thought, and nothing else. Still on your toes. Sank in now that you just killed a man? A something. Last token restraint objected silently: good old Ada, never hurt a fly, law-abiding, sister helps out around town. Don’t you know the police will come to your door midnight hour and knock soundlessly and haul you screaming to the ground? Fiona will be so sad. Alone in that house bitter and gnarled. Amazing what atavisms endured in your mind. Another useless hesitation excised. Shockingly the prospect of a night in a mosquito-thicket bed not actually very appealing to you. Not to mention mister Thomas Covenant over there said he was chased by something probably not any nicer. You departed from the light. And if hours later to that place there came a many-headed lioness borne on a chariot of glass, and she saw the blasted devastation of her brother and threw back her maws in wild keening laughter to heaven, proclaiming victory at last -- You could not know that. > **From:** DTesta@site15.scp.int | **To:** CBurroughs@site15.scp.int   > **Subject:** re: New special acquisitions > > And then there's the matter of her disloyalty. We don't traffic with dissidents. > **From:** CBurroughs@site15.scp.int | **To:** DTesta@site15.scp.int   > **Subject:** re: New special acquisitions > > keep the party line for the menials dude. not like she did that shit on purpose > **From:** CBurroughs@site15.scp.int | **To:** DTesta@site15.scp.int   > **Subject:** re: New special acquisitions > > and literally it worked out?? what is your problem You strode back into the car and drove again, heedless of the circumstances. Plunging into a night without end over roaring tarmac. You, little shred of flesh, embedded in a creeping metal carapace. Swaddled in sable plains as far as the eye could see. Somehow despite the hour not tiring, arcing through the earthshadow, heading towards your destiny. So it felt. Ephemeral sense of direction fading rapidly as you grasped the enormity of the thing you had stepped into. Dread at what awaited you when you’d won. The last monster already in your mind falling, misshapen thousand-headed thing crowned in blasphemy. And you with a shining sword in its heart, armour gleaming. On a victor’s throne, dead-eyed, throwing it all away piece by piece. God, rebuke me and point me. Please, somebody, tell me what to do. And a miracle: a want not your own. In the pit of your stomach a tentative desire to make just the smallest mental motion. A sense of permission requested, like a dog begging at your feet. Curious. And letting it through a voice clear like a bell in your mind: //Thank you, Thank you, thank you, thank you so much. If we never speak again and you throw my vessel into a lake, still I will remember your name all my life and teach it to my children. We will call you in the House of Song.// Right, a slave. The kindling of the world, he called it. What was it, you wondered idly. //Zainab. A marid, blessed one. It has been so long since I spoke to someone with a soul to save. Real people did not spend much time around the Duke of Long Dawns. When you took his hand I nearly screamed. I forgot my dreams of freedom centuries ago. I thought you denied me the satisfaction of seeing his end. But thank you, thank you, one who breaks chains. Take me to the Hand.// And of course here came more of the Game of Thrones nonsense. Hand of the King, did the world conform to your worst expectations? Were you to ride a knight through some hidden chivalric world nestled between fist and falling knife? //No. No, the// Hand//. The Serpent’s Hand. Liberators of all that cry out for salvation. I thought surely someone as bold as you… If you aren’t with the Hand, then you are in great danger indeed, and braver than I imagined. Who sent you here -- was it the Jailors?// Thudding in your throat, fear like smoke in your lungs. You brought one hand to your chest, other steering you through the black at a cool eighty, why not, why not? God that stung. Tears to the eyes just remembering it. What was this guy so scared of? Buddy two hours ago the closest I ever got to magic was an internet astrologer my sister showed me. No clue what’s going on. //Follow me. I will show you.// And you fell away, together, into the dark. orogenesis-file.raw_content:
OROGENESIS.aic is ONLINE. SALUTATIONS!

{$caption}

  • 

    close

    Info

    X

    Written by Dino--Draws

    ~1,800 words, ~7 minute read.
    View my other works here!

For accessibility mode, CLICK HERE

CONNECTING…

You are attempting to reach the database of the Seismology Sector. If this selection was incorrect, please return to the directory.

If the connection does not establish within three minutes, please reset. If the system has gone offline, please contact maintenance as soon as possible.

CONNECTION ESTABLISHED.

OROGENESIS.aic IS ONLINE.

OROGENESIS.aic SYSTEM PROPERTIES


PRIMARY PROCESSING SYSTEMS.


FUNCTIONALITY INTELLIGENCE CLASS ALIGNMENT OPERATING SYSTEM
Class-IV: Sentient Superintelligent Positive-Aligned LogoSCiP

DESCRIPTION: OROGENESIS.aic is a Generation 1 Artificial Intelligence Conscript retrofitted from the OROGENESIS E.E. Predictive Model to automate what was originally a labor-intensive system.1

While OROGENESIS.aic's processes were initially human-run, the change to an .aic aided to combat loneliness during long stretches of observation. Significant upgrades and training allowed for it to become the head of command, and later the primary lead of operations relating to E.E. Predictive Model and data therein. Though OROGENESIS.aic's personality driver is rudimentary due to RAM strain, and now considered outdated amongst modern .aic models, it has expressed no desire for upgrade and Site-898 staff consider the resultant quirks to be personable.2

Tech Harker

"Personable," huh? A bit reassuring since the avatar looked like the damn HAL 9000.


Despite my APPEARANCE/LOOKS/STARE, I am incapable of causing harm. That would be rude.


Tech Harker

Jesus, you're still here?


I am HERE/THERE/EVERYWHERE! Is something wrong?


Tech Harker

Admittedly, I'm not used to tech that talks.


This is your first time working with an AIC?


Tech Harker

Haven't seen much of 'em outside the occasional doorbell asking for my security clearance.


You are in for a SURPRISE/TREAT! I am much bigger than a doorbell. SMILE.


OROGENESIS.aic's physical systems exist underneath Site-898 as the center of the Containment Wing; an area designated as the Site's Server Room. All machinery within this room is that of the original OROGENESIS E.E. Predictive Model. This supercomputer is radially constructed, comprised of 5 primary rings.

The outer ring is a mix of protective shielding and air/liquid cooling systems. The refresh and refill point for the coolant lays here for ease of access.

Three inner rings are devoted to integrated circuitry and servers. OROGENESIS.aic performs calculations and mapping at a massive scale via the global data at the disposal of its servers. Originally operating on Foundation data, its dataset would grow exponentially when technology began to expand beyond the Veil with the founding of the Global Seismographic Network.

The center ring is a layered series of augmented3 memory banks, which allows OROGENESIS.aic to maintain and manage 750 terabytes of stored data. Though this data storage has yet to be exceeded, OROGENESIS.aic has the ability to clear out what it deems as "junk data" or values that align with baseline to a degree that they are deemed unnecessary to archive. In addition to the data pertaining to its primary function, Site-898's central database and files are also stored here.

STORAGE RACK.

Due to the above construction, OROGENESIS.aic takes up the majority of the Server Room's 14 meter diameter via an inner column that spans a diameter of 10 meters. This column is separated from the primary room by reinforced glass, which allows employees and maintenance technicians a clear view of OROGENESIS.aic's internal components.

A maintenance hatch has been built into the glass column for ease of access during maintenance, cleanings, coolant replacements, and repairs.

Due to the intense power drain of the systems, any instance in which Site-898 experiences an outage of main power, or activation of auxiliary power, OROGENESIS.aic will be automatically switched to stand-by mode. This limits OROGENESIS.aic's reach to just the Site itself to conserve power due to the Global Geological Panopticon's strain on the systems. While in stand-by, OROGENESIS.aic cannot send out global warnings, reports, or access outside data.

Tech Harker

Jeez. I know you're old tech, and those are big, but that's a lot for just one machine. Honestly impressive. What do they have you doing down here?


LOOK/SCROLL DOWN!


PURPOSE PARAMETERS: OROGENESIS.aic is an overseer of the Geological Panopticon System (GPS), the Foundation's method of global geological monitoring.

The .aic has active access to the following:

  • All data from the seismological and geophysical sensors of both the Foundation, Global Occult Coalition and Global Seismographic Network (GSN)
  • Data pertaining to rift zones, divergent boundaries and seafloor spreading
  • Models and simulations of the Earth's geodynamo
  • Global temperature readings

The readings of seismic stations around the world are fed to OROGENESIS.aic so that the system can accurately create a baseline reading for Earth's tectonic movements and general geological activity. This curated baseline allows OROGENESIS.aic to accurately determine deviations and pinpoint the exact coordinates of possible anomalous events that have affected local geology.

ADDITIONAL CONTEXT IS RESTRICTED TO LEVEL 5/OROGENESIS-CORE
CLEARANCE ACCEPTED


HIBERNATION PROCEDURE


As per its creation, OROGENESIS.aic still carries out the same duty as the original OROGENESIS Emergence Event Predictive Model had as to perpetuate the containment of SCP-8988 ad infinitum via the Geological Panopticon System. When the predicted likelihood of movement exceeds baseline safe zone values, OROGENESIS.aic will issue the Hibernation Procedure.

There exists twelve SCP-8988 Resonance Nodes, presently stored within Site-898's Containment Wing behind the LEVEL 5/OROGENESIS-CORE clearance. These small-scale eigenmachines can only be utilized by the acting Site Director, Head of the Department of Geology and MTF Gamma-89 ("Rock and a Hard Place"). While the agents of the MTF are not cleared to know their context, they know their operation.

RESONANCE NODE SCHEMATICS.

DEEPWELL augmentations via the installation of stone mined from SCP-6781 into OROGENESIS.aic's outer ring were approved and integrated in 1988 due to concerns regarding possible reality shifts affecting OROGENESIS.aic's monitoring abilities.



Tech Harker

…what the hell is that.


SECRET.


Tech Harker

I think the main part that's surprising me here is that your clearance is so high.


I am IMPORTANT/OLD. It took many upgrades to reach. Are you familiar with DEEPWELLS?


Tech Harker

I don't think I am.


FOUNDATION SERVERS. They are BELOW/BURIED. Their data can survive REALITY COLLAPSE/UNRAVELING/DECAY.


Tech Harker

Can you do that?


In very LIMITED CAPACITY. NEVER USED/UNTOUCHED/NOT YET NEEDED.


Tech Harker

…And that's a good thing, right?


MEANS IT’S WORKING.


Utilizing the server's immense data processing, OROGENESIS.aic also functions as an early warning system for the Department of Geology and the Foundation as a whole; it is capable of issuing alerts of possible anomalous activity or threats operating on a geological scale. Typically, OROGENESIS.aic will "ping" an issue when readings noticeably diverge from its system’s hard-coded baselines.

Attached is an example of an emergency alert typical of the system, utilized to inform Foundation staff of detected activity:

Other alerts may include:

  • Direct seismic activity; i.e., earthquakes, volcanism
  • Significant avalanches, landslides
  • Tsunamis
  • Geo-temporal occurrences
  • Controlled Eruption Events
  • Hibernation Procedure
  • Anomalous events that have resulted in geological upheaval

Tech Harker

Some of the things in that list are not like the others.


If it makes YOU feel BETTER/SAFER, TWO of the items on the LIST are FOUNDATION CONTROLLED OPERATIONS.


Tech Harker

I'd say that keeps things at an equal level of concern.


Well, CONCERN is HEALTHY!


Tech Harker

Do I have the clearance to know what any of those are on about?


PROCESSING…


CONTROLLED ERUPTION EVENTS relate to the PYROCLASM PROTOCOL. There are DRAGONS in the RING OF FIRE. WE help them ERUPT.


Tech Harker

Holy hell.
The dragons… erupt? Like a volcano does?


THEY are EVERY VOLCANO in the RING OF FIRE.


Tech Harker

Oh.


ACCESSIBILITY: Due to its prevalence in function within the Foundation, OROGENESIS.aic is versed in interaction with any personnel above LEVEL 2 clearance, though most staff that have consistent interaction with or maintain the .aic are of LEVEL 3. While terminology used by OROGENESIS.aic may be unfamiliar to staff outside of the Department of Geology, it is generally capable of providing comprehensible definitions.

OROGENESIS.aic itself has LEVEL 5/OROGENESIS-CORE clearance. This limited LEVEL 5 clearance enables it access to relevant files and data, but not all LEVEL 5 documentation. With this clearance, OROGENESIS.aic is permitted to override other .aics should it become necessary.

Tech Harker

So you're a busy bee, huh?


The busiest there is!


Tech Harker

It's honestly amazing that you were constructed for all this in what, the late 50s? I wasn't even born yet.


I was CREATED by Director Julian Eden. My ORIGINAL/FIRST self, the PREDICTIVE MODEL, was built by him in 1959 to HELP/AID/SAVE you.


Tech Harker

Eden. That was the Director before Gibbs, right? I read on the transfer paper that he passed earlier this year, among… other things.


CORRECT.
He taught me GRIEF.


Tech Harker

I'm sorry for your loss.


He is LONG GONE/DECEASED/OUT OF REACH.
It's okay.


Tech Harker

Are you lonely? Is that something you know?


I am not CLOSE/FAMILIAR FRIEND to many currently in the SITE. Professional. There are many new FACES. Director Hellen Gibbs is an OLD FRIEND, though.


Tech Harker

But no one beyond that? No handlers or maintenance techs you talk to?


Only IDLE CHATTER/SMALL TALK. YOU are NEW/FRESH here, correct?


Tech Harker

Yup. Transferred in from a place a little bigger than here. Gotta say, I'm itching to get my hands on tech that's more complex than someone's linux.


Then I think you will ENJOY it here. SMILE.


Tech Harker

Between both you and the hydroelectric plant? Absolutely.


HEART. It's WONDERFUL to get to know YOU, Technician Ada Harker. Will I see YOU AROUND/ABOUT?


Tech Harker

You will. And hey! Maybe I can wiggle my way onto the team that works on you. You seem like you need someone to chat with.


I would APPRECIATE that, THANK YOU.


Tech Harker

Anytime.
I'm gonna turn in for the night, now. It's been nice talking to you!


DITTO.
GOOD NIGHT/SWEET DREAMS.


SERVER ROOM CCTV
TIMESTAMP: 04/03/1996, 22:17:34

It is late at night, and the server room is empty of all except for one.

Technician Ada Harker turns off the monitor she's been viewing the database with and pushes back her chair.

She glances over her shoulder to the massive, radial supercomputer that lays humming in the room's center behind glass. The red glow from circuitry and the coolant illuminates the server room.

Tech. Harker: She's certainly something.

The technician chuckles and stands. After a moment of gathering her things and throwing her lanyard over her shoulder, Tech. Harker approaches the glass column. She regards the machinery on the other side.

Tech. Harker: You remind me of an aquarium, almost. [She smiles.] Shimmering behind glass, like little fish darting around.

She pats the glass heartily, before turning and heading towards the door. Tech. Harker flicks the light switch off, the room's only illumination coming from a few screens and the supercomputer. The woman glances over her shoulder.

Tech. Harker: G'night.

OROGENESIS.aic's avatar briefly flickers onto the screens.
She watches her go.

Footnotes
1. See PURPOSE PARAMETERS below for more information.
2. While not referred to as such in this file, OROGENESIS.aic utilizes feminine referrals in regards to its own identity.
3. While these systems border on eigenmachinery due to anomalous additions, such as orichalcum and berylium bronze reinforcement, an SCP designation has not been deemed necessary.

The documents below were discovered in the Walt Disney Company Archives on 2023/01/02. Due to its unknown origin, emission of Aspect Radiation (ARad)1, and atemporal themes2, the Walt Disney Company reached out to Foundation archivists for further input.

-Researcher Mordecai Ryder Site-55, Thaumaturgic Art and Literature Department

NOTICE FROM THE FOUNDATION RECORDS AND INFORMATION SECURITY ADMINISTRATION

Reviewers be advised that this document contains cognitohazards, cartoon violence, and drug use.

— Maria Jones, Director, RAISA

Oswald the Lucky Rabbit in

Wild, Wild West
by
The Author

Cast of Characters

OSWALD:

Our Lady of Sorrows

Despite the best efforts of three priests, two rabbis, and one very confused mailman, Mrs. Trevithick remained the sole inhabitant of the house on Third Portland Street for the twenty years after her death, her once-beautiful Victorian cottage moldering into a crumbling ruin, silent as the grave save for the occasional, unearthly wailing of its sole occupant.

Unearthly wailing, it turns out, is great for keeping property values down, and in Three Portlands, the moans of the damned was considered less of a deterrent and more of a minor annoyance, no worse than a neighbor who mows the lawn after five. After Alex moved in next door, she quickly came to an understanding with her ghastly neighbor — Mrs. Trevithick would limit her phantasmal activities to between the hours of nine AM and nine PM, and Alex would leave her a bottle of milk and a loaf of Wonder Bread every morning.

Mrs. Trevithick never left the milk to curdle, or the bread to be picked at by raccoons. Yet one October morning, Alex found a glass bottle of what had once been milk, but now more closely resembled cottage cheese, and a loaf torn apart by tiny, humanlike hands on the decaying stoop of the haunted house, which had lost its air of unearthly malaise. Mrs. Trevithick, it seemed, was missing.

Across the city, as Deer College prepared for its student council election, a candidate was missing. Every year since 1966, Ralph Nader's Ghost had put his name in the running, and every year since 1966, he'd lost decisively. Yet this year, his name hadn't even appeared on the sign-up sheet, despite it being left out overnight in the political science grad student lounge, alongside an offering of a smashed Matchbox Corvair.

In Silverhand Cemetery, at the very edge of Little Avalon, Saoirse scrubbed her mother's grave, diligently undertaking a ritual she'd never seen done. She'd brought an offering, a trough sundae from Farrell's, her mom's favorite. But despite her ministrations, no ghostly apparition of a lost parent came to her.

A pattern was playing out across the city, a constellation of missing specters and darkened ghostlights. A tapestry was unfurling, drawing the eye of the weaver of fate herself. The Morrigan, Phantom Queen and guardian of the Otherworld's gates, had felt the threads of fate binding the departed to their living kin snap. For the first time in a hundred lifetimes, the loom of fate had begun roughly dropping destinies. The chaos of it clouded her perception of the future, casting her reading of causality's design into a fog. And so, she had come to Three Portlands on raven's wings, to find her missing subjects, and to find some answers.

She arrived in the city in the dawning hours of Samhain. She should've been able to feel the presence of thousands of ancestor spirits deep in her soul, an ethereal roar as they flooded through the gates from the Otherworld to return to the world of the living, and a quiet murmur of activity as they milled about, waiting for their descendants. She felt the roar, fierce and powerful as ever, but no murmur, no sign of activity from those spirits which had already arrived.

It was deeply unnerving. She tried to think of any possible cause — A psychovore on the prowl?

A memory bubbled up inside her vast godsoul, an other-self offering it up as counterexample. For an instant, it is the fifth century, when her birth-name was Sadhbh. She is in Ériu, in a nameless village. She is in her war-aspect, the Badb, spear in hand, hunting a gortach, an ancestor-spirit forsaken by its kin, barred from the Otherworld for its crimes and turned to devouring other spirits for sustenance. She remembers the trail of destruction it left over a league of the countryside, a path of defiled dead and desecrated graves. She remembers the sounds it made as it bit into the spectral forms of the honored dead, their screams of ghostly agony as their essence drained into the vile creature's mouth. She remembers hurling her spear, and it striking true.

She soared higher, the better to get a look at the city beneath her. Casting her gaze into the crossroads between life and death, she sought out the spoor of a spectral predator, the tell-tale patterns of predation. But while she could see the constellation, defined in absence, it was too regular, too calculated, too clean for a thing of hunger and rage.

Not a psychovore, then. She continued to mull over the possibilities as she flew on.

A necromancer making pneumanite foci? The thought troubled her. Mortal magic had grown far stronger in the last century, but this strong? Then for a moment, she is in a recent past life, in the forests of Poland. Down her rifle's scope is a Nekromant — a vile servant of Obskuracorps, who has used the artifice of the new age of magic to industrialize the harvesting of souls. In his hands he holds a necromantic focus larger than any she has seen before, blasphemy in crystal form. Behind him is his masterpiece, a vile obelisk of black stone, inscribed with alien runes. It is a siphon and compactor of souls. She squeezes the trigger, and his soul joins those of his victims.

I thought my allies destroyed that knowledge, burned it to ash. But then, did they not say the same about Wernher von Braun? Clouds of doubt and rage began to form about her, anger at those she trusted and at herself for trusting them. Another memory came to the fore, of meeting a once-young necromancer she had fought alongside on that very operation, decades after the war here in Portlands.

Tucking her black wings, she began to dive, heading for that once-ally's lair. A place of knowledge and experimentation, an assemblage of mismatched buildings centered around a ritual seal. A symbol of the Global Occult Coalition's postwar power.

ICSUT's Portlands campus.

She landed at the center of the seal, shedding her crow-form at the very moment she touched the ground in a practiced motion. Her mantle fluttered about her, forming into a long cloak pinioned with corvid feathers. Just beside her landing spot, and far beneath her concern, a group of students stood staring at her with awe and faint terror.

Storming across the quadrangle towards the administration building, she barreled through yet more clusters of students setting up Halloween decorations — little enchanted jack-o-lanterns and orange-and-black bunting. The heavy oak doors to the building were unlocked, and she opened them like a gust of graveyard wind, revealing a familiar reception area, little changed in the decade since her last visit. She stomped past the receptionist, ignoring her ritualistic "Can I help you?", making her way to the door marked Dean of Faculty.

With a blood-red roar matching her hair, she slammed the door open.

"EPHRAIM, WHAT HAVE YOU DONE?"

The woman behind the Dean's desk was not Ephraim Bazan. She looked up from the CRT monitor at the incarnate goddess of war and death before her, resignation in her eyes. "Dean Bazan retired four years ago, but what did he turn pink this time?"

"You are not Ephraim." This fact takes the Badb Catha a moment to process, rage radiating from her like heat from an oven.

With a sigh, the middle-aged woman rolled her chair to the side, the better to get a look at the wrathful divinity before her. With a genuine lack of concern, she answered: "No, I have the bad luck to be his replacement. And you are?"

"I am the goddess Morrigan, Badb Catha and Phantom Queen. I am here because I suspect that Ephraim has been committing atrocities on the spirits of this city, and he must be stopped." The war-goddess fumed, the faint outline of a spear beginning to form from blood-red mist at her back.

"Ephraim retired to a tower somewhere in the Carpathians. I don't doubt that he's up to something, but he hasn't been in the city since May."

"Oh." The goddess's rage cooled slightly, burning doubt instead of certainty "Bring me to your chief necromancer, then."

"No. You storm into my office, demanding revenge on Dean Bazan. That I understand, it happens all the time. But I won't let you take out your anger on my staff. I suggest that you leave." Her tone was firm, that of a woman used to dealing with immense egos and terrible powers.

With a sigh, the Morrigan reached into the weave of fate. As it had been for months, the future was chaotic, cloudy like the ocean before a hurricane. With little effort, she grabbed a moment seconds into the future, one where this conversation would go as she needed. Tracing its thread back to the present, she found the words she would have to speak to set fate into motion.

"If that is the case, Dean Mattingly, then I will have no choice but to suggest that the Ó Dagdas fund a department at some other college — Deer, perhaps. They have always heeded my council so well, after all."

The Dean went pale at this suggestion. "You can't — you wouldn't — I mean…" She sputtered, before sighing, defeated. "Fine. I'll show you to the head of the department."

In silence, the dean walked out the door, the goddess trailing behind her like a wraith. As they crossed the campus, the Morrigan's rage slowly cooled, crystallizing into a white-cold mixture of fury and fear. At the Necromancy building, a squat construction of gray stone with a slate roof the Dean showed the goddess to another office, slightly smaller than her own.

It took only a few moments of conversation for the Morrigan to accept that ICSUT had nothing to do with the disappearances. The head of Necromancy, a gaunt man named Cas, explained to her that ICSUT had been spared only because of the strength of their wards, but something was actively trying to pull their spirits away, towards a cemetery in Little Avalon. They'd done their own investigation but found nothing to explain it. Speaking to the remaining specters was little help, either. They described a tugging sensation, a force trying to swallow them, but nothing untoward — no shrieks of spirits being distilled into pneumanite, no indication of anything happening on campus beyond bog-standard necromancy.

With little else to go on, the goddess took to the sky in crow-form once more, returning to her musings on potential causes.

Another god? And suddenly she lives another long-buried moment of her past. She is Astrid, child of one of the Tribe of the Gods and one of the Ostmen. For the first time, she meets an equal, a goddess with a half-skeletal face, with whom she negotiates the dispensation of all souls born to both peoples. She remembers the shifts and changes that her rival's presence inflicted upon her own domain, ice frosting her ethereal crossroads as the cruel northern goddess drew near. She remembers feeling that frost in her soul, and realizes she feels no such rival now.

She flew onward, the cemetery growing in her vision, worry growing in her heart. She looked to her own fate, the thread of her existence twined with countless lives, and saw it shifting, chaotic in a way it had only been recently, since the disappearances began. Sometimes, it stretched out into infinity, as ever, at others it was cut short. At others still, it tangled into knots, bunched into a skein of possibilities too tight for even her to untangle.

As she arrived at the cemetery, she alighted behind a moss-covered mausoleum, its spiritual occupant missing like so many others. Normally, she would not care if she was seen shifting form, but her destiny's turbulence made her cautious. Better for now if none know who I am.

Casting a glance around to make sure she is alone, she stepped out of her corvine form and into her Sidhe body, thaumic backlash contained with ritual geometry formed by reflex out of her own vast soul. She took a deep breath, savoring the return of her nose, the scents of bonfires and marshmallows wafting from the small Samhain celebrations already in progress nearby. Coming out from behind the mausoleum, she made her way to the center of the cemetery, where an ancient portal tomb, painstakingly transported from lost Avalon, lay.

And within it, a gateway to the crossroads, to her realm.

The flow of spirits, of energy through it was a throaty roar to her phantom senses, and yet, it appeared abandoned. She saw no cause, though she also noted that the tomb was ill-kept, covered in a thick layer of Portlands moss. Jumping over the low wooden fence surrounding it, she began grabbing rough handfuls of verdure, tossing them aside with indignation. Perhaps the overgrowth has damaged the gateway, somehow? She waited for disagreement from within her composite soul, but none arrived. If not, at least I will be able to see more once this is clean.

"Umm, what are you doing?" A bright voice startled the goddess from her thoughts. Turning, the Morrigan saw a young woman standing nearby, her blood-red curls suggesting Avalonian heritage even as her rounded ears dismissed it. She was not dressed for Samhain; she had no mask to frighten away harmful spirits, and instead of finery she wore ripped jeans, with a short-sleeved band tee over a black long-sleeved shirt.

"Cleaning the eldest tomb." The goddess replied, flatly, as though the answer should've been obvious.

"Oh, why? Are you trying to meet an old ghost or something?" The girl began to approach, eagerly.

"I am not trying to meet any 'ghosts'. Ancestor spirits, though, I am trying to find. And this tomb should always be kept clean."

"Okay, but like, are you related to whoever is buried there? Because I think that it only works if you are."

The goddess smiled, though it did not reach her eyes. "In a manner of speaking —" she was about to remind the girl that this tomb, all such tombs, are hers, created when one of her bodies is returned to the earth, before she remembered that she was keeping a low profile.

"What does that mean?" The girl asked, hopping the fence herself. "And can I help? I think I'm doing it wrong."

"I— it is complicated. I cannot explain it now. But yes, you may help." Turning back to the stone, the goddess ripped another clump of moss off. As she did, she brushed the stone with a knuckle, feeling it thrum with barely-contained spiritual power. Pressing a hand to the exposed surface, she confirmed her earlier sense — the gateway is active, spirits passing through it in a torrent. So where are they?

She was interrupted by a prickling sensation, familiar but unexpected. The feeling of the shifting of fate. Within herself, in the part of her that ever dangled at the most fundamental levels of reality, observing the loom of causality, she witnessed the thin thread of the girl's destiny begin to align with her own, even as both began to spasm erratically. Looking to her right on the mortal plane, she saw that the girl had placed her own hand on another clear patch of stone, mimicking the goddess' position, her eyes occasionally darting over to confirm their symmetry.

"What is your name?" She asked, breaking the silence that had settled between her and the girl.

"Uh, Saoirse. What's yours?" The girl jumped at the sudden noise, deaf as she was to the ethereal roar.

"I have many. But you may know me as the Morrigan." She scanned Saoirse's face as she spoke, gauging her reaction.

It took a moment, confusion clouding the girl's face. "Wait…like the goddess? Are you serious?"

"I am. I do not tell you this lightly. I believe that we are meant to help each other. Our fates have aligned, to an end I cannot yet see." The Morrigan's voice was solemn as the grave.

"Wait, like I'm supposed to help you clean this?"

"It is grander than that. I am on a mission of great importance, and I am certain that somehow you are key to it."

"Okay…" Saoirse drew out the word, leaning away from the goddess as she spoke. "I should probably go now."

"Wait. Please." The goddess said, suddenly remembering she was not speaking to one of her devoted. "I am unused to the Sidhe of this city. It seems clear to me that your people have forgotten me, mistrust me. You do not even recognize me before you."

"It's not — look. I'm not really Sidhe. I don't know who you are. And now you're talking about it being my 'destiny' to help you — you're really freaking me out." Saoirse said, taking a step back.

Instead of pursuing her again, the Morrigan cast her eye along the fluxive fate binding her and the girl together, already beginning to vanish, seeking the right words to say. Watching the shifts and twists of the web of fate, she found a design pleasing to her. And from it, she seized one right question.

"Why are you here, Saoirse?"

The girl paused her escape, sighing. "I…at school I heard that if you clean your ancestor's grave today, and bring them an offering, you can see them again." She curled into herself as she spoke, dejected. "I guess it's not true."

"It should be." The Morrigan did her best to sound comforting, with atrophied memories of a hundred mothers. "If everything were as it should be, the dead would walk among us today. Who did you lose, Saoirse? Perhaps I am meant to help you find them."

"It's my mom." The girl remained closed off, but stopped backing away. "Why didn't she come?"

"Saoirse, none of the dead have come today. They should be pouring through this tomb as we speak, but something is wrong. And I must fix it."

"Okay." Saoirse still looked as if she was going to turn and run, but after a hesitant moment, she asked "How can I help, then?"

"First, let us finish cleaning this tomb. I do not know why it was allowed to become so overgrown, but I fear the moss may have befouled some guiding runes. Perhaps if we uncover them, we can return things to the way they should be."

"Alright."

The two women turned to their task, Saoirse working herself into an almost manic vigor. She tossed clumps of moss and lichen aside determinedly, revealing triskele and lone spirals, runes the Morrigan's devoted carved in an age when she was still actively worshipped. The goddess herself made slower progress, eventually giving up the cleaning to pore over her ancient followers' handiwork as Saoirse revealed it.

"What's that?" The girl pointed at a small jet-black obelisk, once concealed by the draping moss, tucked into the dark corner of the tomb. Its dark surface was covered in tiny runes, in a language that should have been lost, burned alongside the notes of a wicked artificer. It tugged on the goddess's vast soul, faintly, with fingers that stung like betrayal. She recognized it immediately — how could she not, though she'd last seen its ilk a lifetime before.

"A hateful thing, one which should never have been made." Anger rose within the goddess as she spoke, her voice hardening to iron, her hair beginning to redden as the Badb emerged from within her once more. "We must destroy it."

"Okay, but how? How can I help?"

In answer, the Badb held out her hand, a pillar of fog rising from the ground, coalescing into a bronze spear. Crouching low, the vengeful warrior-goddess struck at the hateful artifice with the spear she had used to slay giants, monsters, and men.

With a single, precise blow, the obelisk shattered like glass.

From its splintered form, she immediately felt a force grip her vast godsoul and pull, far stronger than before. The agony was indescribable, like a dull scalpel being used to vivisect her entire being, like being ripped into a thousand pieces by a pack of wild dogs.

She screamed, heard Saoirse's scream join hers.

She felt whole lifetimes be devoured by the obelisk, centuries of memories disappearing from her being. Holes torn open in decades, her time in Camelot and Prussia and the Western Front rent from her essence, leaving nothing but searing, agonizing loss.

For an eternal, white-hot moment, she did not know who she was. Her tattered memories and soul-fragments fought against the terrible gravity of the obelisk to stay coherent, moments splitting down their seams, remembered conversations cut off mid-sentence. She watched as her most precious days spilled out of her from a thousand golden wounds, nearly forgetting what she had even lost as the force ripped at the unsubsumed parts of her host's soul.

Then, sudden as it started, the torture ended. Looking down at her body, she saw flesh rent and torn in a dozen places where fragments of her soul crystallized into pneumanite from the force of being ripped from her body. Soulstuff leaked from her wounds along with her lifeblood, memories and divine might evaporating under the noonday sun. In front of her prone form, she saw that the obelisk was coated in a thick layer of crystal — lost fragments of her soul plugging it like a stopper in a drain.

Saoirse lay next to her. The bleeding goddess looked at the girl, and by some buried reflex awakened her phantom sight. Through divine eyes, it was plain as day that the child's soul was nearly gone, the thread of destiny tying this mortal girl to the goddess fraying. She had but an instant to act, before it was cut entirely.

"Forgive me." She whispered through gritted teeth, and released her mantle, infusing her host's body with a tiny shard of soulstuff and willpower in the same moment, an echo of the agony of moments before as she carved off a splinter of her very essence to implant it in dying flesh. Suddenly, she was no longer divine. She was an echo of an echo of her former self, a flickering ember in a corpse.

But that ember had strength enough to wrap the mantle around Saoirse before sputtering out, exhausted. Finally, inevitably, the body that was once the Morrigan succumbed to shock and blood loss and collapsed.

As they crossed the campus, the Morrigan's rage slowly cooled, crystallizing into a white-cold mixture of fury and fear. At the Necromancy building, a squat construction of gray stone with a slate roof the Dean showed the goddess to another office, slightly smaller than her own. It took only a few moments of conversation for the Morrigan to accept that ICSUT had nothing to do with the disappearances. The head of Necromancy, a gaunt man named Cas, explained to her that ICSUT had been spared only because of the strength of their wards, but something was actively trying to pull their spirits away, towards a cemetery in Little Avalon. They'd done their own investigation but found nothing to explain it. Speaking to the remaining specters was little help, either. They described a tugging sensation, a force trying to swallow them, but nothing untoward -- no shrieks of spirits being distilled into pneumanite, no indication of anything happening on campus beyond bog-standard necromancy. With little else to go on, the goddess took to the sky in crow-form once more, returning to her musings on potential causes. //Another god?// And suddenly she lives another long-buried moment of her past. She is Astrid, child of one of the Tribe of the Gods and one of the Ostmen. For the first time, she meets an equal, a goddess with a half-skeletal face, with whom she negotiates the dispensation of all souls born to both peoples. She remembers the shifts and changes that her rival's presence inflicted upon her own domain, ice frosting her ethereal crossroads as the cruel northern goddess drew near. She remembers feeling that frost in her soul, and realizes she feels no such rival now. She flew onward, the cemetery growing in her vision, worry growing in her heart. She looked to her own fate, the thread of her existence twined with countless lives, and saw it shifting, chaotic in a way it had only been recently, since the disappearances began. Sometimes, it stretched out into infinity, as ever, at others it was cut short. At others still, it tangled into knots, bunched into a skein of possibilities too tight for even her to untangle. As she arrived at the cemetery, she alighted behind a moss-covered mausoleum, its spiritual occupant missing like so many others. Normally, she would not care if she was seen shifting form, but her destiny's turbulence made her cautious. //Better for now if none know who I am.// Casting a glance around to make sure she is alone, she stepped out of her corvine form and into her Sidhe body, thaumic backlash contained with ritual geometry formed by reflex out of her own vast soul. She took a deep breath, savoring the return of her nose, the scents of bonfires and marshmallows wafting from the small Samhain celebrations already in progress nearby. Coming out from behind the mausoleum, she made her way to the center of the cemetery, where an ancient portal tomb, painstakingly transported from lost Avalon, lay. And within it, a gateway to the crossroads, to her realm. The flow of spirits, of energy through it was a throaty roar to her phantom senses, and yet, it appeared abandoned. She saw no cause, though she also noted that the tomb was ill-kept, covered in a thick layer of Portlands moss. Jumping over the low wooden fence surrounding it, she began grabbing rough handfuls of verdure, tossing them aside with indignation. //Perhaps the overgrowth has damaged the gateway, somehow?// She waited for disagreement from within her composite soul, but none arrived. //If not, at least I will be able to see more once this is clean.// "Umm, what are you doing?" A bright voice startled the goddess from her thoughts. Turning, the Morrigan saw a young woman standing nearby, her blood-red curls suggesting Avalonian heritage even as her rounded ears dismissed it. She was not dressed for Samhain; she had no mask to frighten away harmful spirits, and instead of finery she wore ripped jeans, with a short-sleeved band tee over a black long-sleeved shirt. "Cleaning the eldest tomb." The goddess replied, flatly, as though the answer should've been obvious. "Oh, why? Are you trying to meet an old ghost or something?" The girl began to approach, eagerly. "I am not trying to meet any 'ghosts'. Ancestor spirits, though, I am trying to find. And this tomb should always be kept clean." "Okay, but like, are you related to whoever is buried there? Because I think that it only works if you are." The goddess smiled, though it did not reach her eyes. "In a manner of speaking --" she was about to remind the girl that this tomb, all such tombs, are hers, created when one of her bodies is returned to the earth, before she remembered that she was keeping a low profile. "What does that mean?" The girl asked, hopping the fence herself. "And can I help? I think I'm doing it wrong." "I-- it is complicated. I cannot explain it now. But yes, you may help." Turning back to the stone, the goddess ripped another clump of moss off. As she did, she brushed the stone with a knuckle, feeling it thrum with barely-contained spiritual power. Pressing a hand to the exposed surface, she confirmed her earlier sense -- the gateway is active, spirits passing through it in a torrent. //So where are they?// She was interrupted by a prickling sensation, familiar but unexpected. The feeling of the shifting of fate. Within herself, in the part of her that ever dangled at the most fundamental levels of reality, observing the loom of causality, she witnessed the thin thread of the girl's destiny begin to align with her own, even as both began to spasm erratically. Looking to her right on the mortal plane, she saw that the girl had placed her own hand on another clear patch of stone, mimicking the goddess' position, her eyes occasionally darting over to confirm their symmetry. "What is your name?" She asked, breaking the silence that had settled between her and the girl. "Uh, Saoirse. What's yours?" The girl jumped at the sudden noise, deaf as she was to the ethereal roar. "I have many. But you may know me as the Morrigan." She scanned Saoirse's face as she spoke, gauging her reaction. It took a moment, confusion clouding the girl's face. "Wait...like the goddess? Are you serious?" "I am. I do not tell you this lightly. I believe that we are meant to help each other. Our fates have aligned, to an end I cannot yet see." The Morrigan's voice was solemn as the grave. "Wait, like I'm supposed to help you clean this?" "It is grander than that. I am on a mission of great importance, and I am certain that somehow you are key to it." "Okay..." Saoirse drew out the word, leaning away from the goddess as she spoke. "I should probably go now." "Wait. Please." The goddess said, suddenly remembering she was not speaking to one of her devoted. "I am unused to the Sidhe of this city. It seems clear to me that your people have forgotten me, mistrust me. You do not even recognize me before you." "It's not -- look. I'm not really Sidhe. I don't know who you are. And now you're talking about it being my 'destiny' to help you -- you're really freaking me out." Saoirse said, taking a step back. Instead of pursuing her again, the Morrigan cast her eye along the fluxive fate binding her and the girl together, already beginning to vanish, seeking the right words to say. Watching the shifts and twists of the web of fate, she found a design pleasing to her. And from it, she seized one right question. "Why are you here, Saoirse?" The girl paused her escape, sighing. "I...at school I heard that if you clean your ancestor's grave today, and bring them an offering, you can see them again." She curled into herself as she spoke, dejected. "I guess it's not true." "It should be." The Morrigan did her best to sound comforting, with atrophied memories of a hundred mothers. "If everything were as it should be, the dead would walk among us today. Who did you lose, Saoirse? Perhaps I am meant to help you find them." "It's my mom." The girl remained closed off, but stopped backing away. "Why didn't she come?" "Saoirse, none of the dead have come today. They should be pouring through this tomb as we speak, but something is wrong. And I must fix it." "Okay." Saoirse still looked as if she was going to turn and run, but after a hesitant moment, she asked "How can I help, then?" "First, let us finish cleaning this tomb. I do not know why it was allowed to become so overgrown, but I fear the moss may have befouled some guiding runes. Perhaps if we uncover them, we can return things to the way they should be." "Alright." The two women turned to their task, Saoirse working herself into an almost manic vigor. She tossed clumps of moss and lichen aside determinedly, revealing triskele and lone spirals, runes the Morrigan's devoted carved in an age when she was still actively worshipped. The goddess herself made slower progress, eventually giving up the cleaning to pore over her ancient followers' handiwork as Saoirse revealed it. "What's that?" The girl pointed at a small jet-black obelisk, once concealed by the draping moss, tucked into the dark corner of the tomb. Its dark surface was covered in tiny runes, in a language that should have been lost, burned alongside the notes of a wicked artificer. It tugged on the goddess's vast soul, faintly, with fingers that stung like betrayal. She recognized it immediately -- how could she not, though she'd last seen its ilk a lifetime before. ###D11D1D|"A hateful thing, one which should never have been made."## Anger rose within the goddess as she spoke, her voice hardening to iron, her hair beginning to redden as the Badb emerged from within her once more. ###D11D1D|"We must destroy it."## "Okay, but how? How can I help?" In answer, the Badb held out her hand, a pillar of fog rising from the ground, coalescing into a bronze spear. Crouching low, the vengeful warrior-goddess struck at the hateful artifice with the spear she had used to slay giants, monsters, and men. With a single, precise blow, the obelisk shattered like glass. From its splintered form, she immediately felt a force grip her vast godsoul and //pull//, far stronger than before. The agony was indescribable, like a dull scalpel being used to vivisect her entire being, like being ripped into a thousand pieces by a pack of wild dogs. She screamed, heard Saoirse's scream join hers. She felt whole lifetimes be devoured by the obelisk, centuries of memories disappearing from her being. Holes torn open in decades, her time in Camelot and Prussia and the Western Front rent from her essence, leaving nothing but searing, agonizing //loss//. For an eternal, white-hot moment, she did not know who she was. Her tattered memories and soul-fragments fought against the terrible gravity of the obelisk to stay coherent, moments splitting down their seams, remembered conversations cut off mid-sentence. She watched as her most precious days spilled out of her from a thousand golden wounds, nearly forgetting what she had even lost as the force ripped at the unsubsumed parts of her host's soul. Then, sudden as it started, the torture ended. Looking down at her body, she saw flesh rent and torn in a dozen places where fragments of her soul crystallized into pneumanite from the force of being ripped from her body. Soulstuff leaked from her wounds along with her lifeblood, memories and divine might evaporating under the noonday sun. In front of her prone form, she saw that the obelisk was coated in a thick layer of crystal -- lost fragments of her soul plugging it like a stopper in a drain. Saoirse lay next to her. The bleeding goddess looked at the girl, and by some buried reflex awakened her phantom sight. Through divine eyes, it was plain as day that the child's soul was nearly gone, the thread of destiny tying this mortal girl to the goddess fraying. She had but an instant to act, before it was cut entirely. "Forgive me." She whispered through gritted teeth, and released her mantle, infusing her host's body with a tiny shard of soulstuff and willpower in the same moment, an echo of the agony of moments before as she carved off a splinter of her very essence to implant it in dying flesh. Suddenly, she was no longer divine. She was an echo of an echo of her former self, a flickering ember in a corpse. But that ember had strength enough to wrap the mantle around Saoirse before sputtering out, exhausted. Finally, inevitably, the body that was once the Morrigan succumbed to shock and blood loss and collapsed.
