pointtwo3.raw_content:
BROKEN CROWN

STEP ███/███:
Proceed.


Returning to the darkness felt different, this time. They weren’t reassuming their roles as phantoms ruling the corridors. They weren’t predators stalking through the metal wild. They were rats, hiding in the alcoves, scurrying down the hallways.

“For we walk by faith, and not by sight,” Dault whispered to himself through his mask, standing next to Mark. “Corinthians.”

Shouting came from down the hall behind them. Mark glanced backwards and so did some other soldiers, but mainly the detachment carried on, as though unbothered.

Most of them likely feared no ambush at all. When the Foundation found them, it would go as they all expected. They would hear a request for the Insurgency’s surrender, not sudden gunshots. The Foundation were not hitmen, after all. The request for surrender would go ignored by the Sergeant, of course, but also ensured that no bullets would speed from the shadows and kill them without warning. At least there’s that, thought Mark meekly.

Even in times like this, the Insurgency steadfastly held on to one belief; that the Foundation was bound by its image in a way that they were not. They had to do things the right way, or look as though they were, at least. The Insurgency had no such compunction. That gave them, even in dire straits, a small but measurable advantage. Even if it was just to —

A shot exploded behind them.

Bullets from the shadows.

A soldier of the Insurgency collapsed. Dead.


STEP ███/███:
Proceed.


Like lightning, shots bathed the hall in white flashes. The sound of thunderous explosions, sharp and stinging, bounced off metal walls and gathered speed. It surrounded the detachment within moments, wrapping them in a flurry of overwhelming noise.

Mark was part of the flank team, closest to the enemy; before he could even react, a shot whizzed past his ear, and another grazed his leg. Whirling, his heart surging with adrenaline, he clenched his jaw against the pain and fired back.

Across the corridor, briefly lit up by their own rifles, stood members of the Foundation’s MTF. One line crouched, another line standing. A firing squad.

In this lighting they looked oddly like the Insurgents; their mouths covered, their brows obscured, their heads encased in their helms. But the difference was in the eyes. Every time they shot, the light was reflected in their eyes.

Mark shot once, shot twice, backing away. He was the front line; he needed cover, but they were in a corridor. There was no cover.

Another shot sliced open the armor on his left bicep, and blood burst out from it in spurts. Grunting, Mark aimed, and an MTF soldier fell. Then another. And another. Their formation had its advantages, but their mobility was restricted. He had to lean on that.

Another two enemies fell as the flank team kept returning fire, backing away. But too many of the Insurgency were dying already. Mark resisted the urge to look backwards. They had to reach a corner, a crossroads, something. And then get the hell out of here. They likely had to be just moments from being surrounded.

“Flank team!” shouted the Sergeant. “With me! Center team, cover us!”

What? Mark frowned at that. The Sergeant and the rest of the detachment began backing away even faster. That made no sense. The flank team did have the better gunmen. They’d certainly get the Sergeant to safety, but if they left the center team behind, those men would be fodder. Bait. Buying time.

And Philip would be one of them.


STEP ███/███:
Cull at necessity.


There was no time to argue. And if there had been, no one would’ve listened.

The center team had been those guarding One and Two. Even that meager physical proximity to Research and Development had redoubled their fanatical loyalty to the Chaos Insurgency, so Mark wasn’t shocked when doomed men appeared beside him, rifles in hand, somehow not recognizing the face of death.

Mark was in the flank team. They’d been called to retreat. Protect R&D. Protect the Sergeant.

But he didn’t move.

“Mark fucking Shane!” shouted the Sergeant. “Flank team comes with me! That’s an order!”

Rifle in hand, Philip appeared next to Mark. He raised his gun and shot wildly, frantically. Mark couldn’t tell if he was hitting anything.

He heard a final curse in the Sergeant’s voice. When Mark glanced behind him, the Sergeant — and the rest of the detachment — were gone.

This is it.

Mark shot and shot. He hit one more gunman, but another stepped out from the shadows to fill the gap. The soldiers of the MTF were dying, but it wasn’t fast enough. And in the time it took to kill one, two more CI soldiers hit the floor.

He had to think. Quickly. In a firefight, they were outmatched. As he aimed, he tried to observe them. For anything, any idea he could have. Something to save him. Something to save Philip.

The enemy started breaking formation.

They were advancing on them, finally. Shouts rose from their side of the battlefield; it seemed they’d realized most of the detachment was retreating.

They were scared, too. They were rushing. They weren’t careful.

They’d shot first, without warning. This entire place, this entire facility reeked of fear, of haste, of scrambling to fix things.

In the military, soldiers were taught something to use as a last resort — as a Hail Mary.

Mark and Philip were on the leftmost extremity of the little makeshift front line that had been created. It wasn’t much of a front line, more like a front cloud, made up of scattered corpses and soldiers.

“Philip,” Mark shouted to his brother. “Middle of the line. Come!”

Philip blinked out of his firing. He probably had no idea what Mark meant. But he came anyway. He was scared.

Still shooting, they backed up slightly and made their way behind the rest of the center team.

And the instant they were behind the others, obscured from the MTF, Mark shoved Philip to the ground.

Then he, himself, collapsed backwards.

“The… fuck?!” cried Philip, groaning. “Fuck… my shoulder…”

“Don’t move,” Mark said. “Lay on your stomach.”

“What?”

“Do you have a wound? Are you bleeding?”

“My… my hand…”

“Put it under you. Under your chest.”

“That’s… I’m going to bleed a lot.”

“Good. When it gets quiet, don’t breathe.”

It got quiet fast. Staring blankly at the ground next to him, Mark felt the ground rumble as body after body came crashing to join him.

One fell on top of him. From the pain and shock, Mark guessed he might’ve just fractured a rib. But he kept staring forwards, and made not a sound.

Footsteps rung behind them. Mark wished for a moment that the masks of the Insurgents showed their eyes. It would make the subterfuge harder, but it would’ve let him see Philip’s. Perhaps calm him down. He knew his brother. Behind that mask, his eyes were wider than ever, weren’t they?

“Cover all the exits,” yelled some voice. “All of them! We’ll call reinforcements from outside. We can deal with that thing later. Get everyone here! Now!”

Mark’s heart hammered in his chest. But they paid no mind to Philip, laying motionless in a pool of his own blood, nor to Mark, hidden underneath his comrade’s corpse.

They marched past the dead.

It worked.


STEP ███/███:
Proceed to final marker.


Grunting, Mark shoved the body off of him. His rib wailed in protest, and he gasped, clutching his chest. He was bleeding from at least five different wounds — thankfully all minor, save the one on his left bicep. He needed to bandage it. Now.

While Philip crawled to his feet, Mark faced the body that had fallen on top of him. He stripped off armor and ripped up the dead man’s shirt, before —

It was Dault.

Mark paused.

His hand shook for a moment. His jaw tightened.

Then, slowly, he ripped up the dead man’s shirt, before using the cloth — unclean though it was — to at least slow his own bleeding. He tore some more of Dault’s shirt off and turned to Philip.

“Don’t move so much,” he said. “Show me your hand.”

Philip stretched out his hand. “Can’t believe that worked.”

“Long shot,” Mark said. “Rule 113 of customary International Humanitarian Law.”

“I don’t know,” Philip said, staring at his own blood, “what that means.”

Mark glanced at his brother’s masked eyes. “The unnecessary mutilation of dead bodies is prohibited.” He paused. “Most people don’t care, you see. But this is the Foundation, and they were in a hurry. They would’ve needed a good reason to dead-check us, I think.”

“Yeah.”

“And, well, they had a far better reason to just ignore us. If they’d searched us, or stopped, the Insur— the rest of us would’ve gotten away. If they’d split up, they would’ve lost the next firefight. You saw them. Heard them. They just now called for reinforcements — that was just a scout team, investigating the noise.”

“Scout team,” Philip repeated slowly.

“Mhm.”

Philip winced at the bandage. “This… is this Dault’s shirt?”

Mark nodded. “If it were up to me, we would all have backpacks with primitive med-kits. First aid. But, we make do with what we have.”

Philip looked at Dault’s body for a while. Then, he looked to where the MTF detachment had gone. “Those… If we chased them now… they wouldn’t expect it.”

“We’re both wounded,” Mark said, “Our wounds are going to get infected. Fast. We’d die. And, technically, if we chase after them now, that also could be a war crime. It’s called perfidy.”

“Who fucking cares,” Philip muttered. But he let it go.

They set off in a direction opposite where the MTF had gone. They had to find an exit. Fast. And, somehow, navigate the maze without getting lost, cornered, or surrounded.

“They said,” Philip mumbled, straining as they walked, “that they were going to cover all the exits. How… do we even get out?”

“We might be able to get out fast enough if we go away from the fight,” Mark said. “Get out before they close in.”

“I don’t know if I could run,” Philip said.

Mark looked at him. He’d taken a pretty bad shot to the leg. Thankfully the bullet had only grazed him, but still. The cut was deep.

He was right. Not only would they have trouble even finding an exit, but they’d be too late. They’d be captured or gunned down.

He needed to find an exit that they wouldn’t expect. And one he was already aware of.

And he thought of it.

“Come with me,” Mark said. “I have an idea.”


STEP ███/███:
Exit via southern passage. Cf coordinates C025.


“Breaking the window?” Philip mumbled.

Thankfully, the conference room they’d abandoned earlier was still vacant. The curtains were still open, the bodies still on the floor. The door to the room had been ajar, so likely the MTF had come to investigate and then rushed to meet the Insurgency in combat. Mark had been worried that they might’ve left a man or two guarding it, but, thankfully, they’d saved him the trouble.

“Won’t that make noise?” Philip asked as Mark walked, hand on his chest, towards a rolling chair near the large conference table.

“Yes,” Mark said, grunting as he pulled it towards the window, “but they’re all distracted. You heard them, they’re… gah, scrambling. They won’t notice this.”

Philip came close to the glass and craned his head to the side. “There better be a way around this stupid crater. It’s a long way down.”

“We have to take that chance.” Mark prepared to throw the chair through the window. He braced himself for the pain in his ribs, and —

“Wait,” Philip said. “Wait. Mark. Look.”

One of the four scientists was still alive.

Somehow, even with a shot to the chest, he was breathing. No one had noticed during the earlier commotion. The opening curtains, the violent Sergeant, but now they could see. He was face down on the floor, sputtering slightly.

“He’s dead anyway, Phil,” Mark said softly.

Philip glanced at Mark, then back at the scientist. Then he pulled something out of his pocket, the picture. Charlie’s picture.

For fuck’s sake, Phil, thought Mark. But he didn’t stop him.

Philip crouched next to the dying man. He flipped him over; the man’s eyes widened and he coughed blood.

“This woman,” Philip said. “Charlie Callin. Who is she to you? Why do you want her? Tell me, and I can help get you to safe… I mean to safety.”

The scientist looked up. “Charlie…”

“Or her sister,” Philip said, holding him up. “Her sister. Her sister Harper. Charlie and Harper? Who are they to you?” Philip paused. “Where… where are they?”

Still a shit liar, Mark thought.

The man coughed again.

“Answer me,” Philip said. “Please. I care. About her.”

The man shook his head. “You chose… a good… fucking day.”

“Huh?”

“We’re all… s—so turned around,” the man mumbled. “So much loss, so much pain… and you just walk in while the fire’s burning and do what you want. I guess that’s why… they call you that, hm?”

“Help me,” Philip said, “and we’ll get you out of here. We’ll help.”

“Outside,” the man said suddenly, doubling up. “Don’t go outside. Or, do go outside. It’s dark outside. She’s outside.”

“She?” Philip leaned in. “She?”

The man nodded. “Get… get…”

“Get what?”

He fell backwards, his chest heaving. “Get the fuck away from me.”

Philip tried a few more questions — even tried to shake the man awake. But he didn’t rise, didn’t say anything, didn’t open his eyes. He was still breathing, still coughing. But he chose to die there, quiet, alone, in the dark.

“Fine,” Philip said. “Let’s go.”

With a wail of pain so bad he nearly fainted, Mark heaved the chair over his head and threw it against the window. He had the foresight to duck out of the way, in case the window was too thick to break and the chair bounced back towards his face, but the glass broke just fine.

The pain in his ribs was truly bad now. He’d been able to ignore it before, but that throw had sparked it alive and he now had to strain to avoid doubling up in agony.

Mark kicked pieces of glass off, making the opening big enough for himself and Philip. When it was done, he nodded to his brother, and they climbed out.

Thankfully, the Foundation had left some margin between the beginning of the crater and the station walls, so — crouching and moving slowly — Philip and Mark were able to creep soundlessly along the sides of the countless, rectangular metal buildings, ducking under windows and going completely still when they heard shouting.

Neither of them spoke. They walked with the Foundation on their left and the largest abyss they’d ever seen on their right, night falling upon them, silent as mice.

Eventually, they rounded the final corner, and they were faced with a large open space and a good, clear view of the facility. The entire thing sprawled out like some strange, metal spiderweb, but still it seemed to hug the crater as much as it could, with some parts of it looking almost serpentine as a result.

On one side of it, the crater; on the other, a large, sprawling wooded expanse. A forest. Tall pines, motionless against the night sky. Mark remembered getting a glance of it when climbing out of the truck on arrival, though they’d moved so fast and so close together that, as part of the detachment’s flank, he didn’t see very much at all.

Philip nudged him. “Look.”

MTF soldiers were rushing out of the forest in droves. Through the woods, Mark could see their flashlights — most of them were searching the trees for something, but were being recalled back. Presumably to fight the Insurgency.

“We could wait,” Philip said. “Then walk through the forest to the truck. I think I remember where it is.”

“If we wait too long,” Mark said, “they’ll come back before we reach it. Then we’re in the forest, alone, outmanned, outgunned, and shit out of luck. We have to time it right.”

“What do you think they’re looking for in there? In the forest?”

“Don’t know. Not our problem.”

The forest shuddered as he said that. Mark shoved his own uncertainty to the side. After all, they had no other option. Only a pale imitation of choice remained, mimicking it, goading them forwards.


WALK TEN PACES AND DIE

STEP ███/███:
Follow procedure for scenario A7 if condition Theta is met.


When the timing was right, they walked into the open.

It was dark now; dark enough that the lights surrounding the facility and the enemy’s flashlights were the only things protecting the world from going pitch black. That meant that ‘the open’ was actually fairly safe, so long as they kept close to the ground, kept moving, and moved fast.

His rib wailed. Doubling up helped somewhat with the pain, but moving quickly was a struggle — Mark ended up in a sort of half-gallop, whilst Philip behind him shuffled and panted and coughed trying to keep up.

When they reached the treeline, Philip gasped, hands on his knees, and Mark groaned at his wound. He pulled his arm away from his chest. It was soaked red.

“We have to keep going,” he heard himself say.

“Fuck,” Philip said. “Give me a second, will you?”

Mark grimaced.

But he said nothing. He leaned back against a tree, too, but one facing the facility. He followed every blink of light, every flash, every shout. They needed to get back to the truck. Fast.

“Always on the job?” Philip said between pants.

“When the job’s keeping us alive, then, yes.”

Philip pursed his lips.

Distant bangs wafted into earshot. Mark looked past the trees, trying to spot the fighting, but saw nothing. It was probably still happening inside the facility.

“Think they’ll… make it?” Philip asked, following his gaze.

Mark turned to him. “Maybe,” he lied.

The truth was, if the fighting was still happening inside the facility, that meant the Insurgents had not managed to escape before MTF reinforcements arrived. It meant they were outnumbered, outgunned, outmaneuvered, and stranded in unfamiliar territory. Their knowledge of Foundation tactics might’ve served them, but the Foundation felt off today. They should have never fired from the dark like that, without warning. And with a firing squad?

Despite everything he constantly told Philip, Mark couldn’t stop himself from wondering.

Something had happened here. Something had changed. The Foundation and the Insurgency both were rushing against each other, almost sloppily, thirstily. Why?

And, for all he’d said, they did have a picture of Charlie.

How long had it been since he’d seen her? He couldn’t quite tell. Although he’d pretended the picture barely resembled her, Mark had recognized it from across the room. Seeing it from up close, eyes blacked out, stuck to a Foundation whiteboard with arrows and scrawled notes crowding around her.

Of course he’d recognized her. She looked just like her sister, after all.

No. He couldn’t think like this.

Philip had crumpled to the ground in front of him, sitting with his back against a tree, eyes closed and panting. They had to be focused if they wanted to make it back. Mark had to be focused. Mark had no choice.

He straightened up, groaning. “We have to go.”

“Give me a second,” Philip said again.

“You had one.”

His brother, in a heap on the floor, looked up at him. His face softened somewhat, but his eyes did not. “I don’t get it.”

“We don’t have much time,” Mark explained, grunting and holding his side. “If we don’t make it back to the truck —”

“I get that,” Philip said. “I just don’t get you. How you can just… not care.”

“Philip, not now.”

“Fuck off,” Philip growled, standing with a wince. “How can you just… carry on? How does nothing get to you? Spent all this time with the Insurgency, and you defect like… like that was your plan from day one. Even met Dault, spoke to him, I saw it and… and you fucking loot his body or whatever. Like you didn’t even know him…”

“This isn’t the time.”

“Even… all those years, when we were kids. Charlie, Harper… we grew up together. You too. When Harper vanished, I thought you’d rip apart the Earth to find her, but you did nothing. And when Charlie went after Harper, I thought you’d at least let me go with her… and then she vanished, too, and you said you were coming after her with me, but… That was a lie. You didn’t go after her, or Harper. You went after me.” Philip shook with an odd mixture of a cough and a sob. “You always go after me…”

“You want to cry about this?” Mark asked. “Now? Really? You were going to die, Phil. You were —”

“You don’t know that!” Philip shouted. “But you know what I know? That Dault… all those men… they’re really dead. Because you couldn’t just trust that things were going to turn out fine. That other people had it handled. You’re such a jackass… always need to be in charge.”

Mark’s nostrils flared. “And you always need someone in charge.”

“Huh?”

“You don’t think,” Mark said, “before you do. You don’t question the insanity of your choices. You seem to ambiently piss off everyone who’s ever had authority over you. You walk into danger like crawling into bed, and you want me to just watch? You can’t do that.”

“It’s my call,” Philip muttered. “It’s my call if I want to be in danger. It’s my call if I want to fight. I have that choice!”

“No, you don’t!” Mark shouted at him.

Philip’s mouth hung open. He didn’t answer. His face was still scrunched up, turning red, but his eyes widened slightly.

“We’re getting out of here,” Mark said, turning. “Someone might’ve heard us. You remember where the truck is?”

Philip blinked, glancing at him. “Yeah.”

“Let’s go.”

Mark started forwards. And, although he was stumbling, Philip came too. In silence.

The woods were turning darker by the minute. They were cold. Damp. Mark had expected them to smell of tall pines, of earth and oak and life, but… he barely smelled anything at all. Just the lingering scent of nighttime moisture that follows early fall evenings.

If there had been wildlife beneath that canopy, it did not make itself known. They heard the occasional ruffle from above them, or a scuttle in the dead leaves littering the forest floor, but no chirping of crickets, no birds, no bats, no shuffling in the bushes, no shadows in the corners of their eyes. Mark had been on assignment in forests before, stalking through greenery, a rifle in hand. Through his tinted visor, he’d watched squirrels and magpies scatter away and he advanced. He remembered how much he’d felt like an intruder then. Having to watch the forest empty beneath the rumble of his march. He’d held his weapon in his hands, and felt like a devout sinner walking into church, all eyes on him.

But this time, he didn’t feel like an intruder at all. He felt worse — the forest wasn’t emptying, it was already empty. The church was in ruins, and it didn’t matter if he was a sinner or not. Under the gaze of those wordless pines, he felt too tall, too clumsy, too bold. Although the sounds of fighting grew distant with every step, he felt very eerily like he wasn’t escaping anything at all.

“How much further are we from the truck?” he asked under his breath.

Philip shrugged, not meeting his eyes. “I don’t know. Dozen more minutes.”

His heart began to beat faster again, like it had when the Sergeant had threatened his brother. He felt like they’d been sailors aboard a burning ship, and to save themselves they’d jumped overboard into the water only to realize, right as the ship vanished beneath the waves, that they were surrounded by nothing but vast, solitary, open ocean.

And what if there was something else under the water?

Something in the trees.

He set his jaw even harder. He felt the muscles in his neck tense up against his camo.

He couldn’t do this. He’d made the call. Now they would survive.

Besides, if he was feeling this way, who could tell what Philip was feeling? Mark couldn’t let it show.

He turned his anxiety into a lump in his throat, and he swallowed.

“Did you hear that?” Philip asked suddenly, looking off to the side.

Mark glanced. “Nothing.”

“I think I heard someone…”

“Then walk faster.”

Maybe one of the other Insurgency soldiers had managed to escape. Or maybe one of the MTF was still trekking through the forest, on their way to provide reinforcements. Bad either way.

The fighting behind them, past the trees, had fallen rather silent, or perhaps they were far enough now to not hear the gunshots. But he doubted that. No, Mark was certain of something else: the Sergeant had finally been backed into a corner.

He tried to listen as intently as he could, glancing every so often behind them to try and make out what was happening.

And suddenly, he did hear something. A rustle in the leaves coming from the other side, away from the facility.

Deeper in the woods.

“You heard that one, right?” Philip asked.

Mark didn’t answer. He just stared into the leaves, motionless. His grip on his gun tightened.

“Mark?”

“Quiet.”

Philip obeyed; so did the forest. Silence fell, and Mark strained, motionless, to hear it break. But nothing happened.

“What was it?” Philip asked, whispering.

Mark frowned. “I… don’t know.” He was getting a very odd sensation, all of a sudden.

“This place… have we been here before?” Philip looked around, up at the canopy, down at the ground, then back at his brother. “It feels so familiar.”

Mark nodded slowly. “Maybe we took a wrong turn. Walked in circles.”

“We’ve been walking in a straight line,” Philip said. “I think we’ve been here before.”

“We haven’t,” Mark said, in a firmer voice than he intended. “Keep going. We’re close now.”

But it did feel familiar. Every step they took, every time Mark looked around, he felt it, creeping onto his arms, settling in his mouth so familiar. It’s like he could taste the feeling itself, and it wasn’t altogether unpleasant.

What was this place? Where were they?

The sun had vanished now, and the shadows went with it, blurring out into darkness, into black ink oozing onto the forest floor. Nighttime had come, though the forest did not seem to react to it. Though the dull glow of twilight kept them company, it wasn’t comforting, no. It was just enough light to see the trees against the sky when they looked up, to see them crowding around like stone giants, their faces obscured and dripping with solemnity.

“It feels like Charlie,” Philip said quietly.

“What?”

“I know it’s weird to say. But… doesn’t it? Did we come here with her?”

Mark paused. “Maybe.” But they couldn’t have. It made no sense. And there was no point in thinking about it. “Focus. Keep walking.”

Philip cursed quietly.

Forward. Forward. Forward. Eventually, Mark let Philip lead. He had the better sense of where the truck was, anyway. Rifle in both hands, Mark watched his brother traipse through the wilderness, upending dead leaves with every step, glancing around at the slightest pause.

Crack.

Mark aimed without a second thought, whirling.

But it was too dark. He caught nothing, saw nothing. The scope turned up blank.

Philip had kept walking. Had he not heard…?

“We’re close now,” Philip mumbled when Mark caught up. “I can feel it.”

“Feel it?”

“Can’t you?” His brother’s eyes were turned skywards. “It’s obvious.”

He could. It was obvious. This was the right way. This was where they had to go.

“Soldiers,” came a voice from the woods.

Mark stopped. Extending a hand, he stopped Philip, too.

“What?” Philip asked.

“Quiet.”

“Patrol ended,” the voice said again. “Regroup! Come together…”

It was distant. Far away.

But unmistakable.

“The Sergeant,” Philip said, eyes wide. “They made it out.”

“Impossible,” Mark said. “They might’ve made it close to the forest. But this far?”

“See?” Philip said, grinning. “See? Fucking see, Mark? If you’d just trusted them…”

Philip stumbled forwards. Towards the Sergeant’s voice.

Mark did not. He held his rifle up.

“Mar…” Philip turned around. “The… the fuck’s wrong with you? Put that away! You’re in enough trouble —”

“If that’s him,” Mark said, “then stay fucking put.”

“He’s on our side.”

“Side?” Mark lowered his weapon, gritting his teeth. “And you honestly, truly, after everything you’ve seen, think he cares?”

“It’s not up to him,” Philip said. “He’s not R&D. He’s not Delta command. He can’t just execute us for something that you didn’t even admit to —”

“Keep your goddamn voice down,” Mark hissed.

“God, you’re so cynical!” Philip said. “And you call me arrogant. Well, guess what, Mark. You defected, and you’re bleeding out. They followed the plan. The same kind that never let us down, and they made it out, even when you didn’t think they could. Could you, for once in your miserable life, just have some faith?”

“Faith in the plan. And what’s the plan?”

“Again with that question. It doesn’t matter. Faith —”

“You must’ve read it,” Mark said, pressing his palm against his head. “You must have, right? You must’ve read the whole thing. And there’s a line at the bottom that says, ‘All infantrymen must survive the mission, as unit cohesion is the most important thing to the Insurgency. We, of course, pride ourselves on our low turnover rate.’” Mark’s words dripped with venom, but he didn’t care. “You read that, right? You read those words?”

Philip looked at him. Then looked away. He took a deep, shaky breath. “If only we could all care so little, and think so much of ourselves.”

“Alright, you wanna know?” Mark asked finally.

Philip didn’t answer.

Mark clenched his jaw, but continued. “Think about it, Phil. R&D, they don’t give a shit about us. You think Delta Command does? No. We’re infantry. Sent into a place with almost no intel, barely any training — fuck’s sake, you and I pretty much just joined this thing, and with so many ways it might go wrong?” Mark shook his head. “Only explanation is that it was a suicide mission. Meant to cause…”

Philip turned back at him.

“You know the word,” Mark said. “It’s in their name.”

His brother looked down. “Chaos,” he mumbled.

“Right,” Mark said. “Kill Foundation scientists. Gather intel, which One and Two probably reported back without us even noticing. Big uproar while leaving. Death toll on both sides, sure, but important personnel lost to the Foundation. There. Because, what’s the alternative? Do you think they could’ve predicted all of this? Every level of it, everything, written out in their little Step-compilations? Turn left, turn right, walk ten paces and die? It’s smoke and mirrors.”

“It’s not impossible. Not in their world.”

“Then they would’ve predicted me defecting, too,” Mark said. “And this is all still… according to plan.”

Philip didn’t meet his eyes.

“Philip,” Mark said slowly. “I just —”

Crack.

Mark’s head swiveled. The trees swayed, staring at him.

“I have to believe in it, Mark,” Philip said. “Because otherwise…”

“Quiet,” Mark said quickly.

“What?”

“Quiet.”

There was shuffling in the trees before them. Actual movement. In front of them. Then next to them. How…? It was as if… as if the sounds were coming from all directions.

And then silence.

Movement again, further away, off to the right.

Then suddenly to the left.

“The hell…” Philip stuttered. He held up his gun. His grip on it wavered for a moment.

“We won!” the Sergeant’s voice said. Mark turned to face it. “Homebound. Get in! We’re going.”

He sounded… cheery?

“Did something happen to him?” Philip asked under his breath. “He’s so… happy.”

“Delirious,” Mark said. “He has to be.”

“Off we go!” the happy Sergeant said again. “This way! This way! This way! This way! This way! THIS WAY! Now.”

“Mark,” Philip whispered. “You’re right. Let’s… let’s go the other way. Leave.”

Mark nodded.

“That’s an order,” the Sergeant said. His voice was fading suddenly, then growing louder again as though he were rushing around them. Fast. Very fast.

They took slow, careful steps back. Dead leaves surrounded them, and they tried their best to avoid them, but every so often a soft crush would resound from the ground.

They kept going. Something was wrong. The Sergeant had never been so jovial. Never. And yet everything was…

…so familiar.

Mark shifted before he even registered what happened. He’d seen something move for the first time, he was sure something else in this godforsaken forest had just moved.

He’d seen it through the scope. Mark stood, holding his breath, still as he could be, gun touching his shoulder and cheek against metal.

In the faraway shadows, a red blur. Dashing through the woods.



Nothing

Point Two

One More Part of It All

BROKEN CROWN

STEP ███/███:
Finish relay.”


She was she was and I am.

Leaves and twigs and dead things crack and snap and splinter under me. They break and split and stab but I bury them long before they can hurt me.

There is no wind, but the air howls when I run. There is no sound, but the ground whimpers when I stalk. There is no light, but I see everything, everything, EVERYTHING lurking in the dark.

I can feel them. They’re close. They’re loud.

Every sense I have, every limb I operate, every tendon and muscle and bone jubilates in unison, singing to me. Like it’s the first time. Like I’ve never done it before.

It’s all so legible. It’s all so together. I can see my thoughts in front of me, like webbed nodes, leading each other, one to the other to the other to the other. Once, my thoughts were hidden deep inside an ever-heavier head, pumped with whirring and awful noise, but no longer. Now they speak to me in soothing tones, in lilting sing-song tongues. It all makes sense. It all makes sense. It all makes sense.

She was she was and I am.

Shouting that way! I dash, and monoliths of wood can’t stop me. Footsteps! I double back, and jagged rocks on the ground, hungry for blood, can’t pierce me. A scent! A gorgeous, wonderful, exquisite scent. Beloved interloper of the forest, intruder among the pines, monsters, I CAN FEEL YOU.

Something wriggles inside of me. It’s them, the little selves I collect, squirming like butterflies. Which one? The frightened soldiers, who held her captive? The invaders, horrified, who’d been too MUDDLED to stay away?

The commander. The Sergeant. I can feel my blood warming at the thought of him. He makes sense right now. I can taste their fear, those two lonely boys hiding from me in the woods… they’re too far to make out everything, but I can tell. They’re invaders. They came with the commander, with those white-robed cowards, storming around in their trucks. They’ll listen to his voice.

Voice. Someone once tried to take away my voice. But they gave me hundreds instead.

I speak, I howl, I sing with many, many, many voices.

One thought leads to another leads to another leads to another. I don’t even have to keep track of it anymore.

His voice flows out of me, righteous, authoritative.

“Soldiers!” Listen. “Patrol ended!” Yes. “Regroup.” Keep close to each other. “Come together!”

Don’t move.

I have to be careful when I speak in my other voices. It is delicate. I know this, but when I run, the world turns to a blur, and my heart beats so fast, and my bones vibrate, and my muscles burst with power, and I am no longer delicate.

I remember being very delicate indeed. Conversely, I remember being frightened.

I remember white rooms, and having a throat of one voice. The world was clear as glass but my thoughts were a blur, rushing around in whirlwinds, sinking into my skin, making me tremble.

I wanted, I craved, I pleaded. I could not hunt for what I wanted, because I could not hold it. I could not savor what I had, because I could not eat it. And the three people I wanted most in the world, the three voices I prayed to in my solitude. They did not speak back to me, and they did not hear me. They were very far away.

All was silence and blinding lights. White coats and thrashing monsters.

They all thought I had forgotten. It made them feel safer. They had to imagine I was not the same, they had to focus on my blistering red skin, my jagged spine, my jaw…

They gave me names I didn’t like.

They gave me a number.

I heard…

But I know my number. I know my name. I remember everything.

She was she was and I am.

Today is my triumph. Nothing has stopped me today. I have wounds and I hurt, but I have more voices, so many more voices, and that is a happy thought. When I turn inwards, I can feel them all dancing within me, living with me, excited to come out. I would smile at them if I could — but they are buried down deep and I am not.

“We won!” the Sergeant says, coming out of my jaws, through my bloodsoaked teeth. “Homebound. Get in! We’re going.”

This place has been a blessing. I don’t quite know what happened, or why I was called here; I simply followed the things I felt. My body is stronger than I am now. When it guides me, I listen, instead of locking myself into my own head in a scramble for answers. Yes… A consequence of power, I think, is accepting some sporadic uncertainty.

Something has changed. Unrelated to me, but close to me, brushing against my soul. I felt it in the Earth. I felt it everywhere and in everything — a great tremor in the Universe, something that should not have happened. And now, panic. Panic. Panic. Fear for everyone, fear for the little gods in their little metal houses and their white coats. And in the meantime, here I am, swimming in their panic.

Swimming…

I am close to them now. The two I hunt. The little soldiers in the woods.

I feel them.

Their breathing is heavy. Their pores call out to me.

They are more careful than others have been. Perhaps they don’t care for the Sergeant? Still, I let him speak through me a few more times, prodding them. But I don’t hear movement.

I slow down.

Close to the ground I crouch, and then advance, my claws gliding under the leaves noiselessly.

I can see them now. A man stands, metal death-bringer in hand, pointed near where I hide… a ways behind him, another, hands shaking. Two. Similar height. Similar eyes. Similar scent…

Scent…

The soldier closest to me sweeps the trees with his scope. He passes over me several times, but I do not blame him for his inattention. There are worse failings to have.

Their scent…

I recognize it.

I recognize it.

Strangers they are not, but brothers. And only one of them is a soldier. He is aiming at me.

I wonder: would he aim at me if he knew my names?

I could speak to him. My eldest voice is one I have not used in a long time. It would be a joy.

The brother, standing some distance behind him… his sorrow, I can smell. Layers of fear dilute it, but it is there.

The brothers. We were four once. The soldier and I, and his brother and… and my sister. Charlie. Charlie. Charlie.

The brothers whose voices I wished for, those long eons in darkness.

The soldier… Once, in a muddled mind and among blurred thoughts, he stood sharp and clear against the chaos.

And now they both remind me of her. Dear, sweet sister. Charlie…

How I would love to speak in your voice.

I will take you with me, out of mourning, out of pain. I will look inwards and find you dancing in peace. You look for me, but you think of my skin, and my hair, and my hands. Think instead of my eyes. Think instead of my smile. Think instead of my voice.

She was, she was, but only I am.


ONE MORE PART OF IT ALL

STEP ███/███:
Report success.


“Mark,” Philip whispered. “What’s happening?”

Still nothing. He saw nothing.

His eyes told him to calm down. His mind urged him to continue towards the truck. His bones rattled, begging him to squeeze the trigger and blindly sweep over the forest. But somehow, he stood still.

“Mark,” Philip said again.

“Shush.”

The bushes moved again. He swiveled, tracking the movement, better this time. He still couldn’t see the thing dashing around them. But bullets might find it.

“A boar?” Philip asked. But from his voice, Mark could tell he didn’t believe that. Just like he didn’t believe it either.

The world is made of patterns. If you’ve seen something a dozen times before, and you know steps one through ten, then odds are when you see steps one, two, and three, you can see step four coming. That had kept Mark alive. That had kept Mark moving forwards. That had kept Mark sane, no matter where he was. The Chaos Insurgency had begun to break from those rules in odd, little ways. Their patterns were not right. They were too perfect, or too random.

But randomness is rarer than people say. If something looks random, it may just be part of a larger pattern that they don’t yet understand.

That knowledge electrified Philip; recognizing patterns was euphoria to him. But to Mark, recognizing patterns was breathing. Not in the sense that he was particularly talented at doing so, but because he was always afflicted with a silent, assassin anxiety that whispered that if he ever stopped, he would choke, collapse, and die.

The Chaos Insurgency was the very first part of a pattern he’d never seen before. A very, very large pattern, hooded in the Earth, hiding from everything. The other parts of it were locked away behind metal walls and lab coats.

But Mark knew of one more thing. All the soldiers of the CI knew of one more part of it all — the light above the anglerfish.

Philip wavered next to him a little. “Fuck, Mark…” He’d figured it out too, it seemed. “It’s one of them.”

The dead leaves on the floor rattled again, and Mark imagined claws like scythes raking them. Bushes trembled in the still night and Mark imagined a face overflowing with eyes, staring at him. Movement again, to the right, and Mark —

— pulled the fucking trigger.

The quiet and black night came alive. Philip’s hands flew to his ears in shock. For a moment, in the lightning-like light of the rifle, Mark could see his brother’s face clear as day, scrunched up in fear.

The bullets ripped into the trees in front of them, tearing into bark. Mark strained to see what they hit. He thought he saw something, a dark shape, momentarily slowed, but the next instant it was gone.

“F… fuck, man,” Philip groaned.

Mark glanced at him. “Next time, shoot with me.”

“What? I… I can barely aim.”

“Phil,” Mark said. “I trust you. Shoot with me.”

His brother raised his weapon, and waited.

Movement. Mark traced it with his gun, but didn’t fire. It was testing him, he knew. His ammo was limited. He couldn’t just empty rounds into the empty darkness over and over. He had to wait. Wait until it came closer.

Philip shook, but followed his movements. Mark wanted to glance at him. But he couldn’t. He had to stay —

Sound. Something was —

Bullets erupted from Mark’s rifle, and then Philip’s, burrowing into a thing. In the brief moments the bullets lit it up, Mark gasped.

A claw on a tree, pulling it forwards. Flesh so red, it looked like the forest was bleeding. Eyes fixed, fixed, unmoving, on them.

The bullets… it didn’t… it wasn’t… it felt nothing, nothing, it just… continued —

But when the dust settled, it had vanished again.

Mark glanced at Philip.

His brother didn’t even move. He just stood, feet planted, saying nothing. He looked at Mark for a split second, and his mouth shook itself open.

“Shots fired!” The Sergeant’s voice again. “Shots fired!”

Philip stumbled backwards. So did Mark.

And then, another voice came out of the trees.

But it wasn’t the Sergeant’s.

“Mark?” it whispered.

Mark froze.

Philip glanced around wildly. “Is that —”

“Mark,” it said. “Is that you?”

Mark didn’t move. Didn’t speak.

“I need your help, Mark.” The voice slithered around him, directionless. “I need you to say something, Mark. I need you to speak to me, Mark.”

“No,” Mark breathed.

“You’re so tired, Mark. You used to tell me all about it. You used to like being carried, but you lied. Do you remember? Do you remember?” The voice grew hushed. “Do you remember?”

Despite everything, Mark’s rifle wavered, shaking, lowering ever so slightly.

“What are you?” Mark whispered.

“I am,” it said.

“It’s not her,” Philip said.

Mark didn’t answer. The encroaching familiarity, the voice, he was tired.

Its eyes flashed in his mind.

Mark raised his rifle again.

“Do you remember?” it asked again.

“Mark,” Philip said. “We have to go.”

“Phil,” the voice said suddenly. “Phil?”

Philip closed his eyes. “We have to go.”

“Where’s Charlie?” the voice asked. “Where’s Charlie? Where’s Charlie? I miss her. She misses me.”

“I don’t know,” Philip mumbled. “I lost her.”

“I’ll find her,” the voice said happily? “I’ll find her. Very soon. Then we can go. We can go, all four of us, we can go.”

The voice was off, just like the Sergeant’s had been.

“Harper?” Mark asked.

The forest stood still. Then wind blew across his face, and the trees recoiled, and dead leaves curled around his legs.

“You remember,” the voice said.

A streak of red lashed out from the woods.

Mark tried to aim, but his guard was down and he was too late. His leg was split open with pain and he collapsed.

Behind him, Philip screamed.

Mark twisted in the ground, seeing his leg — his mangled, twisted, horrible leg, shred apart in moments — and tried to raise his rifle. But it slipped out of his hands.

Philip’s headless body collapsed in front of him.

The impact with the ground caused blood to spurt from his neck into Mark’s face. He didn’t even make for his rifle.

The creature, blocking out the night sky, crouched over him, soundless.


EPILOGUE


Very far away from those woods, a clock ticked.

She stared at it. Without its incessant clicking, it’d be hard to tell that any time had passed at all.

“Thank you, Charlie.” Looking up, the interrogator smiled softly at her. “That will be all for now. I need to convene with my associates before I ask any more questions. Would you like some water? Or perhaps something to eat?”

“No.” Charlie didn’t meet his eyes. Arms still crossed, she stared at the table between them, blinking. “No. After all this, I’m just… I’m tired.”

“I understand,” he said. Standing up, he collected his clipboard, and his mug.

Charlie’s eyes turned upwards at him as he left. “I can leave?”

“Of course.”

Charlie nodded slowly.

The doctor turned away, and he was moments before exiting the room. But he paused for a moment, eyes on his clipboard. He flipped a page, then flipped it back. His hand fell to the inside of his lab coat, and something clicked.

“I do have a final question,” the doctor said, “if you don’t mind.”

Charlie stared up at him. “About Harper?”

“In a manner of speaking.” Dr. Olson sat back down, placing his clipboard before him, and taking a sip from his mug. “There’s been a recent development.”

“With Harper.”

He ignored her. “I assume you’re familiar with the Chaos Insurgency, yes?”

Charlie shrugged. “I don’t have files on them or anything.”

“But you know them.”

“I know of them.” She pointed through the one-way glass behind him. “I know you don’t like each other very much.”

“The relationship is more one-sided than that,” Olson said. “But very well. And?”

“And they raid you,” Charlie said. “They shoot you, you shoot them back. That sort of thing.”

“And?”

“And what about them?”

Dr. Olson tapped his pen to his clipboard absent-mindedly, then continued. “One such raid was performed on a Foundation facility, some time ago. As you so succinctly put it, they shot us, and we shot them back.”

“Well done.”

“It seemed,” he said, “that the Insurgency placed some importance on you, during that raid.”

Charlie coughed. “What?”

“Apparently.”

“I’m… not sure why they would.”

“You haven’t been in contact with any Insurgency agents in recent memory?”

“No.”

“Have you noticed being surveilled in any way by the Insurgency?”

“No. Not by the Insurgency.”

“Not the Insurgency?”

“With respect,” she said, “It’s not the Insurgency that snatched me up, put me in a box, and interrogated me.”

“You went after us, Miss Callin.”

“And you’re telling me you let me do that unsupervised?” Charlie made a tsk sound, shaking her head.

He ignored her. “Have you any object or piece of knowledge that might have drawn the Insurgency’s ire? Aside from your relationship with your sister?”

“Not to my knowledge.”

“Can you think of anything?”

“No. And please don’t go poking around in my head to make sure.”

"We're not wizards, Miss Callin.”

She shrugged.

“Well, these were all long shots,” Dr. Olson said, flipping another page. “Intel suggests this was the isolated work of a few agents. Does the name Mark Shane mean anything to you?”

She looked up, quicker than she meant to.

“Mark Shane?” she asked.

“Yes. Or Philip…”

“They’re brothers,” she mumbled.

“Yes, that’s it.” Dr Olson smiled. “Who are they to you?”

“Friends,” she said. “What were they doing there? They joined the Insurgency?”

“I’m afraid I have no answer for you,” Dr. Olson said, writing. He looked up. “You think it’s credible that these were just two isolated individuals looking for you?”

Fucking idiots, she thought to herself. Idiots, idiots, idiots. “Yeah.”

Dr Olson nodded again. “I think I agree. We have reason to believe the Insurgency had far more important reasons to raid that facility.”

Charlie didn’t answer. Philip might’ve, that stupid bastard, she thought. But Mark? Mark was supposed to keep Philip safe. What the hell was going through his head?

“Miss Callin. I’m going to ask you one more question. I apologize for being so insistent, but this facility that the Insurgency raided is of… considerable importance to the Foundation. I need your absolute word that what you say to me is true and accurate, so I can exonerate you of any involvement. Understood?”

She nodded, staring blankly ahead.

“When I say the words ‘Site 19,’” Dr. Olson said very, very slowly, “does that mean anything to you?”

Charlie met his gaze. “No.”

“Nothing at all?”

“No, doctor.”

Dr. Olson nodded, and finally closed his clipboard. “Good. Very well. If you need anything from us, Mr. Grames will be happy to assist you.”

He started to get up.

“Doctor,” Charlie said, watching him. “Mark and Philip. Where are they now? Are they alive?” She paused, then added, “I know you… you can’t really say much. But — please.”

Dr. Olson paused for a little while. “We lost track of them during the assault. Neither of their bodies were recovered, so they may still be…”

A breath of relief escaped her. “They’re alive?”

The doctor pursed his lips. “Certainly, certainly. I see no reason… why they wouldn’t be.” He smiled at her. “Have a nice day, Miss Callin.”

The door closed.

So Mark and Philip had come after her. Despite everything, the thought did warm her up a little bit. She just had to find them, get them out of the Insurgency. They had no idea what they had just joined.

Harper was somewhere out there, too. She’d been close, right before the Foundation had picked her up. Charlie had to stay close to them. If she had any chance of finding her way into this world, it was here, and it was now.

She played the interrogation over in her head. What she did know about the Foundation is that their secrets tended to all fit into each other, locking together like puzzle pieces. And the more of the picture she had, the easier it would be to find her way around.

Harper, Mark and Philip, the Insurgency, the Foundation, and little old Charlie Callin. All related to one raid.

Maybe that was the place to start. She could figure out where to go from there later. Right now she just needed a general direction, a goal, something concrete. A mystery.

So then, she thought to herself, tapping the table. What’s Site-19?

Absent-mindedly, she grabbed her cup and took a sip.

She rubbed her forehead for a moment. The room felt more sterile by the minute, the cold white light above her needling into her skin, the metal chair stabbing at her shoulder blades. Leaning back, she sighed, and she still wanted to prod at the Foundation, but honestly, right now? Right now she actually just wanted to go home. She didn’t even —

That’s when she suddenly looked up, and blinked.

She shielded her eyes from the blinding white light on the ceiling, and glanced around, frantic. Nothing in the room had changed, but she examined it anyway. She twisted in her chair and looked under the table, she shifted uncomfortably in her seat, she peered down at the contents of her cup. A clock ticked. She stared at it. She narrowed her eyes at the suspiciously troubled mirror, embedded into the back wall of the room.

From the other side of it, Olson clicked his tongue and pressed a button. “Good?”

Another voice popped in, muffled by static. “Good.”

Something in his stomach tugged at him a little, but Olson rolled his shoulders, picked up his clipboard, and walked back into the room.

The girl at the table jumped slightly at seeing him enter. He smiled at her.

“Miss Callin, right?”

She nodded slowly.

“I’m Doctor Olson, of the SCP Foundation. Have you ever heard of us?”

She shook her head.

“I see.” He took a quick note, then looked back up at her, his gaze warm. “You’ve been through a traumatic event, Charlie. We’re here to help.”



Walk Ten Paces and Die

Point Two

BROKEN CROWN

PROLOGUE

Maddening, that’s what it was.

He simply couldn’t keep them under his gaze. His hands turned the knobs on the microscope as diligently and carefully as he’d been trained, but as soon as he had them under his eyes… they vanished again.

“I swear,” he muttered. “It’s not possible.”

From the other end of the room, David looked up. He narrowed his eyes, hidden behind thick safety glasses. “Careful with that, Will.”

“Yeah, thanks.” Will tore his eyes free and turned to his notepad, scribbling something down — Definite change. “How thorough does this have to be?”

David shrugged. “As usual.”

“I don’t exactly have the resources to get it done as usual.” Will looked through the microscope again. “Jesus. It’s impossible.”

“You keep saying that. Just write down impossible.”

“You serious? They’d tar and feather me, for God’s sake.” He sighed. “That word’s worse than taboo here.”

He adjusted the left hand knob and the lens slid to the right; he adjusted the right one and it slid downwards. With a curse whispered under his breath, he adjusted both at the same time, and it zoomed out.

“I’m starting over,” he said.

David didn’t even look up, this time. “Your funeral.”

He continued to adjust the knobs as needed. It was interesting — what made the cells so difficult to work with also made them… oddly hypnotic to look at. They were moving, he knew. But from afar… it looked like they were one solid whole — pulsating. Beating. Breathing.

From the corner of his eye, he noticed a red light turn on. It started blinking.

“David.”

“Mhm?”

“Management’s calling.” Will gestured hap-hazardly towards the light without looking up.

David groaned and stood, walking across the room. Will continued his work.

Yes, it was consuming to watch. But… the more he zoomed, the less magical it seemed. The cells were just excited, that was all. They were moving and jumping around. But nothing mystical was happening here. Biology was working as intended; it just wasn’t a biology he was entirely familiar with. Yet.

“Will.”

One moved slower than the rest. Forgetting to breathe, he worked his microscope like a surgeon would a scalpel and followed it on its path. It was… growing. The cell was growing.

Now that was strange. How was matter… just… appearing?

“Will,” David said again. His voice had gotten very quiet.

“Mm?”

“It’s not management.”

“Whoever it is, handle it for a second,” Will muttered under his breath. “I think I might have…”

The cell was gone.

Will raised an eyebrow. Had he missed it? He hadn’t looked away, not for a moment.

“Seriously,” David said.

The knobs flew and spun under his fingers. He scoured the area, his gaze flying across the pane, but… it was just gone. “Will, something’s wrong.”

“For God’s sake, Dave,” Will said, spinning around. “I might actually have found…”

His breath caught in his throat.

“See?” David said.

Will’s hands abandoned the microscope. He joined his colleague at the terminal where he stood, hands hanging loosely at his side.

“What’s happening?”

“I don’t know,” David said. “But look at that. Nine-point-three. That’s… that’s got to be wrong, right?”

Will’s eyes settled on the Kant counter. It was funny — on a table with such advanced technology, with sensors and buttons and knobs most people could only gawk at, that counter was oddly mundane. A little dial whose needle barely ever moved, and just sat there, staring. Although now… now, it had moved.

“The anchor gives false readings, sometimes,” Will said. Does it? “I’ll run a diagnostic.”

“Okay.”

“Meanwhile, tell Alan. Have him go grab Lammiel, if he’s still awake.”

“Sure.” David turned to leave, then hesitated. “You sure you don’t want to re-run it? Make sure it’s not actually… telling the truth?”

“And displaying nine-point-three Humes? Below half-norm? Come on. Let’s not waste our time.”

“I don’t know,” David said. He turned to leave. “I’d do it. It’s on your head, if you don’t.”

The door to the lab closed softly behind him.

Damn the man. He was right. Not that a re-run of the counter was needed — but, if it was, and he was the man who hadn’t done it, then… It was better if he did, just in case. His fingers flew over the control terminal. He’d done this a hundred times. Sort of.

His stomach grumbled a little. Was he hungry? He’d just eaten.

After a little while, he stood back, his fingers leaving the keyboard. A little screen staring at him from the corner of the terminal finally showed the words:

| INIT- diag_irrC0. INIT- run_irrC0.

Messages flew up on the screen, too fast for him to read. From behind his glasses, his eyes widened. His mouth fell open, and his veins turned to ice.

Well, he was right. It wasn’t displaying a nine-point-three anymore.

The door opened behind him.

“Alan says Lammiel transferred to 02 last night,” David said. “Did you know that? Figures. I had him fetch the others, though. He…” David reached his side. “What is it?”

“Dial’s broken,” Will said.

“You ran the diagnostic?” David squinted at the computer screen. “It doesn’t say it’s done yet.”

“Negative zero-point-two,” Will said.

David paused. “There aren’t any negative numbers on the dial.”

“It’s broken,” Will mumbled. “Tell Management. Tell god. What’s ?”

Potato Leek Soup

Ingredients:

  • 2 Large Leeks
  • 2 Cloves of Garlic
  • 6 Large Potatos
  • 2 Tbsp Salted Butter
  • 2 Teaspoons of Salt
  • 1 Teaspoon of Black Pepper
  • 1 Cup of Cream
  • 6 Cups of Chicken Broth/Stock
  • 1 Sprig of Thyme
  • 2 Bay Leaves
  • 1 Teaspoon of Garlic Powder

Preparation:

Cut your leeks at the root end and halfway up the greens and chop each leek in half. Thoroughly wash between each and every layer of the leeks, as they will have plenty of dirt trapped within. Chop your leeks. Peel both cloves of garlic and crush.

Peel, then dice your potatos and let them sit in a bowl of water for at least 15 minutes.

Cooking

In a Dutch oven, throw in your butter and let melt at high heat. Then, add crushed cloves of garlic and your chopped leeks and let simmer for approximately 3 minutes at medium heat. Add in your potatoes and let simmer for a further minute. Then add in your salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Add in all of your chicken broth/stock. Increase the temp to bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to a simmer and add your thyme and bay leaves. Let simmer for 15 minutes.

After 15 minutes, try to pierce the potatos with a fork. If you can pierce them with no resistance, turn off the heat. Fish out the bay leaves, and mash the soup. After fully mashed, add the whole cup of cream to the soup and mix.

Enjoy!

- Clarke Family Recipe

Potato Leek Soup

Ingredients:

  • 2 Large Leeks
  • 2 Cloves of Garlic
  • 6 Large Potatos
  • 2 Tbsp Salted Butter
  • 2 Teaspoons of Salt
  • 1 Teaspoon of Black Pepper
  • 1 Cup of Cream
  • 6 Cups of Chicken Broth/Stock
  • 1 Sprig of Thyme
  • 2 Bay Leaves
  • 1 Teaspoon of Garlic Powder

Preparation:

Cut your leeks at the root end and halfway up the greens and chop each leek in half. Thoroughly wash between each and every layer of the leeks, as they will have plenty of dirt trapped within. Chop your leeks. Peel both cloves of garlic and crush.

Peel, then dice your potatos and let them sit in a bowl of water for at least 15 minutes.

Cooking

In a Dutch oven, throw in your butter and let melt at high heat. Then, add crushed cloves of garlic and your chopped leeks and let simmer for approximately 3 minutes at medium heat. Add in your potatos and let simmer for a further minute. Then add in your salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Add in all of your chicken broth/stock. Increase the temp to bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to a simmer and add your thyme and bay leaves. Let simmer for 15 minutes.

After 15 minutes, try to pierce the potatoes with a fork. If you can pierce them with no resistance, turn off the heat. Fish out the bay leaves, and mash the soup. After fully mashed, add the whole cup of cream to the soup and mix.

Enjoy!

- Clarke Family Recipe

Ingredients:

  • MSG

  • Salt
  • Brown Sugar

  • 1 Sprig of Rosemary

Tools:

  • Dutch Oven/Soup Pot
  • Spatula
  • Ladle
  • Cutting Board
  • Knife
  • Mixing Bowl
  • Immersion Blender

Preparation:

Place your cold pot on your stovetop. Do not turn on the heat.

Take the salami and cut into chunks. Peel and dice all six of your garlic cloves. Make sure that you have at least six cups of chicken broth/stock available, although have more ready if you can.

Slice off the root of your leeks. Then, cut your leeks once length-wise down the middle. Chop all of your leeks from the whites up until the greek stalks become dry. Place all of the chopped leeks in the mixing bowl, and bring them to the sink. Begin to fill the bowl with water as you use your hands to massage the chopped leeks, doing so to remove all of the dirt and sediment. Fill up to the top of the bowl with water. The leeks should float at the top of your bowl.

(Optionally peel your potatoes). Wash off your potatoes thoroughly to remove dirt and excess starch. Chop into small chunks.

Cooking:

In your cold pot, place all of your diced salami. Make sure that there is no water or oil in the pot. Turn the temperature up to medium-high (As the temperature of the pot increases, fat will render out of the salami. This should produce enough fat to dually cook the salami and all other ingredients you need to fry before putting in stock. Any other fatty meat would work as a substitute.). Let simmer for 2 - 5 minutes, until a thin layer of fat covers the pot. Begin stirring salami after one minute.

After roughly a minute, add in your garlic. Let simmer for a further minute before removing the leeks from your bowl and place them into the pot (As said before, all of the leeks should float. Try to minimize the amount of water going into the pot. While some water is inevitable, putting in too much water with the leek will prevent the leeks from frying.).

DO NOT pour remaining water in the bowl down your sink. There should be visible amounts of sand and debris that sink down to the bottom of your bowl, which may be harmful for your drainage. The water is great to use for watering your plants. If not, simply pour the water outside.

Stir frequently and let simmer for around three more minutes. After the time has passed, add in your potatoes. Stir roughly twice a minute for three minutes. (Cooking the potatoes and leeks ahead of boiling them helps the entire dish cook faster, as well as giving them browning and flavor.)

When the potatoes are done simmering, add in enough chicken broth/stock. If you like thicker soups, make sure to add enough stock to just barely cover the other ingredients. If you like lighter soups, add in enough stock to cover the ingredients by one or two inches.

With the stock in, turn the temperature up to high. While the soup begins to boil, add in both bay leaves and a tablespoon of brown sugar (Brown sugar makes every recipe taste better). Frequently stir and scrape the bottom of the pot to avoid burning.

Once the soup has reached a boil, reduce the heat to low/medium-low and stir until the soup is reduced to a simmer. Let simmer for 15 - 30 minutes. Check your potatoes every 2 - 3 minutes starting at around ten minutes. Once your potatoes are easily piercable with a fork, they are ready.

Add in your seasonings. You can choose different seasonings depending on your personal taste preferences. If you choose to add both salt and celery salt, make sure to minimize the amount of standard salt you apply accordingly to how much celery salt you put in (I personally only put half as much salt in as I do celery salt).

Use your spatula to fish out both bay leaves. Add in your cup of cream. Add more or less cream depending on your desired coloration. No matter how much you add, let your cream simmer for a few minutes until it separates and a thin layer forms on the soup. This should also be accompanied by the soup thickening.

Turn off your heat and take out your immersion blender. Puree the soup to your desired consistency.

After you are done pureeing, add in your rosemary.

Serve the soup in a bowl with a side of sourdough bread. Rip off chunks of the sourdough and dip in the soup to eat.

Enjoy!

- Andie Clarke

Grabbing two towels, he picked up the Dutch oven and moved it to the dining room. His mother hurried around, grabbing a heat-safe placemat to set the Dutch oven on. Watch a movie? Play a board game? Something. Anything, really." "Maybe." "Heh. That's not a no!" "Yeah..." Their spoon is dipped into the soup. Andy eased the spoon into their mouth to taste it. //Hot. It is too hot.// "This is really good." He stated. "Thank you." "Same recipe as always?" "Oh, you caught me!" She laughed. ... "Do you ever talk to your Aunt Shelly?" "Sometimes." "How is she going along?" "Alright." "When was the last time you two talked?" "A week ago." "Ah." A torn chunk of sourdough bread was dipped into the soup. He blew on it in a feeble attempt to cool it down before eating it. "What about you?" "Hm?" "When was the last time you and her-" "Oh. A few weeks ago. Or a few months ago. You know?" "Yeah." Minutes passed until the soup was gone. //Tasty, as it had always been.// He used the remaining sourdough to soak up all of the remaining soup in his bowl. "I can take that if you're done with it." She said, outstretching her hand. "It's alright." "You sure?" "I can get it." "Okay, then." Plates and bowls clanked against each other as they were moved to the kitchen. When he was done, he emptied the Dutch oven into boxes of Tupperware and then into the fridge. The sink water rushed out of the faucet. He grabbed a sponge to vigorously scrub at the Dutch oven until every single speck of dirtiness was cleansed. Looking over at his mother, he saw her scrape chunks of food off of the plates into the trash can before they got crammed into the dishwasher. ... //Tap. Tap. Tap.// Footsteps rung as Andy Clarke ascended the staircase. He rested upon his bed as he finally entered his room. Andy allowed the warmth and heat of his body to be drained by the cool, soft bedsheets he rested on. And yet, a light shone directly on his eyes. A turn later, Andy glanced at his curtain. //A curtain that had never quite actually fully closed.// Several groans later, Andy rolled over on his side away from the light. He closed his eyes and tried to sleep. After twenty-three minutes, Andy's eyes opened. An urge overwhelmed him which drove him to grab his phone. [[div class="blockquote"]] [[=]] ---- +++ Boarding Pass ---- [[/=]] ||~ Flight ||~ Date ||~ Origin ||~ Destination ||~ Seat|| || 823 || 12/AUG/2023 || Pittsburgh, PA || Denver, CO || 17B || **Departure:** 05:30 **Passenger Name:** Andy Clarke [[/div]] Three hours. [[div class="blockquote"]] [[=]] ++++ Mom +++++ Phone Call Record ---- [[/=]] **Susan:** Andy? **Andy:** Hey Mom. **Susan:** Hi! **Andy:** How are you holding up? **Susan:** Oh, you know. Just awful! **Andy:** Uh huh? **Susan:** I know it's only been a week, but it has felt like forever. It truly turned out as a horrid meal. Not when his mother made it, of course. But this was his first-ever attempt at even trying to cook. Ignore the noodles he boiled or the eggs he fried, this was a full-blown meal. His family's prized meal. A mean which he completely messed up. The pantry revealed next-to-nothing aside from salt, pepper, butter, and garlic powder. Luckily, the grocery store was around a five-minute walk away. Inside, he grabbed as much as he could remember as he hadn't bothered to write anything down. //A cheap can of dried thyme,// //A single, four-cup carton of chicken stock,// //The first six potatoes he saw,// //And a single head of garlic.// His biggest pain was that he did not have or buy a vegetable peeler. Resorting to using a flimsy knife to cut off any skin or eyes, he chopped off at least a tenth of his total worth of potatoes. The potatoes were unwashed. Before, during, and after they were prepared. Dirt which clung to the potato's skin clung to the knife, which rubbed off on the clean interiors of the potatoes as they were cut. All with the flawed reasoning that he had convinced himself of being that the potatoes would be cleaned off in the bowl of water. While a rough chop was called for the leeks, they were given an impatient hacking-at by Andy. No care was given to ensure that the leeks were clean. Large chunks of soil and earth remained attached to the leeks as they were finished being prepared. At the very least, Andy didn't waste anything. He used //all// of the leeks. The roots, dried inedible leaves, and all. A realization dawned upon him at the last moment; he had no garlic crusher. Instead, he elected to use a mug to smash the garlic that was by some miracle peeled by him. Without a Dutch oven he was left no choice other than to use a simple, standard pot. The temperature was far, //far// too high. Garlic and leeks burned the second they touched the pot. Even as he smelled smoke, he let the aromatics burn for the whole three-minutes as the recipe described before he added potatoes. Thankfully, the potatoes still had some water with them and didn't burn. Whatever little chicken stock he bought was not enough. It failed to cover all of the potatoes without even being simmered down yet. A second forgotten memory came back. He had not purchased bay leaves at the store. Pushed to the back of his mind, he added in all of the spices. For all three seasonings he used, they all were produced at such a fast speed that he had to have poured in at least twice of the seasonings that the recipe called for. Unstirred, the boiling potatoes overflowed twice after he tried to cover them. The one thing Andy had remembered to purchase was a masher. He exerted nearly his full body weight on the masher to, unsuccessfully, grind the potatoes and leeks into chunks. After the fifteen minutes had passed, Andy turned off the heat and took the soup off of the burner. It was hot. It was salty. It was peppery. It tasted charred. At times it felt like he was drinking sand. He would find long strands of poorly-chopped leeks that got stuck in his teeth. It was a struggle to choke down his pathetic excuse of a soup. While he did, he opened his phone. [[div class="blockquote"]] [[=]] +++ Lauren [[/=]] ---- [[>]] > Heyyy. I just got back. [[/>]] [[<]] > welcome back! [[/<]] [[>]] > I'm going to be working most of next week, but should be free for the weekend. [[/>]] [[<]] > nice. [[/<]] [[<]] > do you want to hang out at my apartment over the weekend? [[/<]] [[>]] > You have an apartment? [[/>]] [[<]] > yea [[/<]] [[>]] > That'd be cool. [[/>]] [[<]] > alright [[/<]] [[>]] > Maybe Saturday after I get off work? [[/>]] [[<]] > sure. I can pick you up if you'd like [[/<]] [[>]] > Alright. [[/>]] [[<]] > see you then [[/<]] [[/div]] Leftover portions of the soup were placed in containers and then into the fridge. Even if the food was awful, he wouldn't let it go to waste. Despite his hardest attempts, he couldn't fully clean up. A residue wound up being stuck to the bottom of the pot that would never quite come off. //Likely some mix of burnt butter, garlic, and leeks.// Looking into the shopping bag, Andy remembered an impulse buy they had made. //An ice cube.// Although not much, it would at the very least make the tap water he hated taste cold. [[div class="blockquote"]] [[=]] **Date Range:** ##transparent|..................................................## AUG/20 | AUG/26 [[/=]] ---- [[size 200%]] Potential Earnings [[/size]] + $457.65 [[size 125%]] //Before Taxes & Deductions// [[/size]] ---- [[size 200%]] Total Time Punched [[/size]] + 30:01 [[size 150%]] //__- View Time Punch Details -__// [[/size]] ~ 21/AUG/2023 - 04:07 Hours Worked ~ 22/AUG/2023 - 06:01 Hours Worked ~ 24/AUG/2023 - 06:15 Hours Worked ~ 25/AUG/2023 - 08:32 Hours Worked ~ 26/AUG/2023 - 05:36 Hours Worked [[size 150%]] //- Hide Time Punch Details -// [[/size]] ---- [[/div]] Andy grabbed a backpack and hastily shoved his nametag into it. He adorned a non-company sweater and left the breakroom. He walked to the parking lot. A car horn blared as it drove in front of him. "Andy!" "Hey." "You ready to leave?" "Yep. Andy throws their backpack into the backseat and sits in the passenger seat. "So how have you been?" "Good, good. How'd your summer go." "Oh, you know. Just spent it here-" The car drives out of the parking lot. "-and you're still down to head to my place, by the way?" "Yep." "Rad." "How's your sister holding up?" "Probably good. I don't really know." "Oh?" "We haven't really talked since the start of the summer." "//Oh.//" "Yeah... But what about you. How's your mom hanging in there?" "She's getting better. Quit smoking, drinking, and all that stuff. But at this point..." "The damage is already done?" "Yeah." "Jesus. Sorry for you. "Thanks, Lauren." "Ah shit." "What?" "I haven't told you yet." "Told me what?" "I don't really go by the name 'Lauren' anymore. I started going by 'Quint' over the summer." "Oh. Sorry." "You're good." "Where'd you get the name Quint, anyway." "I saw it in an old movie." ... "Was it Jaws?" "... Yeah." "Fair enough." ... "So... what prompted you - to start going by Quint." "Do you know what being non-binary is?" "Yeah." "So..." "I'm going to take a wild fucking guess and ask if you're non-binary." "Bingo. And you're chill with that?" "Of course." "Thank you." "No problem." Two car doors opened at once. Then, Andy and Quint walked into Quint's apartment.
