"I think you'll be happy with it," Heather said, winking.]] ===== [[include :scp-wiki:theme:blankstyle]] [[include :scp-wiki:theme:queerstyle]] [[>]] [[module rate]] [[/>]] [[=]] + Preordained Diagnosis [[/=]] ----- "So do you have everything you need? I'm not sure they've sent someone back through this before, so you may be stuck there until we can figure out how to pull you out." Hana Thompson usually enjoyed Adams' attempts at humor, though there was something unsettling about being teleported into the void to be lost forever. Her father's love of Star Trek had only reinforced that a transporter room should be sleek, flashy, with buttons and monitors everywhere. The Foundation, however, prided itself on practicality. Hana and Adams stood in a tiny, bland room with only a stiff chair to decorate the space. The room itself was hardly large enough for the two of them, what with Hana's duffel and backpack and Adams' imposing figure. "I should have everything, yeah. I don't plan on getting lost but-- you know my luck." Adams placed a hand on Hana's shoulder. "I've worked out everything with Garrison ahead of time, kid. Don't worry. Just focus on your work and try to have some fun this summer, yeah?" She removed her hand. "And don't forget to call! Kondraki will probably be bored to tears without you around to bother him." The pair shared a laugh, as Adams began to make her way out of the room. "Oh, I almost forgot. Catch." Hana dropped her duffel in an attempt to catch a small, baby blue gift box with her name on it. Inside was a thick silver cuff, slightly larger than her wrist, with instructions that simply read '//Put me on and sit down//'. Hana inspected it for a moment before sitting down, placing her bags on her lap, and put the band around her wrist. The metal felt cool against her skin as she waited, not knowing what should happen next. As she continued inspecting it, she felt a sharp pinch as the band grew tighter and tighter, shrinking to snugly conform to her skin. "//Fuck!//" She shook her wrist, attempting to loosen it, but found herself swallowed by a feeling of vertigo. Overwhelmed, she closed her eyes, and leaned forward, placing her face in her bag. //Do not throw up. Do not throw u--// "You alright in there, Hana?" Hana looked up, finding herself still within the room; despite that, she was greeted by Heather, laughing at her misfortune. "Wait," Hana said, "what's going on? How did I--" "Oh right, first time. Sorry. Welcome to SITE, you should be feeling better shortly." Hana nodded, grabbing onto the back of the chair for support, shakily standing upright; as she did, she noticed that the chair did not budge; it was bolted to the floor. "Heather, what the fuck did you do?" "//Me//?" Heather held up a hand, faux offended. "How could you accuse me of being responsib--" "Heather," Hana said, scowling as much as she could muster between the wooziness. "Okay, fine, fine. You are one of the first staff members to use a Spoke Room, so congratulations on that." "Thanks." Hana gagged. "I feel great." "Yeah, well," Heather said, laughing, "That's the price of conceptual transportation." "What?" "Come on, let's start walking and I can explain it as we go." Hana nodded, finally letting go of the chair. She wobbled, for a second, but stabilized, grabbing her duffel bag and slinging her backpack over her shoulder. "Lead the way, //Director//." Heather held the door open, as Hana walked into a lengthy corridor; it was simple, almost liminally so. On either side of the hall were doors, each the same dull grey shade, each with a label. Turning back, Hana read the sign on the door she had just left. //Site-19.// "Well this isn't creepy," Hana deadpanned, gesturing at the monotony. "I'm guessing you still have to finish decorating?" "Ha, funny." Heather began to walk down the hallway, to a large set of double doors at the end. "No, that's on purpose. High level, the room you entered at Site-19, and the room you just walked out of at SITE are the same room. Conceptually, they are the exact same thing -- to ensure that, they are all uniform, and built to exactly match blueprints. One loose bolt and--" "And what? It wouldn't work?" "No, more like 'potentially causing a cascading reality break'," Heather said, nonchalantly, as if she hadn't casually brushed over the potential dangers of what Hana assumed to be an idea Heather and Lillian had cooked up together. "Oh. Fun." Heather smiled, pretending to not hear the sarcasm in Hana's voice as they made their way down the hall. Heather paused at the double doors, turning around to look at Hana. With her letterman jacket and ratty bags, she looked like the epitome of moving into a college dorm. "Okay. Are you ready to enter SITE proper?" "Yeah, I guess. Actually, wait -- where are we? I know you said I 'teleported', but, where is SITE actually located? Are we at Site-43?" "Oh," Heather said, a wicked smile creeping in. "Great question, we're in the Noosphere." Hana stared blankly for a half-second, before her eyes widened. "I'm sorry, did you just say--" Heather spun, dramatically throwing the double doors open. "Welcome to The Hub!" ----- Heather was not used to being a Director, and she most definitely was not used to SITE -- for that matter, nobody was. Her and Lillian had only moved in a few weeks prior, and things had been eerily quiet. But now, bit by bit, she watched as SITE was coming alive. The double doors opened into a large, open rotunda -- the ceiling was far above, almost out of sight, while the plain concrete walls made it feel like a brutalist version of a skate park. In the center of The Hub was a single structure. A glass cylinder stood eight feet high, a metal frame holding it together. It was an elevator, but, there was no elevator shaft. Nor mechanisms. Nor anything, really. //I fucking love this place,// Heather thought, as she let Hana take it all in. When she and Lillian were planning SITE, they kept having new ideas -- it was almost like her site was a test case. Each part, unproven science. Each room, a new way of thinking. Every detail of SITE was impossible, and that was exactly what Heather wanted. "Heather, just how big is SITE?" Hana asked, looking up. "Well, there's five different floors, but also, only a single floor?" Hana stared at Heather with an exasperated look. "Fine, fine," Heather continued, "SITE is fucking big, conceptually. Physically? It's a single floor." "Right," Hana said, nodding. "Sure, fuck it. I'm going to have to be okay with a bunch of weird science, aren't I? "Yeah," Heather said, "A bit. The thing is that SITE is conceptual, and to be within SITE, we too are conceptual versions of ourselves -- ish. The bracelet helps with that, actually -- you'll have to keep that on the entire time you're here." Hana was rubbing her wrist. "Can it be any looser?" "Do you want to get failsafed back into reality, thrown into the physical version of SITE, unconscious and half-stable? If so, feel free to take it off." "Noted," Hana said, her face white as she slowly pulled her hand away from the bracelet, as if it would bite her at any second. Heather looked down at her own wrist, where she wore a matching bracelet. It was uncomfortable at first, but the feeling faded after a day or two. //The price of conceptual science,// she thought, as she gestured towards the elevator-like structure. "There are five floors to SITE," Heather continued, "Well, five floors, not counting The Hub. We have the CEA--" "The sea?" "C-E-A. Conceptual Exclusion Area, it's a part of SITE that is isolated from the rest of the Noosphere, useful for conceptual fuckery. One of my favorite floors--" "Really?" Hana said sarcastically. "How shocking! Heather Garrison, enjoying a floor dedicated to anomalous ideas, I would neve--" "Shut up," Heather said through a smile, gently pushing Hana. "Then there's Defenses and Diversions, Containment and Research, The Nest and The Burrow. Containment and Research is exactly what it sounds like, so that's easy. Think of The Nest like a central command center, and The Burrow is where we have all the dormitories, recreation rooms and general SITE utilities." Hana nodded. "What's Defenses and Diversions?" "DaD?" Heather replied, smiling. "You'll be assigned to there for the summer. That floor has all of the defenses SITE maintains against Noospheric influences, as well as the support systems that keep SITE conceptually intact. It also houses an armory, of sorts, and the main base of operations for our CTF." "CTF?" Hana asked, as the two reached the elevator. "Right! You don't even know what your assignment is in full, do you?" Hana shrugged. "Not a clue." "Well congratulations, Hana. You are the first member of SITE's CTF, the Conceptual Task Force. This summer, you are going to be running missions within conceptual space, testing both your tactical skills, as well as your ability to adapt to conceptual situations influenced by latent contextual memories." "And I have such a //great// track record with memories," Hana said, ignoring Heather's standard conceptual babbling. "Who do I report to?" "Well, for now, I'm the temporary CTF Captain until we can find a better fit; so you'll be reporting to me." "Is anybody else in the task force? Or will it just be me, running your errands?" "Missions, Hana. //Missions//!" Heather said, emphasizing her point for comedy. "You'll be working with a partner the entire tim--" "Ugh," Hana said, rolling her eyes. "Group projects. Who did you pair me with?" "I think you'll be happy with it," Heather said, winking. //Why tell her more? That would ruin the surprise.// Hana just looked back at Heather, a slight smile on her face. "I just... thank you again, Heather. For... this. For helping me come here, for--" "Hey," Heather interrupted. "You earned it. I just wanted to give you the chance to prove yourself to everybody else." Heather held her cuffed wrist out, and the glass doors slid open. The pair walked inside; it was equally minimalist on the inside, with a small panel of 5 buttons. From top to bottom, it read: The Nest, DaD, CEA, C&R and The Burrow. "Let's get you settled in, huh?" Heather pressed the button for The Burrow, and nothing happened. ----- Heather and Hana stood in the unchanged elevator -- a beat later, Hana noticed that their surroundings had changed completely. Where once was the concrete fishbowl, there was now a wide hallways, a warm taupe textured wallpaper covering the walls. It was immediately more welcoming than anything else so far, and Hana soon realized she had wandered out of the elevator, unintentionally. "Oh," Heather said in a teasing manner. "So //now// you know where to go. Feel free, Hana, lead the way!" "Funny," Hana said, "Sorry, I just got pulled into the space, I didn't even--" "Yeah, that's The Burrow," Heather said nodding. "Ontologically welcoming, meant to be a place to foster community and camaraderie between employees. We're still working on a few finishing touches, but this section is mostly finished." Heather walked out and joined Hana, standing beside her. She continued, "So, are you going to do it?" "Do what?" Hana asked, unable to mask the continued confusion she felt. //Heather is acting like this is normal, but... she knows that this isn't what other Sites are like, right?// "Lead the way to your dorm, Hana." "Right, because obviously I know exactly where--" "Actually," Heather corrected her, "you probably do." "Huh?" "Okay look. SITE isn't like other sites, because it is a concept. As we exist in SITE, we actively change the meaning of it, and it changes to conform to us. I wouldn't be surprised if there's a swimming pool kicking around down here somewhere, now that you're here." "So," Hana said, "you don't know all of the rooms in SITE?" "Nope!" Heather said, a little too eagerly. "Arachne keeps an ontological map up to date, and I'm pretty sure that's somewhere around here? But, to be honest, Hana, it's going to keep changing, and isn't that so cool?" "Heather, //I// need to be honest," Hana said, smiling and shaking her head. "This is fucking insane, you know that?" "Thank you!" Heather beamed back. "So, now that you understand SITE a bit better, do you think you can find your room?" Hana didn't fully understand it yet, but somehow, she had a hunch. ----- A hunch that was right. Hana had started walking with purpose immediately, having gone down a series of twisting hallways, passing recreation rooms, common areas, cafés and more -- each was empty, waiting for life to fill it; SITE was barely open, and Hana was one of the first residents. As she walked through the hallways, she trailed her hand against the wall. It felt warm to the touch, and almost seemed to vibrate or purr under her hand. Heather followed behind, nonchalant, humming a tune to herself as she let Hana take her time. At a split, Hana trusted the impulse, and turned right; just a few steps later, she stood in front of a door. It had no sign, no decoration, and no information; still, Hana knew that this was her room. "Here we are," Hana said. "At least, I think." "Your guess is better than mine," Heather said, sounding more and more the part of a Site Director. After a moment of hesitation, Hana grabbed the handle and pushed the door open. The dormitory within wasn't spacious, but it was bigger than her cell -- the lack of locks on the exterior of the door was a welcome addition Hana was quick to revel in. There was everything you could need to survive; a bed, desk, small kitchenette with a mini fridge, microwave and sink. There was an open door further in, leading to a small en-suite bathroom, complete with both a toilet //and// a shower. //Holy shit. This is mine?// "I know," Heather said, following her in. "It's a bit bare bones, SITE should have slightly shifted the room to fit your personality a bit more, I'm not sure--" "No," Hana said. "This is... This is perfect. Seriously. This is incredible!" Hana dropped her bags to the ground, practically skipping as she ran to the bed, throwing herself into it. It was plush, nothing like the antique she slept on at Site-19; the pillows were like clouds, and the blanket threatened to engulf her in comfort. Heather, watching from the doorway, laughed as she saw Hana's display of youth. "How about I give you a bit of time to settle in?" "Sure, okay," Hana said, still taking her space in. "I don't have that much to unpack, so I shouldn't be too long." Heather just waved her off. "No, no, it's fine. There's no rush. I'll let your CTF partner know that you've arrived, they got in a week ago themselves. They'll probably come by to say hey, and then I'll find you two for your first mission. Sound good to you?" "Sounds great!" Hana was bouncing now. "Who is my partner, by the way? You never mentioned." "Yeah, that's //absolutely// correct," Heather said with a signature smile. Hana's eye twitched. "You'll get along, I'm sure of it," Heather continued, her grin only slightly foreboding. "Anyways, I'll see you later, Han." Heather left, and Hana was finally alone. //In my own room. Without cameras. Without locks. I wonder what Meri would think of this...// Hana began to slowly settle in, dreaming of what the next few months might be like. ----- If anything, the room was //too// big. Truthfully, Hana was still getting used to what she jokingly referred to as her 'nomadic lifestyle'. Her parents had set down their roots by the time she was born, but they taught her to pack light for their vacations or day trips. Adams had repeated this advice to her in training; //An agent needs to travel light. They can't be weighed down in the field by excess gear.// It bled into her college life as well, and though the space she had at school //was// hers, she was either among friends or at class or running missions, never bringing more than a light backpack along with her. Hana, atop her bed, looked up at the ceiling, and wondered what it would be like to set down roots, what that would even look like in the context of her life. She was certain she would thrive if she just had enough time to stay in one place, if she was able to just, settle down with someone to rest. She closed her eyes, and began to dream what that would look like; maybe SITE would shift to make it a reality. //Knock. Knock knock. Knock.// Hana opened her eyes, pulled from her short-lived reverie, and sat up. //This must be my partner. I wonder who else Heather dragged into this insanity.// She stood up from her bed, and slowly stepped over to the door, relishing how each step was absent of the cold tile she had grown used to. When she finally made it to the handle, the //click// of the disengaging lock was a victory in itself, and she slowly opened the door to reveal-- "No way. Billie? What are you doing here?" The pale girl, Billie Forsythe, whom Hana had met months earlier and didn't believe she would ever see again, stood on the other side of the door. She nearly swam in her dark clothes and tall boots that almost brought the pair to the same height, and Hana could still hear the steady, yet chaotic rhythm of bass and guitar through the headphones that rest around her neck. Billie's expression was neutral, somewhat out of place for such a small reunion. "Hi, Hana. Good to see you too." Hana stepped to the side, motioning for Billie to enter. "Please, come in. Make yourself comfortable." Hana exclaimed, almost giddy at the words she thought she would never speak in a Foundation site. Billie entered, and Hana closed the door behind her before walking over to the mini fridge. Billie watched her with a quizzical look. "Did you want a water or anything? I think these fridges stock whatever you want, but I have no clue if I have to be the one to think about it or you." Billie kicked off her boots by the door, and planted herself at Hana's desk, slouching slightly. "Hana, what the fuck are you talking about?" "Oh, you know!" Hana said panicking to save face. "Like, how SITE is changing and all that? Heather said something like..." //That's not what normal people sound like, Hana,// she thought, sitting down onto her bed, fighting the urge to lay down and sink into it. //Maybe she didn't notice it?// She peeked over at Billie, who was now tilting her chair back, gently rocking and trying to keep it balanced. As Hana watched, she couldn't help but smile seeing a familiar face. //We didn't have a lot of time to ourselves before. Maybe we can get to know each other now. Take two.// "So how do you feel about SITE so far? I'm surprised you made it here with--" "Without my mom breathing down my neck? Yeah. I am too," Billie said forcing a snort out of her round nose, staring at Hana in deadpan. A tense silence hung over the pair. "Sorry, I didn't mean to..." Hana paused, struggling to finish her sentence. "No," Billie said, shaking her head. "I'm sorry, that was a cunty thing to say." Hana dropped her jaw in mock horror, covering her mouth while gasping. "That's quite a way to put it!" Billie started back, silently. A smile gently crept onto her face, as she relaxed her shoulders, slouching back down into her ocean of black, layered clothing. "Sorry, I... it's weird," Billie said, having leaned forward and paused her music. "I have lived in the shadow of my mother and a week ago was the first time I went to bed and woke up without a 'nurse' to check on me." Billie laughed awkwardly, seemingly trying to defuse things. She continued, "I just don't know how to be..." "Not a teenager?" Hana offered, giggling. "Yeah," Billie said enthusiastically, chair rocking forward and slamming into the floor. "For real, how the fuck are you supposed to do that?" "Don't look at me," Hana offered in return. "My last memory before the Foundation locked me up was prom night, so your guess is as good as mine." The two laughed lightly, each relaxing a bit more into their nests. Hana loosened the fist that she didn't know she had made, and Billie pulled her legs up and sat like a ball. "You got here a week ago?" Hana asked lazily. "How did that happen?" "So this one day, my mom came back to the dorm and told me that Lillian's new thing had dropped by--" "Heather, obviously," Hana added. "Oh, absolutely," Billie nodded. "I asked her what about, she didn't say. Next morning, she tells me to pack my bags and go find Heather. I guess... I don't know what Heather did, but I don't discount brainwashing." Billie smiled at her own joke, catching Hana off guard. //So she can smile. Good to know.// "What about you?" Billie said, picking at her nail polish. "How did she get you away from 19 for the summer?" "Well," Hana leaned back, looking at the ceiling in recollection, "Adams said we were going to spend this summer learning about how to survive in the wilderness, but then, a few days ago, she told me that a 'special assignment' came in for me." She motioned to the space around her. "And now I'm here." The two exchanged a look. "Heather?" "Who else?" The two girls burst into shared laughter that seemed to warm the room up directly. Billie arched her back, while running a hand through her buzzed fade, pushing her hair to the side. In the time it took for her to push the loose strands from left to right, her face had changed from glee, and returned to a neutral composition. "Looks like Heather saved you too, huh?" Billie said, as monotonous as before. "Yeah, from sunburn and mosquito bites maybe." Hana laughed, as Billie let out the smallest glimmer of a smile. "Does it... feel good, to get away from that? I mean, you spend a lot of time at college too, right?" Hana thought for a moment. "Adams can be a bit... overbearing sometimes. She cares a lot, but she tends to go from fun uncle to drill sergeant without warning." She took a sip of her water. "Even when you're at school you never really escape them, not like here anyways. Assuming Heather doesn't put eyes in the walls to watch our every move or something." "Can never escape them, huh?" "God no. How about you? How are you getting used to being here?" Billie paused for a moment, thinking of a response before shrugging. "To be honest, I've been bored as fuck for this past week. Heather and Lillian have been running through SITE, doing... whatever it is that they do, and otherwise it was just me. So, you know, about the same?" Hana laughed, sitting up and nodding, a mental mission lodged. "Maybe this will be a change of pace for both of us then," Hana said. "Plus... I've heard I'm pretty good company." Billie crossed her arms, looked away and looking like she was going to ignore Hana -- if not for the mumbled "maybe" Hana caught the tail end of. Before she could say anything, someone knocked on the door. "Hey, you two. Put your clothes back on and meet me out here, we've got work to do!" The girls looked at each other, and spoke in unison. "Heather." ----- Heather Garrison couldn't stop smirking as she looked at her reflection in the glass of the pseudoelevator at SITE. //They were both so upset with me, it was so easy too.// Heather laughed to herself, and leaned closer to the impromptu mirror. //Is this what being a Director is like? Getting to make jokes and just do whatever you want?// Heather hoped so, as she checked her eyeliner for touch-ups -- a voice chimed from behind. "For the record," Hana said quietly. "Our clothes were on. Who do you think we are, you and Lillian?" "Oh my god," Billie said in false horror, "Heather and Lillian are //dating//?" "Ha ha," Heather said, rolling her eyes. Satisfied with her makeup for now, she turned to the elevator buttons and pressed the one marked 'The Nest'. "Were we just... Sitting in an elevator," Billie began, "while you were checking your makeup?" "One of you could have pushed the buttons," Heather said, teasing. "Hold on." Heather watched out of the corner of her eye, as both Hana and Billie shuddered at the same time, still not used to all of SITE's many new and unproven technologies. That were perfectly safe. //Probably. Good enough, right?// The trick was to watch the corner of your eye; Heather didn't know why, but that kept her stable as the elevator moved through conceptual space. A half-second later, they were in The Nest. The elevator opened out into a massive round command center -- in the middle was a raised dais, surrounded by computer stations. In the center of the platform was a large table, seeming to glow, projections floating in the air. //Not projections,// Heather reminded herself, //those are floating concepts.// Hanging from the ceiling above the table were a number of large monitors; many were powered off, with a single few displaying data printouts; nothing looked off, so Heather paid them little mind. Arranged around the center stage were more stations, arranged in concentric circles, throughout the room. //Enough for twenty pairs,// Heather thought, nodding to herself. Yes, everything was in the correct place. //Perfect.// She gestured to the room with her arms, and in her best ringmistress' voice proclaimed, "welcome to The Nest, our central overwatch at SITE." "Is it... Is it not ready yet?" Hana asked, eyeing the powerless terminals, and empty space. "What? Why would you think that?" Heather turned on her heel, coat whipping around as she stared at Hana in confusion. "I don't know?" Hana said, raising her hands in protest. "I just figured, you know... like at 19, there would be..." "There would be what?" Heather said, cocking her hip. "People?" Billie asked, cutting through the back and forth. Hana nodded. The crab, for its part, seemed to bubble and froth in agreement. ----- After Billie and Hana had finally returned to their equilibrium, the trio returned to SITE -- the conceptual crab bubbled in excitement when it saw Hana, refusing to sit still as she removed the rubber bands. Heather, having been proven right, departed without another word; presumably to find Lillian, so that they could go harass Harry together. "So, what do you want to do now?" Billie asked Hana, hopefully. "I'm not sure what there is to do at SITE, but..." //Why is this so awkward?// Billie worried, biting her lip. She looked at Hana, who was kneeling beside the Crimson Pincer, trying to corral it back into it's containment chamber. She tried to look away, but -- in her uniform, with the way that Hana's hair fell, loosely hanging in her face as she talked quietly to the crab -- Billie couldn't stop staring. //She's... fuck, she's kind of really cute.// Billie could feel how flush her cheeks were getting, and tossed her hood up, to try and hide it. With the crab secured, Hana walked to Billie, nonchalantly. //Maybe she didn't notice me staring?// "Want to wander SITE and find like... a hangout room?" "Su-- Sure!" Billie stuttered, swallowing hard. Hana, the polite young woman she had been raised to be, held out her arm and proffered her elbow to Billie. "Shall we, then?" Hana said, a bright smile on her face. Billie never managed to say yes -- she simply grabbed on, and Hana began to lead the way. ----- The pair headed down to The Burrows, and began to walk in an arbitrary direction. Billie had, somehow, found her cool again, and had walked casually beside Hana, without any issues. At least, she hoped it had come across as casual. After a couple minutes of walking, instead of the standard doors that lined the halls of the Burrows, presumably leading to dormitories, utilities or storage rooms -- they had found a large archway, leading into a large communal space. The room was wide, and placed throughout were mid-century modern style couches, loungers and more -- the warm woods and bright colors contrasted with the dark walls and moody lighting offered by lamps, string lights and slightly glowing walk decorations. It was cozy, filled with a soft, ambient music that seemed to change as the pair walked in, as if tuning itself to their preferences. Nestled in a corner, set into the ground of the room, was a small conversation pit, filled with seats, pillows, blankets and more. Hana, having made a bee-line towards it as soon as they had entered, spun around in excitement, nearly bouncing. "Billie let's hang out over here!" she called from the corner. "I've always wanted to sit in a comfy hole!" Billie laughed, making her way across the room. "Sure, why not?" she said, walking down the few steps and into their own little space -- Hana, barely wasting any time, was right on her heels. She could feel Hana's breath on the back of her neck, lightly dancing through her buzzed fade, her skin prickling. Billie shivered uncontrollably, before sitting down. //It's fine, just be cool! You're hanging out, with a friend. Remember that? Hana is a friend. I just hope she didn't notice--// The look in Hana's eyes said that she had. "Are you cold?" she asked, looking for where she would sit down. "Yeah!" Billie said quickly, jumping at the excuse. "I just-- oh, yeah, you know, with my condition, I have some circulation things and--" "I get it," Hana said, sitting down directly beside Billie with a soft thump. Hana turned, facing Billie, while grabbing around for some blankets. "My mom is a nurse, and my grandma had arthritis, at least, I think? So helping out somebody cold is pretty routine for me." "That's cool," Billie said, only //slightly// panicking on the inside, seeing how close Hana chose to sit. "I'm just so used to being cold in my hands, that I don't really--" "No, no," Hana said, waving off Billie's protestations. "Please. Let me take care of you." //Oh god,// Billie thought, blood rushing to her face. "Su-- sure. Only if you really want to." "You made sure I was safe earlier," Hana said softly. "You... you talked me through something terrifying. You were calming, caring, comforting, and I just... I want to do the same back. Is that... is that okay?" Hana looked at Billie, worry written on her face. Billie melted. "Yeah, okay," Billie managed to say, nodding. Hana began to reach around, looking for something -- a second later, she pulled up a large blanket, fuzzy and big enough to cover three people. Hana threw the blanket over both of them, shuffling along the pit's couch to be nestled up closer beside Billie. //How did I get here?// Billie screamed internally. //Oh my god, she knows. I'm so obvious, I'm--// "Is the blanket alright?" Hana asked, having shifted and preened it to perfection. "I run warm, so I figured you could share my body heat." Hana smiled softly, and if there had been any doubt left in Billie's mind before, it was now absent; she was falling for her, bad. "So, uhh," Billie began, her brain racing to find a new topic as she found herself hyperaware of each part of her body that was touching Hana. "Did Heather really send us after the crab, for a bet?" "For a bet? Not exclusively," Hana said, lips pursed. "I think she was trying to help in her very... //Heather// way of helping." "She calls that helping?" "Well," Hana said, smirking. "Don't you feel better, somehow?" "...a bit," Billie admitted begrudgingly. "Yeah, exactly," Hana responded, stretching her arms and invading Billie's personal space. "With Heather, you never really know how something is going to end, or why it's happening. There's always a reason, she just... doesn't share it unless she needs to." "Well," Billie said, smirking. "At least the crab seems to like you now?" "It so does!" Hana said, laughing. "I was worried, you know? On account of--" "You killing it?" Billie replied, laughing. "I mean, yeah! Would you be happy to see me if I killed you?" //Maybe,// Billie thought, before trying to cover for herself. "I guess not?" she said. "Yeah, right? So I just don't get why it likes me so much?" Hana looked off into the rest of the room, and Billie watched as her thin, long eyelashes fluttered. Hana looked back, and the two locked eyes. "I'm nothing special, I'm... I'm just me." "I think you're pretty cool," Billie said, the words coming out of her mouth before she could stop them. "I mean like... you know, today, during the mission, you were really cool! You just went out there, without any idea of the danger or what to expect, and then you just... figured it out? I... I feel like I'm too scared to go places sometimes, you know?" Hana nodded. "I think it's just like," Billie continued, looking at the pillows resting in the center of the pit. "I've spent so long being told that I'm this porcelain doll, and how I'm fragile -- and yeah, I mean, I get it, my disease is serious." Billie looked up, and realized Hana was right there. Beside her. A foot, maybe less away, her hair falling softly to the side. "It's not contagious, or anything," Billie clarified, worried. "Oh, that's good," Hana said, "I was worried that we wouldn't be able to get this close." Billie swallowed hard, continuing. "I just wish that I could be out there, like you are! I know that I can't do the same things, but..." "Billie," Hana said, interrupting softly, her plump lips curling up into a soft smile. "This summer, do you think... do you think I can help you figure that out, a bit?" "Figure what out?" Billie said, her mouth hanging loosely apart. Hana seemed to be even closer now. "Will you let me help you be brave? Like... like you did for me, today?" Hana smelled like caramel syrup and irises. A loose strand of hair fell in front of Hana's face, as she tilted her head to one side. Without thinking, Billie reached out and brushed the hair behind Hana's ear, gently tracing from the top, down to the lobe. For a second, neither girl spoke. Billie's heart was racing. "Oh my god," Hana exclaimed softly, in mock offense. "Your hands are //literal// ice, how are you okay with this?" "I'm just--" Billie couldn't get any more words out; Hana had taken both of her hands into hers, pulling them under the blanket, and closer together. Their fingers gently interlaced, as the warm radiated from both girls. "There," Hana said quietly, leaning her head back against the couch as she warmed Billie's frozen fingers. "Isn't this nicer?" she asked, closing her eyes and sighing in comfort. "Yeah," Billie said quietly, mentally tracing the lines of Hana's face, taking in her quiet beauty. "Yeah, this is nicer." //It's going to be a long summer, isn't it?// Billie thought, in a mixture of hope, and anxiety. But for now, things were just beginning. ----- [[include :scp-wiki:component:earthworm | first=true | last=false | hub=yes | previous-url=https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/preordained-diagnosis| previous-title=Preordained Diagnosis | next-url=https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/stuck-song-syndrome| next-title=Stuck Song Syndrome | hub-url=https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/forgotten-memories-hub| hub-title=Comorbidities — A Forgotten Memories Series ]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box |author=Queerious & AstersQuill]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box-end]]

For too long you tried to convince yourself you could be hers.

In those brief weeks after the duke, the fire, the dark:

Crawling out of the molt of your old life, into a world bursting with every half-deliberated impossibility ever dreamed by man. Still the same car, same girl, going to the same college but now each star and branch thrumming with possibility. The voice in your head described a world incomprehensible: aliens, demons, ghosts, gods. Men in black, rebels, terrorists, cultists. Every unseen thing real at last. So surely now out there someone like you, but moving with infectious purpose?

The genie told you the true shape of the world. It was self-contradictory nonsense, and it fell to you to glean the meaning from it. Only real advice she had, picked up from old runaway’s chatter, slow-spreading rumour:

Find the Hand. I know where they are. They hide themselves from the cruel, but to us they will be welcoming. They will teach you everything I cannot.

The first time you truly saw her soon after. Seeking out your rebels in the city. She crawled like smoke out of the icy chain about your neck that was her vessel. Still bound there, still obedient, if only you cared to give orders.

Zainab: the fragrant bloom. The idea of incandescence, deep gold and amber, drawn out and annealed. Given the solidity of steel but still somehow the certainty: here is a thing belonging one instant to the heart of some faraway star.

And she directed you. In interrogation, tracking, digging up rats. She found her Hand.

Let her be the thing they feared: fire that consumed, and you the calm beyond the light. Let your arm be her arm, and as she led the conversation feel yourself act on instinct. And the lure: that you could not be true to yourself, but you could be true to her. Be steered as a ship is steered, and what does cedar care if the captain changes her mind?

Recall this: that your own loves led you nowhere, along Escherian paths. So why not be her instrument, and be content to be wielded. Resolve this in the quiet alone, though you suspect she might guess at what changes in you that day.

Done with being the girl who ran from her own success. Now, you thought, you would be someone else’s trophy.

That faraway room would be empty forever.

You remember being Adelaide Pages, normal girl, overachiever, nothing wrong to look at her. Clever, smirk when someone talks to you, diligent and quiet, but surprisingly fun when you get to know her. All those attempts at flattery over the years. As if any of them knew you.

Feel what it was like being her, and become a girl who can live with other people again.

And at Zainab’s encouragement slot in soundlessly to a life at the university. Exactingly formed smiles, only a hint of teeth. The immensity of the place diluting your image such that you were just another woman. Except, unfortunately, that’s not the case at all. Because you: are famous. Prodigies are not exactly obscure; people have heard of you. In their minds images of you carefully chiselled. Idols to some other goddess, in your name.

Nonetheless, you faithfully amalgamated with the greater student body. Literally: tempered yourself mind and soul until you became a placid lake. Indistinguishable in any way. Whoever you used to be lost like a skiff in still water. All who spoke to you saw a kindred soul. Best of all if you were never remembered at all.

Which is not to say you do not effortlessly dominate whatever paltry challenges are thrown at you. There is such a thing as dignity.

Embedded in a peacock-fan of a social circle. Everyone clamouring to know the famous Ms. Pages, then cringing away from the carefully-crafted banality you showed them. Zainab teasingly insisting that you try better to live in the same world as your peers. Bite back whatever expression of disdain comes instinctually. With her encouragement insinuate yourself among actual human beings, speak and laugh and smile so charmingly they are smitten on the spot, and bask in her approval afterward.

Back home you find that your sisters have something to say. Words from a phantom town. Fiona picking up ballet. Hopefully not overshadowed by you to the point of resentment. It would be intolerable to spend nine years rearing her for your absence to unmake her perfect outlook. But looking lovelier already. The distance will be for the better.

And with unspoken nudges from your companion you shrug and read the other messages. Hannah putting her life together apparently. Waiting tables, tolerable wage. Still in that house. All the stars in the sky are called, inexorably, to a great attractor. Your sisters still bound to those four walls.

One nameless night: hacking down with your pals whisky and hideous flavoured vodkas Zainab snatched off unwary passersby. Brief impressions of juddering bass in your sinew and fitfully intermittent lighting.

Followed around half the time by tall Michael, name a hasty anglicisation of something else entirely, Chinese sophomore not as funny as he thinks, but pretty smart in a dress shirt so why not let him lean into you, breath soft and stinking of star-anise, embrace you? Not even sure where your hands should go, his mouth sweet and bitter and sickly, awful first kiss.

(Which you know makes no sense at all because obviously back in nowheretown you should have had the pick of the lot. Not exactly an inspiring cohort but certainly men to outmatch slumping Mr. Li here and surely you would have had your fun with some gentleman, nice photos at a prom in a swanning dress etcetera. Why didn’t that happen?)

And his hand pressing hard into your ass but he’s the wrong height, shape, smell. Fragrant with what might as well be sulphur.

Why can’t you just want what you want —

And you bite down hard and he jerks back pinwheeling to the floor. Taste of blood piquant on your own maimed tongue. Running over and out your lips and down your throat; inverse jugular. His own shirt looking like a murder scene. Floor spotted with sanguine down. About two dozen people see the whole thing. Presumably from here an appropriate distribution of gasps of horror, accusations, whole cycle of young adult social life accelerated into about five minutes.

You decide now is a great moment to abscond. In your room burrow out of your outfit in the muggy air and for a moment sight outside the monistic starfield undimmed by uniform light.

Once your sister lifted you to the roof of the world and you saw every star. To pick apples from a struggling tree in the dying autumn. Young enough words didn’t come easily. Sink into sleep and God willing that memory gone by morning.

(In dreams, the Duke and his scissor-smile.)

Please don’t use this email chain to alleviate your boredom, Chris.
I am coming around to your view, however, so congratulations.

Sunlight screaming through your window, curtains hatefully dredged open by your spirit-attendant. Stood by the door, flesh that blazed. Brief shower to get the stink of actual blood off you, what stupidity. As you leave her smoky violinist’s fingers alighting briefly on your shoulder, arresting movement, whispering that: It gets better, Ada.

Whatever did she mean? Hallucinating some other girl she could not save. Your body a substrate for her imaginings.

But if she thought you other than you were, that was only your failing. A good tool conforms to the intent of the wielder.

So try to discern the shape of the thing she sees. And feel the weight that lingers on your shoulder. The hand rising to cup your face. Eyes almost tearful. She is — your guidestar cannot be pathetic. Smother the thought and leave.

Outdoors you refused your body’s sudden antipathy to sunlight and basked in the amused reproachments Zainab paid you for the hangover. Returning to an appointment to meet the Hand, met by a ratty kid shuffling around suspicious.

And in the back room of a dingy apartment he showed you a hole in the world. As if the entire rest of your life was a screen over some boudoir and now for the first time through it you glimpsed creation as it actually was. The heart is deceitful above all things, and you have known it.

(Here you will be redeemed at last.)

In the Library: perfectly ordinary shelves, stuffed with nonsense text, but quite beautiful. Giltwork of great colossi striding out of the sea, argent sea-mist rising about them in clouds. But no susurration of distant footfalls or studious petitioners whispering their lore just out of sight. Actual and resounding silence, deep as your tomb.

And then ambushed out of exactly nowhere by half a hundred skeletal scuttling things. Robbed from catacombs but so many of the skulls so small. Clutching in their hands an assortment of atrocity from across centuries fifteenth through twenty-third: mace, pike, musket, some kind of ridiculous laser rifle. And behind this horde a girl with a face desynchronised, half-etched in twitching segments of brass. Others: a lanky punk with lizard scales, some kind of monstrous demon-thing whose head was a mass of interlocking keratinous horns, guy simply made of glass.

The girl, hilariously: No fuckin’ words, get that bloody chain on the ground right now, nice and slow, or I blow your head off. Odd Cockney twang, only ever heard on TV.

If you died, it would be fast. But you couldn’t die to such morons. So, fine, lay down Zainab’s chain.

They draw in poured oil of all things a mandala around it and call her out again, muscled frame, shoulders like an ox, and their indignance she meets with anger. They thought you some kind of gloating slavedriver, and back off panicked when they see the truth.

When they hear what you did to that duke the scaled guy actually breaks down crying. Diplomatic mishaps easy to pile as snow apparently. But no, he throws himself into a fullforce hug speaking some alien tongue and the rest of them pull him off you sheepishly. He’s just been through some stuff. And incapable of handling it. Every organisation has it dregs.

Now finally, finally, time for explanations. Since Zainab’s time the world has grown stern and strange and new. She recounted halfremembered tales of the Jailors, who she promised would leave you curled in a concrete cask for all time. But these runaways and rebels painted a much clearer picture: Great world-spanning conspiracy. Empires built in the dark. Your whole life and everyone else’s collated by numberless eyes, ears, hands. Everything sieved and sifted, weevils plucked from grain, all breath given a rigid order. What were those wistful young mornings? They were only a dream.

Zainab’s Hand not a battalion of unsmiling legionnaires. Incoherent cells, guided only by vague principle. This one unmerry band scampered like rats beneath feet. Nipping briefly at the heels of their enemy and occasionally snatching glimpses of the larder. But vermin die when men wake from their stupor. So these few flee and fall and never look back.

But this apparition, this genie, gave them and you a new life. Where in you there was once fire now there must be stone. A cenotaph on which Zainab will carve your cause.

They were filled with grandiose dreams of raid and sabotage that she methodically dissected: even she feared those that moved unseen. Learn to love, she said, the good time of the smaller things. Live truly like mice, and in the cracks of the world find your joy. I will lead you in this, and give you slivers of your revenge.

And that was your life for nearly three years. Learning to forget you were ever that misericorde girl. Shaping yourself to love a cause, if it was commanded of you. Till in you it blossomed and some part of you even learned to motion that you could feel the injustice of the fetid order that choked you all. Cages and chains and charters perhaps had a certain frigid beauty, but to be under that shadow all your life, whip-hand over you: something in your blood refuted it. And constraining your thinking you chose to see in the Hand your only escape, and the constancy you so needed.

That necklace, Zainab’s chain, heavy with woven malice, would not break under any hammer you could find. And still in truth Zainab was yours by its enchantment, very nearly part of your flesh. But never did you exercise that will, and she trusted you not to. She had reached some understanding of who you were. Or at least who you had made yourself. Coyly purred, You are mine, and what you want is what I want, so what should I fear that your desire constrains mine? The words sat thick on her tongue.

Blacksuited men set to flight. Glittering mechanical beasts left for scrap by your ambushes. For this brief moment together you made your corner of the world free, as she desired of you. But it was not enough for her. Something else was gravid in her heart.

Alone with you she smiles sad smiles, sings sad songs, fount of remorse for God knows what. When you lie alone with coruscating strokes she brushes out your hair. Always the soft eyes, the little touches, the whispered promises, You are safe here.

What does she see in you, victim or damsel or pleading wretch? Dreaming of saving you from nothing at all. A sculpture of you in her mind, by now rococoed with false detail. How you wish to smash it.

Your sisters grew old with you. Visited home a few times. Returning find the place exorcised of all its significance. Was this really the thing you ran so far from: only a dusting of buildings planted haphazardly across the plain, with no smiling princes haunting it.

Fiona doing well enough for herself. Can’t be you of course but hasn’t got a complex about it. Teeth missing in her latest photo, unbearably cute. Her whole life will be a gilded cage. Better that she stay inside the bounds of the box they built around her. She is of the world as it is, not the world you strive to make.

And Hannah, God, Hannah. Still that smile, always. Asking after you every so often. Let her remember you fondly. Make your pleasantries at her, stilling your face. And when she says that at her job she found someone —

Good. Let it be done. Let her dedicate herself to someone else and vanish from your life at last. Happy in her own way, bailed out of a deadend job. By a guy in a pressed shirt, ironed pants, ridiculous half-rounded glasses that even now looking back across the years you stifle laughter at. Kind of chubby, ugly beard, lazy eyes listing toward something outside the photo. Of course she couldn’t do better. Who picks up the waitresses at coffee shops these days anyway?

Occurs to you that this sister too might live her life not knowing the true shape of her world. A butterfly who dreamed she was a girl. The thought clotting in your throat, your lungs, your heart. Sarin ideogram.

(Forget it.)

What else? When a tree rots, for a long time, the bark can remain unbroken, and foresters passing by will think it whole. But then some unfortunate brings it crashing down and with bitter imprecations declares it dead.

Thus recall a frosted morning, and therein: you and a surly demonette and a glass man, distorting the view beyond like a lens left in the furnace too long. The three of you at the peak of your ambition. It had been a good year, and the enemy was running scared (you forced yourself to think). So now you aimed for a higher target.

A Coalition facility hidden beyond the hills outside the city awaited your liberation. Together, fifteen of you positioned in a compass-rose around it prepared to strike your first real blow against the hated Bookburners, having wheedled Zainab into it. She begged them to relent, but their hearts were fixed on it.

Hardly needs to be clarified how it went.

Inside four sparse walls a tiny compound dug into the earth, and crawling out of it the moment one of yours first stepped over the threshold: a manylimbed titan of orichalcum and woven adamant. It bore in it the aurora, the secret light at the end of the world, for you. And you cannot recall what happened next, but a great weight passed over you, and a sensation that you were vivisected: all your steps upon the earth accounted for. And voiceless the words, priusquam te formarem in utero novi te, and when next you woke you were back at your camp and half the band were dead.

Dejection hung clear over them, and the seven that fell were arranged in a line for their funereal rites. Their faces were still, their skin unblemished, their tongues swollen till they burrowed out their throats like rats.

The ceremony did nothing to dispel the grief that flourished in the camp. And you knew, These are the first, and God, how many more? How many hours of these rituals, how many nonsense speeches to make, how many sobbing reprobates for you to console? A sculptress was limited by her materials. You could not crown yourself with this common clay.

At last the implacable sense: it was not enough, not Zainab’s perfect art, nor your small part in it as her instrument, her component, her lever toward some greater victory. Why?

One moment struck dumb by your own stupidity.

Because it was nonsense. Because it contradicted itself. Because you could not be her perfect tool and her perfect rebel. Even searching for consistency outside yourself led to that same incoherence. Nothing new under the sun. And these thoughts you had not had, had not let yourself have, because it would be contrary to the spirit of submission. How worthless was obedience!

But there was another Adelaide, somewhere, who would remake herself to fit that niche. If you could be Zainab’s Adelaide, truly become the girl she sought to save, then you would be done with this. Whatever came next. When came the high court with their magic army, you’d face the fire an unmarred whole.

So for the sake of symmetry you came back to her on another black night in spring, outside your room the orchids choked with weeds. Let yourself be one of the things made anew by the season. And let this shroud of self-deception fall away. At last clear what shape she expects you to take. The looks, the gentle hands, her voice in the dark. Call her up from her resting-place and fall weeping into her arms. She gives one last time her watery smile, you’re so brave, you’re going to be fine, it’s alright. Become her Adelaide.

Kiss her and she melts into you. How long did she wait for this? Trite bitch.

Just let it work. God, let it work.

Her fingers clammy like worms on your skin. Lips like brands burning where they lie. Pawing at you clumsy as any drunken boy off the street. This was what she held coiled for you beneath the pity? You would rather —

No. You realise the recollection is coloured by an intervening animosity. This was not what you felt then. The true hatred you feel is a gentle thing, advancing insensibly in silence until it surrounds your apathy.

So let yourself feel the thing that burned in your breast then and sank beneath your belly, which you called hate laughing.

Remember the sight of her above you, slightly waxen skin of something not wholly human. To whom every breath was a performance. Her hair like smoke shrouding you. Forget the world that is not her mouth, her fingers sweetly curled, her teeth at your throat and ears and breasts. And the thundering in your ears, her hands like God’s cleaving you, and in an instant all reason leaves you. Beneath her ecstatic in epiphany.

Coming down trembling to her leaning so close you can feel her breath across your face. Saccharine like honey, no mortal sourness to it, repulsive beyond belief. She drags your hands above your head, and you abhor that binding, wrong, wrong, awful, but still all things and let yourself be hers.

You will be the doll she thinks you, and be done. Your struggle like a caged bird in your heart, and you would make yourself see the beauty in it. The memory does bring some warmth to your blood.

Clasping your head in her hand, feel your skull thin under strength born of no woman. Legs make the twin points of a compass straddling your mouth. And she writhes above you. Undulating like a snake, hastily fashioned muscle spasming unearthly, you lapping at her cunt.

Those sharp soft breaths an affectation. Just for you.

What does she think of you: that you have taken what you want. So let her know it. You whimpering as she comes, or at least her body warping in its imitation. And that look down at you after you will never forget, breath frozen in your lungs at the warmth of it. Abominable.

And later you lie in her arms and she says what she thinks are soothing things to you. In your mind all passion is stifled. Whatever grail you searched for lost. All this theatre, and still not enough. The Adelaide that was hers is dead.

And finally the end of the road. Time to do the obvious thing.

Your travails with the Hand taught you things: marksmanship, espionage, first aid; tradecraft as known by scared teenagers. And it also taught you the true names of your enemies. GOC, UIU, Pentagram. Foundation.

It is not a hard thing to learn how to contact them. They put a lot of thought into making sure people are scared of them. When Zainab sees what you’re doing, she appears, more puzzled than angry. And you say:

“Take no volitional action.”

Her face twists into a withdrawn expression, and you think: it didn’t work. She has broken the binding, and I am dead after all. But she makes no other move and you realise this is an expression of instinctual and genuine terror. And that teases from your lips the first genuine smile in all the time you’ve known her. Let’s see who’s the doll now.

It takes some time laying down the commands you need, so she can move and act in your name, but not warn the Hand, or fight, or do anything. Except beg. The begging is comforting, somehow.

And you come to them in the early morning, when they are gathered in some warehouse, meeting for an all-hands. Ha.

Through one door burst the kevlared and rifled men of the Foundation. From inside gunfire and bisected prayer. Out the back come that same dead horde you remember, equal parts whole and half-sized. Behind them brass-face girl panicking. And a lash of flame engulfs them. The girl’s face runs down the side of her head. The skeletons blacken and shatter and fall hyaloid to the tarpit floor. Acrid fumes choke everything. For a moment you are alone, and the snow that was your comrades falls around you.

Above floats Zainab, her face still as marble, her soul smooth like glass, and simple like despair. What she learnt from her time with the Duke: she will not let you have her care. A spear’s rebellion.

Outside they have six of them in various stages of dying. Lined up and bagged kneeling on the pavement. If they knelt you beside them and shot you all it would not be an unfair punishment for your sin. But they promised otherwise. For you amnesty, and an interview. In return you gave them these: a cell of terrorists, and a stray genie who thought herself in control. A lesson she will take to heart a thousand years more.

The line dividing good and evil cuts through every human heart but yours. And the Foundation is the thing that swallows up all the evil. Where better can there be?

Let will alone be the reason

Every soul a wave

In those brief weeks after the duke, the fire, the dark: Crawling out of the molt of your old life, into a world bursting with every half-deliberated impossibility ever dreamed by man. Still the same car, same girl, going to the same college but now each star and branch thrumming with possibility. The voice in your head described a world incomprehensible: aliens, demons, ghosts, gods. Men in black, rebels, terrorists, cultists. Every unseen thing real at last. So surely now out there someone like you, but moving with infectious purpose? The genie told you the true shape of the world. It was self-contradictory nonsense, and it fell to you to glean the meaning from it. Only real advice she had, picked up from old runaway’s chatter, slow-spreading rumour: //Find the Hand. I know where they are. They hide themselves from the cruel, but to us they will be welcoming. They will teach you everything I cannot.// The first time you truly saw her soon after. Seeking out your rebels in the city. She crawled like smoke out of the icy chain about your neck that was her vessel. Still bound there, still obedient, if only you cared to give orders. Zainab: the fragrant bloom. The idea of incandescence, deep gold and amber, drawn out and annealed. Given the solidity of steel but still somehow the certainty: here is a thing belonging one instant to the heart of some faraway star. And she directed //you//. In interrogation, tracking, digging up rats. She found her Hand. Let her be the thing they feared: fire that consumed, and you the calm beyond the light. Let your arm be her arm, and as she led the conversation feel yourself act on instinct. And the lure: that you could not be true to yourself, but you could be true to //her//. Be steered as a ship is steered, and what does cedar care if the captain changes her mind? Recall this: that your own loves led you nowhere, along Escherian paths. So why not be her instrument, and be content to be wielded. Resolve this in the quiet alone, though you suspect she might guess at what changes in you that day. Done with being the girl who ran from her own success. Now, you thought, you would be someone else’s trophy. That faraway room would be empty forever. > **From:** DTesta@site15.scp.int | **To:** CBurroughs@site15.scp.int > **Subject:** re: New special acquisitions > > We aren’t totally clear about her relationship to the djinni. TboneBerryhill

The vending machine had eaten Dr. Vivienne Graham’s change for the third time that week, and she was ready to commit a Class-A breach just to get her bag of pretzels back.

She slapped the side of the machine. “You know, if this thing were anomalous, it’d at least be interesting about robbing me.”

Across the dimly lit break room, Dr. Lily Pearl looked up from her tablet. “You think a possessed vending machine would hand you snacks? Please. It’d probably launch them at your face and demand blood as payment.”

“That still sounds better than this.” Vivienne crouched to peer into the slot, where her snack had vanished into the void. “God, I hate night shifts.”

They’d both been at Site-16 long enough to know the rhythms, the hum of filtration systems, the muted clink of security boots in the halls, the faint antiseptic tang that clung to every surface. At 22:30 hours, the place felt like a tomb with fluorescent lighting.

Normally, the cafeteria would be open until midnight. Tonight, a maintenance notice had gone out: Closed for deep cleaning until further notice. Translation: no food until morning.

Lily leaned back in her chair and checked the time. “We could run to town. Gas station’s still open.”

Vivienne blinked at her. “You’re suggesting we leave Site-16 in the middle of the night for snacks?”

“I’m suggesting we not starve to death over a broken vending machine.” Lily closed her tablet and stood. “Come on. It’s ten minutes there and back.”

Vivienne hesitated. Technically, they weren’t supposed to leave without clearance. Technically, they should probably radio Security. But the prospect of another four hours with nothing to eat but breath mints was worse.

“Gas station,” said Vivienne, already grabbing her coat.

The fluorescent lights of the gas station buzzed like a dying insect, casting a sickly glow over the shelves of processed junk. The clerk a guy with a name tag that just said "Steve?"—barely looked up from his phone as the door chimed.

Lily nudged a bag of stale pretzels with her boot. "Cafeteria closes at nine. Nine. Who even does that?"

Vivienne tossed a candy bar into her basket. "The same people who think 'nutrition' is a four-letter word."

Lily snorted, grabbing a bag of gummy worms. "I swear, if I have to eat one more—"

The door chimed again.

Two figures stepped inside.

Lily didn’t pay them much attention at first—just a couple of late-night weirdos, same as them. But then the smell hit her.

Rot.

Not garbage rot. Not "left the takeout in the car too long" rot.

Meat rot.

She wrinkled her nose, shooting a glance at Vivienne, who had gone very still.

Vivienne mouthed a single word: "Sarkic."

Lily’s blood ran cold.

The first Sarkic was wrong in a way that made her eyes itch. His skin was too loose, sagging in places where muscle had been reshaped, his fingers elongated, tips fused into boneless tendrils. The second was worse—his jaw unhinged slightly when he breathed, revealing too many teeth.

Before they could react, the door jingled again.

Two more figures entered.

These ones moved with a mechanical precision, their steps too even, too measured. The first Mekhanite had a steel plate bolted across half his face, one eye replaced with a red-lit lens. The second’s left arm was entirely prosthetic, the fingers ending in delicate, buzzing tools.

A faint tick-tick-tick came from his chest.

Vivienne grabbed Lily’s arm. "Clockwork heart," she whispered. "High-ranking Mekhanite."

Lily swallowed hard.

Four cultists. One gas station.

And them—two unarmed researchers in the snack aisle, holding gummy worms like a shield.

They ducked lower behind the isle, peeking over the shelf.

The two pairs of men had noticed each other from across the store.

A silent, hateful stare-off.

Then—

The loose-skinned Sarkic spoke, his voice wet, like words pushed through meat.

"Iron filth."

The Mekhanite with the clockwork heart clicked his tongue, a sound like a wrench tightening.

"Flesh abominations."

Lily grabbed Vivienne’s sleeve. "We are leaving."

They inched toward the register.

CRASH.

The second Sarkic—the one with the unhinged jaw—lunged, his body stretching unnaturally as he slammed into the nearest Mekhanite. The impact sent them both crashing into a display of energy drinks, the Mekhanite’s metal arm screeching as it scraped against the floor.

The store erupted.

Lily and Vivienne hit the deck, crawling toward the exit.

Shelves toppled. Glass shattered. The clerk—Steve?—finally looked up, eyes wide.

"HEY! KNOCK IT OFF OR I’M CALLING THE—"

The Sarkic with the tendril-fingers whipped an arm out, wrapping it around the clerk’s throat. The Mekhanite with the faceplate slammed a fist into the clerks ribs knocking him against the wall.

Lily and Vivienne exchanged a look.

"New plan," Vivienne hissed. "Crawl faster."

They scrambled over fallen snacks, dodging flying fists and the occasional thrown energy drink. They were so close to the door—

Then two of the cultists crashed directly in front of it, blocking their escape.

Lily’s ID slipped from her pocket.

Shit.

The men stopped.

Looked down.

Looked up.

The cultists turned toward them, united in sudden, vicious interest.

"Oh," said one Sarkic, grinning. "Lab rats."

The other Mekhanite cracked his knuckles. "Out of their cage."

Lily forced a smile. "Hey, guys. Don’t mind us. Just gonna… mosey—"

"You burned our temple in Albuquerque," the Sarkic spat, flesh rippling with rage.

"You stole the Gear of Divinity," the Mekhanite snarled, his clockwork heart whirring faster.

Vivienne scoffed. "Oh, come on! You were mutating a whole town! And that thing was gonna fry the power grid!"

The cultists paused.

Then, in unison: "AND?"

Lily and Vivienne shared another look.

"Ugh," Lily muttered. "Fanatics."

What followed wasn’t a fight.

It was a catastrophe.

The Mekhanite with the prosthetic arm unfolded it into a spinning blade. The Sarkic’s jaw split open like a snake’s.

Lily kicked a rack of motor oil—bottles smashed, liquid slicked the floor. The Mekhanite’s metal feet screeched as he lost traction, crashing into his ally.

Vivienne yanked a fire extinguisher off the wall and blasted the Sarkic in the face. Flesh bubbled where the chemicals hit.

The remaining Sarkic howled and charged—only for the last Mekhanite to tackle him mid-lunge. They slammed into the freezer door, glass exploding outward.

"CAR. NOW," Vivienne gasped.

They bolted, shoving past the dazed clerk, sprinting for the parking lot.

Lily fumbled for her keys. "MOVE MOVE MOVE—"

The car unlocked. They dove in, slamming the doors just as the clockwork Mekhanite slammed into the hood, his red eye flaring.

Lily turned the key.

The engine roared.

She meant to reverse.

Instead—

CRUNCH.

The Mekhanite went flying, his metal limbs sparking as he tumbled across the asphalt.

The airbags deployed.

Lily shoved hers down, wheezing. "OH, FUCK YOU—"

Vivienne grabbed the wheel. "DRIVE, YOU IDIOT!"

They peeled out of the lot, nearly clipping the last Sarkic who flipped them off as they sped away, screaming something about "divine retribution" as they sped away.

Lily’s hands were locked on the wheel, her breath ragged.

"This," she hissed, "is why I applied for a gun."

Vivienne slumped in her seat, rubbing her temples. "Next time, we starve."

Behind them, the gas station’s lights flickered.

Steve the clerk sat up, rubbing his throat.

He sighed, picked up his phone, and went back to scrolling.

"Just another night."

They drove on. Site-16’s silhouette rose out of the dark ahead.

Neither of them said it aloud, but they were already in agreement: when the report went in, this night never happened.
