primer.raw_content:
Intercepted GOI communications: Item Number 12-181



Alpha-Commander Taylor,

I am pleased to present to you the updated intelligence assessments of our great enemy and their infrastructure, personnel, and military capabilities. This information was gathered and corroborated by our cells across the globe, along with embedded undercover agents when appropriate. You have my assurances that the enclosed packages are wholly true, and that careful reading will keep you and anyone you share this with fully informed of the great enemy’s strengths and weaknesses.

As you have requested, two separate documents are enclosed: a brief primer, which is written under the assumption that one is not familiar with the SCP Foundation, and a reference work, which contains a detailed list of all known Foundation sites, biographies of persons of interests, lists of MTF and Covert units, dispositions of their forces, and SCPs currently in their containment.

Should there be any questions or need for clarification, it would be my pleasure to answer them at the soonest possibility.

Our light burns ever brighter,
███ ██████1
Commander of Intelligence


A Brief Primer on the SCP Foundation

1. Their Political Structure
2. Their Physical Sites
3. Their Military Capabilities
4. Their Veil Maintenance
5. Their Fronts



1. Their Political Structure

A. The Division of Power

The SCP Foundation’s political structure has been described before as a ‘bastardized mix of corporate and government laws’,2 a crude but apt comparison. Generally speaking, the SCP Foundation is governed along the lines of a quasi-parliamentary system, in the model of the United Kingdom or Germany. Power is distributed unevenly between the Foundation's three main organs: the Office of the Administrator, the O5-Council, and the Ethics Committee. If one squints hard enough, they may see a division of power between an executive, legislative, and judicial branch.

The Office of the Administrator is the most junior branch, created in 195█ in the aftermath of the Pacific Disaster. This event is beyond the scope of this work, but the O5-Council’s inability to come to a consensus and act led to the containment breaches of multiple SCPs, which almost resulted in the breaking of the veil and led to one of the largest cover-ups in the foundation's history, stretching its resources to the breaking point. In light of this, the Office of the Administrator was created to act decisively when time was of the essence. The Administrator was empowered to marshal the military resources of the Foundation in times of crisis without O5 approval and negotiate with governments and other authorities.

Over time, this mandate has changed from emergency to normalcy. Currently, the Administrator manages the Foundation's military forces, handles day-to-day affairs, and negotiates with political authorities when necessary, all without the need for an ongoing crisis. The O5-Council frequently delegates its own duties and powers which it considers frivolous to the Administrator, which has left the office in limbo: in theory, the Administrator has many powers at their disposal to exert their influence; in reality, almost all of them can be revoked at the whim of the O5-Council.3

Additionally, most Administrators are former O5 members: of all the Administrators in the Foundation's history, only four (including the current one) were not members of the O5-Council before their appointment. This has led to an office that never challenges the council, sympathizes with them, and is usually subservient to their wishes.

(Note: The current Administrator has frequently clashed with the O5-Council and challenged them on numerous matters.4 Why they have respected his wishes and not taken any action to rein him in is unknown. This may be the start of a new trend of more independent Administrators, or it may be a rare case of a forceful personality holding the office.)

Administrators are appointed by the O5-Council and are officially selected if they gain the approval of a 2/3rds majority. Likewise, removal from their office requires a 2/3rds majority. Their terms are five years, and there is no term limit for individuals.

If the Office of the Administrator is junior and relatively new, then the O5-Council is ancient. They are the supreme power that commands the Foundation. The history of this body is shrouded in mystery, much like the Foundation itself, but it is assumed that the council was created at the same time the Foundation began to take its first steps. For decades, they were the only sanctioned official group overseeing its operations.5 The creation of the Ethics Committee and the Office of the Administrator may be seen as the O5-Council losing its grip on power, but this would be a faulty assumption.

To get a position on this body is no easy feat—it is the last and top rung of the political ladder in the SCP Foundation. Soldiers, Directors, Researchers, Scientists, Bureaucrats, and Intelligence officers have all made the climb, but it is the researchers and scientists who historically and presently make up much of the council. It should come as no surprise that their needs dominate most of the council’s time.

And such a hold is not easy to break. The O5-Council elects itself—with token input from the Ethics Committee—ensuring that their perfidious cabal6 lives on to stifle any opposition to it. A ¾ majority of the O5-Council is required to be elected as a council member (along with a simple majority of the Ethics Committee), and they all serve 15-year terms, with no term limits, of course. In practice, an appointment to the council is a lifetime commitment, barring the exceptions of those who resign, either due to health issues, disgruntlement, retirement, being 'promoted' to Administrator, or being forced to do so due to political machinations. Only in exceptional circumstances are members voted out of their position.

The O5-Council directs and oversees the overall long-term strategic planning and vision of the SCP Foundation. All power, authority, and legitimacy derive from them; even the Administrator and Ethics Committee are puppets of their will.7 They control the funding of new projects and expansion (new sites, military forces, etc.) and all the monies they make from their many front organizations. The O5-Council has final say over all matters and can overrule the Administrator on whatever it sees fit, even in emergencies. Any treaties, pacts, and agreements with governments and other entities must be ratified by them to go into effect. They alone can approve of the decommissioning of SCPs or their voluntary release. Finally, the usage of any of the Foundation's nuclear arsenal requires the approval of the O5-Council.

Note: All sites are equipped with nuclear warheads in the case of a containment breach that threatens to break the veil; in this situation, the O5-Council and the Site Director must approve their usage (if the Site Director is incapacitated, then their respective Regional Director takes his place). The O5-Council can overrule even the objections of these directors, but the vote must be unanimous.

The Ethics Committee is the final formal body in the SCP Foundation. Unlike the others, it has its own hierarchy and subordinate groups due to its unique role. Therefore, it would be wise to start from the bottom of this hierarchy and work up to the Committee itself.

At the bottom is the so-called ‘Ethics Officers’. These men and women are numerous and are the face of the Ethics Committee. These officers are attached to all Foundation sites (both official and unofficial8) as well as military units to report on their doings, any potential violations of ethics, concerns, and so on. This group is made up of a mix of volunteers and those assigned to it, usually as a form of punishment; inside the foundation, Ethics Officers are seen as busybodies and meddlers. The number of these officers varies considerably from site to site and unit: small facilities like Site-23 have only 15 or so officers, while the biggest ones have hundreds of them. As a rule, military units generally only have a handful of officers attached.

All these reports and findings are relayed up the chain of command to their respective Ethics Councils. Made up of 7 individuals, these local councils are found at all Foundation sites and at the headquarters of larger military garrisons. Their role is exclusively of an adjudicative nature; they do not make new guidelines or offer new interpretations of existing laws. They only offer judgment in cases and mete out punishments to offenders, ranging from censures, docking of pay, and reassignment. As these councils do not have the authority to authorize the use of amnestics, execution, or other severe punishments, there is no way to appeal these decisions. One might imagine this can lead to injustice and corruption, which it certainly does.9

These Ethics Councils send reports of their proceedings, decisions, and any disputes that are outside the scope of their authority to their Regional Ethics Councils, which correspond to the regional directorates. As a result, there are seven of these councils: the North American Council, the South American Council, the European Council, the African Council, the Asian Council, and the Pacific Council.

The regional councils serve as a court that deals with severe cases and consequently heavy punishments. For a case to reach the regionals, it requires serious accusations of wrongdoing, such as murder, negligence, dereliction of duty, and other such offenses. Composed of 9 individuals, the regional councils render judgment and can authorize the usage of amnestics, execution, and demotion. These can all be appealed to the final rung of the ladder: the Ethics Committee.

Composed of 20 people, the Ethics Committee issues final decisions in appeals it decides to hear and regularly reviews the containment procedures of entities in containment to make sure they are in line with what is currently defined as ‘ethical’ or not. What is ‘ethical’ is a moving target that changes depending on whatever is most convenient for the O5-Council.10 The Committee also gives the O5-Council its counsel and opinions regarding decisions involving sentient SCPs, Class-D personnel, and other such humanitarian concerns. The containment procedures of all entities must be approved by the Ethics Committee, as well as any changes made to them.

One may have noticed that the Ethics Committee is composed of an even number of individuals: what happens when there is a tiebreaker? This is another intentional design by the O5-Council to control all other political bodies and preserve their power. In a tiebreaker, the O5-Council casts the decisive vote by a simple majority. Additionally, any case that makes it to the Ethics Committee can be forcefully removed from their hands by the O5-Council if they will it. The council rarely does this to keep up the charade of an independent body, but the truth is there for all who have eyes to see.11

To attain a position on the committee, one must first be added to a list of potential candidates drafted by the O5-Council, which is then presented to the Ethics Committee. The committee votes on who joins their ranks by a 2/3rds majority. This is another charade put up by the O5-Council—the Ethics committee votes for its own members, but the O5-Council decides who can be considered. While the committee members do vote on prospective O5 members, true rejection is relatively rare. Only on two occasions has the Ethics Committee rejected a candidate, and one of them managed to be elected regardless after ‘intense negotiations’.12 Ethics Committee members serve 10-year terms with no term limits.

From a bird-eye's view, these three bodies interact to efficiently run the SCP Foundation. The O5-Council acts as the supreme body, focusing on the big picture while delegating the day-to-day affairs of the organization to the Administrator. The Ethics Committee deals with disciplinary matters and the overall ‘humanity’ of the SCP Foundation and its actions, acting in both a judicial and policing role.

In practice, the O5-Council is an all-powerful body that created these vestiges to give them the task of actually governing while they spend time doing whatever idle things they fancy. Using the plunder of public money and their other ill-begotten gains, they focus on containing anomalous objects for their use in the intimidation and shakedown of the world’s governments.13 Combating this devil was why our organization was created, and why we will continue to do so, so long as we have legs to stand on and gun's in our hands. They use the anomalous to further their own interests, suppressing humanity’s awareness of them to keep themselves in power. After all, what is more powerful than knowledge?

Forward this to Director Ross. She will want to see this.
-C.M

2. This is admittedly not too far off the mark.

9. Does the insurgency even have ways of settling issues without the end of a gun?
10. Astounding ignorance!
11. And no brains either.

In light of this, the Office of the Administrator was created to act decisively when time was of the essence. The Administrator was empowered to marshal the military resources of the Foundation in times of crisis without O5 approval and negotiate with governments and other authorities. Over time, this mandate has changed from emergency to normalcy. Currently, the Administrator manages the Foundation's military forces, handles day-to-day affairs, and negotiates with political authorities when necessary, all without the need for an ongoing crisis. The O5-Council frequently delegates its own duties and powers which it considers frivolous to the Administrator, which has left the office in limbo: in theory, the Administrator has many powers at their disposal to exert their influence; in reality, almost all of them can be revoked at the whim of the O5-Council.[[footnote]]The writer’s ability to take a nugget of truth and exaggerate it to absurdity is impressive.[[/footnote]] Additionally, most Administrators are former O5 members: of all the Administrators in the Foundation's history, only four (including the current one) were not members of the O5-Council before their appointment. This has led to an office that never challenges the council, sympathizes with them, and is usually subservient to their wishes. //(Note: The current Administrator has frequently clashed with the O5-Council and challenged them on numerous matters.[[footnote]]How exactly does the Insurgency know about this? We will have to step up our counterintelligence efforts. Concerning.[[/footnote]] Why they have respected his wishes and not taken any action to rein him in is unknown. This may be the start of a new trend of more independent Administrators, or it may be a rare case of a forceful personality holding the office.)// Administrators are appointed by the O5-Council and are officially selected if they gain the approval of a 2/3rds majority. Likewise, removal from their office requires a 2/3rds majority. Their terms are five years, and there is no term limit for individuals. If the Office of the Administrator is junior and relatively new, then the O5-Council is ancient. They are the supreme power that commands the Foundation. The history of this body is shrouded in mystery, much like the Foundation itself, but it is assumed that the council was created at the same time the Foundation began to take its first steps. For decades, they were the only sanctioned official group overseeing its operations.[[footnote]]So they don't know all of our secrets.[[/footnote]] The creation of the Ethics Committee and the Office of the Administrator may be seen as the O5-Council losing its grip on power, but this would be a faulty assumption. To get a position on this body is no easy feat—it is the last and top rung of the political ladder in the SCP Foundation. Soldiers, Directors, Researchers, Scientists, Bureaucrats, and Intelligence officers have all made the climb, but it is the researchers and scientists who historically and presently make up much of the council. It should come as no surprise that their needs dominate most of the council’s time. And such a hold is not easy to break. The O5-Council elects itself—with token input from the Ethics Committee—ensuring that their perfidious cabal[[footnote]]The bias is just dripping off the page. Whoever wrote this is a raging lunatic.[[/footnote]] lives on to stifle any opposition to it. A ¾ majority of the O5-Council is required to be elected as a council member (along with a simple majority of the Ethics Committee), and they all serve 15-year terms, with no term limits, of course. In practice, an appointment to the council is a lifetime commitment, barring the exceptions of those who resign, either due to health issues, disgruntlement, retirement, being 'promoted' to Administrator, or being forced to do so due to political machinations. Only in exceptional circumstances are members voted out of their position. The O5-Council directs and oversees the overall long-term strategic planning and vision of the SCP Foundation. All power, authority, and legitimacy derive from them; even the Administrator and Ethics Committee are puppets of their will.[[footnote]]The Ethics committee would have something to say about that![[/footnote]] They control the funding of new projects and expansion (new sites, military forces, etc.) and all the monies they make from their many front organizations. The O5-Council has final say over all matters and can overrule the Administrator on whatever it sees fit, even in emergencies. Any treaties, pacts, and agreements with governments and other entities must be ratified by them to go into effect. They alone can approve of the decommissioning of SCPs or their voluntary release. Finally, the usage of any of the Foundation's nuclear arsenal requires the approval of the O5-Council. //Note: All sites are equipped with nuclear warheads in the case of a containment breach that threatens to break the veil; in this situation, the O5-Council and the Site Director must approve their usage (if the Site Director is incapacitated, then their respective Regional Director takes his place). The O5-Council can overrule even the objections of these directors, but the vote must be unanimous.// The Ethics Committee is the final formal body in the SCP Foundation. Unlike the others, it has its own hierarchy and subordinate groups due to its unique role. Therefore, it would be wise to start from the bottom of this hierarchy and work up to the Committee itself. At the bottom is the so-called ‘Ethics Officers’. These men and women are numerous and are the face of the Ethics Committee. These officers are attached to all Foundation sites (both official and unofficial[[footnote]]Do they know about any of our black sites?[[/footnote]]) as well as military units to report on their doings, any potential violations of ethics, concerns, and so on. This group is made up of a mix of volunteers and those assigned to it, usually as a form of punishment; inside the foundation, Ethics Officers are seen as busybodies and meddlers. The number of these officers varies considerably from site to site and unit: small facilities like Site-23 have only 15 or so officers, while the biggest ones have hundreds of them. As a rule, military units generally only have a handful of officers attached. All these reports and findings are relayed up the chain of command to their respective Ethics Councils. Made up of 7 individuals, these local councils are found at all Foundation sites and at the headquarters of larger military garrisons. Their role is exclusively of an adjudicative nature; they do not make new guidelines or offer new interpretations of existing laws. They only offer judgment in cases and mete out punishments to offenders, ranging from censures, docking of pay, and reassignment. As these councils do not have the authority to authorize the use of amnestics, execution, or other severe punishments, there is no way to appeal these decisions. One might imagine this can lead to injustice and corruption, which it certainly does.[[footnote]]Does the insurgency even have ways of settling issues without the end of a gun?[[/footnote]] These Ethics Councils send reports of their proceedings, decisions, and any disputes that are outside the scope of their authority to their Regional Ethics Councils, which correspond to the regional directorates. As a result, there are seven of these councils: the North American Council, the South American Council, the European Council, the African Council, the Asian Council, and the Pacific Council. The regional councils serve as a court that deals with severe cases and consequently heavy punishments. For a case to reach the regionals, it requires serious accusations of wrongdoing, such as murder, negligence, dereliction of duty, and other such offenses. Composed of 9 individuals, the regional councils render judgment and can authorize the usage of amnestics, execution, and demotion. These can all be appealed to the final rung of the ladder: the Ethics Committee. Composed of 20 people, the Ethics Committee issues final decisions in appeals it decides to hear and regularly reviews the containment procedures of entities in containment to make sure they are in line with what is currently defined as ‘ethical’ or not. What is ‘ethical’ is a moving target that changes depending on whatever is most convenient for the O5-Council.[[footnote]]Astounding ignorance![[/footnote]] The Committee also gives the O5-Council its counsel and opinions regarding decisions involving sentient SCPs, Class-D personnel, and other such humanitarian concerns. The containment procedures of all entities must be approved by the Ethics Committee, as well as any changes made to them. One may have noticed that the Ethics Committee is composed of an even number of individuals: what happens when there is a tiebreaker? This is another intentional design by the O5-Council to control all other political bodies and preserve their power. In a tiebreaker, the O5-Council casts the decisive vote by a simple majority. Additionally, any case that makes it to the Ethics Committee can be forcefully removed from their hands by the O5-Council if they will it. The council rarely does this to keep up the charade of an independent body, but the truth is there for all who have eyes to see.[[footnote]]And no brains either.[[/footnote]] To attain a position on the committee, one must first be added to a list of potential candidates drafted by the O5-Council, which is then presented to the Ethics Committee. The committee votes on who joins their ranks by a 2/3rds majority. This is another charade put up by the O5-Council—the Ethics committee votes for its own members, but the O5-Council decides who can be considered. While the committee members do vote on prospective O5 members, true rejection is relatively rare. Only on two occasions has the Ethics Committee rejected a candidate, and one of them managed to be elected regardless after ‘intense negotiations’.[[footnote]]As said before: exaggeration.[[/footnote]] Ethics Committee members serve 10-year terms with no term limits. From a bird-eye's view, these three bodies interact to efficiently run the SCP Foundation. The O5-Council acts as the supreme body, focusing on the big picture while delegating the day-to-day affairs of the organization to the Administrator. The Ethics Committee deals with disciplinary matters and the overall ‘humanity’ of the SCP Foundation and its actions, acting in both a judicial and policing role. In practice, the O5-Council is an all-powerful body that created these vestiges to give them the task of actually governing while they spend time doing whatever idle things they fancy. Using the plunder of public money and their other ill-begotten gains, they focus on containing anomalous objects for their use in the intimidation and shakedown of the world’s governments.[[footnote]]!!![[/footnote]] Combating this devil was why our organization was created, and why we will continue to do so, so long as we have legs to stand on and gun's in our hands. They use the anomalous to further their own interests, suppressing humanity’s awareness of them to keep themselves in power. After all, what is more powerful than knowledge? ------ //Forward this to Director Ross. She will want to see this.// //-C.M// [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box-end]]

protectors-of-inti-001.raw_content:
Protectors of Inti Archive

In 2023, archeologists working for the Ministry of Culture of Peru discovered a subterranean structure near Maras, ~10km north of Cusco. The repository was constructed of large drystone and is dated between 1465–1478, the height of the Inca Empire. Found within were over 800 perfectly preserved quipu, a type of recording device made of knotted strings that was common in pre-Columbean Andean societies. While typically used to record economic, demographic, or military data, these quipu were discovered to possess anomalous properties and were seized by the Foundation.

The anomalous properties of the "Protectors of Inti" quipu activate when an instance is held by a woman over 68 years of age. This subject is drawn into a trance state, in which she begins to recite the information documented on the quipu. This information is spoken in Southern Quechua, and is only audible to women over 36 years of age. The text of the quipu appears to have been composed by an anomalous normalcy organization that was active within the stretches of the Inca Empire. No information on such an organization has been found in the Site-4 archives, suggesting the "Protectors of Inti" fell rapidly alongside the empire.

The "Protectors of Inti" Archive is held in the Site 43 Archives and Revision Section for digitalization and analysis.


Double-spouted ceramic vessel discovered within the Protectors of Inti archive.

PoI Transcript 001

Type: Immovable, Cuntinsuyu

Required resources:

  • 1 mit'a laborer,1 perpetually
  • 4 mit'a laborers, each Aymuray2
  • 10 local men, each Aymuray
  • 12 llamas, each Aymuray

Estimated cost of failure:

  • Year 1: 100 families
  • Year 2: 800 families
  • Year 3: 10,000 families
  • Year 4: 50 families
  • Year 5: 0 families (conclusion)

Control method:

  • Population is warded from the Monkey at all times.
  • Pot is protected by a single man.
  • Ritual is executed yearly, on the 16th day of Aymuray.
  • Mitma3 of Nasca village indefinitely deferred.

Story: After Topa Inca Yupanqui's mighty victory over the Chimu, he traveled back to Cusco through the Nasca Desert, subsuming towns in Cuntinsuyu. Here, his men discovered a geography of angular waves. In the center was a tower 20 ritka4 tall, which curved into an arithmetic spiral of concentric circles, 20 ritka in diameter. When the men stepped on the geography, a mouth appeared from below them and ate them. When the men used their slings to strike the tower, a mouth appeared from below them and ate them.

The Sapa Inca, Topa Inca Yupanqui, sent men to the nearby village for information on the creature. They described the tower as the tail of a monster created by their ancestors. They described it as a huaca5 created by men. The Chimu had attempted to use the force of their great empire to fight it, but lost at least 1,000 men in the attempt. The creature gets hungry and thirsty every year, and its hunger may be unbounded.

Contact: The Protectors of Inti were officially informed of the Monkey 4 days later, but no actions were taken at this time.

The people of the small nearby village, Nasca, resisted Topa Inca Yupanqui's might and refused to pay tributes. The huaca Pot was claimed for the Sapa Inca's collection and the population was subjected to Mitma, resettled in Qullasuyu. The following year, the Monkey awoke and began to eat the inhabitants of nearby towns.

At this time, the Sapa Inca was conquering lands further north, so the magistrate sent runners to inform the Cuya6 of the disaster by use of the great roads. By the time the Protectors of Inti arrived 12 days later, the great Monkey had returned to its resting place. It was angry and hungry, but exhausted. Two small towns (64 families) were destroyed in this attack, and the Cuya saw that the beast would be powerful enough to reach throughout Cuntinsuyu if it became angry again.

This is when the Protectors of Inti established the current control method. Fortunately, the 40 survivors among the resettled Nasca community were easily located by their high-status women wearing fish-patterned garments and the distinctive ancient pottery they took with them. Despite the deaths of their village elders during relocating, communal knowledge proved sufficient to establish control over the Monkey.

Object:

  1. Honoured huaca. Giant Monkey, embedded in a ground of geometric waves. It is not located on a siq'i.7
  2. Honoured huaca. 1000-year old piece of pottery with 2 touts. It shows a killer whale holding a trophy head. Allows a man to approach the Monkey, in order to provide it with 3 pokcha8 of water.
  3. Ritual. The creature is kept alive and dormant through an annual ritual. 12 men drink chicha9 appropriate for a harvest festival, and walk the entirety of the lines drawn at the feet of the Monkey's platform, while 4 men in the designated area perform a 24-beat percussion. The men sing a song similar to the Jailli,10 clapping their hands on the 4-beats. Each time the 12 men reach the end of a segment, 1 man releases the water content of the pottery in the Monkey's mouth. The ritual lasts from noon to sundown. Following the ritual, 12 llamas are to be led to the platform and fed to the creature.
  4. Celebration. The monkey expects to observe freeform dance, music, and chicha consumption following the conclusion of the ritual. Wari-style feasting traditions must be included. If the delegation fails to provide this, the monkey eats all men present.


Update: Estimated cost of failure confirmed following the calamity of the Spanish invasion. Huaca have become inactive.

Concluded.

When the hellgate first opened, Management scrambled ten thousand personnel to divert a river through it, hoping to hold back what was waiting.

  • 

    close

    Info

    X

    Author: whenwerewe
    Here's my page!

Lumi Laine was thirteen when she realised she would harrow Hell, seventeen when she realised how, and twenty-six when she did.

When the hellgate first opened, Management scrambled ten thousand personnel to divert a river through it, hoping to hold back what was waiting. Unfortunately, even the Phlegethon could only buy them a month.

The worst thing about Hell was that it made a habit of cultivating hope. A poor sinner might look up and see the skies darken and pray that the blood-lanterns of the Lightbringer were dimming at last. Only one who looked carefully would notice that what seemed to be clouds, were, in fact, solid seething mats of limb and wing. The most contemptible class of devil flocked sightlessly over the ash-sodden plains of Tophet, emptied of their regular play of tormented and tormentor.

That expanse was shadowed by what rose over the horizon; a monolithic slab of stone lovingly detailed until every sinuous curve and jagged vertex burst with frescoes, faces, fearsome wyrms and horned beasts. It was incoherent, casually making a melange of five thousand years of theme and symbol. Here rose Aeneas with his spear through the heart of Quetzalcoatl, there the surrendering Mordred was devoured by a pack of kappa, and everywhere the serpent, the serpent, the serpent, crawling around heels and whispering in ears and biting into throats. Even the architecture seemed at war with itself: gables, domes, arches; great ivory monoliths and dead concrete idols; marble graven with gold; and above it all a skyscraper whose windows were obsidian. In the penthouse suite its master brooded tightlipped.

Today, Hell was silent.

Flame poured soundlessly through the great gash that hung perfectly still at the centre of the flatlands, and though it did not even murmur like water as it flowed, its light shone with the promise of mutilation. Redirected by the desperate efforts of devilry, the burning fell laminar to the mortal lands, throwing up a great pall of ember-studded fog that drowned all motion. The river flowed, the devils seethed, the Prince of Tophet looked on with sunken eyes, and through that mist stormed a million tons of war-engine.

Vanguard ran an educational service: they livestreamed faerie nominology, memetic inoculants, and necromantic first-aid.

On the adult channel, past a bevy of warnings —

(CONSULT PRIEST BEFORE VIEWING, CONSIDER AMNESTICS, IS THE COALITION RIGHT FOR YOU?)

— they streamed the view of Hell. Someone up the hierarchy correctly calculated that ninety-nine out of a hundred people who saw it would turn away sickened and try never to think of it again, and the other one would forge herself into a spear to pierce the heart of Lucifer. They probably didn’t expect her to be thirteen, but no plan survives first contact with the enemy.

Once she met a kid who told her that people who sold their souls deserved what they got. They had to wheel him down to the hospital to get the fork out of his shoulder.

What she was taught in school had not been adapted to a post-Impasse world. They discussed afterlives like theories, when she could look down through a scrying pool and see exactly what the measure of every man was, herself. Consulting feverishly with the local abbot one day she found out about something new. He looked kindly on her, in the empty church vaulted and ribbed as if a dying whale, and said:

“When Christ was crucified, his soul descended into Hell, and he rescued all the virtuous from their torments.”

His eyes crinkled, amused by the unusual inquiry. He had not seen them. This kind of man, who had been good all his life, lived in a different universe than the idiots who bought five hours of glory in this world with their eternity in the next.

But, she thought, even idiots are virtuous, compared to the Devil. And if Hell can be braved once, why not again?

She roared out into the great outspread ashdrifts. The sweeping iron columns that were her legs pumped madly through the blazing river. The air saturated with elemental fire and took on a grim crimson aspect. It was a vision, of, well —

The earth all around her boiled upward. At the same moment the clouds plunged down, revealing the garish sky above. She and her companion whooped in one sonorous bellow that rumbled across the plain, all the way to the tower in the distance.

The strength of Good Intentions thrummed through her teeth, sang in time with her treacle-beating heart, pierced her breast like a needle. The sheer promise of her sister’s movement was a thrill felt in the marrow. Intentions trusted her perfectly, and nothing could stop them together.

She grinned within her cockpit, muscle moving despite the thousand needles jabbed in haywire and the paralytic coursing through her blood.

There. I’m going to feed you his heart.

A half-kilometre behemoth of steel and woven carbon raised one pendulous arm to point at the lord they’d come to hunt. In its hand was a great length of steel whose hilt was the column of Trajan. It was crowned in the bones of every saint but one. About its shoulders was a cloak of prophecy: the apokalypsis of Patmos, the thousand awakened ones of the fortunate era, the molten mantle of Dhul-Qarnayn. A promise at last fulfilled:

He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.

Good Intentions giggled back her approval up the neurochannel, and they sprang forward.

Rising from the ash; great cambions and lemures, many-limbed and many-horned. On their backs they hefted twisted black steel things that pulsed with awful purpose. Perhaps they might even hurt her, but —

Great carnelians burst into being all over the length of the plain, and the legions of Hell found they had something else to worry about. She wasn’t planning on overthrowing the cosmic order alone.

Perhaps she tuned into goetics channels more than the average teenage girl; maybe she liked to read about UN sanctions on the infernal plane more than the average political scientist. But if you knew her, you’d think Lumi was a pretty average person. She had friends, liked to box, to climb, to get into ill-advised fights outside bars, to walk around under the black sunless Helsinki sky looking for interesting things; and she never really got bored.

When she volunteered for the Coalition’s cadet forces, her parents were unjustifiably surprised. Her mother made a great show of accepting her decision as her lip quivered, but Father grinned wholeheartedly and thumped her on the back.

She had worked out the very first day that she needed to invade Hell. The question, then, was with who?

Vanguard were all smiles and kids playing in fields and old grannies with three eyes looking over them. She didn’t object to them loosening up from the Foundation days — and she was certainly grateful for the propaganda — but what she needed was an army. Artillery, aircraft, angels; gunmen and drones and cannons. Something to direct her hate. The Coalition blazed with the fire of every weapon ever forged by man. Join us, they said, and you will wield them all.

The choice was obvious.

Screaming sleek airwings daubed a defiant blue streaked the sky above her. Their thunder broke the gibbering horde crowding the ether, and all around her long-collected standoff weapons smeared the lesser devilry and their schemes across the cinders.

The easy part was done. The marshals back home had predicted the joke of an ambush, and laid out in millimetre precision how it would be dismantled. Hell had tried anyway — never go for cleverness when callousness might do; that was the principle. Now, at last, the princes of the pit were desperate.

All Tophet flickered with Coalition light, and pulped fiends drenched the earth until it formed a sodden musclemulch. She kept her eyes on the fortress, and the needlelike tower that seemed to reach halfway to the sourceless light of Lucifer.

The ground shuddered.

The sky bulged towards the earth. For a moment, the horizon bent inward. Then it shattered and like a television fractured into manycoloured shards. Out of the broken heaven dripped fat droplets of zodiacal light which fell perspectivelessly, seeming as likely to patter off Intentions’ optics as to drown a distant mountain.

Then they landed calamitously in the middle distance, and out of them rose mirrors of every kind. A fat sprawling hedge, large enough to swallow her, composed of glass: some smooth and clear, some dully coated in static, some blazoned with bloated erythematic faces, and others yet babbling meaningless debasements.

A pulse of toneless alarm from your sister. No, no, idiot, obviously not mirrors —

In the cadet force they have her on cleaning duty as much as possible. Nobody quite takes seriously that this wispy girl really wants to kill people for a living. She just got swept up in the propaganda dragnet. Too many hot chicks in the mech ads; that’s their assessment.

Screens. Amaymon, lord of noise and madness.

Legs drove into the offal-soaked dirt and she thrust toward his heart. Around her the lesser warcraft of the Coalition advanced. A flight of tactically blinded angels ringed her with celestial glory and she pushed through the muck. They could not see the evil in her own spirit or else she’d already be dead.

And as she reached for him and raised the sword —

Could barely handle moron-standard gunnery, couldn’t maintain anything more complicated than a toaster, didn’t have the head for command. When she tried out at airmanship she scored a clean twenty crashes in a row on the sim. Handling a UHEC was like being a toddler again. Everyone she knew looked at her with pity. Fuck them, and she’d break the girls’ noses in the ring if they wanted to say shit about her.

And stomped her feet and twisted, hips core back shoulders, her sister synchronised perfectly with her, and with best intentions fell her fatal stroke toward the heart of the Lord of the South. His hundred bloodless lips yawned open on their portals and he gave a black laughter and said, Come, know Yourself, and let Us be done with this farce, and she felt ice in her nerves as he exegeted her failures and her worthlessness —

She trembled under the feedback, the first time they connected her to Good Intentions, newborn, forged out of some Sumerian idol, still and tense with ecstasy —

Learned to love it, to hunt it, to plead for it from the colossus, mewling like some kitten because what did she have to lose —

Every movement bursting with strength and joy in the first field deployment, the glory of success, of a place at last, a role to play in the great victory, and she did not even notice when an Insurgent thaumaturge dragged half her mechanised escort into the abyss —

And lay cradled in Intentions’ womb, unmoving, and felt the other girl’s contentment, and thought, I could stay here forever —

And screamed and crushed an Orange beneath her splayed fist, and the pilot couldn’t walk for a month —

Suffocated by bitterness when they named some other guy twice her age as the alternate pilot. She needed to feel that alone, the quiet, the unity —

And in the end they named her the first accredited full pilot of the new Apocatastasis-class frames. And she was overjoyed, though she could not appear in public (they would flinch from the new limbs and the old stumps). Her sister spoke to her in their dreams:

Come on! Did you ever think it wouldn’t be you? Who else is bloodyminded enough to be the scourge of Hell? Who else can see through the lies of Amaymon —

And she woke and cast away and expiated her sins by pulling her sword right through his heart.

Around her the screens shattered and burst; flechettes of glass rattled off her armor. The theophanic gilding would need some buffing out. A spray of technicolour blood lent a brief and failing colour to the greying soil.

Her sword felt a little heavier somehow, with something more than mere mass. As if her motions had some other kind of inertia to them. She had broken one of the angles of the world. She plunged it tip-first into the ground, and it stood silently beside her.

Behind the armies of the Coalition continued to pour forth, more by the minute, and she kept her eyes on the tower. She wasn’t so sure of herself she’d try that obvious trap on her own. No further devils arrived, and the men kept following behind into the little pocket of safety they’d carved out in the plain. Nothing tested their borders. Hovercraft and helicopters and trucks and IFVs and MBTs assembled behind her an anthill of activity. As they scurried back and forth setting up layers of thaumaturgic shielding and tartarean sinks her sister rang that muted alarm: something was wrong.

As it stood, they’d won.

Not just in this moment, but totally. Hell had rings within rings, machina ex machina, but it was fundamentally designed to take the weak and the defenceless and break them. Neither Asmodeus nor Abbadon had any answer to the radio, the guided missile, the jet engine. As long as the gate remained open, they could simply shuffle through ammunition and men, strengthen their grasp, and begin a campaign in earnest.

In no sense would it be easy. Thousands would die, but tens of thousands had come; to see off the worst relic of the Veil. All plans had been for the fighting to be most brutal at this beachhead. Without their weaponry, they were only meat for the lowest lare. With it, they feared almost nothing. She was meant to be their answer to the simultaneous appearance of all six Princes (and die in the answering), but instead…

She looked up toward the fortress, and the tower. Still as the grave. She would break open its vaults and arcades and let the million souls inside free. What she’d seen so long ago would end. And then she would climb to the false star of Lucifer and quench it.

As if mocking her, that was the moment she felt it. A sudden horrible lurching in her stomach, a cry of dismay from her sister, and she fell briefly to her knees. She sprang to her feet with a speed that belied her size, but Mammon had not descended from his stronghold. Then what?

Behind her, with no spectacle, the hellgate had vanished.


/

Heaven Shall Be Empty

The Carters bring Dorian to Vegas.

    X

    Info about the article
    Content warning: This article contains graphic suicide, gambling addiction, and substance use.

⚠️ content warning

January 3, 2021

Never in his life did he think he would spend his twenty-first birthday on an all-expenses-paid trip to Las Vegas. Plenty of young men would have killed for that chance.

What a thought…

As Dorian landed, he could imagine how breathtaking the Strip must have appeared at night. However, he arrived in the middle of the afternoon, and those bright lights were muted amid the sand and concrete.

He could appreciate what the city stood for. The careless disregard for inhibition, the performance of it all. It seemed every billboard paraded addiction and carnal pleasure with some law and insurance advertisements sprinkled in. The neon frenzy of activity reminded him of home in a way London’s buttoned-up manners couldn’t hold a torch to.

Maybe he could have enjoyed himself in a place like this. He might've spent the evening chatting up bartenders and showgirls, tipping them well and giving at least the latter the appreciation of a kindred spirit. Vegas always welcomed new money and pretty words.

But despite the calendar date, Dorian Sloan had come to Las Vegas for business, nothing else.

By 8pm, he was on the casino floor of the Bellagio hotel. Golden light and luxury glittered around him, sprawling up to high ceilings. The warmth could barely combat the obnoxiously vibrant screens of the slot machines. He heard murmuring, accompanied by the soft slaps and shuffling of cards. A scan of the room confirmed a rumor he'd heard—there were no clocks or windows in sight.

Before anything else, Dorian flashed his ID to the tuxedoed staff at the front to prove that, as of today, he was allowed to gamble without supervision or interruption. They looked at his fresh license, then at his Armani attire, before graciously sending him into the casino with happy birthday wishes.

He got the same look when he went to trade his one-hundred thousand in cash for chips, though the teller was better at concealing her amusement. No doubt, this hotel has seen countless boys just like him cough up their allowances. But as Dorian stepped onto the smooth paisley carpet, he intended to make money, not burn it.

He spotted the man of the hour at the roulette table. As Dorian approached, he saw his target’s face sour with a loss.

A shock of worry went through him that Bernard Morris might quit before he reached him, but of course, that wasn’t how gambling addictions worked.

Dorian took advantage of the short break and found a spot at the table to the man’s right. He was in his forties, though he wore those years hard. His hairline crept back, and his eyes—narrowed in concentration—sunk into his face, ringed by discoloration.

“Forty bands on black,” Dorian said casually, pushing his chips forward, then flashing Morris a smile. “Match me on red. That way, one of us has to win.”

“I like the way you think, stranger,” Morris replied, and with no hesitation, made his bet.

God had blessed Dorian with a silver tongue, and the devil herself had seen fit to hire him for it. Watching Morris gamble, however, he doubted any anomalous persuasion was needed to make him keep playing.

The ball spun, then landed on red. Dorian bit the inside of his cheek, even as he reminded himself that he wasn’t betting with his own money.

“You’re on a roll. You’ve got to go again.” He urged in a velvety voice. “Might as well double it—see what happens.” Even as Dorian declined to repeat his bet, Morris stacked one hundred sixty thousand dollars in chips on the table.

Dorian wondered what it meant for him that over the past year, he'd come to see this as a small sum.

The man blanched at the loss, almost surprisingly. Panic struck his face like a deer the moment it realizes the car wasn't going to stop. Before Dorian could get a word in—which was not an easy feat—he’d gone all in, moving chips with furious, decisive movements.

Lady Luck slighted him once more. The neon light bounced off his glassy, bewildered eyes.

How could the bastard possibly be shocked? Dorian was certain that even if he'd grown up with enough funds to spare on blind trust for the odds, he'd still find roulette abhorrently stupid. How could anyone come to Vegas and think they could beat the house?

“Holy shit, my wife’s gonna kill me,” Morris said, bringing a hand up to his forehead.

"Hey, I'm walking into my hotel," Robert cut off the lawyer at last, "let me call you right back."

He hung up and got out of the car. Before going in, Dorian waited for him in front of the door to ask:

"Am I off work for the night?"

"Mm? Oh, yeah, just … don't do anything stupid."

Dorian looked at him in bewilderment.

"Yeah, course not. I'm just going back to my room," he put his hands in his pockets. "Might grab a drink, now that I'm actually legal."

"Americans are so odd for that…" Robert mused.

Dorian gave a quick, hollow laugh. After a few more moments under the overhang, they continued inside. Robert expected him to go toward the bar in the lobby, but he instead went directly to the lift with him.

They rode up the elevator in silence, and only once the doors opened to the floor with their suites did Dorian murmur a quick: "Cya."

Robert returned the sentiment and went back to his room. There, he spent a solid hour on the phone with various people, his patience and energy draining with each call. When things finally calmed down, all he could do was walk over to the bed and collapse.

He was tired. More tired than he had any right to be. Hadn't everything gone right today? There was the issue in Texas, but the engineers and demons had practically already salvaged that.

Dad's right. You'll always find something to mope about.

Disposing of Morris had caulked a massive leak in funds. Was he really allowing the tedium of a few follow-up calls to take that away from him?

What's more, it had been infinitely more satisfying a solution than a sniper. Such thorough humiliation and punishment of someone who dared to think he could steal money from Robert and get away with it was almost gratifying enough to make up for the rest of tonight's events.

Almost.

Still, Robert enjoyed good theatre, and Dorian had delivered a delightful show.

He won't be asleep, Robert decided as he forced his body upright. And you should go check on him, at least.

He got out of bed and moved from his suite into the hallway. Stalking over to Dorian’s room, his emotions stirred together into an ugly and exhausting brew in his chest.

He rapped his knuckles on the door three times in quick succession. When Dorian didn’t answer, he used the spare key. Why wouldn’t he have one? He'd paid for the room, after all.

The suite was far from lived-in, but there were signs of life. A briefcase on the sofa, a coffee cup by the sink, a suit coat and tie slung over the back of the couch, and a newsprint of the Las Vegas Review he'd taken from the lobby, the crossword half-finished in pencil.

Robert could also hear music, and he moved through the suite trying to find the sound.

The music got louder, but was still muffled. Robert realized Dorian was outside on the balcony, sitting against the rail and staring out at the city below.

Freddie Mercury’s voice resonated melodically through the glass door: Beelzebub has a devil put aside for me…

Robert gently pushed open the door, and Dorian raised his head. A bottle of house red and a matching carton of Marlboros sat by his left hip, two crumpled white butts snuffed out into the concrete. There was also a small takeout box with a serving of marbled chocolate cake from Harlo, a fork stuck upright in the dessert.

Haven't quite made a hardened hitman out of you yet, have we? Robert thought bemusedly.

“Robert,” he greeted in a measured tone. “Hi. May I help you?”

“Hi. I wanted to …” 'Check on you? Make sure you were okay?' Those sounded trite, sentimental. Not the sentences he wanted. “You're not jumping or anything, are you?"

Dorian gave a dismissive wave of his hand and replied sardonically. "Jump? Oh, come on, Robert—can't I just be dramatic in peace?"

“Of course," Robert granted, a bit relieved. "You’ve earned that right. You were a good sport today."

"Thanks," he said. “You’ve not come out here to judge a man for having vices in Vegas, have you?"

“Not at all,” Robert said, tail still swaying in uncertainty as he assessed the scene before him.

Dorian put on a good show, but even in the best of performances, there were cracks, and Robert knew tonight put more pressure on him than he would ever outright admit. But hell, even this reaction seemed too curated—a superficial, artistic rendition of turmoil.

Maybe he really was just celebrating his twenty-first, and Robert’s misery was seeking company where it didn’t exist. In the wake of Ruprecht's outburst over dinner, Robert was acutely aware of Chrysophilius and Iris being absent.

"Am I still off the clock for the night?" Dorian tilted his head, wondering if that was what brought Robert here.

"Yes," he confirmed, shifting his weight between his feet once. "Inshallah, we both are. If I have to speak to another lawyer tonight, I'm jumping off the balcony myself."

Dorian gave a quick, dry laugh.

"Oh, don't do that," he replied simply. "Not while there are fast cars and pretty women in the world."

This got a laugh out of Robert, and though the sound was quiet, it was real. It felt good to laugh like that.

"I'd like to add good food and music to the list," Robert contributed.

"Hear, hear," Dorian chuckled, picking up the wine bottle by its neck and toasting toward Robert with it.

"Say," Robert tilted his head. "Are you drunk yet?"

Dorian considered it, then held up a finger in pause. He swished it around to try to gauge how much was left before just tipping it back against his already-stained lips. About six seconds later, he set it down with finality, wiped his mouth, and looked back up.

“Yes,” he said with a flash of smile before licking the wine off his teeth and sitting back against the rails, still holding Robert's gaze.

"That was stupid," he remarked lightly.

"Probably," Dorian conceded. "Are you going to sit, or do you want to go inside? I'm fine with either, but you're killing my neck."

“Do you want company?” He realized he might have asked this before dropping by unannounced, but Dorian didn't seem too bothered.

“By all means,” he said pleasantly, reaching for the box of cigarettes on the ground beside him. “Doesn’t feel right to smoke alone, anyway. You’re welcome to whatever’s here, of course…” Not that anything he had to offer would work for Robert, and he knew as much.

“The sentiment is appreciated,” Robert said, wrapping his tail around the balcony railing for balance as he lowered himself to the floor, sitting with one knee to his chest.

Dorian went to light himself another cigarette. He had trouble sparking the lighter, but managed to catch the end of the dart on the flame on the third try.

"You know, I get it's a difference in biochemistry and all—" Dorian exhaled smoke in the other direction. "—but I feel like if you put a starfish in a pool of vodka, it should still get drunk. Or the starfish-equivalent of drunk."

Robert made an amused noise. "Pretty sure that would just kill the starfish."

"Mm, well then, on the bright side, at least you're not lethally allergic to it."

"Mm. Rather the opposite," Robert informed him. "If we had a bottle of eighty-proof right here, I could chug it for the price of a stomachache."

"Damn, on god?" Dorian raised his brows. "We could try to get you a bottle from the lobby."

Robert shook his head. "It's a better trick if you're sober, honestly."

"Mm, good. Cause I don't terribly want to get up right now," Dorian admitted, then turned his head to lean his temple against the bars. "Not that it couldn't be a very quick trip down," he mused morbidly.

Robert didn't react for a moment, but Dorian didn't seem to mind, satisfied to just stare out at the city below. It was just past midnight, which made it prime time to people-watch the degenerates on the neon-lit streets.

“Does it still bother you?" Robert broached the subject cautiously.

“What, going to dinner with you and your father?” Robert couldn’t help a dry chuckle, and though Dorian tried to smile in return, the expression was more of a grimace. After a pull of his cigarette, he answered more seriously. “I'm fine—just in my head tonight."

"If you say so," Robert shrugged. After a long pause and another drag, Dorian said—

"I stopped bothering to feel bad about it when I realized violence has inelastic demand." He tapped the ash off with his index finger. “Doesn't seem to matter to any of you that I keep raising my price for it—and so long as you're willing to pay, I'll keep taking the jobs. Simple at that."

“I think my father would take out a bloody loan just to see all his enemies die in naked and mysterious ways,” Robert said.

“A loan…” Dorian almost laughed. “Please—doesn’t he own a bank?”

“Yeah, a few.” Robert's tail swept in slow arcs back and forth across the floor. "Sorry you had to sit in on some of that."

Dorian shook his head. "Nothing to apologize for. It was worse for you, anyway."

"It's fine, really. He's just like that. But that doesn't make dealing with it is part of your job."

“No,” Dorian conceded, bitterness lacing into his tone. “But still. If you … can’t get the help you need, the least he could do is not make it worse.”

It startled Robert more than he liked, being read like that. However, he got the sense that the comment hadn't entirely been about him.

“What happened to your father, anyway? If I can ask."

“Casualty of the oh-eight crash,” Dorian replied casually. "Why?"

"Dunno. I'm sure we have it on file somewhere. I just have never heard you mention him."

Dorian shrugged. "Just not really worth mentioning."

"Well, a ladies' man all the way through then, ay?" Robert asked in an attempt to lighten the mood.

Dorian gave a wry smile and ground out his cigarette.

"Something like that."

"… Do you think he'd be proud of you?" Robert realized as he asked it that he probably shouldn't have, though Dorian luckily seemed unaffected by the question.

"Why does it matter?" The wine had given a wistful quality to his voice. "I'm not particularly proud of him."

He said it completely casually, having no idea the sledgehammer it slammed into Robert's chest.

In that moment, he thought of Ruprecht, then of his real father. Worse, those thoughts were followed by ones of his mother, and it all seemed to spiral until he was sure he had to speak of it just to get it out.

Rather than say a word, Robert stood up.

Dorian's brow furrowed. "Everything okay?"

"Fine," Robert said. "One second—I just need to make a call."

It was not that he was averse to admitting certain facts and feelings to Dorian, but he worried if he started down that road tonight, he wouldn't be would be able to stop.

Dorian had an insidious way of getting others to feel comfortable opening up to him. Insidious was by no means synonymous with malicious, but still. It was a rare thing for someone to be both a good speaker and a listener—a dangerous thing.

Robert didn't want to regret oversharing in the morning. Believing anyone took him seriously was difficult enough, even without spilling his guts. He would feel a lot more comfortable knowing Dorian wouldn't remember anything he said.

He called downstairs and requested another bottle of the house red. The staff here knew better than to make him wait for long.

When Robert finally returned, he found Dorian had resumed his content observance of the city below. He turned around, not staring at Robert so much as right through him. Then his amber eyes landed on the bottle.

He watched patiently as Robert jabbed the ruby tip of his tail into the cork and drew it out with a careful, practiced motion.

"Cool trick," was all he said.

"Drink this," Robert said, placing the bottle before Dorian.

"Thanks," he said a bit awkwardly, taking a sip as Robert sat down again.

Robert shook his head. "No. Finish it."

Dorian gawked. "Right now? Are you mad?"

"Does it matter?"

"Robert," he said, giving a soft, exasperated laugh. "I'm already drunk."

"Already? Thought you were Irish."

Dorian looked at Robert in clear contempt, then rolled his eyes. With a heavy sigh, he started on its contents. Halfway through chugging, he set it down to catch his breath and to declare—"You're a fucking tyrant of a boss."

After another minute, Dorian set the second empty bottle next to the first. A deep flush colored his pale, olive face, his expression set in a slight grimace.

"Now—" he hiccuped. "You wanna tell me what that was about? Or are you just trying to give me alcohol poisoning for fun?"

Robert began to doubt if this was even worth it. He hesitated for a long few seconds, and despite his patience, Dorian looked at him with utter bewilderment.

"Happy birthday," Robert at last said ironically.

"Unbelievable," Dorian mumbled as he lit another cigarette, keeping his breath and even. He burned through it quick, then laid over his knees, going utterly still. Eventually, he moved to gaze back through the railing, the glittering city lights mirroring off his eyes. Robert observed all of this in complete silence over the course of fifteen minutes.

At last, Robert brought his hands up to his head. His fingers worked the complicated latches, and Dorian turned at the sound.

"Don't stare." Robert snapped the moment he felt eyes on him. With a respectful nod, Dorian averted his gaze.

Robert felt the cool night wind brush against the hole in his face. Gently, he set the mask on the ground, sighing deeply.

"This is what Ruprecht has to be proud of." Robert whispered. Dorian hummed quietly, peaking up quickly through his lashes before tentatively raising his head.

His amber eyes were wide and glassy, but there was no horror toward Robert's gaping visage. It was closer to wonder than anything.

"Well don't be weird about it," Robert said after a few seconds.

"Sorry," Dorian mumbled, looking at the ground again. "Just thought the colors were pretty…"

Robert flinched, the ruby edge of his tail scraping the ground, the noise quick and harsh.

"What'd you expect?" Robert hissed. A loathsome self-consciousness gnawed insistently in his chest.

"I didn't." Dorian mused plainly. It didn't sound like mockery, but Robert couldn't help the anger and shame that flared up. "I never know what to expect in this job. Stopped trying to guess. Reality's always stranger."

"Ah." Robert said, tail lashing to and fro with an aggravated mind of its own. "So you'll write this off as just another freak you have to deal with on the job. Got it."

Dorian stared at him in equal parts alarm and remorse, like Robert's shift in tone had kicked him.

"That's not what I said at all." Dorian protested, tilting his head. "I think all my bosses are freaks."

The blunt honesty caught Robert off guard, causing him to go still. Concern passed over Dorian's expression, and the tension broke when Robert let out a noise between a scoff and a laugh.

"Don't throw stones in a glass house." Robert replied, not even sure he meant it.

Dorian shrugged. "Mm, I guess…"

Robert sighed pensively before tilting his head back to stare up at the heavens. He wasn't upset at Dorian; he was just upset. Upset at Ruprecht, at himself, at the fact that the light pollution had so thoroughly washed out the stars that he couldn't even count five among the visible void.

"I just wish he didn't yell." Robert whispered. "I mean, after everything, doesn't he feel any shame at all? How can he say he loves me, yet treat me as he does?"

Dorian didn't respond at first. Robert wasn't sure he even wanted him to. He'd not have shared the thought if not for his certainty that Dorian wouldn't remember this vulnerability.

"…I won't pretend the know the deal with you and your old man just because I sat in on one dinner." Though hoarse, Dorian's voice took on a soothing affect. "I doubt anything I say will help, but if you want me to listen and let you talk about it, I'm here all night."

Dorian clumsily shuffled two cigarettes out of the carton. Robert was confused until Dorian passed it to him with a smile; not as a tool to chase a buzz, but as a universal token of camaraderie.

Why does it say about your upbringing, Robert wondered, when one of the most genuine people you know is a career charlatan?

Robert took the cigarette silently and twirling it idly through his fingers. He realized acutely how easy it would be to stay and sit here, both of them stewing in their sadness until sunrise.

Robert consumed the whole dart in one go, the unlit Marlboro disappearing into the hole of his face. Dorian betrayed his surprise by coughing briefly on his own smoke.

"Bloody hell, we are mopey, aren't we?" Robert mused sardonically.

Dorian's coughing turned to laughter. "Fuck… Granted, there are less comfortable spaces to mope in than a suite at the Palms Casino Resort."

"True, I guess," Robert conceded, turning his gaze back toward the invisible stars for a moment before perking with sudden inspiration. "What about a warehouse, though?"

Dorian looked at him in confusion. "A warehouse?"

"Misery loves distraction. I can't in good conscience bring you all the way to Vegas and not show you a better time than this. Get up, we're going to a rave."

Dorian squinted at the Movado on his wrist as Robert pulled himself back to his feet by his tail.

"It's almost one," he pointed out.

"Exactly—night's young." Robert countered as he picked up his mask.

"And I thought New York didn't sleep," Dorian grinned, the idea clearly growing on him. He killed the half-burnt cigarette, pocketed his lighter and pack, then extended a hand. "Help me up."

Robert pulled him to his feet, and after a moment, was pleasantly surprised to see he was decently steady.

"Is this the part where you take me to hell?"

Robert barked a laugh. "Yes, it is."

"Mm, might as well get acquainted," Dorian said half to himself as both of them ventured back inside.

"That's the spirit," his tail swished with a lighter mood. "Leave your wallet here. Just bring cash—just in case."

"I don't need an ID or anything?" Dorian checked.

Robert saw no arrogance in the simple truth: "Not if you're with me."

♦♢♦♢♦

Robert gave directions to their drivers, then had him stop down the street from the venue. He saw Dorian search for their destination, but come up with only confusion. No matter—entrances to these things were usually inconspicuous.

The only thing of note on the dark street was a scantily dressed woman leaning against a wall, minding her business and smoking a long cigarette holder dangling from her dark, manicured fingers.

"Hey—what's your rate per hour?" Robert asked mildly.

"Pssh—you're an ass, Mr. Carter," she smiled, molten eyes flickering over to Dorian. "Who's your friend?"

"My employee," he replied, as much to emphasize his sphere of protection as anything else. The bouncer looked him up and down, razored teeth glinting as her lips curled up further.

"Hello gorgeous."

"Hello yourself," Dorian replied. Even with the energy drink he'd bought in the resort lobby, an exhausted monotone had zapped the vivacity from his voice. That did not make the sound the sound of it any less objectively pleasing.

The bouncer chuckled, sufficiently amused by the exchange. She moved off the wall and turned to lift a board off the door behind her.

"Right this way, gentlemen."

They went down a short, lightless hallway before opening the next door, which served mainly the role of soundproofing the event within.

Bright lights and loud music mixes hit them like a tidal wave. Dorian momentarily brought his hands to his ears. Robert couldn't blame him, angry at himself for having rushed out and forgotten protection for his hearing.

Dorian leaned in, cupping his hand next to his mouth so Robert could hear. Emphasizing each word as well as he could amidst the noise.

"Do you buy new eardrums often?"

Robert just laughed, though the sound was swallowed up in the EDM. He shook his head, tail swishing as comfortably as it could without knocking into anyone.

He leaned in to speak directly into Dorian's ear in the same manner, though luckily, the DJ commanded a lull in the music in time for his soft voice to be somewhat audible.

"Listen, if we get separated, you meet me back here at three no matter what, got it?"

Dorian took note of his surroundings, and Robert was pleased by the fact that even if he was doubtlessly intoxicated, if not still blacked out, he wasn't entirely without his wits.

"Got it," he said with an added thumbs-up.

"Have fun, just be smart." Robert told him with a wave of his hand. "Follow me, if you'd like."

Dorian, wisely, was not too keen to break from Robert's side at the start of the night. It was not a place for formal introductions, anyway, which took some pressure off both of them. Despite the noise and chaos, the rave-goers were, for the most part, surprisingly courteous.

The lights pulsed a cherry red in time with the music, and the color filtered through a thick haze of flavored smoke. Everyone danced, and no one cared if you were any good at it.

Robert's mind was never quiet. His nervous system—or the saltwater-starved network squirming through his body as substitute—never pacified.

But all of this noise drowned out most of that noise.

He wondered: was it the same sublime effect for Dorian? Robert looked to his right to try and tell, only to find he'd slipped away.

Anxiety tugged momentarily at his chest, and he glanced around the undulated crowd. He spotted Dorian standing against the wall a ways off from the source of the music. He was conversing with a woman who looked like she'd already made up her mind to eat him alive. If this even remotely bothered him, it didn't show.

Anxiety quickly gave way to bemusement. Good for you, he thought as the woman led Dorian out of sight by his tie. You and your penchant for getting into things without understanding them.

He went back to enjoying the EDM, the movement of human and not-so-human bodies around him until the devil's hour came around.

Though Robert had had his doubts, Dorian had miraculously returned to their designated rendezvous spot by the time their watches struck 3am.

Scarlet patches were wiped across his skin from his collarbone to his brow, smeared heavily across his mouth. Blood or lipstick, Robert couldn't tell. He leaned against the bar, transfixed by a fire-dancer on the stage.

Dorian barely noticed Robert's approach, but when he did, he immediately started speaking hurriedly at him. Robert was used to his rapid cadence, and even during auctions, he could make out most of the words. But holy shit.

"Shush," he said after a few seconds, holding up a palm. "I didn't catch a word of that."

Dorian faltered, looked suddenly embarrassed. Robert noticed only the thinnest of gold rings around blown pupils.

"Ah. What'd you take?" Robert asked, tail twitching in amusement.

"I… don't … know," he admitted, staggering his words slowly to overcompensate.

Robert cocked his head. "Pretty girl give it to you?" He guessed teasingly.

Dorian's grin glinted in the rave lights. He was swaying on his feet, and though his gaze was fixed on Robert, it seemed hopelessly unfocused.

"No shame in that." Robert mused. "Are you feeling alright?"

"Yes," he answered quickly. "Too alright. Probably not so alright in the morning."

"Probably not," he chuckled. "Now, what were you saying?"

At this, Dorian went quiet, almost sullen. His gaze went back to the stage, but not to any of the dancers. After several silent seconds, Robert concluded that he'd lost his train of thought. He'd been about to laugh it off and ask something new when Dorian spoke up.

"You know, my father was a singer," he confessed. "Or so I heard growing up. Obviously, he wasn't exactly star material, cause I don't remember him ever making a real living off of it, but I—" his quickening words were cut short when the bartender slid a highball glass across the counter toward him. He stared at in confusion, like he hadn't recalled ordering it.

The admission, meanwhile, caught Robert off guard. What does one say to that? I'm sorry? That's cool? Is that where you get it from? Before he got a chance to work out a response, Dorian said in a brisk, dismissive manner—

"I dunno—I'm tone-deaf. Say, do you want this?" He tried to put the drink in Robert's hand. He took it just so it wouldn't drop.

"… Do you want to stay here longer or go back to the hotel?" Robert asked.

Dorian's answer was instant: "Back. Please."

January 4, 2021

What was the Las Vegas tourist experience if not waking up and immediately vomiting your guts out?

Had he even really slept at all? Or had he just laid in bed and vibrated until the crash hit?

Remnants of wine and dinner came up tasting bitter in Dorian's mouth. His throat burned all the way down, and his head ached in ways he did not know it could ache.

For a while, he just knelt on the tiles, taking stock of his memories. Last night came back in disjointed and water-damaged moments. After that second bottle, it was all black, interrupted by bright flashes in slow-motion. Trying to think about any of it too hard only exacerbated the painful throbbing behind his eyes.

When he could stand again, he forced himself to take a miserably cold shower. Then, he called downstairs to the kitchen and ordered double hash browns and an electrolyte water.

He answered the door in a bathrobe and sunshades, tipping the busboy six hundred dollars in cash. He sat down and devoured his breakfast while attempting to finish the crossword puzzle he'd left out on the table. Rather than answers for any of the remaining clues, his brain provided only a film of static over his thoughts.

Walking back into the bedroom, he found his suit from the night before crumpled on the floor next to his bed. He picked it up and dug around his pockets. The loot consisted of fifty dollars, a black poker chip, someone's phone number on a cocktail napkin, and a pack of Marlboro Reds just one dart short of being empty.

Ugh, Dorian thought, lighting the last cigarette and tossing the carton into the bin along with the napkin. Don't do drugs, kids.

He turned on the TV and flipped it over to the news to let it run as background noise as he went about packing. Luckily, he'd travelled light and hadn't bothered unpacking all that much for his overnight stay, and yet the undertaking seemed impossibly arduous.

When he was done, he took a moment to sit atop his luggage and check his phone. Specifically, his bank account.

The rest of the wire had gone through. Robert had even thrown in a few shares of the relevant oil and gas shell company as gratuity.

So, that's what a human life is worth to us, huh?

He'd done more for less.

Have we?

Without doubt.

Dorian pocketed his phone, did one more pat down—cell, wallet, watch, laptop—and left the room, empty save for the cash tip he'd left on the mantle for housekeeping.

There was still a sinusoidal pulse in his temples by the time he reached the elevator, steadied by the extended handle of his garment bag. He was about to shoot his boss a text about his departure when, as luck would have it, Robert caught him getting into the lift.

"Someone's up early," he said, not bothering to hide his surprise.

"Don't talk to me," Dorian groaned, shaking his head, though making sure to crack a smile to let Robert know his irritability was not personal so much as it was the nasty effects of the comedown.

Robert gave a half-laugh. "How do you feel?"

"Like I just fell from thirty-six stories up," Dorian said dryly. "Gonna grab some Tylenol from the lobby and head out. Give my regards to Ruprecht if you see him." His words, though not slurred, seemed to weigh down his tongue.

"You sure you don't want to stay and rest a bit more first? I don't think our drivers would appreciate you throwing up in the car to the airport."

"Already out of my system. Besides, I just … I've got a flight to catch."

"Flight to catch?" Robert cocked his head. "You flew private—it's not leaving without you."

"Still," Dorian resolved. "Gonna head out." Robert would not try to convince him to stay any longer, thank god.

He bought some painkillers, new cigarettes, and a pack of cherry cough drops at the mini-pharmacy. No luck on finding Dramamine. In hindsight, he could have found something for his nausea if he'd looked harder, but he didn't care. He just wanted to check out of that fucking hotel.

Armed with a black drip coffee from the breakfast buffet, Dorian made it to the valet, then to the airport. He felt the caffeine hit his system, but knew he would be asleep before they were even in the air. The pilot or attendant would probably have to wake him up when they touched down in New York. Should he tell them to go to London, just so he could sleep over the Atlantic? No. Definitely back to New York.

"Good morning, Dorian," the flight attendant greeted him with a sparkling smile. Tracy was in her fifties or sixties, but he would not have guessed if not for her silver hair, braided into a neat crown around her head.

Any time he found himself on a company plane, he wondered how many secrets the carefully selected crew had been privy to. He did his best to stay friendly with them.

"Good morning, miss," he said with a poor attempt at his usual liveliness.

"What? Not your sweetheart today?" He lowered his shades for a painful moment to exaggeratingly look her up and down.

"Looking especially fine in your uniform today, sweetheart." She barked a laugh before batting him lightly on the arm.

"Scoundrel, you," she smiled knowingly as he pushed his sunglasses back over his eyes. "I trust you had a happy birthday."

"Something like that," he said, tucking his briefcase into an overhead compartment before taking a seat on the plush leather couch.

"We have champagne on board for you," she offered, then tilted her head. "And a box of chocolates."

"I think I'll pass," he said with a small smile. "Thank you, though."

"Not even a cough drop?" Lord, had he really burned his voice that much? He didn't even speak all that much compared to a regular auction, but he supposed the chain-smoking hadn't helped matters.

"I think I'm just going to sleep," Dorian admitted. "I'll take you up on the chocolates when we get to Manhattan, though."

"Of course, hun. Enjoy the flight."

She dimmed the lights in the cabin on her way to the cockpit. Dorian laid across the sofa, strapping one of the seatbelts over his waist. Setting his shades on the table, he closed his eyes and felt the plane starting to speed up on the runway.

A lot of emotions and sensations fought for his attention. Not one of them was regret.

Because no way in hell could he regret the bottom line: he was leaving forty million dollars richer than he had arrived.
