[[include :scp-wiki:info:end]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:info-cw]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:sigma-plus]] [[include :scp-wiki:theme:black-diamond]] [[module CSS]] /*     Infinite Riches Theme     [2025 Wikidot Theme]     by Fish^12 */ @import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=STIX+Two+Text:ital,wght@0,400..700;1,400..700&display=swap'); @import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Roboto+Flex:opsz,wght@8..144,100..1000&display=swap'); @import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Zen+Old+Mincho&display=swap'); @import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css?family=EB+Garamond:500&display=swap'); @import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=IM+Fell+French+Canon:ital@0;1&display=swap'); .fancytext { font-family:"EB Garamond"; font-size:120%; } .elevator { font-family:"IM Fell French Canon"; font-size:150%; } [[/module]] [[div class="fancytext"]] + January 3, 2021 Never in his life did he think he would spend his twenty-first birthday on an all-expenses-paid trip to [*https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/what-happens-in-vegas-stays-in-vegas Las Vegas]. Plenty of young men would have killed for that chance. What a thought. . . As Dorian landed, he could imagine how breathtaking the Strip must have appeared at night. However, he arrived in the middle of the afternoon, and those bright lights were muted amid the sand and concrete. He could appreciate what the city stood for. The careless disregard for inhibition, the performance of it all. It seemed every billboard paraded addiction and carnal pleasure with some law and insurance advertisements sprinkled in. The neon frenzy of activity reminded him of home in a way London’s buttoned-up manners couldn’t hold a torch to. Maybe he could have enjoyed himself in a place like this. He might've spent the evening chatting up bartenders and showgirls, tipping them well and giving at least the latter the appreciation of a kindred spirit. Vegas always welcomed new money and pretty words. But despite the calendar date, Dorian Sloan had come to Las Vegas for business, nothing else. By 8pm, he was on the casino floor of the Bellagio hotel. Golden light and luxury glittered around him, sprawling up to high ceilings. The warmth could barely combat the obnoxiously vibrant screens of the slot machines. He heard murmuring, accompanied by the soft slaps and shuffling of cards. A scan of the room confirmed a rumor he'd heard—there were no clocks or windows in sight. Before anything else, Dorian flashed his ID to the tuxedoed staff at the front to prove that, as of today, he was allowed to gamble without supervision or interruption. They looked at his fresh license, then at his Armani attire, before graciously sending him into the casino with happy birthday wishes. He got the same look when he went to trade his one-hundred thousand in cash for chips, though the teller was better at concealing her amusement. No doubt, this hotel has seen countless boys just like him cough up their allowances. But as Dorian stepped onto the smooth paisley carpet, he intended to make money, not burn it. He spotted the man of the hour at the roulette table. As Dorian approached, he saw his target’s face sour with a loss. A shock of worry went through him that Bernard Morris might quit before he reached him, but of course, that wasn’t how gambling addictions worked. Dorian took advantage of the short break and found a spot at the table to the man’s right. He was in his forties, though he wore those years hard. His hairline crept back, and his eyes—narrowed in concentration—sunk into his face, ringed by discoloration. “Forty bands on black,” Dorian said casually, pushing his chips forward, then flashing Morris a smile. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Match me on red. That way, one of us has to win.”[[/span]] “I like the way you think, stranger,” Morris replied, and with no hesitation, made his bet. God had blessed Dorian with a silver tongue, and the devil herself [http://https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/a-wolf-at-the-door had seen fit to hire him for it.] Watching Morris gamble, however, he doubted any anomalous persuasion was needed to make him keep playing. The ball spun, then landed on red. Dorian bit the inside of his cheek, even as he reminded himself that he wasn’t betting with his own money. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“You’re on a roll. You’ve got to go again.”[[/span]] He urged in a velvety voice. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Might as well double it—see what happens.”[[/span]] Even as Dorian declined to repeat his bet, Morris stacked one hundred sixty thousand dollars in chips on the table. Dorian wondered what it meant for him that over the past year, he'd come to see this as a small sum. The man blanched at the loss, almost surprisingly. Panic struck his face like a deer the moment it realizes the car wasn't going to stop. Before Dorian could get a word in—which was not an easy feat—he’d gone all in, moving chips with furious, decisive movements. Lady Luck slighted him once more. The neon light bounced off his glassy, bewildered eyes. How could the bastard possibly be shocked? Dorian was certain that even if he'd grown up with enough funds to spare on blind trust for the odds, he'd still find roulette abhorrently stupid. How could anyone come to Vegas and think they could beat the house? “Holy shit, my wife’s gonna kill me,” Morris said, bringing a hand up to his forehead. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Oh? Why?”[[/span]] He inquired. Morris shook his head, but Dorian leaned forward with a smile. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“C’mon, tell me.”[[/span]] “Because that was my daughter’s tuition," he admitted, trembling. Any scraps of pity and hesitation dissolved instantly. Dorian thought of the little sister he'd be moving into Columbia in a few months' time. For years, he'd pained over how to pay for her education, only to be saved the trouble by his generous employer and her full-ride offer. Meanwhile, here was an executive actively whittling away his progeny's future with each bad bet. His smile and eyes a bit colder now, Dorian clapped Morris’ shoulder.  [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“It’s gonna be okay, man.”[[/span]] “I can go take out more—” He started toward an ATM, but Dorian gently held onto him. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Shh, don’t worry about that now,”[[/span]] Dorian said. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Just follow me, why dontcha?”[[/span]] Supplemented by a small beckoning motion of his hand, Dorian had Morris trailing on his heels out of the casino in a devastated trance. “Where are we going?” Each of Morris' steps seemed to catch a fall, and Dorian half-wondered if he'd been drinking, or if he was simply weighed down by the consequences of his actions.  [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Oh, just upstairs.”[[/span]] Dorian said, subtly glancing around to make sure no one was paying attention to their exit. All clear. “Your room?” Morris asked, some skepticism slipping into his voice.  [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“No, you’re not really my type, sorry. But that’s okay. We’re still gonna spend the evening together. You seem like you could use a friend right now. Right this way. I promise, you’ll feel a lot better soon.”[[/span]] They stepped into the elevator, wooden doors closing them in. The rest of the walls were panelled with mirrors, reflecting this damning exchange back at Dorian in his periphery. For this reason, among others, he appreciated the high-speed design. “Bernard Morris, right?" Dorian asked. The last thing he needed was to show up with the wrong guy. “Yes,” he paled, blinking as if waking up, if only for a moment. “How did you—” The elevator dinged softly, the small box with the floor number lighting up: [[/div]] [[div class="elevator"]] [[=]] //2// [[/=]] [[/div]] [[div class="fancytext"]] [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“You know, when I first heard your name, I thought it sounded familiar,"[[/span]] he said.  [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]"You were in London last month, weren’t you? And while you were, you made some people upset. You do a lot of that, don’t you? Your wife, your brothers, your father, your bosses—” [[/span]] “Did Carter send you?” Morris’ voice quivered like a scared child, almost failing him. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Oh, sweetheart, what makes you think you get to ask me questions?”[[/span]] Dorian purred. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Now, quit interrupting me. What did you think was going to happen?”[[/span]] [[/div]] [[div class="elevator"]] [[=]] //9// [[/=]] [[/div]] [[div class="fancytext"]] [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Here's how this works: you're not going to speak, sure as hell not going to scream, and above all, you're not going to move unless I tell you specifically. Do we understand each other? Nod if yes." [[/span]] Morris nodded mechanically as tears welled up along the bottom of his sky-blue eyes. //"Please,"// he mouthed. //"I'll pay."// [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]"Oh, please, we both know you can't afford me."[[/span]] Dorian said. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]] "But that you offered doesn't shock me. You couldn't even afford that oil painting you won at my auction in London last month. I remember—it was this beautiful Veskoti, and yet, you threw a fit when the house told you that you couldn't return it. Don’t you know that Sotheby’s doesn’t do refunds?" [[/span]] Dorian watched a shudder go through Morris as he realized he recognized the voice from the show. He closed his eyes, a silent string of words falling from his lips. A prayer? A curse? An accusation? Dorian didn't care to speculate. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]"We thought it was odd behavior, of course—why wouldn't an oil exec be able to afford a painting? So we checked your books, and what do we find, if not good, old-fashioned embezzlement? What nerve, to cry about how you can’t afford what we’ve charged you, just to come here and blow at least five times that. That wasn’t your money to throw onto the pyre, you know."[[/span]] The Carters made it clear to Dorian that they couldn't have cared less about Morris' behavior or proclivities. Actively chipping away at their bottom line, however, was inexcusable. One way or another, his bosses would always get their pound of flesh. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]"Settling your gambling debts with more gambling is foolish enough, but to think you could do so in this god-forsaken city without the Carters finding out? The bill always comes around at the end, Mr. Morris. Tonight, I’m your debt collector. It’s nothing personal."[[/span]] He frantically shook his head, but it didn't matter. [[/div]] [[div class="elevator"]] [[=]] //17// [[/=]] [[/div]] [[div class="fancytext"]] [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Myself, it’s my first time in Vegas. Lovely city you’ve got here, not that you’re a native either. I’m sure natives must have even less pity for gamblers than I do. That's wise of 'em. No one beats the odds. Those who do get kicked out for playing the game too well. The house didn't gamble, and anyone who understands an inkling about profit would understand that. But people just love to play the wrong games with the wrong people and still want to be shocked when they win stupid prizes? Ridiculous.”[[/span]] It didn’t matter what he said, just that he kept speaking. Just so long as his words continued to worm into his quarry’s ears and head. Morris stared straight ahead, body rigid. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“I mean, I told my boss just this week that if I wanted to risk my life savings on red and black, I’d rather just do it at the New York Stock Exchange. I mean, that’s the gambling capital of the world right there. Not that I don’t invest, of course, but blackjack doesn’t pay dividends, does it? Suppose it doesn’t have bubbles, either, though, so pick your poison, right?”[[/span]] [[/div]] [[div class="elevator"]] [[=]] //23// [[/=]] [[/div]] [[div class="fancytext"]] [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“That’s one of the reasons suicide is astonishingly common in the City. It’s practically a plague among investors. A few bad bets or a crash will ruin you. Sometimes the only way to cut your losses is to end it all before you have to live with being broke. You understand, don’t you? All too well. It helps that we’ve got all those bridges and skyscrapers everywhere. Makes killing yourself a rather scenic event.”[[/span]] [[/div]] [[div class="elevator"]] [[=]] //26// [[/=]] [[/div]] [[div class="fancytext"]] A small sob choked out of Morris as he tried to tell Dorian he didn't want to die. None of them ever did, naturally. Dorian reminded himself that it didn't matter to him. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“No fancy high-rises for me, though! No corner offices or framed diplomas. No class rings to do my networking for me. I was raised by the rats in the sewers of the FiDi.”[[/span]] In recent months, Dorian had found plenty of joy in telling everyone a different version of the truth. This was closer than most. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“And when I was offered a chance to be dragged up in the world for the price of a soul and a silver tongue, how could I have refused?”[[/span]] [[/div]] [[div class="elevator"]] [[=]] //29// [[/=]] [[/div]] [[div class="fancytext"]] [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“But you—you seem like the kind of guy under the impression that everything in the world is yours for the taking. Are all oil brats like that, or are you just especially stupid? The inheritors of the world were determined long before we entered the scene. The more time I spend in this role, the more I realize it’s just the six of them and all the rest of us. Ants unto them in their castles in the sky.”[[/span]] Dorian smiled and winked as if letting him in on a secret. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“That’s not to say I don’t prefer being a well-paid drone to being thrown off the side of that ivory tower.”[[/span]] [[/div]] [[div class="elevator"]] [[=]] //34// [[/=]] [[/div]] [[div class="fancytext"]] At the end of the day, the decision between death and wealth had never been difficult for Dorian, no matter how grisly the job could get. Morris swayed on his feet, tears fully falling in fat droplets down ruddy cheeks. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Ah, finally! Here we are. Thank you for indulging me, Mr. Morris. You’ve been wonderful company on the long ride up, but our time together is almost at an end. Now, this door is going to open, and you’re going to follow me out, because the very least you can do after wrecking your life is be cooperative.”[[/span]] [[/div]] [[div class="elevator"]] [[=]] //36// [[/=]] [[/div]] [[div class="fancytext"]] A string of chanted instructions like [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]//come on//[[/span]], and [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]//one step, two step, one step—//[[/span]] left him in a comfortable auction chant. He’d stopped bothering trying to estimate the speed of his words, though he knew the elevator ride could not have lasted more than a minute. Through the unadorned concrete halls, the staff staircase, and the fire escape, they went. The keycard the Carters had given him did its job without a hitch. At last, he reached and unlocked the final maintenance door to the rooftop. Both Carters were already up there waiting. Their only job for this part had been to ensure no one else was. Dorian ignored them both, too focused on Morris, who seemed like a zombie already. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Oh, one more thing before you go,”[[/span]] Dorian added, recalling Ruprecht’s special request with a snap of his fingers. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Who wears velvet suits? And in the middle of the desert in August? Not that it would be less hideous any other time of the year, but then maybe it’d be practical. Take that ugly shit off.”[[/span]] One by one, articles of clothing fell to the floor until Morris stood there shivering in his undergarments. Dorian would have done this earlier, but he hadn’t wanted to leave the clothes in the elevator, and Ruprecht seemed to delight in seeing the spectacle as it occurred. Dorian could think of at least a hundred more economical ways to assassinate a man than this—none, apparently, matched this entertainment value. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Good boy,”[[/span]] Dorian said patronizingly. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“Now, the rest of it.”[[/span]] Morris stepped out of boxers. Ruprecht started to laugh, but Robert swatted him quickly with his tail, as if worried any noise would risk ruining the spell. But Dorian knew Morris was too entrenched for that, and as fun as that last bit had been, he was ready to get this over with. [[span style="color:#DAA520;"]]“This is a tall building. I wonder if you’ll hit terminal velocity on the way down. I hear it’s euphoric, falling like that. It’s why people decide they want to live halfway down. But not you. You want to fall. Isn’t it funny, how badly you want to? Why shouldn’t you want to die? I would want to die if I were you. So, first, you’re going to climb up there—there you go, grab the rails. Great! Just a bit further, don't be afraid of the edge—and off you go.”[[/span]] Morris’ feet scraped across the shingles. Then his body folded forward and disappeared. He heard the low //whoosh// getting quieter until— //Thump.// Even in his numbness, the combination of blunt impact and shattering bones created a distinctly unpleasant sound. After a stretch of silence, a satisfied chuckle bubbling up from Robert’s chest. His tail swayed in content as he approached the edge, reaching up to grab the rails so he could hoist himself up and peer over the North-West side of the building. The tail's swishing sped up with the delight of seeing Morris' body on the ground. “Dead?” Ruprecht asked. “Very,” Robert replied, pulling back so as not to be spotted. “Dorian, my boy, you’ve just made an old man’s week,” Ruprecht said with a laugh, clapping his shoulder so hard that his body rocked. “Thank you, sir,” he smiled. “I’ll have the second half of your payment wired to you by morning,” he said. “In the meantime, the least I can do is treat you to dinner. We ought to celebrate a job so well //executed//.” He seemed exceptionally proud of that pun. “Maybe we should go back inside, then,” Dorian suggested. The wind roared in his ears up here. “I think the bar’s still serving.” “No, that won’t do. The food here is overrated,” Ruprecht said dismissively. “Besides, it’s your first time in Las Vegas, is it not? We’ve got to make a better impression than that.” He paused, though started up again right as Robert went to give a suggestion. “Does Harlo still have those caviar tacos?” “I’m sure,” Robert replied. “Though they’re closed by now.” “Closed?” Ruprecht laughed. “Perfect! No other customers to worry about.” As they walked back inside, he casually rang up the owner and asked for a private dining room. Robert leaned over to Dorian and said in a low voice: “Well, that was relatively painless, all things considered." “Agreed," Dorian murmured. He felt Robert’s gaze scrutinizing him, despite a lack of expression. "Are you okay?" "Oh, yeah," Dorian said, bringing his fingertips to his throat. "Just need a glass of water." “Pfh— //wooder//,” Robert playfully mocked his accent. “//Wawtur//,” Dorian replied in a mimicry of the posh British pronunciation. "Kiya aap majhe abhi kapi kar sakte hen?[[footnote]] Urdu - Can you copy me now? [[/footnote]]" The headfirst switch into his mother tongue gave a quickness and comfort to his quiet words. It made Dorian wish he had a better reply to the retort than— "Huh?" Oh well. Within ten minutes, Dorian was sipping Fiji water in the backseat of a Cadillac with Robert to his left. Ruprecht sat shotgun, chatting familiarly with the driver the whole way to the restaurant. No one acknowledged the three SUVs of bodyguards that tailed them the whole way. Dorian preferred the condition of motion to the alternative of stillness. The last thing he wanted to do right now was sit around in a hotel room. Unfortunately, the second to last thing he wanted to do was any more speaking. With Chrysophilius, it was easy to get him started on a topic, allowing Dorian to sit back and listen to him ramble. Robert, however, was considerably quieter. The ability to shut up and listen was respectable in a businessman, but it meant Dorian couldn’t easily get him started on a tangent about oil or occultism. Prior to his employment, Dorian’s knowledge of the energy industry had been limited to a few stock pitches—better than his nonexistent awareness of magic at large. Still, he understood the breadth of power that came with Robert holding most of the world’s cartels on strings. As Robert stared melancholically out the window at the night passing them by, Dorian took the cue to simply put his head to the warm glass and do the same. “Dorian, don’t tell me Robert’s rubbing off on you,” Ruprecht said with a huff. “I can’t send you back to the Marshalls so mopey.” Robert blatantly ignored this shot, and Dorian felt an obligation to respond in this case. “No sir," Dorian replied. "Jet lag, sorry." “Mm.” Ruprecht seemed to take this explanation. “Well, that's understandable. Still, here I was thinking kids your age never ran out of energy! Well, you'll feel better after a proper meal." "Yes, I'm sure that's it," he said. "Thank you, sir." "Thank me? For what?" Ruprecht laughed, shaking his head. "I swear, I can't imagine how you've kept any manners about you, given how much time you spend with Chrysophilius—oh, I need to take this." //Someone's found the body.// The thought seized Dorian with more abruptness than he'd been prepared for. As he listened, however, he realized it was nothing of the sort. Some real estate deal, a lawyer dragging his feet. . . Dorian couldn't hash out all the details, just that it upset Ruprecht enough that he was shouting into his phone the rest of the way to the restaurant. "Call me back when your head finds its way out of your arse." The call ended, and he let out a heavy sigh before his voice suddenly resumed its previous jollity. "Let's go in, shall we?" They left the car with the valet and made their way inside the closed restaurant. If the hostess was upset at having to stay late, she didn't let it show. Chances were the staff all knew they were being tipped well for their time. She brought them to their booth—a cushioned semi-circle the color of warm caramel around a table draped in starched ivory cloth. Dorian wasn't sure how he ended up in the middle, but he cared little about the seating arrangement. They were automatically brought waters by a waitress. "Can I start you gentlemen off with any other drinks? Appetizers?" Her voice had a slight fry, and her dark hair was swept out of her face in twin braids. "I'll take a daiquiri," Ruprecht said firmly. "And—Dorian, you're a caviar fan, yes?" "For sure," he replied. As some sort of sick joke, Dorian could have eaten the stupidly expensive black beads for every meal and not gotten sick of them. A few months ago, he’d done just that for a week after finding himself at a loss at what else to do with his commission payout from a lucrative art auction. Funny how expensive tastes can become affordable overnight. "We'll do one of each of your caviar bites for the table," Ruprecht told the waitress. "Of course, wonderful choice. For you, sir?" “Have you got hot tea with honey?” Dorian requested. “Yes sir,” the waitress replied. “Do you have a preference? We have green, jasmine—" “Jasmine’s perfect. Put a splash of bourbon in that, and keep them coming, please.” Robert tried to order, but was interrupted by Ruprecht. “Tea in Vegas,” Ruprecht mused, shaking his head. “Though I suppose it still counts as a cocktail.” Robert sighed quietly in annoyance. He tried again, only for Ruprecht to suddenly remember something else. "Wait! Aren't you going to ID the young man?" He said too enthusiastically, waving toward Dorian. The waitress, a bit confused, played along. Dorian smiled indulgently, taking out his wallet and  passing her a newly minted card. Her eyes lit up. "Happy birthday!" "Thank you," he said softly. A free dessert was in order, if he had to guess. "I think we should sing," Ruprecht declared. Dorian grit his teeth and patiently bore through being serenaded for about ten seconds. When it was over, Robert at last managed to send the waitress away with an order for a Tito's and soda. "Now, Dorian," Ruprecht continued, "I'm hardly one to judge a man for his tastes, and of course, any time is tea time in London, but I maintain that that's an odd cocktail. Some New York delicacy I'm missing out on?" Dorian shrugged with a small laugh. “More remedy than cocktail. It's for my voice. A cough drop would work about the same." “Ah," Ruprecht replied, "So there are adverse effects." He leaned back with his hands on his stomach. “Of course,” Dorian said, “but it’s not much of a price to pay, and a cheap fix at that.” “Hmm. . .” Ruprecht studied him for a moment before his eyes glittered with a more morbid curiosity. “Tell me, my boy, what’s the worst thing you’ve ever done with that silver tongue of yours?” The question made his skin crawl. “Talked rich folks into buying drinks for me,” he lied, flashing a smile as he raised his water glass to Ruprecht. He gave a hearty laugh, and Dorian hoped the joke would satisfy him for an answer. No such luck. Ruprecht cocked his head. "What about what Percival's tasked you with?" Dorian suddenly went very still, the smile on his lips leaving like the flame of a snuffed-out candle. "You would sit here and ask me to spill a dead man's secrets?" A silent beat passed before Ruprecht laughed again, as if there had been any joke made at all. "You're impressively tight-lipped for someone we pay to run his mouth," he said, still wearing a friendly smile. "So then, what about before we hired you? It's not as if you discovered your abilities only once we started paying you for them." Dorian knew he would not go without hearing some grizzly answer or another. He stared contemplatively at his place settings. A hundred incidents of dubious moral standing occurred to him, but everything paled in comparison to what he’d done in the past year. “Every day, I went to work and committed daylight robbery," he replied. "And every day, I called it sales." “Oh, don’t get coy with me, Dorian. Secrets are no fun, you know." The last thing Dorian wanted to do was upset Ruprecht, but that didn't mean he wanted to provide a wealth of information, either. For one, he didn't want to betray the confidence of his other bosses, but on a more selfish note, he just didn't want to hear his deeds relayed back to him in gibes and jokes moving forward. “Dad—” Robert interjected. Dorian suddenly realized how stiff he was in his seat. "Come now, it’s just us,” Ruprecht continued to press. “And cocktail hour is the best place for stories!" For a split second, Dorian was thirteen again, squaring up with a brat twice his size trying to take his older sister for a ride. He heard the crack of him breaking his own nose when Dorian said he should. It overlapped with the sound of Morris' body landing at the base of the Bellagio. “Fine, fine, I’ve got one for you,” Dorian relented to ease the tension. "Maybe you hoped for something grizzlier, but I think you'll still appreciate this. So, I used to go to a lot of open houses. Free food, and during the summers, free AC." Ruprecht furrowed his brow. "Anyone can walk into an open house. That's why they're open." "That's how it started," Dorian said. "But there was one summer where I just started doing all kinds of shit to see what I could get away with. I'd tell people I was a real estate agent, or that I was on lists to view properties. It's one thing to observe how wealthy people act over dinner, but I considered this practice, in a way." "Well, I'd say it paid off," Ruprecht said in mild amusement. "Yes, it did," Dorian agreed. "Except that I tried to go to an open house in Tribeca last month to kill time, and the agent recognized me and kicked me out at the door." "He did?!" Ruprecht looked as angry as he was appalled, and Dorian was suddenly worried he'd just sentenced some real estate agent to death. "That's unacceptable." "No, not really," he grinned at the memory. "The last time he saw me, I snuck out of the place with about ten croissants in my jacket." Ruprecht gave another boisterous laugh, though it quieted as his eyes settled on his son across the table. "Robert, it's terribly rude to be on your phone at dinner," he said playfully. Dorian could hear the tension in the quiet inhale, the noise softly mechanical as the air moved through the gas mask's filters. "The world doesn't stop just because we're at dinner," Robert replied, his voice even despite any irritation. "What's happened?" Ruprecht asked as their waitress unobtrusively brought their drinks. "Just had to shut down a rig down in Texas," he answered vaguely. "Fluid backflow." Ruprecht's eyes widened. "Sabotage?" "Worse. Plain human error." "Doesn't matter to the bottom line, does it?" Ruprecht said. "No," Robert agreed. "No, it doesn't—but the demons are eager to clean this one up for free." By the time Dorian had been thrown that particular curveball, the existence of the demonic hadn't even been remotely surprising. He actually wondered if he'd meet some more of them while here in Sin City. "Ah, you'll get it handled," Ruprecht said in a manner that towed the line between encouraging and dismissive, lifting his drink as to Robert as he said so. "Always so efficient at handling things, this one. I mean, take today's stunt, for example." Neither of them knew how to respond to this. Robert muttered something like a thanks and went back to silently typing, and when the waitress brought their appetizers, Dorian was quick to swipe a caviar latke so he had at least had an excuse not to speak. "On that," Ruprecht said, "any calls about Morris yet?" //Thump.// Dorian heard it again. 200 pounds of meat hitting asphalt. Bones snapping like pencils. Obviously, he wasn't exactly star material, cause I don't remember him ever making a real living off of it, but I—" his quickening words were cut short when the bartender slid a highball glass across the counter toward him. He stared at in confusion, like he hadn't recalled ordering it. The admission, meanwhile, caught Robert off guard. What does one say to that? //I'm sorry?// //That's cool?// //Is that where you get it from?// Before he got a chance to work out a response, Dorian said in a brisk, dismissive manner— "I dunno—I'm tone-deaf. Say, do you want this?" He tried to put the drink in Robert's hand. He took it just so it wouldn't drop. ". . . Do you want to stay here longer or go back to the hotel?" Robert asked. Dorian's answer was instant: "Back. Please." + January 4, 2021 What was the Las Vegas tourist experience if not waking up and immediately vomiting your guts out? Had he even really slept at all? Or had he just laid in bed and vibrated until the crash hit? Remnants of wine and dinner came up tasting bitter in Dorian's mouth. His throat burned all the way down, and his head ached in ways he did not know it could ache. For a while, he just knelt on the tiles, taking stock of his memories. Last night came back in disjointed and water-damaged moments. After that second bottle, it was all black, interrupted by bright flashes in slow-motion. Trying to think about any of it too hard only exacerbated the painful throbbing behind his eyes. When he could stand again, he forced himself to take a miserably cold shower. Then, he called downstairs to the kitchen and ordered double hash browns and an electrolyte water. He answered the door in a bathrobe and sunshades, tipping the busboy six hundred dollars in cash. He sat down and devoured his breakfast while attempting to finish the crossword puzzle he'd left out on the table. Rather than answers for any of the remaining clues, his brain provided only a film of static over his thoughts. Walking back into the bedroom, he found his suit from the night before crumpled on the floor next to his bed. He picked it up and dug around his pockets. The loot consisted of fifty dollars, a black poker chip, someone's phone number on a cocktail napkin, and a pack of Marlboro Reds just one dart short of being empty. //Ugh,// Dorian thought, lighting the last cigarette and tossing the carton into the bin along with the napkin. //Don't do drugs, kids.// He turned on the TV and flipped it over to the news to let it run as background noise as he went about packing. Luckily, he'd travelled light and hadn't bothered unpacking all that much for his overnight stay, and yet the undertaking seemed impossibly arduous. When he was done, he took a moment to sit atop his luggage and check his phone. Specifically, his bank account. The rest of the wire had gone through. Robert had even thrown in a few shares of the relevant oil and gas shell company as gratuity. //So, that's what a human life is worth to us, huh?// He'd done more for less. //Have we?// Without doubt. Dorian pocketed his phone, did one more pat down—cell, wallet, watch, laptop—and left the room, empty save for the cash tip he'd left on the mantle for housekeeping. There was still a sinusoidal pulse in his temples by the time he reached the elevator, steadied by the extended handle of his garment bag. He was about to shoot his boss a text about his departure when, as luck would have it, Robert caught him getting into the lift. "Someone's up early," he said, not bothering to hide his surprise. "Don't talk to me," Dorian groaned, shaking his head, though making sure to crack a smile to let Robert know his irritability  was not personal so much as it was the nasty effects of the comedown. Robert gave a half-laugh. "How do you feel?" "Like I just fell from thirty-six stories up," Dorian said dryly. "Gonna grab some Tylenol from the lobby and head out. Give my regards to Ruprecht if you see him." His words, though not slurred, seemed to weigh down his tongue. "You sure you don't want to stay and rest a bit more first? I don't think our drivers would appreciate you throwing up in the car to the airport." "Already out of my system. Besides, I just . . . I've got a flight to catch." "Flight to catch?" Robert cocked his head. "You flew private—it's not leaving without you." "Still," Dorian resolved. "Gonna head out." Robert would not try to convince him to stay any longer, thank god. He bought some painkillers, new cigarettes, and a pack of cherry cough drops at the mini-pharmacy. No luck on finding Dramamine. In hindsight, he could have found something for his nausea if he'd looked harder, but he didn't care. He just wanted to check out of that fucking hotel. Armed with a black drip coffee from the breakfast buffet, Dorian made it to the valet, then to the airport. He felt the caffeine hit his system, but knew he would be asleep before they were even in the air. The pilot or attendant would probably have to wake him up when they touched down in New York. Should he tell them to go to London, just so he could sleep over the Atlantic? No. Definitely back to New York. "Good morning, Dorian," the flight attendant greeted him with a sparkling smile. Tracy was in her fifties or sixties, but he would not have guessed if not for her silver hair, braided into a neat crown around her head. Any time he found himself on a company plane, he wondered how many secrets the carefully selected crew had been privy to. He did his best to stay friendly with them. "Good morning, miss," he said with a poor attempt at his usual liveliness. "What? Not your sweetheart today?" He lowered his shades for a painful moment to exaggeratingly look her up and down. "Looking especially fine in your uniform today, sweetheart." She barked a laugh before batting him lightly on the arm. "Scoundrel, you," she smiled knowingly as he pushed his sunglasses back over his eyes. "I trust you had a happy birthday." "Something like that," he said, tucking his briefcase into an overhead compartment before taking a seat on the plush leather couch. "We have champagne on board for you," she offered, then tilted her head. "And a box of chocolates." "I think I'll pass," he said with a small smile. "Thank you, though." "Not even a cough drop?" Lord, had he really burned his voice that much? He didn't even speak all that much compared to a regular auction, but he supposed the chain-smoking hadn't helped matters. "I think I'm just going to sleep," Dorian admitted. "I'll take you up on the chocolates when we get to Manhattan, though." "Of course, hun. Enjoy the flight." She dimmed the lights in the cabin on her way to the cockpit. Dorian laid across the sofa, strapping one of the seatbelts over his waist. Setting his shades on the table, he closed his eyes and felt the plane starting to speed up on the runway. A lot of emotions and sensations fought for his attention. Not one of them was regret. Because no way in hell could he regret the bottom line: he was leaving forty million dollars richer than he had arrived. [[/div]]

queen-of-sheboygan.raw_content:
"What's your name? Where are your parents?"
"It's a party," she repeats.

"What's your name? Where are your parents?"
"It's a party," she repeats.



The Queen Of Sheboygan


I fall out into the half-light, confused. Although I'm not blind the crumbled walls and faded half-signs my eyes fall on tell me nothing. I search for context in my memories but find a dreadfully inchoate sensation, as if clawing at dreams.

I see, caught in a ray of honey-colored light, a small, singular figure, potentially human. Coming closer I make out a child, dancing alone on the broken flagstones. She is wrapped in layers of cloth, a swaddling of soft fleece blankets, embroidered quilts, and what might be real, heavy furs. These loop even around the top of her witch-like, uncombed hair, drape over her skinny outstretched arms that wiggle in the ecstatic dance, giving her the solemn dignity of a veiled Mahadevi.

I approach, unsure of my place. The child has no such reservations.

Her gait as she comes close is bird-like, hopping along on the balls of her feet. Her eyes are bright and keen beneath the makeshift headscarf, staring into mine before darting away. She chirps loudly, “I am the Queeeen of Sheboygan!” Drawing it out proudly, looking quickly to me for confirmation. I am struck by how bizarre it is that this is what she cares about, in the midst of this rubble. Am I dreaming after all?

“No, you aren’t,” I say, chiding her, but playfully. Her reaction is strong and immediate: she screams, sounding not like a person in distress but like a screeching tea kettle. I clap my hands over my ears, my eyes watering as I feel a migraine coming on. The scene wavers in front of me. But instead of what should follow, the flashing lights, the pain, there is nothing. Not even the blackness you see behind your eyelids, or the sensation of falling asleep.



An overgrown pagoda on stilts, used as a shelter by the Queen.
✖




God, am I unwell, comatose, piecing these images together? No, apparently not comatose, because there is again a world. When I next claim consciousness she is staring at me, dirty face inches from mine. She is older than she first looked, maybe ten or twelve, but small for her age.

I sit up, and she falls backwards onto her hands, crawling away in a hurried crabwalk. In the layers of fuzzy blankets she resembles a colorful caterpillar, only her face peeking out. She thumps down cross-legged on the ground, gazing off imperiously into the distance.

I am the first one to speak. "What happened here? Where is everybody?"

The Queen thinks about it, her brow wrinkling. She opens and closes her mouth, then abandons the effort. Finally she takes a scrap of paper from the ground and folds it into a hat, her small fingers carefully smoothing the folds, and places it on my head. "Don't be sad," she tells me solemnly. "It's a party."

"What's your name? Where are your parents?"

"It's a party," she repeats. "It's a party." Her expression is unconcerned as she stands and skips away. The breeze is picking up, and scraps of paper swirl around her like confetti.



A television sits in an abandoned intersection, playing cartoons.
✖



I wander through a world that seems abandoned. Numb, but cataloguing. The Queen doesn’t seem to mind when I go off on my own — sometimes I think she forgets I exist.

It’s quicker to list what’s left.

1. Paper. All colors, in boxes, flying loose on the streets, folded into origami. I'm glad I can write down my thoughts, it helps me organize what I do remember. The Queen doesn't understand why I keep a journal, but she finds me incomprehensible in general.

2. Birds. Not only the birds in the sky, some of the paper lying around the streets has been folded into origami birds. It’s not that crane you think of right away; it's a different one, a crow. I’ve been unfolding the pattern to procure paper, and only needed to see it twice to remember how to make one. I have a feeling that might be useful.

3. Sugar. Someone has a sweet tooth. All kinds of buildings have fallen down — schools, banks, government buildings, even grocery stores — but bakeries and ice cream stores are just fine.

4. Cartoons. Working televisions stand among the rubble, broadcasting the same few cartoons repeatedly. I think there's something off about the scripts (they keep repeating the same lines back to each other) but maybe that's what cartoons are like these days.

5. Rubble and ruins. Lots of fragments of plastic and stone. The city I remember Sheboygan being is hard to credit: was it that bright, that loud, that full of life? It seems too strange to be real, but I miss it too much for it to be imagined.

6. Ecological balance. For everything that's missing it's not as off as it should be. How did only the birds survive what happened? (And what happened??) Even the birds are changed somehow, evolved maybe; I just realized they're quieter. Haven't woken me up once. I would do a better survey of the environment if I had a drone, but besides the TVs and fridges the highest tech around seems to be the lighter I use for campfires.

7. The Queen of Sheboygan. (Are we the only people left?)

Once, I hiked as far as Lincoln Park Zoo to see what animals had survived. Days of traveling over cracked roads devoid of the rusting hulks of cars. There was nothing there but empty cages pulled apart by vines, not even bones for the birds to pick at. I wonder what it is they eat: they don't like ice cream. Maybe it's each other.

It's a good thing the Queen likes sweets.



Figures found in a garden. Too small to be human bodies.
✖



It’s all a bit unreal, what’s left, like a painting of itself. I noticed it first with the ice cream: it’s a perfect spiral on top of the waffle cone. And it's this uncanny color — almost too pretty to eat. It's the same color as the sky, which is never bright or dark.

There’s something else about the ice cream, something about how it doesn’t change even though it’s usually warm here. The Queen doesn’t like getting sticky… and she doesn't like change. But how do I know that?

It’s not always warm here. It can be cold when the wind is blowing, and you’re wet. The Queen doesn’t like getting wet. I know that much because I saw it.

I saw her swimming once, in the great violet body of water beside the shore where the seabirds peck. It is not the ocean; the taste is sour but not salty, though the waves are high. I glimpsed her little face between one wave and the next, thinking at first the water had taken her. But of course she was exactly where she wanted to be.

She had gone swimming in all her clothes, the layers of cloth trailing like the fins of tropical fish when she paddled. Her expression was much unchanged from usual, serene but serious. I waited for her to be ready to hold court.

Once she had returned to the shallows where she could walk the Queen trudged grandly towards me, nodding twice as she sometimes does to acknowledge my existence. But she stopped suddenly, shivering and scrunching her face in distress. She plucked at the wet cloth wrapped around her shoulders, her breathing rapid and agitated.

I don’t remember how I got over to her so quickly, maybe I ran. I don’t think I would have rushed her. But I was there next to her, kneeling so I wasn't looming over her, offering her the warm blanket I was wearing around my own shoulders. Patting her face with it to get her attention.

“Here,” I said, “Let’s get dry.”

The Queen bared her teeth in a grimace, looking not at me but through me. She thrashed wildly, limbs windmilling, but I wasn't trying to grab her: I had ducked backwards to give her more space, she was fighting air. Finding herself still wet, she shrieked piteously, throwing herself to the ground, and flailed everything. Her face was bright red from the effort of her despair.

She reached for me and I heard what she was asking, giving her my outstretched hand to hold. That calmed her enough that I heard her muttering under her breath. I leaned in a bit, enough to hear her saying, "Dry. Dry. Get dry." There was a smell in the air like lightning, like petrichor, like a young storm finding its feet. A sonic thunderclap followed that made both of us reach for our ears, failing because we were still holding hands, and -

-And everything was dry. Her hair and robes steamed lightly in wisps. The bed that had once held Sheboygan Lake (how did I forget, of course it was Sheboygan Lake) was as empty as a tooth socket.

The Queen caught her breath, then exhaled slowly and relaxed her shoulders. She was unsmiling when she looked back in my direction, so maybe I was only imagining the satisfaction I read on her face. “I don’t like swimming,” she informed me.

“Oh?” I asked. “It looked like you were having fun in the water.”

She considered this gravely, and announced, “I like water. I don’t like wet.” She shrugged elaborately. “I am never ever trying that again!”

“Well,” I cajoled, “maybe you can try again another day.” Quickly, the double nod.

“Again another day.” I got the sense that she was happy with me. But I did not see her or the lake again for days.



A beach with birds. The sky is the color of ice cream.
✖



I started thinking today: why me? Why am I left? It can’t be random. This isn’t luck. What is different about me?

I cannot remember. There is almost certainly a reason why. But I can work out a theory.

I am a logical person. In her way, so is the Queen. So this is a trait about me she may appreciate. The things remaining in this world have a common feature: they are things she may appreciate.

The Queen likes me. But does not like me to remember why.

I think….

I might have taught her how to fold a paper crow. Is that how I met her? Was I a teacher?

The birds are very quiet over the beach today, and the ice cream is sweet and wonderful. All is right in the Kingdom of Sheboygan. Hail to the Queen.

qusbbxbjqiuakskmz.raw_content:
1. Scarlet King was once bitten by Nahash the Serpent; after seven whole excruciating days, Nahash died.
  2. Scarlet King once wanted to count for SCP-033 seconds and sneeze; it had scared SCP-033 to the point of deleting itself.
  3. Scarlet King stared at Pattern Screamer once for him being too noisy; in light of this, Pattern Screamer invented π and hid himself in its last digit.
  4. The Cosmic Starfish had been terrestrial before Scarlet King ridded him into the ocean.
  5. There is no Foundation database, just a list of anomalies Scarlet King allows to live.
  6. To make interaction between SCP-055 and SCP-579 is essentially to make a phone call to Scarlet King.
  7. SCP-2845 had been the most intelligent creature in the universe before he began pondering the weaknesses of Scarlet King.
  8. Scarlet King changes his horns twice a year.
  9. Mekhane once challenged Scarlet King for having the slimest build; the Broken God won in the end.
  10. Scarlet King is red.
  11. It's believed that SCP-500 is made of Scarlet King's tears, albeit he never cries.
  12. Scarlet King has seven to the seventh power ways to destroy the world, but he usually only uses the first one — getting up on the wrong side of the bed.
  13. The brides of Scarlet King were chosen in an audition on a multiversal online dating site.
  14. The seven King's Spears are actually Scarlet King's toothpicks.
  15. Antimemes exist because they're afraid of being memorized by Scarlet King.
  16. Scarlet King has vowed to destroy the Tree of Knowledge for it blocked the sight between himself and Sanna.
  17. The word "normalcy" means "Scarlet King doesn't give a fuck".
  18. Yaldabaoth is an escapee from Scarlet King's breakfast.
  19. The Two Trees of Valinor were grown out of the two horns of Scarlet King.
  20. Scarlet King praises Procedure 110-Montauk for being a great ASMR for sleep.
  21. The devouring of Scarlet King's brother has been recorded by historians as the first family dinner in the history.
  22. Scarlet King leaves those six chains of SCP-2317 broken because he thinks that's more fashionable.
  23. Scarlet King is an official unit used by the Foundation; 1 Scarlet King = ∞ XK end-of-the-world scenarios.
  24. In Scarlet King's eyes, "Special Containment Procedures" means gift boxes waiting for him to open.
  25. Scarlet King doesn't exist; he only allows "existence" to exist so that he gets a place to put his little crown down.
  26. Scarlet King has deleted all weekdays between Sunday and Monday.
  27. Scarlet King prefers strawberry pudding to screaming souls and fresh blood.
  28. Scarlet King once ordered a cup of SCP-3999 via SCP-294, then drank the cup and left the content intact.
  29. Cosmic microwave background is just the snores of Scarlet King.
  30. Scarlet King keeps the other half of SCP-529 as his pet.
  31. The reason for all lives to exist is a joke made by Scarlet King; all their hearts have to laugh until they die.
  32. Scarlet King doesn't need concepts; concepts need Scarlet King.
  33. This is Scarlet King's favorite joke: Knock Knock! — Who's there? — Whoever he is, he's not your brother.
  34. Scarlet King turns a random concept red whenever he yawns.
  35. SCP-140 is a fanfiction written by the young Scarlet King.
  36. Scarlet King uses SCP-096's picture as wallpaper on his phone.
  37. Every month, Scarlet King goes to Walmart to buy brighteners for his horns.
  38. When Scarlet King can't finish his summer homework, time stops and apologizes to him.
  39. Sometimes laws of physics compare with each other, saying, "I did a more important thing for Scarlet King today than you!"
  40. All internet disconnections are Scarlet King's fault.
  41. All toes-kicking-at-the-corner-of-cabinet are also Scarlet King's fault.
  42. All bad stuff are Scarlet King's fault; those aren't done by Scarlet King are still Scarlet King's fault.
  43. Scarlet King owns an alternative Foundation for containing everything that hasn't been destroyed by him.
  44. The three Brothers of Death used to have a fourth member, until he tried messing with Scarlet King.
  45. Even so, Brothers of Death still play cards with Scarlet King at the seventh day of every month.
  46. Scarlet King writes his programs in base-seven.
  47. Sometimes Scarlet King braids his tentacles into pigtails.
  48. Before coming into existence, everything shall ask Scarlet King for permission, "would this be acceptable?"
  49. The Children of Night did become extinct at Scarlet King's hands; all because he wanted to pick a flower as a present for Sanna.
  50. Scarlet King once looked into the eyes of Chuck Norris.
  51. Scarlet King created SCP-999 in order to test if the absolute cuteness can balance out the absolute horror.
  52. Scarlet King knows you're reading this page; thankfully he doesn't care.
  53. All books in the Wanderers' Library are diaries by Scarlet King.
  54. Scarlet King actually suffers from severe erythrophobia.
  55. Scarlet King is Nian.
  56. Scarlet King is Santa Claus.
  57. Scarlet King's wikidot ID is scarletking123!.
  58. Scarlet King has never received a greeting card on Father's Day.
  59. Scarlet King wanted some home-made cured meat, hence the Hanged King was born.
  60. Linguists use "the smile of Scarlet King" to describe something not able to happen.
  61. In the beginning there was nothing, until Scarlet King slapped at nothing's face and yelled, "Do something you piece of shit!" And that was the beginning of everything.
  62. Everything was the same, until getting beaten up by Scarlet King into different shapes.
  63. SCP-8900-EX once told Scarlet King that red isn't the best color.
  64. Scarlet King will win and lose the same war at the same time; or course, that is a thing Scarlet King does and doesn't do.
  65. The higher narrative wrote Scarlet King — Thus spake and wrote Scarlet King.
  66. Scarlet King's food at Holy Communion is fried chicken that hasn't thawed before being put into the fryer.
  67. Scarlet King's holy water is lukewarm Coca-Cola without bubbles.
  68. Scarlet King responds to all prayers from his believers by leaving them on read.
  69. Scarlet King hasn't invaded our world yet, mainly because he has a bad procrastination problem.
  70. Scarlet King's throne is implemented with an intelligent massaging and grilling function.
  71. The last question of your math exam was created by Scarlet King.
  72. Scarlet King once tried to be merciful for a split second; this has directly caused the extinction of dinosaurs.
  73. Scarlet King once formed a band with the Witch of Obliteration and Sevenfold Destroyers; eventually they disbanded because of disagreement on musical concepts.
  74. Scarlet King once took part in and won a Presidental Election in the United States.
  75. The worst nightmare to Scarlet King is hearing someone asking him, "Mister, who are you?"
  76. The true name of Scarlet King is not Scarlet King. It's his name only because he unintentionally bit his tongue on his self-introduction and he was too embarrased to correct it, and that has been continously mistaken for his true name till today.
  77. Scarlet King can't make more of this shit up.
  78. This is Scarlet King's favorite joke: Knock Knock! — Who's there? — Whoever he is, he's not your brother (Duplicated for he really likes this joke).
  79. Scarlet King's favorite wish is world's peace, as he can destroy all those worlds with the reason "you failed to fulfill this particular wish".
  80. Scarlet King's code of law consists of 7777777 articles, all of them are "you are guilty".
  81. Scarlet King once discovered a world that meets all of his requirements perfectly, but he accidentally destroyed it out of habit upon descending into that world.
  82. Scarlet King considers "hope" as the most flawless calamity he has ever created.
  83. Every sentence said by Scarlet King is a horned Pan pun.
  84. Scarlet King's hair contains all colors of the rainbow: rose, salmon, burgundies, vermilion, incarnadine, crimson, scarlet.
  85. Scarlet King is a President Emeritus of the Ethics Committee.
  86. Scarlet King searches for fan arts with tag "scarlet_king" and hits the like button anonymously.
  87. Does the black moon howl? — Yes, ever since he met Scarlet King.
  88. Scarlet King doesn't really want to destroy all worlds; he is just panhandling so that he can gift money to friends on his wedding.
  89. Scarlet King can put people into pregnancy via his sight.
  90. It is widely considered that Scarlet King gives the greatest sense of security among all gods, for there is no god more dangerous than him.
  91. Scarlet King recalls all embarrassing things he has done before he sleeps.
  92. Scarlet King destroys a world on every birthday. Incidentally, his birthday is on every day.
  93. The true self of Scarlet King is a giant red kaktus1.
  94. The true self of Scarlet King is an axolotl.
  95. Scarlet King never stops giving birth to children because he wants to pull for the rarest limited character.
  96. Scarlet King loves broccoli.
  97. The Scarlet King is a mysterious being from the online science/horror fiction collaborative writing project SCP Foundation, appearing in a large number of its articles.
  98. Scarlet King has a little blanket to hug and sleep with.
  99. Only 77 of the lines above are genuine facts.
  100. This article isn't actually written by any authors; the words assemble themselves out of fear.

rainbow-in-the-night.raw_content:
TboneBerryhill

Just past 7 p.m., after a scorching summer day gave way to a heavy, humid night, Joe sat on the rooftop of Site-16 with a half-empty beer gone lukewarm. The skyline shimmered in the distance, stars barely visible through the haze.

The rooftop hatch creaked open behind him.

"Hey," Trevor said, easing onto the rooftop. "Figured you’d be up here."

Joe offered a tired glance. "Only quiet spot beside my windowless temp office. And that place smells like expired printer ink."

Trevor sat beside him, close enough for warmth but not quite touching. "Rough day?"

Joe took a sip. "Containment briefing. One of the anomalies got philosophical again. Then off to Site-16-1 tomorrow. I barely unpacked."

Trevor chuckled. "Always somewhere else, huh? Same old Joe. Always in motion until he burns out."

Joe smiled faintly. "You still talk like that. Like everything's poetry."

"You’re still drinking lukewarm beer on rooftops like everything's tragic." Trevor nudged him gently. "You okay?"

Joe hesitated. "It’s been five years since college. Deadlines, danger. I'm still waiting for something to feel different. I'm tired of waiting on everyone and everything"

"You waited on me."

That landed heavier than either of them expected. Joe didn't deny it.

"You could’ve called. Even once."

Joe looked away. "I thought you moved on."

"I never wanted to." Trevor paused, voice soft. "You mattered. You still do."

Silence hung between them, thick with memory.

Trevor scanned the perimeter, sharp eyes tracing the edge of the site. A guard on the ground spotted them and lifted his radio to his mouth.

Trevor called down casually, “It’s all good, Luke we’re fine!”

Joe arched a brow. “You know him?”

“Yeah. We used to date.”

“You used to?”

Trevor shrugged. “Dad wasn’t thrilled about me dating an MTF.”

“Ah.” Joe turned back toward the site, letting the silence fill in the rest.

"Do you remember the UTA rooftop?" Joe asked quietly.

Trevor smiled. "Of course. You wore that ridiculous hoodie. The city lights in your eyes made you look" He stopped himself.

Joe turned to him. "Made me look what?"

"Like I loved you. Because I did." Trevor’s voice barely rose above a whisper.

For a long moment, neither of them moved. Then, deliberately, Joe leaned his head against Trevor's shoulder.

"I still do," Joe murmured.

Trevor didn’t pull away. Instead, he reached over and linked their fingers together. “Then maybe… this time, we don’t run.”

And for once between secrets and silence, fear and flame the rooftop stayed quiet.

The elevator doors closed with a soft hiss, humming as it descended beneath Site-16. Trevor stared ahead, jaw tight. He hadn’t meant to pick this fight tonight but after the rooftop, it was inevitable.

His father, Keith, sat in his office, eyes locked on a tablet full of redacted damage reports. Trevor stepped through the door.

“Why didn’t you want me seeing Luke?” he asked, no preamble.

Keith didn’t look up. “Is this the time?”

“It’s well overdue.”

Keith sighed, set the tablet down, and leaned back in his chair. “Because he was MTF.”

Trevor’s lips parted, incredulous. “So what? That’s it? He chooses the wrong job?”

Keith stood. “It’s not just about the job. It’s about the fact that you already work one of the most dangerous jobs in this building. And Luke volunteered to walk into hell, weekly, with no hesitation. You think I wanted to see you attach your heart to a walking funeral?”

“I chose him, Dad. That was mine to decide.”

Keith’s voice tightened. “You’re right. But you’re my son. You think I can just stand by and watch you tie your life to someone with a half-life in breach zones?”

“You don’t get to protect me by wrecking what made me happy,” Trevor said. “You pushed us apart, and had him sent away.”

Keith looked genuinely pained. “Because I didn’t want to lose you twice first to this job, then to grief.”

Trevor hesitated.

“You didn’t trust me to handle the risk,” Trevor said. “You took away something good because you were scared.”

“I was,” Keith admitted, quiet and rough around the edges now. “Terrified. Of getting the call."

Trevor swallowed. “He made me feel alive, even in all this. And you made it feel like that wasn’t worth fighting for.”

Keith looked down like that hit somewhere deep. “I never stopped wanting you safe. I just forgot that safe and happy aren’t always the same.”

Trevor lingered at the doorway, torn between bitterness and love. Keith didn’t say anything just stood there, older than he looked a minute ago.

“I love you, Dad,” Trevor said softly. “But sometimes… you make that hard to do.”

Keith gave a small nod, eyes glassy. “I know, I love you too.”

And with that, Trevor turned and left grief and love trailing behind him in equal measure.

Personnel transfer and permanent position
Good morning, Xavier. I'm writing today to request a transfer of a member of personnel by the name of Joe Thompson to Site-16, and to assign a permanent position suited for him for effective work. I believe that he would be a great addition to the staff, I remember you were having trouble looking for a new personnel replacement. I have known Dr. Thompson for a significant amount of time and can vouch for him and his skill along with his work ethic. If we could fast-track this, that would be much appreciated. We cannot allow another site or group to snatch him away to our detriment.
Sincerely, Dr. Trevor Berryhill
Researcher
Secure, Contain, Protect
