secondhand-smoke.raw_content:
"There is comfort in routine."

.

My Dearest Iris,

I'm not sure how to write a letter like this, nor do I know if you are ever going to read this, but I thought these words would be more valuable here than if they remained unspoken. To say a lot has happened in these past few years would, frankly, be an understatement. The world has changed so much, and even though I was never a part of it the way you were, even though I lack a frame of reference to compare it to, its rippling effects have surely reached me; the walls meant to keep me safe from the world, or rather the world safe from me, were not able to protect me.

I read once that nature tends towards entropy, disorder, decay. I've often taken comfort in the idea that all I did, then, was hasten a natural process. When I was first brought to Site-17, I must have destroyed dozens of devices in testing. I wonder what other damage I've unknowingly been responsible for.

I wonder if it is simply the nature of things to fall apart around me…



November 2025, The Present:

There is comfort in routine.

Iris Thompson had not thought this was something she would ever concede. For as long as she could remember, routines had been forced upon her: first by her parents, then by the Foundation.

Before, her life had been monotonous: wake up, eat, sleep. Train every day except Sunday, psych eval on Tuesday, medical on Wednesday. The odd experiment, mission with Alpha-Nine, or Adams dragging her along to some ill-fated social outing in an attempt to make her feel marginally more like a person. Now, in retrospect, it all blurred together— one long, dull, repetitive stretch of time which had not been hers to spend, in which her life had not been her own.

After the Impasse, after it had become hers, instinct propelled her as far away from the Foundation as possible. She threw herself into the deep end, and, as a result, found herself strangely adrift. Some traitorous part of her yearned for it, the way her life had been laid out for her in the past.

Lost in thought, she watches Meri — no last name as of yet — as she stands at her kitchen counter, chopping home-grown scallions.

When it came to building a life outside of the Foundation, Meri had taken the opposite approach of her: she’d not gone very far away from the Foundation at all — whether for lack of options, or because she chose to, Iris didn’t know. What she did know, or at least suspected, was that it was the same thing that brought them back together, on nights like these:

There is comfort in routine.

"When are you leaving again?" Meri asks.

Tok tok tok tok tok.

Her knife knocks rhythmically against the cutting board, the sound filling the entirety of the small apartment.

"Tomorrow," Iris mumbles from the doorway behind her. "Early, probably. I won't wake you." She pauses. "Seriously, if you need help with—"

"It's fine." Meri doesn’t turn around.

Tok tok tok.

"Where are you going this time?"

Iris sighs, burying her hands in the pockets of her jacket. She'd elected to just keep it on, rather than trying to cram it onto crowded coat rack next to the door.

"Does it matter? It's all the same."

Tok tok tok tok tok.

"It matters to me," Meri says. "I want to know what you're up to."

"They wanted me to speak at another convention. Your, ah—" Iris clears her throat. "Clef is going to be there."

Tok tok tak!

"Oh." The chopping stops.

"Are you guys still not on speaking terms?"

A pause. Iris looks past Meri, at the post cards of faraway places pinned to the kitchen wall: bustling cities and vast landscapes on glossy paper. Their backs were blank— no one had sent them. Meri had explained she simply liked to collect them, that she liked knowing just how many different kinds of places there were in the world.

Meri sets her knife down and grabs onto her cane, gripping its head tightly.

"You're right." Iris didn’t know her to sound curt often, but she did now. "I don't want to talk about that."

"Right. Right, yeah. I figured."

The ensuing silence is somewhere between awkward and familiar. Iris continues to watch as Meri maneuvers around her kitchen. There's an elegance to it, Meri's familiarity with the space readily on display. She collects twigs of herbs from the hanging pots adjacent to her stove, only ever taking as much as she needs, chops them into small pieces, and throws them into the pot, bubbling gently on the stove.

Iris couldn’t tell the herbs apart. Cooking was a skill she'd not had time to brush up on since she’d gotten out, subsisting entirely on takeout, canned meals, and the occasional fried egg. It was for the better, she supposed, that Meri didn’t let her help, even if she offered each time.

Dinner, as always, is uneventful. The two sit on wooden chairs at Meri's wooden table, eat stew from wooden bowls with wooden spoons, and outside of the occasional comment about the food or attempt at small talk, the only noises filling the apartment are the scraping and sloshing and satisfied ahhhh that marks the end of the bowl. Meri couldn't eat animal products, so she made up for the lack of available ingredients with an unwavering dedication to bring out the best in each and every one she could use— it was the best meal Iris had had since, well, the last time she’d been here.

But, at the same time, seeing her misshapen and miscolored reflection on the soup's surface, Iris searches past the minced garlic and chunks of celery for something that may or may not have been in it at all:

Love.

✽✽✽

"Listen," Iris begins after they've finished eating, "at least let me do the washing up. It's the least I can do to make up for bothering you like this."

"You're not bothering me," Meri insists, as always. "I like when you visit. No one else does, really. Let me play host.”

Iris sighs. There was comfort in routine, but it all had a way of leaving her with a guilty conscience— for not visiting more often, for visiting at all. It felt like she was taking advantage of Meri, of her loneliness and lingering affection for her. They'd both agreed to go their separate ways after all, four years ago, when it had occurred to them that they could. She could've stayed with Meri then, but she hadn't, couldn't, and Iris felt like she only ever came back when she needed something from her.

They’d had sex twice, on nights like this one. The first time had been a year and a half after the Impasse, shortly after Iris had begun visiting again. Both of them had been lonely, neither of them had been having any luck with other women. It felt like the world had left them both behind, and as Meri leaned in to kiss her, Iris had remembered what had first drawn her to the other woman: Meri, too, was something inhuman, unsure how to exist among real people.

The guilt, ever-present, had caught up with her in the morning. There had been a conversation, awkward, and not as emotional as it should have been. It had been Iris who had asked not to let it happen again. In the dull light of the morning, the enormity of what she’d felt the night prior scared her. She had meant to only visit for one night. She couldn’t stay here. She could not stay here.

Meri, of course, had nodded and smiled and understood, the way she always did.

The second time had been when Iris had let it happen again. She’d fallen asleep next to Meri afterwards, in her bed, the fur that covered most of her body soft against Iris' bare skin.

She’d woken with the first light, dressed and collected her things as quietly as she could, so as not to wake Meri. Then, out on the stairwell, she'd had what her therapist had taught her to identify as a 'panic attack'.

She stayed away for six months afterwards, terrified. When she did come back, finally (because of course she came back, she always came back) they didn’t speak of it.

They'd yet to speak of it, even now.

As Iris fills the sink with water and olive oil soap, Meri goes to collect a spare blanket from her room. The pair move around the space, around each other, with a practiced ease. They didn't need to speak; they had done this dance many, many times before: dinner, dishes, changing clothes, and retiring to their respective corners of the small apartment, careful not to get too close, not to speak too much.

Before long, Meri retires to her bedroom.

"I'll see you tomorrow," she says with a shy smile, and there is a moment where she stands in the doorway, lit from behind, that Iris feels like she should say something. She doesn't.

Meri closes the door behind her. A thin beam of light still seeps through the crack beneath it and into the room. Iris turns away from it to stare up at the ceiling. The room is silent, except for the occasional sound of a page turn from the other room, and Iris tries to let the rhythmic sound lull her to sleep.

But sleep doesn’t come to her tonight.

The couch feels softer than she's used to, like she's sinking into it, being swallowed whole by the woolen blanket. She tries to relax, tries to close her eyes and calm her breathing, but there is something threatening, suddenly, in not being able to see the space around her.

She opens her eyes back up and looks around. The apartment feels too small and too large at once. Somehow, it's as there is something ominous in dangling flowerpots, something urgent in the ticking of the grandfather clock on the wall. The air feels stale, despite Meri having left the window open while cooking.

Iris feels sweat beading down her back. She is overcome an acute sense of being trapped, that she's been deceived. Something is wrong, a part of her says, the part that expects blinking red lights and shrill alarm bells. Something is wrong.

She throws off the blanket and turns on the lampshade on the side table. Warm, yellow light floods into all corners of the room, turning dark shadows back into familiar household objects. Iris breathes in, then out. She is safe here. She is safe, and she can leave any time she likes.

After gathering her bearings, Iris shuffles to the kitchen. She drinks water straight from the tap, splashing some of it into her face.

She knows what would calm her nerves; she'd taken up smoking, shortly after she'd first struck out on her own. It had been some belated teenage rebellion, perhaps, that had induced it, despite the fact that she’d been well over thirty. Slowly, sneakily, it had turned from an indulgence to a habit to a need-– there was, after all, comfort in routine.

The lack of nicotine made her anxious, twitchy, more prone to losing her shit the way she just had, and she hadn't had any in several days. She held off on smoking before visiting Meri. The lingering smell of it on Iris made Meri's throat itch and her eyes water, like an allergic reaction, like Iris was blowing the smoke right into her face.

She deliberates, for a moment. She could take a shower, after, change her clothes. Meri didn't need to know. Or, if all else failed, Iris would simply leave before she woke up, an old reliable for when she fucked something up.

As quietly as possible, she collects her jacket and taps over to the porch, moving aside the curtains to the glass door. Taking one more glance behind her, she reaches into her pocket and pulls a cigarette from the pack.

She tucks it between her lips and raises her lighter up to her face. She can feel the dull warmth of the small flame on her skin as she waits for the smoke to fill her lungs.


I felt it was only right I remain alone in my chamber, to deprive myself of the few bits of connection I was afforded, with faith as my only comfort; I left the convent I was raised in, so how sure could I be that this new life would remain, either?

But then you came along, and for once, I began to feel like maybe, just maybe, something would last. Fate, obviously, wasn't kind to us; It never has been, to me. I'm sure you know the circumstances that led to my containment well by this point. It was… a mercy, if you can put it that way. I wish I knew my mother. Sometimes I wish I had a better relationship with my father. I wonder if I would have loved to walk the world as you once did, before you too made your way into the custody of the Foundation. I imagine you were as scared as I was, when I first arrived there, but you've never been one for fear, at least in front of me. Your bravery was something I almost envied once; you always seemed to be immovable in those difficult times.

Envy. Not quite the sin I thought I'd fall for.

And then came the Impasse, and suddenly the world was plunged into a new type of darkness. It was naive of me to think it would have passed me by. Suddenly, everything that made me special disappeared. For once, I was normal; not a half-deer, not an agent of decay, but Meri Clef, finally someone normal. Along with that normalcy, though, came something else: fear. Fear of the unknown, fear of the world just outside the walls, fear that I would lose my legs. But for a moment, none of that seemed to matter. You were around, you were here, and it felt like we could weather whatever the world threw at us.

I was such a fool for believing we would have lasted forever.


March 2017:

Site-17's inner courtyard is still quite barren, despite the coming spring. Nature always seems to take a bit longer to return here; the sparse bits of greenery, meant to create at least an imitation of a recreational space for the anomalous humanoids and staff, were perhaps still too exhausted from the impossible task demanded of them— it wasn't really possible to make a place like this look nice, try as they might.

Meri might've been able to help it along, Iris thinks. If only it had been any other time, if things were the way they'd always been, if something extremely unprecedented wasn't happening to Meri, to all of them, right at this moment.

"I don't think you have to worry so much," Meri assures her as Iris pushes her wheelchair through the garden. "Consider it a vacation of sorts. We have no reason to think this isn't temporary."

Iris sighs, glancing down at her. Meri had gotten thinner, smaller. The antlers she'd shed in January, that usually made her seem so much taller than she was, never grew back in. Everything about her seemed duller, and the cheery, polite temperament she continued to maintain despite it only served to make things more unbearable.

"You're right." Iris tries her best to not sound morose. "I just don't like this inaction. I'm not used to sitting back and letting someone else do the important work. I should be out there, trying to find some sort of solution. Figuring out why this is happening at all."

Meri gives a short laugh that quickly turns into a cough.

"A task force comprised entirely of anomalies isn't really cut out to be dealing with the end of everything anomalous. I think you're allowed to sit this one out, dear."

"I know, I'm just— I worry about you, you know? What if there's no solution? What if this is just how things are now?"

Meri tilts her head upwards, giving her a look, that look, the one of endless and insufferable patience. "Then we'll just have to make do. It's what we've always done, isn't it?"

The last sentence hangs in the air for a moment. She was right. During their time on site, the pair always did what they could to maintain their bond, oftentimes skirting within the rules of their respective confinements just to catch a glance of the other. But those small waves and smiles were what provided them with hope that maybe fate would be kind to them. That maybe things would get better.

But it seemed impossible to hold on to that hope now, with how intent fate had seemed on fucking them over lately. Their luck was bound to run out eventually— Iris just hadn't expected it to happen like this. Iris can't shake a sudden wave of frustration at the other woman. She tightens her grip on the wheelchair's handles.

"God, I really wish you weren't so fucking Catholic sometimes, y'know?"

A pause. Meri adjusts herself in the chair, turning ever so slightly to lean closer to Iris in an attempt to meet her eyes.

"Is this about the operation?"

It was a sore subject between the two of them, and a tired one.

It had started early on into the Impasse, before Iris had noticed any substantial effects on her own anomaly. Meri had been raked with pain, muscle spasms, and a creeping atrophy of her legs, until one morning she'd found herself unable to move them at all. They'd taken it to be some sort of illness at first; maybe Meri, almost thirty, having simply gotten far older than any deer was ever meant to get. Once more humanoids contained at the site began to be affected, though, the bigger picture began revealing itself: Meri's body, in and of itself, was an anomaly. People were simply not meant to have hooves and antlers. With reality aligning itself to how things were "supposed" to work, her body, as if realizing its own wrongness, rejected a part of itself; her legs were a foreign object, some unknown creature that Meri had become conjoined with in the womb.

It had been Site-17's own medical staff that had brought up the possibility of amputation. They said it was the safe choice, with her situation being an unprecedented one. There was no way to tell how her body would continue reacting to the Impasse. It was entirely possible it would continue waging war on itself until it simply stopped functioning entirely.

Iris inhales sharply. "I mean, it's not not about the operation," she says, begrudgingly. "It's your call; I told you, I don't want to make that choice for you."

"No, I know that," Meri says, sounding tired.

Iris bites her lip.

"… Y'know what the fucked up thing is?" she asks, knowing she probably shouldn't.

Meri tilts her head.

"I used to pray for something like this, that one day I'd wake up and just be normal. My camera would take photos, and that would be it. That I'd just get to… go home."

A silence follows, one that slowly brings a smile to Meri's face. "Pray, huh?"

Iris snorts. It sounds bitter. "I know it was stupid. The vain hopes of a little kid. You don't get to home from somewhere like here. Things don't just go back to normal, but—"

"But you were homesick."

"I— " Iris hesitates, "I guess so. Either way, things are different now. I'm not— I've got—" She falters. "I've got you now. Which has to count for something."

"Thanks," Meri says, quietly. "I'm glad that I've got you too."

Iris smiles at her, tired but soft.

They find a patch of crocuses on their way back inside, white and purple against the dull spring dirt.

When the world started healing, when my body stopped the war within itself, I found that my heart could not heal. My antlers grew back, and I couldn't help but think of the person who used to be there to help me brush out the mats and knots from between them. I learned to walk again, and I imagined someone besides the site medical staff guiding me down the parallel bars. When I finally moved out of my cage and into this small halfway house I've turned into a home, I imagined there would be someone to help me decorate and make the space feel lived in. You were there, yes, but I found myself wondering if you truly were there. I know this must have been hard on you as well, and I feel so guilty for feeling like I needed more from you, but I felt so alone.

And then you left.

Though I've had time to cultivate quite an active imagination, it brings me no joy to see the ghosts of you in shadows or mirrors or in sudden movements at the edges of my vision. I wanted I needed I prayed you were there. I was so lonely. I missed you.

And out of every prayer to answer, it seemed God wanted to curse grace me with this one.

September 2024; A Little Over a Year ago:

"Iris! Over here!"

Adams had barely changed since Iris had last seen her, outside of a few gray hairs that had begun to make themselves more visible. She'd opted out of her usual pantsuit, as she tended to when the occasion was pleasure rather than business. Instead, she was wearing a short jacket and silk neckerchief over a black dress, making Iris feel under-dressed in her work pants and jeans jacket.

She makes her way over to Adams, weaving through tables before climbing onto the bar stool next to her.

"Hi," Iris says, simply.

"It's good to see you," Adams raises her hand, evidently some attempt at a greeting, but seems to think better of touching her. "Can I order you anything? My treat."

Iris scans the blackboard above the bar: Cosmopolitan, Moscow Mule, Negroni, and dozens of other fancy and utterly incomprehensible names scribbled out in colorful chalks.

"I'll, uh—" Iris squints. "Do they just have a pint of beer?"

Adams gives her a look, something insufferably amused hiding within it.

"You sure? You can order something expensive, you know. Vanguard's paying."

There it was. Vanguard. That was what they were calling themselves now, wasn't it?

"I thought you said this wasn't a business meeting."

"It's not!" Adams holds up three fingers in a mock scout's honor. "Honest! It's just that, if I, hypothetically, wasn't strictly using my company credit card for business purposes only, they wouldn't need to know."

"Right," Iris says. She can't help but smile slightly. "Y'know what, why not. Harming their finances does seem tempting."

She shoots a skeptical look at the cocktail glass in front of Adams. An orange peel floats lazily atop a sugary-looking amber liquid.

"What's the, ah— least girly thing they have?"

"Oh, so it is about that, huh?" Adams says, slyly. "My girly drink has about twice the alcohol of the pint I would've ordered you, and then some. You're worse about this sort of thing than Clef sometimes, you know?"

"Fuck off. We both know how elaborate Clef gets with his drink orders."

Adams laughs and places a hand on Iris' shoulder, amicably. Iris finds herself surprisingly alright with it.

"I'll surprise you. You wouldn't know what to get anyways."

"Sure." Iris loathes to admit that she's right. "Just don't get me too drunk. I've got work in the morning."

"No worries." Adams swirls the remaining liquid in her glass around before downing it, undoubtedly to get herself another drink, too. "This won’t be a repeat of last time. No undercover GOC agents either— I checked."

"Isn’t the point of being undercover supposed to be that you can’t tell?" Iris asks, flatly.

"I can." Adams puffs out her chest, jabbing it with her thumb. "I’m a professional."

Iris snorts, scanning the room while Adams orders, just to make sure. It seems Adams was right, though. The other patrons appear wrapped up in their own conversations, not giving them a second look.

"Sooooo…" Adams puts on a sing-song voice, "What have you been up to? God knows it’s been a while. You look different."

"Yeah?" Iris asks, somewhat surprised.

"Good-different," Adams assures her. "More like an adult. Little shabby, though, not going to lie."

"Figures." Iris rubs at her eyes. "I’ve been sleeping on a lot of couches."

Adams smiles sympathetically. "I know it may not be my place to offer, but if you're ever in the area and miss having a place of your own—"

"No," Iris says, quickly. "No, I know what you're going to say. I'm not going to indebt myself to the Foun— to Vanguard, I guess, further. I'm not giving them anything else to hold over my head."

Adams opens her mouth, but stops when the bartender returns with their drinks. Iris mumbles a thanks. Adams idly swirls her drink for a moment.

"You’re entitled to their help, you know," Adams says, finally. "You’re entitled to more than that. You have every right to bleed them dry if you ask me. Just, y'know, until you find something else."

Iris hesitates. She thinks of Meri’s arm, warm and fuzzy, draped over her under the covers that morning. Prying herself out, dressing, leaving at the crack of dawn, the morning air cold on her face as she dialed a taxi with shaking fingers, desperate to go anywhere else.

Meri, who’d moved from one form of confinement to another. Meri, who was still stuck so firmly underneath the Foundation’s thumb.

"What if I don’t find anything else? What if I don’t make it out of there, and then nothing will have changed? I’ll still be in containment, but it’ll be my own fault this time."

"I don’t think any of this is something you should blame yourself for," Adams says, quietly.

There’s a pause. Iris takes a sip of her drink. It is, in fact, sweeter than what she’s used to, but there’s a tangy aftertaste to it that she finds she likes quite a bit. Damn you, Andrea.

"Listen, I just- I need to have something outside of the Foundation, before I’m comfortable going back to them. Something of my own."

Iris glances back at Adams to find her looking into her glass, contemplative. The warm lights above the bar paint kaleidoscopic patterns onto the liquid’s surface.

"I can't tell you what to do," Adams says, carefully. "Just make sure you don't forget about yourself in the midst of everything, yeah?"

I never expected you to return to me. Truthfully, after we parted ways, I just assumed that you would have forgotten about me, left me as a memory of the world you suffered in for so long, the one you wanted to escape. I think a small part of me wanted you to remember, though. Did you think of me when you saw deer in the forest? Did you think of me when you stumbled upon crocuses or lilies or any of the other myriad of flowers or plants we used to surround ourselves with in the garden at Site-17? Why did you come back to me? It matters not; you returned, after all, and although my initial reaction may have seemed tame, when I opened the door, it felt like I fell in love all over again.

But part of me knew I could not keep you forever, and just as quickly as you came back, you were gone again. And you did it again. And again. And again. And again. This torment torture routine of you coming and going has become incredibly difficult. Some days I wish we could go back to the way things were between you and me. Some days I wish that, when you return to my apartment, you'll stay, and I can learn more about your world together. I would be lying, though, if I didn't say this whole matter was unbearable. So while some days I wait and clean and keep track of your belongings for if you'll be returning, some days I find myself wishing you simply wouldn't return at all.

My heart aches, Iris, and as much as I want to rid myself of this cycle, I know, ultimately, that means ridding myself of you.

So I will play whatever part you need me to. I will greet you at the door and cook you dinner because I am a gracious host, I will keep you company and ask you about your travels because I care about you, and, in those truly lonely times, when I have not felt a friendly or loving touch in months, I will invite you into my bed because because

But even then you'll leave, as you have before.


January 2022:

The apartment is on the ground floor of a building block that had been raised out of what used to be one of Site-17’s military training grounds. It still smells like fresh paint when Iris helps Meri move in. It makes Meri’s eyes water, gives her rashes on her skin, so Iris helps her strip the walls down to the brick, watches it grow back over with vines and flowers over the next few days.

She watches Meri recover, switching from a wheelchair to crutches to a cane. They walk to the freshly-opened grocery store, exchange food stamps for vegetables; Iris assembles furniture from inscrutable instructions and Meri knits a blanket for the couch. It’s new to them both, getting to choose what food to prepare, what clothes to put on, which matter of everyday objects to clutter their space with, but it's altogether manageable, quaint even. Like playing house.

It lasts all of five weeks before Iris leaves. It’s for purely pragmatic reasons: she’s needed elsewhere. With the Impasse reversing and various nexuses recovering, thousands of displaced anomalies were beginning to make their ways back home. The world seemed awash with people searching for fragments of lives shattered by what seemed like it would be the end of the world.

Iris spends two months in Three Portlands, being shown pictures of lost loved ones, relaying their locations, writing notes to them through photographs to establish contact. She watches people reunite, closing their arms around each other with a kind of hunger Iris isn’t sure she’s ever felt.

A woman named Marcia, who told her to call her 'Marcy', offers Iris her son's old room to stay in, after finding out she'd been sleeping in the emergency shelter they'd set up. She says it’s the least she can do for her, with Iris having helped find her wife and all.

Iris isn’t sure if she can tell. She must, with the way Iris’ hair is cropped short, the way she'd stolen one of her son's old varsity jackets to wear to work once it had started getting colder, instead of taking the women's coat Marcia offered her. Either way, she doesn’t comment. Iris appreciates it.

She goes to a gay bar one night, sitting in the corner like a frightened animal. She leaves as soon as she finishes her drink.

Meri doesn’t call. She can’t. She doesn’t have a phone, and Iris hasn’t given her an address to send letters to. Iris won’t have an address for her to send letters to for the next four years.

Iris doesn’t write to Meri in turn.

She goes to work one day to find them breaking camp. It’s over, they say. Things are back to normal, more or less. They can all go home. Iris tries not to feel envious of them for having a baseline for what "normal" means.

Marcia offers her couch for if Iris is ever in town again.

"Sure", Iris says, and "Thank you."

So Iris returns to Meri, because where else would she go? She takes the Greyhound, falling asleep with her forehead on the cold glass, vague shapes rushing past in the darkness outside. She wakes in the early morning hours, watching lights turn on in windows carved into silhouettes by the side of the road. The world had seemed so small to her until just a while ago - it was humbling, the way people seemed to be able to make their home almost anywhere.

With each stop she wonders: what would it be like to get off here? What would it be like to have someone waiting for her, on what used to be the outside?

Meri, of course, welcomes her with open arms. She isn’t cross with her for being gone for so long. She's never cross with her for anything, even when Iris can tell she’s hurt. She asks what she’s missed, and Meri shrugs. It isn’t until later that she finds out Meri had found out about Clef in her absence. It isn’t until later that she finds out how poor of a job Clef had done at living up to the idea of a father Meri had envisioned for herself all these years. It isn’t until later that she finds out Meri had put together that Iris had known this whole time and not said a word.

She lasts another week in Meri’s little apartment — their apartment, back then, together — before it all becomes too much. She wishes Meri would get mad at her, allow for some sort of release for the guilt that’s been building up inside of her since she'd gotten back, maybe even since she left.

Instead, she gets mad at Meri. Meri apologizes, frightened tears in her eyes that she tries to wipe away before Iris can see them, and Iris wishes she'd never come back at all. Even still, she comforts Meri, the way she’s always done, when it wasn’t her who had hurt her, when it was still them against the world. They talk about it in the morning. It’s excruciating, how matter-of-fact it is, both of them too used to adapting to crises, to being the ones making sacrifices for the greater good.

When Iris leaves for the second time, she takes her belongings. She buys a travel backpack to carry them. It doesn’t fill up all the way to the top.

She's only gone for ten days when Marcia opens her door to find Iris before it, again. She doesn't seem surprised to see her.

Five months pass before Iris sees Meri again. It’s Light who asks for her at Site-17, to help locate a person of interest. She doesn’t have to come, doesn’t have to help Vanguard, but old habits die hard. She’s offered a bed at the Site, but refuses, staunchly, despite not really having a backup plan, despite it being February, and cold out at night.

She sits in a little kebab shop, four street corners from where Meri lived alone now, until closing time, before resigning herself to her fate. On her way over, a part of her hopes that the apartment might be empty, that Meri might not be in, but really, where else would she be?

Meri welcomes her gently, warmly. She makes her a bed on her couch.

"Be here earlier, next time," she says, "and let me know in advance. We can have dinner."

When next time comes, Iris finds her way to the little apartment of her own accord. The third time, she leaves some clothes and a toothbrush.

Two years later, she wakes up in Meri’s arms, leaving without waking her, feeling like the biggest piece of shit on earth.

It must be easy for you to leave. It must be so easy for you to move from place to place while I'm rooted here. I think sometimes that if only I too had been a field agent, that I could have accustomed myself to it, and then now I could come with you. But, really, I know that's not true. Because what is out there for me? You are all I've ever had.

How am I supposed to feel, watching you leave after those nights, Iris? How am I meant to feel when your warmth leaves me in the night without a word? How am I supposed to feel, opening my eyes and not seeing that slight smile you used to give me, or even just the comforting reassurance that someone sleeps softly besides me?

I felt a million things when you left me that night, and even now you do not know how deep that blade has been plunged into my heart. I prayed that day, not even knowing for what, gripping my rosary so tightly I thought the pearls would crack and shatter in my shaking hands. And the only thing I could think was why? Why did you leave me? Why? Why? Why?

Even now, you haven't told me. Does it bring you shame, are you ashamed of me? Do you even want to apologize, but cannot find your words? Or, I find myself thinking sometimes, cynically, are you waiting for the day I fall for you again, turning our entanglement into a routine where the only constants are me and an empty bed? I know that if you'd let me, I would fall for you again and again and again and again and again because you are the only thing I know for certain…

I'm sorry, Iris, but I am so tired. I feel… wrong. Even as I write this, my hand shakes and teardrops stain the page and muddle the ink. And even still, in all this pain and frustration, excruciating frustration, I can't seem to let you go. Even this letter has lost its purpose, even words fail. But I would rather lay my sins bare, just for once. I hope you can forgive me.

Love, Yours,
~Meri

The Present:

The cold night's air does little to provide Iris relief, and her cigarette, still a good thumb's length from her knuckles, only seems to stain her and her surroundings with the smell of smoke. That would fade in time, much like Iris' imprint on the couch cushions, or the smoothed wood on the coat rack from where her jacket, now long discarded, once hung. It was the nature of things to slowly fade away, but Iris was unsure she ever would.

How many times had she been here before? How many times did she dine with Meri? How many times did her ex-lover's smile greet her at the door? And still, Iris returned. Maybe Meri would have forgotten me by now, she thinks, if only I stayed away. But Iris knew that wasn't true.

Even now, leaning against the railing of Meri's porch, still minding the many plants that sat neat and manicured in their planters, Iris knew she would have another night just like this one. For, below all of Iris' frustration, all of her regret, all of her guilt, were the embers of comfort, stoked only by Meri and this routine.

Tap tap, thud.

Behind her, she hears the quiet, steady rhythm of footsteps, and the hollow reverberation of a cane along the floor.

Tap tap, thud. Tap tap, thud.

Meri slides open the curtain, one hand gripping the wall, and the other, the decorated sheet separating her domain and the outside world. They lock eyes; Meri's are red. Tears stream down her face, but Iris can't tell if it's because of the smoke or something else entirely. Her expression is painfully neutral, bereft of her usual soft smile. It's strange, almost uncanny. Iris hadn't thought her able to make any other face, even if she wanted to.

And in the starry night, on the porch of the halfway house outside of Site-17, Iris and Meri stand in silence; there is simply nothing to be said at all.

    Tale - Sehnsucht
    Author: local lesbian commie
    local lesbian commie's author page

Let the monsters belong to the absence.

A girl stands alone in unmatched darkness,
Surrounded by the gold she cannot reach.
She asks if she is going to be there forever,
But nothing that exists answers back.

All she can hear now is a distant song,
An out-of-tune melody her mind plays to her.
Always there, rotting away along her ears,
Until the strings finally break apart and rest.

Selling an Idea

Dezi Sutton, despite her professional proclivities, often found herself in the same situation; one that many queer folx around the world often ended up in.

In her cozy, eclectic apartment in Three-Portlands, with the warm glow of an amber lamp, Dezi stared at the letter in her hand and said one word:

"Fuck," Dezi checked her calendar. How is rent due again, already?

Throwing the letter into a pile of fellow discarded notices, she went to her bedroom, pressing a non-descript panel on the wall. It moved with her hand, sliding forwards, and then gliding to the right with ease, revealing a cache hidden behind the panel. There were a handful of items, none more significant than a porcelain mask that sat in a cradle, nestled in the middle; but that wasn't what she was here for.

Her manicured hands found a small metal box, brass and tarnished, tucked in the back. With practiced ease, she slid it out, careful not to disturb any of the other trinkets that decorated the pseudo-safe, least of all the bone china brush. The box opened with a satisfying click, to a deeply disappointing sight.

Five, ten, fifteen… shit, I'm four hundred short. Dezi looked around, trying to see if she had squirreled any other cash away, but, no — as happened nearly every month, putting off selling items to collect more led to only problems. At least at this point, she mused, I'm used to the stress of it by now?

She considered her options.

I could pull a job? No, I don't have anything ready to go. I don't have anybody who owes me, and it's not like my bank account exists in any meaningful way… She frowned, the honest part of her having known what the answer was from the onset. She shook her head, returning the box to the designated corner, grabbing a few of the smaller, more innocuous trinkets on the way out, wrapping them in silk with care and stuffing them into her satchel.

She looked in the mirror, seeing her brown skin, manicured eyebrows, wicked smile and flowing hair, nodding.

Better get into character, Dezi turned back to the hidden compartment. With a careful reverence, she lifted the mask from its home, holding it before her in the air. As she looked upon Marginalia, she smirked, trying her best to summon the bravado that the idea thief so effortlessly exuded. Her fingers began to sparkle, light glowing out and casting a pearlescent hue across the hidden treasures, as a warmth began to fill her chest.

A second later, the glow faded, and Marginalia returned the empty mask to the place of honor in the wall, closing the panel up behind her.

She spun on her heel, smiling to herself on the way out.

Time to go fence some ideas.

As Marginalia walked into Fabnormality, the premier queer bar in Three Portlands, she grinned, feeling the eyes that were immediately drawn to her. It's not that she was here to meet anybody, but — well, who doesn't like being desired? With renewed confidence, she strode across the dance floor, turning down a hallway and descending a flight of stairs.

As the thumping music gave way to muffled bass, she set her eyes on her destination. At the end of the hallways was a plain door that to any but the initiated, would be summarily ignored. This was the kind of place where you needed to know somebody to get in. Luckily, Marginalia knew many people.

The person sitting on a stool by the door watched as she approached, casually, yet, overt in their observation. The market paid extra for tight security, and you couldn't get in unless you had a pass—

Fuck! Marginalia realized, blinking and trying to not let it show. My pass is still in the wall, god damn it. I… I'm not walking all the way back just to come here, I can… I can figure this one out.

Marginalia had grown up around those who found wallets, lifted unnoticed baubles, done what they could do make their way in life, and, as much as she respected them, it wasn't her style. No, the idea of picking a pocket felt… uninspired.

I'm not that dull, she reminded herself. There was always another way, and she loved finding it. Pausing against the wall, to 'tie' the laces of her thigh-high boots, she considered her options. I'm going to have to let them know that I should be allowed in; I don't have my pass, but you don't need one to get in. It just makes it easier, rather than having to prove your friend is really inside, waiting for you.

As she methodically laced each layer, pulling them tight against her fishnets, the door opened, two rich assholes walking out, acting as though they owned the world.

Of course, she rolled her eyes. Clients.

That did, however, present an opportunity. As they passed her by, Marginalia's hands shimmered beneath a pair of red leather gloves, tipping forward and bumping into the close one.

"Fuck, I'm sorry!" She mimed platitudes as the two men leered at her. "Didn't mean to get in the way of you two boys having your… fun."

The close one sneered in disgust, shaking her off and motioning with his head towards the stairs; the other followed after, having forgotten all about Marginalia. She grinned, tying a practiced knot and striding towards the door.

Shame, she thought, looking over her shoulder at them cockily walking away. I won't get to see the looks on their faces when he gets kicked out of his own penthouse.

She could imagine it, though, and that was still pretty good. As she neared the doorperson, they stood, clearly recognizing her, opening the door and tilting their head.

Of course they would recognize me, she thought, laughing to herself. After all, I 'deserve to be here'.

As the sound of music was replaced with a familiar din, she breathed a sigh of relief. It was good to be back in her element.

"I'll have a Caesar," she said casually as she approached the bar, locking eyes with the muscular woman behind the counter. Marginalia quirked her eyebrow, and the bartender returned the look with a nod and a smile. As she watched the bartender's shoulders flex, as the cocktail was shaken, a voice came from her left.

"— believe somebody else would actually order a fucking Caesar!" a cloaked figure said, laughing openly. "It's just so—"

"Cut it out," another hidden figure beside her replied in a sultry, feminine tone, swatting at the first one's shoulder playfully. "We're in public, babe."

"Fine," the first intoned, as the pair looked up, finally noticing that Marginalia had been staring.

If you're going to talk about me, at least do it to my face.

Before she could move any closer, the second figure held out a hand in apology, nodding and trying to resolve things amicably. Luckily for them both, the bartender had returned, and Marginalia was far more interested in her.

"Here you go, darling." The bartender set down her glass, speaking in a husky tone, ragging out each consonant with a mischievous lilt. "You have to be an interesting woman to order a drink like that. Can I get your name?"

"What, are you flirting, or just a fae trying to trick me into dropping my guard?" Marginalia tittered. "For what it's worth, your appearance did pull me in, but you'll have to do more than just that to earn my name."

"You're too smart for this place." The bartender pressed her arms against the bar and flexed her muscles. "My name's Mina. What are you doing down here, in our little chaotic den?"

Marginalia smiled at the woman, turning her back to the bar, attempting to appear aloof as she scanned the crowd, drink in her hand.

"You seem to be on a roll, Mina," Marginalia emphasized, "why not keep guessing?"

"Oh, that's your kind of thing, is it? Fair play." Mina began to clean behind the bar, as she kept the majority of her focus on Marginalia. "Obviously, you belong here."

"Obviously," Marginalia said, the concept burning a hole in her pocket, metaphorically.

"You don't seem like a buyer." Mina shook her head.

"Oh?" Marginalia looked back and watched Mina from the corner of her eye.

"You're not an asshole," she stated simply, chuckling to herself. "Are you here to find somebody to hire?"

"Almost there, sweetheart." Marginalia lit up as the woman turned pink. "I'm more of a facilitator."

"You're a thief," Mina said simply, as if it was always a fact that both had known.

"What? Have a problem with my career choice?"

Marginalia held her breath. As cool as she was playing it, the same doubt she had felt many times crept back in. A moment later, she felt Mina's breath on the nape of her neck.

"Not at all, honey," Mina whispered. "I like a woman who knows how to use her hands."

Fuck, Marginalia waited a second for her mind to reboot, hot under the collar, sipping from her cocktail..

"Speaking of, I do need to get down to business." Marginalia set down her drained glass, sliding it across the bar towards Mina. "Maybe I'll see you around?"

"Here's hoping," Mina leaned forward and posed one last time. "See you later, thief."

As Marginalia began to walk into the crowd, determined to find a buyer, she paused. Turning, ever so slightly, she winked at Mina over her shoulder.

"It's Marginalia, by the way. See you next time, Mina."

By the look on Mina's face, it seemed her reputation had proceeded her. That, or she had affected Mina more than she had thought. Either way, she counted that as a win.

Things had certainly been easier on other nights, and Marginalia found herself running into dead ends more often than not. It seemed she arrived right after a concept shipment arrived, and stock was full at nearly every concept vendor. Anybody who made an offer lowballed her laughably; she might need the cash, but she wasn't desperate.

Not yet.

Not as long as I still have Ernie to see, Marginalia had saved her favorite idea trader for last. That status wasn't because he was the best, nor was it because he gave her the best prices. He had helped her out when she was in a rough spot, and she did the same. Other thieves and vendors might vie for notoriety or power, but Ernie?

Ernie was happy in his corner, and she loved him for that.

Approaching the warm tent, a lean-to that Ernie had decorated with trinkets carrying concepts, ontologic cores and more, Marginalia saw his bald head poking out from behind a workbench.

"Ernie," she called in a sing-song voice. "Have I got something you'll want."

When he popped his head up, it was not wearing the welcoming grin she expected.

He looks anxious. Her eyes narrowed. Why?

"Marginalia! So— Sorry, I'm just a bit busy tonight." His attention was still clearly elsewhere.

"What?" Marginalia walked lazily into his makeshift stall. "Don't have time for your favorite idea mover?"

"I just—" Ernie paused, looking around, eyes darting to and fro. He nodded his head, telling Marginalia to come closer. She obliged, and as she neared, Ernie continued in a whisper. "Look, I've got a big ticket item tonight. I sell this? I'm set for months. Sorry, I'm just not in a place right now where I can spare the— "

As Marginalia craned her neck over his bench, she caught the edge of a box before he snapped it shut, glaring at her.

"Keeping secrets now, are we?" Marginalia scoffed, turning to look at a trinket on the wall. What does he have? I would have heard about anything major, or at least, rumors would have spread. There haven't been any major heists lately, so…

"Do you mind?" Ernie said more firmly, making it clear that she should leave.

Thankfully, Marginalia was not the kind to follow directions.

"How dangerous is it?" She took a swing — and struck gold.

"You're killing me here." Ernie begged, sweat pouring down his brow. "What can I do to get you to leave?"

Marginalia smirked, opening up her bag and removing the few concepts she brought with her. They were gnarled, hand carved figurines, exotic and unrecognizable. The stones shimmered with flecks of crystal, embedded into the form.

"Okay." Ernie was frantic. "What am I looking at here? Luxury, brand names?"

"Those are exclusive luxury concepts." She gestured at the small statuettes. "Guaranteed to make any item one-of-a-kind."

"Anything more interesting?" Ernie dismissed her baubles. "You and I both know that's nothing."

Marginalia rolled her eyes, putting them back into her bag. She gently lifted another piece, stone, ancient and significant. "What about this?"

"Margie." A nickname Marginalia hated, that only he could get away with using. "So what? What is this, just a museum concept? An artifact?"

"Ernie, it's better than just a museum artifact." She leaned in, conspiratorially. "It's an ancient artifact, stolen and displayed within the British Royal Museum. Anything you want to falsify provenance on, use this and you're guaranteed to get away with it."

Ernie paused, looking conflicted. On any other night, Marginalia knew that she would have caught him, but… he just couldn't take his eyes off of his prize.

"I just… can you come back in a week?" Ernie was apologetic, but unwilling to waver. "Tonight's just bad timing."

"I can't." Marginalia was worried, her honed mask cracking. "Look, I need to make rent. Can we cut a deal here?"

Ernie hemmed and hawed for a few seconds more, before shaking his head.

"Marginalia, you know that I will always go to bat for you," Ernie said, apologetic. "Listen, my buyer is coming sometime soon; if you hang around at the bar, come back when they're gone and then we can talk, okay?"

Marginalia acquiesced. Instead of picking up her artifact, she left it on the tabletop.

"Don't forget your—"

"Keep it for now." Marginalia interrupted him in a less-than subtle maneuver. "That way, if anything happens to it before I come back, you'll owe me. More."

Ernie laughed, nodding and squirreling the piece within a hidey-hole as Marginalia drifted away from his stall.

That box… Marginalia was unable to ignore a mystery that interesting. Just how bad is that concept of his?

As Marginalia wandered her way through the weaving corridors of stalls, carts and displays she made sure to steer clear of a few that were… objectionable. Not that she was one to talk, but, there were always degrees of morality.

There were vendors who found rare concepts, those who worked with thieves to secure items for buyers, those who treated things like it was a flea market — all of those were reasonable, and generally, pretty good people. You had identity forgers and other specialty artisans, each living and dying by their morals and reputations. And then, there were the stalls that stole concepts as you walked by, those that employed more… violent tactics in their recovery. And worst of all? Some stalls had recently started to sell mass-produced, simple concepts: ideas like 'sharp', 'shiny', or 'toxic'.

Marginalia didn't know exactly how they 'mass-produced' an idea, but — any solution she could think of was exploitative or dangerous.

I'm not stupid enough to get into bed with somebody like that, no matter how gorgeous, she thought, passing one such stall with a very pretty man behind the counter. She didn't have a 'code of honor', per se, Marginalia preferred flexibility in her approach.

Her one rule, the one that had saved her time and time again?

Don't take stupid risks, she reminded herself, or you'll get stupid prizes.

Reaching the end of the cluster of stalls, leading back into the bar, she caught sight of a few people she had seen here before, running into them as she came to buy or sell an concept: idea thieves, like her. She paused, considering approaching them to say hello.

As much as I keep to myself, a little networking never hurt anyone.

Before she could make her way over, however, a figure bumped into her from behind. Immediately, Marginalia's hands began to shimmer as she mentally checked her sense of self, searching for any incongruence. If you lose sight of who you are, then you won't even notice when somebody steals part of you.

Things seemed to check out, though.

Letting her guard down, glow fading, she recognized the person who had tripped into her. As they sat, dazed on the floor, blushing and rubbing their elbow where they hit it, Marginalia frowned.

"Inoh." Marginalia shook her head. "Haven't you learned to look where you're going yet?"

Inoh shrugged, and gave her a sheepish, still relatively-innocent look. "Sorry, Marginalia, didn't see you there. I was just—"

"Rushing?" Marginalia said, hand on her hip.

"Yeah." They rubbed the back of their neck. "You know me," they offered, as if it explained everything. Unfortunately, it did.

Inoh was a young idea thief, one she had given a few tips to during visits to the market — they weren't very careful, nor were they talented, but Inoh was kind. Marginalia had seen what happened to people who were kind down here; she did what she could to prevent that from happening again.

Extending her hand, and helping Inoh to their feet, she continued. "What are you in such a rush for?"

"Oh!" They bounced excitedly, buzzing uncontrollably. "I was just heading back to a few people I met, we're…"

Inoh looked around, surreptitiously.

They're not subtle, Marginalia rolled her eyes.

"We're pulling a job. A big one. Do you want in?"

No, her gut instinct told her immediately, before the rational brain interjected. Well, I do need rent… maybe I'll hear them out?

"I'll consider it." Marginalia still kept her guard up. "Who are you working with?"

"They're just over there," Inoh pulled towards the group she had spotted earlier. Sighing, Marginalia followed behind.

As she did, she began to riffle through her bag, looking for a small metal rectangle; finding it with ease, she opened the clasp on the end, as it opened like an accordion, revealing many blank white cardstock cards, and a single card at the front, embossed with a cursive 'M'. Her idea thief 'concept card', a little thing concept thieves had started a few years back, for when they met others like them.

Each concept card was embedded with a powerful ontological core, representing the thief; one that could replicate and sustain itself, even if the idea was taken from it. The blanks were just that: empty surfaces, ready for an idea.

As they approached the group, Marginalia saw a few members reach for their waists.

Guns? Marginalia tensed, ready to flee. Or their own cards?

Maybe they hadn't decided which to grab yet, either.

"Hey, guys," Inoh said, brimming with enthusiasm. "This is Marginalia, I was telling her about the job."

A larger, older thief who looked like he belonged at a dock scowled. "Inoh. What did I tell you about talking about our plans?"

"I just—" Inoh stammered, before Marginalia took pity on them. She cut forward, extending her concept card.

"You can trust me," Marginalia acted uninterested, allowing the gathered thieves to reach out and pull her concept from the card. It wasn't just a way of identifying them, it also served as a record of their exploits, previous jobs, and other notable details.

In other words, Marginalia was showing off.

If that's not enough, then they're too slow for me anyways.

A girl with a rat's nest for hair spoke next.

"I've heard of you before, you pulled that Hoarder job, right?"

"The weapon?" Marginalia knew exactly what they meant. "That was me."

The group closed in, whispering amongst themselves. Marginalia picked at her nails, casually and disinterested.

God, they take their time, don't they? She dug an imagined fleck of dirt from under her index nail. I'm about ready to leave this generic rogues gallery and go back to something more fun. Like Mina.

Before she gave up, however, it seemed they had reached a consensus.

"We need somebody who can move big ideas," the gruff one said, crossing his arms. "Interested?"

"How big?" Marginalia dug for information. "Actually, scratch that. Who's the buyer?"

"You don't care what we're stealing?" The man failed to mask his surprise. Marginalia had fun, where she could, and this was no exception.

They're all the same. Marginalia was unimpressed by Inoh's 'friends'. The same buttons, the same triggers, and the same tricks to catch them off guard.

It was a bit boring, she would admit, working with people at this level, but… maybe the job would be worth it.

"What we're stealing isn't relevant, because I know that I'll be able to do it." Marginalia crossed her arms. "The employer is far more meaningful for me to know before signing up. So?"

"We're stealing a shipment of refugees, anomalous ones." The man spoke casually, as if it was a daily occurrence. "The CI wants those cover stories to infiltrate the… kinder groups, to get their people on the inside more easily."

"No thanks," Marginalia immediately dismissed the group and snapped her card case shut. "Not quite my speed."

"Are you sure?" The gruff tone was now wavering, the slightest hint of desperation leaking in. "It pays well, you'll get a fair cut."

"I don't 'do' war crimes," Marginalia tossed her hair to the side. Ignoring the man, she turned to Inoh. "Look after yourself, okay? Remember what I told you."

Inoh looked conflicted, but nodded slightly. "Th— thanks," They made no move to leave the group.

"Fine." The man riffled through his pockets, and pulling out his card case. "If you ever decide that your 'morals' are less important than, you know, living the good life? Come find me."

She grabbed his concept, sticking it onto an offered blank. 'Porter Black', it meant. A man who would do anything, for the right price.

For a moment, Marginalia considered crumpling it up — but she knew it was better to stay neutral, than make more enemies. There may be no conceptual honor amongst idea thieves, but she still had manners.

She slid the card into her bag, forcing a smile, and departing for the bar. As she turned, she began to frown, thinking about Inoh.

You can't save them all, she reminded herself. The best you can do is save yourself.

By the time Marginalia had returned to the bar, unfortunately, Mina had been replaced by not only somebody far less interesting, but one who did not know what a Caesar was. Even when explained, he struggled with the idea of it, asking 'why would you want to drink that?'

Oh well. Marginalia looked him up and down once more, leering. At least the idiot is pretty to look at.

As she idly sipped on her drink, and wondered if Ernie was finished with his deal, she watched the cloaked figures out of the corner of her eye. They hadn't moved, nor done anything to warrant further suspicion, but, Marginalia felt off.

They're here for something, so, what is that something? A beat later, a thought crossed her mind. Or, who is that someone?

Before she could think on the topic any longer, the relative consistent murmur of the bar-cum-bazaar was interrupted by shouts, screams, and a vortex of noise. Her eyes darted around trying to identify the source.

God damn it. Marginalia slammed her drink down and stood up. This better not be fucking Er—

The familiar baritone scream that cut through the crowd only confirmed it: this was Ernie's fault.

Weaving through the fleeing crowds and curious onlookers alike, Marginalia stalked purposefully towards the back corner that housed Ernie's stand. As she did, light began to bend in strange ways, the images of the world beginning to bend and distort. Pausing, Marginalia took a breath, and centered herself ontologically.

You are Marginalia, thief extraordinaire. Marginalia felt all extents of her body, physical and conceptual. You cannot be forgotten, nor will you forget yourself.

Mantra ingrained in her mind, Marginalia continued into the chaos of the market, repeating it mentally as she did.

She turned a corner, and where Ernie's stall had been was— well, yes, one could argue it was still 'Ernie's Stall', conceptually, but, in practice?

The world seemed to be folding in on itself there, radiating fractals extending from Ernie's workbench, where the box had been placed on top. She saw Ernie, hunkered down in the back of his stand, struggling to remain conscious, let alone to maintain his grip on reality. Shape and colors distorted in a kaleidoscope of noise, bright enough to burn her eyes, as Marginalia considered her next steps.

"What the fuck did you do now, Ernie?" she yelled, her voice echoing, distorting and seeming to bend along the curves of shifting reality.

"I swear!" He sounded as if he was behind her. "It just did that on its own!"

"What? What fucking concept did you bring here?" Marginalia edged closer towards Ernie, as best as she could given the ever-changing non-Euclidian space the stall now resembled. Objects twisted, shifting in meaning, morphing between connected and disconnected ideas all the same. It extended out, like an aurora, strongest centered around the dangerous concept, weakening as it went further out.

Marginalia grabbed a piece of chalk from her bag and marked a line on the ground, where she best guessed the field of influence stopped; a few seconds later, she looked back.

The line had been replaced with a deep, red gouge in the floor, as if laughing at her.

Fuck. She dropped the chalk. It's growing.

"It's not important!" Ernie still protested, but Marginalia'd had more than enough bullshit for one night.

"Ernie. Tell me what the fuck that is this fucking second, before your mind is too abstracted to remember. What were you selling?"

Ernie froze, brow creasing as he concentrated, trying to dig up the ever-drifting memory. The twisting fractals grew larger now, threatening to engulf him.

"Instability!" he shouted in a moment of fleeting lucidity. "It's 'instability'."

Who the fuck would bring a concept that dangerous to a place with so many fucking people?

But, of course, she already had her answer. Ernie would.

"I—" Marginalia took a step back, staggered by the expanding nexus of change. What the fuck do I do? I'm… I'm not fucking prepared to handle something like this, if I had time, sure, but—

From the other side of the stall, Marginalia saw a woman striding towards the swirling chaos: the cloaked individual from earlier.

"Hey, wait!" Marginalia tried to warn the woman. "You don't know how dangerous this—"

Seemingly ignoring her warning, Marginalia watched as the woman carelessly walked into the field of fractal shifting, shaking her head. As Marginalia held her breath, waiting for the worst to happen, the woman spoke.

"Fucking idiots." The woman reached a hand into her cloak as she strode towards the box in the center. "Can't even manage a simple fucking idea. This was supposed to be a cute date, not… whatever the fuck this is."

The cloaked woman had reached the center of the sphere of influence, and as the light, sound and objects distorted around her with the intensity of a winter maelstrom — nothing happened to the woman.

What the fuck is she? Marginalia was horrified. The only beings with that much conceptual stability are deities, extraplanar entities, or… no, she couldn't be an Icon, right?

Of course, as Marginalia would later realize, it didn't quite matter what the woman was; that wasn't relevant. What was relevant was what the woman pulled out of her cloak.

Her hand emerged with something that looked like a metal, skeletal frame of a cube, one foot wide in all dimensions, braces leading towards a spherical void in the center that seemed to distort all light that passed through it. Marginalia didn't recognize what it was, and she made it her business to know about things like that.

With a lazy flick of her wrist, the woman flung the cube at the center of the instability. It hovered in the air, looking like it might shift and change. Instead, the colors, lights, surfaces and sounds began to normalize, reverting to their intended meanings. The sphere of chaotic influence shrunk, constrained by the small spherical void in the center; the box shrunk, compressing the entropy until it was almost the size of a fist.

The box disappeared with a perfunctory 'pop', and the bazaar had returned to normalcy, in as much as the bazaar was normal, mind you.

Ernie stood up gingerly, glancing between Marginalia and the woman, face stuck fluctuating between fear and gratitude. The cloaked woman, seemingly, paid him no mind; she had turned, and was advancing on Marginalia.

Shit. Marginalia panicked. What the hell is she doing?

She considered her escape routes, but— the crowds had come to see the commotion, crisis having been seemingly averted, and she wouldn't be able to make a break for it in time. She was out of options.

"You were trying to help him, weren't you?" The concealed woman stood before her, neutral but intrigued.

"I— I wasn't just going to watch." Marginalia shrank into herself. a bad habit from her past. "Not with this many people around."

Despite the roar of the crowd, there was a distinct moment of silence. A beat later, the woman tilted her head.

"Interesting." The woman acted casually, as if there hadn't just been a disaster unfolding. "Let me buy you a drink."

That wasn't a question, Marginalia, nevertheless, nodded in cautious agreement. "Lead the way," she managed.

The cloaked figure turned, and walked towards the bar, Marginalia hesitantly following in tow, giving a passing shrug of confusion to Ernie.

I can yell at him about his stupidity another time. It's not like I have a choice in this. Maybe if I play things right, I can still salvage tonight.

As she caught up with the cloaked woman, Marginalia saw her companion sitting at the bar, her face no longer concealed. She was pretty, silver hair and green eyes, smiling like the cat who ate the canary. She reached out her right hand to the approaching woman, and Marginalia spotted a gemstone on her right ring finger.

The other woman, sitting and turning back was also visible now. She had dark wavy hair, flowing inside the back of her hood, like smoke, her sharp sculpted brows quirked.

She looked like a woman.

That fact, in context, deeply scared Marginalia.

Who the fuck is she?

"Sit," the dark-haired woman said, patting a seat at their tall table, again, not providing a choice.

"How can I—" Marginalia sat, before the silver-haired woman cut her off.

"We dropped our conceptual filters. Just for you. Feel special?"

"Honored," Marginalia quipped in pseudo-sarcasm. "Why… who… what do you want from me?"

The dark-haired woman seemed to ignore her question. "You were drinking Caesars, right?"

Marginalia nodded, and the woman signaled to the bartender to mix another for her. As she waited, she looked between the two women, who had locked eyes, and seemed to be engaged in a silent conversation. Marginalia tried to assess her options, but, from where they sat, she had no way out.

They planned this. Marginalia felt like the proverbial rat in a cage.

"You know," the dark-haired woman began abruptly. "I liked the trick you pulled."

"The trick?" Marginalia turned slightly to pick up the proffered cocktail from the bartender. If I can just bide enough time to figure out—

"You know, the one you pulled with the railgun? Pretty elegant, we thought."

Fuck. Fuck, fuck, fuck, fuck—

"Little mistake," the woman smirked. "You left your ontological signature behind when you forced the final reset of the system. It was buried in pretty deep, but—"

"We know all about digging up dirty little secrets," the silver-haired companion smiled wickedly. "Not to mention, we have the best conceptual bloodhound in the biz. Tracking you down was trivial."

They're Hoarders, Marginalia realized, every cell in her body screaming to run. I can't let them catch me, otherwise—

She couldn't spend her life in a box, Marginalia had made her choice. She kicked the table with her knee, sending the cocktails flying. At least, her own; it seemed the dark-haired woman had anticipated something like that, holding the other two drinks in the air.

When Marginalia turned to try and flee, she saw the silver-haired woman standing, blocking her way.

"Oh, don't worry about running." The silver-haired woman rolled her eyes.. "We don't give a shit about 'justice'. Hell, I was impressed, that was fucking hilarious. You know they think it's a toaster?"

Marginalia was completely out of her element, and despite every instinct telling her not to, she gave up.

"Well then." Marginalia sat back down and wiped up her spilled drink, begrudgingly. "What the fuck is going on here?"

"We should probably introduce ourselves." The dark-haired one pushed her hood down, hair cascading out as she did. "My name is Heather, and that's Lillian."

"And… you work for the Foundation?"

"Ehh?" Lillian tilted her hand back and forth. "We work at the Foundation."

"There's a difference?" Marginalia came across more dismissively than she meant it. Thankfully, the women shared a glance and laughed.

"Yeah, there is." Heather relaxed and leaned back in her chair, sipping from her fruity cocktail. "Namely, I get to make the choice I want to make, no matter what the higher-ups say."

"Then, pray tell," Marginalia said, trying to find her calm. "What do you want?"

Heather looked like the cat around her cage, leaning in. "How would you like a permanent position? I could use somebody as fearless and talented with concepts as you on my team. You're the first concept thief we've met who is competent enough without being a massive piece of shit. Interested?"

"What's in it for me?" Marginalia's curiosity betrayed her suspicion.

"You mean, other than a salary and a place to stay?" Lillian kicked her feet up on the stool beside Marginalia, heels thudding onto the padding. "You'll get to do things you could only ever dream of."

"Plus," Heather added, "we'll keep your little secret. Nobody needs to know that you are Marginalia, you can just be whatever cover story you want; and as long as you stay loyal, that never has to change."

"So…" Marginalia considered her options, if she had any. "You're blackmailing me into a job?"

"Partially?" Heather quirked her head and started laughing. "But you still have the final choice. Say no, and we'll give you a few days head start."

I… Marginalia was stuck, trying to figure out the right answer. As much as I fucking hate working for 'the man'… She paused, looking at Heather. They do seem like they hate it as much as I do. Obviously, if they're going to blackmail an idea thief into secret employment, but… I'm not seriously considering this, am I?

"You are absolutely considering this," Lillian's green eyes were piercing, as if she reading her mind. "You were good by yourself. With Heather and I? You'll be the best."

It seemed, to Marginalia, that she could only do what a thief did when presented with an unprotected gem: even if it was a trap, you still took it..

"Tell me how you did that trick, and you've got yourself a deal."

"Just one of the many toys you'll get to play with." Heather extended her hand, which Marginalia grabbed. "Welcome to the team."

Marginalia grinned, leaning back in her chair with renewed confidence. Obviously, these two understand the level of professional and talent I have, and they can see just how uniquely skilled I am. After all I—

Marginalia froze, the rest of her self catching up. That wasn't her true self, no, that was the part that knew it 'deserved to be here'. Isolating the rogue concept mentally before it could integrate fully into her sense of self, she held a hand to her temple, fingers shimmering as she extracted the errant idea.

Looking for a host, and noticing the bartender coming over to yell at Lillian to get her boots off the seat, Marginalia made a quick choice, pushing the concept onto Lillian's heeled boots. In a blink, the feeling was gone, and the bartender stopped in his tracks, seeing that everything was exactly where it was meant to be.

"Actually." Marginalia blinked, hesitating. "I…"

"Cold feet already?" Lillian rolled her eyes. "What'd I tell you, babe, you were never—"

"It's not that." Marginalia unfolded her hands, interrupting Lillian's aside. "But I want to make sure I earned this job. On my own merits."

"What are you talking about?" Lillian was, uncharacteristically, confused. "Did you not steal the railgun?"

"No, I did, I just—"

Heather, who had been watching this exchange with raised brow, took that moment to interject.

"What did you just get rid of, there?"

"You noticed?" Marginalia hadn't expected a non-thief would see anything. "I left my pass at home, so I stole an idea off of some rich prick outside. I moved it onto her heels," inclining her head at Lillian's feet.

"Oh my god! Lils, she made your boots 'deserve to be on the stool', that's—"

"That's fucking great!" Lillian immediately joined in the shared bemusement. "So, what's your problem, Marginalia?"

"I…" She paused, taking a breath in. "Look, I just wanted to make sure that you actually wanted me, not just the woman who you 'knew' 'deserved to be here'. Does that make any sense?"

"Crystal clear," Heather gave her a soft smile. "You're speaking our language. In fact, I'd say that proves that we picked the right person; you'll fit right in."

Huh. Marginalia hesitated, before the corners of her mouth turned up. "In that case, when do I start?"

Retrocausal Provenance

Forgotten Memories

To Be Continued...
