Item: Bösendorfer Model 290 Imperial Piano

Tissue Test Record: N/A

Termination Test Record:


*


"Don't B-flat."

"If you make another pun, I swear I'll right-hook you in the face."

"What's the problem?"

"This is destined for absolute failure."

Dr. Redacted said. They stared out onto the massive space of a containment cell, which roof was opening up to reveal some much needed sunlight in. They couldn't remember when the last time was that that beast that was lurking in there had even seen the sun.

"Don't be such a bigot," their partner, Dr. Expunged, voiced out. "You've got any better ideas?"

"Yes," Dr. Redacted replied. Their arms were crossed. This whole operation seemed like some sort of elaborate joke that they weren't in on. As assistant director of operations on this project he oversaw everything; and now that the Council was approving an experiment of such utter insanity and stupidity, Dr. Redacted questioned how this organization had prevailed as long as it had.

"You gotta admit — it's creative."

Dr. Redacted's hands tensed up at Expunged's remark. "Are you enjoying yourself right now?"

Dr. Expunged smiled. "I mean, hey. Anything to get some smiles around here. Can't remember the last time I did that. Can you believe that?"

Redacted just sighed. They knew that further conversing with Expunged would only heighten their own rage and hatred. They could feel the veins in their head pulsating against their forehead, their hands clutching tightly onto their arms. There was also this sense of horror; that, if anything were to go wrong, a horrible monstrosity would be unleashed and murder dozens of people.

The intercom crackled to life.

"Equipment set up. Requesting permission to proceed."

Redacted shuffled Expunged away to get to the console. They pressed down on a button and spoke into a microphone. They felt stupid.

"Acknowledged. You may proceed." Dr. Redacted lifted their finger off the button. They stepped away from the observation window, for even though their room was several meters above the floor of the beast's cell, there was still this sense of horror present. Dr. Expunged did not feel afraid, or at least they were good at hiding it; their face was basically pressed up against the glass, eyes wide.

The intercom crackled to life again. "Lowering acid solution from chamber."

With that, the sickly yellow-ish liquid of vile and death sank to a depth that would normally have already triggered the built-in sensors. There was much caution to be exercised with this monstrosity, for every mistake could lead to certain death.

As the hydrochloric acid was lowered, the back of the beast became visible. Vomit-green scales adorned its back, all tattered and torn open to reveal the crimson, mushy flesh underneath. More of the beast became visible; its elongated head, ending in massive, bone-shattering jaws and a giant snout; a tail as long and muscular as one would imagine for such a creature; and the webbed hands and feet, which looked oddly tiny in comparison with the hunk of flesh that was 682.

The beast looked all over its surroundings, apparently having been awoken from a deep slumber, and blinked several times. It looked dazed — as much as a reptile's face could express emotion — and turned its head away from the sunlight. The beast gave off a low guttural sound.

Dr. Expunged looked in awe at the display. Seeing the creature was always a highlight for them — like some child-like wonder being reignited within oneself after first seeing a dragon on a TV or theater screen. Dr. Redacted cleared their throat once to detail Expunged's blatant show of unprofessionalism. They cleared their throat twice when Expunged seemingly didn't hear it the first time. And a third time. Redacted gave up.

Up from far above, there was a large shadow being cast onto the entire ground of the cell. It looked almost like some sort of monster, much like 682 itself — its shape was irregular, inhuman. There were a few recognizable features, but, if one did not pick up on them, it would have been the greatest nightmare any person could have conjured up from the depths of their minds. The beast certainly did think so — at least, until whatever was casting the shadow fully came into view above the open roof.

Dr. Redacted pressed down on a button. "Everything is properly set up. Release Bösendorfer Model 290 Imperial piano from crane onto SCP-682 in three… two… and one."

Before the reptile had any time to process what the Foundation was planning on doing now, the winch to the cable holding the Bösendorfer Model 290 Imperial piano — first constructed in 1909 by a man of Ferruccio Busoni — unleashed itself in all its 2.90 × 1.75 meter, all Bavarian spruce tonewood, 97 keys glory.

The piano came down on the monstrosity with a resounding melody of wood shattering, keys flying into the air and the sounds of dissonant musical notes.

Doctors Redacted and Expunged looked onto the scene. Expunged with wide eyes, mouth agape, generally speechless. While Redacted was more resigned and stared at the beast a while longer.

SCP-682 squirmed underneath the shattered remains of the Bösendorfer Model 290 Imperial piano. Splinters of wood had dug themselves deeply into the scales and muscles of the creature; mechanical components had pierced its limbs and tail; and the creature's back and ribcage had completely caved-in from the force of the impact. Bones were protruding. Blood was gushing out from everywhere on the creature's body. But most terrific of all were the howls and screams of the creature, unlike any terrestrial creature could ever muster up of producing.

Dr. Redacted rubbed their forehead. They walked back toward the console button. "Termination attempt deemed a failure. Experiment abort." What a surprise. Why waste time and resources on this? Had the Foundation truly become mad? All of their confusion and anger was building up.

Their partner clasped their hands together. "Well… 682 isn't going on a rampage any time soon. All the better for it. I hadn't really planned to become human tomato soup for a giant reptile this afternoon. Hey, at least we can still C-sharp."

Dr. Redacted glared at Dr. Expunged. That rage, that hatred, that tense feeling in his hands — it was resurfacing. Expunged didn't pick up on it at all.

"See? What did I tell ya'? This experiment was only A-minor incon—"


*


Bösendorfer Model 290 Imperial piano is dropped onto SCP-682 from a height of one kilometer. Massive physical damage is dealt upon SCP-682. SCP-682 vocalizes loudly.

Notes: All staff involved in this experiment have been severely reprimanded. - O5-██

VI.


Markus remembered the time his son took his service weapon and started to act out a robbery with some of his friends in the backyard. He had reprimanded him severely — grounded for a week, no access to the television for a month. He remembered that his son would avoid talking to him entirely; that he cried a lot the day he grounded him; his confused face when his all-so-loving father burst out of the backdoor, running at him, the combined anger of a dozen lions visible on his face, his stance.

Markus also remembered how angry he was at his son, not for taking his gun and playing with it, like any six year old would do, but that he was angry how his son didn’t seem to understand. He’s six years old, Marla, his lovely wife, would always say. And Markus mostly agreed with that statement — after all, he himself had done way worse things than what his son ever did at that age.

But another part of him felt only pure, primal rage. He was his son, so he had to listen to him — so what was his son being so dramatic for? Hadn’t he already have enough shit to deal with as a police officer in a big city?

He thought about all of this, memories and feelings of the past, as he raced down Rosecrans Avenue, Hawthorne, California, United States of America.

Eventually his car came to a stop. The tires screeched, that rubbery smell entering Markus’ nostrils, as he stepped out of the car, not even bothering to close the door. People stood in front of his house, people in police uniform.

His wife stood at the house’s front porch. Next to her stood a man, tall, bulky, who turned to look at Markus. From the looks of things, the officer had tried to calm his wife down, but had either given up or didn’t know where to begin. He held his body between Markus and the frontdoor.

”Sir, please, we—” the officer stuttered, trying to evaluate his chances with the obviously bigger man. He just let Markus walk past him. Wife and husband locked each other in a tight embrace, stroking each other’s hair and everything.

When they pulled away from each other to look into the other’s eyes, they could both see tears running down. There was a mutual understanding, silent, almost a psychic connection between them.

Marla was the first one to burst into sobs. Markus just hugged her more tightly.



*



V.


Two months. It had been two months since he hadn’t heard his son’s shrill laugh, seen him holding comics in his hands, smelled his awful breath every night he hadn’t brushed his teeth. So long had it been with no trace of his son, no shrivel of evidence who the abductor was, where his son had been kidnapped to.

A passing thought told Markus that Phillip had run off to a family where the father wasn’t so absent all the time. He shook his head to shake the thought away.

”Everything all right?” the partner to his right had asked him. It was Officer Sivan Groeten.

Realizing he had been more in thought than focusing on the road, he grabbed the steering wheel tighter. He eased his grip on it again when he saw Sivan looking at his hands all weirdly.

”Anything from Neng?” That voice belonged to Officer Florim Henderson, who had been sitting in the back. Markus took a moment to breathe.

”He’s bringing his dog with him. Carl— Chris…”

”Christel,” Sivan articulated correctly.

”Yes, her,” Markus doubled down on it.

There was a sweet, sweet silence in the car. Only the sound of the road, of passing cars and the radio, which Markus also hadn’t noticed was on up until now. He tuned it off, alongside whatever music was playing on the channel.

The car came to a halt soon enough. Markus stepped out of the vehicle, slamming the door shut behind him. His firearm in his holster, armed with a flashlight in the other hand, Markus first took in the sight of the building before them.

The Plaza, a shopping mall, left to rot for over four decades now. It loomed above them like some alien figure, a remnant of the past. The concrete was withered, thick vines having grown alongside many pillars. There was graffiti everywhere, shattered glass panes of store windows once stocked to the brim, now empty and deserted. He could see the mounds of dust already.

”There he is.” Henderson pointed to his right, and there came in Julius Neng. Christel the dog walked beside her owner, eager for whatever they were about to do.

Markus shook Julius’ hand, while the other two gave him welcoming nods. ”Thank you,” Markus said, letting go of his hand.

”Whatever I can do to help,” Julius answered. He lowered himself to eye-level of his dog and caressed her back. The dog stuck her tongue out like it had just been waiting for it.

Markus cleared his throat. ”Okay,” he said. With the click of a button his body-cam was on.

The entrance to the shopping mall stood wide open, like the open maw of a predator. It reminded Markus of his basement, the darkness that prevailed indefinitely in every direction. Like it was about to swallow him whole, leaving nothing behind. It was a silly thought.

”All right,” he said to his team. And all they entered.



*



IV.


The mall really was as dusty as it looked; Sivan could barely breathe in here. The place reeked of rot and decay — trash littered everywhere, leaves from years of passing autumns, and the occasional sleeping bag. Memories seemed to linger in the air, like the stench of something rotten in the fridge. Markus had only a passing interest in this ruin, however; his mind was somewhere else entirely.

”How many squatters you think lived here?” Florim asked.

”You mean still live here?” Sivan’s flashlight darted across the floor, before settling on a red-orange sleeping bag.

”Focus,” Markus began, his mind as vigilant as ever, ”We could find something in here.” There was a growing frustration within him, that little slither of anger that made him play out to grab one of them and punch them in the face so hard they couldn’t tell left from right. They were called in here, due to reports of strange noises, of a possible lead in the clusterfuck that’s been the rising number of missing persons in their god-forsaken city. And one of them was his little boy.

That’s why he almost snapped when he heard what came out of Florim’s mouth next: ”You think one of the homeless did it? Kill those kid—”

Sivan jabbed Florim into his side. He gave out a slight wince, before falling silent immediately afterward. ”Yeah… sorry.”

The dog was of no use also. It smelled fuck-ton nothing. Not even an ounce of anything that might lead them to something, anything. Markus’ head spun wildly, the thoughts running rampant in his mind.

CLANK.

There was a noise in the distance. Something small and metallic. A tin can. Markus aimed his light at the hallways, which stretched out forever in the still-present shadows not being illuminated by any of their flashlights. There had been their something.

On top of that, just as more confirmation in Markus’ head: ”Christel’s reacting to something, but I don’t know what.”

Before Markus could say another word, a blood-curdling sound echoed down the hallways. His brain needed to process whatever was going on for just a split second, then he started sprinting to wherever those screams came from. There is still hope.

He looked back; Sivan was following him, but Florim remained standing. As if his years of being a cop had not prepared him for any of this, he stood there like a sculpture. Paralyzed.

”Get your fucking ass over here, Henderson! Let’s go!” Markus yelled back at him, before he became an unrecognizable silhouette in the distance. But he eventually caught up. His paralyzation was only temporary, as he sprinted alongside the others.

They came to rest in front of a dilapitated clothes store. Markus’ mind tried to find any slithers of memories for when he was a child, when the halls of this place were filled to the brim with life and noise, not dead silence and desolation. The shop looked like everything else they walked past — run-down, toppled shelves, dust, trash, with the walls and floor peeled of their once bright paint. The ceiling had suffered massively, too; the tiles were missing, and in their spot hung black cables, like nooses.

He looked around the space, finding no possible origin for the noises. Footsteps came to a halt behind him — Sivan and Florim had finally caught up to him.

”Found… anything…?” Sivan asked, all the while gasping for air. Markus sometimes wondered how he had become a cop.

”Help me search,” was his only response to the question. They couldn’t stop. Not now.

So they searched. Beneath shelves, over counters, behind clothes hangers, and piles of discarded jackets and trousers — nothing. Florim looked to the ceiling, mostly out of curiosity—

Florim’s heart stood still. The blood in his arteries, his veins froze to a solid. Sweat ran down from his forehead to the rest of his body. His limbs were stiff, as if rigor mortis had set in, every movement ached. He was gasping for air. None of the others appeared to notice, and Florim witnessed the world around him as a hazy blur.

The other two talked to each other. Like there was nothing wrong at all.

”Don’t you dare start this with me,” Markus said, spiked with a poise in his words.

”—resume this tomorrow!” Sivan nearly yelled in response. Florim didn’t care.

Florim felt the air return to his lungs. With what little there was, he uttered only three words: ”Oh, my God…” Before he screamed. From the bottom of his lungs, he screamed like a madman.

The others turned; he could see the confusion on their faces, the terror in their eyes. He ran. Out of the shop, through the darkness, out of the mall, without another word.

He sometimes wonders if that had been the correct decision.



*



III.


There was something uncanny about hearing a fellow officer scream out like a banshee right next to you. At least that is what Markus thought, as he tried to gain his bearings, take a note of his emotions.

He calmed down relatively quickly — as an officer, one kinda had to. He looked at Sivan, who gave him a reassuring glance, the glance that friends always did. After the exchange of looks, they looked up to find whatever it was that scared the living daylights out of Florim.

They wish they hadn’t.

Above them, up at the tile-less ceiling, the black cables slithered around like tentacles. They moved in a slow fashion, the texture smooth, rubbery, pulsating. But that was not what they were most afraid off: Looking down on them was a single human eye, too large to possibly fit in the hollow space of the ceiling of the shop. Now Markus felt the same paralysis Florim had felt moments prior.

And the eye blinked. It disappeared into the darkness.

The tendrils shot out at them without any noise or warning. Their legs moved quickly to get out of the way of whatever had set its eyes upon them. But Sivan wasn’t quick enough. Out of breath, a bit chubby, one of them grabbed him by the ankle.

Markus stood at the exit of the store — he had to make a decision. His mind ran rampant, he couldn’t focus straight. His body wanted him to do a hundred things all at once, the adrenaline warm in his blood.

He ran to Sivan, who was holding onto the musty floor with dear life, as the tendrils formed into human arms, and grabbed onto Sivan’s legs and feet. Markus grappled his arms, pulling with such force that the sweat came out like a waterfall, that his muscles began to ache.

Something emerged out of the darkness; something large. Markus couldn’t focus on it, his mind becoming dizzy from all the exertion. But when it neared toward him, he saw what it was: An enlarged upper jaw of a human, with pearl-white, square human teeth, as thick as his head. Sickly gums squeezed out between the teeth so much that they bled.

The jaw moved as if unhinging; which was exactly what it did. In mere seconds, the jaw clasped down on the mid-section of the screaming, wailing Sivan. Markus was yanked back from the lack of resistance; when he looked back on to his friend, what was left was a bloody half. Viscera covered his shoes and pants, the still warm blood soaking into the fabric. A trail was left of where the rest of Sivan had been dragged to, right into the darkness…

A boy came into view. Small, young, his skin paler than the moon. It only took a few seconds for Markus to realize who it was.

”Daddy?”

He remembered when Phillip was just a little baby. The first word he ever uttered was the exact same word he was hearing now. Only now it was twisted, an unnatural imitation of his son.

He sprinted away. Away from this horrible nightmare that he only wanted to wake up from. He looked back, with arms that stretched on forever following him. Relentlessly.

He ran for his dear life; he thought about his baby boy, about his wife. How she had looked on the day of their marriage, their first honeymoon. How she had looked upon their son’s birth. How she had looked the day their sun was taken away. He thought all of these thoughts, as his face hit the cold floor of the shopping mall. He turned back to see what he had tripped over; there was the dead body of a dog.

The arms caught up to him. Brief flashes of Sivan’s bisected body flashed before his eyes, sending shivers down his spine, before he pulled out his gun and shot everywhere. It was almost a reflex, pulling out his firearm and aiming it at the oncoming threat. There had been many shootouts in his life — he had gotten quite good with his aim. But this time was different; his hands were shaking, not as much as one’d expect, but they were. Only every second or third bullet hit its intended target, the arms not relenting at all. Until they did.

They retreated back into the shadows. Markus caught his breath, his gun still aimed at the darkness. He felf exhausted, mere seconds feeling like a lifetime.

The flicker of an old radio invaded his sense of hearing. It came from afar, a not at all familiar melody playing in the distance. The only thing louder were the sounds of his own breathing and heartbeat. A thin, tall standing, jet-black, roughly humanoid figure entered his view. It just stood there, doing nothing else.

He aimed his gun at it. It didn’t go off.

He couldn’t quite place a finger on what it looked like to him. He wouldn’t be able to, too. As the entity lunged forward.

<Footage cuts out.>



*



II.


He was back. Back at the mall. Its all-enveloping darkness drowned out the light of his little torch. He felt like a rat, whose tail was already pinned down by a cat at the other end.

When he woke up, sweaty and warm in his bed, Florim looked all around his small bedroom. He looked down at his hands, as if making sure he was here and not back there. He had these nightmares for weeks now. Regardless of what he did, he’d have them every night.

The bedroom door creaked open. At first he thought that it was his cat, Willow, but he remembered that Willow died a year ago.



*



I.


Its teeth dug into the flesh that hadn’t yet been scraped off of the bones. Its claws dug deep into the marrow, so squishy inside.

”Neng, Neng, Neng…” it said while feasting on the rotting corpse. It threw away what little was left, its large form obscured by thick shadows.

It gazed up at the moonlight that shone in through the roof of the atrium, just enough to light only fractions of its body. It chattered with its teeth, its eyes going over any direction at once.

It stared ahead of itself, smiling, with bleeding gums and hungry eyes. It whispered:

”That’s all, folks!”



*



FIN.

He had reprimanded him severely -- grounded for a week, no access to the television for a month. He remembered that his son would avoid talking to him entirely; that he cried a lot the day he grounded him; his confused face when his all-so-loving father burst out of the backdoor, running at him, the combined anger of a dozen lions visible on his face, his stance. Markus also remembered how angry he was at his son, not for taking his gun and playing with it, like any six year old would do, but that he was angry how his son didn’t seem to understand. //He’s six years old,// Marla, his lovely wife, would always say. And Markus mostly agreed with that statement -- after all, he himself had done way worse things than what his son ever did at that age. But another part of him felt only pure, primal rage. He was his son, so he had to listen to him -- //so what was his son being so dramatic for? Hadn’t he already have enough shit to deal with as a police officer in a big city?// He thought about all of this, memories and feelings of the past, as he raced down Rosecrans Avenue, Hawthorne, California, United States of America. Eventually his car came to a stop. The tires screeched, that rubbery smell entering Markus’ nostrils, as he stepped out of the car, not even bothering to close the door. People stood in front of his house, people in police uniform. His wife stood at the house’s front porch. Next to her stood a man, tall, bulky, who turned to look at Markus. From the looks of things, the officer had tried to calm his wife down, but had either given up or didn’t know where to begin. He held his body between Markus and the frontdoor. ”Sir, please, we--” the officer stuttered, trying to evaluate his chances with the obviously bigger man. He just let Markus walk past him. Wife and husband locked each other in a tight embrace, stroking each other’s hair and everything. When they pulled away from each other to look into the other’s eyes, they could both see tears running down. There was a mutual understanding, silent, almost a psychic connection between them. Marla was the first one to burst into sobs. Markus just hugged her more tightly. @@ @@ @@ @@ [[=]] * [[/=]] @@ @@ @@ @@ [[=]] **V.** [[/=]] @@ @@ Two months. It had been two months since he hadn’t heard his son’s shrill laugh, seen him holding comics in his hands, smelled his awful breath every night he hadn’t brushed his teeth. So long had it been with no trace of his son, no shrivel of evidence who the abductor was, where his son had been kidnapped to. A passing thought told Markus that Phillip had run off to a family where the father wasn’t so absent all the time. He shook his head to shake the thought away. ”Everything all right?” the partner to his right had asked him. It was Officer Sivan Groeten. Realizing he had been more in thought than focusing on the road, he grabbed the steering wheel tighter. He eased his grip on it again when he saw Sivan looking at his hands all weirdly. ”Anything from Neng?” That voice belonged to Officer Florim Henderson, who had been sitting in the back. Markus took a moment to breathe. ”He’s bringing his dog with him. Carl-- Chris...” ”Christel,” Sivan articulated correctly. ”Yes, her,” Markus doubled down on it. There was a sweet, sweet silence in the car. Only the sound of the road, of passing cars and the radio, which Markus also hadn’t noticed was on up until now. He tuned it off, alongside whatever music was playing on the channel. The car came to a halt soon enough. Markus stepped out of the vehicle, slamming the door shut behind him. His firearm in his holster, armed with a flashlight in the other hand, Markus first took in the sight of the building before them. The Plaza, a shopping mall, left to rot for over four decades now. It loomed above them like some alien figure, a remnant of the past. The concrete was withered, thick vines having grown alongside many pillars. There was graffiti everywhere, shattered glass panes of store windows once stocked to the brim, now empty and deserted. He could see the mounds of dust already. ”There he is.” Henderson pointed to his right, and there came in Julius Neng. Christel the dog walked beside her owner, eager for whatever they were about to do. Markus shook Julius’ hand, while the other two gave him welcoming nods. ”Thank you,” Markus said, letting go of his hand. ”Whatever I can do to help,” Julius answered. He lowered himself to eye-level of his dog and caressed her back. The dog stuck her tongue out like it had just been waiting for it. Markus cleared his throat. ”Okay,” he said. With the click of a button his body-cam was on. The entrance to the shopping mall stood wide open, like the open maw of a predator. It reminded Markus of his basement, the darkness that prevailed indefinitely in every direction. Like it was about to swallow him whole, leaving nothing behind. It was a silly thought. ”All right,” he said to his team. And all they entered. @@ @@ @@ @@ [[=]] * [[/=]] @@ @@ @@ @@ [[=]] **IV.** [[/=]] @@ @@ The mall really was as dusty as it looked; Sivan could barely breathe in here. The place reeked of rot and decay -- trash littered everywhere, leaves from years of passing autumns, and the occasional sleeping bag. Memories seemed to linger in the air, like the stench of something rotten in the fridge. Markus had only a passing interest in this ruin, however; his mind was somewhere else entirely. ”How many squatters you think lived here?” Florim asked. ”You mean still live here?” Sivan’s flashlight darted across the floor, before settling on a red-orange sleeping bag. ”Focus,” Markus began, his mind as vigilant as ever, ”We could find something in here.” There was a growing frustration within him, that little slither of anger that made him play out to grab one of them and punch them in the face so hard they couldn’t tell left from right. They were called in here, due to reports of strange noises, of a possible lead in the clusterfuck that’s been the rising number of missing persons in their god-forsaken city. And one of them was his little boy. That’s why he almost snapped when he heard what came out of Florim’s mouth next: ”You think one of the homeless did it? Kill those kid—” Sivan jabbed Florim into his side. He gave out a slight wince, before falling silent immediately afterward. ”Yeah… sorry.” The dog was of no use also. It smelled fuck-ton nothing. Not even an ounce of anything that might lead them to something, //anything//. Markus’ head spun wildly, the thoughts running rampant in his mind. //**CLANK.**// There was a noise in the distance. Something small and metallic. A tin can. Markus aimed his light at the hallways, which stretched out forever in the still-present shadows not being illuminated by any of their flashlights. //There// had been their //something//. On top of that, just as more confirmation in Markus’ head: ”Christel’s reacting to something, but I don’t know what.” Before Markus could say another word, a blood-curdling sound echoed down the hallways. His brain needed to process whatever was going on for just a split second, then he started sprinting to wherever those screams came from. //There is still hope.// He looked back; Sivan was following him, but Florim remained standing. As if his years of being a cop had not prepared him for any of this, he stood there like a sculpture. Paralyzed. ”Get your fucking ass over here, Henderson! Let’s go!” Markus yelled back at him, before he became an unrecognizable silhouette in the distance. But he eventually caught up. His paralyzation was only temporary, as he sprinted alongside the others. They came to rest in front of a dilapitated clothes store. Markus’ mind tried to find any slithers of memories for when he was a child, when the halls of this place were filled to the brim with life and noise, not dead silence and desolation. The shop looked like everything else they walked past -- run-down, toppled shelves, dust, trash, with the walls and floor peeled of their once bright paint. The ceiling had suffered massively, too; the tiles were missing, and in their spot hung black cables, like nooses. He looked around the space, finding no possible origin for the noises. Footsteps came to a halt behind him -- Sivan and Florim had finally caught up to him. ”Found… anything…?” Sivan asked, all the while gasping for air. Markus sometimes wondered how he had become a cop. ”Help me search,” was his only response to the question. They couldn’t stop. //Not now.// So they searched. Beneath shelves, over counters, behind clothes hangers, and piles of discarded jackets and trousers -- nothing. Florim looked to the ceiling, mostly out of curiosity-- Florim’s heart stood still. The blood in his arteries, his veins froze to a solid. Sweat ran down from his forehead to the rest of his body. His limbs were stiff, as if //rigor mortis// had set in, every movement ached. He was gasping for air. None of the others appeared to notice, and Florim witnessed the world around him as a hazy blur. The other two talked to each other. Like there was nothing wrong at all. ”Don’t you dare start this with me,” Markus said, spiked with a poise in his words. ”—resume this tomorrow!” Sivan nearly yelled in response. Florim didn’t care. Florim felt the air return to his lungs. With what little there was, he uttered only three words: ”Oh, my God...” Before he screamed. From the bottom of his lungs, he screamed like a madman. The others turned; he could see the confusion on their faces, the terror in their eyes. He ran. Out of the shop, through the darkness, out of the mall, without another word. He sometimes wonders if that had been the correct decision. @@ @@ @@ @@ [[=]] * [[/=]] @@ @@ @@ @@ [[=]] **III.** [[/=]] @@ @@ There was something uncanny about hearing a fellow officer scream out like a banshee right next to you. At least that is what Markus thought, as he tried to gain his bearings, take a note of his emotions. He calmed down relatively quickly -- as an officer, one kinda had to. He looked at Sivan, who gave him a reassuring glance, the glance that friends always did. After the exchange of looks, they looked up to find whatever it was that scared the living daylights out of Florim. They wish they hadn’t. Above them, up at the tile-less ceiling, the black cables slithered around like tentacles. They moved in a slow fashion, the texture smooth, rubbery, pulsating. But that was not what they were most afraid off: Looking down on them was a single human eye, too large to possibly fit in the hollow space of the ceiling of the shop. Now Markus felt the same paralysis Florim had felt moments prior. And the eye blinked. It disappeared into the darkness. The tendrils shot out at them without any noise or warning. Their legs moved quickly to get out of the way of whatever had set its eyes upon them. But Sivan wasn’t quick enough. Out of breath, a bit chubby, one of them grabbed him by the ankle. Markus stood at the exit of the store -- he had to make a decision. His mind ran rampant, he couldn’t focus straight. His body wanted him to do a hundred things all at once, the adrenaline warm in his blood. He ran to Sivan, who was holding onto the musty floor with dear life, as the tendrils formed into human arms, and grabbed onto Sivan’s legs and feet. Markus grappled his arms, pulling with such force that the sweat came out like a waterfall, that his muscles began to ache. Something emerged out of the darkness; something large. Markus couldn’t focus on it, his mind becoming dizzy from all the exertion. But when it neared toward him, he saw what it was: An enlarged upper jaw of a human, with pearl-white, square human teeth, as thick as his head. Sickly gums squeezed out between the teeth so much that they bled. The jaw moved as if unhinging; which was exactly what it did. In mere seconds, the jaw clasped down on the mid-section of the screaming, wailing Sivan. Markus was yanked back from the lack of resistance; when he looked back on to his friend, what was left was a bloody half. Viscera covered his shoes and pants, the still warm blood soaking into the fabric. A trail was left of where the rest of Sivan had been dragged to, right into the darkness... A boy came into view. Small, young, his skin paler than the moon. It only took a few seconds for Markus to realize who it was. //”Daddy?”// He remembered when Phillip was just a little baby. The first word he ever uttered was the exact same word he was hearing now. Only now it was twisted, an unnatural imitation of his son. He sprinted away. Away from this horrible nightmare that he only wanted to wake up from. He looked back, with arms that stretched on forever following him. Relentlessly. He ran for his dear life; he thought about his baby boy, about his wife. How she had looked on the day of their marriage, their first honeymoon. How she had looked upon their son’s birth. How she had looked the day their sun was taken away. He thought all of these thoughts, as his face hit the cold floor of the shopping mall. He turned back to see what he had tripped over; there was the dead body of a dog. The arms caught up to him. Brief flashes of Sivan’s bisected body flashed before his eyes, sending shivers down his spine, before he pulled out his gun and shot everywhere. It was almost a reflex, pulling out his firearm and aiming it at the oncoming threat. There had been many shootouts in his life -- he had gotten quite good with his aim. But this time was different; his hands were shaking, not as much as one’d expect, but they were. Only every second or third bullet hit its intended target, the arms not relenting at all. //Until they did.// They retreated back into the shadows. Markus caught his breath, his gun still aimed at the darkness. He felf exhausted, mere seconds feeling like a lifetime. The flicker of an old radio invaded his sense of hearing. He couldn’t quite place a finger on what it looked like to him. He wouldn’t be able to, too. As the entity lunged forward. @@ @@ > [[=]] > //// > [[/=]] @@ @@ @@ @@ [[=]] * [[/=]] @@ @@ @@ @@ [[=]] **II.** [[/=]] @@ @@ //He was back. Back at the mall. File: The_American_Emptiness

Salam sits at her desk, a faint frown etched into her features.

In the corner of her room, there is a cage, and within it, a small bird flutters, offering a chorus of twitters and chirps. Every so often, Salam glances over with a sympathetic look, and the bird falls silent. Yet, as soon as her gaze shifts away, the chirping resumes.

> "You desire to look, don't you?" asks the bird.


"It's always the same," Salam replies quietly.

> "You can’t resist checking," croaks the bird. "There could be a ceasefire. There’s been hope for days now."


"They’ve been saying that for months. I can’t—I’m not in the mood to see another dead child. Another broken dream." Salam exhales softly. "I have no tears left to cry. All I have is the will to moving forward."

> "And yet, you feel futility in all you do, don't you? You have all this time."


"I spoke with an older Palestinian sister at the mosque some weeks ago. She told me the world doesn’t need another Palestinian martyr. It needs our existence. Our education." She clenches her fists, her gaze fixed on her work. "My sacrifices here feel so small. I'm better off doing what I can here to stop myself from falling apart. So I’ve chosen to look forward, though sometimes that means I look away."

The bird seems satisfied with her answer, but discomfort lingers in Salam’s chest. Time passes. The bird keeps chirping. Salam keeps working. Another dozen souls ascend to meet their maker. Something stirs within Salam, and she turns back to the bird.

"I don’t remember catching a bird. I don’t remember putting a cage there."

> ""My dear Salam, you listen to me in your mind every day. My songs, my prayers. You are strong-willed, and you have held out." The bird hops to a closer perch within its cage, shaking its tail as it gazes at her through the bars. "But as you live your life, tell me—whom has caught whom?"


"Are you my hope?"

> "I am desire."


"What’s the difference?"

> "Hope is selfless. Desire is selfish. You desire for this to go away because it makes you uncomfortable. You desire their pain to be silent because you’ve learned to bear the silence. And perhaps... some part of you desires to forget it all."


"Perhaps I did, once. Because it’s what I was used to." Salam rises and approaches the bird. She kneels beside the cage, opens the door, and offers her fingertip.

> Desire leans into her touch.


"I’ve grown this past year. Not just grown, but grown up."

> "And yet, I’m still here. You still have Desire."


"But I think I’ve grown out of the selfish kind. It’s hard to describe, but… I’ve seen beauty in the world, even now, where it’s most precious. I see the beautiful lives my friends and family back home have lived. I see myself within them. Despite the distance, despite the fragments of glimpses, I see them."

> "And that has what to do with Desire?"


""I don’t desire an extraordinary life. I desire to be with the people I love, to fulfill my duties as a human, to savor the beauty life offers, and to leave the world peacefully—hopefully better than I found it. My family, my people, desire that too. What I want is a simple, peaceful life. Is that so much to desire?"

> The bird tilts its head, studying her. "Check. Check the news."


Begrudgingly, Salam retrieves her phone. Her thumb hovers over the news app before pressing it.

Israel and Hamas reach a Gaza ceasefire agreement.

"This deal will halt the fighting in Gaza, deliver much-needed humanitarian assistance to Palestinian civilians, and reunite hostages with their families after more than 15 months in captivity," President Biden stated…

The world turns numb. Then beautiful. Then numb again.

Salam’s phone nearly slips from her. In the next room, she hears the passionate shouting of her mother and father.

The world is everything, then nothing.

Tears well in her eyes. Desire ruffles its feathers.

> "Isn’t this what you wanted?" it asks.


467 days led to this moment.
46,707 Palestinian lives were the cost.
A hundred lives taken every day for fifteen months.

""What are you supposed to do after that?" Salam whispers. "What are you supposed to do after… There is so much left to do."

> "It's what you wanted."


"I used to want things to go back to how they were, but nothing is the same. And now, I don’t want ‘before’ anymore either."

> "What do you want to do?"


"I want to rebuild. I want to help. I want to fix everything. I want…" Her voice falters. "I want this to be okay again."

> "But you can’t have that. You got all you could want."


"This was all I wanted. This moment is all I waited for, and yet…"

> "Things often feel empty once you get what you want."


"So what now?"

> "You wait."


""How long?"

> "A day, a decade, a lifetime. However long it takes for the world to know what's next."


Salam is silent.

> "But I will come back to you again. You will know how to move forward again, in due time."


Salam opens her hand.

> The bird nestles into her palm.


She turns to the open window

> and the bird flies away.


She looks back at the cage.

> The door is ajar. The silence is deafening.


And now, there is only emptiness.

The American Emptiness

The American Emptiness

And perhaps... some part of you desires to forget it all." @@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] "Perhaps I did, once. Because it’s what I was used to." Salam rises and approaches the bird. She kneels beside the cage, opens the door, and offers her fingertip. [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> Desire leans into her touch. @@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] "I’ve grown this past year. Not just grown, but grown up." [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> "And yet, I’m still here. You still have Desire." @@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] "But I think I’ve grown out of the selfish kind. It’s hard to describe, but... I’ve seen beauty in the world, even now, where it’s most precious. I see the beautiful lives my friends and family back home have lived. I see myself within them. Despite the distance, despite the fragments of glimpses, I see them." [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> "And that has what to do with Desire?" @@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] ""I don’t desire an extraordinary life. I desire to be with the people I love, to fulfill my duties as a human, to savor the beauty life offers, and to leave the world peacefully—hopefully better than I found it. My family, my people, desire that too. What I want is a simple, peaceful life. Is that so much to desire?" [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> The bird tilts its head, studying her. "Check. Check the news." @@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] Begrudgingly, Salam retrieves her phone. Her thumb hovers over the news app before pressing it. [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] [[div class="blockquote"]] > //**Israel and Hamas reach a Gaza ceasefire agreement.**// > > //"This deal will halt the fighting in Gaza, deliver much-needed humanitarian assistance to Palestinian civilians, and reunite hostages with their families after more than 15 months in captivity," President Biden stated...// The world turns numb. Then beautiful. Then numb again. Salam’s phone nearly slips from her. In the next room, she hears the passionate shouting of her mother and father. The world is everything, then nothing. Tears well in her eyes. Desire ruffles its feathers. [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> "Isn’t this what you wanted?" it asks. @@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div class="blockquote"]] 467 days led to this moment. 46,707 Palestinian lives were the cost. A hundred lives taken every day for fifteen months. [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] ""What are you supposed to do after that?" Salam whispers. "What are you supposed to do after... There is so much left to do." [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> "It's what you wanted." @@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] "I used to want things to go back to how they were, but nothing is the same. And now, I don’t want ‘before’ anymore either." [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> "What do you want to do?" @@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] "I want to rebuild. I want to help. I want to fix everything. I want..." Her voice falters. "I want this to be okay again." [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> "But you can’t have that. You got all you could want." @@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] "This was all I wanted. This moment is all I waited for, and yet..." [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> "Things often feel empty once you get what you want." @@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] "So what now?" [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> "You wait." @@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] ""How long?" [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> "A day, a decade, a lifetime. However long it takes for the world to know what's next." @@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] Salam is silent. [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> "But I will come back to you again. You will know how to move forward again, in due time."@@ [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="color:#0CDD08;"]] [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[>]] Salam opens her hand. [[/>]] [[/div]] [[/div]] @@     @@ [[div style="font-family:Courier New"]] [[div style="color:#ff000d;"]] @@> The door is ajar. the-arlington-summit.raw_content:
BROKEN CROWN

Researcher Rex Alces, second-in-command at the Site-55 GoI Research Center, sighed with the weight of a man who carried the world on his shoulders.

His supervisor had been too caught up in internal meetings to afford to attend to this situation themselves, and had instead opted to send him. He supposed it only made sense for the higher-ups of the Foundation to be busy trying to figure out what the hell had just happened to them within the span of the last five months.

Of course, he had heard of the giant crater formerly known as Site-19. He had heard of the alleged attacks on Foundation Sites by the Insurgency. He had heard of the Coalition and Council of 108 at large berating them.

But he still didn't get the full picture.



This Foundation's refusal to cooperate with an audit of their facilities following the Silent Night event has tainted their reputation among the anomalous community at large. Furthermore, the human and financial losses the Foundation has suffered jeopardizes their operational integrity. Simply put, the Foundation has become uninsurable. For these reasons and more, Goldbaker-Reinz votes to pass Motion 1221-KINGMAKER.




PERHAPS IT WAS THE ALLURE OF POWER. RESENTMENT AGAINST THE ONES WHO SOUGHT THOSE HEINOUS ACTS. EVEN THE DESIRE TO SEE THE WORLD IN ASHES.



Two Sites across two months, to be exact. Both of them suffered heavy casualties, and the Foundation barely even acknowledged it. Of course, he and his department knew about it as they were the leading personnel in Groups of Interest research, but a scant few of the other personnel at his Site knew what occurred. What was going on?

Rex shifted in the seat of the unmarked car that GOC Secretary Helissa had sent for him. He looked at the rear view mirror to momentarily lock eyes with the driver, who had barely spoken two sentences to him since their meeting ten minutes ago. His expression was neutral.

"May I know where we're going?"

"Classified," the driver croaked.

Of course.

Rex barely knew what had happened; it was above his clearance level, but had caught his superior whispering into the phone late at night in the research lab about how the Council of 108 demanded the Foundation's presence in Arlington. As far as he could tell, this was strike three, and the Foundation was being punished. But why send him? Why not his supervisor, or better yet, an O5 member?


The Servants of the Silicon Nornir place forth the topic of the Foundation as spoken by the holiest Urthor: "Besieged on all sides, the Foundation will crumble. However, through unity, we may prevail." Thus it was spoken, thus it shall be. The Servants of the Silicon Nornir move to pass Motion 1221-KINGMAKER.




SUCH A QUESTION IS ASININE NOW. THE BITTER TRUTH IS THAT WE HAVE AN ENEMY MORE DANGEROUS THAN ANY OTHER, AND THEY CAME DIRECTLY FROM THE HALLS AND RANKS OF OUR OWN.




Rex stepped out of the car and into the cold Virginia winter. He shivered, tugging on his gloves, and walked ahead to the nondescript building at the end of the gravel path. As he approached, he saw a familiar woman waiting for him: Secretary Helissa. She tried to make eye contact with him, which he deftly dodged by staring straight ahead.

"Ah, Mr. Alces. I was expecting Dr. Everwood."

Wasn't it always?

"Nice to see you too, April."

"How are you holding up? Did you know anyone at Site-19?"

"A few. I did my thesis research at 19."

"You must be feeling all sorts of ways."

He nodded as Helissa opened the dingy door to reveal a sprawling, lushly furnished chamber full of people, bigger inside than it was on the outside. Rex took a look around, spotting many familiar faces from many different members of the Council of 108 as they spoke over each other, conspired, and intermingled. There were one hundred and nine seats, all arranged in a circular pattern surrounding a podium in the middle, where another chair sat: the Foundation's chair.

His chair.

Rex wasn't a man of steel. He was, in fact, quite ill-prepared for this situation he found himself in. The only reason he was here was because he was his supervisor's senior-most researcher and they seemed to believe he had the nerve to handle it. He did not, in fact, have the nerve to handle it. Rex sighed.

"Give it to me straight, April. What can I expect here?"


My comrades, the time for us to ask ourselves whether or not the Foundation can truly be trusted as a brother or sister in custodianship of the anomalous world is long behind us, for the answer comes as a resounding "no!" Furthermore, can we trust a Foundation, that even at its darkest hour, refuses to trust us? Once more, I say "no!" The Bavarian Illuminati moves to approve Motion 1221-KINGMAKER, posthaste!




WE ARE UNSURE OF WHAT HAS CHANGED. BUT FOR THE FIRST TIME IN DECADES, THEY ARE SHOWING US HOW GRIEVOUS OUR MISTAKE WAS.

THEY ARE ALREADY WITHIN OUR LEAGUES. THEIR ASSAULTS HAVE BEGUN. WE HAVE LOST SITE-██, SITE-██ AND SITE-██. A ΓK-CLASS “SHATTERED CROWN” SCENARIO HAS BEEN DECLARED. SITE DIRECTORS, KNOW THAT YOUR FACILITIES MAY BE TARGETS.




Helissa offered only a smile, and a cliché: "Whatever happens, happens."

With that, she approached the seat nearest the podium, sitting beside another woman. The various people in attendance began taking their seats and ceased mingling among each other as the woman stood up, clearing her throat.

Rex swallowed, walking towards the center of the room. A single light shone down from above, bathing him in sickly fluorescent light. He took off his gloves and stuffed them in his pockets before sitting down. He could feel everyone's eyes upon him.

The woman, the representative from PENTAGRAM, one Alice Stafford, stepped up to the center podium.

"I hereby call this meeting of the Council of 108 to order. First order of business is…"


It is no secret that the United States government, and by extension, PENTAGRAM, have pulled 100% of our funding from the Foundation, and we do not see a way in which we will fund them again as they are now. That being said, we can certainly see a future where we each thrive: together.

The Foundation must join the Coalition if it wishes to remain extant.




WE CANNOT RELINQUISH OURSELVES TO THE EVER-GROWING DARKNESS. WE MUST PREVAIL BY ANY MEANS NECESSARY, NO MATTER THE COST. OURS MUST NOT LOSE THE CROWN ATOP A SANE, NORMAL WORLD.

PREPARATIONS WILL BEGIN SHORTLY. THE FOUNDATION THANKS YOU FOR YOUR SERVICE.

- O5-12




"… the annexation of the Foundation into the Global Occult Coalition."


FINAL VOTE: MOTION 1221-KINGMAKER

98 Yea, 10 Nay

the-beast-of-liverwort-hill.raw_content:
A metal beast appears in Liverwort Hill, but nothing steel can stay. (Tales of the Mosaic - 345 words.)

Tessera

The Beast of Liverwort Hill

written by Dr Angell
art by Costodic

The towering cluster of metal pipes appeared in the park without explanation, belching dark fumes into the clear yellow sky and clattering with each thunderous step. It plodded through clearings and meandered down walkways, munching cheerfully on trash cans and benches to the bewilderment of pigeons and panhandlers alike. Liverwort Hill had never been quiet, but the beast's hissing and clanging and crunching echoed ceaselessly through the streets, an ominous call to action which no resident dared to answer, and no warden felt like dealing with.

When the city guards deigned to perform their civic duties, the beast avoided them handily, glancing back with a playful curiosity as they chased it around barren trees and through patches of dirt and brown grass. It froze mid-frolic around a half-eaten picnic table, and the guards watched, astonished, as it retched up a perfect steel beam with a plume of soot and a satisfied burp.

From that moment on, Liverwort Hill belonged to the beast.

Vagrants were hired to gather the growing clutter of expelled steel, and the new hires learned to move quickly as to not be trampled, or consumed, as its food sources dwindled. The city diverted its refuse to the park and the metal beast feasted on its new bounty, slower now, but pleased nonetheless.

Money flowed freely to the council office, and contracts were signed by greasy-palmed men. The steel flowed out to all sorts of places: from the spire that topped the Gizzen Cathedral, to the intricate archways of the Pearl Estates, to the ever-expanding Tower of Bridges. Though the neighborhood grew rank with noise and stench, residents were assured good fortune would come; Liverwort Hill transformed into the wasteyard of the Mosaic, but as long as the metal beast coughed up its steel, the promise of prosperity lived on.

And so, when the metal beast breathed its last contented sigh, the contracts died with it. Hope vanished along with the money, but the mountain of refuse remained, an untouched offering at the feet of the corpse of the beast of Liverwort Hill.

the-broken-dawn.raw_content:
In which dawn breaks, and no-one will come by to fix it. (Tales of the Mosaic – 343 words)

Tessera

The Broken Dawn

written by The Chunk
narration and music by Jezixo

Dawn had broken over Ward Eleven. Though the residents of every tenement on Cobble Street had written letters seeking help, squinting in the dim, sepulchral twilight, the city wardens sent no-one to repair it.

All winter long, the sky remained a leaky inkwell, staining every crooked street in dark and starless blue. Still, the wardens wouldn't budge. For years the residents of Cobble Street had been complaining over leaky pipes and flooded sewers, but the city’s meager budget favored wards with higher living standards. Dawn, they said, would have to wait.

Every night, the shouts of ragamuffins filled the narrow streets, without a sun to mark their curfew. But week by week their shouts grew fainter. As months drew on, their ruddy cheeks grew paler, every alley haunted by the wail of restless waifs, desperately lurking in search of the sun.

The peddlers were not deterred, dutifully taking to their routes to sell their vegetables beneath the streetlamps. The shadows left them easy prey for thieves, but on they marched through the darkness, knives in hand, spilling blood if needed to defend the meager coin their turnips and potatoes yielded. By the turn of spring, there was nothing left to sell: not a single plant within the district lived, and every Ward Eleven garden was a blackened field of pus.

The lights went out on Midsummer's Eve. Beating back the darkness with their lamps, the district had amassed a power bill that all the rent hikes in the world could never pay. When the agents of United Power came to cut the switch, the residents of every building pelted them with bricks pulled from the district’s crumbling facades, and in the stifling heat that night the still-clogged sewers overflowed with blood.

By autumn, every tenement on Cobble Street had been condemned. The residents had been condemned as well, shipped away to prison for the riots, or committed to the workhouse for their squalid way of life.

As the first leaves fell, the bulldozers came, gleaming bright and golden in the early morning sun.

the-carters-in-piscataquis.raw_content:
It is 2023, July 8th, at 10:34 P.M., and

Mayhew Carter sits in a windowless room ensconced by numerous cavernous hallways from the wooded nothing of Maine’s vast north. In the morning he will venture into an interior courtyard that abuts a private lake, and he will allow himself to be taken out upon the water, but there is only him tonight, his wife Layla in the next room doing whatever she does with her time, and the help stacked like sardines in their quarters far away.

He is reading a book; it is open on his desk; he looks down and thinks with a start that he does not remember what book it is or why he is reading it, nor does he know quite where he is or why he is there, or who he is, and

It is 10:34 and he wants to get up but

a bright wind is blowing from Heaven

He wouldn’t have thought himself able to get there. He was Reformed on his mother’s side and the mark of predestination is virtue in this world and he has never been the type of man who jealously guarded his innocence, no, and in the course of his life and his ascendance it is also the case that the world has darkened somewhat in his esteem, such that it seems childish that a soul could indeed be redeemed or purified by actions within this realm of night that grew ever darker, grew ever darker, and now is literally dimming before his eyes, as

a bright wind is blowing from Heaven

He feels goosebumps and the cold that comes when sensation ceases and he feels the thoughts roll slower through his head, and maybe he could scream and be heard, if only by Layla; he could dispel all this for an instant and roar and allow himself to be swept back up by the rush and crash of the storm that he had made, all of his wealth, or an arbitrary amount thereof, suddenly funneled to the cause of the preservation of his person; and his reinforcements, his cavalry, would be summoned by Layla. His whore, he thinks. His bluebird. Well, should she save him, his bluebird tonight – though not even he can foresee his emotions, as who can know what tomorrow will bring? Although he is unsure whether he desires to scream. He cannot quite unite that will with his mouth which moves fluid and strange, not really his, and his head, at once made heavy, slams down on his desk like a fallen tree, and his fading eyes yet behold his discolored slobber as it seeps into the leaves of his book, and it might be that he could cry out even now, if he summoned his incomprehensible strength, that strength with which he had built ships and buildings and ferried great things far from their place of creation, was it not he himself who had raised those great towers? And he at last cries out, just once, as

a bright wind is blowing from Heaven

bringing with it no pain

It was 2014, May 10th, at 10:34 P.M., and

It was Mayhew Carter’s birthday extravaganza, the precise age that he was turning a secret to all but those closest to him; and helicopters, alongside shielded crafts of various and fascinating designs, descended upon one of his favorite rural properties, a colossal mansion in Piscataquis County, Maine. Many remarked, upon entrance, about the quaintness of the location – the beauty of the surrounding woods, the splendor of the lake – but they were people for whom physical location was of minute concern, for whom one place was like any other place, and they said it only in order to make conversation.

It had been only three months since Mayhew’s marriage to the young – perhaps scandalously young – Layla Carter.

(Once Layla Rosen, a few of the folks from Valravn observed, whispering out of propriety. Gosh, they really were everywhere, weren’t they?)

(And others whispered, out of propriety, that it was nice that he’d found someone so soon after his prior wife passed, especially since he’d lost her after only seven months together, and – this too they whispered – Mayhew had been truly unlucky in love, having married his previous and now-departed spouse only a few weeks after the equally premature departure of his prior spouse…)

(And others observed, whispering out of propriety, that a certain anonymous attendee of the prior wedding had sent Mayhew a splendid assortment of objects belonging to King Henry VIII, and that Mayhew was now devoting considerable investigative resources to identify the person who had insulted him so…)

(And others observed that an especially inebriated buy-sider from the Deer College Management Corporation had been loudly inquiring as to whether other guests had heard the tale of Bluebeard, and been discreetly ejected…)

(And still others feared that perhaps there was trouble in Paradise, as Mayhew and the lovely Layla Carter had been heard to have an animated conversation beside one of the outlying cocktail-tables, at the conclusion of which Mayhew had slapped her quite hard on the cheek and barked something at her, at which point she fled…)

And Layla Carter was quivering, weeping, standing some distance down the manicured path that originates just east of the great lawn. Her mascara was running. She did not know whether the handprint showed on her face. This was the first time but she knew already that it would not be the last. She felt a raw and acrid anger move through her. She didn’t totally know where she was, but knew that in a few days they would be going back to New York City, and that once she was there she would… it would take time, she would have to wait for the current rage to pass so that she could think, she didn’t get this far being helpless, no, or being irrational. But this was a life that she could and would leave. She knew how to cut her losses. She had the world before her, and whatever he said to her, whatever he tried to make her believe, she knew that there was nothing that she could not do.

But he told her to get out of his sight, and she still wasn’t ready to go back into that house. She took a handkerchief from her clutch and wiped her eyes. She breathed in, breathed out. Counted her breaths. Felt her heart slow. Five things you can see. Four things you can touch. Three things you can hear, two things you can smell, nothing to taste.

She could take her time, here. There were a pair of footsteps far behind her, but when they caught up to her she could turn around and greet them and say, oh, I was just collecting my thoughts. It’s so good to see you. Yes, sometimes I like to step out and take some time to myself and just think about how lucky I am. She had thirty seconds to gather herself, and then turn around and face the person approaching. And, from then, the world.

She turned. A woman was standing there, quite tall. Kindly eyes. Beautiful shawl. Mid-fifties, if she had to guess? She smiled – automatic – and extended her hand.

“Good evening!” Layla said. “I hope you’re enjoying yourself on this fine night?”

  “Yes, absolutely,” said the woman. “I’m sorry that we haven’t met. You can call me Stephanie. Stephanie Kimball. I’m with… ah, well, one of those. But it’s nice to see that someone else has gone out walking.”

  “Oh, absolutely,” said Layla. “You know, when the weather is getting warm like this, I really hate to waste it indoors. I hope my presence hasn’t been missed?”

“I wouldn’t worry,” said Stephanie. “You know, events like this are for enjoyment. If the spirit moves you to go for a little walk in between drinks, then that is exactly what you should do.”

  “So what brings you here?”

More footsteps in the distance. Perfect. Layla thought that if another few people joined her throng, then by the time she arrived back at the house, it would be as though they had left as a group in order to see the gardens, and it would seem as though she had not run away at all.

  “Ah, well, my organization is a diversified one. A little bit of this, a little bit of that."

 “But anomalous?” asked Layla.

 “Entirely. But don’t let me keep you; we can keep walking together."

 “That’d be lovely. You know, it’s really good to just talk to someone. You get in so many huge, twelve-person dialogues around here. What city are you based out of?”

 “Well, that’s an embarrassingly complicated question. The association I’m part of is very location-independent. I can tell you that we do a lot of business in the major metro areas: New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, for instance. I find myself showing up essentially wherever there are people.”

 “And, tonight, you’re even where they aren’t.”

 “Oh, exactly! I mean, how did he ever land on Piscataquis?”

 “He didn’t. The property’s been in the Carter family for generations. He just made a number of additions. Almost 80% of the floor-plan was added on by him.”

 “I’m impressed that you know all that. Do you work with MC&D?”

 “No, but I am associated with them, I suppose. Oh, I haven’t introduced myself at all, have I?”

 “That’s entirely my fault. I guess I didn’t even ask your name.”

“Well, my name is –“

 A short distance away, a man coughed from the darkness.

Layla stopped, then turned to face him. “Oh, evening! We’re just walking together; would you care to join us?”

 “Not tonight,” said the man, facing Layla. “I’m not sure we’ve ever met properly, but I’m Judd Marshall. I, too, am associated with MC&D.”

“Oh, good evening, Judd!” said Stephanie.

Marshall turned toward Stephanie, with an expression that bordered on amusement. “Eat your face.”

“Excuse me?” Stephanie asked.

 “Eat your face.”

 “I’m sorry, Mr. Marshall. Is it offensive to you?”

 “Not terribly. Has she given you her name?”

 “Why, no,” says Stephanie, looking at Layla. “No, come to think of it I suppose that you haven’t.”

 “I assumed she hadn’t,” said Marshall. “Given how well she looks.”

 Stephanie smiled, but the smile was strained, and the voice that issued from her lips was breathy, deep and dry. “You’re coming between a hawk and its game, Mr. Marshall.”

 “Oh, apologies,” said Marshall. “Would you like to know her name?”

“It only works if it comes from her. And not if I ask for it.”

“Indulge me. Carter. Her last name is Carter.”

 “She’s his daughter?”

 “Not quite. I…” He looked up, snickered. “I think that before I do anything else, I am going to take this coin, this one right here, and I am going to flip it into the air. I expect it to come up at an ordinary pace and down at an ordinary pace, unaffected by any anomalously generated force, and for it to proceed to hit the ground. After it hits the ground I might take certain steps. But until it hits the ground, presuming accordance with my aforementioned expectations, I will abstain from any further action. Do you understand me?”

 “Forgive me, Mr. Marshall, but did you want me to eat my current face?”

 “I don’t give a damn what you do or don’t do,” said Marshall.

Then he took the coin and placed it on his finger, and he flicked it in the air, and it went up in a two-foot arc and banked slightly westward and when it landed it was half-swallowed by the soft dirt.

When Layla looked up there was nobody on the path but Marshall.

 “Who was that?” Layla asked.

“Something from somewhere.”

“Thank you.”

 “Don’t mention it. Really, don’t.”

 “Will it come back for me?”

 “I strongly doubt it.”

 “And why are you out here?”

 “I wanted to go for a walk," said Marshall.

 “You just wanted to go for a walk?”

 “No.”

 “Did Mayhew send you?”

 “No. No, he’s already upstairs.”

 “Should I join him there?”

 “I wouldn’t recommend it.”

 “He has company?”

 “Not my place to say.”

 “Well, surely it’s my business.”

 Marshall kept walking.

“I mean, I’m his wife.”

 “Is that what you are?"

 “Yes, I’m his wife! You know I’m – God, what should I do? I don’t – you don’t need to answer. I just don’t know what I should do.”

“If I were you, I would apologize to him.”

 “For what?”

 “For something. Make something up.”

 “He slapped me in the face. And… and he’s upstairs with…”

 “Then you’ve got a hard road ahead of you. He must be very angry. You might have to beg. But he wouldn’t have married you if you didn’t know how to make him happy.”

“Look, I know we barely know each other, but I don’t have an apology in me.”

 “You don’t have to mean it. Hell, cry a little. He’d like that.”

 “I don’t mean to say what I don’t mean.”

 “You know, uh, Lily, I’ve seen corpses that piss and shit themselves shortly after they die. And then as they deteriorate, you know, those parts decay first, because there’s a pile of organic matter within them that acts almost like fertilizer, and, well, all corpses that are left out to the elements start stinking just terribly, but those, well, those really–“

“Why the hell are you telling me this?”

 “Don’t interrupt me again.” He walked a few paces in silence, then continued. “I’m telling you that dignity dies when the body does. It recedes to nothing in an instant. That’s all.”

“Are you implying that he would kill me if I left him?”

 “It wouldn’t be out of anger.”

 “What?”

 “It would be as a matter of course.”

 “Why do you… why do you think that?” 

“Half the people in that room have killed for vastly less.”

 “That’s insane. You sound… completely insane.”

 “God, you sound just like the last one. Walk slower, will you? I’m an old man.”

“How far are we from the house right now?” 

“About a quarter of a mile, now. Why?”

“If I ran away into the woods, right now, what would you tell him?”

“I’d tell him exactly where you are,” said Judd.

“Oh, is that what friends do for friends?”

 “Not even that. It’s what colleagues do for colleagues. You had chances to get away. But now all of those chances are behind you forever. I guess I’m sorry that no-one told you. Keep walking, Lily.”

Her breathing was heavy and her vision swam.

“Keep walking.”

It is 2023, July 8th, at 10:56 P.M., and

Layla sits on the porch and sees the gibbous moon reflected in the lake’s calm waters. It is a summer night, but even so, the breeze comes with a pleasant chill, and she wraps her shawl around her and cradles her steaming teacup. The crickets chirp loudly, and will continue until seven hours pass and the birdsong supersedes them. She will call for help, she thinks. The first thirty minutes are the crucial ones. But first she will finish her cup, slowly, staring out over the water. Then she will run to the servants’ house. In such a terrible hurry. Tears in her eyes.
