    This is an art exchange gift for my good friend 🗿 stormbreath!

    This was a tough article for me to write, because I've never written anything remotely like it before. That being said, I hope I did crewtime justice! They're a fun character to read about and write for, and I had a blast figuring out what kind of story I wanted to tell. Enjoy!

    Your Friend,
    youseeinthedark

crewtime 12/25/24 (WED) 14:21:28 #94926937

Merry Christmas and happy holidays, Parawatch. I hope you're all bundled up this winter season, as I have quite the cold case to share with you all. The records on this one are very few and far between, but I had a friend in Canada help me with some ground research.

At 7:56 PM on December 24th, 1999, a woman was kidnapped by two robed figures in front of one Mrs. Laura Chance's residence in rural Canada. Within two hours a manhunt unveiled a secret cult, merely moments after a ritualistic killing deep in the Yukon woodlands. Suspects were locked up, cleanup crews called, the incident tucked away, and the town utterly shaken to its core. A frightening and chilling case for sure — but, ultimately, a mundane one.

What makes this case cold is the fact that, in spite of the tiny size of the town, no one knew who the kidnapped woman was.

crewtime 12/25/24 (WED) 14:21:50 #94926938

Mrs. Laura Chance, age 62 and recently widowed, lived by herself in a three bedroom home just on the edge of Watson Lake, Canada. She spent most of her time knitting, reading, and watching television, occasionally visiting friends in the neighborhood. On this particular Christmas Eve in 1999, however, she's busy cleaning her home as the holiday spirit begins to set in, dutifully setting plates and hanging up decorations.

At precisely 7:56 PM MST — known only because Mrs. Chance checked her watch moments earlier — a woman's scream echoes across the house. Dropping everything, Mrs. Chance runs to her front door, and is met with a terrifying sight: a cloaked figure dragging a screaming, kicking woman across her front lawn towards an unmarked black van. After a few moments of shock, she dashes for the landline and dials emergency services.

Mrs. Chance speaks frantically into the phone. Although her report is sporadic and takes random turns, the dispatcher seems to pick up exactly what she's saying. Within mere minutes, a cop car is already set and ready to go. The hunt is on.

Surprisingly, officers in the area are quite quick to respond. Although a majority of them are off for the holidays, several are still on duty and eager for some action. Within another fifteen minutes, two more police cars mobilize and began the search, with several more gearing up for action behind them.

Watson Lake, being a small Yukon town, is directly on the Alaska Highway. Getting in and out undetected is no simple feat this time of year. That meant that, with their quick work, the police could lock down the region fast and begin searching for the van with a high confidence of catching it quickly.

They would not have to look for long. The van is found rapidly, within an hour of the call, abandoned by the side of the road on the edge of town. The officers step out of their car and begin examination, immediately spotting three sets of clear footprints, trailing deep into the woods.

One set was uneven, and smaller than the other two. A perfect match, with not a second to lose. They had found a path straight to the perpetrators… and the victim.

crewtime 12/25/24 (WED) 14:22:02 #94926939

Hot on the culprits' tails, the two officers at the scene — Christopher Cooper and Gwenda Dalton — set off without waiting for backup, relaying their plans to dispatch. The darkness and freezing snow means their progress is slow and difficult. However, the two persevere, even while the wind begins to pick up around them.

As the tracks deepen and become more defined, Officer Dalton notices a faint glow directly ahead of them, which she immediately mentions to dispatch. When they approach, the officers soon fall completely silent, and stop walking entirely. Christopher later commented:

It was nightmarish — something you'd see out of a cheap horror film, but gritty and physical. Me 'n Gwenda just about stopped and stared for a minute, trying to comprehend what the hell we were witnessing. If what we were lookin' at was even real.

The officers' bodycams show several robed, hooded figures standing in a circle, their hands raised as the wind howls around them. In frame are the bones of several animals littering the area, and various objects hang from the nearby trees in a circle. In other words, a cliche cult circle, complete with a ringleader standing above a corpse.

The moment they catch their bearings, the duo draw their weapons and promptly jump into action. Startled, several of the figures flee into the woods at the sight of the officers, while several others seem to double over or clutch their heads. The leader, in the middle, is too preoccupied with their ritual to notice.

Dalton and Cooper make quick work of the group. Within minutes, nearly all the suspects still present are safely in custody, all having gone willingly. Save for one, that is: the aforementioned cult leader, who only began to struggle as the pair moved to arrest them. The other officers, arriving minutes later, help take the group in. The other cultists, however, are long gone — a prospective manhunt is called off almost immediately due to the weather.

Records on the suspects in custody are sparse. There is, however, a throughline between all the records that are public: the cultists either suffer from amnesia, or are all very good at pretending to. No one at the cult site — save for the leader, whose transcripts aren't anywhere I can find — could remember why they were there, or what they were trying to do.

The leader was one Ms. Catherine Polley, a 25-year-old who lived in the area. I couldn't find anything particularly noteworthy about her life, though apparently she had been caught stealing signs from the Sign Post Forest, a local tourist trap, several weeks earlier. Similar — though heavily damaged — signs were found near the cult site. Besides that, though, all I could find was that she'd lived in the town her whole life, and apparently was an extremely bitter and spiteful person.

All these details on their own would be eyebrow-raising. A mass hysteria case led by a vindictive psychopath or people strung too far in over their heads, perhaps, but not necessarily supernatural.

What seals the deal for me is not the cultists. It's the body.

crewtime 12/25/24 (WED) 14:22:08 #94926940

It took almost no time for the police to determine that the woman was dead. Her body sat lifelessly in the now-darkened center of the cult site, snow beginning to bury her limbs. With the lead suspect in custody and the weather potentially causing issues, the shift supervisor gave approval for the body to be transferred to a nearby morgue for analysis.

The autopsy of the body took place on the 26th, after the holidays. Much to the surprise of the resident pathologist, no cause of death could be determined. There was no sign of physical injury (besides a broken wrist), blunt force trauma, toxicity buildup, or anything indicating foul play. Although hypothermia was the most likely cause of death, there was also nothing on the corpse that indicated death by exposure — save for some frostbite in the arms — and it seemed unlikely the cult would let her die naturally. The cause of death would ultimately be labeled as "Unknown, likely hypothermia."

What's even more mysterious is that, in the ensuing days, the woman could not be identified at all. Her DNA, fingerprints, and dental records did not match anyone in any known registry. No one interviewed in the region could identify her, nor had ever even seen her before. Even a vehicle found near the location of the kidnapping — believed to be owned by the victim — could not be traced to a specific owner.

It was though she had simply materialized from thin air, for the sole purpose of being killed.

At this point, records become practically non-existent. My best guess is that CSIS (Canada's FBI-equivalent) got involved and shut their investigation under a tight lock. That, unfortunately, gives us almost nothing to work with. Whether they're just as puzzled as us or have long solved the case, I have no idea. What I do know, though, is that within a week, every single outlet that had previously been following the story completely dropped it. Within a year, no one was talking about it anymore at all.

My own efforts to unravel this mystery — or, at least, write about it — have been mostly fruitless. No missing persons cases across Canada or the US even remotely match her description. No one's come forward online claiming to have known her. Her car has no prior sightings or records associated with the license plate. Barely anyone even mentions the case anymore, even the content farms that pump out true crime stories. Dead end after dead end.

Was she from a parallel universe? Was the cult? Did the cult's ritual somehow partially summon her into existence? Why? Is the government involved? Is the victim a foreign government agent, attempting to infiltrate some random Yukon town? Did she even know how she got there? Did the fact it happen on Christmas have anything to do with it at all?

I have no idea. Truthfully, I don't think we'll ever really know. The whole thing reeks of conspiracy or a supernatural phenomenon. Whatever the case may be, we can only hope that she's at peace now, whoever she was.


crewtime 12/25/24 (WED) 14:25:29 #94926943

But that's not really a satisfying ending, and I wouldn't leave you all with nothing of substance to chew on.

About a year after I initially shelved this post, a friend of mine — who wishes to remain anonymous — told me they were taking a trip through the Yukon. I remembered this case, and asked them if they'd do some ground research for me. They said yes.

I wish I could say they cracked the case open, but all I've got is more questions. Still, I think the questions are different enough to make this case worth sharing now.

To start off, some newspaper clippings in the local library reveal the ultimate fate of Ms. Polley: first-degree murder, kidnapping, and property theft charges, incurring a life sentence. That feels a little overkill to me personally, especially since we don't even know who the victim is or how she died. But, I'm not Canadian, so who can say.

Her current whereabouts are unknown, though presumably she's behind bars.

A different clipping — buried deep in the library's archives — reveals more about the cult site itself, though I don't know how much it illuminates. There were several urns containing ground-up bones, crow feathers, and other cult-adjacent items. There was a single burnt Polaroid, though it was too damaged to be legible.

Perhaps most baffling, though, were several license plates, road signs, and other similar landmark items stolen from the aforementioned Sign Post Forest, scattered around the area. All of them seem to have had the names of places they were from removed, almost seamlessly. No clue what to make of that, personally.

After that, my friend didn't seem to make much further progress. Asking the townsfolk was mostly a dead end; no one knew anything more than we did, in spite of the fact that it happened in that very same town.

There was still one more lead that we wanted to follow through on, though: Laura Chance is still alive. She lives in the same three bedroom home, alone, twenty-five years later. She is currently eighty-seven, though is — from what I'm told — in relatively good health.

When they met, she invited my friend inside for tea, and they had a pleasant chat. I have a recording of the conversation. While I don't think all of it is particularly pertinent — Mrs. Chance only had a passing role in the whole affair, after all — I do think there was one particular comment that caught my eye. I'll leave it off on this note.

Hm. After everything… I still don't know what to make of it, honestly. But I can tell you, my life's been emptier ever since it happened. I think seeing it on Christmas must've drained all the optimism out of me. A young girl pulled to her death right in front of my home, only years after my husband's passing… it hurt a fundamental part of my soul, I think.

A few days after the whole affair, the police came to ask me a couple of questions. I don't remember everything they said to me — I was just in so much shock — but… they showed me a picture of her face, and asked me, and I quote, "do you recognize her?". And as soon as I saw it, I just started breaking down, sobbing uncontrollably.

In all honesty… I still don't know why, all these years later. I had never seen her before in my life.

Still, I think the questions are different enough to make this case worth sharing now. To start off, some newspaper clippings in the local library reveal the ultimate fate of Ms. Polley: first-degree murder, kidnapping, and property theft charges, incurring a life sentence. That feels a little overkill to me personally, especially since we don't even know who the victim is or how she died. But, I'm not Canadian, so who can say. Her current whereabouts are unknown, though presumably she's behind bars. A different clipping — buried deep in the library's archives — reveals more about the cult site itself, though I don't know how much it illuminates. There were several urns containing ground-up bones, crow feathers, and other cult-adjacent items. There was a single burnt Polaroid, though it was too damaged to be legible. Perhaps most baffling, though, were several license plates, road signs, and other similar landmark items stolen from the aforementioned Sign Post Forest, scattered around the area. All of them seem to have had the names of places they were from removed, almost seamlessly. No clue what to make of that, personally. After that, my friend didn't seem to make much further progress. Asking the townsfolk was mostly a dead end; no one knew anything more than we did, in spite of the fact that it happened in that very same town. There was still one more lead that we wanted to follow through on, though: Laura Chance is still alive. She lives in the same three bedroom home, alone, twenty-five years later. She is currently eighty-seven, though is — from what I'm told — in relatively good health. When they met, she invited my friend inside for tea, and they had a pleasant chat. I have a recording of the conversation. While I don't think all of it is particularly pertinent — Mrs. Chance only had a passing role in the whole affair, after all — I do think there was one particular comment that caught my eye. I'll leave it off on this note. > //Hm. After everything... I still don't know what to make of it, honestly. But I can tell you, my life's been emptier ever since it happened. I think seeing it on Christmas must've drained all the optimism out of me. A young girl pulled to her death right in front of my home, only years after my husband's passing... it hurt a fundamental part of my soul, I think.// > > //A few days after the whole affair, the police came to ask me a couple of questions. I don't remember everything they said to me — I was just in so much shock — but... they showed me a picture of her face, and asked me, and I quote, "do you recognize her?". And as soon as I saw it, I just started breaking down, sobbing uncontrollably.// > > //In all honesty... I// still //don't know why, all these years later. I had never seen her before in my life.// [[/div]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box]] > **Filename:** scent of night - myuu (extended).mp3 > **Name:** Scent of Night - Myuu > **Author:** Myuu > **License:** "Royalty-Free Music | Just give credit" > **Source Link:** [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ma3BFoEwjPI Youtube] > **Additional Notes:** Audio file repeats track four times. the-cologne-massacre.raw_content:
by Letova

crewtime 03/11/14 (Mon) 18:53:29 #84985910

The demise of the Baumann family is among the most puzzling and obscure cases I have come across during my True Crime investigations. Despite the severity of the tragedy, and the absolutely unusual circumstances, it seems that no one outside of a few local newspapers from Cologne has even attempted to cover it, until now. It was only brought to my attention a couple of weeks ago by request of a friend from a village near where the case had taken place. I was only able to dig up anything on it from a few newspaper scans forwarded by her.

The Baumann family were, by all accounts, a quirky but happy family. At the time of the incident, the family was made up of Andreas Baumann, his wife Ursula, their thirteen year old son Theodore and their six year old daughter Angela. They lived in the suburbs of Cologne, North Rhine-Westphalia and were heavily engaged in their community, regularly going to local events and visiting their neighbors every couple of days. Their children were getting high grades in school and the family was financially stable, they were pretty much a model German family. Well, with one exception. Their near-militant atheism, with the family never attending any local churches, non-secular holiday celebrations and even, at one point, cutting off a close family friend after he announced his intentions of becoming a priest. Otherwise, however, there didn't seem to be anything notable about them.

At least from the outside.

crewtime 03/11/14 (Mon) 19:00:42 #84985910

In the weeks leading up to the tragedy, the behavior of the children was noted by their peers and teachers to have changed drastically. The usually social and energetic Theodore had become withdrawn and nervous, with his teachers even having raised this issue to his parents. The usually reserved and quiet Angela meanwhile had become cheerful and excited, telling her classmates that "Mommy and Daddy said we'll be together forever", before claiming that they had banned her from elaborating further.

Their parents, meanwhile, began to meet with groups of individuals with non-local license plates almost daily, their neighbors reporting seeing up to 5 cars in their driveway every evening. It wasn't the first time this happened, similar packs of guests having visited the family every few weeks, although this was seldom paid attention to at the time. We all have extended family, after all. At the same time, the Baumann parents cut off all contact with their previous friends and co-workers, remaining casual at work but refusing to talk to or meet anyone outside of it. All of this finally culminated on the 13th of November, 2005, when a tragedy finally struck the family.

On that morning, Ursula drove both of their children to school, before stopping at a butcher's shop on her way home. There, she bought a total of 10 kilograms of various animal meats, including pork, chicken and beef, then headed back home. This was the last time anyone had seen her.

Andreas left his house a few hours later, in order to pick up his daughter from school. After arriving, he struck up a short conversation with one of the teachers, who noted that he seemed exceptionally happy on that day, though he refused to say why. His son left school only an hour later, coming home by foot. Neither of the children were seen again after this point.

crewtime 03/11/14 (Mon) 19:03:16 #84985910

On the evening of the same day, a neighbor unnamed by the newspapers alleged to have heard a loud bang coming from inside the house, followed by the sound of glass breaking. Only a few minutes later, Andreas emerged from the building, before proceeding to stretch his limbs, look down at his hands and pace around. A short conversation followed, during which Andreas claimed he was just going for a walk, before he walked away from the house and onto the nearby street. Sensing something was wrong, he was followed for a short time and last seen entering a white van parked a few streets down from the family's residence and, unfortunately for investigators, far outside the view of any cameras. And with that, the last member of the family had now vanished, never to be seen again.

It took 5 days for anyone to raise alarms at their neighbor's disappearance, at which the building was finally breached by police. What they uncovered inside was quite a gruesome scene. A glass table in the kitchen had been smashed to pieces, while a hole had been punched in the nearby wall. The door leading to the guest room had been ripped off its hinges, while blood had seeped out of it and stained the carpet. The guestroom itself was a scene that, while horrific, sounds straight out a cheesy 80s horror movie.

The floor had been lined with a white tarp, almost fully covered in partially dried blood. The furniture had been replaced with tables bearing knives, surgical tools and notebooks, while symbols of unknown origin had been painted across the walls. Though no photos exist, the newspapers gave vivid descriptions of figures with multiple heads, long six-fingered hands and spirals, in addition to writing visually similar to the mongolian script. Clumps of hair and small pieces of flesh, later identified as belonging to each member of the family, were found strewn across the room. Not a single body was found.

crewtime 03/11/14 (Mon) 19:07:31 #84985910

And here, we get to the strangest part of the story. The notebooks. Inside them was a mixture of normal German writing and presumed words in the unidentified script covering parts of the guest room's walls, none of which have been deciphered. The german parts themselves were hardly discernable, although they seemed to be a kind of suicide note. Here is a fragment provided by one of the newspapers.

Tonight, it is time we join together, forever. May our [UNINTELLIGIBLE], as was shown by the Great K[UNINTELLIGIBLE]. May this night be remembered onwards. From now, to the day the skies turn pink. [UNINTELLIGIBLE]

And… that is where evidence ends, as much as it hurts me to say it. At one point, the police had claimed to have discerned a fragment of the writings alleging the family to be members of a new religious movement by the name of "Brotherhood UNITY", although the they proceeded to retract it in an interview a week later, owing it to confusion while trying to decipher the writing. Otherwise? There's no known motive, no traces of the family, nothing.

Andreas couldn't have hidden them on the property, it was flipped upside down multiple times during the search, Nothing, not even digging up the backyard provided any leads. Nor, if the neighbor is to be believed, could he have discretely disposed of them while on his way out. He wasn't spotted carrying any bags with him, after all. And what about the damage in the living room? And the growl? If the family had fought back, the damage would have surely been more extensive. And most importantly, why? Andreas was not undergoing a mental health crisis from what we know, and the family seemed to be aware that something was going to happen to them.

I really hate to end an investigation like this, with so many questions and not even a shred of evidence that could point us towards what may have happened. There is, however, a fragment of one of the reports covering it that I have found interesting. I am not sure what to think of it either, but figured I might as well copy and paste it here. For context, it was from an interview with the same neighbor who had last seen Andreas.

He was walking weird, you know? I used to be a nurse, I have seen people get up for the first time after days of laying down. He was walking like that, almost like he was learning to walk again. That's when I called out to him, asked him what he's doing. He looked away from his hands and yelled to me in this… this very young, high-pitched voice, he didn't sound like himself at all. And he said:

"Oh, hey there! Don't mind us, we're just going for a walk."

the-containment-of-arsene-lupin.creator: Uncle Nicolini
the-containment-of-arsene-lupin.raw_content:
≡

The Containment of Arsène Lupin

It wasn't often that Site-19 security guards were forced to exit the impenetrable fortress to check up on something outside its perimeter.

When they did, it usually turned out to be an animal, like a coyote or a hare that had wandered too close to the movement sensors. As such, it was always the rookie guard's duty to go outside and brave the heat of the Mojave. Today, such misfortune fell upon Maurice Lagrange, a guard fresh out of training and stationed at Site-19 only two weeks prior.

Lagrange took a few steps out of the gates of the Site, then looked up at the night sky. For the first time ever, he could see the stars shining above. He gawked in admiration for a moment before command bellowed the order in his earpiece to get moving. Sighing, he trudged ahead to take a look at the sector where the motion sensors had gone off.

He rounded the corner of the complex and—

THUNK!

"Lagrange? Come in, Lagrange! You've been sitting still for three minutes, what the hell are you doing out there?" command barked through the earpiece.

"Sorry. I tripped and my earpiece went flying," the man replied as he dusted himself off.

"Your earpiece's microphone must have broken too, you sound weird."

"It is very likely. Apologies."

"Whatever, we'll let tech figure that out. What's out there?"

"Nothing I could see. Probably just a coyote." Lagrange put on his helmet and continued onward.

"Just hurry up and get back."

"Yes, sir."

The earpiece went silent. He picked up the gun that lay on the ground, an overdesigned automatic rifle that miraculously hadn't gone off when it fell. He looked back a moment and smiled, then continued.

Lagrange entered Site-19 and looked around. There were a few guards idling about, their faces hidden by their helmets. He spotted the elevators in the distance and started toward them.

Suddenly, a voice behind him called his name.

"Lagrange! Where are you going?"

He turned around to spot the source of the voice: a large, barrel-chested man with thin legs and a beard that poked out from underneath the helmet.

"I was just heading to my quarters."

"Well, I guess you earned an early night by going out and dealing with the heat. Sorry for doing that to you, but you know how it is around here." The bearded guard nodded and walked off.

Once he was gone, Lagrange approached the elevators. He pressed his keycard to the reader, and a few minutes later, a cabin had come up. The doors opened to reveal a few scientists looking over their clipboards and speaking to one another. Lagrange allowed them to exit before getting in, alone.

He shot a glance to all the numbers on the control button panel and thought a moment. Lagrange would have stroked his chin had he not been carrying a weapon and wearing a helmet. Eventually, the elevator cab started moving again; someone on one of the lower floors had called it. Oh well. He had to go down anyway.

"I hate all these new stupid security measures," one of the scientists entering the elevator grumbled. He was gruff and old, wearing a grey beard and equally greying hair.

"Same," his companion, a thin, young man with blond hair agreed. "I can't believe they're making us use snail mail for intra-Site communications because of that damn thief."

Lagrange nodded. "At least us guards still have our earpieces. Can't take that away from us."

"Yeah? Lucky you. I have to deal with everyone's godawful handwriting. Do they no longer teach proper handwriting in schools?" the older one prattled. "Bunch of halfwits they've got me working with."

"I resent that, Doct—"

"Oh please. You of all people? After you fell for that thief Lupin's obvious phishing scam, telling him where SCP-268 is stored? You're lucky we literally cannot fire you."

Lagrange raised his hand quietly, clearing his throat. "Pardon me, gentlemen, but isn't SCP-268 the hat that allows one to vanish without a trace?"

Both researchers nodded.

"Well, I think there should be a guard stationed outside its chamber, just in case that Lupin fellow comes sneaking along." Lagrange shrugged. "After all, it is my job to make sure these things are looked after."

"If only some other people showed the same initiative this fine young man does." The older doctor shot his younger counterpart a nasty look. "Good thinking. Do you know where it is?"

Lagrange nodded. "Sublevel 43, room 3803-B."

The elder doctor shook his head. "Ah, no, the research team moved it after this idiot's 'accident.' It's on sublevel 55, room 1221-A now."

"I am not an idiot…" the younger doctor mumbled.

1219-A

1220-A

1221-A

Finally. He reached for the keycard at his hip, grinning as he pressed it to the scanner.

ACCESS DENIED.

"Darn." This was unexpected; he had anticipated that security guard clearance would get him wherever he needed to go. He turned around to spot a scientist rounding the corner of the hallway nearby.

"Excuse me," he called. "Care to open this door for me? My keycard seems to be malfunctioning."

"SCP-268's containment chamber? I didn't know it was scheduled for testing tonight," she replied, stopping beside Lagrange.

"Yes, well, you know how it is around here." Lagrange laughed, eyeing the lanyard around her neck which contained her keycard.

"I… what? No! Let me see your ID." She swatted his hand away and held out her own.

They were cut off by the Site-wide alarm system, which went off before Lagrange could open his mouth again.

WARNING. WARNING. THERE IS AN INFILTRATOR IN THE SITE. ALL PERSONNEL MUST REPORT TO THE SITE BUNKER WITH IDENTIFICATION HANDY.

"Ah, merde." he grumbled. "Looks like I ran out of time."

The woman began backing away slowly. The man followed.

"Who are you?!" she demanded.

"My name, mademoiselle, is Arsène Lupin…" He grinned, and in one fell swoop, his disguise fell away. The guard helmet was tossed aside to reveal a face with long sideburns, a thin mustache, and a monocle. The fatigues were dropped to reveal he was sharply dressed in a dark suit. Lupin laughed, dropping the gun he had acquired earlier, and held up the woman's keycard in his free hand. "… And you have just played your part in my latest heist."

She fumbled around her chest with her hands, searching for her keycard. A look of horror etched itself upon her face upon finding that it was missing.

Lupin took a few steps backwards and pressed the pilfered ID to the scanner.

ACCESS GRANTED. WELCOME, RESEARCHER FUJIKO.

The door slid open.

"Thank you, mademoiselle Fujiko!" Lupin laughed and dashed into the room, shutting the door behind him. He turned to investigate the room, glancing around the multiple cabinets and lockers that occupied it.

He stroked his chin. "Mon dieu," the thief grumbled as the Site alarm continued to sound. “It is so hard to concentrate with that blasted alarm going off…" He extended his left arm, and a fancy, golden cane with an equally elegant emerald topper emerged, sliding down his sleeve until it came to rest in the palm of his hand.

"Now where are we, SCP-268…" Lupin stroked his chin, curling at his mustache with a free finger. He glanced around the room, eventually spotting a locker labeled '268'. "Hmph. Silly Foundation. They make it so easy." The thief approached, noticing a lock on the door. It was too loud to pick it because of the alarm, so he would have to improvise.

He swung the cane against the lock, bashing it until it fell. "It's not that I don't appreciate a good lock; there is an art to the practice, but I simply have no time. Apologies, Foundation." Lupin sighed, pressing on the handle of the locker. It swung open to reveal a black top hat, at which he smiled.

"Très bien!" He picked up the hat. "And now, I wa—"

The door behind him exploded off its hinges and soared through the room, narrowly missing him and smashing straight into the opposite wall, leaving a sizeable hole. A floodlight brightly illuminated the room, obscuring the men who had knocked the door down.

"Well, well, well. You're a long way from your quarters, Maurice Lagrange." A voice emerged from the smoke that occupied the newly formed entrance.

"What can I say, this place is a labyrinth."

"I'm afraid so, Mr. Lagrange. Or should I say, Arsène Lupin?"

"Ah, I see you know of me." Lupin smiled.

"Of course I know of you, Mr. Lupin."

"Please. Monsieur will do just fine."

A man with a big beard and a guard uniform, sans helmet, entered the room: the very same man from before. He pointed his gun at the thief, the same gun Lupin had tossed aside earlier. Though it was hard to see through the floodlight behind him, Lupin could tell the guard was grinning, as widely as he was himself.

"Whatever you say, Monsieur Lupin. But I'm afraid this will be the last time you get what you want. Arrest him!"

A group of men rushed into the room, all of them holding beryllium bronze handcuffs and pistols. Lupin laughed briefly before making a run for it into the next room via the hole. He was followed by a hail of bullets and the floodlight's bright illumination. After he had escaped into the hallway, he could hear the guard roaring and stomping: "After him!"

Clutching his cane and newly pilfered hat, Lupin ran towards where he remembered the elevators were. He wasn't surprised to find that there were guards there, all of them with guns and more beryllium bronze handcuffs. The thief looked around him; the guards following still hadn't rounded the corner of the hallway and the ones by the elevator hadn't seen him yet. He doffed the top hat and put it on, immediately becoming narratively indistinguishable from a background character. Lupin then approached the elevators wearing a smile.

"ID please," one of the guards stopped him.

"But of course." The thief pulled out the ID he had previously stolen and showed it to the towering brute in front of him.

"… Researcher Fijuko Mine? You don't look like a Fujiko," the guard, faceless behind his helmet, grumbled at Lupin.

"Pray tell, what do I look like then?" he fired back.

"Oh, uh. Sorry. I didn't mean anything by it. Are you taking the elevator up to the shelter?"

"Indeed."

"Please, right this way."

The guard stepped aside and allowed for Lupin to pass. Just as he did so, the group of guards that had been chasing him from the containment chamber caught up and breathlessly yelled, "Where is Lupin?!" The men guarding the elevator collectively shrugged while Lupin slinked away into the elevator.

"I thought tracking him was your job," one of the elevator guards said.

"It's all our jobs!" the bearded guard roared, running up from behind. "Have you seen anyone else around here?!"

"Only that one researcher." The brutish guard thumbed backwards to the closing elevator.

Just before the doors of the elevator shut, Lupin removed the top hat and winked at the guards, whose jaws all hung agape. The doors shut, and Lupin leaned against the walls of the cabin. He adjusted his monocle with one hand, and with a flick of his other wrist, his cane disappeared.

"Well that was simply too easy. This won't do."

"What do you mean SCP-268 is 'public domain' now?" Detective Quinn Roscoe yelled over the Site alarm into his communicator. "Does that mean he actually stole it?"

"One of your AICs picked it up on a public domain dump site. And by the way, security confirms that Lupin is at large with SCP-268 and is currently somewhere in the Site."

The detective grumbled a curse, pressing the button to call the elevator.

"Well that's just great. What does it mean for an SCP object to be in the public domain anyway?"

"Knowing how we anomalies work, probably something Veil-breaking."

The elevator doors dinged and opened to reveal someone within, who stepped out and stopped directly in front of Roscoe.

The detective blinked.

"Bonsoir." Lupin smiled at him, holding the hat in his right hand.

"Who's there with you, Quinn?"

"Lupin." Roscoe stuffed the communicator into his coat pocket and pulled out his sidearm.

"It's Dupin. Come, you should know how to pronounce my name by n—"

"No, it's Lupin!"

"What?! Get him, Quinn!"

"Arsène Lupin, you are under arrest. Place SCP-268 on the ground."

"Yes, yes, as you say. I suppose I have been caught. I prefer to craft my own disguises myself, rather than rely on something else, anyway." The phantom thief set the object on the floor in front of him between both men.

"On your knees. Hands behind your back."

Lupin obliged.

Roscoe quickly got behind Lupin and handcuffed him, then spoke into his communicator again.

"Dupin, you still there?"

"Yeah. You got him?"

"Yes. Tell security to get up to Sublevel 20."

"On it." The communicator switched off.

"Aren't you going to read me my Letter of Rights?" Lupin asked.

"There will be no trial for you."

"That's good, because I have a bad habit of missing those."

Roscoe laughed.

Lupin grinned.

"Well, either way, I have something to say, monsieur. Let it be known that I, Arsène Lupin, plan on mounting the greatest heist the Foundation has ever seen! One month from now, you will come to know a loss so severe, you will simply be unable to continue as you were."

"You are a mile underground," the detective blinked, "and you'll be even deeper once we get you in containment. How do you intend on getting out of here?"

"I guess we shall have to wait and see, oui?"

"Either you have something planned or you are a fool, and I'm willing to bet it's the former. So I will make sure that you are locked up tighter than the lizard." Roscoe chuckled sensibly at the threat of Lupin attempting to breach the most secure fortress in the world. Though he had just infiltrated it today… Something for the containment engineers to think about when they drafted his conprocs.

"Before you take me to what will no doubt be the least attractively furnished room in existence, I have something to give you. Here, take this."

Lupin flicked his wrist as best he could while handcuffed, and produced a card. Roscoe took it, and flipped it over.

the-coronation-of-judd-marshall.raw_content:
There is a price that comes with change, and it may not be one that Judd Marshall is willing to pay.

habaniah & xexnoncores

This work contains CWs for: misogyny, and antisemitic/homophobic/transphobic slurs.

The Coronation of Judd Marshall by habaniah and xexnoncores

⚠️ content warning

Judd Marshall is on the forty-third minute of a thirty-minute meeting. He is a single sip of whiskey deep; he’s barely been able to metabolize the stuff since he went on new meds around his 130th. Twenty feet up, the abstract, swooping crow-shaped logo of Valravn Corporation looms in white paint on a vast pinewood wall, its eyes glaring without beholding, and hating without knowing, even at someone like him, one of the three most important executives of Marshall, Carter, and Dark Ltd.

Nate Hansen, Midwestern Regional President of Valravn, finishes signing the last of a stack of papers. A collection of vacant glasses sits beside him like trophies, courtesy of the office’s open bar diplomacy. Ian Whitten, of Valravn’s legal team, has worked through his pile of forms and is attacking a smorgasbord beside him at a steady, deliberate, and impressive pace.

Marshall smiles, attempting a joke. “I see why Wisconsin needs to make so much cheese.”

Hansen looks up, drilling three fingers with heavy rings on them. They’re all made of bronze and silver. “What the hell else is he supposed to do with his mouth?”

Whitten, down a tongue from a long-ago involuntary secondment with the Serpent’s Hand, glances over at Hansen with a look of disgust. He eats another cube of cheddar.

Hansen pulls out the final page and passes it along the table to Marshall, who signs and gives it back without a word.

“Won’t you need some other sign-offs, Judd? Of the other two keys to the kingdom?” Hansen asks.

“Pardon?”

“You know. Layla and Iris. Iris and Layla.”

“We’re not a vetocracy,” Marshall replies curtly. “I have the final say-so over projects in my purview. And it’s Mayhew. Iris and Mayhew. Layla’s just his wife.”

“Oh, you can keep your little shibboleths,” Hansen spits. “We know Layla’s calling the shots over there. At least, since May-hew Car-ter decided thinking was too strenuous for him.”

Mayhew’s heart attack. Ah, it feels like it happened just yesterday—in actuality, it occurred eighteen months ago. The change in authority was as swift as it was without any time to mourn; Layla had the yoke broken upon her as soon as she was able to say yes to the prospect, most likely not entirely aware of what she agreed to.

Marshall smiles. It is not only fake but obviously so, not only obviously so but intentionally enough as to communicate its falsity. His reminiscence makes it all the more so. “I’m just here to protect our interests at the Cortez site. I only ask for your typical arsenal, and your Valkyries… That’s all. You know how much the ore mines matter here.”

Hansen bolts upward; Whitten turns toward him, evident anger in his eyes. Marshall turns toward him, also—there’s a bubbling beneath the waves he’s seen many a time between partners at other meetings. Valravn had its splendid facilities, within which the High Table carried on its fine practice of corporate administration, but the truth was that it filled those facilities with animals. And those animals often stank up whatever room they were allowed to fill unless collared by someone with more silver in their pockets.

“Well, as long as you’re here, I’ll tell you what’s really going on.”

Marshall wants to roll his eyes. But the night is young, so he’ll let himself be drawn in. Mayhew used to be really good at taking these kinds of leads on, tempting bulls like this. “What’s really going on?”

“A lot of us here at Valravn are starting to chafe. Grumble. Regarding the new MC&D.”

Marshall clears his throat. “I’m not sure what you mean, Nate. Especially by new. We’ve had the same basic contract for six years.”

Hansen clicks his tongue. “You know what I mean.”

“I don’t think I do. We’re your largest client by a factor of four, and we’ve been very good to the High Table. Mercenary work is an industry where demand is a lot harder to come by than supply, especially since Constellis launched that hub office in the Portlands.”

“It’s not about the bottom line,” Hansen says, a deep hatred riding in his voice.

Whitten, silent always, remains so. But his expression darkens.

“That’s news to me," Marshall says. He didn't even know he could smile so wide. "Then what are these complaints for?”

Hansen waves his hand, scowls, shows his teeth for the first time.

What ugly veneers, Marshall thinks. A maid could do better.

“Let me tell you a little about the way things were a few years ago,” Hansen starts, pointing at Marshall. “You and Mayhew, you two, well, you were the type of people that guys like me and my men could feel proud about working for. We liked you, we liked your strides, your attitude.”

Another sip of whiskey. Behind him, Whitten bites his lip.

“And Iris, well, Iris we could tolerate. She could show face to the press. Someone approachable. Nice…" Hansen laughs a little. "Nice cheekbones. Though I'll admit I'm not much for the Adam's apple.”

Whitten rises, slaps Hansen, grabs his arm. The two trade blows on the floor for a moment. Marshall stares, impassive, soon a micrometer from laughter. They wouldn't kill each other—not here, not yet.

He checks his watch. Within a minute, Hansen, bruised, stands again before him; Whitten, less bruised, slinks back to the cheeseboard.

Violence accomplishing little. But what else could he possibly be here for? The unprofessionalism Valravn could have was why you could trust them not to obey national treaties going into less-than territories.

“…Iris has been called a great many things,” he begins. “But I’ve never heard anyone call her approachable.”

“Our boys think women are born approachable. Despite what’s between their legs.”

“If you can have sex with her, I guess it doesn’t matter what she is, hm?”

Marshall lets out a short, cruel laugh.

Hansen smiles. His teeth are too perfect, too square for what they should be. “Knew we could work with you.”

“So,” Marshall begins, “let me get this straight—you’re saying opinions us within Valravn’s rank-and-file have deteriorated somewhat since Mayhew’s…incapacitation. Correct?”

“That’s right,” says Hansen. “It’s not about the projects. It’s not about the pay.”

“You just don’t want to work for Layla and Iris.”

Hansen leans forward. “Yeah. Our boys call them the K. and the D."

Whitten's knuckles dig hard into the table again.

"Gosh," Marshall says, almost like a child at a birthday party asking for the big surprise from their parents. "What does that stand for?"

"The kike and the dyke. Some folks say faggot. Not me, though," Hansen says, giggling like a rattlesnake. "Because that doesn't rhyme."

“Ah,” Marshall says.

"Well, doesn't the shoe fit?"

He shrugs. “Well…you’re certainly right about Layla Rosen-Carter’s heritage.” He cracks his knuckles, taking a deep breath. “I believe her great-grandfather was a deck-rat on the Exodus. But Iris Dark prefers the company of men, you’re aware of that, yes?”

“Maybe she does,” says Hansen. “Doesn’t really change who she is.”

"I don't get it," replied Marshall. "I have seen your Valkyries. You guys have no problem working with them."

"Valkyries are not women. Not fully at least." Hansen flashed a repugnant smile. "Don't get me wrong, they are one of our finest products. But still a product at the end. We don't work with them, they serve us. You may want to take some note there."

Marshall sighs, running sore hands down the side of his face. “So what do you expect me to do about this, Nate?” He again stills what trickles down through his head; he’s not lived this long without learning to offer up his irrationality upon the crucible, his contemplative notions that may align against what Iris wants. “About this dissatisfaction in your ranks? What makes you think I can change anything?”

“Don’t talk to me as if this is just Valravn, Judd,” Hansen says, pointing at him again. “They’re deadweight, as everyone can see them. You could, and should cut them both, and strike out on your own.”

“Strike out on my own?”

Hansen nods. “Mhm.”

Marshall simply shakes his head, putting in only the bare minimum effort to dissuade those thoughts from intrusively latching upon his mind. “Do you have any idea what the enterprise value of MC&D is?”

“I don’t,” Hansen replies.

“Of course.” Marshall stands up, wiping imaginary dust off his clothes like he was some kind of royalty. “Regardless, I will take your comments under advisement. In the meantime, seeing as the contract is signed, I’d like to wish you both good evening.”

“Hey, don’t brush this off so easily!” Hansen yells, rising from his stool and stepping toward Marshall. His breath is rank. “Advisement? I think you should consider this a warning, honestly. This stuff filters upstream faster than you think; you’re bleeding reputation here. You’ve got nowhere to go.”

“Nate, please.” Marshall’s head is buzzing. “I am here to get your help with Cortez. Only that.”

Hansen shakes his head.

It would be better, professionally, for Marshall to leave. Better yet to have left ten minutes ago. But he got where he was by nodding – to Mayhew, to Iris – and assent is a difficult habit to break.

“Faster than you think,” Hansen repeats, waltzing over unsteadily to poke Marshall in the ribs. “You know what our hires for you are saying in the barracks?”

Marshall looks down at Hansen’s outstretched finger. Swollen diamonds glint in the incandescent light.

“No,” Marshall replies. “What are they saying?”

“They’re saying they work for the Three Queens.”

“…Three?”

“Yeah. Three.” Hansen cackles like a hyena. “You’re running with a pack of bitches. Why shouldn’t you be crowned with them?”

"Ah," says Marshall. But it's deeper. Lower. It's only once it's through his lips that he realizes he is genuinely pained.

Why can’t Marshall bring himself to leave?

Hansen smiles, wicked and unapologetic.

“Ha, look at him. Snake got his tongue.”

Behind Hansen, a cracker splinters in Whitten's tensed hand. But Marshall feels heavy, immobile. Like there's a cannonball in his chest.

“…I take it these difficulties aren’t affecting performance,” he begins. So dull. So flat. “Since you had no issues last month in Khartoum."

Valravn stays on the books, Iris had told him before he came here. Their services are expensive, but the intimidation they produce is plentiful and cheap.

“…You seem to be suggesting a problem to something which I cannot solve.”

“Says who? Just backstab the whores."

Marshall can only roll his eyes. This wine’s dryness is getting on his nerves. Hansen grabs his drink as soon as he sets it down to finish a shaky, paltry swig, and it takes everything, with everyone watching– his own long-forgotten frailty, his own self-preservation– not to take a fist to his head.

But that’s what Mayhew would have done. He slapped Layla in the face at the autumn ball. Even in front of her parents, both younger than him.

Marshall swallows his sour spit and exhales cleanly.

“Alright, well…I shall consider your words for tonight.”

“You better.”

“But I must be going now."

“I’m pleased this is going so smoothly,” Iris says while eating an apple. “Layla, this might have been before your time, but last time we… played around there, there was no end to the difficulty.”

“Well, Valravn can easily level a town or two down there, right?” Layla puts a perfect grape into her mouth. “With those…what did they call them? Valkyrie machines?”

"Valkyrie models,” Iris corrects her. “And mechanically, yes. Politically, no. The troubled lands of Colombia still contain horrible things, and Valravn has given them more of an understanding of their precarity."

His coworkers. Judd is silent. They’re his equals in every way, allegedly, on paper, on every transaction and sign-off, but tonight he can’t tell how he feels about it. Everything they touch, eat, and talk about is made of porcelain, of million-dollar signatures, as shiny as their faces and strong as their wills.

With fingernails polished, colored red and purple, Layla eats like she’s always been here, Iris as if she never knew Mayhew was gone.

“I’m surprised they take me seriously,” Layla says with a bite of her lip. She wipes juice off her chin and cranes her head to the ceiling.

“I’m surprised they took Mayhew Carter seriously.” Iris peels back a marble-colored piece of cheese. “But then again, you two never looked as far apart in age as you actually were.”

Layla was twenty-two when Mayhew took her hand in marriage, he a ripe seventy-nine. She was thirty-four now, and though she looked younger than that, like the twelve years had not fully passed her by. Mayhew had promised magic, but he had never even been able to get it to work for himself – not as well as he had wanted it to work. Mortality had advanced upon him and rendered him a frozen husk. Judd and Layla would go that way eventually, though it would take them longer. Far longer.

It was Iris who would outlast the rocks.

It was Iris who would keep the gears of Marshall, Carter, and Dark going after those preceding names faded, no doubt eager to exchange them when that time came.

It was Iris who would stay.

Judd feels like he should say something. He feels like he needs to push the air out here, for some reason. Everything is too quiet.

Layla looks at Iris with blank, untilled eyes; their vibrant brown hasn't quite given way to life yet. But the longer she stares, the more alike their images become to him. Two women sitting in velvet-sewn chairs, surrounded by floralesque wallpaper that feels just a decade out of fashion. Skinny, prim, perfumed and trimmed. No different from him and his starched suit. His salt-and-pepper hair, optimized for respectability.

“Judd, any word on your contractors from Valravn yet?”

Iris looks up at him from her laptop, her eyes diaphanous and glassy, like waning lilacs.

“No,” he replies blankly. He maintains steady eye-contact with her as easily as he breathes. “There seems to be no dissent or concern among them about the job. Layla’s plans will come to fruition soon.”

Indeed. Her plans. Layla loved the beach, and therefore asked so innocently if there was any way for the company to invest in some upscale accommodations. She was a traveler at heart, even before her husband’s heart attack, and the world called to her, in all things, without resistance or reservation.

And just like him, she too had grown fond of subjugation. Of taking, taking, taking. Extracting as she took, savoring it in her mouth, making numbers out of mincemeat and people as she took.

Does he resent her for that? For taking Mayhew’s place? Their sons weren’t yet old enough for the family business. And Judd would be a liar if he said he wouldn’t have preferred one of their kingly visages here over her…

Layla bows her head. Judd sighs. Iris closes her laptop, and stands up.

“It’s settled then. Layla, you should go home and get some rest. You’ve done enough for this week.”

“Have I?”

Judd watches Iris’s gaze peel over to her.

“For now. You are adjusting to your new workload quite quickly.”

“I was in marketing before this, I hope you know…”

“I’m aware.” Iris’s voice turns stagnantly acrid. “You didn’t know of what we did before then though. Your husband—”

“He kept it from me, yeah, yeah. G’valt, you don’t need to bring him up every time we see each other…!”

Judd watches Layla put on black satin jacket, tightening her ponytail. She leaves quickly, her auburn-brick hair leaving a void where she once stood despite everything. It is quiet void.

Now, Iris’s eyes turn to him.

His phone rings.

She doesn’t say anything. He has to answer it.

Turning around, Judd’s voice declines to a whisper. He does not consider himself to be afraid of Iris. Not even in Mayhew's day. But one lowers one's voice for a reason.

“Yes?”

"I hope you don't intend to call me about every package I receive. I told you to open them and set them aside."

“…Oh. I see.”

“Really? You’re sure it’s from them?”

“Yes, I agree. It's very peculiar. It still has the rings on it?”

"No, it's not a threat. Maybe it's like Freud. Sometimes a finger is just a finger?"

"Old joke. Ordinarily it's… oh, forget it."

“From a business partner, most likely.”

From the sound of it, Nate.

Judd is relieved. And impressed. They want the brutality of this “apology” to reinforce their contracts. They want their hatred to remain under the table, insulated from the good grace of their well-off clients. Valravn thinks about the "other" as the cat thinks about the mouse, touches them solely through thaumic fires. Through snipers guided by fae sights, dressed in dragonskin-reinforced armor.

“…Throw it away,” he says, finally. This is obeisance to who crowned him with his money and good fortune. Iris’s eyes are boring into his back and he cannot cut them away.

He thinks of the many wives he's had and lost for some reason, like a man upon the noose. The children to whom he does not speak. The heir and the spare and the spare and the spare and the…

“In the end it means nothing,” she says. Her word is final.

Dial tone. Judd clicks off the call and turns around. Iris is staring and her face has nothing readable upon it.

“…You knew.”

“Don't state the obvious.” Her voice shifts to its factual tone. “I knew. Yes. But I knew before I knew.”

His eyes bore into her, but they go no deeper than a foothold. A deep breath fills his chest involuntarily with the ferrous scent of her rather masculine cologne, stitched together by its cobblestone high notes and asphalt lows.

“…Valravn have impressive anti-magic capabilities.”

“I'm pleased to see you read the first paragraph of the briefing.”

She says her words with such a butchering tone that Judd relents quickly, in both mind and soul, pursing his lips together as he runs a hand through his hair. It’s weighed down by an invisible concrete crown.

“Layla is going to give you pushback on this.”

“Well, she will understand quickly how little this matters. Stray words aren’t going to kill her.”

He raises an eyebrow, a lump catching in his throat at the sheer audacity. “You really don’t mind what they said about you?”

“What do you think of me, Judd?”

Judd blinks several times. He knows it is the kind of question that must be answered quickly, if it is to be answered at all. But he racks his mind for several long moments. For the level of sincerity required. For the latent intent in the query.

Until she steps back, and at last a series of words drip out of his mouth like tar.

“…What you do is your own business,” he replies stolidly.

“And that extends to who I am,” she says, hanging herself up in a manner Judd has seen before. He knew of her transition, and had no opinion on it. Iris treated it with great privacy, one which only mattered on the rare occasions she needed to remind someone what the minuscule rune on her left shoulder was. It was an archaic Sarkic “E”, at least its closest equivalent.

Pure neutrality was the cleanest way to live. Bow your head and ignore who your neighbor was, for it was none of your business. It would never be any of your business. It’s not your business to know their troubles, of the belligerents who threaten them and pound on their doors. It’s not your business to know what the words created to specifically harm them mean, just keep quiet if something happens.

If the glass breaks, sweep it up and throw it away.

It’s only your business to make money, after all. Raze down others, bleed their veins, and watch their blood dye your field until next year’s harvest of jewels came in. Who gave you the right to pry into their personal life, their personal histories?

“And how long do you think it will take Layla to get used to this?”

The banality stings him for the first time in a while. Thinking about Layla coming into work every day like he and Iris do, like Mayhew once did, the color in her eyes fading as a line went up and her circle of influence grew.

“Mayhew had mud slung at him for marrying her. He got used to it rather quickly.”

You’d be willing to ask that of her so easily? is what he would say if he was a more recalcitrant man, but he’s not.

“And if she doesn’t?”

Iris scoffs. “Weren’t you poor once?”

Both of them quiet as soon as the words finish. Judd realizes quickly it’s a non-sequitur meant to put him in his place, but instead it brings up reminiscences that he had longer buried under a mine of gold.

Lucky for him, they do not mean much as they wash over. But the polluted water erodes unto him the understanding from his past circumstances he, Iris, and Layla are only afforded this great privilege by virtue of their money acting as the most perfect of insulators. If Iris were a more common street rat like what he had been once, she’d be squeaking a different tune.

He doesn’t laugh at the image in his head. He would if he was alone, though.

“Also, Judd?”

Oh, she seems to have one last thing to say. Good, he needs to be getting home for dinner. He needs to be throwing away this gift of uneasiness as soon as possible.

“Her grandfather was on the Exodus,” she finishes. “Not her great-grandfather.”

Judd sighs. He runs another hand through his hair as he flattens his lips. “My mistake, of course. Do I want to know how you found that out?”

Iris taps her foot and slides her laptop into a slick dragon-leather purse. If you put your ear close enough to it, you could still hear its soul lingering.

“No more answers. This is a matter in which our interests are adverse.”

Judd relents finally. Enough relevancy has been extinguished. Enough tiresomeness has been wrung.

“I’m sorry. For what I said.”

Why is he saying that?

Who is he saying that for?

Himself? The unseen Layla? Her husband he’d been partners with for fifty years? If Mayhew was here, this wouldn’t be ending so somberly… He always knew a way to make Iris stare at the both of them silently before dropping the inane subject all together.

Iris shakes her head, almost mournfully. “Oh, Judd.”

“Why do you keep Layla around if you think she will fail?”

“You only miss Mayhew now that he’s gone.”

He hesitates. “That’s…That’s always the way.”

“That’s right.”

“And what will you say about me, if I go? And someone comes around missing me?”

He knows he shouldn’t have asked that. He knows this conversation shouldn’t be happening.

But he’s already been weak enough today. Weak in ways indescribable, undescribed actually, for there was a void where his actions were, not an outpouring of thought and notion.

He shouldn’t be here. They shouldn’t be here. Iris should be gone. He should be home for dinner. The schedule’s important; the way out is to do things as they’ve always been.

Always been, always been.

Has there always been a crown upon his head? Was he coronated when he joined this company, his fate sealed when he watched Mayhew take as his bride a young nothing star who was barely old enough to drink?

“When you go,” she corrects him.

Iris started this company, and by whatever god exists in this universe, if one existed at all, she will be here if it ever sees its end.

She grabs everything of hers and leaves without a word. He is now left alone, alone, alone in the Darkless dark, a Rosenless room, without the chartering of the Carter that used to light it up.

And like he has done many times and will do many times again, Judd Marshall blanks his mind. It is an easy thing to do when he can occupy himself with asking what car will be taking him to what house of his tonight. There’s three here just in town.

He eats another cube of cheddar. Hansen pulls out the final page and passes it along the table to Marshall, who signs and gives it back without a word. “Won’t you need some other sign-offs, Judd?
