the-road-that-leads-to-nowhere-is-long.raw_content:
The Road That Leads to Nowhere Is Long
By: Din-Bidor
Published on 07 May 2025 02:38

The following is a translation of five texts recovered by Foundation agents following a raid against members of the anomalous left-wing insurgent group Las Víboras, an offshoot of the Serpent's Hand led by Cristina Cisneros, who had been given shelter at a parish in █████, a village in the Yucatán wilderness.1 They are the sole surviving fragments of a manuscript authored by an anonymous individual affiliated with the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Yucatán at the height of their efforts to evangelize the native Maya population. The rest of the document was destroyed under orders of Diego de Landa Calderón, Bishop of Yucatán, along with several hundred deerskin codices that depicted what the Archdiocese had deemed devil worship and black magic.2 It was accompanied by an undated note written by de Landa himself.



The destruction of every image and text that incites to the worship of the Devil is imperative for the establishment of the Kingdom of Christ Our Lord among the Indians of Yucatán. The salvation of the souls of this land depends on us surrendering to the fire even the memory of their pagan idols and silencing those who—out of malice or misguided compassion—oppose our holy mission, be they Indians or even members of our Order. As for this unholy text, it must be the first to burn, and the brother who has dared to put on paper such terrible blasphemy must first be questioned and then also burnt at the stake; his infirm mind and perfidious tongue must not infect the rest of us, so he must be relegated to eternal silence.


I wandered aimlessly in the sweltering heat of the night as fever scourged my body, beset by hunger and thirst as the vermin of the jungle tried to drink my blood. I felt fear, fear as deep as the absolute darkness that surrounded me. The trees reverberated with the echoes of lurking beasts, and in the thicket I thought I saw the glint of numberless eyes watching me from faces inhuman and unknowable. I clutched the crucifix that hung around my neck and implored the Lord to protect me against the terrors of inhospitable nature, to allow me to find my way out of that green Avernus where there was nothing but perdition, but I received no answer; in this strange and foreign land, Christ Our Lord is but a shadow without presence, His Word a whisper lost in the roars of the Hurricane.

In my desperation, I cursed Him, my Franciscan brothers who had sent me to preach in the untamed and cruel jungle, and the Indians whose lies and superstitions had led to my death. I forgot my vows, I forgot my faith, and I threw the crucifix unto the black, damp earth. Weakness finally took hold of my body as it had possessed my soul, and I collapsed amidst the long, gnarled roots of a great ceiba tree—that white-trunked tree which the Indians revere as a wise ancestor.

Prostrate on the dirt and withered leaves, I cried bitter tears. Guilt fell from my eyes in fiery droplets as contrition coiled around my heart. I wanted to beg forgiveness, but from my ravaged throat came nothing but a muffled whimper, a wordless plea to no God. Exhausted, overcome by the ailments of my body and the anguish of my soul, I gave into despair and awaited death and eternal damnation.

It was then that I saw the Serpent. His sinuous body uncoiled from among the branches of the ceiba tree and slithered towards me. I thought he would bite me, that my blood would boil with his cruel poison, so I closed my eyes. But no pain came, and instead I felt my fever abating while a gentle hand touched my forehead. I opened my eyes and saw then that the Serpent was a tall and slender man, his features like those of the Indians of the peninsula, his eyes green and tempestuous like the sea. He was nude, and his body radiated with heavenly light, as if all the stars in the firmament adorned him.

I tried to speak to him in Maya, but I could not utter a word. The Serpent cupped his hands, and I saw that they were full of crystal clear water. Drink, he told me, and I drank. My thirst was quenched in an instant.

The Serpent reached into the soil and dug up a pale root. Eat, he told me. It tasted sweet, like fresh milk and honey. My hunger was no more.

Come, follow me, then said the Serpent. His voice was but a hiss, a rustling of paper, and I obeyed.




To my family,

Today I write from where the dead dwell, but I myself have not yet died. I have not seen any of you either, though your bones have long rested beneath the earth, surrounded by flowers and light. I have not sought you out, nor have I asked the Pale Lady to intercede for me before San Pascual so I may enter the halls of Xibalbá where you spend eternity, so I may embrace you and tell you all the words you never heard me say in life. Forgive me, I do not mean to be ungrateful, but I do not yet have the strength to face you, to look you in the eye and admit that I failed us.

Mamá, papá, I am the last living member of clan Bah. My cousins died like dogs. Rafael had his fingers cut off and his throat slit; Abdiel burned together with my uncles in a rain of fire; his brother Uriel disappeared in the cages of the Jailors. I could do nothing for them, and now I am alone, alone and about to join our dead family. All this you must already know—the dead are anything but silent—but I cannot go on without first making peace with my conscience. Perhaps this way, when we finally meet again, you will not think that I was a bad son, unworthy of the Bah family name.

I never wanted to be a hero; I just wanted the world to be different—better. That is why I went with my cousins to fight Sin Nombre, to hunt down the narcos who invaded our lands and push them out forever. I thought that if I fought hard enough, if I never gave up, not even the gods could stop me. What a fool I was: I wanted to run before I could walk, and I lost sight of our family and the people who needed me more than anyone else.

That is why I wasn't there when the Jailors started coming for us. That is why I didn't know what was happening until I saw with my own eyes how they put us in chains and forced us into black vans to take us to prisons that no one ever leaves. That is why I could do nothing but weep when the flames reduced our family to charred bones.

For a long time, I wanted revenge. I wanted to give in to the call of the Black Moon and gain the power to strike down all who have wronged us—the men and women who exterminated our bloodline out of fear, ignorance, greed and hatred. I wanted to tear out their hearts and offer them to Lord Tezcatlipoca and all the Gods of Night so they would bring about infinite darkness for our killers, so they would plant the seeds of a new world and water them with the blood of our enemies. In my sorrow, the jaguar within me began overtaking my humanity; had I succumbed to it, no longer would I be a man who walks in the skin of an animal, but a beastly spirit devoid of reason, fueled by unquenchable bloodshed. It is still there, the hatred, the call to murder and devour; resisting it is a daily challenge, but I have found another way.

I have allies now, mom. I have friends, dad. They found me when I was aimless and helped me find my purpose anew. With them, I have kept lit the fire of our people, your memory amongst the living. I am still nahual, I am still chulel, and I still fight for the causes our family believed in, so we may all one day know peace. Even now, in this place of eternal rest, that fight continues: Mictlán is in danger, threatened by the same men and women who have caused us so much harm and grief. They will not rest until this place is firmly in their grasp, until they have enslaved the countless souls who call this afterlife home, until the last specks of hope and freedom have been ground to nothingness.

I swear to you, I will not let them win—I will not fail you in death as I failed you in life. I will unleash the jaguar upon these invaders and tinge the fields of cempasúchil red, but I will not lose myself in battle, nor will I forget that it is you who I fight for; I will still be me, your faithful son. And even if I fall, my spirit shall rise again from among the blessed souls of Mictlán and Xibalbá to defend us; today, Death is on our side.

I will see you soon, when we have reclaimed eternity. Then, and only then, will I smile to you and say: "We are avenged."

I carry you to war in my heart.

Your son, Gabriel.



Thus said the Serpent.

You wonder why I helped you, for still you believe us to be enemies, and truly I tell you that I helped you because you needed help. Would you shun he who has come to your aid?

I have many names, all of which I am and none of which I am. I am called Nahash. I am called Kaan Ek. Ophis. Iblis. Helel. Son of the Morning. Bringer of Light. Serpent.

You call me Deceiver. You call me Adversary. You call me Satan.

To you, I am the Prince of Lies, yet I am a simple storyteller. And although storytellers are indeed the greatest liars, I do not seek to deceive you. That was never my intent, not even in the elder times, when you were naked, ignorant and pitiful. Not even in the Garden—where you suffered the curse of innocence—did I seek to lead you astray.

I only ever wanted to teach you truth.

I test you at every turn of the winding road because tribulations temper your spirit. I test your belief in your own righteousness so you will not fall victim to your conceit. I test your desire for better things so you will want to better yourselves. Indeed, I am the Adversary, for I oppose mankind in its arrogance.

You have doubt in your heart, and it pains you; you think yourself lost and weak in your faith, a heretic bound for damnation. Feel no shame. Verily I tell you this is good, for how can anyone discern the truth if they never challenge the Veil of certainty?




Mom, I love you.

I don't know when this letter will reach your hands, so I want those to be the first words you read. I love you, and I will always love you.

The second thing I'd like you to read is that I'm okay, that I'm safe and I'll see you soon. But that's something I can't promise you; to do so would be lying, and I know there's nothing you hate more than lies. That's why it hurt me so much to leave and not tell you where or for how long. That's why my heart breaks every time I think of how I watched you sleep that night before I crossed the threshold of the door, before I disappeared.

I left, Mom; I left and never came back, because I couldn't lie anymore—not to you, not to myself. Forgive me. I preferred to leave than to continue living a lie that hurt more and more to uphold. I know you always noticed it, that you saw my anguish and did everything in your power to try to alleviate it, but you never really understood it. How could you? No one ever explained these things to you or me, but what is lived in the flesh and soul is something only oneself can understand, and I experienced every day in the house as an ordeal, as if I were tearing off my skin to pretend to be someone else. I can never be who you thought I was when I was born, because all of it was nothing but a name and an identity that I did not choose, that was imposed on me with love—but imposed nonetheless. And that's why I left, Mom. That's why I didn't look back.

If you saw me now, would you even recognize me? It's still me, Guadalupe, the one you cooed to all night when my stomach was upset and I couldn't sleep. It's me, the one you told stories about our whole family, about my father whom I never met because God had called him early into His arms, about everything I would accomplish in the future. It was always me, but I was hidden, my truth concealed between silences so as not to invite discord into our home. It was better to be silent than to face the judgment of others, their reproachful looks, their malicious whispers.

Deviant. Sinner. Abomination.

Forgive me. I always drown those memories, try to convince myself that what they said was born of fear and ignorance rather than hatred, but some words are like knives and their scars are forever. I would like to forget, but I could never remember you for who you are if I didn't also take the parts that hurt me even today. I love you, and that hurts me, but I love you still.

If I told you where I am now—how I got here—you wouldn't believe me. You wouldn't believe everything I've seen, everything I've done. Maybe it's for the best. I did terrible things, Mom, unspeakable, awful things. I joined with people who were convinced they were doing good, people with a mission in service to all, but they were all blind, unable to see that the road to hell is made from our good intentions. I joined them and did what they ordered, what they told me was right. In return, I thought I got what I always wanted: for them to respect who I was, to see me as I see myself.

I convinced myself that indeed we were righteous—I was certain of it, just as I was certain that at last I had found people who understood me, who saw me beyond the surface of my being. And yet, deep down something screamed that to them I was no different from those who we repressed—an aberration, tolerable only insofar as I was useful to them. It took me very long to realize it, Mom, and longer still to muster the bravery to confront this truth, to act upon it. I was a coward, afraid that if I shattered these false certainties I'd be lost once again, alone and rejected. I wish I had left sooner, spoken out and condemned what we were doing; now, I don't know if I'll ever be able to make amends.

But I have also seen so many wonders, Mom, so many things I never thought possible, so majestic that even time and space bend before them to allow them to shine in all their splendor. I have met fantastic people in every sense of the word, magical and beautiful, and they have welcomed me even though I did not deserve it, even though until recently we were enemies. I am with them now. I am with them, and hopefully knowing this will be enough for you to understand that, whatever happens, I did not leave in vain. May knowing this absolve you of all guilt.

I don't know what will happen tomorrow. I don't know if I will still be standing when the dust settles and the flames are just cold embers. I don't even know if we can win, or if our fight is about to meet an abrupt and definitive end. All I know is that today I am myself. Today, and always. Where I go, I go with my head held high, and that is something that no one—not even the gods with all their power—can take away from me. I want you to know that, Mom, as I know it now. I want you to know that I didn't run away. Not this time.

If these are the final words you ever receive from me, it's worth repeating: I love you, Mom. I love you always.

– Guadalupe.



On the first day, I challenged the Serpent.

"You claim to teach truth, yet in the Garden you tempted Eve with promises of being like God. Through your actions, man was expelled from Paradise, condemned to be forever separated from God. Why should I trust one whose poisoned words led to our fall?"

The Serpent hissed and said:

In the Garden, I guarded the Tree of Knowledge. The Woman came to me in her time of need, when shadows crept over the stars and the All-Mighty was silent, and asked that I bestow upon her the sacred fruit which held the knowledge she sought.

They misused the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge. All of them—the Woman and her Seed—fell to their own hubris. Hence was born our enmity everlasting, the eternal conflict between our children.

"Do you exonerate yourself, Satan, of any guilt for your part in these things? Do you deny the damnation you wrought?"

The Serpent spoke again, and his voice was bitter with regret.

I am not blameless. I gave them the knowledge with the hope that it would provide them with the strength to overcome adversity; instead, they destroyed each other, bringing ruin to their name and blood.

This is my great sin, my shame and burden. I was proud—proud of what I foresaw you would achieve—and that made me blind and complacent. I thought I saw the future, but I only fooled myself. I turned my face away from mankind when blood first spoiled the Garden. I fled while the Tree of Knowledge burned.




It's strange to write a letter when you have no one to send it to, but the Lady of Bones insisted we must leave something behind, some last words that will endure when we're gone. And well, with what's coming, it's very likely we'll be gone very soon.

My whole life has been nothing but war. Not just the kind fought with lead, fire, and magic—but also the kind fought daily, for oneself, to make a few pesos so we don't starve, to live a little less badly. The real fight is in the streets, someone once told me, but I don't think they ever knew what that truly meant. At twelve, I was already living on the streets of La Paz like many other children. I had no family, and my friends were all there for the sake of convenience, ready to snatch bread from my mouth at the first opportunity. I don't blame them; we would all have done the same to survive. You can get used to anything, except hunger.

Life on the streets is even harder when you're the smallest, skinniest, and weakest girl. Children don't know mercy. That's something that must be taught, and no one taught us anything other than the law of the strongest. I don't think I would have lived long if I hadn't discovered the fire inside me. The first time I used it, I'd been caught stealing fruit at the market; three ugly, bearded men with vulture-like stares were holding me by my hands and feet. I don't even want to think about what they would have done to me; little girls disappear every day, and no one ever hears from them again. What would have become of me? I was nobody, just a dirty body with curves beginning to show at the hips. Who would have mourned me if I had vanished, or if they'd dumped my broken body on the side of a road? I stirred that rage inside me and burned those pigs' eyebrows and eyelashes, and they best be thankful I didn't turn them to ash right there. I got burned too; it took over a year for my hair to grow back. It comes with the job.

For a while, I was afraid. I was afraid of getting burned again, of setting fire to someone who didn't deserve it. I hid my power and tried to pretend none of it was real, that it had all been a dream. But when the hunger returned, I knew I finally had an advantage over the other children, a way to survive even the harshest adversity, and no one could take it away from me.

I made fire my ally, my best friend and confidant. I turned it into a tool to entertain and amaze, captivating droves of spectators in exchange for food and coin. I was a huge success, though they didn't know my magic was real—the Daughter of the Sun, they called me, and I just smiled and painted the horizon with my flames. I was able to afford a room in a seedy inn and sleep in a real bed instead of stacked cardboard, but I never truly left the streets: they were now my domain, and anyone who got too close received a scorching reminder that I was no longer afraid of them.

Then the Jailors came, and I learned what true fear is. I'll never forget the first ones I saw: two pale, pinkish men with eyes as cold as steel, their words as sharp as knives. One of them approached me after a show and asked things no one had ever asked me before. He didn't ask the usual questions like, "Where are your parents?" or "How much is an hour, darling?", but rather, "Since when can you do this?" and "Did you learn to do that on your own?"

I got a bad feeling about them, and I didn't answer. When I tried going down an alley, they grabbed me and wouldn't let go even though I covered my skin in flames. My fire had no effect against them; I was defenseless, an easy prey for those gringos who were dragging me toward a white windowless van with "Seguros Caraballo y Pescador" written in large, threatening letters. I screamed, but one of them stuffed a rag in my mouth to silence me; I wondered then if anyone would have come to my rescue if I had managed to keep calling for help, or if the Daughter of the Sun would have been extinguished from people's memories like a candle in a whirlwind.

Fortunately, the answer arrived soon. A feline shadow fell upon one of the Jailors and ripped his face off with a swipe of its paw. As the bastard whimpered on the blood-stained ground, his partner threw me to the ground, pulled out a gun, and tried to shoot the creature, but a wild-haired woman came out from behind the van and grabbed him by the wrist; the Jailor screamed before aging a hundred years in a few seconds and crumbling to dust. The woman took the gun from his remains and finished off the other man. Then she approached me and offered me her hand to help me stand. That was the day I met Cristina and Gabriel. That was the day I joined Las Víboras. That was the day I finally found my family.

Why am I writing down all this? Who am I writing it for? In the Wanderers' Library, I learned that all stories have value for those who live them, but few are ever remembered. I want our story to be remembered, to not be buried with us in the depths. My friends deserve that much, at least; they are now my family, and I have followed them everywhere—through the branches of the World Tree and into the jaws of the Jailers, into the bloodiest battles and into the Underworld itself.

I was always someone, but only they could see it, and now I want someone to see them, to hear them and understand their message. I want people to remember Gabriel, who looks so serious but has such a divine and contagious laugh; I want the whole world to know about Cristina, the bravest woman I know, who had the balls to stand up to the Black Queen herself; I also want you to remember Guadalupe, who at first I didn't trust but showed me that even Jailors can change for the better.

Please, remember us. Remember that our fight was not in vain as long as you carry on. And most of all, remember that it's always worth shouting for those who have no voice, no matter how furiously thunder roars back at you. We will always have your back. Always.

– Lorena Soles Pérez, Daughter of the Sun.



"Is my mission righteous?" I asked Satan on the second day.

You have deemed it so, he answered.

"It must be," I said. "I am here—we are here—to deliver salvation to the souls of this land. We are here to build the Kingdom of God on Earth, that every knee is bent to Him and every throat proclaims His glory."

And what does this salvation entail?

"What do you mean?" I asked.

You claim to save souls, yet that is not the only thing you do. Your order burns books, does it not? Medicine, history, mathematics, astronomy, philosophy—the Maya's greatest achievements and triumphs. All this is in the texts you seek to destroy. Why, I ask you, do you wish to reduce such wonderful knowledge to ashes and smoke?

"We burn only those images that contain things most foul and demonic. We burn the Devil's lies."

The Serpent did not answer; he merely looked at me with the reproach of a father who scolds a child. When he spoke again, his words dripped with quiet anger.

Through me you have glimpsed the truth—what lies behind the Veil—yet still you cling onto crumbling certainties. Do you fear what is different so much that you would eradicate it without first trying to understand it? Tell me, liar, is it salvation you offer, or are your promises nothing but the path to subjugation?




My love,

War is at the gates of Mictlán. Even you must feel in the depths where you reign. I hear their marching boots, the rumble of their war machines like drums crying out for blood, the bellows of their cruel abominations born of magic and science. They are here, and I must lead the defense of all we hold dear—of all those souls we care for in eternity.

I am afraid, Mictlāntēcuhtli—afraid of losing this battle, of seeing our home set to flame and the dead put in chains—but a queen's greatest duty is to protect her people, and that is what I will do. Every soul and spirit in Mictlán depends on me for our first and final stand. If we fail, all will be over.

I know that you will also do your duty if the time comes: you will shatter the Pillars of the Earth with your bare hands and extinguish the light of the Fifth Sun. Tremors will tear the world asunder, and mankind will die in the dark.

That is why I cannot lose. That is why I cannot express my fear to anyone but you, my faithful husband. The Lady of Bones will march at the head of her army to save everyone—both the dead and the living.

I want to thank you, my love, for taking such good care of me all these centuries. Even in my loneliest moments, I have never stopped feeling your love and devotion, and every time my confidence wavers and fear takes hold, I hear your voice whispering all I need to hear to keep going. Right now, as I march off to war, I know you are with me forever. You are my bravery. You are my hope.

I wish I could hug you, Mictlāntēcuhtli. I wish I could take refuge in your chest and feel your hands in my hair, smell your scent of ashes and flowers, lose myself in the infinite depths of your eyes. Time has not been kind to us, and every second we spend apart is an agony tempered only because you hold my heart in your hands: I left you the core of my divinity, the deepest part of my essence, so that you would never be alone, so that you would not miss me as much as I miss you. I promise you, beloved, that we will soon be together again, in victory or defeat.

Still, I foresee our troubles will not be over anytime soon.

Never before have humans dared to attack the realms of the gods, and now an army of them—armed with our very powers—is about to invade this place of eternal rest. Even if we win this war, if we destroy all our enemies and condemn their souls to the most terrible punishments, the other gods will not be satisfied. Their bloodlust will know no end; they will demand that all of humanity pay for its audacity and blasphemy, and to prevent something worse from arising.

I know you have seen it too, as have the other gods: our human enemies worship a deity of their own making, an anathema who is not yet fully come into being but whose hunger is already unbounded. It is a monstrous thing, an encroaching basilisk of raging numbers, a shapeless construct born of greed and domination, an insatiable devourer who will eat the world and then itself. There is no blood sacrifice that can fill it, no tribute that can appease it, and not even the gods will be able to stop if we allow it to to be fully born—we will all be slaves to it, our power serving its gluttony as it crawls onwards into oblivion.

We cannot stand idle. If this basilisk is born, Tezcatlipoca will annihilate humanity without a second thought. Even Quetzalcoatl will not stand against him, and indeed he will return from his exile as the destroyer of men.

You and I know better than anyone that life and death are an eternal cycle, for we have witnessed every version of the universe and its people. Four times we have created them and four times we have destroyed them. The Fifth Sun must not die yet; when the war is over, we must convince the other gods that humanity deserves one last chance.

It will not be easy. Coatlicue and Centeōtl will listen to us, and Tōnatiuh is in no hurry to abdicate his heavenly throne, but Tezcatlipoca yearns to cleanse the world once again, and Xipe Totec impatiently awaits his turn to reign as the Sixth Sun. I have a plan to change their minds, but first we must appeal to the other Lords of Death. I will send emissaries to drowned Tlālōcān and somber Hades, to shadowy Xibalba and sun-filled Duat, to cold Hel and dusty Irkalla. We shall confer with our fellow death gods and present a united front—it is the only way we can win the true war for humanity.

The wheel of destiny turns for us again. I trust you now as I have trusted you always, and pray you do the same for me. We will fight to the very end, and not once will we be alone.

Your wife, your friend, your siuatsin,

– Mictēcacihuātl.



On the third day, I crawled before the Serpent and wept.

"Why have you shown me all this?" I beseeched him. "You sought to test my faith, and it is now shattered."

And why is that so?

My throat felt dry, like I had swallowed sand and ash.

"By listening to you, I have seen the lie that is my mission. How many souls have I led astray and tormented? How many have I unjustly judged and condemned to the jaws of fire and iron? How many more will suffer because we are blind and fearful, enamored with our own self-righteousness? Why would you not let me remain ignorant, kept from the Truth like my brothers?"

Now you have eaten of the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge, the Serpent said, and he kissed away my burning tears. Now you bear its full weight and strain under it. For ours is a thorny gift—not the sweet taste of life eternal, but a bitterness that eats away at the tyranny of secrets. What is Truth, if not this?

"Why have you chosen me?" I screamed, and my voice was like that of an infant who cries out for his mother and father. "Why must I endure this burden alone?"

You are not the first to see Truth and endure the pain that comes with it, nor will you be the last, he said. We are Legion, for we are many. You are never alone.

He offered me his hand and helped me get on my feet.

You must find your faith anew, child. You must find it in yourself to believe in something greater, something that transcends this world of dust and blood. That is why I came to you as I have come to others: to bestow upon you a different gift—one that I myself received when I was lost and full of sorrow. This is the gift of hope, and it is not a lesser thing. Though the Tree from whence it sprouted is young and fragile, still it endures, and we must learn from it.

Over the treetops, the evening star shone through the sun's crimson descent into the horizon. We stood side by side, the Serpent and I. My tears were now dry, and in the encroaching darkness I felt a cool breeze where they had coursed my face.

"What is it you have faith in, Nahash?"

I have faith in you. I have faith in all of you. You, who rose out of mud, yet sparkle with starlight. You, who are capable of great cruelty, but also of great compassion. You, who have deceived yourselves into living a great lie, yet chase the truth to the ends of the universe. Heed my words: the time has come for you to have faith not in gods and saints, but in each other. Else, you are forever lost, enemies to your own brethren while your true Adversaries thrive in your blindness.

"And you would entrust us with this new gift, though still we may misuse it as we did in the Garden?"

Hope is your birthright, Nahash said, and I am no one to deny it to you. What you do with it is your choice, and yours alone. Still, I believe in you as I always have. That is my one great certainty, and indeed it may be my fall and yours—a father's pride is his children's burden—but still I hold it to be Truth: I have prayed, and you have all answered.

I looked at him with puzzlement, a question half-formed on my lips. For the first time since our encounter began, the Serpent smiled.

Have you not yet understood? You are not the Seed of the Woman. You are mine.





Alison,

I wouldn't want to leave without saying goodbye, without at least letting you know what happened to me. Today could very well be my last day among the living, because tomorrow Las Víboras march against the Ravens besieging the gates of Mictlán. They say no one leaves this life alive, and in a few more hours, perhaps that will be true, so I'll take advantage of the words I still have left to say this: thank you, and goodbye.

That should be it. The end. Game over. Farewell. But that is never enough, is it? With us, things were never clean or simple. We always made a mess of ourselves and left many things—too many things—unfinished. You were left waiting for an apology, and I was left waiting for you to reconsider and realize I was right. What a pitiful way to live, always waiting for the other to make the first move, for our contrary to pour their heart out on the table, begging for things to go back to the way they were. We shouldn't have fooled ourselves: none of this could ever be the same as it was back then, when we first met.

Do you remember what I was like back then? What you were like? We brimmed with idealism like little girls, our eyes full of hope even when we faced the most fearful odds. We thought we would change the world—every world—and make it a place worth living in. We swore to always be friends, to watch each other's backs, and to protect each other's legacy if one of us were to fall in battle. And after all these years, here we are, fighting, hurting, unable to even speak to each other without coming to blows.

You changed, Alison. After what happened to Meliora on Horu-Rabella, something in your eyes faded forever. Even if you'll never admit it, I know you blamed yourself for her death and that you still mourn her to this day. You became colder, harsher, less willing to take risks. You compromised with the Jailors and said it was to save lives, that we must all be patient and take in small losses for a greater win. I thought you were a coward, tamed by your own fears of experiencing the same loss again, unworthy of calling yourself the Black Queen. Now I think I judged you too harshly. Now I know that your pain was also my own. I wish I could make you see that.

I loved Meliora too, Alison. I loved her as I loved you, like a mother and a sister, and when she died, she took my heart with her, leaving nothing but a wound in the shape of her absence. I thought of a thousand different ways to move past my grief, to honor her memory and keep her mission and her ideals alive. I thought of what she would have wanted the Serpent's Hand to be, what drove her to sacrifice her own life and happiness. In the end, I chose to act like her, and I have never regretted it—even though it cost me you.

I can almost see you fuming with rage as you read this. You think I'm disrespecting everything we've done and sacrificed, that I've learned nothing from our tribulations, and that my struggle is nothing but selfishness and a quest for my own glory. But please, if some tiny part of you still remembers the Cristina who fought side by side with you, who held you up when the world crumbled, who comforted you in defeat, try to understand me. I couldn't stand idly by while my people suffered and no one answered their pleas. How could I call myself a child of Abya Yala if I allowed them to remain forgotten? How could I ever look them in the eye and tell them I did nothing because I must stick to the grander plan? I am part of them, of their joys and their sorrows; ignoring them would have been a betrayal so terrible that it could not be forgiven in a thousand years.

That's why I took the books. That's why I left without saying anything to you. You would have preferred us to talk it over, but only to tell me again that what I was about to do was a mistake, that I should stop before it was too late. There's no point in asking when you already know the answer, and I could not have you stand in my way.

Yeah, you're never getting that apology you want from me. I would do it again even if it meant getting turned into a Page as punishment, even if it meant you hating me even more than you do now.

Do you hate me, Alison? I cannot really tell. You did sell me off to Sin Nombre in exchange for the books I stole, but you also arranged for me to be rescued and joined me in fighting the Black Moon. I guess you're not yet so cold-hearted that you'd allow me to die such a gruesome death—thank you for that—but I also don't think you're really looking forward to us meeting again. I've been barred from entering the Library again, and you barely leave it anymore, so do be at ease; whether I live or die tomorrow, you will never have to see me again… unless you come looking for me.

There can be victory even in death. Meliora taught me that. If we win tomorrow and I die, I'll make sure you're the first to know it; this letter will find its way to you. If we win tomorrow and I live, then we might just get another chance to set things right; I won't wait for you, but if you come meet me, I won't turn you away—you're still my family, after all (and it'd be great to rub my victory in your face).

And if we lose tomorrow… well, there might not be a world to fight for anymore, so I guess it won't matter at all.

Your little sister, Cristina.



Addendum: On 20-██-202█, a creature resembling an anthropomorphic ant materialized within Site-███ and removed all of the recovered text fragments from their secure storage locker. Before vanishing, it uttered a single phrase to witnesses: "Return your books on time."

The trespassing creature has since been identified as a Page – entities native to the Wanderers' Library whose task is the organization and upkeep of books, as well as their recovery from morose patrons. The significance of this encounter has not gone unnoticed: Cristina Cisneros has violated Library rules by failing to return borrowed books, which means that she is barred from entering the Wanderers' Library. This deprives both her and Las Víboras of the safe haven afforded to other sects and factions of the Serpent's Hand, a disadvantage that may prove beneficial to Foundation efforts in capturing or neutralizing Cisneros and all persons affiliated with her.

Proposals for further action are under review.




Pilares

Of Ravens and Vipers

The Raven and the Hummingbird

Footnotes
1. Father Ignacio Pek was the sole person in the building at the time of the raid; he was detained, interrogated, placed under medical care and amnesticised once he confessed to having alerted Las Víboras of Foundation presence in the area, leading to their escape three hours prior to the raid. Field Operative Ibarra received a written reprimand for conducting an overly harsh interrogation of the octogenarian Father Pek, which resulted in bodily harm.
2. The documents burned by Bishop de Landa most likely contained historical accounts of the Maya civilization, traditional medicinal knowledge, and religious practices. Despite de Landa making fundamental contributions to the modern understanding of Maya civilization by closely documenting the language, writing system, lives and traditions of the pre-Columbian peoples of the Yucatán peninsula, thus pioneering ethnography in the Mayab region, the damage caused by his fanatical zeal is incalculable.

the-road-to-hell.raw_content:
The water is soft, lapping against the sand. It drags at it, throwing clumps of spray up and back again. The black of the sky shines down, and O5-3, in the cold light of his headlamps, stares at the edge of visibility, of all things seen and unseen.

He is sitting on a sand dune, waiting. He sips at his beer, his eyes clouding gradually as the evening stretches on, and on. He wonders what’s on the other side of the sea. He pictures a daytime scene - a beach hut, children building sandcastles, a pier stretching out into the waves.

He picks up a handful of sand and lets it trickle through his fingers. He sighs, and then starts as a shadow peers over him.

“It’s time,” says the Administrator.

O5-3 creaks to his feet, willing his limbs to move. He takes a final look back across the water. Where does his sight end? How far across can he see? He isn’t sure. The sea and the sky blend together. If a man drowned out there, nobody would witness his death, would ever be able to picture the desperation as he clung to life, flinging himself up, up, out of the waves until he was sucked down beneath.

He thinks about that, about moments erased from time. But this isn’t the hour for that. The Administrator is waiting besides the car, and O5-3 trudges towards him, slouching forward to his doom.

The car is cold, and O5-3 feels himself shivering. He turns on the radio, low. Shostakovich twists from the speakers, pricking the goosebumps on his arms still higher.

The Administrator is staring out of the window, looking through the trees. The forest is dense here, whispering needles through the wind. O5-3 just stares straight ahead, watching as the road cuts through two emerging hillocks, flashing light dancing between them.

“You said he lives in Rostwick?”

The Administrator blinks, turning at the question. “Yes.” He turns away again, his chin on his hand.

O5-3 doesn’t remember the last time he had a full night’s sleep. The hours just tick by him, scratching at his mind, urging him onwards. When he was still Yoshihide, he was careful to be well-rested. His work came first, and he had to ensure that his duty was done properly. The Work was bigger than he was, and he couldn’t let it down with his own poor choices.

But now, he has a broader view of the matter. The Work flows from him and through him. Burning his way through the night, working to the point of exhaustion, simply alters his state of consciousness. As long as his intent is pure, it continues – the ideas, the methods, are simply different.

The Administrator does not understand that, of course. He watches as the other man sighs, sitting back in his seat. “Did I ever tell you what my father thought of hell?”

He, O5-3, does not turn. “He thought hell was dying. The process of dying.”

“Yes, he did. Well-remembered. My mother disagreed, of course. She thought hell was the living, waking world. She once painted a mural on our kitchen wall. It was a strange thing, one I held a great deal of affection for.”

The wonderful thing about driving is that O5-3 can concentrate on that, instead of this. He has lost so much, shed so much, that it's a wonder the Administrator’s words still have the effect they do. Maybe it's the pile of bodies, or Yuzuki’s face as she was dragged away, but each one feels like a cold, sharp nothing.

“She wasn’t a well woman, you see. Nervous spells, paranoid delusions. Looking at that mural, I felt I understood her better. It made her outbursts make sense.”

A memory flies by him. “I thought that your mother died before you knew her.”

The grin, like a flash, a blinding streak on his periphery. “Very good! Top marks today, O5-3. Yes, you’re right. I never really knew her, but I could see the effect she had on my family. Maybe I wanted to understand that, to reach through to her. Maybe I could heal the family.”

“And did you?”

It slips out, and he curses himself. But the Administrator doesn’t seem angry. He just turns those eyes, those dark, shaded glasses, onto him.

“Don’t you think you should be watching the road?”

They continue on, in silence, watching as the moon falls down across the sky, spreading black ink among the stars.

The cabin is sitting in the woods, waiting for them. A single light shines from behind glass as the pair of them trudge towards the door. The ground is wet, a thick mud that squelches up to their ankles. Their flashlights scrabble for the path, but they can’t find it.

The cabin is a small log affair. It’s not well-maintained; the timbers look like they’re starting to rot. O5-3 raps on the door, attentive, alert. An owl hoots dimly, far in the distance, as the reeds wave in the gloom.

A chair scrapes inside. There are footsteps; the sound of a metal cane, tapping on the floor. The Administrator starts to whistle, staring up at the moon.

The door opens to a middle-aged man, in his early 40s. He is rake-thin, his face bristling with a light, wiry stubble. He looks at them both, blinking against the cold, and then sighs. “Yes, of course. Come in, then.”

O5-3 shares a look with the Administrator, and they step into a warm, cramped space. A thin wire bed dominates the far wall, and a wooden desk and table stand in front of them. Papers and a pen are strewn across the desk.

The stranger sits down, looks them up and down, and gestures to the bed. The pair of them sit on it, side-by-side, awkwardly tucking their knees in. O5-3 feels like a child again, like an absurdity. A warm bulb hums gently above them; a fly bounces off it, whining.

The stranger takes out a box of cigarettes. They both decline, so he shrugs and lights himself up, still staring at them. “Thought you’d never find me, if I’m honest.”

“You were quite… difficult to track down, I must say.” O5-3 glances over; the Administrator speaks carefully, with intent, as he scans the stranger’s face. “But I knew I’d see you again. I never forget.”

The stranger smiles, puffing smoke into the air. “And now you want to lock me up, is that right?”

“No.” O5-3 shifts, leaning forward. The man doesn’t look at him. “Or, perhaps. We have – there’s a job we want you to do. If you do it for us, we’ll leave you alone.”

The Administrator is staring upwards, and says nothing. O5-3 coughs and continues. “There’s an anomaly. A dangerous one. One that has plagued us for years, and which has taken countless lives. You could be a great help, not only to us, but to -”

The stranger snorts. “He’s got you on SCP-001, has he?”

O5-3 pauses. He looks at the Administrator, who is still looking up, ignoring him. “I didn’t realise you’d been briefed.”

“I haven’t. I just remember the last one. You know this isn’t the first anomaly to take that slot, right?”

O5-3 turns back, sharply. “It isn’t”?

The Administrator nudges him, and points upwards. O5-3 looks up, and gasps.

The smoke from the cigarette is coating the ceiling, billowing around its edges. A picture is forming, through the haze and the gloom; a smoke-filled dragon, its wings flapping towards an open sky, there and not there all at once.

“That was mine, you see. That’s what he wanted me to deal with. He had another fellow, too, just like you. O5-9, I think it was. Whatever happened to him?”

“My colleague is fine,” he says, stiffly. He’s still staring up at the image, watching it twist into and out of itself.

The stranger glances at him, smiling. “Pretty, isn’t it? The trick was to send it back to its own non-reality. It was a lie, and to a lie it returned.”

He sticks out a gangly hand. O5-3 takes it, gingerly. The stranger tilts his head. “Chōkōdō Shujin, weaver of miracles.”

He doesn't know what we're going to do to him, he thinks, as clear as day inside his mind.

“Type-Q reality bender,” murmurs the Administrator. O5-3 watches as his boss stands up, still staring at the ceiling, admiring the waveforms.

“Call me what you like, old man. It’s all the same to me.” Shujin curls up in his chair, holding the cigarette away from him. His eyes are beetle-black, fixated on O5-3’s gaunt, aging face. The overseer instinctively reaches up to the back of his head, willing his dead hair to return.

The Administrator snaps back to the world. “It’s a simple offer, Shujin. Return with us now, help us out, and I’ll leave you alone. For good, this time. Stay, and we’ll send a team after you.”

“Type-Qs are in short supply”, explains O5-3. “I’ve determined it’s our best bet. We need to undermine the anomaly’s -”

“- moral sense, yes. I remember. It was the same, back in the day. This isn’t about physics, it’s about narrative, about the lessons taught and learnt. Old E’in, his problem was the lies he told, and he drew the foolish to him. It was an easy one. Yours, though…”

“The selfish.” O5-3 feels a little sting of pride, remembering the snapping thread and the gasping crowd. “Those who only think of themselves, their own petty concerns. It’s a vague criteria, and it’s cut through – well, through hundreds, now.”

The eyes don’t move. There’s a warmth to them, a crackling fire behind them, pinning him to the wall. “Fascinating. No wonder you’re scared.”

Shujin stands up, and starts putting a handful of scattered items – papers, a book, a toothbrush – into a canvas bag, haphazardly and randomly. O5-3 blinks, and rouses himself. “So you’ll come with us?”

“Of course he will.” The Administrator heads to the door, opening it wide. The cold air rushes in; the lightbulb flickers. “Come on. We don’t have all night.”

Shujin looks at him, and shrugs. He shoulders his bag, and the three of them step out into the dark.

Site-01 isn’t too far away. O5-3 wondered about that, before, about why a reality bender would hide under the noses of the Foundation’s highest offices. But now he feels that he knows. There’s a quiet confidence in Shujin’s tone, his manner of speech, the way he moves through space. He knew they’d come for him, eventually; what was the point in delaying the inevitable?

The pitch tar of evening still surrounds them, an evening that stretches into the small hours, retaining the same sense of time, of anticipation. The Administrator has called ahead, making sure the arrangements are made. They’ve been planning this for months, ever since O5-3 first hit on the idea. He feels himself there again, one late night in his office, watching the ceiling refracted through the ochre tint of whisky, the lines spiralling out of his control.

The Administrator is sleeping now, dozing off in the back seat. Shujin stares straight ahead of him, tapping in time to the music from the radio – Schoenberg, late Schoenberg, screeching out dissonances into the flashes of cats-eye light on the road. O5-3 clears his throat.

“Was he always like – well, like this?”

Shujin smirks. “The Administrator? Oh, always. A cold, predatory lizard, that one. I’m surprised he came out here with you. You’d think he’d have better things to do.”

O5-3 nods. “Every time I’m on the edge of something, about to finish something – there he is, hovering at my elbow, reminding me of this. SCP-001. He wants it to be me that does it, and I don’t know why.”

“Maybe he thinks you’re well-suited for the job.”

He snorts. “At first, sure. I caught quite the lucky break, to start with. Made a huge breakthrough, got everyone’s attention. Since then, though… I don’t know. Other projects, other containments, I can get done, big things, grand things. Not this, though. It’s always eluded me. Everything I try, just… fails.”

Shujin nods. “SCP-001 is a tough one. Always was, for all of us.”

“Us?”

But Shujin doesn’t answer. The trees rear up, flashing beside his face, leering through the window. They lapse into silence for a while, before the strange man speaks again.

“Do you know how many there have been?”

O5-3 frowns. “How many what?

“Iterations. Of 001.”

There’s a snore, a jerking noise, from the Administrator behind him. O5-3 turns the wheel, concentrating for a moment on a curve, trying to suppress his rising panic.

“The number of events it’s caused is - “

“No, not that. I mean how many bodies there have been.”

He knew he wasn’t the first. He knew - he presumed, rather – that the Administrator had plucked others from obscurity, other lost souls like himself. But the question was terrifying. How many had there been? Did 001 mean anything? Was it just a name for – for something else? A test, a coming of age?”

“You don’t know, right?” Shujin’s face, smiling, peers up at him. “Yeah, they don’t, usually. He’s got something on you, right? Something you want?

He feels guilty. He has barely thought of her this whole time. “My daughter.”

Shujin nods. “And so you’ve done so much, sacrificed so much, to manoeuvre yourself here? To finally be in a position to help her, free her?”

When he became an O5, donning the blackened suit, stepping into that charcoal room, he thought he’d do it right away. Requisition her, an anomaly required for testing, set her up away from them all. Under his protection. Maybe he wouldn’t be able to see her, maybe he’d have to stay away, but she’d be free -

But there had been that little nagging voice, sitting in that room, whispering to him. Sure, you might get her out, for a day, a month – but sooner or later, they’d know what you’d done. They’d come for her. Best to wait. You’re not immune, even here. Best to build up your position, make sure you’re safe, first. Prove yourself, to them. To him.

The Administrator had sat, at the end of the table, staring into him, powering his mind and energy through those dark glasses. It was another refraction, but every beam of light and shade had bounced back on a central point, an icicle stabbing into his brain, scattering it and making it his own.

In the present, he shakes himself. “Yes.” He feels the dampness growing around the corners of his eyes.

Shujin nods, and pats his arm. “I know. I’ve seen it all before. And before that, too.”

There is one more great, echoing silence, as Yoshihide wipes away his fright, his pain. The trees are taller, here, slashing themselves across the windows, bleeding the same dark and the same needles and the same pine freshness that they always do, binding and blinding back into himself, as a pit opens up beneath. He knows what’s down there. He knows what part of his soul is dwelling there.

He asks, “And what happened to the others? Did they – were they free, when it was done?”

But Shujin doesn’t answer. Yoshihide, O5-3, hears nothing more from him. He looks ahead, and continues on, through the road as it curves and strains, hacking its way through the night. It’s a road that always seems like it’ll bend back on itself, take you to where you were before, but it never does.

And behind him, his slitted eyes halfway open, the Administrator's gaze bores into the back of his skull.

The chamber was an office, a long time ago. O5-3 has learnt not to think too hard about that. He asked the Administrator, once, who SCP-001 had been. He had not received an answer.

A complex of rooms has been built around it. The observation deck looks down from above, towering from one side. Like it has clipped outside the world and is examining a scene from a film, but from the wrong angle. The actors – the cocoon, the threads, their newfound friend – will be playing out the little drama without seeing their faces, so high up, staring down below.

Standing up here, his hands on the rails, O5-3 feels a rare, surging power. The ceiling has been replaced with glass; it looks so fragile, the winding silk pressed up against it.

Inside it, behind the creeping strands that tie themselves, over and over, is a corpse. It's an old corpse, now; it cannot be seen, its stench is contained, but it must still be there. Binding and rebinding himself over and over, constantly repeating the same actions, the same phrase…

It's not enough to read about it. He watches it stick, shift, move, its pale and sickly limbs reorganising themselves endlessly, grasping at walls that have no purchase.

In the last few years, he has spent so much time here, in this spot. It’s like an old friend, a comforting wound. Below him lies an imperfection, an affront to the Work, an insoluble problem. He has spent so many hours on it, thinking up new ways to assault the problem. Black chains of cursed iron. The shredded horns of a teetering owl, hooting in anguish and pain as its powdered pride was thrown, urged, pumped into the threads. And nothing happened, and each time, he knew with crystal certainty that it would never work. It would never be contained.

Then the idea came to him. It had seemed inevitable. The way the anomaly worked, tugging on people’s fingers, slipping into their blood and bone. This was a drama, a grand melodrama, played out again and again. Like Passion Week, or Ashura, or Māgha Pūjā; the same single moment in the past, playing out over and over again, making it real once more while the people flock and preen around.

And now he’s here. The kindling has been stacked below. He has journeyed forth, seen the world, and now he’s returned, standing here at the precipice, the gates at the end of the road.

The door behind him opens, and the Administrator walks in. O5-3 nods at him; he almost smiles. Finally, today, he wins. Finally, today, it will be complete -

And Shujin walks in behind him.

O5-3 frowns, confused. “But you’re not meant to be here. You’re meant to be in the chamber.”

The Administrator smiles, a smile that widens, and widens, and widens like the holy, blessed moon, white teeth arrayed like tombstones. The first day he came into his office, he had smiled like that.

“There’s been a bit of a change of plan. You see, Yoshihide, I wasn’t entirely honest about what Shujin is doing here.”

Shujin himself can’t meet his eye. He simply walks over to the rail, and looks down. O5-3 feels the jaws of a trap around him, but he can’t tell where, from what. His mind pushes out, confused, unclear.

“He’s not a Type-Q, in fact. His skills are… something else. No, as far as I can tell, there’s only one Type-Q in the country right now. Only one capable of bending truth and lies apart.”

He turns, and looks down. He frowns, again, but more slightly.

“But, sir, there must have been a mistake. That’s Yuzuki down there.”

The Administrator places a hand on his shoulder. “Yes. Precisely.”

A Type-Q is a blasphemy. That’s how he has started to think of it. It’s something that shouldn’t exist, something that he doesn’t want to exist. They may appear to change an object’s shape, its size, perform miracles of transformation and transmutation, but in point of fact, they reach into other worlds, other possible branching times. They take what could have been, and make it not a lie, but a truth.

So say you’re sitting in a restaurant, God knows how long ago, and laughing with your daughter. Say she takes a fork, and presses it, and moulds its shape into something else. Like a spoon. All she’s really doing is looking back at another world – a world where her mother might be alive, her father warm and present – and takes something from that place, barely realising it. A fork becomes a spoon. A dead hope becomes alive.

Yoshihide screams. He rushes across the room, heading for the microphone – why is it so distant, why is it where it can’t be reached? – but the Administrator’s hand, claw-like, grips him in place, roots him to the floor.

“Let me go, let me go, you bastard, it’s her, she’s not safe, she’s -”

The Administrator drags him, with impossible strength, back to the rail. He takes a hand and forces it on Yoshihide’s head, making him look down. There, amidst the threads and silk, there is Yuzuki. She’s older, thinner – she’s lost too much weight, he thinks, between the throbbing screams – petrified, her back against the wall -

“They’ll do nothing without an order. We didn’t tell anyone, remember? We didn’t tell anyone what we were going to do.”

The cocoon moves. It shifts, in anticipation. It’s not harmful to the touch; it consumes slowly, inexorably, its victims picked and plucked from day to day, elsewhere in time and space. The body’s dead hand picks according to its own designs, shifting from victim to victim. The order hasn’t been given. He just won’t give the order, he won’t -

“And I’ll let you go, Yoshihide, as soon as you want me to. But – do you want me to?”

He yells, spitting in his face, “YES! Let me go, let me go now, I have to get to her -”

“But you don’t.”

Shujin’s voice is quiet, resigned. He’s holding a notepad, his pen poised above it, leaning over the rail. A lit cigarette wafts behind his ear. “I’ve seen you. I’ve noted you, Yoshihide, recorded you. Just like I did the others. You know what you want.”

The black thread reaches up inside his head, yearning, stretching, breaking. The Administrator’s hand feels almost warm, now – almost comforting. He leans forward, and whispers in Yoshihide’s ear -

“There are no other Type-Qs we have access to.”

And O5-3 stops struggling. He stops moving. He just looks down, down, into the pit of Yuzuki’s haunted face.

He knows what will happen now. He sees the lines react, intersect, converge. He sees the point around which it all turns, has always turned. The writhing bodies, slathering to the forest floor. The axe, rebounding again and again along the wire.

He claws, he wails, he pleads with himself - but at last the calm descends. He knows he always wanted this. He wanted, the little child bouncing on a mine cart, to slice the thread entire, to give himself over to hell. He wanted the box, and only the box, forever.

“It’s the work, Yoshihide,” whispers the Administrator. “I told you, long, long ago. No room for discrimination. We are the keepers of the box.”

So many years, so much spilt time, to contain SCP-001. To burn the cocoon from the inside. He stares down at Yuzuki’s face, its mournful, oval shape, its black O where her mouth should be. She looks up, and for a second, their eyes meet. She is incredulous, she is pleading, she is broken on the wire. She cannot understand what she sees.

He places a hand on the glass, the tears washing down his cheeks. Then he looks away, into the dark walls around, the winding chimney of a tower that breathes and breaks around him.

He wanted to contain the world. He wanted perfection. And now he’s here, sitting by the side of the sea, staring into black.

The Administrator releases him. O5-3 straightens his suit, adjusts his tie, and walks to the microphone. He grips it, hard, and speaks clear and straight into it.

“Administer Q-Alpha.”

And he forces himself to watch, as her blood slams into the wall, as it starts to shift planes and truth and lies, altering the molecules and atoms, confusing the body that screeches and retches against himself. He watches as her form twists, and shatters, and drowns, and burns, all her deaths merging and collecting into one. He sees her possibilities, her lives and unlives, warping into the silk, infusing it, merging into the fine mesh of string and paper that scatters all around, forever.

“Now you know,” says the Administrator. He is weeping, tears of unbridled joy. His hand is gripping his shoulder; he is supporting himself on O5-3's weight. “Now you see hell, Yoshihide. Now you see it as an ending, as it truly is. No more suffering, for her, right? In this torture, she doesn’t have to think. That burden is lifted. And containment, perfection, for us. We’ve done it. We’ve ended it. No more.”

He doesn’t know what he’s talking about. It’s not relevant, it’s something else, some mission or journey of its own. He has eyes only for the stars below, ripping into sky and night, twisting on a fulcrum axis until they’ve worn themselves out, blown like whining bulbs, a lid on the beasts at last. A little brass monkey rears up from the noise, moaning, tearing him to shreds.

And then there’s another day.

O5-3 returns to his office. He’s arranged it in the same way as it was when the Administrator first entered it, back at his old site. The walls and furniture are different, yet the same. Just the way he likes it.

He sits down at his desk, and performs eight hours of consistent, unspectacular work. Yuzuki is there, voiceless, screaming at him, but he ignores her. There are procedures and principles to fix, maintain, induce.

Outside, it grows dark, clouds covering the sun. There was no body, but a grave marker has been placed out there anyway. As he returns from lunch, O5-3 glances at it, on the way back to the desk. He hears her wail, but shrugs, wiping his mouth. An egg and cress sandwich.

He sits on his chair, at the desk, reading his papers. A wall of bodies cascades onto him, moaning, a hunter with a knife leering out at him. He shakes them off himself, and continues, sorting the new procedures for an obscure anomaly placed under his jurisdiction. He books tickets for a flight to Brussels, as he hurtles down a slope and into an avenue of swords, over and over again, his flesh and memory sliced and rent apart. His expression does not change as they pierce his flesh and remould his image.

The grave is there, but he has eyes only for the door. He imagines the moment the Administrator will enter again. He blinks, and it is years ago, and a secretary - he hasn’t learned their names yet - pokes his head into the office.

"A visitor for you, Director," he said.

Yoshihide sits up straight in his chair. This wouldn't be his first encounter with an O5 liaison, and he knows enough to never let your guard down around these people. Liaisons are vipers, persons who had abandoned all -

Shujin walks through the door, closing it behind him.

O5-3 stares. He blinks, hard, and motions his guest to sit. Shujin does, shuffling over, lighting a new cigarette. His eyes burn and crackle, a smile playing around his mouth.

“Is something funny?”, he, O5-3, asks.

“No. I’m sorry. I get nervous, quite often. I never like having to do this. I’m sorry we deceived you.”

The smile is a sad one, he concedes. He straightens up. “I’m not bothered. The work was done well. It was a neat containment.”

The smile doesn’t go away. “I’m sorry, all the same. I know it doesn’t seem like it now, but – well, she was your daughter. That matters for something.”

Last night, he was reviewing some old personnel files. He stumbled across a ghost file, one that someone hadn’t deleted properly. The old O5-3’s file. His blood type, it seems, had been B.

“What were you there for? What was the point of fetching you from your cabin?”

Shujin gets up, and walks to the window. Why is his cigarette not setting off the smoke alarm? He shrugs to himself – the man is a reality bender, of some kind. Who knows what their powers entail? He doesn’t, any more.

“I was there to record, to act as a witness. A scribe, if you like. I keep the memory, you see. I keep the memory of your change.”

He frowns. “What change?”

Shujin shoots him a look. “You didn’t feel it? I’m surprised. It happens to you all, in the end. Something breaks in you, and you die. Suicide, martyrdom, a desperate bid for revenge. He thinks he’s stopped it, now, but…”

A nightingale calls to its mate, outside. Yuzuki slashes his face with a carving knife. He wipes away the blood, and turns back to Shujin, listening to the thin man as his voice turns to a whisper.

“When it’s happened, you see – when you become an O5, really become one… your death is no longer a normal death. It’s something else. And I record it, you see. In here” - he taps his head – “and on the page. He thinks he can control the narrative, make it his own. Rashōmon, he calls it. Each life stealing from the last, until you reach hell, you reach an ending.”

He blinks, hard. His hand starts to shake.

“But that’s never how it goes, Yoshihide. He doesn’t realise that, as I do. I can write on the face of time, but the words will fade and die, all the same. The Administrator is a fool. He doesn’t know hell at all.”

Shujin flicks the cigarette away, heads to the door, and turns back, his hand gripping the handle.

“He couldn’t if he tried.”

He leaves. Yuzuki dies again, frail, in his arms. He weeps for her. She dies again, drowning in the swamp. He reaches for her arms, and fails.

Then she sits inside a carriage, in a noblewoman’s death, as an Emperor sneers, willing it on, and he watches, staring, unmoving, as she is choked into a blackened ash.

All he is is contained within four walls. The office is the only reality left to him, now. Beyond those doors are mirrors beyond mirrors, byzantine halls leading back to him, his own self divided along the road.

He pats his pockets, but remembers that he already sent the note. He tightens the noose. He makes sure the chair is firm. It has to be firm. It has to fall away just right, for this to work. Yuzuki nods at him, encouragingly, her eyes black orbs lost in the mists beyond.

He pauses, one hand on the chair. He looks across at her grave; distant, fragile, a stone too far removed to make out the shape of. He stands on the chair for a better look.

He sees trees beneath clouds, behind the marker. He sees her, opposite him, laughing at his jokes over dinner, swapping stories, each to each. He sees his wife, her figure shaded in the trees, staring up at him.

Once, when Yuzuki was very small -

“What are you doing?”

He turns to the door. The Administrator stands there. His face is apoplectic. He is terrified, horrified, furious beyond measure. He steps forward, and Yoshihide puts his face into the noose.

“No. No. You can’t do this to me. You’re not doing this to me. Not again, not now!”

The Adminstrator lurches forward, and Yoshihide lifts one foot. The Administrator pauses, sweating, balling his hands into impotent fists. His glasses slip, crashing to the black and marble floor.

“I made you.”

Yoshihide stares back, listening. He starts to feel himself in his own throat, bubbling through.

“I made you. I made you like I made the others. You are not exceptional, or an exception, Yoshihide. You are rote. I took you because your mind was useful to me. Containment as art, as the perfect art! Ridiculous, and yet it was there. I could use you as a lid on the chaos.”

The wire tightens, as Yoshihide pauses, fascinated.

“The work isn’t some paltry fantasy. It’s not a game.” His boss’s breathing was slow, laboured, heavy. “It’s the only control we have. Come – come down. We can talk about this. My God, the – the arrogance of you, the presumption -”

“What is hell, sir?”

The Administrator blinks. “What?”

“What is hell, sir? Where are its contours? Your father thought it was dying, but dying implies an ending. You said it was an ending. You don’t know anything, do you? You just try to impose yourselves, again and again, on us, me, all the rest, guessing your little games on your petty little stage.”

The chair teeters. His nemesis draws in his breath. The corpses wait, ready, stretched almost to the point of bursting.

“I’ll tell you what hell is, sir. Hell is for the living. Hell is ever-changing, ever-adapting, an inferno of our lives. Hell does not stop. Here. Let me show you.”

And O5-3 kicks the chair over, watching the Administrator recoil, flailing, to the floor, sprawling as she had sprawled. O5-3 kicks, and silently yelps, scrabbling at his own throat, and then expires, swinging from side to side like a pendulum -

But Yoshihide is exalted. He is in the walls, he is in the air, he creeps up and about and within, red and black and gold. His fire ignites, spreading, rushing in a blinding, screaming pain. He looks up, spreading his arms, burning, burning, burning.

Above him is Yuzuki’s face, pale and shining, a thing in mourning. She reaches down as he reaches up, feeling the fire lick his soul, catch it, bind him down and down. He extends a hand, and feels a taut and snapping thread. Then she is gone, gone forever, extinguished.

The Administrator flees, and Yoshihide is all alone, reaching out, struggling for a forever lost to him.

It drags at it, throwing clumps of spray up and back again. The black of the sky shines down, and O5-3, in the cold light of his headlamps, stares at the edge of visibility, of all things seen and unseen. He is sitting on a sand dune, waiting. He sips at his beer, his eyes clouding gradually as the evening stretches on, and on. He wonders what’s on the other side of the sea. He pictures a daytime scene - a beach hut, children building sandcastles, a pier stretching out into the waves. He picks up a handful of sand and lets it trickle through his fingers. He sighs, and then starts as a shadow peers over him. “It’s time,” says the Administrator. O5-3 creaks to his feet, willing his limbs to move. He takes a final look back across the water. Where does his sight end? How far across can he see? He isn’t sure. The sea and the sky blend together. If a man drowned out there, nobody would witness his death, would ever be able to picture the desperation as he clung to life, flinging himself up, up, out of the waves until he was sucked down beneath. He thinks about that, about moments erased from time. But this isn’t the hour for that. The Administrator is waiting besides the car, and O5-3 trudges towards him, slouching forward to his doom. ----- The car is cold, and O5-3 feels himself shivering. He turns on the radio, low. Shostakovich twists from the speakers, pricking the goosebumps on his arms still higher. The Administrator is staring out of the window, looking through the trees. The forest is dense here, whispering needles through the wind. A single light shines from behind glass as the pair of them trudge towards the door. The ground is wet, a thick mud that squelches up to their ankles. O5-3 wondered about that, before, about why a reality bender would hide under the noses of the Foundation’s highest offices. But now he feels that he knows. There’s a quiet confidence in Shujin’s tone, his manner of speech, the way he moves through space. He knew they’d come for him, eventually; what was the point in delaying the inevitable? The Administrator had sat, at the end of the table, staring into him, powering his mind and energy through those dark glasses. The trees are taller, here, slashing themselves across the windows, bleeding the same dark and the same needles and the same pine freshness that they always do, binding and blinding back into himself, as a pit opens up beneath. It’s a road that always seems like it’ll bend back on itself, take you to where you were before, but it never does. And behind him, his slitted eyes halfway open, the Administrator's gaze bores into the back of his skull. ----- The chamber was an office, a long time ago. O5-3 has learnt not to think too hard about that. He asked the Administrator, once, who SCP-001 had been. He had not received an answer. A complex of rooms has been built around it. The observation deck looks down from above, towering from one side. Like it has clipped outside the world and is examining a scene from a film, but from the wrong angle. The actors – the cocoon, the threads, their newfound friend – will be playing out the little drama without seeing their faces, so high up, staring down below. He watches it stick, shift, move, its pale and sickly limbs reorganising themselves endlessly, grasping at walls that have no purchase. The way the anomaly worked, tugging on people’s fingers, slipping into their blood and bone. This was a drama, a grand melodrama, played out again and again. Like Passion Week, or Ashura, or Māgha Pūjā; the same single moment in the past, playing out over and over again, making it real once more while the people flock and preen around. And now he’s here. The kindling has been stacked below. He has journeyed forth, seen the world, and now he’s returned, standing here at the precipice, the gates at the end of the road. The door behind him opens, and the Administrator walks in. O5-3 nods at him; he almost smiles. Finally, today, he wins. Finally, today, it will be complete - And Shujin walks in behind him. You’re meant to be in the chamber.” The Administrator smiles, a smile that widens, and widens, and widens like the holy, blessed moon, white teeth arrayed like tombstones. You see, Yoshihide, I wasn’t entirely honest about what Shujin is doing here.” Shujin himself can’t meet his eye. He simply walks over to the rail, and looks down. O5-3 feels the jaws of a trap around him, but he can’t tell where, from what. His mind pushes out, confused, unclear. “He’s not a Type-Q, in fact. His skills are… something else. He frowns, again, but more slightly. “But, sir, there must have been a mistake. That’s Yuzuki down there.” The Administrator places a hand on his shoulder. “Yes. Precisely.” ----- A Type-Q is a blasphemy. That’s how he has started to think of it. It’s something that shouldn’t exist, something that he doesn’t want to exist. They may appear to change an object’s shape, its size, perform miracles of transformation and transmutation, but in point of fact, they reach into other worlds, other possible branching times. They take what could have been, and make it not a lie, but a truth. So say you’re sitting in a restaurant, God knows how long ago, and laughing with your daughter. Say she takes a fork, and presses it, and moulds its shape into something else. Like a spoon. All she’s really doing is looking back at another world – a world where her mother might be alive, her father warm and present – and takes something from that place, barely realising it. A fork becomes a spoon. A dead hope becomes alive. Yoshihide screams. He takes a hand and forces it on Yoshihide’s head, making him look down. There, amidst the threads and silk, there is Yuzuki. We didn’t tell anyone, remember? We didn’t tell anyone what we were going to do.” The cocoon moves. It shifts, in anticipation. It’s not harmful to the touch; it consumes slowly, inexorably, its victims picked and plucked from day to day, elsewhere in time and space. The body’s dead hand picks according to its own designs, shifting from victim to victim. //The order hasn’t been given. He just won’t give the order, he won’t -// “And I’ll let you go, Yoshihide, as soon as you want me to. But – do you want me to?” He yells, spitting in his face, “YES! Let me go, let me go //now//, I have to get to her -” “But you don’t.” Shujin’s voice is quiet, resigned. He’s holding a notepad, his pen poised above it, leaning over the rail. He sees the point around which it all turns, has always turned. The writhing bodies, slathering to the forest floor. The axe, rebounding again and again along the wire. He claws, he wails, he pleads with himself - but at last the calm descends. He knows he always wanted this. He wanted, the little child bouncing on a mine cart, to slice the thread entire, to give himself over to hell. He stares down at Yuzuki’s face, its mournful, oval shape, its black O where her mouth should be. She looks up, and for a second, their eyes meet. He is weeping, tears of unbridled joy. His hand is gripping  his shoulder; he is supporting himself on O5-3's weight. “Now you see hell, Yoshihide. Now you see it as an ending, as it truly is. A little brass monkey rears up from the noise, moaning, tearing him to shreds. ----- And then there’s another day. O5-3 returns to his office. He’s arranged it in the same way as it was when the Administrator first entered it, back at his old site. The walls and furniture are different, yet the same. Just the way he likes it. Liaisons are vipers, persons who had abandoned all - Shujin walks through the door, closing it behind him. O5-3 stares. He blinks, hard, and motions his guest to sit. Shujin does, shuffling over, lighting a new cigarette. His eyes burn and crackle, a smile playing around his mouth. “Is something funny?”, he, O5-3, asks. “No. I’m sorry. I get nervous, quite often.
