RAISA NOTICE: The following SCP database file has just been updated because of a recent related incident, new information highlighted in blue. Presented information may be subject to further changes in the near future.

Main file abridged.

SCP-1213.

Item #: SCP-1213

Object Class: Safe

Description: SCP-1213 is a wooden and steel catapult, medieval in design. SCP-1213 is capable of autonomous locomotion on its four wooden wheels and of operating its firing mechanism by an unknown method.

Should SCP-1213 encounter a suitable subject, SCP-1213 will transport the subject into the basket on its firing arm by unknown means. SCP-1213 will then launch the subject at the nearest flat vertical surface. After a launching it will remain stationary, emitting a sound similar to the contented purring produced by felines while it resets its firing arm. SCP-1213 favors infant to prepubescent mammalian subjects that weigh between 15 and 50 kilograms.

SCP-1213 was found in █████, a farming town in England, after several unexplainable cases of dead children and small animals that were reported as having been "hurled into walls at high velocity". A search of the town found SCP-1213 in the bushes of a school playground. Further investigation of the town led to the discovery of an improvised laboratory in an abandoned farmhouse. Much of the laboratory was destroyed by an explosion, presumably caused by the large defunct device that was the focus of the laboratory. The device was the experimental work of Dr. ████████, who could not be located.

Addendum: On the night of 16/12/2025 a severe extradimensional and spatio-temporal disruption occured centered on the ruins of the abandoned farmhouse in the town of █████, the building was the site of SCP-1213's creation over 10 years prior. The civillian population of the town has been successfully evacuated under the pretense of newfound geological instability.

Research and containment efforts are ongoing under supervision of the Emergent Threat Tactical Response Authority (ETTRA).

The town of █████, England, United Kingdom

16th December, 2025

The early morning sun coated the English coastline in pink and orange hues, shining through the rooftops and windows of small, cutesy buildings. The town — humble, yes, but once lively — was now more than desolate, for it met with an unimaginable fate. A destroyed farmhouse on the outskirts now standing tall and overlooking the town with a sinister presence, twisted beyond recognition into a hotchpotch of its previous parts, as if dozens and dozens of itself were crushed together into one barely coherent mess by some unthinkable force.

The sight of an old, dilapidated building, one abandoned by everything and everyone, was not a pleasant one for sure, but now it was something different, something much more foul. What was once a simple ruined farmhouse gave birth to an imposing fortress of evil and wickedness, incomparable to even the worst nightmares of the town's gone populace.

If the Specter were to have just one sense, if everything was stolen from his face aside from one thing, he'd be left with his nose. His nose is all he needs to know the smell of villainy, he was never wrong.

This place reeked like none other.

However, he still had all of his face left intact to perceive wretchedness in all of its perverted glory. Staring down at the fortress with revenge in his eyes and wind fluttering his cape, SCP-4494 pondered.

"Alright, that's everyone evacuated. You learned something from just standing like this?"

The Specter turned to see Doctor Dan of the SCP Foundation's Emergent Threat Tactical Response Authority behind him. While they didn't agree on everything, their limited cooperation was for the best of both of them, and the worst of the forces of evil.

"Justice learns all what it needs from but a single glimpse!" With this declared the Specter struck a dramatic pose, and continued on. "A staredown is an enforcement of its will to fight for what's right, doctor."

"Figures. Just so you know, this place is not random." Dan said, handing over a piece of paper to SCP-4494. "Around a decade ago the Foundation recovered an anomaly here, SCP-1213. Nothing all that special, from what I know that project's been sitting untouched for like six years, with just one minor development a year ago. Around this time, interestingly enough. Probably a coincidence."

Skimming over the abridged SCP-1213 file, the Specter locked eyes with Doctor Dan. "So you're admitting to carelessness? That's why we're here?" He handed the paper back with a slightly mocking motion, at the same time glancing over the Foundation's research teams swarming around them.

"Not really. Look, this all happened just over 4 hours ago, and we've been here for 3 already. There are procedures in place for active monitoring of anomalous recovery sites, specifically for this very occasion. If anything, we're too careful, as we should be. Wouldn't you agree?"

"I would, my sincere apologies."

"Sure. Judging by your staring contest against a building, I suppose you have a plan."

"Delivering justice is a plan in and of itself, the steps do not matter if you have convictions! It's evil that gets caught up in schemes and plots. Blinded by arrogance, it wouldn't know what to do at the tiniest inconvenience!"

With a swift motion SCP-4494 turned away, again facing the mind-breaking collage of walls, and doors, and wooden support beams all in rainbow colors, and walked right into the mouth of the beast, disappearing. The Specter's elongated cape fluttered in anticipation of his triumphant return, before vanishing just as him, in a flash of light.

Dan had no idea if the Specter's last words were supposed to be a dig at him or not. Either way he didn't really care, and he had no time for that, he saw a scientist walk up to him, and had to prepare for news.

"Doctor Dan, sir. The narrative assessment is complete."

As soon as SCP-4494 showed up on the coast, he asked for one. This wasn't really a standard, but he sometimes lets his gut feeling take hold.

"So?"

"A lot of narrative structures in place here seem to be consistent with tropes associated with '1950s one-off comic book supervillains'. I'm personally not really an expert on the topic."

"Well, then compared to you I very much am." Doctor Dan said with a slight grin appearing on his face. "This could get interesting."

The Specter should've expected that the inside of the den of darkness would be even more treacherous than its outside would suggest. An impossible structure sure does have an impossible interior, each turn could plunge him into the inescapable darkness of twisting wooden planks and staircases spiraling up and down and sideways all at the same time.

It was eerily quiet in there, but this quietness was interspersed with the cracking of wood under the Specter's determined and heroic gait, coupled with some other distant and unclear sounds. He couldn't quite make out what he was hearing there, from time to time he stopped in place and tried to listen.

Gusts of air, mechanical clicking, bursts and cracks and slams.

Wherever these sounds originated from, something was clearly being destroyed there. Destroyed with excessive force.

The whole structure was a mess, the Specter suspected that maybe he's already gotten lost, but even if so, that doesn't really matter. He's now in enemy territory, an cut-and-dried evil hideout, and he knows damn well how these stories go, he's lived through this countless times. The mastermind doesn't just flee, they have to show themselves to the hero, then and only then can they attempt escape. Evil is predictable.

And then something unpredictable happened, the hallway the Specter was in came to an end, just like that. There was absolutely nothing special about it, a wooden and twisted corridor like every single one he's been in already, but this time it ended in a door.

The door had a label, too. It read "The Meat Packing Room" in ominous blood red lettering. The only room that could've felt more evil than this in this scenario the Specter's found himself in would be something like "The Murdering People With An Axe Room".

And what would this be doing in a farmhouse? He thought to himself, before composing and quickly rushing towards the door.

At the halfway point he suddenly felt a sharp pain in his right leg. Something stabbed him. He looked down, and saw something that at first glance looked like a mousetrap, but it clearly wasn't one, its true shape was just distorted by the surrounding darkness.

No, it was not a mousetrap. It was a miniature catapult, or was it a trebuchet? He didn't know the difference, and didn't care. Either way what struck him in the leg was a weapon of destruction, the fruit of humanity's often monstrous ingenuity. He kicked the contraption into the wall, and then heard cracks louder than before, now with a clear source — beneath his feet.

It seems "The Meat Packing Room" was a trap.

And then the floor collapsed.

The Specter woke up to whole-body pain and rhythmic noises. He suspected that this was what he heard earlier, the cracks and slams, but now the sounds were not muffled, he was at their source. He found himself laying down, he tried standing up, but was strapped with rope to some sort of wooden contraption, probably a bigger catapult than the one he saw before falling.

Then, instead of trying to force his way out immediately, he tried to carefully analyse his surroundings, pretending to still be unconscious. Instantly he understood that he was where he needed to be, this was the heart of darkness he's been searching for.

He was in the middle of a huge, dimly lit chamber. Around him were hundreds of catapults, trebuchets, and other ballistic devices of different makes and sizes — some freakishly large and others so small that they could fit into his hand with room to spare. Everything seemed very neatly organized, it looked as if he was in the middle of a military compound. The contraptions seemingly all had their duties to carry out, some were transporting boxes, some were surrounding him, and others were busy launching different projectiles into a designated wall, as if training for combat. That's what he kept hearing.

There was a single platform near the ceiling of the room, overlooking everything from above. There, he saw a human silhouette, after a moment of staring he could make out more details — a lab coat, goggles, gloves, unkept hair. It was clear this was a mad scientist, and not of the Albert Einstein sort, rather the sort that's driven mad with evil. Behind the figure there was a big, bulky machine emanating some sort of aura, this was probably the reason for the dimensional shenanigans of today.

And now, he was ready.

"You should've known mere ropes won't hold back your punishment…" SCP-4494 began, and with a single display of strength tear down the ropes that bound him, jumped into the air, and landed victoriously. "For instruments of evil can't hold back… the specter!"

"Oh, you're awake." The scientist figure said with a mix of confusion and indifference.

"That I am, fiend! Your meat packing was no match for the likes of me, the trap was obvious at first glance! I allowed myself to get caught, and in your arrogance you lead me right where I needed to be!"

A few seconds of silence went by.

"Your nefarious Meat Packing Room! I've seen many sinister room before, but none as sinister as that! What are you plotting behind its doors!?"

"That's food storage." A devious smile appeared on the scientists face. "It seems you didn't need my help getting caught! There was no trap, frankly I don't even know who you are! If it wasn't for you falling out of the ceiling I wouldn't have known you were here."

The scientist made a swiping motion with their hand, the previously idle catapults began swarming around SCP-4494.

"Since your name doesn't ring any bells, do you mind actually introducing yourself?"

"I am the Specter, the keeper of good, embodiment of justice itself!" His spiel would've been much longer if he didn't have to fight off all the catapults, and also if the scientist didn't interrupt him.

"Very impressive." This response was accompanied by a clearly sarcastic clap. "I am Orphan Crusher, doctor of multiversal sciences. My old name is of no concern to you, and anyone else for that matter."

A punch to the wheel, a kick to another, all the twisted contraptions quickly began overwhelming the Specter, as he nearly nodded his head in acknowledgement of the name, but then did a swift double take.

What the hell did they just say?

"I know your type well enough! Only pure evil would call itself something so depraved!"

"I did not choose this life, or this name! Society made me into a monster!"

Getting them to monologue was a chance at turning the tables of the fight. The Specter knew that, and very much liked using this trick to his advantage. Evil can't resist an evil monologue when given the opportunity.

"I was supposed to help everyone! I invented a machine that could do just that! It could see into every possible alternate dimension, humanity could've had everything it wanted!" Orphan Crusher's tone became more somber for a while. "I was lonely. I found a dimension of sentient catapults, and I adopted one as my son. How was I supposed to know it would just disappear one day and throw little Bobby into a wall?!"

The Specter wasn't really listening to all this, he was busy thinking of a plan while jumping from one catapult to another, he tried to remember the file Doctor Dan showed him before the mission. He had to think of a way to somehow reach Orphan Crusher, the constant onslaught of attacks prevented him from just going up there himself.

Although, from what he did gather of the monologue, it was pretty stupid.

"The townsfolk were furious! But they didn't listen to me! They didn't want to listen, and it's them who gave me my new name!" Orphan Crusher kept screaming and screaming at the top of their lungs. "It wasn't my fault, it was these hellish catapults! I had to flee from the town because of them!"

The Specter finally got an idea. The Foundation has only had just two SCP-1213s. Here, he had an unlimited supply, so what if…

"I used my machine to go to their dimension, and I tamed them! I now have an army, and everyone will pay for what they did to me!"

"You've done that to yourself! In your pursuit of glory, you failed to realise the consequences of what you were doing!" The Specter started his concluding speech, his movements way more focused than his chaotic jumping from before. "You should only blame yourself! Instead you're shifting the blame onto everything else! That's what true evil is!"

Orphan Crusher tried to think of a response, but froze when they looked down at the Specter and his movements. His cape was elongated and stretched across the entire room, meticulously attached to some of the catapults attacking him.

The Specter then landed in the center of the room, but his cape went flying, and with it a series of catapults, each one smaller and smaller. A catapult was loaded into a catapult, then another, then another, like a matryoshka of ballistic weaponry. Then the biggest fired the rest, kickstarting a chain reaction. Each catapult fired in succession, their projectile, a baseball sized catapult made of sticks, accelarating to incredible speeds.

And then it hit the target.

ETTRA Area-09, Great Basin Desert, Central Nevada, USA

17th December, 2025

"It hit them right in the head, I supposed knocked them out, and they fell onto the machine. This is probably why I was spit back into reality, and everything went back to normal." The Specter said, finishing his explanation.

"So what you're saying is you did a good job. Then why are you so…"

Dan couldn't quite find the right word to use here, which is not usual occurence for him. Luckily he didn't need to think any longer, as the Specter interrupted his silence. "Weirded out?"

"Maybe." Doctor Dan concurred, waiting for SCP-4494 to say anything else after he finished his summary of the fight against the Orphan Crusher.

Post-mission debriefings weren't always awkward moments. Of course it depends on the team dynamics and success rates, but generally after a mission well done these meeting were more like cynical joking sessions at the expense of the just stopped self-proclaimed bad guy of the week, rather than anything actually productive.

Especially considering the Specter's usual highly dramatic demeanor, this uneasy silence of the conference room was nothing short of bizarre.

"Speak up then, what is it?"

"How am I supposed to explain to anyone that I fought a guy named Orphan Crusher?" SCP-4494's cadence was that of an annoyed young adult, not his usual over-the-top superhero manner of speaking one could mistake for intentional parody.

This response prompted Doctor Dan to raise an eyebrow. "Are you sure you even have to explain this to anyone? Besides, even if you did have to, it's not like the guy specifically sought you out. You were there because there was evildoing in the area." Dan's imitation of the Specter came out as more mocking than he wanted it to.

"What if they come back?"

"So what? It's not like they're going to hit you with 'we're not so different, you and I'. You said it yourself, they don't even know who you are. I also highly doubt they're ever coming back."

"How so?"

"These types are usually a one-and-done." With that said Dan opened a briefcase he brought for the meeting, revealing some items from his personal collection of vintage superhero comic books. "You can borrow some, might just cheer you up. You're not the only one dealing with weirdos."

With a swift motion and a wave of his cape, the Specter rose up from his seat and swiped one of Dan's books.

"Well, I must say I needn't have worried about it this much. Of course while delivering justice you have to fight awkwardness as well, for the awkwardness of evil knows no boundaries it won't cross! I lost a battle against awkwardness today, but thanks to your kind words, I won the war!" The Specter said, flipping throught the pages of the comic book. "I am personally a fan of the more modern takes on my dignified profession, but I must say this really is a considerate gift!"

SCP-4494 then jumped onto the table, and from there to the windowsill. While the window was previously closed, during his leap he managed to perfectly open it using his cape.

"Justice thanks you! We will meet again when evil comes crawling out! As for now…" He jumped out of the window. "The Specter departs! "

Although the Specter's performance just now was actually somewhat impressive, there was one other thing on Doctor Dan's mind.

He's probably not getting his comic book back.

Look, this all happened just over 4 hours ago, and we've been here for 3 already. There are procedures in place for active monitoring of anomalous recovery sites, specifically for this very occasion. If anything, we're too careful, as we should be. Wouldn't you agree?" "I would, my sincere apologies." "Sure. Judging by your staring contest against a building, I suppose you have a plan." "Delivering justice is a plan in and of itself, the steps do not matter if you have convictions! It's evil that gets caught up in schemes and plots. Blinded by arrogance, it wouldn't know what to do at the tiniest inconvenience!" With a swift motion [[span class="shadow"]]//SCP-4494//[[/span]] turned away, again facing the mind-breaking collage of walls, and doors, and wooden support beams all in rainbow colors, and walked right into the mouth of the beast, disappearing. The [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]]'s elongated cape fluttered in anticipation of his triumphant return, before vanishing just as him, in a flash of light. Dan had no idea if the [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]]'s last words were supposed to be a dig at him or not. Either way he didn't really care, and he had no time for that, he saw a scientist walk up to him, and had to prepare for news. "Doctor Dan, sir. The narrative assessment is complete." As soon as [[span class="shadow"]]//SCP-4494//[[/span]] showed up on the coast, he asked for one. This wasn't really a standard, but he sometimes lets his gut feeling take hold. "So?" "A lot of narrative structures in place here seem to be consistent with tropes associated with '1950s one-off comic book supervillains'. I'm personally not really an expert on the topic." "Well, then compared to you I very much am." Doctor Dan said with a slight grin appearing on his face. "This could get interesting." [[div]] [[=]] @@ @@ [[image http://scp-sandbox-3.wdfiles.com/local--files/collab%3Akarpin-blank-resurrection-chapter-2/A9Asterisk.png]] @@ @@ [[/=]] [[/div]] The [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] should've expected that the inside of the den of darkness would be even more treacherous than its outside would suggest. An impossible structure sure does have an impossible interior, each turn could plunge him into the inescapable darkness of twisting wooden planks and staircases spiraling up and down and sideways all at the same time. It was eerily quiet in there, but this quietness was interspersed with the cracking of wood under the [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]]'s determined and heroic gait, coupled with some other distant and unclear sounds. He couldn't quite make out what he was hearing there, from time to time he stopped in place and tried to listen. Gusts of air, mechanical clicking, bursts and cracks and slams. Wherever these sounds originated from, something was clearly being destroyed there. Destroyed with excessive force. The whole structure was a mess, the [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] suspected that maybe he's already gotten lost, but even if so, that doesn't really matter. He's now in enemy territory, an cut-and-dried evil hideout, and he knows damn well how these stories go, he's lived through this countless times. The mastermind doesn't just flee, they //have// to show themselves to the hero, then and only then can they attempt escape. Evil is predictable. And then something unpredictable happened, the hallway the [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] was in came to an end, just like that. There was absolutely nothing special about it, a wooden and twisted corridor like every single one he's been in already, but this time it ended in a door. The door had a label, too. It read "The Meat Packing Room" in ominous blood red lettering. The only room that could've felt more evil than this in this scenario the [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]]'s found himself in would be something like "The Murdering People With An Axe Room". And what would this be doing in a farmhouse? He thought to himself, before composing and quickly rushing towards the door. At the halfway point he suddenly felt a sharp pain in his right leg. Something stabbed him. He looked down, and saw something that at first glance looked like a mousetrap, but it clearly wasn't one, its true shape was just distorted by the surrounding darkness. No, it was not a mousetrap. It was a miniature catapult, or was it a trebuchet? He didn't know the difference, and didn't care. Either way what struck him in the leg was a weapon of destruction, the fruit of humanity's often monstrous ingenuity. He kicked the contraption into the wall, and then heard cracks louder than before, now with a clear source -- beneath his feet. It seems "The Meat Packing Room" was a trap. And then the floor collapsed. [[div]] [[=]] @@ @@ [[image http://scp-sandbox-3.wdfiles.com/local--files/collab%3Akarpin-blank-resurrection-chapter-2/A9Asterisk.png style="margin-top: 1em"]] @@ @@ [[/=]] [[/div]] The [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] woke up to whole-body pain and rhythmic noises. He suspected that this was what he heard earlier, the cracks and slams, but now the sounds were not muffled, he was at their source. He found himself laying down, he tried standing up, but was strapped with rope to some sort of wooden contraption, probably a bigger catapult than the one he saw before falling. Then, instead of trying to force his way out immediately, he tried to carefully analyse his surroundings, pretending to still be unconscious. Instantly he understood that he was where he needed to be, this was the heart of darkness he's been searching for. He was in the middle of a huge, dimly lit chamber. Around him were hundreds of catapults, trebuchets, and other ballistic devices of different makes and sizes -- some freakishly large and others so small that they could fit into his hand with room to spare. Everything seemed very neatly organized, it looked as if he was in the middle of a military compound. The contraptions seemingly all had their duties to carry out, some were transporting boxes, some were surrounding him, and others were busy launching different projectiles into a designated wall, as if training for combat. That's what he kept hearing. There was a single platform near the ceiling of the room, overlooking everything from above. There, he saw a human silhouette, after a moment of staring he could make out more details -- a lab coat, goggles, gloves, unkept hair. It was clear this was a mad scientist, and not of the Albert Einstein sort, rather the sort that's driven mad with evil. Behind the figure there was a big, bulky machine emanating some sort of aura, this was probably the reason for the dimensional shenanigans of today. And now, he was ready. "You should've known mere ropes won't hold back your punishment..." [[span class="shadow"]]//SCP-4494//[[/span]] began, and with a single display of strength tear down the ropes that bound him, jumped into the air, and landed victoriously. "For instruments of evil can't hold back... [[span class="shadow"]]//the specter!//[[/span]]" "Oh, you're awake." The scientist figure said with a mix of confusion and indifference. "That I am, fiend! Your meat packing was no match for the likes of me, the trap was obvious at first glance! I allowed myself to get caught, and in your arrogance you lead me right where I needed to be!" A few seconds of silence went by. "Your nefarious Meat Packing Room! I've seen many sinister room before, but none as sinister as that! What are you plotting behind its doors!?" "That's food storage." A devious smile appeared on the scientists face. "It seems you didn't need my help getting caught! There was no trap, frankly I don't even know who you are! If it wasn't for you falling out of the ceiling I wouldn't have known you were here." The scientist made a swiping motion with their hand, the previously idle catapults began swarming around [[span class="shadow"]]//SCP-4494//[[/span]]. "Since your name doesn't ring any bells, do you mind actually introducing yourself?" "I am the [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]], the keeper of good, embodiment of justice itself!" His spiel would've been much longer if he didn't have to fight off all the catapults, and also if the scientist didn't interrupt him. "Very impressive." This response was accompanied by a clearly sarcastic clap. "I am Orphan Crusher, doctor of multiversal sciences. My old name is of no concern to you, and anyone else for that matter." A punch to the wheel, a kick to another, all the twisted contraptions quickly began overwhelming the [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]], as he nearly nodded his head in acknowledgement of the name, but then did a swift double take. What the hell did they just say? "I know your type well enough! Only pure evil would call itself something so depraved!" "I did not choose this life, or this name! Society made me into a monster!" Getting them to monologue was a chance at turning the tables of the fight. The [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] knew that, and very much liked using this trick to his advantage. Evil can't resist an evil monologue when given the opportunity. "I was supposed to help everyone! I invented a machine that could do just that! It could see into every possible alternate dimension, humanity could've had everything it wanted!" Orphan Crusher's tone became more somber for a while. "I was lonely. I found a dimension of sentient catapults, and I adopted one as my son. How was I supposed to know it would just disappear one day and throw little Bobby into a wall?!" The [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] wasn't really listening to all this, he was busy thinking of a plan while jumping from one catapult to another, he tried to remember the file Doctor Dan showed him before the mission. He had to think of a way to somehow reach Orphan Crusher, the constant onslaught of attacks prevented him from just going up there himself. Although, from what he did gather of the monologue, it was pretty stupid. "The townsfolk were furious! But they didn't listen to me! They didn't want to listen, and it's them who gave me my new name!" Orphan Crusher kept screaming and screaming at the top of their lungs. "It wasn't my fault, it was these hellish catapults! I had to flee from the town because of them!" The [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] finally got an idea. The Foundation has only had just two SCP-1213s. Here, he had an unlimited supply, so what if... "I used my machine to go to their dimension, and I tamed them! I now have an army, and everyone will pay for what they did to me!" "You've done that to yourself! In your pursuit of glory, you failed to realise the consequences of what you were doing!" The [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] started his concluding speech, his movements way more focused than his chaotic jumping from before. "You should only blame yourself! Instead you're shifting the blame onto everything else! That's what true evil is!" Orphan Crusher tried to think of a response, but froze when they looked down at the [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] and his movements. His cape was elongated and stretched across the entire room, meticulously attached to some of the catapults attacking him. The [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] then landed in the center of the room, but his cape went flying, and with it a series of catapults, each one smaller and smaller. A catapult was loaded into a catapult, then another, then another, like a matryoshka of ballistic weaponry. Then the biggest fired the rest, kickstarting a chain reaction. Each catapult fired in succession, their projectile, a baseball sized catapult made of sticks, accelarating to incredible speeds. And then it hit the target. [[div]] [[=]] @@ @@ [[image http://scp-wiki.wdfiles.com/local--files/the-bowe-decommission-part-one/Asterisk.png style="margin-top: 1em"]] @@ @@ [[/=]] [[/div]] [[=]] ++ __ETTRA Area-09, Great Basin Desert, Central Nevada, USA__ //17th December, 2025// [[/=]] [[div style="border-top: 1px solid rgb(200, 200, 200); margin: 1em 0"]] [[/div]] "It hit them right in the head, I supposed knocked them out, and they fell onto the machine. This is probably why I was spit back into reality, and everything went back to normal." The [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] said, finishing his explanation. "So what you're saying is you did a good job. Then why are you so..." Dan couldn't quite find the right word to use here, which is not usual occurence for him. Luckily he didn't need to think any longer, as the [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] interrupted his silence. "Weirded out?" "Maybe." Doctor Dan concurred, waiting for [[span class="shadow"]]//SCP-4494//[[/span]] to say anything else after he finished his summary of the fight against the Orphan Crusher. Post-mission debriefings weren't always awkward moments. Of course it depends on the team dynamics and success rates, but generally after a mission well done these meeting were more like cynical joking sessions at the expense of the just stopped self-proclaimed bad guy of the week, rather than anything actually productive. Especially considering the [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]]'s usual highly dramatic demeanor, this uneasy silence of the conference room was nothing short of bizarre. "Speak up then, what is it?" "How am I supposed to explain to anyone that I fought a guy named Orphan Crusher?" SCP-4494's cadence was that of an annoyed young adult, not his usual over-the-top superhero manner of speaking one could mistake for intentional parody. This response prompted Doctor Dan to raise an eyebrow. "Are you sure you even have to explain this to anyone? Besides, even if you did have to, it's not like the guy specifically sought you out. You were there because there was //evildoing in the area//." Dan's imitation of the Specter came out as more mocking than he wanted it to. "What if they come back?" "So what? It's not like they're going to hit you with 'we're not so different, you and I'. You said it yourself, they don't even know who you are. I also highly doubt they're ever coming back." "How so?" "These types are usually a one-and-done." With that said Dan opened a briefcase he brought for the meeting, revealing some items from his personal collection of vintage superhero comic books. "You can borrow some, might just cheer you up. You're not the only one dealing with weirdos." With a swift motion and a wave of his cape, the [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] rose up from his seat and swiped one of Dan's books. "Well, I must say I needn't have worried about it this much. Of course while delivering justice you have to fight awkwardness as well, for the awkwardness of evil knows no boundaries it won't cross! I lost a battle against awkwardness today, but thanks to your kind words, I won the war!" The [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]] said, flipping throught the pages of the comic book. "I am personally a fan of the more modern takes on my dignified profession, but I must say this really is a considerate gift!" [[span class="shadow"]]//SCP-4494//[[/span]] then jumped onto the table, and from there to the windowsill. While the window was previously closed, during his leap he managed to perfectly open it using his cape. "Justice thanks you! We will meet again when evil comes crawling out! As for now..." He jumped out of the window. "[[size 150%]][[span class="shadow"]]//The Specter departs!//[[/span]][[/size]] " Although the [[span class="shadow"]]//Specter//[[/span]]'s performance just now was actually somewhat impressive, there was one other thing on Doctor Dan's mind. He's probably not getting his comic book back. the-spiciest-pizza.raw_content:
It is 9:56 at night at your town’s local Spicy Crust Pizzeria. Just four more minutes before closing, and you are itching to get your shift over with. You never anticipated that you would work until closing, but it somehow managed to sneak up on you, like it had yesterday, and the day before that.

You had thought the job to be a good way of earning some extra cash to sling around during the later years of high school, but you always thought it to be a temporary arrangement, one you’d cast aside when faced with something better. Four years of community college later, and something better never came, and you stuck around the greased floors of this hole in the wall. Only now, you were here full time. Something’s gotta pay the bills.

As the minute hand ticked over the twelve, you put up your last chair and locked the door behind you. Technically, you shouldn’t be leaving just yet, as there was still a table and a half’s worth of chairs still sitting on the ground. Bill might be paying you to close, but he wasn’t paying you a cent after ten o’clock, so as far as you were concerned, the chairs were his problem now. It wasn’t like he was the shining picture of a protestant work ethic himself, as he seemed fond of taking off on a shift whenever he damn well felt like it.

You quickly stopped ruminating on the topic. You were free now, this job wasn’t going to take up any more of your time than it already had to. Thankfully, you finally arrived at the front door of your apartment.

Quickly, you tossed the full weight of your body onto your bed, not bothering to change out of your uniform, as sweet oblivion was all you could think about at that moment. As you felt yourself drifting off into the ether, quite a rude awakening presented itself to you in the form of your landline ringing.

Groaning, you pulled a pillow over your head and waited for the piercing beeping to subside.

And you waited.

And waited.

And you waited.

H- hello? Who is this?

Yeah, hi, it’s Bill. Listen, I know you just got off of your closing shift, which thank you for, by the way, but there- there’s this other thing that I you- we uh, gotta do. See, there’s this customer that ordered a pizza pretty dang close to the closing time, which, heh- yeah, it’s a dick move, I know, but an order’s an order, and it looks like it slipped past us, and they still haven’t gotten their pizza. So you’re gonna have to- to do that. Yeah.

You almost hung up on him right then and there. Bill was always a little aloof, but he must be near delusional if he thought you were going to deliver a pizza, off the clock, past closing, to some random fatass in god knows what part of this stupid hick town.

You also resisted the urge to call Bill a liar, as you were at the pizzeria the entire day, and had not heard that phone make a beep past 9:25. As a matter of fact, you could call him a liar, what did he know, he wasn’t in the pizzeria at all since 4:00, he wouldn’t know jack.

Luckily for your job, these thoughts stayed in your head, and before you had the chance to self-terminate, Bill presented you with an offer most peculiar.

I know this is probably like a real- really bad time for you, but you’re the only one that’s available at this hour right now. So look, just- deliver this one pizza for us, and tell ya what, I think a promotion could be in store for you.

A promotion?

Yeah, pay raise and everything. Right hand to god.

The offer of a promotion surprised you enough to where you forgot to think about if he even had the authority to give you one. If you did get that promotion, which was practically being offered on a silver platter, you could finally pay your rent on time, and actually have a decent bit of money left over. Maybe getting promoted would look good enough on his resume for you to finally look for a better job.

Bill’s still an asshole, though.

Okay. Where am I delivering?

Can’t really say right now, but I’ll call you at the pizzeria in about 20 minutes. Bye.

And with that, Bill hang up on you. With your prospective promotion in arms reach, you don’t have the energy or patience to question why Bill was being so secret about what was probably just a very cold pizza by now. You simply grab your coat, and walk back out into the night.

Walking back to the pizzeria, you only just begin to notice how eerie your trek to and from work can be. Your town is, after all, quite small and out of the way, which means that it had none of the lights and noise that would come from the bustling downtown of a major city.

No, for you your trek to work meant an awkward 15 minutes shuffling through the quiet hinterlands of your town's suburbs. It wasn’t like you were feeling your way through the pitch black of the country or anything, the streetlamps which lined the empty roads gave you enough light for you to see where you’re going, but also illuminated just enough for you to look into the precipice of places where you couldn’t see.

Your town isn't doing the best, finance-wise, which reflected in the quality of housing on this side of town, which fell short of stellar, to say the least. More than a few windows were boarded up, the wood of the porches were rotting and being eaten by moss and fungi, and of course, there were no working lighting fixtures to be seen, leaving the streetlamps to just barely light up the fronts of the house, giving you the feel that they were almost staring at you from beyond the pale. You wonder if anyone is looking right back at you from the shroud of darkness.

You think about how fast a human is able to run.

Shoving that thought to the back of your mind, you finally cross the street and come into view of the empty strip mall where your town’s very own Spicy Crust Pizzeria was located. As you step between the shuttered nail salon and convenience store with your keys in hand, you stare through the glass walls of the establishment and peer into the pitch darkness which began right around where the second table on the left was. You know, the one where you hadn’t finished stacking-

The three chairs which you flippantly left all over the ground now sat neatly in a row, upside down on that table. A shard of ice runs up your back as you try and parse who possibly could’ve done that, because it sure as hell wasn’t you.

None of the other high schoolers that helped run this place cared a smidgeon more than you did about whether or not the chairs were stacked correctly come closing, and you were the only one closing that night anyways. The only set of keys were in your hand, which you quickly found out needn’t be the case when you discovered that the door was already unlocked.

It would be a lie to say that you weren’t at least a little nervous at the prospect of the pizzeria not being completely empty, but the logical half of your brain decided enough was enough, and you dismissed your wild fantasies about axe murderers or roaming skinwalkers.

Ordering yourself into a relative sense of security, you flick on the lights, which still made you jump as a tiny part of yourself still expected a humanoid silhouette to be standing off ominously in a corner. Aside from the chairs, everything is as expected.

Before you were able to search for the nondescript pizza you were meant to be delivering, the phone at the front began to ring, and as embarrassing as it is to admit, you hurriedly picked up the phone to hear Bill’s dopey voice so that you would have at least one familiar face with you.

Hey, so the pizza’s on the first table in the back. You’re delivering to 423 Hefford Avenue. Be there in less than thirty minutes. Company policy and all that.

Yeah, got that, and I just got a question about- about the pizzeria, cause I closed at around ten, and I was just wondering if you ever came back after, or-

Also, when you get the pizza, don’t open it at any point.

Although he started off in his usual informal, dopey way of speaking, you felt as though Bill was being uncharacteristically– stern, was the right word? He enunciated his words far more clearly and had far more bass in his voice than you had ever heard him speak with, and spoke with the conviction you would expect a SWAT responder to have, not the middling manager of an irrelevant pizza chain in the middle of nowhere.

And you already weren’t going to open the pizza, so you really didn’t get the urgentness in which he barked that last command at you.

The way to 423 Hefford is pretty confusing, and it's a bit of a ways there, so I want you to take- ahem- there’s a prepaid cellphone in the safe in the back, take it in case you ever get lost or anything, I’ll answer. The code to the safe’s on the pizza box.

Once again, before you could question what exactly Bill just said, he hung up on you, but this time, you were too bewildered to be angry at him for essentially ordering you around. You thought about the peculiarity of the orders you had just received, you were delivering a pizza, not meth, so you question the need to use a burner phone like you were a drug dealer.

Besides, he put his phone number on the list pinned up on the wall with all the other employees. If you really needed to call him, you could just use your regular phone, the one that was made in the last decade.

You shove those thoughts aside as you perform your last twist of the safe’s dial, cracking it open, expecting there to be a modestly sized stack of cash or the property deed that you would have to resist stealing, instead you see two lonely items– a prepaid cell phone, and a small handgun.

Mildly surprised, you take the phone. It’s not that seeing the gun itself was that surprising to you, you just didn’t peg Bill as that type of guy. Closing the safe door, you still haven’t shaken how oddly specific Bill worded this specific order. He’d never expressed that much concern for if the delivery drivers knew where they were going, probably because he trusted them enough to know how to use a GPS.

And even if you didn’t, you knew where Hefford Avenue was. Right by the Stevenson & Carson Projects.

As you take a sharp left into your municipality’s infamous housing tract, you feel remarkably less safe than you feel you should be, even with a car protecting you, and a small revolver poking into the side of your pocket.

Your town has had the unfortunate distinction of having the highest mortality rate in the area, and a large portion of that statistic is thanks to the Stevenson & Carson Projects. Almost monthly, like it’s a scheduled event, some sort of massive tragedy would befall the denizens of this town, and it would always come out of this seemingly cursed neighborhood.

A kidnapping here, a mass shooting there, an attempted terrorist attack one time, even a falling satellite, all were events that had occurred within or out from the Projects. It’s a wonder anyone still lives there, a fact a bit more bewildering than the speed in which the local news covered each incident that happened in the Projects, way before word of mouth can even have an opportunity to spread. If you didn’t know any better, you’d wager that they were orchestrating these events so they’d have a story to tell.

Either way, you felt uneasy driving past the Projects even at day, let alone at a hair’s width of midnight. Pulling over off to the side, you notice how eerily empty the entire neighborhood seemed to be. Even the derelict hinterlands you brushed past earlier had signs of habitation, with rustbucket cars, and indented stairs that showed at least somebody was in the area relatively recently.

Not here. The houses, although much nicer than the ones on your side of town, were barren of any personality. No lawn decorations, no cars in the driveway, and not even any window dressings. Some houses didn’t even have any paint.

The streets were better paved than anywhere else in town too, with the asphalt not having one dent or pothole taken out of it anywhere, as far as your eyes can see. It made sense for the area, as there wasn’t a single car accompanying yours on either side of the road, anywhere. The entire neighborhood had a perpetual feeling of being constructed last week, which gave it an air of indifferent unease which made you ask if there was anyone around to hear you scream. Maybe the nearby elementary school would, if it wasn’t the middle of the night.

You suppose that’s what the gun is for.

Before stepping out of the car, you lifted up the mysterious pizza box, the odd weight distribution of what was allegedly a pizza in there throwing you off again, making you almost drop the box on the spotless road.

Wanting to get out of this passively hostile environment as soon as possible, you quickly shuffle over to 432 Hefford Avenue, which was about as remarkable as the rest of the neighborhood.

You gave the blank white door a knock, to no response. Suddenly, your burner phone came to life in a flurry of beeps and vibration, breaking the veil of silence.

Drop the pizza off in the backyard of the house.

What?

In the backyard. The gate’s locked, but it's just a latch, so you should be able to let yourself in. When you enter the yard, you should see a pretty big tree by the center. Just leave the box somewhere by the base of the tree and you’ll be done. Customer request.

Why-

Your inquiries were met with silence as Bill hung up on you once again. You had almost grown desensitized to how weird he had been recently, dismissing the nightly delivery out of nowhere, the weird burner phone instructions, and the gun in the safe, but the latest batch of instructions pulled you violently back into reality as you question whether you’re delivering a pizza or feeding a lion.

Of course. A crushing realization befell you like a bunch of weights on your shoulders that all of this must have been some sort of shitty prank. Just a ruse to waste your time because he felt like it.

But what if it wasn’t? Your promotion was one step away, practically in your hands, and if you walk away now, you risk potentially squandering the opportunity, wasting the last hour of your life.

You contemplate just leaving the box at the doorstep and saying you did all that weird shit, but if the customer did request the box in the backyard you could risk a complaint…

If this really is a prank, you don’t really have much time left to waste, right?

Walking across the perfectly trimmed lawn and over to the latch gate, you notice the first outlier you’ve seen here all night. Although the gate's materials seemed to be in perfect condition, the structural integrity of the gate very much wasn’t, with what seemed to be a modestly sized hole punched through it, big enough to fit a large dog, or a goat or something.

You’re torn between a sense of distress at what possibly could’ve happened here or a strange sense of relief that this neighborhood was more normal than you gave it credit for. Whichever way you end up leaning, you let yourself through the gate.

Turning on your phone’s flashlight, and you start to think you may have been right to have been distressed. There was indeed a tree by the center of the yard, but what Bill neglected to tell you was that there seemed to be an impromptu tree fort sitting on top of its branches. You cannot see into the fort itself.

You turn left, and you see where the material for the tree fort came from. The back of the house was almost completely mutilated, with bricks, planks, window panes, insulation, and roof shingles all haphazardly ripped out of the walls by what looked like was without any tools, like someone had simply ripped them out of there with their bare hands.

You hold your breath, and resolve to quickly make your delivery and not give this fever dream of a night a second thought once you make it home.

You somewhat crudely toss the pizza box on the floor, the impact of which forces the cover open, spilling the contents onto the grass.

There wasn’t any pizza in that box.

An assortment of roadkill, with all manner of birds, rats, and even an opossum or two came sprung from the flimsy cardboard box. There was so much roadkill you were surprised that it fit that snugly in the box. The cacophony of dead mammals were in various states of mutilation. Some you could see were mostly intact, sans a leg or two, quite a couple of lone heads dotted the foul stew before your eyes, and the rest was a mulch of various muscle tissue and organs that all blurred together in a sea of viscera.

You felt the fingers on your left hand. Earlier you had felt a wet spot at the bottom of the box you just assumed was the grease. Holding it up to the light, you now see that it was blood.

After staring at what you’ve just done for what felt like an eternity, you finally remember to get the hell out of here. But before you could bolt out of the yard, you heard a low rumbling sound coming from inside the house.

And before you could devote a single neuron to what it was, you felt a crushing blow to the chest. Next thing you knew, you found yourself crumpled on the floor, with a thud and a crack. You find yourself immobilized by the extreme agony you are in.

After the crushing pain falls to tolerable levels, you open your eyes to find your phone. You almost don’t comprehend the present danger you are in, as you desperately search for the one thing that can bring back your primal sense of sight, so you can even begin to defend yourself.

After far too much feeling around, you sense a small metal rectangle, which gives you a modicum of relief. With some of the focus taken off, you remember to pay attention to the ambience of the surroundings, and quickly find out that it is not as quiet as it was when you arrive.

You pick up your phone, and you quickly find the source of the wet sounds of chewing you had just been hearing.

Caught, bright as day, like a deer in the headlights of your phone’s flash, you see what looks to be a small child, ravenously shoving the desiccated remains of a rat down its throat like it was its last meal ever.

Unfortunately, it also saw you.

It momentarily paused from its sickly feast and opened its little mouth the widest it could, and let out a sound that was somewhere in between a growl and a hiss. Its first course of action was to desperately retreat to the makeshift fort on the center tree, but the wood planks stapled to the trunk serving as ladder rungs were not prepared for the amount of force the creature put into each step, with the third one quickly collapsing.

It fell to the ground in short order with a thud, quickly turning its gaze to meet you once again.

You didn’t wait to see what its second course of action was.

With each step sending shockwaves of pain down your spine, you sprinted off of this godforsaken property as quickly as your legs could move.

It was with such desperate vigor you ran back to your vehicle that you momentarily forgot to maintain decent running form. This cost you dearly as your center of mass came careening down to the pavement.

Terrified, you turn around to face the inevitable, the child-thing a mere foot away from you, with its mouth caked in blood, and its eyes wide and pitch black. It leaped like an animal, with its arms positioned like a leopard’s paws, and its mind ready to do god knows what to you.

With speed you didn’t know you possessed, you quickly pulled out the petite revolver and squeezed the trigger rapidly.

All six bullets found their way into the child’s center of mass, but they might as well have missed, as it only seemed to piss it off even more.

The feral eight year old landed on your stomach, pinning you to the ground as you vomited blood up and back into your eyes. After taking a bite out of your shoulder, it wailed on your head with the force of five men, with your will to fight dissipating more and more with each blow, until you had subconsciously accepted your ultimate fate.

You awoke in a blaze of light. Not the light of the gates of heaven, or any other afterlife for that matter, but the light of a burning jet of fire which engulfed the small child almost totally, who immediately abandoned your bloody torso to escape the black silhouette you saw direct the streaming inferno onto it.

Of course you were not completely spared from the effects of the flamethrower, with your legs being bathed in second degree burns, but the situation felt so unreal that the pain almost didn’t register.

As you turned, you saw the monster child being subdued by several more black silhouettes and carted off in the back of a black van, the first vehicle you saw in the neighborhood other than your own.

As your vision begins to fade from the excruciating pain your legs are in, you hear the black silhouette, someone you now see as a man clad in black armor talk about “skips” and “containing chambers”. You think you hear him say your name, followed up with something about a “level zero”.

You open your eyes for the last time in a while and see your own reflection in the visor of the man’s helmet.

The last thing you hear is him chuckling, and then going on to say,

I think you’re going to be delivering a lot more pizzas with us.

You really should have stayed home.

[[module Rate]]

[[/>]]



It is 9:56 at night at your town’s local Spicy Crust Pizzeria. Just four more minutes before closing, and you are itching to get your shift over with. You never anticipated that you would work until closing, but it somehow managed to sneak up on you, like it had yesterday, and the day before that.



You had thought the job to be a good way of earning some extra cash to sling around during the later years of high school, but you always thought it to be a temporary arrangement, one you’d cast aside when faced with something better. Four years of community college later, and something better never came, and you stuck around the greased floors of this hole in the wall. Only now, you were here full time. Something’s gotta pay the bills.



As the minute hand ticked over the twelve, you put up your last chair and locked the door behind you. Technically, you shouldn’t be leaving just yet, as there was still a table and a half’s worth of chairs still sitting on the ground. Bill might be paying you to close, but he wasn’t paying you a cent after ten o’clock, so as far as you were concerned, the chairs were his problem now. It wasn’t like he was the shining picture of a protestant work ethic himself, as he seemed fond of taking off on a shift whenever he damn well felt like it.



You quickly stopped ruminating on the topic. You were free now, this job wasn’t going to take up any more of your time than it already had to. Thankfully, you finally arrived at the front door of your apartment.



Quickly, you tossed the full weight of your body onto your bed, not bothering to change out of your uniform, as sweet oblivion was all you could think about at that moment. As you felt yourself drifting off into the ether, quite a rude awakening presented itself to you in the form of your landline ringing.



Groaning, you pulled a pillow over your head and waited for the piercing beeping to subside.



And you waited.



And waited.



And you waited.



> {{H- hello? Who is this?}}



> {{Yeah, hi, it’s Bill. Listen, I know you just got off of your closing shift, which thank you for, by the way, but there- there’s this other thing that I you- we uh, gotta do. See, there’s this customer that ordered a pizza pretty dang close to the closing time, which, heh- yeah, it’s a dick move, I know, but an order’s an order, and it looks like it slipped past us, and they still haven’t gotten their pizza. So you’re gonna have to- to do that. Yeah.}}



You almost hung up on him right then and there. Bill was always a little aloof, but he must be near delusional if he thought you were going to deliver a pizza, off the clock, past closing, to some random fatass in god knows what part of this stupid hick town.



You also resisted the urge to call Bill a liar, as you were at the pizzeria the entire day, and had not heard that phone make a beep past 9:25. As a matter of fact, you could call him a liar, what did he know, he wasn’t in the pizzeria at all since 4:00, he wouldn’t know jack.



Luckily for your job, these thoughts stayed in your head, and before you had the chance to self-terminate, Bill presented you with an offer most peculiar.



> {{I know this is probably like a real- really bad time for you, but you’re the only one that’s available at this hour right now. So look, just- deliver this one pizza for us, and tell ya what, I think a promotion could be in store for you.}}



> {{A promotion?}}



> {{Yeah, pay raise and everything. Right hand to god.}}



The offer of a promotion surprised you enough to where you forgot to think about if he even had the authority to give you one. If you did get that promotion, which was practically being offered on a silver platter, you could finally pay your rent on time, and actually have a decent bit of money left over. Maybe getting promoted would look good enough on his resume for you to finally look for a better job.



Bill’s still an asshole, though.



> {{Okay. Where am I delivering?}}



> {{Can’t really say right now, but I’ll call you at the pizzeria in about 20 minutes. Bye.}}

 

And with that, Bill hang up on you. With your prospective promotion in arms reach, you don’t have the energy or patience to question why Bill was being so secret about what was probably just a very cold pizza by now. You simply grab your coat, and walk back out into the night.



Walking back to the pizzeria, you only just begin to notice how eerie your trek to and from work can be. Your town is, after all, quite small and out of the way, which means that it had none of the lights and noise that would come from the bustling downtown of a major city.



No, for you your trek to work meant an awkward 15 minutes shuffling through the quiet hinterlands of your town's suburbs. It wasn’t like you were feeling your way through the pitch black of the country or anything, the streetlamps which lined the empty roads gave you enough light for you to see where you’re going, but also illuminated just enough for you to look into the precipice of places where you couldn’t see.



Your town isn't doing the best, finance-wise, which reflected in the quality of housing on this side of town, which fell short of stellar, to say the least. More than a few windows  were boarded up, the wood of the porches were rotting and being eaten by moss and fungi, and of course, there were no working lighting fixtures to be seen, leaving the streetlamps to just barely light up the fronts of the house, giving you the feel that they were almost staring at you from beyond the pale. You wonder if anyone is looking right back at you from the shroud of darkness.



You think about how fast a human is able to run.



Shoving that thought to the back of your mind, you finally cross the street and come into view of the empty strip mall where your town’s very own Spicy Crust Pizzeria was located. As you step between the shuttered nail salon and convenience store with your keys in hand, you stare through the glass walls of the establishment and peer into the pitch darkness which began right around where the second table on the left was. You know, the one where you hadn’t finished stacking-



The three chairs which you flippantly left all over the ground now sat neatly in a row, upside down on that table. A shard of ice runs up your back as you try and parse who possibly could’ve done that, because it sure as hell wasn’t you.    



None of the other high schoolers that helped run this place cared a smidgeon more than you did about whether or not the chairs were stacked correctly come closing, and you were the only one closing that night anyways. The only set of keys were in your hand, which you quickly found out needn’t be the case when you discovered that the door was already unlocked.



 It would be a lie to say that you weren’t at least a little nervous at the prospect of the pizzeria not being completely empty, but the logical half of your brain decided enough was enough, and you dismissed your wild fantasies about axe murderers or roaming skinwalkers.



Ordering yourself into a relative sense of security, you flick on the lights, which still made you jump as a tiny part of yourself still expected a humanoid silhouette to be standing off ominously in a corner. Aside from the chairs, everything is as expected.



Before you were able to search for the nondescript pizza you were meant to be delivering, the phone at the front began to ring, and as embarrassing as it is to admit, you hurriedly picked up the phone to hear Bill’s dopey voice so that you would have at least one familiar face with you.



> {{Hey, so the pizza’s on the first table in the back. You’re delivering to 423 Hefford Avenue.  Be there in less than thirty minutes. Company policy and all that.}}



> {{Yeah, got that, and I just got a question about- about the pizzeria, cause I closed at around ten, and I was just wondering if  you ever came back after, or-}}



> {{Also, when you get the pizza, don’t open it at any point.}}



Although he started off in his usual informal, dopey way of speaking, you felt as though Bill was being uncharacteristically– stern, was the right word? He enunciated his words far more clearly and had far more bass in his voice than you had ever heard him speak with, and spoke with the conviction you would expect a SWAT responder to have, not the middling manager of an  irrelevant pizza chain in the middle of nowhere.



And you already weren’t going to open the pizza, so you really didn’t get the urgentness in which he barked that last command at you.



> {{The way to 423 Hefford is pretty confusing, and it's a bit of a ways there, so I want you to take- ahem- there’s a prepaid cellphone in the safe in the back, take it in case you ever get lost or anything, I’ll answer. The code to the safe’s on the pizza box.}}



Once again, before you could question what exactly Bill just said, he hung up on you, but this time, you were too bewildered to be angry at him for essentially ordering you around. You thought about the peculiarity of the orders you had just received, you were delivering a pizza, not meth, so you question the need to use a burner phone like you were a drug dealer.



Besides, he put his phone number on the list pinned up on the wall with all the other employees. If you really needed to call him, you could just use your regular phone, the one that was made in the last decade.



You shove those thoughts aside as you perform your last twist of the safe’s dial, cracking it open, expecting there to be a modestly sized stack of cash or the property deed that you would have to resist stealing, instead you see two lonely items– a prepaid cell phone, and a small handgun.



Mildly surprised, you take the phone. It’s not that seeing the gun itself was that surprising to you, you just didn’t peg Bill as that type of guy. Closing the safe door, you still haven’t shaken how oddly specific Bill worded this specific order. He’d never expressed that much concern for if the delivery drivers knew where they were going, probably because he trusted them enough to know how to use a GPS.



And even if you didn’t, you knew where Hefford Avenue was. Right by the Stevenson & Carson Projects.



As you take a sharp left into your municipality’s infamous housing tract, you feel remarkably less safe than you feel you should be, even with a car protecting you, and a small revolver poking into the side of your pocket.



Your town has had the unfortunate distinction of having the highest mortality rate in the area, and a large portion of that statistic is thanks to the Stevenson & Carson Projects. Almost monthly, like it’s a scheduled event, some sort of massive tragedy would befall the denizens of this town, and it would always come out of this seemingly cursed neighborhood.



A kidnapping here, a mass shooting there, an attempted terrorist attack one time, even a falling satellite, all were events that had occurred within or out from the Projects. It’s a wonder anyone still lives there, a fact a bit more bewildering than the speed in which the local news covered each incident that happened in the Projects, way before word of mouth can even have an opportunity to spread. If you didn’t know any better, you’d wager that they were orchestrating these events so they’d have a story to tell.



Either way, you felt uneasy driving past the Projects even at day, let alone at a hair’s width of  midnight. Pulling over off to the side, you notice how eerily empty the entire neighborhood seemed to be. Even the derelict hinterlands you brushed past earlier had signs of habitation, with rustbucket cars, and indented stairs that showed at least somebody was in the area relatively recently.



Not here. The houses, although much nicer than the ones on your side of town, were barren of any personality. No lawn decorations, no cars in the driveway, and not even any window dressings. Some houses didn’t even have any paint.



The streets were better paved than anywhere else in town too, with the asphalt not having one dent or pothole taken out of it anywhere, as far as your eyes can see. It made sense for the area, as there wasn’t a single car accompanying yours on either side of the road, anywhere. The entire neighborhood had a perpetual feeling of being constructed last week, which gave it an air of indifferent unease which made you ask if there was anyone around to hear you scream. Maybe the nearby elementary school would, if it wasn’t the middle of the night.



You suppose that’s what the gun is for.



Before stepping out of the car, you lifted up the mysterious pizza box, the odd weight distribution of what was allegedly a pizza in there throwing you off again, making you almost drop the box on the spotless road.



Wanting to get out of this passively hostile environment as soon as possible, you quickly shuffle over to 432 Hefford Avenue, which was about as remarkable as the rest of the neighborhood.



You gave the blank white door a knock, to no response. Suddenly, your burner phone came to life in a flurry of beeps and vibration, breaking the veil of silence.



> {{Drop the pizza off in the backyard of the house.}}



> {{What?}}



> {{In the backyard. The gate’s locked, but it's just a latch, so you should be able to let yourself in. When you enter the yard, you should see a pretty big tree by the center. Just leave the box somewhere by the base of the tree and you’ll be done. Customer request.}}



> {{Why-}}



Your inquiries were met with silence as Bill hung up on you once again. You had almost grown desensitized to how weird he had been recently, dismissing the nightly delivery out of nowhere, the weird burner phone instructions, and the gun in the safe, but the latest batch of instructions pulled you violently back into reality as you question whether you’re delivering a pizza or feeding a lion.



Of course. A crushing realization befell you like a bunch of weights on your shoulders that all of this must have been some sort of shitty prank. Just a ruse to waste your time because he felt like it.



But what if it wasn’t? Your promotion was one step away, practically in your hands, and if you walk away now, you risk potentially squandering the opportunity, wasting the last hour of your life.



You contemplate just leaving the box at the doorstep and saying you did all that weird shit, but if the customer did request the box in the backyard you could risk a complaint…



If this really is a prank, you don’t really have much time left to waste, right?



Walking across the perfectly trimmed lawn and over to the latch gate, you notice the first outlier you’ve seen here all night. Although the gate's materials seemed to be in perfect condition, the structural integrity of the gate very much wasn’t, with what seemed to be a modestly sized hole punched through it, big enough to fit a large dog, or a goat or something.



You’re torn between a sense of distress at what possibly could’ve happened here or a strange sense of relief that this neighborhood was more normal than you gave it credit for. Whichever way you end up leaning, you let yourself through the gate.



Turning on your phone’s flashlight, and you start to think you may have been right to have been distressed. There was indeed a tree by the center of the yard, but what Bill neglected to tell you was that there seemed to be an impromptu tree fort sitting on top of its branches. You cannot see into the fort itself.



You turn left, and you see where the material for the tree fort came from.
