It had belonged to a previous site director, and another director before them, stretching back to when they laid down the concrete pad the original building once sat on. That building, like so many other systems within the Foundation, was now buried underneath a growing network of structures and bureaucracies that stretched out around it, the epicenter of a web spun by a great invisible spider. Here at its heart, Yoshihide could see every twist and tangle, every humming thread, each unknowing participant walking across the latticework. He wondered if the last director had seen him, as well, slowly working his way inwards towards this office. The last director had, like many other directors, left suddenly when a new appointment was selected for them. Yoshihide remembered a time early in his career when a fellow researcher, one several years his senior, had cautioned him about the nature of careers in the Foundation. "//Don't get thinking you have any say in the matter,//" he had said, a smoldering cigarette clutched in his fingers. "//The Foundation offers you opportunities like you'd never believe, but the choice you have is an illusion. They'll put you where they want to put you, and make you think it was your idea. You get to think you're the master of your own destiny, but they will get what they want. In the end, they win either way.//" He couldn't help but feel, though, that he'd somehow broken the mold. The bookshelves, the desk, the engraved nameplate on the door. //Akutagawa Yoshihide - Site Director//. The trappings of success, certainly, but all of them every bit his own. He was a containment specialist - the //best// containment specialist, he often heard his peers say, and this was his reward for that talent. In this site were teams of doctors, researchers, clerks; all of them answering to him directly. There was no longer a medium he needed to answer through, no more taskmasters who had to be compelled to action. Sure, there were faceless directors and overseers above him, somewhere - but as he'd climbed up the ladder to this office those names had become less and less tangible, and further away. He reported to someone, somewhere - but did it matter? If you never saw them, did they even exist? This rise hadn't come without sacrifice. Choices he had been forced to make to reach the room he now sat in. He'd felt a keen sense of cameraderie with his coworkers at the beginning - assistants and junior researchers who had all come up in the Foundation around the same time as he. Back then the world had seemed so much bigger than it was now, and that companionship had been a life raft on a wild and uncertain sea. Over time his work had filled more of the space where those friendships had lived, until one day he woke up and realized they were all gone. Yoshihide didn't mind it, though. The cost of his success, he reasoned. If the worst of it was losing a few drinking buddies, then that wasn't the end of the world. There had been other costs, though, greater and lesser. He had been away when his father had died, at a conference about staff reorganization. They had never been close, but as he'd gotten older his old man had begun opening up more and more to Yoshihide. "//Making up for lost time, if you'll let me,//" he used to say through a crooked smile and missing teeth. They had shared a few moments years before, after his mother died. He had always intended to go see him before the end, but those meetings seemed so important at the time. "//This will look very good to senior leadership,//" an executive personnel manager had told him, so he went. When he got the call from the hospital that his father had passed, he had his affairs managed remotely to avoid having to leave the conference. He didn't have the heart to ask the nurse if his father had died alone. He knew the answer. The worst, though, had happened long before he had ever walked into his new office. She was an agent assigned to the local branch of the Global Occult Coalition when Yoshihide had been stationed in a little research site outside of Okazaki. He was taken by her immediately - she was clever, funny, sharp. Her eyes were cutting; he used to say that there was nothing he could hide from her that she couldn't just see through. Her laughter was a song and her touch a warm breeze in summer. When they were together, Yoshihide made excuses to get away from work - something unthinkable now - so they could spend the afternoons together. They had plans to get a place in the city, to start a family. Plans that didn't include the Foundation. When their daughter was born, Yoshihide thought he might have finally found something that filled the hole in his heart. Then she was killed - of all things, in a car accident - and Yoshihide was alone again. In the days and weeks that followed her funeral, he convinced himself there was no deeper pit of despair a man could suffer, no lower agony. Eventually he threw himself back into his work -  a welcome reprieve from his despair that helped to silence the screaming he heard when he closed his eyes at night. He took his daughter, only a child at the time, and moved to Europe. He found the pathway to promotion ready and available, and seized after it. At no point had he ever noticed the strings pulling at him, or the hands on the marionnette. He was too busy looking forward to ever look up. So no, he thought, that old researcher had been wrong. The Foundation had opened doors for him, undoubtedly, but he was the one who chose which to walk through. It had been his own efforts that put his name on the door, and it would be by his own hand that he climbed to even higher offices than this. His meditations were disrupted by a knock on the door. A secretary - he hadn't learned their names yet - poked his head into the office. "A visitor for you, Director," he said. "O5 clearance." Yoshihide sat up straight in his chair. This wouldn't be his first encounter with an O5 liaison, and he knew enough to never let your guard down around these people. Liaisons were vipers, persons who had abandoned all career ambition in order to offer total subservience to a single person. In doing so they were allotted authority beyond their station, but at the cost of their agency. They made his skin crawl. The figure who passed through his door, though, was not a liaison at all. In fact, it wasn't anyone he'd ever seen before. It was a man, relatively tall but otherwise nondescript, in a sharp black suit with matching tie over a white shirt. Behind his dark glasses Yoshihide could just barely make out his eyes, keen and aware - like a raptor. Something about him felt queer. "Director!" the man said, extending a hand and complementing it with a wide grin. His voice was rich and genial, and Yoshihide was caught off guard by it. "Welcome to your new station. Sincerest apologies on my delay in getting here - I wanted to come offer my congratulations before you'd broken the place in, but business being what it is, ah. Couldn't be helped." Yoshihide took his hand. It was firm, and abrupt, but not inconsiderate. "I appreciate the consideration, nonetheless," he said. "I have to beg your apology, though. I don't believe we've met." The man helped himself into a chair opposite Yoshihide's desk, and the director followed suit. He paused for a moment, surveying the room. "Ah, yes, well, that's where I must apologise. I like to try and get out ahead of these things, make inroads as early as I can. Our working relationship is of paramount importance, you see, but my schedule has gotten the better of me again." He tapped the side of his chin with an extended finger. "I am the Administrator. Think of me as a go-between for Directors and Overseers. The grease that keeps the wheels moving. I'm here to help facilitate your transition to this new post, as well as make sure your interactions with our esteemed O5 Council are as seamless as possible." Yoshihide instinctively raised an eyebrow. "Really? I didn't know such a position existed." The man's smile didn't move an inch. Yoshihide could feel the hair on the back of his arms standing on end. "Oh yes," the Adminstrator said. "I've been at this for some time now. My job here, aside from ferrying tidings of goodwill down from Overwatch Command, is to ensure a sort of linearity in our ideals. The staff of our Foundation, the researchers and task forces, they have their own goals and objectives. There are too many of them to address individually, so we rely on our site directors to maintain that sense of direction. Once you get to this level, there's an expectation of... call it synchonicity. The Overseers set the line, the directors are expected to stay within it, and I help to make sure everyone knows where the line is. It is a narrow path, but it's one we all march together. We are, after all, here for the same reason, wouldn't you say?" Yoshihide's brow furrowed. "I suppose. But humor me, if you would - what reason would you say that is?" The Administrator placed his hands on the edge of Yoshihide's desk and leaned forward slightly. "Containment, Director. We are the keepers of the box. There are things in this world that, as you know, simply should not be. Were we gods, it would be enough to simply make them vanish, as if they were never there at all. There are some in our ranks who would seek to do just that, to use the mechanisms of man to accomplish a task ordained for God alone. They fail, of course. Every one of them. We are not gods, Director. So we must do what we can while we wait for God to act. The irregularities in our world, the things that go bump in the night - we put them into boxes, and then we watch the boxes. We do not discriminate; we've learned too many hard lessons to know how badly that can go. If we do this, we achieve our goal. It is thankless, certainly, and never-ending. But it is important, and it is right. I'm sure you agree." A bead of sweat began to run down Yoshihide's back. He knew the Administrator could not see it, but it did not change the fact that he felt as if the man somehow knew it was there all the same. He straightened up and nodded curtly. "Indeed," Yoshihide said. "That is the Work, after all." The Administrator sat back in his chair. His smile softened somewhat, but not in a reassuring way. "I am glad to hear it. My job and yours becomes so much simpler when we have a good sense of synergy." He laughed. "I hope you'll forgive my corporatism. Old habits die hard. But the truth of the matter remains - if I continue to illuminate the path, and you stay on the path, and your subordinates follow your direction, then we will be a successful unit, all of us." He looked down at his watch. "Ah, and there's my time. Apologies for departing as quickly as I arrived - my schedule is a fickle puppeteer, and I am just another marionette dancing at the end of a rope." He stood, and Yoshihide followed suit. The Administrator extended a hand and Yoshihide shook it. The hand was strangely warm. "We will be in touch, Director, as you settle into your new role. I am excited to see you rise to this new challenge!" He turned to leave, but as he opened the door he stopped and turned back over his shoulder. "Just don't forget - containment is our ultimate purpose. At whatever cost, yes?" Yoshihide said nothing, but nodded slightly. The Administrator grinned, and then closed the door behind him as he left. ----- "You didn't tell me you were going to be in the city this month," Yoshihide said, a scowl desperately trying to mask his happiness at seeing her face. "You need to be better at communicating your schedule, I could have arranged to have you stay at a nicer hotel." She laughed as she idly poked at her lunch. "You would think after all your hard work to be a Director you could stand to finally relax a little bit." He sighed. "Ahhhh, but don't you see! That's how they get you. You dream of freedom, but each new rung on the ladder is another shackle! More responsibilities, more meetings, more phone calls. It never ends. Even now, I have had to block out a whole hour to spend time with my inconsiderate daughter." "Inconsiderate!" She turned up her nose and jabbed at him with her fork. "Here I thought I was doing you a favor, getting you out of that stuffy office. If you stay there too long you're going to end up pickled, or worse." Yoshihide snickered at the thought. "Pickling might not be the worst outcome, if I'm being honest. It would do wonders for my skin." He paused for a moment, taking her in. She was every bit the picture of her mother - a blessing, considering the alternative. Her laughter was music and her presence was light. When she was with him he could almost forget about the burden of his work, the time spent endlessly poring over notes and reports and files. Those thoughts consumed him, but whenever she was near she seemed to so easily cast them away. She was clever, as well - almost too clever. While he could not help himself but feel pride in her when the Foundation had come calling for her expertise in exotic high-tension metamaterials, it was cocooned in stifling, suffocating dread. It must have shown on his face, and she frowned. "What's wrong?" she said, surveying him with her mother's eyes. "Are you having indigestion? Do you need a laxative?" He wanted to laugh, but the moment was lost on him. "No, Yuzuki. I'm fine. I just worry about you, is all. You need to let me know if you're ever in trouble, I can help you out. More now than I've ever been able to before - but I won't know if you need it unless you say something." She snorted. "What is there to say? I have a great job, a comfortable home, I get to work on some of the most fascinating projects I've ever seen in my life - and my father is only a couple hours train ride away; when he can find time for me, that is." This time he laughed, but only a little. "What are you worried about?" He closed his eyes, and saw another pair looking back at him from behind dark glasses. "You need to stay aware, all the time. This is dangerous work we do, you know. There are always people watching, waiting to take advantage of us in our moments of weakness. We can't afford to be caught off guard." She popped a grape in her mouth and spoke while she chewed. "I have a hard time imagining someone starting trouble with the daughter of a Site Director. Even if she is //inconsiderate//." He heard her mother's voice again, in her words. They were so similar. "It's not just about starting trouble. It's just about being aware. You need to promise me, if you see anything suspicious or hear of anything that makes you uncomfortable, you let me know, alright?" She rolled her eyes. "Yes, yes, very well. If it helps you sleep better at night, then I promise. Last thing I need is for you to keel over dead now from the stress." He relaxed for a moment, until he looked at her hands. She had picked up her fork and held the tines between her thumb and middle finger. With a firm but gentle motion, she pushed against the metal, and the metal danced under the pressure of her fingertips. It spread out, connecting with the other tines until they were a solid piece, and then she pushed into it with her thumb. The metal bent backwards like it was soft clay. When she released it, she was holding a spoon. His eyes darted to meet hers, but she was looking across the restaurant, hardly paying attention at all. Panic gripped him in an instant. His hand darted across the table and grabbed the spoon out of her hand, stashing it in his jacket pocket as quickly as he could. She jumped back in alarm, her other hand trying to slap his away. "Hey, what was that for?" she shouted at him. "I'm not finished with my food!" "//Quiet!//" he hissed as he frantically scanned around the room. "What have I //told// you about doing that, daughter? And out in the open like this?" She blinked twice, stunned at his sudden turn. "What are you so worried about? It's just a fork, and there's nobody around to see it. Saves me the trouble of getting up to have to get another-" "It's not //just a fork//," he said, his voice quiet and viscious. "It's never //just a fork//. Don't for a //second// think that there aren't always people watching. Even if they're not watching you //right now//, they will be soon. Don't you understand?" She grabbed a spoon from his side of the table and glared at him. "You worry too much, father. Nobody cares about a fork, or a spoon. It's helpful to me, sure, but it's not important." Dark glasses. Piercing eyes. "You need to make another promise to me," he said, his voice quivering now. "You must promise me that you will never do this again. Now more than ever, it is important that nobody knows what you-" he hesitated, "what you are capable of. They can't know, do you understand me?" Her stare could have cut him to his core. //Just like her mother//. "Are you worried them finding out I can... can change things... will disrupt your career progression? Is that what this is? God, am I that much of an embarrassment to you?" His heart broke. He saw her as a child, taking a little brass monkey and turning it into a snake, and then back again. She laughed, and looked at him for approval. He had smiled. //Why had he smiled?// He had to have known better then, why hadn't he done something sooner? He straightened himself and looked across the table at her. She seemed about to speak, but the indignation caught in her mouth. "I need you to promise me," Yoshihide said in short, measured words. "You need to promise me that you will give that up, forever. It is not about me, Yuzuki. It is about your safety. You may feel comfortable now, and you may very well be safe - now. But all it takes is the wrong person noticing, or saying something to someone else. The only way you can be safe is if they have no reason to suspect you are capable of anything other than the great work you do." He paused. "I love you, daughter, and I want you to be safe. I will continue to work to keep you safe, even if I must climb all the way to Overwatch Command to do it. But I need your help. Please help me." She held still for a moment, as if determining whether or not she wanted to lash out at him again. Then the moment passed, and she relaxed. She smiled a little smile, and reached across to take his hand. He hadn't realized it was shaking until just then. "Don't worry," she said to him. "Everything will be alright. I'll be alright." //Blood coated his hand as he felt hers go cold. Even as she lay dying in the dim light of the headlamps, her eyes saw straight into his soul. She smiled a little smile. "Everything will be alright. I'll be alright. Don't worry."// ----- Months passed. The days, if they ever had a notion of individuality before, abandoned it entirely now as they blurred together in a ceaseless barrage of new tasks and obligations. He would, at times, laugh at the naivety of his youth, when he had imagined himself rising to the level of Site Director to have his pick of great and important projects to work on. He had been among the best containment specialists when he was younger - //the// best, some had claimed, and he knew it every bit as well as they did. He saw intricacies and subtleties that the others missed, and knew how to exploit them. He was occasionally able to convince himself that his rise to the chair he sat in now had been for noble reasons, but deep down he knew the truth. Containment was what he did well. But now his time was filled with endless approvals and reviews, inspection and training. Periodically he would have moments where he was asked his thoughts on a new process, or had a chance to investigate a problem that was troubling his subordinates. Through it all, he began to feel a terrible gripping thing - this was not the work he should be doing. Pushing papers and sorting files was administrative work, surely the Foundation had people who could do that? The chair he sat in, the office, the desk - what was it, actually? Was it a position for him to exert influence? Was it a means by which to change the world? Was it a cage? So it was that a mere three years into his residency as a Site Director, Yoshihide found himself requested to fly out to a place he knew nothing about at the behest of the Overseers. He studied this location as much as he could, but all he gathered was that it was a small, unimportant house deep in the forests of Eastern Europe. Yet, the Overseers would not have called on him for something so meager. There had to be something there that required someone like him. A task that needed his keen intellect and judicious hand. //Actual work//, he thought. He left within the day. It was, as he had presumed, not much more than a tiny wooden house in the middle of the forest. It sat in a small clearing at the end of a long, narrow drive. The clearing was cleared, and a small stack of firewood sat outside the door of the house. The trees stretched tall in all directions around it, and in the dying light of day he almost felt like they were bending in above him, choking off what little of the sun was left before opening up to a deeper darkness. There was a light on inside, and smoke from a chimney. He entered the house. It was modestly furnished. Wooden furniture, woolen rug. Pictures hung on the walls. The most striking thing, aside from the person sitting across from the doorway near the fire, were the many taxidermied heads of animals that filled every other possible inch of wallspace that was not treasured family heirloom or window. Not just taxidermies, either - skulls, in many cases. Some he had never seen before. The animals themselves, whatever was left of them, were strange. Eerily magnificent. Deer, elk, ram, wolf, and then skulls and skins of things he could not name. They stared out with glassy black eyes. Not at him. Not at anything. Then, of course, was the Administrator. Yoshihide had almost forgotten his face from their meeting years before, though his words had never been too distant. He was looking into the fire, his hands folded neatly in his lap. He did not speak as Yoshihide entered, but gestured to another chair beside him. The scene was so bizarre, Yoshihide's mind was too busy racing to realize his body was acknowledging the courtesy and sitting down. "I realize my offer may have left you with expectations that are not currently being met," the Administrator said. His voice was soft, not nearly so bright and genial as it had been that day in his office. "I apologize for any discourtesy, I had only meant to not raise the concerns of anyone who might intercept the message. This place is, by my own design, not a place that one can be so easily followed to." Yoshihide moved to speak, but the words were absent. He had questions, endless questions, and growing concerns, but something in his better nature held his tongue. He distinctly had the feeling as if he was in the presence of something very dangerous, and needed to be very careful. A few moments later, the Administrator continued. "I have been watching your work for some time, Director. You have risen to the challenge of your station, and your staff are dutiful in their fulfillment of the goals of the Foundation. I have no reason to feel anything but satisfaction in your selection to this position." He felt the other man looking at him now. He dared not look back. "And yet," the Administrator said, "I cannot help but feel as if you are not reaching your full potential. I don't mean this as a criticism, of course. The limits of your office are such that, perhaps you are not in the position to best carry out the work at which you are the most capable. Would you agree?" It was a trap. Yoshihide knew it. He saw the snare and felt the tension humming on the line. But the gnawing inside him suddenly flared and he saw a long life lived sitting behind that desk, mindlessly rubber stamping the better work of better men. He was good at what he did. //The// best, some had claimed. The gnawing consumed his growing apprehension. "Yes," he said quietly. The Administrator smiled again. "That's what I thought. Come with me. Grab a jacket if you have one, it's cold out there tonight." ----- The forest around them was still. The energy of distant cities and all the lights of mankind were foreign to a place like this - none of the noise permeated the tall trees and the dense growth below them. The path they walked on was well maintained, though, and the only sound at all was the soft padding of their shoes on dirt. The Administrator carried a lantern, "//an antique, if you can believe it,//" he'd said with a laugh. The light was sufficient to see their path but little beyond it. The forest was everything. "My grandfather always said, //hell is the dark//." The Administrator lifted the light up slightly higher. "He hated these woods. Hated the things in them. Hated the dark. He was paralyzed by the fear of it. This lantern was his, back when the house was as well." He paused for a moment at a large tree. He ran his hand across its surface. The bark was broken - something had been by here. An animal, maybe, something with antlers that had brushed against it. He continued. "He only came out here when he needed food for his family. He would hunt, though he loathed it. The best hunting was at dusk, and if he was out too late, well. Then there was the dark." "Why live in a place like this, then?" Yoshihide asked. "Surely he could've had somewhere closer to a town?" He couldn't see his face, but he knew the Administrator was smiling. "I asked myself the same question, Director. But then, men are drawn to their antithesis, I think. They find comfort in believing they are exposing themselves to something frightful, to them. It makes them feel strong." He took a breath. "My father said //hell is dying//. He didn't mind the dark. Embraced it, actually. He was a hunter, you see - not in the way my grandfather was, out of necessity. My father hunted because he liked it. He enjoyed the chase, enjoyed pitting his wit against the instincts of a beast. He would come home from a hunt - successful or not, with such a //look// on his face. He's been gone for many years, but I can still see his expression. It was rapture. I think he found religion in these woods." He halted, gathering his thoughts, and turned to Yoshihide. "But my father realized what you and I both know. The chase is thrilling, no doubt, but the joy is in //winning//. It's not enough to just follow the beast. A beast can follow a beast. To be able to have the life of something in your hands, well. That's something altogether different, isn't it? That was his work." He turned back to the trail. "When I was very young, I remember being in town with my father when a woman came screaming into the square. Her child had gotten lost in the woods, and some manner of creature had found them. A jackal, maybe, or a wildcat. Maybe even a great boar. Whatever it was, the child had only just survived the encounter, with //survived// being a choice word. The thing, the beast, had chewed off most of the face and much of the skin on the arms raised to defend itself. The soft meat - though I suppose at that age most of the meat is soft. They had managed to escape and run, and by luck had blindly found their way back to their own home. Can you imagine that? Knowing your child is lost in the forest and then feeling the joy at hearing them running back, and then..." He broke off, his gaze turned towards the trees around them. "The thing that came out of the forest was not her child anymore. Not really. It had been changed by the beast. It was a heaving, wretched thing. One ruined eye staring out in horror from behind a face that was little more than strips of meat clinging desperately to shattered bone. A mouth that would have screamed if it was not full of blood. A miserable thing." They carried on in silence for a while longer. After a time, the Administrator paused and knelt down. He picked up something from the path below them - a tooth, something cervid. He put it in his pocket. "My father carved this trail after that child was attacked," he said. "It stretches far and wide across these woods. He spent days, months, years, studying how the creatures in this forest move throughout it. From his hunting posts he watched them, and he noted their behaviour. He kept extensive records. Truthfully, it was how we spent most of our time together, growing up. Together, in silence, up in a tree. Watching the beasts move." He held out his hand and moved it around, as if tracing something in his mind. "They were blameless, of course. Beasts are just beasts, they can't reason the same way you and I can. They aren't //evil//, certainly. But they are dangerous. One of them got a hold of that child, just one, and changed its life forever. I remember seeing it years later, no longer a child but a ghastly, haunted thing. They died young, as I remember, but lived long enough to know true agony. Not just the pain of their injuries, though I'm certain it was severe. No, I believe the greatest pain they felt was the loneliness that followed. They were horrible to look at, and were avoided by neighbors, friends, family. The beast did kill them, in the end, but the dying was not the worst of it. Death is not hell." They came to a fork in the path. The Administrator lifted his lantern again, looking in both directions. "So my father cut this path. He found that they tended to follow on the edge of cleared spaces, and would follow these trails to wherever they would lead. In his mind, I believe, my father had always intended to just shephard them away from the town, somewhere deeper into the forest. But this trail is just a box without a lid, Director. It is not enough to put them in a cage if the cage has no door." They turned left at the fork and continued forward. "One night he was maintaining this trail, and a bear found him. I wonder sometimes if, in his last moments, he regretted simply delaying what had suddenly become inevitable for him. It was not as if he did not enjoy hunting. Maybe he thought this simply was not sporting. I doubt the bear cared either way." He let out a sigh, pausing briefly. "Do you see now, Yoshihide? Do you understand? We are all the children of our fathers. He learned from his father, who learned from his before him. All of them flawed men. My father had vision, but lacked execution. He cut this trail for beasts knowing they would get caught in it, but did not live long enough to realize for himself the true fulfillment of that vision. That's what we are. We are that fulfillment-" They came to a clearing. In the dark he saw nothing, but felt something moving in the space in front of him. Something writhing. Something foul. The Administrator lifted his lantern, and Yoshihide gasped. "-and this is the lid on the box." A mountain of corpses. Some old, some new. Some still wriggling in agony from their butchery, desperately clinging to the meager life remaining in them. All of them stacked together in a groaning, heaving pile. Eyes that stared out at nothing. Beasts of all shapes and sizes, but not just beasts - men as well, white jackets stained with blood that soaked into the groundwater. Some of them gunned down, perhaps. Others cut apart by cruel instruments. A tower of torment and despair, of misery that could not be understood, and across the entire forest not a single sound to be heard. "In the end, we are just problem solvers," the Administrator said. His voice felt very far away, and every bit of the geniality of their first encounter had long fled. "The problem is that the world is sick. For my father, for this town, it was beasts. Beasts that can devour a mother foraging for food. Beasts that can bite and poison you until you long for a quicker death than you are afforded. Beasts that tear the soft meat off a child's bones. But for us, the beasts are more insidious. They are not always beasts we can see. But we are careful, and we are patient. We have cut our own path in the woods. We lead them to the clearing, and then we solve the problem." He lowered the lantern, and the light cast over the high grave retreated. "There have been others like you. Like me. Those who could not handle this knowledge. Presented with the scope of what we must do they would quake and quiver and beg to return to their meager lives of tepid normalcy. They were a problem, too - in their own way. You are very good at what you do, Yoshihide. There is no questioning that you are competent. What I want to know is whether you are //capable//." His voice was barely a whisper now. "//This// is how we keep the world safe - we complete the work of our fathers. They were men of limited vision. We are not. We will preserve the world - //that// is our Work." He was suddenly in front of Yoshihide. His face was a mask and behind it was something with //intention//. Yoshihide felt his skin go cold. "We cannot make exceptions, Director," he said softly. "Exceptions lead to pain, and horror. A rabid dog must still be put down, regardless of whether or not it once came when you called. We do not have the luxury to choose. We can only perform the task in front of us." He paused, considering the director. "I asked you once if you were prepared to do the Work, and you said you were. You have performed your task. Now, look at what we must do. See what is required for us to keep this world safe. I ask you again - are you prepared to do the Work?" Yoshihide felt the panic rising inside him again. His heartbeat quickened. His vision began to swim and shimmer, but something else now rose within him to accompany the anxiety. He would have felt sick, but this new sensation overwhelmed all else. The fear slipped away, and then he thought of nothing but the desk, and the papers, and the chair. Despite himself, he was lost in his own grim desire. "Yes." He had never meant anything more in his life. "Let's go back, then," the Administrator said. "I have something I need you to do." They turned back down the trail. If Yoshihide had been aware of anything other than the sea of thoughts he was lost in, he may have noticed the Administrator staring at him from behind. His skin may have prickled at the malice radiating off him. He might have felt the tension in the line. @@ @@ @@ @@ [[=]] ++++ ACT II ++ [[[the-path-of-swords|THE PATH OF SWORDS]]] [[/=]] @@ @@ @@ @@ [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box |author=djkaktus]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:license-box-end]]

the-unseen-that-lurks.raw_content:
"My name is Dr. Dan, greatest cryptid hunter in the state of South Dakota."

Cleanup on Aisle Five

The Unseen That Lurks

{$next-title}

Fort Pierre National Grassland

South Dakota

Night.

The wind howled through the tall grass of the prairie. Little could be seen in the pitch-black darkness, save for silent shadows that crept across the brush. With nothing but the dim light of the crescent moon to illuminate the landscape, there was no doubt that all sorts of horrors would be out prowling the grasslands.

When the biting winds died down, the only sound left that could be heard was of footsteps. Boots crunched on the late autumn foliage — boots belonging to a hunter by the name of Dr. Dan. An ex-military cryptozoologist, nothing had ever escaped Dan's hawk-like sights — and the cryptid he was hunting today was no exception.

The Unseen That Lurks.

Every so often, a hiker in the grasslands of South Dakota would go missing without a trace. The residents said it was because of a local cryptid — eight foot frame, pale gray skin, grotesquely long arms, and a blood-curdling scream. No photos of it existed, supposedly all covered up by the FBI. But that wouldn't stop Dan. He had spent the last twenty years searching for The Unseen That Lurks, but he knew today was the day he'd find it — and put an end to its terror.

A bush rustled. A lesser hunter would have overlooked such a minute detail, but Dan's fine-tuned instincts alerted him to the noise instantly. Donning his state-of-the-art SCRAMBLE Visor, Dan scanned the landscape up and down for signs of his target. He carefully unholstered his scoped Blaser R93, cradling the heavy sniper rifle in his arms.

In the corner of his eye, a shadow moved. The hunt was on.

Dan moved methodically, a shadow among shadows. He made no sound, creeping through the brush as he stalked his prey. Even the slightest motion, the slightest scent, would alert him. He crouched low in the grass, heart hammering harder than the time he fought apex predators in the Amazon. Each breath was slow and deliberate, fogging in the biting cold. His eyes, narrowed beneath the visor, scanned the horizon, mentally marking each feature of the landscape.

Then he saw it. Just beyond the edge of a dried cornfield, about five hundred feet away. Tall. Lanky. Eight feet tall, skin like gray leather. Dan's eyes narrowed, and a smile grew on his face. Visual acquired. That's my target.

He flicked the safety off. Raised the rifle. Scoped in.

The figure didn’t move. Didn’t breathe.

It's toying with me.

Dan hesitated. His breath stilled. Something in his gut tightened.

He pulled the trigger.

The sound of the gunshot echoed throughout the hills, alerting all of his victory. Without even a moment to scream, the target fell over sideways, landing in the grass.

…

A sense of triumph filled Dan's heart and mind. After two decades of relentless pursuit, he, Dr. Dan, had finally brought an end to to the ceaseless struggle between man and cryptid. Long thought to be nothing more than an urban myth, he had now proven to all that The Unseen That Lurks had always been there — at least, until the brave hunter had brought it to a swift end.

With trembling hands, Dan removed his visor, and gripped the rifle with which he had shot the creature. Uncrouching from his position to his full height, he approached the fallen target carefully. Every sleepless night, he thought, every goddamn mile I trekked, every fucking time I thought I had the beast, only to lose it at the last moment. It wasn't all for nothing. He began to cackle as he crept toward the culmination of twenty years of sweat and tears, knowing his prize was waiting.

But as Dan approached the body, illuminating it with his flashlight, the laughter died in his throat. The body was wearing ripped flannel and jeans. The smell was not of animal musk, but of dirt, grime, and time.

His mouth went dry. He lowered the rifle, hands trembling slightly now.

"God," he breathed. "Oh, god."

His eyes scanned the limbs. One arm was twisted beneath the body. The head was tilted at an unnatural angle, but not unnatural enough.

That’s a fucking person.

The thought hit him like a blow to the chest. His knees buckled. He staggered back a step, mouth ajar, heart pounding.

No. No no no no. He looked around, eyes wide in panic. He shouldn’t have been out here. Why would — why would anyone be dressed like that?

A low panic started bubbling in his chest. "Are you kidding me?!" he yelled at the man, who was mortally wounded if not already dead.

All of Dan's muscles tensed up. He felt a feeling he hadn't felt since a hodag scratched his arm down in the town of Sloth's Pit. He felt rage. I thought I had my target, but it turns out it was some dumbfuck standing around at night!

No. Dan froze. I need to think logically. Dan surveyed the area, eyes lingering at every swaying stalk of corn reaching just barely below his head. I have the instincts of a bloodhound and the mind of Socrates. He crept toward the fallen man, approaching his limp body, cloaked amidst the corn stalks. Now is the time when I must ignore the former and follow the latter. He grasped his rifle in a white-knuckle grip. And my logical mind says…

Leave no witnesses.

Dan positioned himself so that neither could see the other's head. He aimed his rifle for a second shot. The Unseen That Lurks is my life. His finger flush against the trigger, Dan gritted his teeth, his heart racing and sweat pooling within his camo clothing. So what's one life for another?

A second shot rang out. A grin crept up onto Dan's face. If it weren't for the fact that he'd just killed a man he'd be cackling, swimming in his own single-minded determination like a snallygaster through its hoard of treasure. Shoving aside stalks of corn in his way, he strutted up to his quarry, equal parts delighted and horrified to see the fatal blow he had inflicted upon it.

Only to find a man made of straw.

A third sound reverberated through the area — the howls of the great cryptid hunter, Dr. Dan.

Dr. Dan’s knuckles turned white as he gripped his Jeep’s steering wheel. He stared blankly into the nothingness of the prairie night, engine idling as the second shot still echoed in his head.

A scarecrow.

A motherfucking scarecrow.

He slammed his fist on the dashboard. The glove box popped open. He ignored it.

He'd been fooled.

Again.

Dan had planned this hunt for weeks. Days mapping out the terrain, consulting wind charts, compiling decades of local folklore into a single spiral-bound notebook — one he was now scrawling into pathetically. Target uses misidentification tactics to evade capture.

He snapped the book shut.

Enough was enough.

Two Days Later

Dr. Dan sat hunched on a folding chair in front of a map duct-taped to the inside of his three-person tent. Strings — some yarn, some twine, some made from whatever fibers he could pull from the Jeep’s upholstery — connected pins that marked "Likely Lurking Zones," "Possible Hideouts," and “Suspicious Crop Patterns.”

All of it pointed to here.

So he would force The Unseen to make a move.

Dan had spent the past two days preparing the prairie with traps: tripwires, snares, and hidden pits. The grasslands were no longer a safe place for anything foolish enough to take a step. And to make sure nothing could escape undetected, Dan set up a costly, but foolproof series of trail cameras — every inch of the area was covered in surveillance. If that thing made a move, he would know. If The Unseen That Lurks took so much as a single breath, Dan would catch it.

Each trap was more elaborate than the last. He had spent a full two days laying them out in concentric rings around his tent, muttering equations to himself. When it was done, he limped back to his chair, bone-tired and shivering.

Dr. Dan sat in his tent, scribbling into the crumpled notebook. He munched his half-eaten hot dog, the stale meaty taste rotating the well-oiled cogs of his mind. He had vanquished every cryptid in North America, from the common jackalope to the elusive Loveland frogman, and they all followed a pattern. His time in the Congo, the Jersey Pine Barrens, even that regrettable week at Bradshaw Ranch — it always started with a sighting.

Cryptids act out when exposed. When their face is seen.

He stared out into the dry grass as it rustled to and fro in the light winds.

What I need… is a photo.

Pierre

South Dakota

Dan exited the Jeep and beelined toward the nearest convenience store. The bell above the door jingled weakly as he entered, sweat-soaked and grimy. He rushed toward the rack of newspapers, grabbing every one in sight.

The cashier stared at him. "You gonna pay for those?"

Dan stared back, and threw his last ten dollars on the counter. "Knowledge has no price," he muttered.

He crouched behind a shelf in the back, dropped his pile, and began to sift. With his hunter's gaze, he scanned the pages up and down for anything that could be of use. Hell, even a few fucking pixels will do it.

Missing hiker. No photo.

Weird footprints. No photo.

UFO sightings. Not relevant.

He was about to give up when something strange caught his eye — an ad, tucked between listings for pest control and psychic readings.

"SCP Foundation," it read, "Cleanliness Guaranteed!*"

Beneath the ad was a black-and-white photo of a crudely-made, peanut-shaped sculpture, with the floor beneath it covered in what looked like viscous liquid shit. Gross, he thought, but serviceable. The ad said something about a federal contract. The logo struck a chord, too — three inward-facing arrows, a code scrawled faintly in the center.

Dan’s eyes widened. Cryptid code. He leapt to his feet, nearly overturning the booth. His chair slammed against the wall. The cashier blinked. Dan pointed to the photo.

“This is it,” he whispered.

Dan dashed out of the store and climbed into his Jeep. Wrenching the keys into the ignition switch, he slammed his foot on the accelerator. The battered vehicle sputtered to life.

Not long after, Dr. Dan pulled into the parking lot of 1630 Lowell Avenue, Pierre, South Dakota — referred to in the ad as "Site 19." How many facilities does this company have, anyway? The building was unremarkable on the outside, with various trailers parked in its sizable lot, as well as a howitzer for some reason. If they have more than nineteen locations, and each building is this size… I could be out of my league here — if that's even possible.

Dan climbed out of his Jeep, gritted his teeth, and walked slowly toward the nearest entrance, pausing for a moment.

He breathed in. He breathed out. As he had done several times in the past sixty seconds, he stared menacingly at the laminated sheet of paper taped above the double doors, "SAFE CLEANUP PROFESSIONALS FOUNDATION" printed in bold font. Dan squinted at the secret message placed upon the logo of three inward-facing arrows. Barely visible, the silhouette nonetheless lit up his eyes. Now what could 'AWCY? STOCK' mean? Cryptids have, in the past, been known for leaving secret messages, and since a hunter must think like his prey, an experienced cryptid hunter must leave secret messages as well. Clearly, these were professionals.

Dan readied his fist. He calibrated the amount of strength he would project onto the front door of the establishment. Enough to create a commanding presence, enough to show that he meant business, enough to demonstrate to this rival organization that Dr. Dan was currently the top cryptid hunter in the entirety of Pierre, South Dakota, and that he would get answers goddammit. He accelerated his fist toward the door in the same motion one might stab an assailant, spittle flying as he clenched his jaw. By the end of it all, the Foundation would know his name.

The door opened at just the right moment for him to punch the air.

"Hello?" a man with scruffy brown hair and a fedora replied, standing tall in the middle of the now-open doorway. Dan grunted, wiping the dust from his 'borrowed' clothing. A smile crept back onto his face as he stood tall, a full head above the man standing in front of him. The corner of his face twitched.

"My name is Dr. Dan, greatest cryptid hunter in the state of South Dakota," he replied, enunciating each syllable with the force of a '50 caliber round. A twinge of doubt racked his eyes, as he debated internally whether he should have expanded the scope of his superlative to encompass the entire continental United States. He held out a hand to shake, to which the man in the fedora obliged. The man sucked in air as Dan's vice-like grip turned his palm a bony white before rattling his arm two and fro like a chew toy in the jaws of the Michigan Dogman.

The man in the fedora exhaled with relief as Dan released him, shaking his hand. Something clicked. "Oh, hey, you're the guy that called earlier!" he exclaimed, beckoning him to enter the establishment. Dan steeled himself as he crossed the front desk into the building proper.

"I'm the Administrator. But people here just call me Fritz." He grinned as he led Dan through Site 19. "I suppose you don't need to introduce yourself — I mean, top cryptid hunter in the state, right?"

Dan responded with only a grunt. His attention was on the building itself — his analytical mind was already calculating where and how he might uncover his next clue to The Unseen That Lurks.

"You called cuz' you wanted to see our collection of cryptids? Well, we're no stranger to anomalies here!"

The musty warehouse that surrounded Dan sent a tingle down his spine. He had seen shacks. He had seen log cabins. He'd seen a storage unit a rival of his rented out because his wife didn't want the jackalope skull in the living room. Serves him right. The damn thing's just a rabbit with deer antlers glued to it. He'd seen apartments and he'd seen McMansions and he'd seen local businesses adorned with the paraphernalia and the spoils of his trade. And he'd catalogued all his findings in his head, in his mental ledger, in his strict, objective ranking of all the hunters across the world whom thus far had had the displeasure to host him.

But a cryptid warehouse?

Never had he seen a warehouse.

As Fritz led him down a corridor, passing various offices and whatnot, Dan's predatory eyes scanned across the Safe Cleanup Professionals' abode in a full 360 degrees. The hair on the back of Fritz's neck stood on end as the image of Inspector Cimmerian flashed through his head, superimposed on top of the stone-faced man now standing in front of him.

Dan's gaze flitted back and forth as they entered the storage area. The air smelled vaguely of coffee and beer. Mops and brooms and buckets were piled in a corner. Cardboard boxes were strewn about the floor. Industrial-size barrels of concentrated bleach lay stacked in a pattern resembling a stone-age ruin. A pile of orange slime was festering in the corner, emanating a scent of deodorant. Most impressively, an entire fallen-over forklift with both windows broken was plopped at the far side of the room like the carcass of a megafaunal creature.

Phew. They're just janitors, in over their heads. Their skills must pale in comparison to my complete mastery of the art of the hunt.

Dan maintained his stone face. He would have to betray no emotion, lest he intimidate these feeble custodians.

"Alright, Fritz. Show me where you keep the good stuff. Who knows — I might take interest in, ah, endowing your operations."

Fritz inhaled quickly, nodding. "Of… of course. Let's get started." He led Dan down the corridor to the other side of the building. To their left and right were four rooms, each furnished with a heavy door.

Fritz motioned to the first one on the left. "We'll start with the one that put us on the map. Plug your nose."

He opened the door to reveal one of their storage rooms. The air was filled with a putrid scent that assaulted Dan's nostrils. Inside, a shipping container sat in the middle of the room, the bulkhead open. Viscous brown sludge poured out of the opening, coating the floor. The source of the foul substance was the statue from the newspaper ad — now clearly visibly made of pale brown concrete and pieces of rebar.

"Here's our first — I mean, one-hundred-and-seventy-third cleanup," Fritz said proudly. "SCP-173, The Sculpture, The Peanut — it goes by many names. I'd make it a local attraction if it weren't for the feds, hah."

He squinted. "It’s not moving." A cheap parlor trick.

"It only moves when you’re not looking," Fritz said with a forced chuckle. "If we both blink at the same time we can — actually, that's probably not a good idea. Right! On to the next!"

Fritz quickly ushered him out through the door, slamming it behind them. Fritz darted across the hall as Dan followed, boots echoing on concrete.

"Behold — cleanup number six-eighty-two! The Lake Oahe Monster!" Fritz threw open a second door. An industrial-size vat, seven feet tall or so, sat squarely in the center of the room.

Dan peered in. "That’s a dead alligator."

"It’s molting," Fritz grumbled, flicking a switch. Bubbles filled the vat. The decomposing creature within sloshed about lazily in the tank.

“It’s still not doing anything." Charlatans. I've bagged creatures bigger than this.

"Hmm. Must be a little shy today." Fritz shut the door faster this time. "Oh wait — that's it!"

A smirk bled through Dan's emotionless face as Fritz scampered off down the hall like the timid Sasquatch. And I thought my position was under threat, he mused while Fritz accelerated to a jog. Dan kept up near effortlessly with his sweeping strides. Though this likely means they'll have no useful intel about The Unseen That Lurks. Oh well. I'll build my rapport and ask when the time comes.

"GERALD, STOP THE TRUCK!" Fritz shouted as the two neared the loading bay, barely cutting above the deafening sound of the semi-truck's engine. The sound abruptly halted.

"Geez Louise!" came from the driver's seat. "Scared the fuckin' daylights outta me, Big Willie! Whatcha got here?" A six-foot man in a tank top exited the vehicle.

"Stay here for just a moment," Fritz said to Dan with his signature toothy grin. He stormed toward the truck driver.

"Gerald," Fritz whispered, "First thing, don't call me 'Big Willie.' Second—" He pointed at the truck. "Is this thing awake?"

Gerald recoiled from Fritz's coffee breath. "It's moping in the corner, but if you rattle the cage I'm sure it'll—"

"This is serious, Gerald," Fritz interrupted, shaking the Foundation's driver like a ragdoll. He stared him in the eyes. "That man is the top cryptid hunter in the state. If we want him to put in a good word for us we need our anomalies to be… well… anomalous! Can you guarantee that —"

"Look, Fritz," Gerald replied. "That thing reminds me of me back in seventh grade. It hates people and'll happily do anything to avoid the attention. If that means playing dead or—"

"I know that Dan guy is a hardass but—"

"Fritz, you moron, I'm talkin' about the thing in the truck!"

"Fuck it," Fritz said, sprinting back towards Dan. "Sorry to keep ya waiting!"

Fritz frantically messed with the locks of the trailer's door, Dan's gaze a baleful scourge upon his back. "C'mon," he muttered, undoing the both of them.

Once again, thought Dan as Fritz floundered around like a hapless chupacabra with one of its legs stuck in a bear trap, the doors of the truck stuck on a deadbolt he had yet to open. Once again my opponents prove themselves mere amateurs, dabbling in things far exceeding their understanding, desperately attempting to convince the world that their hubris does not exceed their sham discoveries. I am a true pioneer — a true explorer — a true hunter — the only one with the grit to venture beyond that which humanity considers 'normal.' It's a damn shame that there aren't others like me, that there aren't others willing to seek answers in the unknown. It's almost disappointing, dare I say. It's quite—

The doors to the truck slammed open.

Within a cage sat a pale, gangly, roughly human-shaped creature with a paper bag over its head, butt naked, huddling in the corner. It whimpered like a child with the sunlight shining on its body. Dan eyes widened as he examined the beast, the gears in his mind turning through the multitude of possibilities by which it could be considered to be less impressive than the most outrageous of his own hunts. But as the trickle of possibilities ran dry and as he finished matching the physical characteristics of the beast to his mental database of cryptid lore, the answer dawned upon him, sending bile into his throat.

The Unseen That Lurks.

…

…

…

"H- how— how did you acquire the…?" Dan stammered, his words falling over themselves like the legs of a freshly-shot buck.

"Oh, we didn't acquire it," Fritz replied nonchalantly. "We caught it. Don't know what it is other than that the feds didn't want it in Pierre."

Dan attempted to match the potential cryptid capturer to the faces he had seen within the past ten minutes. "W- wh- who- who did—"

"Oh, just the intern. Kid's got a knack for it," Fritz said.

Dan fell to his knees.

"One of our easier jobs, to be honest. Can't even break out of a zip tie."

Moisture welled up in his eyes.

"We're dropping it off somewhere in Minnesota. Controls the deer population and all."

His stomach wrung itself like a wet towel.

"Twenty years." Dan whimpered. A tear dripped from each of his eyes. "Twenty fucking years. All for nothing."

"You doing alright?" Fritz said, nervously approaching the distraught Dr. Dan.

Dan did not move from his position.

"Hello? Earth to Dan? Earth to Dr. Daniels? Earth to the top cryptid hunter in South D—"

"In America," Dan snapped, standing up as straight as a pole. He wiped the tears from his eyes.

No. Dan thought, surveying the surroundings with his eagle eyes. Not like this. He took a deep breath. Think. Think logically. These people were simply lucky. They were at the right place at the right time.

"Riiight," Fritz trailed off. "Can I get you a tissue? You seem a tad… congested."

They didn't put in the work. They didn't put in the effort. They're simply a group of amateurs who stumbled across it when it was weak and exhausted from the twenty years it's spent running from me.

"No," Dan replied.

"A— are you sure?" Fritz asked. He adjusted his hat and his shirt. "It's really no problem at all, we have some antihistamines that—"

"The creature in the truck," Dan blurted out.

"Wh- what about it?" Fritz replied, averting his eyes from Dan's piercing gaze.

"I mean. You've clearly spent… a great deal of effort attempting to catch this creature, have you not?"

Fritz forced a chuckle. "Well, I don't mean to toot my own horn, but it really wasn't that hard." Dan flinched. He took a deep breath.

"Well," Dan added, the corners of his mouth twitching as he resisted the shit-eating grin spreading across his face, "As a show of goodwill toward your organization, would you be open to… me… taking it off your hands?" Dan gestured to the truck.

"Wait just a moment right there, buddy," Gerald growled from behind Fritz, "I ain't lettin' my gig get replaced by an upstart like you."

Dan silently pulled his credit card out of his wallet. "Compensation can be arranged."

"Gerald, shut it. We're discussing business," Fritz replied.

"I see how it is," Gerald barked, "I'm gonna go ask the cops if this is even legal." The man stormed off into the loading bay.

"Sorry about him," Fritz chuckled.

"So…" Dan said, swallowing his sobs.

"Okay. Right," Fritz said, "Oh-ninety-six. Listen, we're honored to have the best cryptid hunter in America interested in one of our cleanups, but, you see…"

"Explain," Dan growled.

"We, uh, can't just hand it off to anyone. We wish we could! And I don't mean to imply that you're just any old cryptid hunter. I mean, if we were able to hand it off, we'd hand it off to you, but—"

"What?" Dan barked. "So what's stopping you from handing it over?" He loomed over Fritz's meek figure.

"I- I mean, we can't just put oh-ninety-six anywhere. There's laws we have to follow here. The feds only gave us authorization to send it off to Minnesota, and, on the off chance that you—"

Dan forced a chuckle from his trembling throat, which came out more like a wheeze. "I fully intend on taking it to, ah, Minnesota."

"But," Fritz replied, "If you don't, then we're getting in trouble. And while I respect the highly courageous approach you take to the business of cryptid hunting… we, unfortunately, need to keep our contract with the FBI. That we get 90% of our revenue from."

"You misunderstand," Dan replied coldly. He clenched his fists in his pockets. "Cryptozoological law is of utmost importance to me." He forced a smile, his yellowed teeth showing. "So hand over the creature."

Fritz sighed. "Out of curiosity, why do you want oh-ninety-six so much in particular? I don't mean to question your taste in cryptids, it's just— we have a lot of other ones you could have, so, why this one? This one's not that interesting—"

"Not. That. Interesting?" Dan said through gritted teeth. "The Holy Grail of cryptids is not that interesting?"

"Wait, wait, wait," Fritz faltered, "Sorry, sorry, didn't mean to hit a nerve. But… are you saying this thing's actually worth something?"

"No, no, no, no, no," Dan stammered. "I jest. I mean, it's like you said. It's worthless. It's weak. It's. Easy. To capture. Really, it'll just look tacky in your collection of—"

"In that case…" Fritz said. Dan's heart pounded with anticipation. "…why do you want it so much if it's worthless?"

Neither Fritz nor Dan said a word for the next few moments. A tension filled the air. It was as if tripwires surrounded the two of them, and any move could spring hundreds at once.

"Can I have it?" Dan said. His eyes darted back and forth. Something.

"Unfortunately, I can't think of a way to make it happen," Fritz replied, sighing. "I wish I could, but—"

"But I need it!" Dan exclaimed, restraining himself from shouting. Anything.

"I hate to say it," Fritz replied, "But this isn't something we can do. I realize your time is valuable, and I don't want to keep you here for longer."

Dan swallowed. He inhaled deeply.

"Fine," he spat. "If you’re content to check the boxes and toss it in a forest, be my guest. But some of us… like to do something worth remembering."

Fritz's mouth opened, then closed. "I— I don't know if—" He exhaled slowly.

"Okay. You… can have it."

"I— can?" Dan enunciated, hunter instincts on the alert for any surprises.

"Yeah," Fritz sighed, "oh-ninety-six is yours." He looked over his shoulder toward Gerald, two police officers from the dock flanking him. He leaned in, lowering his volume. "Just— as far as the cops are concerned, it ended up in Minnesota."

"Thank you," Dan said, grinning widely. The hunt is back on.

"I'll put in a good word for your organization at the next cryptid conference. What was your company called again? I—"

"Hold it," a voice sounded from behind him. There stood Gerald, accompanied by two policemen.

"What's the problem, officer?" Dan hissed. His heart pounded.

"Fritz, what's Dan doin' by the truck?" Gerald barked. "I thought ya said you weren't lettin' 'im have it!"

"Oh, I changed my mind! He can have it." Fritz said.

"Fritz, we don't even know this guy!" Gerald shouted. "You're withholdin' my pay and givin' away a potentially dangerous animal to some rando you never met? I'm not givin' him the keys!" He turned to the cops. "There's gotta be somethin' illegal 'bout this!"

"Legally, you're all in the clear," one officer said, a clipboard and pen in his hands. "As long as he has a valid driver's license — and I don't see why he wouldn't — we don't care who drives the animal to Minnesota. S'long as it gets there."

"Gerald, he's the top cryptid hunter in the US!" Fritz said. "And he said he'd compensate us for the effort. Give Dan the keys, Gerald."

"Okay, fine," he grumbled. He rummaged through his pocket and pulled out a keychain. "It's the silver one. Just don't total the damn thing. Rental company's already on my ass about it."

"Glad we're all on the same page," Fritz sighed.

Finally, Dan thought, as Gerald reached out his arm, the keychain nearly within his grip. Finally, The Unseen That Lurks is in my grasp. The culmination of twenty years of effort. The sum total of my life's work, a demonstration of my razor-sharp wit, honed to perfection. And, really, I wouldn't have it any other way than this. Because the best professionals become leaders. And the best leaders don't do. They delegate. And delegate I have done. With my silver tongue I have lured The Unseen That Lurks directly into Pierre, where I tricked a group of amateurs into capturing it for me. I am truly the ringleader of a cryptid empire, and the 'Safe Cleanup Professionals' are naught but puppets hanging from—

"Actually, just so we don't get one of y'all whinin' 'bout it later," one of the officers said, gesturing towards Dan, "how 'bout we check your ID first?"

"Sounds alright with me," Fritz chimed in.

Dan leered at Fritz, before sighing and retracting his arm. He pulled out his driver's license from his wallet. The officer squinted at the plastic card.

"From Florida, male, name is… Daniel Daniels?"

"That sounds fake."

"Indeed it does. No way in hell is that real."

The first cop turned the license over in his hands. "Expired, too. Says here you’re 70? You don’t look a day over 55."

"I try to live healthy," Dan said through his teeth.

The cop didn’t smile. "Hm. You know, I think I saw a bulletin come through last night — something about a guy in camo and sunglasses, six-five, seen laying illegal traps off Highway 14."

"Big dude," the second cop added. “Sound familiar to you?”

"Nope," Dan said. "Could’ve been anyone. Lotta tall cryptid hunters around these parts."

"With barbed caltrops?" the first officer asked, nodding to the pouch on Dan’s belt.

"That’s a collector’s item."

The cop raised an eyebrow. "It’s also illegal as hell. Especially outside city limits."

Dan took a step back. "Now, hold on. I’m trying to help. You don’t understand the importance of what’s inside that truck."

"No," the officer replied, hand resting on his cuffs. "I do understand. I just don’t trust you with it."

Dan swallowed.

"I understand that you both do an important public service."

"Now, don't try an' butter us up, that ain't gonna—"

He pulled out his wallet. "And a public service needs proper compensation."

The two officers glanced at one another, and then back at Dan's wallet. They both nodded. "Well," one of them said after a brief pause, "I suppose we could let you off with a warning."

"That'd be wonderful," Dan said, grinning. He opened the wallet.

Only to find it devoid of cash.

His smile faltered. He began to rummage through the wallet's many folds of leather, sifting through long-expired gift cards and random memorabilia and photos of his most prized kills.

He pulled out two coins.

"These are antique, limited edition…" Dan finally proclaimed, squinting at the coins…

"2006 quarters."

The cops' expressions narrowed.

…

"Come with us, bud."

Decades of cryptid hunting had gotten Dr. Daniel Daniels into numerous altercations — twenty outstanding warrants in fifteen counties, a laundry list of enemies, and several scars, only about a third of which were from wild animals.

"You're…"

His grief was replaced by a surge of adrenaline. No. Not like this.

"under…"

He dug the tips of his combat boots into the gravel…

"arrest."

…and bolted.

"HEY!"

Dan sprinted through the Site 19 parking lot, making a beeline for his Jeep. His decades of experience trekking through the woods more than outmactched the minimal exercise his pair of pursuers had undertaken. He leapt into the driver's seat and jammed in the key, the engine coughing and wheezing as the vehicle roared to life, splattering droplets of oil all over his parking spot. Feeling his lunch slosh around in his stomach, he twisted his jeep around the parking lot and out onto the main road, performing the left turn that Fritz always hated with near-perfect precision.

Dan floored the gas as alternating flashes of red and blue filled his rear- and side-view mirrors like dots on a night-vision scope. Several curses exited his mouth in rapid succession. Oh well, he thought, clenching his jaws as he weaved between sluggish seventy mile-per-hour traffic. The hunt isn't over. As soon as those pompous garbagemen deliver The Unseen, I'll be there waiting.

"M I N N E S O T A," he typed into the GPS receiver, vibrating on his dash.

TURN LEFT. The blood rushed to the right side of his head. His heart pumped louder.

TURN RIGHT. Five seconds later the cops followed suit, struggling to match Dan's precision. He snickered, glancing at the county line on the GPS. Their jurisdiction only extended so far.

A sharp pop-pop-pop rattled from beneath the Jeep's tires. Dan's eyes turned wide. He nearly bit his cheek, as his vehicle jerked to a slow with an audible hiss. All over the asphalt were caltrops — his caltrops, placed to prevent The Unseen from escaping. Now, of course, they worked perfectly — on him.

With his margin more than cut in half, Dan slammed his full weight on the accelerator. The Jeep jerked and shuddered as it barreled down the road. As he wrenched vigorously for control over the vehicle, his eyes darted back and forth between the road and the GPS display, mentally crossing off each unpaved service road one after the next. Sweat pooled in his armpits. Too short. Too hilly. This one's flooded. This one's gated. This one's—

A star-shaped icon appeared on the map, a campfire placed within it.

A gasp left Dan's mouth.

He twisted the steering wheel to the right in one sharp motion, kicking up enough gravel to furnish an aquarium for the Loch Ness Monster. Should've done this in the first place, Dan thought, Police cars can't handle this terrain. He chuckled as the red-and-blue strobe dimmed from a piercing flash to a comfortable glow. Several forks in the road littered the GPS readout, as Dan barreled toward the oncoming ditch. Perfect.

Wait.

Ditch?

The Jeep lurched downwards, sending Dan careening into the steering wheel. The metallic twinge of blood spattered across his tongue. The sound of the vehicle's chassis crumpling echoed beneath him with a sickening crunch. It was his ditch, dug two summers ago to catch The Unseen That Lurks — and forgotten afterwards.

Dan gathered himself, and kicked the door open, his rifle in tow. He scampered out the door and into the prairie, abandoning the Jeep. His hair stood on end as he heard the sound of rubber screeching behind him. Six car doors slammed shut. Foliage rattled.

Dan trampled through the thick vegetation. His stomach churned. His eyes were bloodshot. His heart pumped faster than it had any right to be at his age. Slimy strands of saliva dripped from his mouth like a rabid dog as he pushed onward, dragged along only by the yoke of certain freedom. A triumphant sneer took shape on Dan's face as his boots clomped along the… unstable soil. Soil that gave way to his two-hundred-eighty pounds of body weight.

His stomach dropped.

His ankle crunched.

The rest of his body hit the ground, ten feet below the surface of a false blanket of fallen leaves and sediment.

If the loud thump hadn't already alerted the cops, his ensuing howl of pain made his presence known to every living thing within a mile.

He clawed his way up one hand at a time, his fingers gripping into the soil, his already-injured right ankle throbbing with enough pain to just barely poke through the surge of adrenaline running through him. Barely managing to scale over the edge, he galloped forward on all fours before stumbling into a pathetic limp, hopping on one foot while a man clad in a deep blue uniform emerged from the bushes, five more in hot pursuit.

Before the cop had the chance to say "FREEZE," Dan's forty-year-old muscle memory had already activated. He'd pulled the trigger on his rifle, which he'd squarely placed at the precise angle for a headshot.

The sight would've been more gruesome if he'd had any ammunition to load it with.

Dan dropped the rifle. Six standard-issue pistols stared him down.

"Wait! Don't shoot! — You'll blow the proximity mines!"

The cops went silent, eyes darting around in panic.

Dan broke out into a hacking cackle. "Just kidding," he choked. "I forgot where I buried them."

"Looks like you're comin' with us," grumbled the same officer from before. "You're under arrest."

Dr. Daniel Daniels sat handcuffed to a cheap plastic chair, his eyes glazed over as the half-dead fluorescent bulb flickered overhead. Another chair sat opposite to him on an equally cheap table. His eyes darted around. A knife. A pencil. A paperclip. Anything. Anything. He grunted as he pushed himself against the chair, scooting around in no direction in particular like a beached megalodon flopping about on land.

A tired, middle-aged man stamped into the room, rubbing his temples. "I'm giving Williams an earful after this," he muttered. Dan squinted his eyes. Senior Inspector Jeremiah Cimmerian, his nametag read, FBI Unusual Incidents Unit. The agent plopped himself into the unoccupied chair.

"Daniel… Daniels, was it?"

"That's Doctor Daniel Daniels," Dan muttered under his breath.

"You got a PhD, son?"

"In cryptozoological studies."

Cimmerian raised an eyebrow, folding his hands on the table. "Explains a lot."

He slid a manila envelope across the table.

"Open this."
