February 2, 1987

The stale scent of smoked cigars, sweat, and cheap coffee hung heavy in the air of the Serbian safe house. The house's walls were empty save for a pinup calendar on the wall, depicting a grinning white blonde woman holding both of her breasts in her hands with the text “GOOD FOR LIFE!" for February plastered across her bikini like a twisted affirmation.

Agent Ukulele tapped his worn leather boot against the concrete floor. His thoughts weren't on the previous mission, they weren't on the safe house, and they weren't on the blood that was still lodged under his short, bitten fingernails.

They were on Lilly.

She was a knot twisting and turning around in his stomach, a snake wrapping around a mouse. Each day that passed, she seemed to only get worse, and it horrified him.

He feared her. It was a shameful thing for him to admit, he was a man he was supposed to be the strong Casanova who sweeps the woman off her feet, slaps her to the ground when she disrespects him. he couldn’t ever quite shake this feeling in his gut that one night, he'd wake to find her looming over him with a knife to his throat and he wouldn't be able to protect himself against her.

He was trained to disarm, to subdue, and to eliminate, but with Lilly? He wasn't the one holding the knife, not really. She overpowered him easily, and he was so tired and so scared.

His ever-winding thoughts are interrupted by another agent, Pepper, with a hit on the back and salutes him on defeating his toughest set of reality benders yet, a family of three, a child, a father, and a mother.
The mother was certainly the most difficult of all; she scratched him and bit him and kicked and threatened him with her gun, and he met her fury with a bullet squarely between her eyes.

"Ukulele, you old bastard! Another job down. Toughest yet, I heard," Pepper’s voice boomed, filling the room with a sound that grated on one's nerves. "Whole damn family, no less. Father, child, and mother. Heard she was a real hellcat."

"Mhm. She put up a fight," Ukulele mumbled, his voice flat. "A real wild one. You know I always pull through, though."

Pepper chuckled and smiled, flashing his yellowed teeth. "That's what you get for dealing with all the toughest snakes. But you crushed it as always. Now, get some rest. You've earned it."

Pepper clapped him on the shoulder again, a gesture that felt less like a 'good job' and more like an iron branding searing through him. As Pepper walked away, the hum of the lights seemed to intensify, vibrating through his skull.

All he could think about was Lilly. And the fear that was eating him alive.

Following the Cornwall Incident, during the subsequent search and containment sweep of the residence formerly shared by SCP-4231-A and SCP-4231-B, Foundation personnel recovered a handwritten letter. The document was discovered concealed beneath a section of loose floorboards in the northwest corner of the main bedroom. Analysis confirmed the letter was authored by SCP-4231-B.

My Lilly,

I don't even know how to start these anymore.

I can’t shake this feeling that one day, you’ll be nothing more than another threat I’ll be forced to confront—and that terrifies me in a way I can’t put into words. I wish we could go back to how we were.

Why can’t things go back to the way they were? You used to be so gentle, so kind. I believed deep in my soul that you would always protect me, always care for me. What happened? What changed? Why are you doing this to me? You used to hold me like I mattered, and you'd smile at me and kiss me like I was something precious.

Why, why, why, why?

Why now do you look at me like you own me, not like you love me? Not like I'm precious?

Why do you touch me when I say no, and then act like I’m the one who’s wrong for flinching?

Why do you hurt me when all I ever wanted was to love you?

I wish you would tell me why.

I wish you would give me some kind of explanation, solace. I’m exhausted, Lilly. I am utterly and completely drained from living in fear of the person I love most. And I’m tired of pretending this is normal, of dreading when you want my body again, and of waiting for when you might care for me like you used to.

I love you. I have always loved you, and you know that.

Yours, now and forever,

Francis Wojciechowski

April 3, 2010, 12:30

Alto Clef is absentmindedly clicking a pen against his teeth as he scribbles something out on a Post-it note. It's been a rough 60- something years for him, anyone could tell that just by looking at him, his sunken eyebags and deep wrinkles decorating his face.

Clef takes a swig of a cigar, blowing a thick smoke that obscures his unfortunate features, sinking deep into his chair, and clicking on a record.

February 31, 1987

Francis Wojciechowski dreads getting back home, stopping in a bathroom and looking at bruises covering his thighs and stomach under the flickering light and he dreads what'll happen to him next, how he'll piss off Lilly next, how delectable he'll look in his sleep. He's so tired and he doesn't dare to look any further down his bruised body.

“God. God, fuck, god. Why?” he mutters to himself frantically, just out of pure shock at how his life spiraled out of his control and where he is right now. He feels his stomach churn, bends over the toilet, and he retches up a mix of blood and stomach acid.

After he washes out his mouth and hands and stares at his sweaty reflection in the mirror for a good while, he opens the door and Agent Ukulele leaves the room.

April 3, 2010, 12:32

Alto Clef begins to speak, his groggy voice and unidentifiable accent filling the air, he kicks his feet up on the table in front of him, illuminated only by the weak flickering fluorescent light above him.

"Have you ever met a man who’s a walking contradiction? With one eye shadowed by war crimes, a deep yearning for love in the other—a tragic jester cloaked in the ashes of his past—"

koff
koff
koff!

A young man, perhaps around 30, with thin, greasy blond hair tied back in a braid, barged in and interrupted the carefully crafted ritual of self-loathing that Clef had only just begun.

"Are you alive in here? What's all this?" He walked in and settled himself in, plopping rudely into the worn leather chair in front of Clef's desk.

Clef sighed, running his hand over his face before putting out his cigar and clicking the record off and snapping a lamp on. "Don't tell me you're doing the existential poetry again… Haven't I been through enough already?"

The young man, Francis, settled himself into the room, plopping rudely into an old leather chair in front of Clef's desk, which had long outlived its usefulness. The leather was peeling from the sides, and frankly, it was releasing a rather unpleasant odor, but that could just be excused as an effect of being in his office for years and accumulating his smell.

“You know, you come off as a pretentious jackass,” he scoffs, coughing. “Not so much a tortured poet, if that’s your intention. This whole atmosphere is pitiful, and the room reeks.”

Clef sighs, and he sinks into his chair, flicking his lamp on and stubs out his cigar.

November 12, 1978

Francis is just a teenager, and he is walking through the forest he's spent probably half of his life in with his best friend in the entire world. She holds his hand and tells him she's bringing him to see something beautiful, more beautiful than he could ever possibly imagine.

He believes her because he always believes her, and he follows her even though he feels her sharp nails digging into his palm, and he feels this sinking pit in his belly, and her antlers only seem to get bigger.

May 8, 2009

Clef lies in bed, staring at the ceiling, feeling an emptiness that weighs heavier than usual.

April 3, 2010, 12:43

Clef uncrosses his legs and rubs his temples, and asks Francis why he can't just let an old man have his moments, his hobbies. He owes at least this to him for the fact that people think he's insane after being caught talking to him or a wall one too many times.

Francis shrugs. "Well, you're the reason we still flinch at perfume counters." He fiddles with the vase on Clef's desk as he speaks. "…and maybe if you weren't so busy…I don't know really know what you're doing with yourself, sitting here writing sad stories about yourself and staring at a wall and projecting onto busty blonde babes and maybe tried to actually figure out whatever the fuck is wrong with you I wouldn't be here."

Clef's mood shifted as he spoke. "I don't ever project. I only… test the waters." He chuckled. "Drown in them, actually, heh. And, I don't HAVE anything TO project about anyways, I'm not a high school girl."

"Is that why I walked in on you calling yourself a tragic clown?" Francis continued, "You don’t drown in repressed feelings you've been pushing away for what? 30 years. You ferment in them."

Clef bites his lip.

January 20, 1984.

Francis sits in the living room on the couch, watching Lilly through the doorway of the kitchen as she slices vegetables at the counter and drops them into the broth boiling on the stove top. Her knife taps are slow and deliberate.

He ponders, just for a moment, how simple it would be to rise once she's done, grab that knife out of the sink, and catch her off guard.

He wonders if he could split her belly open like a ball of threads, or if he'd have to carve her open. He wonders if she'd spray blood onto his clothes or bleed downwards, slowly building a puddle. He wonders if her blood would cause rot beneath the wooden floorboards.

The thought inside him twisted and turned.

He doesn’t know if what he feels is hate for her, for what she put him through, the constant insults and assaults—or for himself, for enduring it. But he knows he hates. That much is certain to him as he stares through that doorway and shakes the thought away.

March 12, 1985.

Agent Ukulele slides a gun into the back of the farthest hallway closet, nestling it behind a row of old coats and their umbrella stand. As the door clicks shut, he lingers, staring at the grain of the wooden door like it might give him some kind of answer for 'why'. He wonders what kind of man he must've been in another life to end up here. Karma, maybe. Some crooked decision echoing. Something has to have happened—some sin, some slip—for this to be his life now. He must've done something wrong. He just can’t remember what.

He won't ever know what he did to deserve this fate of his.

April 3, 2010, 1:08

Francis taps his foot. “So? I guess we're still pretending this emotional dysfunction of yours is classified? Why don't you just see a therapist here or something. I just don't get you at all,” Francis spoke, pointing at him.

Clef sighed loudly at the remark and smacked his hand out of his face. "It's not a dysfunction. Its structure.”

Francis could only mutter a non-committal mhm before a knock at the door stopped their conversation in its tracks.

"Ohh, who could it be at this time?" Francis mused. Clef shook his head, pinching between his eyebrows.

Clef spoke again as he went to open the door for their visitor, "They’ll just think I’m talking to the wall again. Institutional madness — just another byproduct of working in this shithole."

Clef clicks the door open, and Andrea Adams walks into his office holding a clipboard and a pen.

"Dr. Clef. Sorry to interrupt, your signature is needed on the containment for …ah?" She realized that Clef was the only person in the room and scratched her head with her free hand. “You were speaking with…?"

Clef bluntly responded to her, "God. I was talking to God, and he said you’re annoying, what do you want?"

She chuckled uncomfortably at his remark and continued on, "Right… is now a bad time?"

Francis mused, "Tell her no, now’s perfect. Let’s talk about containment and sign our little papers while unraveling decades of abuse-induced psychosis."

Clef groaned loudly and sank his fingers into his temples.

"You know, sometimes I wish I could exorcise you like a proper demon."

Adams glanced to the left, then to the right, and finally back at Clef. After a moment’s hesitation, she continued, "Sir… you’re aware that no one else can hear whatever—"

Clef cut in on her. "Say 'voices' and I’ll staple that board to your forehead. I’m not schizophrenic."

Francis chuckled. "Tell her about your ex-girlfriend. That always clears a room."

Clef shot a look at her and the irritating blonde ghost (hallucination? Clef isn't really sure) who was grinning smugly behind her, a muscle twitching in his jaw. "Just give me the damn thing so I can sign it, Adams. I haven't got all day to listen to your insightful observations about my mental state." He snatched the clipboard, scribbled his musical note signature with a flourish that bordered on violent, and shoved it back into her hands.

"There. Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have a… theological debate to resume."

Adams, looking thoroughly bewildered and slightly frustrated, retreated towards the door. "Right, of course, Dr. Clef. I’ll just… leave you to it. Try not to… argue too much." She slipped out, closing the door and leaving the two alone yet again.

March 17 ██████

Francis is eight years old. He ventured deeper into the forest than he ever should have, and he feels very lost. His mother had warned him not to wander too far, but he had mindlessly kept going further and further chasing a bunny rabbit he saw. Just as he was about to cry, he heard a rattle nearby. A single lock of golden hair sprang out of view behind a bush.

“Hello?” he called out, only to be met with silence.

He waited for a moment, then tried again. “Hello…? Is anyone there? I saw your hair..You don’t need to be afraid, I promise I wont do anything.”

From the foliage, a young child emerged—a pale deer girl with delicate hooved feet, large brown eyes, and long golden hair that shimmered in the sunlight like waves upon the water. Her hair was adorned with dirt and twigs. She wore a white layered dress, intricately decorated with lace and bows, which made Francis wonder if she might be a princess.

She held his gaze, saying nothing at first, then began to wag her small brown tail as she cautiously stepped closer, her hooves crunching all plants and flowers beneath her.

April 3, 2010, 1:25

As soon as she was gone and he heard the door click, Francis burst out laughing. "Oh god, that was funny… 'Theological debate'! You’re incorrigible, you know that?"

"Unf. Shut the hell up…" Clef grumbled, sinking back into his chair lazily and defeated. He drank the last of his whiskey, the cheap spirit burning a path down his throat.

"She’s probably halfway to the cafeteria right now to say how weird Dr. Clef was acting, that he might need to be put back into containment, and report me to somebody who can do something about it."

"You are acting paranoid, and besides, it's not like they don't already think you’re halfway to Crazy Town? A little arguing with yourself in a room, then getting defensive about it, never hurt anyone. Adds character, like a good seasoning."

Francis leaned back in his chair, crossing his arms and tapping his foot. "Plus, it's not like she hasn't seen you talking to yourself before. I’m basically a fixture here."

"You're a fixture? A fixture like a shit stain on an otherwise clean carpet maybe" Clef retorted, though the edge had gone out of his voice. He knew Francis was right, and that was what really irked him.

"Oh, how you wound me.” Francis responded.

Clef let out another long groan, the sound somewhere between a rusty hinge and a deflating party balloon. He ran a hand across his forehead, messing his already disheveled hair, then he stood up abruptly, pushing himself away from his desk. "I need a drink. A real one. And preferably somewhere I don't have to listen to your incessant commentary."

"Running away again?" Francis sighed dramatically, following him to the door. "Fine, let's go. But don't think you can drown me in the nearest cheap seedy bar. You're stuck with me."

Clef didn't respond, just slammed the door open and strode out into the fluorescent-lit hallway. Francis trailed behind, the click of his shoes a contrast to Clef's heavy steps.

May 18, 2012

Clef lies in his bedroom yet again, he can't seem to stop replaying every bad thing that's ever happened to him in his mind. It wasn't a singular event that plagued him, not a glaring, catastrophic failure. It was the slow, insidious accumulation of everything.

He decides to get up and make himself some tea to maybe calm his nerves, even a little. He slips on some cute pink bunny slippers and voyages.

As he fills up the pot with water and readies the stove ██████ thinks about Cornwall.
He thinks about the water searing through his feet,
He thinks about all the IVs in his skin,
He remembers how intensely he felt everything enter his veins,
He remembers how the bandages on his legs felt,
He remembers how he had to relearn how to walk because his legs were so badly mutilated.

██████ reaches for the tea bags, his hand trembling slightly. A few slips from his grasp, scattering across the counter. He picks them up, carefully replacing them in the packet. A knot of anxiety clenches his stomach. In another life, in another time, such clumsiness would have earned him a crack of a hand to his face. A shadowed corner of his mind still anticipates the strike.

██████ does understand intellectually that Lilly is gone, she's probably fully rotted by now, her body returned to the earth, but somewhere in his belly, he fears he'll turn around and she'll be there. He'll lay down and feel an arm creep up his stomach and pull his zipper down.

He'll burn something on the stove and she'll poke holes in his skin.

He'll walk into the bathroom and see her brushing her gorgeous blonde hair, he'll see her thin body illuminated against the lights on the mirror and watch her gentle smile disappear as soon as she sees him. Sometimes he felt she would smile at everyone but him.

He thought that was hurt most about the things she did, it was never out of love or wanting him; he didn't know what it was, and something about that was worse than knowing.

██████ turns off the stove and lets the tea cool down, and pours it into an old Garfield-shaped mug.

On the fourth week of containment, during his weekly interview, in Dr Henderson's interview with SCP-4231-b, B seemed to show more neurosis signs and signs of mental decomposition. SCP-4231 has been discovered to be tearing bits of his flesh off his legs through the stitches and casts he is in, as well as picking the skin on his face, palm, and fingertips. He has also bitten his nails down to their core and ripped out multiple patches of hair from his head. Dr. Henderson was sent to do a cognitive test on B, and the following interaction was recorded and transcribed:

Begin Log

“Dr. Henderson: SCP-4231-B, please stop picking at the stitches in your legs. I’m not here to hurt you; you don’t need to be so nervous, okay? I’m just here to conduct a brief test with you. Tests are okay, aren’t they? You've been harming yourself—we can’t ignore that.

[5 minute lapse of silence]

SCP-4231-b: What happened to my Meri?

Dr. Henderson: That particular information is classified and cannot be disclosed at this time. I'm sorry.

Scp-4231-b: Don’t even pretend to be sorry. That’s just bullshit coming from you. What happened? Can you at least let me know if Lilly is alright and if my baby is safe? I’m pleading with you, please. I won't ask for anything else, I swear to god I won't.

Dr. Henderson: That information is classified, I'm sorry. Please try to cooperate with me.

Scp-4231-b: What a load of shit. You can’t tell me if my baby is alive or dead? You're lying to me. You're lying to me right now, that’s what you’re doing. You just want to hurt me. Is that it? You want to hurt me, so I break and fucking give you what you want.

Dr. Henderson: SCP-4231-b I assure you-

SCP-4231-b: Where is my Meri?

> End Log

Note: Subject B remained silent for the duration of the interview session. Requesting authorization for increased monitoring and potential administration of mild tranquilizers to mitigate self-harm tendencies. - Dr. Henderson

Following the interview, SCP-4231-b’s self-harming behavior intensified. Subject B was observed repeatedly banging his head against the padded wall before restraints could be fully reapplied. While the padded walls prevented serious injury, the behavior indicates a significant escalation in his level of distress. SCP-4231-b is currently secured to his bed, restricting movement of his arms and legs save for carefully monitored feeding times and physical therapy sessions in which he is actively relearning how to walk after injuries sustained during the Cornwall incident.

December 3, 2005

Alto Clef sits on a couch with Benjamin Kondraki watching some shitty sitcom show Ben put on that Alto tolerates, and things are good. He had bought some meat and cheeses and made a pretty good charcuterie board for his little date night, he was quite proud of himself. Alto had managed to arrange the meat into a little rose and the cheese into little leaves.

Alto suddenly pulls Ben's arm off from around his shoulder and nearly skips into the kitchen. “Wuh- had to go piss huh?” Ben said, a little dumbfounded at the suddenly energetic and running middle aged man hopping away from him.

“I forgot to pour us the wine! I paid 50 dollars for that stuff, we can't just skip it Konny!” Alto shouted from the kitchen, followed by the loud clanking of glasses and pans and god knows what else in the kitchen.

Ben scratched his chin and just waited, hoping he didn't smash anything. Just when he was just gonna get up and get the cups for him, Alto emerged from the kitchen with two wine glasses.

“The fuck did you do in there? You didn't… break anything, did you?” Ben was afraid to see what happened next time he had to go cook something.

“I wanted to do something fancy, y'know a salt coat on the rim, but I couldn't find your plates –gave up halfway through. By the way your cabinets really suck, you need to organize them better. I don't know how you live like this.”

Ben chuckled and shook his head as he lifted the blanket back up. “Come on, get back in here, you cabinet critic.”

May 8, ██████

Francis hands the newborn baby to his girlfriend, watching her smile so sweetly and hold her with such gentleness for a moment, he felt every reason he ever loved her flood back to him at once. He wonders how much humanity is left in her, if she lies awake at night thinking of what she did, or if he's just a functional punching bag. He wonders how somebody could do all these things to him and still be so beautiful in his eyes.

He knew what he had to do, for himself, for her, and for his baby girl. He had known for a while now. But the sight of her, holding their daughter, the little life they had created more or less together, made the decision feel so heavy for him again.

This feeling hung heavy in the air as he watched her cradle the baby, watched her hold her little hands in her own.

He watched the baby coo and gurgle, and he watched Lilly's eyelashes flutter as she drifted off to sleep.

Francis’s gaze remained fixed on her.

Her face was bathed in the soft glow of the nursery lamp, and Francis sees a ghost of the woman he fell in love with. Her cheeks are red and streaked with dried tears, yet her thin pink lips remain beautiful. Her hair is styled in a bun wrapped in a braid, and shes reminiscent of the princess he imagined her to be all those years ago.

Subject: Transcript of Auditory Traumatic Imprint from the Shared residence of SCP-4231-A and SCP-4231-B; specifically, the downstairs kitchen of the aforementioned residence.
Date Recovered: ██/██/████

Begin Log

SCP-4231-A: Are you stupid or do you just do these things on purpose to piss me off? Is that it? Because I honestly cannot fathom how you could be this… incompetent. We’ve been over this countless times. You’re just… useless. Absolutely stupid and utterly useless. I think you enjoy making me feel miserable.

SCP-4231-B: I really didn't try to do anything. I don't- I don't ever try to do-

SCP-4231-A: Oh, of course you don’t try! That’s abundantly clear! Is there anything you’re capable of doing right? You just fail me constantly, and then, you lie to me. 'I didn’t mean to.' I'm sure you didn't.

SCP-4231-B: I'm not lying. I can fix this. It isn't huge. This doesn't have to be – this!

SCP-4231-A: It's not about fixing it. This is about YOU, this is about the stupidity YOU keep having.

SCP-4231-B: I don't know what you want me to say, Lilly.

SCP-4231-A: You don't ever fucking know. You don't know anything.

SCP-4231-B's breath hitches, escalating into ragged, silent sobs. A sharp slap is audible, followed by a stifled whimper.

SCP-4231-B: I’m sorry… I’m so sorry… I’ll be better, I swear, please don't be mad at me I-I'll fix it.

SCP-4231-A: You're not sorry. You're just scared.

SCP-4231-B: I-I can do better! I promise, I can! I'll do anything you want, please…

SCP-4231-A: I don’t want your promises. I want you to stop wasting my time. But you can't even manage that, can you?

Silence for approximately 14 seconds. SCP-4231-B's hiccuping sobs continue.

SCP-4231-A: Clean yourself up. You're disgusting to look at right now.
> End log

Transcript Review — Auditory Traumatic Imprint ██/██/████
Filed by Dr. ███████

Throughout the recorded exchange between SCP-4231-A and SCP-4231-B, B displays expected behavioral patterns consistent with previous observations. SCP-4231-A engaged in verbal aggression, culminating in physical assault (confirmed audibly via impact noise and subsequent distress from B).

The recorded interaction suggests B has undergone sustained, significant psychological degradation, resulting in heightened dependency and compliant responses. A's demeanor remained consistently hostile and emotionally disengaged throughout the interaction.

— Dr. ███████

June 12, 2012

Clef runs a hand over a large and deep scar on his leg and doesn't feel very alone. Francis haunts the room without saying anything for a while until he finally speaks.

“Well.”

Clef didn’t look up. He knew Francis was there, just beyond the reach of his peripheral vision. He knew what that single word meant. It was an invitation. "Well" was the beginning of a conversation they had been skirting around for years.

"Well, what, Francis?" he asked, his voice rough with disuse. He could almost see Francis shifting, becoming slightly more defined, the shimmer solidifying into something almost, but not quite, tangible.

"Well," Francis repeated, the word laced with melancholy. "Well… are you finally ready to talk about it? Or are we just going to keep pretending those scars are from a nasty coffee spill?"

Clef remained silent, his fingers tracing the jagged bits of the scar, dipping his fingers into the deep crevices where his flesh came clean off.

"There's nothing to talk about."

Heavily inspired by the rituals canon [[include :scp-wiki:info:end]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:info-cw]] + February 2, 1987 The stale scent of smoked cigars, sweat, and cheap coffee hung heavy in the air of the Serbian safe house. The house's walls were empty save for a pinup calendar on the wall, depicting a grinning white blonde woman holding both of her breasts in her hands with the text “GOOD FOR LIFE!" for February plastered across her bikini like a twisted affirmation. Agent Ukulele tapped his worn leather boot against the concrete floor. His thoughts weren't on the previous mission, they weren't on the safe house, and they weren't on the blood that was still lodged under his short, bitten fingernails. They were on Lilly. She was a knot twisting and turning around in his stomach, a snake wrapping around a mouse. Each day that passed, she seemed to only get worse, and it horrified him. He feared her. It was a shameful thing for him to admit, he was a man he was supposed to be the strong Casanova who sweeps the woman off her feet, slaps her to the ground when she disrespects him. he couldn’t ever quite shake this feeling in his gut that one night, he'd wake to find her looming over him with a knife to his throat and he wouldn't be able to protect himself against her. He was trained to disarm, to subdue, and to eliminate, but with Lilly? He wasn't the one holding the knife, not really. She overpowered him easily, and he was so tired and so scared. His ever-winding thoughts are interrupted by another agent, Pepper, with a hit on the back and salutes him on defeating his toughest set of reality benders yet, a family of three, a child, a father, and a mother. The mother was certainly the most difficult of all; she scratched him and bit him and kicked and threatened him with her gun, and he met her fury with a bullet squarely between her eyes. "Ukulele, you old bastard! Another job down. Toughest yet, I heard," Pepper’s voice boomed, filling the room with a sound that grated on one's nerves. "Whole damn family, no less. Father, child, and mother. Heard she was a real hellcat." "Mhm. She put up a fight," Ukulele mumbled, his voice flat. "A real wild one. You know I always pull through, though." Pepper chuckled and smiled, flashing his yellowed teeth. "That's what you get for dealing with all the toughest snakes. But you crushed it as always. Now, get some rest. You've earned it." Pepper clapped him on the shoulder again, a gesture that felt less like a 'good job' and more like an iron branding searing through him. As Pepper walked away, the hum of the lights seemed to intensify, vibrating through his skull. All he could think about was Lilly. And the fear that was eating him alive. ------ > //Following the Cornwall Incident, during the subsequent search and containment sweep of the residence formerly shared by SCP-4231-A and SCP-4231-B, Foundation personnel recovered a handwritten letter. Analysis confirmed the letter was authored by SCP-4231-B.// > > My Lilly, > > I don't even know how to start these anymore. > > --I can’t shake this feeling that one day, you’ll be nothing more than another threat I’ll be forced to confront—and that terrifies me in a way I can’t put into words.-- I wish we could go back to how we were. > > Why can’t things go back to the way they were? It's been a rough 60- something years for him, anyone could tell that just by looking at him, his sunken eyebags and deep wrinkles decorating his face. Clef takes a swig of a cigar, blowing a thick smoke that obscures his unfortunate features, sinking deep into his chair, and clicking on a record. ------ + February 31, 1987 Francis Wojciechowski dreads getting back home, stopping in a bathroom and looking at bruises covering his thighs and stomach under the flickering light and he dreads what'll happen to him next, how he'll piss off Lilly next, how delectable he'll look in his sleep. After he washes out his mouth and hands and stares at his sweaty reflection in the mirror for a good while, he opens the door and Agent Ukulele leaves the room. ------ + April 3, 2010, 12:32 Alto Clef begins to speak, his groggy voice and unidentifiable accent filling the air, he kicks his feet up on the table in front of him, illuminated only by the weak flickering fluorescent light above him. "Have you ever met a man who’s a walking contradiction? Clef sighed, running his hand over his face before putting out his cigar and clicking the record off and snapping a lamp on. "Don't tell me you're doing the existential poetry again... Haven't I been through enough already?" The young man, Francis, settled himself into the room, plopping rudely into an old leather chair in front of Clef's desk, which had long outlived its usefulness. The leather was peeling from the sides, and frankly, it was releasing a rather unpleasant odor, but that could just be excused as an effect of being in his office for years and accumulating his smell. “You know, you come off as a pretentious jackass,” he scoffs, coughing. “Not so much a tortured poet, if that’s your intention. This whole atmosphere is pitiful, and the room reeks.” Clef sighs, and he sinks into his chair, flicking his lamp on and stubs out his cigar. ------ + November 12, 1978 Francis is just a teenager, and he is walking through the forest he's spent probably half of his life in with his best friend in the entire world. She holds his hand and tells him she's bringing him to see something beautiful, more beautiful than he could ever possibly imagine. He believes her because he always believes her, and he follows her even though he feels her sharp nails digging into his palm, and he feels this sinking pit in his belly, and her antlers only seem to get bigger. ------ + May 8, 2009 Clef lies in bed, staring at the ceiling, feeling an emptiness that weighs heavier than usual. ------ + April 3, 2010, 12:43 Clef uncrosses his legs and rubs his temples, and asks Francis why he can't just let an old man have his moments, his hobbies. He owes at least this to him for the fact that people think he's insane after being caught talking to him or a wall one too many times. Francis shrugs. "Well, you're the reason we still flinch at perfume counters." He fiddles with the vase on Clef's desk as he speaks. "...and maybe if you weren't so busy...I don't know really know what you're doing with yourself, sitting here writing sad stories about yourself and staring at a wall and projecting onto busty blonde babes and maybe tried to actually figure out whatever the fuck is wrong with you I wouldn't be here." Clef's mood shifted as he spoke. "I don't ever project. I only… test the waters." He chuckled. "Drown in them, actually, heh. And, I don't HAVE anything TO project about anyways, I'm not a high school girl." "Is that why I walked in on you calling yourself a tragic clown?" Francis continued, "You don’t drown in repressed feelings you've been pushing away for what? 30 years. You ferment in them." Clef bites his lip. ------ + January 20, 1984. Francis sits in the living room on the couch, watching Lilly through the doorway of the kitchen as she slices vegetables at the counter and drops them into the broth boiling on the stove top. Her knife taps are slow and deliberate. He ponders, just for a moment, how simple it would be to rise once she's done, grab that knife out of the sink, and catch her off guard. He wonders if he could split her belly open like a ball of threads, or if he'd have to carve her open. He wonders if she'd spray blood onto his clothes or bleed downwards, slowly building a puddle. He wonders if her blood would cause rot beneath the wooden floorboards. The thought inside him twisted and turned. He doesn’t know if what he feels is hate for her, for what she put him through, the constant insults and assaults—or for himself, for enduring it. But he knows he hates. That much is certain to him as he stares through that doorway and shakes the thought away. ------ + March 12, 1985. Agent Ukulele slides a gun into the back of the farthest hallway closet, nestling it behind a row of old coats and their umbrella stand. "It's not a dysfunction. Its structure.” Francis could only mutter a non-committal //mhm// before a knock at the door stopped their conversation in its tracks. "Ohh, who could it be at this time?" Francis mused. Clef shook his head, pinching between his eyebrows. Clef spoke again as he went to open the door for their visitor, "They’ll just think I’m talking to the wall again. Clef shot a look at her and the irritating blonde ghost (hallucination? Clef isn't really sure) who was grinning smugly behind her, a muscle twitching in his jaw. He snatched the clipboard, scribbled his musical note signature with a flourish that bordered on violent, and shoved it back into her hands. "There. He ventured deeper into the forest than he ever should have, and he feels very lost. His mother had warned him not to wander too far, but he had mindlessly kept going further and further chasing a bunny rabbit he saw. Just as he was about to cry, he heard a rattle nearby. He decides to get up and make himself some tea to maybe calm his nerves, even a little. He slips on some cute pink bunny slippers and voyages. As he fills up the pot with water and readies the stove ██████ thinks about Cornwall. He thinks about the water searing through his feet, He thinks about all the IVs in his skin, He remembers how intensely he felt everything enter his veins, He remembers how the bandages on his legs felt, He remembers how he had to relearn how to walk because his legs were so badly mutilated. ██████ reaches for the tea bags, his hand trembling slightly. He'll walk into the bathroom and see her brushing her gorgeous blonde hair, he'll see her thin body illuminated against the lights on the mirror and watch her gentle smile disappear as soon as she sees him. Sometimes he felt she would smile at everyone but him. He thought that was hurt most about the things she did, it was never out of love or wanting him; he didn't know what it was, and something about that was worse than knowing. ██████ turns off the stove and lets the tea cool down, and pours it into an old Garfield-shaped mug. ------ > //On the fourth week of containment, during his weekly interview, in Dr Henderson's interview with SCP-4231-b, B seemed to show more neurosis signs and signs of mental decomposition. Alto had managed to arrange the meat into a little rose and the cheese into little leaves. Alto suddenly pulls Ben's arm off from around his shoulder and nearly skips into the kitchen. “Wuh- had to go piss huh?” Ben said, a little dumbfounded at the suddenly energetic and running middle aged man hopping away from him. “I forgot to pour us the wine! This feeling hung heavy in the air as he watched her cradle the baby, watched  her hold her little hands in her own. He watched the baby coo and gurgle, and he watched Lilly's eyelashes flutter as she drifted off to sleep. Francis’s gaze remained fixed on her. Her face was bathed in the soft glow of the nursery lamp, and Francis sees a ghost of the woman he fell in love with. Her cheeks are red and streaked with dried tears, yet her thin pink lips remain beautiful. Her hair is styled in a bun wrapped in a braid, and shes reminiscent of the princess he imagined her to be all those years ago. ------ > Subject: Transcript of Auditory Traumatic Imprint from the Shared residence of SCP-4231-A and SCP-4231-B; specifically, the downstairs kitchen of the aforementioned residence. > Date Recovered: ██/██/████ > > **Begin Log** > > SCP-4231-A: Are you stupid or do you just do these things on purpose to piss me off? theoldmasters.raw_content:
Clear it and move on. Don't stop to talk. Don't look where you shouldn't. Text your mother.

The Old Masters


Click. Click. Click. Click.

There was a sense of power in how Officer Calloway’s boots rang out against the silence. Perhaps it was the raw individuality of it, a solo performance — Jules was the only source of sound now — or perhaps it was the memories of their schooldays, of sharp-dressed administrators and the heel clicks they'd come to match. Whatever the case, they stepped proudly, surveilling the halls and knowing nothing would dare to cross them on a night like this.

Though, judging by the buzz in their pocket, that didn't mean that nobody would. Their pacing halted with a click-ksh as they checked their notifications.

There was a line an older coworker of theirs had said: it's nice to have someone worry about you. Except Jules was nearing twenty-four, and it was all getting to be a bit much.

Besides, it’d been almost a year since anyone had wanted them dead.

Sighing sharply, they jammed their phone back into their pocket and continued on their route.

Click. Click. Click.

The beam of their flashlight made the frames on the walls shine. Some of these paintings were hundreds of years old, some worn enough to need restoration. On their unluckier nights, Jules had to share their domain with the man who headed up such efforts, Adam Morrows. The lucky bastard got to actually touch the paintings. They had to settle for just quietly admiring them. They clicked their way over to an empty space at the wall and aimed their torch at the poster that hung there.

Martin Drolling's Interior of a Kitchen has been taken down for restoration.

We apologize for the inconvenience.





—The High Museum



Even a photo displayed how cracked the surface was. He was right, the old thing needed fixing. And once he was done, it'd look as perfect as ever. On one hand that was good, because history and culture and preservation very well did matter, but on the other it meant Adam wouldn't be fired any damn time soon. Even in spite of being an insufferable prick.

Jules stood for a while in front of the piece, glaring at the figures smiling back at them. At least this job was giving him some trouble. Issues with one of the paint colors being hard to match. They’d tried talking with him about it when he’d first undertaken the project about two weeks prior.

"What, so you just don’t mix some colors and slap 'em on?" they'd jeered, leaning over his shoulder as he took notes.

"Not quite, no." He'd pushed up his stupid magnifiers and smiled at them. "We have a mastery of several pigments — Egyptian Blue, even, though it was lost for so long — but this one is difficult to emulate. Its rich tones are largely due to its…well, unsavory composition."

"Y'mean…?” They'd gestured vaguely towards their lower regions.

"Wh- no! Goodness. It's perhaps a bit more… sinister."

"…I’m not followin’.”

He'd paused for a moment. "Nothing you need to concern yourself with."

"Well, you're bein' a lil' too quiet about it."

He'd stood, looming a few extra inches over them. Something of a sense of superiority. "I'll leave it at this: art and its history are complicated matters, Jules. If we tried to measure the past by the ethics of the present, we'd deem everyone a criminal. It's best not to judge the old masters, and better to simply appreciate what they gave us."

Jules understood. But it didn't mean they had to like it.

"I know there's somethin' up with you," they told the poster. "I don't really know what, but there's somethin'. And it feels a lil' spooky."

If the picture had opinions, it kept them to itself.

Jules was a person of many talents. At least, this was what they mused to themself as they circled around the staff area and checked the entry logs. These talents included their security work, of course. The one time someone had broken in, he hadn't stood a chance, and then there was the work back in… hell, they were beating around the bush. Their real talent was extreme patience. So much patience, in fact, that when the log displayed a sign-in from Dr. Adam Morrows just two hours earlier, they didn't kick the damn display console.

So much for solitude. They noted down the activity in their logbook and pushed open the door to the restoration space. That saintly patience came into play once more as they caught themself before they flicked on the harsh fluorescent lights, instead just turning up their torch beam and aiming it square at the cloth-covered workstation.

"Protocol says you owe me a heads-up before waltzin' in here."

The beam glinted off his glasses, tossing shards of light at the wall as he looked up at them. "Apologies, Officer Calloway. I couldn't sleep a wink. I thought I might get a little extra work done on the Drolling piece."

They scowled. If he could see it, he didn't react. "Guess I better head out, then. I'd hate to disturb all your high-tech efforts."

"Oh, they're hardly high-tech." He reached over to adjust the lampshade, letting the bulb cast a faint, warm glow across his face. "You're welcome to take a look if you'd like. I've made some progress mimicking the old pigmentation. Nothing can quite match the original, of course, but I believe it should suffice."

Jules raised an eyebrow, but after a moment's pause, they crossed the room to join him at the broad table. Secured to its surface was Interior of a Kitchen. Now that they were up close and personal, its cracks were all the more apparent. There was some level of poetry in here, they mused. A beautiful piece tarnished with time, cracking to reveal… well, something Morrows obviously knew, but something Jules was still in the dark about.

Those faces were mocking them. They were sure of it.

"Not bad." They examined where cracks had been carefully sealed and colors had been precisely matched. God only knew what kind of concoctions he'd used to patch up the damn thing. The fume traps — really just large fans — were on full blast, but Jules could still pick up traces of a chemical cocktail. "Still fuckin' creepy, especially with your being on some kicker about the paint comp. But I guess that's not changin' any time soon."

"Comp?"

"Composition. It's, what, 2 AM? I stop bein’ a wordsmith past 12. You want a sonnet, go talk to Billy Shakespeare."

He stared at them, his expression steadily growing more disturbed. "…William Shakespeare.”

"You got it." Jules stepped back from the table, giving the flashlight a twirl. "See, I know some things. I'd know more, if you weren't so weird about shit."

Adam bristled, closing his eyes and taking what Jules felt was an over-exaggerated deep breath. "Is this about the conversation we had the other day?"

"You should try for MENSA."

"Look, Jules…" He trailed off, pinching the bridge of his nose and heaving another deep sigh. God, what was it with that stance? Seemed like every guy who thought he was something big struck it to make a point. "There's a lot of complexity behind the history of that painting. Things that horrified artists like Drolling. You wouldn't believe some of the things people come across in this job."

They raised an eyebrow. "You work with paint, dude. Past fume-induced hallucinations, I doubt you're goin' up against much."

"…Huh."

For one long, disturbing moment, he was silent. And Adam wasn't a man who did silence. He did quiet, sure, in that little voice of his that both demanded you respect him and begged you to listen to him, but never silence. And never the blank silence Jules was being met with— calculating, ice-cold.

"Perhaps there is just a bit more you should learn, then, Jules."

"Past shelterin' me on paint? I'm honored. Next you'll be teachin' me about shapes— hey!"

But Adam was not listening. Their rant had bought him the time needed to shut off the fume fans, and now there was stark silence, the only sounds being Jules' struggles as he grabbed them by the back of the collar and dipped them towards the surface of the painting. They flung out a hand to catch the edge of the table and keep from plowing into the damn thing, but now their nose was practically touching the still-drying surface. The faces below blurred out of focus as they strained to regain sense. Struggled to regain posture, too, but couldn't find a weak point behind them, couldn't pull the collar away from their neck enough to not gasp for air, couldn't lash out for fear of damaging a priceless artifact.

And in all of this, all Adam offered was one word: "Listen."

They listened.

But he wasn't speaking.

He was at least kind enough to ensure they fell back when they collapsed.

At least, above all else, Jules was dutiful.

After the Shit With The Painting, as they had dubbed it, they'd finished their shift and returned home without another word to or from anyone. They'd slept for five hours, gone to the store, straightened up their apartment, and… well, and then just sat back and stared at the ceiling for a while.

How were you supposed to deal with things like this? Contacting the police, probably. At the very least contacting the museum to let them know their restoration specialist was batshit insane. But HR complaints were mounds of paperwork and legal proceedings were time and money, and Jules was exhausted just existing these days.

So after another nap that afternoon, they did what they always did when times were rough and money was tight: they went to work.

Click. Click. Click. Click.

Flashlight. Poster. Hallways. Art. Check-ins. Adam — No! Kitchen. Paint.

Clear it and move on. Don't stop to talk. Don't look where you shouldn't. Text your mother.

Although they'd tried convincing themselves several times over that they weren't concerned for Adam, they couldn't quite master the lie. Elitist he was, and condescending, but not violent. Never before violent. And if they'd heard those voices at his insistence, he'd heard them too, so they were either really there or they were both screwy.

A few nights of pondering these matters prompted Jules to call a therapist. A night awake prompted them to cancel the appointment. Something like this was likely to get them medicated or worse, and mandatory reporting would come back to bite both of them.

Besides, the museum at night was their domain, and it was that thought above the rest that kept drawing them back to pace through the halls. Flashlight shining, boots click-ing. In the moments where all they thought about was the silence itself and not what lay underneath it, it felt like they were back in control. Jules knew these halls. They knew these paintings. And they knew that if Adam Morrows grabbed them like that again, they were going to have a hell of a lot more than something to say about it.

But every night they felt the urge to return, to listen to what the choir had to tell them and to understand who and what they had been. When had ghosts become a thing? Jules had explored abandoned places as a kid, had hopped fences to walk through houses and tag their walls. Even the spots that gave the local tough kids a pause barely fazed them. So why, why did things have to become real now, right when they were trying to put their life back together?

"Are you joining us?"

A year ago, maybe. They'd been a hotshot young detective assigned to an art theft case that nobody took too seriously. Just another painting to be intercepted on eBay, and the damn thing wasn't worth that much anyway. The Art Theft Detail had welcomed it as a break after going on a months-long goose chase for a painting that had been in some grandma's closet.

Then people had started getting killed.

It'd escalated fast. Jules had been on the online side of things, grabbing details, and intercepting emails. But suddenly they'd been stumbling across the names and numbers of people working the case, details about their homes and families, all up for grabs for interested parties. They'd done what they could, but soon enough their own name had popped up, and nobody wanted the department rookie's death on their conscience. They'd been not-so-gently instructed to disappear.

They had. They'd hunkered down in a nice little job below both their pay grade and their skill level and now had to worry about getting choked out in a restoration workshop while a bunch of ghosts ranted at them. Rock bottom was beginning to feel like a fragile surface.

A stinging sensation in their palm dragged Jules out of their sulking. They pried their fingernails from their skin and eased their grip on the flashlight as they approached the screen. No names. No Morrows. Good. They cracked open the door, doing a quick once-over with the torch. Coast still seemed clear. They stepped back and pulled the door shut. Continued on their way. All routine these days, everything as quick as possible.

Except… except the issue was the routine. They'd been dodging around the room ever since the attack, doing their best to avoid running into Adam. The museum at night was supposed to be their domain, damn it, but here they were tiptoeing around Mr. X.

It all had to stop. They at least had to know, had to figure out what the hell was going on with that painting. And if he wasn't there, this was as good a time as any.

They took a deep breath and pushed the door open. It all felt like signing in at their old desk, hands trembling as they brought up news of the dead and soon-to-be. Now the dead had spoken, and Jules felt they owed it to them to listen.

Click. Click. Click. Click-ksh.

Even the voices quieted at the sound of the far door opening.

"Jules? I thought you might be here, I… I'm terribly sorry about the other day-"

Go.




Jules ran, boots pounding on steady floorboards, flashlight beam swinging wildly. Before Adam could even register their movements they had reached the opposite door, tugging on its handle to escape to freedom.

It wouldn't budge.

And now, alone with a madman in the dark, that stubborn thought rose to the surface again: there were more people in that painting than the three women it depicted. More, probably, than had even spoken to Jules thus far.

And they were in the paint.

Jules wiped a sweaty palm on their slacks and adjusted their grip on the flashlight.

"Was, uh, jammin' the door part of your apology, Adam?" They gave a nervous chuckle, turning to face the interior of the room. "Most people do this kinda thing over coffee."

In softer lighting, they might've been convinced of his side. His smile was small and meek, and he walked slowly. The torch's sterile beam was unforgiving, though, and Jules could see how he just looked wrong. His smile was paired with dead eyes, and his walk was deliberately slow — like a fox approaching a rabbit.

"A necessity, I'm afraid. You do have a bit of a… let's say, tendency to run when things get complicated."

Their nails were beginning to break skin. "Fuck off."

Adam stopped and held up his palms. "My sincerest apologies for hitting a sore spot, but I do my research on the things that fascinate me. You happen to be one of them."

"Yeah, your pals said somethin' similar." They took a few steps to the side, trying to keep him an even distance away. "Told me a bit about themselves, too, actually.

"Your 'unsavory composition' was just, y'know, human lives — I guess that ain't much to you. But you talk a lot of shit for someone restorin' a painting created with ground-up mummies."

They expected a reaction from that line. Something, at least, anger or denial, something that made him feel human. But he simply shrugged.

"It isn't as if I can change the past."

"At least have a little fuckin' shame for it, Adam!"

He stepped forward. Jules stiffened.

"And yet you have no shame for interfering with my work, Officer Calloway. I would think someone like you would understand the inherence of loss in art."

"The fuck do you-"

"Think about it." He began to pace. "Art— art always requires loss, does it not? Money spent on paints leaving one in the gutter, trying to appeal to the masses to earn their keep. Gorgeous portraits of wartime scenes — and there, there you can even see the loss right on the canvas, hm?

"So what is the next step, Jules?" He turned to face them. "Pouring human emotion, humanity into a painting is the start. Is putting in actual humans not the next logical step? Is it not the purest form of love to those we do not know to include them in what we deem beautiful? Is it not the best expression of admiration to turn our muses into our medium?"

Jules stared at him, eyes wide with shock. It took a moment for them to recover, but once they did, they said the one line they could think of:

"Bless your fuckin' heart, Adam, you're screwier than I thought."

He smiled broadly, stepping forward to close the gap and putting a hand on their shoulder.

"It's that Southern charm that draws me to you, Jules, it really is."

Drawing back with a grimace, they raised their arms to shove him back. But before they could react, they found themself staring up at him, their legs swept out in less than a second. Their head hit the ground with a crack. They tasted blood.

"Disappointing, considering your prior training. I suppose even the pros get rusty."

They spat, rolling over to try and push themself up. But now he had their legs, and they felt a ripping pain through their elbows and hands as they tried to brace against being dragged back. Adam simply hoisted them up like a fallen toy, holding them close, whispering an apology for their struggles. Assuring them the pain would be temporary.

And then the world tilted sharply, the edge of the table catching Jules in the back of the legs and making them crumple back onto it. The room felt like it was spinning. Their ears were ringing. Their palm, their tongue, God only knew what else was bleeding, and they could barely string together a coherent thought other than I don't wanna die.

They tried to get up. Couldn't. Could only look around the dark, wide-eyed, and disoriented.

But the room was now mockingly quiet, forcing them to hear their own whimpers and gasps and pleas for Adam to just stop this. But there was no response from him now. He was off by his supplies, getting something, and even though they had precious seconds there was nothing they could do.

They closed their eyes and willed the world to stop.

And for a brief moment, it felt like it did.

I Think I See The Sun

They opened their eyes, glancing over to the painting.

And the flashlight next to it.

I don't wanna die.

The sheer effort of moving nearly knocked them down again. They grit their teeth against the pain, felt a gasp slip out, heard Adam begin to rush back over. But the torch was theirs, and as they steadied themself on the table, they felt a strange clarity among the chaos.

"Come on, Jules, this is pitiful. You're only making this harder for us bo—"

They dragged him down and against them. Slammed him against the table.

Stared down at his shock.

Wondered which city they'd head to next.

Then slammed the torch against his head until he stopped moving.

"…Say hi to the old masters for me, Adam," they wheezed. "I think y'all might be in the same place now."

The room was silent.

They weren't sure how much time had passed. An hour? Two? Granted, five minutes could feel like an eternity with a corpse in the room. Whatever the case was, they knew they had time before anyone would arrive on the scene.

In spite of their nerves being shot, in spite of the shaking, Jules felt eerily calm. Deep down they knew they had expected something like this. Had seen it coming from the moment he'd first attacked them. The panic would come later, they were sure, but for now, they embraced the numb tranquility.

They leaned against the table, tilting their head back and closing their eyes. This was borrowed time, borrowed peace. But they had done what they had to do.

It's best not to judge the old masters, and better to simply appreciate what they gave us."// Jules understood. But it didn't mean they had to like it. "I know there's somethin' up with you," they told the poster. "I don't really know //what,// but there's somethin'. And it feels a lil' spooky." If the picture had opinions, it kept them to itself. [[/div]] ------ [[div style="text-indent: 25px;"]] Jules was a person of many talents. At least, this was what they mused to themself as they circled around the staff area and checked the entry logs. These talents included their security work, of course. The one time someone //had// broken in, he hadn't stood a chance, and then there was the work back in... hell, they were beating around the bush. Their real talent was extreme patience. So much patience, in fact, that when the log displayed a sign-in from {{Dr. Adam Morrows}} just two hours earlier, they didn't kick the damn display console. //So much for solitude.// They noted down the activity in their logbook and pushed open the door to the restoration space. That saintly patience came into play once more as they caught themself before they flicked on the harsh fluorescent lights, instead just turning up their torch beam and aiming it square at the cloth-covered workstation. "Protocol says you owe me a heads-up before waltzin' in here." The beam glinted off his glasses, tossing shards of light at the wall as he looked up at them. "Apologies, Officer Calloway. I couldn't sleep a wink. I thought I might get a little extra work done on the Drolling piece." They scowled. If he could see it, he didn't react. "Guess I better head out, then. I'd hate to disturb all your high-tech efforts." "Oh, they're hardly high-tech." He reached over to adjust the lampshade, letting the bulb cast a faint, warm glow across his face. "You're welcome to take a look if you'd like. I've made some progress mimicking the old pigmentation. Nothing can //quite// match the original, of course, but I believe it should suffice." Jules raised an eyebrow, but after a moment's pause, they crossed the room to join him at the broad table. Secured to its surface was //Interior of a Kitchen//. Now that they were up close and personal, its cracks were all the more apparent. There was some level of poetry in here, they mused. A beautiful piece tarnished with time, cracking to reveal... well, something Morrows obviously knew, but something Jules was still in the dark about. Those faces were mocking them. They were sure of it. "Not bad." They examined where cracks had been carefully sealed and colors had been precisely matched. God only knew what kind of concoctions he'd used to patch up the damn thing. The fume traps — really just large fans — were on full blast, but Jules could still pick up traces of a chemical cocktail. "Still fuckin' creepy, especially with your being on some kicker about the paint comp. But I guess that's not changin' any time soon." "Comp?" "Composition. It's, what, 2 AM? I stop bein’ a wordsmith past 12. You want a sonnet, go talk to Billy Shakespeare." He stared at them, his expression steadily growing more disturbed. "...//William// Shakespeare.” "You got it." Jules stepped back from the table, giving the flashlight a twirl. "See, I know some things. I'd know more, if you weren't so weird about shit." Adam bristled, closing his eyes and taking what Jules felt was an over-exaggerated deep breath. "Is this about the conversation we had the other day?" "You should try for MENSA." "Look, Jules..." He trailed off, pinching the bridge of his nose and heaving another deep sigh. God, what //was// it with that stance? Seemed like every guy who thought he was something big struck it to make a point. "There's a lot of complexity behind the history of that painting. Things that horrified artists like Drolling. You wouldn't believe some of the things people come across in this job." They raised an eyebrow. "You work with paint, dude. Past fume-induced hallucinations, I doubt you're goin' up against much." "...Huh." For one long, disturbing moment, he was silent. And Adam wasn't a man who //did// silence. He did quiet, sure, in that little voice of his that both demanded you respect him and begged you to listen to him, but never silence. And never the blank silence Jules was being met with-- calculating, ice-cold. "Perhaps there //is// just a bit more you should learn, then, Jules." "Past shelterin' me on paint? I'm honored. Next you'll be teachin' me about shapes-- //hey!//" But Adam was not listening. Their rant had bought him the time needed to shut off the fume fans, and now there was stark silence, the only sounds being Jules' struggles as he grabbed them by the back of the collar and dipped them towards the surface of the painting. They flung out a hand to catch the edge of the table and keep from plowing into the damn thing, but now their nose was practically touching the still-drying surface. The faces below blurred out of focus as they strained to regain sense. Struggled to regain posture, too, but couldn't find a weak point behind them, couldn't pull the collar away from their neck enough to not gasp for air, couldn't lash out for fear of damaging a priceless artifact. And in all of this, all Adam offered was one word: "Listen." They listened. But he wasn't speaking. @@@@ @@@@ [[span style="color:#af6836"]] [[/div]] [[div class="speak"]] [[>]] {{(hello)}} [[/>]] [[<]] [[div style="font-family:Georgia; font-size:110%"]] Hel- [[/div]] [[/<]] [[=]] [[div style="font-family:Baskerville; font-size:140%"]] //Hello There You Seem New You Seem A New Face Seem To Be// [[/div]] [[/=]] [[>]] {{(can i ask you something)}} [[/>]] [[<]] [[div style="font-family:Georgia; font-size:110%"]] Does he often treat you in such a way? [[/div]] [[/<]] [[>]] {{(are you going to bury me again)}} [[/>]] [[=]] [[div style="font-family:Baskerville; font-size:140%"]] //Your Eyes Open Wide Wide Eyes Moon Sky Like The Sky// [[/div]] [[/=]] [[<]] [[div style="font-family:Georgia; font-size:110%"]] I would have little patience for such a thing. [[/div]] [[/<]] [[>]] {{(it keeps getting darker)}} [[/>]] [[=]] [[div style="font-family:Baskerville; font-size:140%"]] //Higher Than My Soul The Sun The Son The Father The// [[/div]] [[/=]] [[>]] {{(are you joining us)}} [[/>]] [[/span]] [[/div]] [[div style="text-indent: 25px;"]] @@@@ @@@@ He was at least kind enough to ensure they fell //back// when they collapsed. [[/div]] ----- [[div style="text-indent: 25px;"]] At least, above all else, Jules was dutiful. After the Shit With The Painting, as they had dubbed it, they'd finished their shift and returned home without another word to or from anyone. They'd slept for five hours, gone to the store, straightened up their apartment, and... well, and then just sat back and stared at the ceiling for a while. How were you //supposed// to deal with things like this? Contacting the police, probably. At the very least contacting the museum to let them know their restoration specialist was batshit insane. But HR complaints were mounds of paperwork and legal proceedings were time and money, and Jules was exhausted just existing these days. So after another nap that afternoon, they did what they always did when times were rough and money was tight: they went to work. //Click. Click. Click. Click.// Flashlight. Poster. Hallways. Art. Check-ins. Adam — //No!// Kitchen. Paint. //Clear it and move on. Don't stop to talk. Don't look where you shouldn't. Text your mother.// Although they'd tried convincing themselves several times over that they weren't concerned for Adam, they couldn't quite master the lie. Elitist he was, and condescending, but not violent. Never before violent. And if they'd heard those voices at his insistence, he'd heard them too, so they were either really there or they were //both// screwy. A few nights of pondering these matters prompted Jules to call a therapist. A night awake prompted them to cancel the appointment. Something like this was likely to get them medicated or worse, and mandatory reporting would come back to bite both of them. Besides, the museum at night was //their// domain, and it was that thought above the rest that kept drawing them back to pace through the halls. Flashlight shining, boots //click//-ing. In the moments where all they thought about was the silence itself and not what lay underneath it, it felt like they were back in control. Jules knew these halls. They knew these paintings. And they knew that if Adam Morrows grabbed them like that again, they were going to have a hell of a lot more than something to say about it. But every night they felt the urge to return, to listen to what the choir had to tell them and to understand who and what they had been. //When had ghosts become a thing?// Jules had explored abandoned places as a kid, had hopped fences to walk through houses and tag their walls. Even the spots that gave the local tough kids a pause barely fazed them. So why, //why// did things have to become real //now//, right when they were trying to put their life back together? {{"Are you joining us?"}} A year ago, maybe. They'd been a hotshot young detective assigned to an art theft case that nobody took too seriously. Just another painting to be intercepted on eBay, and the damn thing wasn't worth that much anyway. The Art Theft Detail had welcomed it as a break after going on a months-long goose chase for a painting that had been in some grandma's closet. Then people had started getting killed. It'd escalated fast. Jules had been on the online side of things, grabbing details, and intercepting emails. But suddenly they'd been stumbling across the names and numbers of people working the case, details about their homes and families, all up for grabs for interested parties. They'd done what they could, but soon enough their own name had popped up, and nobody wanted the department rookie's death on their conscience. They'd been not-so-gently instructed to disappear. They had. They'd hunkered down in a nice little job below both their pay grade and their skill level and now had to worry about getting choked out in a restoration workshop while a bunch of ghosts ranted at them. Rock bottom was beginning to feel like a fragile surface. A stinging sensation in their palm dragged Jules out of their sulking. They pried their fingernails from their skin and eased their grip on the flashlight as they approached the screen. No names. No Morrows. //Good//. They cracked open the door, doing a quick once-over with the torch. Coast still seemed clear. They stepped back and pulled the door shut. Continued on their way. All routine these days, everything as quick as possible. Except... except the issue //was// the routine. They'd been dodging around the room ever since the attack, doing their best to avoid running into Adam. The museum at night was supposed to be their domain, damn it, but here they were tiptoeing around Mr. X. It all had to stop. They at least had to //know,// had to figure out what the hell was going on with that painting. And if he wasn't there, this was as good a time as any. They took a deep breath and pushed the door open. It all felt like signing in at their old desk, hands trembling as they brought up news of the dead and soon-to-be. Now the dead had spoken, and Jules felt they owed it to them to listen. //Click. Click. Click. Click-ksh.// Just a couple gals on an old, old canvas. "Hello." @@@@ @@@@ [[span style="color:#af6836"]] [[/div]] [[div class="speak"]] [[>]] {{(hello again)}} [[/>]] [[<]] [[div style="font-family:Georgia; font-size:110%"]] We were waiting for when we'd see you again. I don't know what's up with him, honestly. He's never been this bad." Speaking to the damn thing didn't make the whole situation feel any less weird, but it was nice to know that the weird painting ghosts seemed concerned for their wellbeing. Or one was, at least.
