Unexpected Ramifications

On their third day of living in the clubhouse, Avys had finally reclaimed enough of the ostentatious chapel through rampant application of posters, ratty couches, tattered pillows, carpets and draped sheets, such that it no longer felt like living in a museum exhibit.

The rest of the clubhouse? To put it lightly, it could use some work.

Avys stood in their makeshift bedroom, a tripod set up on the other side, pointed towards the decorated wall. Their phone sat in the tripod, and using it like a mirror, they brushed the misplaced hairs out of their blurred, unrecognizable face.

That looks better than I thought it would. They grinned, happy with their uncertain appearance, stepping back from the camera. Satisfied with the framing, they nodded.

"Record."

As the phone began to capture them standing in front of their bedroom, they counted in their mind.

One, two, three, fo—

They began to move, a practiced and choreographed dance routine, humming along to imagined music. They danced with a balance of poise and enthusiasm, a style developed out of dancing alone in a bedroom, for an audience of strangers.

Each step found its mark, and each motion of the arm flowed with a freedom, happiness expanding to fill the empty, echoing halls of what was once a dull, monotonous guildhall.

Unbeknownst to them, they had gathered an audience.

"What all this, Avys?"

Avys stumbled, the interruption breaking their focus, tripping on their own feet, tangling in the carpet and falling to the floor unceremoniously. As they looked up to the source of the judgement, they saw Leokadia Krzysztof standing in the doorway to their bedroom.

"How long were you watching?" Leokadia walked in, helping Avys to their feet, teasing smile on ner face.

"I didn't know you were a dancer. Did you make that routine?"

"Oh, that?" Avys shook their head, bouncing over to their phone to stop the recording. "It's a Tiktok dance."

Leokadia stared back, blinking. "A what dance? Is that… is that a new anomalous dance troupe?"

"What?" A beat later Avys put the pieces together. "Oh! Right, you've been locked up for a bit."

"Yeah, 'a bit' is a bit of an understatement."

"Right. Tiktok is a lot of things?"

"Mhm."

"Sorry, it's just — you care about the dancing part, right? Not the social media thingy?"

Leokadia inclined ner head, cracking ner joints. "Am I that obvious?"

"Don't worry, you're in good company." Avys swiped to their feed, showing Leokadia videos. "Okay, so, basically, somebody will choreograph a routine to a specific sound, and then share that on Tiktok. If it's good, then a lot of people will start to copy the dance, to the same sound."

"Oh! It's a cognitohazardous dance?"

"What? No, that's… no this is like, public stuff."

"Oh," Leokadia said, slightly dejected. "I had hoped that there would be more who moved like I do. I'm sure there are, elsewhere, but—"

"Hey," Avys said, putting their hand onto ner shoulder. "Do you want me to teach you the dance? It's not going to make somebody's balls explode, but it's still pretty fun!"

"Pffft." Leokadia reached out and ruffled Avys' hair, laughing. "I bet I could still figure out a way to explode somebody's balls with it anyways. But… I'd love to learn if you don't mind?"

"Of course not!" Avys' unstable features settled on joy. As they put their phone on a nearby surface, music began to play. "Okay, so, it's…"

On their fifth day of living in the clubhouse, Avys' field of comfortable influence had extended beyond their room, a common area now filled with furniture of questionable origin, fascinating conditions, and a sense of community. The 'revolution', so to speak, gathered here often, enjoying their collective freedoms and time off while they waited for their next assignment.

Thank god we have wifi. Avys scrolled through their Instagram feed, scrolling past photos of those they didn't really know from college, and things they didn't really care about. Passing the time takes many forms and, well, endless scrolling was a modern innovation that was phenomenal at it.

"Who was that?" Faruq Zikry, wearing leggings and a loosely wrapped top, was draped over the arm of the couch, hand supporting his head as he gazed at Avys' phone.

"Huh? Sorry, I just zoned out there, should I go back?"

"Yes, yes!" Faruq reached out with urgency, scrolling through Avys' feed, stopping shortly above on a tabloid post that Avys had ignored. "Him. Who is that man?"

"Oh, that? That's Rami Malek, he's an actor." Avys sat up, their focus now captured by something other than waiting. "Why? Does he look familiar?"

"No. But I wish he was."

Ohhhhh.

"You think he's hot." In retrospect, Avys realized they could have framed it as a question, but—

"Undoubtedly. Can you… can you show me more photos of him?"

"Ye— yeah, sure. Here, let me just find his account and—" Before they could finish, Faruq had snatched the phone out of their hand, and was looking through Rami Malek's account.

"Do you know… is he?"

"I don't think he's ever actually said that, publicly, you know?"

Faruq looked sad, just for a second, before once again being captured by Avys' phone. "Ah. I understand. Still… don't you agree?"

"Agree what?"

"That he is delicious?"

"I… I mean I get it." Avys patted the cushion beside them, and Faruq joined them on the couch. "Here, sit down, let's see what we can dig up."

As the latest shipment of supplies arrived, Faruq was waiting impatiently, looking decades younger than he truly was. Digging through the piles, he located a poster tube, and took it off to his bedroom.

Once he made sure that nobody else was watching, he opened the package, and quickly pasted the Mr. Robot poster on his wall, letting out a sigh.

God, he's dreamy.

On their eighth day of living in the clubhouse, Avys had decided that having a wifi signal in here was actually quite a bad idea, as they glared at their phone.

"What's eating you, Avys?"

Thank God for distractions. Avys turned away from their phone on the table, stifling a small giggle seeing the speaker. Brury Regevoy was one of their favorite people in the clubhouse. Avys, given their current abstraction, was more or less shielded from his comedic effects, a fact that he was quite pleased about.

They still found him funny, though. Just not, you know, for something he hadn't said.

"Oh hey, Brury." His eyes lit up with the casual ease Avys had shown, and they continued. "Sorry, I'm just pissed off at some idiots online."

"What are they doing now? Are they still on about the 'Queer Gender'?" Brury sat down at the table across them, as Avys laughed.

"Honestly? You're not that far off." Avys unlocked their phone, showing Brury the screen. "No, some fucking idiot on Twitter keeps misgendering me."

"Right," Brury said casually, pausing. "And Twitter is…"

"A hellhole, bought by a fucking dumbass, full of idiots." Avys clarified. "Sometimes, it's funny, I guess?"

"So you were…"

"Right. I was getting into a fight with somebody over the idea that there are more than two genders, and when they finally agreed, they fucking called me a girl!"

"But, don't they know you're not?"

"You would think so, right? It's even in my fucking username!" Avys sighed. "Whatever, it's not like anybody even reads or thinks about who somebody is on the other side of the screen."

As Avys closed Twitter, mindlessly tapping on a time-wasting mobile game, Brury sat with a thoughtful look on his face. A beat later, his voice cut through Subway Surfer as they died.

"Sorry, just—" Avys looked as Brury was piecing everything together, trying not to laugh at his face. It's a very goofy face.

"What's on your mind?" Avys asked, snorting.

"You said nobody really cares about who you are on Twitter?"

"Yeah," Avys nodded, "Nobody even looks at your name, they just talk to you directly. It's infuriating."

"Is it?" Brury dug through his pockets, pulling out a slightly battered smartphone. "How do I sign up?"

"Oh, uhh…" Avys tried to recall a process that was like breathing to them. "You download the app, create a new account, and pick a username. Some people use their own name, but—"

"What?" Brury seemed distressed and incredulous at the same time. "I don't…"

"What's up?"

"The name I chose was taken."

"Oh? Just choose another one."

"No, Avys, it doesn't make any sense." Brury shook his head. "My username was taken."

"What… What did you put? There's plenty of reasons somebody might have a username cho—"

"Really? Can you explain why @BruryRegevoy was already fucking taken?"

Okay, Avys thought through a full belly laugh, as Brury glared at his phone. I get it now, that's a funny fucking name.

Hours later, Brury had finally chosen a username, and followed Avys.

Just as they had finally gotten over the username debacle, the notification they got on their phone sent them right back into a giggle-fest.

@BradSmelt followed you.

To think something so small could create so much. Zwist surveyed the guildhall's kitchen, desperately trying not to let the guilt take hold.

He took a deep breath, surrounded by the fruits of his labor. From wall to wall, there were cooling racks, filled with breads of all kind. Baguette, challah, ciabata and sourdough as far as the eye could see, each freshly baked, crafted by his masterful wizened hands.

After so many years of working with his hands, Zwist deserved a break. What else, rather than kneading his way through leavened history?

As he fed the culture, adding sugar by hand, he smiled, relaxed for the first time in many, many years.

I bet Avys would like to try the new loaf, I added a bit of honey, just like they like.

Avys: he won't fucking stop

On the twentieth day of living in the clubhouse, Avys knew that they weren't the only one going a little stir-crazy. It hadn't been coined yet, but they were sure this was the first recorded instance of 'Noösphere Fever'.

So, when Avys walked into the common area, and saw Dorothy Bradbury and Alis Rydderech at each other's throats, they nearly squealed in delight.

Where's the popcorn when you want it?

"As if," Dorothy said, turning their nose up, and shaking their head. "Your work is like carving ice with a sledgehammer. You're lucky everything doesn't fall apart."

"You're one to talk, 'Dorothy', haven't you had enough credit from other people's contributions to the cause?"

Alis stomped off, throwing herself down on the couch beside Avys.

"Back me up here, Avvy, I would win, right?"

Avys looked between the two skilled writers and erasers, before making the biggest mistake of the week. "Who would win what?"

They should never have gotten involved.

"Okay, so." Dorothy grabbed a chair, spinning it backwards and sitting on it, facing them. "We were arguing about who's done more."

"More what?"

"More damage to the idiots on the right with a single word."

Alis rolled her eyes. "And Dorothy thought that their little 'tweaks' to meaning were more effective than my complete obliteration of terms. Huh, even saying it out loud, it seems pretty obvious, doesn't it?"

"Are you still on about that?" Dorothy rolled their eyes. "You can't really think you'd win."

"Win what?" Avys, once again, would learn that around their friends, they would need to be much more careful with their choice of words.

"So, we figured out a test, and we wanted an impartial judge."

"And I am…"

"Impartial?" Alis shrugged. "I mean, you think both of us go too far, so… yeah, about as impartial as we'll get."

"So, what's the challenge? I don't think Lillian would be okay with us actually editing word meaning—"

"We already solved that," the two said in unison. Dorothy continued, "we promise, no word magic here, just normie shit."

"So." Alis butted back into the conversation. "One week, one entry on Urban Dictionary. Whoever can do more damage to the enemy wins."

"How will you decide that?"

The two stared at Avys, dumbfounded.

"That… That's your problem, judge."

Fuck. As the two pulled out their phones and began to furiously type, Phoebe sat down beside Avys, a fresh bowl of popcorn in her hands.

"Want some?"

Avys grinned, taking a handful, deciding to worry about how to judge them later.

A week later, conservative social media had fully adopted Dorothy's term 'brainthot', a word 'meaning' an idea that is inherently valuable, the opposite of brain rot. On the other hand, rightwing pundits proudly began to refer to white Americans with Alis' term, 'second first nations peoples'. So, when Avys declared the results as a tie, neither could bring themselves to disagree.

On the eve of their first month of living in the clubhouse, Avys walked into the middle of a confrontation that had been long brewing. While the venue may have changed, their animosity remained: Nirav Oberoi and Bianca Cimarosa glared at each other, from opposite sides of the kitchen.

I picked the worst time to grab a snack.

"You cannot really think your taste in cuisine is superior, Bianca." Nirav tutted from his chair, pushing his glasses up. "What bland food would you rather we eat tonight? Noodles in butter? Perhaps, something exotic, an American dish, meatloaf?"

"Pretentious fuck," Bianca muttered under her breath. "No, I would rather have my girlfriend's specialty."

"And that is?"

"Curry."

The pair was silent, as Avys made themselves known. "I like curry."

Both turned to look at them, each wearing a puzzled and uncertain look. Nirav was the first to look away from Avys.

"You like curry? I assume you are limited to butter chicken—"

"My preference is actually paneer pasanda, but, sure, chicken tikka will do in a pinch." As she saw Nirav staring with his mouth open, she laughed. "Careful you don't catch Noöspheric flies."

Nirav wheeled around the kitchen island, stopping in front of her.

"Oh, wow, you actually like curry curry? I just… I have been dreaming about palak paneer partha since I left home!"

Bianca's eyes lit up. "Oh! That would go so well with a goat korma, my mouth is watering…"

The two shared an uneasy look, each hesitating. It seemed, however, that while their animosity had been great, curry healed all wounds.

"Would you…" Nirav blushed. "Would you want to cook some curry with me?"

"You think I would trust you enough to eat anything you made without me supervising?"

"How crass." Nirav rolled his eyes. "The colonizer must ensure the native creates their cuisine authentically."

"Move over, drama queen, let me see the recipe you want to work off of."

That's good… I think? Avys frowned, grabbing some fruit and sneaking back out of the kitchen watching the argumentative pair. Nirav maneuvered to a properly-sized tabletop, while Bianca gathered ingredients from around the kitchen. Amidst the sniping, the two nattered excitedly about their preferences. I mean, cooking together is better than the two of them fighting all the time. How bad could it be?

After two weeks of eating nothing but assorted curries, Avys truly learned that they needed to be much more careful with what they said. In the Noösphere, it seemed that irony was both more literal, and had a much more wicked sense of humor.

They laughed, sending one more set of messages to Lillian.

Avys: they're still fighting, but through curry
Avys: the entire clubhouse smells like it

Dr_L: Oh? Is that good?

Avys: I mean
Avys: at least we have something to eat the fucking sourdough with

unreal-real-surreal.raw_content:
Anyar

A companion tale for SCP-8403.

A week after she left, Alfie tried reading his poems to lab rats. They skittered and squeaked and cheese-nibbled about the same, and a couple of them had fur that almost matched her particular shade of brown. In the end, though, they were just regular boring rats, and none of them ever decided to turn human.

In time, he got tired of their squeaking, tired of writing stupid poems nobody would ever care about, and so he returned to his old routine. The Foundation never ran out of busywork, and one quiet researcher disappeared easily among the bustle of the anomalous and those sworn to contain them. He clocked in on time, did the experiments, wrote the papers, and ended the day with nothing gained and another little part of him lost.

It was on one of those days, several months later, that he wrapped up the day's work and walked out the door. Snow crunched underfoot and a chilly breeze ruffled his hair, and he pulled his coat tighter around himself without thinking.

And that's when he saw her, waiting outside with her hands clasped to her chin.

She was so easy to miss, just the faintest wisp of a silhouette against a darkening sky. He squinted and rubbed his eyes, expecting her to disappear and shocked when she didn't. He slapped his palms against his temples, and when that didn't wake him up, he pinched himself until his skin turned crimson.

But it was her, alright. Noria and her bright hazel eyes, staring at him curiously through a tangle of cinnamon brown hair. Her mouth moved as though to speak, yet not a sound came out.

His eyes watered, and he reached his hand out to grasp at her. It went right through like she was a Noria-shaped cloud of mist with just the faintest hint of warmth. She tilted her head with a weak, disoriented smile, and for a moment, he stopped being able to breathe.

Then she looked away, and his mind started racing again.

It should've been impossible. She had been Neutralized, they'd tested it—not a single errant Hume left in her wake. Even now, she seemed barely real. All he heard was an indistinct whisper, and even that was probably just his imagination.

Voices from behind jolted him back to reality, and he hurriedly began walking, his breath puffing into little white clouds. Nobody else seemed to notice her, and by some miracle, Noria followed diligently after him despite her apparent confusion.

Well, for the most part. Every once in a while, she would startle and chase after a passing car or hopping bunny or drifting snowflake, and he'd have to chase her to lead her back. Other times she simply stopped in place and stared at him with such a strange expression and for so long that he felt as if he was going to burst.

Eventually, they reached his home. He watched with more than a little embarrassment as she hopped around his pigsty of an apartment, moving her hands along the dusty countertops and peeking at the crumpled blankets. Once, she tripped over a stack of clothes (which didn't budge an inch) and simply lay there dazed for a while.

It was admittedly cute, and Noria seemed to trust him, but he was almost cerain she didn't really recognize who he was. Not consciously, at least. That hurt him a little.

Still, having her home was… overwhelming. Desperate for a distraction, he snatched up a napkin and began wiping dust off the table; soon, he was staring blankly at the faded wood with his mind awhirl.

Was she real? Could he really trust his eyes? Thinking logically, he could be under the effects of a cognitohazard or who knows what other mind-affecting anomaly. Or maybe it was entirely mundane, and the stress and guilt and burning regret that had suffocated him all this time had finally congealed into this faint hallucination of his failures. Maybe he could take a pill and this damning vision of her would disappear for good.

Ice ran down his spine. He whirled around just in time to see her flop onto the couch. The sight brought him no relief as a roaring thunder echoed in his skull, for he was certain of it now—the next time he looked away, Noria would vanish completely. She would be replaced by nothing but the dismal, barren apartment and he'd finally break. He fell to his knees, straining to keep his eyes open though they burned and trembled and his nails dug into his palms until they bled, but anything, any pain would be worth seeing her for one moment more.

Then she stretched her arms and rolled off the couch with an entirely silent thud. Noria shook her head, her hair falling wildly over her eyes, and looked up at him with a sheepish grin. He blinked, smiled back, and the world was good again.

Over time, her voice became clearer. Disjoint syllables pieced together into complete sentences, faint as they were.

"You look really familiar, you know?" She liked to wonder out loud. Then, every morning: "Huh? Why can't I come with you?"

Alfie hated leaving her alone, but he couldn't risk bringing her near the site. So, he tried to make her comfortable. He bought vivid paintings, the kind you could stare at for hours, and hooked up a TV to play drama shows all throughout the day. He set up an automatic answering machine so he could call her from on-site, huddled in the bathroom stall with his hand cupped over the phone, desperately praying that nobody overheard.

After work, he would sprint home with his whole body aflame and collapse in the doorway, gasping for air so she could fuss over him. Then after he could breathe again, they'd do exciting things like reading poems, watching movies, and dressing up. She had pleaded for the last one until he'd relented, even though it brought back terrible memories of whiskers peeking out of a bundle of clothes. They played around with all the colors of the rainbow and crafted crazy, impossible hairstyles, but in the end, the lilac braids were still her favorite.

Noria was still a ghost when she remembered his name. There had been a containment breach that day, and he had watched a coworker die before his eyes. He had returned home shaken, his lab coat still dripping ooze, and she'd popped her head out from behind the couch, looked him up and down, and asked, "Alf? Are you okay?"

And it was the first time he'd let himself cry.

The neighborhood was quiet after midnight. They walked along a glassy lake that reflected the few dim stars yet visible in the sky; blooming pink camellias lent a faintly sweet aroma to the otherwise still air. Hardly a mote of moonlight passed through her anymore, which was the only reason they dared to go outside.

She was humming to herself when all of a sudden she stopped and announced, too loudly, "I'm gonna go jump in the lake."

Hands in his pockets, Alfie replied, "You're joking, right?"

She shook her head, her hair flying about. They had cut it together, which meant the ends were terribly uneven, but she claimed it looked perfect. "It'll be fun! I wanna see how cold the water gets. Look here, I'm already getting goosebumps just thinking about it." She pointed at the little dots on her arm. "Wouldn't it be cool if I froze into a big, me-shaped block of ice? Oh wait, you should totally jump with me! We'll freeze together!"

"I'd rather keep my blood running, thanks." He rubbed his head. "Also, I don't know how to swim."

"Then I'll teach you, I mean, even babies can do it, Alf. You just put your hands in front of you like you're praying and push them to the sides and kick your feet hard. You'll put all the fishies to shame."

"That… doesn't really help. Why can't we just keep walking and talking about deep meaningful things instead of voluntarily turning into ice cubes?"

She pursed her lips. "Don't you ever get tired of talking?"

"Well, sure, but—"

"Because I don't," she said, bouncing on the balls of her feet. "Talking's fun. But it's even more fun to do fun things while you talk."

"I-I don't know, I—"

Noria lunged at him and he instinctively jumped to the side. Her hands went right by him, her eyes went wide and she windmilled her arms for a second before falling into the lake with a thunderous splash.

"Um, you okay?" He asked, leaning over the side.

Her head popped out of the water and she yelled, flailing around. "Help! I actually did—" she bobbed below the surface "—forget how to swim!"

In the next moment, Alfie was airborne. The cold hit him like a stone wall, and then his hands crashed into the actual wall of the lake floor. He surfaced with a gasp and climbed to his feet, heart pounding in his chest like dynamite.

The water rippled against his waist. Beside him, Noria laughed, floating on her back and kicking icy droplets into his face. "Come on, you can't forget how to swim, it's like, part of your human DNA."

"I don't know why I dived in," he said, shivering violently and shielding himself with his hands. "If you'd actually been in trouble, we would've both drowned."

"All the more reason to learn this valuable skill, huh?" She reoriented herself upright and grinned. "Come deeper in and clap your hands together. I'll work you through it."

To hell with it. His clothes were already soaked, he was slowly warming up, and she was just too excited and smiley to refuse.

Alfie proceeded to, despite his best efforts, do his best impression of an anchor. After ten or twenty minutes of his hopeless struggling, Noria stomped out of the lake, tossing her hair over her shoulder in a big wet clump, and declared him a lost cause.

She brought it up over dinner one day. They had worked together to make a big pot of soup with carrots and celery and cheese (yes, cheese), and it was the first time they'd managed to get the salt and seasonings just right. Gnawing on a loaf of sourdough, she said almost offhandedly, "Eventually, you know, I'm gonna have to go poof again."

Alfie froze, spoon halfway to his mouth. He took a deep breath, then slowly set it down. "…yeah, I know. They aren't going to let me take an SRA off-site either, so you'll have to go back at some point."

"That's okay." She idly stirred her soup. "This time you know I'll be back, so it won't be so bad, right? I just want to make sure you'll be fine."

"I'll survive. But what about you?" He put his hands in his lap and searched her eyes. "It must be scary even thinking about it."

She blinked and looked away. "Don't worry about me. It'll just be like a long nap and I won't remember any of it."

He leaned over the table. "Do you want to talk about it?"

She waved her hand in the air. "I'll be okay. It's not important. I was asking about you."

"Of course it's important. You don't have to hide it if you're—"

She stood up abruptly. "I shouldn't have brought it up."

"Wait, Noria—"

"I've been human for a while now," she interrupted, still refusing to make eye contact. "It won't be too long before I'll become more than human, and it's not something I have a choice in, but it's fine, and you should be, um, prepared for it. So we should decide now. When I should go back and turn myself in."

"Can't avoid this any longer, huh?" He closed his eyes and sighed. "Logically, and to be safe, we should return before you start getting any real abilities. That way we can show that you don't mean to be a threat, otherwise they might just try to kill you outright. So judging from last time, starting from now, it'll take… maybe a couple weeks? I don't know for sure."

"Okay." Her voice came out as a whisper, and she looked at her feet. "Three weeks, then."

"Maybe four."

"Five, you mean?"

She tried to smile, but her eyes were glassy. He picked up his bowl and sipped the soup, but it was too salty.

Two months later, they caught him smuggling an SRA through the very first security checkpoint. It was confiscated immediately and he was detained for questioning, but fortunately, he was a good researcher and it was only a minor infraction. They let him off with an understanding headshake and a warning not to do it again.

Then he returned holding hands with a high-level Type Green, and they were a little less lenient this time.

Heated discussions were held. SCP-8403's file was brought out from dusty archives and pored over by countless eyes, and MTF squads equipped with experimental paratech were once again called to action. All the while, terrain, structures, and animals nearby flickered intermittently between real and unreal.

Researcher Xiao was one voice in this debate that would normally be overlooked. Yet the unusual circumstances, his repeated vows that the anomaly would willingly neutralize itself like before, plus a certain senior researcher's unexpected support, eventually led to a single SRA being airdropped to their location. Even still, a wide array of esoteric weaponry locked onto the pair as they held the device between them, clothes swaying in the breeze.

He cradled her face in his hands, breathing shakily and trembling up a storm. Yet her smile held firm and her eyes twinkled like moonlight. His thumb touched her lips, he leaned in, and for a brief moment before she pulled away, their faces heated up hotter and brighter than the sun.

"I'll see you in a few," Noria grinned through her blush.

Then she was gone.

Her hands went right by him, her eyes went wide and she windmilled her arms for a second before falling into the lake with a thunderous splash. "Um, you okay?" He asked, leaning over the side. Her head popped out of the water and she yelled, flailing around. "Help! I actually did—" she bobbed below the surface "—forget how to swim!" In the next moment, Alfie was airborne. The cold hit him like a stone wall, and then his hands crashed into the actual wall of the lake floor. He surfaced with a gasp and climbed to his feet, heart pounding in his chest like dynamite. The water rippled against his waist. Beside him, Noria laughed, floating on her back and kicking icy droplets into his face. "Come on, you can't forget how to swim, it's like, part of your human DNA." "I don't know why I dived in," he said, shivering violently and shielding himself with his hands. "If you'd actually been in trouble, we would've both drowned." "All the more reason to learn this valuable skill, huh?" She reoriented herself upright and grinned. "Come deeper in and clap your hands together. I'll work you through it." To hell with it. His clothes were already soaked, he was slowly warming up, and she was just too excited and smiley to refuse. Alfie proceeded to, despite his best efforts, do his best impression of an anchor. After ten or twenty minutes of his hopeless struggling, Noria stomped out of the lake, tossing her hair over her shoulder in a big wet clump, and declared him a lost cause. ---- She brought it up over dinner one day. They had worked together to make a big pot of soup with carrots and celery and cheese (yes, cheese), and it was the first time they'd managed to get the salt and seasonings just right. Gnawing on a loaf of sourdough, she said almost offhandedly, "Eventually, you know, I'm gonna have to go poof again." Alfie froze, spoon halfway to his mouth. He took a deep breath, then slowly set it down. "...yeah, I know. They aren't going to let me take an SRA off-site either, so you'll have to go back at some point." "That's okay." She idly stirred her soup. "This time you know I'll be back, so it won't be so bad, right? I just want to make sure you'll be fine." "I'll survive. But what about you?" He put his hands in his lap and searched her eyes. "It must be scary even thinking about it." She blinked and looked away. "Don't worry about me. It'll just be like a long nap and I won't remember any of it." He leaned over the table. "Do you want to talk about it?" She waved her hand in the air. "I'll be okay. It's not important. I was asking about you." "Of course it's important. You don't have to hide it if you're—" She stood up abruptly. "I shouldn't have brought it up." "Wait, Noria—" "I've been human for a while now," she interrupted, still refusing to make eye contact. "It won't be too long before I'll become more than human, and it's not something I have a choice in, but it's fine, and you should be, um, prepared for it. So we should decide now. When I should go back and turn myself in." "Can't avoid this any longer, huh?" He closed his eyes and sighed. "Logically, and to be safe, we should return before you start getting any real abilities. That way we can show that you don't mean to be a threat, otherwise they might just try to kill you outright. So judging from last time, starting from now, it'll take… maybe a couple weeks? I don't know for sure." [[size smaller]]"Okay."[[/size]] Her voice came out as a whisper, and she looked at her feet. "Three weeks, then." "Maybe four." "Five, you mean?" She tried to smile, but her eyes were glassy. He picked up his bowl and sipped the soup, but it was too salty. ---- Two months later, they caught him smuggling an SRA through the very first security checkpoint. It was confiscated immediately and he was detained for questioning, but fortunately, he was a good researcher and it was only a minor infraction. They let him off with an understanding headshake and a warning not to do it again. Then he returned holding hands with a high-level Type Green, and they were a little less lenient this time. ---- Heated discussions were held. SCP-8403's file was brought out from dusty archives and pored over by countless eyes, and MTF squads equipped with experimental paratech were once again called to action. All the while, terrain, structures, and animals nearby flickered intermittently between real and unreal. Researcher Xiao was one voice in this debate that would normally be overlooked. Yet the unusual circumstances, his repeated vows that the anomaly would willingly neutralize itself like before, plus a certain senior researcher's unexpected support, eventually led to a single SRA being airdropped to their location. Even still, a wide array of esoteric weaponry locked onto the pair as they held the device between them, clothes swaying in the breeze. He cradled her face in his hands, breathing shakily and trembling up a storm. Yet her smile held firm and her eyes twinkled like moonlight. His thumb touched her lips, he leaned in, and for a brief moment before she pulled away, their faces heated up hotter and brighter than the sun. "I'll see you in a few," Noria grinned through her blush. Then she was gone. ⚠️ content warning


Untitled Paratech Company | Untitled Parable >>

SIGNAL RECEIVED.

…

SYSTEM STARTUP.
ENGAGING JOINT LOCKS.

…

MOTOR SKILLS: FUNCTIONAL.

COGNITIVE SOFTWARE: FUNCTIONAL.

FLUID PUMPS: FUNCTIONAL.

SSD: FUNCTIONAL.

CONNECTION: STABILIZED.

…
…
…

ENGAGING BIOS.UNTITLED

Untitled's screen lit up, its cameras flashing red lights before its display began. It felt probes behind the baseplate of its back, plugged in from this morning. A base firmware update to enhance its performance. Its frame rattled, titanium scraping against iron as it stepped out of its upholstery. Untitled's feet echoed against the concrete as it walked around the workshop, scanning the current board of projects that Roman had to work on. The amount of overlapping pages and blueprints that were pinned probably would’ve exceeded the weight of the board itself if it hadn’t been bolted to the wall.

Roman had always made paratech to sell to anyone who had a need for it. The human side of this business has been legally questionable due to how he gathered his information on what he'll have to build next to please the market. He might just be an old man who can craft things, but one thing is for sure, he knows his way around every other party there is. He said that someone taught him, but he has never elaborated further. That someone is most likely dead at this point. Roman is a frail, old man. How he had the energy to keep going is something only he'll know.

It paced forward, metal screeching as dust moved its way inside its machinery. Their warehouse was filthy, debris pushed to the walls instead of properly disposed of. Metal supports were evenly spaced out across the warehouse, and were built onto with large chain link walls which helped give a sense that this is a place meant to be lived in. Each sectioned off space had a purpose. Around Untitled were rows of tables with pieces of tech in their production stages as well as boxes, filled with sold pieces that had to get shipped. Its thoughts waned.

"Sigh."

It wishes it could exhale air instead of having to pronounce it. While Roman and Sykes were out, busy doing who knows what, it'd be a good idea to keep working on its side of the company in peace. Untitled got down on one knee, brushing away stains as it lifted up the hatch in the floor in front of its upholstery. It climbed down before it slammed the hatch shut above itself, a creak greeting its sensors while dirt and sand sprinkled down like snowflakes from the hinges. A corroded ladder down to the bunker welcomed it like an old friend.

Down here is its domain. Entirely its. The bunker had to have been one of the most unpleasant places to turn into a workplace … for a human, that is. From a robot point-of-view, it did what it was meant to do. Damp and oppressive, an atmosphere most likely born out of Untitled's intentions. As a machine, it didn't have a need to breathe. The air is noxious and deadly, due to all the active fumes produced across numerous chemistry sets and machines. A single ventilation unit was near the entrance to ensure nothing would escape when the hatch was open.

As it stepped across cracked concrete, it pulled back a ragged curtain that hid a section of its lab, revealing a half-built endoskeleton, with spools of wires and plugs flowing outwards from its chest like a still life of a man getting shot. Untitled did not properly know how to clean up after itself in this regard. The pros & cons list that it computes every time it enters this place always says sorting this plastic mess will be a waste of time.

Before the robot could do anything meaningful, it heard the sound of the Way opening upstairs. It grabbed the curtain and dragged it together. The hydraulics in it hissed as it made its way up the rusty ladder, opening the hatch yet again.

The first thing it saw was Roman, dropping off a saggy duffel bag on a granite tabletop as he pushed away a pile of electronics that he had previously tinkered with. Sykes had ran off to the bathroom. The man drinks too many energy drinks while he walks about. Roman takes a puff from his inhaler as he speaks.

"Hey, U. Glad to see that … you are awake."

Untitled made its way around, gliding a hand against the edge of the table. "Yes, Roman. I appreciate the WORK," it raised a palm up, "I feel refreshed and INVIGORATED." It looked at Roman, the cameras in its head tightening as it zoomed in on his face. Untitled's distorted voice was like a relic of that which Roman had worked with to make the machine. Crude and harsh. Every few words crashing unceremoniously into itself was something the two of them got used to. Some bugs in the code can't be squashed.

"Uh-huh." The man was busy, digging through the bag as he placed an assortment of items out on the table. For an old man like Roman, his raspy voice did have the power to travel quite a bit. The echo of the building did help. "Definitely. Please, just remind me to fine tune anything that's off. Sykes!"

"What?!"

"The veritas headset, the one the gawker gave us— where is it?!"

The flush of a toilet rang out. Sykes came out and leaned against the doorway of the workshop. Gloved hands run leather fingers through slicked back, dark hair.
"In my bag! Don't get your panties twisted, man."
Sykes chuckles, dirtied boots leaving slight stains as he steps in, squatting down as he grabs the headset from his backpack. He carefully hands it over to Roman.

The robot took a few steps closer, looking down at the odd device. "Your status with the SERPENT’S HAND. Are they aware?" Its head cleanly rotated to look at Roman, the expression on its facial panel showing a neutral glare.

"Bah—" He bluntly exclaimed, "I can always just give them another hint or tip on what the … the GOC or Foundation is doing next. Everyone needs this thing just as much as we do, considering the innovations that have been happening at Eurtec. My inside man is getting antsy." Roman grasped for his inhaler as he spoke.

"Whatever you say, Rome … "
Sykes grabbed his bag, heading off to the kitchen to fill his stomach.

"We need to improve upon their design; make it compact enough, cheap enough. The GOC's engineers … cannot design jack shit efficiently." Roman sits down on a comfortable mattress chair, the cover scratched and worn. "U, I know we were just out, but … yes, would you mind fetching me an order I placed in Three Portlands? It's food and medicine." He shook his inhaler around. "I heard there is a parade of sorts going around across the entire city … lots of outsiders and such … you'll blend in with those augmented people, forgot their names."

"Do I get a pass?"
Sykes stood behind, hands placed at the neck rest of the chair.

"Yes, you can go too. Just make sure to be quick … I am sure both storefronts close in two hours. Didn’t you just go to make lunch?"

Untitled placed its cold hands on Roman.
"We will go with GREAT HASTE, father."

♔

A Way is a form of travel that requires a method to access it, known as a Knock. In exchange for free orders on all future products, Roman made a deal with a human that possessed incredible thaumaturgy. They created an illegal way to Three Portlands as well as several other Free Ports and Nexus's so that the company may conduct business without intervention. The police force that works in Three Portlands, nicknamed the Fireflies, are specifically looking out for Sykes & Roman, both for their own reasons. They work to keep the island clean from filth like them.

… Who was that human?

Untitled stepped out of the Way, with Sykes close behind. Their little pocket dimension filled with doors folded into itself as they exited. Out into the same spot they always have, the empty upper floors of a skyscraper currently owned by some random company that didn't matter to them. They just needed free space so they could do their travel uninterrupted. Bribing is the best option they had. Failing businesses needed any cash flow they could get to survive in this world.

"I wonder … will anyone try to turn me in to the fireflies if they recognize me?"
Sykes's mind was always on the wrong things.

The robot gripped his shoulder tightly. "Look out for POSTERS, Sykes. We must be careful here." Untitled turned, walking through stale air and down musty, molding corridors. The workers knew not to pay much attention to them if they knew what would happen to their jobs.

"You know I can handle myself if things get messy, tin can."

"Do not shake the HORNET'S NEST."

The two of them stay close together, with Untitled leading the way. They make their way down a fire exit and walk out into the alleyway next to the building. Fresh air at last. The city was radiating with noise, and looking to the exits of the alleyway showed crowded streets. Trash didn't pile these dumpsters as much, but with the parade, confetti and litter became noticeable among the hundreds of feet stomping on the ground. Workers make sure to stick to a tight schedule while maintaining the beauty that this city holds. With the water around them, most people prefer to give their trash to the fauna that makes good use of it. The outsiders who visit Three Portlands aren't very aware of this tradition.

The screen on its head flashed an ellipsis. "Decoding GEO.Node … Sharp's Special Souls AND Dali Pharma."

"That's going to be one long walk—"

"Apply your BUFFER and stop complaining. I would like a clean EXPEDITION from you." Untitled raised a finger at Sykes as it began walking, not bothering to turn around.

Robots like Untitled were very uncommon in Three Portlands, albeit they were always confused for devoted Maxwellists. No one bothered to look for flesh, because you'd never know if the only thing left was a heartbeat. Men like Sykes blended into the background due to the far more interesting anahumans you'd see roaming about. Navigating through the dense crowds allowed them to see winged men and children, horns and teeth in places where they don't belong, and humans who are part machine. Squeezing past tightly packed stalls selling paraphernalia made movement through the main city streets slow. It was not long before the two of them passed by Sykes's posters, signed by the United States Domestic Security Court. A detailed poster with Sykes's prison mugshot was pinned to an intricate bulletin board, as well as several more on the surrounding lampposts. A lot of it was covered up by advertisements for the current festival alongside UIU and Anderson Robotics recruitment campaigns.

He ripped the poster from the board, looking down at it. The buffer somewhat muffled his voice. "My jawline is sharper than that. I swear they didn't angle the lights properly while I was in there"

"Get a MOVE ON, Sykes. Before THEY notice."

It'd be a good idea to fetch Roman's medication before dinner, Untitled thought. Roman neglected to mention that nearly everyone had some form of green apparel on for this event. The two of them stuck out like sunlight reflecting off of snow. Luckily, so did the people who put the posters up. The long, crystalline barrels of a Firefly's weapon was easy to spot from a distance, and they navigated around them in the crowds to avoid any altercation. It was barely an hour before they arrived at Dali Pharma. Clinical, clean and handcrafted. A knock on the floral pattern shutter under the overhang, simple proof of payment and they were off with a brown carton bag. Untitled twitched the visible gears on its back as a thank you. This was one of the only shops not flooded with outsiders.

His stiff neck cracked as he rolled his head. "How many people do you know in this damn city?"

"The perfect LIFEFORM is a fungus, due to its mastery in CONNECTION. It can teach you things, Sykes."

"Oh, fuck you."

To the other side of the city on a normal day, it would be 35 minutes. With this crowd, it would likely take 53. Margin of error leaves 7 minutes. Expert navigation using backstreets to the best of their ability … 15. As they quickly walked through a narrow alley, Untitled suddenly grabbed Sykes by his collar, placing their backs against a spray-painted brick wall.

"HALT."

He stuck close to the wall and peeked around as he got close to the robot. Untitled had its reasons, so Sykes did not struggle. "What do you see? Anyone in our debt?" Untitled heard the bolt of Sykes’s hidden rifle slide open.

"Refrain. It's REINVELD," It looks up, seeing a fire escape ladder out of reach, "Up there."

Sykes balls his fist and sighs before Untitled turns around, crouching as it extends a hand. The man steps up, the joints locking in place to sustain Sykes's weight. In a moment, the ladder falls down, and the two of them carefully climb up to the roof.

Reinveld is an engineer working for one of the many successful companies that moved to Eurtec, specifically, LifeSynth. Or, at least, he is on paper. A massive reactor meltdown and eventual explosion caused by "system malfunctions" occurred in another facility not too far from their headquarters that had a body count in the triple digits. Paratech companies are willing to hire terrorists and mercenaries to get rid of their enemies if it means they'll get more time to experiment and find solutions to problems that wouldn't exist if it weren't those same companies creating those problems in the first place. The competition is fierce. Untitled sought to work alongside Roman and play both sides.

"How much did he pay you to develop that bomb?" Sykes spoke flatly; his rifle squared against his hip as he held on to the stock.

"I don't sympathize with LOSS OF LIFE that I have not personally met. We do business with those that PAY rather than the ones that don't." Untitled looked over towards Sykes, its rigid fingers pushing the black barrel down. "Not now. We plan for it when it BENEFITS us."

"Does it matter if it benefits us if we know it'll benefit everyone else?" He folds his rifle together, hiding it in his backpack.

"Do you VALUE strangers more than the bounty your own hide is worth, Cristobal?" One could barely make out a robot similar to Untitled speaking to the Fireflies between the decorated washing lines and banners before disappearing into the cheering groups of the festival. It seemed to carry an instrument with it in a guitar case. Performers are common … robotic ones, not at all.

"I value the peace I'd get knowing that someone who has probably killed thousands is dead." Sykes turns his back to Untitled before he begins to climb down the fire escape opposite the one they previously climbed.

The two of them pushed past entranced civilians who look onwards to the annual Portland Prairie Festival main event, meant to harmonize land & sea together through a thrilling display of thaumaturgy where the backlash causes beautiful alterations to the greenery and sea life. A massive stage is built in advance in the main plaza, similar to an amphitheatre. There's a lot more anomalous properties to the festival than just the show itself. The blind see the artistic display of talent, the deaf hear the rhythmic melody of the talented orchestra and the voiceless sing their praises. It unites all those that oppose each other yet love that which nature gives them. It is with much thanks to The Mayor that everyone gets a chance to experience this event every year.

"Hey … what the hell are they celebrating really?"

"I just had it open in my database. ONE MOMENT—"

Sykes pulls Untitled closer by the shoulder, standing aside as he leans in, hushing his voice. "Don't you think it's a big coincidence to see Reinveld here the same day they're doing this bullshit?!"

"Relax. He is most likely SIGHTSEEING with his daughter. He would not do it twice in the same quarter, nevertheless with HER witnessing. Besides. What would his motive be? ANDERSON'S plaza is further away. PROMETHEUS left months ago. Who'd RUIN this lovely event?"

"You sold him more than one, didn't you? I know you are fine with your 'I DON'T CARE ABOUT ANYONE' mindset, but this is just … fucked up. I can't believe you!"

Untitled grabbed Sykes by the back of the neck, raising him up and carrying him on his shoulder as he walked to Sharp's Special Souls. Sykes tried resisting for a moment, but he knew he could never be as strong as the robot even if he tried. Onlookers laughed briefly before the two disappeared behind brick and stone.

"Stay quiet in front of the public eye before we have to BREAK YOU OUT again. You're attracting UNWANTED ATTENTION."

After a burdened walk, It put Sykes down on the ground as they entered Sharp's shop. Wooden beams held up a large thatch roof, with large logs stretching across. The floor tiles had intricate geometrical patterns and the seats were worn down. Squishy and relaxing. The commotion outside brought a lot more business to this quaint restaurant, and people are, without a doubt, enthralled. The line is long, and some people won't get served in time. Luckily, the man of the hour is free to serve them.

"Unty, my boy! Just in time. What can I get for you and your friend'o there?" Sykes paced to the left, slightly hiding behind the robot. Sharp grinned, happy to see one of his favourite recurring customers amongst the crowd of new faces.

Untitled stepped forward. "CAESER placed an order. I am picking it up."

Sharp's crooked blue horns began to glow before he flicked his tatted blue fingers at them, flaming sparks flying through the air. “Right'o, right'o. I'll give you an extra bottle of Sirpa on the house, how's that? I owe the man, after all!” Roman's favourite alcohol. The ASCII smile formed on Untitled’s screen.

"That would be PLEASANT to deal with. Thank you very much, Sharp." Untitled saw Sykes looking off through the windows, so it quickly slipped the flyer it had hidden in its forearm to Sharp underneath the bill. The two of them nodded to each other before the robot stored the packages in its rug sack compartment which opened up like a shutter on its back.

"LET'S GO. Our tasks are finished."

"Thank god, I was just beginning to think I'll have to pitch a tent here."

"QUIET."

Untitled was thankful for once that Sykes's attention could easily be taken off of it and onto the crowds around them. Slipping that paper was important. Customers of its side of the Untitled Paratech Company had to get its list of available products one way or another, right?

Both make their way through the chanting groups and back to the same office building, climbing up the same flight of dilapidated stairs. As they stand near massive, thick framed windows, walking down the grungy hall that leads to the Way, the echo of a rifle rings out nearing the festival centre. At least, it sounds that way to Untitled. Two more shots ring out before the screams of all the crowds begin to exceed the music that abruptly stops. People begin to disperse like ants, all hording against each other to get away from the gunfire. Some with powers don't hide but instead seek. Buildings block their view of people that are most likely dead, but nothing blocks its line of sight to the perpetrator.

The robot that spoke to the Fireflies. Its design was minimalist and practical. Steel plates blocked its vital components. Its legs and arms were stripped to their core for efficiency. Spring counterweights were attached within cylinders that jutted out from its shoulders. Why here? Why now? Did they have a deal? They wouldn't hire mercenaries, would they?

Its weapon. A modified instrument that could be built into a lightweight rifle with ease. The motors within Untitled began to whir with excitement. A fellow robot doing what it does best? They exist?
"I have never seen someone use such a CREATIVE method for hiding a weapon in plain sight."

"What the fuck are you talking about, tin can?"

"OH, right." Untitled began to point with its left hand. "To the LEFT of the office block on our right, look UP to the ventilation units. Right THERE. Armed shooter. MARVELOUS!"

The man immediately reached behind his bag without hesitation. Sykes unfolded his rifle and placed the barrel of his gun on Untitled's shoulder, chambering a round as he began zeroing the scope. "Distance to target?"

Untitled processed for a second before answering. Interfering could cause problems … but after the run in with Reinveld, Sykes was most likely itching to shoot anything he could. This could be seen as heroic to the public, and the Fireflies could take credit for a third party's silent involvement. Distance.
"ONE THOUSAND metres."

He adjusts his scope before carefully aiming. His breath steadies, his hands jittery. Another shot rings out. Leather gloves squeeze tightly against the glass fibre stock of the rifle, and a drop of sweat rolls down Sykes’s forehead before he swallows the spit in his mouth.

"Shoot the top of its thigh. It won't be able to ESCAPE without control of its legs."

All of the sound dissipates in Sykes's ears but for a moment. The last breath exits his lungs, and he relaxes. The rifle rattles against his shoulder as a shot is fired, and all of Sykes's senses return to him like a floodgate of stimulation. Untitled's shoulder slightly heats up as smoke trails the gun barrel. Sykes takes another breath in before slinging it away.

"Hit?"

"… Down."

"EXCELLENT."

♔

Untitled roamed the building before settling in the living quarters, watching Roman scroll along on the laptop, reading an issue of Magpie Swoops. All old men have their own forms of entertainment. Before the robot could speak, Sykes walked in, taking a seat at the far end of the mahogany table.

"Hey, tin can. Did we ever look at what actually happened the other day?"

"From what I can gather on VOID & other sources, it appears that the ASSASSIN … "

Roman looked up from the screen. "Yes? Keep going, U."

" … shot Reinveld. He'll be getting JAILED when he recovers. One bullet to the shoulder. One to the INTESTINES. One to his leg. Another shot apparently GRAZED his daughter's hand. Despite SYKES and I interfering, the assassin got away."

"Looks like someone did my job for me." Sykes chuckles, leaning back as he interlaced his fingers behind his head. "So much so for that shitty mindset, huh?"

"Yes. It would APPEAR so.”

With Reinveld off the board for now, companies are going to want to find his supplier. One man can’t make such chemicals alone. but they fail to consider it's not a human doing it. Perhaps that robot was doing Untitled a favour in that regard. The thought didn’t cross Sykes’s mind, but it definitely crossed Untitled’s.

And that thought made its binary flutter with glee.

@import url('https://fonts.bunny.net/css2?family=IBM+Plex+Sans:ital,wght@0,400;0,500;0,600;0,700;1,400;1,500;1,600;1,700&display=swap');
 
/* VARIABLES */
 
:root {
 
    /* VARIABLES > Core */
 
    --header-title: "SCP Foundation";
    --header-subtitle: "SECURE, CONTAIN, PROTECT";
    --logo-img: url(https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/local--files/theme:foxtrot/fxtrt-scp_logo_lightmode.svg);
    --darkmode-logo-img: url(https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/local--files/theme:foxtrot/fxtrt-scp_logo_darkmode.svg);
    --logo-opacity: 14%;
 
    --head-font: 'Sans Normalcy';
    --ui-font: 'IBM Plex Sans';
    --mono-font: 'JetBrains Mono', 'Fira Code', monospace;
    --page-font: 'Inter', 'verdana';
    --base-font-size: 0.9rem;
    --page-font-size: 1rem;
 
    /* VARIABLES > Misc */
 
    --header-txt-color: #333333;
    --subheader-txt-color: rgb(var(--accent));
    --misc-txt-color: #464646;
    --link-txt-color: #E6283C;
    --link-hover-txt-color: white;
 
    /* VARIABLES > Color Accents */
 
    --accent: var(--acc-default);
 
    --acc-default: 59, 59, 59;
    --acc-wyoming: 142, 0, 18;
    --acc-canada: var(--acc-default);
    --acc-poland: 87, 44, 17;
    --acc-slothspit: 27, 60, 133;
    --acc-vanguard: 0, 153, 75;
    --acc-threshold: 121, 113, 130;
    --acc-overwatch: 28, 37, 56;
    --acc-spc: 0, 165, 200;
    --acc-fishing: 67, 111, 145;
    --acc-nightfall: 151, 0, 2;
    --acc-hybrasil: 27, 60, 133;
    --acc-goc: 39, 84, 149;
    --acc-spooky: 252, 112, 40;
 
    /* VARIABLES > BetterFootnotes */
 
    --fnColor: var(--link-txt-color);
    --fnLinger: 1s;
 
}
 
/* VARIABLES > Info Bar */
 
.info-container {
    --barColour: rgb(var(--accent));
    --linkColour: #EDEDED;
}
 
/* MAIN */
 
html {
    scroll-behavior: smooth;
    overflow-x: hidden;
}
 
body {
    font-family: var(--ui-font), sans-serif;
    font-size: var(--base-font-size);
    color: rgb(51, 51, 51);
    background-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, #e0e0e0, #fff 200px);
    text-rendering: optimizeLegibility;
    overflow-wrap: break-word;
}
 
div#container-wrap {
    background: none;
}
 
#content-wrap {
    margin: 2em auto 0;
}
 
#page-content {
    font-family: var(--page-font), var(--ui-font), sans-serif;
    font-size: var(--page-font-size);
    font-weight: 440;
}
 
#page-content strong {
    font-weight: 700;
}
 
tt,
.page-source,
pre,
#edit-page-textarea {
    font-family: var(--mono-font);
}
 
ol li {
    margin: 0 0 1em;
}
 
ul {
    margin: 1em 0;
}
 
li,
p {
    line-height: 1.5;
    text-underline-offset: 40%;
}
 
::selection {
    background: rgb(var(--accent));
    color: #fff;
}
 
/* Clicky links */
a,
a.newpage,
a:visited,
#side-bar a:visited {
    color: var(--link-txt-color);
}
 
a:hover,
a.newpage:hover,
a:visited:hover,
#side-bar a:visited:hover {
    color: var(--link-hover-txt-color);
    text-decoration: none;
    background-color: var(--link-txt-color);
}
 
a {
    transition-duration: 0.1s;
}
 
/* patch for sidebar media, collapsibles, ACS, info button and ayers module so link doesn't override */
#page-content .collapsible-block-folded a:hover,
#page-content .collapsible-block-unfolded-link a:hover,
#page-content .rate-box-with-credit-button .fa-info:hover,
#side-bar .side-block.media a:hover,
.danger-diamond a:hover {
    background: transparent;
}
 
.info-container .collapsible-block-folded .collapsible-block-link,
.info-container .collapsible-block-link {
    background: var(--linkColour) !important;
}
 
/* MAIN > Header */
 
div#header {
    background: none;
    height: 160px;
}
 
#header h1 span,
#header h2 span {
    font-size: 0;
    display: none;
}
 
#header h1 a::before,
#header h2::before {
    color: var(--header-txt-color);
    letter-spacing: 1px;
    font-family: var(--head-font), sans-serif !important;
    font-weight: 900;
    text-shadow: none;
}
 
#header h1 {
    margin-top: -0.3rem;
}
 
#header h1 a {
    width: fit-content;
    margin: auto;
}
 
#header h1 a::before {
    content: var(--header-title);
    font-size: 1.3em;
}
 
#header h2::before {
    content: var(--header-subtitle);
    font-family: var(--ui-font) !important;
    font-weight: 700;
    font-size: 1.4em;
    color: var(--misc-txt-color);
    line-height: 26px;
    margin-top: 0.35rem;
    display: block;
    text-transform: uppercase;
}
 
#header h1,
#header h2 {
    margin-left: 0;
    float: none;
    text-align: center;
}
 
#header h1 span,
#header h2 span {
    font-size: 0;
    display: none;
}
 
div#extra-div-1 {
    height: 160px;
    width: 100%;
    top: 7px;
    position: absolute;
    background: var(--logo-img) 10px 30px no-repeat;
    background-size: 130px;
    background-repeat: no-repeat;
    background-position: 50% 50%;
    z-index: -1;
    opacity: var(--logo-opacity);
}
 
/* MAIN > Header > Search Box */
 
#search-top-box-form>input[type=text] {
    display: none;
}
 
#search-top-box-input,
#search-top-box-input:hover,
#search-top-box-input:focus,
#search-top-box-form input[type=submit],
#search-top-box-form input[type=submit]:hover,
#search-top-box-form input[type=submit]:focus {
    border: none;
    background: rgb(var(--accent));
    box-shadow: none;
    border-radius: 5px !important;
    color: #efefef;
    font-family: var(--ui-font);
    font-size: calc(var(--page-font-size) - 10%);
}
 
#search-top-box input.empty {
    color: #999999;
}
 
#search-top-box {
    position: absolute;
    top: 47px;
    width: unset;
}
 
/* MAIN > Header > Top Bar */
 
#top-bar,
#top-bar a {
    top: 10rem;
}
 
#header #top-bar ul {
    border-radius: 10px;
    border: none;
    background: rgb(var(--accent));
    padding-left: 15px;
    padding-right: 15px;
}
 
#header #top-bar a {
    color: white;
    background: rgb(var(--accent));
    font-weight: bold;
}
 
#header #top-bar ul li ul {
    padding: 0px;
    border-radius: 0px;
}
 
#top-bar ul li.sfhover a,
#top-bar ul li:hover a {
    border-left: solid 1px #FFF;
    border-right: solid 1px #FFF;
}
 
#top-bar ul li ul li a:hover {
    color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.83) !important;
    line-height: 230%;
    text-indent: 3px;
}
 
#top-bar {
    display: flex;
    justify-content: center;
    right: 0;
}
 
.mobile-top-bar {
    left: unset;
}
 
/* MAIN > Header > Login Info */
 
#login-status {
    top: 19px;
}
 
#login-status,
#login-status a {
    color: #333333;
}
 
@media (max-width: 767px) {
    #header .printuser {
        font-size: 0;
    }
}
 
.printuser a {
    margin: 0;
}
 
.printuser img.small {
    width: 18px;
    height: 18px;
    padding: 1px 4px 0 0;
 
    background-image: none !important;
}
 
@media (max-width: 767px) {
    #header .printuser img.small {
        transform: translate(0, 4px);
    }
}
 
#my-account {
    display: none;
}
 
@media (max-width: 767px) {
    #account-topbutton {
        margin: 0 0 0 5px;
    }
}
 
/* MAIN > Header > Side Bar */
 
#top-bar .open-menu a {
    border-radius: 0px;
    border: none;
    background: rgb(var(--accent));
    color: white;
}
 
#side-bar {
    background: #FFF;
}
 
@media (min-width: 768px) {
 
    #side-bar {
        padding: 0.3em 0.6em 0 0.6em;
        width: 18.75em;
        transition: left 0.2s ease-in-out;
        direction: rtl;
        text-align: left;
        border-right: none;
    }
 
}
 
#side-bar .side-block,
#side-bar .side-block.resources,
#side-bar .side-block.media,
#interwiki .side-block {
    border: 2px solid rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2);
    border-radius: 0px;
    box-shadow: none;
    margin-bottom: 6px;
    direction: ltr;
    background: transparent;
}
 
#side-bar .side-block.resources {
    text-align: center;
}
 
#side-bar .heading {
    color: var(--misc-txt-color);
    border-bottom: solid 2px #cfcfcf;
    font-size: 9pt;
    font-family: var(--head-font);
    font-weight: 800;
    text-transform: uppercase;
}
 
/* CONTENT */
 
/* CONTENT > Blockquotes, Custom Divs */
 
.blockquote,
div.blockquote,
blockquote {
    border: solid 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.15);
    background: #f7f7f7;
}
 
.jotting {
    padding: 1.3em;
    margin: 1em 4.5em;
    border: dashed 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2);
    background: #f7f7f7;
}
 
.notation {
    padding: 1em 1.5em;
    margin: 1em 3em;
    border-left: solid 3px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.35);
    border-right: solid 3px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.35);
    background: #f7f7f7;
}
 
.modal {
    padding: 1.2em;
    margin: 1em 3em;
    border: solid 5px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.15);
    background: #fbfbfb;
}
 
.quote {
    padding: 0.4em 2em;
    margin: 3em auto;
    border-left: solid 3px #bbb;
    max-width: 500px !important;
}
 
.paper {
    padding: 1.5em;
    margin: 2em;
    background: #FFF;
    box-shadow: 0px 4px 9px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2);
}
 
.box {
    padding: 1px 9px;
    border: solid 3px #bbb;
    margin: 0.5em 1em;
}
 
div.note {
    font-size: unset;
    border: 2px solid #afafaf;
    background-color: #fff;
}
 
.round {
    border-radius: 10px;
}
 
/* CONTENT > Headings, Titles */
 
#page-title,
.meta-title {
    font-family: var(--ui-font), sans-serif;
    font-weight: 800;
    color: #3b3b3b;
    border-bottom: solid 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2);
    width: fit-content;
    margin: 0 auto 1.5rem;
}
 
#page-title,
.meta-title,
#breadcrumbs,
.pseudocrumbs {
    text-align: center;
}
 
h1,
h2,
h3,
h4,
h5,
h6 {
    font-family: var(--head-font), sans-serif;
    font-weight: 800;
    color: #3b3b3b;
}
 
h1,
h2 {
    font-weight: 800;
}
 
.footnotes-footer .title {
    font-family: var(--head-font), sans-serif;
    color: #3b3b3b;
    font-weight: 800;
}
 
/* CONTENT > Rate Module */
 
#page-content .creditRate {
    margin: unset;
    font-family: var(--ui-font);
    float: unset !important;
}
 
#page-content .rate-box-with-credit-button {
    background-color: #fff;
    border: solid 1px #bbb;
    box-shadow: none;
    border-radius: 0;
}
 
#page-content .rate-box-with-credit-button .fa-info {
    border: none;
    color: #333;
}
 
#page-content .rate-box-with-credit-button .fa-info:hover {
    background: #333;
    color: #fff;
}
 
.rate-box-with-credit-button .cancel {
    border: solid 1px #fff;
}
 
.page-rate-widget-box {
    box-shadow: none;
    border: solid 1px #bbb;
    margin: unset;
    margin-bottom: 4px;
    border-radius: 0;
    font-family: var(--ui-font);
}
 
.page-rate-widget-box .rate-points {
    background-color: #fff !important;
    color: #333 !important;
    border: none !important;
    border-radius: 0;
}
 
.page-rate-widget-box .rateup,
.page-rate-widget-box .ratedown {
    background-color: #fff;
    border-top: none;
    border-bottom: none;
}
 
.page-rate-widget-box .rateup a,
.page-rate-widget-box .ratedown a {
    background: transparent;
    color: #333;
}
 
.page-rate-widget-box .rateup a:hover,
.page-rate-widget-box .ratedown a:hover {
    background: #333;
    color: #fff;
}
 
.page-rate-widget-box .cancel {
    background: #fff;
    border: none;
    border-radius: 0;
    display: inline-block;
}
 
.page-rate-widget-box .cancel a {
    color: #333;
}
 
.page-rate-widget-box .cancel a:hover {
    background: #333;
    color: #fff;
    border-radius: 0;
}
 
#page-content .rate-box-with-credit-button .page-rate-widget-box {
    border: none;
}
 
/* CONTENT > Rate Module > Author Label */
 
.authorlink-wrapper {
    --author-top-adjust: 0;
    --author-bottom-adjust: 0;
    --author-right-adjust: 0;
    font-family: var(--ui-font);
    font-size: var(--base-font-size);
}
 
/* CONTENT > Side Box */
 
.anchor {
    position: sticky;
    height: 0;
    top: 0;
}
 
.sidebox {
    padding: .14rem;
    margin-top: 0;
    margin-bottom: 8px;
    width: calc((100vw - 870px)/2);
    max-height: calc(100vh - 18rem);
    position: absolute;
    top: 0;
    left: 103.5%;
    z-index: 5;
    overflow: auto;
    box-sizing: border-box;
}
 
@media (max-width: 1290px) {
    .sidebox {
        display: none;
        visibility: hidden;
    }
}
 
/* CONTENT > Image Block */
 
.scp-image-block .scp-image-caption {
    background-color: #f4f4f4;
    color: #3b3b3b;
    border: solid 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1);
    margin-top: 8px;
    box-sizing: border-box;
    border-radius: 4px;
}
 
.scp-image-block {
    border: none;
    box-shadow: none;
}
 
.scp-image-block img {
    border: solid 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1);
    box-sizing: border-box;
}
 
.imagediv {
    float: right;
    margin: 15px
}
 
@media (max-width: 540px) {
    .imagediv {
        float: unset;
        text-align: center;
        margin: 1.3rem auto 1.3rem auto;
    }
}
 
@media only screen and (max-width: 600px) {
    .scp-image-block.block-right {
        float: none;
        margin: 10px auto;
    }
}
 
/* CONTENT > Tables Base */
 
#page-content tr th {
    padding: 6px;
    border: 2px solid rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2);
}
 
#page-content tr td {
    padding: 12px;
    border: 2px solid #bfbfbf;
    line-height: 1.4;
}
 
#page-content .sidebox tr td,
#page-content .sidebox tr th {
    padding: 0.35em;
}
 
/* CONTENT > Tables Customization (Table Coloring System) */
 
/* CONTENT > Tables Customization (Table Coloring System) > Table Headings, Image Captions */
 
#page-content .table1 tr th,
#page-content .table1 .scp-image-block .scp-image-caption {
    background-color: #E0FFD4;
}
 
#page-content .table2 tr th,
#page-content .table2 .scp-image-block .scp-image-caption {
    background-color: #D8ECF4;
}
 
#page-content .table3 tr th,
#page-content .table3 .scp-image-block .scp-image-caption {
    background-color: #FDF6D7;
}
 
#page-content .table4 tr th,
#page-content .table4 .scp-image-block .scp-image-caption {
    background-color: #FFDFCD;
}
 
#page-content .table5 tr th,
#page-content .table5 .scp-image-block .scp-image-caption {
    background-color: #FFCFCF;
}
 
#page-content .table6 tr th,
#page-content .table6 .scp-image-block .scp-image-caption {
    background-color: rgba(146, 0, 255, 0.2);
}
 
.tableb .wiki-content-table {
    border-collapse: separate;
    border-spacing: 2px;
}

.table5 .blockquote,

    background: rgb(255, 218, 255);
}
 
/* CONTENT > Tabs Base */
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav a,
.yui-navset .yui-navset-top .yui-nav a {
    background-color: inherit;
    background-image: inherit
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav a:hover,
.yui-navset .yui-nav a:focus {
    background: inherit;
    text-decoration: inherit
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav .selected a,
.yui-navset .yui-nav .selected a:focus,
.yui-navset .yui-nav .selected a:hover {
    color: inherit;
    background: inherit
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav,
.yui-navset .yui-navset-top .yui-nav {
    border-color: inherit
}
 
.yui-navset li {
    line-height: inherit
}
 
/* CONTENT > Tabs Customization */
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav,
.yui-navset .yui-navset-top .yui-nav {
    display: flex;
    flex-wrap: wrap;
    width: calc(100% - .125rem);
    margin: 0 auto;
    border-color: #333333;
    box-shadow: none;
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav a,
/* ---- Link Modifier ---- */
.yui-navset .yui-navset-top .yui-nav a {
    color: #333333;
    /* ---- Tab Background Colour | [UNSELECTED] ---- */
    background-color: #efefef;
    border: unset;
    box-shadow: none;
    box-shadow: none;
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav a:hover,
.yui-navset .yui-nav a:focus {
    color: #ffffff;
    /* ---- Tab Background Colour | [HOVER] ---- */
    background-color: #333333;
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav li,
/* ---- Listitem Modifier ---- */
.yui-navset .yui-navset-top .yui-nav li {
    position: relative;
    display: flex;
    flex-grow: 2;
    max-width: 100%;
    margin: 0;
    padding: 0;
    color: #ffffff;
    background-color: #ffffff;
    border-color: transparent;
    box-shadow: none;
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav li a,
.yui-navset-top .yui-nav li a,
.yui-navset-bottom .yui-nav li a {
    display: flex;
    align-items: center;
    justify-content: center;
    width: 100%;
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav li em {
    border: unset;
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav a em,
.yui-navset .yui-navset-top .yui-nav a em {
    padding: .35em .75em;
 
    text-overflow: ellipsis;
    overflow: hidden;
    white-space: nowrap;
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav .selected,
/* ---- Selection Modifier ---- */
.yui-navset .yui-navset-top .yui-nav .selected {
    flex-grow: 2;
    margin: 0;
    padding: 0;
    /* ---- Tab Background Colour | [SELECTED] ---- */
    background-color: #333333;
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav .selected a,
.yui-navset .yui-nav .selected a em {
    border: none;
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav .selected a {
    width: 100%;
    color: #ffffff;
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-nav .selected a:focus,
.yui-navset .yui-nav .selected a:active {
    color: #ffffff;
    background-color: #333333;
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-content {
    background-color: #ffffff;
    box-shadow: none;
}
 
.yui-navset .yui-content,
.yui-navset .yui-navset-top .yui-content {
    padding: .5em;
    border: 1px solid #333;
    box-sizing: border-box;
}
 
/* CONTENT > WORDS NO BROKEY. CROQ HAS SPOKEY. and other things */
 
span,
a {
    word-break: normal !important
}
 
.avatar-hover {
    display: none !important;
}
 
#main-content .page-tags span {
    max-width: 100%;
}
 
/* CONTENT > Dustjacket Assets */
 
.fancyhr hr {
    border-top: 2vw solid transparent;
    background-color: rgba(var(--bright-accent), 0);
